\subsection{Source 08: the question, disambiguated}\label{swo:sk:sec:question}

The phrase ``well-orders of surreal numbers'' has two independent
ambiguities. First, is the carrier a set of surreal numbers or the whole
proper class? Second, is a well-order required to be the restriction of
the numerical order, or is it a new ordering of the labelled carrier?
A third choice enters when the well-orders themselves are compared:
which data are read lexicographically?

This paper uses the following principal convention. An arbitrary
well-order on a labelled carrier is represented by its exhaustive
increasing enumeration \emph{in that well-order}. Two enumerations are
then compared at their first unequal entry, using the \emph{numerical}
order of their surreal values. The enumerations themselves need not be
numerically increasing. This distinction is indispensable.

For example, the two lists $(0,1,-1)$ and $(0,-1,1)$ represent two
well-orders of the same three-element set. The second list is smaller in
our lexicographic order, since $-1<1$. Both underlying relations have
ordinal type $3$. Passing to ordinal isomorphism types would identify
them and destroy the object being studied.

\subsubsection{Five different carriers}

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.18\textwidth}Y Y@{}}
\toprule
Object & Elements or parameters & Foundational size \\
\midrule
$\W(X)$ & Exhaustive enumerations of one fixed set $X$ & A set in $\ZFC$ \\
$\I(\No)$ & Injective ordinal-length, set-sized words in $\No$ & A class of sets \\
$\Hsl$ & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ & A virtual collection of classes \\
$\Psupp(b)$ & Set codes for set-supported changes of a fixed $b$ & A class of sets \\
Arbitrary class well-orders & Class relations, possibly not set-like & A virtual collection; another comparison rule is needed \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

A \emph{virtual collection} is notation for a condition on class
variables, not a new object whose members are proper classes. Thus
``$e\in\Hsl$'' abbreviates ``$e$ is a class bijection from $\Ord$ onto
$\No$.'' All statements involving several such parameters can be
translated into the two-sorted language of class set theory. Whenever a
family of classes is used, it is represented by one uniform class
relation. This convention is made precise in \cref{swo:sk:sec:global}.

\subsubsection{Main conclusions}

The central distinction is between a very large ambient order and its
class-sized dense skeleton. Fix a global enumeration $b:\Ord\to\No$.
Write $\Psupp(b)$ for canonical set codes for permutations $\sigma$ of
$\Ord$ that equal the identity outside a set, ordered by the numerical
lexicographic comparison of $b\circ\sigma$. We prove
\[
                 (\Psupp(b),<_{b})\cong(\No,<).                 \tag{S08.1}\label{swo:sk:eq:t1}
\]
Moreover, if uniformly given set-sized families $L,R$ of arbitrary global
enumerations satisfy $L<_{\lex}R$, then some $b\circ\sigma$ strictly
separates them. The separator is in the same fixed skeleton regardless
of the supports, or lack of supports, of the input enumerations.

This yields a useful answer to the embedding question. Every
\emph{set} linear order, every ordinal, and indeed every
\emph{class linear order whose elements are sets} embeds into
$\Psupp(b)$. In particular, $\Ord$, $\Ord+1$, $\Ord+\Ord$, their reversals,
$\No$, and each set-indexed lexicographic power of $\No$ embed. This does
not say that the full virtual order $\Hsl$ is itself a class order or is
isomorphic to $\No$.

At a fixed set-sized carrier $X$, the answer is different. If
$|X|=\kappa$ is infinite, then
\[
 |\W(X)|=2^\kappa,
 \qquad
 \beta\emb\W(X)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \beta<\kappa^+.
                                                               \tag{S08.2}\label{swo:sk:eq:t2}
\]
Thus making the carrier larger changes the allowed ordinal spectrum;
there is no legitimate substitution of a ``cardinal $|\No|$'' into \eqref{swo:sk:eq:t2}.

\subsubsection{Relationship to existing work}

The set-sized part extends the exhaustive-enumeration viewpoint of the
prior working manuscript on the continuum \cite{Batch76Source02}. Its results are
reproved here in a form that does not assume separability of the
alphabet. The standard surreal background is the sign-sequence and
cut-filling viewpoint associated with Conway, Gonshor, and Alling
\cite{Conway,Gonshor,Alling}; Ehrlich's work places the surreal continuum
in a broader universality framework \cite{Ehrlich2012}.

The immediate formalization base is the inspected ProveIt sign-sequence
construction and its small-cut theorem \cite{ProveItSigns,ProveItCutFill}. We do not
need the repository's field arithmetic or stronger research claims.
The resemblance to the Kanovei--Shelah definable hyperreal construction
is real but limited: their actual index consists of fixed-length maps
whose ranges are ultrafilters, not literally all well-orders of the
reals \cite{KanoveiShelah}. We return to this distinction in \cref{swo:sk:sec:KS}.

\subsection{Source 08: the Kanovei--Shelah connection, carefully stated}\label{swo:sk:sec:KS}

Kanovei and Shelah's definable nonstandard model uses an index $A$ of
maps
\[
                 a:\mathfrak c\longrightarrow\mathcal P(\mathbb N)
\]
whose ranges are ultrafilters. They compare these maps lexicographically
using the binary characteristic-function order on subsets of
$\mathbb N$. Repetitions are allowed; the index is not a well-order
\cite{KanoveiShelah}. It is therefore not literally the order of all bijective
well-order enumerations of $\mathbb R$.

The relevant common idea is that ordinal-indexed codes can be linearly
compared at their first unequal value even when no definable choice of
one representative from each coded object is supplied. Our paired
codes, terminal codes, and virtual relations explore that order-theoretic
idea in the surreal setting. They do not provide a class ultrapower or
a transfer theorem.

An extension to a class-sized ultrapower would need separate decisions
about admissible predicates, function families, equivalence-class
coding, truth or satisfaction, and the exact size of saturation.
Neither a dense index order nor a surreal-sized skeleton settles these
questions. In particular, the set-cut interpolation theorem is an
order-theoretic theorem, not a claim of saturation for every language
or every class-sized family of types.

uniform constructions it suggests are research questions here
(\cref{swo:n16.10}; source~09's and source~08's last directions).

\subsection{Source 13: scope, provenance, and the main advances}\label{swo:fs:sec:scope}

The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of surreal
numbers'' does not determine a single object. There are three independent
choices: what is being well-ordered, how that well-order is represented,
and in what universe the collection of representations is allowed to
exist. A fourth choice appears when representations can have different
lengths: the position of a termination symbol.

The ProveIt repository already contains a substantial report on these
issues, assembled from four independent manuscripts. Its maintained
\code{article.pdf} is described as 115 pages, and the report explicitly
distinguishes written proofs from machine-checked results
(this report and its README at the pin; \merge\ the page count and the number
of sources have grown with the batch-81 addition, and the report is still not
formalized). We use the snapshot \texttt{0ecd158fd163bc4aca0ee40ccf6479ca6cf5f2a8}.
The earlier report supplies the fixed-alphabet theory, the surreal-sized
dense core, the direct comparison of raw class well-orders, and several
nonembedding and coding arguments. These are credited below and, where
needed for the new proofs, re-established in a compact form.

The present investigation addresses four of that report's proposed
continuations rather than relabeling its existing results as discoveries.
The term ``new'' below means an extension developed in this manuscript
relative to the inspected material; it is not a bibliographic priority
claim.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Main conclusions.}
A normalized cut comes from an injective $\Ord$-word exactly when it
crosses a unique prefix cylinder at every set-ordinal length. It comes
from a global enumeration exactly when these prefixes eventually include
every label. Nonbranch cuts stop either at a successor step, where they
separate whole next-letter cylinders, or at a limit step, where they lie
on the boundary of one cylinder.

For the virtual order $\Hsl$ of all class bijections $\Ord\to\No$,
\[
 \Hsl\cong\No\times_{\lex}\Hsl,
\]
but $\Hsl\times_{\lex}2\not\emb \Hsl$ in the full inaccessible model and in
the specified uniform $\KM+\GC$ sense. This is not a contradiction:
$\No$ is an ordinary class of sets, whereas the full $\Hsl$ is a domain of
class objects.

An order automorphism can send a prefix cylinder to a non-cylinder.
Consequently the numerical linear order on enumerations does not, by
itself, canonically specify the prefix tree. Central termination, on the
other hand, repairs the small one-sided characters of ordinary dictionary
words and produces an order isomorphic to $\No$.
\end{resultbox}

\subsubsection{What is proved, and what remains conditional}

The cut-reconstruction, product-absorption, recoding, and central-word
results are proved in $\GBC$. The product obstruction is proved in two
separate interpretations: ambient $\ZFC$ with a strongly inaccessible
universe, and a fixed-formula uniformity schema in $\KM+\GC$. The
latter proof identifies its impredicative comprehension step. We do not
claim that the same argument works over bare $\GBC$.

This separation also prevents a false ``absolute'' assertion about the
full global order. In an externally countable model, the available global
enumerations form an externally countable dense order without endpoints,
hence a copy of the rationals. Arbitrary external maps and internally
uniform constructions therefore answer different embedding questions.

\subsubsection{Reading paths}

\Cref{swo:fs:sec:interpretations}--\ref{swo:fs:swf:sec:fixed} survey the
interpretations and size constraints. \Cref{swo:fs:sec:core}--
\ref{swo:fs:sec:failure} establish the dense-core and cut machinery.
\Cref{swo:fs:sec:products}--\ref{swo:fs:sec:central} contain the other
main extensions. \Cref{swo:fs:sec:foundations,swo:fs:sec:lean} specify foundational and proof-assistant interfaces.
The final research agenda distinguishes questions resolved here from
stronger problems still to be investigated.

\subsection{Source 14: the continuation and its main conclusions}
\label{swo:tc:sec:overview}
The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of surreal
numbers'' does not specify one mathematical object. It leaves open what
is being well-ordered, how it is represented, how termination is compared,
and which logical universe supplies the word ``all.'' These choices are
not cosmetic: they change cardinality, adjacency, completeness, and even
the logical sort of the objects under study.

The present article continues the merged ProveIt report
(this report and its README), inspected at commit
\texttt{0ecd158fd163bc4aca0ee40ccf6479ca6cf5f2a8}.
That report combines four earlier manuscripts and already proves a large
body of results. In particular, its Section~19 (\merge\ Part~IV here) supplies the dense
set-supported skeleton, and its research agenda explicitly asks which
cuts of that core represent exhaustive branches. Repeating the skeleton
isomorphism or the set-sized ordinal spectrum would not answer that
question.

Our main ambient theory is $\GBC=\GB+\GC$, with Power Set and ordinary
set Foundation. The letters $\Hsl$, $\Jinj$, and $\Hall$ denote predicates
on classes, not classes whose members are proper classes. Fix a class
bijection
\[
 b:\Ord\longrightarrow\No.
\]
The ordinary class $\Psupp(b)$ consists of set codes for permutations of
$\Ord$ with set support, evaluated against $b$. The virtual order $\Hsl$
consists of all admitted class bijections $\Ord\to\No$.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Four main results.} (\merge\ Five are listed below.)

\textbf{Cut classification and recognition.}
Every proper normalized class cut of $\Psupp(b)$ is uniquely a cylinder
edge, a numerical gap after a set prefix, or an $\Ord$-long injective
branch. Such a cut is the trace of an element of $\Hsl$ exactly when its
crossing prefixes occur at every ordinal length and together contain
every surreal (\Cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy} and~\ref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}).

\textbf{No newly filled old cuts.}
For two $\GBC$ class realizations with the same sets and the same $b$,
an old skeleton cut is realized by a global enumeration in the larger
realization if and only if it already was in the smaller one
(\Cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute}).

\textbf{Exact support threshold.}
For every infinite set cardinal $\kappa$,
\[
 \mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)\text{ is }\eta_{\cf\kappa}
 \quad\text{and is not }\eta_{(\cf\kappa)^+}.
\]
A witnessing omitted configuration has a minimum possible support cost
of exactly $\kappa$ in the full core (\Cref{swo:tc:thm:support}).

\textbf{What unrestricted tails hide.}
Two labelled class well-orders have the same trace on $\Psupp(b)$ exactly
when they have the same canonical initial $\Ord$-enumeration. Above a
fixed injective branch $F$, the fiber is precisely the family of
well-orders of $\No\setminus\ran F$
(\Cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers}).

\textbf{Bare-order cut orbits.}
Character pairs completely determine the automorphism orbits of
normalized cuts, yet exhaustive representability is not preserved by
those automorphisms (\Cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits}).
\end{resultbox}

The results are complementary. The first determines the missing boundary
points; the second studies dependence on the admitted classes; the third
measures the amount of permutation support needed for interpolation; and
the fourth distinguishes the full relation order from its set-like part.
No one of these conclusions identifies the full collection of class
well-orders with an ordinary surreal-sized class.

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 102-158
\subsection{Source 15: scope, notation, and the audit boundary}\label{swo:cb:sec:scope}

The useful starting point is to specify what the entries of the proposed
order actually are. A well-order relation on a fixed set, an enumeration of
that set, an isomorphism type, a relation table, and a naturally increasing
subclass of $\No$ are different kinds of data. Some determine one another,
but their natural-looking lexicographic comparisons need not agree.

The ProveIt report \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Well-Orderings of the Surreal
Numbers} combines four earlier manuscripts into a 115-page document (\merge\ at
that revision). We
inspected its source, guide, the related real-alphabet report, and the
sign-sequence foundation at revision \texttt{0ecd158fd163bc4aca0ee40ccf6479ca6cf5f2a8}. The surreal report's source blob
is \texttt{f20837b76f8d981cb1dce3da79f633e280edad41}; the same source was present
at the earlier search-index revision
\texttt{491ed8411cccf7bd57916eb7666bbba762e92f96}. This article uses the newer
revision as its audit boundary (this report; \cite{ProveItReals,ProveItSigns}).

The prior report already establishes general set-sized cardinal and ordinal
spectra, direct comparison of labelled class well-orders without abstract
class ordinals, the global-choice equivalence, a dense bounded-support core
isomorphic to $\No$, an omitted-range construction, and the singular
minimal-slice dichotomy. We preserve those results as background. The main
continuation consists of the block decomposition in \Cref{swo:cb:sec:blocks},
the cut classification in \Cref{swo:cb:sec:cuts}, and the longer fixed-type
calculation in \Cref{swo:cb:sec:fixed}. The interpretation obstructions in
\Cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives} explain why these results cannot simply be
transferred to every other coding.

\paragraph{Foundational convention.}
$\GB$ means G\"odel--Bernays set theory with Power Set and with no choice
axiom built into the notation. $\GBC=\GB+\GC$, where global choice provides a
class choice function on nonempty sets. Set-sized results are in ZFC unless
stated otherwise. A class well-order is a class strict linear order in which
every nonempty available subclass has a least element. This explicit
convention avoids silently confusing internal class well-foundedness with
well-foundedness in an external metatheory. The standard equivalent
formulations under global choice are discussed in \Cref{swo:cb:sec:foundations}.

\paragraph{Order notation.}
An embedding preserves and reflects strict order. $L\equi M$ means that
there are embeddings in both directions; it does not mean that $L$ and $M$
are isomorphic. The product $L\times_{\lex}M$ compares the $L$ coordinate
first. Ordinary ordinal multiplication keeps its usual convention:
$\alpha\cdot\beta$ is $\beta$ consecutive copies of $\alpha$.
We write $\B_\theta=(2^\theta,<_{\lex})$, where $0<1$.
The binary coding length $\bl(L)$ is the least ordinal $\theta$ for which
$L\emb\B_\theta$, when it exists. Birthday is written $\bd(x)$.

\paragraph{An essential size distinction.}
Symbols such as $\Hsl(\No)$ and $\Hall(\No)$ name predicates on class variables,
with a comparison formula. They are not assertions that an ordinary GB
class has other proper classes as its elements. A statement about a uniform
family means one class relation whose rows are indexed by sets, possibly
by a proper class of set indices. A larger universe may instead make the
whole collection into an external set. The two readings are related but
must be kept explicit.

\subsection{Source 16: main conclusions and relationship to the earlier report}\label{swo:ds:sec:overview}

There is a coherent and quite rich theory here, but it is essential to say
which objects are being compared. A well-order on surreal labels need not
agree with their numerical order. An ordinal-indexed enumeration of the
whole surreal class is necessarily a class function. An arbitrary class
well-order need not possess such an enumeration. Finally, even when each
well-order is a legitimate class, a collection having those classes as its
elements is not an ordinary class of the same two-sorted theory.

The ProveIt manuscript (this report, read at revision \code{491ed8411}) already establishes the basic
distinctions, exact ordinal embedding bounds for set alphabets, the
surreal-sized bounded-support core, direct comparison of non-set-like
orders, and a full-universe nonembedding result. Its merged source contains
four earlier manuscripts and explicitly leaves several sharper questions.
The present article develops those questions rather than treating the
earlier conclusions as new. The principal additions are as follows.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Topology at every enumeration length.}
For an infinite linearly ordered set $X$ of cardinality $\mu$ and an
ordinal $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|=\mu$,
\[
 \dens(\WO_\alpha(X))=\cell(\WO_\alpha(X))=
 \begin{cases}
 \mu^{<\mu},&\alpha\in\{\mu,\mu+1,\mu+2\},\\
 2^\mu,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
For the full order, both invariants equal $2^\mu$. Every infinite
stratum, and the full order, has a countable witness to failure of
conditional Dedekind completeness.
\item \textbf{Regular-stage gap spectrum.}
If $X$ is an $\eta_\mu$ order of size $\mu$, for regular infinite
$\mu$, the unfilled two-sided cuts of $\WO_\mu(X)$ have exactly the
characters $(\mu,\lambda)$ and $(\lambda,\mu)$, where $\lambda$ ranges
over infinite regular cardinals at most $\mu$.
\item \textbf{Represented cuts.}
A lower cut of the bounded-support core represents an injective
$\Ord$-branch exactly when it is straddled by a prefix cylinder of every
set ordinal length. The branch is exhaustive exactly when those prefixes
collectively contain every label. A failed test has a first successor or
limit obstruction; arbitrary non-set-like well-orders do not remove either
obstruction.
\item \textbf{All ordinal-class blocks at once.}
Every class well-order $R$ admits the canonical decomposition
\[
 (X,R)\cong\left(\sum_{j\in J_R}\Ord\right)+\alpha_R,
\]
where the summands are precisely the equivalence classes for set-sized
closed intervals, and $\alpha_R$ is the optional final set block. The block
index can itself be any class well-order. The construction is elementary in
$\GB$, and directly defines the entire family of residual tails.
\item \textbf{Word conventions and formal strength.}
For the shorter-prefix-first convention, arbitrary, injective, and
numerically increasing set-length words are isomorphic in $\GBC$ by maps
preserving lengths and prefixes. Other placements of a termination symbol
can instead make the whole unrestricted or injective word order isomorphic
to $\No$. For elementary relationally specified transformations, a uniform
nonembedding theorem needs only $\Sigma^1_1$ class comprehension over
$\GBC$, rather than all of $\KM$.
\end{enumerate}

These are extensions relative to the inspected report, not announcements
that previously catalogued problems in the literature have been solved.
The proofs below are intended to be independently readable. When a longer
existing theorem is only summarized, its provenance and exact scope are
stated. We separate mathematical proof, finite diagnostic checks, and
formal proof throughout.

\subsection{Source 18: main results and the scope of the continuation}
\label{swo:sh:sec:main}

The current \texttt{ProveIt}\ report on surreal well-orders (this report, read at
revision \code{83befe707})
merges four earlier manuscripts. It already distinguishes set and class
interpretations, proves the set-sized ordinal spectrum, analyzes binary
coding at singular birthdays, compares arbitrary class well-orders
directly, characterizes adjacency, and constructs a dense bounded-support
core in the set-like global order. Repeating these conclusions would not
answer the request for further study. We use them as a starting point,
prove the elementary tools needed below, and address the outstanding
questions on cuts, block decompositions, termination conventions, and
model dependence.

Here is the principal bounded result. Throughout the article,
$\kappa$ is an infinite initial cardinal and
\[
  \mu=|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa},\qquad
 r=\cf\kappa,\qquad q=\cf\mu.
\]
Let $P=\WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})$ consist of all bijections
$\mu\to \No_{<\kappa}$, ordered by their first unequal values. We prove
\[
 |P|=2^\mu,\qquad \dens(P)=\cell(P)=\mu^{<\mu},\qquad
 \cf(P)=\ci(P)=r,
\]
and every point has left and right character $q$. The order fills all
cuts specified by fewer than $r$ points. Its proper Dedekind gaps have
exactly the character pairs
\[\tag{S18.1}\label{swo:sh:eq:main-gap-spectrum}
 \{(r,r),(q,q)\}
 \ \cup\
 \{(\theta,r),(r,\theta):
           \theta<\mu\text{ is an infinite regular cardinal}\}.
\]
This is a gap spectrum, not an isomorphism classification. Orders with
the same spectrum can still have different global arrangements of cuts.
There are exactly $2^\mu$ proper gaps of character $(q,q)$,
and exactly $\mu^{<\mu}$ of every other character in the displayed
spectrum. Thus the Dedekind completion has cardinality $2^\mu$.

For every infinite ordered alphabet $X$ of size $\mu$, a separate
fixed-type result gives
\[\tag{S18.2}\label{swo:sh:eq:main-third-tail}
 \dens(\WO_\alpha(X))=\cell(\WO_\alpha(X))=
 \begin{cases}
 \mu^{<\mu},&\alpha=\mu,\mu+1,\mu+2,\\
 2^\mu,&\mu+3\le\alpha<\mu^+.
 \end{cases}
\]
The third terminal position is the first that supplies an interior point
of a finite permutation fiber. This is an order-topological transition,
and its numerical values need not differ when $\mu^{<\mu}=2^\mu$.

On the class side, let $R$ be any supplied well-order of a proper class.
Declare two labels equivalent when the closed interval between them is
a set. Every block has an actual least label, which represents it without
making a class an element. In GB this gives
\[\tag{S18.3}\label{swo:sh:eq:main-division}
 R\cong(B_R\times\Ord)_{\lex}+\theta_R,
\]
with all proper blocks of type $\Ord$ and at most one final set block
of type $\theta_R$. The block index $B_R$ can be any class well-order;
it can even be isomorphic to $R$. Thus simultaneous decomposition is
elementary, while repeated quotienting need not lower isomorphism type.

A class cut of the bounded-support core comes from a raw global
well-order precisely when, at every ordinal length, one prefix cylinder
meets both sides. These prefixes uniquely reconstruct an injective
$\Ord$-word by elementary comprehension. The cut has a set-like
representative exactly when that word is onto. A cut that would require
the first two entries to be the same surreal is represented by no raw
well-order. Allowing arbitrary class well-orders therefore does not
fill all class cuts, even though it fills the omitted-range branch cuts.

A further theorem concerns an external, countable model of the class
theory. If the model is $\omega$-standard, the full admitted order
$\Hall$ is a dense shuffle of finite chains of sizes
\[
 1,2,6,24,120,\ldots.
\]
Its finite-condensation quotient is the rational order with every
factorial size appearing densely as a color. The admitted set-like order
$\Hsl$ is externally isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$, but it is not definable
in the pure full order, even with finitely many parameters. These are
external statements; they do not supply an internally coded embedding
of all global orders into a class of sets.

The final new group of results concerns set-length words. Ordinary
dictionary comparison puts a proper prefix first. Under GBC, arbitrary,
injective, and strictly numerically increasing words with this convention
are isomorphic as prefix trees and as linear orders. Centered termination
over $\No\setminus\{0\}$ instead makes arbitrary and injective words
isomorphic to $\No$. Increasing words retain a precisely identified
limit-prefix obstruction. Keeping the actual digit $0$ immediately above
a distinct terminator creates adjacent pairs. Hence ``lexicographic''
must include a termination rule.

\subsubsection{What is established here}

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1532-1544
\subsection{Source 14: the precise Kanovei--Shelah connection}
Kanovei and Shelah's definable nonstandard-model construction uses a
lexicographically ordered family of maps from the continuum cardinal to
$\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters; the maps may
repeat values \cite{KanoveiShelah}. That index set is not literally the
set of all well-orders of $\mathbb R$. Its relevance is methodological:
a linear order on an entire family of presentations can organize a
construction without selecting one privileged presentation. Importing
that method into a surreal setting must still state the indexing sort,
support restriction, and evaluation relation. The diagonal theorem
prevents replacing all global enumerations by one exhaustive ordinary
class of set presentations.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 1715-1739
\subsection{Source 17: the Kanovei--Shelah connection, with its size boundary}
\label{swo:gs:sec:ks}

The definable nonstandard-real construction is a useful motivation for
ordering many presentations rather than selecting one preferred
presentation. Its actual index should be stated accurately. In
Section 1 of Kanovei--Shelah \cite{KanoveiShelah}, the index consists of
maps from the continuum cardinal into $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose
ranges are ultrafilters; the maps need not be injective. The authors order
this \emph{set} of maps by first difference, using the binary lexicographic
order of subsets of $\mathbb N$, and then use finite-support functions.
It is therefore not literally the order of all well-order relations on
$\mathbb R$.

The methodological analogy remains valuable: a specified linear order of
codes can organize a construction without a definable choice of one
special code. In the present setting, $\WO_\mu(X)$ is a legitimate set
index, and a uniform subfamily of global enumerations can be indexed by
an ordinary class of set codes. Neither observation makes the full
higher-order predicate $\Hsl$ into a set index. Any proposed surreal
analogue must state where its functions, supports, evaluation maps, and
ultrafilters live. The diagonal obstruction of
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:diagonal} rules out one tempting shortcut, while leaving
many bounded or explicitly uniform constructions available.

\merge\ The Kanovei--Shelah distinction is thus made by all ten sources, in
the same terms (\cref{swo:sk:sec:KS} and the note after it).

\section{Surreal order facts and foundational conventions}\label{swo:sec:prelim}

\subsection{Signs, birthdays, and set cuts}

A surreal number is represented by a sign sequence
\[
 s:\alpha\longrightarrow\{-,+\}
\]
of set-ordinal length \(\alpha\), its birthday \(\bd(s)\). Numerical
comparison at the first disagreement uses
\[
 -\ <\ \text{termination}\ <\ +.
\]
This differs from dictionary order with every proper prefix smaller
than every extension. A sign sequence can be on either side of an
extension, depending on its next sign.

For an ordinal \(\theta\), let
\[
 \No_{<\theta}=\bigcup_{\alpha<\theta}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}.
\]
It is a set. The full \(\No\) is proper-class-sized, because all-plus
sequences embed all ordinals. Every set of surreals has bounded birthdays
by Replacement.

\begin{definition}\label{swo:n3.1}
A class linear order \(L\) has the \emph{set-cut property}, called
\(\eta_{\Ord}\) here, if for all sets \(A,B\subseteq L\) with \(A<B\)
there is \(x\) with \(A<x<B\). Empty sides are allowed. For a cardinal
\(\kappa\), the set-sized notation \(\eta_\kappa\) requires the same
property when \(\card{A\cup B}<\kappa\).
\end{definition}

The surreal cut construction supplies this property for \(\No\)
\cite[Section 2]{BagayokoHoeven}. A separator can be chosen canonically
as the unique simplest separator. This statement concerns \emph{sets}
of options; applying it to the whole class against the empty right side
would be inconsistent.

\begin{lemma}[Deleting a set]\label{swo:lem:delete}
If \(S\subseteq\No\) is a set, then \(\No\setminus S\) has the
set-cut property. Every nonempty open interval of \(\No\) is a
proper class.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let \(A<B\) be sets in \(\No\setminus S\). First choose \(x\) with
\(A<x<B\), and put
\[
 S_-=\{s\in S:s\leq x\},\qquad S_+=\{s\in S:x<s\}.
\]
Then \(A\cup S_-<B\cup S_+\). A separator of this new set cut
avoids both parts of \(S\). The argument allows empty sides.
If an interval \((a,b)\) were a set \(S\), applying the result to
\(\{a\}<\{b\}\) in \(\No\setminus S\) would be impossible.
\end{proof}

Choosing both separators by simplicity makes the deletion argument
uniform in the set parameters without global choice.

% ---- source 12, lines 580-589
\begin{lemma}[Avoiding a forbidden set]\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:avoid}
If $A<B$ are sets of surreals and $D$ is a set, then some separator
$z$ of $A,B$ lies outside $D$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $u$ between $A$ and $B$, and then $v$ between $\{u\}$ and $B$.
Every point of $(u,v)$ separates $A,B$, and that interval is a proper
class. It cannot be contained in $D$. With a fixed global well-order,
choose the first acceptable point, making the operation uniform.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Source 08: surreal order and size, the minimal toolkit}\label{swo:sk:sec:toolkit}

We take a surreal number to be a sign sequence
\[
 s:\alpha\longrightarrow\{-,+\},\qquad \alpha\in\Ord.
\]
Its birthday is $\bd(s)=\alpha$. To compare two sequences, extend them
by a termination symbol $0$ and compare at the first disagreement using
$-<0<+$. This is the numerical order. The simplicity relation is proper
initial-segment extension, and is not the numerical order.

\begin{proposition}\label{swo:sk:prop:size}
Every birthday-bounded collection of surreals is a set, every set of
surreals has bounded birthdays, and $\No$ is a proper class. Neither the
numerical order nor ``birthday first, then numerical order'' is a
well-order of $\No$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed ordinal $\lambda$, the sign sequences of length below
$\lambda$ form the set $\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}$.
Replacement bounds the birthdays of any given set. Conversely, the
all-plus sequences give a distinct surreal for every ordinal, so a set
containing all surreals would bound all ordinals.
The negative integers already descend numerically. For the second
claim, let $s_n$ have birthday $\omega$, with $n$ initial minus signs
followed by plus signs forever. At coordinate $n$ one has
$s_{n+1}(n)=-<+=s_n(n)$, so
$s_0>s_1>s_2>\cdots$ within a single birthday level.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{A birthday-controlled separator theorem}

We record a proof of the exact order-theoretic fact used later. It also
explains the repository's bounded-word implementation \cite{ProveItCutFill}.

\begin{lemma}\label{swo:sk:lem:binarycomplete}
For every set ordinal $\beta$, the binary lexicographic order
$\B_\beta=(\two^\beta,<_{\lex})$ is a complete lattice.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The least and greatest elements are the constant $0$ and $1$ words.
Given a set $A$ of words, form $w$ recursively. At coordinate $\xi$, put
$w(\xi)=1$ exactly when some $a\in A$ agrees with the already constructed
prefix $w\restr\xi$ and has $a(\xi)=1$; otherwise put $0$.
If some $a\in A$ exceeded $w$, its first disagreement would contradict
the rule for a $0$ coordinate. If $v<w$, then at their first
disagreement $\xi$ we have $v(\xi)=0$, $w(\xi)=1$, and a witness
$a\in A$ agreeing with $w$ through that $1$ coordinate. Thus $v<a$ and
$v$ is not an upper bound. This proves that $w=\sup A$, including
$A=\varnothing$. Infima follow by reversing all bits.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Birthday-controlled cut filling]\label{swo:sk:thm:cut}
Let $A,B$ be sets of surreals with $A<B$, meaning $a<b$ for all
$a\in A$, $b\in B$. If $\beta$ is an ordinal strictly greater than every
birthday in $A\cup B$, then a surreal $z$ of birthday exactly $\beta$
satisfies $A<z<B$. Either side may be empty.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a shorter word $x$, let $u_\beta(x)$ be the word of length $\beta$
obtained by appending a plus to $x$ and then filling all remaining
coordinates with minuses. It is the least full-length word strictly
above $x$. Dually, let $v_\beta(x)$ be $x$ followed by a minus and then
pluses; it is the greatest full-length word strictly below $x$.
These assertions follow by inspecting the first differing sign: an
extension above $x$ must choose plus when $x$ terminates, and the
least possible continuation then uses only minuses.

If $x<y$ and both have length below $\beta$, then
$u_\beta(x)\leq v_\beta(y)$. Indeed $u_\beta(x)\leq y$ by the same
first-disagreement check; equality is impossible because their
birthdays differ. Applying the dual greatest-word property gives the
claim. By \cref{swo:sk:lem:binarycomplete}, full-length sign words have a
supremum, and
\[
       z=\sup\{u_\beta(a):a\in A\}
\]
satisfies $a<u_\beta(a)\leq z$ for every $a\in A$ and
$z\leq v_\beta(b)<b$ for every $b\in B$. All words in this complete
lattice have birthday exactly $\beta$. If $A$ is empty, its supremum
is the all-minus word. The vacuous case $\beta=0$ causes no problem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Fresh separators]\label{swo:sk:cor:fresh}
If $A<B$ are sets and $S$ is a set of forbidden surreals, a separator
$z\notin S$ exists. It can be required to have any specified birthday
strictly exceeding all birthdays in $A\cup B\cup S$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}\label{swo:sk:def:eta}
A class linear order is an $\eta_{\Ord}$-order if every pair of
\emph{sets} $A<B$ has a strict separator, including empty sides. For an
infinite cardinal $\kappa$, an $\eta_\kappa$-order satisfies the same
condition when $|A\cup B|<\kappa$.
\end{definition}

The notation $\eta_\kappa$ here uses a cardinal bound directly; it should
not be confused with conventions in which the subscript is the index
$\alpha$ in $\aleph_\alpha$. By \cref{swo:sk:thm:cut}, $\No$ is an
$\eta_{\Ord}$-order. Every interval is a proper class: if $(a,b)$ were a
set, a separator of $\{a\}\cup(a,b)$ and $\{b\}$ would be a new member
of the same interval above all its members. No set is cofinal or
coinitial in $\No$.

% ---- source 11, lines 309-329
\subsection{Which recursion principle is used?}

Here \(\GB\) has a \(\ZF\) set part, elementary class comprehension,
and class replacement; choice is stated separately.
We use \(\GBC=\GB+\GC\), which includes set choice.
Cardinality calculations and cardinal-valued cofinality statements
throughout the article are read in \(\ZFC\), or in the set part of
\(\GBC\). The explicitly definable sign code and the direct
set-cut constructions retain their stated choice-free strength.

Ordinary recursion along \(\Ord\), with a \emph{set} output at every
stage and a rule using the set of earlier values and fixed class
parameters, is available in \(\GB\). On each set ordinal perform the
usual recursion with those parameters. Uniqueness makes the local
solutions agree; elementary comprehension assembles their graph.

This is different from arbitrary elementary transfinite recursion,
\(\ETR\), whose stages may themselves be classes. The latter supports
iterated truth predicates and is stronger than \(\GBC\)
\cite{GitmanHamkins}. The prefix searches, partial permutations, and
back-and-forth maps used here have set-sized stages.

\subsection{Source 12: the surreal carrier and the foundational conventions}
\label{swo:st:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Sign sequences}

We use the sign-sequence presentation
\[
 \No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}.
\]
Each individual sequence is a set. Its length $\bd(s)=\lh(s)$ is its
birthday. At the first difference, signs and termination are compared by
\[
 -\ <\ \End\ <\ +.
\]
This is the usual numerical order, not the ordinary ``shorter comes
first'' dictionary convention. Simplicity is the separate relation of
being a proper sign prefix. The standard surreal construction and its
simplicity structure are treated by Gonshor and Ehrlich
\cite{Gonshor,Ehrlich2012}.

We shall use the following standard feature, also obtainable directly
from the construction: whenever $A,B$ are \emph{sets} of surreals with
$A<B$, there is a surreal $z$ with $A<z<B$. There is a unique such
separator of minimum birthday. Moreover, if every member of $A\cup B$
has birthday less than an ordinal $\gamma$, a separator can be constructed
with birthday at most $\gamma$. This is interpolation, not Dedekind
completeness: no least upper bound is being asserted.

Every set of surreals has a birthday bound, by Replacement. Every
nonempty numerical interval contains a proper class of surreals. To see
the latter without arithmetic, start with $a<b$ and recursively choose
$x_\alpha$ between $\{a\}\cup\{x_\xi:\xi<\alpha\}$ and $\{b\}$.
The previous values form a set at each stage. Thus one obtains distinct
points for all ordinals $\alpha$.

\subsubsection{Well-orders and set-likeness}

A class well-order on a class $X$ is a strict linear class relation $R$
for which every nonempty subclass has an $R$-least element. In GBC this
agrees with the usual formulations using nonempty set subsets or absence
of descending $\omega$-sequences; the relationship is discussed in
\cite[\S3]{HamkinsWoodin}. We use strict relations throughout.

It is \emph{set-like} if
\[
 \pred_R(x)=\{y\in X:yRx\}
\]
is a set for every $x$. A proper-class set-like well-order is isomorphic
to $\Ord$: map $x$ to the ordinal type of its set of predecessors. The
range is an initial segment of $\Ord$, and cannot be a set ordinal when
$X$ is proper. This construction uses only set-sized order types.

Not all class well-orders are set-like. The ordered sums
$\Ord+1$, $\Ord+\Ord$, and $\Ord+\Ord+1$ are examples. Their notation
means ordered sums of class orders, not new von Neumann ordinals.

\subsubsection{Foundational levels}

Our set-sized results are theorems of ZFC. Our global results are in GBC,
meaning Gödel--Bernays set theory with global choice. When analyzing the
necessity of choice we work over GB plus ordinary, set-level AC.
The full collection of global well-orders is handled by formulas with
class variables, not by pretending that a proper class is an element of
another GBC class.

Kelley--Morse theory allows stronger comprehension, but its classes still
have sets, not proper classes, as members. Moving from GBC to KM does not
by itself create a powerclass object of all subclasses of $\No$.
One can instead use a larger set-theoretic universe, a set model with a
specified collection of classes, or an explicitly higher-order theory.
These are distinct interpretations and will be kept distinct.

\subsubsection{Why an ordinal-length recursion here need not invoke ETR}

A recursion on $\Ord$ that produces one \emph{set} at each stage and uses
the set of previous values is available by the ordinary recursion theorem
with class parameters in GB. In contrast, ETR permits a genuinely
class-valued recursive stage, represented by a class of pairs of a stage
and an arbitrary set. Even a truth hierarchy brings stronger principles
into play \cite[\S2]{HamkinsWoodin}. Our forth constructions, block lengths, and
canonical enumeration of a class with set-sized initial segments are
set-valued recursions. We do not invoke a universal satisfaction predicate
or unrestricted class-valued recursion.

\subsection{Source 09: foundational conventions and the surreal order}
\label{swo:ec:sec:foundations}
\subsubsection{Sets, classes, and the meaning of a family}
All set-sized results are in $\ZFC$. Global results are in $\GBC$, here
meaning G\"odel--Bernays class theory with global choice. Classes have sets
as members. A proper class cannot be an element of another class. An
expression such as ``the set of class functions $E_i$'' is therefore
replaced by a \emph{uniform family}: a class relation
\[
       F\subseteq I\times\Ord\times\No
\]
whose $i$th section is the graph of $E_i$. The index $I$ may be a set or a
class of sets. If $I$ is a set, this is a uniformly set-indexed family,
not a literal set of proper classes.

This distinction does not prevent quantification over individual class
variables. For example, ``for every two class bijections $E,F$, there is
a least ordinal where they differ'' is a legitimate $\GBC$ assertion.
What is unavailable is a class having all such bijections as members.
Rangel and Mariano explicitly distinguish the set-subsets of a class
from a nonexistent class of all its subclasses \cite[\S1.1.1]{RochaRangelMariano}.

Global choice will be used in its standard consequence that a proper
class can be enumerated by $\Ord$ with set-sized initial segments. One
way to obtain this consequence is to well-order each rank layer using a
global choice function, concatenate the layers, and collapse the resulting
set-like well-order. Restricting such an order to any proper subclass
again gives order type $\Ord$.

\subsubsection{Sign sequences and the cut property}
Use the sign-sequence realization
\[
   \No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}.
\]
Each displayed element is a set function. Its domain is its
\emph{birthday}, denoted $\bd(x)$. Numerical order compares the first
different sign using
\[
                  -\;<\;\text{termination}\;<\;+.
\]
It is different both from ordering by birthday and from the dictionary
order on arbitrary surreal-valued words used later. The all-plus word
of length $\alpha$ represents the ordinal $\alpha$.

The standard simplicity/cut theorem says that, for sets $A,B\subseteq\No$
with $A<B$, there is a unique simplest surreal strictly between them.
Here $A<B$ means $a<b$ for every $a\in A,b\in B$, with empty sides
allowed. We write this simplest separator as $\{A\mid B\}$. A useful
birthday bound is
\begin{equation}
 \bd\{A\mid B\}\le
       \sup\{\bd(x)+1:x\in A\cup B\}.
 \label{swo:ec:eq:cut-birthday}
\end{equation}
These are standard sign-sequence facts \cite{Gonshor}; the inspected
repository also contains explicit small-cut and birthday-bound
statements on its sign carrier \cite{ProveItCuts}.

In particular, every set of surreal numbers has strict upper and lower
bounds. No set is cofinal or coinitial in $\No$, and no set is the whole
of $\No$. These assertions do not authorize a cut constructor with
arbitrary proper-class option families.

\begin{definition}\label{swo:ec:n2.1}
A class linear order $D$ has the \emph{set-cut property} if every pair of
sets $A,B\subseteq D$ satisfying $A<B$ has an element $d\in D$ with
$A<d<B$. Empty sides are allowed.
\end{definition}
The surreal order has the set-cut property. In terminology used in the
literature this is an absolute or class analogue of an $\eta$-order.
We use the explicit definition rather than relying on potentially
ambiguous subscripts such as $\eta_{\Ord}$.

\begin{lemma}[Avoiding a prescribed set]\label{swo:ec:lem:avoid}
If $D$ has the set-cut property and $U\subseteq D$ is a set, then
$D\setminus U$ also has the set-cut property.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $A,B\subseteq D\setminus U$ be sets with $A<B$, and put
\[
 U_0=\{u\in U:A<u<B\}.
\]
Then $A\cup U_0<B$. Choose $x$ with $A\cup U_0<x<B$. This $x$ is in the
original open cut. If it belonged to $U$, it would belong to $U_0$, giving
$x<x$. Thus $x\notin U$.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The precise recursion strength used here}
We repeatedly construct a sequence of \emph{sets} indexed by ordinals,
where the next value is a uniquely specified set obtained from the
set-sized previous history and fixed class parameters. This recursion
is available in $\GBC$: set recursion with class parameters constructs
all set-length approximations, uniqueness makes them compatible, and
elementary class comprehension joins them.

This is not the principle $\ETR$, whose stages can themselves be proper
classes. The latter is genuinely stronger than $\GBC$ and must not be
silently invoked by saying ``perform class recursion''
\cite[\S2]{GHHSW}. Every global recursion in the proofs below is explicitly
of the former, set-valued kind.

\subsection{Source 08: class foundations and set-like well-orders}\label{swo:sk:sec:foundations}

From this section onward, the default theory is $\GBC$: G\"odel--Bernays
class set theory with Global Choice. Sets are the objects that may be
members; classes are collections of sets. A class function maps set
arguments to set values. Its image of a set is a set by class
replacement. Elementary class comprehension allows formulas with
class parameters but only set quantifiers in the defining formula.

\subsubsection{Why Global Choice is named explicitly}

Global Choice supplies a set-like global well-order of the universe.
Restricting it to any class gives a set-like well-order, and every
proper class can then be enumerated by $\Ord$. We use this to choose
one baseline $b:\Ord\to\No$, to enumerate class carriers during
back-and-forth, and to select witnesses uniformly. Ordinary set Choice
alone does not justify these global choices.

Many local results need less. Pairwise lexicographic comparison, the
extension of one specified set prefix relative to a given $b$, and the
set-cut argument use only class replacement, elementary comprehension,
set Choice, and the displayed class parameters. Keeping $b$ as an
explicit parameter is therefore useful in weaker foundations.

\begin{definition}\label{swo:sk:n8.1}
A class well-order $\prec$ is \emph{set-like} when, for every element
$x$, its predecessor class $\{y:y\prec x\}$ is a set. By a class
well-order here we mean a linear class relation such that every
nonempty subclass available in the model has a least element.
\end{definition}

For a set-like relation, it suffices to require well-foundedness on
sets: a nonempty subclass has a witness $x$, and one may search the
set of predecessors of $x$ together with $x$ for its least member.
Over $\GBC$, well-foundedness of any fixed class relation is equivalent
to the absence of a set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence. Keeping the
sets and the relation fixed while enlarging the class collection therefore
does not change its internal well-foundedness. What may change is which
class relations are available; internal and external well-foundedness
must also be distinguished.
\merge\ (This replaces one sentence of source~08; see the note before
this section.)


% ---- hand chunk n08enumclass

\begin{note}[Source~08, Theorem~8.2]\label{swo:sk:thm:enumclass}
\emph{Every set-like well-order of a proper class has a unique order
isomorphism from $\Ord$. Conversely, every class bijection $e:\Ord\to\No$
induces a set-like well-order of $\No$.} This is the last paragraph of the
proof of \cref{swo:cf:choice} and source~09's
\cref{swo:ec:prop:global-equivalence}, proved by the same rank map: the
predecessors of $x$ form a well-ordered set of ordinal type $r(x)$; the range
of $r$ is downward closed, and it cannot be a set ordinal, since the inverse
of $r$ would then map a set ordinal onto a proper class, contradicting class
replacement. Conversely the predecessors of $e(\alpha)$ form the set
$e[\alpha]$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 08, lines 786-809
Thus all set-like proper-class well-orders have the same abstract order
type. The interesting lexicographic structure lies in their labels,
not in distinct ordinal types. It is incorrect either to introduce a
set ordinal equal to ``the order type of all ordinals'' or to quotient
away the enumerations and expect the lexicographic information to
survive.

\subsubsection{The recursion principle actually used}

All transfinite constructions below have \emph{set-valued} stages and
set-sized histories at each ordinal stage. In $\GBC$, fix the class
parameters and a rule assigning a unique set to each set history.
The ordinary set recursion theorem with those parameters constructs a
solution through each set ordinal. Uniqueness makes these initial
solutions compatible, and elementary comprehension forms their union
as a class. This is the set-valued recursion needed here.

It is not the principle of elementary transfinite recursion with
\emph{class-valued} stages. For example, constructing a new truth class
at each stage is a substantially different task. The distinctions among
$\GBC$, $\GBC+\ETR$, and $\KM$ are genuine; the class-recursion and class
forcing literature documents their strength \cite{HamkinsOpenDet,HamkinsClassForcing}.
No equivalence with those stronger principles is claimed for the
constructions in this paper.

\subsection{Universality and uniqueness of the saturated class order}

\begin{proposition}\label{swo:prop:universal}
In \(\ZFC\), every set linear order embeds into \(\No\). In
\(\GBC\), every class linear order embeds uniformly into \(\No\).
Any two proper-class \(\eta_{\Ord}\) orders are isomorphic in
\(\GBC\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate the source in a cardinal-length well-order, or in type
\(\Ord\) for a proper class, using global choice. At stage \(\alpha\),
the earlier images form a set. Separate the images of earlier points
below the new point from those above it, and choose a separator.
This extends an order embedding. Each partial map is a set.

For uniqueness, globally enumerate both class orders and alternately
insert the first unused point from each enumeration. The appropriate
set cut in the other order is fillable. Global choice selects a
separator when none is distinguished. The union of the partial
isomorphisms is a surjective class order isomorphism.
\end{proof}

The same construction, started from a specified set-sized partial
isomorphism, gives set homogeneity. These are the order-theoretic
universality and homogeneity features of \(\No\)
\cite{Ehrlich2012}. The assertion that every \emph{class} order embeds
is made with global choice; it is not used as an unproved converse
to global choice.

\begin{lemma}[Surreal universality, with the size of the recursion exposed]
\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:universalNo}
In GBC, every class linear order admits a class order-embedding into
$\No$. For a set order enumerated in type $\lambda$, one can arrange
that the image of its $\xi$th enumerated element has birthday at most
$\xi$, for each $\xi<\lambda$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use a global-choice enumeration of the carrier, either by an ordinal or
by $\Ord$. When the next element is considered, its previously embedded
predecessors and successors form two sets $A<B$. Send it to the simplest
surreal separator. It is distinct from all previous images and preserves
order. Every stage has set-sized history. Induction gives the birthday
bound, because the earlier birthdays are less than the current stage.
This is the standard forth argument behind surreal universality
\cite{Ehrlich2012,HamkinsUniversal}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Deleting a set does not change the numerical class order]
\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:delete}
In GBC, $\No\setminus A$ is order-isomorphic to $\No$ for every set $A$.
Every nonempty open numerical interval is also order-isomorphic to $\No$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each target has interpolation for arbitrary separated sets, by
\cref{swo:st:lem:avoid}, adding interval bounds when needed. Each is a proper
class and has an $\Ord$-enumeration by global choice. Carry out a
back-and-forth between the two enumerations. At each ordinal stage,
extend the partial isomorphism to the next unused domain point and then
to the next unused target point. The previous partial map is a set, and
the required cut can be filled while avoiding its set-sized range.
At the end the class map is onto and order-preserving.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Source 09: the classical universality mechanism, with proofs}
\label{swo:ec:sec:universality}
The following facts are classical features of the surreal order; we
include the arguments because the same mechanism will identify our
lexicographic core. The class-universal and set-homogeneous viewpoint
appears, for example, in \cite{RochaRangelMariano}.

\begin{theorem}[Class universality]\label{swo:ec:thm:class-universal}
In $\GBC$, every class linear order embeds into $\No$. More generally,
every class linear order embeds into any class linear order with the
set-cut property.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a set-sized domain, choose a well-ordering and enumerate it by an
ordinal. For a proper-class domain $L$, use global choice to fix a class
bijection $a:\Ord\to L$. At stage $\alpha$, assume the values $h(a(\xi))$
for $\xi<\alpha$ have been selected. Form the two sets
\[
 A_\alpha=\{h(a(\xi)):\xi<\alpha,
                         \ a(\xi)<_L a(\alpha)\},
 \qquad
 B_\alpha=\{h(a(\xi)):\xi<\alpha,
                         \ a(\alpha)<_L a(\xi)\}.
\]
Earlier choices preserve order, so $A_\alpha<B_\alpha$. Choose a separator
in the target, using its set-cut property and a fixed global well-order
for a definite choice. The new value is different from every earlier
value and has exactly the required comparisons. At each stage the
partial map is a set. The resulting class function is the embedding.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness and set-homogeneity]\label{swo:ec:thm:backforth}
In $\GBC$, any two class linear orders with the set-cut property are
isomorphic. Moreover, an order isomorphism between set-sized suborders
of these orders extends to a class order isomorphism.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Neither order is a set: applying the set-cut property with the entire
carrier on the left would otherwise be contradictory. Fix $\Ord$-length
enumerations of both carriers. Start with the given set partial
isomorphism. At each ordinal stage, first put the least not-yet-mapped
element of the first enumeration into the domain. Its required image
is constrained by two sets of already mapped elements; the set-cut
property supplies an image. Next put the least omitted element of the
second enumeration into the range by the symmetric construction. Take
unions at limit stages. Every initial partial map is a set, so the
recursion is of the permitted kind. The final map is total and onto.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{swo:ec:cor:removed}
For every set $U\subseteq\No$, $\No\setminus U\cong\No$. Every nonempty
open interval of $\No$ is likewise isomorphic to $\No$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use \cref{swo:ec:lem:avoid,swo:ec:thm:backforth}. For an interval $(a,b)$, add $a$ to
every lower constraint set and $b$ to every upper constraint set.
\end{proof}
These isomorphisms concern numerical order alone and need not preserve
simplicity or arithmetic.

\section{Well-order codes on a fixed set alphabet}\label{swo:sw:fixed}

Let \(X\) be an infinite linearly ordered set, and put
\(\lambda=\card{X}\).  We work in \(\ZFC\) throughout this section.
A well-order on the whole carrier \(X\) has a unique increasing
enumeration \(f:\alpha\longrightarrow X\), where increasing refers to
that well-order, not to the native order of \(X\).  Its domain satisfies
\(\card{\alpha}=\lambda\), and hence \(\alpha<\lambda^+\).
Write \(\WO(X)\) for these bijective enumeration codes, and introduce
two related sets:
\[
 \mathcal I(X)=
 \bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda^+}\{f:\alpha\hookrightarrow X\},
 \qquad
 \WO_\lambda(X)=\{f:\lambda\longrightarrow X:
                                      f\text{ is bijective}\}.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal I(X)\) codes well-orders of arbitrary subsets of \(X\),
including the empty subset, whereas \(\WO(X)\) always uses the whole
carrier.  All three sets inherit the lexicographic order defined
earlier.  A proper prefix is smaller than its extension in
\(\mathcal I(X)\).  Two distinct members of \(\WO(X)\) cannot be proper
prefixes of one another: the shorter enumeration would already have
used every element of \(X\).

The repository's real-well-ordering report already proves the
exhaustive and cardinal-length statements for arbitrary infinite
alphabets \cite{ProveItReals}.  We record those results together
with the injective-word variant, and include a common proof
to keep the size distinctions explicit.  Neither density nor
completeness of the native order is needed.

\begin{theorem}[Cardinality and exact ordinal spectrum]\label{swo:sw:setspectrum}
Each of \(\WO_\lambda(X)\), \(\WO(X)\), and \(\mathcal I(X)\)
has cardinality \(2^\lambda\), contains a copy of every linear order
of cardinality at most \(\lambda\), and contains neither
\(\lambda^+\) nor \((\lambda^+)^*\).
Consequently the ordinals embeddable in any of them are exactly
the ordinals \(\alpha<\lambda^+\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
There are at most \(\lambda^+\) permitted domains.  For each domain
there are at most \(\lambda^\lambda=2^\lambda\) functions, so
\(\card{\mathcal I(X)}\leq\lambda^+\cdot2^\lambda=2^\lambda\).
For the reverse inequality, partition \(X\) into pairs
\(\{a_\xi,b_\xi\}\), \(\xi<\lambda\), with \(a_\xi<b_\xi\).
The lexicographic order on \(\lambda\times\{0,1\}\), taking
\(\xi\) first, has order type \(2\cdot\lambda=\lambda\).
For \(\varepsilon\in2^\lambda\), list the \(\xi\)-th pair as
\((a_\xi,b_\xi)\) if \(\varepsilon(\xi)=0\), and as
\((b_\xi,a_\xi)\) otherwise.  The resulting map
\[
                 2^\lambda\longrightarrow\WO_\lambda(X)
\]
is an order embedding when \(2^\lambda\) has lexicographic order.
This proves all three cardinality assertions.

Let \(L\) be any linear order of cardinality at most \(\lambda\),
and fix an injection \(\iota:L\hookrightarrow\lambda\).
Associate to \(t\in L\) the binary function \(c_t\) whose value at
\(\iota(s)\) is \(1\) precisely when \(s<t\), and whose remaining
coordinates are \(0\).  If \(t<u\), then \(c_t\leq c_u\)
coordinatewise, and the inequality is strict at \(\iota(t)\).
Their first difference therefore has the correct direction.
The preceding pair construction embeds \(L\) into
\(\WO_\lambda(X)\).

It remains to exclude longer monotone sequences.  Suppose that
\((f_\xi)_{\xi<\lambda^+}\) is strictly increasing or strictly
decreasing in \(\mathcal I(X)\).
We recursively construct eventual common prefixes \(p_\alpha\)
of length \(\alpha\), for \(\alpha<\lambda^+\).
At a limit stage, take the union of the earlier prefixes.
Regularity of \(\lambda^+\) ensures that a tail of the original
sequence extends that union.  At a successor step, at most one
member of this tail equals \(p_\alpha\); discard it and all earlier
indices.  The values at coordinate \(\alpha\) are now monotone.
A monotone sequence indexed by a tail of \(\lambda^+\), taking
at most \(\lambda\) values, is eventually constant: the first
occurrence indices of all its values have a supremum below
\(\lambda^+\).  Append this eventual value to \(p_\alpha\).
Every constructed prefix is injective because it occurs in
members of the original sequence.  The union of the prefixes
through \(\lambda^+\) would therefore be an injection
\(\lambda^+\hookrightarrow X\), a contradiction.
Finally, an ordinal at least \(\lambda^+\) contains
\(\lambda^+\), whereas every smaller ordinal has cardinality
at most \(\lambda\).
\end{proof}

The distinction between the models also affects their elementary
order topology.  The order \(\WO_\lambda(X)\) is dense.
Indeed, let \(f<_{\lex}g\), with first difference at \(\xi\).
If the tail of \(f\) after \(\xi\) has an ascent, interchanging
the two entries produces a point strictly between \(f\) and \(g\).
If the tail of \(g\) has a descent, the corresponding interchange
works in the other direction.  If neither exists, the first
remaining tail is strictly decreasing and the second strictly
increasing.  Their common set of entries, after removing the two
entries at \(\xi\), is infinite and would be both well-ordered
and reverse-well-ordered.  This is impossible.

By contrast, \(\WO(X)\) has adjacent pairs.  Choose \(a<b\) in \(X\),
enumerate \(X\setminus\{a,b\}\) as a prefix \(p\), and compare
\(p\cat\langle a,b\rangle\) with
\(p\cat\langle b,a\rangle\).  Any intervening enumeration would have
to share \(p\), after which only these two orders remain.
Thus a cardinal-length convention changes the resulting linear
order even though it does not change its cardinality or ordinal
embedding spectrum.

\begin{proposition}[Exactly where jumps occur]\label{swo:sw:adjacency}
Suppose \(f<_{\lex}g\) in \(\WO(X)\), with common prefix \(p\)
up to their first difference.  Put
\(Y=X\setminus\ran(p)\), \(a=f(\dom(p))\), and
\(b=g(\dom(p))\), so \(a<b\).
The pair is adjacent precisely when \(Y\) is finite,
\(a,b\) are consecutive in its native order, the tail of
\(f\) after \(a\) lists \(Y\setminus\{a\}\) decreasingly,
and the tail of \(g\) after \(b\) lists
\(Y\setminus\{b\}\) increasingly.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If an unused element lies strictly between \(a\) and \(b\),
start an enumeration with that element after \(p\) and
complete it; this lies between \(f\) and \(g\).
Likewise, an ascent after \(a\), or a descent after \(b\),
can be interchanged to create an intervening enumeration.
Adjacency thus forces the two remaining tails to be
decreasing and increasing, respectively.
Their common native suborder \(Y\setminus\{a,b\}\) is then
both well-ordered and reverse-well-ordered.
It must be finite: an infinite well-order contains its
first \(\omega\) elements, a subset with no greatest element.
This proves necessity.
Conversely, an intervening enumeration must share \(p\).
There is no possible next entry strictly between \(a\)
and \(b\).  Among enumerations beginning with \(a\), the
displayed decreasing continuation is the largest; among
those beginning with \(b\), the increasing continuation
is the smallest.  Neither branch admits an intervening point.
\end{proof}

This description also identifies the finite components generated
by adjacency.  Write the domain of an enumeration uniquely as
\(\theta=\delta+n\), with \(\delta\) a limit ordinal and
\(n<\omega\).  Its component consists of the \(n!\) permutations
of the final \(n\) entries, keeping the prefix of length
\(\delta\) fixed.  In particular, words of limit length have
no immediate neighbor.  A jump cannot cross from one such
component to another, because its common-prefix remainder
would be infinite.

Endpoints can be classified just as concretely.
The least element of \(\WO(X)\), if one exists, must always
choose the least unused native element: otherwise interchanging
that entry with a later smaller one decreases the enumeration.
Hence a least element exists exactly when the native order
on \(X\) is a well-order, and is its increasing enumeration.
The greatest-element statement is the reverse assertion.
For \(\WO_\lambda(X)\), the same argument shows that
a least element exists exactly when the native order type is
the initial ordinal \(\lambda\), not merely an arbitrary
ordinal of cardinality \(\lambda\).
For example, an alphabet of native type \(\lambda+1\)
has a least full enumeration, but no least
\(\lambda\)-length permutation.

\subsection{Source 12's route: a general set-sized spectrum theorem}
\label{swo:st:sec:bounded}

We temporarily forget the surreal structure. Let $X$ be any infinite
linearly ordered set, and write $|X|=\mu$, an initial cardinal.
The spectra below depend only on the cardinality, not on density,
separability, or field operations of $X$.

\begin{lemma}[Prefix-freeness of exhaustive enumerations]\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:prefixfree}
Two distinct exhaustive injective ordinal enumerations of $X$ are never
proper prefixes of one another. Hence first-difference lexicography is
unambiguous on $\WO(X)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An exhaustive prefix has already used every element of $X$. An injective
proper extension would have to use a new element, which is impossible.
\end{proof}

For any ordinal $\gamma$, let $\BB_\gamma=(2^\gamma,<_{\lex})$.
For linear orders $L,M$, write $L\emb M$ for an order-embedding and
$L\equim M$ for embeddings in both directions. Define
\[
 \bl(L)=\min\{\gamma:L\emb\BB_\gamma\}
\]
when such a binary coding ordinal exists. This is an ordinal-valued rank,
not a cardinal invariant.

\begin{lemma}[Strict binary hierarchy]\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:strictcube}
For ordinals $\alpha,\beta$,
\[
 \BB_\alpha\emb\BB_\beta\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\alpha\leq\beta.
\]
In particular $\bl(\BB_\alpha)=\alpha$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Zero-padding proves the forward construction when $\alpha\leq\beta$.
It suffices to rule out an embedding
$f:\BB_{\beta+1}\to\BB_\beta$.

Recursively construct an input prefix $s_\xi$ of length $\xi$ and an
output prefix $t_\xi$ of length $\xi$, so that every input extending
$s_\xi$ is sent to an output extending $t_\xi$. At a successor stage,
split the input cylinder into its two next-bit halves and split the
output cylinder likewise. The two input halves have strictly ordered
images. They cannot both have images meeting both output halves:
an image point in the upper output half from the lower input half would
exceed an image point in the lower output half from the upper input half.
Thus one input half has image contained in a single output half.
Choose those halves to continue.

At a limit take unions; the corresponding cylinders are nonempty and
the containment persists. At stage $\beta$, two inputs remain, differing
in their last bit, but their images have the same full $\beta$-long
output. This contradicts injectivity. For $\alpha>\beta$, padding embeds
$\BB_{\beta+1}$ into $\BB_\alpha$, giving the general impossibility.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Characteristic-cut coding]\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:cutcode}
Every linear order of cardinality at most $\mu$ embeds in $\BB_\mu$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate its carrier by distinct coordinates $d_\xi$, padding unused
coordinates if necessary. Send $x$ to the bits
$\mathbf1[d_\xi<x]$. For $x<y$, every differing coordinate changes from
$0$ to $1$, and the coordinate representing $x$ does change. Thus the
least difference gives the correct order.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pair orientation coding]\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:pairs}
$\BB_\mu\emb\WO_\mu(X)$. More generally,
$\BB_\gamma\emb\WO(X)$ for every $\gamma<\mu^+$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Partition $X$ into $\mu$ unordered pairs, sort each pair by $X$'s order,
and orient the pair according to its bit. The ordinal sum of $\mu$
two-element blocks has type $2\cdot\mu=\mu$.

For a general $\gamma<\mu^+$, choose $|\gamma|$ disjoint pairs and retain
a disjoint reserve of size $\mu$. Such a choice is possible even when
$|\gamma|=\mu$. List the pairs in type $\gamma$, then well-order all
remaining labels in type $\mu$. The resulting enumeration has length
$2\cdot\gamma+\mu<\mu^+$. Its comparison is decided by the first
oriented pair at which the inputs differ.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[No $\mu^+$-long monotone chain]\label[lemma]{swo:st:lem:nochain}
Neither $\mu^+$ nor its reverse embeds into $\WO(X)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $(e_i)_{i<\mu^+}$ is strictly increasing. We recursively stabilize
its entries on final segments of the index set. Assume that a final
segment agrees on a prefix $p$ of length $\delta<\mu^+$. No enumeration
in a further infinite final segment can end there, by
\cref{swo:st:lem:prefixfree}. Their $\delta$th entries form a nondecreasing
$\mu^+$-sequence in a set of size $\mu$.

Such a sequence is eventually constant: choose one first occurrence for
each value in its range; their at most $\mu$ indices have supremum below
$\mu^+$ by regularity. Past that supremum no larger value can first
appear. At a limit stage $\delta<\mu^+$, take the supremum of the earlier
stabilization indices, still below $\mu^+$, and the union of the earlier
prefixes.

This would produce an injective sequence of labels from $X$ of length
$\mu^+$: every set-sized earlier part is shared by a final segment of
injective enumerations. That contradicts $|X|=\mu$. Replace
nondecreasing by nonincreasing for the reverse order.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cardinality and exact spectra]\label{swo:st:thm:setspectrum}
For every infinite linearly ordered set $X$ of cardinality $\mu$,
\begin{align*}
 |\WO(X)|=|\WO_\mu(X)|&=2^\mu,\\
 \beta\emb\WO(X)\quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta<\mu^+,\\
 \beta\emb\WO_\mu(X)\quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta<\mu^+,\\
 \BB_\gamma\emb\WO(X)\quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma<\mu^+,\\
 \bl(\WO(X))&=\mu^+.
\end{align*}
The ordinal statements also hold for reversed ordinals, and every
linear order of cardinality at most $\mu$ embeds even into
$\WO_\mu(X)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Pair coding gives $2^\mu$ elements, while all well-orders are relations
on $X$, giving the upper bound $2^{|X\times X|}=2^\mu$.
The lower ordinal bounds and universality follow from
\cref{swo:st:lem:cutcode,swo:st:lem:pairs}; \cref{swo:st:lem:nochain} gives the upper bounds.
The same characteristic coding applies to reversed ordinals.

For the cube spectrum use \cref{swo:st:lem:pairs}. If $\gamma\geq\mu^+$,
$\BB_\gamma$ contains an increasing chain of type $\mu^+$: use the
sequences that are $1$ before a moving cut and $0$ afterward. Thus it
cannot embed into $\WO(X)$.

Embed $X$ into $\BB_\mu$ using \cref{swo:st:lem:cutcode}. Encode an exhaustive
enumeration of length $\alpha<\mu^+$ by concatenating its $\mu$-long
entry codes, then pad with zeroes to length $\mu^+$. The unpadded length
$\mu\cdot\alpha$ has cardinality at most $\mu$, so is less than $\mu^+$.
Distinct enumerations disagree before either ends, and their encoded
first disagreement preserves the order. This proves
$\WO(X)\emb\BB_{\mu^+}$.

If it embedded in $\BB_\rho$ for $\rho<\mu^+$, then the copy of
$\BB_{\rho+1}$ supplied by \cref{swo:st:lem:pairs} would contradict
\cref{swo:st:lem:strictcube}. Hence the rank is exactly $\mu^+$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the rank does not say]\label{swo:st:n9.7}
Although $\bl(\WO(X))=\mu^+$, the cube $\BB_{\mu^+}$ does \emph{not}
embed back into $\WO(X)$. An order can first admit a binary encoding at
an ordinal without containing the full cube of that ordinal.
Nor is the absence of $\mu^+$ and its reverse claimed sufficient for an
arbitrary order to embed in $\WO(X)$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Source 09's route}\label{swo:ec:sec:setcase}

\merge\ Source~09's Section~4 works for any linearly ordered set. Its first
statements are recorded in notes; its stabilization lemma and its proof of the
ordinal spectrum are a second route and are printed in full.

\begin{note}[Source~09, Definition~4.1]\label{swo:ec:n4.1}
$\WO_\alpha(X)=\Bij(\alpha,X)$ and $\WO(X)$ is the union over all ordinals
$\alpha$; if $\card X=\kappa$ is infinite, the possible lengths are exactly
$\kappa\le\alpha<\kappa^+$. This is the $\WO(X)$ of \cref{swo:sw:fixed} and of
the reals report.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~09, Lemma~4.2, ``Exhaustiveness removes the prefix ambiguity'']\label{swo:ec:lem:prefixfree}
\emph{Distinct members of $\WO(X)$ have a first unequal coordinate strictly
below both of their lengths}, so $e<_\lex f$ at that coordinate is a strict
linear order (for transitivity compare the two first-disagreement ordinals of
$e<f$ and $f<g$). This is \code{lwo:lem:prefix-free} and
\cref{swo:st:lem:prefixfree}, by the same argument.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~09, Theorem~4.3, ``Cardinality and universality'']\label{swo:ec:thm:set-universal}
\emph{For every infinite linearly ordered set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$,
$\card{\WO_\kappa(X)}=\card{\WO(X)}=2^\kappa$; the lexicographic cube
$2^\kappa$ embeds into $\WO_\kappa(X)$; consequently every linear order of size
at most $\kappa$ embeds into $\WO_\kappa(X)$ and hence into $\WO(X)$.} This is
\cref{swo:sw:setspectrum}, \code{lwo:prop:cardinality} and
\code{lwo:thm:ordinal-spectrum}(a), with the same pair-orientation and
characteristic-function codes. Source~09 stresses that $2\cdot\kappa=\kappa$
is ordinal multiplication.
\end{note}

\paragraph{Second route (source~09): eventual stabilization at a regular cardinal.}

% ---- source 09, lines 435-483
\begin{lemma}[Eventual stabilization]\label{swo:ec:lem:stabilize}
Let $\mu$ be a regular infinite cardinal and let $X$ have cardinality
less than $\mu$. Every nondecreasing map $f:\mu\to X$ is eventually
constant.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Some fiber must be unbounded: otherwise the union of fewer than $\mu$
bounded fibers would be bounded. Once a value in such a fiber is reached,
monotonicity and the unboundedness of the fiber prevent any subsequent
strict increase.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact ordinal spectrum]\label{swo:ec:thm:ordinal-spectrum}
For $|X|=\kappa$ infinite and any ordinal $\beta$,
\[
 \beta\emb\WO(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta<\kappa^+.
\]
The same equivalence holds for $\beta^*$, the reverse order of $\beta$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The positive direction follows from \cref{swo:ec:thm:set-universal}.
For the negative direction put $\mu=\kappa^+$ and suppose that
$(e_\xi)_{\xi<\mu}$ is strictly increasing in $\WO(X)$. We construct an
injective common eventual prefix of length $\mu$, which is impossible
in the alphabet $X$.

Assume a prefix $p$ of length $\delta<\mu$ is shared by all $e_\xi$ beyond
some index $t_\delta<\mu$. At limits this holds by taking the supremum of
the earlier cutoffs; regularity ensures that the new cutoff remains below
$\mu$. If $p$ exhausts $X$, every enumeration on this tail is exactly $p$,
contrary to strict increase. Otherwise each tail enumeration has an entry
at coordinate $\delta$. As the words share all earlier coordinates,
these entries are nondecreasing in $\xi$. By \cref{swo:ec:lem:stabilize} they
eventually have one common value. Add it to $p$. Injectivity of the
enumerations makes this a new value, not used earlier in $p$.

Continuing for every $\delta<\mu$ gives $\mu$ distinct elements of $X$,
a contradiction. An embedding of any $\beta\ge\mu$ would restrict to
one of $\mu$. Reversing the alphabet proves the negative statement for
$\mu^*$ and its longer extensions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{swo:ec:n4.6}
The absence of $\kappa^+$ and its reverse is not asserted to characterize
all linear orders embeddable in $\WO(X)$. Indeed $\WO(X)$ already contains
the binary cube of cardinality $2^\kappa$, so ``size at most $\kappa$'' is
a universality guarantee, not a necessary cardinality condition for an
individual order to embed.
\end{remark}

% ---- hand chunk n09set_b

\begin{note}[Source~09, Proposition~4.7]\label{swo:ec:prop:endpoints}
\emph{$\WO(X)$ has a least element exactly when the alphabet order on $X$ is a
well-order, and a greatest element exactly when its reverse is.} This is the
paragraph on endpoints after \cref{swo:sw:adjacency} and
\code{lwo:lem:extrema}, by the same argument (a least enumeration must take the
least unused element at every position).
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~09, Proposition~4.8, ``Finite residuals are exactly the adjacency mechanism'']\label{swo:ec:prop:adjacent}
\emph{If $e<f$ in $\WO(X)$ have common prefix $p$ before their first
disagreement and $R=X\setminus\ran(p)$, they are adjacent precisely when $R$ is
finite and their remaining words are consecutive permutations of $R$ in finite
lexicographic order.} This is \cref{swo:sw:adjacency} and
\code{lwo:thm:adjacency}, by the same argument through
\cref{swo:ec:prop:endpoints}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 09, lines 521-524
Even for a dense alphabet $X$, the full space $\WO(X)$ can therefore have
adjacent points. This finite-tail phenomenon disappears for global
enumerations: deleting a set prefix from $\No$ never leaves a finite
remainder.
