\section{The set-coded skeleton and its cylinders (source 14)}
\label{swo:tc:sec:core}
For the remainder of the class-level development we work in $\GBC$ and
fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. All occurrences of a class
parameter mean a class belonging to the chosen class realization.

\subsection{Canonical support codes}
A \emph{support code} is a set bijection $\sigma:S\to S$ with no fixed
points, where $S$ is a set of ordinals. The empty code is permitted.
Extend it by the identity to a class permutation $\widehat\sigma$ of
$\Ord$, and set
\[
 E_\sigma=b\circ\widehat\sigma,
 \qquad \supp(\sigma)=S.
\]
Let $\Psupp(b)$ be the ordinary class of these codes, ordered by
$\sigma<\tau$ if $E_\sigma <_{\lex} E_\tau$. The codes are canonical:
two of them have the same extension exactly when they are equal.
Every class permutation with set support is represented, because its
support is invariant under the permutation and its restriction has no
fixed points. A set of ordinals is bounded, so ``set support'' and
``bounded support'' are equivalent here. This does not mean finite support.

Let $\Hsl$ stand for the virtual collection of class bijections
$\Ord\to\No$, and $\Jinj$ for that of class injections. A statement
quantifying over $\Hsl$ or $\Jinj$ is a statement with class variables;
these symbols do not name additional class objects. Two distinct members
of $\Jinj$ have a least differing ordinal. Their common initial segment
has set length, so first-difference comparison is unambiguous.

\begin{lemma}[Fresh separators]\label{swo:tc:lem:fresh}
If $A,B,U$ are sets of surreals and $A<B$, there is a surreal
$x\notin U$ such that $A<x<B$. Consequently $\No\setminus U$ has
no endpoints and fills all cuts specified by sets of its elements.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The ordinary surreal set-cut theorem supplies a separator
(\cite{Ehrlich2012}; \cref{swo:lem:delete}). In fact there
are more than $|U|$ separators: recursively for $|U|^+$ many steps choose
a separator above the earlier choices and $A$, and below $B$.
Every stage uses set options, and the resulting choices are distinct.
At least one is outside $U$. The same argument permits either option
set to be empty. This uses set recursion and the usual surreal cut
existence theorem, not a purported cut with proper-class options.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Completion of a set prefix]\label{swo:tc:lem:completion}
Every injective set word $p:\lambda\to\No$ extends to some
$E_\sigma$ with $\sigma\in \Psupp(b)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose an infinite initial cardinal $\nu$ strictly greater than
$\lambda$ and all the ordinals in $b^{-1}[\ran p]$. The map
$\alpha\mapsto b^{-1}(p(\alpha))$ is a partial injection from $\nu$
to itself with domain of cardinality $<\nu$ and equally small range.
Both complements have cardinality $\nu$. Choose a bijection between
them to extend the partial map to a permutation of $\nu$, and fix every
ordinal outside $\nu$. Restricting the resulting permutation to its
moved points gives the required canonical code.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Cylinder and residual alphabet]\label{swo:tc:n4.3}
For an injective set prefix $p:\lambda\to\No$, put
\[
 C_p=\{\sigma\in \Psupp(b):E_\sigma\res\lambda=p\},
 \qquad A_p=\No\setminus\ran p.
\]
The empty prefix has cylinder $C_\varnothing=\Psupp(b)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Cylinder geometry]\label{swo:tc:prop:cylinders}
Every $C_p$ is a nonempty convex proper class. It has neither an endpoint
nor a set-sized cofinal or coinitial subset. Its immediate subdivisions
are
\[
 C_p=\bigcup_{x\in A_p}C_{p\cat(x)},
\]
in increasing order of $x$. The union is an elementary class statement,
not a set-indexed union. Cylinders of two prefixes are either nested or
disjoint and strictly ordered.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Completion proves nonemptiness. If a word between two extensions of $p$
first differed from $p$ before $\lambda$, it would lie on the same side
of both extensions, proving convexity. The child cylinders partition
$C_p$ by the value at coordinate $\lambda$, and first difference puts
them in numerical order. \Cref{swo:tc:lem:fresh} and completion give a
child below or above any specified set of child labels. Thus a set of
members of $C_p$ is neither cofinal nor coinitial: take their next
labels, choose a fresh label above or below all of them, and complete.
In particular $C_p$ cannot itself be a set. Finally, incomparable
prefixes first differ at a set coordinate, which orders their entire
cylinders; comparable prefixes give nested cylinders.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Density around injective branches]\label{swo:tc:lem:branchdensity}
If $F,G\in \Jinj$ and $F<_{\lex} G$, there is a code $\sigma\in \Psupp(b)$
with $F<_{\lex} E_\sigma <_{\lex} G$. For every $F\in \Jinj$ and every set
ordinal $\alpha$, there are codes below and above $F$ agreeing with
$F$ before $\alpha$ and differing from it at $\alpha$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the first assertion use the first disagreement $\delta$, choose
$x$ strictly between $F(\delta)$ and $G(\delta)$ outside their common
prefix range, and complete $(F\res\delta)\cat(x)$. For the second,
choose fresh values below and above $F(\alpha)$ and complete the two
prefixes. A fixed global well-order of set codes makes all these
choices uniform when a uniform family is needed.
\end{proof}

These elementary cylinder facts, rather than a powerclass completion,
are the main engine of the next result. The predecessor proves the
stronger statement that $\Psupp(b)$ interpolates every uniformly
set-indexed strict cut of $\Hsl$ (\cref{swo:gl:interpolation}; Section~19
of this report at the pin).
We will also recover the ordinary set-cut property of $\Psupp(b)$ from
our cut classification and its character calculation.

\begin{note}[\merge; Part~IV counterparts of source~14's Section~4]\label{swo:viii:note:core}
Source~14's support codes are source~09's coding $\Psupp(b)$
(\cref{swo:sec:notation}); its \cref{swo:tc:lem:fresh} is \cref{swo:lem:delete},
its \cref{swo:tc:lem:completion} is \cref{swo:gl:completion} with the

\subsection{Source 13: surreal cuts and the size of the universe}\label{swo:fs:sec:surreal}

\subsubsection{Signs, birthdays, and small cut filling}

We use the sign-sequence presentation of the surreal numbers. A surreal
$x$ is a sequence of signs $-$ and $+$ indexed by a set ordinal $\bd(x)$.
Extend the sequence by $0$ after its domain; comparison is at the first
unequal coordinate using $-<0<+$. Here $0$ in the sign alphabet is a
termination value, not an extra sign before the birthday. This is also
the representation used by the inspected Lean carrier
\cite{ProveItSigns}. General context for the universal ordered-continuum
viewpoint is given in \cite{Ehrlich2012}.

For sets $A,B\subseteq\No$ with $A<B$, a surreal lies strictly between
them. More precisely, if an ordinal $\gamma$ strictly exceeds all their
birthdays, there is such a separator of birthday exactly $\gamma$.
The stronger statement is implemented at the source level by
\code{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt}
\cite{ProveItCutFill}. We use it in the following form.

\begin{lemma}[Fresh set-cut separator]\label{swo:fs:lem:fresh}
Let $A,B,S$ be sets of surreals and suppose $A<B$. There is an
$x\notin S$ with $A<x<B$. Empty sides are allowed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $\gamma$ strictly larger than every birthday occurring in
$A\cup B\cup S$. A separator of birthday $\gamma$ cannot belong to $S$.
\end{proof}

The adjective ``set'' cannot be removed. There is no surreal above every
ordinal: any surreal is smaller than a sufficiently long all-plus sign
sequence. Likewise, a proper-class sign sequence is not another surreal
at a larger birthday.

\subsubsection{Set-cut orders and class back-and-forth}

Call an ordinary class linear order \emph{set-cut saturated} when every
pair of sets $A<B$ has a strict interpolant, including when a side is
empty. This is sometimes expressed by an $\eta_{\Ord}$ terminology; we
use the explicit condition rather than assigning a set cardinal to it.

\begin{lemma}[Class universality and uniqueness in $\GBC$]\label{swo:fs:lem:backforth}
Every ordinary class linear order embeds into $\No$. Any two nonempty
set-cut saturated ordinary class orders are order-isomorphic. In
particular, for every set $S\subseteq\No$,
\[
                    \No\setminus S\cong\No.
\]
The complement isomorphisms can be chosen as a single uniform class
family $h_S:\No\to\No\setminus S$, indexed by sets $S$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Global choice supplies a set-like enumeration of any proper class of
sets; for a set carrier use a set well-order. At a stage of the usual
order-embedding recursion, the images already chosen form a set. Their
lower and upper parts determine a set cut in $\No$, and a fresh
interpolant gives the next image. The recursion has a set partial map
at each set-ordinal stage.

For uniqueness, alternate the two enumerations. A forth step puts the
next unused source point into the target cut determined by the current
partial isomorphism; a back step does the same for the inverse. Strict
interpolation keeps each map injective. Every point on both sides is
visited, so the union is an isomorphism. A set-cut saturated nonempty
order cannot be a set, since using all its points as a lower side would
require a point above itself.

\Cref{swo:fs:lem:fresh} says that $\No\setminus S$ has the same set-cut
property. To make its isomorphism uniform, fix the global well-order
and always choose its least eligible witness. For each set parameter
$S$ and each set stage, the partial history is a set satisfying a fixed
recursive specification. Its existence and uniqueness are established
by set-length recursion. Elementary class comprehension, quantifying
over such set histories, gives one relation $h(S,x,y)$. No choice of a
class witness for each $S$ is being assumed.
\end{proof}

This is not an appeal to elementary transfinite recursion with
\emph{class-valued} stages. Our stages are sets, even though their total
union is a class. Keeping that distinction explicit will matter in
source~13's sections on asymmetric products and on foundational
interpretations (\merge\ its Sections~10 and~13, printed in Part~IX as
\cref{swo:fs:sec:products,swo:fs:sec:foundations}).

\subsubsection{Global choice is a real assumption}

The earlier report proves, over $\GB$ without set choice, that the
existence of a class well-order of $\No$ is equivalent to global choice
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}; Theorem~13.1 at the pin). Thus a global enumeration is not a
choice-free consequence of the numerical order of surreals. We work in
$\GBC$ for the main global constructions and fix a baseline bijection
\[
                         b:\Ord\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\No.
\]
The particular $b$ affects the chosen dense core but not the definition
of the full enumeration comparison.

% ---- source 13 (batch-81 manuscript 01), lines 624-807
\subsection{Source 13: the global enumeration order and its dense core}\label{swo:fs:sec:core}

\subsubsection{Uniformity and the code carrier}

Let $\Jinj$ denote the virtual domain of injective class functions
$F:\Ord\to\No$, and let $\Hsl\subseteq \Jinj$ require surjectivity. Their
lexicographic comparison is at the least disagreement ordinal. A
nonempty class of ordinals has a least member: find one member and take
the least member below it. Thus this comparison is elementary in its
class parameters.

A \emph{uniformly set-indexed family} $(F_i)_{i\in I}$ means a set $I$
and a single class relation coding all values $F_i(\alpha)$. A phrase
such as ``choose a class $F_i$ for each $i$'' is not a substitute for this
uniform family. We consistently use the latter.

Fix $b:\Ord\simeq\No$. A set-supported permutation $\sigma$ of $\Ord$
is the identity except on a set of ordinals. Code it by the set graph of
its moved points, omitting all fixed points. Such normalized codes form
an ordinary class $\Psupp(b)$, and a code $d$ evaluates to
\[
                             E_d=b\circ\widehat d.
\]
Equivalently, a code is a set bijection $d:S\to S$, where $S$ is a
set of ordinals and $d(\xi)\ne\xi$ for every $\xi\in S$; the empty
code is allowed. This is an elementary condition on sets, so defining
$\Psupp(b)$ does not require quantification over a collection of class
permutations. Different normalized codes have different evaluations.
Order $\Psupp(b)$ by these evaluations. The support of each code is bounded by a set ordinal,
but there is no common set bound for all codes.

For an injective set word $p$, define
\[
 C_p=\{E\in \Hsl:E\restr\dom(p)=p\},\qquad
 \Psupp(b)_p=\{d\in \Psupp(b):E_d\restr\dom(p)=p\}.
\]
$C_p$ is virtual notation; $\Psupp(b)_p$ is an ordinary class of set codes.
Both are convex in their respective orders.

\subsubsection{Completion with the missing cardinality check}

\begin{lemma}[Set-prefix completion]\label{swo:fs:lem:completion}
Every injective set prefix $p:\alpha\to\No$ has a completion in $\Psupp(b)$.
The completion can be chosen uniformly from $p$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The class inverse of $b$, restricted to the set range of $p$, gives a
set injection $f=b^{-1}\circ p:\alpha\to\Ord$. Choose an infinite
initial cardinal $\delta$ strictly above $\alpha$ and every member of
$\ran(f)$. Both $\delta\setminus\alpha$ and
$\delta\setminus\ran(f)$ then have cardinality $\delta$. A bijection
between these complements extends $f$ to a permutation of $\delta$.
Extend it by the identity outside $\delta$ and retain only its moved
points as a code. Global choice makes the choices uniform.
\end{proof}

It would be incorrect to assert that every partial injection of a set
into itself extends to a permutation without checking the complements.
For instance, a bijection from a proper subset onto the entire carrier
has no such extension. Enlarging to the cardinal $\delta$ is exactly
what prevents this obstruction.

\subsubsection{The active-prefix interpolation argument}

The next theorem is the earlier dense-core interpolation result
(\cref{swo:gl:interpolation}; Section~19 at the pin). We include the algorithm because both
cut classification and the central-word theorem depend on its logic.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform set-cut interpolation]\label{swo:fs:thm:interpolate}
Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(B_j)_{j\in J}$ be uniform set-indexed
families in $\Jinj$, with $A_i<B_j$ for every cross pair. There is an
injective set prefix $p$ such that all its global completions lie
strictly between the two families. In particular, a code in $\Psupp(b)$
interpolates the cut.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a cross pair let $d(i,j)$ be its least disagreement. Class
replacement gives a set of these ordinals. Put
\[
               \theta=\sup\{d(i,j)+1:i\in I,\ j\in J\},
\]
with supremum $0$ for an empty set. We construct an injective common
prefix, keeping as \emph{active} the rows that agree with it so far.
Every inactive lower row is already strictly below all completions;
every inactive upper row is already strictly above them.

At stage $\beta$, let $L_\beta$ and $U_\beta$ be the sets of next
letters of the active lower and upper rows. Every $l\in L_\beta$ is
at most every $u\in U_\beta$, since otherwise the corresponding
cross pair would be reversed. There are two cases.

If $L_\beta\cap U_\beta$ is nonempty, it is a singleton $\{t\}$.
Append $t$, which is fresh because the active rows are injective.
Keep only the rows whose next letter is $t$. A dropped lower row has
next letter less than $t$, and a dropped upper row has next letter
greater than $t$, so the invariant is maintained.

If the intersection is empty, then $L_\beta<U_\beta$, allowing empty
sides. Choose a fresh strict separator $x$ outside the earlier range
by \Cref{swo:fs:lem:fresh}, and append it. Every remaining active
comparison is now strict. This prefix is the required $p$.

At a limit stage take the union of the earlier set prefixes and keep
exactly the rows agreeing with it. The construction cannot continue
with a shared letter through stage $\theta$: surviving active rows on
both sides would agree beyond their first disagreement. It therefore
stops by that stage. The prefix has length at most $\theta+1$.
Apply \Cref{swo:fs:lem:completion} to obtain a code.
\end{proof}

The histories in this proof have set length and set entries. Nothing
requires collecting a set of class-valued choices, taking a surreal
cut with proper-class sides, or invoking a class-valued recursion
principle.

\begin{corollary}[The core and its cylinders]\label{swo:fs:cor:core}
$\Psupp(b)\cong\No$, and every $\Psupp(b)_p\cong\No$. The core is order-dense
among global enumerations and among distinct injective class words.
Every interval specified by a uniform set cut in $\Hsl$ contains a
whole cylinder $C_p$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The theorem says that $\Psupp(b)$ fills all its set cuts, so
\Cref{swo:fs:lem:backforth} applies. To keep a prescribed prefix $p$,
run the same active-row construction after $p$, forbidding $\ran(p)$
as well as the later used values; all forbidden values at a stage
still form a set. This proves the set-cut property of $\Psupp(b)_p$,
including empty sides. The other assertions follow directly from the
strict cylinder conclusion of the theorem.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Approximating one branch}

\begin{lemma}[Two-sided ordinal approximants]\label{swo:fs:lem:approximants}
For $F\in \Jinj$ there are uniform sequences of codes $a_\alpha,b_\alpha$
indexed by $\Ord$ such that, for $\alpha<\beta$,
\[
 E_{a_\alpha}<E_{a_\beta}<F<E_{b_\beta}<E_{b_\alpha}.
\]
They are respectively cofinal and coinitial among code evaluations
strictly below and above $F$. Neither punctured side has a set-sized
cofinal or coinitial family.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Complete $F\restr\alpha$ followed by a fresh letter below $F(\alpha)$
to obtain $a_\alpha$, and use a fresh letter above for $b_\alpha$.
The inequalities are decided at the earlier index. A code differing
from $F$ at $\xi$ lies on the appropriate far side of every
approximant with index greater than $\xi$. Uniform choices come from
the least completion code in the fixed global well-order. Finally,
\Cref{swo:fs:thm:interpolate}, with $F$ on one side, puts a code
strictly beyond any proposed set family on the other side.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The diagonal limitation on all set codes}

\begin{theorem}[No exhaustive uniform evaluator]\label{swo:fs:thm:diagonal}
No single class relation with set indices can have, among its rows,
every class bijection $\Ord\to\No$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Extend an alleged evaluator to all set indices by giving unused
indices empty rows. Fix a class bijection $\alpha\mapsto c_\alpha$
from $\Ord$ to the universe of sets. Partition $\Ord$ into pairs
\[
                    (2\cdot\alpha,\ 2\cdot\alpha+1).
\]
The multiplication is ordinal multiplication with $2$ on the left;
these adjacent pairs partition all ordinals.

On pair $\alpha$, use the two values
$b(2\cdot\alpha),b(2\cdot\alpha+1)$. Put the second value first if
the row $c_\alpha$ reports $b(2\cdot\alpha)$ at coordinate
$2\cdot\alpha$; otherwise put the first value first. Put the other
value second. This elementary class construction defines a bijection
$E$. Whenever the row $c_\alpha$ is the graph of a function, it differs
from $E$ at that even coordinate. Thus every valid row misses $E$.
\end{proof}

The theorem does not say that $\Psupp(b)$ is too small to be dense. It says
that density and exhaustive representation are different notions. It
also does not prohibit defining some enumerations from set parameters;
it prohibits one uniform evaluator from covering \emph{all} of them.

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 892-937
\subsection{Source 15: the ordinary class of bounded-support codes}\label{swo:viii:sub:cb-core}

Fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. A set-supported permutation
of $\Ord$ equals the identity outside some ordinal. Code it by a
permutation $\pi:\gamma\to\gamma$ and extend it by the identity.
Normalize
$\gamma=\sup\{\xi+1:\overline\pi(\xi)\ne\xi\}$,
using $\gamma=0$ and the empty code for the identity. This makes codes unique.
Let $\Pbd(b)$ be the ordinary class of these set codes, with evaluation
\[
 E_d(\xi)=b(\overline\pi_d(\xi)).
\]
The values of an evaluation are sets; the whole evaluation is a class
function uniformly given by a class relation.

\begin{lemma}[Every injective set prefix has a core completion]\label{swo:cb:lem:completion}
Every injective set word $p:\alpha\to\No$ extends to some $E_d$,
$d\in \Pbd(b)$, and a completion can be chosen uniformly.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The map $q=b^{-1}\circ p$ is a set injection into $\Ord$. Choose an
infinite initial cardinal $\nu$ greater than $\alpha$ and every member
of $\ran(q)$. The complements of $\alpha$ and of $\ran(q)$ in $\nu$
both have cardinality $\nu$. A bijection between them extends $q$ to
a permutation of $\nu$. Extend by the identity and normalize.
The least permissible $\nu$ and a fixed global well-order choose a
particular complement bijection, so the construction is uniform.
\end{proof}

We use the following established core theorem from the prior report:
$\Pbd(b)$, with the induced native lexicographic order, fills every set cut
and is class-order-isomorphic to $\No$ (\cref{swo:gl:interpolation} and
\cref{swo:gl:pbd-no}; Theorem~19.10 and Corollary~19.15 at the pin, which
source~15 cites as ``Theorems 19.10 and 19.15'').
Its proof combines prefix completion with fresh separators and then
applies the ordinary class back-and-forth theorem. This is a statement
about a class of sets, so it falls within surreal universality.

For an injective set word $p:\alpha\to\No$, its cylinder is
\[
 C_p=\{d\in \Pbd(b):E_d\res\alpha=p\}.
\]
Cylinders are nonempty and convex. Those of a fixed length partition
$\Pbd(b)$ and are strictly ordered by their different prefixes. Each
cylinder has no set cofinal or coinitial subset: given a set of its
codes, choose a fresh label above or below all their values at coordinate
$\alpha$, append it to $p$, and complete it using \Cref{swo:cb:lem:completion}.

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 1325-1437
\subsection{Source 16: the bounded-support core of global enumerations}\label{swo:ds:sec:core}

Work in GBC and fix a baseline bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. A normalized
bounded-support code is a set permutation $\sigma:\lambda\to\lambda$
of an ordinal satisfying
\[
 \lambda=\sup\{\xi+1:\sigma(\xi)\ne\xi\}.
\]
The empty permutation is permitted. Extend $\sigma$ by the identity above
$\lambda$, obtaining $\widehat\sigma$, and evaluate the code as
$E_\sigma=b\circ\widehat\sigma$. Let $\Pbd(b)$ be the ordinary class of
these set codes, ordered by comparison of their evaluations. Normalization
makes the coding injective. The evaluations are class functions, but their
codes are sets; the distinction is essential.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform completion of every set prefix]\label{swo:ds:lem:completion}
Every injective set function $p:\delta\to\No$ extends to an evaluation
$E_q$ with $q\in \Pbd(b)$. A completion can be selected uniformly in $p$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The function $b^{-1}\circ p$ is a set injection into $\Ord$. Choose
an infinite initial cardinal $\gamma$ strictly above $\delta$ and all
the ordinals in its range. The unused positions and unused values below
$\gamma$ both have cardinality $\gamma$. A bijection of their
complements extends this injection to a permutation of $\gamma$.
Extend by the identity and normalize. Choose the least suitable set
bijection in a fixed global well-order to make the construction uniform.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform set-cut interpolation]\label{swo:ds:thm:interpolation}
Let $(F_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(G_j)_{j\in J}$ be uniformly set-indexed
families in $\Jinj$ satisfying $F_i<G_j$ for all cross pairs. Either side
may be empty. Some injective set prefix $p$ has every continuation in
$\Jinj$ strictly between the families. In particular, a member of $\Pbd(b)$
interpolates them.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
When both sides are nonempty, their cross first-disagreement ordinals
form a set by Class Replacement. Bound them strictly below $\beta$;
otherwise put $\beta=0$. Follow a prefix $p$, calling an input row
active if it agrees with the whole prefix. Discarded lower rows are
below every continuation and discarded upper rows above every
continuation.

At coordinate $\delta=\dom(p)$, let $A$ and $B$ be the sets of next
values of the active lower and upper rows. Every value of $A$ is at
most every value of $B$. If they are disjoint, use
the fresh-separator lemma (\cref{swo:lem:delete}) to append an unused value strictly between them
and stop. This also handles empty sides. If they meet, their intersection
is a singleton; append that forced value and retain only the rows using
it. A surviving injective row guarantees freshness. At limits take
unions of the set histories.

The process cannot retain both a lower and an upper row through length
$\beta$, since such rows would agree beyond their bounded first
disagreement. Thus it stops at a set stage, with all comparisons decided.
\Cref{swo:ds:lem:completion} provides the bounded-support completion.
Surjectivity was not used for any input row.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A surreal-sized dense core]\label{swo:ds:cor:coreiso}
The ordinary class order $\Pbd(b)$ satisfies the set-cut property and is
isomorphic to $\No$. It is dense in both $\Jinj$ and $\Hsl$ in the sense of
their definable comparisons. It has no set cofinal or coinitial subset.
The interpolation theorem works for every chosen baseline, including
constraints whose rows do not belong to that baseline's core.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \Cref{swo:ds:thm:interpolation} to evaluations of sets of codes.
The core is proper, since transpositions of position zero with arbitrary
ordinal positions give distinct codes. Class universality and uniqueness (\cref{swo:prop:universal,swo:ec:thm:backforth})
then gives the isomorphism. The remaining assertions are instances of
the same interpolation theorem.
\end{proof}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Status.} The completion and interpolation theorems, and the core
isomorphism, are results of the earlier report (Part~IV:
\cref{swo:gl:completion,swo:gl:interpolation,swo:gl:pbd-no}). They
are proved here because they are the inputs to the new recognition theorem
below. Neither $\Pbd(b)\cong\No$ nor its density says that all global
enumerations can be coded by sets.\par\smallskip

\subsubsection{Canonical first cores and residual fibers}

For $R\in \Hall$, the first block of source~16's canonical block decomposition
(its Theorem~10.1, \merge\ \cref{swo:ds:thm:blocks}) is
\[
 I_R=\{x\in\No:\{y:yRx\}\text{ is a set}\}.
\]
It is always a proper class and has a unique enumeration
$F_R:\Ord\to I_R$. If $I_R$ were a set, the least point outside it
would have exactly that set of predecessors, a contradiction.

Conversely every $F\in \Jinj$ occurs as such a first core: enumerate its
range by $F$ and then append any class well-order of its complement.
The points in the range have set predecessors; every residual point
has that whole proper range before it. Restriction and concatenation
therefore identify the fiber over $F$ with
\[
 \WO(Y_F),\qquad Y_F=\No\setminus\ran(F),
\tag{S16.12}\label{swo:ds:eq:fiber}
\]
where for a proper $Y_F$ the notation denotes the raw class comparison.
Each fiber is convex. Distinct fibers are ordered by the first ordinal
disagreement of their cores. Symbolically,
\[
 \Hall\cong\sum_{F\in \Jinj}\WO(Y_F).
\tag{S16.13}\label{swo:ds:eq:rawsum}
\]
This is a summary of uniform relational constructions, not a same-level
class sum whose index elements are proper classes. The set-like order
$\Hsl$ consists precisely of the exhaustive, empty-residual fibers.
A singleton fiber need not be exhaustive: omitting one label produces
a unique raw completion of type $\Ord+1$.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 996-1143
\subsection{Source 17: the ordinary class core inside the global comparison}
\label{swo:gs:sec:core}

From now on work in $\GBC$ and fix $b:\Ord\to\No$. Let $\Jinj$ be the
predicate of injective class functions $\Ord\to\No$, and let $\Hsl$ be its
surjective subpredicate. Comparisons are made at the least ordinal of
first disagreement. These are predicates on class variables, not classes
whose members are proper classes.

\subsubsection{Canonical codes and interpolation}
A \emph{support code} is a set bijection $\sigma:S\to S$, where
$S\subseteq\Ord$ is a set and $\sigma(\xi)\ne\xi$ for every $\xi\in S$.
The empty code is allowed. Extend it by the identity off $S$ and put
$E_\sigma=b\circ\widehat\sigma$. Let $\Psupp(b)$ be the ordinary class of
these codes, ordered by the associated enumerations. The fixed-point-free
condition makes the coding unique. A global enumeration has such a code
exactly when it agrees with $b$ at every sufficiently large ordinal.
By \Cref{swo:gs:cor:optimal-prefix}, every injective set prefix occurs
in this core.

We recall the central interpolation theorem of the source, with its proof
because the later recognition results depend on its full strength for
\emph{injective, possibly nonexhaustive} rows.

\begin{lemma}[Avoiding a set of labels]\label{swo:gs:lem:avoid-set}
If $L,R,Z$ are sets of surreal numbers with $L<R$, there is
$z\notin Z$ with $L<z<R$. Either side of the cut may be empty.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The surreal set-cut property supplies a strict separator of any two
separated sets. Repeat that construction $|Z|^+$ times, each time adding
all earlier chosen separators to the lower side. Every stage has a set
history and gives a new separator below all of $R$. The resulting set
has more elements than $Z$, so one separator is not forbidden. This is
set-valued recursion with class parameters, not class-valued recursion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Core interpolation; source result]\label{swo:gs:thm:core-interpolation}
Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(B_j)_{j\in J}$ be uniformly set-indexed
families in $\Jinj$, with $A_i<_{\lex}B_j$ for every $i,j$. There is an
injective set prefix $p$ such that every row in $\Jinj$ extending $p$ lies
strictly between both families. In particular there is such a row with
a code in $\Psupp(b)$. Empty index sets are permitted.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
When both sides are nonempty, Class Replacement collects their cross
first-difference coordinates into a set. Choose an ordinal $\beta$
strictly above all these coordinates. If one side is empty take
$\beta=0$.

Build an injective prefix, retaining as \emph{active} the rows agreeing
with it. At stage $\alpha$ form the sets of active next labels
\[
 L_\alpha=\{A_i(\alpha):A_i\text{ active}\},\qquad
 R_\alpha=\{B_j(\alpha):B_j\text{ active}\}.
\]
Every lower label is at most every upper label. Their intersection has
at most one member. If it is empty, choose a fresh strict separator by
\Cref{swo:gs:lem:avoid-set}, append it, and stop. All active inequalities
are now strict. If the intersection is $\{z\}$, append $z$ and keep only
rows with next value $z$. This value is fresh because a surviving row is
injective. A discarded lower row is below every later extension; a
discarded upper row is above every later extension. This is the invariant
throughout the construction. At limits take unions of the set histories.

Both sides cannot still be active after a common prefix of length
$\beta$, since an active cross pair would disagree only at or beyond
$\beta$. Thus the procedure stops by the next step. Complete the final
prefix in $\Psupp(b)$ using \Cref{swo:gs:cor:optimal-prefix}. All recursions
and collections in this proof have set-sized stages and values.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A dense surreal order core; source result]
\label{swo:gs:cor:core-isomorphism}
The class order $\Psupp(b)$ is isomorphic to the numerical order of $\No$.
It is order-dense in the global comparisons of both $\Hsl$ and $\Jinj$:
between any two distinct rows there is a coded row. Every uniformly
set-indexed separated cut of those comparisons has a core interpolant.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The last statements are \Cref{swo:gs:thm:core-interpolation}. In particular
$\Psupp(b)$ has the same set-cut interpolation property as $\No$. Under
Global Choice enumerate each of these proper classes in a set-like
well-order. Construct a back-and-forth partial order-isomorphism along
$\Ord$. At each stage its domain and range are sets, so the required
cut is a set cut; interpolation provides a fresh image or preimage.
Global choice selects a least permissible choice. Every history at a
set ordinal is a set, so elementary class comprehension together with
set-valued transfinite recursion gives the full class map. Alternating
forth and back ensures exhaustiveness on both sides.
\end{proof}

This is an isomorphism of \emph{linear orders}, not of surreal fields or
of structures with the simplicity relation. The additional structure
studied in \cite{BagayokoHoeven} cannot be inferred from numerical order
alone. Nor is the core exhaustive in $\Hsl$.

\begin{corollary}[Universality for ordinary class linear orders]
\label{swo:gs:cor:class-universality}
Every given linear order on a class of sets embeds by a class map into
$\Psupp(b)$, hence into $\No$, $\Hsl$, and $\Hall$ in their stated senses.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Global choice supplies a set-like enumeration of the given class
(or a set enumeration if its carrier is a set). At each stage, previous
images form a set. Partition them by whether their source labels are
below or above the next source label; interpolation in $\Psupp(b)$ supplies
a fresh image. This forth-only recursion gives the required embedding.
The core inclusion and \Cref{swo:gs:cor:core-isomorphism} give the other
targets. This is the source's class-universality argument.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis ``class of sets'' cannot be dropped and replaced with
``all class well-orders''. The latter is the higher-order predicate
$\Hall$, not a carrier to which this recursion theorem applies.
This distinction is compatible with the no-coding theorem that follows.

\subsubsection{Why a dense class of codes is not a universal list}
\begin{theorem}[Uniform diagonal obstruction; source result]
\label{swo:gs:thm:diagonal}
No ordinary class of set indices with one uniform evaluation relation
lists all class well-orders of $\No$. A missing order can always be
chosen set-like.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Global choice permits reindexing a proposed nonempty list by $\Ord$;
a set-sized list can be extended by repetitions. Write its rows as
$R_\alpha$. Partition the baseline labels into the pairs
\[
 \{b(2\cdot\alpha),b(2\cdot\alpha+1)\}=\{a_\alpha,c_\alpha\},
 \qquad a_\alpha<c_\alpha.
\]
The products here are ordinal products with $2$ on the left, so these
successive two-element blocks partition $\Ord$. In block $\alpha$, list
the two labels in the order opposite to their relative order under
$R_\alpha$. Keep the blocks in increasing $\alpha$ order. Elementary
comprehension defines a class bijection $E:\Ord\to\No$. Its induced
well-order disagrees with $R_\alpha$ on that pair, for every $\alpha$.
The empty-list case is immediate.
\end{proof}

Each input row and the diagonal output are legitimate classes. The
forbidden object is a same-level exhaustive decoder, not an individual
large relation. Strengthening comprehension does not make a class into
a permissible element of another class of the same two-sorted theory.
An external set universe, a higher sort, or a stated uniform operator
provides a different, legitimate interpretation.

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 2640-2752
\subsection{Source 18: the set-like global order and its ordinary class core}
\label{swo:sh:sec:global-core}

Assume GBC and fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$.
The set-like global order can be studied through its ordinal
enumerations: if $e\ne f$, the nonempty class
$\{\alpha:e(\alpha)\ne f(\alpha)\}$ has a least ordinal. Numerical
comparison there agrees with source~18's Theorem~12.3 (\merge\
\cref{swo:sh:thm:class-lex}; \cref{swo:st:thm:fulllex}).

\subsubsection{Canonical bounded-support codes}

A permutation $\pi$ of $\Ord$ with set-sized support can be encoded
by the set graph of its nonfixed pairs; it is the identity elsewhere.
This representation is unique. Let $\Psupp(b)$ be the genuine class of all
such set codes, ordered by their evaluated global enumerations
$b\circ\pi$. The notation distinguishes the set code from the class
function that it evaluates.

\begin{lemma}[Completion of every set prefix]
\label{swo:sh:lem:core-completion}
Every injective set word $p:\delta\to\No$ extends an evaluated
member of $\Psupp(b)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The $b$-indices of the labels in $\ran p$ form a set. Choose an
infinite initial cardinal $\lambda$ greater than $\delta$ and all
these indices. The first $\lambda$ values of $b$ contain $\ran p$.
List $p$ first, followed by a bijection of the unused values of this
initial block in length $\lambda$. Since $\delta+\lambda=\lambda$,
the result permutes that entire block. Leave all later positions
unchanged. This is a bounded-support permutation extending $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform set-cut interpolation]
\label{swo:sh:thm:global-interpolation}
Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ be uniformly presented
set-indexed families of global ordinal enumerations, and suppose
$e_i<f_j$ for all $i,j$. There is $g\in \Psupp(b)$ strictly between them.
In particular, $\Psupp(b)$ fills every set cut and is order-isomorphic
to $\No$ in GBC. It is order dense in $\Hsl$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
When both families are nonempty, the first disagreements of all pairs
$(e_i,f_j)$ form a set of ordinals by Class Replacement. Take a bound
on them. Run a common-prefix search: keep only the family members
extending the current prefix; numerical next values on the lower side
are at most those on the upper side. If the sets of next values meet,
they meet in a unique value, which is appended. If they do not meet,
choose a fresh surreal strictly between them, append it, and stop.
At a limit stage take the union of the preceding set prefixes.

The search cannot continue through the bound on all pairwise first
disagreements while both active sides remain nonempty. When a side
becomes empty, the surreal set-cut property also supplies a fresh
next value. If one original side is empty, the search stops at the
first step. Each inactive lower member is below the whole current
cone, and each inactive upper member is above it. Thus the resulting
successor prefix puts every completion strictly between the given
families. Apply \Cref{swo:sh:lem:core-completion}.

For the isomorphism, perform set-valued back-and-forth along fixed
set-like enumerations of the two proper classes $\Psupp(b)$ and $\No$.
At each stage only a set of previously matched points must be respected,
and interpolation supplies the next point. Taking singleton families
in the first assertion proves density in $\Hsl$.
\end{proof}

The conclusion is stronger than pairwise density and weaker than
filling arbitrary proper-class cuts. For example, choose an injective
$\Ord$ word that enumerates $\No\setminus\{x\}$. It determines a
cut of $\Psupp(b)$ but cannot itself be a global enumeration of $\No$.
The next section makes the distinction exact.

Class universality of $\No$ now implies that every supplied class
linear order embeds into $\Hsl$, through $\Psupp(b)$. The same is true
inside any nonempty open interval of $\Hsl$: a sufficiently long
set prefix and a free numerical interval place a copy of the same
core inside it. This is a statement about uniform class-indexed
subfamilies. It does not say that $\Hsl$ itself is an ordinary class.

\subsubsection{An elementary obstruction to exhaustive class coding}

\begin{theorem}[No ordinary class of codes for all global well-orders]
\label{swo:sh:thm:noncoding}
There is no class-indexed uniform evaluator whose values include every
class well-order of $\No$. The same holds if only set-like orders are
required as values.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Under Global Choice any class of set codes can be listed in an
$\Ord$-indexed family, repeating values if the code class is a set.
Suppose $(R_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Ord}$ were exhaustive. Split the
fixed baseline $b$ into consecutive pairs
\[
 \{b(2\cdot\alpha),b(2\cdot\alpha+1)\},\qquad\alpha\in\Ord.
\]
In pair $\alpha$, choose the orientation opposite to the relative
order of these two labels in $R_\alpha$. Keep the pair blocks in
their original ordinal order. This is a class bijection
$\Ord\to\No$, hence a set-like well-order. It differs from
$R_\alpha$ on the relative order of its designated pair, for every
$\alpha$, contradicting exhaustiveness. The orientation class is
defined elementarily from the proposed evaluator.
\end{proof}

This is the relevant Cantor-style diagonal. It blocks a uniform
``all codes are sets'' shortcut. Individual global well-orders can
still be parameters, and any specified uniform family can be studied.
Kelley--Morse comprehension strengthens which classes exist; it does
not make proper classes into members of other ordinary classes.

% ---- hand chunk trichotomy
% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 571-733
\section{A trichotomy for class cuts of the skeleton (source 14)}
\label{swo:tc:sec:cuts}
\subsection{Normalization and the three constructions}
A \emph{proper normalized cut} of $\Psupp(b)$ is a class
$D\subseteq \Psupp(b)$ which is nonempty, proper, downward closed, and has
no greatest member. Its complement is allowed to have a least member.
Thus the point $\sigma$ is represented by the lower set
$\{\tau:\tau<\sigma\}$, not by the lower set that includes $\sigma$.
This convention is essential when we calculate characters.

We write $D_p^-$ and $D_p^+$ for the two edges of a nonempty-prefix
cylinder:
\begin{align*}
 D_p^-&=\{\sigma:(\forall\tau\in C_p)\ \sigma<\tau\},\\
 D_p^+&=\{\sigma:(\exists\tau\in C_p)\ \sigma<\tau\}.
\end{align*}
Since $C_p$ has no endpoints, $D_p^-$ consists of the codes below the
whole cylinder, whereas $D_p^+$ consists of those codes together with
all of $C_p$. Both are proper normalized cuts. The empty-prefix edges
are the improper endpoint cuts and are excluded.

For a set prefix $p$ and a nonempty proper initial class $H\subset A_p$
with no greatest member and with $A_p\setminus H$ having no least
member, define a \emph{numerical-gap cut}
\[
 D_{p,H}=D_p^-\ \cup\
 \{\sigma\in C_p:E_\sigma(\lambda)\in H\},
 \qquad \lambda=\dom p.
\]
Here $D_\varnothing^-=\varnothing$ by convention. The nonprincipality
conditions prevent this notation from duplicating the two edges of a
child cylinder.

Finally, for $F\in \Jinj$ define the \emph{branch trace}
\[
 D_F=\{\sigma\in \Psupp(b):E_\sigma <_{\lex} F\}.
\]
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:branchdensity} shows that it is a proper normalized cut.
The branch need not be exhaustive. If $F=E_\sigma$, the cut is principal
in the normalized sense; otherwise it has no point of the skeleton at
its boundary.

\subsection{Crossing cylinders and reconstruction}
\begin{definition}\label{swo:tc:n5.1}
A prefix $p$ \emph{crosses} $D$ if its cylinder meets both sides:
\[
 \operatorname{Cross}_D(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (\exists\sigma\in C_p\cap D)(\exists\tau\in C_p\setminus D).
\]
Let $T_D$ be the class of crossing set prefixes.
\end{definition}
All displayed witnesses are sets. Therefore $T_D$ is obtained by
\emph{elementary} class comprehension from $D$ and $b$.

\begin{lemma}[The crossing-chain lemma]\label{swo:tc:lem:crosschain}
For every proper normalized cut $D$, the class $T_D$ contains the empty
prefix, is downward closed under prefix restriction, and is a chain
under prefix extension. It contains at most one prefix of any given
length. Its union is an injective function with domain either a set
ordinal or all of $\Ord$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Properness gives the empty prefix, and any ancestor of a crossing
cylinder also crosses. If incomparable prefixes $p,q$ both crossed,
order their disjoint cylinders as $C_p<C_q$. An excluded point of $C_p$
would then lie below an included point of $C_q$, contradicting downward
closure. Thus they are comparable, which also proves uniqueness at each
length. Their union is a function and is injective because every two
of its coordinates occur together in a sufficiently long member of the
chain. Its domain is an initial subclass of $\Ord$. Such a subclass is
all of $\Ord$ or a set ordinal. In the latter case, class Replacement
on that set domain makes the union a set function.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Boundary trichotomy]\label{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}
Every proper normalized class cut $D$ of $\Psupp(b)$ has exactly one of
the following forms:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item a cylinder edge $D_p^-$ or $D_p^+$ for a nonempty injective set
prefix $p$;
\item a numerical-gap cut $D_{p,H}$ with the nonprincipality conditions
specified above;
\item a branch trace $D_F$ for an injective class function
$F:\Ord\to\No$.
\end{enumerate}
The data within the appropriate form, including the edge direction, are
unique. The alternatives and their data can be recovered from the
crossing-prefix class by elementary formulas with class parameters.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We distinguish whether the lengths occurring in $T_D$ are unbounded.

\emph{Unbounded case.} Let $F=\bigcup T_D$. Its domain is $\Ord$.
For a code $\sigma$ with $E_\sigma\ne F$, let $\delta$ be their first
disagreement. Take a crossing prefix of length greater than $\delta$.
If $E_\sigma <_{\lex} F$, then $\sigma$ is below that entire cylinder and
in particular below one of its included points, so $\sigma\in D$.
If $F<_{\lex} E_\sigma$, it is above an excluded point of that cylinder
and cannot belong to $D$. If $E_\sigma=F$, membership in $D$ would make
$\sigma$ its greatest member, since all larger codes have just been
excluded. This is prohibited by normalization. Therefore $D=D_F$.

\emph{Bounded case with no longest crossing prefix.} The union $p$ has
nonzero limit length $\lambda$. It does not cross, so either
$C_p\subseteq D$ or $C_p\cap D=\varnothing$. For every code outside
$C_p$, its first disagreement with $p$ occurs before $\lambda$; a
longer crossing prefix then decides its membership exactly as in the
unbounded case. Hence $D=D_p^+$ in the first alternative and $D=D_p^-$
in the second.

\emph{Bounded case with a longest crossing prefix $p$.} No child
$C_{p\cat(x)}$ crosses. Each child is consequently wholly included or
wholly excluded. Let
\[
 H=\{x\in A_p:C_{p\cat(x)}\subseteq D\}.
\]
It is an initial class of $A_p$. Because $C_p$ crosses and the child
cylinders partition it, $H$ is nonempty and proper. Points outside
$C_p$ are below all of it or above all of it; the crossing witnesses
show that exactly those below belong to $D$. Thus $D$ has the formula
used to define $D_{p,H}$. If $H$ has a greatest member $x$, that formula
is $D_{p\cat(x)}^+$. If $A_p\setminus H$ has a least member $x$, it
is $D_{p\cat(x)}^-$. Both possibilities cannot occur, since $A_p$ is
dense. If neither occurs, we have precisely alternative (ii).

For uniqueness, in alternative (iii) the crossing prefixes are exactly
all set restrictions of $F$; in alternative (ii) they are exactly $p$
and its restrictions; and at an edge they are exactly the \emph{proper}
restrictions of its prefix. If the last chain has no longest member,
its union recovers the limit prefix and membership of its cylinder
recovers the direction. If it has a longest member, the included child
labels have a maximum or the excluded child labels have a minimum;
that endpoint recovers the additional label and the direction. For a
numerical gap neither endpoint exists. These descriptions distinguish
the alternatives, and also recover every parameter uniquely.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the theorem does not construct]\label{swo:tc:n5.4}
It does not collect all class cuts into an ordinary class, nor insert
an $\Ord$-length sign sequence as a surreal number. The theorem is a
statement about an arbitrary supplied class $D$. Its elementary formulas
can be used uniformly in models, but the virtual family of every such
$D$ still occupies a higher logical level.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Examples distinguishing the alternatives}
For the one-letter prefix $(0)$, the cut $D_{(0)}^-$ lies just below all
core enumerations beginning with $0$. There is no numerical ``largest
first entry below $0$.'' It is a cylinder boundary, not a branch trace.
At the empty prefix, take the numerical gap
\[
 H=\{x\in\No:(\exists n\in\mathbb N)\ x<n\}.
\]
Its complement is the class of surreals at least as large as every
natural number. It has no least member: from such a surreal $y$, the
number $y-1$ is still in the complement and is smaller. The class $H$
has no greatest member. This produces a cut of type (ii), with a
countable cofinal left side but no set-sized coinitial right side.
Finally $F(\alpha)=\alpha$ is an injective branch of type (iii) which
omits, for example, $-1$. Its trace is coherent at every set length but
is not realized by any member of $\Hsl$. Exhaustiveness is not implied
by coherence.

\begin{note}[\merge; the three examples in the repository]\label{swo:viii:note:examples}
The first-label cut at $0$ (with its upper-edge twin) is printed also by
sources~15 and~16 (\cref{swo:cb:ex:firstlabelcut} and source~16's table after
\cref{swo:ds:thm:firstfailure}); the numerical gap
$\{x:\exists n\ x<n\}$ also by sources~15 and~17 (\cref{swo:cb:n7.7,swo:gs:n9.3}).
The branch $F(\alpha)=\alpha$, which omits $-1$, is source~09's
\cref{swo:ec:thm:class-gap} (printed in Part~IV), which source~14 does not
cite; source~13 recovers it as \cref{swo:fs:n8.5}, crediting this report,
and source~15 prints it again (after \cref{swo:cb:n7.7}). Its one-label
variant, a bijection $\Ord\to\No\setminus\{r\}$, is source~11's
\cref{swo:gl:omitted}, printed again by sources~16 and~17 (source~16's
table, \cref{swo:gs:n9.5}), which do not cite it. The limit boundary below
the cylinder of $p(n)=n$ ($n<\omega$), which source~14 does not use, is
printed by sources~13 (end of its Section~9), 15 (\cref{swo:cb:n7.7}),
16 (its table) and~17 (\cref{swo:gs:n9.4}, for any injective $p$ of
length~$\omega$).
\end{note}

\section{Characters, saturation, and principal cuts (source 14)}
\label{swo:tc:sec:characters}
We use $\Ord$ as a \emph{character symbol}: it means that a uniform
ordinal-indexed cofinal or coinitial family exists, while no set-sized
one exists. It is not an ordinary cardinal. For any nonempty class
linear order with no set-sized cofinal subset, global choice permits
an increasing cofinal $\Ord$-sequence: at each set stage dominate the
earlier choices and the elements seen so far in a global enumeration.
If no such upper choice existed, the already considered set would be
cofinal. This is set-valued recursion. The dual argument handles
coinitiality. A set-sized character is the least cardinality of a
cofinal or coinitial subset; if there is a corresponding endpoint it
is $1$.

\begin{theorem}[Cut-character calculation]\label{swo:tc:thm:characters}
Write the character of a normalized cut as
$(\cf D,\ci(\Psupp(b)\setminus D))$. For the alternatives of
\Cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}, the following formulas hold.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Yl@{}}
\toprule
Cut & Character\\\midrule
$D_F$, with $F=E_\sigma$ for some core code & $(\Ord,1)$\\
$D_F$, with $F$ not represented by a core code & $(\Ord,\Ord)$\\
$D_p^-$, $\dom p=\lambda$ a nonzero limit & $(\cf\lambda,\Ord)$\\
$D_p^+$, $\dom p=\lambda$ a nonzero limit & $(\Ord,\cf\lambda)$\\
$D_p^-$ or $D_p^+$, $\dom p$ a successor & $(\Ord,\Ord)$\\
$D_{p,H}$ & $(\cf H,\ci(A_p\setminus H))$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
For the last row both characters cannot be set-sized. At every actual
point of $\Psupp(b)$, both \emph{strict} local characters are $\Ord$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a branch $F$, complete a prefix agreeing with $F$ before $\alpha$
and taking a fresh smaller entry at $\alpha$; call the result
$a_\alpha$. Similarly obtain $b_\alpha$ with a larger entry. If
$\alpha<\beta$, first difference gives
\[
 a_\alpha<a_\beta <_{\lex} F<_{\lex} b_\beta<b_\alpha.
\]
Every code below or above $F$ is surpassed on the appropriate side by
one of these approximants, once $\alpha$ exceeds its first disagreement.
A set of codes differing from $F$ has a set of first disagreements and
hence a common ordinal bound; a later approximant defeats its alleged
cofinality or coinitiality. If $F$ itself is a core point, the complement
of $D_F$ has that point as its least member. This gives $(\Ord,1)$,
not $(\Ord,\Ord)$; only the strict right side has character $\Ord$.

At the lower edge of a limit-length prefix $p$, take a cofinal sequence
of coordinates $\alpha<\lambda$ and complete a word that first differs
from $p$ there by a smaller entry. These codes are cofinal below the
cylinder. Conversely the first-disagreement coordinates of any cofinal
family must be cofinal in $\lambda$: a code which follows $p$ longer
would otherwise be above the entire family. This proves the character
$\cf\lambda$. On the other side the cylinder has no set-sized
coinitial subset by \Cref{swo:tc:prop:cylinders}, and lies below
all other points of the complement. Its character is $\Ord$. The
upper-edge calculation is dual.

For a successor-length prefix $p=q\cat(x)$, any set of points below
$C_p$ that first differ before the last coordinate can be surpassed by
one following $q$. Among those which follow $q$, their entries at the
last coordinate form a set below $x$. \Cref{swo:tc:lem:fresh} provides a
fresh entry between that set and $x$. Completion again surpasses the
whole family while remaining below $C_p$. Thus the lower side of the
lower edge has no set-sized cofinal subset. The opposite side follows
from the cylinder property. The upper edge is the dual case.

For a numerical gap, project included points in $C_p$ to their
next-coordinate labels in $H$. A cofinal set of labels, with one
completed word above each chosen label when necessary, produces a
cofinal family of codes. Conversely a cofinal family of codes must
have cofinal projected labels: otherwise a child cylinder with a
larger label in $H$ surpasses it. The absence of a greatest member of
$H$ removes any dependence on the internal character of one child.
The dual argument proves the right character. If both were sets,
cofinal labels on the left and coinitial labels on the right would
constitute a set cut of $A_p$ with no separator, contradicting
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:fresh}. Finally the branch argument at a core point
already proves the assertion about strict local characters.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Recovery of the core saturation theorem]\label{swo:tc:cor:coreeta}
Every separated pair of sets of codes $A,B\subseteq \Psupp(b)$ has a
strict separator in $\Psupp(b)$. In particular the core is an
$\eta_{\Ord}$-order: it fills all set-sized strict cuts, including
those with an empty side.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Empty-side bounds follow by choosing a first label above or below all
first labels in the specified set. Suppose both sides are nonempty
and no separator exists. If $A$ has a greatest point $a$, then $B$
would be coinitial in the strict right side of $a$, contradicting its
local character. The dual argument applies if $B$ has a least point.
Otherwise let $D=\{\sigma:(\exists a\in A)\ \sigma<a\}$. It is a
proper normalized cut with $A$ cofinal. Absence of a separator makes
$B$ coinitial in its complement: any point there below all of $B$
would be strictly above all of $A$. The character table has no
nonprincipal cut with two set-sized characters, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The known surreal order type]\label{swo:tc:cor:coreNo}
There is a class order isomorphism $\Psupp(b)\cong\No$ in $\GBC$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Both are proper class linear orders filling all set cuts. Fix set-like
global enumerations and perform back-and-forth along $\Ord$. At a set
stage the existing partial map has set domain and range; the next
point's lower and upper constraints are sets and admit a fresh image.
The union is an elementary definable class bijection preserving order.
This is the standard argument, also used by the predecessor; the
isomorphism statement itself is inherited, not claimed as a new result.
\end{proof}

The character calculation explains why the core is not Dedekind complete.
For instance the increasing core points whose first entries are natural
numbers have upper bounds but no supremum. Filling \emph{strict} set
cuts supplies another point between all those entries and any proposed
upper bound. The countable/non-set-sized numerical-gap character above
records this failure rather than contradicting saturation.

\begin{note}[\merge; which rows are new]\label{swo:viii:note:characters}
The branch rows of \cref{swo:tc:thm:characters} are source~11's
\cref{swo:gl:local} and source~09's \cref{swo:ec:thm:class-gap}
($(\Ord,\Ord)$ at a non-core branch); \cref{swo:tc:cor:coreeta} is
\cref{swo:gl:interpolation} for sets of codes and \cref{swo:tc:cor:coreNo} is
\cref{swo:gl:pbd-no}, both stated by source~14 as recoveries. New are the
characters of the edge and numerical-gap cuts and the statement that no
nonprincipal cut has two set-sized characters. The same table is proved,
case by case, by source~13 (\cref{swo:fs:prop:characters}), source~15
(\cref{swo:cb:prop:cutcharacters}), source~16 (the paragraph after its
table) and source~17 for non-core branches (\cref{swo:gs:prop:class-characters});
those statements are printed with their sources' recognition theorems in
\cref{swo:viii:sec:routes}.
\end{note}

\section{Recognizing exhaustive cuts and preserving old cuts (source 14)}
\label{swo:tc:sec:recognition}
\begin{theorem}[Exhaustive-cut recognition]\label{swo:tc:thm:recognition}
Let $D$ be a proper normalized class cut of $\Psupp(b)$. There exists
$E\in \Hsl$ with $D=D_E$ if and only if both conditions hold:
\begin{align}
 &\forall\alpha\in\Ord\ \exists p\,
   [\dom p=\alpha\ \wedge\ \operatorname{Cross}_D(p)],
       \tag{C}\label{swo:tc:eq:coherence}\\
 &\forall x\in\No\ \exists p\,
   [\operatorname{Cross}_D(p)\ \wedge\ x\in\ran p].
       \tag{X}\label{swo:tc:eq:coverage}
\end{align}
Such an enumeration is unique, and its graph is given by
\[
 E(\alpha)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists p\,[\operatorname{Cross}_D(p)\ \wedge\ \alpha\in\dom p
                         \ \wedge\ p(\alpha)=x].
\]
All quantifiers in the criterion and reconstruction range over sets;
only $D$ and $b$ are class parameters.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For an exhaustive $E$, every restriction $E\res\alpha$ crosses its
trace by the smaller and larger completions in
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:branchdensity}. Every surreal occurs in one of these
restrictions, giving (C) and (X). Conversely (C) and
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:crosschain} produce an injective union $F$ on all of
$\Ord$. Condition (X) makes it surjective. The unbounded case of
\Cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy} gives $D=D_F$. The displayed graph formula
is exactly the union of the crossing chain; its functionality and
uniqueness follow from the chain lemma.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{A logical simplification.}
For this proper-class alphabet, (X) by itself already implies (C).
Indeed, the union of the crossing chain then has range all of $\No$;
if its domain were a set ordinal, class Replacement would make that
range a set. Its domain is therefore $\Ord$, and prefix closure gives
(C). We retain the two conditions in the theorem to distinguish
coherent nonexhaustive branches from failures that stop at a set stage;
we do not claim that the conditions are logically independent.

This answers the predecessor's question ``Which cuts of the core
represent exhaustive branches?'' (\cref{swo:n16.1}; source~09's third direction in \cref{swo:ec:sec:research})
\emph{in the prefix-enriched structure}. A bare linear-order isomorphism
of the core does not come equipped with its prefix cylinders or the
label evaluation. The theorem does not show that those enrichments are
definable from the order relation alone. \Cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic} below proves that an automorphism-invariant
bare-order criterion cannot recognize exhaustiveness: some core
automorphisms carry exhaustive traces to nonbranch cylinder edges.

The criterion also separates two notions of completion. An injective
branch always gives a cut coherent through every set stage. It gives
a global enumeration only if it eventually visits every label. No
condition at a single bounded stage can enforce the latter assertion.
For the branch $F(\alpha)=\alpha$, (C) holds and (X) fails at $x=-1$.
The two cylinder-edge alternatives fail (C) at a bounded length; a
numerical-gap alternative also fails (C), because there is no crossing
child after its last crossing prefix.

\merge\ The second half of source~14's Section~7, on preserving old cuts
under class extensions (its \cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute}, the corollary and
the remark after it), is printed in \cref{swo:viii:sec:extensions}.

% ---- hand chunk routes
\section{Five further proofs of the represented-cut theorem (sources 16, 15, 13, 17 and 18)}\label{swo:viii:sec:routes}

\begin{note}[\merge; one theorem, six proofs]\label{swo:viii:note:sixfold}
The theorem that a normalized class cut of the core is the cut of an
injective class word exactly when a crossing (straddling) prefix exists at
every set length, that the word is then unique and elementary in the cut,
and that it is exhaustive exactly when the ranges of these prefixes cover
$\No$, is proved independently in all six batch-81 sources:
source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}(iii) and \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition},
source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:cutrecognition}, source~15's
\cref{swo:cb:thm:cutcriterion} with \cref{swo:cb:cor:kernel}, source~13's
\cref{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction}, source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}
and source~18's \cref{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut} with
\cref{swo:sh:cor:elementary-cut-recognition}. Each source presents it as its
own answer to source~11's \cref{swo:n16.1}; it answers that question
(\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}), and no source has priority over another. The
six proofs are the same argument: uniqueness of a crossing prefix at each
length, coherence under restriction, the elementary union, and the first
disagreement with a code. They are printed as routes because each source
builds different examples and corollaries on its own proof.

The analysis of a failing cut is likewise proved five times. Source~14
partitions the proper cuts by their form (edge, numerical gap, branch:
\cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}); sources~13, 15, 16 and~18 partition the
failing cuts by their first failed length (successor or limit:
\cref{swo:fs:thm:failure,swo:cb:thm:terminal,swo:ds:thm:firstfailure,swo:sh:thm:cut-first-failure}).
The two partitions are equivalent: a limit failure is an edge of a
limit-length cylinder, and a successor failure is an edge of a child cylinder
or a numerical gap. Source~15's successor case is the finest, separating a
\emph{forbidden repeated label} (the unused alphabet split at a label already
used by the prefix, \cref{swo:cb:n7.7}, source~16's second table row and
source~18's \cref{swo:sh:ex:repeated-label-cut}) from a numerical gap with no
surreal separator; in source~14's terms both are numerical-gap cuts
$D_{p,H}$, the first with $A_p\setminus H$ and $H$ separated by a point of
$\ran p$.

Source~18 states its theorem ``in $\GB$ with the fixed baseline''. A baseline
$b:\Ord\to\No$ already yields global choice over $\GB$
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}), so the hypothesis is not weaker than $\GBC$; the
theorem's own content is that no class choice and no $\ETR$ are used beyond
the baseline. Sources~13, 14, 15, 16 and~17 say $\GBC$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 1438-1611
\subsection{Source 16: exact recognition of cuts represented by branches}\label{swo:ds:sec:cutrecognition}

Fix the core $\Pbd(b)$ and its evaluation. For an injective set prefix
$p:\alpha\to\No$ write
\[
 C_p=\{q\in \Pbd(b):E_q\res\alpha=p\}.
\]
These cylinders are nonempty and convex, and at each fixed length they
form an ordered partition. Each cylinder has no endpoint: change the
next coordinate of one completion to a fresh smaller or larger surreal
and apply \Cref{swo:ds:lem:completion}.

A \emph{lower cut} here means an available class
$\varnothing\ne L\subsetneq \Pbd(b)$ that is initial and has no greatest
member. Put $U=\Pbd(b)\setminus L$. A prefix \emph{straddles} the cut if
$C_p\cap L$ and $C_p\cap U$ are both nonempty. This is a property with
only set quantifiers and the class parameters $L,b$.

\begin{theorem}[Prefix-cylinder recognition]\label{swo:ds:thm:cutrecognition}
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is an injective class function $F:\Ord\to\No$ such that
\[
 L=\{q\in \Pbd(b):E_q<_{\lex}F\}=:L_F.
\]
\item At every ordinal length $\alpha$ some injective prefix straddles
the cut.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, the prefix at each length is unique and is
exactly $F\res\alpha$. The branch is exhaustive if and only if every
surreal occurs in the range of some straddling prefix.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a given $F$, choose fresh values below and above $F(\alpha)$ and
complete the corresponding one-letter extensions of $F\res\alpha$.
They lie on opposite sides of $F$, so its prefix straddles.

Two different prefixes at the same length cannot both straddle an
initial cut. Their cylinders are entirely ordered one before the
other, and an upper witness in the earlier cylinder would be below a
lower witness in the later one. This contradicts initiality.
Restrictions of straddling prefixes still straddle. Hence the prefixes
$p_\alpha$ supplied by condition 2 are unique and coherent.

Define the branch directly, by elementary comprehension:
\[
 F(\alpha)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists p\,[p\text{ straddles},\ \dom(p)=\alpha+1,\ p(\alpha)=x].
\tag{S16.14}\label{swo:ds:eq:recognitionformula}
\]
Here the prefix and the witnesses from both sides are sets. Coherence
proves that this is a total injective class function and that
$F\res\alpha=p_\alpha$. This is not a class-valued recursion.

If $E_q<F$ first differ at $\delta$, every point of
$C_{p_{\delta+1}}$ is above $q$. One such point is in $L$, so $q\in L$.
If $F<E_q$, an upper witness in the same cylinder lies below $q$, so
$q\in U$. Finally, if $E_q=F$, placing $q$ in $L$ would make it the
greatest member of $L$ by the preceding two implications. Thus it is
in $U$, and $L=L_F$. The prefixes determine $F$ uniquely, and their
range union gives exactly the stated exhaustion criterion.
\end{proof}

The no-greatest convention matters only at a represented core point:
without it, both $\{q:E_q<F\}$ and $\{q:E_q\le F\}$ would straddle
every level when $F=E_q$ for a code. The two improper cuts fail already
at the empty prefix and represent no injection.

\begin{theorem}[Complete classification of the first failure]
\label{swo:ds:thm:firstfailure}
If a lower cut is not represented, let $\lambda$ be the least length
with no straddling prefix. Then $\lambda>0$, and exactly one of the
following occurs.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Successor failure.} If $\lambda=\alpha+1$, let $p$ be
the unique straddling prefix of length $\alpha$. The unused labels
$\No\setminus\ran(p)$ split into nonempty initial and final classes
$A+B$, with
\[
 C_{p\cat(x)}\subseteq L\ (x\in A),\qquad
 C_{p\cat(x)}\subseteq U\ (x\in B).
\]
All codes below $C_p$ are in $L$ and all codes above it in $U$.
\item \textbf{Limit failure.} If $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit, the
coherent earlier prefixes have an injective set union $p$ of length
$\lambda$. The cut is exactly the lower or upper edge of its cylinder:
\[
 L=C_p^-\quad\text{or}\quad L=C_p^-\cup C_p,
 \qquad C_p^-:=\{q:\forall c\in C_p\ (q<c)\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Minimize below any ordinal witnessing failure; this uses no ordering of
classes. The empty prefix straddles. At a successor, every nonempty
child cylinder is wholly on one side, and the children partition the
parent cylinder, which straddles. Both parts of the label split are
therefore nonempty, and their order follows from that of the children.
The outside-code assertion follows by comparison with a lower and an
upper witness in the parent.

At a limit, Class Replacement applied to the unique prefixes indexed
by the set $\lambda$ makes their union a set. Coherence ensures
injectivity, and completion ensures a nonempty cylinder. Since the
length fails, that cylinder is wholly on one side. Any code outside it
first differs from $p$ at $\delta<\lambda$; the shorter prefix of
length $\delta+1$ still straddles. Its witnesses force the code to the
lower side if it differs downward and to the upper side if upward.
Including or excluding the entire limit cylinder gives exactly its
two edges.
\end{proof}

A successor failure need not be a numerical gap with both sides lacking
endpoints. It can be an edge of a whole child cylinder, or a cut for which
the numerically suitable next label has already been used. The theorem
distinguishes these from a failure of coherence at a limit length.

\subsubsection{Explicit cuts and their meaning}

The following table gives concrete, fully defined examples.

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.49\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.12\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.32\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Lower side & First failure & Interpretation\\
\midrule\endhead
$\{q:E_q(0)\le0\}$ & $1$ & Upper edge of the entire zero-first
cylinder.\\[5pt]
$\{q:E_q(0)<0\}\cup\{q:E_q(0)=0,\ E_q(1)<0\}$ & $2$ & The apparent
second separator would repeat the already used zero.\\[5pt]
$C_p^-$ or $C_p^-\cup C_p$, with $p(n)=n$ for $n<\omega$ & $\omega$ &
Every finite prefix straddles, but the whole countable-prefix cylinder
lies on one side.\\[5pt]
$L_F$ for $F:\Ord\overset{\sim}{\to}\No\setminus\{r\}$ & None &
A genuine injective branch, failing only the exhaustion test.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

All displayed lower sides have no greatest member. For a nonzero limit
prefix length $\lambda$, its lower cylinder edge has lower cofinality
exactly $\cf(\lambda)$ and no set coinitial family on its upper side.
To see this, make a fresh downward deviation at cofinally many positions
of $p$. The completions increase cofinally below $C_p$; any cofinal
family must have unbounded deviation coordinates. On the upper side,
the initial portion $C_p$ has no set coinitial family, since one can
choose a fresh next value below any set of next values. The upper
edge has the dual characters.

\begin{corollary}[Exactly what raw tails add]\label{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}
For a raw order $R\in \Hall$, its strict lower cut in $\Pbd(b)$ is
$L_{F_R}$. Thus the cut image of all raw orders consists exactly of
the cuts passing the straddling test. Over the cut of $F$, the fiber
is the convex order $\WO(\No\setminus\ran F)$.
Neither successor nor limit first-failure cuts are filled by any raw
class well-order.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A bounded-support enumeration unequal to $F_R$ first disagrees at a
set ordinal, before any non-set-like tail begins. Its comparison with
$R$ is therefore its comparison with $F_R$. Equality is possible
only when $F_R$ is exhaustive, in which case it determines $R$.
Conversely every injection occurs as a first core, by
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:fiber}. Distinct cores give different cuts by
\Cref{swo:ds:thm:cutrecognition}, proving exactly the asserted image
and fibers.
\end{proof}

This resolves the earlier report's represented-cut question using the
prefix tree with its numerical labels. It does not claim that the tree
is recoverable from the bare order on $\Pbd(b)$. Since $\Pbd(b)\cong\No$,
forgetting those additional predicates can lose precisely the information
used by the recognition test.

\begin{note}[\merge; on source~16's last paragraph]\label{swo:viii:note:ds-resolves}
Source~16's sentence that this ``resolves the earlier report's
represented-cut question'' is true of the theorem, which all six batch-81
sources prove (\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold}). Its \cref{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}
is the statement about raw orders that sources~13, 15, 17 and~18 make in
\cref{swo:fs:cor:rawtraces}, \cref{swo:cb:cor:kernel},
\cref{swo:gs:prop:raw-lifts} and \cref{swo:sh:cor:cut-representation-levels};
the fibre description in it is source~12's \cref{swo:cf:fibers}, and the
image of all raw orders, exactly the cuts passing the straddling test, is the
new part. Part~IX prints source~14's trace-fibre theorem
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers}).
\end{note}
