% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 211-250
\subsection{Source 15: sign sequences, properness, and cut filling}

We realize a surreal as a sign sequence $s:\alpha\to\{-,+\}$ of ordinal
length $\alpha$. At a first difference the comparison is
$-<\text{undefined}<+$; the birthday is the length. The all-plus sequences
give an increasing copy of $\Ord$, so $\No$ is a proper class. Every set of
surreals has a set bound on its birthdays, by replacement.

The numerical surreal order fills every set cut: if $L,R$ are sets and
$L<R$, some $x$ satisfies $L<x<R$, with either side allowed to be empty.
This is the familiar Conway construction. It implies density and no
endpoints, but it does not assert filling for arbitrary class cuts.
The numerical order and the simplicity relation are distinct: extending a
sign string makes it more complicated in simplicity, but may increase or
decrease its numerical value \cite{Conway,Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}.

\begin{lemma}[Fresh separators]\label{swo:cb:lem:fresh}
If $L<R$ are sets of surreals and $S$ is a set, there is
$x\notin S$ with $L<x<R$. In particular, deleting a set from $\No$ leaves
a dense order without endpoints.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If every separator belonged to $S$, the class $I=\{x:L<x<R\}$ would be
a set, by separation from $S$. It is nonempty. Apply set-cut filling to
$L\cup I<R$: every member of $I$ is less than every member of $R$.
A resulting separator belongs to $I$ and exceeds all of $I$, a contradiction.
Thus the interval has a point outside $S$. The same proof allows empty
bounding sides.
\end{proof}

In $\GBC$, a forth construction embeds every ordinary class linear order
in $\No$: enumerate its underlying class by $\Ord$, and at each stage
separate the sets of earlier lower and upper images. A back-and-forth
construction shows uniqueness, up to class order isomorphism, of a proper
class order with this set-cut property. Each stage has a set of earlier
values; these are ordinary set-valued ordinal recursions. This is the
classical universality and absolute-linear-continuum phenomenon
\cite{Ehrlich2012,HamkinsUniversal}. It does not apply to a collection whose
elements are themselves class functions.

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 277-381
\subsection{Source 16: foundations and surreal order facts}\label{swo:ds:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Conventions about sets, classes, and choice}

Here $\GB$ has ZF as its set theory and no choice principle built into its
notation. We write $\GBC=\GB+\GC$; global choice implies ordinary set choice.
The set-sized theorems are proved in ZFC. A \emph{class well-order} is a
strict class linear order for which every available nonempty subclass has
a least element. A relation is \emph{set-like} if each predecessor class is
a set. A proper set-like class well-order is uniquely isomorphic to
$\Ord$: send each point to the ordinal type of its predecessor set.

An individual class function $F:\Ord\to\No$ is legitimate. The notation
``$F\in \Hsl$'' below abbreviates that this class function is a bijection; it
does not make $F$ an element of a GB class. Likewise, a uniform family
$(F_i)_{i\in I}$ means one class of triples $(i,\alpha,x)$ whose rows are
the graphs in question. Its index $I$ may be a set or a class of sets. One
cannot silently choose a class for each set index and assume that the rows
assemble into an available uniform family.

\subsubsection{Sign sequences, small cuts, and bounded stages}

We use the sign presentation
\[
 \No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^\alpha,
\]
with numerical comparison at the first different or missing sign, using
$-<\text{missing}<+$. The birthday $\bd(x)$ is the length of the sign
sequence. Every set of surreals has bounded birthdays, whereas all birthdays
occur. Thus $\No$ is proper. The basic separation property is:
\[
 A,B\text{ sets},\quad A<B
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists x\in\No\ (A<x<B),
\tag{S16.1}\label{swo:ds:eq:setcut}
\]
with either side allowed to be empty. These are standard facts about the
surreal order \cite{Conway,Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}; the corresponding
smallness-sensitive primitives in ProveIt are audited in
\Cref{swo:ds:sec:lean}.

\begin{lemma}[Fresh separators]\label{swo:ds:lem:fresh}
If $A<B$ are sets of surreals and $S$ is any set, some
$x\notin S$ satisfies $A<x<B$. Every nonempty numerical interval is a
proper class. Deleting a set from $\No$ preserves the set-cut property.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First choose $u,v$ with $A<u<v<B$ by two applications of
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:setcut}. The interval $(u,v)$ cannot be a set: if it were, choose
an element above all of $(u,v)$ but below $v$, a contradiction. Hence the
set $S$ cannot exhaust this interval. Any remaining point works. The same
argument gives the assertions about intervals and deletion.
\end{proof}

For infinite cardinal $\kappa$, put
\[
 \No_{<\kappa}=\{x:\bd(x)<\kappa\},\qquad \mu=2^{<\kappa}.
\]
Then $\No_{<\kappa}$ is a set of size $\mu$. For regular infinite $\kappa$ it is
an $\eta_\kappa$ order: every separated pair of sets with total cardinality
less than $\kappa$ has an interpolant in the same birthday stage. Bound the
option birthdays below $\kappa$ using regularity, and use the usual
birthday-controlled separator. At singular $\kappa$ this argument fails
because a small set can have birthdays cofinal in $\kappa$.

\subsubsection{Which uses of recursion are elementary?}

A recursion producing a set at each ordinal stage, with a set history
before each stage and fixed class parameters, is available in GB. One
constructs each set-length approximation by ordinary recursion and joins
the compatible approximations by elementary comprehension. This applies to
the forth and back-and-forth constructions used below.

By contrast, a recursion whose stages are classes is an instance of
elementary transfinite recursion when its defining formula has only set
quantifiers. Such a recursion may exceed GBC even along $\omega$; truth
recursion is a standard example. ETR supplies abstract class well-order
comparability by initial-segment isomorphisms, but we neither identify
comparability with ETR nor assert a necessity result for our particular
constructions \cite{HamkinsWoodin,GitmanHamkins}. Size of the stage and
history, rather than the mere appearance of the symbol $\Ord$, is decisive.

\begin{proposition}[Universality and uniqueness]\label{swo:ds:prop:universal}
In GBC every class linear order embeds into $\No$. Any two proper class
linear orders satisfying \eqref{swo:ds:eq:setcut} are isomorphic, provided they
have set-like global enumerations. The construction can be made uniform in
set parameters when the carrier and order predicates are uniform.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate the source by an ordinal or by $\Ord$ using global choice. At
each stage insert its next point between the images of its earlier lower
and upper points. These are sets. For an isomorphism alternate forth and
back steps through fixed global enumerations of the two orders, inserting
the next unused point on the appropriate side at each step. Each partial
map is a set. Choose the least permissible point under fixed global
well-orders to make every stage unique. Its graph is the union of the
set-length approximations. With an extra set parameter carried throughout,
the same defining formula gives a uniform class relation for the whole
parameterized family. This is the classical mechanism of surreal
universality and homogeneity \cite{Ehrlich2012,HamkinsEmbeds}.
\end{proof}

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 302-390
\subsection{Source 18: surreals as sign sequences}

Represent a surreal number by a function
$s_x:\bd(x)\to\{-,+\}$, where $\bd(x)$ is an ordinal. Numerical order
is comparison at the first unequal sign, counting an absent sign as
strictly between $-$ and $+$. Sign extension is the simplicity relation,
which is a tree order, not a total order. This presentation and its
substructures are developed in the standard surreal literature
\cite{Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}.

We shall repeatedly use the following elementary consequences.

\begin{lemma}[Surreal order tools]
\label{swo:sh:lem:surreal-tools}
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $L,R$ are sets of surreals and $L<R$, some surreal lies strictly
between them. Either set may be empty.
\item The separator can avoid any prescribed set of forbidden values.
\item For infinite initial $\kappa$, every nonempty open interval of
$\No_{<\kappa}$ contains a sign-prefix cone isomorphic to $\No_{<\kappa}$; hence it
has cardinality $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$.
\item $\No_{<\kappa}$ fills every cut with fewer than $r=\cf\kappa$ input
values. Its cofinality, coinitiality, and both characters at every point
are $r$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For (1), choose an ordinal strictly above all birthdays in $L\cup R$.
Comparison in a sufficiently long full binary level supplies a sign
sequence separating the two sets; equivalently use the usual simplest
surreal cut construction. To get (2), the separator interval contains
a proper class of values: an interval is order-isomorphic to $\No$,
or one can extend a sign prefix by arbitrary ordinal lengths. A set of
forbidden values cannot exhaust it.

For (3), first choose a sufficiently long but still $<\kappa$ prefix
whose whole cone lies inside the given interval. Prefix concatenation
preserves numerical order. If $\beta,\gamma<\kappa$, then
$\beta+\gamma<\kappa$, since this sum still has cardinality below the
initial cardinal $\kappa$. This works at singular cardinals too.
Thus concatenating the chosen prefix with every sign word of length
$<\kappa$ gives the required copy. Counting levels gives
$|\No_{<\kappa}|=\sup_{\alpha<\kappa}2^{|\alpha|}=2^{<\kappa}$.

For (4), fewer than $\cf\kappa$ birthdays are bounded below $\kappa$,
so the construction in (1) stays below $\kappa$. Ordinal labels along a
cofinal sequence in $\kappa$ give a cofinal sequence; their negatives give
a coinitial one. No smaller family is cofinal, since its birthdays are
bounded. At a fixed point, append a negative sign and then arbitrarily
long positive tails to approach from below; use the dual construction
above. These give character at most $r$. The small-cut property gives
the reverse inequality.
\end{proof}

Part (2) is also available in the bounded setting when the forbidden
set has size $<\mu$ and a whole interval of separators is available.
This distinction matters: a used prefix in a minimal permutation can
have length much greater than $\kappa$, but it still uses fewer than
$\mu$ labels.

\subsection{Source 18: set and class theories}

Set-sized results are proved in ZFC. In class arguments, GB denotes
G\"odel--Bernays theory over ZF with elementary class comprehension and
Class Replacement. GBC adds Global Choice. A class is a collection of
sets, never an element of another ordinary class. We regard a class
well-order $R$ as a strict class linear order for which every nonempty
available subclass has an $R$-least element. This definition is internal
to the specified two-sorted model.

A class order is \emph{set-like} if every predecessor class is a set.
A proper set-like class well-order is isomorphic to $\Ord$: map a point
to the ordinal type of its predecessors. The range is an initial
subclass of $\Ord$, and if it were a set, Class Replacement would make
the whole carrier a set. Conversely, an $\Ord$ enumeration is set-like.

All uses of class back-and-forth below choose one new set label at each
ordinal stage. The preceding history at a stage is a set, and the next
choice is determined using a fixed global well-order. This is ordinary
set-valued recursion with class parameters. We do not infer that arbitrary
class-valued recursions follow from GBC. Elementary transfinite recursion
has substantially greater strength in general \cite{GHHSW}.

An expression such as $\Hall$ is initially notation for a domain of
class variables, not a class whose members are class relations. A
uniform family $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ means one class relation
$F(i,x,y)$ with set labels $i,x,y$. A set-indexed family of class
relations is not silently replaced by a set of classes.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 325-427
\subsection{Source 17: foundations and direct comparison without a class of classes}
\label{swo:gs:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Four safe levels}
Our set theorems use $\ZFC$. Our global theorems use $\GBC$, meaning
G\"odel--Bernays set theory with Global Choice; $\GB$ alone includes no
choice principle. This agrees with the conventions in the source and in
Hamkins's account of Global Choice \cite{HamkinsGC}.

A class well-order here is a linear class relation for which every
nonempty admitted subclass has a least element. Set-likeness is an
additional property, not part of that definition. Which subclasses are
admitted is specified by the surrounding class theory or model.

There are four distinct safe ways to interpret a higher-order-looking
statement. One may work with ordinary sets such as $\WO_\mu(X)$; with an
ordinary class of \emph{set codes} such as $\Psupp(b)$; with finitely many class
variables or a uniform class relation coding a family; or externally in a
larger universe in which the objects from the smaller universe are sets.
None permits forming an unrestricted same-level set or class of all
proper classes.

A uniform family indexed by a class $I$ of sets is a single relation
$F\subseteq I\times\Ord\times\No$, with each row $F_i$ an enumeration.
A uniform transformation of enumerations is a formula which defines an
output class from an input class and for which output existence and
uniqueness are proved. It is not a GB function with proper classes as
arguments stored in its graph.

\subsubsection{The direct common-prefix formula}
For a strict class well-order $R$ let
$P_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$. Given two class well-orders $R,S$ of the same labelled
carrier $X$, define
\[\tag{S17.2}\label{swo:gs:eq:commonprefix}
 C(R,S)=\{x:P_R(x)=P_S(x)\text{ and }
 R\res P_R(x)=S\res P_S(x)\}.
\]
Equality and restriction here expand to quantifiers over elements of $X$;
no class quantifier is hidden in the defining formula.

\begin{proposition}[Direct labelled comparison; background with proof]
\label{swo:gs:thm:rawcomparison}
The class $C(R,S)$ is the largest common labelled initial segment of $R,S$.
If $R\ne S$, its complement is nonempty and the two least residual labels
$a=\min_R(X\setminus C)$ and $b=\min_S(X\setminus C)$ are different.
Declaring $R<_{\lex}S$ exactly when $a<b$ gives a strict linear comparison
of all admitted class well-orders of $X$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $x\in C$ and $yRx$, the equality of predecessor classes puts $y$ before
$x$ in both orders; agreement below $x$ then gives equal predecessor
classes and equal predecessor orders for $y$. Thus $y\in C$. The same
argument works with $S$, and proves agreement on $C$. Every common labelled
initial segment satisfies the defining condition, so is contained in $C$.
If $C=X$, the relations agree. Otherwise well-foundedness provides the least
residual elements. If $a=b$, both its predecessor classes are $C$ and the
orders there agree, contradicting $a\notin C$.

For transitivity compare $C(R,S)$ and $C(S,T)$ as initial segments of $S$.
Initial segments of a linear order are comparable by inclusion. If one is
properly shorter, its first disagreement is the first disagreement relevant
to comparing $R,T$, and has the same orientation. If the two prefixes are
equal, the three next labels $a<b<c$ give $a<c$. Trichotomy and asymmetry
are immediate. This is an elementary proof; it does not compare arbitrary
abstract class order types by a recursive isomorphism construction.
\end{proof}

This result is already in the merged report (\cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}).
Its inclusion is important: it eliminates a false dilemma between restricting
to $\Ord$-enumerations and introducing a stronger class recursion theory
merely to define the comparison.

\subsubsection{Choice, recursion, and external semantics}
Global Choice supplies a baseline bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. The source
also proves the converse strength statement: existence of any class
well-order of the sign-sequence surreals implies Global Choice over
choiceless $\GB$ (\cref{swo:cf:choice}). That converse is not needed in
our proofs; we explicitly assume $\GBC$ for the global results.

Recursion whose value at each ordinal stage is a set is available with
class parameters in $\GBC$: set recursion constructs compatible histories
on each set ordinal, and elementary comprehension collects them. This is
not the assertion that arbitrary class-valued recursions have solutions.
The latter territory is governed by principles such as $\ETR$, whose
strength is substantially more than elementary comprehension
\cite{GitmanHamkins}. We will reconstruct branches by a uniqueness formula,
so that even the appearance of such a class-valued recursion is avoided.

In a transitive two-sorted model $(M,\mathcal X)$, ``all classes'' means
$\mathcal X$. An external observer may have more subclasses of $M$. With a
strongly inaccessible cardinal $\lambda$ in an ambient universe,
$(V_\lambda,\mathcal P(V_\lambda))$ provides a useful full-class
interpretation. Externally, its set-like surreal enumerations are the
$\lambda$-length permutations of $\No_{<\lambda}$, while its unrestricted
well-orders allow all external ordinal types of cardinality $\lambda$
(\cref{swo:st:thm:model}). This is a conditional model construction,
not an assertion that $\ZFC$ proves an inaccessible cardinal exists.

Finally, neither passing to $\KM$ nor enumerating formula strings gives an
internal universal class decoder. The latter would need a uniform truth
predicate, not merely syntax. \Cref{swo:gs:sec:core} gives an independent
diagonal explanation for the failure of exhaustive same-level coding.

% ---- source 13 (batch-81 manuscript 01), lines 534-623
\subsection{Source 13: direct comparison of unrestricted class well-orders}\label{swo:fs:sec:raw}

The class $\No$ itself is fixed throughout this section. A class
well-order $R$ is a strict linear order for which every nonempty
subclass has an $R$-least member. A set-like class order additionally
has a set of predecessors at every point. The totality $\Hall$ is
notation for the domain of such class parameters, not an ordinary
class whose members are relations.

\subsubsection{The largest common labeled prefix}

The following construction is from the earlier report
(\cref{swo:cf:lex}; Section~14 at the pin); its explicit formula is useful because
it does not demand an enumeration of a non-set-like order by $\Ord$.

\begin{proposition}[Elementary labeled comparison]\label{swo:fs:prop:rawlex}
Two distinct class well-orders $R,S$ of $\No$ have a largest common
labeled initial part $G$. There are distinct labels $r,s$ that are the
respective first points after $G$. Defining
\[
                         R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r<s
\]
gives a strict linear comparison on $\Hall$ by an elementary formula
with $R,S$ as class parameters. No class-well-order comparability
principle is required.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Define $G$ to consist of those $x$ such that
$\pred_R(x)=\pred_S(x)$ and the two relations agree on that common
predecessor class. Equality and agreement here abbreviate formulas
quantifying over set elements. They do not form the predecessor
classes as elements of a larger collection.

If $x\in G$, all its predecessors belong to $G$. The restrictions of
$R$ and $S$ to $G$ agree, and any common labeled initial part is contained
in $G$. If $G$ were the whole carrier, the relations would agree.
Otherwise take the least points $r,s$ of the complements in the two
orders. Their predecessor classes are both $G$. They cannot coincide,
since their common value would then be a member of $G$.

Trichotomy follows from numerical trichotomy of $r,s$. For transitivity,
consider $R<S<T$. The common prefixes of $(R,S)$ and $(S,T)$ are both
initial parts of $S$, hence one contains the other. If one is properly
shorter, its first disagreement also decides the comparison of $R,T$.
If they are equal, the three next labels satisfy $r<s<t$, which gives
$R<T$. This proves transitivity without assigning an ordinal length
to a proper-class prefix.
\end{proof}

This is not comparison of abstract class order types by initial-segment
isomorphisms. For that different problem, elementary transfinite
recursion is a known sufficient principle \cite[Theorem 6]{HamkinsWoodin}.
Our formula compares identical labels on one carrier, rather than
constructing an isomorphism between unrelated carriers.

\subsubsection{The ordinal head and the residual fiber}

\begin{proposition}[Canonical head; prior structural lemma]\label{swo:fs:prop:head}
For $R\in\Hall$, the points with a set of $R$-predecessors form a
proper-class initial part $H_R$, uniquely enumerated by a class injection
\[
                             F_R:\Ord\longrightarrow\No.
\]
Conversely, for every injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$, appending
any class well-order of $Y=\No\setminus\ran(F)$ produces a raw order
whose head is $F$. All raw orders with this head form a convex fiber,
with their internal comparison equal to the labeled lexicographic
comparison of well-orders of $Y$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$H_R$ is initial. Were it a set, the least point outside it would have
exactly $H_R$ as its predecessor class and would belong to it, a
contradiction. Ranking each point by the ordinal type of its set of
predecessors gives the unique enumeration: its ranks form a proper
initial subclass of $\Ord$ only if they are a set, so they are all of
$\Ord$.

After an $\Ord$-head is listed, every residual point has a proper class
of predecessors, whereas each head point has a set of predecessors.
This proves the converse. Distinct heads disagree at a set ordinal,
and that disagreement places one entire fiber below the other. Equal
heads leave only the tail comparison, proving convexity. A well-order
on $Y$ is available from global choice, also when $Y$ is proper.
\end{proof}

This is the earlier report's decomposition (\cref{swo:cf:core,swo:cf:fibers};
Section~15 at the pin).
We shall identify exactly which cuts of a fixed dense core these fibers
represent, thereby supplying an additional characterization not contained
in the decomposition alone.

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 366-489
\subsection{Source 15: native lexicography on class well-orders}\label{swo:cb:sec:classlex}

\subsubsection{Existence, set-likeness, and the first proper block}

A class relation $R$ on $\No$ is \emph{set-like} when
$\pred_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$ is a set for every $x$. An already-given
set-like class well-order of a proper class has a unique order isomorphism
with $\Ord$: assign to each point the ordinal type of its predecessor
set. The image is initial in $\Ord$ and cannot be a set, since the
inverse map would make the whole carrier a set. This collapse needs GB,
not a separate global choice assumption \cite{HamkinsGC}.

Existence is different. Over GB, the existence of any class well-order of
$\No$, even a non-set-like one, is equivalent to global choice
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}; Theorem~13.1 at the pin). One direction restricts a set-like global
well-order of the universe. For the other, a well-order of $\No$ orders
the sign codes for every $\mathcal P(\alpha)$. Starting with an ordinal
enumeration of a rank stage, transport this order to its power set;
at limits combine the already constructed orders by rank. This set-valued
ordinal recursion produces well-orders of all rank stages and hence a
global well-order. This explains why merely assuming a convenient global
baseline already carries substantive choice information.

An arbitrary class well-order can have type $\Ord+1$, $\Ord+\Ord$, or
much more complicated class types. The final element of an $\Ord+1$
order has a proper class of predecessors. It is still an ordinary
surreal label; the new size occurs in its position in the chosen order.

\subsubsection{A first disagreement after a proper class of agreement}

If $R,S$ are class well-orders of the same labelled carrier $X$, put
$\pred_R(x)=\{y\in X:yRx\}$. A common labelled prefix is initial in
both orders and carries the same restricted relation. The comparison
below is the prior report's elementary construction
(\cref{swo:cf:lex}; Section~14 at the pin); we include its proof because it makes the
foundational advantage precise.

\begin{theorem}[First unequal labels without class ordinals]\label{swo:cb:thm:rawlex}
If $R\ne S$, there are unique distinct $a,b$ such that
\[
 \pred_R(a)=\pred_S(b)=C,
 \qquad R\res C=S\res C.
\]
The class $C$ is their maximal common labelled prefix. If the labels
carry a fixed linear order $<$, declaring $R<_{\lex}S$ when $a<b$
defines a strict linear comparison on the class-well-order predicate.
Its formula has only set quantifiers with $R,S$ as class parameters.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $a$ be the $R$-least point whose predecessor classes in $R$ and $S$
differ, and put $C=\pred_R(a)$. For $y\in C$, these predecessor
classes agree. Such $y$ must also precede $a$ in $S$: otherwise $aSy$
would imply $aRy$. If $zSy$ for $y\in C$, agreement of predecessor
classes gives $zRy$, so $C$ is also $S$-initial. The restricted orders
agree, and $C\subsetneq\pred_S(a)$. Let $b$ be the $S$-least point
outside $C$. Then $bSa$, $b\ne a$, and $\pred_S(b)=C$.
Any other first-disagreement pair must have its first member equal to
the $R$-least point with changed predecessors, proving uniqueness.

For transitivity, suppose $R<S<T$. Their two common prefixes with the
middle order $S$ are initial segments of that same order, hence comparable.
If one is shorter, its first difference also decides $R$ versus $T$;
if they are equal, the next labels satisfy $a<b<c$, which decides the
comparison. Totality and asymmetry follow from unique first disagreement.
Finally the formula can be written directly as
\[
 \exists a,b\ \bigl[a<b\ \land\ \forall z(zRa\leftrightarrow zSb)
 \ \land\ \forall u,v((uRa\land vRa)\Rightarrow(uRv\leftrightarrow uSv))\bigr].
\]
No quantification over a collection of prefix classes is required.
\end{proof}

For example, enumerate $\No\setminus\{a,b\}$ in type $\Ord$, where
$a<b$, and append either $a,b$ or $b,a$. Their first unequal labels occur
after every ordinal stage of the common enumeration. The displayed formula
still compares them. It is not necessary to invent a set ordinal
``beyond $\Ord$'' to name their first difference.

For one given class index order $J$, bijections $J\to\No$ may instead
be compared at the $J$-least unequal coordinate. This agrees with the raw
comparison, but restricts the allowed order type. Two different index
orders should be compared through the induced labelled relations unless
an explicit alignment has been supplied.

\begin{proposition}[Prefix convexity and initial-word fibres]\label{swo:cb:prop:fibres}
In $\GBC$, orders extending a common labelled prefix form a convex family. For an
arbitrary class well-order $R$ of $\No$, let
\[
 I_R=\{x:\pred_R(x)\text{ is a set}\},
 \qquad F_R:\Ord\longrightarrow I_R
\]
be its unique increasing enumeration. Then $I_R$ is a proper class.
Every injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$ occurs as $F_R$, and its
fibre is a convex copy of the well-order space of
$Y_F=\No\setminus\ran(F)$. Distinct fibres compare at the first
unequal coordinate of their words.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A comparison that first diverges inside a common prefix puts the competing
order on the same side of every extension, proving convexity. The class
$I_R$ is initial and set-like. If it were a set, the least point outside
it would have precisely $I_R$ as its predecessors, a contradiction.
Its enumeration is therefore by all ordinals.

Given $F$, order its range by its ordinal indices and append any fixed
well-order of $Y_F$. Every point of the range has set predecessors, and
every residual point has the proper range of $F$ among its predecessors.
Thus the resulting initial word is exactly $F$. Restriction to $Y_F$ and
concatenation with $F$ give inverse order-preserving maps on the fibre.
For unequal words, first ordinal difference precedes both residual tails.
\end{proof}

If $F$ omits $m$ labels, its fibre has $m!$ elements. An exhaustive word
and a word omitting just one label both have singleton fibres; only the
first is set-like. The unrestricted space has adjacent finite residual
permutation blocks, whereas the set-like space is dense and has no
endpoints. These distinctions are already established in the prior report.

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 1064-1173
\subsection{Source 16: global choice and direct comparison of arbitrary class well-orders}\label{swo:ds:sec:raw}

Write $\Hsl$ for the predicate of class bijections $\Ord\to\No$, and
$\Hall$ for that of all class well-order relations on $\No$. These are
notations for assertions about class variables. We will also use $\Jinj$
for class injections $\Ord\to\No$, allowing nonexhaustive ranges.

\begin{proposition}[Existence has a precise choice strength]\label{swo:ds:prop:gc}
Over GB, the following are equivalent: global choice; a class bijection
$\Ord\to\No$; a set-like class well-order of $\No$; and an arbitrary
class well-order of $\No$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Global choice gives a set-like global well-order of the universe. Its
restriction to the proper class $\No$ has order type $\Ord$, yielding
the bijection. A bijection induces a set-like well-order, which is an
arbitrary class well-order as well.

For the reverse implication suppose $R$ well-orders $\No$. Every
$\mathcal P(\delta)$ injects into $\No$ by sign sequences of length
$\delta$, so $R$ gives it a well-order. One can now well-order the
hierarchy $V_\beta$ uniformly by set-valued recursion, starting with
$w_0=\varnothing$. At a successor, use the existing well-order
$w_\beta$ of $V_\beta$ to identify it with an ordinal
$\delta$, transfer subsets to $\mathcal P(\delta)$, and use the
restriction of $R$ on their sign codes. At a nonzero limit $\lambda$,
order the disjoint rank layers by their ranks, using
$w_{\gamma+1}\res(V_{\gamma+1}\setminus V_\gamma)$ on layer $\gamma$,
where $\gamma+1<\lambda$. Each history is a set; no choice of an unspecified family
of well-orders is used. Finally order all sets first by rank and then
by the resulting well-order on that rank layer. This is a set-like
global well-order of the universe and supplies global choice. This
expands the choice-equivalence argument recorded in the prior report
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}).
\end{proof}

For distinct $F,G\in \Jinj$, their first unequal ordinal coordinate exists:
minimize the disagreement class below any one witness. Compare
$F(\delta)$ and $G(\delta)$ numerically. This is a total, transitive
lexicographic comparison. For general $R,S\in \Hall$, however, a first
disagreement may occur after a proper class of common labels.

\begin{lemma}[A common labelled prefix without class ordinals]
\label{swo:ds:lem:rawprefix}
Let $R\ne S$ be class well-orders of the same class $X$. There are
unique distinct labels $a,b$ such that
\[
 \{x:xRa\}=\{x:xSb\}=C,
 \qquad R\res C=S\res C.
\]
The class $C$ is their largest common labelled initial segment.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $a$ be $R$-least among the labels whose predecessor classes in
$R$ and $S$ differ. For every $xRa$ the two predecessor classes of
$x$ agree. Consequently $C=\{x:xRa\}$ is also $S$-initial and the
relations agree on it. Moreover $C$ is a proper subclass of the
$S$-predecessors of $a$. Let $b$ be the $S$-least label outside $C$.
Then $bSa$, $b\ne a$, and its $S$-predecessor class is $C$.
In any pair satisfying the displayed conditions, every earlier label
has identical predecessor classes, while the next $R$-label does not.
It must therefore be $a$, and then both $C$ and $b$ are determined.
\end{proof}

Define $R<_{\lex}S$ if the corresponding next labels satisfy $a<b$ in
the numerical or other fixed native order of $X$. In a triple $R,S,T$,
the common prefixes of $(R,S)$ and $(S,T)$ are initial segments of $S$
and are inclusion-comparable. Whichever ends first decides the comparison
of $R$ and $T$; if they end together, transitivity of the next numerical
labels decides. Thus the definition is a strict linear comparison.

The first-pair condition can be expressed using only set quantifiers:
\[
\begin{split}
 a\in X\land b\in X\land a\ne b
 \quad&\land\quad\forall z\,(zRa\leftrightarrow zSb)\\
 &\land\quad\forall x\,\forall y\,
 ((xRa\land yRa)\Rightarrow(xRy\leftrightarrow xSy)).
\end{split}
\tag{S16.9}\label{swo:ds:eq:rawpredicate}
\]
This is why no abstract comparison of class order types and no ETR is
required. On an injectively indexed uniform family of class well-orders,
it gives an ordinary class linear order on the set-valued indices.

\begin{proposition}[Convexity and finite residual jumps]\label{swo:ds:prop:rawjumps}
Fix any labelled common prefix, possibly a proper class. Its completions
form a convex suborder of $\Hall$. Two distinct raw orders are adjacent
exactly when the labels remaining after their largest common prefix form
a finite set and their residual permutations are consecutive.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
An order that disagrees before a fixed common prefix ends compares in
the same direction with all its completions, proving convexity.
If $R<S$ were adjacent and the remaining set or class of labels were
infinite, $R$ would have to be maximal in its next-letter cylinder and
$S$ minimal in its next-letter cylinder. As in
\Cref{swo:ds:lem:nojump}, swapping an ascent or descent forces the
respective suffixes to be numerically decreasing and increasing. If $Y$
is the residual carrier and $a,b$ the first unequal labels, the numerical
order on $Y\setminus\{a,b\}$ is consequently both a well-order and a
reverse well-order. Such a class is finite: otherwise repeatedly taking
its least remaining member produces a set-coded increasing
$\omega$-sequence, contradicting reverse well-foundedness. Thus $Y$ is
finite, and convexity reduces adjacency exactly to that of
its finite permutation list. Conversely consecutive residual
permutations have no intervening completion, and convexity excludes
an intervening order outside the prefix cylinder.
\end{proof}

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 2180-2350
\subsection{Source 18: global well-orders: existence and elementary comparison}
\label{swo:sh:sec:class-comparison}

\subsubsection{Existence is exactly a global choice issue}

No set-length function exhausts $\No$, since its range is a set. A
well-order of the whole surreal carrier must therefore be a class
relation. It need not be set-like: $\Ord+1$, $\Ord\cdot2$, and more
complicated class concatenations can be transported to the carrier under
Global Choice. Here these expressions denote explicitly constructed
class orders, not set ordinals.

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a global well-order; repository result]
\label{swo:sh:thm:choice}
Over GB with ZF as its set theory, the following are equivalent:
Global Choice; the existence of a set-like global well-order of $\No$;
the existence of any class well-order of $\No$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Global Choice gives a set-like global well-order of the set universe and
hence of $\No$. The second statement implies the third. For the reverse
implication, let $R$ be a class well-order of the sign-sequence surreals.
For every ordinal $\theta$, the length-$\theta$ binary sign sequences
form a set, and the restriction of $R$ well-orders that set. It thereby
well-orders $\mathcal P(\theta)$, uniformly in $\theta$.

Construct a well-order of each $V_\alpha$ by set-valued recursion with
parameter $R$. Start with the empty set. Given a well-order of
$V_\alpha$, use its unique ordinal enumeration to identify subsets of
$V_\alpha$ with subsets of an ordinal; pull back the already specified
well-order of that power set. At a limit stage, order the disjoint rank
layers first by their ordinal rank and then by the relevant previously
constructed well-order. These orders need not extend one another;
uniform existence is what the argument requires. Finally order the
whole universe first by rank and then by the chosen well-order of each
rank layer. Its predecessor classes are sets, so it is a set-like
global well-order and supplies Global Choice. This is the choiceless
argument used in the repository (\cref{swo:cf:choice}).
\end{proof}

The theorem is distinct from asking whether universality of the
\emph{numerical} surreal order for all class linear orders implies
Global Choice. Our arguments use Global Choice for that universality;
they do not establish its converse. Under Global Choice, the usual
forth construction embeds a class linear order in $\No$: enumerate its
carrier in type $\Ord$, and at each stage place the next point between
the already embedded lower and upper sets. Hamkins gives a research-paper
account of this class universality \cite[\S5]{HamkinsEmbeds}.

\subsubsection{Comparing orders after a proper-class common prefix}

Let $R,S$ be class well-orders on the same linearly ordered class $X$.
The numerical order on $X$ need not coincide with either well-order.
Write $\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$. Define $C(R,S)$ to consist
of the labels $x$ such that
\[\tag{S18.4}\label{swo:sh:eq:common-prefix}
 \operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\operatorname{Pred}_S(x)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 R\restr\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=S\restr\operatorname{Pred}_R(x).
\]
Both equalities expand to formulas quantifying only over set labels,
with the two relations as class parameters.

\begin{lemma}[Largest common labelled initial segment]
\label{swo:sh:lem:class-prefix}
$C(R,S)$ is an initial segment of both orders, on which they agree.
It contains every common labelled initial segment. If $R\ne S$, it is
proper, and the first remaining labels $a$ in $R$ and $b$ in $S$ satisfy
\[
 \operatorname{Pred}_R(a)=C(R,S)=\operatorname{Pred}_S(b),\qquad a\ne b.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $x$ satisfies \eqref{swo:sh:eq:common-prefix}, each of its predecessors does
too: the two orders agree below $x$, and therefore assign identical
predecessor classes below any such label. Thus $C$ is initial in both,
and agreement follows by testing a pair below its larger label. Every
common labelled initial segment satisfies the displayed conditions.
If $C=X$, the two relations agree everywhere. Otherwise their
well-order property supplies least labels outside $C$. Their
predecessor classes are exactly $C$. If those labels were equal, that
label would satisfy \eqref{swo:sh:eq:common-prefix}, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Elementary full lexicographic order]
\label{swo:sh:thm:class-lex}
For distinct $R,S$, declare $R<_{\lex}S$ if $a<b$ in the numerical
order, with $a,b$ as in \Cref{swo:sh:lem:class-prefix}. This is a strict
linear order on the available well-orders of $X$. It is elementary in
the two class parameters. It requires neither a system of abstract class
ordinals nor a principle comparing arbitrary class order types.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Trichotomy and asymmetry are immediate. For transitivity, compare the
common prefixes for $R,S$ and for $S,T$. They are initial segments of
the same order $S$, hence nested. If the first prefix ends earlier,
$S$ and $T$ still agree at its next label, so the comparison of $R,T$
is the comparison of $R,S$. The opposite strict containment gives the
comparison of $S,T$. If the prefixes agree, the three next labels are
numerically ordered and transitivity follows in $X$.

For explicit elementary definability, use the formula defining $C$,
assert that the predecessors of $a$ under $R$ and of $b$ under $S$
are exactly the labels satisfying that formula, and assert $a<b$.
No existential quantification over an additional class is needed.
\end{proof}

The theorem extends the usual first-ordinal-difference rule. In the
case of distinct set-like orders, $C$ is a set and has an ordinal length. In the full
case, it may already have type $\Ord$, $\Ord\cdot2$, or a more
complicated type. The comparison still exists because the two orders
use the same labels. Abstractly isomorphic but differently labelled
prefixes are not declared equal.

\subsubsection{Residual cylinders and finite adjacency}

Fix a labelled well-order $Q$ of $C\subsetneq X$. Its cylinder is the
family of all global orders beginning with $Q$. Put $Y=X\setminus C$.
Restriction to $Y$ and concatenation with $Q$ are inverse,
order-preserving operations. The cylinder is convex: any order that
diverges before finishing $Q$ lies on the same side of every extension
of $Q$.

This gives the following useful size-sensitive reading of a cylinder.
If $|Y|=n<\omega$, its tails form the $n!$ permutations of $Y$.
If $Y$ is an infinite set of size $\lambda$, its tails form
$\WO(Y)$, of cardinality $2^\lambda$ and ordinal spectrum
$\beta<\lambda^+$. If $Y$ is proper, its tails form a predicate on
class relations. Under GBC this last family contains a uniformly
presented copy of every class linear order. Indeed, characteristic
functions of initial segments embed any class linear order into binary
$\Ord$ words; independent pair swaps in a fixed enumeration of $Y$
then embed those words into set-like well-orders of $Y$.

Even when $Y$ is a set, the corresponding full orders of $X$ are class
relations. The statement is a set-parameterized isomorphism with their
tails, not the assertion that those class relations themselves form an
ordinary set.

\begin{theorem}[Adjacency is finite residual adjacency]
\label{swo:sh:thm:adjacency}
Let $R<S$, with common prefix $C$, next labels $a<b$, and residual
carrier $Y=X\setminus C$. Then $R,S$ are adjacent if and only if
$Y$ is finite and their residual permutations are consecutive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $R,S$ are adjacent, no remaining numerical label lies strictly
between $a,b$, or it could be put next to produce an intermediate
order. The tail of $R$ after $a$ must be lexicographically greatest:
otherwise a greater replacement remains below $S$. A greatest
well-order tail must list its labels in decreasing numerical order,
since any numerical ascent can be transposed to increase the code.
Dually, the tail of $S$ after $b$ must be numerically increasing.
On $Y\setminus\{a,b\}$, numerical order and its reverse would
therefore both be well-orders. Such a carrier is finite: otherwise
successively taking the least remaining element produces an increasing
$\omega$ sequence with no greatest member, contradicting reverse
well-ordering. Conversely, convexity of the cylinder reduces a finite
residual carrier exactly to finite permutation adjacency.
\end{proof}

For example, choose $a<b$ in $\No$ and give
$\No\setminus\{a,b\}$ a set-like order $Q$. The two orders
$Q+(a,b)$ and $Q+(b,a)$ are adjacent and have type $\Ord+2$.
Neither is set-like. The set-like global order has no adjacent pairs,
because a set prefix leaves an entire proper class of unused numerical
separators. It is consequently not dense in the full global order:
intervals inside a six-point terminal permutation fiber contain only
non-set-like orders.

% ---- hand chunk blocks
\section{The canonical block decomposition (source 15; routes of sources 16 and 18)}\label{swo:ix:sec:blocks}

\begin{note}[\merge; one theorem, three proofs]\label{swo:ix:note:blocks}
Three batch-81 sources decompose an arbitrary class well-order at once by the
same relation: $x\sim y$ exactly when the closed interval between $x$ and $y$
is a set. Each proves that $\sim$ is an elementary convex equivalence, that
every block is set-like of type $\Ord$ or a set ordinal, that at most one block
is a set and it is final, and that the whole order is canonically the
lexicographic sum of $\Ord$ over the class of proper-block representatives,
followed by the optional final set block; each realizes every nonempty class
well-order as a block-index order in $\GBC$. The statements are source~15's
\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition,swo:cb:cce:cor:profiles,swo:cb:cce:thm:allindices},
source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:blocks,swo:ds:thm:blockindices} with
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:blocknormal}, and source~18's \cref{swo:sh:n13.2},
\cref{swo:sh:thm:class-division} with \eqref{swo:sh:eq:main-division}, and
\cref{swo:sh:thm:block-spectrum}. Source~15 is printed first because it also
writes out the coordinate map $x\mapsto(\pi_W(x),r_W(x))$ and the realization
of every block profile; the other two follow as routes, whole, because each
adds statements of its own: source~16 the largest set final segment
(\cref{swo:ds:cor:finalset}) and the uniform family of residual tails;
source~18 the functoriality of the decomposition (\cref{swo:sh:n13.4}), the
cofinality of $R$ read off its blocks (\cref{swo:sh:n13.5}), uniform removal of
the first $\alpha$ blocks by one closed definition, and a class well-order
isomorphic to its own block quotient (\cref{swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block}).
The first block is source~11's canonical initial part (\cref{swo:cf:core}), as
all three say. The sources do not cite one another (source~18 was written
before sources~15 and~16 arrived), and no source has priority. All three state
that the decomposition is elementary in $\GB$, without global choice or
$\ETR$, and that $\GBC$ is used only to transport an abstract order to $\No$.
The block decomposition answers the block-index clause of \cref{swo:n16.3}
(\cref{swo:ix:sec:status}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 490-681
\subsection{Source 15: canonical condensation into proper-class blocks}
\label{swo:cb:cce:sec:blocks}\label{swo:cb:sec:blocks}

The preceding extraction of the initial set-like part can be extended to
\emph{all} blocks at once.  This resolves an ambiguity in the question of
how much recursion is required: constructing the canonical first-level
decomposition is elementary; enumerating its blocks by a prescribed
index order, or iterating the decomposition on an arbitrary input, is a
different request.

Interval condensation is a standard construction in order theory \cite{BrownSuarez}.  Here
the size ideal consists of sets, not of countable subsets.  Thus the
construction belongs to class theory and depends on which collections
are sets in the underlying model.  Its comparison with familiar
countable-interval condensation is structural, not an identification of
the two notions.

Work first in GB, with no choice assumption, and let $(X,W)$ be a class
well-order.  We use the formulation that every nonempty available
subclass of $X$ has a least element.  Put
\[
 [x,y]_W=\{z\in X:x\leq_W z\leq_W y\}
 \qquad(x\leq_W y).
\]

\begin{definition}[Condensation by set intervals]\label{swo:cb:n5.1}
For $x,y\in X$, write $x\sim_W y$ when the closed interval between them
is a set.  Let
\[
 B_W=\{b\in X:\text{there is no }aWb\text{ with }a\sim_W b\}.
\]
The \emph{condensation} of $W$ is the induced order on $B_W$.
\end{definition}

This definition is elementary.  For example, ``$[x,y]_W$ is a set''
can be written
\[
 \exists u\ \forall z\,
 \bigl(z\in u\longleftrightarrow
       (z\in X\land x\leq_W z\land z\leq_W y)\bigr),
\]
where $u,z$ are set variables and $X,W$ are class parameters.  Neither
the equivalence classes nor a collection of those classes is being used
as an element of another class.  Their least representatives are sets
and form the legitimate class $B_W$.

\begin{theorem}[Elementary canonical block decomposition]
\label{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}
In GB, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The relation $\sim_W$ is a convex equivalence relation.  Every
      equivalence class has a least element, and the class function
      $\pi_W:X\to B_W$ sending an element to that least representative
      is elementary and unique.
\item The order $(B_W,W)$ is a class well-order.  Each fiber
      $C_b=\pi_W^{-1}(b)$ is set-like in its induced order.  It therefore
      has the order type of a nonzero set ordinal if it is a set, and
      has order type $\Ord$ if it is a proper class.
\item Every nonfinal fiber is a proper class.  Consequently at most one
      fiber is a set, and such a fiber must be final.
\item There is a uniform class order isomorphism
      \[
       x\longmapsto\bigl(\pi_W(x),r_W(x)\bigr),\qquad
       r_W(x)=\operatorname{otp}([\pi_W(x),x)_W),
      \]
      onto a lexicographically ordered subclass of $B_W\times\Ord$.
      Every nonfinal vertical section is all of $\Ord$; a final
      section is either all of $\Ord$ or a nonzero set ordinal.
\end{enumerate}
No elementary-transfinite-recursion principle is required.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate.  In a linear order the interval
between $x$ and $z$ is contained in the union of the intervals between
$x,y$ and between $y,z$.  A subclass of a set is a set by Separation
with class parameters; hence $x\sim_W y$ and $y\sim_W z$ imply
$x\sim_W z$.  If $x\leq_W z\leq_W y$ and $x\sim_W y$, the intervals
from $x$ to $z$ and from $z$ to $y$ are subsets of $[x,y]_W$, proving
convexity.

For any $x$, its equivalence class is nonempty and elementary in the
parameters, so it has a $W$-least element $b$.  Such $b$ belongs to
$B_W$, and conversely every member of $B_W$ is the least member of its
equivalence class.  The graph of $\pi_W$ is therefore given by one
elementary formula.  Every nonempty available subclass of $B_W$ is also
a subclass of $X$, and its $W$-least member belongs to it.  This proves
the quotient's well-order property without any theorem comparing
abstract class well-orders.

Fix $b\in B_W$ and $x\in C_b$.  The predecessors of $x$ in $C_b$ are
exactly $[b,x)_W$, a set.  Thus $C_b$ is set-like.  Its set-sized
predecessor ranks form an initial subclass of $\Ord$.  If this initial
subclass were a set ordinal while $C_b$ were proper, the inverse rank
map and class Replacement would make $C_b$ a set.  Therefore the rank
range is all of $\Ord$ precisely in the proper-class case.  In the
set case it is the ordinary ordinal order type of $C_b$.

Suppose now that $C_b$ is a set and is not final.  Let $d$ be the least
point after this fiber.  More explicitly, choose the least member of
the nonempty class
\[
 \{z\in X:bWz\text{ and }z\not\sim_W b\}.
\]
Convexity and minimality give $[b,d)_W=C_b$.  Hence
$[b,d]_W=C_b\cup\{d\}$ is a set, contradicting
$d\not\sim_W b$.  This proves the final-fiber assertion.

For each $x$, the set well-order $[\pi_W(x),x)_W$ has a unique ordinal
order type.  Its order-isomorphism witnesses are sets, so $r_W$ is
defined by elementary comprehension.  Elements in different fibers
are compared by their representatives; elements in one fiber are
compared by their ranks.  The displayed map is therefore a class order
isomorphism.  Its image is defined directly as the class of pairs that
occur, so no symbol denoting a ``class ordinal'' has to be treated as
a set-valued section length.
\end{proof}

The first fiber is exactly the familiar initial part consisting of
elements with set-sized predecessor classes.  If $X$ is proper, the
following equivalence is particularly useful:
\[
 W\text{ is set-like}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |B_W|=1.
\]
This is an invariant of the individual class well-order.  It does not
claim that set-likeness is definable in the \emph{bare lexicographic
order of all labeled well-orders}; that reconstruction question remains
separate.

\begin{corollary}[Allowed block profiles]
\label{swo:cb:cce:cor:profiles}
Every proper-class well-order is canonically a sum of $\Ord$-blocks
indexed by a class well-order, with the sole possible exception of a
final block of nonzero set-ordinal type.  The index order need not be
set-like, or even have type $\Ord$.
\end{corollary}

The word ``canonically'' refers to the least-representative quotient and
the rank map above.  It does not assert that arbitrary class index
orders have canonical set codes or admit an ordinal classification
inside GB.

\begin{theorem}[Every class well-order occurs as a block index]
\label{swo:cb:cce:thm:allindices}
Assume GBC.  Let $J$ be any nonempty class well-order, with a set or
proper-class carrier.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is a class well-order of $\No$ whose canonical condensation
      is order-isomorphic to $J$ and whose every block has type $\Ord$.
\item For every nonzero set ordinal $\alpha$, there is one whose block
      index is $J+1$, whose blocks indexed by $J$ have type $\Ord$,
      and whose final block has type $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
More generally these realize every profile allowed by
\Cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}, subject only to the whole carrier
being a proper class.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Order $J\times\Ord$ lexicographically, comparing the $J$ coordinate
first.  This is a class well-order: a nonempty subclass has a least
first coordinate and then a least ordinal coordinate.  It is proper
because $J$ is nonempty.  The interval between two points of the same
row is a set.  Between points of different rows lies a final segment
of the earlier $\Ord$-row, which is proper.  Consequently the rows
are exactly the equivalence classes, with representatives $(j,0)$.

Global Choice supplies a class bijection between this proper carrier
and $\No$.  Transfer the relation along it.  A class bijection takes
sets to sets by class Replacement, and the same is true of its inverse;
it therefore preserves the set/proper-class distinction used in the
condensation definition.  This proves the first assertion.

For the second, append the set ordinal $\alpha$ to
$J\times_{\mathrm{lex}}\Ord$.  This final tail is one new equivalence
class.  It does not merge with any preceding row because an interval
crossing into it contains a proper final segment of an $\Ord$-row.
Transfer again to $\No$.

For a desired profile with final set block, remove the final index
from its proposed index order and apply the second construction.
The remaining order must be nonempty: otherwise the whole carrier
would be a set.  Profiles with no set block use the first construction.
\end{proof}

For instance, the formal class-order expression
$\Ord\cdot(\Ord+1)$ has an $\Ord+1$ block index.  Its final block
occurs after a proper class of complete $\Ord$-blocks.  No procedure
that lists only set-ordinally many initial blocks reaches it.  Here
the product denotes the explicitly described ordered sum; it is not
an ordinal object larger than every ordinal.

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 1174-1324
\subsection{Source 16: simultaneous canonical decomposition into ordinal-class blocks}
\label{swo:ds:sec:blocks}

The earlier report extracts the first set-like part of a class well-order
and asks how to organize the successive residual parts. A direct interval
definition answers this question without carrying out a class-valued
recursion. In this section GB suffices; assume that the given relation
already is a class well-order in the sense of
\Cref{swo:ds:sec:foundations}.

For $x,y\in X$, let $[x,y]_R$ mean the closed interval between them,
regardless of which comes first. Put
\[
 x\sim_R y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [x,y]_R\text{ is a set}.
\tag{S16.10}\label{swo:ds:eq:blockequiv}
\]
Formally the right side is $\exists s\,\forall z\,
(z\in s\leftrightarrow z\in[x,y]_R)$, with $s$ a set variable.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical block decomposition]\label{swo:ds:thm:blocks}
The relation $\sim_R$ is a convex equivalence relation. Every block has
a least member and is set-like in its inherited order. Each block is
therefore either a set well-order of ordinal type or a proper class
well-order of type $\Ord$.
There is at most one set block, and it is terminal.

Let $J_R$ be the class of least representatives of the proper blocks,
ordered by $R$, and let $\alpha_R$ be the ordinal type of the terminal
set block, or zero when it is absent. There is a canonical class order
isomorphism
\[
 (X,R)\cong\left(\sum_{j\in(J_R,R)}\Ord\right)+\alpha_R.
\tag{S16.11}\label{swo:ds:eq:blocknormal}
\]
All the data and the isomorphism are definable by elementary
comprehension. The sum is the ordinary class $J_R\times\Ord$ ordered
lexicographically, not a class whose members are classes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The interval between $x$ and $z$ is contained in the union of the
intervals between $x,y$ and between $y,z$. Finite union and separation
therefore prove transitivity; the other equivalence properties and
convexity follow immediately.

Each block is an available nonempty subclass and has an $R$-least point
$m(x)$. The formula saying that $j\sim_R x$ and no $R$-earlier point
is equivalent to $x$ defines $m$ elementarily. Thus representatives
form a subclass of $X$, avoiding a quotient carrier made of proper
classes. If $j=m(x)$, the predecessors of $x$ within its block are
exactly the set $[j,x)_R$. Define
\[
 \rho_R(x)=\otp([j,x)_R,R).
\]
This uses only a set well-order and its unique ordinal type. The range
of $\rho_R$ on the block is an initial subclass of $\Ord$. If that
range were a set, Class Replacement applied to its inverse would make
the block a set. Hence a proper block has rank range all of $\Ord$;
a set block has an ordinal rank range.

Suppose a set block $B$ were not terminal. Let $c$ be the least point
strictly above all of $B$. There is nothing between $B$ and $c$.
For $b\in B$, the interval $[b,c]_R$ is contained in $B\cup\{c\}$,
a set. This contradicts maximality of the equivalence block. Thus a
set block is terminal, and there is at most one.

On proper blocks, $x\mapsto(m(x),\rho_R(x))$ is the desired
isomorphism; on the optional final block use its ordinal rank. All
assertions defining these graphs quantify over sets with $R$ as a
fixed class parameter, so elementary comprehension suffices.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Every residual tail is now available uniformly}

For $j\in J_R$ put
\[
 T_j=\{x:j\le_R x\},\qquad B_j=\{x:m(x)=j\}.
\]
The family of tails is one class relation of pairs $(j,x)$. Within
$T_j$, a point $x$ has a set of predecessors exactly when $[j,x)_R$
is a set, equivalently when $x\in B_j$. Hence $B_j$ is precisely the
canonical initial set-like part of $T_j$. The tail $T_j$ is what
remains after all earlier blocks have been deleted. This supplies the
whole successive residual family even when $J_R$ is non-set-like.

\begin{corollary}[Largest set final segment]\label{swo:ds:cor:finalset}
The class
\[
 A_R=\{x\in X:\{y:x\le_R y\}\text{ is a set}\}
\]
is always a set. It is the largest set-sized final segment of $R$,
and is exactly its optional terminal block.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $A_R$ is nonempty, let $a$ be its least point. Every later point
has a tail contained in the set tail above $a$, so $A_R$ is precisely
that tail, a set. Every set final segment is contained in $A_R$ by
definition. Conversely, a block containing a point of $A_R$ is the
union of a set of block predecessors and a subset of its set tail,
and so is a set block. \Cref{swo:ds:thm:blocks} identifies it.
\end{proof}

Deleting $A_R$ leaves a labelled prefix consisting of all the proper
blocks and having no nonempty set-sized final segment. If that prefix
is fixed, its completions form a convex copy of $\WO(A_R)$. Appending
any well-order on $A_R$ leaves it the largest set final segment, since
a tail meeting an earlier $\Ord$ block would already be proper. This
refines the earlier first-block decomposition: after every proper block
is removed, the residual carrier is always a set.

\begin{theorem}[All block-index orders occur]\label{swo:ds:thm:blockindices}
Every nonempty class well-order $J$, whether its carrier is a set or a
proper class, occurs as the index of the proper blocks of a class
well-order. An arbitrary set ordinal can be prescribed as its final
block. In GBC the resulting order can be carried by surreal labels.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Order $J\times\Ord$ with the $J$ coordinate primary. A nonempty
subclass has a least occupied $J$ coordinate and then a least ordinal
in that section, so this is a class well-order. Intervals inside one
section are sets; an interval crossing two sections contains a proper
tail of $\Ord$. Its blocks are exactly the sections. Appending a set
ordinal gives the stipulated final block. The product is proper, and
global choice supplies a class bijection of its carrier with $\No$,
along which the relation can be transported.
\end{proof}

If $J_R$ is a set of type $\gamma$, formula~\eqref{swo:ds:eq:blocknormal}
means $\Ord\cdot\gamma+\alpha_R$. If $J_R$ is proper and set-like, it
means $\Ord\cdot\Ord+\alpha_R$. The example
$\Ord\cdot(\Ord+1)+\alpha$ has block index $\Ord+1$: an
$\Ord$-indexed list of its initial blocks would miss its last full
block, whereas \eqref{swo:ds:eq:blockequiv} finds it directly.

\subsubsection{What this does and does not require from ETR}

The construction resolves successive residual extraction for one original
order. Repeatedly condensing the \emph{quotient order itself} is another
operation. If $C_R(D)$ denotes the least representatives of set-interval
blocks in the induced order on $D\subseteq X$, a tower such as
\[
 D_0=X,\qquad D_{\beta+1}=C_R(D_\beta),\qquad
 D_\lambda=\bigcap_{\beta<\lambda}D_\beta
\]
is an elementary class-valued recursion. Each specified finite iteration
is elementary; appropriate ETR supplies a uniform transfinite tower.
No necessity or exact reversal is established here. Also, since the
block-index order can be an arbitrary class well-order,
\Cref{swo:ds:thm:blocks} does not solve abstract class well-order
comparability or give a universal class ordinal.

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 2382-2639
\subsection{Source 18: a simultaneous decomposition into ordinal-class blocks}
\label{swo:sh:sec:simultaneous-blocks}

The repository asks how much class recursion is needed to iterate the
extraction of the initial set-like part of a class well-order.  A direct
definition organizes all of these blocks simultaneously.  It avoids a
recursion whose successive states are proper classes.

Work in GB and let $R$ be a class well-order on a proper class $X$.
Here ``class well-order'' means that every nonempty available subclass
has an $R$-least element.  For $x\le_R y$, write
\[
 [x,y]_R=\{z\in X:x\le_R z\le_R y\}.
\]
The assertion that this interval is a set is the elementary formula
\[
 \exists a\ \forall z\,[z\in a\longleftrightarrow
      (z\in X\wedge x\le_R z\le_R y)].
\]
In particular, no quantification over candidate classes is needed.

\begin{definition}[Set-interval equivalence]\label{swo:sh:n13.1}
Put $x\sim_R y$ when the closed $R$-interval with endpoints $x,y$ is
a set.  Let $m_R(x)$ be the $R$-least element of the equivalence class of
$x$.  A block is represented by this least label, never by placing a
proper class inside another class.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Block structure]\label{swo:sh:n13.2}
The relation $\sim_R$ is an elementary, convex equivalence relation.
Every one of its blocks is set-like in its induced order.  Every
nonfinal block is a proper class.  Consequently there is at most one
set-sized block, and if present it is final.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate.  For transitivity, the interval
between two of three points is contained in the union of the intervals
from those points to the third; separation and the union of two sets
give the result.  Convexity follows by taking subsets of an interval.

Fix a block $C$.  Its least element $b$ exists by the assumed class
well-ordering.  If $x\in C$, its predecessors within $C$ form the set
$[b,x]_R\setminus\{x\}$.  Thus the block is set-like.  Suppose now
that $C$ is a set and is not final.  There is a least point $d$ after
all of $C$.  Convexity and this minimality imply
$[b,d]_R=C\cup\{d\}$.  This is a set, so $d\sim_R b$, contradicting
$d\notin C$.  The final assertion follows because two distinct final
blocks are impossible.
\end{proof}

Let $B_R$ be the class of least labels of the proper-class blocks,
ordered by $R$.  If there is a final set block, let $\theta_R$ be its
ordinal order type; otherwise put $\theta_R=0$.  Since $X$ is proper,
$B_R$ is nonempty.  It may be a set or a proper class.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical division by the ordinal class]
\label{swo:sh:thm:class-division}
In GB, every class well-order $R$ on a proper class has a canonical
class isomorphism
\[
 (X,R)\ \cong\ (B_R\times\mathrm{Ord})_{\rm lex}+\theta_R,
\]
where the product compares the $B_R$ coordinate first.  All proper
blocks have type $\mathrm{Ord}$.  The block map, the block index order,
and the isomorphism are elementary and uniform in $R$.  No global
choice or elementary transfinite recursion principle is used.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A proper, set-like class well-order has type $\mathrm{Ord}$: assign
to each point the ordinal type of its set of predecessors.  The ranks
form an initial subclass of the ordinals; if that subclass were a set,
the inverse rank map and class replacement would make the domain a
set.  Hence the rank range is all of $\mathrm{Ord}$.

Apply this observation to each proper block.  More explicitly, define
\[
 \rho_R(x)=\operatorname{otp}
 \bigl(\{z:m_R(x)\le_R z<_R x\},R\bigr).
\]
The displayed predecessor interval is a set.  Its restricted relation
and its unique ordinal order type are sets as well.  Thus the graph
of $\rho_R$ is elementary with class parameter $R$, and $(m_R(x),
\rho_R(x))$ gives the desired coordinate in a proper block.  The
same rank map identifies a final set block with $\theta_R$.  Convexity
of the blocks proves order preservation and exhaustiveness.

The class $B_R$ consists of actual elements of $X$, characterized by
an elementary formula.  Class well-foundedness restricts to it.  None
of the construction forms a collection having the blocks themselves
as elements.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Uniqueness and functoriality]\label{swo:sh:n13.4}
A class order isomorphism preserves set-interval equivalence, induces
an isomorphism of the proper-block index orders, and preserves the
final ordinal $\theta_R$.  Hence the pair $(B_R,\theta_R)$ is unique
up to class order isomorphism of its first coordinate.  The construction
works simultaneously for any uniformly coded set- or class-indexed
family of input relations.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A class isomorphism and its inverse send sets to sets by class
replacement.  They therefore preserve whether an interval is a set,
and send block minima to block minima.  Ordinal order types of set
tails are unique.  Conversely an isomorphism of block indices and
equality of the final ordinals combine, using the displayed coordinates,
to produce an isomorphism of the original orders.  Uniformity follows
by inserting the family index into the same elementary formulas.
\end{proof}

The first proper block is exactly the repository's canonical initial
set-like part $I_R$.  Thus the theorem is a simultaneous form of the
successive residual decomposition.  It does not prove comparability
of arbitrary abstract class well-orders: the remaining index order
$B_R$ can be as complicated as any class well-order.

\begin{corollary}[Set-sized cofinality from the blocks]\label{swo:sh:n13.5}
If $\theta_R>0$, the least size of a set cofinal in $R$ is
$\operatorname{cf}(\theta_R)$.  If $\theta_R=0$ and $B_R$ has a
greatest element, no set is cofinal in $R$.  If $\theta_R=0$ and
$B_R$ has no greatest element, $R$ has a set cofinal subset exactly
when $B_R$ does, and the least sizes agree.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A nonempty final set tail determines cofinality.  A final proper
block has type $\mathrm{Ord}$, so every set of points in that block
is bounded, while earlier blocks cannot help with cofinality.  In
the remaining case, projecting a set cofinal subset to block minima
gives a set cofinal in $B_R$.  Conversely a set cofinal in $B_R$
provides a cofinal set of least block labels in $R$: because $B_R$
has no maximum, a cofinal family includes a block strictly beyond
the block of any prescribed point.  Class replacement preserves
the relevant size inequalities.
\end{proof}

In a full containing-universe interpretation based on an inaccessible
$\kappa$, the theorem agrees with ordinary ordinal division.  The
internal ordinal class is externally $\kappa$.  An internal class
interval is an internal set exactly when its external order type is
less than $\kappa$: regularity bounds the ranks of fewer than
$\kappa$ labels, and internal sets have size less than $\kappa$.
Thus a well-order of external ordinal type $\gamma$, with
$|\gamma|=\kappa$, decomposes as
\[
 \gamma=\kappa\cdot\beta+\rho,
 \qquad \rho<\kappa.
\]
The elementary internal argument does not require the existence of
such a containing universe.

\begin{theorem}[Exact spectrum of block index orders]
\label{swo:sh:thm:block-spectrum}
In GBC, every nonempty class well-order $\Gamma$ on a class of set
labels occurs as $B_R$, up to isomorphism, for a class well-order $R$
of $\mathrm{No}$.  Any prescribed set ordinal can simultaneously be
realized as the final remainder $\theta_R$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Form $(\Gamma\times\mathrm{Ord})_{\rm lex}+\theta$.  It is a
class well-order: a nonempty subclass either meets the product, in
which case choose its least first coordinate and then its least ordinal
coordinate, or lies in the final ordinal.  Within one product fiber,
closed intervals are sets.  Between distinct fibers, an interval
contains a proper final part of an $\mathrm{Ord}$ fiber and is proper.
The proper blocks are exactly the fibers, and the final $\theta$,
when nonzero, is one set block.  Global choice supplies a class bijection
from this proper carrier to $\mathrm{No}$; transport the order.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Uniform removal through ordinary ordinal stages}

The direct decomposition also answers a narrower recursion question.
Let $K_R$ be the initial set-like part of $B_R$ (all of $B_R$ if it is
a set), and let $r_R(b)$ be the ordinal type of the predecessors of
$b$ in $B_R$, for $b\in K_R$.  For every set ordinal $\alpha$, put
\[
 U_\alpha=\{x\in X:m_R(x)\in K_R\ \wedge\
                     r_R(m_R(x))<\alpha\}.
\]
The family $(U_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathrm{Ord}}$ is one elementary
class relation.  Its complement carries the residual order after
removal of the first $\alpha$ proper blocks.  At a successor stage,
if a proper residual carrier remains, its initial $\mathrm{Ord}$
block is removed; at a limit stage the removed domain is the union
of the earlier removed domains.  If $B_R$ is a set, removal stops
after its ordinal type, leaving $\theta_R$.

Thus even this uniform ordinal-indexed instance of apparently
class-valued recursion is already available in GB through a closed
definition.  This is a statement about this particular operation,
not a claim that arbitrary class-valued recursions are provable in GB.

\subsubsection{A class well-order isomorphic to its own block quotient}

Let $\mathcal P$ consist of all functions $f:\omega\to\mathrm{Ord}$
with finite support.  For distinct $f,g$, put
\[
 f\triangleleft g
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 f(n)<g(n),\qquad
 n=\max\{i:f(i)\ne g(i)\}.
\]

\begin{proposition}[Self-similar block quotient]
\label{swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block}
The order $(\mathcal P,\triangleleft)$ is a class well-order.
Its set-interval blocks consist precisely of functions that agree
at every coordinate $i\ge1$.  Every block has type $\mathrm{Ord}$,
and its block index order is isomorphic to $(\mathcal P,
\triangleleft)$ itself.  In GBC the example can be transported to
a class well-order of $\mathrm{No}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a nonempty class of functions, the zero function is least if
present.  Otherwise choose its least possible largest nonzero support
index $d$.  Among functions with that index, minimize the coefficient
at $d$, then at $d-1$, and so on through $0$.  A nonempty class of
ordinals has a least element, and there are finitely many steps.  The
result is least among functions of degree $d$, and every larger degree
is greater.  This proves class well-foundedness.

If $f,g$ agree above coordinate $0$, every function between them has
that same tail, and its zeroth coordinate lies in the set ordinal
interval between $f(0)$ and $g(0)$.  Their interval is a set.  If their
tails differ and $f\triangleleft g$, keep the tail of $f$ fixed and
let the zeroth coefficient run through all ordinals greater than
$f(0)$.  The resulting proper class lies strictly between $f$ and
$g$.  This proves the description of blocks.

The least label in a block has zeroth coefficient $0$.  Deleting that
coordinate identifies the class of block minima, with its inherited
order, with all of $\mathcal P$.  Varying the zeroth coefficient
identifies each block with $\mathrm{Ord}$.  Finally apply global choice
to transfer the proper carrier to $\mathrm{No}$.
\end{proof}

This example is a rigorous class analogue of the finite-polynomial
presentation informally denoted by $\mathrm{Ord}^{\omega}$.  The
notation is not needed in the construction.  It shows that passage to
the block quotient need not reduce the order to a simpler isomorphism
type.  It does not assert nontermination of every possible limit-stage
condensation convention; a limit operation must be defined separately.

\subsubsection{What remains open after the direct decomposition}

The repository's question about uniformly organizing successive
initial $\mathrm{Ord}$ blocks has an elementary answer above, including
an exact unrestricted spectrum of block index orders.  A distinct
question remains: what is the strength of uniformly iterating the
\emph{quotient operation itself} through arbitrary class well-orders,
with an explicitly specified limit convention?  General ETR is a
sufficient framework for suitable elementary class recursions, but
the present arguments establish neither its necessity for this
specific operation nor the strength of alternative limit conventions.
The self-similar example rules out a proof based merely on a claimed
strict decrease of quotient isomorphism types.
