\section{An exact external classification in countable models (source 18)}
\label{swo:sh:sec:countable-factorial-shuffle}

The distinction between an internal class and an external collection of
classes leads to a surprisingly uniform external order type. The statement
below concerns the raw labelled comparison of all admitted class well-orders,
including those that are not set-like. It does not concern their abstract
order types. It strengthens the observation that an external countable
collection of admitted orders can embed into the external rational line.

For a linear order $L$, write $x\sim_{\mathrm{fin}}y$ when the closed
interval between $x$ and $y$ is finite. These equivalence classes are the
\emph{finite-condensation blocks}. For a nonempty countable collection
$\mathcal A$ of linear order types, its \emph{shuffle}
$\sigma(\mathcal A)$ is obtained by densely colouring $\mathbb Q$ with one
colour for each member of $\mathcal A$, then replacing a point by the order
type of its colour. A colour-preserving back-and-forth proves that the
resulting order type is independent of the chosen dense colouring. These
are standard order-theoretic constructions; see, for example,
Dimitrov--Harizanov--Morozov--Shafer--Soskova--Vatev,
\emph{On cohesive powers of linear orders}, Definitions 3.3 and 6.2,
\cite{CohesivePowers}. The identification with the
well-order space below is derived here.

\subsection{Terminal tails and finite-condensation blocks}

The next arguments can first be carried out internally in $\GBC$. Let
$X$ be an infinite linearly ordered class, and consider the predicate of
all class well-orders of $X$, with the raw labelled lexicographic comparison.
It is enough that the required well-orders and constructions exist; for
$X=\No$, global choice supplies them.

\begin{lemma}[The maximal finite terminal tail]
\label{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence}
Every class well-order $R$ on an infinite carrier has a unique finite
terminal segment $T_R$ such that $R$ restricted to $X\setminus T_R$ has no
greatest element. Write $n(R)=|T_R|$. Every finite terminal segment of $R$
is contained in $T_R$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $R$ has no greatest element, take $T_R=\varnothing$. Otherwise start at
the greatest element and repeatedly take its immediate predecessor, for
as long as one exists. If this process did not terminate at a finite stage,
ordinary set-valued recursion with parameter $R$ would produce a
descending $\omega$-sequence. Class Replacement makes its range a set,
contradicting well-foundedness. At termination the selected finite chain
is terminal and the remaining prefix has no greatest element. Any finite
terminal segment is obtained by finitely many of the same uniquely
determined predecessor steps, proving maximality and uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Adjacency forces a finite residual carrier]
\label{swo:sh:lem:adjacency-finite-residual}
Suppose $R<S$ are adjacent in the lexicographic order of all class
well-orders of $X$. Let $C$ be their common labelled prefix, and let
$a=\min_R(X\setminus C)<\min_S(X\setminus C)=b$ in the ambient label
order. Then $Y=X\setminus C$ is finite.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Keep the prefix $C$, then the next label $a$, fixed. The $R$-tail must
be the greatest available well-order in that prefix cylinder: any greater
tail gives an order strictly between $R$ and $S$. At each subsequent
position, therefore, its label must be the greatest remaining label.
Otherwise choose a larger remaining label and well-order the remaining
carrier to obtain a greater tail. Consequently the reverse ambient
label order on $Y\setminus\{a\}$ is a class well-order.

The symmetric argument, fixing $C$ then $b$, shows that the ambient
label order on $Y\setminus\{b\}$ is a class well-order. On
$Z=Y\setminus\{a,b\}$, both an order and its reverse are therefore
well-orders. This forces $Z$ to be finite. Indeed, if $Z$ were infinite,
repeatedly choosing the least unused point in one of those well-orders
would produce an ascending $\omega$-sequence in that order, hence a
descending $\omega$-sequence in the other. Thus $Y$ is finite.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Factorial blocks]
\label{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks}
The finite-condensation block containing $R$ consists exactly of the
orders obtained by keeping $R$ fixed on $X\setminus T_R$ and permuting
the $n(R)$ labels in $T_R$. It is a finite chain of size $n(R)!$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The common-prefix cylinder with residual carrier $T_R$ is convex and
contains exactly its $n(R)!$ permutations. In lexicographic order they
form a finite chain, so they lie in one finite-condensation block.

Conversely, any adjacent order $S$ has a finite residual carrier at the
first disagreement, by the preceding lemma. That residual is a finite
terminal segment in $R$, hence lies in $T_R$. Thus an adjacent step
cannot leave the displayed permutation cylinder. A finite interval is a
finite chain of adjacent steps; no member outside this cylinder can be
at finite distance from $R$. This proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ both give a singleton block. The maximal
finite-tail length distinguishes these as labelled well-orders, but their
block sizes do not distinguish them in the pure linear order.

\subsection{Every factorial block size occurs densely}

\begin{lemma}[An interval across different blocks contains an infinite
residual cylinder]
\label{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder}
If $R<S$ belong to different finite-condensation blocks, there is a
labelled prefix cylinder lying entirely inside $(R,S)$ whose residual
carrier is infinite. The prefix may be a proper class.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be the common prefix, $Y=X\setminus C$, and let $a<b$ be the
first unequal labels. The class $Y$ is infinite, since a finite residual
would put the two orders in one finite permutation cylinder.

Consider the following two possible changes. In $R$, at a position
$x\in Y\setminus\{a\}$ outside $T_R$, keep the whole earlier prefix
and replace $x$ by a larger unused label. In $S$, at a position
$x\in Y\setminus\{b\}$ outside $T_S$, keep the whole earlier prefix
and replace $x$ by a smaller unused label. A change of the first kind
gives a prefix cylinder above $R$ and below $S$, because the earlier
first label $a$ remains fixed; a change of the second kind gives the
same conclusion with the first label $b$ fixed. The unused carrier
before such a change is infinite, since the changed position lies
outside the maximal finite terminal tail. Removing one label leaves
the new cylinder with infinite residual carrier.

At least one such change must be possible. Otherwise let
\[
 Z=Y\setminus\bigl(\{a,b\}\cup T_R\cup T_S\bigr).
\]
This class is infinite. In $R$, every $x\in Z$ must be numerically
greater than each of its $R$-successors in $Z$, since any larger unused
successor would permit the first change. Thus $R\restriction Z$ is
the reverse ambient label order. In $S$, every $x\in Z$ must be
numerically smaller than each of its $S$-successors in $Z$, since a
smaller one would permit the second change. Thus $S\restriction Z$
is the ambient order. Both restrictions are class well-orders,
contradicting the infinitude of $Z$ as in the preceding proof.
The orders in this cylinder also lie in blocks different from both endpoint
blocks. For an upward change, its first disagreement with $R$ occurs while
the residual is infinite, and its first disagreement with $S$ occurs at
the original infinite residual $Y$; the downward case is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Prescribing the finite tail]
\label{swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail}
For every $n\in\omega$, every interval joining different
finite-condensation blocks contains an order $W$ with $n(W)=n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take the cylinder from \Cref{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder}, with prefix
$P$ and infinite residual carrier $Y$. Choose $n$ distinct labels
$F\subseteq Y$. Well-order $Y\setminus F$ without a greatest element:
if it is a set, use its infinite initial cardinal as order type; if it
is a proper class, use a set-like well-order of type $\Ord$. Both are
available in $\GBC$. Append these labels after $P$, and then append
the $n$ labels of $F$ in any order. The resulting well-order belongs
to the cylinder, and its maximal finite terminal tail is exactly $F$.
\end{proof}

These arguments are parameterwise constructions of individual classes.
They do not assert that the collection of all orders, or its quotient,
is an internal class whose elements are classes.

\subsection{The external classification}

Let $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)$ be an externally countable two-sorted
model of $\GBC$. Write ${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ and
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ for the external sets of its admitted
set-like and arbitrary class well-orders of its internal surreal
carrier. Comparisons are those computed in $\mathcal M$.

\begin{theorem}[Countable-model factorial-shuffle theorem]
\label{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}
If $\mathcal M$ is $\omega$-standard, then, externally,
\[
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}
 \ \cong\ \sigma\bigl(\{1,2,6,24,120,\ldots\}\bigr)
 =\sigma\bigl(\{n!:n\in\omega\}\bigr).
\]
Its finite-condensation quotient is a copy of $\mathbb Q$, and each
factorial block size occurs densely in that quotient. In particular,
the pure external order type is independent of the particular countable
$\omega$-standard model and its admitted collection of classes.

For every externally countable model of $\GBC$, even without
$\omega$-standardness,
\[
 {\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}\cong\mathbb Q.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Internal linearity gives an actual external linear order on each
admitted collection. The collections are countable because the entire
class sort is externally countable. Internal nonemptiness and
variation of the first surreal label make them infinite and give no
endpoints.

In an $\omega$-standard model, the number $n(R)$ of
\Cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence} is a standard natural number.
Its $n(R)!$-element permutation cylinder is therefore genuinely
externally finite. \Cref{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks} identifies
all external finite-condensation blocks. Its converse is also external:
an external finite interval is a standard finite chain of adjacent
steps, and adjacency has its literal external meaning because the
class sort ranges over precisely the admitted orders.

The quotient is countable, has no endpoints, and is dense by
\Cref{swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail}. The same lemma makes every block-size
colour dense. The countable colour-preserving back-and-forth identifies
it with the densely coloured rational order used in the definition of
the shuffle. Each finite block is a rigid chain, so this quotient
isomorphism lifts uniquely within each block to the claimed order
isomorphism.

For the set-like orders, their internal lexicographic order is dense:
at the first unequal ordinal position, the common prefix is a set;
choose an unused surreal strictly between the next two labels and
complete the prefix to a global enumeration. The surreal cut-filling
property permits avoidance of the set of used labels. There are no
endpoints by varying the first label. Thus its external order is a
countable dense linear order without endpoints, hence isomorphic to
$\mathbb Q$. This part does not use $\omega$-standardness.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[An explicit computable presentation]\label{swo:sh:n16.7}
For $q\in\mathbb Q$, let $d(q)>0$ be its denominator in lowest terms,
and set $c(q)=(1+v_2(d(q)))!$. Then the lexicographically ordered set
\[
 \bigl\{(q,i):q\in\mathbb Q,\ 0\leq i<c(q)\bigr\}
\]
is an explicit computable copy of the factorial shuffle. For each fixed
$k\geq0$, reduced rationals with denominator of $2$-adic valuation $k$
are dense: choose a sufficiently large odd denominator factor and an
odd numerator inside the desired interval. Cancelling common odd
factors does not change that valuation. This computable presentation
does not supply a computable decoder for the model's class relations.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The hypothesis cannot simply be dropped]\label{swo:sh:n16.8}
If $\mathcal M$ is $\omega$-nonstandard, choose a nonstandard
$N\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$ and append an internally $N$-element tail
to a global well-order without a last element. The corresponding
internal $N!$-element permutation cylinder is externally an infinite
discrete interval with endpoints. Starting at its first element and
taking the immediate successor any standard finite number of times
produces infinitely many points in one external finite-condensation
block. Consequently the external blocks need not be finite, and the
displayed factorial-shuffle classification fails. The proof requires
standardness of $\omega$, not external well-foundedness of every
admitted class relation; no $\beta$-model assumption is needed.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[External embeddings and intrinsic automorphism orbits]\label{swo:sh:n16.9}
In an externally countable $\omega$-standard model, the unrestricted
order is not externally isomorphic to its set-like suborder: it has
adjacent pairs. Nevertheless it externally embeds into that suborder,
since every countable linear order embeds into $\mathbb Q$.

The automorphism group of the unrestricted external order is the
automorphism group of the rational quotient coloured by factorial
block size. Its point orbits are indexed by a factorial block size
and a position within that block.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Only the automorphism assertion needs comment. Finite-distance blocks
and their sizes are preserved by every order automorphism. Every
colour-preserving quotient automorphism lifts uniquely because finite
chains are rigid. Conversely, the colour-preserving back-and-forth is
transitive on the quotient points of each fixed colour. Hence two
points lie in the same orbit exactly when their block sizes and
within-block positions agree.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Set-likeness is not definable from the external order]
\label{swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable}
In the countable $\omega$-standard setting, the distinguished subset
${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ is not first-order definable, even with a
finite tuple of parameters, in the pure linear order
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set-like orders have no last element and hence lie in singleton blocks.
Orders of type $\Ord+1$ also lie in singleton blocks, since their
maximal finite terminal tail has size one, but they are not set-like.
The preceding automorphism description can exchange any two
singleton-block points.

To allow finitely many parameters, take a surreal label smaller than
the first labels of all the parameter orders. There are both a
set-like order and an order of type $\Ord+1$ starting with that label.
They lie below all the parameters and occupy singleton blocks. A
colour-preserving quotient back-and-forth sends one to the other while
fixing each parameter block, and its lift fixes the parameter points.
No formula with those parameters can distinguish the two points.
\end{proof}

The natural inclusion of ${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ in
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ is not dense. For example, fix a proper
class prefix of type $\Ord$ leaving three labels, and vary the final
three labels. The resulting six-point cylinder has a nonempty open
interval containing no set-like order. More substantially, leaving an
infinite set of labels gives whole intervals between different
finite-condensation blocks that contain no set-like order. Thus the
pure order classification does not classify the expanded pair
$({\Hall}^{\mathcal M},{\Hsl}^{\mathcal M})$, or the external
evaluation relation connecting these orders to their surreal labels.
Those richer structures remain appropriate further research targets.

\begin{note}[\merge; relation to sources~13 and~17 and to Part~V]\label{swo:ix:note:countable}
The second clause of \cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}
($\Hsl\cong\mathbb Q$ externally in every externally countable model) is
source~13's \cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}, with the same proof; source~11
already observed, after \cref{swo:thm:km-nonembedding}, that in such a model
the external set-like order can admit an external copy of the unrestricted
order, which source~18's \cref{swo:sh:n16.9} makes precise.
\Cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence,swo:sh:lem:adjacency-finite-residual,swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks}
are a second proof of source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation}. New in this
section are the factorial-shuffle classification of the full order in
countable $\omega$-standard models, its computable presentation, the failure
without $\omega$-standardness, the description of the automorphism orbits,
and the non-definability of set-likeness in the pure order
(\cref{swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable}).
\end{note}

\subsection{Source 13: a formalization plan tied to the inspected Lean code}\label{swo:fs:sec:lean}

\subsubsection{What already exists at the pinned snapshot}

The inspected source
\code{Surreal/Foundations/SignSequence.lean} defines
\cite{ProveItSigns}:
\begin{lstlisting}
structure SignSequence : Type (u + 1) where
  birthday : Ordinal.{u}
  signAt : Ordinal.{u} -> SignType
  signAt_ne_zero_iff :
    forall i, signAt i != 0 <-> i < birthday
\end{lstlisting}
This display is an ASCII schematic rendering of the actual declaration,
not a new compiled Lean file. The source uses Lean's native logical
notation. Its numerical linear order is lifted from the lexicographic
order of zero-extended sign functions.

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.43\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.49\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Inspected declaration & Role in this development\\
\midrule\endhead
\code{SignSequence.lt\_iff} & First-disagreement characterization of
numerical comparison.\\[4pt]
\code{ordinalOrderEmbedding} & The all-plus embedding of the ordinal
carrier into the sign carrier.\\[4pt]
\code{birthdays\_bounded} & A strict birthday bound for a family with
an explicit lower-universe smallness instance.\\[4pt]
\code{not\_small} & The whole sign carrier is not small in the
universe indexing its birthdays.\\[4pt]
\code{small\_bounded} & Each fixed birthday-bounded fragment is small
relative to that lower universe.\\[4pt]
\code{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt} & A separator of
exactly a prescribed birthday above all option birthdays; the fresh
separator lemma's direct input.\\[4pt]
\code{small\_cut\_fillers} & The constructed carrier realizes every
small strict cut.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The last two are in \code{SignSequenceCut.lean}
\cite{ProveItCutFill}. They are not merely postulated field axioms: the
inspected source constructs them from fixed-length Boolean
lexicographic words. We inspected the files, not a fresh build of the
project. No theorem in this manuscript is thereby automatically a
kernel-checked theorem.

\subsubsection{Relative smallness must stay visible}

\code{SignSequence.\{u\}} and \code{Ordinal.\{u\}} both live in
\code{Type (u + 1)}, while bounded sign sequences and initial segments
are small relative to \code{u}. A \code{Set SignSequence} is merely
a predicate on the larger carrier. It need not be an admissible small
family of options. The formal counterpart of ``set cut'' therefore
requires an index type with \code{Small.\{u\}}, not just the word
\code{Set} in a declaration.

The same applies to supports and prefix lengths. A support that is a
predicate on a larger type is not automatically a small support.
A code should carry a small graph or an explicit smallness proof.
Otherwise the completion bound, the dense-core distinction, and the
diagonal interpretation can silently change meaning.

A universe-relative approach may take a baseline equivalence
\[
                 b:\code{Ordinal.\{u\}}\simeq
                            \code{SignSequence.\{u\}}
\]
as an explicit parameter. Its existence is not inferred merely because
the types occupy the same universe. A formal project must either
construct the required equivalence, with the intended small-initial-
segment properties, or retain it as a stated assumption.

\subsubsection{Suggested modules and their proof obligations}

The following names are proposals, not claims about existing files.

\paragraph{Exhaustive orders and finite predicates.}
A first module should define exhaustive ordinal enumerations on a
small carrier, prove prefix-freeness, and compare the relation-based
and enumeration-based first-disagreement definitions. These proofs do
not require surreal arithmetic or class theory. The finite checker
included here provides examples, not a substitute for this module.

\paragraph{Prefix codes and completion.}
Represent a moved-point graph canonically and prove evaluation
injective on codes. Prove the complement-cardinality extension lemma
before using any prefix-completion operation. Formulate cylinders by
restriction equality and prove convexity and same-level disjointness.

\paragraph{Small-family interpolation.}
Use an explicit small index type for the two families. Establish a
bound on cross first-disagreement coordinates, then implement the
active-row invariant with a set-sized history. The stopping lemma,
not a generic unbounded recursion tactic, is the critical finite-
length formal obligation at this stage.

\paragraph{Cut traces and failure.}
Define crossing by two existential code witnesses. Same-level
uniqueness and restriction coherence are purely order-theoretic.
Under all-level existence, reconstruct the value at $\alpha$ from the
unique prefix of length $\alpha+1$. Prove trace equality with the
no-greatest-lower normalization stated explicitly. For first failure,
split successor from limit ordinals and prove the boundary formula
rather than assuming that crossing commutes with limit intersection.

\paragraph{Products and recoding.}
First formalize \Cref{swo:fs:lem:split} for ordinary set types and
an order-dense subset. It has no class-theoretic ambiguity and should
be a small, reusable result. The uniform complement-map interface
then supports prefix insertion and finite-block automorphisms. The
$\KM$ inverse evaluator belongs in a model or syntax layer, not in an
unqualified theorem about arbitrary Lean functions on a larger type.

\paragraph{Central words.}
Represent termination by an option type or by a reserved symbol with
an explicit proof that it is not a letter. For injective words,
retain injectivity as an invariant when selecting the shared next
letter. The explicit sign-block embedding can be formalized
independently of the class back-and-forth isomorphism.

\subsubsection{Three complementary formalization routes}

The \emph{cutoff-first route} proves the fixed-set and density-bound
lemmas inside ordinary types. It requires the least foundational
infrastructure and makes cardinal hypotheses explicit.

The \emph{universe-relative route} abstracts a large ordered carrier
with a lower-universe small-cut operation, a set-like enumeration,
and support codes. It can certify the local combinatorics and many
of the new constructions relative to those interfaces. It should not
be described as a proof of every $\GBC$ or $\KM$ metatheorem merely
because it uses two universes.

The \emph{deep model route} formalizes a two-sorted class theory or a
specified model $(M,\mathcal C)$. This is the route for the exact
comprehension schema, the external countable contrast, and the
full-model interpretation. Taking all predicates on an arbitrary
carrier as ``classes'' does not by itself establish the intended
replacement or universe axioms; the model assumptions must be proved
or supplied.

\subsubsection{Verification boundary}

A completed formalization should pin both the repository revision and
its dependency revisions, compile the new modules, and audit theorem
axioms and unfinished proofs. None of those actions is claimed here.
The deliverable is a proof manuscript, a reproducible LaTeX build, and
finite consistency checks. Existing Lean inputs are identified by
actual declarations and source hashes in the audit appendix, so that
a future formalization has concrete starting points.

\subsection{Source 14: a realistic formalization plan}
\label{swo:tc:sec:formal}
The new proofs admit a modular formalization in which most of the work
is ordinary order theory. A full class-theoretic metamodel should not
be the first dependency. The finite checks shipped with this article
are useful regression tests, but do not discharge any infinite or
class-level theorem.

\subsubsection{A generic set-level kernel}
Start with a type $X$ carrying a linear order and a chosen ordinal or
well-ordered index type. An exhaustive presentation is a bijection from
that index type to $X$. For arbitrary well-order types on one fixed
carrier, relations are often easier than a dependent sum over every
ordinal: a relation together with linearity and well-foundedness proofs
is already a set-sized object at the carrier's type level.

Prove the labelled common-prefix comparison before importing surreal
arithmetic. Its main obligations are initiality, agreement of the
restricted relations, existence and inequality of the two next labels,
and transitivity via nested initial segments. For fixed-domain words,
prove the equivalent least-disagreement formulation. Finite relation
matrices and permutation words give independently checkable examples.

A second module handles partial-injection extension. Its specification
must retain \emph{agreement on a prescribed prefix} and the
\emph{support cardinality bound}; bare existence of an extension is not
enough for the compression theorem. The finite case and the infinite
buffer case should be separate lemmas, since equality of infinite
cardinalities of domain and range alone does not imply equality of their
complement cardinalities.

\subsubsection{An abstract saturated alphabet interface}
The core theory needs an ordered alphabet with set-cut filling and fresh
separators, a global baseline in the class version, and set-prefix
completion. Numerical surreal field operations are not required.
A bounded preliminary development may use a regular-cardinal saturated
set order and prefix lengths below that cardinal, with all relevant
smallness hypotheses explicit. It proves the crossing-chain and bounded
versions of the trichotomy without formalizing surreal addition.

For actual sign sequences, the pinned repository already supplies
simplicity lemmas. The inspected declaration
\texttt{existsUnique\_simplest\_separator} requires a proof that a
separator exists. The appropriate architecture imports an independent
small-cut existence theorem and then applies this uniqueness result;
it does not erase the hypothesis to manufacture saturation.
\merge\ The pinned tree already has this architecture: \texttt{small\_cut\_fillers}
in \path{SignSequenceCut.lean} proves that small cuts have fillers, and
\texttt{cut} in \path{SignSequenceCutOperation.lean} is defined from
\texttt{existsUnique\_simplest\_separator} applied to it
(\cref{swo:sec:formal}; the same remark in source~14's audit section,
\cref{swo:tc:sec:foundations}).

\subsubsection{Proposed modules and theorem dependencies}
\begin{longtable}{@{}p{.26\textwidth}p{.64\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Principal obligations\\\midrule\endhead
\texttt{LabelledCommonPrefix} & Initiality, next labels, lexical linearity;
comparison with ordinal enumerations.\\
\texttt{SupportExtension} & Finite extension; infinite buffer; preservation
of fixed positions; cardinal bounds.\\
\texttt{CoreCylinders} & Canonical support codes, prefix completion,
convex cylinders, ordered children.\\
\texttt{CrossingPrefixes} & Elementary crossing predicate; chain and
uniqueness by length; union graph.\\
\texttt{CutTrichotomy} & Unbounded branch; bounded limit edge; terminal
numerical gap; uniqueness.\\
\texttt{ExhaustiveTrace} & Coherence and coverage; graph reconstruction;
trace injectivity.\\
\texttt{SupportSaturation} & Support compression; union bound at
$\cf\kappa$; sharp forced-prefix configuration.\\
\texttt{RawTraceFibers} & Canonical set-like initial branch; tail
concatenation; equality and convexity of trace fibers.\\
\texttt{ClassRealizations} & Same-set structures and elementary
absoluteness with old parameters.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
These are proposed modules, not files claimed to exist or compile.
A dependency path is
\[
 \text{completion}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{cylinders}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{crossing chain}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{trichotomy}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{recognition}.
\]
Support compression can instead import the predecessor's verified-in-writing
core interpolation theorem while that path is being formalized. The
character theorem and support threshold then provide two largely
independent audits of the prefix machinery.

\subsubsection{Class-level interfaces and avoiding a hidden third sort}
A formal metatheory of $\GBC$ can express cuts and enumerations as class
variables and use elementary comprehension explicitly. An alternative
is to formalize the external inaccessible model, where all relevant
collections are sets in a larger type universe. These routes have
different assumptions and should not be conflated.

The central reconstruction specification can be written schematically as
\begin{lstlisting}
Crosses(D, p) :=
  exists a b, InCylinder(a,p) and InCylinder(b,p)
              and D(a) and not D(b)

RecoveredGraph(D, alpha, x) :=
  exists p, Crosses(D,p) and alpha in domain(p) and p(alpha)=x

Coherent(D) := forall alpha, exists p,
  domain(p)=alpha and Crosses(D,p)

Covers(D) := forall x, exists p, Crosses(D,p) and x in range(p)
\end{lstlisting}
This is logical pseudocode, not Lean syntax and not compiled code.
Its purpose is to display the quantifiers: $a,b,p,\alpha,x$ are set
objects. No line chooses a class as an element of a class family.
The proof of functionality precedes any use of the recovered graph as
a function, and the coverage theorem is a separate proof of surjectivity.

\subsubsection{What must be checked before a kernel-verification claim}
A completed formalization must pin its Lean and Mathlib revisions, compile
all files, expose any axioms beyond the chosen foundations, and connect
the generic ordered alphabet to the actual surreal carrier. It must
also verify that internal ordinals, universe lifts, and prefix domains
match the statements. None of those steps has been completed for the new
theorems in this package; the package contains conventional written
proofs and executable finite diagnostics only.

\subsection{Source 15: a concrete Lean architecture}

The inspected ProveIt declaration is
\[
 \texttt{SignSequence.\{u\} : Type (u+1)}.
\]
Its birthday belongs to $\texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}}$. The file provides
\path{ordinalOrderEmbedding}, \path{birthdays_bounded},
\path{small_bounded}, \path{not_small}, and a well-founded
simplicity relation, among other declarations \cite{ProveItSigns}.
The essential statement is relative smallness: the entire sign carrier is
not $u$-small, even though it is a legitimate type one universe higher.
The official Lean universe rules support this distinction
\cite{LeanUniverses}. This article has inspected those declarations but
has not rebuilt the repository or certified any new theorem in Lean.

A practical development should use the following dependencies.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Generic set layer.} Define exhaustive ordinal enumerations
of an arbitrary linearly ordered carrier; prove prefix-freeness,
first-difference comparison, pair orientation, and the successor-cardinal
obstruction. Surreal arithmetic is unnecessary.
\item \textbf{Bounded surreal layer.} Reuse sign order and birthdays.
Formalize the $00/11$ code with terminal $01$, ordinal concatenation,
the max-coordinate scheduler, and the three coding-length cases.
Track ordinal products explicitly instead of replacing them by cardinalities.
\item \textbf{Relative-smallness layer.} For a relation on a higher-universe
carrier, express the assertion that an interval or predecessor type is
$u$-small. Implement the least-representative condensation and its rank
map. This models the chosen set/class boundary without a type of all types.
\item \textbf{Prefix and cut layer.} Define one uniform evaluation relation
on small support codes. State crossing using quantification over small
prefixes and codes, and reconstruct a persistent branch. Quantify over
the cut as a parameter at the permitted universe level.
\item \textbf{Model layer.} To claim a theorem about GB, GBC, or KM itself,
formalize a model or an axiomatic interface for that theory. Universe
polymorphism alone is not a proof that a chosen type-theoretic encoding
satisfies precisely those set-theoretic axioms.
\end{enumerate}

Each layer should record its universe parameters, smallness assumptions,
choice use, and available recursion principle. A relation on the entire
higher-universe sign type with ordinary Lean well-foundedness may encode
external well-foundedness stronger than a Henkin model's internal class
condition. These should be separate definitions, linked only by proved
translation theorems.

\subsubsection{Inspected primitives and actual status}

\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/}; the pinned sources
are recorded in the bibliography \cite{ProveItSigns,ProveItCutFill,ProveItCuts,ProveItSize}.
No Lean build was performed for this article, and no proposed module name
below should be read as an existing theorem declaration.

\subsubsection{Two formalization routes}

The most economical first route is ordinary type-theoretic order theory.
Use a bounded birthday carrier known to be small, transport it with
\code{Shrink} if convenient, and prove the set-alphabet theorems. Store
the numerical label order separately from the well-order being encoded.
A proposed \code{WellOrderOn X} can store the binary relation, strict
linearity, and \code{WellFounded} evidence; an enumeration stores an
ordinal domain with a bijection to $X$. Prove the relation/enumeration
correspondence, prefix-incomparability, and first-disagreement comparison
before taking any quotient. Quotienting first by abstract isomorphism
would destroy the required labels.

The second route explicitly formalizes a model of class theory. Introduce
separate carriers of set and admitted-class codes, membership, formula
semantics, and internally admitted family relations. State elementary
comprehension, replacement, and any GC or ETR assumptions at that level.
This route is appropriate for exact axiom-strength claims and Henkin
models. It is heavier than proving the bounded combinatorial theorems, but
it prevents an accidental use of all ambient predicates as internal classes.

\subsubsection{Universe levels and logical levels are different}

ProveIt's actual carrier is
\[
 \code{SignSequence.\{u\}}:\code{Type (u + 1)},
 \qquad \code{birthday}:\code{Ordinal.\{u\}}.
\]
Its small-cut interfaces explicitly require \code{Small.\{u\}} for the
index families. A bounded birthday subtype is small at that level, while
the full sign carrier is not.

One must not say that every power set automatically forces the next
syntactic Lean universe. If $S:\code{Type (u + 1)}$, then both
\code{Set S} and \code{S -> S -> Prop} also inhabit
\code{Type (u + 1)}. Being well-typed does not make them
\code{u}-small, nor does it identify them with the class collection of
an internal GBC model. Native quantification over all such predicates
is an ambient full-type interpretation. Likewise, native
\code{WellFounded R} asserts ambient well-foundedness, which is not
automatically a model's internal assertion
\cite{LeanUniverses,MathlibSet,MathlibOrdinal}.

For a direct universe-relative global development, keep a baseline
$b:\Ord^{u}\simeq\No^{u}$ as an explicit parameter until its existence
is separately established. Encode supported permutations by genuinely
small data, and represent families of their evaluated graphs uniformly.
This gives meaningful theorems without pretending that every ambient
type is an internal set or every function on class predicates is a
same-level class function.

\subsubsection{Suggested milestones}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Finite and set-alphabet layer.} Formalize first disagreement,
prefix convexity, pair coding, and the stabilization bound. This isolates
the ordinal-spectrum theorem from all surreal-specific facts.
\item \textbf{Topological layer.} Formalize the no-cross-fiber-jump lemma,
prefix families meeting every open set, and disjoint finite-tail
cylinders. Then prove the countable incompleteness construction and the
regular-stage gap spectrum.
\item \textbf{Small-support layer.} Formalize normalization, completion
of a small prefix, and the bounded common-prefix interpolation search.
Reuse the existing small-cut separator rather than postulating a new
unrestricted cut operation.
\item \textbf{Cut recognition.} Define straddling on set codes, prove
uniqueness and coherence at each length, and implement the direct
formula \eqref{swo:ds:eq:recognitionformula}. Only then package the exhaustive
branch criterion and first-failure classification.
\item \textbf{Class semantics layer.} In an explicit model interface,
formalize set-interval equivalence, least representatives, local rank,
and the terminal set. These are elementary constructions; a general
class-recursion engine is unnecessary for them.
\item \textbf{Higher comprehension.} State the inverse evaluator with
its exact syntactic complexity before invoking a comprehension axiom.
Prove the elementary diagonal theorem independently, and use it as the
final contradiction in the nonembedding theorem.
\end{enumerate}

These milestones deliberately separate ordinary mathematics about a large
type from metatheorems about a two-sorted model. No new consistency axiom
is needed for the bounded results, and the inaccessible model is an
optional explicit interpretation rather than a prerequisite for the
whole subject.

\subsection{Source 17: formalization routes and a practical verification plan}
\label{swo:gs:sec:formalization}

\subsubsection{Start with the alphabet interface, not surreal arithmetic}
The new set-sized results depend on a small interface. A formal development
can begin with a linear order $X$ of infinite cardinality $\mu$, with
$\mu$ elements in every nonempty open interval and ray. It should record
its ray and point character $r$ and the gap spectra of deletions of fewer
than $\mu$ elements. Prefix completion, clopen cylinders, divergence
bounds, the cut trichotomy, and fusion can then be proved abstractly.
The birthday sign alphabet is one implementation of this interface.
This organization prevents arithmetic lemmas about surreal addition or
multiplication from obscuring a proof that uses only order and signs.

The exact gap theorem has four independently testable mathematical
interfaces: a gap is a two-sided partition without endpoints; a
straddling prefix is a set witness; the first stopping stage is a
successor, a proper limit, or full length; and each resulting character
is computed separately. Separating them makes it difficult to accidentally
substitute point character $q$ for cylinder character $r$.

The support theorem is another independent target. Its statement needs
only a set partial injection, the necessarily moved domain and range,
cardinal addition, and a complement bijection. No surreal construction
appears until the final composition with a baseline.

\subsubsection{Proposed modules and proof obligations}
The following names describe a proposed architecture, not files claimed
to exist in the repository or in this package.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.37\textwidth}Y@{}}\toprule
Proposed module & Principal obligation\\\midrule
\path{WellOrders/CommonPrefix.lean} & Elementary predecessor formula,
maximality, first residual labels, transitivity\\[3pt]
\path{WellOrders/PartialSupport.lean} & Mandatory support, deficiency
balance, exact reserve cardinal and extension\\[3pt]
\path{WellOrders/PrefixTopology.lean} & Completion, convex clopen cylinders,
point versus cylinder character, base cardinality\\[3pt]
\path{WellOrders/CutTrichotomy.lean} & Unique straddling path, first failure,
limit boundary, nonexhaustive branch\\[3pt]
\path{Surreal/CutoffGapSpectrum.lean} & Sign-path classification of alphabet
gaps and stability under small deletion\\[3pt]
\path{WellOrders/Fusion.lean} & Dense-open refinement with explicit coverage
of the alphabet\\[3pt]
\path{ClassOrders/BranchRecognition.lean} & A chosen model or size interface;
elementary reconstruction from unique set witnesses\\[3pt]
\path{ClassOrders/CoreAutomorphisms.lean} & Represented-cut preservation,
uniqueness of extension, nonextension witness\\\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

For the topology modules, one should formalize the definition of
cellularity as a supremum before claiming an exact cardinal value. A
supremum of disjoint-family sizes need not be attained. Likewise the gap
spectrum should not include point cuts of character $1$, and the
recognition module should not quietly switch between open and closed
principal lower cuts.

\subsubsection{Universe-relative type theory}
Lean's universes offer a practical way to keep a fixed smaller universe
separate from a larger carrier. A type, a type of relations on it, and a
universe of all smaller types must have their levels checked explicitly.
Function types do not automatically jump one level merely because they
represent a mathematically large collection: their levels are computed
from the domain and codomain. Universe polymorphism supplies a family of
declarations, not an internal type of all universes; and universe lifting
is explicit rather than an automatic cumulative coercion
\cite{LeanUniverses}.

For this project, choose a lower notion of ``small'' and an ordinal index
which well-orders the intended large carrier with small proper initial
segments. State the cut operation only for lower-small families. A
back-and-forth argument along an arbitrary choice well-order of the large
type is unsafe: its proper initial segments may be too large for the
assumed cut operation. The correct interface is the small-history property
used in the proof of \Cref{swo:gs:cor:core-isomorphism}.

A set-sized cutoff implementation avoids this difficulty entirely. Every
object is an ordinary type with explicit cardinal bounds, and a formal
proof can be instantiated at many cardinals. A universe-relative version
then transports the argument, without equating an ordinal type from one
universe with all ordinals from every universe.

\subsubsection{A deep model-theoretic alternative}
To study exactly which comprehension principles suffice, formalize a
specified two-sorted model $(M,\mathcal X)$ and its elementary
comprehension and replacement axioms. Each theorem about global rows is
then a theorem about admissible class relations of that model. This is
the most direct route for \Cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension} and for
questions comparing $\GBC$, $\ETR$, and $\KM$.

The two routes should not be conflated. A successful theorem about types
in a fixed universe does not, without an interpretation theorem, prove a
conservativity or axiomatic-strength statement about class theory.
Conversely, a GBC proof with explicit class variables is not automatically
a compiled theorem about the repository's current sign-sequence carrier.

\subsubsection{Verification boundary}
No Lean code accompanies this article and no kernel-verification claim is
made. The source's foundation modules were not rebuilt. A future
formalization should pin both the repository and Mathlib revisions,
compile the modules, reject unfinished proofs, and audit theorem axiom
dependencies. The companion Python checks test only finite mechanisms.
They cannot decide the existence of class maps, prove cardinal cofinality
formulas, or certify the infinite support obstruction.

\label{swo:sh:sec:formalization}

\subsubsection{What the inspected source actually provides}

\texttt{83befe707f2840c2b53e0606701d8a2b28598e47}.

\end{center}

The declaration $\texttt{SignSequence.\{u\}}$ living in
$\texttt{Type (u+1)}$ is crucial. It contains the surreals with
$u$-small birthdays; the theorem \texttt{not\_small} says that this
whole type is not itself $u$-small. The existence of a Lean type is
therefore not the same as being a set at the intended smaller size
level. Lean's universe hierarchy enforces these distinctions
\cite{LeanUniverses}. A Tarski--Grothendieck implementation is another
well-developed option; P\k{a}k and Kaliszyk's Mizar formalization
illustrates a concrete universe-based route \cite{PakKaliszyk}.

This article does not assert that the new spectrum, condensation, or
shuffle theorems are already formalized in these files. No Lean build
or complete imported-axiom audit was performed for this article.
Reading a proof file is not equivalent to running its elaborator and
kernel in the pinned environment.

\subsubsection{The first set-level modules}

The most reusable initial target is independent of surreal arithmetic.
Represent a labelled well-order by a relation on a fixed carrier and
its well-order proof, or by a bijection from an ordinal domain. Prove
the equivalence of these representations and the absence of proper
prefixes for exhaustive enumerations. Keep ``increasing by numerical
order'' as an extra predicate on words, not as part of the definition
of a well-order code.

The suggested sequence is:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Ordinal words.} First disagreement, concatenation,
prefix cones, alternative terminators, and the finite permutation
adjacency criterion.
\item \textbf{Set spectra.} Pair coding, eventual coordinate
stabilization, and the $\mu^+$ obstruction. The central induction is
on a regular successor cardinal, with the domain and range
cardinalities stated separately.
\item \textbf{Permutation topology.} Order topology, dense sets,
disjoint interval families, $Q_n(X)$, and the density/cellularity
transition. Include global endpoints in dense-set constructions for
arbitrary alphabets.
\item \textbf{Surreal cutoff interface.} Large sign cones, preservation
of cut characters after deleting fewer than $\mu$ labels, and
$\cf(2^{<\kappa})\ge\cf\kappa$.
\item \textbf{Cut classification.} Encode the chain of straddling
prefixes and prove its three cases. The multiplicity theorem then
uses explicit injections and the cardinalities of the prefix tree
and full branch set.
\end{enumerate}

This order gives a checkable sequence of finite dependency boundaries.
The proof of the gap spectrum depends only on order, ordinal words,
cardinal arithmetic, and the cutoff interface. It does not require
surreal addition, multiplication, or real closedness.

\subsubsection{The class-level modules}

There are two sensible implementations.

\emph{Semantic set/class models.} Define a first-order set universe
and a collection of admitted class predicates, with the GB axioms
made explicit. A class well-order is a relation in that collection
with the internal well-order property. Then prove the elementary
common-prefix theorem, set-interval decomposition, uniform branch
criterion, and factorial-block facts as statements about that model.
An external countability hypothesis subsequently gives the shuffle
classification. This route preserves the exact meaning of internal
set size and available classes.

\emph{Universe-relative carriers.} Fix the smallness level $u$, work
with a larger carrier type, and formulate set-likeness using
$u$-small predecessor types. Relations on that carrier live in an
appropriate larger universe. This is convenient for a concrete
containing-universe development, but theorems must say which subsets
are admitted and which smallness level ``set'' means. Merely forming
the type of all relations in the next universe does not identify it
with a particular GBC class realization.

In either route, give quotient blocks actual representatives. For
set-interval condensation use the least label of a block; for the
external finite-condensation quotient use the usual set quotient in
the ambient universe. Their types and their purposes differ.

\subsubsection{Suggested proof obligations and trust reporting}

For a mechanized milestone, require the following explicit outputs:
the precise theorem statement with universe levels; a compiling source
file against the pinned toolchain; an imported-axiom report; and a
short explanation of the semantic correspondence with the article.
Finite examples can test a comparator implementation, but they do
not verify the $\mu^+$ argument, Global Choice equivalence, or any
claim about proper classes. The current deliverable supplies
conventional proofs and source provenance, rather than presenting
finite computations as certificates for infinitary assertions.

well-order, followed by at most one final set block; every nonempty class
well-order occurs as the index, with any final set ordinal
(\cref{swo:ix:note:blocks}); explicit condensation histories of every class
length exist (\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:anyhistory}). In particular all the
subpredicates $\Ord\cdot\gamma+\alpha$ of \cref{swo:st:n14.4} are nonempty and
are recognized by their block profile. Open: the strength needed to iterate the
condensation of an arbitrary input uniformly (\cref{swo:cb:n13.3},
\cref{swo:ds:n16.7}, \cref{swo:sh:n19.5}), and, for \cref{swo:st:n14.4}, the
embedding and nonembedding theorems between those subpredicates and the
set-like order, of which only the full-model separation
$\WO_{\kappa+2}\not\emb\WO_\kappa$ (\cref{swo:ds:thm:externalnonembedding}) is
proved.
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.2}, weakest comprehension for the uniform
nonembedding}: answered in part. For transformations defined by formulas with
only set quantifiers, $\GBC$ with $\Sigma^1_1$ class comprehension suffices
(\cref{swo:ds:thm:sigma}); whether it is necessary, and whether $\GBC$ alone
suffices, is open (\cref{swo:ds:n16.6}). The question's bounded variant,
comparing density and cellularity of all well-orders of $\No_{<\kappa}$ with
the minimal stratum, is answered by \cref{swo:ds:thm:density} (Part~VI).
\item \emph{Source~08's question~7, full virtual lexicographic products}
(\cref{swo:sk:sec:research}): \textbf{answered} for the interpretations it
names. In $\GBC$, $\Hsl\cong\No\times_\lex\Hsl$ and every ordinary class-indexed
lexicographic sum of copies of $\Hsl$ embeds into $\Hsl$
(\cref{swo:fs:thm:absorption}); in the full inaccessible universe
$\Hsl\times_\lex2\not\emb\Hsl$, hence $\Hsl\times_\lex\Hsl\not\emb\Hsl$
(\cref{swo:fs:thm:fullsplit}); no fixed definable uniform embedding exists in
$\KM+\GC$ (\cref{swo:fs:thm:kmsplit}); in externally countable models
$\Hsl\times_\lex\Hsl\cong\Hsl$ externally (\cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}). The
negative half already followed from the proofs of
\cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding,swo:thm:km-nonembedding}
(\cref{swo:ix:note:products}). A finer absorption spectrum (source~13's
\cref{swo:fs:n15.6}) is open.
\item \emph{Source~12's \cref{swo:st:n14.7}, automorphisms and finite
condensation}: answered in part. The maximal finite components of the
unrestricted order are the $n!$ permutations of the maximal finite final
segment, and the condensed order is dense without endpoints
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation}, \cref{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks}); in every
countable $\omega$-standard model the full order is externally the factorial
shuffle and its automorphism orbits are known
(\cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}, \cref{swo:sh:n16.9}). The
internal classification of the condensed order (source~17's
\cref{swo:gs:n15.9}) is open.
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.8}, source~12's \cref{swo:st:n14.8} and
source~08's question~12, class realizations}: answered further. In addition to

model, so it records nothing about the class realization there, and

(\cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle,swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable});
among $\GBC$ realizations with the same sets, internal well-foundedness of a

structures with the set-like predicate or the label evaluation are open
(\cref{swo:sh:n19.7}).
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.4}, recovering prefix structure from the
bare order}: a further negative part. Set-likeness is not first-order
definable, even with finitely many parameters, from the pure order of all

(\cref{swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable}); within one class well-order
it is recognized by the number of blocks (source~15: $W$ is set-like exactly
when it has one block). With \cref{swo:viii:sec:status}~(c), the question's
negative half is settled; the positive question, which extra predicates
suffice, stays open.
\item \emph{Comprehension questions} (source~12's \cref{swo:st:n14.6},
source~09's direction~2, source~08's question~10): bear. The direct comparison,

\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.10}, source~09's direction~9 and

\part{Set-sized strata, topology and permutation groups}\label{swo:part:topology}

\merge\ (3 October 2026.) The first Part of the batch-83 addition, sources~19--30
(provenance in \cref{swo:b83:sub:batch83}, notation in

Part~VI (\cref{swo:part:strata}) determined the density, cellularity, point
characters and gap spectra of the set-sized strata and the coding lengths of the
types $\mu\cdot\gamma+n$; it left open the topology of these spaces beyond their

isomorphism type and homogeneity of the minimal slice (\cref{swo:vi:sec:status},
items~(b) and~(e)). Nine batch-83 sources continue exactly there. This Part prints
what they prove about set-sized enumeration orders as ordered and topological

of prefix completion:
\begin{itemize}
\item thick alphabets, prefix cylinders and the prefix topology, with the sources'
re-proofs of Parts~I and~VI as notes (\cref{swo:x:sec:prefix});
\item residual cylinders, the weight and the point characters of every fixed-length
stratum (source~22, \cref{swo:x:sec:weights});
\item the exact binary-cube spectrum of every fixed enumeration type, and its coding
sandwich (source~19, with source~30's independent route, \cref{swo:x:sec:tails});
\item three completions of the minimal slice: forward prefix completion (source~24),
the closure of the minimal stratum in the full order (source~21) and normal forms
for the Dedekind completion (source~19) (\cref{swo:x:sec:completion});
\item a generalized Baire model of the minimal slice at every regular size
(source~24, \cref{swo:x:sec:regular});
\item the countable cutoff, printed once from source~24, with the other six proofs
and source~21's homogeneity theorem (\cref{swo:x:sec:countable});
\item the countable strata of types $\omega+n$ (sources~29 and~30,
\cref{swo:x:sec:omegan});
\item singular cardinalities: continuity of the permutation operations, the exact
complete-metrizability classification, non-Borel boundaries and closed universality
(sources~24 and~26, \cref{swo:x:sec:singular});
\item maximality, self-normalization and the canonical group envelope of the

\Cref{swo:x:sec:status} records which questions of this report, of its batch-81

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 127-405
\subsection{Source 19: scope, sources, and the meaning of further study}
\label{swo:rs:sec:scope}

\merge\ Source~19's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Its $X_\kappa$ is
printed $\No_{<\kappa}$, its $r_\kappa$ is printed $\rho_\kappa$ (this report's
$r$ is $\cf\kappa$, \cref{swo:sub:notation81}), and its weighted lower and upper
lengths $R$, $U$ are printed $\varrho_{\mathrm{lo}}$, $\varrho_{\mathrm{up}}$, since $R$ names raw
class orders here (\cref{swo:b83:sub:notation83}).

The repository already establishes a substantial foundation for this
problem. Its merged surreal report \cite{swoAtPin} treats fixed set
alphabets, birthday cutoffs, set-length words, set-like global
enumerations, and arbitrary class well-orders. Its elementary
largest-common-labelled-prefix comparison is particularly useful: it
compares raw class relations directly, even when their common prefix is
a proper class. It therefore avoids any preliminary assignment of
``class ordinals.''

Three same-day continuation manuscripts \cite{swoSrc16,swoSrc15,swoSrc18} go further.%
\footnote{\merge\ These are sources~16, 15 and~18 of this report, printed in
Parts~VI--IX; source~19 read them as unplaced manuscripts and saw this report at
\code{d5bd4a67b}, with Parts~I--V only.} Among other things, they analyze bounded gap
characters, simultaneous decomposition into set-interval blocks,
representability of core cuts, fixed types with finite tails, and the
external order in countable $\omega$-standard models. These are treated
as prior work here. In particular, the exact identification of a
persistent cut fiber with a residual well-order space is a starting
point, not a new claim of this article.

The present continuation asks what those results leave unresolved.
The principal advances are a stronger analysis of infinite residual
types; completion formulas retaining the residual fibers; extension
criteria for automorphisms; the nonstandard countable-model case and a
common elementary theory; a full restriction-map theorem; and a normal
form for points in the bounded Dedekind completion. The last sections
explain how each result can be formalized without identifying objects
from different size levels.

Throughout, ``new'' means developed in this continuation relative to
the sources just identified. No claim of historical priority in the
literature is made. A proof supplied here is a conventional mathematical
proof. Existing Lean lemmas are named only when their source declarations
were inspected; no new Lean development is asserted.

\subsubsection{A precise historical connection}

The motivation from Kanovei and Shelah should be stated accurately.
Their construction \cite[\S2]{KanoveiShelah}%
\footnote{\merge\ Section~2 of the published paper; the index is defined in
Section~1, page~2, of the preprint, which the other sources and this report's
bibliography cite.} lexicographically orders
maps from the continuum cardinal into $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose
ranges are ultrafilters. The maps need not be injective. It is not,
literally, the set of all well-order relations on $\mathbb R$.
The relevant common mechanism is ordinal-indexed first-disagreement
comparison of labelled codes. Passing to surreal labels introduces
proper-class and representation questions absent from that set-sized
index construction.

\subsubsection{Notation and conventions}

For a linear order $X$ and an ordinal $\alpha$,
\[
 \WO_\alpha(X)=\{f:\alpha\longrightarrow X:f\text{ is bijective}\},
 \qquad
 \BB_\alpha=(\{0,1\}^\alpha,<_{\lex}).
\]
We write $L\emb M$ for an order embedding and $L\equim M$ for
embeddings in both directions. Equimorphism is weaker than
isomorphism. All sums, products, and inequalities between ordinal
indices are ordinal operations unless explicitly called cardinal.
Thus $\kappa\cdot\kappa$ and $\kappa$ have the same infinite
cardinality and different ordinal meanings.

For an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$, put
\[\tag{S19.1}\label{swo:rs:eq:parameters}
 \mu=|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa},\qquad
 \rho_\kappa=
 \begin{cases}
 \kappa\cdot\kappa,&\kappa\text{ singular and strong limit},\\
 \mu,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
A strong limit cardinal $\lambda$ satisfies $2^\rho<\lambda$ for
every cardinal $\rho<\lambda$. The exceptional ordinal $\rho_\kappa$
is the repository's singular birthday transition
(\cref{swo:st:thm:transition}).

We use $\GB$ for G\"odel--Bernays set theory with ZF in its set
sort and no choice assumption built into the notation. We use
$\GBC$ for $\GB$ with Global Choice. Purely set-sized results are
proved in ZFC. Results involving all admitted class relations as an
actual domain are stated externally over a specified set-sized
two-sorted model. This distinction is repeated wherever it affects
a theorem.

\subsubsection{The main conclusions at a glance}

The complete fixed-type cube spectrum is stated in
Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:thm:tail-cubes}. Divide the residual ordinal
into finitely many decreasing cardinal layers,
\[
 \alpha=\mu\gamma+\sum_{i<k}\lambda_i\eta_i+n,
 \qquad \mu>\lambda_0>\cdots>\lambda_{k-1},\quad n<\omega.
\]
Give a singular strong-limit layer weight $\lambda_i\cdot\lambda_i$
and every other residual layer weight $\lambda_i$, and add those
weighted lengths to $\rho_\kappa\gamma$ to obtain $\varrho_{\mathrm{lo}}$. Then
\[
 \BB_\theta\emb\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\kappa})
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \theta\le \varrho_{\mathrm{lo}}+\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor.
\]
When the explicitly computed coding upper bound agrees with $\varrho_{\mathrm{lo}}$,
the least binary coding length is
$\varrho_{\mathrm{lo}}+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil$. This agreement holds for every
enumeration type when $\mu\le\aleph_\omega$.

The global reconstruction theorem, Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction},
works externally over any set-sized GBC model. It replaces each cut of
the core by the completed interval of its admitted raw-order fiber,
or by one point when the fiber is empty. Retaining this decoration is
exactly what is needed to decide extension of core automorphisms
(Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:rf:thm:aut}). The at-most-two trace ambiguity for general
residual alphabets is isolated in Proposition~\ref{swo:rs:rf:prop:doubleton}.
Proposition~\ref{swo:rs:rf:prop:alphabetcriterion} characterizes its occurrence
by a set deletion exposing numerical initial and final segments of types
$\Ord$ and $\Ord^*$.

For externally countable models, Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types}
gives the two pure order types
\[
 \sigma(\{1,2,6,24,\ldots\})
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \sigma(\{1,2,6,24,\ldots\}\cup\{K\}),
 \qquad K=\omega+\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]
The second occurs in the $\omega$-nonstandard case. The two orders
are nonisomorphic but satisfy the same first-order sentences; indeed
the same complete theory arises from every externally set-sized GBC
model (Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:thm:cm-common-theory}).

Two more concrete conclusions are the exact restriction classification
(Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:ia:thm:restriction-classification}) and the first-cutoff
topology (Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:ia:thm:countable-topology}): its permutation
order is homeomorphic to Baire space and has real-line completion,
while omitting continuum many completion points in every interval.


\subsection{The interpretations that must be distinguished}
\label{swo:rs:sec:interpretations}

The ambiguity has several independent sources. One may fix a set of
surreal labels or use the entire proper class; fix an enumeration type
or vary it; keep labels or quotient by isomorphism; compare labels in
their numerical order or compare relation bits in a background schedule;
and regard a collection externally or attempt to represent it internally.
There are arbitrarily many artificial encodings, so no finite list can
exhaust every possible meaning. The following table covers the natural
mathematical interpretations and makes their differences explicit.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.23\textwidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Objects & Comparison and size\\
\midrule
Fixed set, fixed type & Bijections $\alpha\to X$, with $X\subset\No$ a set
& First unequal numerical labels; a set\\
Fixed set, all types & All well-orders of the same $X$
& Compare their unique ordinal enumerations; a set\\
Variable set support & Injective ordinal-length surreal words
& Must specify proper-prefix rule; a class of sets\\
Induced numerical well-orders & Increasing ordinal-length words, or subsets
well-ordered by the numerical order & A special family of labelled words;
termination still matters\\
Set-like global orders & Class well-orders of all $\No$ with set predecessors
& Equivalent in GBC to bijections $\Ord\to\No$; predicate on classes\\
Fixed class index & Exhaustive enumerations indexed by a specified class
well-order $J$ & Comparisons depend on $J$; may go beyond $\Ord$\\
All global orders & Arbitrary class well-orders of the entire carrier
& Common labelled initial segment; predicate on classes\\
Unlabelled order types & Well-orders modulo order isomorphism
& Set case reduces to ordinals; label lexicography does not descend\\
Rank or relation codes & Inverse rank functions, or characteristic functions
of order relations & A different lexicographic order, dependent on a
background coordinate well-order\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{The numerical order is not a global well-order}

The surreal line is densely ordered and has no endpoints. It contains
descending sequences such as $0,-1,-2,\ldots$. Consequently the phrase
``a well-order of the surreal numbers'' cannot mean the numerical
ordering of the whole class. It means an additional relation imposed on
the labels, or a restriction to a numerically well-ordered subclass.
Every set ordinal embeds numerically into $\No$, but $\No$ itself
is not an ordinal.

For set-supported numerical well-orders, each subset has exactly one
increasing enumeration. Allowing different well-orders of the same subset
gives many distinct words, one unique ordinal enumeration per relation.
A prefix such as $\langle 2,-1\rangle$ is a valid
injective well-order code and cannot be an increasing numerical code.

For a proper subclass, even numerical well-ordering need not be set-like.
For instance,
\[
 a_\alpha=1-\frac1{\alpha+2}\quad(\alpha\in\Ord)
\]
is a strictly increasing proper-class sequence below $1$. Adjoining
$1$ yields a numerically well-ordered class of type $\Ord+1$;
the new last point has a proper class of predecessors. The arithmetic
is ordinary surreal field arithmetic, and $\alpha$ denotes its
ordinal surreal representative.

\subsubsection{What happens when labels are forgotten}

For a set $X$ of infinite size $\mu$, the isomorphism types of
well-orders of $X$ are exactly the ordinals $\alpha$ with
$\mu\le\alpha<\mu^+$. Their natural comparison is the ordinary
ordinal order. It has little to do with the lexicographic order of
their labelled representatives. Two different permutations of a fixed
ordinal type are isomorphic as well-orders while occurring in different
positions in the label order. In fact the isomorphism classes need not
be convex. On the natural-number labels,
\[
 R=(0,1,2,\ldots),\qquad
 S=(1,2,3,\ldots,0),\qquad
 T=(2,0,1,3,4,\ldots)
\]
satisfy $R<S<T$ and have types $\omega,\omega+1,\omega$.
Thus numerical lexicography does not induce an ordered quotient by
unlabelled order type.

For arbitrary class well-orders the situation is more delicate: the
existence of an isomorphism or comparison between two abstract class
orders is a separate class-theoretic problem. The elementary labelled
comparison below never requires that problem to be solved.

\subsubsection{Termination is part of the definition}

When supports vary, one word can properly extend another. The
shorter-first convention declares $p<p\cat q$ for nonempty $q$.
A centered convention introduces a termination token $\dagger$ and
compares it with the next actual label. With $0$ excluded from the
alphabet, one can use
\[
 \No_{<0}<\dagger<\No_{>0}.
\]
For increasing words this can reverse the comparison of a word with
one of its extensions: appending a negative allowed label places the
extension below its prefix, while a positive label places it above.

The previous continuations prove that arbitrary and injective centered
set-word orders are isomorphic to $\No$ in GBC, whereas increasing
words have additional limit-prefix obstructions \cite{swoSrc18}
(\merge\ printed in Part~VII:
\cref{swo:vii:sub:sh-centered,swo:vii:sec:centered}).
Under shorter-first comparison, arbitrary, injective, and increasing
words are mutually isomorphic as ordered prefix trees in GBC. Their
order is still not $\No$: if $p$ has nonzero limit length, its proper
prefixes have supremum $p$. A set of surreals in the full numerical
line has no least strict upper bound, by the set-cut property.

Keeping an actual zero and placing a distinct terminator immediately
below it creates adjacent increasing words
$p<p\cat\langle0\rangle$ when every entry of $p$ is negative.
Identifying a terminator with zero instead identifies distinct words
unless a quotient convention is imposed. These are actual mathematical
changes, not different notations for one order.

\subsubsection{Inverse ranks and relation-bit codes}

For a set carrier $X$, fix a well-order $j$ as a coordinate schedule. A well-order
$R$ of $X$ can be encoded by the ordinal rank of each label, and
these ranks can be compared in $j$-order. This inverse-rank comparison
need not agree with the comparison of the forward enumerations.
Alternatively, well-order the coordinate set $X\times X$ and compare
the bits $1_{xRy}$. The result is again a linear order on codes, but
it depends on the chosen pair schedule and on which bit is called
smaller. Such encodings remain useful for implementation, provided
their order is not silently identified with the numerical label order.

Ordinal-valued inverse ranks extend to set-like global well-orders,
but are not available for arbitrary proper-class predecessor segments.
Relation-bit coding remains available for supplied raw class orders
when a genuine class well-order scans the pair coordinates. The code
is then a class of bits. This changes none of the size boundaries: a
class code is not an element of the set universe.

\merge\ Source~20's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Its bounded-support core

The ProveIt report \cite{swoAtPin} already gives an extensive account of

The main advances concern information that is lost when a rich
enumeration structure is replaced by its underlying linear order.
They also explain which limiting procedures genuinely recover global
objects. The distinction is productive: the same family of bounded spaces
supports a directed system recovering a surreal-sized core and a coherent
restriction system recovering every admitted class well-order.
