The contributions are intentionally stated at their actual foundational
level. A theorem about a class of set codes is not automatically a theorem
about a collection whose individual members are proper classes. An
external classification of a countable model does not create an internal
enumeration of its class objects.

\subsection{The interpretations, separated}
\label{swo:lm:base:interpretations}

\subsubsection{The choices that determine the question}

A complete formulation specifies six things: the carrier, whether its
labels are retained, whether its given numerical order must be respected,
the allowed enumeration types, the comparison convention, and the
universe in which the collection is formed. Varying these choices produces
the following natural interpretations. There are infinitely many
artificial coding conventions; ``all interpretations'' here means an
account of these mathematically distinct choices, not an enumeration of
every possible arbitrary encoding.

\begin{longtable}{@{}P{0.22\textwidth}P{0.35\textwidth}P{0.35\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Object & Meaning of one point & Size and comparison\\
\midrule\endhead
$\WO(X)$ for a set $X\subseteq\No$ & An arbitrary labelled well-order
of the same carrier $X$ & A set; compare exhaustive ordinal enumerations\\[5pt]
$\WO_\alpha(X)$ & Such an order with specified ordinal type $\alpha$ &
A set stratum, nonempty exactly when $|\alpha|=|X|$\\[5pt]
Injective set words & A well-order of a variable set of surreal labels &
A proper class of sets; a rule for termination is necessary\\[5pt]
Numerically increasing set words & A set well-ordered by the numerical
surreal order & No arbitrary permutation of the chosen subset\\[5pt]
$\Hsl(\No)$ & A set-like well-order of the whole surreal class &
A predicate on classes; equivalently a bijection $\Ord\to\No$\\[5pt]
$\Hall(\No)$ & Any class well-order of the whole surreal class &
A predicate on classes; common prefixes may be proper classes\\[5pt]
Variable class domains & A class well-order on an arbitrary subclass of
$\No$ & A class-variable predicate; one whole order may be a proper prefix
of another\\[5pt]
Numerical class well-orders & A subclass well-ordered by the inherited
numerical order & Can have proper predecessor classes; not restricted to
set-like orders\\[5pt]
Isomorphism types & Labels are forgotten & Numerical lexicography does
not descend to the quotient\\[5pt]
Relation-table words & Membership bits of the order relation, scanned in
a fixed order of pairs & A valid different lexicographic comparison\\[5pt]
Objects of a smaller universe & All orders available in a specified
model or universe & Sets externally; the answer depends on the chosen
notion of ``available''\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\subsubsection{Fixed labels and forgotten labels}

For a set $X$ with its numerical order, a well-order has a unique
increasing enumeration relative to that well-order,
$e:\alpha\to X$. The word ``increasing'' here refers to the new well-order,
not to the numerical order used to compare the entries of two enumerations.
If two exhaustive enumerations of the same $X$ are distinct, neither is a
proper prefix of the other. Thus their first differing entries determine
their comparison without a termination rule.

Forgetting the labels changes the problem completely. On $\{0,1\}$ the
orders enumerated by $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ are isomorphic, yet the first is
lexicographically smaller. Consequently lexicography is not invariant
under arbitrary relabelling and gives no induced order on well-order
isomorphism types. If one instead orders set well-order types by their
ordinals, the resulting order is simply the usual ordinal order; that is
a different construction.

Nor does ``all well-orders'' mean that the lexicographic order itself is
a well-order. Even on an infinite fixed alphabet it contains descending
chains. Numerical negation of every label gives an order reversal between
the spaces for $X$ and $-X$; when $X=-X$, this is a self-duality of the
enumeration order.

\subsubsection{Inherited numerical well-orders}

The numerical order of $\No$ is not well-founded. For example, the negative
integers form a descending sequence. Its well-ordered subclasses are
therefore a restriction on the domain, not choices of a new order on the
entire domain.

They need not be set-like. For each ordinal $\alpha$, let $s_\alpha$ be
the surreal whose sign sequence has length $\alpha+1$, begins with a
minus sign, and has only plus signs afterward. These labels strictly
increase with $\alpha$ and remain below $0$. Their class followed by $0$
has numerical order type $\Ord+1$. The last point has a proper class of
predecessors. More generally, under Global Choice the universality of the
surreal line realizes every supplied class linear order as a numerical
suborder, so inherited numerical class well-orders realize all supplied
class well-order types as well. This is an existence statement, not a
canonical choice of a representative for every type.

\subsubsection{Variable domains and termination}

For set words, the usual dictionary convention puts a proper prefix
before every proper extension. This convention has an empty least word
and permits small cofinal sequences at limit-length words: the proper
prefixes of a word of length $\omega$ increase to that word. Hence this
word order is not isomorphic to the set-cut-saturated surreal line.

For a variable-domain order the carrier is part of the object; an empty
strict relation alone would not distinguish an empty domain from a
one-point domain. The same prefix-first convention works for variable
class domains. Use
the largest common labelled initial segment. If both remainders are
nonempty, compare their least labels numerically; if just one is empty,
put the exhausted order first. A proper-class order of type $\Ord$ can
then be a proper prefix of one of type $\Ord+1$. This possibility is absent
when both orders exhaust the same carrier. The elementary common-prefix
argument below proves transitivity in this variable-domain setting as
well, with an exhausted branch treated as a least terminator.

An alternative is to place a terminator at a numerical cut of the digit
alphabet. In particular, a terminator between the negative and positive
nonzero surreal digits behaves like the undefined sign in a surreal sign
sequence. The earlier continuation proves that arbitrary and injective
set words with this centered convention are isomorphic to $\No$ in
GBC, while increasing words retain a limit-prefix obstruction
\cite{swoSrc18} (\merge\ \cref{swo:vii:sub:sh-centered,swo:vii:sec:centered}). If the digit $0$ is also retained immediately
above a distinct terminator, the empty suffix and the suffix $(0)$ become
adjacent. Endpoint and gap conclusions therefore require the convention
to be stated.

Reversing the significance of coordinates introduces another issue.
Two infinite words need not have a last differing position, so a proposed
``compare the last difference'' rule is not a total order without a
support restriction. Comparing order types before labels also changes
the order: it is a type-priority sum of strata, rather than native
enumeration lexicography.

\subsubsection{The Kanovei--Shelah connection}

Kanovei and Shelah use a definable lexicographic order of maps
$a:\mathfrak c\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters;
repetitions are allowed. The entries are compared by their characteristic
functions. This is not the collection of all well-orders of the reals,
and their construction does not identify it with one of the orders above
\cite[\S1]{KanoveiShelah}. The shared idea is to retain many ordered
codes instead of selecting one privileged representative. Transferring
that idea to class-sized indices requires a separate account of uniformity
and support.


% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 143-433
\subsection{Source 21: the problem and the further results}\label{swo:fu:sec:introduction}

\merge\ Source~21's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Its $\mathcal T$ (macro
\verb|\Words|), the class of \emph{all} set-length words, is printed
$\WordsAll$; this report's $\Words$ is the injective class. Its internal labels
\code{gl:} stay under its own prefix (\code{swo:fu:gl:}) and are unrelated to
source~11's \code{swo:gl:}.

The surreal numbers supply an unusually effective testing ground for
lexicographic constructions. Their numerical order can interpolate every
set-sized strict cut, yet the collection of all surreals is a proper
class. Thus a finite or set-sized argument may remain perfectly valid
while an apparently harmless change from ``each'' to ``all'' crosses a
logical size boundary. The order of presentations introduces a second
source of complexity: labels, enumeration lengths, and terminal tails
can survive in a lexicographic order even when the presented well-orders
are abstractly isomorphic.

The pinned ProveIt treatment \cite{swoAtPin} is a substantial synthesis of
four earlier manuscripts. It proves general set-alphabet spectra,
surreal birthday-stage results, word codings, a direct comparison of
class well-orders, dense bounded-support cores, and size obstructions.
Its open-question list asks about prefix recovery, automorphisms,
noncardinal cutoffs, coherent embeddings, and changes of the class
realization. The present paper concentrates on these directions.%
\footnote{\merge\ Source~21 read this report at \code{109aaca15}, before
Parts~VI--VIII were written. Part~VIII has since answered the prefix-recovery,
automorphism and class-realization questions in part
(\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}); noncardinal cutoffs (\cref{swo:st:n14.2}) and
coherent embeddings (\cref{swo:st:n14.9}) were still open there, and
source~21's Sections~5 and~6 answer them in part (\cref{swo:b83:sec:qstatus}).}
Canonical block decompositions and represented-cut criteria also arose
in the preceding research; we include the versions needed for the
new arguments rather than treating every restatement as a new result.

The main conclusions are these.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{An exact obstruction to extending core automorphisms.}
The bare order of a surreal-sized dense core does not distinguish the
large cuts arising from exhaustive global enumerations, those arising
from nonexhaustive injective branches, and certain cuts arising from no
class well-order at all. An automorphism can interchange these kinds.
Consequently some core automorphisms admit no extension to an order
embedding from the set-like space into the full class-well-order space.
Preservation of exhaustive represented cuts is the exact criterion for
automorphism extension within the set-like space.
\item \textbf{A concrete failure of prefix recovery.}
For $P=\WO_\omega(\mathbb{Q})$, all nonempty open intervals and open rays have
order type $P$. Every finite increasing partial map extends to an
automorphism, but the family of positive-length prefix cylinders is not
preserved by all these automorphisms. No such cylinder is definable from
the pure order using finitely many parameters.
\item \textbf{A precise topology behind the countable example.}
The order topology of $P$ is its topology of finite agreement. It is
homeomorphic to $\omega^\omega$, but its order is not that of the
irrationals. There are continuum many missing cuts even inside each
prefix cylinder, caused both by numerical cuts and by failure to
enumerate every label.
\item \textbf{Fibers and closure for set-sized alphabets.}
Every well-order of an infinite $X$ starts with an injective word of
length $|X|$. Fixing this word leaves exactly the lexicographic order of
all well-orders of the unused labels. Under a natural large-interval
hypothesis, the closure of the minimum-length stratum consists of that
stratum together with the existing endpoints of these fibers.
\item \textbf{Further bounded and model-theoretic information.}
We compute basic invariants at noncardinal birthday cutoffs, construct
coherent embeddings over bounded chains of equal cardinality, and
separate standard finite permutation blocks from the externally infinite
blocks hidden in nonstandard models. The abstract countable set-like
order is always $\mathbb{Q}$, while the distinguished core retains information
that this bare order forgets.
\end{enumerate}

The conclusions are deliberately sensitive to interpretation. A dense
class isomorphic to $\No$ does not turn the entire family of class
enumerations into an ordinary class. A homeomorphism does not imply an
order isomorphism. An internally finite terminal block need not be
externally finite. These distinctions are mathematical content, not
merely precautions about notation.

\subsubsection{The relation to Kanovei--Shelah}

The motivating analogy should be stated accurately. In
Kanovei--Shelah's construction \cite[\S1]{KanoveiShelah}, the index set is
\[
 A=\{a:\mathfrak c\longrightarrow\mathcal P(\mathbb{N}):
                 \ran(a)\text{ is an ultrafilter on }\mathbb{N}\}.
\]
They order these maps by first disagreement, using the characteristic
function order on $\mathcal P(\mathbb{N})$. The maps can repeat values. This is
not literally the set of all well-orders of $\mathbb{R}$, and their resulting
index order is not itself a well-order. What carries over to our problem
is the usefulness of a linear order on a sufficiently rich family of
presentations. Their definable hyperreal construction is not a theorem
identifying any of the surreal spaces studied below.


\subsection{Interpretations and the logical size boundary}\label{swo:fu:sec:interpretations}

\subsubsection{Surreals as sign sequences}

We use the sign representation
\[
 \No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}.
\]
The union is class notation. Each individual sign sequence has a set
ordinal as its length, called its birthday $\bd(x)$. At the first place
where two sequences differ, termination is compared by
\[
 -\;<\;\text{undefined}\;<\;+.
\]
This is the numerical order of the surreals, not the rule that a shorter
word always comes first. The sign construction and its relation to the
simplicity tree are classical \cite{b83EhrlichTree,Gonshor}.

For an ordinal $\theta$ put
\[
 \No_{<\theta}
        =\{x:\bd(x)<\theta\}
\]
(source~21's $X_\theta$). This is a set. If $\kappa$ is an infinite initial ordinal, then
$|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}$, where
$2^{<\kappa}=\sup_{\lambda<\kappa}2^{|\lambda|}$.
Each set of surreals has bounded birthdays. Conversely, allowing all
birthdays produces a proper class, since the all-plus sign sequences
already give a copy of $\Ord$.

The cut property used in this paper is:
\[\tag{S21.1}\label{swo:fu:eq:smallcut}
 A,B\text{ sets},\quad A<B
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists x\in\No\ (A<x<B).
\]
Empty sides are allowed. This is often called the $\eta_{\Ord}$ property
or the absolute linear continuum property \cite{Ehrlich2012}. It does
not assert interpolation for arbitrary class-sized sides. For example,
there is no surreal greater than every ordinal.

\subsubsection{The main natural readings}

No finite list exhausts every artificial coding convention. The
following table covers the natural readings that change the mathematical
problem. Independent choices in different rows can also be combined.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}P{.23\textwidth}P{.37\textwidth}P{.34\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Reading & Objects being ordered & Size and principal distinction\\
\midrule\endhead
Fixed carrier & All well-order relations on a fixed set $X\subseteq\No$ &
A set $\WO(X)\subseteq\mathcal P(X^2)$; labels matter.\\[4pt]
Fixed enumeration type & Bijections $\alpha\to X$, where $|\alpha|=|X|$ &
A stratum $\WO_\alpha(X)$; different $\alpha$ need not have the same invariants.\\[4pt]
Varying set carrier & Well-orders of arbitrary set-sized subsets of $\No$ &
An ordinary class of set-coded objects; equivalent to injective set-length words after choosing a termination rule.\\[4pt]
Arbitrary words & Functions $\alpha\to\No$, possibly with repetitions &
An ordinary class; repetitions make these words different from well-order presentations of their ranges.\\[4pt]
Numerically increasing subsets & Sets or classes well-ordered by the inherited numerical $<$ &
An additional monotonicity restriction; an auxiliary well-order is no longer being chosen.\\[4pt]
Set-like global well-orders & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$, or their induced relations &
Each object is a class. Their totality is a predicate on classes, denoted $\Hsl(\No)$.\\[4pt]
Unrestricted global well-orders & Class well-order relations on all of $\No$, with possibly proper-class predecessor segments &
A predicate on classes, denoted $\Hall(\No)$; ordinal enumeration need not exist.\\[4pt]
Relation-table lexicography & Characteristic functions of well-order relations, read in a separately chosen order of $X^2$ &
A different order on the same relations; depends on the coordinate code.\\[4pt]
Unlabelled order types & Isomorphism classes of the preceding well-orders &
Numerical first disagreement does not descend to this quotient. For set well-orders, the usual comparison gives ordinals instead.\\[4pt]
Universe-relative collection & All well-orders of the surreals small in a fixed universe &
A larger-universe set or type; smallness must remain fixed throughout a theorem.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

\subsubsection{Set presentations and termination}

For a set $X$ with a fixed linear order $<$, a well-order relation $R$ on
$X$ has a unique increasing enumeration
$e_R:\alpha_R\to X$ in the order $R$. Here ``increasing'' refers to $R$,
not to the numerical order on $X$. For two different relations on the
same $X$, their enumerations cannot be proper extensions of one another:
the shorter enumeration would already have used all of $X$. Thus they
have a first disagreement, and
\[
 R<_{\lex}S
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 e_R(\delta)<e_S(\delta)
 \quad\text{at their first disagreement }\delta.
\]
No termination convention is needed in this fixed-carrier situation.

For varying carriers, a word can be a proper prefix of another. Three
different choices should be kept separate: shorter-first lexicography,
longer-first lexicography, and a termination symbol at a specified cut
of the alphabet. Shortlex, which first compares lengths and only then
uses lexicography, is another order altogether. The usual surreal sign
order uses a termination symbol between $-$ and $+$; that special
three-way convention should not be imported silently into words whose
letters are arbitrary surreals. The repository gives explicit
prefix-safe embeddings of set-length words into $\No$ and analyzes the
one-sided limit-word cuts \cite[Sections 9--11]{swoAtPin} (\merge\ Part~II,
\cref{swo:part:words}).

\begin{example}[The unlabelled quotient is incompatible with lexicography]\label{swo:fu:n2.1}
Let $X=\mathbb{Q}$. Choose minimum-length enumerations beginning with $0$ and
$2$, and an enumeration of type $\omega+1$ beginning with $1$. In
lexicographic order the third lies between the first two. The two outer
well-orders are isomorphic, while the middle well-order has a different
type. Therefore equality of abstract order type is not a convex
equivalence relation. There is no induced linear order on order types
obtained by comparing arbitrary representatives in numerical lexicography.
\end{example}

The inherited numerical order on all of $\No$ is not a well-order,
as the sequence $0,-1,-2,\ldots$ witnesses. Nevertheless, each set
ordinal occurs as the type of a numerically increasing subset of $\No$,
using ordinal surreals. The proper class $\Ord\subset\No$ is a
numerically well-ordered class. These facts concern one inherited order,
not the many auxiliary well-orders of the whole numerical line.

Under $\GBC$, every given class well-order has a numerical copy in
$\No$, by the class-order universality proved below. Such a copy need
not be set-like. For example, using surreal field operations,
\[
 \left\{-\frac{1}{\alpha+1}:\alpha\in\Ord\right\}\cup\{0\}
\]
has numerical type $\Ord+1$: the negative points increase with
$\alpha$, and the last point has a proper class of predecessors.

One can also fix a particular class well-order $J$ and compare class
bijections $J\to\No$ at the $J$-least disagreement. This is a legitimate
fixed-domain stratum, for example with $J=\Ord+2$. It does not supply
a common ordinal coordinate system for all possible class domains. The
labelled-relation comparison in \cref{swo:fu:gl:comparison} avoids that need.

Relation-table coding is different even on two labels. With
$0<1$, the word $(0,1)$ is lexicographically before $(1,0)$. But if the
first off-diagonal table coordinate is $(0,1)$ and $0<1$ is the bit
order, the first relation has bit $1$ and the second bit $0$, reversing
this comparison. At the class level a fixed enumeration of $\No^2$
similarly makes first-bit comparison legitimate, but it remains an
auxiliary-coordinate order. Its binary-class equimorphism result in
the repository does not identify it with the labelled-prefix order
\cite[Section 17]{swoAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:sk:prop:relationcode}).

\subsubsection{Sets, classes, and predicates on classes}

Our class theory convention is explicit. $\GB$ has the usual set and
class axioms with elementary class comprehension and class replacement,
but no choice principle by definition. $\GBC=\GB+\GC$, where global
choice includes a set-like global well-order of the set universe. Set-only
results are proved in $\ZFC$. The class constructions below use $\GBC$
unless a weaker hypothesis is stated.

In these theories classes contain sets, not proper classes. A class
relation $R\subseteq\No^2$ is a legitimate single class. The notation
``the class of all such $R$'' is not legitimate as an ordinary class.
Instead, write a formula $\mathrm{CWO}(R)$ with a class variable, and
write a formula $\mathrm{Lex}(R,S)$ for comparison. A theorem such as
\[
 \forall R,S\bigl(\mathrm{CWO}(R)\wedge\mathrm{CWO}(S)
          \longrightarrow\text{exactly one comparison holds}\bigr)
\]
is a second-order theorem. It requires no object having all those
classes as elements. We use the symbols $\Hsl$ and $\Hall$ as readable
shorthand for this predicate-level language.

An ordinary class family of global enumerations must have an explicit
uniform code, for instance a class $E\subseteq I\times\Ord\times\No$
whose sections $E_i$ are enumerations and whose indices $i$ are sets.
Quantifying over such a coded family is different from quantifying over
every externally conceivable family of classes. Every interpolation and
back-and-forth statement below respects this distinction.

\subsubsection{What stronger foundations do and do not provide}

$\KM$ permits class quantifiers in class comprehension. It still does
not make proper classes into elements of an ordinary class. A genuine
collection of all classes requires a third sort, a suitable hyperclass
theory, or a larger surrounding set universe. Higher-order comprehension
and choice principles then have to be stated for that additional level.
Global choice chooses sets from nonempty classes; it is not an unrestricted
choice principle for selecting one class from each family of classes.
This remains a real distinction even over $\KM$ \cite{ClassChoice2026}.

Likewise, an ordinal-stage construction does not automatically require
$\ETR$. If the state at each stage is a set and the previous stages form
a set, ordinary set-valued recursion suffices in $\GBC$. In contrast,
$\ETR_\Ord$ permits class-valued slices at each ordinal stage and is a
substantive strengthening \cite{GHHSW}. Our set-sized partial
isomorphisms and prefix reconstructions belong to the former situation.
We do not assert a uniform isomorphism-comparison theorem for arbitrary
unlabelled class well-orders from this observation.

The universe-relative alternative is equally precise. Fix a universe
$\mathcal U$ of small sets and form surreals whose birthdays and cut
families are $\mathcal U$-small. The encompassing surreal object belongs
to a larger universe. The HoTT construction states this shift explicitly
\cite[\S11.6]{b83HoTT}. In an inaccessible-universe model, $V_\Omega$
plays the role of the small universe and its classes can be treated
externally as subsets of $V_\Omega$. This is a model for a specified
interpretation, not a proof that every abstract $\GBC$ model has its full
external power set as its class part.

Its README explicitly distinguishes mathematical manuscripts from formalized declarations. We inspected the revision

The maintained report is a union of four manuscripts, not a sequence of superseding editions. Its current guide describes a 116-page compiled text.%
\footnote{\merge\ True at the pin \code{d5bd4a67b}, which has Parts~I--V. The

We also consulted two previous continuation manuscripts supplied through the user's Library: \emph{Lexicographic Well-Orders of the Surreal Numbers, II} \cite{swoSrc17}, and \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Surreal Well-Orderings: Cut reconstruction, asymmetric products, prefix non-rigidity, and size-safe foundations} \cite{swoSrc13}. Their results are not presented here as new.%
\footnote{\merge\ They are sources~17 and~13 of this report (printed in
Parts~VI--IX). Source~22's audit says that they ``are not assumed to have been

They explicitly ask about nonminimal enumeration types, whether unranked cylinders suffice, and how much of a class realization can be reconstructed.

The present work answers substantial versions of those three questions. ``Extension'' means relative to the inspected manuscripts, not a claim of priority in the literature.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{The principal advances.} The cardinal topological invariants of \emph{all} fixed-length strata are classified, with a sharp transition at two and three extra positions. Local characters are computed for $\mu+n$ and $\mu+\omega$. Prefix heights are recovered from cylinder inclusion rather than supplied as additional data. A labelled trace structure faithfully recovers the available class predicates over a fixed set universe.
\end{resultbox}

\subsubsection{What is deliberately not asserted}
We do not classify all nonprincipal cuts at every nonminimal length, the full automorphism group of the global enumeration order, or the order type of every unrestricted class-well-order quotient. The reconstruction theorem retains labels and fixed coding parameters; it does not recover a class model from the bare linear order alone. No unrestricted class-cut filling principle is assumed. No existence assertion about all proper-class well-orders is smuggled into an ordinary set or an ordinary class.

\subsubsection{Reading paths}
For the new set-sized mathematics, read \cref{swo:rg:sec:alphabet,swo:rg:sec:residual,swo:rg:sec:finite,swo:rg:sec:infinite}. For the global reconstruction results, read \cref{swo:rg:sec:core,swo:rg:sec:unranked,swo:rg:sec:realization}. \Cref{swo:rg:sec:interpretations,swo:rg:sec:foundations,swo:rg:sec:formalization} specify the interpretation and formalization boundaries. Every new result is proved within its stated framework.

\subsection{The interpretations that must be kept separate}\label{swo:rg:sec:interpretations}
\subsubsection{A numerical order is not a chosen well-order}
The numerical order on $\No$ is a dense linear order, not a well-order. For example, $0,-1,-2,\ldots$ is descending. A well-order $R$ of a labelled set $X\subseteq\No$ is generally unrelated to the numerical order. Its unique exhaustive $R$-increasing enumeration
\[
 e_R:\alpha\longrightarrow X
\]
need not be numerically increasing. To compare $R$ and $S$ lexicographically, we compare $e_R$ and $e_S$ at their first unequal label, using the \emph{numerical} order of those labels.

For a fixed carrier $X$, distinct exhaustive enumerations cannot be proper prefixes of one another: a proper prefix that already exhausts $X$ leaves no unused label for the longer enumeration. Thus the first-disagreement comparison is independent of an end-marker convention in this case.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.24\textwidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Mathematical representation & Size and comparison issue\\
\midrule
A fixed set, fixed order type & $\WO_\alpha(X)=\{e:\alpha\simeq X\}$ & A set; numerical first disagreement.\\
A fixed set, all order types & All well-order relations on $X$ & A set; varying exhaustive enumeration lengths cause no prefix ambiguity.\\
Varying set-sized carriers & Injective ordinal-length words in $\No$ & An ordinary proper class; a termination convention is needed.\\
Numerically well-ordered subsets & Strictly increasing words, or class well-ordered suborders & Not arbitrary labelled well-orders; variable carriers again require a convention.\\
Set-like global well-orders & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ & A predicate on class variables, not an ordinary class of objects.\\
Unrestricted global well-orders & Class relations on $\No$ & Proper-class predecessor segments may occur; compare common labelled initial parts directly.\\
Unlabelled order types & Quotient by order isomorphism & Lexicography of labels does not descend to this quotient.\\
Relation-code or shortlex orders & Bit strings, or length first and then labels & Different orders depending on the coding or primary key.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{Words, repetitions, and terminal markers}
All set-length words, injective words, and strictly increasing words are three different carriers. A word with repeated entries is not an exhaustive enumeration of a well-order on its range. It can instead describe a well-ordered family with repeated labels.

If lengths vary, an end-first convention declares a proper prefix smaller than its proper extensions. The empty word is then a least element. End-last gives a greatest element. A central terminal marker, placed between negative and positive labels after reserving $0$, produces a different order. The earlier continuation \cite{swoSrc13} proves surreal-line isomorphism results for this central convention under its stated class foundations (\merge\ \cref{swo:fs:sec:central}). They must not be transferred to end-first lexicography.

Even when the empty word is deleted, the convention matters. Under end-first comparison, a word $p$ of nonzero limit length $\lambda$ can be approached from below by its proper prefixes. Any word below $p$ either is such a prefix or has a first smaller label, and then lies below a sufficiently long prefix. Hence its left character is $\cf\lambda$. The full surreal line has no set-sized cofinal family below a point: the set cut between such a family and that point would be fillable. This is an explicit obstruction to identifying these word orders.

Restricting to numerically increasing words does not restore well-foundedness of the lexicographic order: singleton words already contain a copy of $\No$. A numerically increasing enumeration of the \emph{whole} surreal class cannot exist, since it would provide a numerically least surreal. Proper subclasses can, of course, be numerically well-ordered; the ordinal surreals are a basic example.

\subsubsection{Quotients and alternative codes}
If labels are forgotten, set well-orders are represented by ordinal order types. All set-like global well-orders of the whole surreal class have order type $\Ord$, so their unlabelled quotient has one type, even though their labelled lexicographic comparison is highly nontrivial. An order on relations obtained by reading membership bits according to a chosen well-order of pairs is another legitimate construction. Its first differing bit need not correspond to the first differing element in the two exhaustive enumerations.

These distinctions are structural, not merely notational. There are indefinitely many possible coding conventions, but the table separates the independent choices responsible for the principal mathematical interpretations.

\subsubsection{The Kanovei--Shelah connection}
Kanovei and Shelah's definable nonstandard-model construction \cite{KanoveiShelah} uses a lexicographically ordered set of maps from the continuum cardinal to $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters. The maps need not be injective, and the index set is not itself a well-order. Thus ``the lexicographic order of all well-orders of the reals'' is not a literal description of that construction. The relevant methodological connection is to retain presentations and order them definably, rather than select one presentation of each object. Their construction is set-sized; a proposed surreal analogue must state separately where its functions and index families live.

\subsubsection{What this article adds}

Write $A$ for a class order having the small-cut property of $\No$, and let
$A=L\sqcup R$ be a class cut determining the position of a new termination
symbol $\varepsilon$. All letters in $L$ precede $\varepsilon$, and $\varepsilon$ precedes all
letters in $R$. Both arbitrary and injective words are allowed to have any
set ordinal length, including zero.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Termination criterion.}
The word order is set-cut saturated if and only if $L,R$ are nonempty and
\[
\begin{split}
&L\text{ has a greatest element, or no set is cofinal in }L,\\
&R\text{ has a least element, or no set is coinitial in }R.
\end{split}
\]
This holds for arbitrary words and for injective words separately.
Under global choice, either saturated order is isomorphic to $\No$.
\end{resultbox}
\noindent\merge\ This is source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:terminator} for an
abstract alphabet with the set-cut property; the condensation hierarchy below
is source~15's (Part~IX).

The endpoint exceptions in this statement are essential. An immediate
neighbor of $\varepsilon$ can be replaced by a whole continuation cylinder,
which has room above and below every set of its elements. A mere
``the augmented alphabet must itself be saturated'' criterion is false.
Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:characters} supplies exact point characters, not merely a
sufficiency argument.

Strictly increasing words behave differently. Once an increasing word has
entered the region above the marker, it cannot extend downward relative to
its termination point. A countable increasing word then yields an explicit
unfilled countable cut. Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:increasing} proves this for every
fixed marker placement.

The second development concerns the order \emph{being encoded}, not merely
its code. For a raw class well-order $H$, identify two points when the closed
interval between them is a set. Every equivalence class has a least element,
so the quotient is representable by an ordinary class of set objects. For a
given class well-order $\Gamma$, let $P(\Gamma)$ consist of finitely
supported functions from $\Gamma$ to the ordinals, compared at their greatest
coordinate of disagreement. The functions are represented by finite graphs;
we never turn a proper-class total function into a set.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Prescribed condensation hierarchy.}
For $t\in\Gamma$, put
\[
 p\equiv_t q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p(\gamma)=q(\gamma)\quad\text{for all }\gamma\geq_\Gamma t.
\]
Adjoin a final stage $\top$ with universal equivalence.
This is exactly the set-interval condensation hierarchy of
$P(\Gamma)$: successor stages condense set intervals and limit stages
are unions. Every stage before $\top$ is nontrivial.
The whole family is given by one elementary definition in $\GBC$.
\end{resultbox}

For example, deleting the first $n$ coordinates gives a quotient of
$P(\omega)$ isomorphic to itself for every finite $n$, yet the limit
stage $\omega$ collapses it to a point. For $\Gamma=\Ord$, every set stage
has the original quotient order type, but the union of all those stages
collapses. Thus repeated isomorphism of successive quotients does not imply
that a limit stage has stabilized.

The lexicographic relevance is concrete: between any two distinct set-like
exhaustive enumerations of $\No$, there is a raw well-order isomorphic to
$P(\Gamma)$ for any prescribed nonempty $\Gamma$
(Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:densecomplexity}). This asserts arbitrary \emph{internal
well-order complexity} in those intervals. It does not assert that the
complexity is recoverable from the bare outer linear order.

\subsubsection{Conventions about size and proofs}

Our default class theory is $\GBC=\GB+\GC$, with ordinary set Foundation and
Power Set. The name $\GB$ itself is not used to imply choice. All members of
classes are sets. An ``ordinary class'' below is a class of set objects.
A ``virtual order'' is a predicate on class variables with a definable
comparison; it is not a same-level class whose members are proper classes.

A class well-order means a class linear order in which every nonempty
admitted subclass has a least element. We use the global-choice consequences
needed for class enumerations and for producing a descending sequence from a
nonempty subclass with no minimum. No arbitrary class-valued recursion is
silently included in $\GBC$.

The symbol $\Ord$ in a character pair means ``no set-sized cofinal family''
or its dual. It is not an additional cardinal. Under global choice, the
relevant nonempty class orders have cofinal or coinitial sequences indexed
by $\Ord$, so this notation also records their class-sized character.

\subsection{Source 24: the continuation and its main results}\label{swo:pc:sec:scope}

\merge\ Source~24's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Its $\mathcal P_\mu(X)$
and $\mathcal I_\mu(X)$ are printed $\WO_\mu(X)$ and $\I_\mu(X)$ (the
length-$\mu$ layer of this report's $\Words(X)$; this $\mathcal P$ is not $\Psupp$), its core
$\mathcal C_b$ (normalized permutation codes) is printed $\Pbd(b)$, and its
$\mathfrak E$, $\mathfrak I$ are $\Hsl$, $\Jinj$.

There is no unique object denoted by ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of the surreal numbers.'' Even after the size level is fixed, one must choose whether labels matter, whether the carrier is fixed, whether the enumeration length is prescribed, and how termination is compared with the next label. At the class level, there is the additional distinction between a well-order whose every proper initial segment is a set and a well-order that has a proper-class initial segment.

The merged ProveIt report~\cite{swoAtPin} develops the foundational taxonomy, embedding spectra, finite-tail adjacency, and a set-coded dense core of the global enumeration order. Three subsequent research drafts~\cite{swoSrc17,swoSrc13,swoSrc14}%
\footnote{\merge\ Sources~17, 13 and~14 of this report.} study cut reconstruction, automorphisms, asymmetric products, support thresholds, and model dependence. The present article does not count these as new results. Instead, it addresses a different question: \emph{what exactly converges when longer and longer initial parts of an enumeration stabilize?}

For a set $X$ of infinite cardinality $\mu$, regarded as an initial ordinal, write
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)=\Bij(\mu,X),\qquad
 \I_\mu(X)=\Inj(\mu,X).
\]
The first is the minimal-length slice of the labelled well-ordering space. The second allows a well-order of a proper subset whose cardinality is still $\mu$. Both carry the topology generated by initial-segment cylinders. For the surreal alphabets treated below, this is also their lexicographic order topology.

\subsubsection{A precise statement of the advances}

\begin{theorem}[Main results, with hypotheses explicit]\label{swo:pc:thm:main}
Let $|X|=\mu$ be infinite.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The Hausdorff completion of $\WO_\mu(X)$ for agreement on bounded initial segments is $\I_\mu(X)$. Surjectivity is the intersection of the $\mu$ open dense requirements that each label occur.
\item If $\mu$ is regular and $\lambda=\mu^{<\mu}$, then
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\ \cong_{\mathrm{top}}\ \lambda^\mu,
\]
where the right side has the bounded topology. This is a homeomorphism, not an asserted order isomorphism or a forward-uniform isomorphism.
\item If $X$ is countable and densely ordered without endpoints, the lexicographic order on $\WO_\omega(X)$ has a complete compatible metric and is homeomorphic to $\omega^\omega$. Its Dedekind completion is $\mathbb{R}$, and its complement there is a dense meager $F_\sigma$ set of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$. In particular, this order is not isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.
\item In the bounded-prefix topology on $\Sym(\mu)$, right translation by $\sigma$ is continuous exactly when $\sigma$ takes bounded subsets of $\mu$ to bounded subsets. Inversion is continuous at $\pi$ exactly when $\pi^{-1}$ has that property. These conditions hold automatically for regular $\mu$ and can fail for singular $\mu$.
\item In $\GBC$, every uniformly set-indexed prefix-Cauchy net of global enumerations is eventually constant. The coherent class-length prefix completion, formulated as a scheme about individual class parameters, consists of injective $\Ord$-words. Requiring inverse stabilization as well yields exhaustive enumerations.
\end{enumerate}
For (i), (ii), and (iv), the topology depends only on the alphabet as a set. To identify it with a lexicographic order topology at uncountable sizes, we use the thickness hypothesis in Definition~\ref{swo:pc:def:thick}.
\end{theorem}

The proof of (ii) is constructive in the order-theoretic sense: a node is extended until the least still-unused label, relative to a fixed baseline enumeration, first appears. This produces a full tree with $\mu^{<\mu}$ successors at every node. Regularity keeps all intermediate prefixes short. The very step that makes this construction work identifies its singular-cardinal obstruction.

Part (iii) answers the complete-metrizability question in~\cite{swoSrc17} for the countable-size case. It does \emph{not} settle that question for uncountable singular $\mu$ with $\cf\mu=\omega$. Those spaces are metrizable, but the incompleteness of their most obvious metric is not a proof that every compatible metric is incomplete.%
\footnote{\merge\ Source~26, which read source~24, settles it negatively in
$\ZFC$: for uncountable $\mu$ of countable cofinality $\WO_\mu(X)$ is not
Borel in $\I_\mu(X)$, hence not completely metrizable
(\cref{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification}; \cref{swo:x:note:q131}).}

\subsubsection{How to read the article}

Sections~\ref{swo:pc:sec:taxonomy}--\ref{swo:pc:sec:basic} provide the interpretations and reusable elementary order theory. Sections~\ref{swo:pc:sec:uniform}--\ref{swo:pc:sec:singular} contain the principal set-sized results and their proofs. Sections~\ref{swo:pc:sec:global}--\ref{swo:pc:sec:foundations} treat the class problem, including non-set-like orders and universe-sensitive interpretations. The formalization plan and research agenda are in Sections~\ref{swo:pc:sec:lean} and~\ref{swo:pc:sec:questions}.

Set-sized arguments use $\ZFC$. For class arguments, $\GB$ means G\"odel--Bernays theory without a choice convention silently built into the abbreviation, and $\GBC$ means $\GB$ with Global Choice. A statement about a family of classes always specifies a uniform coding relation; it never means that proper classes have become elements of an ordinary class.

\subsection{The interpretations that must remain distinct}\label{swo:pc:sec:taxonomy}

\subsubsection{Fixed carriers, labels, and enumeration length}

Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set. A \emph{labelled well-ordering of $X$} is a well-order relation $R$ on that very carrier. It has a unique exhaustive enumeration
\[
 f_R:\alpha_R\longrightarrow X
\]
that is an order isomorphism from the ordinal $\alpha_R$ to $(X,R)$. Its enumeration is not usually increasing in the given numerical order of $X$. The external well-order $R$ says when a label is listed; the original order of $X$ says which first differing label is smaller.

If $R\ne S$, neither exhaustive enumeration can be a proper initial segment of the other. Once one has listed every element of $X$, an injective continuation on the same carrier is impossible. Thus there is a first index $\delta$ at which they differ, and
\[
 R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_R(\delta)<_X f_S(\delta).
\]
There is no termination convention to choose in this fixed-carrier comparison.

The full order $\WO(X)$ allows all ordinal lengths $\alpha$ of cardinality $|X|$. Its fixed-length slice is $\WO_\alpha(X)=\Bij(\alpha,X)$. The minimal slice $\WO_\mu(X)$, where $\mu=|X|$ is initial, is especially uniform: after every prefix of length less than $\mu$, the remaining domain still has order type $\mu$ and the remaining labels still have cardinality $\mu$. Several conclusions below fail without this qualification. In particular, the full order can have adjacent pairs produced by finite residual permutation tails~\cite{swoAtPin}.

\subsubsection{Varying set carriers and the end marker}

An arbitrary set-sized labelled well-order of a set of surreals is represented by an injective word $p:\alpha\to\No$, with both $\alpha$ and the word's graph sets. Two such words can stand in the proper-prefix relation. Three natural conventions are genuinely different:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}p{.22\linewidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Convention & Comparison at termination & Immediate consequence\\
\midrule
End first & Termination precedes every actual label. & A proper prefix is smaller; the empty word is least.\\
End last & Termination follows every actual label. & A proper prefix is larger; the empty word is greatest.\\
Central termination & Termination lies at a specified cut of the alphabet. & Extending a word can move either left or right.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

For example, on a nonzero ordered alphabet with negative and positive letters, a termination symbol placed at zero gives
\[
 p\cat(-1)<p<p\cat(1).
\]
The sign-sequence presentation of a surreal uses precisely a central convention on the \emph{sign} alphabet: $-<$ termination $<+$. This should not be confused with end-first dictionary comparison of \emph{surreal-valued} words. Length-first comparison, or shortlex, is yet another order. Allowing repeated labels produces an arbitrary word space rather than a space of labelled well-orders.

\subsubsection{Numerically increasing well-orders}

One may instead ask that a subset of $\No$ be well-ordered by the \emph{inherited numerical order}. Its increasing enumeration is then a special injective word. This is a far smaller and more constrained problem than arbitrarily well-ordering its labels. The whole numerical order of $\No$ is not a well-order: it contains $0>-1>-2>\cdots$.

At the class level, even a numerically increasing well-ordered subclass need not be set-like. Ordinal surreals give a copy of $\Ord$. The ordered-field identity
\[
 \frac{v}{v+1}-\frac{u}{u+1}
 =\frac{v-u}{(u+1)(v+1)}>0\qquad(0\le u<v)
\]
shows that $\{\alpha/(\alpha+1):\alpha\in\Ord\}$ is an increasing, numerically bounded copy of $\Ord$. Appending the surreal $1$ gives a well-ordered subclass of type $\Ord+1$. The final point has a proper-class predecessor collection. Numerical boundedness is therefore not a substitute for set-likeness.

\subsubsection{The whole surreal class}

A \emph{set-like} class well-order is one in which each element has only a set of predecessors. A set-like well-order on a proper class has a canonical enumeration of type $\Ord$: the index of an element is the ordinal order type of its predecessor set. In $\GBC$, fix a baseline class bijection
\[
 b:\Ord\longrightarrow\No.
\]
We write $\Hsl$ for the \emph{virtual domain} of all class bijections $f:\Ord\to\No$, ordered by numerical first disagreement. Each $f$ is a class; $\Hsl$ is not declared to be a class whose members are those classes.

An \emph{arbitrary} class well-order of $\No$ can have type $\Ord+1$, $\Ord+\Ord$, or more complicated class-order types. These are not covered by $\Hsl$. Their lexicographic comparison requires a largest common labelled initial segment that may itself be a proper class; Section~\ref{swo:pc:sec:raw} supplies an elementary formula.

\subsubsection{Codes and quotients are different constructions}

Fixing a class enumeration of $\No\times\No$ permits comparison of the characteristic functions of two well-order relations at the first differing \emph{relation bit}. This relation-code order is legitimate, but it depends on that chosen enumeration and need not agree with numerical first-disagreement comparison of the exhaustive label lists.

Quotienting by unlabelled order isomorphism is more drastic. All set-like global well-orders have the same type $\Ord$, so their quotient has one element. The rich order $\Hsl$ is a structure of labelled presentations, not a structure of those unlabelled types. Numerical lexicographic order generally does not descend to the quotient.

The same caution applies to the Kanovei--Shelah construction of a definable nonstandard model~\cite{KanoveiShelah}. Their published index set consists of functions from the continuum cardinal into $\mathcal P(\mathbb{N})$ whose ranges are ultrafilters, ordered lexicographically. The functions need not be injective. This motivates definable fixed-length indexing, but it is not literally the present order of all well-order relations on $\mathbb{R}$ or $\No$.

\subsection{Source 25: the continuation and its main conclusions}\label{swo:ph:sec:intro}

\merge\ Source~25's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Its core $\mathcal D_b$
(support codes) is printed $\Psupp(b)$, its node class $\mathcal T$ of
injective set-length words is $\Words$, and its two-sorted reduct $\mathscr C_b$ is printed
$\Cyls_b$, as in Part~XIII (sources~20, 24 and~26 write $\mathcal C_b$ for
the core itself).

The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of surreal numbers'' leaves several independent choices unspecified. The word \emph{well-order} may describe an additional relation on a fixed carrier or the numerical order inherited by an increasing subset. The carrier may be a set or the whole proper class $\No$. A representation may be an enumeration, a relation code, or an unlabelled order type. Finally, the word \emph{all} must be interpreted at an explicit logical size level. These distinctions are mathematical, not merely notational.

The maintained ProveIt report \cite{swoAtPin,swoReadmeAtPin} develops these layers and the set-supported dense core of the global enumeration order. Subsequent continuation manuscripts investigate cut reconstruction, prefix completion, termination conventions, residual geometry, and condensation \cite{swoSrc13,swoSrc22,swoSrc23}.%
\footnote{\merge\ Sources~13, 22 and~23 of this report; source~25 also read
source~17. It saw this report at \code{7ff7736ec}, with Parts~I--VIII.} In particular, the residual-geometry continuation recovers prefix heights from unranked cylinder inclusion but explicitly leaves open whether the label information used to recognize exhaustiveness can be discarded. The present article answers that question negatively, in a stronger form that still preserves the entire core and all its cylinders.

Our new arguments are concentrated in Sections~\ref{swo:ph:sec:extension}--\ref{swo:ph:sec:singular}. The supporting material is re-established where it enters those proofs. The preliminary fixed-set spectrum and raw-class comparison are included to make clear which interpretation each conclusion concerns; they are not presented as new discoveries.

\subsubsection{The principal objects}

Fix, in $\GBC$, a class bijection
\[
 b:\Ord\longrightarrow\No.
\]
Let $\Psupp(b)$ be the ordinary class of normalized \emph{set codes} for set-supported permutations of this enumeration. Its evaluated branches are exhaustive, but the codes themselves are sets. Let
\[
 \Words=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\operatorname{Inj}(\alpha,\No)
\]
be the ordinary class of set-length injective words. A node $p\in\Words$ determines a cylinder
\[
 C_p=\{d\in{\Psupp(b)}:p\sqsubseteq d\}.
\]
Here and below a core code is identified notationally with its evaluated class word; the coding distinction is maintained in the proofs.

Write $\Jinj$ for the \emph{virtual domain} of admitted class injections $\Ord\to\No$, and $\Hsl$ for the subdomain of bijections. These are predicates on class variables, not ordinary classes whose members are themselves classes. An automorphism of the core-and-cylinder structure acts on its ordinary classes of set codes and induces an elementary transformation of any supplied class branch.

\subsubsection{The main result in one statement}

\begin{theorem}[Configuration classification; precise version in Section~\ref{swo:ph:sec:homogeneity}]\label{swo:ph:thm:overview}
Let $(f_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(g_i)_{i\in I}$ be uniformly set-indexed families of pairwise distinct members of $\Jinj$. There is an order automorphism of ${\Psupp(b)}$ preserving the entire unranked cylinder family and carrying every $f_i$ to $g_i$ on the induced branch action if and only if, for all applicable indices,
\begin{align*}
 f_i\in{\Psupp(b)}&\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g_i\in{\Psupp(b)},\\
 \delta(f_i,f_j)&=\delta(g_i,g_j),\\
 f_i<_{\lex}f_j&\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g_i<_{\lex}g_j.
\end{align*}
Here $\delta(f,g)$ is the least ordinal at which distinct branches disagree.
\end{theorem}

Several consequences are worth distinguishing. An arbitrary noncore exhaustive branch and an arbitrary nonexhaustive injective branch lie in the same orbit. Thus exhaustiveness is not invariant under the unlabelled cylinder structure. This also produces cylinder-preserving core automorphisms with no order-automorphism extension to $\Hsl$. On the other hand, preserving the equality of labels across different extension edges forces a single alphabet automorphism. Requiring that automorphism to preserve ${\Psupp(b)}$ forces it to be the identity.

These are statements about particular reducts and expansions. They do not say that the original, fully labelled definition of a global enumeration is ambiguous. They identify exactly which information was lost when labels were forgotten.

\subsubsection{What is not claimed}

The word ``new'' means an extension relative to the inspected repository and continuation material, not established historical priority. We do not classify all automorphisms of the \emph{bare} order $\Hsl$, nor all automorphisms of ${\Psupp(b)}$ after forgetting cylinders. We do not transfer the regular-cardinal theorem to arbitrary singular birthday fragments. We do not infer a proper-class theorem from finite experiments. Every such stronger question is separated from the proofs below.

\subsection{A taxonomy of the interpretations}\label{swo:ph:sec:taxonomy}

\subsubsection{Fixed carriers and canonical ordinal enumerations}

For a linearly ordered set $X$, a well-order $R$ on the labelled carrier $X$ has a unique increasing enumeration with respect to $R$,
\[
 e_R:\alpha_R\longrightarrow X.
\]
The word ``increasing'' here refers to $R$, not to the pre-existing numerical order on $X$. For distinct well-orders on the same carrier, neither enumeration can be a proper prefix of the other: an exhaustive proper prefix leaves no new label available for an injective extension. Consequently there is a first disagreement, and one may define
\[
 R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 e_R(\delta)<_X e_S(\delta).
\]
Different ordinal lengths are allowed; no termination convention is needed for two exhaustive words on the same carrier.

We use $\WO(X)$ for all such well-orders and $\WO_\alpha(X)$ for those of enumeration type $\alpha$. The latter is nonempty exactly when $|\alpha|=|X|$. In particular, ``all well-orders on $X$'' and ``all bijections $|X|\to X$'' need not be the same domain.

\subsubsection{Varying the carrier or allowing repetitions}

An arbitrary injective set-length word represents a well-order on its range. If the ranges can differ, a word can be a proper prefix of another. An extra convention is then indispensable. Placing termination before every letter gives end-first dictionary order. Placing it after every letter gives the opposite prefix convention. Placing it inside an alphabet cut gives a third family of orders. Equal words are, of course, compared as equal.

Allowing repetitions produces all ordinal-length words, but these are no longer enumerations of well-orders on their ranges. They are still useful as comparison and coding spaces. The recent termination manuscript \cite{swoSrc23} studies how different termination cuts affect set-cut saturation (\merge\ as source~16 does, \cref{swo:ds:sec:termination}). Its results do not make those conventions interchangeable.

Shortlex orders compare length before letters and change the construction again. A right-to-left or ``last disagreement'' comparison is generally undefined on infinite words: the disagreement positions need not have a largest element. Sign expansions of individual surreal numbers have their own central termination convention, $-<0<+$; that order must not be confused with an end-first order on words whose letters are themselves surreals.

\subsubsection{Numerically increasing words}

A set $A\subseteq\No$ can already be well-ordered by the numerical order. Its increasing enumeration is then an injective, numerically increasing ordinal word. This is a much smaller domain than arbitrary labelled well-orders on $A$: for a given $A$ there is only one inherited numerical order.

For example, the finite list $(3,-1,2)$ specifies a perfectly good additional well-order of three surreal labels, but it is not numerically increasing. Our principal homogeneous structure contains all injective prefixes; restricting it to increasing prefixes removes the freedom that makes the one-point extension argument work. Section~\ref{swo:ph:sec:raw} returns to this distinction for class-sized increasing subsets.

\subsubsection{Global set-like and unrestricted class well-orders}

A class well-order is \emph{set-like} when every proper initial segment below an element is a set. On the proper class $\No$, a set-like class well-order has type $\Ord$ and is equivalent to a class bijection $\Ord\to\No$. This is the interpretation represented by $\Hsl$.

An unrestricted class well-order can have proper-class initial segments. A copy of $\Ord+\Ord$ illustrates the difference. Such a well-order has no exhaustive ordinal-class enumeration of type $\Ord$, so it is not an element of $\Hsl$. It can nevertheless be compared directly with another labelled class well-order through their largest common labelled initial part; the definition is recalled in Section~\ref{swo:ph:sec:raw}.

\subsubsection{Relation codes and unlabelled order types}

A relation can instead be encoded as a binary characteristic word using a chosen well-order of the ordered pairs of labels. The resulting lexicographic order depends on that auxiliary coding and need not agree with enumeration lexicography. It is a valid but different construction.

Quotienting by order isomorphism discards labels. For a fixed infinite set $X$ of cardinality $\mu$, the possible unlabelled types are the ordinals $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|=\mu$. Ordering these types by ordinal comparison is not the labelled lexicographic order. For global set-like well-orders, the unlabelled type is always $\Ord$, so this quotient has only one type. Arbitrary class well-order types require additional care: a class of proper-class isomorphism classes cannot simply be formed as an ordinary class in GBC.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.24\textwidth}p{.30\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Objects compared & Logical size in the stated setting\\
\midrule
Fixed set $X$ & Well-order relations or exhaustive ordinal words & An ordinary set in ZFC\\
Variable set ranges & Injective set-length surreal words & An ordinary class of sets\\
Repeated words & All set-length surreal words & An ordinary class, but not all are well-orders\\
Inherited order & Numerically increasing words or subsets & Set/class distinction still applies\\
Global set-like & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ & A predicate on class variables\\
Global unrestricted & Class well-order relations on $\No$ & A predicate on class variables\\
Relation-code order & Binary codes under a selected pair order & Set or higher-level domain, depending on carrier\\
Unlabelled types & Isomorphism types rather than labels & A different quotient problem\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{The Kanovei--Shelah motivation, accurately scoped}

The construction in Kanovei and Shelah \cite[Section~1]{KanoveiShelah} uses lexicographically ordered maps $a:\mathfrak c\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters; those maps may repeat values. It is not literally the order of all well-order relations on $\mathbb R$, and it is not a construction involving the proper class of all surreal labels. Its relevant methodological idea is to order presentations even when selecting one distinguished presentation would be undesirable. We retain that motivation without conflating the index spaces.

\subsection{Source 26: the continuation and its principal results}\label{swo:nb:sec:intro}

\merge\ Source~26's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Source~26 writes $\kappa$
for the cardinality of the alphabet and $\theta$ for a birthday cutoff; they are
printed $\mu$ and $\kappa$, as for source~16 (\cref{swo:sub:notation81}), so
its $\mu=2^{<\theta}$ reads $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$. Its $\mathcal P_\kappa(X)$,
$\mathcal I_\kappa(X)$ are printed $\WO_\mu(X)$, $\I_\mu(X)$.

The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of surreal numbers'' does not determine a single object. A well-ordering of a fixed set of surreal labels is a set relation. A well-ordering of the entire surreal class is a class relation. Its totality is not an ordinary class of objects in a two-sorted set/class theory. Moreover, a numerical increasing enumeration and an arbitrary enumeration carrying a different well-order are different constructions, even before these size issues arise.

The repository report~\cite{swoAtPin} already develops much of this foundational separation, together with embedding spectra, birthday-cutoff phenomena, global support cores, and comparison of non-set-like class well-orders. The subsequent manuscript~\cite{swoSrc24}%
\footnote{\merge\ Source~24 of this report.} identifies the forward-prefix completion with injective words and asks, in its Question~13.1, whether an uncountable minimal-length permutation space of countable cofinality might nevertheless admit some other compatible complete metric. Incompleteness of the displayed prefix metric did not decide that question. Neither did the construction of a finer complete two-sided uniformity.

Here that question is answered negatively, by a stronger descriptive obstruction. Throughout the set-sized part, cardinals are identified with initial ordinals, and set choice is available. Write
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)=\Bij(\mu,X),\qquad
 \I_\mu(X)=\Inj(\mu,X),\qquad |X|=\mu\ge\aleph_0.
\]
The topology has basic neighborhoods prescribing a whole initial segment of length $\alpha<\mu$. It is not, at uncountable lengths, the usual finite-coordinate product topology.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Main classification.} In the bounded-prefix topology,
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\text{ is metrizable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\cf\mu=\omega,
\]
whereas
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\text{ is completely metrizable}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu=\omega.
\]
If $\mu>\omega$ and $\cf\mu=\omega$, the stronger assertion
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\notin\operatorname{Borel}\bigl(\I_\mu(X)\bigr)
\]
holds in $\ZFC$, without a continuum-hypothesis assumption.
\end{resultbox}

The classification concerns the \emph{minimal} ordinal enumeration length $\mu$. It does not silently include all other ordinals of cardinality $\mu$. The distinction is essential: at a successor enumeration length, fixing the entire proper prefix can leave a unique final label and isolate a point.

The second main result is a closed-subspace universality theorem. If additionally $\mu>\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}$, then every zero-dimensional separable metrizable space is homeomorphic to a closed subspace of $\WO_\mu(X)$. For any prescribed subset of binary Cantor space, the construction can preserve binary lexicographic order when $X$ is linearly ordered. Thus the missing boundary is not a technical nuisance that disappears after a simple completeness repair; it can carry arbitrary Cantor traces.

The surreal specialization uses two different cardinal parameters. For an infinite birthday cutoff $\kappa$,
\[
 \mu=|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}.
\]
The relevant permutation length is $\mu$, not automatically $\kappa$. Every interval and ray of $\No_{<\kappa}$ has size $\mu$, so its minimal enumeration order has the prefix topology as its order topology. In particular, $\kappa=\beth_\omega$ supplies an unconditional example with $\mu=\kappa>\mathfrak{c}$ and $\cf\mu=\omega$.

\subsubsection{What is inherited, and what is developed here}

The interpretation taxonomy, the basic set-alphabet embedding results, the support-core framework, direct common-prefix comparison, and the earlier forward-completion theorem belong to the preceding reports~\cite{swoAtPin,swoSrc24}. Their elementary mechanisms are reproved below when they are needed for a self-contained argument. The main developments of this continuation are the compact omitted-label coding theorem, its non-Borel consequence, the resulting exact complete-metrizability classification, closed universality, and their simultaneous application to singular surreal birthday fragments. The bounded-image refinement in Section~\ref{swo:nb:sec:bounded} gives a further localization of the obstruction.

This is a statement of dependence and of what the present manuscript contributes relative to the inspected drafts, not a claim that no related result exists elsewhere. Classical descriptive set theory supplies the perfect-set property for uncountable Borel subsets of Cantor space~\cite{Kechris1995}. The newer singular-cardinal descriptive-set-theoretic framework of Dimonte and Motto Ros~\cite{b83DimonteMottoRos} is relevant context, but its generalized Borel hierarchies are not identified with the ordinary Borel sigma-algebra used in our theorem.

\subsubsection{Conventions and logical scope}

The set-sized proofs take place in $\ZFC$. In the class-sized part, $\GB$ denotes G\"odel--Bernays theory without an included choice principle, and $\GBC=\GB+\GC$. We explicitly distinguish a theorem about two class relations from an assertion that a collection of all such relations is itself a class. A uniformly coded family means one admitted class relation whose sections are the family members; it never means an arbitrary set whose members are proper classes.

The words ``well-order'' and ``well-founded'' in a class model are internal unless an external viewpoint is stated. ``Borel'' throughout the main theorems means generated from open sets by \emph{countable} unions and complements. ``Closed-universal'' means that the specified spaces occur as closed subspaces; it does not mean that all of them admit complete metrics. ``Equimorphic'' means mutually order-embeddable and does not mean order-isomorphic.

\subsection{An atlas of the main interpretations}\label{swo:nb:sec:atlas}

There is no finite list of every artificial coding one could call lexicographic. The following axes isolate the standard mathematically distinct meanings. Their combinations cover the principal interpretations of the question without imposing a misleading single answer.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.21\textwidth}Yp{.23\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Objects and comparison & Foundational level\\
\midrule
Fixed labelled carrier & Well-orders of a set $X\subseteq\No$, compared through their ordinal enumerations & A set in $\ZFC$\\
Fixed enumeration length & Bijections $\lambda\to X$; especially the minimal slice $\lambda=|X|$ & A set in $\ZFC$\\
Varying set carriers & Injective ordinal-length surreal words; termination must be ordered & A class of set codes\\
Inherited numerical order & Strictly increasing words, or subsets well-ordered by $<_{\No}$ & A class of set codes\\
Relation-code order & Characteristic functions of well-order relations, along a separately chosen coordinate order & Set codes, or virtual class relations\\
Order-type quotient & Forget labels and retain ordinal or class order type & Different quotient problem\\
Set-like global orders & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ & A predicate on class variables\\
Unrestricted global orders & Class well-orders, possibly with proper-class predecessor segments & A predicate on class variables\\
Higher-universe version & The preceding objects interpreted inside a specified smaller universe or class model & Sets externally; size shift explicit\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{Fixed sets: arbitrary well-orders are not numerical increasing orders}

Let $X$ be a set of surreal numbers, equipped with its numerical linear order. A different relation $R\subseteq X^2$ can well-order $X$. Its unique ordinal enumeration is
\[
 e_R:\otp(X,R)\longrightarrow X.
\]
The values need not increase numerically. For instance, $\langle 1,0\rangle$ is a legitimate enumeration of a two-element labelled well-order, but is not increasing in surreal numerical order. Numerical order is used to compare \emph{different enumerations}, not to constrain each enumeration.

Two unequal enumerations of the same carrier cannot be related by proper initial-segment extension. If one exhausted $X$ before the other ended, the latter would have no unused label for its next position. Hence their first disagreement occurs at a coordinate belonging to both domains, and its two labels determine their lexicographic comparison. No end marker is needed on a fixed exhaustive carrier.

For an infinite $X$ of cardinality $\mu$, the possible order types are exactly the ordinals $\lambda$ with $\mu\le\lambda<\mu^+$. Thus
\[
 \WO(X)=\bigcup_{\mu\le\lambda<\mu^+}\WO_\lambda(X),
 \qquad \WO_\lambda(X)=\Bij(\lambda,X).
\]
These slices need not be convex in the full lexicographic order. First labels can already place members of different lengths on either side of each other. Our principal topological theorem is about the minimal slice $\WO_\mu(X)$, not an assertion about this entire union.

\subsubsection{Variable carriers and termination conventions}

If the carrier is allowed to vary, one word can be a proper prefix of another. For an ordinary class of all set-length injective words, the most familiar convention puts a proper prefix first. Equivalently, the termination symbol is below every genuine label. The empty word is then least. Putting termination above every label reverses the prefix comparison and makes the empty word greatest. Inserting termination at a chosen cut in the alphabet gives further inequivalent orders.

The standard sign presentation of a surreal uses the special convention
\[
 -\;<\;\End\;<\;+.
\]
It therefore cannot be identified without proof with a surreal-labelled word order using termination below all letters. With the three binary words $\langle-\rangle$, $\langle\rangle$, $\langle+\rangle$, the central-termination order places the empty word in the middle, whereas prefix-first puts it before both nonempty words.

Allowing repeated labels changes injective words into arbitrary ordinal-length functions. Sorting by length before comparing labels is another construction, often called shortlex. A reverse-coordinate comparison at the \emph{last} disagreement is not automatically defined for infinite words: two words may differ at all natural-number coordinates and have no last disagreement. These alternatives need their own definitions, rather than being treated as harmless notational changes.

\subsubsection{Inherited well-orders, simplicity, and quotienting}

A set $A\subseteq\No$ well-ordered by numerical order has a unique increasing enumeration. This gives a natural restricted suborder of the varying-carrier word order. It excludes almost all arbitrary permutations. The numerical surreal order itself is not a well-order, as witnessed by
\[
 0>-1>-2>-3>\cdots.
\]
The simplicity order on sign sequences, by proper prefix extension, is well-founded but partial. Birthday order is only a rank comparison, and equal birthdays require an additional tie-breaker to produce a linear well-order. None of these is the numerical lexicographic order on all well-order presentations.

Forgetting the labels removes the information on which enumeration lexicography depends. All bijections $\mu\to X$ represent the same abstract order type $\mu$, although their first values can be arbitrary elements of $X$. Therefore the strict lex order does not descend to their order-isomorphism quotient. Ordering the resulting ordinal types in their usual ordinal order is legitimate, but it answers a different question. At the global level all proper-class set-like well-orders have type $\Ord$; their type quotient collapses an especially rich labelled order to one type.

\subsubsection{Relation-code lexicography}

Choose a well-order $q$ of the coordinate set $X^2$. A relation $R$ is coded by its indicator function $\chi_R:X^2\to\{0,1\}$, and two relation codes can be compared at their $q$-least disagreement. Restricting to well-order relations produces another linear order. It depends on $q$ and compares incidences, not next enumeration labels.

For example, let $X=\{0,1,2\}$, let $R$ enumerate $0,1,2$, and let $S$ enumerate $1,0,2$. Enumeration lexicography gives $R<S$. If the first differing coordinate in $q$ is $(0,1)$ and $0<1$ is the bit order, then $\chi_R(0,1)=1$ and $\chi_S(0,1)=0$, so relation-code lexicography gives $S<R$. Both constructions are rigorous, but they are not the same construction.

The Kanovei--Shelah definable-hyperreal construction provides related motivation for lexicographically ordered presentations~\cite{KanoveiShelah}. Its displayed indexing family consists of maps from the continuum into $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters, with lexicographic comparison of maps. That is not literally the set of all well-orders of $\mathbb R$. Repeated presentations there are part of a definability device; this distinction should be retained when transferring the idea to surreal labels.

The numerical order on $\No$ is not a well-order: already the finite

The second decision is the object to be compared. A well-order relation
can be replaced by its increasing enumeration \emph{in that well-order},

lexicographic orders. A third decision is size: a set of surreals is a

members are arbitrary proper-class relations is not an ordinary class of
sets in two-sorted set theory.

set would not by itself constitute meaningful further study. Our main
extensions instead concern information discarded by encodings and
unlabelled prefix structure, sharper support optimization, and the
difference between an ordinary class family and the whole raw order.

\subsubsection{Notation and conventions}

A surreal number is represented by a sign sequence
$s:\alpha\to\{-,+\}$ for a set ordinal $\alpha$. Its birthday is
$\bd(s)=\alpha$. At the first disagreement we compare signs using
$-<\dagger<+$, where $\dagger$ means that the sequence has ended. Thus
termination is distinct from both signs. We write
\[
 \No_{<\theta}=\{s\in\No:\bd(s)<\theta\}.
\]
This is a set for every set ordinal $\theta$.

A word over a linearly ordered alphabet $X$ is a function
$p:\alpha\to X$. Unless stated otherwise, its length is a set ordinal.
The notation $p\concat q$ denotes ordinal concatenation; ordinal
multiplication in all scan and block lengths is genuine ordinal
multiplication, not cardinal multiplication. The order $L\times_{\lex}M$
compares the $L$ coordinate first. The sum $\sum_{l\in L}M_l$ is the
corresponding lexicographic sum. We write $L\equi M$ for mutual order
embeddability; this never asserts $L\cong M$.

We use $\GB$ for G\"odel--Bernays theory without a choice axiom,
$\GBC$ for $\GB$ with Global Choice, and $\KM$ for Kelley--Morse class
theory. A \emph{uniformly class-indexed family} $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ means
that $I$ is an ordinary class of sets and one class relation
$\mathcal R(i,x,y)$ gives every section $R_i$. The word ``uniformly''
is a mathematical requirement, not a convenience of notation.

\subsection{Source 28: what is being continued}\label{swo:ge:sec:intro}

\merge\ Source~28's Sections~1 and~2, printed whole. Its $\mathcal P_\mu(X)$,
