The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of surreal numbers'' does not determine a unique mathematical structure. A well-order may have a fixed set of labels, a varying set of labels, or the entire surreal class as its carrier. It may be arbitrary or inherited from the numerical order. Labels may be retained or forgotten. A global well-order may or may not have only set-sized proper initial segments. A word may terminate, and the rule for comparing termination with a further label matters.

The ProveIt report~\cite{swoAtPin} develops this taxonomy, set-sized embedding spectra, the singular birthday transition, global supported-permutation cores, and direct comparison of arbitrary class well-orders. The subsequent manuscript~\cite{swoSrc24}%
\footnote{\merge\ Source~24 of this report. Source~28 did not see source~26.} distinguishes forward prefix completion from Dedekind completion and derives exact continuity criteria for permutation operations. The present paper takes the latter criteria as a starting point, reproves them in a more general form, and answers several of that manuscript's questions about the boundedness-preserving subgroup and natural topology refinements. It does not present the earlier completion or regular-cardinal Baire-space theorems as new discoveries.

\subsubsection{The principal developments}

Let $\mu$ be an infinite initial cardinal. On $S_\mu=\Sym(\mu)$, let ${\tau_{\mathrm b}}$ be the topology of agreement on bounded initial segments. Put
\[
 {H_\mu}=\{p\in S_\mu:p\text{ and }p^{-1}\text{ send bounded sets to bounded sets}\}.
\]
The following statements summarize the principal contributions relative to the inspected predecessor material.

\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Main results.} For singular $\mu$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item ${H_\mu}$ is the largest subgroup containing the finitary permutations on which the inherited ${\tau_{\mathrm b}}$ topology is a group topology. Its normalizer in $S_\mu$ is exactly ${H_\mu}$.
\item Its ${\tau_{\mathrm b}}$-closure consists of all permutations preserving bounded sets in the forward direction. This closure is nowhere dense. Its forward uniform completion consists of all boundedness-preserving injections.
\item The inverse-boundedness locus is dense and is an intersection of $\cf\mu$ explicit open sets in the injection completion. If $\cf\mu=\omega$, it is a dense completely metrizable $G_\delta$ subspace.
\item The coarsest group topology containing ${\tau_{\mathrm b}}$ is ${\tau_{<\mu}}$, agreement on arbitrary subsets of $\mu$ of cardinality less than $\mu$. Its character is
\[
 \chi(S_\mu,{\tau_{<\mu}})=\cof([\mu]^{<\mu},\subseteq)>\mu.
\]
\item The group $(S_\mu,{\tau_{<\mu}})$ is complete for its two-sided group uniformity. This is a topology-changing repair, not a proof that the original lexicographic topology was already a group topology.
\end{enumerate}
\end{resultbox}

The numerical application uses $\No_{<\kappa}$, the surreals with sign-sequence length less than an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$. Its cardinality is $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$. The topology of its minimal exhaustive-enumeration slice $\Bij(\mu,\No_{<\kappa})$ is precisely the prefix topology. The singularity relevant to the main results is therefore the singularity of $2^{<\kappa}$, not merely that of $\kappa$.

\subsubsection{Assumptions and limits}

All set-sized results are proved in $\ZFC$. We write $\GB$ for G\"odel--Bernays class theory without building a choice principle into the abbreviation, and $\GBC$ for $\GB$ with Global Choice. Our global constructions use $\GBC$ and a specified baseline enumeration. An assertion about a family of proper classes is stated using one uniform class relation, or explicitly in an external metatheory. Neither $\GBC$ nor $\KM$ makes a proper class an element of another class.

The remaining complete-metrizability question for the \emph{full} singular forward permutation space is not settled by the dense complete subspace constructed here. We state that question precisely in Section~\ref{swo:ge:sec:questions}.%

\subsection{The interpretations that must not be identified}\label{swo:ge:sec:taxonomy}

\subsubsection{Fixed sets of labels}

Let $(X,<)$ be a linearly ordered set. A labelled well-ordering $R$ of $X$ has a unique exhaustive ordinal enumeration
\[
 f_R:\alpha_R\longrightarrow X,
\]
which is an isomorphism from the ordinal $\alpha_R$ to $(X,R)$. There are two orders here: $R$ tells us when a label is listed, whereas $<$ tells us which differing label is numerically smaller. The enumeration need not be increasing for $<$.

Two different exhaustive enumerations of the same carrier cannot be proper prefixes of one another. A completed enumeration has already used every available label. Hence, for $R\ne T$, a first disagreement $\delta$ exists and we define
\[
 R<_{\lex}T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_R(\delta)<f_T(\delta).
\]
The standard least-disagreement argument proves a linear order. For example, in a comparison of three words, the smaller of the first-disagreement indices for the first two comparisons determines the outer comparison; when those indices agree, transitivity of the alphabet order applies. No end-marker convention is required.

We distinguish the full order
\[
 \WO(X)=\{R:R\text{ is a well-order on }X\}
\]
from a fixed-length slice $\WO_\alpha(X)=\Bij(\alpha,X)$, and especially from the minimal slice
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)=\Bij(\mu,X),\qquad \mu=|X|\text{ initial}.
\]
The full carrier is a set: it is a subclass of the set $\mathcal P(X\times X)$. The apparent union over ordinal lengths does not make it a proper class. The minimal slice, however, has a uniform supply of unused labels after each proper prefix, which need not hold for other slices.

\subsubsection{Varying set carriers and termination}

A labelled well-order on some set of surreals is represented by an injective set-length word $p:\alpha\to\No$. Such words themselves have set codes, so the collection of all of them is an ordinary class. Now proper-prefix comparisons occur. End-first dictionary order places a word below every proper extension; end-last places it above every proper extension. In particular, the empty word is respectively least or greatest.

A central termination convention puts an end symbol at a chosen cut of the alphabet. On nonzero surreal labels, for example, one may place termination between the negative and positive labels. For fresh labels this gives
\[
 p\cat\langle-1\rangle<p<p\cat\langle1\rangle.
\]
The sign representation of an individual surreal uses the central convention $-<\text{termination}<+$ on the \emph{two-sign alphabet}. It is not the same as end-first dictionary order on \emph{surreal-valued} words. Allowing repeated labels makes a word space rather than a space of labelled well-orders. Comparing length first makes a shortlex-type order rather than first-disagreement lexicography. These are legitimate alternatives, not interchangeable notations.

\subsubsection{Inherited numerical well-orders}

A different question asks for subsets that are already well-ordered by the numerical order of $\No$. Their increasing enumerations form a restricted collection of injective words. The full numerical surreal order is not well-founded, since it contains
\[
 0>-1>-2>\cdots.
\]
Even a numerically bounded class well-order can fail to be set-like. For nonnegative surreals $u<v$, ordered-field arithmetic gives
\[
 \frac{v}{v+1}-\frac{u}{u+1}
 =\frac{v-u}{(u+1)(v+1)}>0.
\]
Thus $\{\alpha/(\alpha+1):\alpha\in\Ord\}$ has increasing type $\Ord$ and lies below $1$. Appending $1$ gives type $\Ord+1$; the last point has a proper class of predecessors. Numerical boundedness does not imply set-likeness.

\subsubsection{Global class orders, codes, and quotients}

A class order is \emph{set-like} when every element has a set of predecessors. A set-like well-order of a proper class has an ordinal-class enumeration. For the whole surreal class, this produces the virtual domain of class bijections $\Ord\to\No$. Arbitrary class well-orders can have proper-class initial segments and types such as $\Ord+1$ or $\Ord+\Ord$; ordinal-class words do not exhaust them.

There are also representation-dependent alternatives. After choosing an enumeration of pairs of labels, one can compare the characteristic functions of the well-order relations themselves. This compares the first differing \emph{relation bit}, not the first differing label in an exhaustive list. Section~\ref{swo:ge:sec:raw} gives an explicit finite discrepancy.

Finally, forgetting labels and taking order-isomorphism types changes the problem drastically. All set-like global well-orders have type $\Ord$, so their unlabelled quotient has one element. The rich lexicographic structure belongs to presentations. Lexicographic order generally does not descend to the quotient: differently labelled presentations of the same ordinal may occur on both sides of another presentation.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}P{.25\linewidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Objects & Essential qualification\\
\midrule
Fixed set $X$ & Well-order relations or exhaustive ordinal lists & No proper-prefix ambiguity.\\
Minimal slice & Bijections $\mu\to X$, $\mu=|X|$ & The subject of the topology and group results.\\
Varying set carriers & Injective set-length surreal words & A termination rule is needed.\\
Inherited order & Numerically increasing enumerations & Not arbitrary labelled well-orders.\\
Set-like global orders & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ & A virtual higher-order domain.\\
All class well-orders & Possibly non-set-like relations & Common prefixes can be proper classes.\\
Relation-bit codes & Characteristic functions of relations & Depends on a coordinate enumeration.\\
Order-type quotient & Unlabelled isomorphism types & Numerical lexicography is not inherited.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsection{Source 29: the question, the audit, and the new results}\label{swo:bw:sec:introduction}

\merge\ Source~29's Sections~1 and~3, printed whole except Subsection~3.3; its
interpretations (Section~2) and Subsection~3.3 are printed in Part~XII
(\cref{swo:bw:sec:interpretations,swo:bw:sub:scans}). Its $\mathbf T$ (the
shorter-first order of all set-length surreal words, the type $\mathbf T_{\min}$
of source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}) is printed $\mathbf T_{\min}$ and
its $\mathbf P=\mathbf T\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ is printed $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$;
its $\otimes_{\lex}$ is printed $\times_\lex$. Its internal labels \code{gl:}
stay under its own prefix (\code{swo:bw:gl:}).

Lexicographic comparison combines two orders with different jobs.
An auxiliary well-order says which label is visited first, second, and
so on. The numerical order on the labels decides which of two visits
comes earlier at their first disagreement. There is no reason for the
resulting order on presentations to be a well-order. When the labels
are surreal numbers, a further issue intervenes: all surreal numbers
form a proper class. The well-orders of a fixed set of surreals and the
well-orders of the entire surreal class therefore have fundamentally
different logical sizes.

These observations do not prevent a substantial theory. They tell us
which carriers, parameters, and axioms must be written into a theorem.
The present continuation develops that theory in several directions
that are not settled by the inspected merged article. Its main theme
is the amount of information that a chosen order or presentation keeps.
The numerical birthday alphabet remembers its exact cutoff; some
permutation-stratum embedding invariants forget it. An ordered prefix
tree remembers every local numerical comparison but can still forget
whether a class branch visits every label. A class condensation history
has a finite description at each individual point, while its existence
for all class well-orders has nontrivial foundational strength.

\subsubsection{What was actually inspected}

The source audit used the GitHub repository at a fixed commit, not a
moving branch name. Sixteen source files were retrieved and their bytes
checked against the Git blob hashes returned by GitHub. The central
research file is
\begin{quote}\small

\path{surreal-well-orders/article.tex}.
\end{quote}
At the pin, its blob is
\texttt{f3f69663cd63682ad2e1db808bcb3c6e8fd940ce} and its size is
903,287 bytes. The research README still describes an earlier
116-page, four-source merge.%
\footnote{\merge\ True at \code{7ff7736ec}; the README is updated with this
addition.} The actual article already incorporates
substantial additions from six further manuscripts, called sources
13--18 in its editorial apparatus. Its Parts VI--VIII supersede several
entries in the older research-question list. The introduction also
mentions an intended Part IX that is absent from the pinned body
(\merge\ Part~IX was written before this addition).
Accordingly we use actual theorem statements and proofs, together with
explicitly identified earlier manuscripts, rather than infer established
results from a roadmap or README \cite{swoAtPin,swoSrc19,swoSrc21,swoSrc20}.%
\footnote{\merge\ The three earlier manuscripts are sources~19, 21 and~20 of
this report; source~29's manifest
(\path{data/29-birthdays-source_manifest.json}) records their SHA-256, which
equal the delivered texts. Source~29 did not see sources~22--28 or~30.}

This distinction changes what counts as further study. The pinned
article already proves the general set-alphabet ordinal cutoff,
substantial binary-cube spectra, fixed-stratum density and cellularity,
minimal-stratum gap spectra, word-termination classifications, a raw
comparison of arbitrary class well-orders, and a detailed represented-cut
theory for a bounded-support core. Those results are recalled as
background. We do not present them again as new discoveries.

\subsubsection{A guide to the extensions}

The following results organize the continuation.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exact numerical birthday spectra.}
For every pair of set ordinals $\beta,\theta$,
\[
 \B_\beta\emb\No_{<\theta}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta<\theta.
\]
This gives the exact numerical embeddability hierarchy and its least
binary coding lengths, including noninitial ordinal cutoffs.

\item \textbf{Residual strata at noninitial birthdays.}
We extend the earlier variable-residual analysis to every noninitial
birthday cutoff. In particular, without the continuum hypothesis,
all countable noninitial birthday alphabets have the same fixed-stratum
equimorphism type at each common admissible enumeration length.
This is a statement about mutual embeddings, not order isomorphism.

\item \textbf{An exact centered-word product.}
Increasing words split at their termination cut. At a numerical
threshold this yields ${\mathbf{T}_{\min}}^{\mathrm{op}}\mathbin{\times_\lex}{\mathbf{T}_{\min}}$, and a small
finite-fiber calculation classifies the zero conventions up to
isomorphism. Translation disposes of thresholds at other actual
surreal numbers; nonprincipal class cuts remain genuine parameters.

\item \textbf{New behavior at proper-class carriers.}
Numerically well-ordered proper subclasses can have unattained surreal
suprema. Exactly these create adjacent pairs under shorter-first
comparison. This destroys a symmetry present for all set-length words
and obstructs extending the set-prefix tree isomorphism to full class
carriers.

\item \textbf{Topology and Borel structure after finite tails.}
Over a countable dense alphabet, the types $\omega$, $\omega+1$,
$\omega+2$, and $\omega+n$ for $n\ge3$ exhibit different relations
between native lexicographic topology and coordinate topology.
The resulting distinction is measurable as well as topological.

\item \textbf{Prefix-tree and foundational limitations.}
Uniform tree automorphisms can exchange exhaustive and nonexhaustive
class branches. Separately, canonical terminating condensation histories
are equivalent over $\GBC$ to strong class-well-order comparability.
Neither statement conflates the existence of a class object with the
existence of a class containing all such objects.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{The Kanovei--Shelah connection}

The historical motivation needs a precise formulation. In the preprint
of Kanovei and Shelah, the relevant index set consists of maps
\[
 a:\mathfrak c\longrightarrow\mathcal P(\mathbb{N})
 \quad\text{whose ranges are ultrafilters on }\mathbb{N}.
\]
The maps are compared at their first unequal coordinate, using the
characteristic-function order on $\mathcal P(\mathbb{N})$. Repeated values are
allowed. These are redundant ultrafilter presentations, not literally
all well-orders of the real line. The index order is linear but is not
itself required to be well-founded. Its role is in the definable
nonstandard-real construction \cite[\S1 of the preprint]{KanoveiShelah}.
What transfers here is the method of comparing sufficiently rich
presentations lexicographically. No identification of the present
surreal orders with that index order is assumed.

\subsection{Source 29: the fixed-set baseline and what it does not identify}\label{swo:bw:sec:baseline}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~3, printed whole. Its fixed set has cardinality
$\kappa$; following \cref{swo:sub:notation81} it is printed $\mu$ in the first
two subsections (the birthday-fragment formulas keep $\kappa$ as a cutoff).
Its Theorem~3.1 is \cref{swo:sw:setspectrum} and is recorded as a note.

\subsubsection{Exhaustive enumerations}

For a linearly ordered set $(X,<)$, let
\[
 \WO_\alpha(X)=\{f:\alpha\longrightarrow X:f\text{ is a bijection}\},
 \qquad
 \WO(X)=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\WO_\alpha(X).
\]
If $|X|=\mu$ is infinite, only
$\mu\le\alpha<\mu^+$ can occur, so this union is a set.
No exhaustive enumeration can be a proper prefix of another. Thus
for distinct $f,g$ there is a least coordinate at which both are
defined and differ, and
\[
 f<_{\lex}g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(\delta)<g(\delta)
 \quad\text{at that coordinate }\delta.
\]
The termination convention is immaterial here. It becomes relevant as
soon as incomplete words or different carriers are admitted.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Theorem~3.1, ``Inherited fixed-set spectrum'']\label{swo:bw:thm:baseline}
\emph{For every infinite linearly ordered set $X$ of cardinality $\mu$,
\[
 |\WO(X)|=2^\mu,
 \qquad
 \beta\emb\WO(X)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \beta<\mu^+
\]
for set ordinals $\beta$. Every linear order of size at most $\mu$
embeds in the minimal stratum $\WO_\mu(X)$.
The reverse of every ordinal below $\mu^+$ embeds as well, while
neither direction admits a monotone sequence of length $\mu^+$.}
This is \cref{swo:sw:setspectrum} (the reals report's
\code{lwo:thm:ordinal-spectrum} for every infinite alphabet), as source~29
says: ``This is established in the repository \cite{swoAtPin,ProveItReals}; we include
the main mechanism because it underlies the later distinctions.'' Its
summary of the mechanism follows; it is source~09's stabilization route
(\cref{swo:sw:setspectrum} and the note after it), not a new proof.

\smallskip\noindent
Partition $X$ into pairs $\{a_\xi,b_\xi\}$, with $a_\xi<b_\xi$, indexed
by $\xi<\mu$. A binary word chooses whether each pair is listed as
$(a_\xi,b_\xi)$ or $(b_\xi,a_\xi)$. Their concatenation has length
$2\cdot\mu=\mu$ and preserves first-difference comparison.
Hence $\B_\mu\emb\WO_\mu(X)$.

If $L$ is any linear order of size at most $\mu$, enumerate its
points among $\mu$ coordinates and map $x\in L$ to the bits recording
whether the corresponding point is strictly below $x$. Unused
coordinates are fixed at zero. For $x<y$ all changing bits move from
zero to one, and the coordinate naming $x$ changes. This embeds
$L$ into $\B_\mu$. It also gives the lower cardinality bound
$2^\mu$ for the minimal stratum. The upper bound follows because
well-orders are relations on $X$ and there are only $2^\mu$ such
relations.

For the upper ordinal bound, suppose a strictly increasing sequence
$(f_i)_{i<\mu^+}$ existed. The first coordinates form a nondecreasing
sequence in a set of size $\mu$ and therefore are eventually constant.
Continue by transfinite induction: after a common prefix of length
$\gamma<\mu^+$ has been fixed on a tail, the next coordinates are
eventually constant on that tail. At a limit, regularity of $\mu^+$
allows the at most $\mu$ preceding tail bounds to be combined.
The chosen labels are distinct. If a common prefix exhausts $X$,
all subsequent $f_i$ are identical, a contradiction. If none does,
the construction chooses $\mu^+$ distinct elements of $X$, also
a contradiction. Reverse all comparisons for descending sequences.
The lower ordinal assertion follows by embedding any order of
cardinality at most $\mu$.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Why cardinality and abstract types are insufficient}

The same theorem applies to many numerically different alphabets.
For birthday fragments,
\[
 |\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}\quad(\kappa\text{ infinite initial}),
 \qquad
 |\No_{<\theta}|=2^\kappa\quad(\kappa<\theta<\kappa^+).
\]
The second formula follows because the full sign level of length
$\kappa$ is present and there are at most $\kappa$ levels, each of
size at most $2^\kappa$. It does not imply that the numerical
alphabets are equimorphic. The next section proves exactly the contrary
(\merge\ \cref{swo:bw:bs:sec:spectrum}, Part~XI).

Nor does enumeration lexicography descend to abstract well-order types.
Two presentations of the same type can fall on opposite sides of a
third presentation after a change in the early labels. Ordering the
possible types themselves by ordinal comparison gives the interval of
types $\mu\le\alpha<\mu^+$, whose order type is $\mu^+$.
By \Cref{swo:bw:thm:baseline}, that type cannot embed in the labelled order.
For set-like global well-orders, quotienting by abstract class-order
isomorphism collapses all objects to the single type $\Ord$.

\noindent\merge\ Source~29's Subsection~3.3, ``Relation scans and inverse
ranks'', is printed in Part~XII with the scans (\cref{swo:bw:sub:scans}).

\subsection{Source 30: scope, results, and the audited starting point}\label{swo:rt:sec:scope}

\merge\ Source~30's Section~1, printed whole; its interpretations (Section~2)
are printed in Part~XII (\cref{swo:rt:sec:interpretations}). Its $\mathfrak W_{\mathrm{sl}}$,
$\mathfrak W_{\mathrm{all}}$ (macros \verb|\SL|, \verb|\ALL|) are $\Hsl$,
$\Hall$; its $X_\kappa$ is printed $\No_{<\kappa}$ and its countable strata
$P_n=\WO_{\omega+n}(\mathbb Q)$ are printed $P_{\omega+n}$, as in source~29
(\cref{swo:b83:sub:notation83}).

Two choices precede every substantive question in this subject:
\emph{what objects are being ordered}, and \emph{which representation is
scanned}. A well-order of a fixed set can be represented by its ordinal
enumeration, its relation table, or the ranks of labels in a previously
fixed list. These representations give different comparisons. On the
full surreal class, an individual well-order is itself a class relation,
so the collection of all such relations is not an ordinary class of sets.

This article continues the merged ProveIt report
\emph{Lexicographic Orders of Well-Orderings of the Surreal Numbers}
\cite{swoAtPin}, inspected at the fixed revision
\[
\texttt{7ff7736ecf3a0adc8536b2d083cf819e1ba39ace}.
\]
Its location is
\begin{quote}\small
\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/docs/foundations-and-computation/}\\
\path{surreal-well-orders/article.tex}.
\end{quote}
We also inspected its guide and the four foundational Lean files listed
in \cref{swo:rt:sec:formal}. Some questions retained from the first wave are
answered elsewhere in the merged text or in subsequent reports.
Appearance in an old research list is therefore not, by itself,
evidence that a problem remains open.

\subsubsection{The inherited baseline}

The previous work develops fixed-set cardinalities and ordinal spectra;
the singular strong-limit birthday transition; set-length words and
termination conventions; the equivalence of global choice with the
existence of any class well-order of $\No$; direct comparison through
proper-class common prefixes; and a bounded-support core, isomorphic to
$\No$ under global choice, together with cut recognition and
automorphism-extension obstructions. Finite residual permutation
blocks, nonmonotone restrictions, class-model absoluteness, and
countable external classifications have also already been studied.
We do not present these as new findings.

\subsubsection{Four continuations}

Throughout, $\equi$ means \emph{equimorphism}: order embeddings exist
in both directions. It does not mean isomorphism.

\paragraph{Infinite remainders.}
For an infinite cardinal $\kappa$, put
\[
\mu=2^{<\kappa},\quad
\rho_\kappa=
\begin{cases}
\kappa\cdot\kappa,&\kappa\text{ singular strong limit},\\
\mu,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
For every infinite regular $\nu<\mu$, every
$0<\gamma<\mu^+$ and $0<\delta<\nu^+$, and every finite $n$, we prove
\[\tag{S30.1.1}
\WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\nu\cdot\delta+n}(\No_{<\kappa})
\equi
\BB_{\rho_\kappa\cdot\gamma+\nu\cdot\delta}\times n!.
\label{swo:rt:eq:headline-remainders}
\]
Here $n!$ is a finite chain; products of orders are lexicographic;
subscripts use ordinal arithmetic. In particular $\nu=\omega$ handles
every countably infinite remainder. The argument iterates through
finite descending sequences of residual cardinals. A singular
strong-limit block of size $\nu$ instead contributes $\nu\cdot\nu$
per block. Mixing these two regimes gives a complete fixed-type
equimorphism classification under GCH
(\cref{swo:rt:cor:all-types-controlled-cardinals}). The remaining
unconditional boundary is a singular residual cardinal at most $\kappa$
that is not strong limit. Residual cardinals above $\kappa$ also
have uninflated codes, even when singular. In particular, every
fixed type is classified in ZFC whenever $\kappa<\aleph_\omega$,
including $\kappa=\omega_1$ without CH
(\cref{swo:rt:cor:omega-one-all-types-ZFC}).

\noindent\merge\ Source~19 proves the same classification independently and
more generally (cube spectrum also at singular non-strong-limit layers):
\cref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich,swo:rs:thm:tail-cubes}. Source~30's explicit
$\ZFC$ corollary for $\kappa<\aleph_\omega$ is the one statement source~19
does not spell out (source~19 writes $\mu\le\aleph_\omega$). Neither source
saw the other.

\paragraph{Topological and measurable transitions.}
For $P_{\omega+n}=\WO_{\omega+n}(\mathbb Q)$, the order topology is Polish and
homeomorphic to Baire space at $n=0$. At $n=1$ it is still second
countable and metrizable but is meagre in itself. At $n=2$ it is
separable and first countable, but nonmetrizable, and its Borel
structure is not standard. At $n\geq3$ it has continuum many isolated
points forming a dense open set and becomes a Baire space again.
The maps between relation tables and enumerations have different,
sharp measurability thresholds. Since $\No_{<\omega}$ is a countable
dense order without endpoints, the same results hold at the first
infinite surreal stage $\No_{<\omega}$.

\paragraph{Partial relation data and global type.}
A set-sized partial table extends to a well-order of \emph{any supplied
proper-class well-order type} precisely when its forced orientations
are well-founded, together with diagonal consistency. Each admitted
global type is dense for set-supported relation observations. Finite
observations approximate all linear orders; countable observations
already detect ill-foundedness, but cannot detect set-likeness or
the global class order type.

\paragraph{Recovery of the class universe.}
For GBC realizations of the same set model, inclusion of the admitted
labelled global enumeration families is equivalent to inclusion of
their whole class collections. Adjacent pair swaps along one common
baseline already encode every class. The pure external order loses
this information; the evaluation relation is essential.

\subsubsection{The precise Kanovei--Shelah connection}

Kanovei and Shelah lexicographically order maps
$a:\mathfrak c\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters
\cite[Section 2]{KanoveiShelah} (\merge\ Section~2 of the published paper;
Section~1, page~2, of the preprint). Such maps can repeat values. Their
index order is not literally the set of all bijective well-orderings
of $\mathbb R$, or all class well-orders of $\No$. The common idea is
a well-ordered coordinate domain and a linearly ordered alphabet.
Keeping the actual indexing object straight prevents a misleading
identification at the start of the surreal generalization.

\section{Thick alphabets, prefix cylinders and the prefix topology (source 24; sources 26, 28, 21, 22 and 19)}\label{swo:x:sec:prefix}\label{swo:pc:sec:alphabet}

\merge\ Source~24's Sections~3 and~4 are printed, with its re-proofs of results of

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 219-229
A surreal can be represented by a set-length sign sequence; see also Ehrlich\,\cite{Ehrlich2012} for the broader arithmetic and foundational setting. Write $\bd(x)$ for its length, and for an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$ put
\[
 \No_{<\kappa}=\{x:\bd(x)<\kappa\},\qquad
 \mu=2^{<\kappa}=\sup_{\alpha<\kappa}2^{|\alpha|}.
\]
All cardinal arithmetic in this section is external $\ZFC$ arithmetic. There is no assumption that $\kappa$ is regular, that $\mu=\kappa$, or that a birthday cutoff is a subfield.

\begin{definition}[Thickness]\label{swo:pc:def:thick}
A linear order $X$ of infinite cardinality $\mu$ is \emph{$\mu$-thick} if it is dense without endpoints and every nonempty open interval and every ray has cardinality $\mu$.
\end{definition}


\begin{note}[Source~24, Lemma~3.2, ``Cutoff size and thickness'']\label{swo:pc:lem:cutoff}
\emph{For every infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$, the alphabet $\No_{<\kappa}$ has
cardinality $2^{<\kappa}$ and is $2^{<\kappa}$-thick. Removing fewer than $\mu$
points from a $\mu$-thick alphabet leaves a $\mu$-thick alphabet of the same
cardinality.} This is \cref{swo:gs:lem:alphabet-size} (source~17), by the same
sign-cone argument. Source~24 makes the cone explicit in three cases: if neither
of $a<b$ is a prefix of the other, or if $b$ is a proper prefix of $a$, every
extension of $r=a\cat(+)$ lies in $(a,b)$; if $a$ is a proper prefix of $b$, the
next sign of $b$ is plus and $r=a\cat(+)\cat(-)^{\bd(b)+1}$ works, since ``either a
later plus of $b$ gives the first strict comparison, or the negative tail extends
past the end of $b$''. It stresses that ``finite ordinal sums of ordinals below an
infinite initial cardinal remain below it; regularity is not needed here'', and
obtains the deletion clause by applying the cardinality count inside each old
interval and ray. Source~15's three-case construction
(\cref{swo:cb:new:lem:full-size-intervals}) uses $b\cat-$ in the second case.
\end{note}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 251-255
\begin{remark}[What the arithmetic parameters do and do not control]\label{swo:pc:n3.3}
The previous cutoff study (source~17; \cref{swo:gs:lem:alphabet-character,swo:gs:thm:invariants}) distinguishes $\cf\kappa$, which controls several alphabet-side characters, from $\cf(2^{<\kappa})$, which controls prefix-neighborhood characters in the minimal enumeration slice. The topology below uses $\mu=|X|$ as its domain length. Replacing it by the birthday bound $\kappa$ without checking equality would change the problem.
\end{remark}

The proof also explains why the relevant formalization should begin with sign sequences and a linear-order interface, not with the whole surreal field. Addition, multiplication, normal forms, and real closedness are unnecessary for the main results.

\subsection{The minimal slice: prefixes and elementary spectra (source 24)}\label{swo:pc:sec:basic}

\merge\ Source~24's Section~4. Its prefix lemmas hold for every infinite alphabet
and, under thickness, for the order topology; for $X=\No_{<\kappa}$ and the minimal
slice they are \cref{swo:gs:lem:cylinder-base} (source~17). New are the injection
space $\I_\mu(X)$ beside $\WO_\mu(X)$, the metrizability criterion and the
relabelling corollary.

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 259-287
For an infinite $\mu$ and a set $X$ of size $\mu$, let
\[
 \I_{<\mu}(X)=\bigcup_{\alpha<\mu}\Inj(\alpha,X).
\]
For $p\in\I_{<\mu}(X)$, define its cylinders in the two spaces by
\[
 [p]_{P}=\{f\in\WO_\mu(X):p\subseteq f\},\qquad
 [p]_\I=\{h\in\I_\mu(X):p\subseteq h\}.
\]
The subscript will be omitted when the ambient space is clear.

\begin{lemma}[Small-prefix extension]\label{swo:pc:lem:extension}
Every $p:\alpha\to X$ in $\I_{<\mu}(X)$ extends to a member of $\WO_\mu(X)$. Moreover, if $z\notin\ran p$, it extends to a bijection $\mu\to X\setminus\{z\}$, viewed as a nonexhaustive member of $\I_\mu(X)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The unused labels have cardinality $\mu$, even after the one additional deletion. The ordinal tail $[\alpha,\mu)$ has order type $\mu$: its cardinality is $\mu$, its type is at most $\mu$, and $\mu$ is initial. Choose a bijection between the tail and the required unused labels and append it to $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cylinders and order topology]\label{swo:pc:lem:cylinders}
Suppose $X$ is $\mu$-thick. In both $\WO_\mu(X)$ and $\I_\mu(X)$, cylinders are nonempty convex clopen sets without endpoints and form a base for the lexicographic order topology. Both orders are dense without endpoints.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If a word lies lexicographically between two words sharing $p$, it shares $p$; otherwise its first disagreement with $p$ puts it on the same exterior side of both words. Thus cylinders are convex. The complement of a length-$\alpha$ cylinder is the union of the other length-$\alpha$ cylinders.

Let $f$ extend $p$, where $\dom p=\alpha$. Fewer than $\mu$ labels have been used. Choose unused labels $u<f(\alpha)<v$, and complete $p\cat(u)$ and $p\cat(v)$ using Lemma~\ref{swo:pc:lem:extension}. These give points of $[p]$ on both sides of $f$. Hence $[p]$ is open and has no endpoints; its complement is open as well.

If $g<f<h$, take a prefix of $f$ extending beyond its first disagreements with $g$ and $h$. Its cylinder is contained in $(g,h)$. Rays are handled using one disagreement. This proves the base assertion. Finally, at the first differing coordinate of any two words, an unused label strictly between their two labels gives an intermediate exhaustive completion. The same construction gives points above or below any given word.
\end{proof}


\begin{note}[Source~24, Proposition~4.3, ``Cardinality and exact ordinal spectrum'']\label{swo:pc:prop:spectrum}
\emph{For any infinite linearly ordered alphabet $X$ of size $\mu$,
$\card{\WO_\mu(X)}=2^\mu$. Every linear order of cardinality at most $\mu$ embeds
into $\WO_\mu(X)$. An ordinal $\beta$ embeds into this lexicographic order exactly
when $\beta<\mu^+$; the same bound holds for reverse ordinal orders.} This is the
set baseline (\cref{swo:sw:setspectrum}; reals report \code{lwo:prop:cardinality},
\code{lwo:thm:ordinal-spectrum}) on the minimal slice, by the pair-orientation,
initial-segment and coordinate-stabilization argument of \cref{swo:sw:fixed}; it is
\cref{swo:gs:prop:local-universality} without its interval clause. Source~24 adds:
``For comparison, the predecessor report proves that the full fixed-carrier order
$\WO(X)$ also has cardinality $2^\mu$ and exact ordinal spectrum
$\{\beta:\beta<\mu^+\}$. The positive embeddings already occur in the minimal
slice. The upper-bound argument for the full varying-length space is a separate
result, not an automatic consequence of the fixed-coordinate proof above. Equal
cardinality and ordinal spectrum do not identify their topologies or their
adjacency structure.''
\end{note}

\merge\ The character assertion of the next proposition is
\cref{swo:gs:thm:invariants} (point character $q=\cf\mu$) for an arbitrary
alphabet; the metrizability criterion is source~24's.

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 305-321
\begin{proposition}[Local character and metrizability]\label{swo:pc:prop:metric}
In the prefix topology on $\WO_\mu(X)$, each point has neighborhood character $\cf\mu$. The space is metrizable exactly when $\cf\mu=\omega$. The same holds for $\I_\mu(X)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Restrictions to any cofinal sequence of prefix lengths give a base of size $\cf\mu$. Conversely, for every member $U$ of a local base at $f$, choose a cylinder $[f\res\alpha_U]\subseteq U$. If there were fewer than $\cf\mu$ members, the lengths would be bounded by some $\gamma<\mu$. Every such $U$ would contain $[f\res\gamma]$. No one of them could be contained in the strictly smaller neighborhood $[f\res(\gamma+1)]$, a contradiction. The strictness follows by changing coordinate $\gamma$ and completing the resulting prefix.

When $\cf\mu=\omega$, fix increasing cofinal lengths $\alpha_n<\mu$. Give two distinct words distance $2^{-n}$, where $n$ is the least index at which their restrictions to $\alpha_n$ differ. This is a compatible ultrametric. If $\cf\mu>\omega$, the space is not first countable and hence not metrizable.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The topology forgets the numerical labels]\label{swo:pc:cor:relabel}
A bijection $a:X\to Y$ induces a homeomorphism $f\mapsto a\circ f$ of the corresponding prefix spaces. If both alphabets are $\mu$-thick, this is a homeomorphism of their lexicographic order topologies. It is an order isomorphism precisely when $a$ is increasing.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Relabelling carries cylinders to cylinders. An increasing relabelling preserves first disagreement. Conversely, use exhaustive enumerations with prescribed distinct first labels to see that an order-preserving relabelling must preserve the alphabet order.
\end{proof}

This is the first indication that a topological classification and an order classification answer different questions. Numerical comparison is indispensable for the order, but under thickness it is invisible to the topology of the minimal slice.

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 251-256
\begin{proposition}[Basic topology]\label{swo:nb:prop:basic}
The cylinders form a clopen base for a Hausdorff zero-dimensional topology on $\WO_\mu(X)$ and on $\I_\mu(X)$. The former is dense in the latter. Every permutation cylinder is homeomorphic to $\WO_\mu(X)$, after an arbitrary bijective relabelling of its remaining alphabet.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Two prefixes are either incompatible or one extends the other, so cylinder intersections have the required base property. The complement of $N_p$ is a union of cylinders witnessing a disagreement before $\dom p$. Distinct functions have a coordinate of disagreement and disjoint longer cylinders. Density is \cref{swo:nb:lem:extension}. For the final statement, remove the prescribed prefix, increasingly reindex the ordinal tail, and bijectively relabel $X\setminus\ran p$ by $X$. Both this map and its inverse carry bounded-prefix neighborhoods to bounded-prefix neighborhoods.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Residual cylinders and an exact character formula (source 22)}\label{swo:rg:sec:residual}

% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 238-312
\subsubsection{The residual-fibre identity}
For an injective prefix $p:\beta\to X$ of a length-$\alpha$ enumeration, let
\[
 R_p=X\setminus\ran p,\qquad \gamma_p=\otp([\beta,\alpha)).
\]
The prefix is extendible exactly when $|R_p|=|\gamma_p|$.

\begin{theorem}[Residual-cylinder identity]\label{swo:rg:thm:residual}
For every extendible prefix $p$, concatenation is an order isomorphism
\[
 \WO_{\gamma_p}(R_p)\ \cong\ \{e\in\WO_\alpha(X):e\res\beta=p\}.
\]
The image is convex. In particular, if $\alpha=\mu+\nu$ and $R\subseteq X$ satisfies $|R|=|\nu|$ and $|X\setminus R|=\mu$, every length-$\mu$ enumeration of $X\setminus R$ determines a convex copy of $\WO_\nu(R)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Restriction to the remaining coordinate interval and reindexing by its order type are inverse to concatenation. All initial coordinates are equal, so first disagreement occurs in the tail. An enumeration between two extensions of $p$ cannot disagree with $p$ earlier than $\beta$, since such a disagreement puts it on the same outside side of both extensions.
\end{proof}

The theorem is elementary, but its consequence is substantial: after $\mu$ coordinates, the original birthday alphabet imposes no uniform residual-cardinality condition beyond the prescribed tail length. A proof valid only while fewer than $\mu$ labels have been consumed cannot simply be reused.

\subsubsection{Characters and disagreement fibres}
For a point $e$ in a linear order $P$, define
\[
 \chi^-(e;P)=\cf(P_{<e}),\qquad
 \chi^+(e;P)=\ci(P_{>e}).
\]
We assign character $0$ to an empty side and character $1$ to a side with a greatest, respectively least, element. Thus $(1,1)$ means an isolated non-endpoint.

For $e\in\WO_\alpha(X)$ put
\[
 X_\beta=X\setminus e[\beta],\qquad
 A^-_e=\{\beta<\alpha:(X_\beta)_{<e(\beta)}\ne\varnothing\},
\]
with $A^+_e$ defined similarly. These are the coordinates at which a smaller or larger first disagreement is possible. Let $H^-_\beta$ and $H^+_\beta$ be the corresponding fibres.

\begin{theorem}[General first-disagreement formula]\label{swo:rg:thm:characters}
For any infinite set alphabet and any enumeration length,
\[
 P_{<e}\cong\sum_{\beta\in A^-_e}H^-_\beta,
\]
where the index set has its increasing ordinal order. The upper side is the analogous sum in reverse coordinate order. Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item If $A^-_e$ is empty, $\chi^-(e;P)=0$.
\item If $A^-_e$ has no greatest member, $\chi^-(e;P)=\cf(A^-_e)$.
\item If $A^-_e$ has greatest member $\beta_*$, then $\chi^-(e;P)=\cf(H^-_{\beta_*})$.
\end{enumerate}
The dual statements hold on the right. More explicitly, with $\gamma=\otp([\beta+1,\alpha))$,
\[
 H^-_\beta\cong
 \sum_{a\in(X_\beta)_{<e(\beta)}}\WO_\gamma(X_\beta\setminus\{a\}).
\]
Thus, if the next-label index order has no greatest element, its cofinality is the cofinality of the fibre; if it has greatest element $a_*$, the last residual enumeration order supplies the cofinality.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every $f<e$ has one first-disagreement coordinate. If this coordinate is $\beta<\delta$, and $g<e$ first disagrees at $\delta$, then $f<g$, because $g(\beta)=e(\beta)>f(\beta)$. For fixed $\beta$, varying the label $a<e(\beta)$ gives the displayed lexicographic sum, and the remainder is exactly the residual cylinder. Every allowed label has a completion: deleting any one member of the same residual set leaves the required cardinality.

For a sum of nonempty orders indexed by a limit well-order, choosing one point on a cofinal collection of indices yields a cofinal set. Conversely, every cofinal set projects to cofinally many indices. If there is a last index, the last summand is cofinal. Applying these facts twice proves the formula. Reverse the order for the upper side.
\end{proof}

This is an exact reduction, not an assertion that arbitrary residual endpoint cofinalities already have a simple closed formula. Limit prefixes can fail to be extendible even when every shorter prefix is extendible. For example, the decreasing enumeration of $\omega^*$ has length $\omega$; its finite prefixes extend to length $\omega\cdot2$ enumerations of that alphabet, but their union exhausts the alphabet too early.

\subsubsection{Endpoint replacement after the first cardinal block}
\begin{theorem}[Character transfer]\label{swo:rg:thm:transfer}
Let $X$ be $\mu$-rich, $q=\cf\mu$, and $\alpha=\mu+\nu$. Write $e=p\cat t$, where $p$ has length $\mu$, $R=X\setminus\ran p$, and $t\in\WO_\nu(R)$. Then
\[
 \chi^\pm(e;\WO_\alpha(X))=
 \begin{cases}
 \chi^\pm(t;\WO_\nu(R)),&\text{if that intrinsic side is nonempty},\\
 q,&\text{if that intrinsic side is empty}.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A nonempty part of the cylinder below $e$ is cofinal in the entire lower side of $e$: every point below $e$ outside the cylinder lies below all its points. This proves the first case. If $t$ is the cylinder minimum, all lower first disagreements occur before $\mu$. At every $\beta<\mu$, richness supplies an unused smaller label, so the active coordinate set is exactly $\mu$. \Cref{swo:rg:thm:characters} gives $q$. The right side is dual. The proof also covers $\nu=0$, when the cylinder is a singleton.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The finite-tail transition and all fixed-length cardinal invariants (source 22)}\label{swo:rg:sec:finite}

% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 315-360
The order topology is always intended. Density $\dens P$ is the least cardinality of a dense subset, weight $\weight P$ the least cardinality of a base, and cellularity $\cell P$ the supremum of the sizes of families of pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets. A $\pi$-base need only contain a nonempty open subset of each nonempty open set; it need not provide neighborhoods of every individual point.

\begin{theorem}[Topological classification of every fixed-length stratum]\label{swo:rg:thm:topology}
Let $X$ be $\mu$-rich, let $\Delta=\mu^{<\mu}$, and let $|\alpha|=\mu$. Then
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{enumeration length}&\dens\WO_\alpha(X)&\cell\WO_\alpha(X)&\weight\WO_\alpha(X)\\ \hline
\mu\text{ or }\mu+1&\Delta&\Delta&\Delta\\
\mu+2&\Delta&\Delta&2^\mu\\
\alpha\geq\mu+3&2^\mu&2^\mu&2^\mu
\end{array}
\]
Thus this table applies to every ordinal length of cardinality $\mu$, not merely to finite extensions of $\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{The common lower bound.} For each $\beta<\mu$, there are $\mu^{|\beta|}$ injective prefixes of length $\beta$. To verify the lower estimate, partition $X$ into $|\beta|$ disjoint sets of size $\mu$ and choose the $\xi$th entry from the $\xi$th set; the finite and empty cases are immediate. Distinct prefixes of that length have disjoint, nonempty open cylinders by \cref{swo:rg:lem:short}. Consequently
\[
 \cell\WO_\alpha(X)\geq\sup_{\beta<\mu}\mu^{|\beta|}=\Delta.
\]
There are altogether $\Delta$ short prefixes, since $\Delta\geq\mu$.

\emph{The first three lengths.} Suppose $\alpha=\mu+n$ with $n\leq2$. If two distinct enumerations have the same length-$\mu$ prefix, they lie in a fibre of size $n!\leq2$. Their open interval is therefore empty. Hence the endpoints $e<f$ of any nonempty open interval must first disagree at some $\beta<\mu$. Choose an unused label
\[
 e(\beta)<a<f(\beta)
\]
above the common prefix, and extend that prefix by $a$. Richness ensures that deleting the fewer than $\mu$ earlier labels does not exhaust this interval. The resulting short cylinder is contained in $(e,f)$.

The orders have no endpoints, because their first labels can always be moved down or up. Thus every nonempty open set contains such an interval, and the short cylinders form a $\pi$-base. Choose one point from each cylinder. This gives a dense subset of size at most $\Delta$. Since disjoint nonempty open sets require different points of a dense set,
\[
 \Delta\leq\cell P\leq\dens P\leq\Delta.
\]

For $n=0,1$, any two distinct enumerations differ before $\mu$, so the same interpolation argument shows that $P$ is dense as an order. In a dense order without endpoints, intervals with endpoints in a dense subset form a base. Therefore $\weight P=\Delta$ in these two cases.

For $n=2$, fix a two-element subset $R\subset X$. There are $2^\mu$ bijections $p:\mu\to X\setminus R$. Each cylinder of such a $p$ consists of two adjacent points, say $a_p<b_p$. These are pairwise disjoint jumps. For each jump, a base must contain an element $B_p$ with
\[
 b_p\in B_p\subseteq(a_p,\infty).
\]
Different jumps require different base elements: if the $p$-jump precedes the $p'$-jump, then $b_p\leq a_{p'}$, so $B_{p'}$ cannot contain $b_p$. Thus $\weight P\geq2^\mu$. Every order of size $2^\mu$ has an interval base of size at most $2^\mu$, proving equality.

\emph{Every remaining length.} Write $\alpha=\mu+\nu$, where $\nu\geq3$. Choose $R\subset X$ with $|R|=|\nu|$ and $|X\setminus R|=\mu$. There are $2^\mu$ length-$\mu$ enumerations of $X\setminus R$. Their cylinders are pairwise disjoint convex copies of $\WO_\nu(R)$ by \cref{swo:rg:thm:residual}. This residual order has at least three points. Choose $u_p<v_p<w_p$ in each cylinder. Then $(u_p,w_p)$ is a nonempty open interval, contained in that cylinder. We have obtained $2^\mu$ pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets. The inequalities
\[
 2^\mu\leq\cell P\leq\dens P\leq\weight P\leq |P|^2=2^\mu
\]
finish the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[\merge; credits for \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology}]\label{swo:x:note:rg-credits}
The density and cellularity columns of the table are \cref{swo:ds:thm:density}
(source~16; source~18's route in \cref{swo:sh:sec:new-bounded-invariants}), proved

changes at the second terminal coordinate and density and cellularity at the

\end{note}

\begin{remark}[Why the distinction between a base and a $\pi$-base matters]\label{swo:rg:n5.2}
At length $\mu+2$, short cylinders still detect every nonempty open set, but they cannot refine a neighborhood of an upper jump point which excludes its lower partner. Treating the short-prefix $\pi$-base as a neighborhood base would give the false conclusion $\weight P=\Delta$ whenever $\Delta<2^\mu$. Conversely, a length-$\mu$ cylinder is convex, but its two-point endpoints prevent it from being open. Both distinctions are essential.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Birthday-cutoff form]\label{swo:rg:cor:birthday-topology}
For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, put $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ and $\Delta=\mu^{<\mu}$. The table in \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology} holds for $X=\No_{<\kappa}$ without assuming that $\kappa$ or $\mu$ is regular. Moreover, for every $\alpha$ of cardinality $\mu$,
\[
 \cf\WO_\alpha(X)=\ci\WO_\alpha(X)=\cf\kappa.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{swo:rg:lem:rich}. For the last assertion, the first-label projection expresses the order as a lexicographic sum of nonempty fibres indexed by $X$. Since $X$ has neither endpoint, the cofinality and coinitiality are those of the indexing order.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Finite fibres and exact point characters}
Let
\[
 Q_n(X)=\{p:\mu\hookrightarrow X:|X\setminus\ran p|=n\},
\]
with first-disagreement order. Sorting each finite residual set identifies its permutation order with the finite chain of size $n!$.

\begin{proposition}[Finite-tail normal form]\label{swo:rg:prop:finite-normal}
For each finite $n$, there is an order isomorphism
\[
 \WO_{\mu+n}(X)\cong Q_n(X)\times_{\lex} n!.
\]
The order $Q_n(X)$ is dense without endpoints, has cardinality $2^\mu$, and every point has character $(\cf\mu,\cf\mu)$. Its density, cellularity, and weight are $\mu^{<\mu}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The residual-cylinder identity gives the displayed lexicographic sum and hence the isomorphism. Distinct elements of $Q_n(X)$ differ at a coordinate below $\mu$. At that coordinate one can insert an unused label strictly between their labels, then complete a length-$\mu$ injection leaving exactly $n$ labels. This proves density; changing the first label proves the absence of endpoints.

For a fixed $p$, smaller and larger first disagreements are possible at every $\beta<\mu$. The argument of \cref{swo:rg:thm:characters}, applied directly to these prefixes, gives characters $(\cf\mu,\cf\mu)$. The cardinality is $2^\mu$ by fixing a residual set of size $n$. The short-cylinder counting and $\pi$-base argument from \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology} applies to $Q_n(X)$ as well. Density of its order then converts the dense subset into a base of the same size.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All finite-tail point characters]\label{swo:rg:thm:finite-chars}
Let $q=\cf\mu$. The complete character classification for $\WO_{\mu+n}(X)$ is
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
n&\text{characters and positions within each }n!\text{-point block}\\ \hline
0,1&(q,q)\text{ at every point}\\
2&(q,1)\text{ at the first point};\quad(1,q)\text{ at the last point}\\
n\geq3&(q,1)\text{ first};\quad(1,1)\text{ at the }n!-2\text{ interior points};
\\ &\hspace{0pt}(1,q)\text{ last}.
\end{array}
\]
For $n\geq3$, there are exactly $2^\mu$ isolated points, and they form a dense subset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inside a finite chain, each nonempty side has character one. At a block endpoint, the missing intrinsic side acquires character $q$ by \cref{swo:rg:thm:transfer}. Singleton blocks acquire $q$ on both sides.

A point with both an immediate predecessor and an immediate successor is isolated. Hence exactly the interior points of the finite blocks are isolated. There are $2^\mu$ blocks and a fixed positive finite number of interior points per block. To see density, take a nonempty interval. If it lies within a single block, it contains an interior block point. If its endpoints have different blocks, density of $Q_n(X)$ supplies a whole intervening block, which has an interior point.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[One-step derivative]\label{swo:rg:n5.6}
For $n\geq3$, the first Cantor--Bendixson derivative of $\WO_{\mu+n}(X)$ consists exactly of the first and last points of each finite block. The derivative has no isolated points in its subspace topology, so the derivatives stabilize at this stage. For $n\leq2$, the original space has no isolated points.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is the isolated-point classification. Between distinct blocks there are further blocks arbitrarily close in the relevant direction. Consequently each retained first point is accumulated from below by retained endpoints, and each retained last point is accumulated from above. No retained endpoint is isolated after the interior points are removed. For singleton blocks both sides have character $q\geq\omega$; for two-point blocks one side still has that character.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A countable alphabet]\label{swo:rg:n5.7}
Take $\kappa=\omega$, so $\mu=\omega$, $q=\omega$, and $\Delta=\omega$. The orders at lengths $\omega$ and $\omega+1$ are second-countable. At length $\omega+2$ the order is separable and first-countable but not second-countable: it has $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct jumps. At length $\omega+3$ it has $2^{\aleph_0}$ isolated points, densely distributed in six-point blocks. Thus extending an exhaustive enumeration by only two or three ordinal positions changes its topology sharply, although the alphabet cardinality and ordinal embedding spectrum have not changed.
\end{example}

\merge\ Source~30 proves the weight column for every infinite alphabet, with no
density, regularity, saturation or endpoint hypothesis. Its ``established''
inputs are the finite-residual decomposition (\cref{swo:rg:prop:finite-normal},
whose proof does not use richness) and the density theorem
\cref{swo:ds:thm:density}.

\begin{corollary}[Weight for arbitrary infinite alphabets]
\label{swo:rt:cor:finite-tail-weight-general}
Let $X$ be any infinite linearly ordered set of cardinality $\mu$,
and let $n<\omega$.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{w}(\operatorname{Bij}(\mu+n,X))=
 \begin{cases}
  \mu^{<\mu},&n=0,1,\\
  2^\mu,&n\geq2.
 \end{cases}
\]
No density, regularity, saturation or endpoint hypothesis on $X$
is needed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the established finite-residual decomposition and dense-quotient
lemma for arbitrary infinite alphabets.  For $n=0,1$ the fibers have
one point, so the order is dense.  In an infinite dense linear
order, a dense subset gives a base of intervals and endpoint rays;
thus weight equals density.  The established density calculation
is $\mu^{<\mu}$ in these two cases.

For $n=2$, fix an omitted pair.  There are $2^\mu$ bijections from
$\mu$ to its complement, producing $2^\mu$ distinct adjacent
pairs in the full order.  The base-set argument in the preceding
proof gives weight at least $2^\mu$.  For $n\geq3$, the same
argument with a fixed omitted $n$-element set gives $2^\mu$
isolated interior points of finite fibers.  In all cases the
whole order has cardinality $2^\mu$, which bounds its weight above.
\end{proof}

This refines the density and cellularity threshold in the existing
fixed-type analysis.  Weight changes at the \emph{second} terminal
coordinate, whereas density and cellularity change at the third.
The numerical values can coincide when $\mu^{<\mu}=2^\mu$; the
finite-fiber geometry still distinguishes the mechanisms.

\subsection{Infinite tails and the general adjacency mechanism (source 22)}\label{swo:rg:sec:infinite}

\merge\ \Cref{swo:rg:lem:adjacency} is the fixed-stratum form of this report's
adjacency theorems (\cref{swo:cf:adjacency,swo:st:thm:adjacency}); source~22's proof is printed because the next lemma
uses its tail argument.

% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 427-477
\subsubsection{Why infinite residuals cannot make jumps}
The finite-tail origin of adjacency was established in the earlier reports for more general enumeration comparisons (\cref{swo:cf:adjacency}; source~17). The following fixed-stratum form is useful here.

\begin{lemma}[Adjacency forces a finite residual]\label{swo:rg:lem:adjacency}
Let $X$ be an infinite linearly ordered set and write an infinite ordinal $\alpha$ uniquely as $\alpha=\lambda+n$, where $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal and $n<\omega$. The adjacent pairs in $\WO_\alpha(X)$ are precisely the consecutive permutations in a common length-$\lambda$ prefix cylinder. Its maximal finite adjacency components are therefore the $n!$-point cylinders, with singleton components when $n=0$ or $1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $e<f$ are adjacent, and let $\beta$ be their first disagreement. Fixing the prefix through $e(\beta)$, the remaining tail of $e$ must be lexicographically greatest among all exhaustive permutations of its residual labels. Otherwise a larger such tail would produce a point strictly between $e$ and $f$. Swapping entries at an increasing pair of tail positions shows that this greatest tail is numerically strictly decreasing. Dually, the tail of $f$ after its first differing label must be numerically strictly increasing.

Let $R$ be the common set of unused labels before coordinate $\beta$. The inherited numerical order on
\[
 R\setminus\{e(\beta),f(\beta)\}
\]
is both well-ordered and reverse well-ordered. Such a set is finite: if infinite, its first $\omega$ increasing elements have no greatest member, contradicting reverse well-ordering. Hence $R$ is finite, and the remaining coordinate interval $[\beta,\alpha)$ is finite. Therefore $\beta\geq\lambda$.

Conversely, the common length-$\lambda$ prefix cylinder is a finite convex chain of $n!$ permutations. Consecutive points in it are adjacent in the whole order. No adjacency crosses between these cylinders, proving the component assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The tail of order type \texorpdfstring{$\omega$}{omega}}
\begin{lemma}[Countable residual enumeration orders]\label{swo:rg:lem:countable-tail}
For a countably infinite linearly ordered set $R$, the order $\WO_\omega(R)$ has no adjacent pair and is separable. Each nonempty side of a point has character $\omega$. A minimum exists exactly when the numerical order type of $R$ is $\omega$, and a maximum exists exactly when its order type is $\omega^*$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are no jumps by \cref{swo:rg:lem:adjacency}. There are countably many finite injective prefixes. Choose one exhaustive completion of each. Given a nonempty interval, choose an interior enumeration $h$. Its comparisons with the endpoints are both decided at finite coordinates. A sufficiently long finite prefix of $h$ has its entire cylinder in the interval. Therefore the chosen completions form a countable dense set. A nonempty side has no extremal point, because there are no jumps; its cofinality or coinitiality is at most $\omega$ by separability and cannot be finite. It is therefore $\omega$.

If an enumeration is the minimum, every pair of its entries must be numerically increasing; otherwise swapping an inversion produces a smaller enumeration. Thus it is a strictly increasing exhaustive enumeration of length $\omega$, and $R$ has order type $\omega$. Conversely, that enumeration always chooses the least unused label, so is lexicographically least. The maximum assertion is dual.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact $\mu+\omega$ character spectrum]\label{swo:rg:thm:omega-chars}
For a $\mu$-rich alphabet $X$ and $q=\cf\mu$, the complete set of point characters in $\WO_{\mu+\omega}(X)$ is
\[
 \{(q,\omega),(\omega,q),(\omega,\omega)\}.
\]
Repeated pairs are counted only once. The order is dense without endpoints, has no isolated points, and has density, cellularity, and weight $2^\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The length-$\mu$ prefix leaves a countably infinite residual set $R$. Apply \cref{swo:rg:lem:countable-tail,swo:rg:thm:transfer}. A countably infinite order cannot have both an increasing and a decreasing exhaustive $\omega$-enumeration, so its permutation order cannot have both endpoints. This gives exactly the three displayed possibilities.

Each possibility occurs. A rich alphabet contains a countable increasing sequence of type $\omega$, a decreasing one of type $\omega^*$, and a countable dense suborder without endpoints. These can be chosen inside a fixed interval with an outside complement of size $\mu$. Leaving one of these sets as the residual alphabet realizes the first, second, and third cases, respectively. For the dense suborder, recursively satisfy all rational-order requirements inside the interval, using density to place each new point. This requires only countably many choices.

The length $\mu+\omega$ is a limit ordinal, so there are no adjacent pairs by \cref{swo:rg:lem:adjacency}. There are no global endpoints, since the first label can be changed in either direction. The last assertion is \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A sharp contrast even when cardinal invariants coincide]\label{swo:rg:n6.4}
If $\cf\mu>\omega$, the minimal stratum has character $(\cf\mu,\cf\mu)$ everywhere, while the $\mu+\omega$ stratum does not have that character anywhere. Thus local characters can distinguish these strata even in cardinal-arithmetic situations in which their densities and weights happen to coincide. At $\mu=\omega$, the $\omega+\omega$ stratum is first-countable but has continuum many disjoint nonempty open intervals. Unlike the $\omega+3$ stratum, it has no isolated points.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{What remains for longer infinite tails}
For $\alpha=\mu+\nu$ with general $\nu$, \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology} settles the three cardinal invariants, while \cref{swo:rg:thm:characters,swo:rg:thm:transfer} reduce local characters to residual enumeration orders. At $\nu=\mu$, the residual can be any subset $R\subseteq X$ of cardinality $\mu$ with complement of cardinality $\mu$. Its order need not resemble the original birthday fragment. A further classification of point characters or cuts must therefore analyze the actual residual order and not just substitute $\cf\mu$ into the minimal-stratum formulas.

The same distinction controls ordinal-tail refinements. For example, at $\alpha=\mu+\omega+n$, finite adjacency blocks have size $n!$, but the geometry between them is governed by the preceding countable residual enumeration. The residual-cylinder identity provides a recursive description; it is not, by itself, an order-isomorphism classification of all such strata.
