% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 620-1096
The finite-tail theorem in the previous continuation leaves a specific
obstruction: a long initial enumeration can leave a smaller, variably
ordered alphabet for its final infinite tail. We now control that
variation. The result is an exact binary-cube spectrum for every fixed
enumeration type, together with exact equimorphisms for a broad family
that includes every type at alphabet cardinality at most
$\aleph_\omega$.

Throughout this section $\kappa$ is an infinite initial cardinal and
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-parameters}
 X=\No_{<\kappa},\qquad \mu=2^{<\kappa},\qquad
 \rho_\kappa=
 \begin{cases}
  \kappa\cdot\kappa,&\kappa\text{ is singular strong limit},\\
  \mu,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
For a positive finite integer $m$ put
\[
 (\B_{\rho}\times_\lex m)=\B_\rho\times_{\lex}\{0,\ldots,m-1\},
 \qquad \B_\rho=(\{0,1\}^{\rho},<_{\lex}).
\]
The notation $\equi$ always means an order embedding in each
direction. It does not mean order isomorphism. All arithmetic on
enumeration types and binary lengths is ordinal arithmetic.

Write an admissible type as
\[
 \alpha=\mu\cdot\gamma+\zeta,
 \qquad 0<\gamma<\mu^+,\quad\zeta<\mu,
 \qquad\sigma=\rho_\kappa\cdot\gamma.
\]
The previously proved finite-tail result is
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:prior-finite-tail}
 \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+n}(X)\equi (\B_{\sigma}\times_\lex n!)
 \qquad(n<\omega).
\end{equation}
Its proof uses a sign-sequence code and, at singular strong limits, a
first-varying-row scheduler (source~15, \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:block-scheduler}; \cref{swo:st:lem:scheduler}). We first
record exactly which parts continue to apply when infinitely many
labels are reserved.

\subsection{Uniform prefix codes and deletion of a small alphabet}

\begin{lemma}[A prefix-free code for any small alphabet]
\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-entrycode}
Every linear order $Y$ of infinite cardinality $\lambda$ admits an
order-preserving prefix-free binary entry code whose code lengths are
positive and strictly less than $\lambda$. This assertion does not
require regularity of $\lambda$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{swo:rs:lem:insertion}, insert $Y$ into $\No_{<\lambda}$,
with the element inserted at stage $\xi$ having birthday at most
$\xi<\lambda$. Replace each minus sign by $00$, each plus sign by
$11$, and append $01$. The three blocks express exactly
minus $<$ termination $<$ plus. Distinct completed codes cannot be
proper prefixes of one another, and their lexicographic comparison
agrees with the comparison of the surreal labels. The code length is
$2\cdot\bd(y)+2<\lambda$. Padding any completed code with zeros
therefore preserves its comparison with every other completed code.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The main prefix and its small-deletion counterpart]
\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix}
Every lexicographically ordered family of injective prefixes
$p:\mu\cdot\gamma\to X$ embeds into $\B_\sigma$. Moreover, for
every $Y\subseteq X$ with $|Y|<\mu$,
\[
                 \B_\sigma\emb
                  \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma}(X\setminus Y).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the prefix-free sign code of Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-entrycode} for
the labels of $X$, of length less than $\kappa$. If $\mu>\kappa$,
pad each entry to length $\kappa$. A block of $\mu$ entries then
has length $\kappa\cdot\mu=\mu$. If $\mu=\kappa$ is regular,
concatenate the unpadded codes. Every proper partial sum within a
$\kappa$-entry block is below $\kappa$, and its full sum is
$\kappa$. If $\mu=\kappa$ is singular, it is a strong limit:
otherwise an attained equality $2^\rho=\kappa$, $\rho<\kappa$,
would also hold at $\max(\rho,\cf\kappa)$, contradicting
K\"onig's inequality. In this last case pad entries to length
$\kappa$; each $\kappa$-entry block has length
$\kappa\cdot\kappa$. Applying the appropriate construction to
the $\gamma$ consecutive blocks gives length exactly $\sigma$.
Exhaustiveness of the prefix is never used.

For the lower embedding in the nonexceptional cases, partition
$X\setminus Y$ into pairs indexed by $\mu\cdot\gamma$. Orient
each pair by its corresponding bit. Since
$2\cdot(\mu\cdot\gamma)=\mu\cdot\gamma$, this has exactly the
required enumeration type and preserves first disagreement.

Suppose now $\mu=\kappa$ is singular strong limit. The sign cones
with prefixes $+^\xi\cat-$, $\xi<\kappa$, are disjoint copies of
$X$. At most $|Y|<\kappa$ of them meet $Y$. Choose $\kappa$
unaffected cones and index them by $\kappa\cdot\gamma$.
Their complement in $X\setminus Y$ still has size $\kappa$:
it contains all but fewer than $\kappa$ of the all-plus sequences.
Thus the row scheduler used in the prior theorem still applies.

For completeness, its relevant property is the following. Inside a
$\kappa$-row block, schedule row--column pairs $(i,j)$ first by
$\max(i,j)$ and then lexicographically within each level. Every pair
has fewer than $\kappa$ predecessors, so the schedule has type
$\kappa$, including when $\kappa$ is singular. The first occurrence
of row $i$ is $(i,0)$, and these occurrences increase with $i$.
Choose the first entry of each row by an input parameter and enumerate
the rest of that cone in a fixed way depending on that parameter.
Include the complement as a fixed filler row in the first block.
This embeds $X^{\kappa\cdot\gamma}_{\lex}$ in the required
permutation order.

Finally let $\delta=\cf\kappa$ and choose positive lengths
$(\tau_j)_{j<\delta}$ with sum $\kappa$. Since
$\delta\cdot(\kappa\cdot\gamma)=\kappa\cdot\gamma$, group
the input coordinates into $\kappa\cdot\gamma$ successive blocks
of $\delta$ coordinates. In each group restrict coordinate $j$ to
surreals of sign length exactly $\tau_j$. This realizes the cube
of length $\kappa\cdot\kappa\cdot\gamma=\sigma$ inside the
product, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

The small-deletion assertion is necessary: the independent residual
alphabet can have any cardinality below $\mu$. Removing it is not
being treated as if only finitely many cones were affected.

\subsection{Extracting an arbitrary tail factor from one residual fiber}

Let $P$ be the order of injective prefixes
$p:\mu\cdot\gamma\to X$ whose omitted set has cardinality
$|\zeta|$. There is an actual lexicographic-sum isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-sum}
 \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\zeta}(X)
 \cong\sum_{p\in P}\WO_\zeta(X\setminus\ran p).
\end{equation}
The next result shows why this decomposition controls embeddings that
need not initially respect the displayed fibers.

\begin{lemma}[Fusion into one fiber]\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-fiber-fusion}
If $Q\emb\B_\rho$ and $L=\sum_{q\in Q}F_q$, then for every
nonempty linear order $K$,
\[
 \B_\rho\times_{\lex}K\emb L
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K\emb F_q
 \quad\text{for some }q\in Q.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Compose an asserted embedding with the nondecreasing projection to
$Q$ and its binary code. At stage $\xi<\rho$, retain a full source
cylinder with its first $\xi$ bits fixed and with the first $\xi$
target bits fixed. The next target bit makes an ordered split. If the
lower full source child lies entirely on the lower side, retain it.
Otherwise it contains a point on the upper side, and the upper full
source child lies entirely on the upper side; retain that child.
At limits take unions of prefixes. The whole $K$ factor survives.
After $\rho$ stages it has one target binary code and therefore lies
inside a single $F_q$. Restrict the original injective map to that
factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact residual embedding reduction]
\label{swo:rs:thm:tail-reduction}
For every nonempty linear order $K$,
\begin{align*}
 &\B_\sigma\times_{\lex}K
       \emb\WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\zeta}(X)\\
 &\qquad\Longleftrightarrow
 \exists Y\subseteq X\,
 \bigl(|Y|=|\zeta|\ \text{and}\ K\emb\WO_\zeta(Y)\bigr).
\end{align*}
In particular, replacing $K$ by $\B_\tau$ gives the exact test
for whether $\B_{\sigma+\tau}$ embeds into the total order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Forwards, combine the prefix code from
Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix}, the sum
\eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-sum}, and Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-fiber-fusion}.
Conversely fix $Y$ and apply the small-deletion embedding to
$X\setminus Y$. Append the chosen $K$-indexed permutations of
$Y$. Every main prefix exhausts the same complement, so the residual
alphabet is independent of its binary parameter.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Which small orders can occur as residual alphabets]
\label{swo:rs:prop:tail-universality}
For an infinite cardinal $\lambda<\mu$, every linear order of
cardinality $\lambda$ embeds numerically into $X$ if and only if
$\lambda\leq\kappa$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $\lambda\leq\kappa$, \cref{swo:rs:lem:insertion} embeds the
order into $\No_{<\lambda}\subseteq X$. If $\lambda>\kappa$,
the padded sign code embeds $X$ into $\B_\kappa$. This cube has
no increasing sequence of type $\kappa^+$: successive stabilization
of its bits, with bounds taken at the regular cardinal $\kappa^+$,
would make every coordinate constant on a tail of such a sequence.
But the $\lambda$-sized ordinal $\lambda$ contains a
$\kappa^+$-sequence. It cannot embed into $X$.
\end{proof}

Thus residual alphabets at or below $\kappa$ include all small
linear orders, not just a special family of surreal order types.
Above $\kappa$, the inherited global sign code is a real restriction.

\subsection{Finite cardinal layers and the coding sandwich}

Repeated left division by the current infinite cardinal gives
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-decomposition}
 \zeta=\lambda_0\cdot\eta_0+\cdots+
        \lambda_{k-1}\cdot\eta_{k-1}+n,
\end{equation}
where
\[
 \mu>\lambda_0>\cdots>\lambda_{k-1}\geq\omega,
 \qquad 0<\eta_i<\lambda_i^+,\qquad n<\omega.
\]
There are only finitely many layers: otherwise the successive
remainders would give an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of
initial ordinals. Finite $\zeta$ means $k=0$.

Define two weights on infinite cardinals:
\begin{align}
 \xiwt(\lambda)&=
 \begin{cases}
  \lambda\cdot\lambda,&\lambda\text{ singular strong limit},\\
  \lambda,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-lower-weight}\\
 \xiwt^+_\kappa(\lambda)&=
 \begin{cases}
  \lambda\cdot\lambda,&\lambda\leq\kappa
                             \text{ and }\lambda\text{ singular},\\
  \lambda,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-upper-weight}
\end{align}
Finally put
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-RU}
 \xiRlo=\sigma+\sum_{i<k}\xiwt(\lambda_i)\cdot\eta_i,
 \qquad
 \xiRup=\sigma+\sum_{i<k}\xiwt^+_\kappa(\lambda_i)\cdot\eta_i.
\end{equation}
Both are nonzero limit ordinals and $\xiRlo\leq \xiRup$.

\begin{lemma}[Regular-cardinal blocks over any alphabet]
\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-regular}
Let $\lambda$ be an infinite regular cardinal, $|Y|=\lambda$, and
$0<\eta<\lambda^+$. Injective prefixes of length
$\lambda\cdot\eta$ in $Y$ admit an order embedding into
$\B_{\lambda\cdot\eta}$. For every $n<\omega$,
\[
       \WO_{\lambda\cdot\eta+n}(Y)
                  \equi (\B_{\lambda\cdot\eta}\times_\lex n!).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-entrycode}. Regularity makes every proper
partial sum of entry-code lengths within a $\lambda$-entry block
less than $\lambda$, while positivity makes the full sum exactly
$\lambda$. Code the $\eta$ consecutive blocks separately. In an
exhaustive enumeration the last $n$ labels are determined by the
preceding prefix, so append their finite permutation rank. This gives
the upper embedding. For the lower embedding reserve a fixed
$n$-element set, orient pairs of the complement indexed by
$\lambda\cdot\eta$, and append its selected terminal permutation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform coding bounds for every fixed type]
\label{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich}
With the parameters above,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-sandwich}
 \boxed{\quad
 (\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex n!)\emb\WO_\alpha(X)\emb (\B_{\xiRup}\times_\lex n!).
 \quad}
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\xiRlo=\xiRup$, then $\WO_\alpha(X)\equi (\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex n!)$.
Equality holds whenever every residual cardinal is regular, singular
strong limit, or strictly larger than $\kappa$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the upper embedding, code the main prefix in length $\sigma$.
At the beginning of residual layer $i$, the remaining alphabet has
cardinality $\lambda_i$. If it is regular use
Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-regular}. If it is singular and at most
$\kappa$, pad the entry code from
Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-entrycode} to length $\lambda_i$. The next
$\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$ entries then use length
$\lambda_i\cdot\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$. If
$\lambda_i>\kappa$, use the fixed global $\kappa$-bit sign code
instead; its length for this block is
$\kappa\cdot\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i
 =\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.

Choose an entry code for each possible residual alphabet. Such choices
are indexed by a set. Two enumerations that have agreed up to a
layer boundary have the same residual alphabet and use the same code;
if they disagree before that boundary, their comparison is already
decided. Consequently these conditional codes combine to an
order-preserving code of length $\xiRup$. Append the finite permutation
rank, obtaining the upper embedding.

For the lower embedding choose fixed, pairwise disjoint alphabets for
the finitely many residual layers. A singular strong-limit
$\lambda<\mu$ necessarily satisfies $\lambda<\kappa$, for
otherwise
$\mu=2^{<\kappa}\leq2^{<\lambda}=\lambda$.
At such a layer choose an ordered copy of $\No_{<\lambda}$,
which has cardinality $\lambda$, inside a sign cone of $X$.
Finitely many distinct finite prefixes, such as $+^i\cat-$,
make these copies disjoint. The singular scheduler in
Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix}, applied at cutoff $\lambda$,
realizes the factor
$\B_{\lambda\cdot\lambda\cdot\eta}$ there. For all other
layers choose arbitrary disjoint sets of the requisite cardinality
and realize $\B_{\lambda\cdot\eta}$ by pair orientation.
Also reserve a fixed $n$-element terminal set.

Their union has cardinality less than $\mu$. Its complement realizes
$\B_\sigma$ by Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix}. Concatenate all
the independent block enumerations and the selected terminal
permutation. The first changed source factor supplies the first
changed target block. This gives the lower embedding in
\eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-sandwich}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[All regular residual layers]
\label{swo:rs:cor:tail-regularlayers}
If every $\lambda_i$ in \eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-decomposition} is regular,
and $\tau=\sum_{i<k}\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$, then
\[
 \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\tau+n}(X)
                 \equi (\B_{\sigma+\tau}\times_\lex n!).
\]
In particular every countably infinite residual is classified. Every
admissible enumeration type is classified whenever
$\mu\leq\aleph_\omega$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is $\xiRlo=\xiRup=\sigma+\tau$. A countable ordinal is
of the form $\omega\cdot\eta+n$. If
$\mu\leq\aleph_\omega$, every smaller infinite cardinal is one
of the regular cardinals $\aleph_j$, $j<\omega$.
\end{proof}

Even with a singular non-strong-limit residual, ordinal absorption
inside a coefficient $\eta_i$ can occasionally make $\xiRlo=\xiRup$. The
criterion is the equality of the computed ordinals, not merely the
absence of one label in a list of cardinal cases. When they differ,
Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich} leaves a binary coding-length
problem. The next argument nevertheless determines all embedded
binary cubes exactly.

\subsection{A cardinality fusion lemma and the complete cube spectrum}

\begin{lemma}[A constant subcylinder from a small range]
\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-smallrange}
Let $\chi$ be an infinite cardinal and $A$ a linear order with
$|A|<2^\chi$. A nondecreasing map from a binary cylinder with at
least $\chi$ free initial bits, followed by any nonempty factor,
into $A$ is constant on a full subcylinder obtained by fixing fewer
than $\chi$ of those bits.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix all later bits and choose one point in the final factor. This
gives $2^\chi$ ordered test points. Some value has at least three
test preimages $x_0<x_1<x_2$, since a union of $|A|$ sets of at most
two elements has cardinality at most $|A|$. Choose $\delta<\chi$
strictly beyond the first disagreements of $x_1$ with both outer
points. The entire source cylinder determined by the first
$\delta$ bits of $x_1$ lies strictly between $x_0$ and $x_2$,
regardless of its later bits and final factor. Monotonicity forces
the same value throughout it.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The singular non-strong-limit block]
\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-singular-fusion}
Suppose $\lambda$ is singular and not strong limit, and
$0<\eta<\lambda^+$. Consider a putative order embedding whose
target enumerations share their earlier prefix, leaving an alphabet
of cardinality $\lambda$, and whose source has a free initial block
$\B_{\lambda\cdot\eta}$ followed by a nonempty factor $K$.
One can fix the source binary block so that the next
$\lambda\cdot\eta$ target entries are constant on the surviving
whole $K$ factor.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose an exponent $\theta<\lambda$ with $2^\theta\geq\lambda$,
and put $\chi=\max(|\theta|,\cf\lambda)<\lambda$.
Then $2^\chi\geq\lambda$, and equality would contradict
$\cf(2^\chi)>\chi\geq\cf\lambda$. Thus $2^\chi>\lambda$.

Process target coordinates $j<\lambda\cdot\eta$. All earlier
target coordinates have been fixed. The current coordinate is
therefore a nondecreasing map on the remaining source cylinder into
a $\lambda$-element order. Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-smallrange}
makes it constant after fewer than $\chi$ additional source bits.
Before coordinate $j$, the total bits fixed are at most
$\chi\cdot j$. There are still $\chi$ free bits available:
\[
 \chi\cdot(j+1)<\lambda\cdot\eta
 \qquad(j+1<\lambda\cdot\eta).
\]
Indeed, writing $j=\lambda\cdot\beta+\delta$ with
$\delta<\lambda$ gives
$\chi\cdot j=\lambda\cdot\beta+\chi\cdot\delta$, and
$\chi\cdot(\delta+1)<\lambda$. The ordinal
$\lambda\cdot\eta$ is a limit, so $j+1$ stays below it at every
stage.

At limits take unions of the chosen prefixes. The total cost at the
end is at most
\[
 \chi\cdot(\lambda\cdot\eta)=\lambda\cdot\eta.
\]
If fewer bits were used, fix arbitrary additional bits to the exact
block boundary. All target entries in the stated block are now fixed,
and the entire subsequent factor $K$ remains.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact binary-cube spectrum for every fixed type]
\label{swo:rs:thm:tail-cubes}
For every positive finite integer $m$,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-capacity}
 (\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex m)\emb\WO_\alpha(X)
                 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\leq n!.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every ordinal $\theta$,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-cubes}
 \boxed{\quad
 \B_\theta\emb\WO_\alpha(X)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \theta\leq \xiRlo+\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
This includes all singular non-strong-limit residual layers.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The lower embedding in Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich} proves the
forward constructions in \eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-capacity}. Conversely
suppose an embedding of $(\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex m)$ is given. Fuse through the target's
main prefix code, using Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-fiber-fusion}; this
fixes $\sigma$ source bits and the entire main target prefix while
preserving the later source factor.

At each regular residual layer fuse through the prefix code of
length $\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$. At each singular strong-limit
layer fuse through the padded code of length
$\lambda_i\cdot\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$. At a singular
non-strong-limit layer use
Lemma~\ref{swo:rs:lem:tail-singular-fusion}, whose cost is only
$\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$. These are exactly the successive
summands defining $\xiRlo$. After finitely many layers, all target
positions before the last $n$ are fixed. The surviving $m$ source
points must inject into the $n!$ permutations of one fixed residual
$n$-element set. Thus $m\leq n!$.

Put $j=\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor$. The lower construction contains
$\B_{\xiRlo+j}=(\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex 2^j)$, whereas \eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-capacity} excludes
$\B_{\xiRlo+j+1}=(\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex 2^{j+1})$. Every larger cube contains this
forbidden cube, and every smaller cube embeds into $\B_{\xiRlo+j}$
by padding zeros.
\end{proof}

The small-range argument concerns a map on a full binary cylinder,
not merely on the chosen test points. Fixing a prefix of the middle
test point puts every extension between the two outer points. This
is what permits the fusion to retain an arbitrary subsequent source
factor and to pass through limit stages.

\subsection{Exact coding lengths, comparisons, and examples}

Define the binary coding length $\ell_2(L)$ to be the least ordinal
$\rho$ for which $L\emb\B_\rho$. The finite-capacity argument
has the following familiar consequence, recalled with its obstruction.


\begin{note}[Source~19, Lemma~5.12, ``Finite factors over a limit-length cube'']\label{swo:rs:lem:tail-finite-capacity}
\emph{For nonzero limit ordinals $\rho,\tau$ and positive finite integers $m,n$,
$(\B_\rho\times_\lex m)\emb(\B_\tau\times_\lex n)$ if and only if $\rho<\tau$ or
($\rho=\tau$ and $m\le n$); and $\bl(\B_\rho\times_\lex m)=\rho+\lceil\log_2m\rceil$.}
This is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:finite-capacity}, by the same
equal-length fusion; source~19 adds that the one-bit fusion also gives
$\B_\beta\emb\B_\xi$ exactly when $\beta\le\xi$ (``if $\beta>\xi$, fixing $\xi$
source bits to match all target bits leaves at least two source points''), which
is \cref{swo:st:lem:strictcube}. Source~19 calls it ``the familiar consequence
\ldots{} recalled with its obstruction''. Source~29 proves it a third time
(its Lemma~4.1 and Corollary~4.2).
\end{note}

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 1122-1203

\begin{corollary}[Coding bounds and exact classifications]
\label{swo:rs:cor:tail-coding}
For every type in this section,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:rs:eq:tail-coding-bounds}
 \xiRlo+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil
 \leq\ell_2(\WO_\alpha(X))
 \leq \xiRup+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil.
\end{equation}
If $\xiRlo=\xiRup$, both inequalities are equalities. Two such classified
orders with parameters $(\xiRlo,n!)$ and $(\xiRlo',m!)$ embed in the indicated
direction exactly when
\[
 \xiRlo<\xiRlo'\quad\text{or}\quad(\xiRlo=\xiRlo'\text{ and }n!\leq m!).
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-finite-capacity} to the sandwich
\eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-sandwich}. When its two outer orders coincide up
to notation, use the resulting equimorphisms on both sides of a
proposed embedding.
\end{proof}

Under CH, $\kappa=\mu=\omega_1$ and every admissible type has
the form
\[
 \alpha=\omega_1\cdot\gamma+\omega\cdot\eta+n.
\]
It follows that
\begin{align*}
 \WO_\alpha(\No_{<\omega_1})
 &\equi (\B_{\omega_1\cdot\gamma+\omega\cdot\eta}\times_\lex n!),\\
 \ell_2(\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\omega_1}))
 &=\omega_1\cdot\gamma+\omega\cdot\eta
                         +\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil.
\end{align*}
For $n=3$, the largest embedded cube has length
$\omega_1\cdot\gamma+\omega\cdot\eta+2$, while the least
coding length is that limit part plus $3$. The difference follows
from finite-capacity nonembedding, not from cardinality.

For an example with an infinite singular residual, let $\lambda$
be singular strong limit, put $\kappa=\lambda^+$ and
$\mu=2^\lambda$. Then
\[
 \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\lambda\cdot\eta+n}
       (\No_{<\lambda^+})
 \equi (\B_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\lambda\cdot\lambda\cdot\eta}\times_\lex n!).
\]
The singular residual contributes an additional ordinal factor
$\lambda$, despite having smaller cardinality than the main alphabet.

\subsection{What is settled and what remains}

The arbitrary variable residual has now been controlled well enough
to determine the complete embedded binary-cube spectrum for every
fixed type. Exact equimorphism and coding length are also determined
whenever the two computable bounds $\xiRlo,\xiRup$ agree. This includes every
type when $\mu\leq\aleph_\omega$, every countable residual at
any cutoff, and the singular strong-limit residuals described above.

The remaining coding question occurs when singular non-strong-limit
residual layers at or below $\kappa$ make $\xiRlo<\xiRup$. Does the lower
coding bound in \eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-coding-bounds} always hold with
equality? A stronger formulation asks whether the whole order embeds
into $(\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex n!)$. The simplest general-alphabet instance asks whether
\[
       \WO_\lambda(Y)\emb\B_\lambda
\]
for every ordered $Y$ of singular non-strong-limit cardinality
$\lambda$. The argument above proves that its embedded cube
spectrum is exactly $\theta\leq\lambda$, but the direct entry
code only gives an embedding into $\B_{\lambda\cdot\lambda}$.
One must not infer a coding embedding from the absence of the next
larger cube.

Further refinements concern isomorphism instead of equimorphism,
residual gap spectra, and which fiber structures can be recovered
from the pure order. The exact residual reduction
Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:thm:tail-reduction} supplies a useful test: an arbitrary
product embedding with the full main binary factor must already
realize its remaining factor on a single allowed residual alphabet.

\begin{note}[Source~30, Lemmas~4.1--4.3: entry codes, the long prefix, small deletion]\label{swo:rt:lem:regular-alphabet-code}\label{swo:rt:lem:long-prefix-code}\label{swo:rt:lem:small-deletion}
Lemma~4.1 (``Short codes for arbitrary regular-cardinality alphabets''):
\emph{let $\nu$ be an infinite regular cardinal and $Y$ an arbitrary linear order of
cardinality $\nu$; there is an order-preserving, prefix-free binary code $c_Y$ for
$Y$ with $0<\lh(c_Y(y))<\nu$; consequently
$\WO_{\nu\delta+n}(Y)\equi\B_{\nu\delta}\times_\lex n!$ for every $0<\delta<\nu^+$
and $n<\omega$; for $\nu=\omega$ the codes are finite binary words, and the
conclusion holds ``for every countable linear alphabet, regardless of density,
endpoints, jumps, or scatteredness''.} This is \cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-entrycode}
with \cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-regular}, by the same stage-controlled insertion into
$\No_{<\nu}$ (``regularity is not needed for this embedding step'') and the same
$00<01<11$ sign code; for $\nu=\omega$ source~30 notes the alternative embedding
into the dyadic rationals. Lemma~4.2 (``Exact coding length of an arbitrary long
prefix''): \emph{for $0<\gamma<\mu^+$ there is an order embedding
$X^{\mu\gamma}_\lex\to\B_{\rho_\kappa\gamma}$, in particular for all injective
prefixes of that length; no exhaustiveness hypothesis is used}, which is the first
half of \cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix} and the upper construction of
\cref{swo:cb:new:thm:block-types} (``This proves the asserted order embedding even
for functions with repeated entries''). Lemma~4.3 (``Small deletion in the singular
scheduler''): \emph{let $\kappa$ be singular strong limit and $D\subseteq\No_{<\kappa}$
with $\card D<\kappa$; for $0<\gamma<\kappa^+$ and $\lambda=\kappa\gamma$,
$\B_{\kappa\lambda}$ order-embeds into $\WO_\lambda(\No_{<\kappa}\setminus D)$.}
This is the second half of \cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix}: it ``extends the
repository's finite-deletion lemma'' \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:finite-deletion} ``from
finite deletion to deletion of cardinality below $\kappa$'', and it prints the
row scheduler of \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:block-scheduler} in full ``to expose the
order, rather than merely cardinal, requirements'': the sign cones $+^\xi\cat-$,
$\xi<\kappa$, of which fewer than $\kappa$ meet $D$; a filler row for the unselected
labels; rows split into blocks of $\kappa$ and scheduled by $\max(\xi,j)$; and the
regrouping of coordinates into blocks of $\cf\kappa$ restricted to sign words of
lengths $\eta_j$ with $\sum_j\eta_j=\kappa$.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~30, Theorem~4.4 and Corollaries~4.5, 4.6 and~4.8; Remark~4.7]\label{swo:rt:thm:regular-remainder}\label{swo:rt:cor:countable-remainder}\label{swo:rt:cor:regular-remainder-ranks}\label{swo:rt:n4.7}\label{swo:rt:cor:regular-descent}
Theorem~4.4 (``A smaller regular-cardinal block after the long prefix''):
\emph{for an infinite regular $\nu<\mu$, $0<\gamma<\mu^+$, $0<\delta<\nu^+$ and
$n<\omega$, $\WO_{\mu\gamma+\nu\delta+n}(\No_{<\kappa})\equi
\B_{\rho_\kappa\gamma+\nu\delta}\times_\lex n!$; all constructions are set
constructions in $\ZFC$, with no global choice or class comprehension.}
Corollary~4.5 (``Every countable remainder''): \emph{if $\mu>\omega$, then
$\WO_{\mu\gamma+\omega\delta+n}(\No_{<\kappa})\equi\B_{\rho_\kappa\gamma+\omega\delta}\times_\lex n!$
for $0<\gamma<\mu^+$, $0<\delta<\omega_1$, $n<\omega$}; ``Together with the
repository's finite-remainder theorem, this covers every $\alpha=\mu\gamma+\zeta$
with $\zeta<\omega_1$. For a countable alphabet itself, Lemma~4.1 already treats
every admissible ordinal length.'' Corollary~4.6 (``Exact coding and cube
spectrum''): \emph{with $\sigma=\rho_\kappa\gamma+\nu\delta$, the least binary coding
length is $\sigma+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil$, $\B_\theta$ embeds exactly when
$\theta\le\sigma+\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor$, and two instances embed exactly when
$\sigma<\sigma'$ or ($\sigma=\sigma'$ and $n!\le m!$)}, by
\cref{swo:cb:new:lem:finite-capacity}. Remark~4.7: ``At $\kappa=\omega_1$, the
countable-remainder corollary already classifies every fixed type under CH: divide
$\alpha$ by $\omega_1$ and apply the corollary to the countable remainder.
Corollary~5.6 below removes CH entirely.'' Corollary~4.8 (``Finite descent through
regular residual cardinals''): \emph{for regular $\mu>\nu_1>\cdots>\nu_t$,
$\WO_{\mu\gamma+\zeta+n}(\No_{<\kappa})\equi\B_\sigma\times_\lex n!$ with
$\zeta=\nu_1\delta_1+\cdots+\nu_t\delta_t$ and $\sigma=\rho_\kappa\gamma+\zeta$, with
the coding-rank, cube-spectrum and comparison conclusions of Corollary~4.6.} These
are \cref{swo:rs:cor:tail-regularlayers} and \cref{swo:rs:cor:tail-coding}, by the
same upper codes (``ordinary set choice suffices'' to choose one code for each
possible residual alphabet; ``equal earlier prefixes determine the same code'')
and the same reserved alphabets with pair orientations. Source~30's closing
paragraph of its Section~4, ``The remaining boundary'', observes that every
remainder has a finite decomposition into blocks of strictly decreasing infinite
cardinalities followed by a finite term, that ``regularity is the exact step used
to make a block of short entry codes have precisely the cardinal's ordinal length,
and the residual alphabet need not contain all of $\No_{<\nu}$'', and that after its
Section~5 ``the remaining uncontrolled regime is therefore singular, not strong
limit, and at most $\kappa$'', as for source~19.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~30, Theorem~5.1 and Corollary~5.2]\label{swo:rt:thm:singular-remainder}\label{swo:rt:cor:singular-remainder-obstruction}
Theorem~5.1 (``A singular strong-limit residual block''): \emph{if $\nu<\mu$ is a
singular strong-limit cardinal, $0<\gamma<\mu^+$, $0<\delta<\nu^+$ and $n<\omega$,
then $\WO_{\mu\gamma+\nu\delta+n}(\No_{<\kappa})\equi

smaller regular-cardinal formula cannot be extended to all singular residual

strong-limit layer of \cref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich}, where
$\xiwt(\nu)=\xiwt^+_\kappa(\nu)=\nu\cdot\nu$, and its coding consequence
\cref{swo:rs:cor:tail-coding}; source~30's proof is source~19's: $\nu<\kappa$
because $\mu=2^{<\kappa}\le2^{<\nu}=\nu$ otherwise, every residual alphabet of size

$\nu$, and the lower embedding reserves the full smaller cutoff $\No_{<\nu}$ and
runs the singular scheduler at cutoff $\nu$. Source~30 adds: ``The explicit strict
contrast above uses $\delta=1$; for arbitrary $\delta$, ordinal absorption can make
$\nu\cdot\nu\cdot\delta=\nu\cdot\delta$. The smaller-cutoff argument alone does not
classify a residual singular cardinal which is not strong limit. The padded upper
bound remains available, but the smaller full surreal cutoff may have more than
$\nu$ labels, so it cannot be reserved as a residual alphabet of size $\nu$.''
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~30, Corollaries~5.3 and~5.4]\label{swo:rt:cor:mixed-cardinal-descent}\label{swo:rt:cor:all-types-controlled-cardinals}
For an infinite cardinal $\nu$ that is regular or singular strong limit, source~30
puts $\xiwt(\nu)=\nu$ or $\nu\cdot\nu$ respectively. Corollary~5.3 (``Finite descent
through both controlled cardinal regimes''): \emph{if $\mu>\nu_0>\cdots>\nu_k$ are
infinite cardinals, each regular or singular strong limit, then
$\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\kappa})\equi\B_\sigma\times_\lex n!$ for
$\alpha=\mu\gamma+\sum_{i\le k}\nu_i\delta_i+n$ and
$\sigma=\rho_\kappa\gamma+\sum_{i\le k}\xiwt(\nu_i)\delta_i$.} Corollary~5.4 (``All
fixed types when smaller cardinals are controlled''): \emph{if every infinite
cardinal below $\mu$ is regular or singular strong limit, every fixed type of
cardinality $\mu$ is covered by this formula; in particular this yields a complete

singular cardinal is a strong limit. Under GCH, with the canonical decomposition
$\alpha=\sum_{i\le k}\kappa_i\delta_i+n$, $\kappa=\kappa_0>\kappa_1>\cdots>\kappa_k\ge\omega$,
the complete formula reads
\[
 \WO_\alpha(\No_{<\kappa})\equi
 \B_{\sum_{i\le k}\xiwt(\kappa_i)\cdot\delta_i}\times_\lex n!,
\]
and ``every product and sum here is ordinal; replacing a term
$\kappa_i\cdot\kappa_i$ by its cardinality would destroy the claimed
classification''. These are the equality clause of
\cref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich} in the regular and singular strong-limit cases;

The one point source~30 checks separately is that the reserved alphabets of the
singular strong-limit blocks (copies of $\No_{<\nu_i}$ behind distinct prefixes
$+^j\cat-$) are disjoint, as in source~19's lower embedding.
\end{note}

whereas the successor cutoff $\kappa$ is not singular strong limit,

Its exact binary coding length is $\sigma+3$, while its largest

\begin{corollary}[The first uncountable cutoff needs no continuum hypothesis]
\label{swo:rt:cor:omega-one-all-types-ZFC}
Put $X=\No_{<\omega_1}$ and
$\mu=2^{\aleph_0}$.  For every ordinal $\alpha$ of cardinality $\mu$,
write $\alpha=\lambda+n$, where $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal
and $n<\omega$.  Then, in ZFC,
\[
 \WO_\alpha(X)\equi 
 \BB_\lambda\times_{\mathrm{lex}}n!.
\]
More generally the same conclusion holds for
$X=\No_{<\kappa}$ at every infinite initial cutoff
$\kappa<\aleph_\omega$, with $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ and
$|\alpha|=\mu$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For such a $\kappa$, every infinite cardinal at most $\kappa$ is
regular.  Any larger residual cardinal has the uninflated native code
from \cref{swo:rt:prop:residual-above-cutoff}.  Thus every cardinal
in the canonical finite residual decomposition is covered and has
cost equal to itself.  The main cutoff is regular, so
$\rho_\kappa=\mu$ as well.  The mixed formula therefore has binary
length equal to the entire limit part $\lambda$ of $\alpha$.
For $\kappa=\omega_1$, its alphabet cardinal is $2^{\aleph_0}$,
with no condition on the value of that cardinal.  For $\kappa=\omega$,
there are no smaller infinite residual cardinals, and the existing
cardinal-block theorem supplies the same conclusion.
\end{proof}

\section{Completions of the minimal slice (sources 24, 21 and 19)}\label{swo:x:sec:completion}

\merge\ Three different completions of the minimal slice are printed here: the
Hausdorff completion for agreement on bounded initial segments (source~24's
Section~5), the closure of the minimal stratum inside the full order $\WO(X)$
(source~21's Section~4), and normal forms for the Dedekind completion (source~19's
Section~7). Source~24's own summary of the difference: ``Forward stabilization
preserves injectivity but can lose labels. Inverse stabilization prevents that
loss. Dedekind completion is larger again: it also fills cylinder edges and
numerical gaps.'' Sources~26 and~28 prove the forward completion again; source~28
extends it to every admissible coordinate ideal
(\cref{swo:ge:thm:forward-complete}).

\subsection{Forward prefix completion and the missing-label boundary (source 24)}\label{swo:pc:sec:uniform}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 325-409
\subsubsection{The uniformity that remembers only initial segments}

For $\alpha<\mu$, put
\[
 E_\alpha=\{(f,g):f\res\alpha=g\res\alpha\}.
\]
These equivalence relations form a base of entourages for a Hausdorff uniformity on either $\WO_\mu(X)$ or $\I_\mu(X)$. We call it the \emph{forward prefix uniformity}. Its topology is the cylinder topology. No ordering of $X$ is needed to define it.

A net is Cauchy for this uniformity when, for every $\alpha<\mu$, all sufficiently late terms have exactly the same restriction to $\alpha$. The requirement is stronger than merely having many pairwise agreements, and at a singular $\mu$ it must still be stated for every bounded initial segment, not merely for arbitrary finite sets of coordinates.

\begin{theorem}[Exact forward completion]\label{swo:pc:thm:completion}
The uniform space $\I_\mu(X)$ is complete. The inclusion
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\hookrightarrow\I_\mu(X)
\]
is a dense uniform embedding and exhibits $\I_\mu(X)$ as the Hausdorff completion of $\WO_\mu(X)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a Cauchy filter on $\I_\mu(X)$. For each $\alpha<\mu$ it contains a nonempty $E_\alpha$-small set, hence contains a cylinder $[p_\alpha]$ of length $\alpha$. It cannot contain two distinct cylinders of that length, since they are disjoint. These unique prefixes are coherent: if $\alpha<\beta$, the two cylinders in the filter intersect, so $p_\alpha=p_\beta\res\alpha$.

Their union $h=\bigcup_{\alpha<\mu}p_\alpha$ is a function with domain $\mu$. It is injective, because any two proposed equal values occur in a common sufficiently long injective prefix. The filter contains every cylinder neighborhood of $h$ and therefore converges to $h$. This proves completeness.

The entourages on $\WO_\mu(X)$ are the restrictions of the same entourages on $\I_\mu(X)$. Every cylinder of the latter meets $\WO_\mu(X)$ by Lemma~\ref{swo:pc:lem:extension}. Completeness, density, and Hausdorffness give the claimed completion, including its uniqueness up to the usual uniform isomorphism fixing the dense subspace.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exhaustion is an intersection of dense open requirements]\label{swo:pc:thm:exhaustion}
For each $x\in X$, let
\[
 U_x=\{h\in\I_\mu(X):x\in\ran h\},\qquad
 F_x=\I_\mu(X)\setminus U_x.
\]
Then $U_x$ is open dense and $F_x$ is closed nowhere dense. Moreover,
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)=\bigcap_{x\in X}U_x,
 \qquad
 \I_\mu(X)\setminus\WO_\mu(X)=\bigcup_{x\in X}F_x.
\]
Both $\WO_\mu(X)$ and its complement are dense in $\I_\mu(X)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Once $x$ occurs, a prefix extending past that occurrence witnesses membership in $U_x$, so $U_x$ is open. Any prefix can be extended to include $x$, if it does not already include it; then complete the new prefix. Hence $U_x$ is dense, and $F_x$ has the stated properties. The displayed equalities express surjectivity exactly.

Density of $\WO_\mu(X)$ was proved above. Given any short prefix, choose an unused label $z$ and extend to an enumeration of $X\setminus\{z\}$. This gives a nonexhaustive point in the cylinder and proves density of the complement.
\end{proof}

The last result is a generalized dense-intersection description, not automatically an ordinary $G_\delta$ statement. It becomes a $G_\delta$ statement when $X$ is countable. At larger cardinalities, the number of exhaustion requirements matters.

\subsubsection{A concrete failure of forward completeness}

\begin{example}[A label escaping to later and later positions]\label{swo:pc:ex:shift}
On $\mathbb N$, define
\[
 \pi_n(k)=
 \begin{cases}
 k+1,&k<n,\\
 0,&k=n,\\
 k,&k>n.
 \end{cases}
\]
Each $\pi_n$ is the cycle $(0\ 1\ \cdots\ n)$. For every fixed $k$, eventually $\pi_n(k)=k+1$, so the sequence is forward Cauchy and converges in $\I_\omega(\mathbb N)$ to $h(k)=k+1$. The limit omits $0$. Equivalently, $\pi_n^{-1}(0)=n$ never stabilizes. Forward stabilization records where each position goes, but not where each target label comes from.
\end{example}

For arbitrary infinite $\mu$, choose a nononto injection $h:\mu\to X$ and, for every $\alpha<\mu$, an exhaustive extension $f_\alpha$ of $h\res\alpha$. The $\mu$-indexed net $(f_\alpha)$ is forward Cauchy with limit $h$ in $\I_\mu(X)$ and no limit in $\WO_\mu(X)$. Thus the forward uniformity is incomplete for every infinite $\mu$.

\subsubsection{Why this is not Dedekind completion}\label{swo:pc:subsec:ordercompletion}

Assume thickness. Let $\widehat{{P}}$ be the Dedekind completion of the dense order ${P}=\WO_\mu(X)$, using nonempty proper lower sets without a greatest element as the cut convention. For $h\in\I_\mu(X)$, put
\[
 L_h=\{f\in{P}:f<_{\lex}h\}.
\]

\begin{proposition}[The injection space sits strictly inside order completion]\label{swo:pc:prop:trace}
The map $h\mapsto L_h$ is an order embedding of $\I_\mu(X)$ into $\widehat{{P}}$ extending the canonical embedding of ${P}$. If $h$ is nonexhaustive, its image is a nonprincipal cut of ${P}$. This map is not onto: even cylinder-edge cuts need not come from injective words.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $h<k$ in $\I_\mu(X)$, choose an unused label strictly between their values at the first disagreement and complete the resulting prefix exhaustively. This gives $f\in{P}$ with $h<f<k$. Repeating the same argument supplies exhaustive words on either side of any injection and between any injection and a strictly smaller or larger exhaustive word. It follows that $L_h$ is a valid cut, that the map is strictly order preserving, and that a nonexhaustive $h$ has neither a greatest exhaustive word below it nor a least exhaustive word above it. If its cut were the cut of an exhaustive $g$, the same separation argument between $h$ and $g$ would be a contradiction.

Fix $x\in X$. Consider the lower edge of the cylinder $[\langle x\rangle]$:
\[
 L=\{f\in{P}:f(0)<x\}.
\]
This is a nonempty proper lower set with no greatest element. An injection beginning with a label below $x$ is not cofinal in this lower side, by density of the alphabet. An injection beginning above $x$ lies above the entire $x$-cylinder. An injection beginning exactly with $x$ has exhaustive words with that same first label strictly below it. Its lower cut therefore contains words not in $L$. These three cases exhaust the possibilities, so $L$ is not $L_h$ for any injection $h$.
\end{proof}

Thus there are at least two qualitatively different boundaries. A \emph{branch boundary} is an injective full-length word missing labels. A \emph{prefix edge} ends a cylinder without selecting a full continuation. Alphabet gaps create further order-completion points. Earlier cut-classification results (sources~17 and~13; \cref{swo:gs:sec:cuts}) organize these possibilities more finely; Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:completion} identifies exactly the part visible to the forward uniformity.

\begin{note}[Source~26, Theorem~4.1 and Proposition~4.2]\label{swo:nb:sec:completion}\label{swo:nb:thm:completion}\label{swo:nb:prop:exhaustion}
Source~26's Theorem~4.1 (``Forward completion; earlier result reproved''):
\emph{$\I_\mu(X)$ is complete for the forward-prefix uniformity, and the inclusion
$\WO_\mu(X)\subseteq\I_\mu(X)$ exhibits it as the Hausdorff uniform completion of the
permutation space.} Its Proposition~4.2 (``Exhaustion requirements''): \emph{each
$U_x=\{h\in\I_\mu(X):x\in\ran h\}$ is open dense, $\WO_\mu(X)=\bigcap_{x\in X}U_x$, and
the complement $F_x$ is closed nowhere dense and nonempty.} These are
\cref{swo:pc:thm:completion,swo:pc:thm:exhaustion}; source~26 says ``This is the
mechanism of the earlier completion theorem'' (source~24), and stresses that at
uncountable $\mu$ ``a Cauchy filter must eventually stabilize every bounded prefix;
pointwise stabilization of isolated coordinates alone is not the definition''. It
adds: ``The missing points of the uniform completion are therefore precisely the
nonexhaustive injections. This is not a Dedekind completion theorem. Order
completion can add cylinder edges and gaps in the alphabet that are not
represented by a full injective branch \ldots{} the non-Borel theorem below
concerns the branch boundary already present in $\I_\mu(X)$''
(\cref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel}).
\end{note}

\subsection{First-cardinality fibres and the closure of the minimal stratum (source 21)}\label{swo:fu:sec:fibers}

\merge\ Source~21's Section~4, printed whole. Its first-cardinality decomposition
is the set-level form of the fibre decomposition of class well-orders that
source~16 proves in Part~VIII (\cref{swo:ds:eq:fiber}) and of source~22's
residual-cylinder identity (\cref{swo:rg:thm:residual}); the closure theorem is
new. Source~21's $\I_\mu(X)$ is this Part's.

% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 580-694
The set-sized setting already contains a useful prototype of the
proper-class residual-tail phenomenon. No higher-order foundation is
needed for it.

\begin{theorem}[First-cardinality decomposition]\label{swo:fu:set:fiber}
Let $X$ be any infinite linearly ordered set of cardinality $\mu$. There
is a canonical order isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{swo:fu:eq:firstmu}
 \WO(X)\ \cong\
 \sum_{f\in\I_\mu(X)}\WO\bigl(X\setminus\ran(f)\bigr),
\end{equation}
where the index set has its numerical lexicographic order and the sum
is a lexicographic sum. The fiber over an exhaustive $f$ is a singleton;
the set of these singleton points is exactly $\WO_\mu(X)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every well-order of $X$ has an enumeration of ordinal length at least
$\mu$. Take its first $\mu$ entries, an injective word $f$. The rest
of the relation is exactly a well-order of the unused set
$Y_f=X\setminus\ran(f)$. Conversely, concatenate $f$ with the
enumeration of any well-order of $Y_f$. This uses every label exactly
once and produces a well-order of $X$. The two constructions are inverse.

If two first words differ, their first disagreement occurs below
$\mu$ and decides the comparison of all corresponding completions.
If they agree, comparison reduces to the residual well-orders. This is
precisely the lexicographic sum in \eqref{swo:fu:eq:firstmu}. For
$Y_f=\varnothing$ there is one empty residual relation. For
$Y_f\ne\varnothing$, the concatenation has length strictly greater
than $\mu$, so it does not belong to the minimum stratum.
\end{proof}

One should not confuse a singleton fiber with an exhaustive word. A
one-element residual set also has only one well-order. Thus the
unlabelled size of a fiber cannot detect exhaustivity.

\begin{lemma}[Endpoints of a residual enumeration order]\label{swo:fu:set:fiber-ends}
For any set $Y$ with a linear label order, $\WO(Y)$ has a least element
if and only if the label order $<$ well-orders $Y$. It then consists
of listing $Y$ in that order. It has a greatest element if and only if
the reverse label order well-orders $Y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $<$ is a well-order, its increasing enumeration chooses the least
unused label at every stage. Every first disagreement in another
enumeration is larger, so this is the lexicographic minimum. Conversely,
if a lexicographic minimum ever chooses a label while a smaller unused
label remains, interchange the chosen label with that later label.
The resulting well-order is smaller. Hence a minimum always chooses the
least unused label; its enumeration shows that the label order itself
is a well-order. Reverse the inequalities for the greatest element.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Density of exhaustive branches in the index order]
\label{swo:fu:set:branch-density}
If $X$ has uniformly large intervals, the exhaustive words
$\WO_\mu(X)$ are order-dense in $\I_\mu(X)$, and there are exhaustive
words on both sides of every nonexhaustive word.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $f<g$, let $\delta<\mu$ be their first disagreement. Fewer than
$\mu$ labels occur in the common prefix. Choose an unused label
strictly between $f(\delta)$ and $g(\delta)$ and complete that prefix
to an exhaustive $\mu$-word. It lies strictly between $f$ and $g$.
To obtain exhaustive words on both sides of a single branch, choose
unused labels below and above its first label, respectively, and complete.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Closure theorem]\label{swo:fu:set:closure}
Assume $X$ has uniformly large intervals. In the order topology of
$\WO(X)$, the closure of $\WO_\mu(X)$ consists of:
\begin{enumerate}
\item every point of $\WO_\mu(X)$; and
\item the least and greatest point, when they exist, of each fiber over
a nonexhaustive $f\in\I_\mu(X)$.
\end{enumerate}
By \cref{swo:fu:set:fiber-ends}, the added endpoints are exactly the orders
obtained by following $f$ with an increasing or decreasing numerical
well-order of its unused set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
An interior point of a nonexhaustive fiber has a point of that fiber on
each side. The open interval between those two points is disjoint from
$\WO_\mu(X)$, so the point is not in the closure.

Suppose $R$ is the least point of its fiber over $f$. If $A<R<B$, then
$A$ cannot lie in the same fiber. Its first $\mu$ entries form a word
$g<f$. By \cref{swo:fu:set:branch-density} choose an exhaustive word
$h$ with $g<h<f$. Its singleton fiber gives a point of
$\WO_\mu(X)$ between $A$ and $R$, hence inside $(A,B)$. Thus every
neighborhood of $R$ meets the minimum stratum. The greatest-point case
is symmetric. A singleton fiber satisfies both arguments.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Finite and infinite residuals]\label{swo:fu:set:closure-examples}
If $f$ omits a finite set of size $n$, its fiber is an $n!$-element
chain. For $n=1$ the unique point is in the closure; for $n=2$ both
points are; for $n\ge3$ only the two extreme permutations are. If
$X=\mathbb Q$ and $f:\omega\to\mathbb Q\setminus\mathbb N$ is a bijection, the residual
$\mathbb N$ has a numerical well-order but its reverse does not. Exactly the
least point of this infinite fiber is in the closure. If the unused
set has order type $\mathbb Q$, neither endpoint exists, and its entire fiber
is disjoint from the closure.
\end{example}

The closure theorem describes the relative position of strata, not just
their separate cardinalities. It also identifies the information lost
by retaining only the first $\mu$ entries: all residual well-order
choices are compressed to a single index. At the class level the first
$\Ord$-block plays the analogous role, but its fibers are no longer
automatically set-sized.

\subsection{Normal forms for the Dedekind completion of the minimal slice (source 19)}\label{swo:rs:ia:sec:completion}

\merge\ Source~19's Section~7, printed whole. Its three kinds of cut are source~17's
cut trichotomy (\cref{swo:gs:lem:cut-trichotomy}): a branch, an edge at a last
straddling prefix, a limit-prefix boundary. New in source~19 are the uniqueness of
the codes, the order read directly from them, and the sign codes of the residual
splits (\cref{swo:rs:ia:prop:residual-sign-codes}). ``The gap spectrum in the
preceding research'' is \cref{swo:gs:thm:gap-spectrum} (source~17) with source~18's
multiplicities \cref{swo:sh:thm:gap-multiplicities}. Its full-branch cuts $L_f$ are
source~24's trace cuts (\cref{swo:pc:prop:trace}). Source~19's
$\operatorname{Perm}_\mu(D)$ is printed $\WO_\mu(D)$; its alphabet $D$ is thick.

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 1311-1515
The gap spectrum in the preceding research identifies possible
characters and their multiplicities. The same prefix analysis gives
more information: it describes the arrangement of the completion
points through unique decorated-word codes. This construction is
entirely set-sized and therefore takes place in ZFC.

Let $D$ be a dense linear order without endpoints, of infinite
cardinality $\mu$, and assume that every nonempty open interval of
$D$ has cardinality $\mu$. Put
\[
 P=\WO_\mu(D)
   =\{e:\mu\longrightarrow D:e\text{ is bijective}\}.
\]
The application is $D=\No_{<\kappa}$ and $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ for
an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$. For an injective prefix
$p:\delta\to D$, $\delta<\mu$, write
\[
 C_p=\{e\in P:e\restr\delta=p\},\qquad
 D_p=D\setminus\operatorname{ran}(p).
\]
The cylinder $C_p$ is nonempty and convex. Since fewer than $\mu$
labels have been used, $D_p$ still meets every nonempty interval
and is unbounded in both directions. In particular, every cylinder
has neither a first nor a last member.

Use the following convention for the Dedekind completion:
$\overline P$ consists of the nonempty proper initial subsets of
$P$ having no greatest element, ordered by inclusion. The point
$e\in P$ is represented by $P_{<e}$. The two external endpoints
can be added separately when a compactified completion is wanted.

\begin{theorem}[Unique normal forms for the completion]
\label{swo:rs:ia:thm:completion-normal-form}
Every point of $\overline P$ has exactly one code of one of the
following three kinds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A full branch.} An injection $f:\mu\to D$, representing
\[
 L_f=\{e\in P:e<f\}.
\]
If $f$ is onto, this is the original point $f$; otherwise it is an
omitted-branch gap.

\item \textbf{A numerical split.} A pair $(p,I)$, where $p$ has
length $\delta<\mu$ and $I$ is a nonempty proper initial subset
of $D_p$, representing
\[
 L_{p,I}=\{e:e<C_p\}
       \ \cup\ \{e\in C_p:e(\delta)\in I\}.
\]
Here $e<C_p$ means that $e$ lies below every member of the cylinder.
The set $I$ may have a greatest member, and its complement may
have a least member. This kind always represents a proper gap.

\item \textbf{A limit-prefix boundary.} A pair $(p,\varepsilon)$,
where $p$ has nonzero limit length $\delta<\mu$ and
$\varepsilon\in\{-,+\}$, representing respectively
\[
 L_{p,-}=\{e:e<C_p\},\qquad
 L_{p,+}=\{e:e<C_p\}\cup C_p.
\]
Both are proper gaps.
\end{enumerate}
The restrictions in this list eliminate all duplication. In
particular, a successor-prefix boundary is already a numerical-split
code at its predecessor; a principal point is represented only by
its full surjective branch.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $L\in\overline P$, and let $K$ consist of the short injective
prefixes whose cylinders meet both $L$ and $P\setminus L$.
Two incompatible cylinders are disjoint convex sets, so they cannot
both straddle one cut. Thus $K$ is a downward-closed chain under
extension. It contains the empty prefix because both sides of the
cut are nonempty.

If $K$ has a greatest member $p$, no child cylinder straddles.
Partition $D_p$ according to whether its entire child cylinder is
in $L$ or in $P\setminus L$. Both parts are nonempty since
$C_p$ straddles. The lower digit part is an initial subset $I$,
and the cut is precisely $L_{p,I}$. Both sides have no endpoint:
if a digit side has an endpoint, its final or initial child
cylinder still has no endpoint; otherwise the varying next digits
themselves defeat an endpoint. The longest straddling prefix and
its partition are intrinsic to $L$, proving uniqueness in this case.

Suppose that $K$ has no greatest member and its lengths have
supremum $\delta<\mu$. The union $p=\bigcup K$ is injective
and has nonzero limit length $\delta$. Its cylinder does not
straddle, for then $p$ would be a greatest member of $K$.
If $C_p\subseteq P\setminus L$, the cut is the lower boundary
of $C_p$: any point below $C_p$ disagrees with $p$ at an earlier
coordinate, and a longer member of $K$ has a point of $L$ above
it. Every point above or in $C_p$ belongs to the upper side.
The reverse argument gives the upper boundary when $C_p\subseteq L$.
The union $p$ and the side containing its cylinder are intrinsic.

In the remaining case the lengths in $K$ are cofinal in $\mu$.
Their union is an injection $f:\mu\to D$. Every permutation
$e$ different from $f$ has a first disagreement with it. Looking
at a longer straddling prefix shows that $e\in L$ exactly when
$e<f$. If $f$ is onto, it belongs to $P$ and cannot lie in $L$,
because then it would be the greatest member of $L$. Consequently
$L=L_f$ in the onto case as well as the non-onto case. The word
$f$ is uniquely recovered as the union of $K$.

Conversely, the displayed codes have exactly their asserted
straddling patterns. For a numerical split, $p$ is the last
straddling prefix. For a limit boundary, all proper prefixes of
$p$ straddle and $p$ itself does not. To see straddling arbitrarily
late, choose unused smaller and larger next digits and complete the
resulting prefixes. For a full branch, every short prefix straddles
by the same construction. The full-interval-size hypothesis ensures
the requisite fresh digits, and each resulting short injection has
a bijective completion. All displayed lower subsets are nonempty,
proper, and have no greatest member. Their distinct patterns exclude
duplication between the three kinds.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{How the normal forms are ordered}

The order can be read directly from the codes; it need not be
reconstructed from cofinality data. Compare actual entries up to
their first disagreement. If there is such a disagreement, use
the order of $D$. If one code ends at $p$ while the other continues
with next label $x$, a numerical-split token $I$ lies above the
continuing code exactly when $x\in I$, and below it exactly when
$x\notin I$. A boundary token $p^-$ lies below every code
continuing $p$, and $p^+$ lies above them all. Numerical-split
tokens at the same prefix compare by inclusion of their initial
subsets. At a limit prefix, $p^-$ is below all numerical-split
tokens and $p^+$ is above all of them.

There is a necessary distinction at an available next letter $x$:
\[
 I_x^- =\{y\in D_p:y<x\},\qquad
 I_x^+ =\{y\in D_p:y\leq x\}.
\]
These are different initial subsets and represent the two different
boundaries of $C_{p^\frown x}$. Identifying them would collapse a
whole nonempty interval of the completion. In contrast, a successor
boundary must not be added again as a separate boundary code.

The theorem realizes the completion as an explicit decorated tree
order. Every automorphism of $P$ extends uniquely to it through
its action on cuts. This alone does not say that the automorphism
preserves the three kinds of code or the displayed prefix tree.

\subsubsection{Surreal sign codes for the residual numerical splits}

For the surreal cutoff, even the residual-cut parameter has a
concrete sign description.

\begin{proposition}[The exact identifications after deleting labels]
\label{swo:rs:ia:prop:residual-sign-codes}
For $D=\No_{<\kappa}$, initial subsets of $D$, including the two
external ends and both principal cuts at a point, are in bijection
with sign words of length $\kappa$. Initial subsets of $D_p$ are
obtained by restricting these cuts. This restriction identifies
exactly the pair of principal cuts immediately below and immediately
above each deleted point $x\in\operatorname{ran}(p)$, and makes
no other identifications.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Given an initial subset $A$ of $D$, recursively construct
$s:\kappa\to\{-,+\}$ by
\[
 s(\alpha)=+
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 s\restr\alpha\in A.
\]
Every proper prefix is a surreal in $D$. A first-disagreement
comparison proves $A=\{x\in D:x<s\}$. If $x$ is a proper
prefix of $s$, its membership is exactly the defining condition
at its length. At a genuine first disagreement, the membership of
the common prefix and initiality of $A$ give the same conclusion.
Conversely, the cut induced by a length-$\kappa$ sign word
reconstructs that word by this recursion, proving the bijection.

Restriction to $D_p$ is surjective: for an initial subset $I$
of $D_p$, its downward closure in $D$ induces exactly $I$.
Suppose $A\subsetneq B$ are two initial subsets of $D$ with the
same restriction. If $B\setminus A$ contained $x<y$, there would
be $z\in D_p$ strictly between them because $D_p$ is dense in
$D$. Initiality gives $z\in B\setminus A$, a contradiction.
The difference therefore consists of one deleted point $x$.
The two cuts must then be $\{y:y<x\}$ and $\{y:y\leq x\}$.
Each such pair plainly has equal restriction. This proves that
there are no further identifications.
\end{proof}

Thus numerical-split tokens can be coded by length-$\kappa$
sign words modulo these precisely specified deleted-point pairs,
with the two residual endpoints excluded. All branches, prefixes,
quotients, and completion points in this construction are sets.

An unrestricted analogue for global surreal well-orders would
require a collection of arbitrary class cuts. A higher sort, an
external containing universe, or a supplied uniform family must
be specified before forming it. Applying the same first-failure
argument to individually supplied classes does not create a GB
class whose elements are all such cuts, and does not turn the
raw global well-order family into a completion of its core.

\section{A generalized Baire model at every regular size (source 24)}\label{swo:x:sec:regular}\label{swo:pc:sec:regular}

\merge\ Source~24's Section~6, printed whole. It determines the topology, not the
order, of the minimal slice at every regular enumeration cardinal $\mu$: the slice
is homeomorphic to the bounded-topology space $(\mu^{<\mu})^\mu$, with no hypothesis
$\mu^{<\mu}=\mu$ and no GCH. For $X=\No_{<\kappa}$ this answers source~12's question
``Classify the order topology'' (\cref{swo:st:n14.3}) whenever $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ is
regular (\cref{swo:x:sec:status}). Source~28 recalls the construction and its
singular obstruction (\cref{swo:ge:sec:application}).

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 413-493
For a cardinal $\lambda$ and an infinite cardinal $\mu$, the \emph{bounded topology} on $\lambda^\mu$ has basic open sets
\[
 N_s=\{a\in\lambda^\mu:s\subseteq a\},\qquad s\in\lambda^\alpha,
 \quad\alpha<\mu.
\]
When $\mu$ is uncountable this is usually finer than the ordinary product topology, which permits only finitely many coordinate restrictions. Generalized descriptive set theory systematically studies this distinction~\cite{FriedmanHyttinenKulikov}. We keep the topology explicit rather than relying on an ambiguous use of ``Baire space.''

\subsubsection{The exhaustion-adapted prefix tree}

Fix a bijection $e:\mu\to X$. For a short injective prefix $p$, let
\[
 m(p)=\min\{\xi<\mu:e(\xi)\notin\ran p\}.
\]
This exists because $|\dom p|<\mu$. A \emph{child} of $p$ is an extension in which the label $e(m(p))$ first appears at the very end:
\[
 q=p\cat t\cat\langle e(m(p))\rangle,
 \qquad
 t\in\Inj\bigl(\delta,X\setminus(\ran p\cup\{e(m(p))\})\bigr),
 \quad\delta<\mu.
\]
All these extensions are short. Different children are incompatible: neither is a proper prefix of the other, because the earlier one would already have used the distinguished label. Every exhaustive extension of $p$ extends exactly one child, namely the prefix ending at its first occurrence of that label.

\begin{lemma}[Exact branching number]\label{swo:pc:lem:branching}
Each node $p$ has exactly $\lambda=\mu^{<\mu}$ children.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The available labels for $t$ have size $\mu$. For each ordinal $\delta<\mu$, the number of injections from $\delta$ into a set of size $\mu$ is $\mu^{|\delta|}$. For nonzero $\delta$, the lower bound follows by coding an arbitrary function $a:\delta\to\mu$ as the injection $\xi\mapsto(\xi,a(\xi))$ and then using a fixed bijection from $\delta\times\mu$ to $\mu$; the upper bound is immediate. The zero-length case contributes one. Summing over $\delta<\mu$ gives $\mu^{<\mu}$, since that cardinal is at least $\mu$.
\end{proof}

The rule uses a well-order of the \emph{set of labels} only to decide which coverage requirement to enforce next. It is independent of their numerical order. This is why it can classify the topology without classifying the linear order.

\begin{theorem}[Regular-cardinal topological classification]\label{swo:pc:thm:regular}
If $\mu$ is infinite regular, $|X|=\mu$, and $\lambda=\mu^{<\mu}$, there is a homeomorphism
\[
 \Phi:\lambda^\mu\longrightarrow\WO_\mu(X)
\]
for the bounded topology and the prefix topology. If $X$ is $\mu$-thick, the latter is its lexicographic order topology.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Using Choice, label the children of every short injective prefix by $\lambda$. Define prefixes $p_s$ for $s\in\lambda^{<\mu}$ by recursion. Let $p_{\varnothing}$ be empty. At a successor stage let $p_{s\cat\langle i\rangle}$ be the child of $p_s$ labelled by $i$. At a limit $\eta<\mu$, define
\[
 p_s=\bigcup_{\xi<\eta}p_{s\res\xi}\qquad(\dom s=\eta).
\]
Regularity of $\mu$ is used here: the supremum of fewer than $\mu$ prefix lengths, each below $\mu$, is still below $\mu$. The union is injective and hence is a valid node.

For a branch $a\in\lambda^\mu$, put
\[
 \Phi(a)=\bigcup_{\xi<\mu}p_{a\res\xi}.
\]
Every successor step increases the prefix length. Thus these lengths are cofinal in $\mu$, and the union has domain $\mu$. It is injective. At stage $\xi$, the prefix contains every label $e(\zeta)$ with $\zeta<\xi$: prove this by induction. At a successor, either $e(\xi)$ is already present or it is exactly the least missing label and the child adds it. At a limit, take the union. Therefore $\Phi(a)$ is exhaustive.

Conversely, an exhaustive $f:\mu\to X$ chooses a unique child of the empty prefix, then a unique child of that child, and so on. At limit stages take the already-determined prefix union. All intermediate prefixes are short by regularity and remain restrictions of $f$. This defines a unique branch $a$ with $\Phi(a)=f$.

The correspondence satisfies
\[
 \Phi[N_s]=[p_s]_{P}.
\]
Indeed, a permutation extending $p_s$ must have followed the unique distinguished-label choices along the path to $s$. Hence $\Phi$ is an open bijection. To check continuity, take $f=\Phi(a)$ and a prescribed prefix length $\alpha<\mu$. Some $p_{a\res\xi}$ has length at least $\alpha$, so its cylinder lies inside $[f\res\alpha]$. The preimage of every cylinder is open. This proves the homeomorphism, and Lemma~\ref{swo:pc:lem:cylinders} supplies the final order-topological identification.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Size-matched regular cutoffs]\label{swo:pc:cor:regularcutoff}
If $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ is regular, then
\[
 \WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})\cong_{\mathrm{top}}(\mu^{<\mu})^\mu.
\]
In particular, if $\mu^{<\mu}=\mu$, this is the usual bounded-topology generalized Baire space $\mu^\mu$.
\end{corollary}

No continuum hypothesis or generalized continuum hypothesis has been used. The branching cardinal is retained as $\mu^{<\mu}$ rather than being silently replaced by $\mu$. The regularity hypothesis is on the \emph{enumeration cardinal} $\mu$; regularity of the birthday parameter $\kappa$ alone is not the statement of the theorem.

\subsubsection{Why the construction does not contradict forward incompleteness}

The full branch space $\lambda^\mu$ is complete for its own prefix uniformity: a Cauchy filter stabilizes a unique prefix at every height, and the union is a branch. The homeomorphism $\Phi$ transports this complete uniformity to a compatible complete uniformity on $\WO_\mu(X)$.

This is not the forward uniformity of Section~\ref{swo:pc:sec:uniform}. A height in the exhaustion-adapted tree means that a prescribed list of labels has already been covered. The amount of ordinary enumeration needed to achieve that height varies from branch to branch and is not uniformly bounded. In the countable example, the place at which $0$ first occurs can be arbitrarily late. Homeomorphisms preserve topology, not a chosen uniformity or the completeness of every compatible metric.

\subsubsection{The exact point where singularity intervenes}

If $\mu$ is singular, a chain of fewer than $\mu$ short prefixes can have union of length $\mu$. It can therefore reach a full injective word before all $\mu$ coverage requirements have been visited. There is no short node at that limit stage to which the same child construction can be applied. This is a concrete obstruction to \emph{this proof}, not a proof that no other generalized Baire presentation exists.

The distinction will recur in Section~\ref{swo:pc:sec:singular}: at a singular cardinal a small-cardinality set of coordinates may be unbounded. Arguments that control finitely or cardinally few positions do not automatically control one bounded initial segment.
