\section{The countable cutoff (source 24; routes of sources 19, 20, 21, 26, 29 and 30)}\label{swo:x:sec:countable}\label{swo:pc:sec:countable}

\begin{note}[\merge; one theorem, seven proofs]\label{swo:x:note:sevenfold}
For every countable dense alphabet $X$ without endpoints, in particular for the
finite-birthday surreals $\No_{<\omega}$, the minimal slice $\WO_\omega(X)$ is
homeomorphic to Baire space $\omega^\omega$, its Dedekind completion is the real
line, every interval of the completion contains continuum many omitted points,
and the slice is not order-isomorphic to the irrationals. Seven batch-83 sources
prove this independently: source~24 (\cref{swo:pc:thm:completecountable,swo:pc:lem:separable,swo:pc:thm:gdelta,swo:pc:cor:notirrational},
printed below as the base: it alone gives both a complete compatible metric for
the original topology and the exact descriptive form of the complement);
source~19 (\cref{swo:rs:ia:thm:countable-topology}, which adds that every interval
also contains continuum many original points); source~20 (\cref{swo:lm:top:main},
which adds that the slice is not $F_\sigma$ in its completion); source~21
(\cref{swo:fu:ct:topology,swo:fu:ct:completion}, which add a second mechanism of
omitted cuts, and its homogeneity theorem \cref{swo:fu:ct:homogeneity});
source~26 (\cref{swo:nb:prop:countable}, complete metrizability only); source~29
(\cref{swo:bw:tp:thm:category-omissions}, case $n=0$, set beside the slices with
finitely many omitted labels); and source~30
(\cref{swo:rt:prop:cofinite-prefix-category,swo:rt:cor:baire-homeomorphism}). Five
build the homeomorphism with $\omega^\omega$ by the same least-missing-label tree
(sources~19, 20, 24, 30, and source~29 by citation); source~21 uses an even--odd
back-and-forth coding. The $G_\delta$ description through cylinder intervals and
label requirements is common to sources~19, 20 and~24; source~26 obtains complete
metrizability from the $G_\delta$ criterion \cref{swo:pc:nC.1}. In this report the
case was the example \cref{swo:gs:n6.6} (``a Baire, zero-dimensional order'', with
the warning that these facts do not identify it with the real line). No source has
priority over another. The routes are printed after source~24's text, each whole,
because each adds a clause or a different proof.
\end{note}

\merge\ Source~24's Section~7, ``The countable cutoff: a complete metric but a
different order''.

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 497-573
Let $X$ be countable, densely ordered, and without endpoints. This includes $\No_{<\omega}=\No_{<\omega}$, the finite sign sequences. Every nonempty interval and ray of such an $X$ is infinite, so the thickness hypothesis holds with $\mu=\omega$.

\subsubsection{An explicit complete compatible metric}

Fix $e:\omega\to X$ and identify $f\in\WO_\omega(X)$ with the permutation $\pi=e^{-1}\circ f$ of $\omega$. On injections or permutations of $\omega$, define
\[
 d_{\to}(\pi,\sigma)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&\pi=\sigma,\\
 2^{-\min\{k:\pi(k)\ne\sigma(k)\}},&\pi\ne\sigma.
 \end{cases}
\]
This familiar forward ultrametric is not complete on permutations, by Example~\ref{swo:pc:ex:shift}. Instead put
\[
 D(\pi,\sigma)=\max\bigl\{d_{\to}(\pi,\sigma),
                   d_{\to}(\pi^{-1},\sigma^{-1})\bigr\}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Complete metrizability at countable size]\label{swo:pc:thm:completecountable}
The metric $D$ is a complete compatible ultrametric on $\WO_\omega(X)$. This space is homeomorphic to $\omega^\omega$, has no isolated points, and is nowhere locally compact.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The maximum of the two ultrametrics is an ultrametric. To see compatibility, finitely many inverse requirements at a fixed $\pi$ are enforced by finitely many forward requirements: to ensure $\sigma^{-1}(j)=\pi^{-1}(j)$ for $j<n$, require $\sigma$ to agree with $\pi$ at all the finitely many positions $\pi^{-1}(j)$. One sufficiently long forward prefix does this. Hence adding inverse requirements does not change the topology.

For a $D$-Cauchy sequence $(\pi_n)$, each forward coordinate and each inverse coordinate eventually stabilizes. Let their limits be $h$ and $g$. If $h(k)=j$, sufficiently late terms have $\pi_n(k)=j$ and $\pi_n^{-1}(j)=g(j)$ simultaneously. Thus $g(j)=k$. Conversely, if $g(j)=k$, the same argument gives $h(k)=j$. Therefore $g=h^{-1}$ and $h$ is a permutation. The original sequence converges to it in $D$.

Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:regular} gives the homeomorphism with $\omega^\omega$, since $\omega^{<\omega}=\omega$. Every finite prefix admits at least two continuations, so there are no isolated points. Each cylinder is partitioned by its exhaustion-adapted children into countably infinitely many nonempty open cylinders. That cover has no finite subcover, so the original cylinder is not compact. If a point had a compact neighborhood, it would contain a cylinder, which is closed in the whole space and hence would be a compact closed subset of that neighborhood. This contradiction proves nowhere local compactness.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The Dedekind completion is a real line}

\begin{lemma}[A countable order-dense subset]\label{swo:pc:lem:separable}
The order $\WO_\omega(X)$ is separable and dense without endpoints. Its Dedekind completion is order-isomorphic to $\mathbb R$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are countably many finite injective prefixes. Choose one exhaustive extension for each. These chosen points meet every nonempty cylinder and hence every nonempty open interval, giving a countable order-dense subset. Density and absence of endpoints were proved in Lemma~\ref{swo:pc:lem:cylinders}.

The completion is consequently a complete dense linear order without endpoints with a countable order-dense subset. For completeness of the identification, a countable order-dense subset has no endpoints and is itself densely ordered; a standard alternating insertion construction gives an order isomorphism with $\mathbb Q$. Each point of the complete order is uniquely determined by the rational cut below it, and every real cut is realized by a supremum. This extends the countable isomorphism to an isomorphism with $\mathbb R$.
\end{proof}

Fix such an identification of the completion with $\mathbb R$. For a nonempty finite prefix $p$, let $J_p$ be the open interval between the lower and upper completion edges of its cylinder. Then
\[
 J_p\cap\WO_\omega(X)=[p]_{P}.
\]
Both edges exist because a nonempty cylinder is bounded by words with smaller or larger first labels. It has no endpoints and is clopen in the original order, so neither edge lies in that cylinder. For the empty prefix set $J_{\varnothing}=\mathbb R$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact descriptive form of the omitted points]\label{swo:pc:thm:gdelta}
Inside its Dedekind completion $\mathbb R$, the space ${P}=\WO_\omega(X)$ is a dense $G_\delta$ set. Its complement is a dense meager $F_\sigma$ set of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $n<\omega$ and $x\in X$, set
\[
 V_n=\bigcup_{\substack{p\in\I_{<\omega}(X)\\|p|=n}}J_p,
 \qquad
 W_x=\bigcup_{\substack{p\in\I_{<\omega}(X)\\x\in\ran p}}J_p.
\]
All these sets are open and contain ${P}$, hence are dense. We claim
\begin{equation}\label{swo:pc:eq:gdelta}
 {P}=\bigcap_{n<\omega}V_n\ \cap\ \bigcap_{x\in X}W_x.
\end{equation}
The forward inclusion is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, a point $z$ belonging to all $V_n$ chooses a unique length-$n$ prefix $p_n$ with $z\in J_{p_n}$. Distinct same-level intervals are disjoint: a nonempty intersection would be open and meet the dense original order, contradicting disjointness of the corresponding cylinders. The same argument shows that the chosen prefixes are coherent. Their union is an injective $\omega$-word $h$.

Membership in every $W_x$ ensures that each label occurs in one of these prefixes. Indeed, if $z\in J_p$ and $x\in\ran p$, comparison with a chosen prefix of length at least $|p|$ forces compatibility and hence $p\subseteq h$. Thus $h$ is exhaustive. Finally, $z$ is its completion point: if they differed, an original point strictly between them would have to belong to every sufficiently long cylinder of $h$, contrary to its first disagreement with $h$. This proves~\eqref{swo:pc:eq:gdelta}.

The complement is therefore $F_\sigma$ and meager; each closed set complementary to one of the displayed dense open sets is nowhere dense. It is dense as well. Every completion interval contains an original cylinder interval, and every such cylinder contains the trace cut of an injection that extends the prefix but omits an unused label.

For its cardinality, fix a label $z_0$ and partition $X\setminus\{z_0\}$ into countably many pairs. Independently ordering each pair gives $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct injective words with range exactly $X\setminus\{z_0\}$. Proposition~\ref{swo:pc:prop:trace} gives distinct omitted completion points. The opposite bound follows from the cardinality of $\mathbb R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Homeomorphic to, but not ordered like, the irrationals]\label{swo:pc:cor:notirrational}
The minimal enumeration order of the countable surreal cutoff is homeomorphic to the Baire space and hence to the usual irrational-number space. It is not order-isomorphic to the irrationals in their usual order.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The homeomorphism with Baire space was constructed above. The familiar identification of Baire space with irrationals can also be obtained from infinite continued fractions, or from successive countable interval partitions; only the topological assertion is used here. An order isomorphism of dense orders extends uniquely to their Dedekind completions, by transporting lower cuts. The completion of the irrationals omits only the countably many rational points, whereas Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:gdelta} gives continuum many omitted points for our order. An isomorphism cannot have these two different complements.
\end{proof}

The completion description gives a particularly concrete answer to the original question at the first infinite cutoff. It is not a strange topology: it is Baire topology. Its unusual feature is the \emph{placement of that topology in a linear order}, with many more omitted order cuts than the standard irrational presentation. The phenomenon is already visible before any genuinely class-sized issues arise.

\subsection{Source 21's route, with homogeneity and non-intrinsic cylinders}\label{swo:fu:sec:countable}

\merge\ Source~21's Section~7, printed whole. Its \cref{swo:fu:ct:topology} and
\cref{swo:fu:ct:completion} are the theorem above by different proofs: the slice is
a $G_\delta$ in the discrete product $\mathbb Q^\omega$, and an even--odd
back-and-forth coding gives the homeomorphism; the completion theorem adds omitted
cuts from numerical next-coordinate splits to those from nonexhaustive branches.
Its \cref{swo:fu:ct:absorb}, \cref{swo:fu:ct:homogeneity} and
\cref{swo:fu:ct:nonintrinsic} are new: the countable minimal slice is strongly
finitely homogeneous, has $2^{\aleph_0}$ automorphisms, and its proper prefix
cylinders are not definable in the pure order. They answer source~12's question on
the ``degrees of homogeneity'' (\cref{swo:st:n14.3}) at $\kappa=\omega$, which
Part~VI left open (\cref{swo:vi:sec:status}, item~(b)); the corollary is the
set-level counterpart of source~13's class-level prefix non-rigidity
(\cref{swo:fs:thm:nonrigidity}).

% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 1023-1245
Let
\[
 P=\WO_\omega(\mathbb Q).
\]
The rationals here carry their usual numerical order; the points of $P$
are all exhaustive enumerations of them. Every countable dense alphabet
without endpoints gives the same presentation order, by relabelling.
In particular, this treats $\WO_\omega(\No_{<\omega})$, since the
finite-birthday surreals form a countable dense order without endpoints.
It does not assert that the finite-birthday surreals equal the rational
surreals as sets.

\subsubsection{Order topology and an explicit Baire coding}

\begin{theorem}\label{swo:fu:ct:topology}
The order topology of $P$ equals its finite-prefix topology, equivalently
the subspace topology inherited from the product of countably many
copies of \emph{discrete} $\mathbb Q$. It is a zero-dimensional Polish space,
homeomorphic to Baire space $\omega^\omega$, and it is nowhere locally
compact.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The equality of topologies and the clopen-cylinder assertion follow
from \cref{swo:fu:set:prefix-topology}. In discrete $\mathbb Q^\omega$, the
injective words form a closed subspace. The surjectivity requirement is
\[
 \bigcap_{q\in\mathbb Q}\bigcup_{n<\omega}\{e:e(n)=q\},
\]
a countable intersection of open sets. Thus $P$ is a $G_\delta$ subspace
of a Polish space and is Polish.

Here is also a direct homeomorphism with Baire space, so no topological
classification theorem is necessary. Fix a bijection of the underlying
set $\mathbb Q$ with $\omega$ and view a point as a permutation of $\omega$.
Given $c\in\omega^\omega$, build finite partial bijections $p_s$.
At even stage $s$, take the least unused domain element and send it to
the $c(s)$th unused range element. At odd stage $s$, take the least
unused range element and assign it to the $c(s)$th unused domain
element. Unused elements are listed in their natural order.

Every stage adds one pair. The even stages exhaust the domain and the
odd stages exhaust the range, so the union is a permutation. Conversely,
for a given permutation each prescribed even or odd step has a unique
rank among the unused choices, recovering a unique $c$. The forward
map is continuous because each finite construction stage uses only a
finite prefix of $c$. Its inverse is continuous because a finite
construction trace inspects finitely many values of the permutation or
its inverse, and
\[
 \pi^{-1}(r)=d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\pi(d)=r
\]
is a clopen coordinate condition. This proves the homeomorphism.

Finally, a cylinder with a prefix of length $n$ has a continuous
surjection, by its next coordinate, onto the infinite discrete set of
unused rational labels. It is therefore not compact. If a point had a
neighborhood with compact closure, that neighborhood would contain a
clopen cylinder. The cylinder would be a closed subset of the compact
closure, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The adjective ``discrete'' matters. If one uses the ordinary Euclidean
topology on the rational coordinate alphabet, the topology of coordinate
agreement is no longer the product topology being described here. At
uncountable lengths the bounded-prefix topology requires its own
formulation as well.

\subsubsection{Absorption and interval self-similarity}

\begin{lemma}[Countable sums are absorbed]\label{swo:fu:ct:absorb}
For every nonempty countable linear order $J$,
\[
 \sum_{j\in J}P\ \cong\ P.
\]
Every nonempty finite-prefix cylinder of $P$ is also isomorphic to $P$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
After a finite prefix, the unused alphabet is $\mathbb Q$ minus finitely many
points. It is again a countable dense order without endpoints and hence
isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$. Reindex the remaining $\omega$ positions and
relabel by such an isomorphism. This proves the cylinder assertion.
In particular, first-coordinate decomposition gives
\[
 P\cong\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q}P.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \sum_{j\in J}P
 \cong\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q}P
 \cong\sum_{t\in\sum_J\mathbb Q}P.
\]
The index order $\sum_J\mathbb Q$ is countable, dense, and without endpoints:
inside a fiber use density of $\mathbb Q$, and between distinct fibers use
the absence of an endpoint in either relevant copy of $\mathbb Q$. It is
isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strong finite homogeneity]\label{swo:fu:ct:homogeneity}
Every nonempty bounded open interval and every open ray of $P$ is
order-isomorphic to $P$. Every finite increasing partial map from $P$
to itself extends to an order automorphism. Moreover,
\[
 |\Aut(P,<)|=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $e\in P$. Partition the points below $e$ according to their first
disagreement position $n$. At a fixed $n$, the smaller unused labels
form a countable dense order without endpoints, and each such next
label has a completion cylinder isomorphic to $P$. Thus each part is
a $\mathbb Q$-sum of copies of $P$, hence isomorphic to $P$. These parts occur
in increasing order of $n$, giving
\[
 (-\infty,e)_P\cong\sum_{n<\omega}P\cong P.
\]
For the upper ray the first-disagreement parts occur in order $\omega^*$,
and \cref{swo:fu:ct:absorb} again applies.

For $e<f$, let $n$ be their first disagreement. The interval $(e,f)$
splits into the upper ray after $e$ within its length-$(n+1)$ cylinder,
the cylinders whose next label lies strictly between $e(n)$ and $f(n)$,
and the lower ray before $f$ within its corresponding cylinder. These
are respectively a copy of $P$, a $\mathbb Q$-sum of copies of $P$, and a
copy of $P$. Their sum is isomorphic to $P$.

Given finite increasing tuples $e_1<\cdots<e_k$ and
$f_1<\cdots<f_k$, match the points and choose isomorphisms of their
corresponding intervening intervals and two outer rays. Patching the
maps gives an automorphism.

Transitivity on the continuum many points of $P$ gives the lower bound
for the automorphism group. Choose one exhaustive completion of each
finite injective prefix. The resulting countable set is order-dense.
An order automorphism is determined by its values on this set, so there
are at most $|P|^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$ automorphisms.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Prefix cylinders are not intrinsic]\label{swo:fu:ct:nonintrinsic}
The family of proper positive-length prefix cylinders is not invariant
under all automorphisms of $(P,<)$. No individual such cylinder is
definable in the pure order with finitely many parameters.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose two ordered points in one cylinder and two ordered target points
with different first coordinates. By \cref{swo:fu:ct:homogeneity} there is an
automorphism carrying the first pair to the second. The image of the
cylinder cannot be a positive-length cylinder, since its two target
points disagree at their first coordinate. It cannot be the whole
space, since the original cylinder was proper.

For the stronger statement, fix finitely many parameters. The
automorphisms fixing them pointwise act transitively on each open
component of their complement, by the same finite homogeneity theorem.
A proper cylinder has no least or greatest point, and its two boundary
cuts are omitted. Near either boundary one can choose an inside point
and an outside point in the same component of the complement of the
finite parameter set. An automorphism fixing all parameters moves the
first point to the second and changes cylinder membership. A definable
set would have to be invariant under this automorphism.
\end{proof}

This supplies a negative answer to a concrete prefix-recovery question.
The labels and the displayed tree add real structure. An abstract order
automorphism has no obligation to respect that tree.

\subsubsection{Completion: two mechanisms for missing cuts}

\begin{theorem}\label{swo:fu:ct:completion}
The Dedekind completion of $P$ is order-isomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Every
nonempty prefix cylinder has continuum many omitted cuts arising from
nonexhaustive branches and continuum many arising from numerical cuts
in a next-coordinate alphabet. In particular,
\[
 P\not\cong(\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q,<),
\]
although the two spaces are homeomorphic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$P$ is dense, without endpoints, and has a countable order-dense set
as in the preceding proof. Its Dedekind completion is consequently a
complete separable dense order without endpoints, hence has type $\mathbb R$.

Fix $q_0\in\mathbb Q$ and a bijection
$v:\omega\to\mathbb Q\setminus\{q_0\}$. Its first-disagreement comparison
with every member of $P$ is defined. Put
\[
 L_v=\{e\in P:e<v\},\qquad R_v=\{e\in P:v<e\}.
\]
Both sides are nonempty. Each has no endpoint: after any given finite
first disagreement, agree with $v$ for longer and then choose a fresh
smaller or larger rational label. No point of $P$ realizes the cut,
since any different branch can be separated from $v$ at its first
disagreement by a fresh intermediate label. Distinct $v$ give distinct
cuts by the same separation argument. There are continuum many such
bijections. The argument works after any fixed finite prefix by
omitting a still-unused label.

For a different mechanism, take any irrational real $r$ and split $P$
according to $e(0)<r$ or $e(0)>r$. This is a missing cut because no first
coordinate equals $r$; both sides approach it through rational first
coordinates. Distinct irrationals give distinct cuts. Within a prefix
cylinder use the next unused rational coordinate instead. These cuts
do not determine a full rational branch through that level, whereas
the preceding omitted-range cuts do.

An order isomorphism extends uniquely to the Dedekind completions and
preserves the subset of represented points. The irrational order omits
only the countably many rational points of its completion; $P$ omits
continuum many. Hence they are not order-isomorphic. The homeomorphism
assertion follows from \cref{swo:fu:ct:topology} and the standard Baire-space
description of the irrationals, or from their usual continued-fraction
coding.
\end{proof}

Thus separability, complete metrizability, interval self-similarity,
finite homogeneity, and the size of the completion do not suffice to
identify this order with the irrational line. The placement of its
omitted cuts is an additional invariant.

\subsection{Source 20's route: the slice is not \texorpdfstring{$F_\sigma$}{F-sigma}}\label{swo:lm:top:sec}

\merge\ Source~20's Section~9, printed whole. Its proof of the Baire-space
homeomorphism and of the $G_\delta$ description is source~24's; new are the strict
Borel classification (the slice is not $F_\sigma$ in its completion, because Baire
space is not $\sigma$-compact) and the omitted cuts from irrational first
coordinates, which are source~21's second mechanism (\cref{swo:fu:ct:completion}).

% ---- source 20 (batch-83 manuscript 02), lines 2914-3147
At the first infinite birthday cutoff, the space of enumerations admits
an accessible description that also illustrates a limitation of topological
classification.  Put
\[
 X=\No_{<\omega},\qquad
 P=\WO_\omega(X)=\{f:\omega\longrightarrow X:f\text{ is a bijection}\},
\]
with numerical first-difference comparison.  The numerical order on $X$
is countable, dense, and without endpoints.  Thus it is isomorphic to
$\mathbb Q$; fix one such identification when needed.  Everything in
this section is an ordinary set theorem in ZFC.  In fact, the proofs
apply to any countable dense alphabet without endpoints.

For a finite injective word $s$ over $X$, write
\[
 [s]=\{f\in P:s\text{ is an initial segment of }f\}.
\]
Every such cylinder is nonempty: enumerate its countably infinite
remaining alphabet after the prescribed prefix.

\begin{theorem}[Topology, completion, and omitted cuts]
\label{swo:lm:top:main}
The order $P$ has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Its order topology equals the topology of pointwise convergence
when the alphabet $X$ is discrete.  The cylinders $[s]$ are a countable
clopen basis.
\item Its Dedekind completion is order-isomorphic to $\mathbb R$.
Under any such identification, $P$ is a dense $G_\delta$ subset of
$\mathbb R$ that is not $F_\sigma$.
\item As a topological space, $P$ is homeomorphic to Baire space
$\omega^\omega$.  No point has a compact neighborhood.
\item Every nonempty open interval of the completion contains
$2^{\aleph_0}$ omitted points.  Consequently, $P$ is not
order-isomorphic to the irrational numbers with their usual order.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

The last two conclusions are compatible.  A homeomorphism of spaces
need not preserve their displayed linear orders.  Here the order remembers
the omitted Dedekind cuts, while the topology alone does not remember
their number.

\subsubsection{The topology comes from finite prefixes}

\begin{lemma}
\label{swo:lm:top:cylinders}
Every cylinder $[s]$ is convex, has no first or last point, and is
clopen in the order topology.  Conversely, every neighborhood of
$f\in P$ contains a cylinder determined by an initial segment of $f$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Convexity follows immediately from first-difference comparison: a word
that disagrees with $s$ before the end of $s$ lies on the same side of
every member of $[s]$.  Let $n$ be the length of $s$ and let $f\in[s]$.
The residual alphabet $X\setminus\operatorname{ran}s$ remains dense
and without endpoints.  Choose unused labels
$a<f(n)<b$.  Complete $s$ followed by $a$, and $s$ followed by $b$, to
permutations $g,h$.  Then $g<f<h$, and convexity gives
$(g,h)\subseteq[s]$.  This proves openness and also rules out endpoints.
The complement of $[s]$ is the union of all other cylinders of length
$n$, so $[s]$ is closed as well.

For the converse, suppose $g<f<h$.  Let $i$ and $j$ be the first
positions at which $f$ differs from $g$ and $h$, respectively.  If
$n>\max\{i,j\}$, then every word sharing $f$'s first $n$ entries
remains between $g$ and $h$.  The same argument, using one comparison,
handles an open ray.  Hence the finite cylinders form a basis for
the order topology, exactly as they do for pointwise convergence on
the discrete alphabet.
\end{proof}

There are countably many finite prefixes.  Choosing one completion of
each produces a countable dense subset of $P$.  Moreover, $P$ itself
is densely ordered: at the first difference between two permutations,
choose an unused numerical label strictly between their unequal labels
and then complete the resulting prefix.  Varying the first label also
shows that $P$ has no endpoints.

For completeness, these facts identify its completion without a
cardinality argument.  A countable dense subset $D\subseteq P$ is itself
a dense order without endpoints, and the usual alternating extension
of finite partial isomorphisms identifies $D$ with $\mathbb Q$.
Cuts of $D$ then identify the Dedekind completion of $P$ with
$\mathbb R$.  We henceforth use one such identification and regard
$P$ as a dense suborder of $\mathbb R$.

\subsubsection{An explicit homeomorphism with Baire space}

Fix a listing $X=\{x_0,x_1,\ldots\}$.  At a finite injective prefix
$s$, let $x_{m(s)}$ be the first label in this listing that has not yet
appeared in $s$.  Partition $[s]$ according to the finite extension
ending at the first subsequent occurrence of this required label.
The parts are the cylinders $[t]$ with
\[
 t=s\mathbin{{}^\frown}u\mathbin{{}^\frown}\langle x_{m(s)}\rangle,
\]
where $u$ is any finite injective word over
$X\setminus(\operatorname{ran}s\cup\{x_{m(s)}\})$, including the
empty word.  These prefixes are pairwise incomparable under extension:
each ends precisely at that first occurrence.  Their cylinders
therefore form a disjoint partition of $[s]$.  The partition is
countably infinite, and we enumerate its members using a fixed coding
of finite words by natural numbers.

Given $z\in\omega^\omega$, start with $s_0$ empty and take $s_{n+1}$
to be the prefix indexing the $z(n)$-th part of this partition at
$s_n$.  The union
\[
 \Phi(z)=\bigcup_{n<\omega}s_n
\]
is an injective sequence of length $\omega$, because the lengths
strictly increase.  It is surjective as well: after $n$ steps all
of $x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}$ have appeared, since every step inserts the
least missing label.  Thus $\Phi(z)\in P$.

Conversely, any $f\in P$ selects a unique member of each successive
partition and hence determines a unique $z$.  The image of a basic
finite-prefix neighborhood in $\omega^\omega$ is exactly the
cylinder $[s_n]$ reached by that prefix.  These are open, and their
lengths tend to infinity along each branch.  They consequently form
a neighborhood basis at $\Phi(z)$.  This proves directly that $\Phi$
is a homeomorphism.  No compactness theorem or classification theorem
for Polish spaces is needed for this construction.

There is also a direct local compactness obstruction.  For each $s$,
the cylinders $[s\mathbin{{}^\frown}\langle a\rangle]$, as $a$ ranges
over the unused alphabet, are a countably infinite disjoint open
cover of $[s]$ with no finite subcover.  Thus $[s]$ is not compact.
If a point had a compact neighborhood, a sufficiently small clopen
cylinder inside that neighborhood would be a closed subset of a
compact space and hence compact, a contradiction.

\subsubsection{Recognizing the genuine permutations inside the completion}

The $G_\delta$ assertion has an explicit description in terms of
finite prefixes and eventual occurrence of every label.  For each
nonempty $s$, let
\[
 I_s=(\inf[s],\sup[s])\subseteq\mathbb R,
 \qquad I_{\varnothing}=\mathbb R.
\]
The endpoints for nonempty $s$ are finite: comparison of the first
entry with smaller and larger labels bounds the cylinder.  By
convexity and the absence of endpoints in $[s]$,
\begin{equation}
\label{swo:lm:top:cylinder-trace}
 I_s\cap P=[s].
\end{equation}
Intervals belonging to different prefixes of the same length are
disjoint.  Otherwise their open intersection would meet the dense
set $P$, contradicting disjointness of the cylinders.  More generally,
if $I_s$ and $I_t$ intersect, their prefixes are comparable under
extension.

Define open subsets of the completion by
\[
 U_n=\bigcup_{\substack{s\text{ injective}\\|s|=n}}I_s
 \quad(n\geq1),
 \qquad
 V_a=\bigcup_{\substack{s\text{ finite injective}\\a\in\operatorname{ran}s}}I_s
 \quad(a\in X).
\]
Every permutation belongs to all these open sets.  We claim the exact
identity
\begin{equation}
\label{swo:lm:top:gdelta}
 P=\bigcap_{n\geq1}U_n\ \cap\ \bigcap_{a\in X}V_a.
\end{equation}
Indeed, a real point in every $U_n$ determines a unique prefix $s_n$
of every length, and the intersection rule makes these prefixes
compatible.  Their union is an injective sequence $f$.  Membership
in every $V_a$ forces every label to occur in $f$, so $f\in P$.
The real point in question and $f$ both lie in every $I_{s_n}$.
If they were different, a member of the dense set $P$ strictly
between them would lie in every $I_{s_n}$ and hence share all entries
of $f$, an impossibility.  This proves the identity.

The conditions in \eqref{swo:lm:top:gdelta} have distinct purposes.  The
$U_n$ require a genuine label at every position; the $V_a$ impose
exhaustion of the alphabet.  An infinite injective word omitting a
label is excluded by the second requirement.  A cut that separates
possible next labels without selecting one is excluded by the first.
Since each displayed open set contains the dense set $P$, the
complement of $P$ is a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets.

The Borel classification is strict: $P$ is not $F_\sigma$ in its
completion.  First observe that $\omega^\omega$ is not
$\sigma$-compact.  Given compact sets $K_n\subseteq\omega^\omega$,
their projections onto coordinate $n$ are finite; choosing the
$n$-th entry outside that finite projection constructs a point
outside $\bigcup_nK_n$.  The homeomorphism above gives the same
conclusion for $P$.  But an $F_\sigma$ subset of $\mathbb R$ is
$\sigma$-compact, by intersecting its closed pieces with the compact
intervals $[-m,m]$.  This contradiction proves the assertion.

\subsubsection{Continuum many missing points in every interval}

Identify the alphabet with $\mathbb Q$.  For every irrational
$r\in\mathbb R$, split the permutations according to
\[
 L_r=\{f\in P:f(0)<r\},\qquad
 R_r=\{f\in P:f(0)>r\}.
\]
These two sets partition $P$, the first has no greatest member, and
the second has no least member.  Indeed, a rational first entry can
always be chosen closer to $r$ on its own side and completed to a
permutation.  Thus this cut is an omitted point of the completion.
Distinct irrational numbers give distinct cuts, because a rational
first entry between them separates the cuts.  The completion
therefore has $2^{\aleph_0}$ omitted points.

The same argument works inside every cylinder: its residual alphabet
is again a countable dense order without endpoints. Every nonempty open
interval of the completion contains a cylinder, by density of $P$
and \cref{swo:lm:top:cylinders}.  Hence every such interval contains
$2^{\aleph_0}$ omitted points.  In particular, the complement is
both dense and meager.

Finally, an order isomorphism between two dense orders extends
uniquely to an isomorphism of their Dedekind completions, by mapping
cuts.  If $P$ were order-isomorphic to $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$,
this extension would identify the omitted points of their
completions.  One complement has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ and
the other is countable.  This is impossible, and completes the proof
of \cref{swo:lm:top:main}.

This example supplies a specific answer at the level of topology
and descriptive complexity.  It does not by itself classify the
arrangement of all omitted cuts up to order isomorphism.  Extending
the analysis to uncountable birthday cutoffs requires explicit
choices of generalized topology and of the permitted lengths of
prefixes; the countable Polish-space conclusions do not transfer
merely by replacing $\omega$ with a larger cardinal.

\subsection{Source 19's route}\label{swo:rs:ia:sec:countable-topology}

\merge\ Source~19's Section~8, printed whole. Its $G_\delta$ proof reads the
omitted points off the normal forms of \cref{swo:rs:ia:thm:completion-normal-form},
and it counts the original as well as the omitted points of every interval.

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 1520-1632
The first infinite birthday cutoff already distinguishes order
type from topology in a concrete way. Let $D=\No_{<\omega}$ and
$P=\WO_\omega(D)$. The proof below applies to
every countable dense alphabet without endpoints.

\begin{theorem}[A real completion with many omitted points]
\label{swo:rs:ia:thm:countable-topology}
The order $P$ has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item its Dedekind completion is order-isomorphic to $\mathbb R$;
\item its order topology is homeomorphic to Baire space
      $\omega^\omega$;
\item in its real-line completion it is a dense $G_\delta$ subset;
\item every nonempty open interval of the completion contains
      $2^{\aleph_0}$ original points and $2^{\aleph_0}$ omitted
      completion points;
\item it is not order-isomorphic to the irrational numbers.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Finite prefix cylinders form a clopen basis for the order topology.
For $e\in C_p$, choose an unused smaller next digit and an unused
larger next digit at some coordinate at or after the end of $p$,
and complete to obtain $a<e<b$ inside $C_p$. Convexity gives
$(a,b)\subseteq C_p$, proving openness. Its complement is a union
of incompatible prefix cylinders and is also open. Conversely,
an interval around $e$ contains a sufficiently long finite prefix
cylinder of $e$, since both endpoint comparisons are decided at
finite coordinates.

Only countably many finite prefixes exist. Choosing one completion
of each gives a countable order-dense subset. The order is dense
and has no endpoints. Its Dedekind completion is consequently a
complete dense order without endpoints and with a countable dense
subset, hence isomorphic to $\mathbb R$: identify a countable
dense skeleton with $\mathbb Q$ and then identify the two
completions through their cuts. This proves the first assertion.

For an explicit Baire-space homeomorphism, fix an enumeration
$d_0,d_1,\ldots$ of $D$. At a finite injective prefix $p$, let
$m(p)$ be the least-indexed unused label. Split $C_p$ according
to the finite block $q$ that starts immediately after $p$ and
ends at the first occurrence of $m(p)$. Thus $q$ is nonempty and
injective, uses only unused labels, ends with $m(p)$, and has no
earlier occurrence of that label. There are countably infinitely
many such blocks; enumerate them by natural numbers using the
fixed alphabet enumeration.

Their cylinders $C_{p^\frown q}$ are nonempty, clopen, pairwise
disjoint, and cover $C_p$. Two such blocks cannot be proper
prefixes of one another because both end at their first occurrence
of the same required label. Given $s\in\omega^\omega$, at stage
$n$ append the block numbered $s(n)$. The prefix length increases
at every stage, and each stage inserts the least missing label.
The union is therefore an injection of domain $\omega$ using
every label, hence a permutation. Conversely, every permutation
splits uniquely into these successive blocks. These procedures
are inverse. A finite Baire cylinder maps to exactly one of the
corresponding permutation cylinders, and these cylinders form
bases on both sides. This proves the homeomorphism without a
separate classification theorem for Polish spaces.

For the $G_\delta$ assertion, view $\overline P$ as the real
line and, for each nonempty finite prefix $p$, put
\[
 J_p=(\inf C_p,\sup C_p).
\]
These cylinder boundaries exist in the completion. For $n\geq1$
and $d\in D$, define the open sets
\[
 U_n=\bigcup_{\operatorname{length}(p)=n}J_p,
 \qquad
 V_d=\bigcup_{d\in\operatorname{ran}(p)}J_p,
\]
where the second union is over finite injective prefixes. Then
\[
 P=\bigcap_{n\geq1}U_n\ \cap\ \bigcap_{d\in D}V_d.
\]
Indeed, a numerical-split code at a prefix of length $k$ fails
$U_{k+1}$. There are no nonzero short limit prefixes below
$\omega$. A full branch omitting $d$ fails $V_d$. Every
surjective branch belongs to every displayed open set.
Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:ia:thm:completion-normal-form} exhausts all cases.
This is a countable intersection of open sets. Each contains the
dense set $P$, so the representation is a dense $G_\delta$.

Every nonempty interval contains a finite prefix cylinder. Reserve
one unused label $d$. There are $2^{\aleph_0}$ full injective
branches extending that prefix and omitting $d$, for example by
permuting the countably infinite remaining alphabet with $d$
removed. Distinct branches give distinct proper gaps: at their
first unequal coordinate, choose a fresh label strictly between
their two entries and complete to a permutation between them.
Thus the original interval contains continuum many omitted
completion points. The cylinder also contains continuum many
surjective permutations. This proves the fourth assertion.

Finally, the irrational order has real-line completion with
exactly countably many omitted points, namely the rationals.
An order isomorphism extends uniquely to the completions and
preserves their complements. Our continuum-sized omitted set
therefore excludes an order isomorphism with the irrationals.
\end{proof}

The conclusion illustrates a limitation of topological
classification: the explicit Baire-space topology coexists with
a substantially different pattern of Dedekind omissions. The
completion normal forms retain that order information. For
uncountable $\mu$, the same full-size-interval hypothesis makes
bounded-length prefix cylinders a clopen basis, but the countable
Baire-space construction and the real-line completion conclusion
must not be transferred without new hypotheses.

The first countable stage gives a particularly concrete way to distinguish
interpretations that have the same cardinality and the same embedding
spectra.  Let $D$ be a countable dense linear order without endpoints;
the intended example is $D=\No_{<\omega}$ with its numerical order.
For every countably infinite ordinal $\alpha$, put
\[
 P_\alpha=\{f:\alpha\longrightarrow D:f\text{ is bijective}\}.
\]
We compare these functions at their first unequal ordinal coordinate.
There are two topologies on the same set that must be named separately:
\[
 \tau_{\mathrm{lex}}=\text{the topology of the displayed linear order},
 \qquad
 \tau_{\mathrm{coord}}=\text{the subspace topology from }D^\alpha,
\]
where the alphabet $D$ is discrete in the second definition.  The latter
topology specifies finitely many coordinate values, at arbitrary positions
of $\alpha$.  A fixed prefix extending through an infinite ordinal need
not be an open coordinate condition.

The previous countable-cutoff result says that these topologies agree on
$P_\omega$ and give Baire space (sources~21 and~20; \cref{swo:fu:ct:topology,swo:lm:top:main}).  The repository also already determines
density and cellularity for every fixed stratum: in the present case the
first three strata have countable density and all later ones have density
$\mathfrak c$ (\cref{swo:ds:thm:density}).  We use these as background and prove refinements that are
not consequences of the cardinal invariants: the precise topology
comparison, a category distinction at one extra label, and different
Borel sigma-algebras at two extra labels.

\subsection{A common real completion for finite omissions}

Let
\[
 I=\{p:\omega\longrightarrow D:p\text{ is injective}\},\qquad
 E_n=\{p\in I:|D\setminus\operatorname{ran}p|=n\}\quad(n<\omega).
\]
Here $E_0=P_\omega$.  Both $I$ and each $E_n$ carry finite-coordinate
first-difference comparison.  For a finite injective word $s$, its
cylinder consists of all extensions of $s$ in the order under discussion.

\begin{lemma}[A common completion]\label{swo:bw:tp:lem:common-completion}
The order $I$ is dense, has no endpoints, and has a countable clopen
cylinder basis.  Its Dedekind completion $\widehat I$ is a copy of $\mathbb R$.
Every $E_n$ is order-dense in $I$ and in $\widehat I$.  The order topology of $E_n$
is its subspace topology in $\widehat I$, and is also its finite-prefix topology.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
After any finite prefix the unused alphabet is again countable, dense,
and without endpoints.  Given unequal entries at the first difference,
choose an unused entry strictly between them and extend to an infinite
injection.  The same construction on either side of the next entry
proves that each cylinder has no endpoints and is open.  Cylinders of
one fixed finite length partition the order, so they are also closed.
Every order interval containing $p$ contains a sufficiently long finite
prefix cylinder of $p$.  Thus the countably many cylinders form a basis.
Choosing one point of each nonempty cylinder gives a countable dense
subset, whose order is the rational order.  Passing to cuts identifies
the completion with $\mathbb R$.

Every finite injective prefix can be completed with exactly $n$ omitted
labels: reserve $n$ labels outside the prefix and enumerate all the other
unused labels.  Consequently each $E_n$ meets every cylinder.  It is
order-dense in $I$ and $\widehat I$.  Density ensures that the order topology is
the inherited topology; the cylinder proof also works directly in
$E_n$.
\end{proof}

The real completion in this lemma is shared by all $E_n$.  In particular,
it gives an unambiguous setting for comparing the complexity of their
realized points.  No class of proper-class orders occurs in this argument.

For each nonempty finite injective $s$, let
\[
 J_s=(\inf[s],\sup[s])\subseteq \widehat I,
 \qquad J_\varnothing=\widehat I,
\]
where the cylinder is now taken in $I$.  Its finite endpoints exist,
and $J_s\cap I=[s]$.  Put
\[
 U_k=\bigcup_{|s|=k}J_s\quad(k\geq1),\qquad
 V_a=\bigcup_{a\in\operatorname{ran}s}J_s\quad(a\in D).
\]
All these sets are open in $\widehat I$.  Distinct cylinders of a fixed length
give disjoint open intervals: an intersection would meet the dense
order $I$.  More generally, intersecting intervals have compatible
prefixes.  It follows, exactly as in the exhaustive case, that
\begin{equation}\label{swo:bw:tp:eq:I-gdelta}
 I=\bigcap_{k\geq1}U_k.
\end{equation}
Indeed, a point in the intersection determines a compatible infinite
injective branch.  The point equals that branch in the completion,
because otherwise an intervening member of $I$ would share all of its
coordinates.  For a branch $p\in I$, membership in $V_a$ says exactly
that the label $a$ occurs in $p$.

Define, for $n\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:bw:tp:eq:at-most-n}
 G_{\leq n}
 = I\cap
   \bigcap_{A\in[D]^{n+1}}\ \bigcup_{a\in A}V_a.
\end{equation}
This is a dense $G_\delta$ subset of $\widehat I$: it contains $E_0$, which is
dense, and the displayed intersections are countable.  Its branches
omit at most $n$ labels.  Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{swo:bw:tp:eq:exact-n}
 E_0=G_{\leq0},\qquad
 E_n=G_{\leq n}\setminus G_{\leq n-1}\quad(n\geq1).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[The category change at one omission]
\label{swo:bw:tp:thm:category-omissions}
The following statements hold in the common real completion $\widehat I$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $E_0$ is a dense $G_\delta$, homeomorphic to Baire space, and is
      not $F_\sigma$.
\item For every $n\geq1$, $E_n$ is a difference of two dense
      $G_\delta$ sets, and hence is $\Delta^0_3$.  It is neither
      $G_\delta$ nor $F_\sigma$.
\item For every $n\geq1$, $E_n$ is meager in itself, has no compatible
      complete metric, and contains a closed copy of Baire space.
\end{enumerate}
Every nonempty interval of $\widehat I$ contains $\mathfrak c$ points of every
$E_n$.  Thus equal cardinalities of realized and omitted points do not
detect this category distinction.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is the previous $\omega$-enumeration theorem, applied
to $D$.  The explicit least-missing-label block construction gives the
homeomorphism with $\omega^\omega$.  For completeness, this space is
not sigma-compact: if $K_i$ are compact subsets, the projection of $K_i$
to coordinate $i$ is finite, and a diagonal choice outside these finite
projections avoids $\bigcup_iK_i$.  Since an $F_\sigma$ subset of
$\mathbb R$ is sigma-compact, $E_0$ is not $F_\sigma$.

Fix $n\geq1$.  For $F\in[D]^n$, let
\[
 A_F=\{p\in E_n:D\setminus\operatorname{ran}p=F\}.
\]
Within $E_n$ this is the closed condition that no member of $F$ ever
occurs.  It has empty interior.  A finite prefix of a point of $A_F$
can be extended by a member of $F$ and then completed with $n$ different
omissions.  Such a completion lies outside $A_F$ in the same prescribed
prefix neighborhood.  The countable family $(A_F)_{F\in[D]^n}$ covers
$E_n$, proving that $E_n$ is meager in itself.  Each $A_F$, with its
inherited prefix topology, is exactly the permutation space of the
countable dense alphabet $D\setminus F$, hence is homeomorphic to
Baire space.  The Baire category theorem rules out a compatible
complete metric on the nonempty space $E_n$.

Equation~\eqref{swo:bw:tp:eq:exact-n} proves the asserted Borel upper bound.
If $E_n$ were $G_\delta$ in $\widehat I$, it would be a dense $G_\delta$
disjoint from the dense $G_\delta$ set $E_0$, contradicting the Baire
theorem for $\mathbb R$.  If $E_n$ were $F_\sigma$ in $\widehat I$, it would
be sigma-compact, and its relatively closed subspace $A_F$ would be
sigma-compact as well.  This contradicts the preceding diagonal
argument for Baire space.

Finally, inside any fixed finite prefix choose one permissible omitted
set $F$ and vary the permutation of the remaining countably infinite
alphabet.  There are $\mathfrak c$ such permutations.  Every nonempty
interval contains a prefix cylinder, and no $E_n$ has more than
$\mathfrak c$ points.
\end{proof}

The description $\Delta^0_3$ here is an upper bound together with strict
exclusion from both second-level classes.  It does not assert
$\Sigma^0_3$- or $\Pi^0_3$-completeness.  The more precise information
we use is the explicit difference-of-$G_\delta$ representation.

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 1389-1517
The countable birthday stage already distinguishes several notions that
cardinality and ordinal-embedding spectra do not distinguish.  Throughout
this section let $D$ be a countable dense linear order without endpoints,
such as $\mathbb Q$ or $\No_{<\omega}$ with its numerical order.  For a
nonnegative integer $n$ put
\[
 P_{\omega+n}=\operatorname{Bij}(\omega+n,D),\qquad
 E_n=\{p:\omega\hookrightarrow D:|D\setminus\operatorname{ran}(p)|=n\}.
\]
Both sets carry lexicographic orders; $P_{\omega+n}$ carries its order topology.
The topology on $E_n$ will shortly be identified with the subspace
topology inherited from $D^\omega$, where $D$ is \emph{discrete}.
This use of the discrete topology is an encoding convention, and does
not change the numerical order used in lexicographic comparisons.

The additional results in this section concern the progression
\[
 \omega,\quad \omega+1,\quad \omega+2,\quad \omega+3.
\]
At the first added terminal coordinate, complete metrizability fails.
At the second, metrizability and standard Borel structure fail.
At the third, a dense set of isolated points appears and the ranking
map from relation tables ceases to be Borel measurable.  These are
different thresholds.

\subsubsection{The cofinite-prefix model}

For $S\in[D]^n$ write
\[
 E_{n,S}=\{p\in E_n:\operatorname{ran}(p)=D\setminus S\}.
\]
For a finite injective sequence $s$ in $D$, write
$[s]=\{p\in E_n:s\subseteq p\}$.  Every such cylinder is nonempty:
choose $n$ unused labels to omit, and enumerate all remaining labels.

\begin{lemma}[Prefix topology and finite fibers]
\label{swo:rt:lem:cofinite-prefix-model}
For every finite $n$ the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The finite-prefix cylinders form a countable clopen base for
      the order topology of $E_n$.  Consequently this topology is
      precisely its product subspace topology.
\item $E_n$ is densely ordered, has no endpoints, and has cardinality
      $\mathfrak c$.
\item Restriction to the first $\omega$ coordinates identifies $P_{\omega+n}$
      as an ordered set with
      \[
        E_n\mathbin{\overrightarrow\times}\{1,\ldots,n!\},
      \]
      where the displayed finite set has its usual order and the
      product is lexicographic.  The projection $\pi_n:P_{\omega+n}\to E_n$
      is continuous.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $p$ extends $s$, choose two unused labels, one below and one above
$p(|s|)$, and complete the two resulting finite prefixes to elements
of $E_n$.  The interval between these two elements contains $p$ and
lies in $[s]$.  Thus $[s]$ is open.  Its complement is a union of the
other cylinders of the same length, so it is also closed.  If
$a<p<b$, the two first disagreements with $p$ occur at finite
coordinates.  A sufficiently long finite prefix of $p$ therefore
has its entire cylinder in $(a,b)$.  The same argument applies to
rays.  This proves the first assertion.

If $p<q$ first differ at $k$, choose an unused label strictly between
$p(k)$ and $q(k)$ and extend the resulting prefix.  The extension
lies strictly between $p$ and $q$.  Choosing a smaller or larger
first label proves the absence of endpoints.  The upper cardinal
bound is $|D^\omega|=\mathfrak c$.  For a fixed omitted set $S$, the
permutations of $D\setminus S$ already give $\mathfrak c$ elements:
independently switch countably many disjoint pairs.

Finally, a prefix $p\in E_n$ leaves exactly $n$ labels, and its
continuations are their $n!$ permutations in lexicographic order.
Different prefixes are compared before any of these terminal
coordinates.  This gives the displayed order isomorphism.  For
example, for $a<b$ in $E_n$,
\[
 \pi_n^{-1}((a,b))=((a,n!),(b,1)),
\]
and the corresponding ray identities prove continuity.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The category and Borel class of cofinite prefixes]
\label{swo:rt:prop:cofinite-prefix-category}
The space $E_0$ is Polish and Baire.  For each $n\geq1$, $E_n$ is
metrizable and second countable, but meagre in itself and therefore
not Polish.  As a subset of the Polish space
$I=\operatorname{Inj}(\omega,D)\subseteq D^\omega$, $E_n$ belongs
to $\Delta^0_3$ and is neither $F_\sigma$ nor $G_\delta$ when
$n\geq1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Injectivity is a closed condition in $D^\omega$.  Surjectivity is the
$G_\delta$ condition
\[
 \bigcap_{x\in D}\ \bigcup_{k<\omega}\{p:p(k)=x\}.
\]
Thus $E_0$ is a $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space, hence Polish
and Baire.

For $n\geq1$ the countable family $\{E_{n,S}:S\in[D]^n\}$ covers
$E_n$.  Each member is closed in $E_n$, since it is specified there
by the condition that every label in $S$ is omitted.  Each has empty
interior: a finite prefix can always be extended while omitting a
different $n$-element set.  This proves meagreness.  A nonempty
Polish space is Baire, so $E_n$ is not Polish.

The condition ``at most $n$ labels are omitted'' is $G_\delta$:
for each $(n+1)$-element subset of $D$, at least one of its labels
must occur.  The condition ``at least $n$ labels are omitted'' is
$F_\sigma$: some $n$-element set is avoided.  Their intersection
is $E_n$, so $E_n\in\Delta^0_3$.  It cannot be $G_\delta$, since
that would make it Polish.

To rule out $F_\sigma$, fix $S\in[D]^n$ and let
\[
 I_S=\{p\in I:\operatorname{ran}(p)\subseteq D\setminus S\}.
\]
This is a closed Polish subspace of $I$, and
$E_n\cap I_S=E_{n,S}$ is a dense $G_\delta$ in $I_S$.
Its complement is also dense: any finite injective prefix can be
extended while omitting one additional label.  Consequently every
closed subset of $I_S$ contained in $E_{n,S}$ is nowhere dense.
If $E_n$ were $F_\sigma$ in $I$, then $E_{n,S}$ would be a meagre
dense $G_\delta$ in the Baire space $I_S$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}


\begin{note}[Source~30, Corollary~6.3, ``An explicit Baire-space presentation'']\label{swo:rt:cor:baire-homeomorphism}
\emph{The space $P_\omega=E_0$ is homeomorphic to $\omega^\omega$ with its usual
product topology.} This is \cref{swo:pc:thm:completecountable}, by the same
least-missing-label tree (\cref{swo:pc:thm:regular} at $\mu=\omega$): at a cylinder
$[s]$ of full permutations, the first label $a_j$ of a fixed list absent from $s$
splits $[s]$ into the countably many cylinders $[s\cat v\cat(a_j)]$, ``exactly the
possible blocks ending at the first future occurrence of $a_j$''.
\end{note}

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 1543-1549
The preceding argument pinpoints why appending one final label matters.
An enumeration of type $\omega$ must eventually display \emph{every}
label; an enumeration of type $\omega+1$ must leave exactly one label
undisplayed at all finite stages.  The latter condition is a countable
union of closed, nowhere-dense alternatives, one for each possible
final label.  In particular $P_{\omega+1}$ is not homeomorphic to the Baire
space $P_\omega$.

\subsection{Finite tails as finite split orders}

\begin{proposition}[The exact finite-tail reduction]
\label{swo:bw:tp:prop:finite-tail}
For each $n<\omega$ there is an order isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{swo:bw:tp:eq:split}
 P_{\omega+n}\ \cong\ E_n\times_{\mathrm{lex}}\{0,\ldots,n!-1\}.
\end{equation}
It sends an enumeration to its first $\omega$ entries and to the
lexicographic rank of its finite terminal permutation.  For $n=0$ and
$n=1$ the second factor is a singleton.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first $\omega$ entries omit exactly the $n$ labels used in the
tail.  For a fixed prefix $p\in E_n$, the $n!$ possible tails form a
finite chain in numerical lexicographic order.  Different prefixes
first differ at a finite coordinate, so their entire tail fibers are
ordered by the prefix comparison.  This proves bijectivity and order
preservation.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[All the finite successors have different order types]
\label{swo:bw:tp:cor:distinct}
The orders $P_{\omega+n}$, for $n<\omega$, are pairwise
nonisomorphic.  In particular, $P_\omega$ and $P_{\omega+1}$ are
equimorphic but are not isomorphic.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The latter two orders are respectively $E_0$ and $E_1$, and their
order topologies are respectively Baire and meager in themselves.
An order isomorphism is a homeomorphism, so no such isomorphism exists.
Their equimorphism follows from the existing countable binary-cube
classification (\cref{swo:cb:new:thm:block-types}); it is not a new embedding-spectrum assertion.

For $n\geq2$, the equivalence relation saying that the closed interval
between two points is finite has exactly the fibers in
\eqref{swo:bw:tp:eq:split} as its classes.  A fiber has $n!$ elements.
Different fibers have infinitely many whole fibers between them because
$E_n$ is densely ordered.  Thus the size $n!$ of the maximal finite
convex blocks is an intrinsic invariant, distinguishing every $n\geq2$
from every other such $n$ and from $n=0,1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-tail topological classification]
\label{swo:bw:tp:thm:finite-topology}
In its native order topology, $P_{\omega+n}$ has the following
properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $n=0$ it is Baire space.
\item For $n=1$ it is separable and metrizable, but is meager in itself
      and is not completely metrizable.
\item For $n=2$ it is first countable and separable, is meager in itself,
      and is not metrizable.
\item For $n\geq3$ it is first countable and nonmetrizable, and has a
      dense open set of $\mathfrak c$ isolated points.  It is therefore
      a Baire space, although its density is $\mathfrak c$.
\end{enumerate}
For $n\geq2$ its topological weight is $\mathfrak c$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The cases $n=0,1$ have already been proved.  Consider a finite split
order $L=E\times_{\mathrm{lex}}m$, where $E=E_n$ and $m=n!\geq2$.
The projection $\pi:L\to E$ is continuous.  A countable dense subset
of $E$ gives countable sequences approaching every base point from
both sides.  Together with the immediate neighbors inside a finite
fiber, these give a countable local base at every point of $L$.

Let $S=E\times\{0,m-1\}$ be the first and last points of the fibers.
Its complement consists of isolated interior points and is open; hence
$S$ is closed.  The induced topology on $S$ is precisely the order
topology of $E\times_{\mathrm{lex}}2$.  This can also be seen directly
from neighborhoods of the first and last point of each fiber: the first
is approached through earlier base fibers and the last through later
ones.  Removing only the interior of the finite fibers changes neither
of these neighborhoods.

The double split of $E$ is separable.  If $B$ is a countable dense
subset of $E$, then $B\times2$ is dense, since every nonempty open
set contains a point over a nonempty base interval.  It is not second
countable.  For each $x\in E$, choose a basis element containing
$(x,0)$ and contained in the open ray $(-\infty,(x,1))$.  The
chosen basis elements must be distinct: if $x<y$, the one chosen for
$x$ cannot contain $(y,0)$.  Thus every basis has cardinality at least
$|E|=\mathfrak c$.  A separable metrizable space is second countable,
so the double split is not metrizable.  Since $S$ is a subspace, neither
is $L$.  First countability and $|L|=\mathfrak c$ give the matching
upper bound for weight.

When $m=2$, the inverse images of the relatively closed nowhere dense
sets $A_F\subseteq E_n$ remain nowhere dense.  Every nonempty open
set in the double split contains all fibers over a nonempty base
interval, which cannot be contained in $A_F$.  These countably many
inverse images cover $L$, proving that it is meager in itself.

When $m\geq3$, the interior points of every fiber are isolated.  They
form a dense open set: any neighborhood of a first or last point meets
another whole fiber, because the base order is dense and has no
endpoints.  Every dense open subset must contain every isolated point.
Consequently a countable intersection of dense open subsets contains
this same dense set, which proves the Baire assertion.  There are
$\mathfrak c$ isolated points, so density is $\mathfrak c$.
\end{proof}

The threshold for category differs from the threshold for metrizability.
One omitted label destroys complete metrizability.  Two terminal labels
produce uncountably many jumps and destroy metrizability.  Three terminal
labels introduce a dense set of isolated points and restore the Baire
property.  The density transition at three labels is already in the
repository; the category and measurable-structure refinements here
explain additional distinctions it does not record.

nonisolated set $S_n$ (its $D_n$), which is order-homeomorphic to the doubled
order $\operatorname{Split}(E_n)$ and closed nowhere dense for $n\ge3$:

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 1551-1666
\subsubsection{The four topological regimes}

We first isolate the elementary topology of a doubled order.  If $E$
is densely ordered without endpoints, put
\[
 \operatorname{Split}(E)=E\mathbin{\overrightarrow\times}\{-,+\}.
\]
The two points $p^-<p^+$ over each $p\in E$ are adjacent, but neither
is isolated.  The term ``split'' here specifies this exact two-point
construction.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-tail topology]
\label{swo:rt:thm:finite-tail-topology}
The following properties hold for $P_{\omega+n}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $P_\omega$ is zero-dimensional, Polish and Baire.
\item $P_{\omega+1}$ is zero-dimensional, second countable and metrizable,
      but meagre in itself and not Polish.
\item $P_{\omega+2}$ is zero-dimensional, first countable and separable,
      but meagre in itself and nonmetrizable.  Its weight is
      $\mathfrak c$.
\item For $n\geq3$, $P_{\omega+n}$ is zero-dimensional and first countable.
      It has a dense open discrete set of $\mathfrak c$ isolated
      points, and is therefore Baire.  Its density, cellularity and
      weight are all $\mathfrak c$, and it is nonmetrizable.
\end{enumerate}
For $n\geq2$, the nonisolated-point subspace is exactly
\[
 S_n=\{(p,1),(p,n!):p\in E_n\}.
\]
With its inherited topology, $S_n$ is order-homeomorphic to
$\operatorname{Split}(E_n)$.  It is separable, meagre in itself and
nonmetrizable, and has no isolated points.  For $n\geq3$ it is
closed and nowhere dense in $P_{\omega+n}$; moreover $P'_{\omega+n}=S_n=S_n'$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The assertions about $P_\omega$ and $P_{\omega+1}$ follow from the singleton-fiber
cases of Lemma~\ref{swo:rt:lem:cofinite-prefix-model} and
Proposition~\ref{swo:rt:prop:cofinite-prefix-category}.

Consider $E_n$ with each point replaced by two points.  Every
nonempty open subset contains the full inverse image of some
finite-prefix cylinder.  Indeed, a nonempty basic interval cannot
have both bounds in one two-point fiber; between their distinct
prefixes choose an intermediate prefix and then a sufficiently
small finite-prefix cylinder.  Choosing one point in the lift of
each of the countably many finite-prefix cylinders gives a
countable dense subset.  Moreover
\[
 \operatorname{Split}(E_n)
   =\bigcup_{S\in[D]^n}\pi^{-1}(E_{n,S})
 \qquad(n\geq1)
\]
is a countable union of closed nowhere-dense sets.  Closedness
follows from continuity of the projection; the preceding
finite-prefix observation proves empty interior.  This proves
separability and meagreness for all these split spaces.

There are $\mathfrak c$ adjacent pairs in
$\operatorname{Split}(E_n)$.  From any base choose, for each $p$,
a basic set $U_p$ with
\[
 p^-\in U_p\subseteq(-\infty,p^+).
\]
These basic sets are distinct.  If $p<q$, then
$q^-\geq p^+$, so a set contained in $(-\infty,p^+)$ cannot also
contain $q^-$.  Hence the weight is at least $\mathfrak c$; the
family of all order intervals and rays gives the reverse bound.
A separable metric space has countable weight, so the split space
is nonmetrizable.

For completeness, the local topology can be described explicitly.
Let $C_k(p)$ be the length-$k$ prefix cylinder about $p$ in $E_n$,
and put $m=n!$.  At the first point of a fiber with $m\geq2$, the
sets
\[
 \pi_n^{-1}(C_k(p))\cap(-\infty,(p,2))\qquad(k<\omega)
\]
form a clopen local base.  At the last point use
\[
 \pi_n^{-1}(C_k(p))\cap((p,m-1),\infty).
\]
Every interior point of a finite fiber is an open singleton.
This proves first countability and zero-dimensionality.

There are no adjacent points in distinct fibers, because $E_n$
is densely ordered.  Thus the isolated points in $P_{\omega+n}$ are
precisely $(p,j)$ with $1<j<n!$.  For $n\geq3$ these points form
a set of cardinality $\mathfrak c$.  They are dense: a neighborhood
of a fiber endpoint contains points from other fibers on its
nonadjacent side, and hence contains an entire intervening fiber
and an interior point of that fiber.  Every dense open set contains
every isolated point.  Any countable intersection of dense open
sets therefore contains this fixed dense set, proving the Baire
property.

Deleting the interior points leaves exactly the two endpoints of
each fiber.  The displayed local bases show directly that their
inherited topology is the order topology of
$\operatorname{Split}(E_n)$.  This subspace has no isolated
points.  It is closed, and for $n\geq3$ it is nowhere dense
because the isolated points are dense.  Consequently the
Cantor--Bendixson derivative stabilizes after the first step.
Its nonmetrizability also proves that $P_{\omega+n}$ itself is nonmetrizable
for $n\geq3$.  Finally, the open singletons give cellularity and
density at least $\mathfrak c$, while the size of the entire space
gives all upper bounds claimed.
\end{proof}

Thus the Baire property is lost at $\omega+1$ and recovered at
$\omega+3$ for an entirely different reason.  The recovered Baire
space is not completely Baire: it contains the nonempty closed
subspace $S_n$, which is meagre in itself.  There is no conflict
with the minimal-type result, and no implication that the spaces
in the final regime are Polish.  Nor does the theorem assert that
all $P_{\omega+n}$ with $n\geq3$ are mutually homeomorphic.

\subsection{Comparing the two topologies at every countable length}

\begin{theorem}[Exact comparison of native and coordinate topologies]
\label{swo:bw:tp:thm:two-topologies}
For a countably infinite ordinal $\alpha$, the coordinate topology
on $P_\alpha$ is always homeomorphic to Baire space.  The two displayed
topologies satisfy
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c}
 \alpha&\text{comparison}\\ \hline
 \omega&\tau_{\mathrm{lex}}=\tau_{\mathrm{coord}}\\
 \omega+1&\tau_{\mathrm{lex}}\subsetneq\tau_{\mathrm{coord}}\\
 \omega+2\leq\alpha<\omega_1&
   \tau_{\mathrm{lex}}\text{ and }\tau_{\mathrm{coord}}
   \text{ are incomparable}.
 \end{array}
\]
The native order topology is first countable for every such $\alpha$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose any bijection $b:\omega\to\alpha$.  Reindexing by $b$
identifies the coordinate permutation space with the coordinate space
$P_\omega$, which is Baire space.  This reindexing makes no claim to
preserve the native lexicographic order.

For $\alpha=\omega+1$, two distinct exhaustive enumerations must
differ before $\omega$: if their first $\omega$ entries agreed,
the single remaining label would agree too.  Consequently finite initial
cylinders form the order-topology basis, making every native-open set
coordinate-open.  The final-coordinate condition $f(\omega)=a$ is
coordinate-open but has empty interior in the native order: any finite
prefix can be completed with a different omitted label.  The inclusion
is strict.

We give witnesses valid for every $\alpha>\omega$, writing
$\alpha=\omega+\tau$.  First, the coordinate topology is never
contained in the native topology.  Choose a bounded numerical interval in $D$ and a suborder
$Y$ of that interval of order type $\tau$.  Such a suborder
exists because every countable linear order embeds in a countable
dense order.  For finite $\tau$ this just means choosing finitely
many increasing labels.  Enumerate $D\setminus Y$ in the first
$\omega$ positions and enumerate $Y$ increasingly thereafter; call
the resulting point $f$.  It is the least point in its first-$\omega$
prefix fiber.  If $a=f(\omega)$, the coordinate-open set
\[
 O_a=\{g:g(\omega)=a\}
\]
is not a native neighborhood of $f$.  Given $h<f$, the first
difference between $h$ and $f$ occurs at a finite position.  Preserve
a longer finite prefix of $f$, choose the next entry smaller than
the corresponding entry of $f$, and prescribe a value other than
$a$ at coordinate $\omega$.  The finite partial injection extends
to a bijection, producing $h<g<f$ with $g\notin O_a$.
Thus every native neighborhood of $f$ leaves $O_a$.

Second, if $\tau$ has at least two elements, the native topology
is not contained in the coordinate topology.  Keep a first-$\omega$
prefix enumerating $D\setminus Y$, where $Y$ lies in a bounded interval and has
cardinality $|\tau|$; choose two completions $f<h$ of this prefix.
The native ray $(-\infty,h)$ contains $f$.  In every finite-coordinate
neighborhood of $f$, select two unfixed finite positions $i<j$ with
$f(i)<f(j)$ and transpose their values.  These exist arbitrarily late
because $D\setminus Y$ is unbounded above and deleting finitely many
entries does not change that.  The modified enumeration $g$ respects
the prescribed finite coordinates, but its first difference from $h$
is at $i$, with a larger value.  Thus $g>h$.  The native ray is not
coordinate-open.

Finally, no increasing sequence of type $\omega_1$ can occur in
$P_\alpha$, nor can a decreasing one.  To see this directly, suppose
$(f_\xi)_{\xi<\omega_1}$ is increasing.  On a final segment its
first coordinate stabilizes, since it is monotone in a countable
alphabet.  Recursively stabilize each coordinate after stabilizing
all earlier ones.  There are only countably many coordinates, so the
supremum of the stabilization indices is still below $\omega_1$.
The sequence is eventually constant, a contradiction.  If the portion
below any point had no countable cofinal subset, recursion would build
an increasing $\omega_1$-sequence there.  The dual argument applies
above the point.  Countable cofinal and coinitial sets give the required
countable local bases.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Low-complexity comparison is not low-complexity topology]
\label{swo:bw:tp:prop:borel-relation}
For every countably infinite $\alpha$, the relation
\[
 \{(f,g)\in P_\alpha^2:f<_{\mathrm{lex}}g\}
\]
is both $F_\sigma$ and $G_\delta$ in the product coordinate topology.
Nevertheless, for every $\alpha\geq\omega+3$ there are native-open
subsets of $P_\alpha$ that are not coordinate-Borel.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For each $\beta<\alpha$, the condition
\[
 f\restr\beta
 =g\restr\beta,
 \qquad f(\beta)<g(\beta)
\]
is closed in the product coordinate topology: the equality is an
intersection of closed coordinate equalities, and the last condition
is clopen because the alphabet is discrete.  The lexicographic relation
is the countable union of these closed sets, hence is $F_\sigma$.
Its complement is the reverse strict relation together with the
closed diagonal, again $F_\sigma$.  Thus the strict relation is also
$G_\delta$.

For the second assertion, write $\alpha=\omega+\tau$ and choose
$Y\subset D$ with $|Y|=|\tau|$ and infinite complement.  There are
$\mathfrak c$ prefixes of length $\omega$ enumerating
$D\setminus Y$.  Each of their convex tail fibers has at least three
points, since $\tau\geq3$, and therefore contains a nonempty ambient
open interval.  These intervals are pairwise disjoint.  This is the
countable case of the existing cellularity argument (\cref{swo:ds:thm:density}).
Their arbitrary unions yield $2^{\mathfrak c}$ distinct native-open
sets, while the coordinate Polish space has only $\mathfrak c$ Borel
sets \cite{Kechris1995}.  For finite tails, arbitrary subsets of the
$\mathfrak c$ isolated interior permutations give the same conclusion.
\end{proof}

Thus a Borel comparison relation on a standard Borel code space does not
make every open set of the corresponding order topology Borel.  The
order topology permits arbitrary unions; the Borel sigma-algebra
permits only countable iterations of its generating operations.
