% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 1705-1794
\subsubsection{Relation tables as a standard Borel presentation}

Let $\mathrm{Tab}_n$ be the set of strict well-order relations of type
$\omega+n$ on $D$, regarded as a subspace of the Cantor space
$2^{D\times D}$.  Its topology records finitely many answers to
questions of the form ``does $xRy$?''  There are mutually inverse
set bijections
\[
 \Phi_n:P_{\omega+n}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Tab}_n,
 \qquad
 r_n:\mathrm{Tab}_n\longrightarrow P_{\omega+n},
\]
where $\Phi_n(e)$ is the relation induced by $e$ and $r_n$ is its
unique increasing enumeration.  The order topology on $P_{\omega+n}$ and
the table topology on $\mathrm{Tab}_n$ should not be identified.

\begin{proposition}[The fixed finite-tail table domains]
\label{swo:rt:prop:table-domain}
For every finite $n$, $\mathrm{Tab}_n$ is a $\Pi^0_3$-complete Borel
subset of $2^{D\times D}$ and hence is a standard Borel space.
Each coordinate of $r_n$, regarded as a map into the product
$D^{\omega+n}$ with discrete $D$, is Borel measurable.  In fact,
each singleton coordinate fiber is $F_\sigma$ relative to
$\mathrm{Tab}_n$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $\operatorname{FinPred}_x$ say that $x$ has finitely many
predecessors.  This is $F_\sigma$: some finite set contains all
predecessors.  Let $\operatorname{Succ}_k(x)$ say that $x$ has
exactly $k$ successors.  This too is $F_\sigma$, by choosing the
finite successor set and specifying all remaining comparison bits.
The set $\mathrm{LO}(D)$ of strict linear orders is closed.

For $n=0$ the required definition is
\[
 \mathrm{LO}(D)\cap\bigcap_{x\in D}\operatorname{FinPred}_x.
\]
For $n\geq1$ a $\Pi^0_3$ definition is the conjunction of
\begin{enumerate}
\item being a strict linear order;
\item among any $n+1$ distinct elements, at least one has finitely
      many predecessors;
\item some element has exactly $n-1$ successors.
\end{enumerate}
To verify this definition, condition (2) leaves at most $n$ points
with infinitely many predecessors.  The remaining points form an
infinite initial segment of type $\omega$.  Hence the entire order
has type $\omega+k$ for some $k\leq n$.  Condition (3) forces
$k=n$.  The definability bounds follow from the displayed
$F_\sigma$ descriptions.

The $\Pi^0_3$-completeness of the isomorphism class of $\omega$ is
classical; see Miller~\cite[\S2, Example~5]{Miller1983}.  Appending
a fixed $n$-point terminal order, after relabeling $D$ into a
cofinite subset, is a continuous reduction from $\mathrm{Tab}_0$
to $\mathrm{Tab}_n$.  Indeed, appending finitely many points
preserves any failure of well-foundedness, and for ordinals
$\gamma+n=\omega+n$ implies $\gamma=\omega$.  This proves
completeness for every finite $n$.  Miller's full calculation in
\cite[\S3, Lemma~3.5]{Miller1983} gives the same classification as
part of the classification for all countable ordinals.

Finally, $r_n(R)(k)=x$ for $k<\omega$ means exactly that $x$ has
$k$ predecessors.  For $j<n$,
\[
 r_n(R)(\omega+j)=x
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 x\text{ has exactly }n-1-j\text{ successors}.
\]
These are $F_\sigma$ conditions.  They prove the coordinate claim
and product Borel measurability.
\end{proof}

The last assertion does \emph{not} imply Borel measurability into
the lexicographic order topology.  This distinction becomes decisive
below.

There is a third natural topology to keep separate.  For every fixed
countable ordinal $\alpha$, the space
$\operatorname{Bij}(\alpha,D)$ is Polish in the \emph{full discrete
product topology} inherited from $D^\alpha$: injectivity is closed and
surjectivity is $G_\delta$.  The map from this product presentation to
relation tables is continuous, since the relative order of two labels
is determined once their two coordinates have been specified.  For
$\alpha=\omega+1$, observing the terminal coordinate is product-open
but not lexicographically open; its lexicographic fiber is one of the
closed nowhere-dense sets above.  Thus even the two topologies on the
same set of enumerations must be named explicitly.  The pathologies
proved here concern the \emph{order topology}, and do not contradict
the existence of a Polish product presentation.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 2399-2463
\subsection{The exact native Borel sigma-algebra of a double split}

The next elementary split-order lemma provides a full measurable
description at $\omega+2$.  The general split-interval phenomenon is
classical: for the split interval the following formula is Fremlin's
\cite[419L(b)]{Fremlin4}.  Applying it to the finite terminal permutation
fibers supplies the present refinement.  We include the complete
proof so that no classification theorem is needed.

\begin{theorem}[Borel sets in the double split]
\label{swo:bw:tp:thm:double-borel}
Let $E$ be a separable dense linear order without endpoints, identified
with a dense suborder of $\mathbb R$, and let
\[
 L=E\times_{\mathrm{lex}}\{0,1\},\qquad \pi:L\to E.
\]
With the native order topologies,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:bw:tp:eq:double-borel}
 \mathcal B(L)
 =\{\pi^{-1}(B)\mathbin{\triangle}N:
       B\in\mathcal B(E),\ N\subseteq L\text{ countable}\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, a native-Borel set can contain exactly one point of
a split pair at only countably many base points.  If $E$ is uncountable,
$\mathcal B(L)$ is not countably generated and is not a standard
Borel structure.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The projection is continuous.  In particular, inverse images of
Borel base sets are Borel, and all countable subsets of $L$ are Borel
because singletons are closed.  This proves one inclusion in
\eqref{swo:bw:tp:eq:double-borel}.

The family on its right-hand side is a sigma-algebra.  Complements
preserve the form; the union of countably many such sets differs from
the inverse image of the union of their base sets at only countably
many points.  It remains to show that it contains every open subset
$U\subseteq L$.

The order $L$ is separable, by the dense-set argument in the preceding
theorem.  Decompose $U$ into its maximal convex components.  Every
component is open and contains a point of a fixed countable dense set,
so there are only countably many of them.  The projection of a convex
component is a convex subset of $E$, hence a Borel interval of $E$,
allowing any endpoint convention.  A convex component contains either
both or neither points of every fiber except, possibly, at its two
boundary fibers.  Consequently $U$ differs from
$\pi^{-1}(\pi[U])$ at only countably many points, and $\pi[U]$ is
a countable union of Borel base intervals.  This proves the other
inclusion.

Suppose, finally, that $(B_i)_{i<\omega}$ generated $\mathcal B(L)$.
Each $B_i$ distinguishes the two points over at most countably many
base points.  Outside the union of these countable exceptional sets,
the two points have the same membership in every generator, hence in
every set in the generated sigma-algebra.  But their singletons are
Borel and distinguish them.  For uncountable $E$ this is impossible.
A standard Borel structure is countably generated
\cite[424B(a)]{Fremlin4}, so it is excluded as well.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis that $E$ sits densely in its real completion matters for
this formulation.  We are not claiming that every separable linear
order embeds densely in $\mathbb R$; orders with jumps need a different
statement.  Each $E_n$ satisfies exactly the hypothesis used here.

\begin{note}[Source~30, Lemma~6.7, ``Borel sets split only countably many fibers'']\label{swo:rt:lem:split-borel}\label{swo:rt:eq:split-borel}
\emph{Let $E$ be a second-countable dense linear order without endpoints, and
suppose $\operatorname{Split}(E)$ is separable. With $\pi$ the projection, its Borel
sets are precisely the sets $\pi^{-1}(B)\mathbin{\triangle}C$ with $B$ Borel in $E$
and $C$ countable; in particular every Borel set splits only countably many fibers;
if $E$ is uncountable, this Borel $\sigma$-algebra is not countably generated and is
not a standard Borel structure.} This is \cref{swo:bw:tp:thm:double-borel}, by the
same component argument (an open set has countably many maximal convex
components, each splitting at most its two boundary fibers). Source~30 adds: ``For
example, the set of all lower endpoints is not Borel. Its failure is stronger than a
failure to be open: it splits every fiber. For $E=E_n$, the split space has exactly
$\mathfrak c$ Borel sets \ldots, despite the failure of countable generation.''
Source~29 credits the formula to Fremlin \cite{Fremlin4}, 419L(b), for the split
interval.
\end{note}

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 2465-2558
\begin{theorem}[The measurable trichotomy for finite tails]
\label{swo:bw:tp:thm:borel-trichotomy}
Let $\mathcal B_{\mathrm{lex}}$ and
$\mathcal B_{\mathrm{coord}}$ be the Borel sigma-algebras of the
two topologies on $P_{\omega+n}$.  Then
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c}
 n&\text{comparison of Borel sigma-algebras}\\ \hline
 0,1&\mathcal B_{\mathrm{lex}}=\mathcal B_{\mathrm{coord}}\\
 2&\mathcal B_{\mathrm{lex}}\subsetneq\mathcal B_{\mathrm{coord}}\\
 n\geq3&\mathcal B_{\mathrm{lex}}\text{ and }
          \mathcal B_{\mathrm{coord}}\text{ are incomparable}.
 \end{array}
\]
For $n=2$, formula~\eqref{swo:bw:tp:eq:double-borel} with $E=E_2$
describes the native Borel sigma-algebra exactly, and it is not
countably generated.  For $n\geq3$, the native Borel sigma-algebra
has cardinality $2^{\mathfrak c}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $n=0$ the topologies agree.  For $n=1$, native-open sets are
coordinate-open.  Conversely, the extra coordinate events are already
native-Borel:
\[
 \{f:f(\omega)=a\}
 =P_{\omega+1}\setminus
   \bigcup_{k<\omega}\{f:f(k)=a\}.
\]
The events on the right are native-clopen.  A countable coordinate
basis therefore consists of native-Borel sets, proving equality of
the two sigma-algebras.

For $n=2$, use the double-split representation.  The prefix map to
$E_2$ is continuous for the coordinate topology, and countable sets
are coordinate-Borel.  Formula~\eqref{swo:bw:tp:eq:double-borel} therefore
gives $\mathcal B_{\mathrm{lex}}\subseteq
\mathcal B_{\mathrm{coord}}$.  Fix $a<b$ in $D$ and consider the
coordinate-clopen event
\[
 O_a=\{f:f(\omega)=a\}.
\]
For each prefix enumerating $D\setminus\{a,b\}$, the two
possible tails are $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$, and $O_a$ contains exactly
one of them.  There are $\mathfrak c$ such prefixes.  The split-pair
criterion in the preceding theorem shows that $O_a$ is not
native-Borel.  The inclusion is strict.

For $n\geq3$, let $m=n!$ and let
$S=E_n\times\{0,m-1\}$ be the closed endpoint subspace from
Theorem~\ref{swo:bw:tp:thm:finite-topology}.  It is the double split of
$E_n$.  Choose a fixed $n$-element residual set $F$ with minimum
$a$ and with a different maximum.  The coordinate-clopen event $O_a$
contains the first but not the last point over every prefix
enumerating $D\setminus F$: the first tail is increasing and the
last decreasing.  Its trace on $S$ distinguishes
$\mathfrak c$ endpoint pairs, so the double-split theorem shows that
the trace is not Borel in $S$.  If $O_a$ were native-Borel, its trace
on this closed subspace would be Borel, a contradiction.

In the other direction, the isolated interior points form a set of
cardinality $\mathfrak c$, every subset of which is native-open.
There are $2^{\mathfrak c}$ such subsets and only $\mathfrak c$
coordinate-Borel sets \cite{Kechris1995}.  Some native-open subsets are therefore not
coordinate-Borel.  This also proves the asserted cardinality of the
native Borel sigma-algebra.
\end{proof}

There is a slightly fuller normal form when $n\geq3$.  Put
\[
 J=E_n\times\{1,\ldots,n!-2\},\qquad
 S=E_n\times\{0,n!-1\}.
\]
A set is native-Borel exactly when its intersection with $J$ is
arbitrary and its intersection with $S$ has the form
\[
 \pi_S^{-1}(B)\mathbin{\triangle}N,
 \qquad B\in\mathcal B(E_n),\quad N\subseteq S\text{ countable}.
\]
Indeed $J$ is open and discrete, $S$ is closed, and the induced
topology on $S$ is the double split.  This gives an explicit
description of every native-Borel set, not just a cardinality argument.

For comparison, under the same finite-split identification the coordinate
Borel sigma-algebra is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{swo:bw:tp:eq:coordinate-borel}
 \left\{\bigcup_{j<n!}B_j\times\{j\}:
                    B_j\in\mathcal B(E_n)\right\}.
\end{equation}
To verify this without a Borel-isomorphism theorem, the prefix projection
is coordinate-continuous and the finite tail rank is coordinate-continuous.
Conversely, partition $E_n$ into the countably many closed sets $A_F$
of prescribed omissions.  On $A_F\times\{j\}$, every tail value is
fixed.  Thus the inverse image of every coordinate cylinder is a
countable union of Borel pieces in the displayed finite product.

\merge\ Source~30 states the measurable comparison through the ranking map $r_n$
and the table map $\Phi_n$; by its \cref{swo:rt:prop:single-orientation-enrichment},
coordinate Borel sets and relation-table Borel sets agree, so its theorem and
\cref{swo:bw:tp:thm:borel-trichotomy} are one result in two formulations.
Source~30's theorem adds that for $n\le1$ ranking is a pointwise limit of
continuous maps, and that the preimage of every lexicographic ray is $F_\sigma$ for
every $n$.

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 1851-2053
\subsubsection{A sharp, two-direction coding threshold}

\begin{theorem}[Ranking and relation-table maps]
\label{swo:rt:thm:finite-tail-borel-threshold}
With the topologies specified above:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $n=0,1$, $\Phi_n$ is continuous and $r_n$ is Borel
      measurable.  Thus the two presentations have the same
      standard Borel structure.  Nevertheless, $r_n$ is
      discontinuous at every point; it is a pointwise limit of
      continuous maps into $P_{\omega+n}$.
\item For $n=2$, $r_2$ is Borel measurable, but $\Phi_2$ is not
      Borel measurable.  The order-topological Borel structure of
      $P_{\omega+2}$ is strictly smaller than the relation-table Borel
      structure and is not standard Borel.
\item For every finite $n\geq3$, neither $r_n$ nor $\Phi_n$ is
      Borel measurable.  The order topology on $P_{\omega+n}$ has
      $2^{\mathfrak c}$ open sets, whereas $\mathrm{Tab}_n$ has only
      $\mathfrak c$ Borel sets.
\end{enumerate}
More precisely, for $n\leq2$ the inverse image under $r_n$ of
\emph{every open set} is $F_\sigma$ relative to $\mathrm{Tab}_n$.
For every finite $n$, the inverse image of each individual
lexicographic ray is $F_\sigma$, including when ranking is not
Borel measurable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $n\leq1$, at least one of any two distinct labels $a,b$ occurs
at a finite coordinate.  The condition that $a$ precedes $b$ is
therefore
\[
 \exists k<\omega\quad
 [\,e(k)=a\ \text{ and }\ b\notin\{e(0),\ldots,e(k)\}\,].
\]
Both this condition and its complementary orientation are unions
of finite-prefix cylinders.  Every relation bit is consequently
continuous, proving continuity of $\Phi_n$.  The countable
finite-prefix base for $P_{\omega+n}$ and
Proposition~\ref{swo:rt:prop:table-domain} prove Borel measurability of
$r_n$.

To see discontinuity of ranking, fix a relation $R$ and a table
neighborhood determined by finitely many labels $F$.  Move a
finite-rank label outside $F$, distinct from the original first
label, to the first position and preserve the relative order of
all other labels.  The order type remains $\omega+n$ and all
specified comparison bits remain unchanged, but the first
enumerated label changes.  The first-coordinate cylinder is open
in $P_{\omega+n}$, so $r_n$ is discontinuous at $R$.

There is also an explicit sequence of continuous approximations
when $n\leq1$.  Fix an auxiliary enumeration $x_0,x_1,\ldots$ of
$D$.  At stage $m$, sort $\{x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\}$ by $R$ and
complete the resulting finite prefix to an element of $P_{\omega+n}$ by a
fixed deterministic rule.  This map depends on finitely many
comparison bits and is continuous.  Every true finite initial
segment eventually occurs correctly in these finite sorts,
because each of its elements has only finitely many predecessors.
The approximations therefore converge in the finite-prefix
topology of $P_\omega$ or $P_{\omega+1}$ to $r_n(R)$.

For $n=2$, write a Borel set of $P_{\omega+2}=\operatorname{Split}(E_2)$
as $\pi_2^{-1}(B)\triangle C$ using
\Cref{swo:rt:lem:split-borel}.  The map
$R\mapsto r_2(R)|\omega$ is Borel into $E_2$, by its countable
finite-prefix base and the coordinate descriptions above.  The
inverse image of the countable set $C$ is countable and therefore
Borel in $\mathrm{Tab}_2$.  Thus $r_2$ is Borel measurable.

In the reverse direction, fix $a<b$ in $D$.  In every fiber whose
omitted pair is $\{a,b\}$, the lower point has terminal order
$(a,b)$ and the upper point has terminal order $(b,a)$.  Therefore
the inverse image under $\Phi_2$ of the clopen table condition
$aRb$ splits $\mathfrak c$ fibers.  It is not Borel by
\Cref{swo:rt:lem:split-borel}.  This proves all the assertions at
$n=2$, including strictness of the two Borel structures.

For $n\geq3$, arbitrary subsets of the dense isolated-point set
are open.  There are $2^{\mathfrak c}$ such subsets.  Distinct
open subsets have distinct inverse images under the bijection
$r_n$, while a standard Borel space of size $\mathfrak c$ has
only $\mathfrak c$ Borel subsets.  Thus $r_n$ cannot be Borel
measurable.

Finally, restrict to the closed subspace
$S_n\cong\operatorname{Split}(E_n)$.  Fix an omitted $n$-element
set $S$ containing $a<b$.  For each of the $\mathfrak c$ prefixes
omitting exactly $S$, the first terminal permutation is the
increasing one and the last is the decreasing one.  The table
condition $aRb$ distinguishes these two endpoints.  Its inverse
image in $S_n$ splits $\mathfrak c$ fibers and is not Borel.
The trace on a closed subspace of a Borel set would be Borel.
Consequently $\Phi_n$ is not Borel measurable in $P_{\omega+n}$ either.

For the final assertions, fix $e\in P_{\omega+n}$.  The condition
$r_n(R)<e$ is a countable union over finite first-disagreement
coordinates $k$, together with a finite exceptional set of
relations whose enumerations agree with $e$ through all of
$\omega$ and differ only in the terminal permutation.  Each
finite-disagreement condition is $F_\sigma$: it specifies finitely
many exact finite ranks, and then one finite rank carrying any of
countably many labels below $e(k)$.  The exceptional relation codes
are closed singletons.  The same proof treats the opposite ray.

Every open subset of a separable linear order is a countable union
of basic intervals and rays with actual order points as endpoints.
To check the assertion without assuming a countable base, first
decompose it into countably many maximal convex open components.
In each component choose countable coinitial and cofinal subsets,
adding a least or greatest point if present.  Intervals with
endpoints from these countable subsets cover the component except
possibly its least and greatest points; one additional ambient
basic neighborhood covers each such point.  These neighborhoods
exist because the component is open.  Applying this observation
to the separable spaces $P_\omega,P_{\omega+1},P_{\omega+2}$, and using closure of
$F_\sigma$ sets under finite intersections and countable unions,
proves the open-set assertion.  This is a statement about the
inverse images of open sets; no Baire-class terminology for maps
into the nonmetrizable space $P_{\omega+2}$ is required.
\end{proof}

The theorem gives a concrete warning for formalization.  On a fixed
countable carrier, relation tables and enumerations are unambiguously
interconvertible as \emph{sets}.  Their natural topologies and measurable
structures need not be interconvertible, even though every individual
enumeration coordinate has a low Borel description in table codes.
At $\omega+2$ there are too many adjacent pairs for a countably
generated Borel structure; at $\omega+3$ there are too many open
sets for ranking to be measurable at all.

\begin{corollary}[Nonmeasurable ranking at every later countable type]
\label{swo:rt:cor:later-countable-nonmeasurable}
Let $\alpha\geq\omega+3$ be countable.  Equip the well-orders of
type $\alpha$ on $D$ with their relation-table standard Borel
structure, and their increasing enumerations with the lexicographic
order topology.  The ranking bijection from the former to the
latter is not Borel measurable.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The fixed-type table class is Borel by the classical Borelness of
the isomorphism class of a countable structure; for ordinals see
Miller~\cite[\S3]{Miller1983}.  The established fixed-type
cellularity theorem supplies $\mathfrak c$ pairwise disjoint
nonempty open intervals in the enumeration order.  Their arbitrary
unions are $2^{\mathfrak c}$ distinct open sets.  The same counting
argument as in Theorem~\ref{swo:rt:thm:finite-tail-borel-threshold}
applies.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[One orientation predicate restores the standard Borel structure]
\label{swo:rt:prop:single-orientation-enrichment}
For $P_{\omega+2}$, let
\[
 H=\{e\in P_{\omega+2}:e(\omega)<_D e(\omega+1)\},
\]
the set of lower endpoints of the adjacent fibers.  Then
\[
 \sigma\bigl(\operatorname{Bor}_{\mathrm{lex}}(P_{\omega+2})\cup\{H\}\bigr)
 =\operatorname{Bor}_{\mathrm{prod}}(P_{\omega+2})
 =\{r_2(B):B\in\operatorname{Bor}(\mathrm{Tab}_2)\}.
\]
Thus one additional binary predicate suffices, and none suffices.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The equality between the full-product and transported table Borel
structures follows from the coordinate formulas for ranking and
continuity of relation coding in the product topology.  Put
\[
 C_{a,b}=\{e\in P_{\omega+2}:D\setminus\operatorname{ran}(e|\omega)=\{a,b\}\}.
\]
This is lexicographically closed: it says that neither $a$ nor $b$
ever occurs at a finite coordinate.  For each $a\in D$,
\[
 \{e:e(\omega)=a\}
 =\bigcup_{b>a}(C_{a,b}\cap H)
   \ \cup\ \bigcup_{b<a}(C_{a,b}\setminus H).
\]
There is an analogous formula for $e(\omega+1)=a$.
All finite-coordinate observations are already lexicographically
continuous.  These countable unions therefore show that the enlarged
sigma-algebra contains every product coordinate cylinder and hence
the full-product Borel structure.  Conversely, the lexicographic
Borel structure is contained in the product Borel structure, and
$H$ is product-clopen.  This proves equality.  Finally $H$ itself
is not lexicographically Borel, since it splits every adjacent
fiber, so an enrichment is necessary.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Sigma-algebra inclusion is not topology inclusion]\label{swo:rt:n6.11}
The full-product topology on $P_{\omega+2}$ is Polish, but is not a refinement
of its lexicographic topology.  The two topologies are incomparable.
The predicate $H$ is product-clopen but not lexicographically Borel.
In the other direction, the lexicographic ray $(-\infty,p^+)$ is
not product-open at $p^-$.  A product neighborhood fixes only
finitely many finite coordinates, along with possibly the terminal
ones.  At a later finite coordinate one can increase the label,
retain the same omitted pair and terminal order, and complete the
enumeration.  The resulting point still belongs to that product
neighborhood but lies above $p^+$.  The proposition compares the
generated sigma-algebras, not an inclusion of the two topologies.
\end{remark}

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 2560-2691
\subsection{Two different products of the native Borel structure}

At two terminal labels a further distinction appears.  For a topology
on $L$, the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(L\times L)$ of its
topological product need not equal the sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B(L)\otimes\mathcal B(L)$ generated by Borel rectangles.
The equality familiar from Polish spaces fails for the native split
orders.  Related split-interval product phenomena are classical
\cite[419X(g)]{Fremlin4}; the following proof uses only the explicit
Borel normal form above.

\begin{theorem}[Native comparison is not measurable for the rectangle product]
\label{swo:bw:tp:thm:tensor}
Let $E$ be an uncountable dense suborder of $\mathbb R$ without
endpoints and let $L=E\times_{\lex}m$ for a finite $m\geq2$.
Then
\[
 \{(x,y)\in L^2:x<y\}\in\mathcal B(L\times L)
 \quad\text{but}\quad
 \{(x,y)\in L^2:x<y\}\notin
       \mathcal B(L)\otimes\mathcal B(L).
\]
Consequently the two product sigma-algebras are distinct.  This applies
to $P_{\omega+n}$ for every finite $n\geq2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Strict order is open in the product topology of any linearly ordered
topological space.  If $x<z<y$, the product of the rays below and above
$z$ is a suitable neighborhood of $(x,y)$.  If $x<y$ is an adjacent
pair, use $(-\infty,y)\times(x,\infty)$ instead.  Thus the displayed
relation belongs to $\mathcal B(L\times L)$.

First let $m=2$.  Every member of a sigma-algebra generated by a family
uses only countably many members of that family: the sets having such
a countable supporting subfamily themselves form a sigma-algebra
containing all generators.  Hence any member of
$\mathcal B(L)\otimes\mathcal B(L)$ is generated by countably many
rectangles $B_k\times C_k$.

By Theorem~\ref{swo:bw:tp:thm:double-borel}, each $B_k$ and $C_k$ distinguishes
the two points of only countably many fibers.  Choose $p\in E$
outside the union of all these exceptional base sets.  Every generating
rectangle has the same membership value at
\[
 ((p,0),(p,1))\quad\text{and}\quad((p,1),(p,0)).
\]
Equality of membership is preserved by complements and countable unions,
so every set generated by these rectangles has the same value at those
two ordered pairs.  Strict order takes opposite values there.  It
cannot belong to the rectangle-generated product sigma-algebra.

For $m>2$, the closed endpoint subspace
$S=E\times\{0,m-1\}$ is a double split.  Its inclusion in $L$ is
continuous, hence Borel measurable.  Pulling a rectangle-product
measurable strict order on $L$ back along the product of these inclusions
would give a rectangle-product measurable strict order on $S$, contrary
to the case just proved.
\end{proof}

The coordinate coding has none of this product ambiguity: it is Polish,
and its strict lexicographic relation is $\Delta^0_2$ by
Proposition~\ref{swo:bw:tp:prop:borel-relation}.  Thus three separate objects
occur naturally: the coordinate Borel structure, the native Borel
structure, and the Borel structure of a native topological product.
Their distinctions already matter for an elementary question such as
whether comparison of two coded well-orders is a measurable operation.

\subsection{What the countable analysis says about formalization}

All the underlying carriers in this section are ordinary sets, and all
arguments take place in ZFC.  Nonetheless, the choice of coding and
topology changes even the measurable sets.  It is therefore insufficient
to say that a formalization uses ``the Borel structure on well-orders''
without naming the topology.

A proof-assistant development can make the distinction concrete as
follows.  The set of bijections $\alpha\to D$ is one underlying type.
Use two tagged copies of it: one with the induced product topology and
one with the topology of the first-difference linear order.  Prove the
finite-tail order isomorphism before transporting any topological
structure.  The prefix-omission sets $E_n$ should retain the prefix
topology, not silently acquire the finer topology obtained by exposing
the finite residual labels as extra coordinates.  At $n=2$, the
coordinate event $f(\omega)=a$ is a particularly useful negative
regression test: it must be coordinate-clopen and fail to be native
Borel.  Identifying the two Borel structures would contradict an
explicit mathematical theorem.

The comparison relation itself remains low in the coordinate Borel
hierarchy for every countable ordinal length.  This makes that code
space useful for descriptive-set-theoretic questions even when the
native order topology has a much larger family of open or Borel sets.
The native topology is appropriate for order completion and cuts;
the coordinate topology is appropriate for finite observations of
enumerations.  Both are rigorous interpretations, and the results
above state exactly where they coincide and where they diverge.

\subsection{Further questions made precise by these results}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Are the dense base orders $E_n$ and $E_m$ isomorphic for distinct
      positive integers $m,n$?  The finite-tail orders themselves are
      pairwise nonisomorphic, but their finite-condensation quotients
      might forget the exact positive number of omitted labels.  The
      common category and Borel bounds established here do not settle
      this question.
\item What is the exact difference-hierarchy or Wadge degree of $E_n$
      in the common real completion for $n\geq1$?  The explicit
      difference of $G_\delta$ sets is a sharper starting point than
      an unqualified third-level Borel bound.
\item Classify the ordered pairs $(C,E_n)$ and their order
      automorphism groups.  Any automorphism preserving $E_0$ must
      preserve a comeager realized set; for positive $n$ it preserves
      a dense meager realized set.  Determine which features of the
      omitted-label decomposition can be recovered from the ordered
      pair alone.
\item For $\alpha\geq\omega\cdot2$, characterize the native Borel
      sigma-algebra in terms of the first-$\omega$ prefix and the
      varying infinite residual orders.  A low-complexity coordinate
      comparison relation is already available, but the finite
      split-pair normal form no longer describes the fibers.
\item Determine which infinite-length native order topologies are
      Baire, and where compatible complete metrics can exist.  First
      countability holds at every countable length, whereas the
      coordinate topology is always Polish; these facts do not settle
      native metrizability beyond the finite-tail cases.
\item Find a functorial formalization of the two tagged topologies and
      their Borel sigma-algebras.  The exact inclusion at one omitted
      label and failure of Borel measurability at two labels give
      concrete milestones before moving to generalized topologies at
      uncountable birthday stages.
\end{enumerate}
