\section{Singular cardinalities: continuity, complete metrizability and non-Borel boundaries (sources 24 and 26)}\label{swo:x:sec:singular}

\merge\ Source~24's Section~8 and source~26's Sections~4--10. At a singular
enumeration cardinal $\mu$ a set of fewer than $\mu$ positions can be unbounded,
and controlling a bounded initial segment is no longer controlling a small set of
coordinates. Source~24 finds the exact continuity criteria for the permutation
operations and isolates the boundedness-preserving subgroup $H_\mu$; source~26
answers source~24's question whether the minimal slice is completely metrizable
when $\cf\mu=\omega<\mu$: it never is, it is not even Borel in its completion, and
no nonempty open subspace is completely metrizable (\cref{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification}).
Source~26 writes $\kappa$ for $\card X$ and $\theta$ for the birthday cutoff; they
are printed $\mu$ and $\kappa$ (\cref{swo:part:topology}). Source~28's further
results on these groups are in \cref{swo:x:sec:envelope}.

\subsection{The permutation-group obstruction (source 24)}\label{swo:pc:sec:singular}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 577-608
A fixed enumeration of the alphabet identifies $\WO_\mu(X)$ as a set with $\Sym(\mu)$. At countable or regular cardinalities, it is tempting to import the usual topological permutation-group picture. At singular cardinalities that import is invalid unless an additional boundedness condition is checked.

\begin{definition}[Preservation of bounded sets]\label{swo:pc:n8.1}
A function $u:\mu\to\mu$ is \emph{boundedness preserving} if
\[
 \forall\alpha<\mu\ \exists\beta<\mu\quad u[\alpha]\subseteq\beta.
\]
Equivalently, it takes every bounded subset of $\mu$ to a bounded subset. Here ``bounded'' refers to the ordinal order on $\mu$, not to cardinality alone.
\end{definition}

On $\Sym(\mu)$ let $L_\tau(\pi)=\tau\circ\pi$ and $R_\sigma(\pi)=\pi\circ\sigma$. All topology in the next theorem is the forward bounded-prefix topology.

\begin{theorem}[Exact continuity criteria]\label{swo:pc:thm:continuity}
For every infinite $\mu$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Every left translation $L_\tau$ is a homeomorphism.
\item Right translation $R_\sigma$ is continuous at every point if $\sigma$ is boundedness preserving, and is continuous at no point otherwise.
\item Inversion $\pi\mapsto\pi^{-1}$ is continuous at a particular $\pi$ exactly when $\pi^{-1}$ is boundedness preserving.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Left translation is a relabelling of output values. Equality of any forward restrictions is preserved in both directions, proving (i).

For (ii), to determine $(\pi\circ\sigma)\res\alpha$, it suffices to determine $\pi$ on $\sigma[\alpha]$. If that image is contained in a bounded initial segment $\beta$, agreement with $\pi$ below $\beta$ enforces the desired output agreement. Conversely, suppose $\sigma[\alpha]$ is unbounded. Given any input neighborhood $[\pi\res\beta]$, choose $u\in\sigma[\alpha]\setminus\beta$ and a different $v\in\mu\setminus\beta$. Precompose $\pi$ with the transposition of $u,v$. The new permutation agrees with $\pi$ below $\beta$, but its composition with $\sigma$ changes at the coordinate below $\alpha$ whose image under $\sigma$ is $u$. Thus no input neighborhood controls that output prefix, at any $\pi$.

For (iii), determining $\pi^{-1}$ below $\alpha$ is equivalent to fixing the positions $\pi^{-1}[\alpha]$ of those labels. If this set is bounded, a sufficiently long forward restriction of $\pi$ fixes all these preimages. If it is unbounded, given $\beta<\mu$ choose $u\in\pi^{-1}[\alpha]\setminus\beta$ and a different $v\notin\beta$. Again precompose with their transposition. The forward prefix below $\beta$ is unchanged, but the inverse position of the label $\pi(u)<\alpha$ changes from $u$ to $v$. This is precisely failure of continuity at $\pi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Regular and singular cases diverge]\label{swo:pc:cor:groupdichotomy}
If $\mu$ is regular, the forward topology makes $\Sym(\mu)$ a topological group. If $\mu$ is singular, it does not: there are right translations discontinuous everywhere, and inversion has points of discontinuity.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 609-612
For regular $\mu$, every set of size less than $\mu$ is bounded, so every permutation and its inverse preserve bounded sets. Joint continuity of multiplication follows directly: to control $\pi'\circ\sigma'$ below $\alpha$, first require $\sigma'\res\alpha=\sigma\res\alpha$ and then require $\pi'$ to agree with $\pi$ on a prefix containing the bounded set $\sigma[\alpha]$.

For singular $\mu$, let $q=\cf\mu<\mu$. Choose $A=\{a_\xi:\xi<q\}$ bounded in $\mu$ and a disjoint cofinal set $B=\{b_\xi:\xi<q\}$. The involution $\sigma$ exchanging each $a_\xi$ with $b_\xi$ and fixing everything else takes the bounded set $A$ to the unbounded set $B$. It and its inverse fail the criterion in Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:continuity}.
\end{proof}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 613-659

This is not a pathology of surreal multiplication. It already occurs for permutations of a naked singular cardinal, before any numerical alphabet is supplied. Nor does it contradict Corollary~\ref{swo:pc:cor:relabel}: left translation is relabelling, whereas right translation changes the \emph{positions} on which a bounded prefix depends.

\subsubsection{The subgroup where the usual picture survives}

Define
\[
 H_\mu=\{\pi\in\Sym(\mu):\pi\text{ and }\pi^{-1}
                         \text{ preserve bounded sets}\}.
\]
It is a subgroup: boundedness preservation is closed under composition, and the definition is symmetric under inversion. At a regular cardinal $H_\mu=\Sym(\mu)$; at a singular cardinal the involution above shows that it is proper.

For $\alpha<\mu$ define two-sided entourages
\[
 E^{\leftrightarrow}_\alpha
 =\{(\pi,\sigma):\pi\res\alpha=\sigma\res\alpha
              \text{ and }\pi^{-1}\res\alpha=\sigma^{-1}\res\alpha\}.
\]
They define a Hausdorff uniformity on the full permutation set, independently of continuity of the group operations.

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided completeness and the bounded subgroup]\label{swo:pc:thm:twosided}
The full space $\Sym(\mu)$ is complete for the two-sided uniformity. On $H_\mu$, that uniformity induces the forward topology and is complete; with this topology $H_\mu$ is a topological group. On all of $\Sym(\mu)$ the two uniform topologies agree when $\mu$ is regular and differ when $\mu$ is singular.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A two-sided Cauchy filter determines coherent stabilized forward prefixes and coherent stabilized inverse prefixes. Their unions are injections $h,g:\mu\to\mu$. If $h(\xi)=\eta$, choose a filter member on which the forward value at $\xi$ and the inverse value at $\eta$ have both stabilized. Every permutation in that nonempty member witnesses $g(\eta)=\xi$. The converse is identical. Hence $g=h^{-1}$ and $h$ is a permutation. Stabilization on each initial segment gives convergence in the two-sided uniformity.

At a point $\pi\in H_\mu$, an inverse-prefix requirement below $\alpha$ is implied by a forward requirement on a prefix bounding $\pi^{-1}[\alpha]$. Thus the two topologies agree on $H_\mu$. If the original Cauchy filter consists of elements of $H_\mu$, its limiting forward prefix $h\res\alpha$ is a restriction of one such element and therefore has bounded image. The same holds for $g\res\alpha$. Thus $h\in H_\mu$, proving completeness of the subgroup. The proof of joint continuity and the inversion criterion above now apply inside the subgroup.

For regular $\mu$, all permutations belong to $H_\mu$, proving equality of the topologies on the full space. For singular $\mu$, inverse stabilization defines a two-sided neighborhood at the involution in Corollary~\ref{swo:pc:cor:groupdichotomy} that contains no forward neighborhood there. The topology is strictly finer.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A complete metric on the bounded subgroup]\label{swo:pc:n8.5}
If $\cf\mu=\omega$, the forward topology on $H_\mu$ has a complete compatible ultrametric. Choose a countable cofinal sequence of ordinal lengths and take the maximum of the resulting forward and inverse first-disagreement ultrametrics.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The cofinal sequence gives a countable base for the complete two-sided uniformity. On $H_\mu$ that uniformity induces the forward topology by Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:twosided}. Its ultrametric is therefore complete and compatible, exactly as in the countable permutation proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A finer complete uniformity is not a universal group repair]\label{swo:pc:n8.6}
The two-sided uniformity exists and is complete on the full singular permutation set, but this by itself does not make all group operations continuous in its topology. For the unboundedness-preserving $\sigma$ above, right translation is still discontinuous at the identity: at the identity, a sufficiently long fixed forward prefix also fixes that inverse prefix, while $\sigma[\alpha]$ remains unbounded. The subgroup $H_\mu$ is the clean topological-group statement proved here.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{What is established when cofinality is countable}

If $\cf\mu=\omega$, Proposition~\ref{swo:pc:prop:metric} provides a compatible forward ultrametric, and Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:completion} identifies its uniform completion with injections. When $\mu=\omega$, Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:completecountable} supplies a different complete compatible metric. At an uncountable singular $\mu$ of countable cofinality, Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:twosided} provides a complete \emph{finer} uniform topology on the full permutation space, but not a complete metric for its original topology.

The earlier dense-open fusion theorem (source~17, \cref{swo:gs:thm:fusion}) proves that these forward spaces are Baire. Its proof extends a short prefix at stage $n$ to meet the next dense open set and to cover a growing block of labels. This does not automatically give the point-preserving choices needed for a stronger topological completeness argument. Therefore neither forward incompleteness nor the failure of inversion continuity settles complete metrizability. The exact singular question is retained as its Question~13.1 (\cref{swo:x:note:q131}).

\begin{note}[\merge; source~24's singular question, answered (3 October 2026)]\label{swo:x:note:q131}
Source~24 retains the ``exact singular question'' as its Question~13.1:
\emph{for singular $\mu>\omega$ with $\cf\mu=\omega$, is the forward-prefix space
$\WO_\mu(X)$ completely metrizable? Equivalently, can the dense permutation
subspace of its metrizable injection completion be characterized as a $G_\delta$
subset? Determine whether the answer depends on cardinal arithmetic.} Source~26
answers it negatively in $\ZFC$, with no cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis: the
permutation space is not even Borel in $\I_\mu(X)$, and no nonempty open subspace is
completely metrizable (\cref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel,swo:nb:thm:completeclassification,swo:nb:cor:answer}).
Source~24's own results do not settle it, as it says; source~28's dense complete
locus does not either (\cref{swo:x:note:q1-rescoped}).
\end{note}

\subsection{The complete-metric subspace criterion (source 24, Appendix C)}\label{swo:pc:app:gdelta}

\merge\ Source~24's Appendix~C, used in the singular question above and in
source~26's classification: ``For completeness, the characterization used in
Question~13.1 can be proved without a separability hypothesis.''

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 1105-1121
\begin{proposition}[Complete metric subspaces and $G_\delta$ sets]\label{swo:pc:nC.1}
Let $B$ be a completely metrizable space and $A\subseteq B$. Then $A$ has a complete compatible metric if and only if it is $G_\delta$ in $B$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Fix a complete metric $d$ on $B$. First suppose $\rho$ is a complete compatible metric on $A$. For each positive integer $n$, cover $A$ by ambient open sets $U$ that meet $A$, have $d$-diameter less than $2^{-n}$, and have $\rho$-diameter less than $2^{-n}$ on $U\cap A$. Such sets exist by compatibility of the two subspace topologies. Let $O_n$ be their union.

If $z\in\bigcap_n O_n$, choose $U_n\ni z$ from the $n$th cover and $a_n\in U_n\cap A$. Then $a_n\to z$ in $d$. For fixed $N$, the ambient neighborhood $U_N$ of $z$ contains all sufficiently late $a_n$. Their pairwise $\rho$-distances are less than $2^{-N}$. Thus $(a_n)$ is $\rho$-Cauchy and converges in $A$ to some $a$. Compatibility gives convergence to $a$ in $d$ as well; hence $z=a\in A$. Therefore $A=\bigcap_n O_n$.

Conversely, suppose $A=\bigcap_{n\ge1}O_n$ with each $O_n$ open in $B$. Put $F_n=B\setminus O_n$ and, on $A$, set $t_n(x)=1/d(x,F_n)$, with $t_n=0$ if $F_n$ is empty. The denominator is positive because $x\in O_n$. Define
\[
 \rho(x,y)=d(x,y)+\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}
                    \min\{1,|t_n(x)-t_n(y)|\}.
\]
The triangle inequality follows term by term, and positivity follows from $d$. Continuity of every $t_n$, followed by control of the summable tail, shows that $\rho$ induces the subspace topology.

A $\rho$-Cauchy sequence is $d$-Cauchy and has a limit $z\in B$. For each fixed $n$, its $t_n$-values are Cauchy in the ordinary real metric: truncated-distance Cauchyness is ordinary Cauchyness once the required error is less than $1$. They therefore have a finite limit. If $z\in F_n$, the distances to $F_n$ would tend to zero and their reciprocals would diverge, a contradiction. Hence $z\in A$. Continuity of the $t_n$ and the same summable-tail estimate give convergence in $\rho$, proving completeness.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~26, Appendix~A, Theorem~A.1, and source~28, Appendix~B, Proposition~B.1]\label{swo:nb:app:gdelta}\label{swo:nb:thm:gdelta}\label{swo:ge:app:metric}\label{swo:ge:nB.1}
Both sources prove \cref{swo:pc:nC.1} again, by the same two constructions (a
$G_\delta$ from covers of shrinking diameter in both metrics; the complete metric
$d+\sum_n2^{-n}\min\{1,\card{t_n(x)-t_n(y)}\}$ with $t_n=1/d(\cdot,F_n)$), ``without
assuming separability''. Source~26: ``The earlier manuscript also records this
criterion; the proof is repeated to make the logical dependence visible \ldots{}
Only the necessity direction is required to turn Theorem~6.2 into the main
negative conclusion. Its proof does not use completeness of the ambient metric; it
uses the complete compatible metric hypothesized on the subspace. The converse
supplies the positive conclusions for $\mu=\omega$ and for $H_\mu$.'' Source~28
uses it for its dense locus (\cref{swo:ge:thm:dense-locus}) and its own
Question~1. Source~29 cites it in the form ``an $F_\sigma$ subset of $\mathbb R$ is
$\sigma$-compact''; the criterion is classical (Alexandrov).
\end{note}

\subsection{Local character, the countable exception and the Baire property (source 26)}\label{swo:x:sub:nb-local}

\begin{note}[Source~26, Theorem~4.3, ``Local character'']\label{swo:nb:thm:character}
\emph{At every point of $\WO_\mu(X)$ and $\I_\mu(X)$, the least cardinality of a
neighborhood base is $\cf\mu$. In particular, either space is metrizable if and
only if $\cf\mu=\omega$.} This is \cref{swo:pc:prop:metric}, by the same argument;
source~26 adds that the cofinal-length ultrametric is complete on $\I_\mu(X)$ by
\cref{swo:pc:thm:completion}, which its classification uses.
\end{note}

\merge\ Source~26's proof of the countable case is a route through the
$G_\delta$ criterion; its second paragraph is source~24's metric $D$
(\cref{swo:pc:thm:completecountable}):

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 360-369
\begin{proposition}[The countable exception]\label{swo:nb:prop:countable}
For $\mu=\omega$, the space $\WO_\omega(X)$ is completely metrizable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Its injection completion is completely metrizable, and \cref{swo:nb:prop:exhaustion} expresses the permutation subspace as a countable intersection of open sets. The complete-metric subspace criterion, proved in \cref{swo:nb:app:gdelta}, applies.

An explicit alternative is to fix a bijection $X\cong\omega$ and combine the forward first-disagreement metric with the corresponding metric on inverses. Stabilization of both a permutation and its inverse produces mutually inverse limiting injections. At $\omega$, a finite inverse-prefix requirement is already implied, at a given permutation, by a sufficiently long finite forward prefix. Thus the combined complete metric has the original topology.
\end{proof}

The last compatibility argument fails for general singular permutations: a bounded set of labels can have an unbounded inverse image. A finer complete metric on forward and inverse prefixes is not evidence that the forward topology itself is completely metrizable.

\merge\ Source~26's Baire theorem is the fusion theorem \cref{swo:gs:thm:fusion}
(source~17, for $X=\No_{<\kappa}$) for an arbitrary alphabet of every infinite
cardinality, by the same fusion with coverage blocks:

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 371-384
\subsubsection{Baire category survives the failure of completeness}

\begin{theorem}[Baire property]\label{swo:nb:thm:baire}
For every infinite cardinal $\mu$, $\WO_\mu(X)$ is a Baire space in its bounded-prefix topology.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $(O_n)_{n<\omega}$ be dense open subsets and start inside an arbitrary cylinder $N_p$. If $\cf\mu>\omega$, successively extend the prefix so that its cylinder lies inside $O_n$. The union of the countably many prefix domains remains bounded in $\mu$, and its injective union extends to a permutation. This extension belongs to every chosen cylinder and hence to every $O_n$.

If $\cf\mu=\omega$, choose increasing sets $Y_n\subseteq X$ with $|Y_n|<\mu$ and union $X$, and cofinal domain lengths $\gamma_n<\mu$. At stage $n$, first refine the current cylinder into $O_n$, using density and openness. Then append all labels of $Y_n$ not already used, in some order, and lengthen the prefix to length at least $\gamma_n$. Both operations still use fewer than $\mu$ coordinates: a finite sum of ordinals whose cardinalities are below the initial cardinal $\mu$ remains below $\mu$. \Cref{swo:nb:lem:extension} supplies any additional unused labels required. The new cylinder stays inside $O_n$.

The union of the resulting prefixes has domain $\mu$, is injective, and covers every $Y_n$. It is a permutation in the original cylinder and in every $O_n$. The proof includes $\mu=\omega$, using finite $Y_n$ and finite lengths.
\end{proof}

This fusion argument controls both domain growth and eventual coverage. It is not a proof of complete metrizability: it produces one point meeting a prescribed countable family of dense open sets, rather than a complete compatible metric or a $G_\delta$ description inside the completion.

\subsection{Compact coding of omitted labels (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:coding}

\merge\ Source~26's Section~5, printed whole: the central construction of the
singular theory.

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 388-478
This section supplies the central construction. It only uses the cardinality of the alphabet and the countable cofinality of the domain. Surreal arithmetic is not involved.

\begin{theorem}[Compact coding of omitted labels]\label{swo:nb:thm:coding}
Suppose $\mu>\omega$, $\cf\mu=\omega$, and $|X|=\mu$. For every $A\subseteq2^\omega$ with $|A|<\mu$, there exist distinct labels $(y_a)_{a\in A}$ and a continuous topological embedding
\[
 F:2^\omega\longrightarrow\I_\mu(X)
\]
with compact, closed image such that
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:defect}
 X\setminus\ran F(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 \{y_z\},&z\in A,\\
 \varnothing,&z\notin A.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:preimage}
 F^{-1}\bigl(\WO_\mu(X)\bigr)=2^\omega\setminus A.
\end{equation}
If $X$ is linearly ordered, $F$ can also be chosen as an order embedding for the binary and $X$-valued lexicographic orders.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\textbf{Step 1: large finite-stage reservoirs.}
Because $\mu$ is an uncountable cardinal of countable cofinality, it is a limit cardinal. Choose strictly increasing infinite cardinals
\[
 \max\{|A|,\aleph_0\}<\lambda_0<\lambda_1<\cdots<\mu,
 \qquad \sup_{n<\omega}\lambda_n=\mu.
\]
Put $\lambda_{-1}=0$ as an endpoint convention and define consecutive domain blocks
\[
 D_n=[\lambda_{n-1},\lambda_n),\qquad |D_n|=\lambda_n.
\]
Every bounded initial segment of $\mu$ meets only finitely many of these blocks.

Choose a disjoint partition
\[
 X=Y\;\sqcup\;\bigsqcup_{n<\omega}R_n,
 \qquad Y=\{y_a:a\in A\},\qquad |R_n|=\lambda_n.
\]
This is possible because removing fewer than $\mu$ labels leaves cardinality $\mu$, and $\sum_n\lambda_n=\mu$.

\textbf{Step 2: release a label at its first mismatch.}
For $t\in2^{n+1}$, define
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:release}
 A_t=\{a\in A:a\res n=t\res n\ \text{and}\ a(n)\ne t(n)\}.
\end{equation}
Thus $A_t$ consists exactly of the branches of $A$ whose first disagreement with $t$ occurs at coordinate $n$. For any infinite branch $z$, the sets $A_{z\res(n+1)}$ are pairwise disjoint and
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:releaseunion}
 \bigcup_{n<\omega}A_{z\res(n+1)}=A\setminus\{z\}.
\end{equation}
When $z\notin A$, the right side is just $A$. Equation~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:releaseunion} is the entire logical mechanism of the code: distinct infinite binary sequences have a unique finite first disagreement.

\textbf{Step 3: fill each block and mark its bit.}
For every $n$ choose distinct marker labels $r_n^0,r_n^1\in R_n$. If $X$ is ordered, choose them with $r_n^0<r_n^1$. Let $d_n$ and $d_n+1$ be the first two positions of $D_n$. For each $t\in2^{n+1}$ choose a bijection
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:theta}
 \vartheta_t:D_n\longrightarrow R_n\sqcup\{y_a:a\in A_t\}
\end{equation}
subject to
\[
 \vartheta_t(d_n)=r_n^{t(n)},\qquad
 \vartheta_t(d_n+1)=r_n^{1-t(n)}.
\]
The remaining domain and target both have cardinality $\lambda_n$: $\lambda_n$ is infinite and absorbs the smaller released set as well as the removal of two markers. Hence these bijections exist. Only set-sized choice is used.

\textbf{Step 4: assemble the injection.}
For $z\in2^\omega$, define
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:F}
 F(z)\res D_n=\vartheta_{z\res(n+1)}.
\end{equation}
Within a block the map is injective. Distinct blocks use disjoint reservoirs $R_n$, and by~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:releaseunion} each distinguished label $y_a$ is released into at most one block. Therefore $F(z)$ is injective on all of $\mu$. Every reservoir is exhausted, and the union of the released labels is precisely $Y\setminus\{y_z\}$ when $z\in A$, or all of $Y$ otherwise. This proves~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:defect} and~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:preimage}.

\textbf{Step 5: topology and order.}
A prescribed output prefix of length $\alpha<\mu$ is contained in finitely many blocks. It is therefore determined by finitely many input bits. This proves continuity of $F$. Its markers recover every bit: the value at $d_n$ is $r_n^{z(n)}$. Thus $F$ is injective. A continuous injection from compact Cantor space into the Hausdorff space $\I_\mu(X)$ is a homeomorphism onto a compact closed image.

Finally, if $z<w$ first differ at bit $n$, they have the same output on every block before $D_n$. At the very first position $d_n$ of that block, their values are $r_n^0<r_n^1$. This is the first output disagreement, proving $F(z)<_{\lex}F(w)$.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Why countable cofinality is the effective resource}

The construction hides arbitrarily many labels in an early reservoir $Y$, but schedules their release according to a finite first-disagreement test. To make the resulting map continuous, every bounded output prefix must see only finitely many stages. The block decomposition by a countable cofinal sequence guarantees precisely this. Each stage has a reservoir large enough to absorb all currently released labels without changing its domain cardinality.

The markers have a separate role. Release scheduling alone establishes the desired range equation but need not separate all input branches. Two permanent marker positions in each infinite block make the code injective and, with ordered markers, order-preserving. Finite tests check the release partition and first-disagreement markers; they cannot check the infinite cardinal absorption used in~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:theta}.

\begin{remark}[A particularly small defect]\label{swo:nb:n5.2}
Every point in the compact image of $F$ is either exhaustive or omits exactly one label. Thus the complexity established below does not require injections with large or complicated omitted ranges. The zero-versus-one omission distinction already suffices.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The strict cardinal bound]\label{swo:nb:n5.3}
The hypothesis $|A|<\mu$ is used to choose a first reservoir size larger than $|A|$. The theorem does not assert the same construction for $|A|=\mu$. Likewise, a cofinality-$\omega$ decomposition is not replaced without argument by finitely many stages or by stages indexed by a larger regular cardinal. These are genuine boundaries of the present proof.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Non-Borelness and exact complete metrizability (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:nonborel}

\merge\ Source~26's Section~6, printed whole. Its classification answers source~24's
Question~13.1 (\cref{swo:x:note:q131}) and source~28's Question~1
(\cref{swo:x:note:q1-rescoped}); it also answers, for the minimal slices, source~17's
question on complete metrizability beyond the proved fusion length
(\cref{swo:gs:n15.4}), and source~22's
question on descriptive topology when cofinalities are countable
(\cref{swo:x:sec:status}). ``The earlier \emph{Prefix Completions} manuscript'' is
source~24.

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 482-536
\begin{lemma}[A small non-Borel set of branches]\label{swo:nb:lem:nonborelset}
In $\ZFC$ there is a non-Borel set $A\subseteq2^\omega$ of cardinality $\aleph_1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We use the classical theorem that every uncountable Borel subset of Cantor space contains a nonempty perfect subset, and every such perfect subset has cardinality $\mathfrak c$~\cite{Kechris1995}.

If $\mathfrak c>\aleph_1$, take any subset $A$ of cardinality $\aleph_1$. It is uncountable and cannot contain a perfect subset, so it is not Borel.

If $\mathfrak c=\aleph_1$, enumerate all nonempty perfect subsets of Cantor space as $(K_\xi)_{\xi<\omega_1}$. There are exactly $\mathfrak c$ such sets: at most that many because closed subsets are coded by countable trees, and at least that many, for example by fixing one infinite subsequence of coordinates while varying its binary values. Recursively choose two distinct new points $a_\xi,b_\xi\in K_\xi$, avoiding all earlier chosen points. Each stage forbids only countably many points, whereas $K_\xi$ has size $\aleph_1$. Put $A=\{a_\xi:\xi<\omega_1\}$. No $b_\xi$ belongs to $A$, by the continued avoidance requirement. Thus every perfect set meets the complement of $A$, and $A$ contains no perfect subset. Again it is uncountable and not Borel.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The singular non-Borel boundary]\label{swo:nb:thm:nonborel}
Let $\mu>\omega$ have $\cf\mu=\omega$, and let $|X|=\mu$. Then $\WO_\mu(X)$ is not an ordinary Borel subset of $\I_\mu(X)$ in their bounded-prefix topology. This is already witnessed on a compact subspace consisting of injections with at most one omitted label.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An uncountable cardinal of countable cofinality is strictly larger than $\aleph_1$. Choose $A$ from Lemma~\ref{swo:nb:lem:nonborelset} and apply Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:coding}. If $\WO_\mu(X)$ were Borel in $\I_\mu(X)$, continuity of $F$ would imply that
\[
 2^\omega\setminus A=F^{-1}\bigl(\WO_\mu(X)\bigr)
\]
is Borel in Cantor space. Taking its complement would make $A$ Borel, a contradiction. The last assertion is~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:defect}.
\end{proof}

No separability assumption on $\I_\mu(X)$ is being smuggled into this argument. Continuous inverse images preserve the sigma-algebra generated by open sets in arbitrary topological spaces. The perfect-set theorem is used only inside the ordinary separable Cantor domain.

\begin{theorem}[Complete-metrizability classification]\label{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification}
For every infinite cardinal $\mu$ and every set $X$ with $|X|=\mu$,
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\text{ is completely metrizable in the prefix topology}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu=\omega.
\]
For $\mu>\omega$ of countable cofinality, no nonempty open subspace of $\WO_\mu(X)$ is completely metrizable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The countable case is Proposition~\ref{swo:nb:prop:countable}. If $\cf\mu>\omega$, \cref{swo:nb:thm:character} shows that the space is not even first countable, hence is not metrizable.

It remains to consider uncountable $\mu$ of countable cofinality. The injection space has a complete compatible metric by \cref{swo:nb:thm:character}. A completely metrizable subspace of a metrizable space must be $G_\delta$ there; \cref{swo:nb:app:gdelta} gives a proof that does not require separability. Complete metrizability of $\WO_\mu(X)$ would therefore contradict Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel}.

Finally, any nonempty open subspace contains a cylinder. The cylinder is clopen in the full permutation space and is homeomorphic to that space by Proposition~\ref{swo:nb:prop:basic}. If the open subspace admitted a compatible complete metric, its closed cylinder would also be completely metrizable, which is impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Answer to the earlier question]\label{swo:nb:cor:answer}
Question~13.1 of the earlier \emph{Prefix Completions} manuscript (source~24; \cref{swo:x:note:q131}) has a negative answer in $\ZFC$. The answer does not depend on the value of the continuum or on additional cardinal-arithmetic hypotheses.
\end{corollary}

\subsubsection{Why several plausible positive arguments fail}

First, the fact that all exhaustion requirements $U_x$ are open dense gives a $\mu$-indexed intersection, not necessarily a countable one. Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel} shows that there is no replacement by a countable Borel construction at all. Second, the forward metric being incomplete is weaker than the conclusion: another compatible metric can repair that problem at $\omega$, but not at the uncountable singular lengths considered here. Third, imposing inverse-prefix stabilization gives a complete uniformity, but in general changes the topology. Fourth, the Baire fusion proof of Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:baire} does not imply that every closed subspace is Baire or that the original space is completely metrizable.

The precise hierarchy is therefore useful:
\[
 \text{complete compatible metric}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{Baire},
 \qquad\text{but the converse fails here even locally.}
\]
For these spaces, ``the completion is well understood'' and ``the original topology is completely metrizable'' are sharply different assertions.

\subsection{Closed universality and ordered Cantor traces (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:universality}

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 540-577
\begin{theorem}[Every Cantor subset as a closed trace]\label{swo:nb:thm:closedtraces}
Suppose $\cf\mu=\omega$ and $\mu>\mathfrak c$. For every $B\subseteq2^\omega$, there is a closed subspace of $\WO_\mu(X)$ homeomorphic to $B$. If $X$ is linearly ordered, the homeomorphism can simultaneously be an order isomorphism from $B$ with its inherited binary lexicographic order to the image with its inherited enumeration order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $A=2^\omega\setminus B$. Its cardinality is at most $\mathfrak c<\mu$. Apply Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:coding} and put $K=F[2^\omega]$. Then $K$ is closed in the injection space and
\[
 K\cap\WO_\mu(X)=F[B].
\]
This is closed relative to $\WO_\mu(X)$, and the restriction of the embedding $F$ is a homeomorphism from $B$ to $F[B]$. The ordered-marker version of $F$ gives the order statement.
\end{proof}

The theorem does not say that $F[B]$ is closed in $K$ or in the ambient injection space. Such a claim would be false for a nonclosed $B$. It is closed in the \emph{permutation subspace}, precisely because that subspace meets the compact family in the prescribed trace.

\begin{corollary}[Closed topological universality]\label{swo:nb:cor:closeduniversal}
If $\cf\mu=\omega$ and $\mu>\mathfrak c$, every zero-dimensional separable metrizable space is homeomorphic to a closed subspace of $\WO_\mu(X)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A zero-dimensional separable metrizable space has a countable clopen base $(V_n)_{n<\omega}$. Indeed, take a countable ordinary base, refine each of its members by clopen neighborhoods, and use Lindel\"ofness to extract countably many such refinements. The characteristic map
\[
 x\longmapsto\bigl(\mathbf 1_{V_n}(x)\bigr)_{n<\omega}
\]
is a topological embedding into $2^\omega$: the base separates points and recovers the topology. Apply Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:closedtraces} to its image.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Closed rational subspaces]\label{swo:nb:cor:closedQ}
Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{swo:nb:cor:closeduniversal}, the permutation space has a closed subspace homeomorphic to $\mathbb Q$. In particular it is not hereditarily Baire.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The rational line is a zero-dimensional separable metrizable space: intervals with irrational endpoints give a countable clopen base after choosing a countable dense set of irrational endpoints. Apply the corollary. The space $\mathbb Q$ is a countable union of nowhere dense singletons in itself and has no isolated points, so it is not Baire.
\end{proof}

This supplies another obstruction to complete metrizability when $\mu>\mathfrak c$, since closed subspaces of completely metrizable spaces are completely metrizable and hence Baire. The non-Borel proof is stronger in range: it also covers singular cardinals $\mu\le\mathfrak c$. It is therefore important not to replace Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel} with a closed-rational argument whose hypothesis is stronger.

\subsubsection{How much of the order is retained}

The ordered-marker construction gives a true order embedding, not merely an injection continuous for an unrelated topology. When the alphabet is thick, \cref{swo:nb:thm:ordertopology} identifies the ambient topology with the lexicographic order topology, so the closedness statements concern that actual ordered space. A subset is always being given its inherited topology for the topological assertion and its restricted order for the order assertion. The order topology intrinsic to an arbitrary suborder need not be silently identified with every ambient subspace topology; no such general identification is required for our proof.

These results distinguish order-theoretic largeness from completeness. A linear order can have strong embedding properties, can contain arbitrary closed topological traces, and can still fail complete metrizability on every nonempty open piece. Mutual order embeddability with a familiar lexicographic cube would not prevent this: equimorphism preserves neither the missing-cut pattern nor all topological completeness properties.

\subsection{Bounded images and bounded inverses (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:bounded}

\merge\ Source~26's Section~8, printed whole. Its $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$ (its
$\mathcal B^+$) is source~28's $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$, and $H_\mu$ is source~24's
boundedness-preserving subgroup. Part~(ii) re-derives source~24's complete metric
on $H_\mu$ (the corollary to \cref{swo:pc:thm:twosided}) by a $G_\delta$ route;
source~28 proves the closure and completion statements for every infinite $\mu$
(\cref{swo:ge:thm:closure,swo:ge:thm:H-completion}) and the dense inverse locus
(\cref{swo:ge:thm:dense-locus}).

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 581-647
Fix a bijection $X\cong\mu$ so that boundedness of labels is meaningful. A subset of $\mu$ is bounded when it is contained in some $\beta<\mu$. Define
\[
 \I^{\mathrm b}_\mu=\{f\in\I_\mu(\mu):
       f[\alpha]\text{ is bounded for every }\alpha<\mu\}
\]
and
\[
 H_\mu=\{\pi\in\Sym(\mu):
       \pi[\alpha]\text{ and }\pi^{-1}[\alpha]
       \text{ are bounded for every }\alpha<\mu\}.
\]
The boundedness-preserving subgroup $H_\mu$ and its compatible two-sided completeness occur in the earlier manuscript (source~24, \cref{swo:pc:thm:twosided}). The following ambient description and coding refinement separate the two boundedness requirements directly.

\begin{theorem}[The bounded-image completion and its complete subgroup]\label{swo:nb:thm:bounded}
Suppose $\mu>\omega$ and $\cf\mu=\omega$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$ is closed in $\I_\mu(\mu)$, hence completely metrizable.
\item $H_\mu$ is dense and $G_\delta$ in $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$, hence completely metrizable in the forward-prefix topology.
\item $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu\cap\WO_\mu(\mu)$ is not Borel in $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$ and is not completely metrizable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A failure of bounded-image preservation is witnessed by a single prefix $f\res\alpha$ whose range is unbounded. Every injection in that cylinder has the same failure. The complement of $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$ is therefore open, proving (i).

Fix cofinal lengths $\gamma_n<\mu$. For each $n$, let
\[
 V_n=\{f\in\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu:\exists\beta<\mu\;
                \gamma_n\subseteq\ran(f\res\beta)\}.
\]
This is open: a witnessing prefix continues to witness membership throughout its cylinder. We claim
\begin{equation}\label{swo:nb:eq:H-gdelta}
 H_\mu=\bigcap_{n<\omega}V_n.
\end{equation}
A member of the right side covers every label and is thus a permutation. For any bounded label set, choose $\gamma_n$ containing it; its inverse image lies in a witnessing $\beta$, so the inverse preserves boundedness. The forward condition is built into $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$. Conversely, a member of $H_\mu$ has bounded inverse image of each $\gamma_n$, giving the required witness. This proves~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:H-gdelta}.

To see density, start with a prefix $p=f\res\alpha$ of a bounded-image injection. Both its domain and range are bounded. Choose an infinite initial cardinal $\rho<\mu$ strictly above their bounds. The complements of $\dom p$ and $\ran p$ inside $\rho$ both have size $\rho$. Complete $p$ to a permutation of $\rho$ and extend by the identity outside $\rho$. This permutation belongs to $H_\mu$ and extends $p$. Part (ii) follows from \cref{swo:nb:app:gdelta}.

For (iii), repeat the proof of Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:coding} with the distinguished labels $Y$ placed in an initial segment $\eta=|A|<\lambda_0$. Take
\[
 R_0=[\eta,\lambda_0),\qquad
 R_n=[\lambda_{n-1},\lambda_n)\quad(n\ge1).
\]
Each block target is contained in $\lambda_n$, so
\[
 F(z)[\lambda_n]\subseteq\lambda_n\qquad(n<\omega).
\]
Consequently the entire compact coded family lies in $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$. Choosing the non-Borel $A$ of Lemma~\ref{swo:nb:lem:nonborelset} proves (iii) by the same continuous-preimage argument, now in this closed ambient space. Noncomplete metrizability follows from the $G_\delta$ criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[What the inverse condition sees on the code]\label{swo:nb:prop:closuretrace}
For the localized construction in the proof of Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:bounded},
\[
 F^{-1}(H_\mu)=2^\omega\setminus\overline A,
 \qquad
 F^{-1}(\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu\cap\WO_\mu(\mu))=2^\omega\setminus A,
\]
where $\overline A$ is the ordinary Cantor-space closure.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The second equation is already known. If $z\notin\overline A$, some finite prefix $z\res N$ has no extension in $A$. Every distinguished label is then released in a block before $N$. The inverse images of $Y$ are bounded. The inverse images of the finitely many reservoir blocks intersecting any prescribed bounded label segment are bounded as well. Thus $F(z)$ is exhaustive and has bounded inverse images.

If $z\in A$, the code is not exhaustive. If $z\in\overline A\setminus A$, then for every $N$ some $a\in A$ agrees with $z$ on its first $N$ bits. This $a$ is distinct from $z$ and is released at a first disagreement at stage at least $N$. The preimages of the bounded set $Y$ therefore meet arbitrarily late domain blocks and are unbounded in $\mu$. Hence $F(z)\notin H_\mu$.
\end{proof}

This is a useful conceptual refinement. On the coded family, surjectivity tests membership outside $A$, whereas bounded inverse behavior tests membership outside its closure. The forward condition alone does not remove the descriptive complexity; the inverse condition removes exactly the accumulation-branch phenomenon responsible for delayed coverage of a bounded reservoir.

The proof also explains the limit of the group analogy. At a regular cardinal every set of size less than the cardinal is bounded, so every permutation preserves boundedness in both directions. At a singular cardinal a permutation can send a bounded cofinality-sized set onto an unbounded set. Consequently the full permutation space with forward-prefix topology is not automatically a topological group. Nor does merely naming a two-sided uniformity prove continuity of every translation on the full singular permutation set. The subgroup $H_\mu$ is the precise safe statement used here.

\subsection{The minimal surreal slices (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:surreal}

\merge\ Source~26's Section~9, printed whole. Its birthday cutoff $\theta$ is
printed $\kappa$, so that $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ as elsewhere in this report. Its
\cref{swo:nb:lem:surrealthick} is \cref{swo:gs:lem:alphabet-size} with a different
sign trunk; its $\beth_\omega$ example extends this report's $\beth_\omega$
examples (\cref{swo:gs:n6.8}, \cref{swo:st:thm:transition}) to the topology.

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 651-731
We use the ordinal-length sign model of surreal numbers~\cite{Gonshor}. A surreal $x$ is a function from an ordinal $\bd(x)$ to $\{-,+\}$. Numerical comparison uses the first disagreement after extending each sign function by the termination value $0$, with $-<0<+$. The ordinal $\bd(x)$ is its birthday. The model separates numerical order from simplicity, which is proper prefix extension.

For an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$, set
\[
 \No_{<\kappa}=
       \{x\in\No:\bd(x)<\kappa\},\qquad
 \mu=2^{<\kappa}=\sup_{\alpha<\kappa}2^{|\alpha|}.
\]
This is a set of labels. It is not the whole surreal class and is not, without additional closure hypotheses, being treated as a subfield.

\begin{lemma}[Cardinality and thickness]\label{swo:nb:lem:surrealthick}
For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$,
\[
 |\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa},
\]
and every nonempty numerical interval and each ray in $\No_{<\kappa}$ has this same cardinality.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are $2^{|\alpha|}$ sign sequences of each birthday $\alpha<\kappa$. Their union has cardinality at least the supremum $\mu$. Also $\kappa\le\mu$: successor cardinal bounds below a limit cardinal, or Cantor's inequality at the predecessor cardinal in the successor case, give this, and the case $\kappa=\omega$ is immediate. Thus the union has size at most $\kappa\cdot\mu=\mu$.

For thickness, we construct a sign trunk all of whose extensions lie between given $x<y$. Let $\delta$ be their first disagreement, with termination included. If $\delta<\bd(x)$, take $t=x\cat\langle+\rangle$. Every extension of $t$ is above $x$, by the plus at position $\bd(x)$, and below $y$, by the earlier disagreement at $\delta$.

The remaining case is $\delta=\bd(x)$: the lower word terminates and the upper word has a plus there. Start with the common prefix followed by that plus, follow the subsequent minus signs of $y$ until its first later plus or its end, and put a minus at that position. Call the resulting trunk $t$. It lies above $x$ by its plus at $\delta$ and below $y$ by the final minus, compared with either a plus or termination. Both comparisons are witnessed strictly before the end of $t$, so they persist through every extension. The length of $t$ is at most one more than one of the original birthdays, hence is below $\kappa$.

In either case, if the trunk length is $\beta<\kappa$, every sign tail of length $\alpha<\kappa$ gives an element of the interval, since $\beta+\alpha<\kappa$. These extensions are distinct and give at least $2^{|\alpha|}$ elements for each $\alpha$. Taking the supremum yields $\mu$, and the opposite bound is the cardinality of the whole cutoff.

For a ray, choose an ordinal sign sequence above the given birthday, or its all-minus counterpart below it, still with birthday below $\kappa$. An interval between that point and the original point lies in the ray. The interval result supplies the same cardinality.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No hidden regularity]\label{swo:nb:n9.2}
The bound $\beta+\alpha<\kappa$ uses that $\kappa$ is an infinite initial cardinal and that only two ordinals are being added. It does not require $\kappa$ to be regular. This is why the thickness argument remains valid at the singular cutoff central to source~26.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Topological classification of the minimal surreal slices]\label{swo:nb:thm:surrealclassification}
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal, let $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$, and compare the bijections $\mu\to\No_{<\kappa}$ lexicographically by numerical surreal labels. Their order topology is the bounded-prefix topology. In that topology,
\[
 \WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})\text{ is metrizable}
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\cf(2^{<\kappa})=\omega,
\]
and
\[
 \WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})\text{ is completely metrizable}
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\kappa=\omega.
\]
If $\mu>\omega$ and $\cf\mu=\omega$, it is non-Borel in its injection completion and has no nonempty completely metrizable open subspace.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{swo:nb:lem:surrealthick} supplies exactly the thickness interface needed by \cref{swo:nb:thm:ordertopology}. Apply \cref{swo:nb:thm:character} and Theorems~\ref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel} and~\ref{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification} with cardinal parameter $\mu$. For $\kappa=\omega$, the union of all finite sign levels is countably infinite. For $\kappa>\omega$, the level of birthday $\omega$ already contains $2^{\aleph_0}$ signs, so $\mu>\omega$. Thus $\mu=\omega$ holds exactly when $\kappa=\omega$.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Three instructive cutoffs}

At $\kappa=\omega$, the labels are finite sign sequences, equivalently the finite-birthday surreal numbers. The minimal enumeration space is completely metrizable; the forward metric still has nonexhaustive injections as completion points, but the topology admits a different complete metric. The earlier manuscript gives a more detailed Baire-space model and a distinction from the order type of the irrational line (source~24, \cref{swo:pc:cor:notirrational}).

At $\kappa=\omega_1$, one has $\mu=2^{\aleph_0}=\mathfrak c$. K\"onig's cofinality inequality gives $\cf(2^{\aleph_0})>\omega$, so the minimal enumeration space is not even first countable. Indeed, countable cofinality of $\mathfrak c$ would yield a sequence of smaller cardinals whose successor product is greater than $\mathfrak c$ by K\"onig's theorem, but at most $\mathfrak c^\omega=\mathfrak c$, a contradiction. This shows why ``the labels contain real-like objects'' does not make the space metrizable.

At
\[
 \kappa=\beth_\omega=\sup_{n<\omega}\beth_n,
 \qquad \beth_0=\aleph_0,\qquad \beth_{n+1}=2^{\beth_n},
\]
we have a singular strong limit cardinal of countable cofinality. For each $\nu<\kappa$, choose $n$ with $\nu\le\beth_n$; then $2^\nu\le\beth_{n+1}<\kappa$. Hence $2^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, and $\kappa>\mathfrak c$ because $\beth_2>\beth_1=\mathfrak c$.

\begin{corollary}[The unconditional $\beth_\omega$ example]\label{swo:nb:cor:bethomega}
The lexicographic minimal enumeration order
\[
 L=\WO_{\beth_\omega}(\No_{<\beth_\omega})
\]
has all of the following properties in $\ZFC$: it is a dense linear order without endpoints; its order topology is zero-dimensional and metrizable; it is Baire; no nonempty open subspace is completely metrizable; it is non-Borel in its completely metrizable injection completion; and it is closed-universal for zero-dimensional separable metrizable spaces. Every subset of binary Cantor space can be realized as a closed trace by an order-preserving coding.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine Lemma~\ref{swo:nb:lem:surrealthick} with \cref{swo:nb:thm:ordertopology}, Theorems~\ref{swo:nb:thm:baire}, \ref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel}, \ref{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification}, and~\ref{swo:nb:thm:closedtraces}, and Corollary~\ref{swo:nb:cor:closeduniversal}.
\end{proof}

This corollary is about an explicitly defined \emph{set} of surreal-labelled well-orders. It is not obtained by pretending that $\beth_\omega$ is inaccessible or that its birthday fragment is the set universe of a full class-theory model.

\subsubsection{Relation to the earlier singular order-spectrum transition}

The repository report also studies the minimal slices at these birthday cutoffs and gives a different singular transition (\cref{swo:st:thm:transition}). In its notation, if $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$, the minimal enumeration order is equimorphic with the binary lexicographic cube of length $\kappa\cdot\kappa$ when $\kappa$ is singular strong limit, and with the cube of length $\mu$ otherwise. Here $\kappa\cdot\kappa$ is \emph{ordinal} multiplication. This earlier assertion is not used as an input to the proofs above.

The two transitions measure different structures. The repository transition concerns mutual order embeddings into cubes. The present classification concerns the order topology and the descriptive complexity of exhaustiveness inside a prefix completion. They agree that singular strong-limit stages deserve attention, but neither assertion can be substituted for the other. Equimorphism does not identify the topology with that of a compact cube, and the equality $\mu=\kappa$ at $\beth_\omega$ does not collapse ordinal length $\kappa\cdot\kappa$ to $\kappa$.

\subsection{Nonminimal lengths and varying carriers (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:otherlengths}

% ---- source 26 (batch-83 manuscript 12), lines 735-756
The minimality of the ordinal domain is structural, not a convenience in notation. For $\lambda$ of cardinality $\mu$, one can define $\WO_\lambda(X)=\Bij(\lambda,X)$ and its proper-prefix topology, but the cardinalities and order types of residual tails vary with the prefix.

\begin{proposition}[Successor-length isolation]\label{swo:nb:prop:successor}
If $\lambda=\delta+1$ and $|\lambda|=|X|$, the proper-prefix topology on $\WO_\lambda(X)$ is discrete.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a given bijection $f$, fix its prefix of length $\delta$. Exactly one label remains, so exactly one full bijection extends this prefix. Thus the corresponding cylinder is the singleton $\{f\}$.
\end{proof}

Even for a dense numerical alphabet, this prefix topology need not coincide with enumeration order topology at nonminimal lengths: the singleton argument has no two unused choices with which to bracket the last coordinate. This gives a concrete reason that Theorem~\ref{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification} cannot simply be restated with ``all ordinals of cardinality $\mu$'' in place of the initial cardinal.

More generally, if a prefix leaves $m$ positions and exactly $m$ labels for finite $m$, its cylinder is a finite residual permutation order. Its adjacency and endpoints are finite combinatorial data. If it leaves an infinite residual cardinal, cardinal size alone still does not identify the residual \emph{ordinal length}. A systematic theory should retain both the order type of the domain tail and the numerical order on the residual labels. The previous repository reports already analyze several such residual and adjacency phenomena (\cref{swo:cf:adjacency,swo:cb:new:sec:block-types}); the present minimal-slice proofs intentionally use only the uniform residual situation guaranteed by initial-cardinal length.

For varying set carriers, write
\[
 \Words=
 \{p:p\text{ is a set function, }\dom p\in\Ord,
       \ran p\subseteq\No,\ p\text{ injective}\}.
\]
This is an ordinary class of sets. Every individual range has bounded birthdays: take the supremum of its birthday successors. Thus a fixed word belongs to a suitable set-sized fragment, while the class of all words is not bounded in one such fragment. The increasing-word subclass is obtained by requiring $p(\xi)<_{\No}p(\eta)$ whenever $\xi<\eta$.

One can compare words with an explicitly specified termination rule. A prefix-first order has a least empty word and extensions lying immediately on one designated side of every terminating prefix; the numerical surreal sign order instead uses central termination. These endpoint and prefix distinctions prevent an automatic identification with $\No$ even when an order embedding into $\No$ is available. The earlier reports supply explicit sign codings and analyze the relevant limit-length cuts (\cref{swo:part:conventions}). Our new compact coding applies to fixed exhaustive and injective $\mu$-words, and does not purport to classify every variable-length cut.
