\subsection{Coordinate control by an ideal (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:ideal}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 282-329
Fix $S_\mu=\Sym(\mu)$ and use composition $(p\circ q)(\xi)=p(q(\xi))$. A fixed label enumeration $e:\mu\to X$ identifies $\WO_\mu(X)$ with $S_\mu$ by $f\mapsto e^{-1}\circ f$. The prefix topology on $S_\mu$ has basic neighborhoods
\[
 N_\alpha(p)=\{q:q\res\alpha=p\res\alpha\},\qquad \alpha<\mu.
\]
The numerical order on $X$ does not enter this topology; thickness was what identified it with the order topology.

\begin{definition}[Admissible coordinate ideal]\label{swo:ge:n4.1}
An ideal $\mathcal J$ on $\mu$ is \emph{admissible} here if it contains every finite set, is closed under subsets and finite unions, and satisfies $\mathcal J\subseteq[\mu]^{<\mu}$. Define $\tau_\mathcal J$ by the basic neighborhoods
\[
 N_A(p)=\{q:q\res A=p\res A\}\quad(A\in\mathcal J).
\]
Write $\Fix(A)=N_A(\id)$. A map $u:\mu\to\mu$ preserves $\mathcal J$ if $u[A]\in\mathcal J$ for every $A\in\mathcal J$.
\end{definition}

The bounded ideal
\[
 \mathcal J_{\mathrm b}=\{A\subseteq\mu:\exists\alpha<\mu\ (A\subseteq\alpha)\}
\]
gives $\tau_{\mathcal J_{\mathrm b}}=\tau_{\mathrm b}$. The small-set ideal $[\mu]^{<\mu}$ gives $\tau_{<\mu}$. They agree at regular $\mu$ and differ at singular $\mu$. Admissibility ensures that outside every control set there remain $\mu$ coordinates, so transpositions can witness the necessity of continuity conditions.

\begin{theorem}[Exact ideal continuity criteria]\label{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont}
In $(S_\mu,\tau_\mathcal J)$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Every left translation $L_s(p)=s\circ p$ is a homeomorphism.
\item Right translation $R_s(p)=p\circ s$ is continuous everywhere if $s$ preserves $\mathcal J$, and nowhere otherwise.
\item Inversion is continuous at $p$ if and only if $p^{-1}$ preserves $\mathcal J$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Equality of restrictions on a fixed domain is unchanged by applying the same injective map to their values. This proves (i), including continuity of the inverse left translation.

To control $p\circ s$ on $A$, it suffices to control $p$ on $s[A]$. This proves sufficiency in (ii). If $s[A]\notin\mathcal J$, then for every $B\in\mathcal J$ some $u\in s[A]\setminus B$ exists; otherwise downward closure would put $s[A]$ in $\mathcal J$. Choose $v\notin B\cup\{u\}$. The permutation $q=p\circ(u\ v)$ agrees with $p$ on $B$, but $q\circ s$ changes at the coordinate $s^{-1}(u)\in A$. Thus continuity fails at every $p$.

To fix $p^{-1}$ on $A$, it suffices to fix $p$ on $p^{-1}[A]$. If this set belongs to $\mathcal J$, this proves the required local implication. If it does not, use the same transposition construction with $u\in p^{-1}[A]\setminus B$. The inverse position of the label $p(u)\in A$ changes from $u$ to $v$, while the forward restriction on $B$ stays fixed. This proves necessity in (iii).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The ideal-preserving subgroup]\label{swo:ge:cor:idealgroup}
The set
\[
 H_\mathcal J=\{p\in S_\mu:p\text{ and }p^{-1}\text{ preserve }\mathcal J\}
\]
is a subgroup, and its inherited $\tau_\mathcal J$ topology makes it a topological group.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Ideal preservation is closed under composition, and the definition is symmetric under inversion. For joint continuity at $(p,s)$, to control $p'\circ s'$ on $A\in\mathcal J$, require $s'\res A=s\res A$ and $p'\res s[A]=p\res s[A]$. Both are valid control requirements when $s\in H_\mathcal J$. Inversion is continuous by Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont}.
\end{proof}

At a singular cardinal, a bounded set of size $\cf\mu$ can be sent onto a cofinal set by a permutation. Thus Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont} reproduces the predecessor's obstruction (source~24, \cref{swo:pc:cor:groupdichotomy}): the original forward topology need not make the full permutation group a topological group. The ideal formulation also identifies exactly which part of the proof is general and which part depends on ordinal boundedness.

\subsection{Maximality and self-normalization (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:normalizer}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 333-382
\begin{theorem}[Maximal inherited topological subgroup]\label{swo:ge:thm:maximal}
Let $\mathcal J$ be admissible. Among subgroups $G\le S_\mu$ that contain every finite-support permutation and for which the inherited $\tau_\mathcal J$ topology is a group topology, $H_\mathcal J$ is the largest.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{swo:ge:cor:idealgroup} proves that $H_\mathcal J$ is such a subgroup; finitary permutations preserve $\mathcal J$ in both directions because they change a set by only finitely many points.

Suppose $G$ has the stated properties and $p\in G$. If $p^{-1}$ does not preserve $\mathcal J$, the transposition witnesses in the proof of Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont}(iii) all lie in $G$: each is $p\circ(u\ v)$, and $(u\ v)$ is finitary. They show that inversion on the \emph{subspace} $G$ is not continuous at $p$. This contradicts the group-topology assumption. Thus $p^{-1}$ preserves $\mathcal J$. Applying the same argument to $p^{-1}\in G$ shows that $p$ preserves $\mathcal J$. Hence $G\subseteq H_\mathcal J$.
\end{proof}

The finitary hypothesis matters. Discontinuity in an ambient space does not automatically remain a discontinuity after restriction to an arbitrary subgroup. It is precisely the supply of internal transposition witnesses that makes this maximality argument valid.

For the bounded ideal, let ${H_\mu}=H_{\mathcal J_{\mathrm b}}$. The next result answers the normalizer part of the predecessor's subgroup question (source~24; \cref{swo:x:sec:status}).

\begin{lemma}[A bounded part and a cofinal part]\label{swo:ge:lem:parts}
Let $\mu$ be singular and ${q}=\cf\mu$. If $C\subseteq\mu$ is unbounded and $|C|>{q}$, then $C$ contains a bounded subset $D$ of size ${q}$ and, disjoint from $D$, a cofinal subset $E$ of size ${q}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose an increasing cofinal sequence $(\gamma_i)_{i<{q}}$ in $\mu$. If every $C\cap\gamma_i$ had size less than ${q}$, their union would have size at most ${q}\cdot{q}={q}$, contrary to $|C|>{q}$. Some bounded intersection therefore contains a subset $D$ of size ${q}$. The portion of $C$ above a bound for $D$ remains unbounded, so it has a cofinal subset $E$ of size ${q}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Self-normalization at singular cardinalities]\label{swo:ge:thm:normalizer}
If $\mu$ is singular, then
\[
 N_{S_\mu}({H_\mu})={H_\mu}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every element of ${H_\mu}$ normalizes ${H_\mu}$. Conversely, let $s$ normalize ${H_\mu}$. Suppose that $s$ fails to preserve bounded sets. Choose a bounded $A_0$ with $s[A_0]$ unbounded. Since a singular cardinal is a limit cardinal, there is a bounded set $A\supseteq A_0$ with
\[
 \cf\mu<|A|<\mu.
\]
For example, enlarge a bounded initial segment containing $A_0$ to one of cardinality greater than $\cf\mu$. Put $C=s[A]$. It is unbounded and has size greater than $\cf\mu$.

Every permutation supported on $A$ belongs to ${H_\mu}$. Conjugation by $s$ therefore implies that \emph{every} permutation supported on $C$ belongs to ${H_\mu}$. By Lemma~\ref{swo:ge:lem:parts}, choose a bounded $D\subseteq C$ and a disjoint cofinal $E\subseteq C$, both of size $\cf\mu$. Exchange $D$ and $E$ bijectively and fix all remaining coordinates. The resulting involution is supported on $C$ but sends the bounded set $D$ to the unbounded set $E$. It is not in ${H_\mu}$, a contradiction.

Thus $s$ preserves bounded sets. Its inverse also normalizes ${H_\mu}$, so the same argument shows that $s^{-1}$ preserves bounded sets. Consequently $s\in{H_\mu}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the cardinal enlargement is essential]\label{swo:ge:n5.4}
An unbounded set of size exactly $\cf\mu$ may have too few points in every bounded interval for the exchange used above. It is not valid to assert that every unbounded support set carries a permutation violating boundedness. Enlarging $A_0$ to cardinality greater than $\cf\mu$ is what makes the proof work.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Recovering boundedness from the natural action]\label{swo:ge:prop:recover}
For $A\subseteq\mu$, the pointwise stabilizer of $A$ in ${H_\mu}$ is open in the inherited prefix topology if and only if $A$ is bounded.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $A$ is bounded, a bounded initial segment containing it has an open pointwise stabilizer contained in its stabilizer. That larger subgroup is open as a union of cosets. If $A$ is unbounded, then for every $\beta<\mu$ choose $u\in A\setminus\beta$ and $v\notin\beta\cup\{u\}$. The finitary transposition $(u\ v)$ belongs to ${H_\mu}$ and fixes $\beta$, but does not fix $A$. No identity neighborhood can lie inside the stabilizer of $A$.
\end{proof}

This reconstructs the bounded-set ideal from the \emph{topological group together with its specified permutation action}. It does not prove that the bare abstract group alone determines the ideal, nor that every abstract automorphism is induced by a permutation of $\mu$.

\subsection{One-sided boundedness: closure, density and a complete locus (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:onesided}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 386-457
Write
\begin{align*}
 {H^+_\mu}&=\{p\in S_\mu:p[A]\text{ is bounded for every bounded }A\},\\
 {H^-_\mu}&=\{p\in S_\mu:p^{-1}[A]\text{ is bounded for every bounded }A\}.
\end{align*}
Then ${H_\mu}={H^+_\mu}\cap{H^-_\mu}$ and inversion exchanges ${H^+_\mu}$ with ${H^-_\mu}$. By Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont}, ${H^-_\mu}$ is exactly the continuity locus of inversion in the full forward topology. At singular cardinals these two one-sided loci have strikingly different positions in the same space.

\subsubsection{A bounded extension lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Extending a bounded partial injection]\label{swo:ge:lem:reserve}
Let $A,C\subseteq\mu$ be bounded and let $q:A\to C$ be a bijection. There is a permutation $h\in{H_\mu}$ extending $q$, with bounded support.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $D_0=A\cup C$. If $D_0$ is finite, the two residual sets $D_0\setminus A$ and $D_0\setminus C$ have equal finite size, so choose a bijection between them and complete $q$ to a permutation of $D_0$.

If $D_0$ is infinite, put $\nu=|D_0|<\mu$. Choose a bounded ordinal block $R$ of size $\nu$ above $D_0$ and set $D=D_0\cup R$. Such a block remains below $\mu$ because both its starting ordinal and $\nu$ have cardinality less than the initial cardinal $\mu$. Both $D\setminus A$ and $D\setminus C$ contain $R$ and have size $\nu$. Complete $q$ by a bijection between these residual sets.

In either case, extend the resulting bounded permutation by the identity outside its carrier. A bounded-support permutation and its inverse send a bounded set into the union of that set and the bounded support. Hence the extension belongs to ${H_\mu}$.
\end{proof}

The reserve in the infinite case avoids a genuine pitfall: an infinite partial bijection need not extend to a permutation of the union of its domain and range, since the residual sets inside that union need not have equal cardinality.

\begin{theorem}[Exact forward closure]\label{swo:ge:thm:closure}
In $(S_\mu,\tau_{\mathrm b})$,
\[
 \overline{{H_\mu}}={H^+_\mu}.
\]
For singular $\mu$, the set ${H^+_\mu}$ is closed nowhere dense, and therefore ${H_\mu}$ is nowhere dense as well.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $p\notin{H^+_\mu}$, choose $\alpha<\mu$ for which $p[\alpha]$ is unbounded. Every permutation with the same restriction to $\alpha$ also fails the forward condition. Thus ${H^+_\mu}$ is closed, and its closure contains no additional point of $S_\mu$.

If $p\in{H^+_\mu}$, then $p\res\alpha$ has bounded domain and bounded range for every $\alpha<\mu$. Lemma~\ref{swo:ge:lem:reserve} extends this restriction to an element of ${H_\mu}$. Every prefix neighborhood of $p$ consequently meets ${H_\mu}$, proving the equality.

Now assume $\mu$ singular and put ${q}=\cf\mu$. Given any short injective prefix, the unused labels form an unbounded set: fewer than $\mu$ used labels cannot contain a tail of cardinality $\mu$. Choose a cofinal sequence of ${q}$ distinct unused labels and append it to the prefix. The enlarged prefix still has length less than $\mu$, since a finite ordinal sum of ordinals of cardinality less than $\mu$ remains below $\mu$. It has unbounded range on a bounded domain. Its nonempty cylinder, obtained by \cref{swo:ge:lem:prefix}, is disjoint from ${H^+_\mu}$. Thus the closed set ${H^+_\mu}$ has empty interior.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{A dense inverse-continuity locus}

Fix an increasing cofinal sequence $(\mu_i)_{i<{q}}$ in $\mu$, where ${q}=\cf\mu$. On the injection space $\I_\mu(\mu)$ with its forward prefix topology, define
\[
 O_i=\{h:\exists\alpha<\mu\ (\mu_i\subseteq\ran(h\res\alpha))\}.
\]
Here $\mu_i$ denotes the set of all ordinals below that ordinal; the condition requires an entire bounded block of labels to have appeared by some bounded time.

\begin{theorem}[Inverse-boundedness as a dense intersection]\label{swo:ge:thm:dense-locus}
Each $O_i$ is open dense, and as a subspace of $\I_\mu(\mu)$,
\[
 {H^-_\mu}=\bigcap_{i<{q}}O_i.
\]
This intersection is dense. If ${q}=\omega$, it is a dense completely metrizable $G_{q}$ subspace of $\I_\mu(\mu)$ and of $S_\mu$. Its complement is meager in both spaces.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Once the labels below $\mu_i$ have appeared in a prefix, every continuation satisfies the same condition, so $O_i$ is open. Any short prefix can be extended to include the as-yet unused labels below $\mu_i$; there are fewer than $\mu$ of them. The extension remains short, proving density.

If an injection belongs to every $O_i$, it is onto, since these label blocks cover $\mu$. Further, the preimage of each $\mu_i$ is bounded. Every bounded subset of $\mu$ is contained in some $\mu_i$, so the inverse of the resulting permutation preserves boundedness. Conversely, inverse boundedness supplies the required witness $\alpha$ for every $i$. This proves the displayed equality.

For density of the full intersection, start with any prescribed short prefix. At stage $i<{q}$, extend it to include every label below $\mu_i$ and to have length at least $\mu_i$. At a limit stage $j<{q}$, take the union of the preceding prefixes. This union is still short, since fewer than $\cf\mu$ lengths below $\mu$ have been used. At the final stage ${q}$, the union has domain $\mu$, is injective, and covers every label. Each block $\mu_i$ was covered at a short intermediate stage, so the final permutation belongs to ${H^-_\mu}$ and extends the original prefix.

If ${q}=\omega$, agreement along the cofinal lengths $\mu_i$ defines a compatible ultrametric on the injection space. A Cauchy sequence stabilizes a coherent injective prefix at every such length, and their union is its limit. Thus the injection space is completely metrizable. A $G_{q}$ subspace of a completely metrizable space is completely metrizable; a proof not requiring separability is recalled in \cref{swo:ge:app:metric}. Since every $O_i$ is open dense, the complement of the intersection is a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets. Intersecting with $S_\mu$ gives the same conclusion there, because each $O_i\cap S_\mu$ is open dense by the same prefix-extension argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A complete core and the Baire property]\label{swo:ge:cor:baire}
If $\cf\mu=\omega$, then $S_\mu$ with the forward topology is a Baire space, and ${H_\mu}$ has a complete compatible metric. At an uncountable singular such $\mu$, this completely metrizable subgroup is nevertheless nowhere dense in $S_\mu$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The dense completely metrizable subspace ${H^-_\mu}$ is Baire. If $U_n$ are open dense in $S_\mu$, their intersections with ${H^-_\mu}$ are open dense there: every open set in $S_\mu$ meeting ${H^-_\mu}$ meets $U_n$ in a nonempty open set, which again meets the dense subspace. Hence $\bigcap_n U_n$ meets every nonempty open set of $S_\mu$. This proves the Baire property.

By Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:closure}, ${H^+_\mu}$ is closed in $S_\mu$, so ${H_\mu}={H^+_\mu}\cap{H^-_\mu}$ is closed in the completely metrizable space ${H^-_\mu}$. The final assertion is Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:closure}.
\end{proof}

Complete metrizability is not inherited upward from a dense subspace. Consequently this corollary does not settle whether $S_\mu$ itself admits a complete compatible metric when $\mu>\omega$ is singular of countable cofinality. It does supply a concrete large complete locus and another proof of the Baire property in that case.

\begin{note}[\merge; source~28's Question~1, answered by source~26 (3 October 2026)]\label{swo:x:note:q1-rescoped}
Source~28 calls the complete metrizability of the full singular forward space its
remaining question: ``The remaining complete-metrizability question for the
\emph{full} singular forward permutation space is not settled by the dense complete
subspace constructed here'' (its introduction); the paragraph above; its ledger
(``Does not settle complete metrizability of the full forward space''); and its
Question~1, ``Complete metrizability of the full singular space'': \emph{let
$\mu>\omega$ be singular with $\cf\mu=\omega$; is $\Sym(\mu)$, with its
bounded-prefix topology, completely metrizable? Equivalently, is it a $G_\delta$
subspace of the complete forward injection space?} Source~28's own results do not
settle it, as it says: complete metrizability is not inherited upward from the
dense locus $H^-_\mu$. The question is answered negatively in $\ZFC$ by source~26's
\cref{swo:nb:thm:completeclassification}: under the identification of $S_\mu$ with
$\WO_\mu(X)$, $S_\mu$ is not Borel, hence not $G_\delta$, in $\I_\mu(\mu)$, and no
nonempty open subspace of it is completely metrizable. Source~28 read source~24 but
not source~26: both were written at the same repository pin \code{7ff7736ec}, and
source~26 arrived first (commit \code{0d7b2441d}; source~28 in \code{79049d58c}). Source~28's Question~3,
on the descriptive complexity of the one-sided loci, is answered in part by
\cref{swo:nb:thm:nonborel} and \cref{swo:nb:thm:bounded}(iii).
\end{note}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 459-497
\subsubsection{The forward and inverse conditions are independent}

\begin{proposition}[An explicit one-sided permutation]\label{swo:ge:prop:one-sided-example}
At every singular $\mu$,
\[
 {H_\mu}\subsetneq{H^+_\mu},\qquad {H_\mu}\subsetneq{H^-_\mu}.
\]
In particular, ${H_\mu}$ is not closed in the forward topology.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put ${q}=\cf\mu<\mu$. Choose a bounded set
\[
 B=\{b_{i,n}:i<{q},\ n<\omega\}
\]
of distinct coordinates. Above $B$, choose disjoint countably infinite blocks
\[
 A_i=\{a_{i,n}:n<\omega\}\qquad(i<{q})
\]
in successively higher bounded ordinal intervals, with their starting positions cofinal in $\mu$. The intervals can be chosen so that every bounded set meets only blocks with indices bounded in ${q}$.

Define $p$ on these coordinates by
\begin{align*}
 p(a_{i,0})&=b_{i,0},&
 p(a_{i,n+1})&=a_{i,n},&
 p(b_{i,n})&=b_{i,n+1},
\end{align*}
and fix all other coordinates. On each $i$-chain this is a bilateral shift, so it defines a permutation. A bounded input set meets only boundedly many of the high blocks. Its image is contained in the union of that input set, the bounded set $B$, and a bounded initial collection of the high blocks. Therefore $p\in{H^+_\mu}$.

But $p^{-1}[B]$ contains every $a_{i,0}$ and is cofinal in $\mu$. Thus $p\notin{H^-_\mu}$. Its inverse lies in ${H^-_\mu}\setminus{H^+_\mu}$. The nonclosedness assertion follows from $\overline{{H_\mu}}={H^+_\mu}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A discrete subgroup outside the bounded subgroup]\label{swo:ge:n6.6}
There is a subgroup of $S_\mu$ not contained in ${H_\mu}$ whose inherited forward topology is a group topology.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For the permutation $p$ in Proposition~\ref{swo:ge:prop:one-sided-example}, the orbit of $b_{0,0}$ under the integer powers of $p$ has no repetitions. Thus the only element of the cyclic subgroup $\langle p\rangle$ fixing $b_{0,0}$ is the identity. A sufficiently long prefix condition isolates that identity, and left translations isolate every other group element. The inherited topology is discrete, hence is a group topology. But $p\notin{H_\mu}$. This subgroup does not contain all finitary permutations, exactly as Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:maximal} requires.
\end{proof}

This example explains why a single condition such as ``the permutation respects small prefixes'' is insufficient. Forward boundedness concerns where early positions go; inverse boundedness concerns how late one must search to find early labels. They are different constraints at singular cardinalities.

\subsection{The canonical group envelope (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:envelope}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 501-561
The two-sided bounded topology $\tau_{\leftrightarrow}$ has basic neighborhoods at $p$ requiring
\[
 q\res\alpha=p\res\alpha,
 \qquad q^{-1}\res\alpha=p^{-1}\res\alpha
 \quad(\alpha<\mu).
\]
The predecessor proved that its defining uniformity is complete (source~24, \cref{swo:pc:thm:twosided}). This does not make the full singular permutation set a topological group: conjugating bounded control sets can produce unbounded control sets. We now identify the exact coarsest refinement that does make all group operations continuous.

\begin{definition}[Symmetric closure of a coordinate ideal]\label{swo:ge:n7.1}
For an admissible ideal $\mathcal J$, let $\mathcal J^{\mathrm{sym}}$ be the ideal generated by the sets $s[A]$, with $A\in\mathcal J$ and $s\in S_\mu$. Thus its members are subsets of finite unions of such images. It remains contained in $[\mu]^{<\mu}$ and is invariant under every permutation.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Smallest group refinement for an ideal]\label{swo:ge:thm:ideal-envelope}
The topology $\tau_{\mathcal J^{\mathrm{sym}}}$ is the coarsest group topology on $S_\mu$ finer than $\tau_\mathcal J$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every permutation and its inverse preserve $\mathcal J^{\mathrm{sym}}$. Corollary~\ref{swo:ge:cor:idealgroup}, or the direct multiplication argument there, makes $\tau_{\mathcal J^{\mathrm{sym}}}$ a group topology. It contains $\tau_\mathcal J$.

Let $\tau$ be any group topology containing $\tau_\mathcal J$. Each $\Fix(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal J$ is $\tau$-open, and conjugation gives the $\tau$-open subgroup
\[
 s\Fix(A)s^{-1}=\Fix(s[A]).
\]
Finite intersections give open stabilizers of finite unions of these image sets. If $C$ is a subset of such a union $D$, then $\Fix(C)$ contains the open subgroup $\Fix(D)$, and is itself open as a union of its cosets. Thus every $\Fix(C)$ with $C\in\mathcal J^{\mathrm{sym}}$ is $\tau$-open. Translating these identity neighborhoods proves $\tau_{\mathcal J^{\mathrm{sym}}}\subseteq\tau$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The bounded-prefix group envelope]\label{swo:ge:thm:envelope}
For every infinite $\mu$, the coarsest group topology finer than $\tau_{\mathrm b}$ is
\[
 \tau_{<\mu}=\tau_{[\mu]^{<\mu}}.
\]
For regular $\mu$, it equals $\tau_{\mathrm b}$. For singular $\mu$,
\[
 \tau_{\mathrm b}\ \subsetneq\ \tau_{\leftrightarrow}\ \subsetneq\ \tau_{<\mu}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every small set $A\subseteq\mu$ is the image of a bounded initial ordinal under a permutation: take a bijection $|A|\to A$ and extend it over the two complements, both of size $\mu$. Conversely, images of bounded sets have size less than $\mu$. Therefore
\[
 (\mathcal J_{\mathrm b})^{\mathrm{sym}}=[\mu]^{<\mu},
\]
and Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-envelope} applies. At regular $\mu$, small and bounded are equivalent.

For every $\mu$, the two-sided bounded topology contains the forward one. A two-sided bounded requirement at $p$ is enforced by forward agreement on
\[
 \alpha\cup p^{-1}[\alpha],
\]
which has size less than $\mu$. Thus $\tau_{\leftrightarrow}\subseteq\tau_{<\mu}$.

Suppose $\mu$ singular. Choose an involution $s$ exchanging a bounded set of size $\cf\mu$ with a disjoint cofinal set of the same size. At $s$, an inverse requirement on the bounded set has no forward-prefix neighborhood enforcing it, by the transposition proof of Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont}. Hence $\tau_{\mathrm b}\ne\tau_{\leftrightarrow}$.

At the identity, however, fixing $\alpha$ automatically fixes the inverse on $\alpha$. Thus the $\tau_{\leftrightarrow}$ and $\tau_{\mathrm b}$ identity neighborhood bases coincide. Let $C$ be an unbounded set of size $\cf\mu<\mu$. Its stabilizer is $\tau_{<\mu}$-open, but contains no bounded-prefix identity neighborhood: beyond any prescribed $\beta$ one can swap a point of $C$ with another point. It is not a $\tau_{\leftrightarrow}$ neighborhood of the identity. Hence $\tau_{\leftrightarrow}\ne\tau_{<\mu}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Why two-sided bounded control is not enough]\label{swo:ge:prop:twosided-failure}
At singular $\mu$, $\tau_{\leftrightarrow}$ does not make $S_\mu$ a topological group.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the permutation $s$ from Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:envelope}, with $s[\alpha]$ unbounded for some $\alpha$. At the identity, every two-sided bounded neighborhood contains $\Fix(\beta)$ for some $\beta$. Choose a transposition $t$ supported outside $\beta$ that moves a point of $s[\alpha]$. Then $t$ belongs to that input neighborhood, but $t\circ s$ disagrees with $s$ below $\alpha$. Right translation by $s$ is not continuous at the identity.
\end{proof}

The envelope theorem gives a canonical answer to a natural formulation of the problem: retain all original prefix-open sets, keep ordinary permutation composition, and add no more open sets than group continuity forces. Its answer is \emph{not} the original order topology and is \emph{not} merely inverse-prefix control. It is control on all sets of positions with cardinality less than $\mu$.

\subsection{Exact character and the singular cardinal penalty (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:character}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 565-566
For a topological space, the character at a point is the least size of a local neighborhood base. For a poset, $\cof$ denotes the least size of a cofinal subset. Neither should be confused with the ordinal cofinality of the enumeration cardinal, although all three occur here.


\begin{note}[Source~28, Proposition~8.1, ``Character of the forward space'']\label{swo:ge:prop:forward-character}
\emph{Every point of $(S_\mu,\tau_{\mathrm b})$ has character $\cf\mu$. The forward
space is metrizable exactly when $\cf\mu=\omega$.} This is \cref{swo:pc:prop:metric}
and \cref{swo:nb:thm:character}, by the same argument (``Strictness follows by
swapping two coordinates outside $\gamma$, one of them $\gamma$'').
\end{note}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 576-618
\begin{theorem}[Character of the canonical envelope]\label{swo:ge:thm:character}
For every infinite cardinal $\mu$,
\[
 \chi(S_\mu,\tau_{<\mu})=\cof([\mu]^{<\mu},\subseteq).
\]
For singular $\mu$,
\[
 \mu^+\le\chi(S_\mu,\tau_{<\mu})\le\mu^{<\mu}.
\]
In particular, the canonical group envelope is not first countable at any singular $\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A cofinal family $\mathcal A\subseteq[\mu]^{<\mu}$ gives the identity base $\{\Fix(A):A\in\mathcal A\}$. For the reverse inequality, let $\mathcal U$ be a local base at the identity, and choose $A_U$ small with $\Fix(A_U)\subseteq U$. Given any small $A$, choose $U\subseteq\Fix(A)$. Then
\[
 \Fix(A_U)\subseteq\Fix(A)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\subseteq A_U.
\]
Indeed, a point of $A\setminus A_U$ could be transposed with a different point outside $A_U$, contradicting the inclusion. Thus the $A_U$ form a cofinal family. Homogeneity of the topological group gives the formula at every point.

The upper bound is the number of small subsets, $\mu^{<\mu}$. To prove the strict lower bound at singular $\mu$, put ${q}=\cf\mu$ and suppose a family $(A_\xi)_{\xi<\mu}$ were cofinal. Choose increasing infinite cardinals $\kappa_i<\mu$, $i<{q}$, cofinal in $\mu$. For each $i$, the union
\[
 T_i=\bigcup\{A_\xi:\xi<\kappa_i,\ |A_\xi|\le\kappa_i\}
\]
has size at most $\kappa_i$, so choose $x_i\in\mu\setminus T_i$. The set $C=\{x_i:i<{q}\}$ has size less than $\mu$. For any fixed $\xi<\mu$, choose $i$ sufficiently large that $\xi<\kappa_i$ and $|A_\xi|\le\kappa_i$. Then $x_i\notin A_\xi$, and hence $C\nsubseteq A_\xi$. This contradicts cofinality of the family. A shorter family could have been padded to length $\mu$, so the cofinality is strictly greater than $\mu$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A countably based order with a very large group envelope]\label{swo:ge:n8.3}
Take $\kappa=\beth_\omega$ and $X=\No_{<\kappa}$. The cardinal $\kappa$ is a singular strong limit of cofinality $\omega$, and $2^{<\kappa}=\kappa$. Thus the minimal enumeration order has a metrizable order topology with local character $\omega$. Its canonical group envelope has character at least $\beth_\omega^+$. No additional hypothesis such as the generalized continuum hypothesis is needed for this example: strong limit follows because every $\lambda<\beth_\omega$ is below some $\beth_n$, and $2^\lambda\le\beth_{n+1}<\beth_\omega$.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What the character bound does not say]\label{swo:ge:n8.4}
Character is not monotone under arbitrary refinement of a topology. In particular, the discrete topology is a finer metrizable group topology and has character $1$. The theorem says that the \emph{coarsest} group refinement has large character. It does not exclude all other finer metrizable group topologies. Nor does it claim that a different, artificially transported group law could not be placed on the underlying space. The fixed operations throughout are ordinary permutation composition and inversion.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Equal global invariants can conceal different local geometry]\label{swo:ge:prop:weight}
Both $(S_\mu,\tau_{\mathrm b})$ and $(S_\mu,\tau_{<\mu})$ have density and weight equal to $\mu^{<\mu}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
There are $\mu^{<\mu}$ short injective prefixes, giving an upper bound for the weight of $\tau_{\mathrm b}$; choosing one completion of each gives the same bound for density. There are also at most $\mu^{<\mu}$ small-domain partial injections, giving both upper bounds for $\tau_{<\mu}$.

For every cardinal $\lambda<\mu$, all injections from a fixed initial segment of size $\lambda$ into $\mu$ give pairwise disjoint nonempty cylinders in either topology. There are $\mu^\lambda$ such injections: an arbitrary function $a:\lambda\to\mu$ can be coded injectively as $\xi\mapsto(\xi,a(\xi))$, followed by a fixed identification $\lambda\times\mu\cong\mu$ when $\lambda>0$. Every dense set must meet every cylinder. Taking the supremum over $\lambda<\mu$ gives density at least $\mu^{<\mu}$, and weight is at least density.
\end{proof}

Thus density and weight alone cannot detect the topology change. The local character and the continuity of right translations do detect it.

\subsection{Three uniform completions, kept separate (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:completion}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 622-697
Uniform completeness depends on a chosen family of agreement requirements, not only on the induced topology. This is already visible for permutations of $\omega$: permutations can stabilize at every forward coordinate while one label escapes to arbitrarily late positions. The following results organize the analogous phenomena at arbitrary cardinalities.

\subsubsection{Forward completion for an arbitrary coordinate ideal}

For admissible $\mathcal J$, put on $\I_\mu(\mu)$ the uniformity with basic entourages
\[
 E_A=\{(h,k):h\res A=k\res A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal J.
\]
Its restriction to $S_\mu$ is the forward $\mathcal J$-uniformity.

\begin{theorem}[The forward ideal completion]\label{swo:ge:thm:forward-complete}
The injection space is complete for this uniformity, and $S_\mu$ is a dense uniform subspace. Hence $\I_\mu(\mu)$ is its Hausdorff uniform completion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A Cauchy filter determines, for each $A\in\mathcal J$, a unique stabilized restriction $q_A$ on $A$: an $E_A$-small nonempty filter member lies in the cylinder determined by one such restriction, and two different cylinders are disjoint. Taking control on $A\cup B$ proves compatibility of $q_A$ and $q_B$. Since singletons belong to $\mathcal J$, the union determines a function $h:\mu\to\mu$. Control on each two-element set proves injectivity. The filter contains the cylinder of $h\res A$ for every $A\in\mathcal J$, hence converges to $h$.

Every small-domain partial injection extends to a permutation, because both unused domain and unused range have cardinality $\mu$. Therefore every basic cylinder in the injection space meets $S_\mu$. The agreement entourages restrict exactly to those on $S_\mu$, proving density and uniform embedding. Completeness and Hausdorffness give the completion assertion.
\end{proof}

This proof uses stabilization of an entire allowed control set, not merely separate eventual stabilization at each coordinate. For uncountable control sets those are distinct conditions.

\begin{theorem}[Forward completion of the bounded subgroup]\label{swo:ge:thm:H-completion}
For the bounded-prefix uniformity, the Hausdorff completion of ${H_\mu}$ is
\[
 \I^{\mathrm b}_\mu
 =\{h\in\Inj(\mu,\mu):h[A]\text{ is bounded whenever }A\text{ is bounded}\}.
\]
For every infinite $\mu$, the subgroup ${H_\mu}$ is not complete for this forward uniformity.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In the full injection completion from Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:forward-complete}, a failure of boundedness is witnessed by an entire prefix with unbounded range. Its cylinder excludes $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$, so that subspace is closed and complete. Each prefix of a boundedness-preserving injection has bounded domain and bounded range; Lemma~\ref{swo:ge:lem:reserve} completes it inside ${H_\mu}$. Conversely, no prefix with unbounded range can occur in an element of ${H_\mu}$. Hence the closure of ${H_\mu}$ in the injection completion is exactly $\I^{\mathrm b}_\mu$.

For a concrete missing point, send each natural number $n$ to $n+1$ and fix every coordinate in $\mu\setminus\omega$. This is a boundedness-preserving injection omitting $0$. When $\mu=\omega$, bounded sets are finite and the assertion is immediate; when $\mu>\omega$, the changed coordinates lie in the bounded set $\omega$. Thus the complete closure strictly contains ${H_\mu}$.
\end{proof}

There is no conflict between this theorem and complete metrizability of ${H_\mu}$ when $\cf\mu=\omega$. A complete compatible metric can induce the same topology as an incomplete forward metric while defining a different uniformity.

\subsubsection{Two-sided small-set completeness}

On $S_\mu$, define
\[
 E_A^{\leftrightarrow}
 =\{(p,q):p\res A=q\res A\text{ and }p^{-1}\res A=q^{-1}\res A\},
 \qquad |A|<\mu.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Completeness of the canonical group envelope]\label{swo:ge:thm:raikov}
The two-sided small-set uniformity is complete, induces $\tau_{<\mu}$, and is the two-sided group uniformity of $(S_\mu,\tau_{<\mu})$. Thus the canonical envelope is a complete topological group in the two-sided sense.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A Cauchy filter determines coherent stabilized forward and inverse restrictions. As in Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:forward-complete}, their unions are injections $h,g:\mu\to\mu$. If $h(\xi)=\eta$, take a nonempty filter member on which the forward value at $\xi$ and the inverse value at $\eta$ are both stabilized. Every permutation in that member witnesses $g(\eta)=\xi$. Conversely, $g(\eta)=\xi$ implies $h(\xi)=\eta$. Hence $g=h^{-1}$, and $h$ is a permutation. Stabilization on each whole small control set proves convergence in the stated uniformity.

At a fixed $p$, inverse agreement on $A$ is enforced by forward agreement on $p^{-1}[A]$, which is small. Thus adding inverse requirements does not change the topology $\tau_{<\mu}$.

Finally, the two group-uniform conditions associated with $\Fix(A)$ are
\[
 p^{-1}q\in\Fix(A),\qquad qp^{-1}\in\Fix(A).
\]
The first is equivalent to forward agreement on $A$. The second is equivalent to agreement of the inverses on $A$: it says $q(p^{-1}(a))=a$ for every $a\in A$. Their intersection is $E_A^{\leftrightarrow}$. Finite unions combine different control sets, identifying the uniformities exactly.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.23\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.24\linewidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Control convention & Completion or completeness & Singular-cardinal warning\\
\midrule
Forward bounded prefixes & Full injection space; for ${H_\mu}$, boundedness-preserving injections & Surjectivity can be lost.\\
Forward arbitrary small sets & Full injection space, with small-set control & Coordinatewise convergence alone is weaker.\\
Forward and inverse bounded prefixes & Complete on the full permutation set & The induced topology is still not a group topology.\\
Forward and inverse arbitrary small sets & Complete two-sided group uniformity & Its topology is $\tau_{<\mu}$, not the original order topology.\\
Dedekind cuts of the numerical order & Also fills cylinder edges and alphabet gaps & Not a uniform completion of either preceding kind.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

For the last row, even a full injective word cannot represent the lower edge of a first-label cylinder. If $X$ is thick and $x\in X$, consider the lower cut consisting of exhaustive words with first label below $x$. An injection starting below $x$ lies below some words in that cut, one starting above $x$ lies above the entire $x$-cylinder, and one starting at $x$ has exhaustive words with that same first label below it. None gives exactly the cylinder-edge cut. This is the elementary reason the forward injection boundary is only part of the order-completion boundary (source~24, \cref{swo:pc:prop:trace}).

\subsection{What the group results say about surreal lexicography (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:application}

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 701-738
\subsubsection{Changing labels versus changing positions}

A bijection $a:X\to Y$ acts on exhaustive enumerations by $f\mapsto a\circ f$. It takes prefix cylinders to prefix cylinders, and is therefore always a homeomorphism of the prefix spaces. If both alphabets are thick, it is a homeomorphism of their order topologies. It is an order isomorphism exactly when $a$ is increasing: sufficiency follows from first disagreement, and necessity follows by choosing exhaustive words with prescribed distinct first labels.

By contrast, a permutation of positions acts by $f\mapsto f\circ s$. Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont} shows that this is a forward homeomorphism precisely when $s\in{H_\mu}$. The distinction is conceptual: relabelling does not change which positions have been inspected, but reordering positions can move a bounded inspection set to an unbounded one.

\begin{proposition}[Exact filtration invariance]\label{swo:ge:prop:filtration}
The position changes that preserve the bounded-prefix topology in both directions are exactly the automorphisms of the bounded-set ideal, namely ${H_\mu}$. The topology $\tau_{<\mu}$ is invariant under every position permutation. For singular $\mu$, it is the coarsest topology that contains the prefix topology and is a group topology for all position permutations.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont}(ii) applied to $s$ and $s^{-1}$. Every permutation preserves cardinality, so it preserves the small-set ideal and acts homeomorphically for $\tau_{<\mu}$. The final assertion is Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:envelope}.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The permutation structure is relative to a baseline}

The set $\Bij(\mu,X)$ is not intrinsically a group under composition: its members have domain $\mu$ and codomain $X$, so $f\circ g$ need not even be typed. Fixing $e:\mu\to X$ gives the group law
\[
 f*_e g=f\circ e^{-1}\circ g,
\]
with identity $e$. The usual right action of $\Sym(\mu)$ on enumerations is intrinsic, but choosing an identity for a group law is auxiliary. It is useful to regard the enumeration space as a \emph{torsor}, a space on which the permutation group acts freely and transitively, before selecting a baseline.

The subgroup ${H_\mu}$ then corresponds to enumerations that send bounded position sets into bounded portions of the baseline label filtration $e[\alpha]$, and whose inverses have the same property. Its placement inside the surreal enumeration space depends on that label filtration. Self-normalization is a precise theorem about this specified action; it is not a claim that numerical order alone canonically chooses ${H_\mu}$.

\subsubsection{Concrete cutoff consequences}

For $\No_{<\kappa}$ and $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$, the following conclusions are immediate from the proved theorems. The minimal order is dense without endpoints, has size $2^\mu$, and contains every linear order of size at most $\mu$. Its ordinal and reverse-ordinal spectra stop exactly at $\mu^+$. Its local order-topological character is $\cf\mu$. After choosing a baseline, the boundedness-preserving subgroup is maximal in the sense of Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:maximal}, and, when $\mu$ is singular, is self-normalizing and nowhere dense. The least group refinement has character $\cof([\mu]^{<\mu})$ and is two-sided complete.

These conclusions are insensitive to whether the birthday cutoff is a subfield. Arithmetic closure is not needed. Conversely, the statements do not automatically apply to an arbitrary sparse subset of $\No$ with its numerical order. Prefix topology still makes sense there, but its agreement with the order topology required thickness.

\subsubsection{Context from earlier topological classifications}

At regular $\mu$, the predecessor manuscript constructs a homeomorphism
\[
 \WO_\mu(X)\cong_{\mathrm{top}}(\mu^{<\mu})^\mu
\]
with the bounded topology (source~24, \cref{swo:pc:thm:regular}). Its tree forces the least not-yet-used label to appear at each stage. Regularity keeps the union of fewer than $\mu$ intermediate short prefixes short. At singular $\mu$, that specific construction can reach full length before all coverage requirements have been imposed. This is why a regular argument cannot simply be copied.

At the countable thick cutoff, the same predecessor proves that the topology is ordinary Baire-space topology, while the Dedekind completion is a real line with continuum many omitted points. It is therefore not order-isomorphic to the usual irrationals, whose real completion omits only countably many points. This is another warning that topology alone does not classify the numerical order. The bounded-topology setting is part of the broader generalized descriptive-set-theoretic landscape studied in~\cite{FriedmanHyttinenKulikov}; the present ideal arguments neither assume nor establish a general classification of all such spaces.

\section{The class analogue: global prefix completion and its limits (source 24; sources 26 and 28)}\label{swo:x:sec:global}

source~28's Sections~11--12. The class layer re-proves Part~IV: the core $\Pbd(b)$
(the three sources' $\mathcal C_b$), its prefix completion, its density and
universality, the diagonal theorem and direct comparison; these are notes. New are
source~24's small-net rigidity, its global branch-completion scheme and its

the singular obstruction of \cref{swo:x:sec:singular} does not occur globally. All
statements are $\GBC$ schemes about supplied class parameters; source~24's

\subsection{Global prefix completion (source 24)}\label{swo:pc:sec:global}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 663-669
We now work in $\GBC$ with the fixed baseline $b:\Ord\to\No$. Besides the virtual domain $\Hsl$ of class bijections, write $\Jinj$ for the virtual domain of class injections $h:\Ord\to\No$. Both have a well-defined first-disagreement comparison of individual members: a nonempty class of ordinals has a least member, since any one witness bounds a nonempty set in which the least witness can be found.

A set-sized injective prefix is an actual set $p:\alpha\to\No$. The expression ``$[p]$'' means the predicate that a given class word extends $p$. It does not introduce a class with those class words as its members. This distinction is harmless for ordinary pairwise proofs and indispensable for statements about all words.

\subsubsection{A genuinely class-sized core made from set codes}

A permutation of $\Ord$ is \emph{set supported} when its moved coordinates form a set. Such a permutation is the identity above some ordinal. Code it canonically by a permutation of the least initial segment containing its support, extended by the identity outside that segment. The identity has the empty code. The collection of these codes is an ordinary class of sets. Evaluating a code as $b\circ\pi$ gives an exhaustive surreal enumeration. Denote the ordered class of canonical codes by $\Pbd(b)$.

\begin{note}[Source~24, Lemma~9.1 and Propositions~9.2 and~9.3]\label{swo:pc:lem:globalextension}\label{swo:pc:prop:coredense}\label{swo:pc:prop:globaluniversal}
Lemma~9.1 (``Global prefix extension with a reserve''): \emph{every set-sized
injective prefix $p:\alpha\to\No$ extends to the evaluation of a code in $\Pbd(b)$;
the extension can be selected uniformly from $p$ and the fixed baseline and
global-choice parameters.} This is \cref{swo:gl:completion}, by a balanced reserve:
with $q=b^{-1}\circ p$ and $S=\alpha\cup\ran q$, a disjoint block $R$ of size
$\nu\ge\card S$ makes $D\setminus\alpha$ and $D\setminus\ran q$ equinumerous for
$D=S\cup R$. Source~24 comments: ``The reserve is not cosmetic. A naive instruction
to `close every partial-injection chain' can fail for an infinite chain with
unequal endpoint behavior \ldots{} Earlier work optimizes the size of that
reserve; optimality is unnecessary here'' (source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve}).
Proposition~9.2 (``Prefix density and numerical density''): \emph{every set-prefix
cylinder in $\Hsl$ or $\Jinj$ contains a core evaluation; a core evaluation lies
strictly between any two distinct injections, and on either side of each}, which
is \cref{swo:gl:cylinders} with the density in \cref{swo:gl:interpolation}.
Source~24: ``The existing report proves more: with its explicit uniform set-cut
convention, this core realizes all set-sized separated cuts and is
order-isomorphic to the surreal line'' (\cref{swo:gl:pbd-no}). ``The results below
need only the prefix extension and density just proved. In particular, the fact
that a dense core is a surreal line should not be turned into the assertion that
the entire virtual enumeration domain is an ordinary copy of $\No$.''
Proposition~9.3 (``Ordinary class-order universality, recalled''): \emph{in
$\GBC$, every linear order carried by a class of sets admits a class order
embedding into $\No$, and hence into $\Pbd(b)$ and the virtual domain $\Hsl$; the
variable-carrier set-word orders also contain such an image, even when words are
required to be numerically increasing}, which is
\cref{swo:prop:universal,swo:gl:universality}; source~24 uses the set-cut property,
``not an assertion about arbitrary class cuts'', and a first-label embedding
$\No\to\Pbd(b)$, and adds: ``The qualifier `carried by a class of sets' is
essential. The virtual domain of \emph{all} class enumerations is not such a
carrier, so the proposition does not embed that whole higher-order domain into
$\No$. This universality statement is part of the predecessor framework; it is
included to connect the new completion theory to the original embedding
question.''
\end{note}

% ---- source 24 (batch-83 manuscript 06), lines 708-778
\subsubsection{Set-indexed nets cannot make nontrivial global progress}

A \emph{uniformly set-indexed family of class words} is given by one class relation $F(i,\xi,x)$, where $i$ belongs to a fixed set $I$, and the $i$th section defines a class word $f_i$. A directed order on $I$ makes it a net. Forward Cauchyness means
\[
 \forall\alpha\in\Ord\ \exists i_0\in I\ 
 \forall i,j\ge i_0\quad f_i\res\alpha=f_j\res\alpha.
\]
All restrictions displayed here are sets. This is a formula about the one class relation $F$, not a quantification over a set of proper-class objects.

\begin{theorem}[Small-net rigidity]\label{swo:pc:thm:smallnet}
Every uniformly set-indexed forward-Cauchy net in $\Jinj$ is eventually constant. Every uniformly set-indexed net converging in the prefix sense to a specified class word is eventually equal to that word. In particular, both statements hold for $\Hsl$ and for core evaluations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each pair $i,j\in I$ whose sections differ, let $\delta(i,j)$ be their least disagreement, and set $\delta(i,j)=0$ when the sections are equal. This is a class function on the set $I\times I$. Class Replacement gives a set of its values. Thus
\[
 \Gamma=\sup\{\delta(i,j)+1:i,j\in I\}
\]
is an ordinal. Two sections in this family agreeing below $\Gamma$ are identical. Cauchyness at $\Gamma$ makes all sections in a tail identical, proving eventual constancy.

For convergence to a specified word $h$, apply the same argument to the set of first disagreements between $h$ and the sections not equal to it. A bound on those disagreements, together with convergence, makes every sufficiently late section equal to $h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No set-sized accumulation pattern]\label{swo:pc:cor:smallclosed}
Relative to the prefix-neighborhood predicates, any uniformly set-indexed collection of distinct global words is discrete and has no accumulation point, even at a word outside the collection. Every set of core codes is a closed discrete subset of the core's order topology.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a specified word $h$, bound the first disagreements with all indexed words other than $h$. The corresponding prefix neighborhood of $h$ excludes them all. On the core, prefix cylinders form the order-topology base by the same argument as Lemma~\ref{swo:pc:lem:cylinders}, using \cref{swo:pc:lem:globalextension} for completions.
\end{proof}

This is a foundationally meaningful difference from the countable case. A sequence indexed by ordinary $\omega$, or a net indexed by any set, cannot successively explore every ordinal-length prefix in the global problem. Nontrivial global approximation must have a proper-class index range or be interpreted externally in a larger universe.

\subsubsection{The correct global branch-completion statement}

\begin{definition}[A coherent prefix system]\label{swo:pc:n9.6}
A coherent prefix system is one class relation specifying, for every ordinal $\alpha$, a set injection $p_\alpha:\alpha\to\No$, with
\[
 p_\beta\res\alpha=p_\alpha\qquad(\alpha<\beta).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Global branch completion, stated as a scheme]\label{swo:pc:thm:classcompletion}
A coherent prefix system has a unique union $h:\Ord\to\No$ that is a class injection. Conversely, every class injection determines such a system. For each specified injection $h$, there is a uniformly $\Ord$-indexed net of core codes whose evaluations converge forward to $h$. It has a limit in $\Hsl$ exactly when $h$ is exhaustive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Elementary class comprehension forms the union relation. Coherence proves that it is a function on all ordinals; injectivity is witnessed in a single set prefix for any proposed pair of coordinates. The reverse construction is restriction of a class function to each set ordinal, with Class Replacement ensuring that each restriction is a set.

For each $\alpha$, apply the uniform extension procedure in \cref{swo:pc:lem:globalextension} to $h\res\alpha$. Let $c_\alpha$ be the resulting core code and $f_\alpha$ its evaluation. For every $\beta$, all $\alpha\ge\beta$ satisfy $f_\alpha\res\beta=h\res\beta$. This is forward convergence. Any other forward limit must share every set prefix with $h$, hence must equal $h$. Therefore a limit in the exhaustive domain exists exactly when $h$ itself is exhaustive.
\end{proof}

This theorem is the global analogue of Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:completion}, but its formulation is deliberately different. It does not form the collection of all Cauchy filters on a nonexistent ordinary space of all class words. It proves a uniform reconstruction statement about each supplied class-coded system. In a larger-universe set model, it can be read as an ordinary completion theorem; within two-sorted class theory it is a scheme with class parameters.

\subsubsection{Inverse stabilization restores exhaustiveness}

For a global enumeration $f$, its inverse is a class function $f^{-1}:\No\to\Ord$. Relative to $b$, a two-sided prefix comparison requires agreement of $f,g$ below a set ordinal $\alpha$ and agreement of $f^{-1},g^{-1}$ on $b[\alpha]$.

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided global completion]\label{swo:pc:thm:classtwosided}
Let $(f_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Ord}$ be a uniformly class-coded net of exhaustive global enumerations. Suppose that for every set ordinal $\alpha$, both the forward restrictions below $\alpha$ and the inverse restrictions on $b[\alpha]$ are eventually pairwise equal. Then there is a unique exhaustive global enumeration $f$ to which the net converges in both senses.

At each specified enumeration, forward and two-sided neighborhood predicates generate the same topology. No elementary transfinite recursion principle beyond $\GBC$ is needed for this reconstruction.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each ordinal $\xi$, define $h(\xi)$ to be the unique eventual value of $f_\gamma(\xi)$. For each surreal $x$, define $g(x)$ to be the unique eventual value of $f_\gamma^{-1}(x)$. The assumed stabilization makes these values exist; they are defined by an elementary formula using the class parameter for the net. Elementary class comprehension therefore gives both graphs.

If $h(\xi)=x$, choose a stage beyond the stabilization thresholds for that forward coordinate and that inverse coordinate. Since every row is a bijection, $g(x)=\xi$. The converse gives $h(g(x))=x$. Thus $h$ and $g$ are inverse class bijections. Stabilization of entire set prefixes, not just individual coordinates, is part of the hypothesis and gives convergence in both senses. Uniqueness follows from agreement on all set prefixes.

For compatibility at a fixed $f$, the preimage $f^{-1}[b[\alpha]]$ is a set of ordinals by Class Replacement, hence bounded by some ordinal $\beta$. Agreement with $f$ below $\beta$ fixes the inverse on $b[\alpha]$. This is exactly the forward-to-inverse neighborhood implication. The other implication is immediate.

The construction selected eventual values by a formula. It did not perform a recursion with proper-class previous values; consequently no appeal to $\ETR$ is hidden in this argument.
\end{proof}

The global theorem behaves like the regular-cardinal case: every \emph{set} of ordinal positions is bounded. The singular set case differs because a set of cardinality less than $\mu$ need not be bounded in $\mu$. This one quantifier distinction explains both the continuity obstruction and the apparent contrast between small-net rigidity and nontrivial external approximations.

\subsubsection{Four different levels of collection}

The safest practice is to attach a size declaration to every carrier and every family. The following ledger separates constructions that are often written with deceptively similar notation.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}p{.24\linewidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Object & Legitimate status & What must not be inferred\\
\midrule
$\WO_\mu(X),\I_\mu(X)$ for set $X,\mu$ & Sets in $\ZFC$; ordinary topology, filters, and powersets apply. & They need not be sets inside a smaller chosen universe.\\
All set-length surreal words & A definable class of set graphs. & This class is not a set; its powerclass is not an ordinary class.\\
The support core $\Pbd(b)$ & A class of canonical set codes with a uniform evaluation relation. & Its dense image does not exhaust all global enumerations.\\
All class enumerations or all class well-orders & A virtual domain, a higher-sort domain, or a set in an external model. & Proper classes do not become members of a same-level class in $\GBC$ or $\KM$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The first two levels are enough to prove many order embeddings. The third supplies a practical surrogate for global prefixes. The fourth is needed only when one insists on quantifying over, or making functions whose arguments are, arbitrary global enumerations as objects.

\begin{note}[Source~24, Theorem~11.1, ``No uniform class of set codes exhausts the global words'']\label{swo:pc:thm:diagonal}
\emph{In $\GBC$, let $A$ be a class of sets and let one class relation uniformly

the blocks $\{2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+1\}$. Source~24: ``This gives a concrete
reason that $\Pbd(b)$ is a core rather than an exhaustive parametrization. Density
is a local statement about each prefix or each interval. Exhaustive coding would
be a global surjectivity statement, and the diagonal argument forbids it. There is
no contradiction between a surreal-sized dense core and a larger virtual domain.''
Its Example~11.2 below is the inconsistency of unrestricted cuts recorded in the

\subsubsection{Set-like recursion versus recursion with class-valued stages}

Several constructions above are sometimes described informally as ``transfinite recursion,'' but they do not all require the same principle. Recursion of set-length along a set ordinal is ordinary set recursion. A uniform $\Ord$-length construction whose stage values and previous histories are sets can be described by its unique set-length initial solutions, then assembled by elementary class comprehension. This is different from a recursion in which the value at each stage is itself an arbitrary proper class.

The latter is the setting of elementary transfinite recursion principles for classes. Their nontrivial strength is reflected, for example, in the equivalence between suitable clopen class-game determinacy and $\ETR$ studied by Gitman and Hamkins~\cite{GitmanHamkins}. It is therefore not valid to invoke arbitrary class recursion while claiming to work only in $\GBC$.

In source~24, the common-prefix formula is elementary; the supported extension procedure takes set parameters to set codes; coherent-prefix unions are given class relations; and eventual-value reconstruction is an elementary definition from a supplied net. None of these arguments assumes an unrestricted proper-class recursion theorem. A future construction of an automorphism by class-length back-and-forth should be audited anew, rather than inheriting this conclusion merely because it also mentions prefixes.

\subsubsection{An external inaccessible-universe model}

There is a transparent way to turn the virtual global picture into an ordinary set-sized one. Work externally in $\ZFC$ and assume a strongly inaccessible cardinal $\Theta$. Let
\[
 M=V_\Theta,\qquad \mathcal X=\mathcal P(V_\Theta).
\]
Interpret sets as members of $M$ and classes as all external subsets of $V_\Theta$. This full class model satisfies the class-comprehension and replacement requirements of $\KM$ with Global Choice: regularity bounds the ranks of images of internal sets, and strong inaccessibility ensures that the required internal sets and powersets lie below $\Theta$.

Its ordinals are externally the ordinals below $\Theta$, and its surreal class is externally $\No_{<\Theta}=\No_{<\Theta}$, of size $\Theta$. Consequently its full set-like global enumeration domain is externally the ordinary set
\[
 \Bij(\Theta,\No_{<\Theta})=\WO_\Theta(\No_{<\Theta}).
\]
Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:regular} applies to it. In this model $\Theta^{<\Theta}=\Theta$, so the external topological presentation is $\Theta^\Theta$ with the bounded topology. The arbitrary internal class well-orders, because all subclasses are available, correspond externally to all genuine well-orders of the set $\No_{<\Theta}$, not merely its minimal-length slice.

There is no conflict with Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:smallnet}. An internal set-indexed net has an index set in $V_\Theta$ and hence fewer than $\Theta$ indices. An external $\Theta$-indexed net need not have an internal set of indices and can make nontrivial progress. The distinction is exactly the one the theorem requires.

The inaccessible hypothesis is a sufficient external modeling device, not an axiom claimed to follow from $\ZFC$, and not a prerequisite for the elementary set-sized results. Other class models can be used, but their available classes and their external size must then be specified.

\subsubsection{Definable classes, class models, and higher universes}

There are three complementary formalization routes.

\subparagraph{Schematic definable classes.}
In a set-theoretic metatheory, work with explicitly supplied formulas and set parameters defining the relevant classes. Each theorem is a schema about such definitions. This is efficient for fixed examples and elementary comparison. It does not yield a single internal truth predicate for all formulas or an internal enumeration of all semantic classes. Syntax codes are not automatically an exhaustive semantic universe.

\subparagraph{A two-sorted class model.}
Specify a model $(M,\mathcal X)$ of $\GBC$ or a stronger theory. Every assertion about ``all global enumerations'' means all such class relations belonging to $\mathcal X$. Enlarging $\mathcal X$ while preserving $M$ can add new branches and new enumerations. A set-coded core can remain unchanged, but this does not make every assertion about all classes absolute. The previous cut-reconstruction work addresses more refined preservation questions (sources~17 and~14; \cref{swo:viii:sec:extensions}); here we use only the explicit parameter-relative interpretation.

\subparagraph{A universe hierarchy.}
In a type-theoretic or Grothendieck-universe setting, collect the small surreals at one level and their large relations at the next. Their functions and cuts can then be ordinary objects at a sufficiently high level. This is often the easiest route for a proof assistant. It remains essential not to identify a type with a type containing all of its own higher-universe relations. Moving to a higher universe resolves a size problem; erasing the universe distinction recreates it.

\begin{example}[Why all class cuts cannot be filled by surreals]\label{swo:pc:n11.2}
Every surreal is below some ordinal surreal: compare its sign sequence with a longer all-plus sequence. Thus the lower class consisting of all ordinal surreals has no surreal upper bound. The separated class cut with that lower side and empty upper side has no surreal separator. The familiar set-cut interpolation property is therefore not a theorem about arbitrary class-indexed cuts. The word ``set'' or ``small'' in such a theorem is a mathematical hypothesis, not bookkeeping.
\end{example}

\subsection{Global well-orders without a class of classes (source 26)}\label{swo:nb:sec:classes}\label{swo:nb:sec:models}

\subsubsection{Set-like versus unrestricted class well-orders}

Work in $\GBC$. A class relation $R$ on a class $C$ is a class well-order when it is a strict linear order and every nonempty admitted subclass has an $R$-least element. It is \emph{set-like} when
\[
 \pred_R(x)=\{y\in C:yRx\}
\]
is a set for each $x\in C$. For a proper class, a set-like class well-order has a unique ordinal-class enumeration: the position of $x$ is the set ordinal $\otp(\pred_R(x),R)$. Its range of positions is an unbounded initial segment of $\Ord$, hence all of $\Ord$.

Fix a baseline class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. Global choice supplies such a bijection. Set-like surreal well-orders can be represented by other class bijections $e:\Ord\to\No$. Their labels at the first differing ordinal determine their comparison. In contrast, an unrestricted class well-order can have type $\Ord+1$ or $\Ord+\Ord$, after a suitable class bijection of its carrier with $\No$. It cannot be represented by an exhaustive $\Ord$-word: the tail beyond the initial proper-class segment would be lost.

The repository proves the equivalence, over its convention for $\GB$ without set choice, between the existence of a class well-order of $\No$ and global choice (\cref{swo:cf:choice}). We do not repeat the full weak-choice coding proof. All global constructions below explicitly assume $\GBC$, so no additional choice claim is concealed in the selection of $b$.

The expressions ``all set-like class well-orders'' and ``all class well-orders'' below denote predicates on class variables. In two-sorted $\GB$ or $\KM$, a class has \emph{sets} as members. Stronger class comprehension in $\KM$ does not turn classes into allowable members of another class. An actual collection whose elements are class relations needs a higher sort, external semantics, or a separately specified coding restriction.

Class-indexed approximation is different. Given a class injection $h:\Ord\to\No$, for every ordinal $\alpha$ apply \cref{swo:nb:lem:globalreserve} to $h\res\alpha$ and choose a support-code extension uniformly. This $\Ord$-indexed family stabilizes to $h$ on each set prefix. The limit can fail to be exhaustive. For example, relative to a baseline, shift the finite ordinal positions by one and leave positions at least $\omega$ fixed; the resulting injection omits exactly the first baseline label.

If forward and inverse prefixes both stabilize for a uniformly coded family of bijections, their unions are mutually inverse. Indeed, when a stabilized forward value is $h(\xi)=x$, take a common sufficiently late stage at which that coordinate and the inverse coordinate $x$ have stabilized. The bijection at that stage witnesses $g(x)=\xi$. The converse is the same. This is a reconstruction scheme for admitted class graphs, not the creation of a completed class whose elements are all class graphs.

\subsubsection{A fixed class relation versus an enlarged class part}

A model of class theory is written $(M,\mathcal X)$, where $M$ supplies the sets and $\mathcal X$ the admitted classes. The class part need not consist of every externally available subset of $M$. A definition using an external collection of all subsets can therefore change the meaning of a supposed internal theorem.

There is, however, an important preservation fact for an \emph{old fixed relation}. In $\GBC$, internal well-foundedness of a fixed strict class relation is equivalent to the absence of a set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence. One direction is immediate from the range of such a sequence. Conversely, from a nonempty class with no minimal element, global choice selects a predecessor at each point, and recursion on $\omega$ followed by Class Replacement yields a descending sequence that is a set.

Consequently, when $(M,\mathcal X)$ and $(M,\mathcal Y)$ both satisfy the relevant $\GBC$ assumptions, have the same sets, and an old relation $R$ belongs to both class parts, enlarging the class part does not change whether that old relation is internally well-founded. What can change is \emph{which relations exist}, which uniform families and cuts are admitted, and which prospective limits are available. The repository's reviewed scope correction makes this distinction explicit (this report's README, review notes). External well-foundedness of a nonstandard model is a different question: an external descending sequence need not be a sequence coded in $M$.

\subsubsection{Higher universes are a legitimate alternative, not a size eraser}

A universe-relative treatment can fix a strongly inaccessible $\Theta$ and view
\[
 (V_\Theta,\mathcal P(V_\Theta))
\]
from an ambient universe. Its internally proper classes are externally sets. The internal surreal sign carrier is represented externally by signs of length below $\Theta$, and global relations become external relations on that set. It is then legitimate to take an external set of those relations. What is illegitimate is to move that set back down and call it an internal class whose members are internal proper classes.

In type theory, the analogous safeguard is explicit universe levels. A carrier for ordinal-length signs lives above the universe of its ordinal lengths, while every fixed birthday-bounded fragment can be small in that lower universe. A type of all predicates on the carrier lives at a higher level again. These level changes can formalize the objects without paradox, but they alter which families count as small and which cut-filling theorem is applicable.

A singular birthday fragment such as $\No_{<\beth_\omega}$ is a perfectly sound set-level alphabet. It is not a replacement for the inaccessible model just described. Regularity, replacement closure, power sets, and externally full class parts must be checked for a proposed model rather than inferred from an evocative notation.

\subsubsection{Where stronger recursion principles actually enter}

The direct common-prefix comparison in \cref{swo:nb:thm:rawcompare} does not need elementary transfinite recursion. Ordinary set-valued recursion used to select one surreal at each stage is also distinct from a recursion that constructs an entire new class at each stage. The latter is the setting in which $\ETR$ becomes a substantive additional principle. Gitman and Hamkins identify its strength over $\GBC$ through clopen class-game determinacy~\cite{GitmanHamkins}.

A formal development should therefore state the exact recursion rule and the sort of its values. Invoking $\KM$ for every global argument overstates some dependencies; treating arbitrary class-valued recursion as an automatic consequence of elementary comprehension understates others. The present manuscript confines itself to elementary comparison, set-valued recursive constructions, and explicitly uniform family schemes. No theorem here assumes that all higher-order cuts can be filled.

\subsubsection{The virtual enumeration domain}

Work in $\GBC$, and fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. Such a baseline can be obtained by globally choosing well-orderings of the set-sized birthday levels and listing the new surreals level by level. Every proper initial part of this listing is a set. The merged repository report analyzes the precise equivalence with Global Choice over its stated weak base theory (\cref{swo:cf:choice}); the arguments here assume the baseline rather than silently selecting one in bare $\GB$.

Let $\Hsl$ mean the virtual domain of all class bijections $f:\Ord\to\No$. It is notation for the objects over which class variables range under a stated predicate, not a declaration that those proper classes are members of an ordinary class. For two specified distinct class words, the first disagreement exists: choose one ordinal witness, and find the least witness inside the set of ordinals at most that one. Their numerical lexicographic comparison is therefore an elementary class-theoretic assertion.

A uniformly indexed family is represented by a single relation
\[
 F(i,\xi,x),
\]
whose $i$th section is the graph of the relevant word. Quantifying over the set or class index $i$ does not turn each section into a set. This representation is sufficient for the global prefix and continuity arguments below.

\subsubsection{Every set of ordinal coordinates is bounded}

\begin{proposition}[Why the global case has no singular-coordinate obstruction]\label{swo:ge:prop:globalbounded}
For every specified class permutation $s:\Ord\to\Ord$, both $s$ and $s^{-1}$ send bounded sets of ordinals to bounded sets. Forward and two-sided set-prefix neighborhood predicates agree at each specified global enumeration. Left and right translations and inversion satisfy the corresponding continuity formulas.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A bounded collection of ordinals is a set. By Class Replacement, its image and inverse image under a specified class permutation are sets of ordinals. Every such set has an ordinal bound. The proofs of Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:ideal-cont} now apply to each allowed control set, with set-sized images and inverse images. In particular, to enforce inverse agreement on $b[\alpha]$ at $f$, it suffices to enforce forward agreement below an ordinal bounding the set $f^{-1}[b[\alpha]]$.
\end{proof}

This is a statement about formulas and specified class parameters, not an ordinary topology carried by a class whose elements are all the global enumerations. The analogy with regular cardinals is exact at the relevant quantifier: every \emph{set} of ordinal coordinates is bounded. At singular $\mu$, a subset of cardinality less than $\mu$ may instead be unbounded in $\mu$.
