that the coherent-branch approximations are ``the appropriate global analogues of
forward completion; they do not require a class containing all Cauchy filters'' on
$\Hsl$; that a supplied class-indexed net stabilizing forward prefixes and inverse
restrictions to $b[\alpha]$ reconstructs mutually inverse class maps by the
two-coordinate argument of \cref{swo:ge:thm:raikov}, with no ``general recursion
with previously constructed proper classes as values''; and, of unrestricted
orders, that ``an order with type $\Ord+1$ cannot be exhaustively represented by an
order-preserving list with domain $\Ord$'', that two orders sharing a common initial
segment with complement $\{a,b\}$ are adjacent, that relation coding gives a
different order already on two labels, and that ``numerical lexicography is not
compatible with merely quotienting presentations by their unlabelled order types''.
\end{note}

\subsection{Foundations, models and paradox avoidance (source 28)}\label{swo:ge:sec:foundations}

\merge\ Source~28's Section~13, printed whole; it states for the group results
what sources~24 and~26 state above for theirs.

% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 891-929
\subsubsection{Set approximations are ordinary mathematics}

For a fixed set alphabet $X$, well-order relations lie in $\mathcal P(X\times X)$, and the spaces $\Bij(\mu,X)$ and $\Inj(\mu,X)$ are sets. Their topologies, filters, completions, and permutation subgroups are standard set-sized objects. This is the cleanest setting for formalizing the new theorems. A birthday cutoff specifies both the carrier and the relevant cardinal parameters explicitly.

One should not replace $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ by $\kappa$ merely because $\kappa$ is the birthday bound. One should also distinguish subsets of size less than $\mu$ from subsets belonging to a particular inner model. The first is a cardinal condition in the ambient set theory; the second is a membership condition relative to a foundational model.

\subsubsection{Two-sorted class theory}

In a model $(M,\mathcal X)$ of class theory, the sets are the elements of $M$ and the available classes are the elements of the external collection $\mathcal X$. Internally, a class is a predicate on sets, not an element that can be inserted into an ordinary set or class. A formula may assert that a class variable is a bijection $\Ord^M\to\No^M$, and may compare two such variables. It may not silently collect every one of those class variables into another ordinary class.

Global Choice supplies useful baseline listings and uniform choices of set-coded extensions. It is not a license for an exhaustive class list of all class bijections: \Cref{swo:ge:thm:diagonal} rules that out. Stronger comprehension in $\KM$ still does not erase the type distinction between sets and classes.

Elementary comprehension is enough for the common-prefix definition, the diagonal construction, and the eventual-value reconstruction of a supplied stabilized net. General recursions in which earlier values are themselves proper classes require separate analysis. Gitman and Hamkins~\cite{GitmanHamkins} distinguish elementary transfinite recursion over well-founded class relations from the strength of $\GBC$ and relate it to clopen class-game determinacy. We do not use that stronger recursion principle in the proofs just listed.

\subsubsection{Larger universes and full external collections}

There is a second rigorous approach: place the smaller theory inside a larger set universe. Conditionally, let $\Theta$ be strongly inaccessible and take $M=V_\Theta$, with the full external collection of subclasses of $M$. The objects called proper classes inside $M$ are sets externally. One may then form, externally, the set of all internal class enumerations and put an ordinary topology on it.

This is a relative model construction with a stated additional hypothesis, not a proof in bare $\ZFC$ that such an inaccessible exists. The external indexing ordinal is $\Theta$, and the surreals built from sign sequences of length less than $\Theta$ form an external set of size $\Theta$. Since $\Theta$ is regular, the singular-coordinate obstruction disappears for external subsets of size less than $\Theta$. But a general external subset of size $\Theta$ is not an internal set-sized control object, so no claim about arbitrary external cuts follows from internal set-cut interpolation.

A Grothendieck-universe or dependent-type-theoretic presentation makes the same size distinction syntactic: words small in one universe form a type in a larger universe. The larger type is not automatically all-surreal mathematics at the same universe level.

\subsubsection{Changing the available classes}

If $(M,\mathcal X)\subseteq(M,\mathcal Y)$ have the same sets but more available classes in $\mathcal Y$, two old ordinal-class words retain their first-disagreement comparison. Their graphs and numerical labels have not changed. New class words can nevertheless appear, along with new approximation systems and new uniform families. An old proof that a class relation is a well-order must also be assessed relative to the intended available subclasses; internal and unrestricted external well-foundedness are not interchangeable.

In an externally countable model, an external countable sequence may be cofinal in $\Ord^M$, despite the absence of such an internal set sequence. Thus the small-net rigidity theorem does not prohibit external approximations indexed by a set that is not an internal set of indices with the required internal uniform coding. Its quantifiers were internal and explicit.

\subsubsection{Definable orders and syntactic codes}

One can restrict to class orders defined by specified formulas with set parameters, but ``all definable classes'' is not automatically an internally evaluable class-coded family. A uniform evaluator for arbitrary definitions would require an appropriate satisfaction predicate. A safer construction fixes a single formula $\varphi(i,\xi,x)$ and varies the set parameter $i$, or works externally with formula codes and an explicitly provided satisfaction relation. The diagonal obstruction applies to any genuinely uniform exhaustive family once the required evaluations are available.

The same caution applies to definability claims motivated by the Kanovei--Shelah construction~\cite{KanoveiShelah}. Their published index set consists of functions from the continuum cardinal to $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are ultrafilters, ordered lexicographically. These functions need not be injective. That construction motivates definable lexicographic indexing, but it is not literally the order of all well-order relations on the reals or on the surreals.

\subsubsection{A short paradox checklist}

Before using an assertion about ``all'' surreal well-orders, specify the carrier, its size level, whether labels are retained, the permitted enumeration domains, and the comparison rule. For a completion argument, specify the topology or uniformity and the index size of the approximation. For a class construction, identify one uniform relation representing any claimed family, and say whether the statement is internal or external. For a recursion, identify the type of its values and the size of its previous history.

The apparent paradoxes arise when one of these specifications is suppressed. In particular, a class can contain codes for some class functions without containing every class function as an element; realizing every set cut does not mean realizing every class cut; and a universe-polymorphic construction does not collapse all its universe levels into one.

\section{Exactly when restriction preserves the native order (source 19)}
\label{swo:rs:ia:sec:restrictions}

\merge\ Source~19's Section~6, printed whole. Its restriction map $r_Y$ is
printed $\pi_Y$. ``The earlier manuscripts'' of its first sentence are, at
this point of the report, source~15's three-label theorem
(\cref{swo:cb:thm:restriction}) and the reversal $021<102$, $21>12$ printed
with it in Part~VII; source~19 cites sources~15, 16 and~18 as unrefereed
prior manuscripts, which are now sources of this report. The two theorems are
consistent: source~15's concerns all three two-label restrictions of a
three-label carrier at once, under any choice of order on each target, while
\cref{swo:rs:ia:thm:restriction-classification} concerns one specified
restriction between native orders, and its exceptional case $\{a<z<b\}\to\{a,b\}$
is the one restriction of source~15's carrier that is monotone.

% ---- source 19 resumes (Section 6)
The earlier manuscripts exhibit reversals under carrier restriction and
show that no linearization can make all two-label restrictions monotone.
There is also an exact answer for one specified restriction with the
native numerical lexicographic orders on its source and target.

\begin{theorem}[Classification of monotone restrictions]
\label{swo:rs:ia:thm:restriction-classification}
Let $(X,<)$ be a linearly ordered set and $Y\subseteq X$. Compare the
well-orders of each fixed labelled carrier by their ordinal enumerations,
using the inherited label order at the first disagreement. The map
\[
 \pi_Y:\WO(X)\longrightarrow\WO(Y),\qquad R\longmapsto R\restr Y,
\]
is nondecreasing if and only if one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $|Y|\leq1$;
\item $Y=X$;
\item $X=\{a<z<b\}$ and $Y=\{a,b\}$.
\end{enumerate}
For an infinite carrier $X$ of cardinality $\mu$, every proper
restriction retaining at least two labels already has a reversal on
the minimal slice $\WO_\mu(X)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each finite word displayed below is followed by the same fixed
well-order of the unused labels. Both relevant comparisons are decided
inside the displayed words.

Suppose $a<b$ belong to $Y$ and $z\notin Y$. If $z<a$, use
\[
 R=(z,b,a),\qquad S=(a,b,z).
\]
Then $R<S$, while their restrictions start with $(b,a)$ and $(a,b)$,
respectively, so $\pi_Y(R)>\pi_Y(S)$. If $b<z$, the pair
\[
 R=(b,a,z),\qquad S=(z,a,b)
\]
has exactly the same property. Therefore monotonicity requires every
omitted label to lie between every pair of retained labels.

If $Y$ contains $a_0<a_1<a_2$, any omitted $z$ violates this
requirement. For $z<a_1$, use the pair $a_1<a_2$; for $a_1<z$, use
the pair $a_0<a_1$. These alternatives are exhaustive because $z$
is omitted. Consequently, a proper monotone restriction retaining at
least two labels must have $Y=\{a,b\}$, with every omitted label in
$(a,b)$.

If two labels $u<v$ are omitted, then $a<u<v<b$. The four-label
pair
\[
 R=(u,b,a,v),\qquad S=(v,a,b,u)
\]
satisfies $R<S$ because $u<v$, whereas the restrictions again begin
$(b,a)$ and $(a,b)$. There can therefore be only one omitted label,
and the only remaining proper case is $X=\{a<z<b\}$.

For this exceptional case the six enumerations, in increasing
lexicographic order, are
\[
 (a,z,b),\ (a,b,z),\ (z,a,b),\ (z,b,a),\ (b,a,z),\ (b,z,a).
\]
The first three restrict to $(a,b)$ and the last three to $(b,a)$,
so restriction is nondecreasing. The singleton and identity cases
are immediate.

Finally, if $X$ is infinite, choose the common unused tail to have
type $\mu$. Every displayed finite prefix followed by this tail
has type $n+\mu=\mu$. Thus all reversals occur already in
$\WO_\mu(X)$.
\end{proof}

The same finite gadgets work for a supplied proper-class carrier in
GBC: append a fixed set-like enumeration of the unused labels.
They produce set-like global witnesses. In that setting the statement
is interpreted as a theorem about supplied classes and explicit
witnesses, not as the assertion that all class well-orders form an
ordinary class of objects.

This sharpens the obstruction to a backwards system of birthday
cutoffs. Whenever $\No_{<\kappa}\subsetneq\No_{<\lambda}$ are infinite,
unrestricted carrier restriction fails to be monotone, even on the
minimal source slice. Forward extension maps, or specially constrained
families of enumerations, must supply any coherent order-preserving
system.

\begin{remark}[Finite verification]\label{swo:rs:n6.2}
The accompanying script \texttt{check\_restrictions.py} checks every
subset of each carrier of size $0\leq n\leq7$ and every adjacent
pair in the lexicographic list of its permutations. It checks
$695{,}228$ adjacent comparisons. All cases agree with
\cref{swo:rs:ia:thm:restriction-classification}; the respective numbers
of monotone subsets are $1,2,4,6,6,7,8,9$. The JSON report records
the counts and sample reversals. This finite regression check does
not replace the proof for arbitrary carriers.

\merge\ The script ships as \path{code/19-residual-check_restrictions.py}
and its recorded output as \path{data/19-residual-restriction_checks.json}.
The counts $1,2,4,6,6,7,8,9$ are those of $n=0,1,\ldots,7$ and agree with
the theorem: for $n\ge4$ the monotone subsets are the empty set, the $n$
singletons and $X$ itself, and for $n=3$ the extra subset $\{a,b\}$ is added.
\end{remark}

\merge\ The ``forward extension maps'' of the last paragraph are what the next
two sections construct: source~20's append-tail maps
(\cref{swo:lm:lim:direct}) and source~21's fixed-slot insertions
(\cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:coherence}). Source~20's \cref{swo:lm:lim:two-labels}
shows that the reversals of
\cref{swo:rs:ia:thm:restriction-classification} disappear in the limit: for a
fixed pair of well-orders, every sufficiently large restriction compares
them as the originals are compared. Source~19 also records the restriction
theorem as an attractive first formalization target and states that it
``does not forbid carefully designed enlargement embeddings'' (its results
ledger).

$\pi_{\beta\alpha}$; the local ranks $r_\alpha(x)$ are printed
$\xilr_\alpha(x)$; the class $A_R$ of minimum-type cutoffs is printed
$\ximin_R$; the core $\mathcal C_b$ is printed $\Pbd(b)$; and the ordinal
$r=\otp(R)$ in the proof of \cref{swo:lm:lim:direct} is printed $\zeta$.
Its citations of the repository are replaced by cross-references to the
results meant. Its first paragraph is accurate at this report's head: the
correction of ``coherent'' to ``uniform'' is the one recorded in
\cref{swo:rem:answered-choice,swo:st:n14.5} (3 October 2026). The
nonmonotone example of its second subsection is source~15's
(\cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives}).

% ---- source 20 resumes (Section 4)
The distinction between uniformly chosen local well-orders and
restriction-coherent local well-orders is mathematically consequential.
The current repository explicitly corrects an earlier use of
``coherent'' in its global-choice argument: the recursively constructed
orders on $V_\alpha$ are uniform, but need not extend one another
(\cref{swo:rem:answered-choice}). Here we study genuine restriction coherence and obtain
an exact local-to-global description. We also show that the native
lexicographic comparison is eventually recoverable from every increasing
exhaustion, even though individual restriction maps need not preserve it.

Write
\[
 \No_{<\alpha}=\{x\in\No:\operatorname{bd}(x)<\alpha\}.
\]
These are increasing sets, their union is $\No$, and every set of surreal
labels is contained in some $\No_{<\alpha}$. The last fact follows by applying
Replacement to birthdays and then taking a strict ordinal upper bound.
For $\alpha\leq\beta$, restriction gives a set map
\[
 \pi_{\beta\alpha}:\WO(\No_{<\beta})\longrightarrow\WO(\No_{<\alpha}),
 \qquad R\longmapsto R\upharpoonright \No_{<\alpha}^2.
\]
A \emph{uniform coherent profile} is one class function
$\alpha\mapsto R_\alpha$, with set-valued entries, such that
$R_\alpha\in\WO(\No_{<\alpha})$ and
$\pi_{\beta\alpha}(R_\beta)=R_\alpha$ whenever $\alpha\leq\beta$.
This is a class of set-coded local relations, not a class containing
global class relations as members.

\subsection{Local well-foundedness reflects to the whole class}

\begin{theorem}[Coherent birthday gluing in $\GB$]
\label{swo:lm:lim:gluing}
Every uniform coherent profile determines a unique strict class
well-order $R$ of $\No$ with
$R\upharpoonright \No_{<\alpha}^2=R_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$.
Conversely, the restrictions of every supplied class well-order form
such a profile. These constructions are inverse, uniformly in the
supplied class parameters. Set-likeness is not required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Define $xRy$ when $xR_\alpha y$ at any stage containing $x,y$.
Coherence makes this independent of the stage. Every finite collection
of labels is contained in a common stage, so irreflexivity, transitivity,
and linearity follow from the corresponding local properties.
Elementary class comprehension supplies $R$.

It remains to prove that every nonempty available subclass $A$ has a
least element. Suppose otherwise and fix $x_0\in A$. Given $x_n$, let
$\beta_n$ be the least ordinal such that
\[
 A\cap \No_{<\beta_n}\cap\{y:yRx_n\}\ne\varnothing.
\]
Such an ordinal exists because $A$ has no least element. A nonempty
subclass of the ordinals has a least member, by restricting to an
ordinal containing one witness. The displayed intersection is a set
by separation with class parameters. Let $x_{n+1}$ be its unique
$R_{\beta_n}$-least member. This is a uniquely specified set-valued
recursion along $\omega$, available in $\GB$; no global choice of
witnesses is needed.

Class Replacement makes $\{x_n:n<\omega\}$ a set. Its birthdays are
bounded, so the entire strictly descending sequence lies in one
$\No_{<\gamma}$. This contradicts the well-foundedness of $R_\gamma$.
Uniqueness follows because every pair of labels occurs at a stage.
The converse is immediate, and local restrictions are sets by
separation with the supplied relation as a class parameter.
\end{proof}

Thus the inverse-limit notation
\[
 \{
   (R_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Ord}:
   \pi_{\beta\alpha}(R_\beta)=R_\alpha
 \}
 \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{R:R\text{ is a class well-order of }\No\}
 \tag{\ref*{swo:lm:lim:gluing}a}
\]
expresses a correspondence between predicates on supplied classes. It
does not assert that either side is an ordinary $\GB$ class of members.
In a larger universe in which the relevant classes are objects, it
becomes a literal inverse-limit bijection, subject to that universe's
well-foundedness interpretation.

\begin{proposition}[The sharp set-filtration criterion]
\label{swo:lm:lim:cofinality}
Work in ZFC. Let $\lambda>0$ and let $(Y_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}$ be an increasing
ordinal-indexed family of sets with union $Y$. The following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every countable subset of $Y$ is contained in some $Y_\alpha$.
\item Every coherent family of well-orders on the $Y_\alpha$ has a
      well-ordered union.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, (2) holds if $\cf(\lambda)>\omega$. If
$\cf(\lambda)=\omega$ and the family is not eventually constant,
there is a coherent counterexample.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For (1)$\Rightarrow$(2), an ill-founded linear union would admit a
descending $\omega$-sequence, whose countable range would lie in one
well-ordered stage.

Suppose (1) fails. Choose a countable set with no bounded stage of
containment. Its stage indices give a countable cofinal sequence in
$\lambda$. Recursively choose increasing cofinal indices
$\alpha_n$ and distinct labels $y_n\notin Y_{\alpha_n}$, enlarging
$\alpha_{n+1}$ so that it contains all previously chosen labels.
For each fixed $\alpha$, only finitely many $y_n$ belong to
$Y_\alpha$: eventually $\alpha_n\geq\alpha$.
Order $\{y_n:n<\omega\}$ by
$\cdots Ry_2Ry_1Ry_0$, and place it before a fixed well-order of
its complement in $Y$. Every restriction to $Y_\alpha$ consists of
a finite initial block followed by a well-order, so it is a well-order.
The union contains the descending sequence $y_0,y_1,\ldots$.

If $\cf(\lambda)>\omega$, countably many stage indices are bounded.
If $\cf(\lambda)=\omega$ and no stage already equals the union,
the same recursive choice of new labels produces a countable
unbounded subset. This proves the final assertions.
\end{proof}

The familiar reverse-$\omega$ union of finite orders is therefore a
real obstruction, but it does not refute birthday gluing along all
ordinals. In the class theorem every set-sized witness has bounded
birthdays. The proof also explains why Class Replacement matters: an
arbitrary external branch through a small model's stages need not be an
admissible class of a $\GB$ realization.

\subsection{Native lexicography survives as an eventual comparison}

Individual restriction maps are not monotone for native enumeration
lexicography. On $0<1<2$,
\[
 021<_{\mathrm{lex}}102,
 \qquad
 21>_{\mathrm{lex}}12
 \quad\text{after restriction to }\{1,2\}.
\]
Nevertheless, each comparison has an unexpectedly small persistent
witness.

\begin{theorem}[Two labels determine every sufficiently large restriction]
\label{swo:lm:lim:two-labels}
Let $R,S$ be distinct well-orders of the same linearly ordered set or
class of labels. There are distinct labels $a,b$ such that every
subcarrier $Y$ containing $a,b$ satisfies
\[
 R\upharpoonright Y^2<_{\mathrm{lex}}
 S\upharpoonright Y^2
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a<b
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R<_{\mathrm{lex}}S.
\]
The assertion includes proper-class common prefixes and is provable
in $\GB$ for supplied class well-orders.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be the largest common labelled initial segment of $R,S$.
The elementary common-prefix construction for class well-orders
provides $C$; it does not compare abstract class order types
(\cref{swo:cf:first,swo:st:thm:fulllex}). Put
\[
 a=\min_R(\No\setminus C),\qquad
 b=\min_S(\No\setminus C),
\]
with the indicated carrier substituted for $\No$ in the general case.
These labels differ, since otherwise $C$ could be extended by that
common next label. In the restrictions to $Y$, the set or class
$C\cap Y$ is still an initial segment of both orders, and their
orders on it agree. Their next labels are still $a,b$, because those
labels belong to $Y$ and were the least available labels outside $C$.
The first unequal labels of the restrictions therefore coincide with
those of the original pair. This is exactly the displayed comparison.
\end{proof}

The number two is optimal: restrictions to a one-element carrier
cannot differ. The theorem is a persistence statement for restrictions
of a fixed pair. It does not say that knowing only the orientation of
one pair determines the comparison of arbitrary other orders.

\begin{corollary}[Native order on the coherent inverse limit]
\label{swo:lm:lim:eventual}
For two coherent birthday profiles with global unions $R,S$,
\[
 R<_{\mathrm{lex}}S
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists\alpha\ \forall\beta\geq\alpha\;
 R_\beta<_{\mathrm{lex}}S_\beta.
\]
For distinct profiles, the local comparisons are eventually strict
and constant. Consequently eventual local comparison gives exactly
the native global lexicographic order, despite the failure of
monotonicity of individual bonding maps.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose a cutoff containing the two labels from
\cref{swo:lm:lim:two-labels}. Every later cutoff has the same comparison.
Equality of the global orders is equivalent to equality at every
stage. Applying the same argument to the opposite strict comparison
establishes the converse.
\end{proof}

This result is independent of the birthday filtration. Any increasing
exhaustion of the carrier eventually contains the two decisive labels.
Thus changing the exhaustion leaves the eventual order unchanged.
There is also a stronger finiteness statement.

\begin{theorem}[Only finitely many changes of decisive labels]
\label{swo:lm:lim:finite-changes}
Fix two well-orders $R,S$ and any uniform increasing ordinal-indexed family
of subcarriers. Once their restrictions are distinct, the pair of
first unequal labels changes only finitely many times. In particular,
the native lexicographic signs change only finitely often. There is
no uniform finite bound on the number of changes, even for birthday
restrictions of well-orders of $\No$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $Y\subseteq Z$ on which the restrictions differ, write
$(a_Y,b_Y)$ and $(a_Z,b_Z)$ for their first unequal labels. The
pair on $Y$ is reversed:
\[
 a_YRb_Y,\qquad b_YSa_Y.
\]
Neither label can lie in the common labelled prefix $C_Z$. For if
one did, initiality in the order putting the other one first would
force both into $C_Z$, contradicting agreement there. Consequently
\[
 a_Z\mathrel{\leq_R}a_Y,
 \qquad b_Z\mathrel{\leq_S}b_Y.
\]
Each coordinate can strictly decrease only finitely many times.
Otherwise, recursively taking the least later index with a strict
decrease would produce a descending $\omega$-sequence in one of the
given well-orders. In the class setting this is again a set-valued
recursion with ordinal choices and Class Replacement. The union of
the two finite sets of change indices is finite.

To obtain any prescribed finite sequence of strict comparison signs,
choose strictly increasing positive ordinals $\gamma_i$ and take
$a_i=-\gamma_i<b_i=\gamma_i$, for $0\leq i\leq n$. Both labels
in a pair have the same birthday $\gamma_i$. In both global orders put these pairs before all other
labels, with the pair blocks in decreasing order of $i$. Within the
$i$th pair choose opposite orientations for $R,S$, selecting the
orientation in $R$ to give the prescribed sign. Append the same
set-like birthday-respecting baseline on the remaining labels.
At a cutoff containing pairs $0,\ldots,i$ and no later pair, the
first unequal labels are exactly the $i$th pair. Both global orders
are well-orders. Arbitrarily long finite alternating patterns follow.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Detecting set-likeness from local ordinal ranks}

For a profile and a label $x$, at every sufficiently large stage put
\[
 \xilr_\alpha(x)=\operatorname{otp}
 \bigl(\{y\in \No_{<\alpha}:yR_\alpha x\},R_\alpha\bigr).
\]
These are set ordinals, even if the global predecessor class is
proper. Coherence makes $\xilr_\alpha(x)$ nondecreasing, because an
ordered subset of an ordinal has order type at most that ordinal.

\begin{theorem}[Rank stabilization is exactly set-likeness]
\label{swo:lm:lim:ranks}
For the global union $R$ of a coherent profile and each label $x$,
the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the global predecessor class $P_x=\{y:yRx\}$ is a set;
\item $P_x$ is contained in a birthday cutoff;
\item the ordinals $\xilr_\alpha(x)$ are bounded by one set ordinal;
\item $\xilr_\alpha(x)$ is eventually constant.
\end{enumerate}
Thus $R$ is set-like exactly when every local rank profile eventually
stabilizes. The theorem holds in $\GB$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first two conditions are equivalent by boundedness of birthdays
and separation. If $P_x\subseteq \No_{<\delta}$, then every later local
predecessor set is exactly $P_x$, proving (2)$\Rightarrow$(4).
Monotonicity gives (4)$\Rightarrow$(3).

For (3)$\Rightarrow$(1), suppose $P_x$ is proper and all ranks are
at most $\theta$. Using the global well-order supplied by
\cref{swo:lm:lim:gluing}, recursively select the least unused predecessor
through $\theta+1$ stages. Each earlier range is a set and cannot
exhaust $P_x$, so the recursion continues. It gives an increasing
sequence of type $\theta+1$. Its range, together with $x$, lies in
one birthday cutoff. That local predecessor order then has type at
least $\theta+1$, contradicting its asserted bound $\theta$.
Only set-valued recursion along a set ordinal was used.
\end{proof}

Coherence alone therefore does not impose set-likeness. For example,
take a birthday-respecting set-like baseline on $\No\setminus\{0\}$
and place $0$ last. Its type is $\Ord+1$. All birthday restrictions
are well-orders and cohere, but $\xilr_\alpha(0)$ is unbounded. Local
ordinal ranks diagnose the proper predecessor class without treating
its order type as an ordinal.

\subsection{A club dichotomy for minimum enumeration types}

For an infinite strong-limit cardinal $\kappa$, the birthday carrier
$\No_{<\kappa}$ has cardinality $\kappa$. Indeed every earlier stage has
cardinality below $\kappa$, their $\kappa$-indexed union has cardinality
at most $\kappa$, and the ordinal labels below $\kappa$ give the reverse
inequality. Thus $\kappa$ is the least possible well-order type of this
carrier. Define the class
\[
 \ximin_R=\{\kappa:\kappa\text{ is an infinite strong-limit cardinal and }
           \operatorname{otp}(R\upharpoonright \No_{<\kappa}^2)=\kappa\}.
\]
A class $C\subseteq\Ord$ is \emph{club} if it is unbounded and contains
every ordinal limit point of itself. A class is \emph{stationary} if
it meets every available club class. These are predicates on classes,
not collections of classes regarded as ordinary members.

\begin{theorem}[Club reflection detects set-likeness]
\label{swo:lm:lim:club}
In $\GBC$, every class well-order $R$ of $\No$ satisfies exactly one
of the following alternatives.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $R$ is set-like, and a club of infinite strong-limit cardinals
      $\kappa$ satisfies: $\No_{<\kappa}$ is an $R$-initial segment and
      has order type $\kappa$. In particular, $\ximin_R$ contains a club.
\item $R$ is not set-like, and there are a fixed label $x$ and a club
      of infinite strong-limit cardinals $\kappa$ such that
      $x\in \No_{<\kappa}$ and $\xilr_\kappa(x)\geq\kappa$.
      Consequently $\operatorname{otp}(R\upharpoonright
      \No_{<\kappa}^2)>\kappa$, and $\ximin_R$ misses that club.
\end{enumerate}
Hence $R$ is set-like if and only if $\ximin_R$ is stationary, equivalently
if and only if $\ximin_R$ contains a club. In particular, minimum type at
every infinite strong-limit cutoff forces set-likeness.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We first record an explicit closure construction. Let $h:\Ord\to\Ord$
be nondecreasing, with $h(\alpha)>\alpha$. The class
\[
 C_h=\{\kappa:\kappa\text{ is a nonzero limit ordinal and }
                  (\forall\alpha<\kappa)\ h(\alpha)<\kappa\}
\]
is club. For unboundedness, start above any prescribed ordinal and
iterate $\alpha_{n+1}=h(\alpha_n)$; its supremum belongs to $C_h$.
Class Replacement justifies this set-sized iteration. Closure follows
by bounding each fixed $h(\alpha)$ below a member of $C_h$ preceding
the proposed limit. If each $h(\alpha)$ is an infinite cardinal and
exceeds $2^{|\alpha|}$, every member of $C_h$ is a strong-limit
cardinal: cardinals are cofinal below it, and its smaller power-set
cardinals are bounded strictly below it.

If $R$ is set-like, let $f:\Ord\to\No$ be its enumeration. Define
$h(\alpha)$ to be the least infinite cardinal strictly exceeding
\[
 \alpha,\qquad 2^{|\alpha|},\qquad
 \sup_{\xi<\alpha}\bigl(\operatorname{bd}(f(\xi))+1\bigr),
 \qquad
 \sup_{x\in \No_{<\alpha}}\bigl(f^{-1}(x)+1\bigr).
\]
All the suprema concern sets by Class Replacement, and $h$ is
nondecreasing. For $\kappa\in C_h$, forward birthday closure gives
$f[\kappa]\subseteq \No_{<\kappa}$. Conversely, each
$x\in \No_{<\kappa}$ already lies in some $\No_{<\alpha}$ with
$\alpha<\kappa$, so inverse closure gives $f^{-1}(x)<\kappa$.
Thus $f[\kappa]=\No_{<\kappa}$, proving the first alternative, including
initiality.

If $R$ is not set-like, choose $x$ with proper predecessor class
$P_x$. Its first $\Ord$-long segment has an increasing enumeration
$f:\Ord\to P_x$. Concretely, each set-length initial enumeration
is obtained by repeatedly selecting the least unused predecessor;
uniqueness makes these set-valued constructions uniform. Define $h$
as above, omitting the inverse term and adding the fixed bound
$\operatorname{bd}(x)+1$. For $\kappa\in C_h$, the label $x$ and
the increasing sequence $f[\kappa]$ lie in $\No_{<\kappa}$.
This sequence has type $\kappa$ and precedes $x$, so
$\xilr_\kappa(x)\geq\kappa$, and the whole local order has strictly
larger type.

Finally, two club classes intersect in a club: alternate their least
points above successive bounds and take the supremum of the resulting
$\omega$-sequence. Closure places that supremum in both classes.
This proves the stationary reformulation.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Unboundedly many minimum types do not suffice.}
The stationary qualification is sharp. Let
\[
 P=\{\beth_{\beta+1}:\beta\in\Ord\},\qquad
 Q=\No\setminus(P\cup\{0\}),
\]
and order the carrier by $P$, in increasing $\beta$-order, followed
by $0$, followed by a birthday-respecting well-order of $Q$.
This class well-order $R$ is not set-like at $0$.
For any ordinal $\alpha$, put
$\lambda=\alpha+\omega$ and $\kappa=\beth_\lambda$.
Then $\kappa$ is strong-limit and $\lambda<\kappa$.
For infinite $\alpha$, the ordinal $\alpha+\omega$ is not an
initial cardinal, whereas $\beth_\lambda\geq\lambda$ is one;
for finite $\alpha$, use $\beth_\omega>\omega$.
The intersection $P\cap \No_{<\kappa}$ has exactly type $\lambda$.
Removing these fewer than $\kappa$ labels and $0$ leaves
$|Q\cap \No_{<\kappa}|=\kappa$. Its birthday-respecting order has
type $\kappa$: each earlier birthday segment has type below
$\kappa$, while their union has cardinality $\kappa$.
Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{otp}(R\upharpoonright \No_{<\kappa}^2)
       =\lambda+1+\kappa=\kappa.
\]
The cardinals $\beth_{\alpha+\omega}$ are unbounded, so $\ximin_R$
is unbounded, yet \cref{swo:lm:lim:club} supplies a club disjoint from it.

\subsection{Coherent append-tail maps and their direct limit}

Work now in $\GBC$ and choose a baseline well-order $B$ which orders
labels first by birthday and then by a chosen well-order of each
birthday layer. It is set-like. Let $b:\Ord\to\No$ be its unique
enumeration. Every $\No_{<\alpha}$ is an initial segment of $B$; write
$t_\alpha=\operatorname{otp}(B\upharpoonright \No_{<\alpha})$, so
$b[t_\alpha]=\No_{<\alpha}$.

For $\alpha\leq\beta$ define
\[
 j_{\alpha\beta}(R)
   =R+\bigl(B\upharpoonright(\No_{<\beta}\setminus \No_{<\alpha})\bigr).
\]
The plus sign means ordered concatenation on the disjoint carriers.

\begin{theorem}[The direct system is precisely the bounded-support core]
\label{swo:lm:lim:direct}
The maps $j_{\alpha\beta}$ are native lexicographic order embeddings,
satisfy
\[
 j_{\beta\gamma}j_{\alpha\beta}=j_{\alpha\gamma},
 \qquad
 \pi_{\beta\alpha}j_{\alpha\beta}=\mathrm{id},
\]
and their direct limit identifies with the bounded-support core
$\Pbd(b)$: the global enumerations which equal $b$ at every
sufficiently large ordinal. The identification is induced by
\[
 J_\alpha(R)
   =R+\bigl(B\upharpoonright(\No\setminus \No_{<\alpha})\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first disagreement of two well-orders on the same carrier occurs
before the appended tail. Neither exhaustive enumeration can be a
proper prefix of the other. Thus appending the common tail preserves
and reflects comparison. Birthday compatibility of $B$ puts
$\No_{<\beta}\setminus \No_{<\alpha}$ before
$\No_{<\gamma}\setminus \No_{<\beta}$, proving the composition identity.
The retraction identity is immediate.

Let $\zeta=\operatorname{otp}(R)$, and choose an infinite initial cardinal
$\kappa>\zeta,t_\alpha$. If $f$ enumerates $J_\alpha(R)$, then on the
appended tail
\[
 f(\zeta+\delta)=b(t_\alpha+\delta).
\]
For every $\gamma\geq\kappa$ both $\zeta+\gamma=\gamma$ and
$t_\alpha+\gamma=\gamma$: write $\gamma=\kappa+\varepsilon$
and use $\zeta+\kappa=t_\alpha+\kappa=\kappa$. Hence
$f(\gamma)=b(\gamma)$ for every $\gamma\geq\kappa$.
Each $J_\alpha(R)$ therefore belongs to $\Pbd(b)$.

Conversely, let $f$ equal $b$ beyond $\kappa$, and let $R_f$ be its
induced order. The two bijections necessarily have
$f[\kappa]=b[\kappa]$. Choose $\alpha$ with
$b[\kappa]\subseteq \No_{<\alpha}$, so $t_\alpha\geq\kappa$.
Then $f[t_\alpha]=b[t_\alpha]=\No_{<\alpha}$; on the complementary
tail, $f$ agrees with $b$. Consequently
\[
 R_f=J_\alpha(R_f\upharpoonright \No_{<\alpha}^2).
\]
Finally, two local objects have the same global extension exactly
when their images agree at a common later stage. This proves the
asserted direct-limit identification.
\end{proof}

There is no need to make a proper equivalence class of stage codes
into a member of another class. One can use the core's unique
set-supported permutation codes, or choose the least stage at which
a direct-limit object is represented. The direct limit is consequently
an ordinary class order. The repository's core theorem identifies it
with $\No$ under the stated choice assumptions
(\cref{swo:gl:pbd-no,swo:ec:thm:core}).

The same stage spaces thus support two sharply different constructions:
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \text{maps} & \text{limit} & \text{comparison}\\ \hline
 \pi_{\beta\alpha}\text{ by restriction}
   & \text{all supplied class well-orders}
   & \text{eventual native comparison}\\
 j_{\alpha\beta}\text{ by appending }B
   & \Pbd(b)\cong\No
   & \text{compatible native embeddings}
 \end{array}
\]
The inverse-limit side includes non-set-like orders; the direct-limit
side consists of eventual perturbations of one baseline. Each local
order has a direct-limit extension, so every bounded observation of a
global class well-order is already realized in the core.

\begin{note}[\merge; the append-tail maps and the earlier remarks on extension]\label{swo:xi:note:append}
The maps $j_{\alpha\beta}$ are the operation $R\mapsto R+Q$ with a fixed
well-order $Q$ of the new labels, which source~15 records as an order
embedding in \cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives} (subsection on restrictions and
extensions), there for one pair of carriers. New in source~20 is the
coherence: one birthday-respecting baseline makes all of them compose
exactly along all ordinal cutoffs, with $\pi_{\beta\alpha}$ as a left
inverse, and the direct limit is identified with the core. Naively appended
tails need not preserve the minimal enumeration type
(\cref{swo:st:n14.9} warns of this); here no minimality is claimed: the
stage spaces are the full spaces $\WO(\No_{<\alpha})$ of all lengths. The
fixed-slot construction of \cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:coherence} keeps the minimal
type instead, at the price of a fixed cardinality band.
\end{note}

\subsection{A monotone inverse system using relation tables}

There is also a literal monotone inverse system, obtained by changing
the comparison. In $\GBC$, well-order the pair layer
\[
 L_\gamma=\{(x,y):
       \max(\operatorname{bd}(x),\operatorname{bd}(y))=\gamma\}
\]
for every $\gamma$, and concatenate these layer orders in increasing
$\gamma$. The resulting scan $Q$ of $\No^2$ is set-like. Its
restriction to $\No_{<\alpha}^2$ is an initial segment of some ordinal
length $s_\alpha$. The lengths are continuous at limit cutoffs and
cofinal in $\Ord$.

\begin{proposition}[Birthday table quotients]
\label{swo:lm:lim:tables}
Order each $\WO(\No_{<\alpha})$ by the characteristic table of its
strict relation, scanned by $Q\upharpoonright \No_{<\alpha}^2$, with
$0<1$. Every $\pi_{\beta\alpha}$ is then a weakly order-preserving
surjection with convex fibers. The append-tail maps
$j_{\alpha\beta}$ are order embeddings for these table orders as
well. The coherent inverse-limit comparison is exactly global
first-difference table comparison under $Q$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Restriction removes a final segment of the table. Prefix restriction
of binary lexicographic words is weakly monotone, and all words with
a fixed prefix form a convex set. Intersecting with the allowed
well-order tables preserves convexity. Surjectivity follows by
appending the baseline on the complementary carrier. The same
argument shows that an append-tail map preserves the first differing
bit of its input tables. For two global tables, their first differing
pair belongs to some $\No_{<\alpha}^2$; every later restriction has the
same first differing bit. Finally, \cref{swo:lm:lim:gluing} identifies the
compatible local well-order tables with the supplied global
well-orders.
\end{proof}

These table orders depend on the chosen scans inside pair layers.
They are a separate interpretation of lexicography. Their monotone
restriction property does not imply that they agree with native
enumeration comparison. Native comparison instead has the stronger
intrinsic interpretation of \cref{swo:lm:lim:two-labels,swo:lm:lim:eventual}, and
requires no scan of pairs.

\merge\ Relation-table orders are source~15's and source~16's scan orders
(\cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives}, its subsection on relation tables, and
\cref{swo:cb:thm:tableendpoints}); \cref{swo:lm:lim:tables} is the first
statement about how they behave under change of cutoff. It answers in part
source~15's question ``Coherent restricted filtrations'' (its Question~13.9),
which asks for restricted families on which restriction is monotone: a
change of comparison achieves it for all well-orders at once.

\subsection{The existence of a branch is already a choice principle}

Over $\GB$ with set-level AC, each $\WO(\No_{<\alpha})$ is nonempty
and every restriction map is surjective. It still takes a uniform
class to provide a full coherent profile. By \cref{swo:lm:lim:gluing} and
the repository's equivalence between global choice and a class
well-order of $\No$ (\cref{swo:cf:choice}),
\[
 \text{a full coherent birthday profile exists}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathrm{Global\ Choice}.
\]
The forward implication uses the glued well-order; the reverse
implication restricts a birthday-respecting baseline. Thus nonempty
set stages and surjective bonding maps do not by themselves supply
a uniform class branch under the weaker stated assumptions. This
pinpoints an actual foundational requirement, rather than attributing
the difficulty to an informal ``size paradox.''

\section{Coherent embeddings within a cardinality band (source 21)}\label{swo:fu:bs:sec:coherence}

\merge\ Source~21's Section~6, printed whole. Its ``proposed direction in the
repository'' is \cref{swo:st:n14.9}; the cited noncardinal theorem is
\cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal} (\cref{swo:fu:bs:sec:noncardinal} below) and
the cited topology proposition is source~21's \cref{swo:fu:set:prefix-topology},
printed in Part~X. Source~20's append-tail system (\cref{swo:lm:lim:direct}),
written independently, is the other coherent system of this Part; the two
are compared in \cref{swo:xi:note:append} and \cref{swo:xi:sec:status}.
Displayed equation (4) of source~21 is (S21.4).

% ---- source 21 resumes (Section 6)
Another proposed direction in the repository is compatibility between
birthday cutoffs (\cref{swo:st:n14.9}). Appending an arbitrary tail generally changes
the enumeration type. Within a fixed cardinality band, one baseline on an
upper alphabet gives embeddings that keep the minimal type and compose
exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Coherent insertion into fixed slots]\label{swo:fu:bs:thm:coherence}
Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be a set-indexed nested family of ordered subsets of an
ordered set $Y$, with $|X_i|=|Y|=\mu$ infinite. Fix a bijection $b:\mu\to Y$.
There are order embeddings
\[
 J_{ij}:\WO_\mu(X_i)\emb\WO_\mu(X_j)
       \qquad(X_i\subseteq X_j)
\]
such that $J_{ii}$ is the identity and $J_{jk}\circ J_{ij}=J_{ik}$ whenever
$X_i\subseteq X_j\subseteq X_k$.

Each map is a homeomorphism onto its image for the prefix topologies. Its
image is closed, and is clopen when the inserted positions are bounded in
$\mu$; if those positions are unbounded, the image is nowhere dense. These
are also assertions about the order topologies whenever the relevant
prefix and order topologies coincide.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $A_i=b^{-1}[X_i]\subseteq\mu$. A subset of the initial ordinal $\mu$
having cardinality $\mu$ has order type exactly $\mu$: its order type is at
most $\mu$ and cannot be smaller. Let $a_i:\mu\to A_i$ be its unique
increasing enumeration. For $X_i\subseteq X_j$, define
\[
 u_{ij}=a_j^{-1}\circ a_i:\mu\longrightarrow\mu,
 \qquad D_{ij}=\mu\setminus u_{ij}[\mu].
\]
Thus $u_{ij}$ is increasing and cofinal. Set
\[\tag{S21.4}\label{swo:fu:bs:eq:insertion}
 J_{ij}(f)(\eta)=
 \begin{cases}
 f(\xi),&\eta=u_{ij}(\xi),\\
 b(a_j(\eta)),&\eta\in D_{ij}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Every old label occurs once in an old slot, and every new label occurs once
in its fixed baseline slot, so the result is a bijection onto $X_j$.
If $f,g$ first disagree at $\xi$, their images first disagree at
$u_{ij}(\xi)$: earlier variable slots agree, all inserted slots are fixed,
and the numerical comparison at that disagreement is unchanged. Hence
$J_{ij}$ is an order embedding.

The slot maps satisfy $u_{jk}\circ u_{ij}=u_{ik}$. Under either successive
insertion or direct insertion, the oldest labels retain the same ambient
slots in $\mu$, and each additional label has its value prescribed by $b$.
This proves the required equality of functions, rather than merely an
isomorphism between two choices of extension. The identity assertion is
immediate.

For continuity, fix a target prefix length $\beta<\mu$. The source
coordinates whose slots are below $\beta$ form a proper initial segment
$\delta<\mu$, because $u_{ij}$ is increasing and cofinal. Agreement on that
source prefix therefore implies agreement on the entire target prefix;
the other entries there are fixed. Conversely, for $\delta<\mu$, knowledge
of the target prefix of length $u_{ij}(\delta)$ determines all source
coordinates below $\delta$. Both directions use genuine bounds below
$\mu$; no regularity of $\mu$ is required. The map and its inverse on its
image are continuous for the prefix topologies.

The image consists exactly of the target permutations satisfying
\[
 g(\eta)=b(a_j(\eta))\qquad(\eta\in D_{ij}).
\]
Indeed these fixed positions contain exactly $X_j\setminus X_i$, so
bijectivity forces the remaining positions to enumerate $X_i$. A violation
is witnessed by a single coordinate and hence by a prefix neighborhood;
the image is closed. If $D_{ij}$ is bounded, a sufficiently long prefix
checks all its conditions, so the image is open as well.

If $D_{ij}$ is unbounded, take any cylinder meeting the image. Beyond its
prescribed prefix choose an inserted position and a distinct later
position, and swap their entries. The result remains in the cylinder but
violates a fixed-position condition. The image therefore has empty interior
and, being closed, is nowhere dense.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A bounded surreal system]\label{swo:fu:bs:cor:surreal-coherence}
Let $\Theta$ be a set ordinal and let $I$ be a set of cutoffs
$\theta\le\Theta$ such that
\[
 |\No_{<\theta}|=|\No_{<\Theta}|=\mu\qquad(\theta\in I).
\]
A single baseline enumeration of $\No_{<\Theta}$ gives the coherent
minimal-length system of \cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:coherence} for all these cutoffs.
\end{corollary}

In particular, for a fixed infinite cardinal $\kappa$, every cutoff
$\kappa<\theta\le\kappa^+$ has alphabet cardinality $2^\kappa$.
Use the single upper alphabet $Y=\No_{<\kappa^+}$, whose cardinality is
$2^{<\kappa^+}=2^\kappa$. Thus the construction works throughout this
entire set-sized band, including its upper endpoint. The topology
statements are then statements about order topology by
\cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal,swo:fu:set:prefix-topology}. The distinction between a clopen image and a
nowhere dense image records the placement of the new labels in the chosen
baseline; it is not determined by their numerical order alone.

The restriction to one set-sized upper alphabet and one cardinality band is
substantive. The proof gives no assertion that a single baseline works
simultaneously across changing minimal cardinal lengths or across all
proper-class birthday cutoffs. Those compatibility questions require
additional constructions and an explicit foundational level.

\merge\ Here $\kappa$ is a cardinal of the band, not a cutoff of the
convention of Part~VI; the cutoffs $\theta$ of the band are noninitial
except its upper endpoint $\kappa^+$, and at the endpoint ``$\mu$'' is
$2^{<\kappa^+}=2^\kappa$ in either convention. The two coherent systems of
this Part are complementary. Source~20's append-tail maps
(\cref{swo:lm:lim:direct}) run along all ordinal cutoffs and compose
exactly, but act on the full spaces $\WO(\No_{<\alpha})$ and change the
enumeration length; source~21's fixed-slot maps keep the minimal length
$\mu$, are homeomorphisms onto closed images, but live in one cardinality
band below one set-sized upper alphabet. Which of these maps preserve finite
condensation, coding ranks or canonical cylinders, the further properties
that \cref{swo:st:n14.9} asks about, is not stated by either source.

\label{swo:bw:bs:sec:spectrum}

$\otimes_{\mathrm{lex}}$ is printed $\times_\lex$, its $\ell_2$ is $\bl$, and
its termination symbol $\dagger$ is printed $\End$; its displayed equations
(1)--(4) are (S29.1)--(S29.4). The fusion lemma
(\cref{swo:bw:bs:lem:fusion}) is the cylinder fusion mechanism of
\cref{swo:cb:lem:entrycode,swo:cb:new:lem:finite-capacity} and of source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-fiber-fusion}, stated in its cleanest form; it is
printed because every later proof of this Part's last three sections uses

from \cref{swo:bw:bs:prop:finite-tail} on is new against the repository and

% ---- source 29 resumes (Section 4)
The numerical order used as the alphabet already has a rigid embedding
hierarchy.  This remains true when increasing the birthday bound does not
change the cardinality of the alphabet.  We first determine that hierarchy;
the result will then distinguish information retained by the alphabet from
information retained by the lexicographic order of its enumerations.

Throughout this section all lengths are set ordinals.  Write
\[
 \No_{<\theta}
   =\bigcup_{\xi<\theta}\{-,+\}^{\xi},
 \qquad
 \B_\beta=(\{0,1\}^{\beta},<_{\lex}).
\]
The order on $\No_{<\theta}$ is numerical surreal order: at the first
disagreement, termination lies strictly between minus and plus.  This is
the standard sign-sequence description of the surreals \cite{Gonshor}.
The symbol $\equi$ denotes order embeddings in both directions, not
order isomorphism.  For a positive finite integer $m$, put
\[
 \B_\rho\times_\lex m=\B_\rho\times_\lex\{0,\ldots,m-1\}.
\]
Every addition or multiplication of lengths below is ordinal arithmetic.

\subsection{Binary fusion and finite capacity}

The following elementary fusion argument is useful both for the native
alphabet and for spaces of its enumerations.  A full cylinder consists of
all extensions of a fixed initial binary word, with every later coordinate
and every displayed final factor retained.

\begin{lemma}[Equal-length fusion]\label{swo:bw:bs:lem:fusion}
Let $\rho$ be an ordinal, let $K$ be a nonempty linear order, and let
\[
 f:\B_\rho\times_\lex K\longrightarrow\B_\rho
\]
be nondecreasing.  There is an $s\in\B_\rho$ such that $f$ is constant
on $\{s\}\times K$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At stage $\xi\leq\rho$ retain a full source cylinder whose first
$\xi$ bits are fixed and on which the first $\xi$ target bits are
constant.  Suppose $\xi<\rho$.  With the earlier target bits fixed,
the next target bit is nondecreasing on that cylinder.  If the lower
source child maps entirely to $0$ at that bit, retain it.  Otherwise
some point of the lower child maps to $1$, so the whole upper child
maps to $1$; retain the upper child.  At limit stages take unions of
the fixed prefixes.  After $\rho$ stages the entire factor $K$
survives over a single source word, and every target bit is fixed.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~29, Corollary~4.2, ``Cube hierarchy and finite factors'']\label{swo:bw:bs:cor:capacity}
\emph{For ordinals $\beta,\gamma,\rho$ and positive finite integers $m,n$,}
\begin{align*}
 \B_\beta\emb\B_\gamma
   &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta\leq\gamma,
       \tag{S29.1}\label{swo:bw:bs:eq:cube-hierarchy}\\
 \B_\rho\times_\lex m\emb \B_\rho\times_\lex n
   &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\leq n.
       \tag{S29.2}\label{swo:bw:bs:eq:finite-capacity}
\end{align*}
\emph{If $\rho=0$ or $\rho$ is an infinite limit ordinal, the least ordinal
length of a binary cube containing $\B_\rho\times_\lex m$ is
$\bl(\B_\rho\times_\lex m)=\rho+\lceil\log_2m\rceil$.}

\merge\ (S29.1) is \cref{swo:st:lem:strictcube} (reals report
\code{lwo:thm:cube-strict}; source~15's \cref{swo:cb:lem:entrycode}); (S29.2)
and the coding length are \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:finite-capacity} for nonzero
limit $\rho$ (the case $\rho=0$ is the count of finite chains), and source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-finite-capacity} proves the same. Source~29 derives all
three from \cref{swo:bw:bs:lem:fusion}: for (S29.1), if $\beta>\gamma$, split
the source after its first $\gamma$ bits; the remaining factor has at least
two points, and fusion of the composite with the target word makes them
equal. For (S29.2), fusion of the composite with the projection to $\B_\rho$
leaves all $m$ source points over one target binary word, so they inject
into its $n$-point fibre. For the coding length, coding the finite factor
in $j=\lceil\log_2m\rceil$ bits gives the upper bound; a target length below
$\rho$ is excluded by the $\B_\rho$ suborder, and a target length $\rho+i$,
$i<j$, has fibres of only $2^i<m$ points, excluded by (S29.2). The proof is
the argument of \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:finite-capacity}. New in the statement
is only that (S29.2) is stated for every ordinal $\rho$, not only for
nonzero limits.
\end{note}

\subsection{The finite part of a birthday bound}

Every ordinal $\theta$ has a unique expression
\[
 \theta=\lambda+n,
 \qquad n<\omega,
\]
where $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda$ is an infinite limit ordinal.  A
finite tail has an exact effect on the native alphabet.

\begin{proposition}[Finite terminal trees]\label{swo:bw:bs:prop:finite-tail}
If $n\geq1$ and $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda$ is an infinite limit ordinal,
then
\[
 \boxed{\quad \No_{<\lambda+n}\equi \B_\lambda\times_\lex(2^n-1).\quad}
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Consider the strings whose length is at least $\lambda$.  Each is a
length-$\lambda$ sign word followed by a finite sign word of length
less than $n$.  The latter words, with centered termination, form a
finite linear order of size
\[
 1+2+\cdots+2^{n-1}=2^n-1.
\]
Thus this subset of $\No_{<\lambda+n}$ is actually isomorphic to
$\B_\lambda\times_\lex(2^n-1)$, proving one embedding.

For $\lambda=0$ this is the whole alphabet.  Suppose therefore that
$\lambda$ is an infinite limit.  The relevant identities are
\[\tag{S29.3}\label{swo:bw:bs:eq:double-limit}
 2\cdot\lambda=\lambda,
 \qquad 2\cdot\xi+2<\lambda\quad(\xi<\lambda).
\]
Indeed $\lambda=\omega\cdot\delta$ for some nonzero ordinal
$\delta$, and left multiplication by $2$ fixes this product.  Strict
inequality for the proper partial lengths follows because
$\xi+1<\lambda$.  The factor $2$ in \eqref{swo:bw:bs:eq:double-limit} is
on the left; no cardinal multiplication is being substituted here.

Replace each minus sign by $00$ and each plus sign by $11$.  If a
string $x$ has length $\xi<\lambda$, append the termination block
$01$, then pad with zeros to length $\lambda$, and assign it finite
fiber rank $0$.  If $x$ has length $\lambda+j$, with $j<n$, double
its first $\lambda$ signs to form its length-$\lambda$ binary block,
and assign its finite tail its rank in the $(2^n-1)$-point centered
tail order.

The first binary blocks separate any two short strings and every
short string from every long string.  At a termination disagreement the
decisive comparison is precisely
\[
                  00<01<11.
\]
Different long prefixes also compare correctly.  Long strings sharing
their first $\lambda$ signs compare by their finite tail ranks.
Consequently this is an order embedding of the entire alphabet into
$\B_\lambda\times_\lex(2^n-1)$.
\end{proof}

The full sign level $\lambda+n$ has $2^n$ points over each
length-$\lambda$ prefix, whereas the available finite subtree has only
$2^n-1$.  Thus \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:capacity} immediately gives
\[\tag{S29.4}\label{swo:bw:bs:eq:successor-obstruction}
               \B_{\lambda+n}\not\emb \No_{<\lambda+n}.
\]
The limit case requires a different argument: there is no final finite
fiber in which to count points.

\subsection{Fusion at a limit birthday}

\begin{proposition}[The missing full-height cube]
\label{swo:bw:bs:prop:limit}
For every infinite limit ordinal $\lambda$,
\[
 \No_{<\lambda}\emb\B_\lambda,
 \qquad
 \B_\lambda\not\emb \No_{<\lambda}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first embedding is the short-string code from
\cref{swo:bw:bs:prop:finite-tail}: double signs, append $01$, and pad with
zeros to length $\lambda$.

Suppose for a contradiction that $e:\B_\lambda\emb \No_{<\lambda}$.
Recursively construct binary prefixes $p_\xi$, for $\xi\leq\lambda$,
of length $2\cdot\xi$.  Require that the images of all extensions
of $p_\xi$ share $\xi$ actual surreal signs; in particular, none of
these common coordinates is a termination symbol.

At a stage $\xi<\lambda$, the earlier target signs are fixed.  The
target symbol at coordinate $\xi$ is therefore a nondecreasing function
on the retained source cylinder with values in
\[
                  -\ <\ \End\ <\ +.
\]
A nondecreasing map to a three-point chain becomes constant on a full
binary subcylinder after at most two source-bit choices.  To see this
precisely, process the two threshold functions indicating whether the
symbol is at least $\End$ and whether it is $+$.  For each threshold,
the one-bit child rule in the proof of \cref{swo:bw:bs:lem:fusion} makes
its value constant while retaining a full child cylinder.  If fewer than
two choices suffice, fix additional arbitrary bits.  The resulting
prefix has length $2\cdot(\xi+1)$.

The constant target symbol cannot be $\End$.  Since the earlier
actual signs are common, termination at $\xi$ would make every image
the same length-$\xi$ surreal.  The retained source cylinder still
has at least two elements by \eqref{swo:bw:bs:eq:double-limit}, contradicting
injectivity.  Its next common symbol is therefore minus or plus, as
required.

At a limit stage $\xi<\lambda$, take the union of the preceding
prefixes.  Its length is
\[
 \sup_{\eta<\xi}2\cdot\eta=2\cdot\xi<\lambda,
\]
and every earlier chosen target sign persists.  At the final stage
$p_\lambda$ is a full source word because $2\cdot\lambda=\lambda$.
Its image has an actual sign at every coordinate below $\lambda$.
That image has birthday at least $\lambda$, contrary to membership
in $\No_{<\lambda}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact native birthday spectrum]
\label{swo:bw:bs:thm:spectrum}
For all ordinals $\beta,\theta$,
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \B_\beta\emb\No_{<\theta}
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta<\theta.
 \quad}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $\beta<\theta$, the strings of exactly length $\beta$ form the
required copy of $\B_\beta$.  The empty alphabet at $\theta=0$
contains no such cube.  For positive $\theta$, nonembedding at
$\beta=\theta$ is \eqref{swo:bw:bs:eq:successor-obstruction} or
\cref{swo:bw:bs:prop:limit}.  Every larger cube contains $\B_\theta$ by
fixing its later coordinates, so larger $\beta$ are excluded as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A strict hierarchy on every birthday band]
\label{swo:bw:bs:cor:strict}
For all ordinals $\theta,\eta$,
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \No_{<\theta}\emb\No_{<\eta}
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\theta\leq\eta.
 \quad}
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Inclusion proves sufficiency.  If $\theta>\eta$, the exact sign level
$\eta$ embeds $\B_\eta$ into $\No_{<\theta}$.  An embedding of that
alphabet into $\No_{<\eta}$ would contradict
\cref{swo:bw:bs:thm:spectrum}.
\end{proof}

For an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$, every noninitial cutoff
$\kappa<\theta<\kappa^+$ has alphabet cardinality $2^\kappa$.
Nevertheless, \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:strict} distinguishes all these cutoffs
under order embeddability.  This distinction will disappear from the
equimorphism type of several corresponding enumeration strata.

\subsection{Coding length versus embedded cubes}

\begin{corollary}[Exact native binary coding lengths]
\label{swo:bw:bs:cor:coding}
Let $\bl(L)$ be the least ordinal $\rho$ such that $L\emb\B_\rho$.
Then $\bl(\No_{<0})=0$.  For every nonzero limit $\lambda$,
\[
                      \bl(\No_{<\lambda})=\lambda.
\]
For $n\geq1$ and $\lambda=0$ or an infinite limit,
\[
 \bl(\No_{<\lambda+n})
     =\lambda+\lceil\log_2(2^n-1)\rceil
     =\begin{cases}
        \lambda,&n=1,\\
        \lambda+n,&n\geq2.
       \end{cases}
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
At a limit, \cref{swo:bw:bs:prop:limit} supplies the upper code.  Every
proposed shorter target $\B_\rho$ is excluded because
$\B_{\rho+1}\emb \No_{<\lambda}$ and
$\B_{\rho+1}\not\emb\B_\rho$.  At a successor cutoff use
\cref{swo:bw:bs:prop:finite-tail,swo:bw:bs:cor:capacity}.
\end{proof}

For example, $\No_{<\omega}$ and $\No_{<\omega+1}$ both have least binary
coding length $\omega$, but only $\No_{<\omega+1}$ contains
$\B_\omega$.  At a limit birthday, all shorter cubes occur and
their supremum is not attained.  At the next birthday that full cube
appears without increasing the least coding length.  The two numerical
invariants therefore answer different questions.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Birthday bound & Native alphabet information & Least binary code\\
\midrule
$\omega$ & cubes exactly of length $<\omega$ & $\omega$\\
$\omega+1$ & $\No_{<\omega+1}\equi\B_\omega$ & $\omega$\\
$\omega+2$ & $\No_{<\omega+2}\equi \B_\omega\times_\lex3$ & $\omega+2$\\
$\omega+3$ & $\No_{<\omega+3}\equi \B_\omega\times_\lex7$ & $\omega+3$\\
$\omega\cdot2$ & cubes exactly of length $<\omega\cdot2$
  & $\omega\cdot2$\\
$\omega\cdot2+1$ & $\No_{<\omega\cdot2+1}\equi\B_{\omega\cdot2}$
  & $\omega\cdot2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

These arguments use only set-sized sign strings, ordinal recursion, and
canonical choices between two binary children.  The native spectrum
and strict hierarchy can consequently be developed in $\ZF$; no
enumeration of an arbitrary unordered set is needed.  This makes them
particularly suitable as an initial formalization target before the
choice-dependent permutation constructions in the next section.
