The repository explicitly asks what survives when the birthday bound is an
arbitrary ordinal rather than an initial cardinal (\cref{swo:st:n14.2}). There is a
useful simplification in that case: the alphabet becomes strictly larger
than the length of any of its monotone chains. This determines several exact
invariants without any additional cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis.

\subsection{A general permutation lemma}

For an infinite initial cardinal $\mu$ and an ordered set $X$ of cardinality
$\mu$, write $\WO_\mu(X)$ for the bijections $\mu\to X$ in enumeration
lexicographic order. For an injection $p:\delta\to X$, where $\delta<\mu$,
put
\[
 C_p=\{f\in\WO_\mu(X):f\restr\delta=p\}.
\]
The \emph{prefix topology} has these cylinders as a base. Throughout this
section, cellularity means the supremum of the sizes of pairwise disjoint
families of nonempty open sets; the supremum need not be attained.

\begin{theorem}[Short monotone chains in the alphabet]\label{swo:fu:bs:thm:generic}
Suppose that $X$ contains neither an increasing nor a decreasing sequence of
order type $\mu$. Then $P=\WO_\mu(X)$ is dense without endpoints, and its
order topology equals its prefix topology. The cylinders are clopen, and
\[
 \dens(P)=\cell(P)=\mu^{<\mu}.
\]
Every $f\in P$ has left cofinality and right coinitiality exactly $\cf(\mu)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Define the feasible downward and upward divergence positions by
\begin{align*}
 D^-(f)&=\{i<\mu:\exists j>i\ [f(j)<f(i)]\},\\
 D^+(f)&=\{i<\mu:\exists j>i\ [f(j)>f(i)]\}.
\end{align*}
If $D^-(f)$ were bounded, a final part of $f$ would be strictly increasing.
Every final interval of the initial ordinal $\mu$ has order type $\mu$, so
this contradicts the hypothesis. Thus $D^-(f)$ is cofinal in $\mu$, and the
same argument applies to $D^+(f)$. At any feasible position, swap $f(i)$ with
the corresponding later value. This produces a bijection whose first
disagreement with $f$ occurs at $i$, in the desired direction.

For $f<g$, an upward swap of $f$ beyond their first disagreement gives
$f<h<g$. The same construction in both directions shows that every point is
internal to each of its prefix cylinders. Since cylinders are convex, they
are open; their complements are unions of other cylinders of the same
length, so they are closed. Conversely, a prefix longer than the first
disagreements with the endpoints of an order neighborhood lies inside that
neighborhood. The two topologies therefore agree.

Choose a cofinal subset of $D^-(f)$ of size $\cf(\mu)$ and one downward swap
at each of its positions. These permutations are cofinal below $f$, since a
later first disagreement brings a point closer to $f$ from below. Any family
of fewer than $\cf(\mu)$ points below $f$, however, has bounded disagreement
positions; a downward swap beyond that bound lies above the entire family.
The left character is exactly $\cf(\mu)$. Reverse inequalities for the right
character.

There are $\mu^{<\mu}$ prefixes, so one completion per prefix gives a dense
set of at most that size. Every prefix extends: its range has size less than
$\mu$, its complement has size $\mu$, and the remaining coordinate interval
has order type $\mu$. At level $\delta<\mu$ there are exactly
$\mu^{|\delta|}$ injective prefixes. For the lower bound, encode an arbitrary
function $h:\delta\to\mu$ as the injection $i\mapsto\langle h(i),i\rangle$
using a fixed injection $\mu\times\delta\to\mu$. Their cylinders form a
disjoint open family of that size. Taking the supremum over $\delta$ and
using $\cell(P)\le \dens(P)$ proves the formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{swo:fu:n5.2}
The hypothesis is sufficient, not necessary. It fails for $X=\mathbb Q$ and
$\mu=\omega$, even though the conclusion holds there because deleting a
finite prefix leaves a dense alphabet without endpoints. It should not be
silently substituted for that different argument.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-alphabet obstruction]\label{swo:fu:bs:lem:finite-alphabet}
If $|\tau|=\kappa$ is infinite and $A$ is a finite linear order, then the
lexicographic order on $A^\tau$ contains no increasing or decreasing
sequence of length $\kappa^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $(x_\eta)_{\eta<\kappa^+}$ is strictly increasing. Recursively make
each coordinate constant on a final segment. Once all coordinates below
$\beta$ have stabilized, their stabilization indices have a common upper
bound below $\kappa^+$, since $|\beta|\le\kappa$ and $\kappa^+$ is regular.
Beyond that bound, coordinate $\beta$ is nondecreasing and takes only
finitely many values, so it too eventually stabilizes. After $\tau$ steps a
single final segment has every coordinate constant, a contradiction. Reverse
the alphabet order for decreasing sequences.
\end{proof}

\merge\ This lemma is the finite-alphabet case of the stabilization argument
used for source~19's \cref{swo:rs:prop:tail-universality} (no increasing
$\kappa^+$-sequence in $\B_\kappa$); it is stated here for every finite alphabet and every index
ordinal of cardinality $\kappa$.

\subsection{Exact invariants at an arbitrary noninitial bound}

\begin{theorem}[Noncardinal cutoff]\label{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal}
Let $\theta$ be an infinite ordinal that is not an initial cardinal, and put
\[
 \kappa=|\theta|,\qquad X=\No_{<\theta},\qquad \mu=|X|.
\]
Then $\mu=2^\kappa>\kappa$. For $P=\WO_\mu(X)$ one has
\[
 |P|=2^\mu,\qquad
 \bl(P)=\mu,\qquad
 \dens(P)=\cell(P)=\mu^{<\mu},
\]
where $\bl$ is the least ordinal length of a fixed-length
binary lexicographic cube into which the order embeds. The order $P$ is
dense without endpoints, its order topology is its prefix topology, and
every point has left and right character $\cf(\mu)$.

Write uniquely $\theta=\lambda+n$, where $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal
and $n<\omega$. Then
\[
 \cf(P)=\ci(P)=\cf(\lambda).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\kappa<\theta$, all sign sequences of length $\kappa$ lie in $X$.
Thus $|X|\ge2^\kappa$. There are $\kappa$ possible lengths below $\theta$,
each contributing at most $2^\kappa$ sequences, proving $\mu=2^\kappa$.
Pad a sign sequence to length $\theta$ with a symbol $0$, ordered
$-<0<+$. This embeds the numerical order of $X$ into the lexicographic order
on $\{-,0,+\}^{\theta}$: the padding symbol reproduces the centered
termination convention for surreal signs. By
\cref{swo:fu:bs:lem:finite-alphabet}, $X$ has no monotone sequence of length
$\kappa^+$. As $\mu\ge\kappa^+$, \cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:generic} applies.

The number of bijections of an infinite $\mu$-set is $2^\mu$. The upper
bound is $\mu^\mu=2^\mu$; independent swaps in a partition into pairs give
the lower bound. To obtain the binary-rank upper bound, encode the three
padding symbols as $00,01,10$, respectively. This embeds $X$ into binary
words of fixed length $\tau=2\cdot\theta$. Here $|\tau|=\kappa<\mu$, so
$\tau<\mu$ and $\tau\cdot\mu=\mu$. Concatenating the entry codes of a
permutation therefore embeds $P$ into $2^\mu$ with its lexicographic order.

Conversely, partition $X$ into $\mu$ pairs, order each pair numerically, and
let each bit choose one of the pair's two enumeration orders. Since
$2\cdot\mu=\mu$, this embeds the lexicographic cube $2^\mu$ into $P$.
That cube contains every linear order $L$ of cardinality at most $\mu$:
index its elements by distinct coordinates and send $t\in L$ to the
characteristic function of its strict lower set, assigning $0$ elsewhere.
For $s<t$, these characteristic functions are nested, differ at the
coordinate for $s$, and compare in the correct direction at their first
disagreement. Thus, for every infinite $\alpha<\mu$, the order $P$ contains
the ordinal $|\alpha|^+$, whereas $2^\alpha$ does not by
\cref{swo:fu:bs:lem:finite-alphabet}. Finite target lengths are excluded by
cardinality. The binary rank is exactly $\mu$.

It remains to compute the global cofinalities. In fact this argument works
for every infinite birthday bound. If $n=0$, the all-plus words
$+^\beta$, for $\beta<\lambda$, are cofinal in $X$. A family of fewer than
$\cf(\lambda)$ words has birthdays bounded below $\lambda$, so a longer
all-plus word dominates the family. Hence $\cf(X)=\cf(\lambda)$.
Whenever an alphabet $Y$ has no maximum,
\[\tag{S21.3}\label{swo:fu:bs:eq:first-coordinate}
 \cf(\WO_\mu(Y))=\cf(Y),
\]
because cofinal first entries give cofinal permutations, and the first
entries of a cofinal family of permutations must be cofinal in $Y$.

If $n>0$, let $B$ consist of the words in $X$ extending $+^\lambda$.
These form a finite final block of the numerical alphabet, of size
\[
 |B|=1+2+\cdots+2^{n-1}=2^n-1.
\]
Every word outside $B$ terminates or first has a minus sign below $\lambda$,
and hence lies below every member of $B$. The complement $Y=X\setminus B$
has no maximum. The words $+^\beta$, $\beta<\lambda$, are cofinal in it.
For the converse bound assign to each $y\in Y$ its first disagreement or
termination position relative to $+^\lambda$. Fewer than $\cf(\lambda)$
such positions are bounded below $\lambda$; a longer all-plus word then
dominates the corresponding family. Thus $\cf(Y)=\cf(\lambda)$.

The cylinder beginning by listing $B$ in decreasing numerical order is a
final convex suborder of $P$. Deleting this finite prefix leaves coordinate
order type $\mu$, so that cylinder is isomorphic to $\WO_\mu(Y)$.
Equation~\eqref{swo:fu:bs:eq:first-coordinate} gives $\cf(P)=\cf(\lambda)$.
Negating all signs proves the matching coinitiality formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Failure of interval self-similarity]\label{swo:fu:bs:cor:interval}
At every noncardinal cutoff of \cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal}, the whole order $P$
is not isomorphic to any nonempty bounded open interval of itself, nor to
either proper open ray.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
K\"onig's theorem gives
\[
 \cf(P)=\ci(P)=\cf(\lambda)\le\kappa
       <\cf(2^\kappa)=\cf(\mu).
\]
Every interval $(a,b)$ has cofinality and coinitiality $\cf(\mu)$, by the
point-character calculation. A proper open ray has one of these endpoint
characters. The corresponding invariant of $P$ is strictly smaller.
\end{proof}

For example, the cutoffs $\omega+1$, $\omega\cdot2$, and $\omega^2$ all have
$\mu=2^{\aleph_0}$. Their minimal permutation orders have global
cofinalities $\omega$ and point characters $\cf(2^{\aleph_0})>\omega$.
Moving from cutoff $\omega$ to cutoff $\omega+1$ already changes the point
character from countable to uncountable. These calculations answer part of
the repository's proposed question, while leaving full cut spectra,
saturation, and isomorphism classifications open. No historical novelty
claim is attached to these deductions.

\merge\ Two remarks on the comparison with initial cardinal cutoffs. First,
at an initial cardinal cutoff $\kappa$ the global cofinality is
$r=\cf\kappa$ and the point characters are $(q,q)$, $q=\cf\mu$
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:invariants}), with $r\le q$
(\cref{swo:cb:new:lem:power-sup-cofinality}). The argument of
\cref{swo:fu:bs:cor:interval} therefore applies at an initial cardinal cutoff
exactly when $r<q$; at a noncardinal cutoff the corresponding inequality
$\cf\lambda<\cf\mu$ holds always, by K\"onig's theorem. Second, at an initial cardinal cutoff the coding rank is
$\rho_\kappa$, which differs from $\mu$ exactly at singular strong limits
(\cref{swo:st:thm:transition}); at a noncardinal cutoff it is always $\mu$,
because $\No_{<\theta}$ codes into binary words of the fixed length
$2\cdot\theta<\mu$. Source~29's \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:strict} shows that the
noncardinal cutoffs of one band are nevertheless pairwise distinguished by
their alphabets, while \cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal} sees of the cutoff
only $\kappa$ and $\cf\lambda$.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 842-1344
\section{All enumeration lengths at a noninitial birthday bound (source 29)}
\label{swo:bw:ns:sec:strata}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~5, printed whole except for four lemmas that
source~19 proves for initial cardinal cutoffs in its Section~5 (printed in
Part~X, \cref{swo:rs:sec:tails}) and that hold verbatim, for any alphabet, at
noninitial cutoffs; these are recorded in notes carrying source~29's labels
(\cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:entry,swo:bw:ns:lem:scheduler,swo:bw:ns:lem:small-range,swo:bw:ns:lem:singular-fusion}).
Source~29 credits all four to source~19 (``the earlier residual analysis'').
Its main-prefix lemma and residual reduction
(\cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:main,swo:bw:ns:prop:residual}) are source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix,swo:rs:thm:tail-reduction} transferred to
noninitial cutoffs, where the proof is simpler (no singular scheduler is
needed for the main prefix); they are printed in full because their
statements are new. The coding sandwich, the exact cube and birthday
capacity, the coding bounds and the countable-band classification
(\cref{swo:bw:ns:thm:sandwich,swo:bw:ns:thm:capacity,swo:bw:ns:cor:coding,swo:bw:ns:cor:countable})
are new; at initial cardinal cutoffs the corresponding statements are
source~19's \cref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich,swo:rs:thm:tail-cubes,swo:rs:cor:tail-coding},
except the native birthday threshold \eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:birthdays}, which is
new at every cutoff. Renamed (conventions of this Part): $D_{\rho,m}$ is
$\B_\rho\times_\lex m$; the layer weights $r(\lambda)$, $u_\kappa(\lambda)$
are $\xiwt(\lambda)$, $\xiwt^+_\kappa(\lambda)$; the weighted lengths $R$, $U$
are $\xiRlo$, $\xiRup$; $\ell_2$ is $\bl$. Displayed equations (5)--(13) are
(S29.5)--(S29.13). Its first sentence's ``fixed-length results'' of the
repository are \cref{swo:cb:new:thm:block-types} (Part~VI).

% ---- source 29 resumes (Section 5)
The repository's fixed-length results include the minimum stratum and
finite tails after a whole-cardinality prefix (\cref{swo:cb:new:thm:block-types}).  The earlier
residual analysis goes further for initial birthday bounds: it treats
arbitrary smaller residual alphabets and obtains an exact embedded-cube
spectrum, while retaining a specific upper coding gap at singular
non-strong-limit residual cardinals (source~19, \cref{swo:rs:sec:tails}).  We now
extend that analysis to every noninitial birthday cutoff.  The residual
fusion and singular scheduler are inherited mechanisms; the work here
is to verify their hypotheses for the new alphabets and draw the resulting
sharp birthday-embedding consequences.

Work in $\ZFC$.  Fix an infinite ordinal $\theta$ which is not an
initial cardinal, and put
\[\tag{S29.5}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:parameters}
 \kappa=\card{\theta},\qquad
 X=\No_{<\theta},\qquad \mu=\card X=2^\kappa.
\]
The last equality follows because every sign word of length $\kappa$
belongs to $X$, and there are only $\kappa$ possible lengths, each
contributing at most $2^\kappa$ words.  In particular $\kappa<\mu$.
An admissible enumeration type is an ordinal $\alpha$ of cardinality
$\mu$, and $\WO_\alpha(X)$ denotes the bijections $\alpha\to X$
ordered by their first numerical disagreement.

\subsection{Main prefixes and variable residual alphabets}

Write
\[
 \alpha=\mu\cdot\gamma+\zeta,
 \qquad 0<\gamma<\mu^+,\qquad \zeta<\mu.
\]
The difference between an injection of length $\mu\cdot\gamma$ and
a bijection of that length is essential: a proper prefix of the full
enumeration may leave a smaller alphabet, with numerical order depending
on the prefix.

\begin{lemma}[Noninitial main-prefix package]\label{swo:bw:ns:lem:main}
Every lexicographically ordered family of injective prefixes
$p:\mu\cdot\gamma\to X$ embeds into $\B_{\mu\cdot\gamma}$.
For every $Y\subseteq X$ with $\card Y<\mu$,
\[
 \B_{\mu\cdot\gamma}\emb
          \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma}(X\setminus Y).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pad every sign word to length $\theta$ with a termination symbol ordered
between minus and plus, and encode the three symbols by $00,01,11$.
This embeds $X$ into $\B_\tau$, where $\tau=2\cdot\theta$ has
cardinality $\kappa$.  Thus $0<\tau<\mu$ and
$\tau\cdot\mu=\mu$.  Concatenating the fixed entry codes over
$\gamma$ successive $\mu$-blocks yields an order-preserving code of
length $\mu\cdot\gamma$.  Exhaustiveness is never used.

The complement $X\setminus Y$ has cardinality $\mu$.  Partition it
into pairs indexed by $\mu\cdot\gamma$, orient each pair numerically,
and let its corresponding bit choose the order in which the two labels
are listed.  Every label appears exactly once.  The resulting enumeration
has length
$2\cdot(\mu\cdot\gamma)=\mu\cdot\gamma$, and its first changed
bit gives its first changed label in the same order direction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact residual reduction]\label{swo:bw:ns:prop:residual}
For every nonempty linear order $K$,
\begin{align*}
 &\B_{\mu\cdot\gamma}\times_\lex K
       \emb\WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\zeta}(X)\\
 &\qquad\Longleftrightarrow
 \exists Y\subseteq X\,
 \bigl(\card Y=\card\zeta\text{ and }K\emb\WO_\zeta(Y)\bigr).
\end{align*}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
There is an actual lexicographic-sum decomposition
\[\tag{S29.6}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:fibers}
 \WO_{\mu\cdot\gamma+\zeta}(X)
 \cong\sum_p\WO_\zeta(X\setminus\ran p),
\]
where $p$ ranges over the injective main prefixes whose omitted set has
cardinality $\card\zeta$.  The projection onto this prefix order is
nondecreasing, and \cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:main} embeds its range into
$\B_{\mu\cdot\gamma}$.  Apply \cref{swo:bw:bs:lem:fusion} to the
composition with a proposed product embedding.  The whole factor $K$
survives in one target fiber, proving necessity.

Conversely, fix a suitable $Y$.  Use \cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:main} to enumerate
the fixed complement $X\setminus Y$ according to the main binary
factor, then append the chosen $K$-indexed permutations of $Y$.
\end{proof}

This reduction applies to arbitrary product embeddings.  It does not
assume that an embedding respects the displayed fibers.  In particular,
it prevents a variable residual alphabet from being replaced silently
by a preferred copy of a birthday fragment.

\merge\ The decomposition (S29.6) is source~19's \eqref{swo:rs:eq:tail-sum} and,
for the minimal length, the set-level fibre identity of sources~21 and~22
printed in Part~X; the class version is source~16's
\cref{swo:ds:eq:fiber}.

\subsection{The finitely many residual cardinal layers}

Repeated left division of $\zeta$ by its current infinite initial
cardinal gives a finite expression
\[\tag{S29.7}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:layers}
 \zeta=\lambda_0\cdot\eta_0+\cdots+
       \lambda_{s-1}\cdot\eta_{s-1}+n,
\]
where
\[
 \mu>\lambda_0>\cdots>\lambda_{s-1}\geq\omega,
 \qquad 0<\eta_i<\lambda_i^+,
 \qquad n<\omega.
\]
There cannot be infinitely many layers, since their cardinals would
form an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of ordinals.  When
$\zeta$ is finite, $s=0$.

Define the two weights
\begin{align*}
 \xiwt(\lambda)&=
 \begin{cases}
  \lambda\cdot\lambda,&\lambda\text{ singular strong limit},\\
  \lambda,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}\tag{S29.8}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:r}\\
 \xiwt^+_\kappa(\lambda)&=
 \begin{cases}
  \lambda\cdot\lambda,&\lambda\leq\kappa\text{ and }\lambda
       \text{ singular},\\
  \lambda,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\tag{S29.9}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:u}
\end{align*}
Finally set
\[\tag{S29.10}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:RU}
 \xiRlo=\mu\cdot\gamma+\sum_{i<s}\xiwt(\lambda_i)\cdot\eta_i,
 \qquad
 \xiRup=\mu\cdot\gamma+\sum_{i<s}\xiwt^+_\kappa(\lambda_i)\cdot\eta_i.
\]
Both are nonzero limit ordinals, and $\xiRlo\leq \xiRup$.  Their difference,
when present, is an ordinal difference in coding cost; their cardinalities
are both $\mu$.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~5.3, ``Entry codes and regular blocks'']\label{swo:bw:ns:lem:entry}
\emph{Every linear order of infinite cardinality $\lambda$ admits a
prefix-free, order-preserving binary entry code with positive code
lengths below $\lambda$. If $\lambda$ is regular, concatenating these codes
over a block of $\lambda\cdot\eta$ entries has length exactly
$\lambda\cdot\eta$.} The first sentence is source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-entrycode} and the second the coding half of its
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-regular}, by the same argument: insert the alphabet,
in an enumeration of length $\lambda$, into $\No_{<\lambda}$ by simplest
separators (the birthday bound for a surreal cut, \cite{Gonshor}), double
minus and plus to $00$ and $11$ and append $01$; regularity keeps every
proper partial sum of fewer than $\lambda$ code lengths below $\lambda$, and
positivity makes the full sum $\lambda$. The code is source~15's entry code
(\cref{swo:cb:lem:entrycode}) applied after the insertion.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~5.4, ``Inherited singular strong-limit scheduler'']\label{swo:bw:ns:lem:scheduler}
\emph{If $\lambda$ is singular strong limit and $0<\eta<\lambda^+$, then
$\B_{\lambda\cdot\lambda\cdot\eta}\emb\WO_{\lambda\cdot\eta}(\No_{<\lambda})$.}
This is the lower half of \cref{swo:cb:new:thm:block-types} at the cutoff
$\lambda$ (there $\mu=\lambda$ and $\rho_\lambda=\lambda\cdot\lambda$), and
source~29 says ``We recall the construction from the earlier residual
analysis'': the row scheduler of \cref{swo:cb:new:lem:block-scheduler} in
the form given in the proof of source~19's \cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-mainprefix}.
Its steps, as source~29 recalls them: the sign cones with prefixes
$+^i\cat-$, $i<\lambda$, are pairwise disjoint copies of $\No_{<\lambda}$,
indexed by $\lambda\cdot\eta$, and their complement (containing the $\lambda$
all-plus words) is a fixed filler row placed first ($1+\lambda=\lambda$);
row--column pairs are scheduled first by $\max(i,j)$, then lexicographically,
which has order type $\lambda$ even for singular $\lambda$ and lets the
first entry of the first varying row decide the comparison; this embeds
$(\No_{<\lambda})^{\lambda\cdot\eta}_\lex$. Finally, with
$\delta=\cf\lambda$ and positive lengths $(\tau_j)_{j<\delta}$ summing to
$\lambda$, a binary word of length $\lambda$ is encoded by $\delta$
consecutive entries of sign lengths exactly $\tau_j$, so that
$\delta\cdot(\lambda\cdot\eta)=\lambda\cdot\eta$ entries carry
$\lambda\cdot\lambda\cdot\eta$ bits.
\end{note}

\begin{theorem}[Noninitial coding sandwich]\label{swo:bw:ns:thm:sandwich}
With \eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:parameters}--\eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:RU},
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex n!\emb\WO_\alpha(X)\emb \B_{\xiRup}\times_\lex n!.
 \quad}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the upper embedding, code the main prefix in length
$\mu\cdot\gamma$ using \cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:main}.  At the start of a
residual layer its remaining alphabet has cardinality $\lambda_i$:
the remaining coordinate interval has that cardinality, and the
enumeration is bijective.

At a regular layer, \cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:entry} gives cost
$\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.  At a singular layer with
$\lambda_i\leq\kappa$, pad its entry codes to length $\lambda_i$,
giving cost $\lambda_i\cdot\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.  If
$\lambda_i>\kappa$, use the fixed global code of length
$\tau=2\cdot\theta$.  Now $\tau<\lambda_i$, so
$\tau\cdot\lambda_i=\lambda_i$, and the cost is only
$\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.

Choose one entry code for each possible residual alphabet.  These are
set-indexed choices.  Two enumerations agreeing through a layer boundary
have the same residual alphabet and use the same code.  If they disagree
earlier, their comparison has already been decided.  The conditional
codes therefore concatenate to an order-preserving code of length $\xiRup$.
After that prefix, the last $n$ labels are determined as a set; append
the rank of their permutation among its $n!$ possibilities.

For the lower embedding, reserve disjoint fixed alphabets for the
residual layers and a fixed $n$-element terminal set.  If a residual
$\lambda<\mu$ is singular strong limit, necessarily
$\lambda\leq\kappa$: otherwise strong limit would imply
$2^\kappa<\lambda$, contradicting $\lambda<\mu=2^\kappa$.
Thus a copy of $\No_{<\lambda}$ lies in a finite-prefix cone of
$X$.  All its sign lengths stay below $\lambda\leq\kappa<\theta$.
Finitely many distinct prefixes make the alphabets for different such
layers disjoint.  Apply \cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:scheduler} at each of them.

For every other residual layer reserve an arbitrary set of the required
cardinality and orient pairs to realize
$\B_{\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i}$.  The union of all reserved sets has
cardinality below $\mu$, so \cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:main} realizes the main
binary factor on its complement.  Concatenate the independent block
enumerations and the selected terminal permutation.  The first changed
source factor gives the first changed target block, establishing the
lower embedding.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact capacity despite a possible coding gap}

The only discrepancy between $\xiwt$ and $\xiwt^+_\kappa$ can occur at a
singular non-strong-limit residual cardinal at most $\kappa$.  The
following inherited fusion mechanism determines its contribution to
embedded cubes even when a short upper code is unavailable.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~5.6, ``Small-range fusion'']\label{swo:bw:ns:lem:small-range}
\emph{Let $\chi$ be an infinite cardinal, let $A$ be a linear order of
cardinality less than $2^\chi$, and let $K$ be nonempty. A nondecreasing map
from a full binary cylinder with at least $\chi$ initial free bits, followed
by $K$, into $A$ is constant on a full subcylinder obtained by fixing fewer
than $\chi$ of those bits.} This is source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-smallrange}, with the same proof: fixing the later bits
and one point of $K$ leaves $2^\chi$ ordered test points, so some value has
three preimages $x_0<x_1<x_2$; a prefix of $x_1$ of length below $\chi$
beyond its first disagreements with $x_0$ and $x_2$ traps its whole cylinder
between them.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~5.7, ``A singular non-strong-limit layer'']\label{swo:bw:ns:lem:singular-fusion}
\emph{Suppose $\lambda$ is singular and not strong limit, and
$0<\eta<\lambda^+$. In an order embedding, suppose the target enumerations
share their earlier prefix and the remaining alphabet has cardinality
$\lambda$. If the surviving source begins with $\B_{\lambda\cdot\eta}$
followed by a nonempty factor $K$, one can fix that source binary block so
that the next $\lambda\cdot\eta$ target entries are constant on the
surviving whole factor $K$.} This is source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:tail-singular-fusion}, with the same proof: choose
$\rho<\lambda$ with $2^{\card\rho}\ge\lambda$ and
$\chi=\max(\card\rho,\cf\lambda)<\lambda$, so that $2^\chi>\lambda$ by
K\"onig's inequality; fix the target entries one at a time with
\cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:small-range}, each at a cost of fewer than $\chi$ source
bits. Source~29 makes the ordinal bookkeeping explicit: before coordinate
$j=\lambda\cdot\beta+\delta$ ($\delta<\lambda$) the cost is at most
$\chi\cdot(j+1)=\lambda\cdot\beta+\chi\cdot(\delta+1)<\lambda\cdot\eta$,
and the total cost is at most $\chi\cdot(\lambda\cdot\eta)=\lambda\cdot\eta$.
\end{note}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cube and birthday capacity]
\label{swo:bw:ns:thm:capacity}
For every positive finite integer $m$,
\[\tag{S29.11}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:capacity}
 \B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex m\emb\WO_\alpha(X)
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\leq n!.
\]
Consequently, for every ordinal $\beta$,
\[\tag{S29.12}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:cubes}
 \boxed{\quad
 \B_\beta\emb\WO_\alpha(X)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \beta\leq \xiRlo+\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor.
 \quad}
\]
For every ordinal $\nu$, the exact native-alphabet threshold is
\[\tag{S29.13}\label{swo:bw:ns:eq:birthdays}
 \boxed{\quad
 \No_{<\nu}\emb\WO_\alpha(X)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \nu\leq \xiRlo+\lfloor\log_2(n!+1)\rfloor.
 \quad}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The positive direction of \eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:capacity} follows from
\cref{swo:bw:ns:thm:sandwich}.  Conversely, suppose an embedding of
$\B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex m$ is given.  Compose with the main-prefix projection and its
binary code.  Equal-length fusion fixes the main target prefix while
retaining the whole later source factor, as in
\cref{swo:bw:ns:prop:residual}.

At a regular residual layer fuse through its code of length
$\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.  At a singular strong-limit layer fuse
through the padded code of length
$\lambda_i\cdot\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.  A layer with
$\lambda_i>\kappa$ has its short global code and cannot be singular
strong limit, as shown in the sandwich proof.  At a singular
non-strong-limit layer at most $\kappa$, apply
\cref{swo:bw:ns:lem:singular-fusion}; its cost is only
$\lambda_i\cdot\eta_i$.  These are exactly the successive
summands defining $\xiRlo$.

After the finitely many layers all target positions before the last
$n$ are fixed.  The surviving $m$ points must inject into the $n!$
permutations of a single fixed residual $n$-element set.  Hence
$m\leq n!$, proving \eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:capacity}.

Put $a=\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor$.  The allowed finite binary
factor has $2^a$ points, whereas the next one has $2^{a+1}>n!$.
Thus $\B_{\xiRlo+a}$ embeds and $\B_{\xiRlo+a+1}$ does not.  The cube
hierarchy proves \eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:cubes} for every ordinal $\beta$.

For \eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:birthdays}, put
$b=\lfloor\log_2(n!+1)\rfloor\geq1$.  Since $\xiRlo$ is a nonzero
limit, \cref{swo:bw:bs:prop:finite-tail} gives
\[
 \No_{<\xiRlo+b}\equi \B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex(2^b-1),
 \qquad
 \No_{<\xiRlo+b+1}\equi \B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex(2^{b+1}-1).
\]
The first finite factor has at most $n!$ points, and the second has
more.  Equation~\eqref{swo:bw:ns:eq:capacity} permits the first alphabet and
excludes the second.  Inclusion between birthday alphabets supplies
all smaller cutoffs and excludes all larger ones.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Coding bounds and exact equimorphisms]
\label{swo:bw:ns:cor:coding}
One has
\[
 \xiRlo+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil
 \leq\bl(\WO_\alpha(X))
 \leq \xiRup+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil.
\]
If $\xiRlo=\xiRup$, then
\[
 \WO_\alpha(X)\equi \B_{\xiRlo}\times_\lex n!,
 \qquad
 \bl(\WO_\alpha(X))=\xiRlo+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil.
\]
In particular equality holds whenever every residual cardinal is
regular, singular strong limit, or greater than $\kappa$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:capacity} to both sides of the sandwich.  In the
listed cases every lower and upper layer weight agrees.  Ordinal
absorption can also give $\xiRlo=\xiRup$ in additional cases; equality of the
computed ordinals is the precise criterion.
\end{proof}

The distinction in \cref{swo:bw:ns:thm:capacity,swo:bw:ns:cor:coding} is deliberate.
The embedded cube spectrum and the embedded native birthday spectrum
are exact even when $\xiRlo<\xiRup$.  They do not, by themselves, supply an
embedding of the whole order into the shorter upper cube.  The remaining
general-alphabet question is still whether
\[
                    \WO_\lambda(Y)\emb\B_\lambda
\]
holds for every ordered $Y$ of singular non-strong-limit cardinality
$\lambda$.  Neither the present argument nor the earlier residual
analysis settles that question (source~19, \cref{swo:rs:sec:tails}).

\merge\ At $\alpha=\mu$ ($\gamma=1$, $\zeta=0$) the corollary gives
$\xiRlo=\xiRup=\mu$ and $\bl(\WO_\mu(\No_{<\theta}))=\mu$, which is the coding
rank of source~21's \cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal}, there proved by the
finite-alphabet obstruction (\cref{swo:fu:bs:lem:finite-alphabet}) and here by
fusion. The remaining question is source~19's ``remaining coding gap''
(\cref{swo:rs:n14.1}) and source~29's \cref{swo:bw:rq:singular}.

\subsection{A complete classification on the countable birthday band}

\begin{corollary}[Every admissible length, without CH]
\label{swo:bw:ns:cor:countable}
Let $\omega<\theta<\omega_1$, put $\mu=2^{\aleph_0}$, and let
$\alpha$ be any ordinal of cardinality $\mu$.  Write uniquely
\[
 \alpha=\Lambda+n,
 \qquad \Lambda\text{ a nonzero limit ordinal},\quad n<\omega.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
 \WO_\alpha(\No_{<\theta})&\equi \B_\Lambda\times_\lex n!,\\
 \bl(\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\theta}))
       &=\Lambda+\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil.
\end{align*}
Its embedded cubes have exactly the lengths
\[
 \beta\leq\Lambda+\lfloor\log_2(n!)\rfloor,
\]
and its embedded birthday alphabets have exactly the bounds
\[
 \nu\leq\Lambda+\lfloor\log_2(n!+1)\rfloor.
\]
The same statements hold for any noninitial $\theta$ with
$\card\theta<\aleph_\omega$, using $\mu=2^{\card\theta}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a countable noninitial cutoff, $\kappa=\omega$.  There is no
singular cardinal at or below $\kappa$.  A singular strong-limit
cardinal $\lambda>\kappa$ cannot lie below $\mu$, since strong
limit would give $2^\kappa<\lambda$.  Every residual weight is
therefore just $\lambda_i$, so $\xiRlo=\xiRup=\Lambda$.  Apply
\cref{swo:bw:ns:thm:capacity,swo:bw:ns:cor:coding}.

More generally, every infinite cardinal at or below a fixed
$\kappa<\aleph_\omega$ is one of the regular cardinals
$\aleph_j$ for finite $j$.  Again there is no singular layer at or
below $\kappa$, while no singular strong-limit residual can occur
above it.  The identical computation gives $\xiRlo=\xiRup=\Lambda$.
\end{proof}

For a limit $\alpha$, the corollary simply says
$\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\theta})\equi\B_\alpha$.  A final single
label adds no choice, so type $\Lambda+1$ still gives
$\B_\Lambda$.  A final pair gives two choices and hence
$\B_{\Lambda+1}$.  With three terminal labels one obtains
$\B_\Lambda\times_\lex6$: the largest embedded cube has length $\Lambda+2$,
whereas the least binary coding length is $\Lambda+3$.

At the minimum length $\mu$, the sharp birthday threshold is
$\mu+1$.  Thus this stratum contains an ordered copy of
$\No_{\leq\mu}=\No_{<\mu+1}$ and contains no larger birthday
alphabet.  The $+1$ here is ordinal successor, not the successor
cardinal $\mu^+$.

Finally, \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:strict} shows that the native alphabets at
$\omega+1$, $\omega+2$, $\omega\cdot2$, $\omega^2$, and every
other distinct countable noninitial cutoff are strictly ordered under
order embeddability.  Nevertheless, at each common admissible
enumeration length their permutation orders have the same
equimorphism type.  No continuum hypothesis is used.  Whether these
corresponding permutation orders are actually isomorphic is a finer
question about their cuts and local order structure, not one decided
by the spectra proved here.

\merge\ Two comparisons. (1) The initial-cutoff counterpart is source~30's
\cref{swo:rt:cor:omega-one-all-types-ZFC} (Part~X): at $\kappa=\omega_1$, and
at every initial cutoff $\kappa<\aleph_\omega$, every admissible stratum is
$\equi\B_\lambda\times_\lex n!$ in $\ZFC$, by the equality clause of source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:thm:tail-sandwich} (source~19's own
\cref{swo:rs:cor:tail-regularlayers} states the classification under
$\mu\le\aleph_\omega$). So the cutoffs $\omega_1$ and every countable
$\theta>\omega$ give equimorphic strata of each common length, although
their alphabets are strictly ordered by \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:strict}. (2) By
\cref{swo:fu:bs:thm:noncardinal} the minimal strata ($\alpha=\mu$) at the
countable noninitial cutoffs share coding rank, density, cellularity and point
characters, and their global cofinality $\cf\lambda$ is $\omega$ at each of
them; so no invariant computed in this Part distinguishes the permutation
orders of two countable noninitial cutoffs, while their alphabets are
distinguished by \cref{swo:bw:bs:cor:strict}. Source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:n13.2} asks whether they are isomorphic.

\subsection{Source 23: a taxonomy of what can be ordered}\label{swo:tm:sec:taxonomy}

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.19\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.34\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.39\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Construction & Objects & Logical size and main caution\\\midrule
\endhead
Fixed carrier & Well-orders on a fixed set $X\subseteq\No$; equivalently
bijections $\alpha\to X$ & A set in ZFC. Complete enumerations of the same
carrier cannot be proper prefixes of one another.\\[4pt]
Fixed order type & Bijections $\alpha\to X$ for one ordinal $\alpha$ &
A set; it is nonempty exactly when $\card\alpha=\card X$.\\[4pt]
Variable set carrier & Well-orders on arbitrary set subsets of $\No$ &
An ordinary class, represented by injective ordinal-length words.
Termination affects the order.\\[4pt]
Words with repetition & Arbitrary $p:\alpha\to\No$, with $\alpha$ a set ordinal &
An ordinary class of labelled sequences, but not literally well-orders
on their ranges unless one keeps positions as distinct objects.\\[4pt]
Inherited well-orders & Set subsets well-ordered by the numerical $<$ &
Strictly increasing words. The restriction on continuations is substantial.\\[4pt]
Set-like global orders & Well-orders of all $\No$ with set predecessor
classes & Equivalent to class bijections $\Ord\to\No$; a predicate on
classes, not an ordinary class of all such bijections.\\[4pt]
Raw global orders & All class well-orders of all $\No$, with no set-likeness
requirement & Can have proper-class predecessor segments. Comparison must
not assume an ordinal-indexed first disagreement.\\[4pt]
Increasing class subsets & Class subsets well-ordered by numerical $<$ &
May have non-set-like inherited order. A global increasing enumeration
of all $\No$ is impossible.\\[4pt]
Unlabelled types & Well-orders modulo order isomorphism & Numerical
lexicography does not descend to this quotient.\\[4pt]
Relation codes & Characteristic functions of ordering relations, after
choosing an order of pairs & A different lexicographic order; its dependence
on the pair enumeration must be retained.\\\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

\subsubsection{Enumeration lexicography}

For words $p:\alpha\to A$ and $q:\beta\to A$, compare their first different
letter if one occurs before either word ends. If one is a proper prefix of
the other, compare $\varepsilon$ with the next letter of the longer word. We
write $p<_{\varepsilon}q$ for this order. The termination marker is not an
allowed letter, even if one reserves a numerical label to model it.

End-first dictionary order means $\varepsilon<A$. End-last order means
$A<\varepsilon$. A marker at a genuine class gap need not correspond to any
surreal number. A marker immediately before $a\in A$ has right side with
minimum $a$; immediately after $a$ has left side with maximum $a$.

For injective words the ordinal indexing and the labels determine a
well-order on the range. Conversely, every well-order on a set of labels
has a unique ordinal enumeration. Thus injective words are a representation
of all labelled set well-orders, not an additional choice of enumerations
for the same labelled ordering.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Lemma~2.1, ``No prefix ambiguity for complete enumerations'']\label{swo:tm:lem:noprefix}
\emph{If $p:\alpha\to X$ and $q:\beta\to X$ are bijections and $p$ is a prefix
of $q$, then $p=q$.} Source~23's proof: if $\alpha<\beta$, the next value
$q(\alpha)$ already occurs in $p$, since $p$ exhausts $X$; this contradicts
injectivity of $q$. This is \code{lwo:lem:prefix-free}
(\cref{swo:sw:fixed}; source~15's \cref{swo:cb:lem:prefixfree}).
\end{note}

Consequently none of the termination issues of source~23's Part~I (its
Sections~4--7, printed in \cref{swo:xii:sec:termination,swo:xii:sec:increasing})
changes the lexicographic order of exhaustive well-orders of a \emph{fixed}
carrier. They arise when carriers, or word lengths without exhaustivity, vary.

\subsubsection{Other comparisons really are different}

Shortlex first compares lengths and only then letters. Reverse lexicography
requires a greatest disagreement, which arbitrary infinite words need not
have. It is meaningful on finite words or suitable finite-difference
families, but is not automatically a total order on all ordinal words.
End-last lexicography is also sometimes used in tree orders; changing that
convention changes prefix comparisons, not the numerical order of labels.

For relation-code lexicography, choose a set-like enumeration of ordered
pairs of labels and compare the characteristic functions of the two
relations at the first differing pair. Global choice supplies such an
enumeration for a class carrier. This works even when the relations are not
set-like. It is not the direct enumeration comparison of source~23's
Section~9 (\cref{swo:tm:sec:rawcompare}). A change in the schedule of pairs
can change which disagreement decides the answer.

Finally, singleton words $(a)$ and $(b)$ have the same unlabelled well-order
type for all labels $a,b$, yet $(a)<(b)$ whenever $a<b$. Lexicography cannot
be a comparison on unlabelled types that respects these representatives.
Choosing the ordinal itself as a canonical representative gives a different,
well-defined type order, rather than repairing this failure of descent.

% ---- source 27 (batch-83 manuscript 13), lines 197-341
\subsection{Source 27: a map of the principal interpretations}\label{swo:sc:sec:interpretations}

There are arbitrarily many artificial encodings of well-orders, so no
finite survey can enumerate every possible convention. The following
table covers the structural choices responsible for the main differences.
Once these choices are fixed, a further encoding is a new construction to
be analyzed on its own terms.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.19\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.36\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.38\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Objects & Comparison and size \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule Interpretation & Objects & Comparison and size \\ \midrule
\endhead
Fixed carrier & All well-orders of a fixed set $X\subseteq\No$ &
Compare their ordinal enumerations at the first unequal numerical label.
A set-sized linear order. \\
Fixed type & Bijections $\alpha\to X$, for a specified ordinal $\alpha$ &
A stratum of the preceding order; its type can matter beyond $\card\alpha$. \\
Variable carrier & Injective words of every set ordinal length in $\No$ &
Prefix termination must be specified. An ordinary class of set objects. \\
Increasing subsets & Words strictly increasing in the numerical order &
Equivalent to set-sized numerically well-ordered subsets, with an explicit
termination convention. \\
Global enumeration & Class bijections $E:\Ord\to\No$ &
Exactly the set-like class well-orders; comparison is on class variables. \\
Raw global order & Arbitrary class well-orders on $\No$ &
May have proper-class predecessor segments. Use a common labelled prefix,
not an assumed ordinal enumeration. \\
Relation table & A well-order $R$ viewed as a binary function on pairs &
Requires an independently fixed well-ordered scan of pairs. Its order
need not agree with enumeration lexicography. \\
Unlabelled type & Well-orders modulo order isomorphism &
For set relations the quotient is ordinal type. Numerical-label
lexicography does not descend to this quotient. \\
Model-relative & The preceding objects inside $(M,\mathcal X)$ &
The admitted classes $\mathcal X$, internal well-foundedness, and external
size must all be specified. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

\subsubsection{Fixed carriers and the absence of a termination ambiguity}

For a set $X$, let $\WO(X)$ be all strict well-orders of $X$. Each
$R\in\WO(X)$ has a unique ordinal type $\alpha_R$ and an enumeration
$e_R:\alpha_R\to X$. If $R\ne S$, neither enumeration can be a proper
prefix of the other: a proper prefix that is already onto $X$ leaves no
unused label for a longer injective word. Consequently the common domain
contains a least disagreement $\delta$, and
\[
 R<_{\mathrm{en}}S
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e_R(\delta)<_X e_S(\delta).
\]
This is a strict linear order. The familiar proof of transitivity compares
the two first-disagreement positions for three words; the earlier position
decides, and equal positions use transitivity in $X$.

For an infinite set $X$ of cardinality $\mu$, the repository proves
(\cref{swo:sw:setspectrum}; the reals report)
\[
 \card{\WO(X)}=2^\mu,
 \qquad
 \alpha\emb\WO(X)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \alpha<\mu^+,
\tag{S27.1}\label{swo:sc:eq:background-spectrum}
\]
and the same ordinal spectrum holds in the reverse order. Every linear
order of size at most $\mu$ embeds. These statements do not classify
$\WO(X)$ up to isomorphism, do not imply separability, and do not identify
its relation-table version. Its finite residual tails create adjacent
points and finite blocks: after an agreed prefix leaves $n$ labels,
the possible completions form the finite lexicographic order on $n!$
permutations.

For a fixed type $\alpha$, write $\WO_\alpha(X)$ for the bijections
$\alpha\to X$. Some strata have much greater binary coding length than
others even though their cardinalities coincide. Birthday truncation of
$X$ is another independent parameter. At an infinite cardinal $\kappa$,
$\card{\No_{<\kappa}}=2^{<\kappa}$, but neither a singular birthday bound nor
a noninitial ordinal cutoff should be replaced by its cardinality without
proof. The earlier corpus studies these distinctions extensively; the new
scan results of \cref{swo:sc:sec:tables} illustrate another reason why
cardinality alone is insufficient.

\subsubsection{Variable words and distinct terminators}

If the carrier is allowed to vary, one word can be a proper prefix of
another. Three standard conventions insert a distinct terminal symbol
$\varepsilon$ below every letter, above every letter, or at a cut $X=L+R$.
The last convention means
\[
 x<\varepsilon\quad(x\in L),\qquad \varepsilon<y\quad(y\in R).
\]
Using the numerical value $0$ as an ordinary letter \emph{and} as an
undistinguished padding symbol identifies different words: the empty
word and $(0)$ already have the same zero extension. One must either
exclude $0$ from the alphabet, place a distinct terminator immediately
before or after it, or explicitly pass to the quotient defined by
zero padding. These are different definitions.

Every set-length word is still a set. Hence the class of all such words
does not create a class-of-classes problem. By contrast, a word of length
$\Ord$ is itself a class, and treating all such words as members of one
ordinary class would cross a type boundary.

\subsubsection{Numerical well-ordering is much more restrictive}

Every set-sized subset $A\subseteq\No$ whose inherited numerical order
is a well-order has a unique numerically increasing ordinal enumeration.
This is the increasing-word interpretation studied in
\cref{swo:sc:sec:increasing}. It does not include arbitrary permutations of
$A$. For example, the set $\{0,1\}$ supplies two labelled well-orders but only
one numerically increasing enumeration.

There is no numerically increasing class bijection $\Ord\to\No$,
because its range would make the numerical surreal order a well-order.
There are increasing proper-class subclasses, such as the ordinals.
Such subclasses need not be set-like in their inherited order: take an
increasing copy of $\Ord$ inside $(0,1)$ and append the point $1$.
The final point then has a proper class of predecessors. Thus even in
the increasing interpretation, ``ordinal sequence'' and ``arbitrary
class well-ordered subset'' must be distinguished.

\subsubsection{Isomorphism types discard the lexicographic information}

On a set carrier, every well-order is isomorphic to an ordinal. Two
distinct enumerations of the same order type can compare either way
after relabelling. For instance, $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ on $a<b$ have
the same ordinal type $2$, while the first is lexicographically smaller.
Numerical-label lexicography therefore does not descend to the quotient
by abstract order isomorphism. Ordering the quotient by ordinal type is
perfectly legitimate, but it is an additional, different order.

\subsubsection{The Kanovei--Shelah connection}

The historical connection should be stated precisely. Kanovei and Shelah
use maps $a:\mathfrak c\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ whose ranges are
ultrafilters, ordered lexicographically using characteristic-function
order on $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ \cite{KanoveiShelah}.
Injectivity is not part of that definition. Their construction motivates
the use of ordinal-indexed lexicographic codes without choosing a
well-order of the underlying reals. It does not literally define the
order of all well-order relations on $\mathbb R$, still less a collection
of all class well-orders of $\No$.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 271-408
\subsection{Source 29: interpretations and a disciplined choice of foundations}\label{swo:bw:sec:interpretations}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~2, printed whole: its sign conventions, its
interpretation table, its size ledger with the definition of uniform families
(\cref{swo:bw:def:uniform}), used throughout its later sections, and its
operations on orders. Its $X_\theta$ is printed $\No_{<\theta}$ (for an
arbitrary set ordinal $\theta$, as in source~29) and its product $\otimes_\lex$
is printed $\times_\lex$. Its Subsection~3.3, on relation scans and inverse
ranks, follows at the end; the rest of its Section~3 is printed with its
birthday spectra.

\subsubsection{Signs, birthdays, and numerical comparison}

We represent a surreal number by a sign sequence
\[
 x:\bd(x)\longrightarrow\{-,+\},\qquad \bd(x)\in\Ord.
\]
At the first unequal coordinate, including the possibility that one
sequence has ended, compare with
\[
 -\;<\;\text{termination}\;<\;+.
\]
This is the numerical order. For each set ordinal $\theta$, write
\[
 \No_{<\theta}=\{x:\bd(x)<\theta\}.
\]
It is a set. The union over all set ordinals is the proper class
$\No$. Simplicity is a different relation: one sign sequence is
simpler than another when it is a prefix. It is a tree order and is
not a global well-order scan of the numerical line
\cite{Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}.

The basic interpolation principle is the \emph{set-cut property}
(\cref{swo:n3.1}): if $L,R$ are sets of surreals and $L<R$, then some
$z\in\No$ satisfies $L<z<R$. Empty sides are permitted. Deleting a set of
forbidden labels does not destroy this property (\cref{swo:lem:delete}). One
can choose a separator with birthday larger than the birthdays of all the
constraints and forbidden labels; the inspected Lean foundation develops
precisely this bounded-birthday route \cite{ProveItCutFill,ProveItCuts}. It
follows that $\No$ has no endpoints and every numerical interval between two
distinct points is a proper class. The principle applies to sets of
constraints. It does not fill an arbitrary cut between two proper classes.

\subsubsection{The interpretation table}

The following choices cover the natural readings relevant to this
problem. Altering the coding or comparison rule within one row can
produce still further orders; the parameterized constructions below
make those alterations explicit.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.24\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.37\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.31\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Interpretation & Object being compared & Logical size and decisive choice\\
\midrule
\endhead
Fixed set of labels & All auxiliary well-order relations on a set
$X\subseteq\No$, represented by exhaustive enumerations & A set;
numerical first disagreement.\\[4pt]
Fixed enumeration type & Bijections $\alpha\to X$ for a specified
ordinal $\alpha$ & A set; a stratum $\WO_\alpha(X)$.\\[4pt]
Variable set carrier & Injective ordinal-length surreal words & A class
of sets; termination placement matters.\\[4pt]
Inherited numerical well-order & Increasing words or their numerical
carriers & Set carriers form a class of sets; proper-class carriers
require higher-order treatment.\\[4pt]
Set-like global well-order & Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ & Each is
a class; the whole family is not an ordinary class of GB.\\[4pt]
Arbitrary global well-order & Class well-orders on $\No$, possibly
with proper-class predecessor segments & Direct labelled-prefix
comparison, without assigning set ordinal types.\\[4pt]
Variable class carrier & Class well-orders on arbitrary subclasses
of $\No$ & A higher-order collection; proper-class termination and
prefixes must be specified.\\[4pt]
Relation-table encoding & Characteristic bits of a relation under a
fixed well-ordered scan of ordered pairs & Scan-dependent; differs
from enumeration comparison.\\[4pt]
Inverse-rank encoding & Ranks of labels read in a fixed background scan
& Requires ranks to exist in the selected codomain; reverses some
enumeration comparisons.\\[4pt]
Abstract order types & Well-orders modulo isomorphism, or ordinal
notations encoding them & Labels have been forgotten; numerical
lexicography does not descend to this quotient.\\[4pt]
Universe-relative version & Any of the set constructions inside a
specified set universe or type-theoretic universe & A legitimate bounded
model; changing the universe changes the object.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Free words with repeated labels are useful auxiliary objects, but are
not themselves exhaustive well-orderings of their ranges. Likewise a
surreal sign sequence has a well-ordered domain; this fact does not make
it a well-ordering of the surreal class. These auxiliary encodings
become legitimate only after their comparison and intended interpretation
are stated.

\subsubsection{Theories and the size ledger}

Our set-sized arguments use $\ZFC$ unless a weaker basis is explicitly
given. The native sign-spectrum argument uses only $\ZF$. Our class
arguments use $\GBC$: G\"odel--Bernays class theory with set choice and
Global Choice. All classes have sets as their members. An expression
such as ``for every class well-order $R$'' is a quantification in the
two-sorted language; it does not assert that there is a class whose
members are the class relations $R$.

\begin{definition}[Uniform families]\label{swo:bw:def:uniform}
A family of class relations $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ is \emph{uniform} if one
class relation $F(i,x,y)$ codes all its members. Here the index $i$ is
always a set; its index carrier $I$ may be a set or an ordinary class.
A uniformly set-indexed family has a set index carrier. A class of
set-coded words is an ordinary class because each word is a set.
\end{definition}

This definition prevents a hidden appeal to a class choice principle.
Choosing a class independently for each of a proper class of indices
is stronger than exhibiting one elementary formula defining all rows.
The local back-and-forth constructions used below are uniform in the
latter sense: a tuple belongs to the output exactly when it appears in
the unique deterministic set-length history with the indicated parameters.

A class well-order need not be set-like. We call $R$ \emph{set-like}
when every predecessor segment $\{y:yRx\}$ is a set. Under $\GBC$, a
proper-class set-like well-order has a class enumeration of type $\Ord$.
A class well-order of type $\Ord+1$ has a last point with a proper
class of predecessors and admits no such exhaustive enumeration.
Elementary comparison of two labelled orders remains possible; it is
not the abstract comparability principle studied later.

\subsubsection{Operations on orders}

Write $A\emb B$ for an order embedding and $A\equi B$ for embeddings
in both directions. These notions are strictly weaker than isomorphism
in general. Define
\[
 A\times_\lex B=\sum_{a\in A}B,
\]
so the first coordinate is decisive. A natural number in such a product
denotes its finite chain. The full binary cube is
\[
 \B_\beta=(\{0,1\}^{\beta},<_{\lex}),
\]
with the least unequal coordinate decisive. All products and sums of
\emph{lengths} are ordinal operations. For example,
$2\cdot\omega=\omega$, whereas $\omega\cdot2>\omega$.
This distinction is essential to every coding-length calculation.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 500-524
\subsubsection{Relation scans and inverse ranks (source 29's Subsection 3.3)}\label{swo:bw:sub:scans}

A fixed well-ordered scan $\mathsf s$ of $X\times X$ permits another
lexicographic order: compare the characteristic bits of two relations
at the first scanned pair on which they differ. This is a legitimate
order, but it uses the scan and the chosen orientation of zero and
one. A first differing relation bit need not reveal the first differing
enumerated label. The repository supplies finite counterexamples and
scan-dependent endpoint classifications
(\cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives,swo:cb:thm:tableendpoints,swo:cb:cor:tablepatterns}).

Likewise one may scan the labels and compare their ordinal ranks in
the two auxiliary well-orders. Already on $0<1<2$, the enumerations
$(1,0,2)$ and $(2,0,1)$ compare in that order, whereas their rank vectors
$(1,0,2)$ and $(1,2,0)$ show that the decisive scanned rank need not
be attached to the first differing enumerated label. A reversal is
given by $(1,2,0)$ and $(2,0,1)$: enumeration comparison places the
former first, while the rank of label $0$ is respectively $2$ and $1$.
On arbitrary non-set-like class well-orders, predecessor segments
need not have set ordinal order types, so even the proposed rank
codomain requires a further foundational choice.

These encodings are best treated as named additional structures.
There is no canonical rule converting every such code order into the
native numerical first-disagreement order.

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 235-427
\subsection{Source 30: the interpretations and their foundational levels}\label{swo:rt:sec:interpretations}

There are indefinitely many artificial encodings. The following matrix
organizes the natural independent choices rather than claiming to
enumerate every possible coding.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.20\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.34\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.39\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Version & Objects and comparison & Size and distinction\\
\midrule\endhead
Fixed labelled set $X$ &
Well-order relations on $X$, compared by ordinal enumerations &
A set in ZFC. Numerical order compares labels; it is not the order
being enumerated.\\[4pt]
Fixed type $\alpha$ &
Bijections $\alpha\to X$, by first unequal value &
A set; nonempty iff $\card\alpha=\card X$. Fixing type changes the topology.\\[4pt]
Variable set support &
Injective ordinal-length words in $\No$ &
A class of set codes. Proper prefixes require a termination rule.\\[4pt]
Increasing support &
Words or subclasses well-ordered by native surreal $<$ &
A restriction on the numerical order, not arbitrary labelled well-orders.\\[4pt]
Set-like global orders &
Class bijections $\Ord\to\No$ &
A predicate on class variables in GBC. All have class type $\Ord$.\\[4pt]
Arbitrary global orders &
Class well-order relations on $\No$ &
May have proper-class predecessors and common prefixes.\\[4pt]
Relation-table scan &
Characteristic bits in a chosen well-order of pairs &
Depends on the scan; has a different topology and measurable structure.\\[4pt]
Inverse-rank scan &
Ranks of fixed labels in a baseline list &
Directly defined only for set-like class orders; the baseline is least.\\[4pt]
Type-first or quotient &
Compare types first, or identify isomorphic well-orders &
Type-first changes the primary comparison; quotienting erases labels.
Class types need not be ordinals.\\[4pt]
Universe-relative &
Orders of $\No^{\,u}$ in a larger universe &
A higher-universe set/type; smallness remains relative to $u$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

\subsubsection{Fixed sets and enumeration lexicography}

For a linearly ordered set $(X,<)$ define
\[
\WO_\alpha(X)=\{f:\alpha\to X:f\text{ is a bijection}\}.
\]
For distinct $f,g$ of the same length, compare $f(\xi)$ and $g(\xi)$
at their first unequal coordinate. Every well-order relation on $X$
has a unique ordinal enumeration. For infinite $\card X=\mu$ the union
of these representations over $\alpha<\mu^+$, $\card\alpha=\mu$, is a set,
denoted $\WO(X)$.

No proper-prefix tie occurs between distinct bijective enumerations
of the same set: the shorter one would already have exhausted $X$.
Thus the comparison extends across types without a termination rule.
An order-isomorphism $h:X\to Y$ induces $f\mapsto h\circ f$ on
enumerations. Arbitrary relabellings need not preserve the numerical
comparison at the first disagreement.

\subsubsection{Variable support and termination}

When the range varies, $(x)$ can be a proper prefix of $(x,y)$.
Putting the shorter word first, putting it last, comparing lengths
first, or placing termination inside the alphabet produces
inequivalent orders. The usual surreal sign order uses
$-<\text{termination}<+$. A termination marker below every surreal
entry is not that convention. Identifying a marker with the actual
entry $0$ also destroys injectivity unless an additional distinction
is made.

All set-length words form a legitimate class: every individual word
is a set. The prior reports embed these orders into $\No$ and classify
several termination families (\cref{swo:sw:code,swo:ds:sec:termination}).
Those embeddings do not authorize collecting all proper-class words into
another ordinary class.

\subsubsection{Native order, birthday, and simplicity}

The native surreal order is not a well-order, as witnessed by
$0,-1,-2,\ldots$. Simplicity is the initial-segment partial order on
sign sequences; birthday is an ordinal rank with many ties. Neither
supplies a well-ordered scan of all labels.

Ordering first by birthday and then by a selected well-order of each
layer works under global choice. The existence of each individual
layer order in ZFC does not provide that global selection.
Numerically increasing proper subclasses need not be set-like:
\[
\{-1/(\alpha+1):\alpha\in\Ord\}\cup\{0\}
\]
has numerical order type $\Ord+1$. Its final point has a proper class
of predecessors. This example separates increasing support from
set-like global enumeration.

\subsubsection{Three scans of the same six objects}

For labels $0<1<2$, enumeration order is
$012,021,102,120,201,210$.
Scanning inverse ranks of labels $0,1,2$ gives
$012,021,102,201,120,210$.
Scanning relation bits in the pair order
$(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1)$ with $0<1$ gives
$210,120,102,201,021,012$.
All three are abstract six-point chains, but they put the labelled
objects in different positions. Infinite examples below distinguish
their abstract topological and measurable structures as well.
The accompanying script reproduces these finite comparisons.
(\merge\ The script is \path{code/30-tables-verify_finite.py}; the three
orders are those of source~15's table in \cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives}.)

\subsubsection{Inverse ranks, type-first comparison, and quotienting}

The inverse-rank interpretation deserves a separate definition.
Fix a baseline list $b:\mu\to X$ of a set $X$. A well-order $R$
of $X$ assigns each label its ordinal rank
$r_R(x)=\otp(\{y:yRx\},R)$.
Scan the values
\[
 \bigl(r_R(b(\xi))\bigr)_{\xi<\mu}
\]
and compare them as ordinals at the first unequal coordinate.
This is a linear order on the same set of labelled well-orders,
including comparisons between different order types. It generally
differs from comparing the values in their increasing enumerations.

For the whole surreal class the same definition works for
\emph{set-like} well-orders, using a supplied
$b:\Ord\to\No$. It cannot assign ordinal ranks to a label whose
predecessor class is proper. Its comparison is an elementary
formula on two supplied class graphs; no collection of all rank
functions is required.

The baseline order is the least point for inverse-rank lexicography.
Indeed, if $R$ first disagrees with the baseline at label index
$\delta$, every earlier label has its unchanged rank. The rank of
$b(\delta)$ cannot be below $\delta$, because that rank is already
occupied by an earlier baseline label. It must exceed $\delta$.
In contrast, numerical enumeration lexicography on the full
surreal class has no least point: any proposed first label can be
replaced by a smaller one and the rest enumerated using the supplied
global choice. The endpoint distinction alone prevents an order
isomorphism between these two global interpretations.
(\merge\ This is \cref{swo:cb:thm:inverserank}, source~15's theorem, which
also gives the characters of the inverse-rank order.)

Another convention compares order type first and uses enumeration
lexicography only within a fixed type. For a set $X$ of cardinality
$\mu$, this is the ordinary lexicographic sum
\[
 \sum_{\substack{\alpha<\mu^+\\\card\alpha=\mu}}\WO_\alpha(X).
\]
Every fixed-type stratum is convex in this new order.
Direct first-disagreement comparison across types has no such
priority: with two different types, the first labels can be chosen
in either numerical order. Thus these strata need not be convex
in the original comparison.

Quotienting by isomorphism is a different operation. On a fixed
set it leaves precisely the ordinal types
$\{\alpha<\mu^+:\card\alpha=\mu\}$. Ordering those types by their
ordinal order is legitimate, but is not induced by the labelled
lexicographic comparison: changing representatives can reverse
the comparison of two distinct type classes. On the whole class,
all set-like global orders have type $\Ord$, so their
isomorphism quotient has just one member. Arbitrary global
well-orders include such types as $\Ord+1$ and $\Ord+\Ord$;
they cannot all be replaced by set ordinals. A type-first
construction there needs an explicitly specified class-type
representation and comparison principle in an appropriate
metatheory. The direct common-prefix formula
(\cref{swo:cf:lex}; source~30's Proposition~3.2) avoids that requirement.

\subsubsection{Why a reverse scan is not automatically defined}

On finite words one can compare at the \emph{last} unequal
coordinate. On an infinite well-ordered domain a disagreement
set need not have a greatest member. Two enumerations of a
countable carrier which differ by switching every consecutive
pair disagree unboundedly in $\omega$, so there is no last
coordinate to inspect. A reverse-lexicographic rule therefore
needs an additional restriction or completion convention.
Even eventual agreement is insufficient by itself: a bounded
set of disagreements can have limit order type and no maximum.

These examples are why the article fixes the scan, the label
order, the allowed domains, and the treatment of termination
before proving a lexicographic theorem. Allowing repetitions
adds another independent choice: arbitrary ordinal-length words
are legitimate set codes, but their multiplicities no longer
represent a well-order of their range.

What is printed here is not new against the repository:

\subsection{Small cuts and fresh labels}\label{swo:tm:sec:fresh}

\begin{note}[Source~23, Definition~3.1]\label{swo:tm:n3.1}
\emph{A class linear order $A$ is set-cut saturated if for all sets
$B,C\subseteq A$ satisfying $B<C$, there is $x\in A$ with $B<x<C$. Either set
may be empty. A subset of a class order is cofinal if every point is at most
some member of that subset; coinitial is the dual notion.} This is the
set-cut property $\eta_{\Ord}$ of \cref{swo:n3.1}.
\end{note}

The surreal order has this property: a separated set cut has a surreal
separator. In sign-sequence language, bounding the option birthdays first
supplies a separator at a suitably larger birthday. The repository proves a
universe-relative form in \texttt{SignSequenceCut.lean} \cite{ProveItCutFill}.
We use only the order property, not surreal arithmetic.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Lemma~3.2, ``Two cuts give a fresh separator'']\label{swo:tm:lem:fresh}
\emph{Let $A$ be set-cut saturated. Given sets $B<C$ and a forbidden set
$D\subseteq A$, there exists $x\notin D$ with $B<x<C$. Consequently
$A\setminus D$ is set-cut saturated.} This is \cref{swo:lem:delete}, with the
same proof, for an arbitrary saturated alphabet.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~23).} Choose $z$ with $B<z<C$. Split $D$ into
$D_- =\{d\in D:d\leq z\}$ and $D_+=\{d\in D:z<d\}$.
The sets $B\cup D_-$ and $C\cup D_+$ are strictly separated. Any separator
$x$ of this second cut is above every point of $D_-$ and below every point
of $D_+$, so it is outside $D$ and still separates $B,C$.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Lemma~3.3, ``No small bounds'']\label{swo:tm:lem:large}
\emph{A set-cut saturated class has no set-sized cofinal or coinitial subset.
Every nonempty initial or final segment of it is a proper class.} For $\No$
this is in \cref{swo:lem:delete} and the remarks after \cref{swo:n3.1}.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~23).} A set cofinal subset would have a strict
upper bound by the empty-right-side instance of saturation, a contradiction.
The dual is identical. If an initial segment containing $a$ were a set, its
subset $\{x:x<a\}$ would be a set. Saturating the cut consisting of that
subset on the left and $\{a\}$ on the right is impossible. The final-segment
case is dual.

\begin{lemma}[Deletion preserves the relevant side conditions]\label{swo:tm:lem:delete}
Let $L$ be a nonempty initial segment of $A$ and let $D$ be a set.
If $L$ has no greatest element and has set cofinality $\theta$, then
$L\setminus D$ also has cofinality $\theta$. If $L$ has no set cofinal
subset, neither does $L\setminus D$. If $L$ has a greatest element $a$,
then either $a\notin D$ remains greatest, or $L\setminus D$ has no set
cofinal subset. The dual assertions hold for final segments.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
When $L$ has no maximum, $L\setminus D$ is cofinal in $L$: above any
$x\in L$, first choose $y\in L$ with $x<y$, then choose a fresh point
between $x$ and $y$. A cofinal set in $L\setminus D$ is therefore cofinal
in $L$. Conversely, a set cofinal family in $L$ can be moved point by point
to larger fresh points of $L$, preserving its cardinal bound. This proves
the first two assertions.

If $a=\max L$ is removed and $B\subseteq L\setminus D$ is a set, use
\cref{swo:tm:lem:fresh} on $B<\{a\}$ to find a fresh point between them.
It belongs to $L\setminus D$ and is above $B$.
\end{proof}

We apply these lemmas both to $A=\No$ and to a surreal alphabet with a set
of reserved labels removed. This avoids a hidden injectivity problem in
word extensions: all labels already used by a prefix form a set.

% ---- source 23 (batch-83 manuscript 05), lines 385-462
\subsection{Cylinders and bounded straddling chains}\label{swo:tm:sec:cylinders}

\merge\ Source~23 opens here its Part~I, ``Termination and the geometry of
set-length words'' (its Sections~4--7). It says that a prefix
\emph{crosses} a cut when its cylinder meets both sides, i.e.\ straddles it
in the word of \cref{swo:sub:notation81}; its heading ``Cylinders and bounded
crossing chains'' is printed with that word, and its proofs keep its own.

Fix a marker cut $A=L\sqcup R$. Let $\WordsAll_\varepsilon(A)$ be all
set-length words, and $\Words_\varepsilon(A)$ their injective suborder. For a
word $p$, its cylinder is
\[
 C_p=\{w:p\sqsubseteq w\}.
\]
It includes $p$ itself. Concatenation always means ordinal concatenation;
a suffix after a prefix of length $\alpha$ is reindexed by the order type
of the corresponding ordinal interval.

\begin{lemma}[Convex cylinders]\label{swo:tm:lem:cylinders}
Every $C_p$ is convex. Incompatible prefixes have disjoint, ordered
cylinders. For arbitrary words, $C_p$ is isomorphic to $\WordsAll_\varepsilon(A)$.
For injective words it is isomorphic to
$\Words_\varepsilon(A\setminus\ran p)$, with the induced marker cut.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A word outside $C_p$ either disagrees with $p$ before $p$ ends, or is a
proper prefix of $p$. Its comparison with every member of $C_p$ is decided
by the same letter or the same marker comparison. It is therefore entirely
on one side of the cylinder. Deleting the fixed prefix gives the claimed
isomorphisms. For injective words the suffix must avoid exactly the labels
already used by $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cylinders have no small end cofinalities]\label{swo:tm:lem:cylinderends}
Suppose $L,R$ are nonempty. In either word order every cylinder has no
set-sized cofinal or coinitial subset, irrespective of whether the
termination criterion of \cref{swo:tm:sec:criterion} holds.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
It suffices to work in a residual alphabet $A\setminus D$. Given a set of
suffixes, collect their first letters into a set $F$. Choose a label
$r\in R\setminus D$ and a fresh label above $F\cup\{r\}$.
Its singleton word is above all the suffixes, including the empty one.
For a lower bound choose $l\in L\setminus D$ and a fresh label below
$F\cup\{l\}$. Nonemptiness of both residual sides follows from
\cref{swo:tm:lem:large}. Reattach the prefix.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Crossing-prefix reduction]\label{swo:tm:lem:crossing}
Let $B<C$ be nonempty sets of words in either word order. Define
\[
 T=\{p:B\cap C_p\ne\varnothing\text{ and }C\cap C_p\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
Then $T$ is a set and a chain of prefixes. Its union $p_*$ is a legitimate
set word. Every constraint outside $C_{p_*}$ lies on the correct side of
that cylinder. Either $p_*\notin T$, and at most one constraint side meets
$C_{p_*}$, or $p_*\in T$ and no proper one-letter extension of $p_*$
belongs to $T$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
All members of $T$ are prefixes of words in the set $B\cup C$, so they form
a set. Two incompatible crossing prefixes would give a lower constraint
in the higher cylinder and an upper constraint in the lower one,
contradicting $B<C$. Thus $T$ is a chain. Its lengths are bounded by
\[
 \Lambda=\sup\{\dom(w)+1:w\in B\cup C\},
\]
so its union is a set word. In the injective case two repeated entries in
the union would already occur together in some member of the chain.

If a constraint $w$ lies outside $C_{p_*}$, choose a crossing prefix long
enough to decide the comparison between $w$ and $C_{p_*}$. Such a prefix
exists by the union definition, also when $w$ is a proper prefix of $p_*$.
A constraint of the opposite side extending that crossing prefix forces
$w$ to be on the required side of the entire cylinder. The last two
alternatives follow directly from the definition of $T$ and its union.
\end{proof}

This reduction is particularly useful for formalization. Its tree is a set
of prefixes of the supplied data. It is not a recursion that successively
constructs arbitrary classes, and it cannot run for $\Ord$ stages.

% ---- source 23 (batch-83 manuscript 05), lines 463-564
\subsection{An exact termination-marker criterion}\label{swo:tm:sec:criterion}

\begin{definition}\label{swo:tm:n5.1}
An interior marker cut $(L,R)$ is \emph{admissible} if
\begin{equation}\label{swo:tm:eq:admissible}
\begin{split}
 L&\text{ has a greatest element or has no set cofinal subset},\\
 R&\text{ has a least element or has no set coinitial subset}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here ``interior'' means both $L$ and $R$ are nonempty.
\end{definition}

These are conditions~(1)--(3) of \cref{swo:ds:thm:terminator}.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Theorem~5.2, ``Termination classification'']\label{swo:tm:thm:termination}
\emph{Let $A$ be a set-cut saturated class linear order. The following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the marker cut is interior and admissible;
\item $\WordsAll_\varepsilon(A)$ is set-cut saturated;
\item $\Words_\varepsilon(A)$ is set-cut saturated.
\end{enumerate}
The proof is uniform for the two word orders.} For $A=\No$ this is
\cref{swo:ds:thm:terminator} (source~16).
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~23).} \emph{Necessity.} If $L$ is empty, the empty
word is the least element; if $R$ is empty, it is the greatest element.
Either violates saturation with an empty constraint side.

Suppose $L$ has no greatest element but has a set cofinal family $S$.
The singleton words $(s)$, for $s\in S$, all lie below the empty word.
No word lies strictly between all of them and the empty word: such a word
must be nonempty, its first letter must belong to $L$, and that first
letter is exceeded by a member of $S$. This is already a cut in the
injective suborder. The argument for a set coinitial family in $R$, with
no minimum, is dual. Thus either (ii) or (iii) implies (i).

\emph{Sufficiency.} Fix separated sets of constraints $B<C$. When a side
is empty, \cref{swo:tm:lem:cylinderends} at the empty prefix supplies a
separator. Otherwise apply \cref{swo:tm:lem:crossing} and write $p=p_*$.
For injective words replace $A$ by $A'=A\setminus\ran p$; for arbitrary
words put $A'=A$. \Cref{swo:tm:lem:fresh,swo:tm:lem:delete} show that
$A'$ remains saturated and its induced marker cut is still admissible.

If $p\notin T$, at most one constraint side meets $C_p$. Choose a point
in that cylinder strictly above, or strictly below, the active set of
constraints, as appropriate. \Cref{swo:tm:lem:cylinderends} permits this,
and all outside constraints were already correctly oriented.

It remains to consider $p\in T$. Project each active constraint to its
next symbol after $p$, using $\varepsilon$ for the constraint $p$ itself.
Call the resulting lower and upper symbol sets $S$ and $U$. They are
strictly separated: equality at an actual letter would make the
corresponding child cylinder cross, contradicting maximality of $p$;
equality at $\varepsilon$ would put the same word on both sides.

If neither symbol set contains $\varepsilon$, saturate the cut $S<U$ in $A'$,
choose a strict separating letter $a$, and take $p\cat(a)$.

Suppose next that $\varepsilon\in S$. Set $S_0=S\setminus\{\varepsilon\}$;
$U$ consists of actual letters in the right side $R'$. First choose
$a_0\in A'$ with $S_0<a_0<U$. If $a_0\in R'$, the word
$p\cat(a_0)$ works. Otherwise $a_0\in L'$, so every lower actual symbol
is below $\varepsilon$.

If $R'$ has no set coinitial subset, some $a\in R'$ lies strictly below
all of $U$; then $p\cat(a)$ works. If $R'$ has minimum $r$, either
$r\notin U$ and $r<U$, or $r\in U$. In the first case choose any point
of $C_{p\cat(r)}$. In the second case choose a point of this cylinder
strictly below all upper constraints inside it, using
\cref{swo:tm:lem:cylinderends}. All lower constraints have next symbol at
most $\varepsilon$, and all upper constraints outside this child have next
symbol larger than $r$, so both choices separate the full cut.

The case $\varepsilon\in U$ is the order-dual argument. The marker cannot
belong to both symbol sets. This exhausts the possibilities and proves
saturation in both word orders.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Corollary~5.3, ``Surreal order type'']\label{swo:tm:cor:iso}
\emph{In $\GBC$, when the marker is admissible, both $\WordsAll_\varepsilon(A)$
and $\Words_\varepsilon(A)$ are order-isomorphic to $\No$.} This is the last
sentence of \cref{swo:ds:thm:terminator}, by class universality
(\cref{swo:prop:universal}).
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~23).} Each is an ordinary class of set codes and has
a class enumeration by $\Ord$. Back-and-forth along such enumerations
constructs an isomorphism between any two set-cut saturated proper-class
orders. At each stage the previous partial map is a set, the induced cut is a
set cut, and a fresh separator extends it. Global choice selects the least
available extension in fixed set-like well-orders. These are set-valued
stages, so the resulting class map is obtained in $\GBC$. Apply the
construction to $\No$.

\begin{remark}[What the endpoint exception does]\label{swo:tm:n5.4}
If $\varepsilon$ is immediately before $a\in A$, then the augmented alphabet
has an adjacent pair $\varepsilon<a$. The words do not inherit that adjacency:
there are entire cylinders with first letter $a$, and within them points
below any prescribed set of constraints. This is exactly the minimum case
in the proof. Removing $a$ because it was already used in an injective
prefix changes that side into one with no set coinitial family, by
\cref{swo:tm:lem:delete}. It does not create a new obstruction.
\end{remark}

\merge\ This is the two-letter detour of source~16's proof
(\cref{swo:ds:thm:terminator}), and the reason why its adjacent placements
$0^-$ and $0^+$ give $\No$ in (S16.6) (\cref{swo:ds:eq:centered}).
