\subsection{Exact point characters and examples}\label{swo:tm:sec:characters}

For an interior marker define
\begin{equation}\label{swo:tm:eq:chi}
\begin{aligned}
\chi_-&=
\begin{cases}
\cf(L),& L\text{ has no maximum and has a set cofinal subset},\\
\Ord,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\\[5pt]
\chi_+&=
\begin{cases}
\ci(R),& R\text{ has no minimum and has a set coinitial subset},\\
\Ord,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
When a value is a set cardinal, it is necessarily infinite and regular.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Theorem~6.1, ``Uniform point characters'']\label{swo:tm:thm:characters}
\emph{Every point of $\WordsAll_\varepsilon(A)$ and every point of
$\Words_\varepsilon(A)$ has left character $\chi_-$ and right character
$\chi_+$. The whole orders have no set-sized cofinal or coinitial subset. At
most one of $\chi_-,\chi_+$ can be a set cardinal.} For $A=\No$ the
characters are those computed in the proof of \cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}
(source~16), and the last sentence is its observation that both threshold
sides cannot fail.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~23).} Fix a word $p$. Every element below $p$ that
does not extend $p$ lies below every extension of $p$ whose next letter is in
$L$. Thus the cylinders $C_{p\cat(a)}$, for available $a\in L$, are cofinal
below $p$. The available alphabet is $A'=A$ or $A\setminus\ran p$.

If $L'=L\cap A'$ has no maximum and has set cofinality $\theta$, choose
a strictly cofinal family of letters of size $\theta$. Their one-letter
extensions of $p$ are cofinal below $p$. Conversely, the first appended
letters of any set cofinal family below $p$ must be cofinal in $L'$:
otherwise a child with a larger first appended letter dominates the
family. Hence the left character is exactly $\theta$.

If $L'$ has no set cofinal subset, the same projection argument rules out
any set cofinal family below $p$. If it has maximum $a$, its last child
cylinder $C_{p\cat(a)}$ is cofinal below $p$, and that cylinder has no set
cofinal subset. \Cref{swo:tm:lem:delete} identifies these alternatives
with the cases in \eqref{swo:tm:eq:chi}, including removal of the original
maximum. The right-hand proof is dual.

The assertions about the whole orders are \cref{swo:tm:lem:cylinderends}.
If both characters were small, there would be a set cofinal family
$S\subseteq L$ and a set coinitial family $U\subseteq R$, with neither
side having its endpoint. A separator of $S<U$ in $A$ could belong to
neither side, contradicting $A=L\sqcup R$.

\subsubsection{Principal placements and reserved labels}

A marker immediately before or after any surreal $a$ is admissible. The
side not having its endpoint has no small approach to $a$, by surreal
set-cut saturation. Thus the corresponding arbitrary-word and
injective-word orders are both isomorphic to $\No$.

The reserved-central convention uses alphabet $\No\setminus\{0\}$ and
marker $0$. Neither side has an endpoint or a small approaching family,
so it is another admissible case. This recovers the successful special
case in source~13 (\cref{swo:fs:thm:central}), while the adjacent placements
settle the additional case asked there.
(\merge\ Pinned provenance: at this report's text the adjacent placements are
source~16's (S16.6) (\cref{swo:ds:eq:centered}), and source~13's question is
answered by \cref{swo:ds:thm:terminator,swo:ds:thm:alltermination}; see the
opening note of this section.)

\subsubsection{A regular-cardinal family of failures}\label{swo:tm:sub:failures}

For any infinite regular cardinal $\theta$, let
\[
 L_\theta=\{x\in\No:\exists\alpha<\theta\ (x<\alpha)\},
 \qquad R_\theta=\No\setminus L_\theta.
\]
The ordinals below $\theta$ are cofinal in $L_\theta$. A smaller cofinal
set would give, by choosing ordinal upper witnesses for its members, a
smaller cofinal set in $\theta$. Therefore $\cf L_\theta=\theta$.
Neither side has an endpoint. For example, an endpoint in $R_\theta$
would contradict filling the set cut between all $\alpha<\theta$ and
that endpoint. The right side has no set coinitial subset by the last
argument of \cref{swo:tm:thm:characters}.

Putting the marker at this cut gives point character
$(\theta,\Ord)$ everywhere. Reversing the construction gives
$(\Ord,\theta)$. Distinct regular cardinals yield nonisomorphic word
orders. They remain mutually embeddable with $\No$ under global choice,
as discussed in source~23's Section~8 (\cref{swo:tm:sec:spectra}). Point
characters distinguish isomorphism, not bi-embeddability.

\merge\ This is source~16's threshold $(L_\kappa,R_\kappa)$, with $\kappa$ for
the regular cardinal, and the word orders are $\mathbf T_\theta$ and
$\mathbf T_\theta^{\mathrm{op}}$ of \cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}. Source~16
also shows that every termination order is equimorphic with $\No$ without
global choice (the paragraph after \cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}).

\subsubsection{Genuine two-large-sided gaps}

The criterion also permits a marker at a nonprincipal cut with no set
cofinal family on either side. Such a cut need not be realized by a
surreal. For a concrete example, fix an $\Ord$-long sign pattern in which
both signs occur beyond every ordinal, such as alternation in consecutive
two-position blocks. Compare each set-length sign sequence with this
class pattern at its first disagreement or its end. The resulting cut
has both sides nonempty and has no set cofinal or coinitial family:
any set of sequences has bounded lengths, and a sufficiently long
prefix ending just before a suitable sign lies closer to the pattern.
Its marker therefore produces surreal-isomorphic word orders.

This is not unrestricted cut filling inside $\No$. It inserts a new
symbol in the \emph{alphabet presentation}, then studies an ordinary
class of finite- or transfinite-length set codes built from that alphabet.
The isomorphism in \cref{swo:tm:cor:iso} is a new order map, not an
extension fixing every original numerical label.

\section{Increasing words: no saturating marker, a product at the terminator, and the zero conventions (sources 23, 27 and 29)}\label{swo:xii:sec:increasing}

\merge\ Part~VII left two questions about strictly increasing words open
(\cref{swo:vii:sec:status}, items~(b) and~(d)): the isomorphism type of the
centered order $\WordsInc_c$ (source~18's own question), and increasing words
with an interior terminator at a threshold other than zero (source~16's
question ``Centered increasing words''). Three batch-83 sources take them up
independently. Source~23 shows that no placement of a marker, at zero or
elsewhere, makes the increasing-word order set-cut saturated
(\cref{swo:tm:thm:increasing}); for the threshold at zero this was known from
source~16's remark and source~18's cut classification
(\cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-cuts}). Source~27 factors every increasing-word order at
its terminator (\cref{swo:sc:thm:incfactor}), which reduces the centered
order to a lexicographic product of the shorter-first order of all words
with its reverse (\cref{swo:sc:cor:centeredproduct}), classifies the zero
conventions up to isomorphism (\cref{swo:sc:prop:zerotypes}), shows that no
interval is a surreal interval (\cref{swo:sc:thm:incrich}) and computes the
point characters at an arbitrary class gap
(\cref{swo:sc:prop:gapcharacters}). Source~29 proves the factorization, the
product and the zero conventions again, without knowledge of source~27; its
statements are notes below. Its reduction of every actual threshold, under
each zero convention, and of every gap with two large sides
(\cref{swo:bw:wp:thresholds}) is new as a proved statement; source~27 states
its two simplest cases in a remark. The
three results on thresholds other than zero complement one another; what
remains open is recorded in \cref{swo:xii:sec:status}.

In this section, for an alphabet $D$ (a set or a class, linearly ordered),
$\WordsInc(D)$ is the class of strictly increasing set-length words over $D$,
including the empty word; $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(D)$ and
$\WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(D)$ compare proper prefixes first and last; and for
a cut $D=L+R$, $\WordsInc_\varepsilon(D)$ puts a distinct marker
$L<\varepsilon<R$. Source~27 writes $\operatorname{Inc}_\bot$,
$\operatorname{Inc}_\top$, $\operatorname{Inc}_C$; source~29 writes
$\operatorname{Inc}_{\mathrm{sf}}$, $\operatorname{Inc}_{\mathrm{lf}}$,
$\operatorname{Inc}_{\dagger}$; source~23 writes $\mathcal U_{\mathsf e}(A)$.
$\mathbf T_{\min}$ is the shorter-first order of all set-length surreal
words, repetitions allowed and the empty word included
(\cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}; source~27's $\mathcal B$, source~29's
$\mathbf T$), and $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}=\mathbf T_{\min}\setminus\{\varnothing\}$
(source~27's $D$, source~29's $\mathbf P$). The centered order with zero
excluded is $\WordsInc_c$ (source~27's $J$, source~29's $\mathcal C$); with
zero retained and a distinct terminator immediately below or above it, as in
\cref{swo:sh:wv:adjacent-terminator-all}, the orders are
$\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$ (source~27's $J_-$, source~29's $\mathcal C_-$) and
$\WordsInc_{\dagger_+}$ ($J_+$, $\mathcal C_+$); the zero-padding quotient of
\cref{swo:sh:wv:zero-quotient} is $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}$ ($Q_0$,
$\mathcal C_{\mathrm{pad}}$). \emph{False reading:} $\mathbf T_{\min}$ is an
order of \emph{all} words; it is not $\WordsAll$ with a central marker, and it
is not the order of a binary cube.

\subsection{Source 23: naturally increasing words, a universal obstruction}\label{swo:tm:sec:increasing}

Let $\WordsInc_\varepsilon(A)$ be the suborder of all strictly increasing
set-length words, for a set-cut saturated class alphabet $A$ and a marker cut
$A=L\sqcup R$. It represents exactly the set subsets well-ordered by the
inherited numerical order when $A=\No$.

\begin{theorem}[No fixed marker saturates increasing words]\label{swo:tm:thm:increasing}
For every placement of $\varepsilon$ relative to a set-cut saturated class
alphabet $A$, the order $\WordsInc_\varepsilon(A)$ is not set-cut saturated.
The same conclusion holds after deleting the empty word.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $R$ is nonempty. Choose a strictly increasing sequence
$a_0<a_1<\cdots$ in $R$, and let $p=(a_n)_{n<\omega}$ and
$p_n=p\res n$ for $n\geq1$. Then
\[
 p_1<p_2<\cdots<p.
\]
If a word $q$ were above every $p_n$ but below $p$, it could not disagree
with $p$ at any finite position: disagreement below would put it below a
longer $p_n$, and disagreement above would put it above $p$. Nor could it
end at a finite position. Thus it would properly extend $p$.
But any new letter of a strictly increasing extension is greater than
$a_0$, hence lies in $R$. Such an extension lies \emph{above} $p$, again
a contradiction.

If $R$ is empty, the marker is above every letter. Choose any strictly
increasing sequence $(a_n)$ in $A$. Now
$p<p_{n+1}<p_n$ for all $n\geq1$. A point above $p$ and below every
$p_n$ would have to properly extend $p$, but every proper extension is
below $p$ under the end-last convention. This is impossible.
All displayed constraints are nonempty words.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the arbitrary injective case escapes]\label{swo:tm:n7.2}
For an admissible interior marker, an arbitrary injective extension can
append a fresh letter on either side of the marker, independently of the
numerical values of earlier letters. A strictly increasing extension cannot.
The failure is therefore caused by the inherited-order condition, not by
injectivity or by class size alone.
\end{remark}

Every set ordinal is still realized by a strictly increasing surreal word:
use its ordinal labels. Every set or class linear order embeds into
$\WordsInc_\varepsilon(\No)$ under global choice by first embedding it into
$\No$ (\cref{swo:prop:universal}) and then taking singleton words. Thus
universality can coexist with the explicit countable failures of saturation
just proved.

\begin{note}[\merge; what is new in \cref{swo:tm:thm:increasing}]\label{swo:xii:note:increasing}
For the marker at zero (zero excluded, \(\WordsInc_c\)) the theorem is
source~16's remark at the end of its Subsection~8.1 (printed after (S16.7):
``a positive increasing word of length $\omega$ still has its finite prefixes
cofinal below it'') and the obstruction of source~18's \cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-cuts},
which classifies all unfilled set cuts there; the endpoint placements are
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:wordcharacter}. The theorem is new for every other
placement, in particular for the thresholds other than zero left open in
\cref{swo:vii:sec:status}, items~(b) and~(d): no such threshold gives a
saturated order, hence (by the set-cut property of $\No$) none gives an order
isomorphic to $\No$. It does not classify the unfilled cuts at a general
threshold; source~27's \cref{swo:sc:prop:gapcharacters} computes the point
characters and source~29's \cref{swo:bw:wp:thresholds} the isomorphism type
for gaps with two large sides. Source~23's proof uses only an $\omega$-sequence
in $R$ (or in $A$); it needs neither global choice nor a classification of
the threshold.
\end{note}

\subsection{Source 27: increasing words and an exact split at the terminator}\label{swo:sc:sec:increasing}

\merge\ Source~27's Section~5, printed whole. Its notation is replaced as listed
at the start of this section. Its reference to ``the known local behavior''
of the centered order is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-characters}, and its
reference to the uniform residual isomorphisms of its Section~6 is
\cref{swo:sc:lem:uniformresidual}.

The increasing-word interpretation remembers the numerical order much
more directly than an arbitrary well-order enumeration. Its restriction
also creates a useful factorization that arbitrary words do not possess.

\subsubsection{A choice-free two-part factorization}

For an ordered alphabet $A$, let $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(A)$ and
$\WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(A)$ consist of the strictly increasing set-length
words, including the empty word, with proper prefixes respectively smaller
and larger. If $A=L+R$, write $\WordsInc_\varepsilon(A)$ for the version with
a distinct terminator between $L$ and $R$.

\begin{theorem}[Factorization at a terminal cut]\label{swo:sc:thm:incfactor}
For every set or class alphabet $A=L+R$,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:sc:eq:incfactor}
 \WordsInc_\varepsilon(A)\cong
 \WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(L)\times_{\lex}\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(R).
\end{equation}
The isomorphism is canonical and uses no choice principle.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In an increasing word, the $L$ entries form an initial segment of its
ordinal domain, and all remaining entries lie in $R$. Thus it has a
unique form $l\concat r$. Conversely, every such concatenation is
increasing because all $L$ letters precede all $R$ letters numerically.

If $l,l'$ differ at actual entries, that difference decides the full
words. If $l$ is a proper prefix of $l'$, the next token of
$l'\concat r'$ lies in $L$, whereas the corresponding token of
$l\concat r$ is the terminator or lies in $R$. Therefore the entire
block indexed by $l'$ precedes the entire block indexed by $l$, exactly
as in $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(L)$. At equal $l$, every possible tail letter
is above the terminator, so the tails are compared by
$\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(R)$. This proves both bijectivity and order
preservation.
\end{proof}

The first coordinate in \eqref{swo:sc:eq:incfactor} is primary. The
factorization would fail for unrestricted words, which may repeatedly return
from $R$ to $L$.

\subsubsection{The centered surreal order}

Let $\mathbf T_{\min}$ be all set-length surreal words, with repetitions
permitted and proper prefixes smaller. Let $\WordsInc_c$ be the increasing
words over $\No\setminus\{0\}$, with negative letters below the terminator and
positive letters above it.

The following standard construction, used in the repository
(\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism,swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism}), is worth
making explicit. After any increasing positive prefix, its permissible
next letters form the ray above a set of surreals. After any increasing
negative prefix, its permissible negative letters form the interval
above that set and below $0$. Both fill every separated set cut and
have no endpoints. With a fixed global enumeration, set-state
back-and-forth identifies each such class order with $\No$, uniformly
in the prefix. Recursively applying these child isomorphisms to a
set-length word gives an isomorphism of the corresponding rooted word
trees. Every individual recursion has set length; no class of chosen
class isomorphisms is needed. This argument is justified in greater
detail for residual alphabets in \cref{swo:sc:lem:uniformresidual}.

\begin{corollary}[A product description of the centered order]\label{swo:sc:cor:centeredproduct}
In $\GBC$,
\begin{equation}\label{swo:sc:eq:centeredproduct}
 \boxed{\WordsInc_c\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_{\lex}\mathbf T_{\min}.}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The tree construction identifies $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(\No_{>0})$ with
$\mathbf T_{\min}$. It identifies $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(\No_{<0})$ with the
proper-prefix-larger arbitrary-word order. Coordinatewise negation
identifies the latter with $\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}$: it reverses actual letter
comparisons, and taking the opposite reverses the prefix convention.
Apply \cref{swo:sc:thm:incfactor}.
\end{proof}

This is an explicit isomorphism type in terms of an already studied
word order, not an identification with $\No$. It also applies to a
genuine gap $\No=L+R$ when $L$ has no set cofinal subset and $R$ has
no set coinitial subset: the same admissible-child orders fill all
set cuts. A threshold at an actual surreal point, with that point
excluded, is the simpler special case obtained by translation.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:sc:cor:centeredproduct} answers the first open item of
\cref{swo:vii:sec:status}~(b) in part: it reduces the isomorphism type of
$\WordsInc_c$ to that of $\mathbf T_{\min}$, the endpoint type of source~16's
classification (\cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}). It is consistent with
source~18's \cref{swo:sh:wv:cone-types}: the fibre over an all-negative
prefix is a copy of $\mathbf T_{\min}$ and is the positive-tail part of
that prefix's cone. It does not identify $\WordsInc_c$ with $\No$
(\cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-corollary}), and whether
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$ is isomorphic to
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$ is source~27's Question~12.4.

\subsubsection{What happens when zero is retained}

Different ways of retaining zero need not give different abstract order
types, even though they give different labelled words. Set
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}=\mathbf T_{\min}\setminus\{\varnothing\}$. Splitting at
the first letter gives
\[
 \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\No\times_{\lex}\mathbf T_{\min},\qquad
 \mathbf T_{\min}\cong1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}.
\]
Since $\No+\No$ fills all set cuts and has no endpoints, class
back-and-forth gives $\No+\No\cong\No$. Hence
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$ and
$\mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}$. Splitting $\No$ at
zero also gives
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}
\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}$. In particular
\begin{equation}\label{swo:sc:eq:wordabsorption}
 \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+},\qquad
 \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+},\qquad
 \mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}.
\end{equation}

Let $\WordsInc_{\dagger_+}$ retain zero and place $0<\dagger_+$ below all
positives. Let $\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$ instead place all negatives below
$\dagger_-<0$. Let $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}$ be the quotient of increasing
words by equality of their zero extensions. An equivalence class has a unique
representative obtained by deleting a final zero if one is present; an
internal zero before positive entries remains.

\begin{proposition}[Exact zero-convention types]\label{swo:sc:prop:zerotypes}
In $\GBC$,
\[
 \WordsInc_{\dagger_+}\cong\WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}\cong\WordsInc_c,
 \qquad
 \WordsInc_{\dagger_-}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_{\lex}(1+\mathbf T_{\min}).
\]
The adjacent pairs in $\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$ are exactly
$p<p\concat(0)$ for all-negative prefixes $p$, including the empty one.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $\WordsInc_{\dagger_+}$, the negative-or-zero part is either an
all-negative word $p$ or $p\concat(0)$. In the upper-terminator comparison
these form a consecutive pair $p\concat(0)<p$. Therefore the first factor has
type $\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_{\lex}2$ and the second has type
$\mathbf T_{\min}$. Absorption of $\mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}$ gives the
result.

For $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}$, fix an all-negative prefix. Its reduced tails
occur in three successive forms: empty; zero followed by a nonempty positive
word; a nonempty positive word. Their types are
$1,\mathbf T_{\min}^{+},\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$, giving
$1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}$ for each
negative-prefix block.

For $\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$, the nonnegative tail has three successive parts:
the empty word, the cone beginning with $0$, and the cones beginning
positively. Their types are $1,\mathbf T_{\min},\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$, whose
sum is $1+\mathbf T_{\min}$ by \eqref{swo:sc:eq:wordabsorption}. The first two
elements of this tail order are consecutive. All other comparisons admit
interpolation by a fresh numerical letter, proving the exact adjacency
assertion.
\end{proof}

These isomorphisms do not preserve the original labelled words or their
prefix trees. In particular, a quotient that merges $p$ with
$p\concat(0)$ can have the same abstract order type as a convention
that keeps them distinct.

\merge\ The adjacency clause is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:wv:zero-adjacency};
the isomorphism types are new. They answer, up to isomorphism, the comparison
of the zero conventions that \cref{swo:sh:wv:zero-quotient,swo:sh:wv:adjacent-terminator-all,swo:sh:wv:zero-adjacency}
make at the level of cuts: three of the four conventions have one type, and
the fourth differs from it exactly by the adjacent pairs.

\subsubsection{Every interval is rich, but none is a surreal interval}

For a point $x$ of an order, its left character means the cofinality of
the open initial segment below $x$; its right character is the
coinitiality above it. ``Proper'' below means no set cofinal, or
coinitial, family exists. It is not a cardinal named $\Ord$.

The known local behavior in $\WordsInc_c$ is simple: every right character is
proper; the left character is $\cf(\alpha)$ when a word has positive
entries and nonzero limit length $\alpha$, and is proper for the other
words (\cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-characters}). At a positive limit word,
sufficiently long proper prefixes form a cofinal sequence. For a smaller
family, disagreement coordinates are bounded, so it is not cofinal. At a
successor word, the set-cut property supplies a fresh intermediate last
letter above any specified set of lower competitors.

\begin{theorem}[Convex word cones in every interval]\label{swo:sc:thm:incrich}
Every nonempty open interval of $\WordsInc_c$ contains a convex cone isomorphic
to $\mathbf T_{\min}$. Every such interval contains points of left character
$\lambda$ for every infinite regular set cardinal $\lambda$, and
also points with proper left character. No nonempty open interval of
$\WordsInc_c$ is isomorphic to $\No$, and $\WordsInc_c$ has no convex
suborder isomorphic to $\No$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Given $f<g$, choose a prefix whose comparisons with $f,g$ are already
settled strictly. If their first difference is at actual entries, use
an intermediate letter above the common prefix. If $f$ is a proper
prefix of $g$, the next letter of $g$ is positive; use a smaller
admissible positive letter. If $g$ is a proper prefix of $f$, the
next letter of $f$ is negative; use a larger admissible negative letter.
All these choices follow from the surreal set-cut property.

Append a positive letter if necessary, keeping the comparisons already
settled. The resulting prefix $p$ ends positively. Its entire extension
cone is convex, lies inside $(f,g)$, and has only letters above the
terminator available afterward. The rooted-tree construction identifies
that cone with $\mathbf T_{\min}$.

Append to $p$ a strictly increasing positive tail of length $\lambda$.
The resulting length has cofinality $\lambda$, and the local-character
calculation gives left character exactly $\lambda$. A successor-length
extension gives proper left character. Taking $\lambda=\omega$ gives
a set cofinal below a point inside the interval; this is an unfilled
strict set cut with that point as upper endpoint. Every surreal
interval fills all separated set cuts, so no such interval is
isomorphic to $\No$. Finally, a convex copy of $\No$ would contain
a nonempty ambient interval isomorphic to a surreal interval, which
has just been excluded.
\end{proof}

Each convex cone above contains a copy of $\No$ among its one-letter
tails. Thus every interval contains surreal copies, but these copies
are necessarily nonconvex. Universality and convex realization are
different questions even at this very local level.

\merge\ This strengthens source~18's remark after \cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-corollary}
(every nonempty open interval contains a nonconvex copy of $\No$); the convex
cone of type $\mathbf T_{\min}$ is the positive-prefix case of
\cref{swo:sh:wv:cone-types}.

\subsubsection{Genuine gap thresholds produce additional behavior}

The factorization in \cref{swo:sc:thm:incfactor} works for any class gap
$\No=L+R$. A concise exact local classification records what changes.
Assume both sides are nonempty. Let $\lambda_L=\cf(L)$ if $L$ has no
maximum and has a set cofinal subset, and put $\lambda_L=\mathrm{proper}$
otherwise. Let $\lambda_R=\ci(R)$, allowing $1$ for a minimum and
$\mathrm{proper}$ when no set is coinitial.

\begin{proposition}[Characters at a general terminal gap]\label{swo:sc:prop:gapcharacters}
The order $\WordsInc_\varepsilon(\No)$ has no endpoints, and its characters
are as follows. In the last two rows the word has successor length.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}Xll@{}}
\toprule
Word & Left character & Right character\\
\midrule
All letters in $L$, including the empty word & $\lambda_L$ & $\lambda_R$\\
An $R$ letter occurs; length $\alpha$ is a nonzero limit & $\cf(\alpha)$ & proper\\
$p\concat(\min R)$ with $p$ entirely in $L$ & $1$ & proper\\
Every other successor word with an $R$ letter & proper & proper\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The only adjacent pairs are $p<p\concat(\min R)$ when $\min R$ exists.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Above an all-$L$ word, the first new letter must lie in $R$; its
coinitial possibilities give exactly $\lambda_R$. A least such letter
gives the stated immediate successor. After an $R$ letter has occurred,
a new letter can be chosen above the whole prefix and below every
relevant letter of a given set of upper competitors. Thus the right
character is proper.

Below an all-$L$ word, if $L$ has no maximum and its range is not
cofinal in $L$, the possible new $L$ letters form a cofinal tail of
$L$, giving character $\lambda_L$. If the range is cofinal, its length
is a limit of cofinality $\lambda_L$. Increasing the common-prefix
length and then replacing the next letter by a smaller admissible
one gives a cofinal family of that size; bounded disagreement
coordinates exclude a smaller one. If $L$ has no set cofinal family,
append an $L$ letter above all relevant set constraints instead.

When $L$ has a maximum $m$, a word not yet containing $m$ can move
closer from below through the cone beginning with $m$ and then
arbitrarily large $R$ letters. No set is cofinal in that cone. For
a word ending at $m$, replace its final letter by one below $m$ but
above all earlier and competing set constraints. Its left character
is again proper, which explains why a maximum of $L$ does not give
character $1$ in the first row.

After entering $R$, a limit-length word is approached by its long
proper prefixes, giving $\cf(\alpha)$. At a successor word the only
obstruction to interpolation at its last letter is that this letter
is $\min R$ and the earlier prefix is all in $L$. This is exactly
the adjacent pair already identified. Otherwise include an $R$
letter below the last letter among the lower constraints and use
the set-cut property. The same constructions give a point on each
side of every word, proving the absence of endpoints.
\end{proof}

For a concrete gap let
\[
 L_0=\{x:x<n\text{ for some }n<\omega\},\qquad
 R_0=\{x:n\le x\text{ for every }n<\omega\}.
\]
Here $\cf(L_0)=\omega$ and $R_0$ has no set coinitial subset; a set
of such elements would admit a smaller surreal still above all
integers. Reversing and negating this gap gives a right side of
coinitiality $\omega$. The associated increasing-word order has
points of right character $\omega$, and therefore cannot be isomorphic
to the standard centered $\WordsInc_c$, whose right characters are all proper.
Changing only the character of the distinguished empty word would
not by itself prove nonisomorphism of unmarked orders; the right-character
argument uses the full point spectrum.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:sc:prop:gapcharacters} answers in part the second open item
of \cref{swo:vii:sec:status}~(b) and item~(d): it gives the point characters,
and with them the adjacent pairs, at every interior threshold; with source~23's
\cref{swo:tm:thm:increasing} (no threshold saturates) and source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:wp:thresholds} (actual thresholds and gaps with two large sides
give $\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$) it settles the
isomorphism type except at gaps with a small cofinality or coinitiality on one
side. There, characters distinguish such an order from $\WordsInc_c$, as just
shown, but the general cut classification ``was not proved'' (source~27's
audit), and source~27's Question~12.5 asks for the isomorphism types. The
threshold $L_0$ is source~16's ``natural numbers'' threshold printed before
\cref{swo:ds:thm:alltermination}, and its reverse is source~23's
$(L_\omega,R_\omega)$ of \cref{swo:tm:sub:failures}, there for all words.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 1346-1761
\subsection{Source 29: a canonical product and the zero conventions}\label{swo:bw:sec:increasing}\label{swo:bw:wp:section}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~6, printed whole. It proves source~27's
factorization, centered product and zero-convention types independently; those
statements are notes quoting source~29's formulation, followed by its proofs
as second routes. Its threshold reduction (\cref{swo:bw:wp:thresholds}) and its
explicit absorption identity $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong
\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$ are new; the collapsing clause of
\cref{swo:bw:wp:zero-types}, that identifying the adjacent pairs of
$\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$ gives $\WordsInc_c$, is not stated by source~27. The
threshold reduction is printed as a proposition, since source~27 only remarks
on its two cases.
Source~29's local isomorphisms $\theta_p$ are printed $h_p$, as in the proof of
\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism}; its product $\otimes_\lex$ is printed
$\times_\lex$.

All words in this section have \emph{set ordinal length}. Their entries
may range over the whole surreal class, but each individual word is a
set graph. The resulting word spaces and their products are therefore
ordinary classes of sets. They should be distinguished from collections
whose individual points are proper-class well-orders.

The repository already identifies the shorter-first trees of free,
injective, and numerically increasing surreal words, and determines the
set-cut obstructions for centered increasing words
(\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism,swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism,swo:sh:wv:inc-cuts}).
We use those mechanisms to obtain an explicit product description and to
compare the different treatments of the entry zero up to isomorphism.

\subsubsection{Splitting an increasing word at its terminator}

For a linearly ordered alphabet $D$, let $\WordsInc(D)$ be the set or class
of all strictly increasing set-length $D$-words, including the empty
word. The notations $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(D)$ and
$\WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(D)$ mean that proper prefixes come first and last,
respectively; first unequal entries always compare in the order of $D$.
For orders $A,B$, write
\[
 A\times_\lex B=\sum_{a\in A}B.
\]
Thus the first coordinate is decisive. The notation records an
\emph{ordered} product and makes no commutativity assertion.

Suppose $D=L+R$ is an initial/final partition, and put a distinct formal
terminator $\varepsilon$ between its parts:
\[
                         L<\varepsilon<R.
\]
The word order $\WordsInc_{\varepsilon}(D)$ compares the terminator against
the next entry when one word is a proper prefix of another. Either side of
the partition is allowed to be empty.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Theorem~6.1, ``Canonical factorization'']\label{swo:bw:wp:factorization}
\emph{For any such ordered alphabet and terminator,
\[
 \WordsInc_{\varepsilon}(D)\cong
 \WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(L)\times_\lex\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(R).
\]
The isomorphism is the canonical decomposition into the maximal initial
$L$-word and the remaining $R$-word. For a class alphabet, the statement
uses only elementary class definitions and set operations; Global
Choice is not required.} This is source~27's \cref{swo:sc:thm:incfactor}.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~29).} If $f:\alpha\to D$ is increasing, the indices
at which its entries belong to $L$ form an initial segment of $\alpha$, say
$\beta$. The remaining interval of indices has a unique ordinal order type
$\gamma$. Thus $f$ splits uniquely as
\[
                         f=u\cat v,
 \qquad u\in\WordsInc(L),\quad v\in\WordsInc(R).
\]
Conversely, every such concatenation is increasing because $L<R$.
The domains, restrictions, ordinal tail, and concatenation are sets.
This proves the claimed bijection of carriers.

Consider two pairs $(u,v)$ and $(u',v')$. If $u,u'$ disagree at a
common coordinate, their first unequal $L$-entries decide the comparison
of both concatenated words, independently of their $R$-tails. If $u$
is a proper prefix of $u'$, the next entry of $u'$ belongs to $L$.
At that position $u\cat v$ either terminates or has an entry in $R$.
In either case it is larger. Hence the entire $u'$-fiber lies below the
entire $u$-fiber, exactly as required by longer-first comparison on the
first factor. The reverse prefix case is symmetric.

Finally, when $u=u'$, the tails use only entries above $\varepsilon$.
Their comparison is therefore shorter-first lexicography on $R$.
These cases prove the order identity.

This factorization does not require a numerical bound for the entire
alphabet. In particular, it remains valid when the two sides of the
terminator are proper classes. The theorem applies to set-length
words even when the partition itself cannot be specified by an actual
surreal number.

\subsubsection{The two surreal factors}

Let $\mathbf T_{\min}$ be the shorter-first order of all set-length surreal
words, with repetitions allowed and the empty word included. Put
\[
                         \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}=\mathbf T_{\min}\setminus\{\varnothing\}.
\]
The empty word is the minimum of $\mathbf T_{\min}$. We will use the following
form of the repository's prefix-tree construction, including its
uniformity requirement (\cref{swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism}).

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~6.2, ``Uniform isomorphisms of admissible alphabets'']\label{swo:bw:wp:local-isomorphisms}
\emph{Work in $\GBC$ with a fixed set-like global well-order. Suppose a class
of permitted set words contains the empty word and is closed under
restrictions and unions of coherent set-length prefix chains. Suppose
it has, after each permitted prefix $p$, a proper class $D_p$ of
admissible next letters, giving exactly its permitted one-letter
extensions. Assume these classes are uniformly defined from $p$ and fixed
class parameters, and each fills every separated set cut, including cuts
with an empty side. Then its ordered prefix tree is isomorphic to the free
surreal-word tree, preserving word lengths, prefixes, and comparison of first
unequal entries. The same tree isomorphism preserves either shorter-first or
longer-first comparison.} This is the construction of
\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism} (source~16) and
\cref{swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism} (source~18), stated for an arbitrary
uniformly given family of admissible alphabets; source~27 uses it in the
proof of \cref{swo:sc:cor:centeredproduct} and states the residual case as
\cref{swo:sc:lem:uniformresidual}.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~29).} For each prefix $p$, construct an increasing
bijection $h_p:\No\to D_p$ by deterministic back-and-forth. Restrict the
fixed global well-order to the two alphabets. At each ordinal stage,
map the least unused point on the source side to the least unused
point in the cut required by the current partial map, and then do the
reverse insertion. The partial map and all cut constraints at a set
ordinal stage are sets. Set-cut filling supplies each insertion.

This construction is uniform: membership in $h_p$ is expressed
by existence of a set-length initial history of the deterministic
construction. The parameters of that assertion are $p$, the fixed
class definitions, and the global well-order. One elementary class
relation therefore gives all $h_p$ simultaneously. There is no
independent choice of a class isomorphism for each prefix.

Given a free source word $f$, construct a permitted target word $g$
by ordinary set recursion,
\[
                 g(\xi)=h_{g\res\xi}(f(\xi)).
\]
The inverse uses $h_{g\res\xi}^{-1}$ at each coordinate.
Thus this is a length-preserving bijection of the two word trees.
A shared source prefix gives a shared target prefix, and the same
increasing letter map acts at the first unequal coordinate. This
preserves first-entry comparisons. Prefix comparisons are preserved
for either of the two specified conventions.

The lemma applies to increasing words over each half of the surreal
line. After a negative prefix $p$, the admissible negative alphabet is
\[
               D_p^-=\{x:\ran(p)<x<0\}.
\]
For separated sets $A<B$ in this alphabet, add $\ran(p)$ to the lower
constraints and $0$ to the upper constraints. The surreal set-cut
property supplies another point of $D_p^-$. The same argument handles
an empty side. For positive prefixes the admissible alphabet is
\[
               D_p^+=\{x:\{0\}\cup\ran(p)<x\};
\]
add $\{0\}\cup\ran(p)$ to the lower constraints. These classes are
proper: if one were a set, its own elements could be placed on one
side of a cut that would require a point beyond all of them in that
same class.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Corollary~6.3, ``The centered increasing-word product'']\label{swo:bw:wp:centered-product}
\emph{Let $\WordsInc_c$ be the order of strictly increasing set-length words
over $\No\setminus\{0\}$, with
\[
                    \No_{<0}<\dagger<\No_{>0}.
\]
In $\GBC$,
$\WordsInc_c\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$.} This is
source~27's \cref{swo:sc:cor:centeredproduct}.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~29).} By \cref{swo:bw:wp:local-isomorphisms},
$\WordsInc_{\mathrm{sf}}(\No_{>0})\cong\mathbf T_{\min}$.
The same lemma identifies longer-first increasing negative words with
longer-first \emph{free} surreal words. On free words, entrywise
negation reverses comparison of unequal entries and converts a
longer-first comparison into the reverse of a shorter-first comparison.
Consequently
\[
                 \WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(\No_{<0})\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}.
\]
Apply \cref{swo:bw:wp:factorization}. Passing first to free words is essential:
negating an increasing word directly gives a decreasing word.

The factorization explains the two kinds of cones already isolated in
the repository (\cref{swo:sh:wv:cone-types}). An all-negative prefix still
allows both a negative part and a positive part. Once a positive entry has
occurred, only the shorter-first positive-tail factor remains. The product is
an explicit description in previously studied orders. It does not by
itself assert that its displayed factors or fibers can be recovered
from the pure linear order.

\subsubsection{Absorption in the dictionary order}

Some useful ordered-sum identities make the zero conventions much
closer up to isomorphism than their definitions suggest.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~6.4, ``Dictionary absorption'']\label{swo:bw:wp:absorption}
\emph{In $\GBC$,
\begin{gather*}
 \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\No\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min},
 \qquad \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+},\\
 \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+},
 \qquad \mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}.
\end{gather*}}
Three of the four identities are source~27's (\cref{swo:sc:eq:wordabsorption}
and the display before it); the third is equivalent to source~27's
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$, since
$\mathbf T_{\min}=1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~29).} Every nonempty free word splits into its first
letter and its tail, so $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\No\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$.
The two-copy sum $\No+\No$ fills every set cut and has no endpoints. For
example, if lower constraints enter the second copy, interpolate there; if
upper constraints enter the first, interpolate there. In the remaining case
all lower constraints are in the first copy and all upper constraints in the
second, and one can choose in the second copy below its set of upper
constraints. Empty sides cause no problem. Class back-and-forth in $\GBC$
therefore gives $\No+\No\cong\No$, and hence
\[
       \mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong(\No+\No)\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}.
\]

Now split $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$ at the one-letter word $q=\langle0\rangle$.
The part below $q$ consists exactly of the words with negative first
letter, and has type $\No_{<0}\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$.
The part above $q$ consists of the nonempty tails in the zero cone,
followed by the words with positive first letter. Each part has type
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$, so their sum has type $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$ by the
identity just proved. Splitting at $q$ thus gives
$\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$.
Finally $\mathbf T_{\min}=1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$, whence
\[
       \mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}=1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}
       \cong1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}=\mathbf T_{\min}.
\]
All products and ordered sums here have set-coded points.

In particular, the proper-class boundary between two copies of
$\No$ does not contradict set-cut saturation: no set is cofinal in
the first copy or coinitial in the second. The proof never treats
those entire copies as set-sized cut constraints.

\subsubsection{An exact comparison of the zero conventions}

Retaining zero as an actual entry requires a choice in addition to
saying that termination is centered. We compare the following four
orders, always using strictly increasing set-length words:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 \WordsInc_c:
   &\text{zero excluded, with termination in its place};\\
 \WordsInc_{\dagger_+}:
   &\No_{<0}<0<\dagger_+<\No_{>0};\\
 \WordsInc_{\dagger_-}:
   &\No_{<0}<\dagger_-<0<\No_{>0};\\
 \WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}:
   &\text{zero padding, with equal padded words identified}.
\end{array}
\]
The distinct terminators in the middle two cases are formal symbols,
not additional numerical entries. In the last case every word is
extended by zero at all later ordinal coordinates and comparison is
at the first unequal coordinate. On the original words this is a
preorder; taking the indicated quotient is necessary.

For increasing words, a canonical padded representative is obtained
by removing a terminal zero when one is present. Such a zero can only
follow negative entries. No other terminal zero tail is possible in a
strictly increasing word. Equality after padding is exactly equality
of these reduced representatives, so the quotient has an ordinary
class of set representatives.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Theorem~6.5, ``The zero-convention isomorphism types'']\label{swo:bw:wp:zero-types}
\emph{In $\GBC$,
\[
 \WordsInc_c\cong\WordsInc_{\dagger_+}\cong\WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}
       \cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min},
 \qquad
 \WordsInc_{\dagger_-}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_\lex(2+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}).
\]
The first three orders are dense without endpoints. The adjacent pairs
of $\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$ are exactly
\[
                 u<u\cat\langle0\rangle,
                 \qquad\ran(u)<0.
\]
The empty word is allowed for $u$. Collapsing these two-point intervals
and leaving every other point alone gives an order isomorphic to
$\WordsInc_c$.} The isomorphism types and the adjacent pairs are source~27's
\cref{swo:sc:prop:zerotypes} (with $1+\mathbf T_{\min}=2+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$);
the adjacent pairs are also source~18's \cref{swo:sh:wv:zero-adjacency}.
Density without endpoints and the collapsing clause are proved only here.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~29).} Put
$A=\WordsInc_{\mathrm{lf}}(\No_{<0})\cong\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}$.
Nonempty increasing positive words have type $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$, because the
prefix-tree isomorphism used in \cref{swo:bw:wp:centered-product} fixes the
empty root. We examine the fibers over a negative word $u$.

For $\WordsInc_{\dagger_+}$, the initial nonpositive word is uniquely either
$u\cat\langle0\rangle$ or $u$. Under longer-first comparison they occur
in exactly that order. Each has an arbitrary increasing positive tail,
including an empty tail, so each contributes a copy of $\mathbf T_{\min}$.
The fiber over $u$ consequently has type
$\mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\mathbf T_{\min}$.
The order of different negative prefixes is $A$, by the same comparison
as in \cref{swo:bw:wp:factorization}. Thus
$\WordsInc_{\dagger_+}\cong A\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$.

For $\WordsInc_{\mathrm{pad}}$, a reduced representative with negative
prefix $u$ either stops there, has zero followed by a nonempty positive
word, or has a nonempty positive word immediately. These three parts
occur in the displayed order: after $u$, zero agrees with padded
termination, and the next positive entry makes the zero-containing
word larger than the reduced root; an immediate positive entry is
larger still at the earlier coordinate. The fiber therefore has type
\[
                     1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}=\mathbf T_{\min}.
\]
This proves the padded-quotient assertion.

For $\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$, the fiber over $u$ consists, in order, of the root
$u$ itself; the entire cone beginning with $u\cat\langle0\rangle$;
and the nonempty tails whose first new entry is positive. The middle
cone has type $\mathbf T_{\min}$, including its root. Thus the fiber is
\[
                  1+\mathbf T_{\min}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}
                   =2+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}\cong2+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}.
\]
This proves the second product formula.

The order $\mathbf T_{\min}$ is dense: between different first entries choose
an intermediate entry, and between a proper prefix and an extension
choose a first new entry smaller than that of the extension. It has
no greatest point because every word has a proper extension.
Its reverse has no least point. Hence $A\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$ is dense
without endpoints, including at comparisons involving different fibers.

In a $\WordsInc_{\dagger_-}$ fiber, the first two points are adjacent. There is
no point between $u$ and $u\cat\langle0\rangle$: an extension of $u$
whose next entry is positive exceeds the latter, and an extension
whose next entry is negative is below $u$. Any continuation after the
zero also exceeds the latter. The remaining parts of the fiber are
dense, and the second point is followed by a copy of $\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$
with no least point. Different fibers have infinitely many points between
them, since their index order $A$ is dense. There are consequently no
other adjacent pairs and no larger finite-interval blocks.

Collapsing the initial two points of each fiber replaces
$2+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}$ by $1+\mathbf T_{\min}^{+}=\mathbf T_{\min}$ and keeps
the index $A$. The quotient is therefore
$A\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}\cong\WordsInc_c$. One can implement it by
retaining the smaller representative of each adjacent pair; no class of
proper-class equivalence classes is introduced.

The original presentations thus give two types among these four
conventions. The distinction caused by a terminator immediately below
zero survives in the pure order through adjacency. In the other
three cases, the different presentations can be absorbed by the
ordered-sum identities of \cref{swo:bw:wp:absorption}. The isomorphisms are
not assertions that the original words, their entries, or their
negative-prefix fibers are identified pointwise.

\subsubsection{Numerical thresholds and genuine remaining parameters}

\begin{proposition}[Threshold reductions]\label{swo:bw:wp:thresholds}
For every actual surreal $c$, the conventions centered at $c$ transfer
to the corresponding conventions at zero by entrywise translation
$x\mapsto x-c$. This includes deletion of the entry $c$, either
adjacent distinct terminator, and padding by $c$ with its quotient.

More generally, suppose $\No=L+R$ is a partition into nonempty
classes, $L$ has neither a greatest member nor a set cofinal subset,
and $R$ has neither a least member nor a set coinitial subset.
The increasing-word order with terminator at this cut is, in $\GBC$,
isomorphic to $\mathbf T_{\min}^{\op}\times_\lex\mathbf T_{\min}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Translation preserves and reflects numerical inequalities, preserves
strict increase, and sends $c$ to zero. It also sends padding by $c$
to zero padding. All first-disagreement and termination comparisons
are therefore preserved.

For the second assertion, each of $L,R$ fills every separated set
cut relative to itself. For instance, a cut in $L$ with a nonempty
upper side can be filled in $\No$ and its filler lies in $L$; when
the upper side is empty, the absence of a set cofinal subset provides
a point above the lower constraints. The argument for $R$ is dual.
After a set increasing prefix in $L$, its remaining upper part is
still proper and set-cut saturated, by adding that prefix to the
lower constraints. The same holds in $R$. Apply
\cref{swo:bw:wp:local-isomorphisms,swo:bw:wp:factorization}.
\end{proof}

An actual numerical threshold is therefore not an additional
isomorphism parameter. Nor are the two large sides of a nonprincipal
class gap, under the stated hypotheses. A nonprincipal cut with a
one-sided \emph{set} cofinality or coinitiality is different: a set
increasing prefix can then exhaust the available room on one side.
The canonical factorization still holds, but the saturated-alphabet
identifications used above need not apply. This is the remaining
threshold issue; the proof does not transfer the repository's complete
free-word termination classification to increasing words.

Finally, $\WordsInc_c$ is not isomorphic to $\No$. The positive word
$\langle1,2,3,\ldots\rangle$ is the supremum of its finite prefixes
in $\WordsInc_c$: any smaller word disagrees earlier in the smaller
direction or is one of its proper prefixes. Such a nontrivial set
supremum cannot occur in $\No$, since a surreal set cut inserts a
point above the given set and below its proposed supremum. The product
formula retains this obstruction rather than removing it.

\merge\ The last paragraph is the proof of \cref{swo:sh:wv:inc-corollary}
(source~18). The second assertion of \cref{swo:bw:wp:thresholds} is the case of
\cref{swo:sc:cor:centeredproduct} that source~27 states in the paragraph after
it (``It also applies to a genuine gap \ldots''); source~29 proves it, and
extends the translation remark there to all four zero conventions.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 1762-1990
\section{Numerically well-ordered proper-class carriers (source 29)}\label{swo:xii:sec:carriers}\label{swo:bw:sec:numerical-classes}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~7, printed whole; no other source proves its
results. Its comparison of carriers by the least point of the symmetric
difference (\cref{swo:bw:nc:union} and the display after it) is source~15's
characteristic comparison $<_\chi$, printed before \cref{swo:cb:prop:hahn},
where it is stated for sets and classes alike; source~29's longer-first order
$\prec_{\mathrm{lf}}$ is $<_\chi$. The example of a numerically increasing
class of type $\Ord+1$ printed after \cref{swo:cb:prop:hahn} is the case $b=0$
of \cref{swo:bw:nc:every-jump}. New are the adjacency theorem, the two-point
blocks, longer-first density, the cofinal representatives and the
tree non-isomorphism (\cref{swo:bw:nc:adjacency,swo:bw:nc:blocks,swo:bw:nc:longer-dense,swo:bw:nc:cofinal,swo:bw:nc:no-tree-extension}).
Source~29 cites source~19 (its ``EarlierResidual'') for the mention of this
interpretation; the batch-81 maps make it as well (\cref{swo:vii:sec:maps}).

The preceding word constructions use set ordinal lengths. We now admit
all available subclasses of $\No$ that are well-ordered by their inherited
numerical order. Such a carrier need not be set-like, and no set ordinal
enumeration is assumed. This interpretation is mentioned in the earlier
project reports, but its proper-class adjacency behavior is different
from the set-word case.

All assertions in this section are made in $\GBC$ about individual
class parameters, uniformly coded families, or the external collection
belonging to a specified class model. We do not form a GB class whose
members are these proper-class carriers.

\subsection{Comparison without an abstract class ordinal}

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~7.1]\label{swo:bw:nc:union}
\emph{The union of finitely many numerically well-ordered class carriers is
numerically well-ordered. Distinct such carriers $A,B$ have a least
point $d$ of $A\mathbin\triangle B$, and
\[
 C=A\cap(-\infty,d)=B\cap(-\infty,d)
\]
is their common initial segment.} The first two assertions are source~15's
paragraph before \cref{swo:cb:prop:hahn}.
\end{note}

\emph{Second route (source~29).} For a nonempty subclass of a finite union,
intersect it with each carrier for which the intersection is nonempty and take
the smallest of their finitely many least points. This proves the first
assertion and applies in particular to the symmetric difference. Below its
least point the carriers agree. Their inherited numerical relations
agree there automatically.

If both carriers have a point after $C$, compare their least such
points numerically. If one carrier is exactly $C$, a prefix convention
is necessary. Denote the shorter-first order by $\prec_{\mathrm{sf}}$ and
the longer-first order by $\prec_{\mathrm{lf}}$. The latter has the
particularly simple expression
\[
 A\prec_{\mathrm{lf}}B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \min(A\mathbin\triangle B)\in A.
\]
It is characteristic-function lexicography with the bit order $1<0$,
but its scan is the well-ordered union of the carriers being compared,
not the whole numerical surreal line. Transitivity follows by comparing
first differences in the union of three carriers. The shorter-first
version reverses proper-prefix pairs and uses the same genuine
first-difference comparisons.

\subsection{Exact adjacency at an unattained supremum}

For a numerical carrier $A$, define its class of possible next labels by
\[
 U(A)=\{x\in\No:\forall a\in A\ (a<x)\}.
\]
If $A$ is a set, $U(A)$ has no least point by the set-cut property.
For a proper-class $A$, it can have one. (\merge\ For a set $A$ this is the
class $U(q)$ of admissible next letters in the proof of
\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism}.)

\begin{theorem}[Proper-class adjacency]\label{swo:bw:nc:adjacency}
Two numerical well-ordered carriers $A\prec_{\mathrm{sf}}B$ are adjacent
if and only if
\[
 B=A\cup\{b\},\qquad b=\min U(A).
\]
Equivalently, $b$ is a numerical supremum of $A$ that does not belong
to $A$. In every such pair, $A$ is a proper class and has no greatest
member.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose first that there is a genuine mismatch after the shared
initial segment $C$, with next points $a<b$. Numerical density gives
$a<c<b$. The carrier $C\cup\{c\}$ is numerically well-ordered and
lies strictly between the two given carriers. This argument remains
valid when $C$ is a proper class: adjoining one point above all its
members preserves well-ordering.

Thus an adjacent pair must have $A$ as a proper initial segment of
$B$. Let $b$ be the least point of $B\setminus A$. If the remainder
has more than one point, $A\cup\{b\}$ lies strictly between $A$ and
$B$. If some $c\in U(A)$ satisfies $c<b$, then $A\cup\{c\}$ lies
strictly between them as well. Necessity follows.

Conversely, suppose $B=A\cup\{b\}$ with $b=\min U(A)$. A carrier
strictly between $A$ and $B$ must extend $A$: an earlier numerical
divergence puts it on the same side of both, and a proper prefix of
$A$ lies below $A$. Its first new label $c$ belongs to $U(A)$.
If $c>b$, it lies above $B$; if $c=b$, it is $B$ or extends $B$ and
again cannot lie strictly between. The case $c<b$ is impossible.

If $A$ had a greatest member $a$, density would supply an upper bound
strictly between $a$ and $b$, contrary to the minimality of $b$.
Thus the least strict upper bound is exactly an unattained supremum.
If $A$ were a set, the cut $(A,\{b\})$ would have a surreal filler,
giving the same contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A jump over every surreal]\label{swo:bw:nc:every-jump}
For every $b\in\No$, put
\[
 A_b=\left\{b-\frac1{\alpha+1}:\alpha\in\Ord\right\},
\]
where the ordinal values are embedded in $\No$ and the arithmetic is
surreal arithmetic. This is an increasing class of numerical type
$\Ord$, and it is cofinal below $b$. Indeed, if $x<b$, choose an
ordinal $\alpha$ with $\alpha+1>1/(b-x)$. Then
$x<b-1/(\alpha+1)<b$. Consequently
\[
 A_b\prec_{\mathrm{sf}}A_b\cup\{b\}
\]
is an adjacent pair. The upper carrier has type $\Ord+1$.
The example is uniform in the set parameter $b$.
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}\label{swo:bw:nc:blocks}
Every nontrivial adjacency component in the shorter-first numerical
class-carrier order has exactly two members. Contracting these pairs
gives a dense order with a minimum, in an external collection or in
any appropriate higher-order formulation.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
An upper member of a jump has a greatest numerical point. A lower
member has none. Hence one carrier cannot be both the upper member
of one jump and the lower member of another. If two different
contracted blocks had no block between them, their facing endpoints
would be adjacent and would have belonged to the same block.
The empty carrier remains least.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Longer-first density]\label{swo:bw:nc:longer-dense}
The longer-first numerical class-carrier order is dense and has the
empty carrier as its greatest element. Therefore the full shorter-first
and longer-first orders are neither isomorphic nor anti-isomorphic.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A genuine mismatch is interpolated exactly as in
\cref{swo:bw:nc:adjacency}. Otherwise $B$ is a proper initial segment of $A$
and $A\prec_{\mathrm{lf}}B$. Let $a$ be the first point of $A\setminus B$.
If the remainder contains more points, the carrier $B\cup\{a\}$
lies strictly between. If it does not, choose any $c>a$.
It is still above every member of $B$, and
\[
 A=B\cup\{a\}\prec_{\mathrm{lf}}B\cup\{c\}\prec_{\mathrm{lf}}B.
\]
This proves density. The empty carrier is a prefix of all carriers
and is greatest under longer-first comparison. Density is preserved
by both isomorphism and reversal; the shorter-first jumps therefore
exclude either identification.
\end{proof}

\merge\ For set carriers, \cref{swo:cb:prop:hahn} (source~15) embeds the
longer-first order into $\No$; source~15 remarks that the construction does not
admit proper-class supports. \Cref{swo:bw:nc:adjacency,swo:bw:nc:longer-dense}
show what changes at proper-class carriers: the shorter-first order acquires
adjacent pairs, which no set-length word order of
\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism} has, while the longer-first order stays
dense.

\subsection{Every final class segment can occur after a prefix}

\begin{theorem}[Cofinal numerical representatives]\label{swo:bw:nc:cofinal}
Let $L$ be an initial subclass of the numerical surreal line and let
$U=\No\setminus L$. In $\GBC$ there is a numerically well-ordered
subclass $A\subseteq L$, cofinal in $L$, such that
\[
 U(A)=U.
\]
The carrier $A$ can be a set exactly when $L$ has a set cofinal
subset. If no such set exists, $A$ can be chosen as the range of an
increasing class map $\Ord\to L$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The empty $L$ is handled by $A=\varnothing$. Otherwise fix a class
bijection $e:\Ord\to\No$. Construct an increasing sequence, stopping
permanently as soon as its earlier range is cofinal in $L$.
At stage $\alpha$, its earlier range $S$ is a set. If it is not
cofinal, some point of $L$ is strictly above every member of $S$.
Choose, by the $e$-scan, the least candidate $y\in L$ satisfying
\[
 S<y,
 \qquad e(\alpha)\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ e(\alpha)\le y.
\]
Such a candidate exists: take the larger of the available strict
upper bound and $e(\alpha)$ when the latter belongs to $L$.
Each step is a set-valued elementary recursion. A permanent stop
flag can be included in the state, and the class construction is
defined by its set-length histories. No recursion with class-valued
slices is involved.

If the process stops, its range is set-sized and cofinal. If it
does not, the resulting increasing class sequence is cofinal because
every point $x=e(\alpha)\in L$ is passed at its scan stage. Its range
is numerically well-ordered, being isomorphic to $\Ord$.
If $L$ has a set cofinal subset $C$, the set of indices $e^{-1}[C]$
is ordinal-bounded. After that bound all of $C$ has been passed, so
the construction stops. The converse is immediate.

Finally, every point outside $L$ is strictly above $A$, while every
point of $L$ is at most some member of $A$. Thus $U(A)=U$.
\end{proof}

This theorem describes the precise failure of a set-prefix argument
at class length. After a set increasing prefix, the next-letter
order has the full set-cut property. After a proper-class prefix,
it can be any final class segment: empty, with a least point, with a
set coinitial sequence, or with no such sequence. A uniform tree
isomorphism that relied on the same saturated successor alphabet
at every set node cannot simply be continued through every class node.

\subsection{A direct obstruction to extending the set-tree isomorphism}

\begin{theorem}\label{swo:bw:nc:no-tree-extension}
In $\GBC$, the virtual prefix tree of all auxiliary class well-orders
on arbitrary surreal subclasses is not isomorphic to the corresponding
tree of inherited numerical class well-orders. In particular, the
isomorphism between injective and increasing \emph{set-length} word
trees (\cref{swo:ds:thm:wordisomorphism,swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism}) cannot
extend to an isomorphism of these full class-carrier trees.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An immediate extension in either tree appends exactly one unused
label. Global Choice provides an auxiliary class well-order of
$\No\setminus\{z\}$. As a node of the full auxiliary tree, it has
exactly one immediate extension, obtained by appending $z$.

In the numerical tree the immediate extensions of $A$ are indexed
by $U(A)$. This class is either empty or a proper class: with any
$x\in U(A)$ it contains every larger surreal. Thus no numerical
node has exactly one immediate extension. A tree isomorphism would
preserve that property, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The proof can be read as a two-sorted assertion about any proposed
uniform map, or as an ordinary external set-theoretic argument in a
specified class model. It does not require a GB class of all nodes.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:bw:nc:no-tree-extension} limits the word isomorphisms of
Part~VII in length, not in choice: it does not bear on the question of
sources~16 and~18, recorded at the end of \cref{swo:vii:sec:status}, whether
they survive without a global well-order.

\section{Relation-table lexicography: spectra, scans, extensions and density (sources 27 and 30)}\label{swo:xii:sec:tables}

Two batch-83 sources continue this line.
\begin{itemize}

Source~27's scan $q:\theta\to X\times X$ is printed $\mathsf s:\vartheta\to
