% ---- source 27 (batch-83 manuscript 13), lines 475-761
\subsection{Source 27: six delayed comparisons change the topology}\label{swo:sc:sec:tables}

Relation-table lexicography orders the same well-order relations using
different data. Its dependence on the scan is much stronger than a finite
relabelling effect. Throughout the set-sized part of this section we work
in $\ZFC$ and let $\card X=\mu$ be infinite.

\subsubsection{The scan and the information it uses}

Fix a bijection $\mathsf s:\vartheta\to X\times X$, where $\vartheta$ is an
ordinal of cardinality $\mu$. For a relation $R$ define
\[
 t_R(\xi)=\begin{cases}1,&\mathsf s(\xi)\in R,\\0,&\mathsf s(\xi)\notin R.
 \end{cases}
\]
Compare these binary words with $0<1$, at their first disagreement.
Write $\WO_{\mathsf s}(X)$ for the well-orders with this comparison and
$\WO_{\mathsf s,\alpha}(X)$ for the relations of ordinal type $\alpha$.
The numerical order on $X$ does not occur in this definition. It matters
only if an additional rule uses it to select $\mathsf s$.

Diagonal entries are always zero. For an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$, the
two directed entries are complements. Only whichever appears first can
decide a comparison. Deleting diagonal entries and the later directed
entry of each pair produces an \emph{effective scan}: a well-ordered list
of oriented unordered pairs with the same induced order on relations.

The discrepancy from enumeration lexicography is visible on three labels.
Let $a<b<c$, and compare the enumerations $(a,c,b)$ and $(b,a,c)$.
The first is enumeration-smaller. If the table scan first inspects
$(a,b)$, its bits are respectively $1$ and $0$, so the first is
table-larger. There is no contradiction: the two definitions ask different
questions at their first step.

\subsubsection{An invariant spectrum shared by every scan}

\begin{lemma}[Independent adjacent-pair coding]\label{swo:sc:lem:tablecube}
For every scan $\mathsf s$ and every ordinal $\alpha$ with $\card\alpha=\mu$,
the lexicographic binary cube $\B_\mu=(2^\mu,<_{\lex})$
embeds into $\WO_{\mathsf s,\alpha}(X)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose one labelled well-order of type $\alpha$. Its initial
length-$\mu$ segment contains $\mu$ disjoint adjacent pairs at
positions $2\cdot\xi,2\cdot\xi+1$. Swapping either pair changes only
the two directed comparisons internal to that pair and leaves the
ordinal type unchanged.

The first effective coordinates of these pairs form a well-ordered set
of cardinality $\mu$, of order type at least $\mu$. Select its first
$\mu$ pairs. For $s\in2^\mu$, orient selected pair $\xi$ so that
its first scheduled bit equals $s(\xi)$. Leave all other comparisons
fixed. The first disagreement of two inputs is precisely the first
disagreement of their output tables, proving the embedding.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact scan-independent ordinal spectrum]\label{swo:sc:thm:tablespectrum}
For any scan $\mathsf s$ and any fixed type $\alpha$ of cardinality $\mu$,
every linear order of size at most $\mu$ embeds into
$\WO_{\mathsf s,\alpha}(X)$. The ordinal and reverse-ordinal embedding spectra
of both this slice and $\WO_{\mathsf s}(X)$ are exactly
\[
 \{\beta:\beta<\mu^+\}.
\]
Both spaces have cardinality $2^\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a linear order $L$ with $\card L\le\mu$, index some cube coordinates
by its elements and encode $l\in L$ by the bits
$s_l(t)=1$ exactly when $t<l$, fixing unused coordinates at zero.
If $l<l'$, the code increases coordinatewise and changes at $t=l$,
so it increases under any lexicographic coordinate order.
Compose with \cref{swo:sc:lem:tablecube}. This proves the positive spectrum and
the lower cardinality bound; the number of tables gives the upper bound.

For the negative spectrum it suffices to exclude a strictly increasing
$\mu^+$-sequence in $2^\vartheta$. Recursively through the coordinates
of $\vartheta$, pass to a final segment of the sequence on which the current
bit is constant. Once the earlier bits are constant, the current binary
coordinate is nondecreasing and therefore eventually constant. At a
limit coordinate take the supremum of the previously chosen starting
indices. There are at most $\mu$ such indices, so regularity of
$\mu^+$ keeps the supremum below $\mu^+$. After all coordinates,
a final segment consists of the same word, a contradiction. The
decreasing case reverses the two bits. Every ordinal of cardinality
greater than $\mu$ contains $\mu^+$ as an initial segment.
\end{proof}

This spectrum cannot detect the topological distinction proved next.
The argument also explains why agreement on the list of embeddable
ordinals is a weak form of classification.

\merge\ The spectrum is that of enumeration lexicography
(\cref{swo:sw:setspectrum}), and the proofs are the same pair-orientation
coding and the same stabilization argument. At class level the corresponding
statement is source~08's \cref{swo:sk:prop:relationcode}, whose lower embedding
also orients two-element blocks at their first scanned pair.

\subsubsection{Scans of the least possible order type}

Now suppose $\mathsf s:\mu\to X^2$, with $\mu$ the initial ordinal of its
cardinality. All topology below is the \emph{order topology} of the
indicated linear order. Its density $\dens$ is the minimum cardinality of a
dense subset; its cellularity $\cell$ is the supremum of cardinalities of
disjoint families of nonempty open sets.

A realized prefix cylinder is
\[
 N(p)=\{R\in\WO_{\mathsf s}(X):t_R\res\gamma=p\},\qquad\gamma<\mu.
\]
Every order-neighborhood of $R$ contains such a cylinder about $R$.
For a neighborhood $(U,V)$, choose $\gamma$ beyond the first
disagreements of $U,R$ and $R,V$; agreement through $\gamma$ settles
both comparisons. A one-sided neighborhood needs only one bound.
This says that cylinders refine neighborhoods. It does not claim that
every cylinder is itself open.

\begin{theorem}[Dense slices and exact topology]\label{swo:sc:thm:minscantopology}
For a scan of type $\mu$, every slice $\WO_{\mathsf s,\alpha}(X)$ with
$\card\alpha=\mu$ is dense in $\WO_{\mathsf s}(X)$. Neither the full order nor
any such slice has isolated points. Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{swo:sc:eq:minscantopology}
 \dens(\WO_{\mathsf s})=\cell(\WO_{\mathsf s})=\dens(\WO_{\mathsf s,\alpha})=\cell(\WO_{\mathsf s,\alpha})=2^{<\mu}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A prefix of length $\gamma<\mu$ involves a set $C$ of fewer than
$\mu$ labels. If $R$ witnesses its feasibility, $R\res C$ has
ordinal type $\beta<\mu$. Put this restriction first, followed by
any well-order of $X\setminus C$ of type $\alpha$. Since
$\beta+\alpha=\alpha$, the result belongs to the desired slice and
matches the prefix. The complement admits $2^\mu$ such orders, so
every neighborhood contains many members of that slice. The same
argument with neighborhood endpoints in a slice excludes isolated
points in its own order topology.

There are
$\sum_{\gamma<\mu}2^{\card\gamma}=2^{<\mu}$ possible prefixes.
Choosing one representative of each realized prefix gives a dense set
in the full order, or in any fixed slice. Thus $\dens\le2^{<\mu}$ and
$\cell\le \dens$.

For the lower bound use the cube embedding in
\cref{swo:sc:lem:tablecube}. For each $s\in2^\gamma$, choose three distinct
increasing extensions $u_s<v_s<w_s$ of length $\mu$. There are still
at least two coordinates available after $\gamma$. The intervals between
the images of $u_s,w_s$ are nonempty, witnessed by the image of $v_s$,
and are disjoint for different prefixes $s$. Hence
$\cell\ge2^{\card\gamma}$ for every $\gamma<\mu$. Taking the supremum
proves \eqref{swo:sc:eq:minscantopology}.
\end{proof}

In the countable case the scan can have type $\omega$, and there is an
explicit order embedding into the real line:
\[
 R\longmapsto\sum_{n<\omega}\frac{2t_R(n)}{3^{n+1}}.
\tag{S27.2}\label{swo:sc:eq:ternarytable}
\]
The first different digit dominates the entire later tail. This is an
order embedding; no identification of every intrinsic suborder topology
with a product subspace topology is being assumed.

\subsubsection{A finite terminal block creates maximal isolation}

\begin{theorem}[Six delayed coordinates]\label{swo:sc:thm:sixcoordinates}
On the same infinite carrier $X$ there is a scan of type $\mu+6$
for which $\WO_{\mathsf s}(X)$ has $2^\mu$ isolated points. Its density and
cellularity both equal $2^\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Reserve three labels $Z\subset X$ and put $Y=X\setminus Z$.
First scan all pairs except the six off-diagonal directed pairs inside
$Z$, using type $\mu$. Put those six comparisons at the end.

For each well-order $Q$ of $Y$, consider the six completions that place
all of $Y$ in order $Q$, then the three labels of $Z$ in any order.
These have the same initial $\mu$ table bits. Conversely those bits
force exactly this form: only the order inside $Z$ is undetermined.
The fiber is therefore a convex six-point chain. Its middle four points
are isolated in the full order, because their immediate neighbors in
the chain delimit singleton open intervals.

There are $2^\mu$ choices of $Q$, with disjoint fibers. Hence there
are $2^\mu$ isolated points. Their singleton neighborhoods give
cellularity at least $2^\mu$, and any dense set must contain them.
The total cardinality supplies the matching upper bounds.
\end{proof}

For countable $X$, the distinction is absolute: a scan of type $\omega$
is separable with no isolated points, while the displayed scan of type
$\omega+6$ has continuum many isolated points and cannot embed into
$\mathbb R$. An embedding into $\mathbb R$ would turn the disjoint
intervals around these isolated points into disjoint real intervals,
each containing a different rational, which is impossible.

Only the placement of six relation entries has changed. For larger
$\mu$ it is possible that $2^{<\mu}=2^\mu$, so density alone
may not distinguish the two scans. Absence versus presence of isolated
points always does. A scan's order type must therefore be specified;
replacing it by an equicardinal ordinal is not innocuous.

\merge\ Together, \cref{swo:sc:thm:minscantopology,swo:sc:thm:sixcoordinates}
answer the set-level form of \cref{swo:vii:sec:status}, item~(e), and of
source~08's question~9 (``Classification of relation-code orders'',
\cref{swo:sk:sec:research}), negatively: on every infinite set carrier two
scans give non-isomorphic orders, although by \cref{swo:sc:thm:tablespectrum}
their embedding spectra agree. Isolated points are an artifact of the scan,
in the sense of source~08's question; whether two set-like scans of type
$\Ord$ can give non-isomorphic orders on $\No$ is not decided by source~27
(but see \cref{swo:rt:reltable:canonical}).

\subsubsection{A reversal of the global density picture}

\begin{theorem}[Set-like orders are table-dense]\label{swo:sc:thm:class-table-dense}
In $\GBC$, fix a set-like scan $\mathsf s:\Ord\to\No^2$. The ordinary
class of bounded-support codes $\Psupp(b)$, now compared by its relation
tables, meets every nonempty open interval of raw class well-order
tables. In particular, set-like class well-orders are dense there.
The analogous assertion holds for one-sided neighborhoods. Neither
the raw nor the set-like table comparison has isolated points.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Given $U<R<V$, choose a set ordinal $\delta$ beyond the two first
disagreements. The pairs inspected below $\delta$ involve a set $C$
of labels. The restriction $R\res C$ is a set well-order, even when
$R$ has proper-class predecessor segments. Enumerate $C$ in that
order as a set prefix, then complete the prefix by a permutation
of $b$ with set support, using \cref{swo:sc:thm:supportcriterion}. Its
relation table matches $R$ through the required coordinates, hence
lies between $U,V$. Appending differently ordered fresh labels before
completion gives multiple core elements. One-sided neighborhoods
are identical with one bound omitted.
\end{proof}

In the enumeration comparison, the set-like orders miss all interiors
of proper-tail fibers. In the relation-table comparison under an
$\Ord$ scan, they meet every nonempty interval. This is a direct
structural disagreement between the two interpretations. Indeed the
relation-table order has a dense uniform ordinary class of codes,
whereas \cref{swo:sc:thm:omittedcopy} excludes every such dense family for
raw enumeration comparison. The objects agree; their comparison
relations differ. No class containing all set-like orders is being
constructed in either argument.

Placing a few comparisons ``after all ordinal stages'' instead would
give them proper-class predecessor collections. An $\Ord+6$ scan is
not a set-like $\Ord$ scan. A finite-looking change at the end can
therefore change the foundational hypothesis as well as the topology.

\merge\ The convex fibres missed in enumeration comparison are those of
\cref{swo:cf:fibers}. \Cref{swo:sc:thm:class-table-dense} answers source~09's
question ``Does it contain a natural set-coded dense core?'' (its direction
``Non-set-like well-order relations'', \cref{swo:ec:sec:research}) for every
set-like scan: the core $\Psupp(b)$ is one. The rest of that direction (when
cuts of the relation-code order are represented by class well-orders) remains
open. Source~30's \cref{swo:rt:reltable:arbitrary-density} proves the
set-like clause again (its second sentence), adds that the set-like part is
dense in itself, and needs no completion theorem.

\subsubsection{Product topology and a complete ambient order}

For a set $X$, the familiar space of all linear orders
$\mathcal L(X)\subseteq2^{X^2}$ is closed in the product topology: failures
of the linear-order axioms are witnessed by finitely many entries.
This is the classical relation-table space used, for example, in
\cite[Section~4]{JahelTsankov}. Every infinite fixed well-order type
of cardinality $\card X$ is product-dense there, since finite constraints
can be put first and the remaining labels well-ordered afterward.

Order-density for a long scan is different. Inspect
$(x_{n+1},x_n)$ first for $n<\omega$. The all-one initial prefix
forces an infinite descending chain and cannot extend to a well-order,
although it extends to many linear orders. Three such extensions,
differing on reserved labels, delimit a nonempty table-order interval
containing no well-order. Thus finite-coordinate density cannot be
substituted for lexicographic density.

There is nevertheless a useful completeness fact for the \emph{set}
space of all linear-order tables.

\begin{proposition}[Complete ambient table order]\label{swo:sc:prop:tablecomplete}
For every set-length scan $\mathsf s$, the linear order $\mathcal L_{\mathsf s}(X)$
has endpoints and every subset has a supremum and an infimum.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Translate each prescribed off-diagonal table bit into a directed
constraint. A feasible partial table is exactly a constraint set with
no finite directed cycle. It extends to a linear order by orienting
unassigned pairs successively: at least one orientation avoids a cycle,
since two forbidden orientations would give an old cycle. At limits a
new finite cycle cannot appear. Greedily preferring the smaller, or
larger, available bit gives the least, or greatest, completion of any
feasible prefix, including the empty prefix.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathcal L_{\mathsf s}(X)$. Follow the
smallest bit realized by some member matching the current prefix. If a full
member survives, it is the minimum. Otherwise there is a first limit
stage $\lambda$ at which the accumulated prefix $p$ has no matching
member. Every finite part of $p$ is matched, so it is acyclic and has
completions. Let $G$ be its greatest completion. Every member of
$\mathcal A$ first differs from $p$ before $\lambda$, with bit $1$
against $0$, so $G$ is a lower bound. A larger lower bound would first
differ upward from $p$ at some earlier coordinate; a member of
$\mathcal A$ still matches $p$ through that coordinate and lies below
the proposed lower bound. Thus $G=\inf\mathcal A$. Reverse the
construction for suprema; empty subsets use the endpoints.
\end{proof}

This does not identify $\mathcal L_{\mathsf s}(X)$ as the Dedekind completion of
$\WO_{\mathsf s}(X)$: density can fail, and adjacent points require care even
when a dense inclusion is available. Nor is the proposition being
extended to a class-length scan without a separate recursion analysis.

\merge\ The extension of a feasible partial table is the constraint closure of
the proof of \cref{swo:cb:thm:tableendpoints}; for well-orders, source~30's
\cref{swo:rt:reltable:extension} gives the exact criterion
(well-foundedness of the forced relation, not merely acyclicity).

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 2061-2317
\subsection{Source 30: extension, local limits, and invisible order types}\label{swo:rt:reltable:sec}

\merge\ Source~30's Section~7, printed whole; its assembly comments (lines
2056--2059 of its \LaTeX{} source, a ``research fragment'' header) are not
printed. No other source proves its results; source~27's
\cref{swo:sc:prop:tablecomplete} contains the acyclic set-level case of the
extension step.

Relation-table lexicography admits a useful local theory that does not require
aligning the enumeration domains of non-set-like orders. The main result is
stronger than density of the set-like orders: every supplied global
well-order type realizes exactly the same set-sized partial tables.

Throughout this section work in GBC, and supply a proper class $X$ and a
class bijection $e:\Ord\to X$. The application is
$X=\No$. A \emph{class well-order} is a strict linear order under
which every nonempty admitted subclass has a least element; it need not
be set-like. Statements about several orders or an indexed family mean
statements about supplied class parameters or one uniformly represented
class relation. They do not collect class relations into another class.

\subsubsection{An exact extension theorem for partial tables}

Let $D\subseteq X^2$ be a set and let $p:D\to\{0,1\}$ prescribe relation
bits. Write $A$ for the set of labels occurring in $D$. A positive
off-diagonal bit requires its indicated orientation; a negative one
requires the opposite orientation, because the extension must be total.
Thus define a set relation $P_p$ on $A$ by
\[
 uP_pv\ \Longleftrightarrow\ u\ne v\ \text{ and }\
 \bigl(((u,v)\in D\ \&\ p(u,v)=1)
 \ \text{or}\ ((v,u)\in D\ \&\ p(v,u)=0)\bigr).
\]
Well-foundedness of $P_p$ means that every nonempty subset of $A$ has a
$P_p$-minimal element. Transitivity of $P_p$ is not required.

\begin{theorem}[Extension with an arbitrarily prescribed global type]\label{swo:rt:reltable:extension}
Fix any supplied class well-order $J$ of $X$. The partial table $p$
extends to a class well-order $W$ isomorphic to $J$ if and only if
\begin{enumerate}
\item every prescribed diagonal bit is $0$;
\item the forced relation $P_p$ is well-founded.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the conditions for extension to a set-like well-order
are the same as the conditions for extension to any other supplied
global well-order type.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Necessity follows because $P_p\subseteq W$: the $W$-least element of
any nonempty subset of $A$ is $P_p$-minimal.

For sufficiency, rank the set-sized well-founded relation:
\[
 \varrho(v)=\sup\{\varrho(u)+1:uP_pv\}.
\]
Order $A$ lexicographically by the pairs
$(\varrho(v),e^{-1}(v))$. This gives a set well-order $\sigma$ extending
$P_p$. Let $\beta$ be its order type.

The first $\beta$ elements of $J$ form a set initial segment $L$ of
type $\beta$. To see this without invoking class-length recursion,
recursively choose the $J$-least label outside the previously chosen
set, for $\xi<\beta$. Such a label exists because $X$ is proper and
$J$ is a class well-order. This is ordinary set-valued recursion of
set length with a class parameter; class replacement makes its range
a set. No instance of elementary transfinite recursion along a
proper class is being used.

Let $h:(A,\sigma)\to(L,J)$ be the increasing bijection. Both
$X\setminus A$ and $X\setminus L$, in their inherited $e$-orders,
have type $\Ord$. Their increasing enumerations extend
$h$ to a class permutation $\pi$ of $X$. Pull $J$ back along $\pi$:
\[
             xWy\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \pi(x)J\pi(y).
\]
Then $W\cong J$ and $W\res A=\sigma$, so every bit of $p$
is realized. Taking $J$ to be the baseline $e$-order gives a
set-like extension.
\end{proof}

For a finite table, condition (2) is just absence of a directed cycle.
For an infinite table, acyclicity is insufficient: the requirements
$x_{n+1}<x_n$ for $n<\omega$ are acyclic but cannot extend to a
well-order. The theorem therefore gives the exact additional
condition needed at infinite observation scales.

When no particular global type is prescribed, a simpler extension
suffices: place $(A,\sigma)$ first and then append the $e$-ordered
complement. The transport argument is needed to preserve a specified
possibly non-set-like type.

\subsubsection{Finite and countable observations have different closures}

For a supplied class relation $R$ and a set $D\subseteq X^2$, write
\[
 N_D(R)=\{W:W\text{ agrees with }R\text{ on }D\}.
\]
Internally this is a \emph{neighborhood notation}: membership is a
formula about supplied class relations. It does not assert the
existence of a set or class of all its members.

\begin{theorem}[Exact local-approximation criteria]\label{swo:rt:reltable:closures}
Fix a supplied class well-order $J$ of $X$, and let $R$ be an arbitrary
supplied class relation on $X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every finite partial table of $R$ has an extension isomorphic
to $J$ if and only if $R$ is a strict linear order.
\item Every countable partial table of $R$ has such an extension if
and only if $R$ is a class well-order.
\item The criterion in (2) is unchanged if ``countable'' is replaced
by ``set-sized'', or by ``a bounded prefix of a fixed set-like scan
of $X^2$''.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Irreflexivity, totality and transitivity are all tested on finitely
many coordinates. Thus the finite extension condition implies that
$R$ is a strict linear order. Conversely, its restriction to the
finitely many labels of a finite table is a finite well-order, and
\cref{swo:rt:reltable:extension} applies.

If $R$ is a class well-order, its restriction to the set of labels
of any set-sized table is a set well-order. The same theorem again
supplies an extension of the prescribed type.

For the remaining implication, countable extension first gives
linearity. Suppose a nonempty admitted subclass $C$ has no
$R$-least element. Choose $c_0$ by the baseline enumeration, and
recursively let $c_{n+1}$ be the $e$-least member of
\[
                  \{x\in C:xRc_n\}.
\]
Set-valued iteration and class replacement produce the set sequence
$(c_n)_{n<\omega}$. Its consecutive positive bits form a countable
partial table that no well-order can realize. This contradiction
establishes (2). The argument uses the supplied global enumeration
to make the choices; it does not silently appeal to a stronger
class dependent-choice principle.

Finally, any set of scanned coordinates has a set of ordinal
positions and is therefore bounded in the scan. Every bounded
prefix is itself a set. This proves the last equivalence.
\end{proof}

Consequently the finite-support closure of \emph{each} admitted
global isomorphism type consists of all strict linear orders, whereas
its countable-support and set-support closures consist exactly of
all class well-orders. These are equalities of closure criteria;
they do not identify the three neighborhood topologies.

The numerical surreal order illustrates the finite/countable
distinction. Every finite restriction is a well-order, but the
countable chain $0>-1>-2>\cdots$ prevents approximation on every
countable support. Conversely, set-likeness has no such local
obstruction: every set-sized table belonging to a non-set-like
well-order also belongs to a set-like one.

More explicitly, put $A_\alpha=e``\alpha$ and, for a class
well-order $R$, define
\[
 R_\alpha=(R\res A_\alpha)
              +(e\res(X\setminus A_\alpha)).
\]
This is a uniform class family of set-like well-orders. It eventually
agrees with $R$ on every set of coordinates. For example, let $R$
put one distinguished label last and $e$-order all remaining labels.
Then $R$ has type $\Ord+1$, although every $R_\alpha$
has type $\Ord$ and has no last element.

\subsubsection{An ordinary class tree of set approximations}

There is a useful formalization of this local theory that keeps all
nodes set-sized. Let the level $\alpha$ of a class tree consist of
the set well-orders of $A_\alpha$, ordered by restriction between
levels. Every level is a set, and the entire node collection is an
ordinary class of set-coded pairs $(\alpha,\sigma)$.

\begin{proposition}[Branches and stabilization]\label{swo:rt:reltable:branches}
Supplied class well-orders of $X$ correspond exactly to supplied
coherent class branches meeting every level of this tree. The
well-order obtained from a branch is set-like if and only if, for
each label $x$, its predecessor sets in the successive levels
eventually stabilize.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Restriction sends a class well-order to a coherent branch.
Conversely, coherence defines a strict linear order $R$ on $X$.
Every set of labels lies in some $A_\alpha$, so every set restriction
is well-ordered. The countable descending-chain argument from
\cref{swo:rt:reltable:closures} makes $R$ a class well-order.

For $x=e(\xi)$ and $\alpha>\xi$, let $P_\alpha(x)$ be its
predecessor set at level $\alpha$. These are nested sets whose
class union is the full predecessor class. If that class is a set,
its $e$-indices are bounded, so $P_\alpha(x)$ eventually becomes
constant. Conversely, a constant final value is the entire
predecessor class and is a set.
\end{proof}

The limit-level requirement matters. Coherence of finite
well-orders alone can produce an ill-founded limit; requiring a
well-order at every set stage excludes the countable descending
witness. No collection of all branches is introduced by this
description.

\subsubsection{An external topology and the absence of continuous type detectors}

To turn the neighborhood notation into an ordinary topological space,
choose an external set-sized two-sorted realization
$\mathfrak M=(M,\mathcal C)$ of the stated theory. Let
$\Hall^{\mathfrak M}$ be the external set of its admitted class
well-orders. Give it the topology generated by $N_D(R)$ with supports
$D$ that \emph{the model regards as sets}. These cylinders are clopen
and separate distinct admitted relations, so the space is Hausdorff.
Equivalently, one may use the internally bounded scan prefixes.

For an admitted $J$, let $[J]_{\mathfrak M}$ denote the orders
isomorphic to $J$ by an admitted class isomorphism. This explicitly
fixes the meaning of isomorphism when the external realization is
not transitive.

\begin{corollary}[Dense type fibers and continuous invariants]\label{swo:rt:reltable:type-detector}
Every $[J]_{\mathfrak M}$ is dense and codense in
$\Hall^{\mathfrak M}$. The set-like orders and the non-set-like
orders are both dense. Every continuous isomorphism-invariant map
from $\Hall^{\mathfrak M}$ to a $T_1$ space is constant.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The extension theorem, interpreted in $\mathfrak M$, puts a member
of $[J]_{\mathfrak M}$ in every nonempty basic neighborhood. There
are at least two distinct types, $\Ord$ and
$\Ord+1$. Thus every type fiber has a different dense
fiber in its complement. Type $\Ord$ provides the
set-like approximants, while type $\Ord+1$ provides
non-set-like approximants.

If $f$ is invariant and continuous, then it is constant, with value
$f(J)$, on the dense fiber $[J]_{\mathfrak M}$. Since the target is
$T_1$, the preimage of $\{f(J)\}$ is closed. A closed set containing
a dense fiber is the whole domain, so $f$ is constant.
\end{proof}

In particular, the indicator of set-likeness, with values in the
discrete two-point space, is discontinuous at every point. The
same holds for membership in any one type fiber. The full table
does determine its order type; the obstruction concerns recovering
that type continuously from set-sized observations.

The phrase ``model regards as sets'' is essential. Externally the
whole carrier is a set. If all external coordinate subsets were
allowed, observing the entire table would be a permitted basic
neighborhood and the topology would be discrete. The preceding
corollary makes no assertion about that different topology.

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 2318-2491
\subsection{Source 30: the order topology of relation-table lexicography}\label{swo:rt:reltable:order-sec}

Fix a set-like scan of $X^2$, and compare table bits with $0<1$.
The first disagreement exists for any two supplied distinct tables.
Support neighborhoods and order neighborhoods are related, but they
need not generate the same topology.

\subsubsection{Density for every scan on the set-like part}

We first recall the endpoint-transfer argument, which already
appears in the repository (\cref{swo:cb:thm:tableendpoints}, source~15).
Suppose a well-order $W$ is claimed to be an extremum but a strict linear
order $L$ improves its table at the first disagreement. Let $P$ be the set of
oriented constraints from the earlier coordinates. If the desired improvement
puts $y$ before $x$, take the $P$-predecessor closure $D$ of $y$,
including $y$. It is a set and does not contain $x$, since $L$
extends $P$. Moving $D$ to the front of $W$, preserving the old
orders inside $D$ and its complement, respects every earlier
constraint and makes the desired improvement. It remains a
well-order and remains set-like if $W$ was set-like. Hence minima
and maxima among well-orders, or among set-like well-orders, are
also extrema among all strict linear orders.

\begin{theorem}[Scan-independent density of the set-like part]\label{swo:rt:reltable:arbitrary-density}
For every set-like scan, the relation-table order of the set-like
global well-orders is dense. Moreover, set-like well-orders are
topologically dense in the order topology of all admitted class
well-orders.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $R<S$ be set-like and let $\delta$ be their first disagreement.
Start with the set of labels in the scan through $\delta$. Close
it under predecessors in both $R$ and $S$, iterating this operation
$\omega$ times. Class replacement and set-likeness ensure that
the resulting $A$ is a set, and it is an initial segment of both
orders. Put $B=X\setminus A$.

If no set-like order lay between $R$ and $S$, replacing their
$B$-tails independently would imply that $R\res B$ is
greatest and $S\res B$ is least among set-like orders of
$B$, under the induced scan. The endpoint-transfer argument
makes them extrema among all linear orders of $B$. Reversal
complements every nonconstant table bit, so these extrema are
reversals of one another. An order on an infinite carrier and
its reverse cannot both be well-orders. This is a contradiction.

For the final assertion, a point $T$ of any nonempty open order
interval has a bounded table prefix fixing its comparisons with
the interval endpoints. A set-like extension of that prefix
still lies in the interval. The same argument treats open rays.
\end{proof}

The last assertion is topological density, not a claim that every
pair of distinct non-set-like orders has an intermediate order for
an arbitrary scan. That stronger question requires another
argument. The next explicit scan does have the stronger property.

\begin{note}[\merge; one density theorem, two proofs]\label{swo:xii:note:density}
The second sentence of \cref{swo:rt:reltable:arbitrary-density} is the
set-like clause of source~27's \cref{swo:sc:thm:class-table-dense}, which is
stronger: the core $\Psupp(b)$ already meets every nonempty open interval, and
neither order has isolated points. Source~27 completes a set prefix by a
bounded-support permutation (\cref{swo:sc:thm:supportcriterion}); source~30
extends the prefix by \cref{swo:rt:reltable:extension}. The first sentence of
\cref{swo:rt:reltable:arbitrary-density}, that two set-like orders always have
a set-like order strictly between them (no adjacent pairs), is source~30's
only; its proof is the reversal argument of
\cref{swo:cb:cor:tablepatterns}, applied to a tail. Source~30 did not see
source~27.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{A canonical baseline scan with asymmetric local character}

Identify labels with their $e$-indices. Scan the unordered pairs
$(\xi,\eta)$, $\xi<\eta$, in increasing order of $\eta$ and then
$\xi$, and use bit $1$ when $e(\xi)$ precedes $e(\eta)$. This is
a set-like class scan. It can be converted to a full directed-pair
scan by listing the reverse direction immediately after each pair
and inserting the constant diagonal bits.

For a set well-order $\sigma$ on $A_\alpha$, let $C_\sigma$ be the
orders whose restriction to $A_\alpha$ is $\sigma$.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical table characters]\label{swo:rt:reltable:canonical}
For this scan, both the set-like order and the order of all class
well-orders have the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item They are dense, have the baseline order as greatest element,
and have no least element.
\item Every $C_\sigma$ has a greatest element and a strictly
decreasing countable coinitial sequence of set-like elements.
\item No point has a uniformly represented set-sized cofinal family
strictly below it.
\item A nongreatest point $W$ has a uniformly represented set-sized
coinitial family strictly above it if and only if its inversion
class
\[
 \operatorname{Inv}(W)=\{(\xi,\eta):\xi<\eta\text{ and }e(\eta)We(\xi)\}
\]
is a set.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The greatest element of $C_\sigma$ is $M_\sigma$, which puts
$\sigma$ first and then appends the baseline tail: every still
undetermined bit is $1$.

For $n\ge1$, let $W_n$ put
\[
 e(\alpha+n-1),\ldots,e(\alpha+1),e(\alpha)
\]
first, then $\sigma$, then the remaining baseline tail. These
set-like orders form a strictly decreasing sequence in $C_\sigma$.
They are coinitial there. Indeed, their successive new labels are
always inserted before every previously scanned label, the least
possible insertion. An order that were below or equal to every
$W_n$ would have to make all these least insertions and would
contain the descending sequence
$e(\alpha)>e(\alpha+1)>\cdots$. A class well-order cannot do so.
Thus every member of $C_\sigma$ has some $W_n$ strictly below it.

Given $R<S$, choose $\alpha$ large enough that agreement with
$S$ on $A_\alpha$ fixes the comparison $R<\cdot$. A member of
the preceding sequence below $S$ lies strictly between $R$ and
$S$. This proves density and absence of a minimum. The baseline
has all bits $1$ and is the maximum.

For a supplied set family $V_i<W$, bound all first disagreements
with $W$ using class replacement. In a sufficiently long matching
cylinder, choose a set-like element strictly below $W$. It still
lies above every $V_i$, proving (3).

If $\operatorname{Inv}(W)$ is proper, every matching cylinder
$C_{W|A_\alpha}$ has maximum strictly greater than $W$. Bounding the first
disagreements of any supplied set family above $W$ and taking such a later
maximum gives a still closer point above $W$. Thus no such family
is coinitial.

If $\operatorname{Inv}(W)$ is a set, choose $\gamma$ containing the endpoints
of all inversions. Every $U>W$ first differs on a pair lying in
$A_\gamma^2$. Therefore $\tau=U|A_\gamma$ is table-greater
than $\sigma=W|A_\gamma$. There are set-many such set orders
$\tau$. Each cylinder $C_\tau$ lies wholly above $W$ and has
the displayed countable coinitial sequence. Their union is a
uniformly represented set-sized family coinitial strictly above
$W$, proving (4).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The eventual-equality core in the canonical table order]\label{swo:rt:reltable:core}
A class well-order has set-sized inversion support for this scan
if and only if it is set-like and its ordinal enumeration is eventually
equal to $e$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If all inversion endpoints lie in $A_\gamma$, the order puts some
set well-order $\sigma$ of $A_\gamma$ first and then the unchanged
baseline tail. Write $\beta=\otp(\sigma)$.
Choose an additively indecomposable ordinal $\lambda>\gamma,\beta$.
The identities $\gamma+\lambda=\beta+\lambda=\lambda$ align the
two enumerations beyond $\lambda$, proving eventual equality.
Conversely, if an enumeration agrees with $e$ from $\lambda$ onward,
its first $\lambda$ entries are exactly $e[\lambda]$.
All inversions are consequently contained in the set $\lambda\times\lambda$.
\end{proof}

Bounded inversion support thus has an intrinsic description in
this particular table order: away from its greatest point, it is
exactly the existence of a set-sized right coinitial family. The
left side has no analogous small character. These properties are
different from numerical enumeration lexicography and should not
be transferred between the two representations.

The support topology is strictly finer than the order topology for
this scan. Order neighborhoods contain sufficiently long matching
table cylinders. In the other direction, swap the first two
baseline labels and keep the remaining baseline tail. The result
is the nongreatest maximum of its two-label cylinder. Every order
neighborhood of it contains larger points by density, and those
points leave the cylinder. That cylinder is consequently not
order-open, although it is clopen in the support topology.

\merge\ The canonical scan realizes source~15's pattern ``maximum only''
(\cref{swo:cb:cor:tablepatterns}) with the baseline as maximum. With $e$ as
the baseline $b$, the orders of \cref{swo:rt:reltable:core} are exactly the
enumerations $b\circ\pi$ coded by the core $\Psupp(b)$ of
\cref{swo:sc:thm:class-table-dense}: a permutation of $\Ord$ with set support
fixes every ordinal beyond its support, and conversely, as the proof shows, an
enumeration eventually equal to $b$ permutes an initial segment of $b$'s
positions. So the core has an intrinsic description in this table order:
apart from the maximum, its members are exactly the points with a set-sized
coinitial family strictly above them. \Cref{swo:rt:reltable:canonical} is the first
intrinsic, scan-dependent local invariant of a relation-table order on $\No$:
item~(4) separates points by their right character. It does not decide whether
two set-like scans of type $\Ord$ can give isomorphic orders.

\section{What this Part answers}\label{swo:xii:sec:status}

than zero} (\cref{swo:vii:sec:status}, items~(b) and~(d); source~16's question
``Centered increasing words''): \textbf{answered in part}. No placement of a
marker gives a set-cut saturated order, so none gives $\No$
(\cref{swo:tm:thm:increasing}, source~23). Every actual threshold, under each
zero convention, and every gap whose sides have no set cofinal (resp.\
coinitial) subset and no endpoint, gives the centered type of~(a)
(\cref{swo:bw:wp:thresholds}, source~29). At every interior gap the point
characters and the adjacent pairs are known
(\cref{swo:sc:prop:gapcharacters}, source~27); they show that a gap with a
small cofinality or coinitiality on one side gives a type different from
$\WordsInc_c$. Open: the isomorphism types at those gaps and the cut

Question~13.5; source~23's Question~16.2 asks which restrictions repair

\item \emph{The isomorphism question for two scans} (\cref{swo:vii:sec:status},
item~(e)) and \emph{source~08's question~9} (``Classification of
relation-code orders'', \cref{swo:sk:sec:research}): \textbf{answered
negatively on set carriers}, \textbf{open on $\No$}. On every infinite set
carrier there are two scans whose relation-table orders of well-orders are not
isomorphic (\cref{swo:sc:thm:minscantopology,swo:sc:thm:sixcoordinates}), while
the ordinal and reverse-ordinal spectra and the cardinality do not depend on
the scan (\cref{swo:sc:thm:tablespectrum}): isolated points, density and
cellularity are artifacts of the scan, the spectrum is not. For set-like scans

\part{The core and its cylinders: symmetries, decorated completions and class realizations}\label{swo:part:coresym}

\merge\ (3 October 2026.) This Part of the batch-83 addition continues
Part~IV (\cref{swo:part:setlike}), which built the core, and Part~VIII
(\cref{swo:part:corecuts}), which classified its class cuts, recognized the
cuts of global enumerations, and showed that the bare order of the core
forgets which of its cuts are represented. Part~VIII left four things open
(\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}, items (c), (e) and (f)): the stabilizer of the
exhaustive cuts and which extra predicates make the reconstruction unique;
what the external order type of the admitted enumerations remembers about the
class realization; and ordinal support bounds. Eight batch-83 sources take
these up, and this Part prints what they prove.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{The core and its cylinders} (base: source~25). Source~22 shows that
unranked cylinder inclusion recovers prefix heights (\cref{swo:rg:thm:height})
and recognizes represented cuts without ranks (\cref{swo:rg:thm:unranked}).
Source~25 classifies the orbits of every set-indexed configuration of injective
branches under automorphisms preserving the core order and every cylinder
(\cref{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity}): there are exactly two single-branch orbits,
the core and the rest. Hence exhaustiveness is invisible to the core with all
its cylinders, even with set-many parameters fixed (\cref{swo:ph:thm:invisible,swo:ph:thm:parameters}),
and a cylinder-preserving core automorphism need not extend to $\Hsl$
(\cref{swo:ph:thm:noextension}), which strengthens \cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension}.
One cross-node relation, equality of edge labels, makes the structure rigid
(\cref{swo:ph:thm:rigidity}). At a regular $\kappa$ with
$\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$ the set version has exactly $2^\kappa$
automorphisms (\cref{swo:ph:thm:group-size}); a family of $\cf\kappa$
approximants can force a noncore branch, so the bound in the set version is
sharp at regular $\kappa$ and the method fails at singular $\kappa$
(\cref{swo:ph:thm:cofinal-obstruction}).
\item \emph{Ordered prefix trees without the core} (sources~27 and~29): branch
transitivity on injective and on increasing words, the exact local
obstruction, and families that preserve exhaustion
(\cref{swo:xiii:sec:trees}).
\item \emph{Automorphisms of the bare core} (sources~20 and~21): re-proofs of
Part~VIII's orbit classification and extension criterion, a failure localized
inside any interval while fixing any set of core points
(\cref{swo:lm:aut:thm:localfailure}), disjointness of relabelled cores
(\cref{swo:lm:aut:prop:labelmoves}) and an explicit cut with no crossing
first-level cylinder (\cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:vertical-cut}).
\item \emph{Decorated completions} (source~19): the Dedekind completion of the
external raw order is the core completion with every represented fibre replaced
by its interval completion (\cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction}); a core
automorphism extends to the raw order exactly when it preserves fibre types
(\cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:aut}); over residual alphabets at most two initial words
share a trace (\cref{swo:rs:rf:prop:doubleton}); and every countable model
omits continuum many amenable branches (\cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:missingbranches}).
\item \emph{The least ordinal support} of a completion of a partial injection
(source~27, \cref{swo:sc:thm:leastheight}).
\item \emph{Class realizations} (sources~22, 27, 21 and~30): the admitted
labelled traces recover the whole class realization (\cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful},
proved three times); the external order of a countable model is $\mathbb Q$
even with the core coloured and the baseline fixed, and does not detect $\ETR$
(\cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:coloredcore,swo:rt:fnd:prop:etrinvisible}).
\end{itemize}
\Cref{swo:xiii:sec:status} records which questions the Part answers.

\emph{Printed once.} Height recovery is printed as source~22's
