% ---- source 25, Section 3
\subsection{Source 25: baseline embedding results and the set/class transition}\label{swo:ph:sec:baseline}

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 214-256

The following arguments are part of the earlier general-alphabet theory (\cref{swo:sw:setspectrum,swo:prop:universal}; the reals report). They are included because they sharply delimit what changes when one passes from a fixed birthday fragment to the whole surreal line.

\begin{note}[Source~25, Theorem~3.1, ``Fixed-set size and ordinal spectrum'']\label{swo:ph:thm:set-spectrum}
{\itshape
Let $X$ be an infinite linearly ordered set of cardinality $\mu$. Then
\[
 |\W(X)|=2^\mu,
 \qquad
 \beta\hookrightarrow\W(X)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \beta<\mu^+.
\]
Every linear order of cardinality at most $\mu$ embeds already into $\W_\mu(X)$. There is no increasing or decreasing sequence of type $\mu^+$ in $\W(X)$.}
This is \cref{swo:sw:setspectrum} (the reals report's general-alphabet theorem), with its ordinal spectrum; source~25 recalls it with its proof and does not present it as new.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
Partition $X$ into $\mu$ pairs and write the members of the $\xi$th pair as $x_\xi^-<x_\xi^+$. For a binary word $s\in2^\mu$, enumerate each pair increasingly when $s(\xi)=0$ and decreasingly when $s(\xi)=1$, using consecutive positions $2\cdot\xi$ and $2\cdot\xi+1$. Ordinal multiplication is intended; these positions partition $\mu$ for an infinite initial ordinal $\mu$. This gives an order embedding
\[
 (2^\mu,<_{\lex})\hookrightarrow\W_\mu(X).
\]
If $L$ has cardinality at most $\mu$, inject its elements into $\mu$ and associate to $x\in L$ the characteristic word of the elements strictly below $x$, with zero at unused coordinates. For $x<y$ the first word is coordinatewise at most the second and differs at the coordinate of $x$, so the assignment is strictly lexicographically increasing. This proves the lower embedding assertion and the lower cardinal bound. The upper bound follows because each well-order is a subset of $X^2$.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that $(e_\xi)_{\xi<\mu^+}$ is a strictly increasing sequence of exhaustive words on $X$. The indices whose words extend a fixed prefix form a convex set of indices. If this set is unbounded in $\mu^+$, it therefore contains a final segment.

Starting with the empty prefix, recursively construct a common prefix extended by a final segment of the sequence. At a successor stage there are at most $\mu$ possible next labels. Termination cannot occur on an unbounded set of indices, since an exhaustive word cannot be a proper prefix of another exhaustive word. Regularity of $\mu^+$ implies that one next-label cylinder is unbounded, and hence contains a final segment. At a limit stage below $\mu^+$, the intersection of the previously chosen final segments is still a final segment. The construction would give an injective word of length $\mu^+$ in $X$, a contradiction. Reversing the sequence gives the decreasing version.

Every ordinal below $\mu^+$ has cardinality at most $\mu$, and every larger ordinal contains $\mu^+$ as an initial segment. The spectrum follows.
\end{proof}

For an infinite cardinal $\kappa$, let
\[
 \No_{<\kappa}
   =\{x\in\No:\bd(x)<\kappa\}.
\]
The sign-sequence representation gives $|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}$. Thus the preceding theorem applies with $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$. In particular, the size parameter is not automatically $\kappa$. The singular-cutoff results in the repository show why suppressing that distinction can give wrong coding statements (\cref{swo:st:thm:transition}; source~22).

\begin{note}[Source~25, Proposition~3.2, ``Class-order universality, in GBC'']\label{swo:ph:prop:class-universal}
{\itshape
Every supplied class linear order admits a class order embedding into $\No$. It consequently admits an embedding into $\Hsl$ and into the set-supported core $\Psupp(b)$.}
This is \cref{swo:prop:universal} with the core universality of \cref{swo:gl:pbd-no}; source~25's embedding into the core uses one-letter completions (\cref{swo:ph:lem:completion}).
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
Use global choice to arrange the underlying class in a set-like construction order. When treating one element, only a set of earlier elements has been assigned images. Separate the images of its earlier predecessors from those of its earlier successors by a surreal number. The usual surreal small-cut property supplies such a separator. This set-valued recursion gives an order embedding into $\No$.

For each surreal $x$, choose a core completion of the one-letter prefix $(x)$; the existence of this completion is proved in \Cref{swo:ph:lem:completion}. The resulting map $x\mapsto d_x$ is increasing because the first letters already decide the comparison. Composition proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

This explains an important discontinuity. Each fixed set fragment has a bounded ordinal embedding spectrum, but the full global construction contains every set ordinal and every supplied ordinary class linear order. Neither statement asserts that a same-level class of \emph{all} class orders has been collected or enumerated.

% ---- source 25, Section 4
\subsection{Source 25: foundational framework and the supported core}\label{swo:ph:sec:core}

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 259-326

\subsubsection{The background theory}

Throughout the global arguments, GBC means Gödel--Bernays class theory with global choice. Sets and classes are distinct sorts; classes have sets as members. Elementary class comprehension allows class parameters but does not quantify over classes in its defining formula. A uniformly $I$-indexed family of class words means one supplied class relation whose rows, indexed by the set $I$, are the words in question. It does not mean a set containing proper classes.

We use a fixed set-like global well-order of the sets to make constructions deterministic when desired. A recursion along $\Ord$ whose stage values and histories at set stages are sets is available by ordinary set recursion with class parameters and elementary comprehension. The materially stronger principle ETR concerns recursions with class-sized stage values. That distinction is essential and is audited in \Cref{swo:ph:sec:foundations}; see \cite{HamkinsRecursionPrinciple,GitmanHamkins,GHHSW} for the background.

\subsubsection{Fresh small-cut separation}

\begin{note}[Source~25, Lemma~4.1, ``A separator avoiding a prescribed set'']\label{swo:ph:lem:fresh}
{\itshape
Let $L,R,S$ be sets of surreals with $L<R$. Then there is an $x\in\No\setminus S$ with $L<x<R$. Either of $L,R$ may be empty.}
This is \cref{swo:lem:delete} and source~13's \cref{swo:fs:lem:fresh}, in the exact-birthday form.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
The surreal separator theorem permits a separator of any birthday strictly above all birthdays of the options. Choose an ordinal $\gamma$ strictly above the birthdays of $L\cup R\cup S$ and choose a separator of birthday exactly $\gamma$. It cannot belong to $S$. The exact-birthday form is supplied by the sign-sequence construction and by the repository declaration \code{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt} \cite{ProveItCutFill}.
\end{proof}

Only this order-theoretic separation property, not multiplication or analysis on surreals, is used in the new homogeneity argument. In particular, every nonempty numerical open interval has points outside any prescribed set. Removing a set from $\No$ leaves an order with the same small-cut separation property.

\subsubsection{Normalized codes rather than class objects}

A normalized support code consists of a set $S\subseteq\Ord$ and a fixed-point-free permutation $\pi_S:S\to S$. Extend it by the identity outside $S$ to obtain a class permutation $\pi$ of $\Ord$, and evaluate the code as the class word
\[
 d_\pi(\alpha)=b(\pi(\alpha)).
\]
The empty support code evaluates to $b$. Requiring $S$ to be the exact support ensures that distinct normalized codes have distinct evaluations. The collection $\Psupp(b)$ of these codes is an ordinary class of sets. Its lexicographic order is elementary in the parameter $b$.

All sets of ordinals are bounded, so a core branch agrees with $b$ beyond some ordinal. Conversely, an \emph{exhaustive} branch eventually agreeing with $b$ belongs to the core: its transition permutation $b^{-1}\circ d$ has bounded, hence set, support. Exhaustiveness is necessary in this converse. An injective word can omit a label while still agreeing with $b$ on a final segment.

\begin{note}[Source~25, Lemma~4.2, ``Supported prefix completion'']\label{swo:ph:lem:completion}
{\itshape
Every $p\in\Words$, of any set-ordinal length, extends to a core branch. Core completions can be selected uniformly from their set-coded prefixes.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:completion}. Source~25 adjoins a fresh reserve of the size of $A$, the device of \cref{swo:ec:n8.2}; \cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve} computes the least reserve and source~27's \cref{swo:sc:thm:leastheight} the least ordinal support.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
Write $\alpha=\lh(p)$ and let $q=b^{-1}\circ p:\alpha\to\Ord$. This is a set partial injection. Put $A=\alpha\cup q[\alpha]$.

If $A$ is finite, the sets $A\setminus\alpha$ and $A\setminus q[\alpha]$ have the same finite cardinality, so complete $q$ to a permutation of $A$. If $A$ is infinite, choose a fresh set $R$ of ordinals, disjoint from $A$, with $|R|=|A|$. In $U=A\cup R$, both $U\setminus\alpha$ and $U\setminus q[\alpha]$ have cardinality $|A|$. Choose a bijection between them and adjoin it to $q$. This is a permutation of $U$, and extension by the identity outside $U$ is a set-supported permutation of $\Ord$.

Normalize its support. The associated core word extends $p$. Selecting the first valid normalized code in the fixed global well-order gives a uniform selection. All searches and restrictions here involve sets and supplied class parameters.
\end{proof}

The reservoir in the infinite case is not cosmetic. Two complements of equinumerous infinite subsets inside their union need not have the same cardinality. Adding a reserve on both sides avoids an invalid cancellation of infinite cardinals.

\begin{note}[Source~25, Lemma~4.3, ``Core separation of full branches'']\label{swo:ph:lem:dense}
{\itshape
If $f,g\in\Jinj$ and $f<_{\lex}g$, there exists $d\in\Psupp(b)$ with
\[
 f<_{\lex}d<_{\lex}g.
\]
Every cylinder $C_p$ is nonempty and has at least two distinct child cylinders.}
The first assertion is the two-family case of \cref{swo:gl:interpolation}, which is stated for injective words; the second is the nonemptiness of cylinders used throughout Part~VIII.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
Let $\delta=\delta(f,g)$ and $p=f\res\delta=g\res\delta$. Choose
\[
 f(\delta)<x<g(\delta),\qquad x\notin\ran(p),
\]
using \Cref{swo:ph:lem:fresh}. Complete $p\cat(x)$ by \Cref{swo:ph:lem:completion}. The first disagreement with both words occurs at $\delta$. Nonemptiness and the existence of distinct children follow in the same way from fresh labels.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~25, Corollary~4.4, ``Injectivity of the cut trace'']\label{swo:ph:cor:trace}
{\itshape
For a supplied branch $f\in\Jinj$, define its lower core trace by
\[
 L_f=\{d\in\Psupp(b):d<_{\lex}f\}.
\]
Distinct branches have distinct traces.}
This is the uniqueness clause of \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition} and its routes (\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold}).
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
A core branch strictly between two distinct branches belongs to exactly one of their lower traces.
\end{proof}

The core is proper because every surreal occurs as the first letter of a core completion, while the image of a set under evaluation at zero would be a set. Therefore global choice supplies a class enumeration of its normalized codes. This enumeration will be used only to schedule the back-and-forth construction, not as an enumeration of $\Hsl$.

% ---- source 22, Section 7
\subsection{Source 22: global enumerations and their set-coded core}\label{swo:rg:sec:core}

% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 480-531
From this section onward, unless otherwise stated, work in $\GBC$: G\"odel--Bernays set theory with Global Choice. The convention $\GB$ alone includes no choice axiom. A class function is represented by its class graph, and a uniformly indexed family of class functions is one class graph with an additional \emph{set-valued} index coordinate.

\subsubsection{The virtual enumeration order}
Fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. Write
\[
 \Hsl=\{e:e\text{ is a class bijection }\Ord\to\No\}
\]
only as shorthand for a predicate on class variables. This display does not assert that $\Hsl$ is a set or an ordinary class. Distinct enumerations have a least disagreement ordinal: restrict a nonempty disagreement class to one ordinal witnessing a disagreement and use the well-ordering of that set. Comparing the two surreal labels there gives a strict linear order on the available enumerations.

The same comparison applies to injective class words $h:\Ord\hookrightarrow\No$ which need not be exhaustive. Every set-length restriction of such a word is a set by class replacement. This fact will be used repeatedly; a proper-class word itself is not a permissible element of a set-coded family.

\subsubsection{Canonical support codes}
Let $\Psupp(b)$ consist of canonical set codes for permutations $\pi:\Ord\to\Ord$ whose support
\[
 \supp\pi=\{\xi:\pi(\xi)\ne\xi\}
\]
is a set. One canonical code is the set of all moved ordered pairs $(\xi,\pi(\xi))$, with the identity recovered off its domain. The code for the identity is empty. Membership in the code class is elementary: the code is a set bijection from a set onto itself with no fixed points, extended by the identity outside that set. Such codes are unique, so $\Psupp(b)$ is an ordinary class of sets. Evaluate its code as the global enumeration $b\circ\pi$, and compare codes by their evaluations. We occasionally write a code as if it were its evaluation when no ambiguity results.

This distinction between codes and evaluations is indispensable: $\Psupp(b)$ is an ordinary class, whereas its evaluations are class functions. The evaluation relation is a single class with set-coded arguments.

\begin{note}[Source~22, Lemma~7.1, ``Every set prefix has a supported completion'']\label{swo:rg:lem:supported}
{\itshape
Every injective set word $p:\alpha\hookrightarrow\No$ extends the evaluation of some code in $\Psupp(b)$. Completions can be chosen uniformly from the set prefix code and the fixed global-choice parameters.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:completion}, completed inside an infinite initial cardinal as in Part~IV.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~22's proof]
Transport $p$ along $b^{-1}$ to a set partial injection $q:\alpha\to\Ord$. Choose an infinite initial cardinal $\theta$ larger than $\alpha$ and all members of $\ran q$, with $|\alpha|<\theta$. Both complements
\[
 \theta\setminus\alpha,\qquad\theta\setminus\ran q
\]
have cardinality $\theta$. Choose a bijection between them, join it to $q$, and extend the resulting permutation of $\theta$ by the identity outside $\theta$. Its moved-pair graph is a set. This gives the required code. Fixing a global choice of the relevant set bijections makes the construction uniform. Every stage is a set construction with class parameters; no class-valued transfinite recursion is involved.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~22, Lemma~7.2, ``Fresh separators'']\label{swo:rg:lem:fresh}
{\itshape
If $a<b$ are surreal numbers and $S$ is a set of forbidden surreal labels, there is $z\in(a,b)\setminus S$. There are also fresh labels on either side of any prescribed surreal.}
This is \cref{swo:lem:delete} and source~13's \cref{swo:fs:lem:fresh}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~22's proof]
Choose an ordinal birthday bound strictly above the birthdays of $a,b$ and every member of $S$. The small-cut separator theorem at that exact birthday supplies $z$ between $a$ and $b$, and its birthday excludes membership in $S$. For rays, use a small cut with only one nonempty side and again prescribe a sufficiently large birthday. This is precisely the smallness boundary respected by the repository's sign-sequence construction \cite{ProveItSigns,ProveItCutFill}.
\end{proof}

For an injective set prefix $p$, write
\[
 C_p=\{d\in\Psupp(b):\operatorname{ev}_b(d)\text{ extends }p\}.
\]
Every $C_p$ is nonempty and convex. If $h$ is an injective $\Ord$-word extending $p$, then there are points of $C_p$ both below and above $h$: choose at the next coordinate a fresh label on the desired side of $h(\dom p)$ and apply \cref{swo:rg:lem:supported}.

\begin{note}[Source~22, Proposition~7.3, ``Density in all injective global words'']\label{swo:rg:prop:global-density}
{\itshape
For any distinct injective $\Ord$-words $h<k$, there is a code $d\in\Psupp(b)$ with $h<d<k$. In particular, $\Psupp(b)$ is dense without endpoints, and its comparisons separate distinct global words.}
This is the two-family case of \cref{swo:gl:interpolation}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~22's proof]
Let $\beta$ be the first disagreement of $h,k$. Choose a fresh label strictly between $h(\beta)$ and $k(\beta)$, avoiding the set of common earlier labels. Complete the resulting set prefix by \cref{swo:rg:lem:supported}. Both comparisons are decided at $\beta$. The endpoint assertion follows by applying the one-sided construction to the empty prefix.
\end{proof}

The earlier report proves the stronger assertion that $\Psupp(b)$ fills every uniformly set-indexed separated cut of global enumerations, and consequently that $\Psupp(b)\cong\No$ in $\GBC$ (\cref{swo:gl:interpolation,swo:gl:pbd-no}). The classical universality and homogeneity of the surreal order underlie that identification \cite{Ehrlich2012}. Our reconstruction arguments below use only the explicitly proved prefix-completion and separation properties, not an unproved inference from density to saturation.

% ---- source 21, Section 8
\subsection{Source 21: class well-orders, canonical blocks, and a genuine dense core}\label{swo:fu:sec:global}

\merge\ Source~21's Section~8, printed whole. Every numbered statement in it is
a result of Parts~III and~IV or of Part~IX and is printed as a note; source~21
calls two of them ``repository baseline'' and says, of the others, that
canonical block decompositions ``also arose in the preceding research'' and
are included ``rather than treating every restatement as a new result''.
Its \cref{swo:fu:set:fiber} is its set-level fibre theorem, printed in Part~X.

% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 1252-1557
We now pass from set carriers to the entire surreal class. A class
well-order means a strict linear class relation for which every nonempty
admitted subclass has a least element. It is \emph{set-like} if each
predecessor class is a set. In $\GBC$, a set-like well-order of a proper
class has unique order type $\Ord$: sending a point to the ordinal type
of its predecessor set gives an initial subclass of $\Ord$, and
properness forces that subclass to be all of $\Ord$.

Thus $\Hsl(\No)$ can be described using class bijections
$\Ord\to\No$. The unrestricted predicate $\Hall(\No)$ is larger.
For example, enumerate $\No\setminus\{a,b\}$ in type $\Ord$ and
then append $a,b$. Interchanging the final two labels gives a second
well-order. The two agree throughout a proper-class prefix, so no set
ordinal is the first disagreement position of the complete orders.
The comparison nevertheless has a direct elementary definition.

Existence of a global baseline is a substantive choice assumption. The
repository proves, over its choice-free $\GB$ convention, that existence
of a class well-order of $\No$ is equivalent to global choice
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}; Theorem~13.1 at the pin). We use $\GBC$ openly rather than treating
the baseline as a canonical choice-free enumeration.

\subsubsection{Direct comparison of labelled class relations}

For a class well-order $R$ on a fixed linearly ordered class $X$, write
$\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$. Given $R,S$, define a class
$C(R,S)$ by the elementary condition
\begin{align*}
 x\in C(R,S)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad&
 \operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\operatorname{Pred}_S(x),\\[-2pt]
 &R\text{ and }S\text{ agree on this common predecessor class}.
\end{align*}
Equality here expands into quantification over set elements of the
classes. There is no quantification over a class of candidate prefixes.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~8.1, ``Largest common labelled prefix; repository baseline'']\label{swo:fu:gl:comparison}
{\itshape
$C(R,S)$ is the largest common labelled initial segment of $R$ and $S$.
If $R\ne S$, the least labels $a,b$ outside it, in $R,S$ respectively,
exist and are distinct. The rule
\[
 R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a<_X b
\]
defines a strict linear comparison on the class well-orders of $X$.
It uses elementary comprehension and does not require comparing abstract
class order types or invoking $\ETR$.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex} (source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:fulllex}); the source calls it a repository baseline.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
If $x\in C(R,S)$ and $yRx$, the two orders agree below $x$. Thus $ySx$,
its predecessors agree in the two orders, and the restrictions below
$y$ agree; hence $y\in C(R,S)$. The symmetric argument gives
initiality in $S$. Any two members have the same ordering in $R,S$ by
the predecessor equality for the later member. Every common labelled
initial segment is contained in $C(R,S)$ by its defining condition.

If $C(R,S)=X$, the predecessor equalities give $R=S$. Otherwise each
well-order has a least element outside the prefix. If these least
elements were the same $x$, both would have predecessor class $C(R,S)$,
with equal restricted orders, so $x$ would belong to $C(R,S)$, a
contradiction.

Totality and asymmetry now follow from the label order. For
transitivity, suppose $R<_{\lex}S<_{\lex}T$. Their two common prefixes
are initial in the same order $S$ and are therefore comparable by
inclusion. If one is shorter, the earlier first disagreement also
decides the comparison of $R$ with $T$. If they coincide, the three
next labels satisfy $a<_Xb<_Xc$, so again $R<_{\lex}T$.
\end{proof}

This is the direct proof developed in the repository
(\cref{swo:cf:comparison}; Section~14 at the pin). It also proves that completion cylinders of a
fixed labelled prefix are convex. A completion that departs earlier
compares with every extension of the prefix in the same direction.
For ordinal enumerations the definition agrees with the usual
first-coordinate comparison.

\subsubsection{The first ordinal-class block and all residual fibers}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~8.2, ``Canonical first block'']\label{swo:fu:gl:first-block}
{\itshape
For $R\in\Hall(\No)$, put
\[
 I_R=\{x:\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)\text{ is a set}\}.
\]
Then $I_R$ is an initial proper class, possibly all of $\No$, whose
induced order is set-like. It has a unique enumeration
$F_R:\Ord\to I_R$. The remaining labels carry the residual well-order,
and $R$ is their concatenation after $F_R$.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:core}; the paragraph after it is \cref{swo:cf:fibers}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Initiality follows because an earlier predecessor class is a subset of
a predecessor set. If $I_R$ were a set, the least point $x$ outside it
would have predecessor class exactly $I_R$, contradicting its exclusion.
Thus $I_R$ is proper. Its inherited predecessor classes are sets, so
their ordinal types yield its unique $\Ord$ enumeration.
\end{proof}

Conversely, every injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$ has an
extension to a class well-order of the whole carrier: append a chosen
well-order of $\No\setminus\ran(F)$. Its first block is exactly
$\ran(F)$, because all later points have that proper class as a
subset of their predecessor class. The completions of $F$ are a convex
fiber with the order of all well-orders of the unused carrier. This is
the class analogue of \cref{swo:fu:set:fiber}. It is a statement about given
class parameters and their completions, not the assertion that the
displayed fibers form an ordinary class-sized lexicographic sum.

\subsubsection{All set-interval blocks at once}

The canonical first block can be extracted without recursion. In fact,
the same idea gives every such block simultaneously.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~8.3, ``Canonical set-interval decomposition'']\label{swo:fu:gl:all-blocks}
{\itshape
For a class well-order $R$ on $\No$, define
\[
 x\sim_R y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{the closed $R$-interval between $x,y$ is a set}.
\]
This is an elementary convex equivalence relation. Each class has a
least element and, in its induced order, is either a set ordinal or a
copy of $\Ord$. There is at most one set-sized block, and if it exists
it is final. Therefore $R$ has a canonical representation
\[\tag{S21.5}\label{swo:fu:eq:allblocks}
 R\ \cong\ \left(\sum_{b\in B_R}\Ord\right)+\theta_R,
\]
where $B_R$ is the class of least representatives of its proper blocks
with the induced order and $\theta_R$ is a set ordinal, zero when
there is no final set block. The representation uses no $\ETR$.}
This is the canonical block decomposition of sources~15, 16 and~18, printed in Part~IX (\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition,swo:ds:thm:blocks,swo:sh:thm:class-division}); source~21 proves it independently.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. An interval between $x,z$ is
contained in the union of the intervals between $x,y$ and $y,z$, which
proves transitivity. Convexity follows by taking subintervals. The
condition that an interval is a set is expressed as existence of a set
with exactly its members, so elementary comprehension defines the
relation.

A block is a nonempty admitted subclass, hence has an $R$-least member
$m$. The predecessors of $x$ inside its block form the set interval
$[m,x)_R$. Thus its induced order is set-like, and its ordinal-rank
map identifies it either with a set ordinal or with all of $\Ord$.

If a block $A$ were a set and not final, choose the least point $y$
after it. With $m$ its least point, $[m,y]_R=A\cup\{y\}$ would be a
set. Hence $y\sim_Rm$, contradicting its being outside the block.
This proves the assertion about the final set block.

The least representatives are specified directly by the elementary
relation. Within a proper block, the point of any specified ordinal
rank is unique and is found using a set interval. Consequently the
map evaluating $(b,\alpha)$ at rank $\alpha$ in block $b$ is a class
function given by an elementary formula. Together with the ordinary
enumeration of the optional final set block it yields \eqref{swo:fu:eq:allblocks}.
No sequence of class-valued residual states is constructed.
\end{proof}

The index order $B_R$ need not be set-like. For any class well-order
$J$, the class order $\sum_{j\in J}\Ord$, transferred to $\No$ by
global choice, has $J$ as its proper-block index order. Thus the theorem
is a canonical decomposition, not a reduction of every class well-order
to a set ordinal. These set-interval blocks inside $R$ are also different
from the finite permutation blocks in the lexicographic order of all
such $R$, studied later.

\subsubsection{Normalized support codes}

Fix a baseline class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. A normalized code is
a set permutation $\sigma:\gamma\to\gamma$ satisfying
\[
 \gamma=\sup\{\xi+1:\xi<\gamma,\ \sigma(\xi)\ne\xi\}.
\]
The empty permutation is permitted. Extend $\sigma$ by the identity
outside $\gamma$, and evaluate it as $E_\sigma=b\circ\widehat\sigma$.
Let $\Pbd(b)$ be the ordinary class of these codes, ordered by their
evaluations. Normalization makes evaluation injective. Its range is
exactly the exhaustive enumerations eventually equal to $b$.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~8.4, ``Uniform completion of a set prefix'']\label{swo:fu:gl:prefix-completion}
{\itshape
Every injective set word $p:\delta\to\No$ extends to a core evaluation.
The completion can be chosen by one elementary class construction from
$p$ and the fixed baseline and global well-order.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:completion}; the warning after it is \cref{swo:ec:n8.2}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
For each $\xi<\delta$, let $a_\xi=b^{-1}(p(\xi))$. The prescribed
partial permutation is $\xi\mapsto a_\xi$. Choose an infinite initial
cardinal $\nu$ strictly larger than $\delta$ and all the $a_\xi$.
Both the unused domain and unused range inside $\nu$ then have
cardinality $\nu$, so the partial injection extends to a permutation
of $\nu$. Choose a completion using the fixed global well-order,
extend by the identity, and normalize its support. Its evaluation has
prefix $p$.
\end{proof}

Enlarging to a strictly larger cardinal is useful here. A partial
injection cannot in general be completed on the mere union of its
domain and range: the map $n\mapsto n+1$ on $\omega$ is a simple
counterexample. The preceding completion is the version verified in
the repository, and it works uniformly for all set prefixes.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~8.5, ``Uniform set-cut interpolation; repository baseline'']\label{swo:fu:gl:interpolation}
{\itshape
Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(B_j)_{j\in J}$ be uniformly set-indexed
families of injective $\Ord$-words, with $A_i<_{\lex}B_j$ for every
cross pair. There is an injective set prefix every extension of which
lies strictly between the two families. In particular, a point of
$\Pbd(b)$ lies between them. Empty sides are allowed.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:interpolation}, which the source credits; the paragraphs after it are \cref{swo:gl:pbd-no,swo:prop:universal}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
When both families are nonempty, class replacement bounds their cross
first-disagreement ordinals by a set ordinal $\beta$; otherwise take
$\beta=0$. Build a prefix and call a row active when it still agrees
with the prefix. At stage $\alpha$, the next active left and right
values form sets $L,R$. Every member of $L$ is at most every member
of $R$, because active cross rows have agreed so far. Thus their
intersection has at most one member.

If they share a value $z$, append $z$ and retain exactly the rows with
that next value. It is fresh since every retained row is injective.
The discarded rows have their desired strict inequality permanently
decided. If the sets are disjoint, choose a fresh value strictly
between them, using the surreal set-cut property after removing the
set of previously used labels, append it, and stop. Removing a set
does not destroy set-cut interpolation: first obtain more than that
set's cardinality many distinct separators by set recursion, then take
one outside it. This also covers empty sides.

At limit stages take the union of the previous prefixes. Both sides
cannot remain active through length $\beta$, since that would give an
active cross pair agreeing longer than its bounded first disagreement.
So the procedure stops with a set prefix. Apply
\cref{swo:fu:gl:prefix-completion}. All recursion states and restrictions of
the uniformly indexed rows used in the construction are sets.
\end{proof}

This proof records the uniformity and size facts behind the repository
interpolation theorem (\cref{swo:gl:interpolation}; Theorem~19.10 at the pin). In particular,
$\Pbd(b)$ is a proper-class $\eta_{\Ord}$ order without endpoints. A
set-valued ordinal back-and-forth identifies it with $\No$: enumerate
the two genuine classes by $\Ord$, alternately insert the least unused
point from each, and use set-cut interpolation to extend the current
set partial isomorphism. This is the same structural principle as the
classical uniqueness theorem for the surreal order \cite{Ehrlich2012}.

The same insertion argument embeds every given class linear order into
$\Pbd(b)$, because the set of already placed points supplies only set-sized
constraints at each stage. This gives class-order universality of the
core, with the input order and a global choice function as parameters.
It does not produce an ordinary class whose elements are all input
class orders.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~8.6, ``The core sees exactly the first ordinal block'']\label{swo:fu:gl:initial-cut}
{\itshape
For $R\in\Hall(\No)$, let $F_R$ be its canonical word from
\cref{swo:fu:gl:first-block}. Then
\[
 \{d\in \Pbd(b):E_d<_{\lex}R\}
   =\{d\in \Pbd(b):E_d<_{\lex}F_R\}.
\]
Consequently any cut of the core represented by a full class well-order
is represented by an injective $\Ord$-word.}
This is \cref{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage} and source~14's trace-fibre theorem \cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers} (Part~IX).
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
If $E_d\ne F_R$, they first disagree at an ordinal coordinate, before
any residual tail of $R$ begins. That first disagreement also compares
the well-order represented by $E_d$ with $R$. If $E_d=F_R$, the word
is exhaustive, so $R$ has no unused labels or residual tail and equals
the core well-order itself. Both strict comparisons then fail.
\end{proof}

Thus a cut forgets the residual well-order. In particular, the core is
dense in the set-like fragment, but it is not dense inside a
nonsingleton residual fiber of the full fragment. A proof using density
must specify which of these ambient orders it concerns.

\subsubsection{Diagonal size obstruction}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Proposition~8.7, ``No exhaustive uniform set-code family'']\label{swo:fu:gl:diagonal}
{\itshape
There is no class relation with a class of set codes whose evaluations
include every set-like global enumeration of $\No$.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:diagonal}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Under global choice, a class of set codes can be listed by $\Ord$
(with repetitions if it is a nonempty set). Suppose its rows are
$E_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Ord$. Decode from each row a bit at coordinate
$\alpha$, setting the bit to $1$ exactly when
$E_\alpha(2\cdot\alpha)=b(2\cdot\alpha+1)$.
Form a new exhaustive enumeration by swapping baseline pair
$\alpha$ exactly when this decoded bit is $0$. The new enumeration
differs from row $E_\alpha$ on that pair for every $\alpha$.
It is given by elementary comprehension from the proposed uniform
family, contradicting exhaustiveness. An empty family is immediately
nonexhaustive.
\end{proof}

This is the relevant Cantor diagonal argument. The core has set codes
because its support is a set; arbitrary class support cannot be
compressed into an exhaustive uniform family of set codes. Moving to a
larger universe permits the larger collection as a set there, but does
not invalidate the internal diagonal statement.

% ---- source 29, Section 10
\subsection{Source 29: global well-orders, represented cuts, and the higher-order boundary}\label{swo:bw:sec:global}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~10, printed whole. Its three numbered statements
are results of this report, which source~29 marks as inherited; its
subsection on the core-cut theorem summarizes Part~VIII.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 3062-3235

\subsubsection{Raw comparison is elementary}

Let $R,S$ be class well-orders of the same carrier $\No$. Define $C$
to consist of those labels $x$ whose predecessor carriers in $R$ and
$S$ agree and on which the two predecessor orders agree:
\[
\begin{split}
 x\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad&
   \forall u\ (uRx\leftrightarrow uSx),\\[-2pt]
 &\forall u,v\bigl[(uRx\wedge vRx)
                 \Longrightarrow(uRv\leftrightarrow uSv)\bigr].
\end{split}
\]
This is an elementary formula with the supplied class parameters.
The class $C$ is an initial segment of both orders and their
restrictions to it agree. If $R\ne S$, both complements have least
points
\[
 a=\min_R(\No\setminus C),\qquad
 b=\min_S(\No\setminus C).
\]
They are distinct; otherwise the common next point would belong to
$C$. Define $R<_{\lex}S$ exactly when $a<b$ numerically.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Proposition~10.1, ``Inherited direct comparison'']\label{swo:bw:gl:comparison}
{\itshape
This construction linearly orders the available class well-orders of
$\No$ in the virtual sense. It needs elementary comprehension, not
the comparability of abstract class well-orders and not $\ETR$.
For set-like orders it agrees with first disagreement of their
$\Ord$-enumerations.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex}; source~29 calls it inherited.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~29's proof]
Totality and asymmetry follow from the two different next labels.
For transitivity, the common initial segments for $(R,S)$ and
$(S,T)$ are both initial in $S$, so are comparable by inclusion.
At the shorter segment, two of the orders still agree and the
third comparison is inherited from the given strict inequality.
If the segments are equal, the three next numerical labels give
transitivity directly. This is comparison of labelled initial
segments, not construction of an isomorphism between unrelated
class orders. In the set-like case each common initial segment
has an ordinal position unless the orders agree everywhere, and
the description becomes ordinary first-coordinate disagreement.
The full argument is part of the repository baseline (\cref{swo:cf:lex}).
\end{proof}

The formula explains why comparing raw well-orders and comparing
their abstract order types are different foundational tasks.
The latter asks for a new class map witnessing an initial-segment
isomorphism; that map is not supplied merely by numerical comparison
of two labels. The distinction will be central to
source~29's condensation section (\cref{swo:bw:ch:section}).

\subsubsection{Set-like enumerations and an ordinary class core}

Fix a class bijection $e:\Ord\to\No$. A set-like global well-order
has an exhaustive enumeration of this form. Denote the virtual
collection of these enumerations by $\Hsl$ and the larger collection
of all class well-orders on $\No$ by $\Hall$.

The bounded-support core relative to $e$ consists of the enumerations
$e\circ\pi$, where $\pi$ is a permutation of $\Ord$ that is the
identity outside some set ordinal. Such a permutation has a set code.
Using the least possible support bound removes duplicate codes.
The core, denoted $\Pbd(e)$, is therefore an ordinary class of sets.
It is a small-code substructure of a higher-order collection, not
an identification of that entire collection with a class of sets.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Theorem~10.2, ``Inherited core theorem'']\label{swo:bw:gl:core}
{\itshape
In $\GBC$, $\Pbd(e)$ has the set-cut property and is order-isomorphic
to $\No$. It interpolates every strict cut specified by two uniformly
set-indexed families of set-like global enumerations. In particular,
$\Hsl$ is dense and has no endpoints in the corresponding virtual
sense, and every ordinary class linear order embeds in its core.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:interpolation,swo:gl:pbd-no} with \cref{swo:prop:universal}; the source states it without proof and summarizes the repository's proof in the next paragraph.
\end{note}

The proof in the repository bounds the first disagreements relevant
to the set-indexed constraints, chooses a fresh numerical separator,
and completes the resulting bounded modification to a permutation.
The last assertion uses the usual $\Ord$-stage back-and-forth:
every stage has a set of earlier constraints, so the set-cut property
supplies the next value. The same method proves that any two ordinary
class orders with the full set-cut property are isomorphic in $\GBC$
(\cref{swo:prop:universal}) \cite{BagayokoHoeven}.

This universality includes every set ordinal, reverse ordinal, set
linear order, and supplied class linear order with set-valued points.
It does not assert an embedding of every \emph{higher-order collection}
of classes into $\No$.

\subsubsection{What the core-cut theorem records}

The inspected article has a detailed normal form for proper normalized
cuts of $\Pbd(e)$. Its three mechanisms are a boundary of a prefix cylinder,
a numerical cut inside a next-letter alphabet, and a coherent injective
branch. A cut is represented by an $\Ord$-length injection exactly
when it crosses appropriate prefix cylinders at every set length;
exhaustivity additionally requires that the resulting prefixes cover
all surreal labels (\cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy,swo:tc:thm:recognition}). The explicit branch-automorphism
theorem of this article shows why that coverage condition cannot be
discarded even if the full ordered prefix tree is named.

An arbitrary class well-order can begin with a proper-class set-like
segment and continue with a residual tail. Distinct tails can share
the same first-block trace on the core. A faithful completion must
therefore retain residual-order information in addition to a numerical
cut. Earlier project work develops such decorated completions
(sources~19, 21 and~20; \cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction}).

The unrestricted order $\Hall$ is not dense. For distinct labels
$a<b$, enumerate $\No\setminus\{a,b\}$ first, then append $(a,b)$
or $(b,a)$. These two class well-orders are adjacent: every intermediate
presentation would have to share their entire initial class prefix,
and there are only the two permutations of the residual labels.
More generally, a fixed prefix with $n$ unused labels leaves a finite
convex block of $n!$ presentations. These terminal blocks cannot occur
in an exhaustive set-like enumeration of type $\Ord$.

\subsubsection{Why uniform set codes cannot enumerate everything}

\begin{note}[Source~29, Proposition~10.3, ``Diagonal boundary'']\label{swo:bw:gl:diagonal}
{\itshape
No uniformly class-indexed family of set-like global enumerations,
indexed by an ordinary class of sets, exhausts all such enumerations
available in $\GBC$.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:diagonal}, in the guard-step form of source~25's \cref{swo:ph:prop:diagonal}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~29's proof]
An empty proposed family omits the baseline enumeration. For a
nonempty family, Global Choice permits a listing as
$(F_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Ord}$, allowing repetition if its index
carrier is a set. Construct a new enumeration $G$ in pairs of stages.
At $2\cdot\alpha$, choose an unused label different from
$F_\alpha(2\cdot\alpha)$. At $2\cdot\alpha+1$, choose the least
still unused label in the baseline $e$-scan. There are always fresh
labels because only a set has been used. Set-valued recursion gives
one class map $G$.

It is injective by construction. The odd stages make it exhaustive:
by transfinite induction they eventually pass every fixed baseline
index. It differs from $F_\alpha$ at coordinate $2\cdot\alpha$ for
each $\alpha$. Thus the proposed family omits $G$.
\end{proof}

The statement is about uniform coding. It does not quantify over an
imaginary GB class of all enumerations. An even more concrete size
comparison is available in a specified full model. If $\kappa$ is
strongly inaccessible and one works externally with
$(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$, then its surreal carrier has
external cardinality $\kappa$, whereas its set-like global
enumerations have external cardinality $2^\kappa$. They cannot all
be injected into that carrier. Using this full-model semantics is
a conditional modeling choice; it is not a proof in $\ZFC$ that an
inaccessible cardinal exists.

\subsubsection{Class extensions and external countability}

For a fixed set universe and a fixed available class relation, well-foundedness
is absolute between GBC class expansions. Under Global Choice, a
failure of class well-foundedness yields a set-coded descending
$\omega$-sequence. The equivalence is established in the primary
class-theory literature \cite[\S3]{HamkinsWoodin}. Enlarging the
class collection can change which relations or branches are available;
it does not thereby change well-foundedness of an old fixed relation.

A countable class model has only countably many available global
enumerations externally. Its set-like enumeration order is then a
countable dense linear order without endpoints and is externally
isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$. This does not make the class model itself
recoverable from that bare order. Nor does internal class
well-foundedness automatically imply external well-foundedness;
that stronger correctness property belongs to a beta-model
assumption. Internally finite terminal blocks can also be externally
infinite in an $\omega$-nonstandard model
\cite{HamkinsWoodin} (sources~19 and~20).

\merge\ The last paragraph's remark that a countable class model has set-like
enumeration order $\mathbb Q$ is source~13's \cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}
(Part~IX), proved again in source~21's \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational}
below. Its adjacent pairs and $n!$ blocks are \cref{swo:cf:adjacency}.

\section{Unranked cylinders recover prefix heights (source 22)}\label{swo:rg:sec:unranked}

\merge\ Source~22's Section~8, printed whole. Its \cref{swo:rg:thm:height} is
printed here once; source~25 re-proves it as its Proposition~5.1 and credits
source~22 (\cref{swo:ph:prop:cylinders}). Its \cref{swo:rg:thm:unranked} is a
rank-free form of the represented-cut theorem \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}
(\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold}).

% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 534-635
The earlier continuation recognizes global branches when cylinder labels and levels are supplied (sources~13 and~17: \cref{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction,swo:gs:thm:recognition}). It asks whether the level predicate is additional essential structure. The answer is no, provided the full cylinder incidence structure is retained.

\subsection{A size-safe meaning of the cylinder family}
Let $\Words$ be the ordinary class of injective set-length prefixes. Use the class incidence relation
\[
 I(p,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\in C_p,
 \qquad p\in\Words,\quad d\in\Psupp(b).
\]
The nodes $p$ are sets; the cylinder $C_p$ is its class of incident core points. We never collect those class subsets as elements of an ordinary class. To say that the cylinders are \emph{unranked} means that the node sort, the core order, and incidence are retained, but the domain-length map is not supplied as an additional predicate. Inclusion is still expressible by the elementary formula
\[
 C_q\subseteq C_p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall d\in\Psupp(b)\ (I(q,d)\Rightarrow I(p,d)).
\]
All quantified objects in this formula are sets.

\begin{theorem}[Cylinder inclusion recovers prefix and height]\label{swo:rg:thm:height}
For $p,q\in\Words$,
\[
 C_q\subseteq C_p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\text{ is a prefix of }q.
\]
In particular, distinct prefixes have distinct cylinders. The strict ancestors of $C_p$ under reverse inclusion form a set well-order of order type $\dom p$. Consequently, in the ambient class set theory, the ordinal height is definable from the unranked incidence structure, and any available class incidence isomorphism preserves it.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The forward implication for genuine prefixes is immediate. If $p,q$ are incompatible, their cylinders are disjoint and nonempty, so inclusion is impossible. If $q$ is a proper prefix of $p$, choose a fresh label at coordinate $\dom q$ different from the corresponding label of $p$, and complete this alternative prefix. Its code lies in $C_q$ but not in $C_p$. These cases exhaust all possibilities.

The strict ancestors of $C_p$ are therefore precisely
\[
 C_{p\res\beta},\qquad\beta<\dom p.
\]
Their node codes form a set by replacement. Ordered from the largest cylinder toward the smaller ones, their order type is exactly $\dom p$. Equivalently, height is the unique ordinal order-isomorphic to the set of strict ancestors under reverse inclusion. This description uses only incidence and the ambient set theory. It is not a claim of first-order definability of arbitrary ordinal heights in the pure two-sorted incidence language alone. It is not an appeal to a recursively constructed class-valued rank. An available class incidence isomorphism preserves inclusion and restricts to a set bijection on each ancestor set. It therefore preserves the unique ordinal order type. This is an internal statement; an arbitrary external map over a nonstandard model is not silently asserted to be an available class isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The fresh-choice hypothesis is real]\label{swo:rg:n8.2}
The analogous assertion can fail for a finite exhaustive permutation tree. If one unused label remains, appending that forced label does not change the cylinder, so two different prefix lengths have the same cylinder. Here the whole surreal alphabet always leaves fresh labels after a set prefix; \cref{swo:rg:lem:supported,swo:rg:lem:fresh} rule out that collapse. The finite regression suite records both the positive fresh-reserve case and this counterexample.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A rank-free criterion for a represented cut}
A \emph{normalized cut} of $\Psupp(b)$ is an initial subclass $L\subset\Psupp(b)$ such that $L$ and $U=\Psupp(b)\setminus L$ are nonempty and $L$ has no greatest point. The upper class $U$ is allowed to have a least point. This convention agrees with strict lower traces
\[
 L_h=\{d\in\Psupp(b):d<h\}.
\]
Normalization matters when $h$ itself is the evaluation of a core code: it prevents choosing the wrong side of that point.

Say that $L$ \emph{crosses} $C_p$ when both $L\cap C_p$ and $U\cap C_p$ are nonempty. Let
\[
 B_L=\{p\in\Words:L\text{ crosses }C_p\}.
\]
This is an ordinary class of set nodes, defined by elementary comprehension from $L$ and incidence.

\begin{lemma}[Crossed cylinders form an initial branch]\label{swo:rg:lem:crossed}
The class $B_L$ is a chain in the prefix order and is closed under taking prefixes. At most one crossed node has a given height.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Ancestor closure follows from cylinder inclusion. Two incompatible cylinders are disjoint convex subsets of a linear order, with one entirely before the other. They cannot both meet both sides of an initial cut: an upper-side point in the earlier cylinder and a lower-side point in the later cylinder would contradict initiality. Thus crossed nodes are compatible. Nodes of equal length which are compatible are equal.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unranked branch-recognition theorem]\label{swo:rg:thm:unranked}
For a normalized cut $L$ of $\Psupp(b)$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $L=L_h$ for an injective class word $h:\Ord\hookrightarrow\No$.
\item The crossed-node class $B_L$ is proper: it is not contained in any set.
\item The recovered heights of crossed cylinders are unbounded in $\Ord$.
\item For every ordinal $\alpha$, there is exactly one crossed node of height $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
The representing word is unique and is definable by elementary comprehension from $L$ and the labelled node incidence. No $\ETR$ is needed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $L=L_h$, then every prefix $h\res\alpha$ is crossed, by the two-sided completion construction preceding \cref{swo:rg:prop:global-density}. Conversely, a prefix incompatible with $h$ has its cylinder wholly on one side. Therefore the crossed nodes are exactly the prefixes of $h$, proving (i)$\Rightarrow$(iv).

By \cref{swo:rg:lem:crossed}, there is at most one crossed node of each height. If all heights are bounded by an ordinal $\lambda$, class replacement applied to the uniquely specified nodes of heights at most $\lambda$ shows that $B_L$ is a set. This proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii). Unbounded heights together with ancestor closure give exactly one node of every height, proving (iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv). A set of nodes has bounded ordinal heights, so (iv)$\Rightarrow$(ii).

Assume (iv). The unique crossed nodes are compatible and nested. Define
\[
 h(\xi)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists p\in B_L\ (\xi\in\dom p\ \wedge\ p(\xi)=x).
\]
This is an elementary class definition, with set quantifiers only. Existence at each coordinate follows from the crossed node of height $\xi+1$; uniqueness and injectivity follow from compatibility. Thus $h$ is an injective $\Ord$-word.

Fix a core point $d$ whose evaluation differs from $h$, and let $\xi$ be the first disagreement. The cylinder of $h\res(\xi+1)$ lies wholly above $d$ if $d<h$, and wholly below $d$ if $d>h$. Since that cylinder is crossed, initiality of $L$ forces $d\in L$ in the first case and $d\in U$ in the second. If $d=h$ is a core point, it cannot belong to $L$: all larger points lie in $U$, so it would be the greatest member of $L$. Hence $L=L_h$. Distinct words have distinct traces by \cref{swo:rg:prop:global-density}, proving uniqueness.
\end{proof}

The properness assertion in (ii) is itself elementary in the class parameter $L$:
\[
 \forall a\ \exists p\ (p\in B_L\ \wedge\ p\notin a),
\]
where $a,p$ range over sets. Thus ``proper class'' is not concealing quantification over a new sort of classes of cylinders.

\begin{corollary}[Exhaustiveness is label coverage]\label{swo:rg:cor:coverage}
The word reconstructed in \cref{swo:rg:thm:unranked} is exhaustive if and only if
\[
 \forall x\in\No\ \exists p\in B_L\quad x\in\ran p.
\]
Therefore unranked cylinder incidence, together with the label-occurrence relation on nodes, suffices to recognize traces of global well-orders.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The reconstructed range is exactly the union of the ranges of the crossed prefixes. Equality of that range with $\No$ is the displayed condition.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What has, and has not, been reconstructed}
The level predicate is redundant: it is recovered from the ancestor order. Exhaustiveness still uses labels, and the word itself uses the coordinate-value incidence of a prefix. We have not shown that this label information can be discarded. Nor have we reconstructed cylinders from the pure core order. The earlier continuation gives an automorphism showing that the bare linear order does not determine its original prefix cylinders (source~13, \cref{swo:fs:thm:nonrigidity}). These statements are compatible: once an unranked cylinder family is supplied, its levels are forced; without that family, the order alone need not determine it.

The criterion also sharpens the logical form of the earlier branch description. A normalized cut which crosses only set-many nodes is not an injective full-length branch trace. A failure can arise when a next-label cut is not realized, or at a limit-prefix boundary, as analyzed in the earlier reports. The present theorem does not need to choose a first failure recursively; it detects all such failures by the boundedness of the crossed branch.

\begin{note}[\merge; the represented-cut theorem in batch 83]\label{swo:xiii:note:ninefold}
Part~VIII prints six proofs of the represented-cut theorem
(\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold}). Batch~83 adds three: source~20's Theorem~3.10
(\cref{swo:lm:base:recognition}), source~21's
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:reconstruction,swo:fu:fnd:thm:represented-cuts}
(\cref{swo:xiii:sec:coreaut}), and source~22's
\cref{swo:rg:lem:crossed,swo:rg:thm:unranked} above. Sources~25, 27 and~30 use
the theorem and credit it (\cref{swo:ph:prop:trace-extension}, source~27's
display (S27.17), \cref{swo:rt:fnd:cor:cuts}). Source~22's form is the only one
stated without the ranks of the crossing prefixes: properness of the class of
crossed nodes replaces ``a crossing prefix at every length''. Its
\cref{swo:rg:cor:coverage} is the coverage clause of
\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}.

Source~22's sentence ``We have not shown that this label information can be
discarded'' is answered by source~25, negatively: the core with all its
