the single cross-node relation of \cref{swo:ph:sec:labels} suffices.
\end{note}

% ---- source 25, Section 5
\section{What unranked cylinders remember (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:cylinders}

\merge\ Source~25's Section~5. Its Proposition~5.1 is source~22's
\cref{swo:rg:thm:height} and is printed as a note.

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 329-396

\subsection{The two-sorted reduct}

Let $\Cyls_b$ have a core sort $\Psupp(b)$, a node sort $\Words$, the order $<_{\lex}$ on $\Psupp(b)$, the prefix relation on $\Words$, and the incidence relation
\[
 \operatorname{Inc}(d,p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\pre d.
\]
One may equivalently recover prefix order from cylinder inclusion. The structure has \emph{no} coordinate-value relation, no ambient membership relation on the codes, and no predicate identifying equal letters used at different nodes. Those are genuinely additional relations, not silently included.

The two sorts are ordinary classes of sets. A cylinder is represented by its node code, not used as a proper-class element of a new class. This is how the informal phrase ``the family of all cylinders'' is made size-safe.

\begin{note}[Source~25, Proposition~5.1, ``Cylinder recovery'']\label{swo:ph:prop:cylinders}
{\itshape
For $p,q\in\Words$,
\[
 C_q\subseteq C_p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\pre q.
\]
Distinct nodes have distinct cylinders. The proper ancestors of a node of length $\alpha$ form a set-sized chain of order type $\alpha$. Hence the unranked cylinder structure determines all prefix lengths.}
This is source~22's \cref{swo:rg:thm:height}, which source~25 credits in the next paragraph; the proof is the same.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
A prefix extension gives the displayed inclusion. Incompatible prefixes have disjoint nonempty cylinders. If $q$ is a proper prefix of $p$, choose at the next position a fresh letter different from that of $p$ and complete the resulting word to the core. Thus $C_p$ is a proper subset of $C_q$. These observations give the converse and injectivity. The proper ancestors of $p$ are exactly $p\res\beta$, $\beta<\alpha$, and their prefix order has type $\alpha$.
\end{proof}

This reconstruction was established in the residual-geometry continuation (source~22, \cref{swo:rg:thm:height}). We use it to convert the new profile theorem into a result about \emph{unranked} cylinders rather than an expansion with a gratuitously named length function.

\subsection{Automorphisms and first-disagreement profiles}

An automorphism of $\Cyls_b$ is a pair $(F,T)$ of class bijections on its two sorts preserving the displayed relations. An order automorphism $F$ of $\Psupp(b)$ carrying cylinders onto cylinders determines $T$ uniquely by
\[
 F[C_p]=C_{T(p)}.
\]
By \Cref{swo:ph:prop:cylinders}, $T$ preserves lengths and prefixes.

For distinct full words define
\[
 \operatorname{pr}(f,g)=
 \bigl(\delta(f,g),\operatorname{sgn}(f,g)\bigr),
 \quad
 \operatorname{sgn}(f,g)=
 \begin{cases}-1,&f<_{\lex}g,\\+1,&g<_{\lex}f.\end{cases}
\]
These profiles determine every pairwise prefix-equivalence relation:
\[
 f\res\alpha=g\res\alpha
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \alpha\leq\delta(f,g)
 \qquad(f\ne g).
\]
The inequality includes equality: a disagreement at $\alpha$ still permits agreement on the restriction to $\alpha$.

\begin{proposition}[Automatic profile preservation]\label{swo:ph:prop:automatic}
Every automorphism of $\Cyls_b$ preserves the first-disagreement ordinal between distinct core branches. Conversely, an order automorphism of $\Psupp(b)$ preserving these ordinals induces a unique automorphism of $\Cyls_b$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The longest prefix common to distinct core branches is the unique deepest node incident with both. Its height is their first-disagreement ordinal and is recovered by \Cref{swo:ph:prop:cylinders}.

Conversely, for $p$ of length $\alpha$, choose $d\in C_p$ and set
\[
 T(p)=F(d)\res\alpha.
\]
For any other $e\in C_p$, either $e=d$ or $\delta(e,d)\geq\alpha$. Profile preservation makes the formula independent of the choice. Applying the same argument to $F^{-1}$ gives an inverse on nodes. The equality $F[C_p]=C_{T(p)}$ follows in both directions, and the remaining structural relations are preserved.
\end{proof}

Every such $T$ acts on a supplied $f\in\Jinj$ by
\[\tag{S25.1}\label{swo:ph:eq:branch-action}
 \widehat T(f)(\alpha)
   =T(f\res(\alpha+1))(\alpha).
\]
The transformed prefixes cohere, so this is an injective full class word. Its inverse is obtained from $T^{-1}$. It preserves all first-disagreement ordinals and lexicographic comparisons and agrees with $F$ on the core. This is an elementary transformation of supplied class parameters, not the graph of a same-level function whose arguments are proper classes.

% ---- source 25, Section 6
\section{The one-point profile extension theorem (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:extension}

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 399-460

The central issue is not extending a partial permutation of labels. Different nodes may relabel the same numerical value differently. What must be preserved is the ordered tree geometry: the first place at which two branches separate and the direction of that separation.

\begin{lemma}[One-point extension into the core]\label{swo:ph:lem:onepoint}
Let $I$ be a set, and let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(a_i')_{i\in I}$ be uniformly indexed families of pairwise distinct members of $\Jinj$ such that
\[
 \operatorname{pr}(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{pr}(a_i',a_j')
 \qquad(i\ne j).
\]
Given $d\in\Jinj$ distinct from every $a_i$, there is $c\in\Psupp(b)$ such that
\[
 \operatorname{pr}(d,a_i)=\operatorname{pr}(c,a_i')
 \qquad(i\in I).
\]
The witness can be selected uniformly from the supplied class parameters and the set of indices.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $I=\varnothing$, choose any core code. Otherwise let
\[
 \delta_i=\delta(d,a_i),\qquad
 \lambda=\sup_{i\in I}(\delta_i+1).
\]
Class replacement makes the collection of these ordinals a set. We construct a set-length injective prefix $r$ that already decides every required comparison. There are two cases; the second is essential at transfinite lengths.

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 1: the disagreement ordinals have a maximum $\delta_*$.}
Let $I_* =\{i\in I:\delta_i=\delta_*\}$. All the source branches with indices in $I_*$ agree with $d$ below $\delta_*$. Hence their target branches share a common prefix $r_0$ of length $\delta_*$. Partition their next labels according to the required side of the new label:
\begin{align*}
 L&=\{a_i'(\delta_*):i\in I_*,\ a_i(\delta_*)<d(\delta_*)\},\\
 R&=\{a_i'(\delta_*):i\in I_*,\ d(\delta_*)<a_i(\delta_*)\}.
\end{align*}
If a label lies in $L$ and another in $R$, their source branches first disagree at $\delta_*$ and are in that increasing order. Profile preservation implies the same for their target labels. Therefore $L<R$. \Cref{swo:ph:lem:fresh} supplies
\[
 x\notin\ran r_0,\qquad L<x<R.
\]
Put $r=r_0\cat(x)$. It has the required profile against every top-level constraint.

For an index $i$ with $\delta_i<\delta_*$, choose $j\in I_*$. The source branch $a_j$ agrees with $d$ through coordinate $\delta_i$. Consequently the comparison of $a_j$ with $a_i$ has exactly the first disagreement and direction required of $d$ against $a_i$. The target profile transfers this statement to $a_j'$ against $a_i'$. Since $r$ agrees with $a_j'$ through coordinate $\delta_i$, it has the required profile against this lower-level constraint as well.

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 2: the disagreement ordinals have no maximum.}
Here $\lambda$ is a limit ordinal and the $\delta_i$ are cofinal in $\lambda$. For each $\beta<\lambda$, define
\[
 r(\beta)=a_i'(\beta)\quad\text{for any }i\text{ with }\delta_i>\beta.
\]
This is independent of $i$. Indeed, any two such source branches agree with $d$ through $\beta$, so their target branches agree through $\beta$. For $\gamma<\beta<\lambda$, choose one $i$ with $\delta_i>\beta$; both $r(\gamma)$ and $r(\beta)$ occur at the corresponding positions of the injective branch $a_i'$. They are distinct. Thus $r$ is an injective word of length $\lambda$.

Fix $i\in I$ and choose $j$ with $\delta_j>\delta_i$. The source $a_j$ agrees with $d$ through $\delta_i$. The profile of $a_j$ against $a_i$ therefore equals that of $d$ against $a_i$. Transferring this profile to the targets and using the definition of $r$ gives
\[
 \delta(r,a_i')=\delta_i
\]
with the required direction. This notation concerns a disagreement already occurring within the domain of $r$, not a comparison using a termination convention.

\smallskip
In either case \Cref{swo:ph:lem:completion} extends $r$ to a core branch $c$. All prescribed first disagreements occur inside $r$, so completion changes none of them. For uniformity, choose the least successful core code in a fixed set-like global well-order. The existence just proved guarantees that this elementary selection is defined.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why no numerical equality pattern is required]\label{swo:ph:n6.2}
The argument does not preserve equality between a letter occurring in one node and a letter occurring at another depth or on another branch. Its only injectivity obligation is within the new prefix $r$. In Case 1 this is handled by avoiding $\ran r_0$; in Case 2 it follows from coherence inside individual target branches. This is the precise source of the extra symmetries studied below.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[An elementary local distortion]\label{swo:ph:n6.3}
Take the two one-step extensions $(0,1)$ and $(2,1)$ of different first-letter nodes. An ordered-tree transformation can send their final labels to two different values, provided each local map is increasing and avoids the label already used on its own prefix. Nothing in sibling order or common-prefix lengths identifies these two occurrences of the original label $1$. \Cref{swo:ph:sec:labels} isolates exactly the relation that prohibits such a distortion.
\end{example}

% ---- source 25, Section 7
\section{Exact configuration homogeneity (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:homogeneity}

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 463-513

\begin{theorem}[Classification of set-indexed branch configurations]\label{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity}
Let $(f_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(g_i)_{i\in I}$ be uniformly set-indexed families of pairwise distinct members of $\Jinj$. There exists an automorphism $(F,T)$ of $\Cyls_b$ such that
\[
 \widehat T(f_i)=g_i\qquad(i\in I)
\]
if and only if the following conditions hold:
\begin{align*}
 f_i\in\Psupp(b)&\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g_i\in\Psupp(b),\tag{S25.2}\label{swo:ph:eq:member-invariant}\\
 \delta(f_i,f_j)&=\delta(g_i,g_j)\qquad(i\ne j),\tag{S25.3}\label{swo:ph:eq:delta-invariant}\\
 f_i<_{\lex}f_j&\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g_i<_{\lex}g_j\qquad(i\ne j).
 \tag{S25.4}\label{swo:ph:eq:order-invariant}
\end{align*}
The construction uses GBC, not ETR.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows from \Cref{swo:ph:prop:automatic}, the induced branch action, and the fact that $F$ maps the core onto itself.

For sufficiency, start with the prescribed correspondences between the core members among the $f_i$ and $g_i$. Their unique normalized codes form sets by class replacement. The remaining $f_i,g_i$ are retained as fixed external-to-the-core constraints. The word ``external'' here means outside $\Psupp(b)$, not outside the model or its admitted classes.

Choose a class enumeration of all core codes, indexed by $\Ord$. Construct a growing partial bijection $H$ between core codes by back-and-forth. At each set stage $\alpha$, its graph $H_\alpha$ is a set. Maintain the invariant that all prescribed correspondences, consisting of $H_\alpha$ and the noncore markers, preserve the profiles of distinct branches.

At a forth step, take the next enumerated core code $d$ not yet in the domain. It is distinct from every source constraint: the core constraints already lie in the domain, and the other markers are noncore. \Cref{swo:ph:lem:onepoint}, applied to the uniformly set-indexed current constraints, gives a core target $c$ with exactly the required profiles. In particular, $c$ differs from every current target, so adding $(d,c)$ preserves injectivity and the invariant.

At a back step, take the next core code not in the range and apply the same lemma with sources and targets interchanged. At a limit set stage, take the union of the earlier partial maps. This is still a set, and every pairwise requirement appeared together at an earlier stage. Choose the least possible witness at each extension step. Thus ordinary set-valued recursion along $\Ord$ defines the whole construction in GBC.

The union $F$ is a class bijection of $\Psupp(b)$ preserving every core profile. It is an order automorphism, and \Cref{swo:ph:prop:automatic} gives its unique node action $T$.

For a noncore marker $f_i$, fix an ordinal $\alpha$ and choose a core completion $d$ of $f_i\res\alpha$. Since $d\ne f_i$, their first disagreement is at least $\alpha$. The maintained constraint implies that $F(d)$ agrees with $g_i$ below $\alpha$. By the definition of the node action,
\[
 T(f_i\res\alpha)=F(d)\res\alpha=g_i\res\alpha.
\]
This holds at every set-ordinal length, so $\widehat T(f_i)=g_i$. The prescribed core markers were already mapped correctly by $F$. This proves sufficiency.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exactly two single-branch orbits]\label{swo:ph:cor:two-orbits}
Under the induced action of automorphisms of $\Cyls_b$, the virtual domain $\Jinj$ has precisely two orbits:
\[
 \Psupp(b)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Jinj\setminus\Psupp(b).
\]
More explicitly, any two supplied core branches can be carried to one another, and any two supplied noncore injective branches can be carried to one another, but no core branch can be carried to a noncore branch.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \Cref{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity} to a one-element index set. Only the membership condition remains. Both cases are nonempty: $b$ is a core branch, and an injection omitting a label is not.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The logical meaning of an orbit]\label{swo:ph:n7.3}
The corollary abbreviates a quantified assertion about supplied class words and class maps on set codes. It does not construct an ordinary class whose elements are all automorphisms, all branches, or their equivalence classes. In the regular set model of \Cref{swo:ph:sec:sets}, these become ordinary sets and an ordinary group action.
\end{remark}

The theorem also determines all finite and set-indexed tuple orbits. For example, a pair of noncore branches is classified solely by its first-disagreement ordinal and its order orientation. A triple must satisfy the usual compatibility of first-disagreement data, but once both triples exist, no additional cross-coordinate label pattern is an invariant. Repeated entries can be admitted by first matching their equality pattern and then passing to distinct representatives; a set of representatives exists by set choice.

\begin{note}[\merge; how this compares with Part~VIII]\label{swo:xiii:note:twoorbits}
Source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits} classifies cuts of the bare core order by
their characters; the cuts of all noncore injective words have character
$(\Ord,\Ord)$ and lie in one orbit there with every other cut of that
character, for example the edges of successor-length cylinders. An
automorphism that also carries cylinders to cylinders preserves the crossing
condition of \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}, so it maps branch cuts to branch
cuts; \cref{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity} shows that on branches the remaining
invariants are exactly core membership, first-disagreement ordinals and order.
Source~27's
\cref{swo:sc:thm:branchtransitive} and source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity} keep the ordered prefix tree but not the
core, and obtain one orbit of all injective branches; \cref{swo:ph:cor:two-orbits}
shows that retaining the core splits it into exactly two.
\end{note}

% ---- source 25, Section 8
\section{Exhaustiveness is invisible to unlabelled cylinders (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:invisible}

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 516-571

\subsection{An explicit pair of branches}

Let $e$ be obtained from $b$ by swapping each pair of consecutive positions
\[
 2\cdot\xi,\quad 2\cdot\xi+1\qquad(\xi\in\Ord).
\]
The finite factor is on the \emph{left} in ordinal multiplication. These pairs partition $\Ord$. The word $e$ is a bijection onto $\No$ and differs from $b$ at every position, so $e\notin\Psupp(b)$.

Define another class word by
\[
 f(\alpha)=b(1+\alpha).
\]
The map $\alpha\mapsto1+\alpha$ is an increasing bijection from $\Ord$ onto its nonzero ordinals. Thus $f$ is injective and omits exactly $b(0)$. Moreover, $1+\alpha=\alpha$ for every infinite ordinal $\alpha$, so $f$ eventually agrees with $b$. This illustrates why eventual agreement without exhaustiveness does not characterize the core.

\begin{theorem}[Cylinder preservation does not preserve coverage]\label{swo:ph:thm:invisible}
There is an automorphism $(F,T)$ of $\Cyls_b$ and branches $e\in\Hsl$, $f\in\Jinj\setminus\Hsl$ such that
\[
 \widehat T(e)=f.
\]
It preserves the core order, every cylinder as a member of the cylinder family, all prefix lengths, and all first-disagreement ordinals. Nevertheless, it carries an exhaustive branch to one omitting a label.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The preceding $e$ and $f$ are both noncore. Apply \Cref{swo:ph:cor:two-orbits}.
\end{proof}

Here preserving the cylinder family means permuting its members, not fixing every cylinder pointwise. Fixing every cylinder would fix every core branch and every supplied full branch.

\subsection{The obstruction survives set-many parameters}

\begin{theorem}[Parameter-robust non-invariance]\label{swo:ph:thm:parameters}
Let $A\subseteq\Psupp(b)$ and $P\subseteq\Words$ be sets. There is an automorphism of $\Cyls_b$ fixing every member of $A$ and every node of $P$, but carrying some exhaustive noncore branch to a nonexhaustive injective branch.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each $p\in P$, choose a core completion $d_p$. Add these codes to $A$, obtaining a set $A'$. Choose a surreal $x$ outside the set of first labels $\{d(0):d\in A'\}$, and choose a core branch $d_0$ beginning with $x$.

Construct an exhaustive branch $e$ beginning with $x$ by leaving the first position of $d_0$ fixed and swapping a proper class of disjoint consecutive pairs in its tail. It differs from $d_0$, and hence from $b$, on a proper class of positions, so it is noncore. Construct $f$ by
\[
 f(0)=d_0(0),\qquad f(\alpha)=d_0(1+\alpha)\quad(\alpha>0).
\]
This word begins with $x$, is injective, and omits $d_0(1)$.

For each $a\in A'$, both $e$ and $f$ disagree with $a$ at coordinate $0$, and their comparison directions are identical because their first label is $x$. The two configurations consisting of all the fixed branches in $A'$ followed by $e$, respectively $f$, therefore satisfy \Cref{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity}. The resulting automorphism fixes $A'$. It fixes each $p\in P$ because $p$ is the prefix of the fixed $d_p$ at its invariant length.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No invariant unlabelled recognition test]\label{swo:ph:cor:recognition}
Exhaustiveness is not invariantly recognizable from $\Cyls_b$ and any prescribed set of core and node parameters. In particular, an automorphism-invariant definition in this reduct cannot recognize precisely the exhaustive full branches.
\end{corollary}

This is deliberately a statement about the specified reduct and admitted branch action. In an ambient set theory that retains the full coordinate-value relation, exhaustiveness is simply the condition that every surreal occurs. We have not made that condition undefinable in the ambient theory; we have shown that the reduct forgets information needed to recover it. The result also does not assert that every enrichment strictly weaker than the one in \Cref{swo:ph:sec:labels} fails.

\subsection{Other properties lost by forgetting labels}

The branch $\alpha\mapsto\alpha$, viewing each ordinal as a surreal, is numerically increasing and nonexhaustive. It is therefore noncore. \Cref{swo:ph:cor:two-orbits} places it in the same orbit as every other noncore injective branch, including an exhaustive branch. Consequently numerical increasingness is also invisible in the unlabelled cylinder structure. It concerns comparisons between labels occurring at \emph{different} coordinates, whereas the prefix geometry orders siblings at one coordinate after a common prefix.

Similarly, the number or order type of omitted labels is not an invariant on the noncore orbit. This statement applies only to omitted ranges realized by supplied injective class words; it does not posit a same-level collection of all class cardinalities or all class order types.

\begin{note}[\merge; relation to the bare-order results]\label{swo:xiii:note:invisible}
\Cref{swo:ph:thm:invisible} strengthens \cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic},
\cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension} with \cref{swo:gs:n10.4}, and
\cref{swo:cb:thm:automorphism}: those move an exhaustive cut by an automorphism
of the bare core, whereas here every cylinder is carried to a cylinder.
\Cref{swo:ph:thm:parameters} is the cylinder-preserving counterpart of
source~20's \cref{swo:lm:aut:thm:localfailure}, which fixes a set of core
points pointwise in the bare order (written before Part~VIII; source~25 did
not cite it). Source~13's \cref{swo:fs:thm:nonrigidity} is a different
theorem: there an automorphism of $\Hsl$ moves a cylinder to a non-cylinder.
\end{note}

% ---- source 25, Section 9
\section{Extension to the full enumeration order (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:extension-obstruction}

\merge\ Source~25's Section~9. Its Proposition~9.1 is source~17's
\cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}, which source~25 credits; it is printed as
a note with source~25's proof.

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 574-607

The previous sections construct an automorphism of the small-coded core and its full injective prefix completion. Does it extend to an order automorphism of the exhaustive domain $\Hsl$? The answer can fail even when the core automorphism respects every prefix cylinder.

\begin{note}[Source~25, Proposition~9.1, ``Represented-trace criterion'']\label{swo:ph:prop:trace-extension}
{\itshape
Let $F$ be an order automorphism of $\Psupp(b)$. It has an order-automorphism extension to $\Hsl$ exactly when it permutes, in both directions, the cuts
\[
 L_e=\{d\in\Psupp(b):d<_{\lex}e\}\qquad(e\in\Hsl)
\]
that are represented by admitted exhaustive branches. If such an extension exists, it is unique. The statement about an extension is understood as a uniform transformation of supplied class words, or externally in a larger universe.}
This is \cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion} (source~17's Theorem~10.1); sources~20 and~21 prove it again as \cref{swo:lm:aut:thm:extensioncriterion,swo:fu:fnd:thm:extension-criterion}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
Any extension must carry $L_e$ to $L_{G(e)}$. Conversely, assume both $F$ and $F^{-1}$ carry represented traces to represented traces. By \Cref{swo:ph:cor:trace}, the branch representing $F[L_e]$ is unique. Define $G(e)$ to be this branch. The corresponding construction for $F^{-1}$ gives its inverse. Density of $\Psupp(b)$ in $\Jinj$ shows that trace inclusion strictly reflects the order, so $G$ is increasing and extends $F$.

There is no need to choose from a collection of classes to make the uniform statement precise. For a supplied trace $L$, the condition that a prefix cylinder crosses its lower and upper sides is elementary in $L$ and the core codes. When $L$ is represented by an injective full branch, these crossing cylinders are exactly its prefixes: an agreeing prefix has core completions on both sides, while an incompatible prefix has its entire cylinder on one side. The unique prefix of each length is therefore recovered by elementary comprehension, and its union defines the representing branch. Apply this decoder to $F[L_e]$.
\end{proof}

The criterion is a conceptual reduction rather than a local classification of the stabilizing automorphism group. The criterion was already proved in the second continuation (source~17's Theorem~10.1, \cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}); it is re-established here to fix the uniformity convention. The next conclusion strengthens the known obstruction by retaining all cylinders.

\begin{theorem}[A cylinder-preserving automorphism with no exhaustive extension]\label{swo:ph:thm:noextension}
There exists an order automorphism $F$ of $\Psupp(b)$ preserving all prefix cylinders that has no order-automorphism extension to $\Hsl$, even if the prospective extension is not required to preserve cylinders.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $F,T,e,f$ as in \Cref{swo:ph:thm:invisible}. The induced order-preserving branch action gives
\[
 F[L_e]=L_f.
\]
An order-automorphism extension $G$ on $\Hsl$ would also give $F[L_e]=L_{G(e)}$. Trace injectivity on all of $\Jinj$ would imply $G(e)=f$. This contradicts $f\notin\Hsl$.
\end{proof}

For a cylinder-preserving $F$, the action $\widehat T$ on $\Jinj$ is already determined. The precise condition for an extension to $\Hsl$ is therefore
\[
 \widehat T[\Hsl]=\Hsl.
\]
This is not automatic from preserving the core, the lexicographic order, or the entire unranked prefix tree. Exhaustive completion is an additional choice of represented branches inside the injective completion.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:ph:thm:noextension} answers in part Part~VIII's open item
on the stabilizer of the exhaustive cuts (\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}~(c)): not
every cylinder-preserving automorphism of $\Psupp(b)$ lies in that subgroup of
$\Aut(\Psupp(b))$. Source~19's \cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:aut} gives
the exact criterion for extension to the unrestricted order in an external
set-sized model.

% ---- source 25, Section 10
\section{Cross-node label coherence and rigidity (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:labels}

\merge\ Source~25's Section~10. Source~27 proves \cref{swo:ph:thm:coherence}
independently as its Theorem~6.5, printed as a note in
\cref{swo:sc:sec:prefix} (\cref{swo:sc:thm:labelcoherence}).

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 610-670

\subsection{A single additional relation}

An extension edge is a pair $(p,q)$ of nodes such that $q=p\cat(x)$ for one unused label $x$. These are exactly the immediate-successor pairs in the prefix order. Add a relation $\sim_{\mathrm{lab}}$ on edges by
\[
 (p,p\cat(x))\sim_{\mathrm{lab}}(q,q\cat(y))
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=y.
\]
The relation connects occurrences of one label at different nodes. It does not initially name any label, any birthday, or any field operation.

Each equivalence class of edges has exactly one root edge, namely $(\varnothing,(x))$. Thus labels can be represented by these existing set-coded root edges. There is no quotient whose elements would have to be proper classes. The root edges inherit the numerical order from their cylinders, and this reconstructs the ordered alphabet.

For the next theorem, consider the ordered prefix tree by itself: its node sort, prefix order, and the order of immediate successors at each node. This sibling order can either be included directly or recovered from the core cylinders.

\begin{theorem}[Label-coherent tree automorphisms]\label{swo:ph:thm:coherence}
An automorphism $T$ of the ordered injective prefix tree preserves $\sim_{\mathrm{lab}}$ if and only if there is an order automorphism $h$ of $(\No,<)$ such that
\[
 T(p)=h\circ p\qquad(p\in\Words).
\]
The alphabet automorphism $h$ is unique.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The action on root edges defines a unique bijection $h:\No\to\No$ by
\[
 T((x))=(h(x)).
\]
Preservation of their sibling order makes $h$ increasing. If the edge from $p$ to $p\cat(x)$ is considered, it is label-equivalent to the root edge for $x$. Its image must be label-equivalent to the root edge for $h(x)$. Therefore
\[
 T(p\cat(x))=T(p)\cat(h(x)).
\]
Induction along the set-ordinal length of $p$ proves $T(p)=h\circ p$. At a limit length, the node is the union of its proper prefixes, and their images determine it uniquely. Conversely, coordinatewise application of any order automorphism $h$ preserves injectivity, prefix order, sibling order, and edge-label equality. Its inverse is coordinatewise application of $h^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[No nontrivial set-supported alphabet automorphism]\label{swo:ph:lem:small-support-rigid}
If an order automorphism $h$ of $\No$ fixes all points outside a set, then $h=\id$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $x<h(x)$. Choose, by \Cref{swo:ph:lem:fresh}, a point $y$ strictly between them and outside the support of $h$. Monotonicity gives $h(x)<h(y)=y$, contradicting $y<h(x)$. If $h(x)<x$, choose a fixed point $y$ between $h(x)$ and $x$; monotonicity gives $y=h(y)<h(x)$, again a contradiction. Thus every point is fixed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The label-coherent core structure is rigid]\label{swo:ph:thm:rigidity}
Every automorphism $(F,T)$ of $\Cyls_b$ preserving $\sim_{\mathrm{lab}}$ is the identity. No numerical labels need to be named individually.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\Cref{swo:ph:thm:coherence} gives $T(p)=h\circ p$ for an alphabet order automorphism $h$. Hence the induced action on the baseline is
\[
 F(b)=\widehat T(b)=h\circ b.
\]
Because $F(b)\in\Psupp(b)$, there is a set-supported permutation $\pi$ of $\Ord$ such that $h(b(\alpha))=b(\pi(\alpha))$. If $S$ is the set support of $\pi$, then $h$ fixes all labels outside the set $b[S]$. \Cref{swo:ph:lem:small-support-rigid} implies $h=\id$. Thus $T=\id$, and the prefixes of every core branch force $F=\id$ as well.
\end{proof}

There is a sharp contrast here. Without cross-node label equality the core structure has two large branch orbits and is homogeneous for all the configurations in \Cref{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity}. After adding just this one relation, it is rigid. For the ordered tree without the distinguished supported core, the same relation still permits all coordinatewise alphabet automorphisms. The rigidity is therefore a joint effect of label coherence and the chosen eventual-agreement core.

\begin{proposition}[Coverage from coherent edges]\label{swo:ph:prop:coverage}
In the edge-coherent expansion, a supplied full branch is exhaustive if and only if every root edge is label-equivalent to some extension edge on the branch.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Root edges represent every surreal label exactly once. An edge on the branch represents exactly the label introduced at its corresponding coordinate. The condition is therefore equivalent to every surreal occurring in its range.
\end{proof}

\Cref{swo:ph:thm:invisible} and \Cref{swo:ph:prop:coverage} give a negative and a positive recognition result in explicit languages. They do not establish that $\sim_{\mathrm{lab}}$ is the weakest conceivable enrichment that recognizes exhaustiveness; its rigidity is stronger than recognition alone, and weaker intermediate expansions are a natural subject for further study.

% ---- source 25, Section 11
\section{Regular set-sized models and an exact group size (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:sets}

\merge\ Source~25's Section~11. Its set structures are written with a
superscript $\kappa$ (\cref{swo:part:coresym}): $\Psupp^{\kappa}(b)$ is source~25's
$\mathcal D_{b,\kappa}$, $\Words^{\kappa}$ its $\mathcal T_\kappa$,
$\Jinj^{\kappa}$ its $\mathfrak J_\kappa$, $\WO_\kappa(X)$ its
$\mathfrak E_\kappa$, and $\Cyls^{\kappa}_b$ its $\mathcal C_{b,\kappa}$.

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 673-742

The class argument has a useful set-sized analogue. This provides ordinary sets of branches and an ordinary automorphism group, making the size claims and the nondefinability obstruction accessible without a higher-order interpretation.

\subsection{The hypotheses and their purpose}

Let $\kappa$ be an infinite regular cardinal such that $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$. Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set of cardinality $\kappa$ satisfying
\[\tag{S25.5}\label{swo:ph:eq:kappa-saturation}
 L<R,\quad |L\cup R|<\kappa
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists x\in X\ (L<x<R).
\]
Empty sides are permitted. This includes density and absence of endpoints.

The analogous fresh-separator property follows. First choose $z$ between $L$ and $R$. For a forbidden set $S$ of size less than $\kappa$, apply \eqref{swo:ph:eq:kappa-saturation} again to
\[
 L\cup\{z\}\quad\text{and}\quad R\cup\{s\in S:z<s\}.
\]
The resulting point lies above $z$ but below every member of $S$ above $z$, so it avoids $S$.

Fix a bijection $b:\kappa\to X$. Define
\begin{align*}
 \Psupp^{\kappa}(b)&=\{b\circ\pi:\pi\in\operatorname{Sym}(\kappa),\
                      |\supp\pi|<\kappa\},\\
 \Words^{\kappa}&=\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}\operatorname{Inj}(\alpha,X),\\
 \Jinj^{\kappa}&=\operatorname{Inj}(\kappa,X),\qquad
 \WO_\kappa(X)=\operatorname{Bij}(\kappa,X).
\end{align*}
These are ordinary sets. Regularity makes support of size less than $\kappa$ equivalent to bounded support. The code normalization used for the class core may be retained, although here the functions themselves are sets.

Every prefix in $\Words^{\kappa}$ has a core completion: the reserve argument in \Cref{swo:ph:lem:completion} uses fewer than $\kappa$ positions. Also
\[
 |\Psupp^{\kappa}(b)|=|\Words^{\kappa}|=\kappa.
\]
The upper bounds follow from $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, and the lower bounds follow already from distinct one-letter prefixes and their completions.

\begin{theorem}[Regular-cardinal configuration theorem]\label{swo:ph:thm:regular}
Let $\Cyls^{\kappa}_b$ be the set-sized core-and-cylinder structure just defined. For configurations indexed by a set $I$ of cardinality less than $\kappa$, \Cref{swo:ph:thm:homogeneity} holds with $\Psupp^{\kappa}(b)$, $\Jinj^{\kappa}$, and first-disagreement ordinals below $\kappa$ in place of their class counterparts.

In particular, its action on $\Jinj^{\kappa}$ has exactly two orbits, the core and its complement. The exhaustive branches are not invariant. Adding cross-node edge-label equality makes $\Cyls^{\kappa}_b$ rigid.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The one-point proof applies verbatim once its supremum $\lambda$ is below $\kappa$. This follows from regularity because there are fewer than $\kappa$ constraints. The maximum case uses the fresh-separator property above, and the no-maximum case gives a prefix of length less than $\kappa$. Complete it to the core.

Enumerate the core in $\kappa$ steps. At each stage below $\kappa$, the partial map together with the fixed markers has size less than $\kappa$, so back-and-forth can continue. Its union gives the required automorphism and branch action.

For non-invariance, pair-swap $b$ throughout $\kappa$ to obtain a noncore bijection, and use $f(\alpha)=b(1+\alpha)$ to omit $b(0)$. The latter is defined on $\kappa$ and has the indicated omitted range for every infinite initial ordinal $\kappa$. Both are noncore and hence conjugate under the branch action.

For rigidity, an edge-coherent automorphism is coordinatewise application of an order automorphism $h$ of $X$. Preservation of the supported core forces $h$ to have support of size less than $\kappa$. The fresh-separator property supplies a fixed point between $x$ and $h(x)$ whenever they differ, giving the contradiction in \Cref{swo:ph:lem:small-support-rigid}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cardinality of the automorphism group]\label{swo:ph:thm:group-size}
Under the preceding hypotheses,
\[
 \bigl|\Aut(\Cyls^{\kappa}_b)\bigr|=2^\kappa.
\]
After adjoining $\sim_{\mathrm{lab}}$, the automorphism group has cardinality $1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An automorphism is determined by its action on the core, which has cardinality $\kappa$. Thus the group has size at most $\kappa^\kappa=2^\kappa$.

There are $2^\kappa$ injective full words: the upper bound is $|X^\kappa|=2^\kappa$, and independent pair swaps of $b$ give the lower bound. Removing the core, which has size $\kappa$, leaves $2^\kappa$ words. By \Cref{swo:ph:thm:regular}, these form one orbit. A group acting transitively on a set of that size has at least $2^\kappa$ elements. The equality follows. The enriched assertion is the rigidity theorem.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Surreal birthday fragments and the countable example}

If $\kappa$ is regular and $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, the alphabet $X=\No_{<\kappa}$ has cardinality $\kappa$ and satisfies \eqref{swo:ph:eq:kappa-saturation}. Indeed, fewer than $\kappa$ birthdays are bounded strictly below $\kappa$ by regularity, and the exact-birthday separator may be chosen at a still larger ordinal below $\kappa$. The equality $|X|=\kappa$ uses $2^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, which follows from the stated cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis for infinite $\kappa$.

At $\kappa=\omega$, one may take $X=\mathbb Q$, or the dyadic rational alphabet $\No_{<\omega}$. The core consists of the finite-support permutations of a fixed enumeration. Its countable ordered cylinder structure has $2^{\aleph_0}$ automorphisms, and every infinite injective word outside the core lies in one orbit of their induced action. Yet the edge-coherent expansion is rigid. No continuum hypothesis is used.

This countable example is a concrete testing ground for the group-theoretic questions below. Its infinitary branch space is still indispensable: a complete ordered injection tree over a \emph{finite} linear alphabet is rigid, since every finite sibling order is rigid. One should not expect an exhaustive finite-alphabet model to exhibit the same symmetries.

\merge\ The bare countable order $\WO_\omega(\mathbb Q)$ also has $2^{\aleph_0}$
automorphisms (source~21's homogeneity theorem, Part~X); that is a different
structure, without cylinders.

% ---- source 25, Section 12
\section{Cofinality obstructions and singular lengths (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:singular}

\merge\ Source~25's Section~12. Here $X$ is any linearly ordered set of size
$\kappa$ with a bijection $b:\kappa\to X$; $\Psupp^{\mathrm{bd}}(b)$ and
$\Psupp^{<\kappa}(b)$ are source~25's $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{bd}}$ and
$\mathcal D_{<\kappa}$, its bounded-support and small-support cores. At a
singular $\kappa$ they differ, as source~14's support hierarchy
(\cref{swo:tc:sec:support}) shows for the class core.

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 745-773

The regularity restriction in the preceding proof is not cosmetic. A family of approximants cofinal in the word length can determine a noncore full word completely, leaving no core point with its profile.

\begin{theorem}[Cofinal profiles force the missing branch]\label{swo:ph:thm:cofinal-obstruction}
Let $\kappa$ be any infinite cardinal and let $b:\kappa\to X$ be a bijection onto any linearly ordered alphabet of size $\kappa$. Let $\Psupp^{\mathrm{bd}}(b)$ be its bounded-support core and $\Psupp^{<\kappa}(b)$ its support-of-size-less-than-$\kappa$ core. There are a bijection $d:\kappa\to X$ outside both cores and a family $(a_i)_{i<\cf\kappa}$ lying in both cores such that the only full word $z$ satisfying
\[
 \delta(z,a_i)=\delta(d,a_i)\qquad(i<\cf\kappa)
\]
is $z=d$. In particular, no member of either core realizes that profile over the fixed family.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $d$ swap every consecutive pair of $b$, with pair blocks indexed by $\xi<\kappa$. Choose pair-boundary ordinals $\beta_i=2\cdot\xi_i<\kappa$ strictly increasing and cofinal in $\kappa$, for $i<\cf\kappa$. Such boundaries are cofinal because the ordinal map $\xi\mapsto2\cdot\xi$ is continuous and cofinal in every infinite initial ordinal.

Define $a_i$ by performing the same swaps below $\beta_i$ and leaving all positions at or above $\beta_i$ fixed. Its support is bounded and has size less than $\kappa$, and
\[
 \delta(d,a_i)=\beta_i.
\]
If $z$ has the indicated first-disagreement ordinals, then $z\res\beta_i=a_i\res\beta_i=d\res\beta_i$ for every $i$. Cofinality forces $z=d$. But $d$ moves all $\kappa$ positions, so it belongs to neither core.
\end{proof}

For regular $\kappa$, the obstruction occurs at $\kappa$ constraints, immediately beyond the less-than-$\kappa$ extension theorem. This establishes sharpness of that bound for the one-point core-realization mechanism. It does not by itself classify every possible larger partial automorphism.

For singular $\kappa$, the obstruction already occurs at $\cf\kappa<\kappa$ constraints. Consequently the less-than-$\kappa$ one-point extension statement fails even if one replaces bounded support by support of cardinality less than $\kappa$. The failure is not repaired merely by adopting a larger small-support core.

\begin{remark}[A second singular obstruction: unbounded prefix images]\label{swo:ph:rem:singular-prefix}
At a singular $\kappa$, not every injective prefix of length less than $\kappa$ extends to the bounded-support core. Choose an injection $q:\cf\kappa\to\kappa$ with cofinal range and put $p=b\circ q$. A bounded-support permutation extending $q$ would have to move positions to cofinally many ordinals above its support bound, which is impossible. In contrast, the reserve construction does extend this $q$ to a permutation of support cardinality less than $\kappa$. Thus bounded support, small support, and prefix completeness must be separated at singular lengths.
\end{remark}

The global GBC theorem has no analogous set-sized obstruction: every set of disagreement ordinals has a strict ordinal bound. A uniformly proper-class family of approximants can, however, force an entire noncore branch by the same argument. The set-indexing hypothesis is exactly what prevents this cofinality failure in \Cref{swo:ph:lem:onepoint}.

% ---- source 27, Section 6
\subsection{Source 27: prefix symmetries, exhaustiveness, and repeated labels}\label{swo:sc:sec:prefix}

% ---- source 27 (batch-83 manuscript 13), lines 1043-1325

The corpus shows that the bare order of the bounded-support core does
not recognize exhaustive branch cuts (\cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic,swo:gs:thm:nonextension}). A natural
response is to retain the prefix tree as additional structure. We show
that even this response is insufficient unless the structure also
remembers which labels at different nodes are the same surreal.

Work in $\GBC$ with a fixed baseline $b:\Ord\to\No$. Let $\Words$
be the ordinary class of all injective set-length surreal words. Its
tree order is initial segment, and the children of $p$ are
$p\concat(x)$ for $x\in\No\setminus\ran p$, ordered by numerical $x$.
An automorphism of this ordered tree is a class bijection preserving
prefixes and each sibling order. It automatically preserves ordinal
height, since the proper predecessors of a node of length $\alpha$
have order type $\alpha$.

Every class injection $E:\Ord\to\No$ determines a maximal branch
consisting of all $E\restr\alpha$. It is maximal whether or not $E$
is onto: a compatible set-length node must be the corresponding
prefix of $E$. Thus maximality is not exhaustiveness.

\subsubsection{A uniform isomorphism lemma with only set states}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform pointed residual isomorphisms]
\label{swo:sc:lem:uniformresidual}
There is one class graph, definable from $b$, which for every pair of
sets $S,T\subseteq\No$ and points $a\notin S$, $c\notin T$ gives
an increasing bijection
\[
 J(S,T;a,c):\No\setminus S\longrightarrow\No\setminus T,
 \qquad J(S,T;a,c)(a)=c.
\]
There is also an unpointed version. The graph has set tuples as its
elements; it is not a class whose elements are class maps.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Deleting a set from $\No$ preserves its ability to fill every separated
set cut. To avoid a deleted set of cardinality $\mu$, first construct
$\mu^+$ distinct points between the two sides, using the surreal
set-cut property at each set stage. At least one remains outside the
deleted set. The same argument permits avoidance of the values already
used by a set partial map.

Start with the increasing partial map $\{(a,c)\}$, or the empty map
in the unpointed version. At ordinal stage $\beta$, handle the source
label $b(\beta)$ if it is eligible and unused. Its image must lie
between the images of its earlier lower and upper domain elements.
Choose the feasible fresh target of least $b$-index. Next handle
$b(\beta)$ on the target side by the symmetric extension of the
inverse. The preceding cut argument ensures both steps are possible.
At limits take unions. Every stage is a set partial increasing
bijection, and every eligible label on both sides is eventually handled.

For each set ordinal $\delta$, the run through $\delta$ is a unique
set sequence. A pair belongs to the final map exactly when some such
set run contains it. This is an elementary formula with parameters
$b,S,T,a,c$. Elementary class comprehension therefore defines one
uniform graph for all allowed set parameters. No stage of this
construction chooses or collects a proper-class object as a state.
\end{proof}

The same proof works for the permissible next-letter orders of
increasing words used in \cref{swo:sc:sec:increasing}: those orders also fill
every set cut, and their restrictions of the baseline enumerate them.
The distinction between set-state recursion and a recursion whose
individual values are classes is essential to the axiom count.

\subsubsection{Every tree automorphism is governed by local residual maps}

For an ordered-tree automorphism $A$, define its local map by
\[\tag{S27.8}\label{swo:sc:eq:localmap}
 A(p\concat(x))=A(p)\concat\bigl(\lambda_p(x)\bigr).
\]
Then $\lambda_p$ is an increasing bijection from
$\No\setminus\ran p$ onto $\No\setminus\ran A(p)$, uniformly in $p$,
and
\[
 A(p)(\xi)=\lambda_{p\restr\xi}(p(\xi)).
\]

Conversely, suppose one class rule $\Lambda(p,q;x,y)$ gives an
increasing residual bijection from $\No\setminus\ran p$ onto
$\No\setminus\ran q$ for every equal-height pair $p,q$. Define the
image $q=A(p)$ by the set recursion
\[\tag{S27.9}\label{swo:sc:eq:localevaluation}
 q(\xi)=\Lambda(p\restr\xi,q\restr\xi)(p(\xi)).
\]
The prefixes cohere by uniqueness. Inverting the residual maps in a
recursion on a target word constructs its unique preimage, so $A$ is
a bijection at every height. It preserves prefixes and sibling orders.
Thus \eqref{swo:sc:eq:localevaluation} is a precise way to construct an
ordered-tree automorphism without selecting unrelated class maps at
each node.

\begin{theorem}[Transitivity on all injective ordinal branches]
\label{swo:sc:thm:branchtransitive}
Given any class injections $E,F:\Ord\to\No$, there exists an
ordered-prefix-tree automorphism $A$ such that
\[\tag{S27.10}\label{swo:sc:eq:branchtransport}
 A(E\restr\alpha)=F\restr\alpha\qquad(\alpha\in\Ord).
\]
It preserves ordinal levels, all prefix incidences, and numerical
order among the children of each node.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For equal-height $p,q$ of length $\alpha$, use the pointed residual map
\[
 J(\ran p,\ran q;E(\alpha),F(\alpha))
\]
when $p=E\restr\alpha$ and $q=F\restr\alpha$. Its distinguished
points are fresh by injectivity. In every other case use the
unpointed residual map. This is a single elementary rule with class
parameters $b,E,F$. Apply \eqref{swo:sc:eq:localevaluation}. Induction on
each set ordinal forces the pointed case along the designated branch,
which proves \eqref{swo:sc:eq:branchtransport}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Ordered prefixes do not recognize exhaustiveness]
\label{swo:sc:cor:nonintrinsic}
Exhaustiveness of an $\Ord$-branch is not invariant under automorphisms
of the ordered prefix tree, even if levels and sibling numerical order
are retained.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $E=b$ and define
\[
 F(n)=b(n+1)\quad(n<\omega),\qquad
 F(\xi)=b(\xi)\quad(\xi\ge\omega).
\]
The map $F$ is injective and omits exactly $b(0)$. Apply
\cref{swo:sc:thm:branchtransitive}. The exhaustive branch is sent to a
nonexhaustive branch, so no property invariant under this structure's
automorphisms can distinguish the two.
\end{proof}

The displayed branches even agree outside a bounded set of coordinates.
Agreement outside a set is not the same as being related by a
permutation supported on that set: the infinite one-sided shift loses
a label. This is the same boundary phenomenon measured by the reserve
in \cref{swo:sc:sec:support}.

For a set alphabet $X$, the full injective-word tree has a different
answer. Its terminal nodes are exactly the exhaustive words, and any
tree automorphism preserves terminal nodes. Every maximal branch has
such a terminal node, because an injective word has length below the
Hartogs number of $X$ and a missing label would allow extension. This
argument does not apply to a truncated set tree that stops before the
terminal height, nor to the full proper-class tree.

\subsubsection{An exact obstruction and useful sufficient bounds}

An automorphism acts on a supplied class branch by the elementary formula
\[
 A_*E(\xi)=A(E\restr(\xi+1))(\xi).
\]
It acts on exhaustive branches precisely when it preserves coverage of
the alphabet. A local formulation makes the obstruction explicit.
For a target label $y$, put
\[
 \Words_y(A)=\{p:y\notin\ran A(p)\}.
\]
This is a downward-closed subtree. At a node in it, exactly one available
input child is forbidden if the branch is to continue omitting $y$,
namely $\lambda_p^{-1}(y)$. Therefore $A_*$ sends every exhaustive
branch to an exhaustive one exactly when none of these subtrees has
an exhaustive $\Ord$-branch. To obtain a bijection on exhaustive
branches, impose the same condition on $A^{-1}$. This criterion is
exact, but it deliberately leaves a substantial branch problem.

\begin{theorem}[Set-bounded local inverse images]
\label{swo:sc:thm:localbounds}
Suppose for every label $y$ there is a set $K_y\subseteq\No$ such that
\[
 y\notin\ran A(p)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \lambda_p^{-1}(y)\in K_y
\]
for every node $p$. Then $A_*$ preserves exhaustive branches.
If additionally for every input label $x$ all possible local values
$\lambda_p(x)$ lie in a set $L_x$, then $A_*$ is a bijection on the
exhaustive branches.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $E$ be exhaustive. The elements of the set $K_y$ all occur in $E$
before some set ordinal $\alpha$, by Class Replacement applied to
their unique occurrence times. If $y$ were absent from
$A(E\restr\alpha)$, its local inverse image would have to belong
both to $K_y$ and to the unused source alphabet. This is impossible.
Thus every $y$ occurs in $A_*E$. The second hypothesis is exactly
the first hypothesis for the inverse automorphism, giving the converse.
\end{proof}

A useful equivalent formulation bounds the birthdays of all possible
local inverse images of labels of birthday below $\beta$ by one set
ordinal $\mu(\beta)$. The bounded sign stage is a set. Conversely,
per-label set bounds have ordinal birthday bounds, and Class Replacement
over a bounded sign stage gives such a uniform modulus. The symmetric
forward condition is analogous.

A uniformly given action of a \emph{set} group of numerical
automorphisms supplies examples: if each local map is the restriction
of a group element, every possible inverse image lies in the set orbit
of $y$, and every forward image lies in the set orbit of $x$.
This is a sufficient criterion, not a classification of all permissible
local dynamics.

\subsubsection{Independent transformations after a chosen prefix}

Let $P$ be a uniformly presented prefix antichain. Suppose that for
every $p\in P$ an increasing class bijection $\varphi_p:\No\to\No$
is given by one class graph, and
$\varphi_p[\ran p]=\ran p$. Keep $p$ fixed and apply $\varphi_p$
to every later letter in its extension cone; fix words in no such cone.
The antichain makes the choice unique, the used set is preserved, and
the inverse uses $\varphi_p^{-1}$. This is an ordered-tree automorphism
preserving exhaustion in both directions. A branch meeting a cone has
its remaining alphabet bijectively relabelled, and a branch meeting no
cone is fixed.

For example, fix a length-$\omega$ prefix enumerating the embedded
ordinary integers $\mathbb Z$. Above that prefix add $1$ to every
later letter, and act identically elsewhere. Since
$\mathbb Z+1=\mathbb Z$, this is a valid transformation. It fixes
all first-level nodes but is not the identity, so it is not a single
global relabelling.

The bounds in \cref{swo:sc:thm:localbounds} are not necessary. Choose a
transformation after each first letter $z$; for $z>1$ use
\[
 \varphi_z(x)=zx-z(z-1),
\]
and for $z\le1$ use the identity. The affine map is increasing and
fixes $z$, so the antichain construction applies. It preserves
exhaustiveness, but $\varphi_z^{-1}(0)=z-1$ ranges over a proper
class. There is no single set $K_0$ bounding all these local inverse
images. Once a first letter is fixed the tail behavior is simple;
uniformity over all first letters is much stronger.

\subsubsection{The additional predicate that gives an exact classification}

Enrich the ordered tree by equality of labels on different successor
edges:
\[\tag{S27.11}\label{swo:sc:eq:edgelabel}
 (p,p\concat(x))\sim(q,q\concat(y))
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=y.
\]
This predicate does not name individual surreals. It remembers which
occurrences at different nodes refer to the same label.

\begin{note}[Source~27, Theorem~6.5, ``Automorphisms after retaining label equality'']\label{swo:sc:thm:labelcoherence}
{\itshape
The automorphisms of the ordered prefix tree preserving
\eqref{swo:sc:eq:edgelabel} are exactly
\[
 A(p)=\varphi\circ p
\]
for increasing class bijections $\varphi:\No\to\No$. They all
preserve exhaustive branches. If the alphabet is also fixed pointwise,
the only such tree automorphism is the identity.}
This is source~25's \cref{swo:ph:thm:coherence}, with the trivial case of \cref{swo:ph:thm:rigidity} in which the alphabet is fixed pointwise; source~27's proof is the same root-edge argument. Source~25 adds that preserving the core as well forces the identity (\cref{swo:ph:thm:rigidity}) and that coherent edges recognize coverage (\cref{swo:ph:prop:coverage}).
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~27's proof]
The local map at the root is an increasing bijection
$\varphi:\No\to\No$. Every edge appending $x$ is equivalent to
the root edge appending $x$. Preservation of the edge equivalence
forces every such edge to append $\varphi(x)$ after transformation.
Thus every local map is the restriction of $\varphi$, and induction
on a set word gives the formula for $A$. Conversely, coordinatewise
relabeling by $\varphi$ preserves every indicated relation and is
inverted by relabeling with $\varphi^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

This answers a precise version of the question ``what extra structure
restores the labels?'' It does not claim that cross-node label equality
is minimal among all possible enrichments. Between the arbitrary tree
automorphisms of \cref{swo:sc:thm:branchtransitive} and the global relabellings
of \cref{swo:sc:thm:labelcoherence} lies a substantial subgroup preserving
exhaustiveness, of which the bounds and antichain constructions describe
useful parts.

All these tree automorphisms preserve first-disagreement comparison on
full $\Ord$-branches, which never stand in a proper-prefix relation.
On set words they preserve the prefix-first and prefix-last orders.
An interior terminator would additionally require the local maps to
preserve its cut; that condition is not automatic.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:sc:lem:uniformresidual} is the uniform construction of
source~18's \cref{swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism} and of source~13's family $h_S$
(\cref{swo:fs:lem:backforth}), with one prescribed point matched; source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ta:residual-isomorphisms} below allows any set partial match and
the increasing alphabets as well. The ``reserve in \cref{swo:sc:sec:support}''
mentioned after \cref{swo:sc:cor:nonintrinsic} is source~27's ordinal support
theorem (\cref{swo:sc:sec:support}).

% ---- source 29, Section 9
\subsection{Source 29: ordered prefix trees do not determine their exhaustive class branches}\label{swo:bw:ta:section}

\merge\ Source~29's Section~9, printed whole. Its \cref{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity}
is, for the injection tree $\Words$, source~27's \cref{swo:sc:thm:branchtransitive}
(a second proof); its case of the increasing-word tree $\WordsInc$ is new.
Its Corollary~9.3 is source~27's \cref{swo:sc:cor:nonintrinsic} with another
target branch and is printed as a note. Its \cref{swo:bw:ta:set-alphabet} is
source~27's remark on set alphabets after \cref{swo:sc:cor:nonintrinsic}.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 2697-3058
The ordered prefix tree contains much more information than the pure
lexicographic order. It records the length of every set word, all
extension relations, and the numerical order of the possible next
entries. Even this structure does not recognize which proper-class
branches exhaust the surreal labels. We prove this by constructing
automorphisms that carry any one supplied branch to any other.
The same method applies to increasing branches and can exchange a
numerically cofinal range with a bounded one.

\subsubsection{The structures and the required uniform isomorphisms}

Let $\Words$ be the class of all injective functions
$p:\alpha\to\No$ with $\alpha$ a set ordinal. Let $\WordsInc$ be
its strictly numerically increasing subclass. Both include the empty
word. Each carries word length, the prefix relation, and shorter-first
lexicographic order. At a node $p$, the one-step extensions have the
order of their next entries. The respective admissible alphabets are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_p^{\Words}&=\No\setminus\ran(p),\\
 D_p^{\WordsInc}&=\{x\in\No:\ran(p)<x\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The inequalities in the second line mean that every entry of $p$ is
less than $x$.

These are structures on a genuine class of set-coded nodes. A
proper-class branch will be supplied separately as a class function
$F:\Ord\to\No$ all of whose set restrictions are nodes of the
relevant tree. The assertion below quantifies over such class
parameters; it does not form a class whose members are all branches.

\begin{lemma}[Residual alphabets and a prescribed match]
\label{swo:bw:ta:residual-isomorphisms}
Work in $\GBC$ with a fixed set-like global well-order. Each of the
alphabets $D_p^{\Words}$ and $D_p^{\WordsInc}$ is a proper class
filling every separated set cut, including cuts with an empty side.
For two nodes $p,q$ of the same tree and any set partial order
isomorphism between their residual alphabets, there is an increasing
bijection
\[
                          h:D_p\longrightarrow D_q
\]
extending it. If the nodes and the initial partial match are specified
uniformly from set parameters and fixed class parameters, these
bijections can be given by one elementary class relation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First recall set avoidance in the surreal line. Given sets $A<B$ and
a forbidden set $S$, choose $z$ with $A<z<B$. If $z\notin S$, it is
already a suitable filler. Otherwise apply the set-cut property again
to obtain
\[
       A\cup\{z\}<y<B\cup\{s\in S:z<s\}.
\]
All constraints are consistent: $z<B$, and every newly imposed upper
constraint is larger than $z$. The point $y$ is larger than every
forbidden element at most $z$ and smaller than every forbidden element
above $z$, so $y\notin S$. This proves set-cut filling in
$D_p^{\Words}$. It is proper because removing a set from $\No$
cannot leave a set.

For $D_p^{\WordsInc}$, append $\ran(p)$ to the lower constraints of
any set cut in the residual alphabet. Every upper constraint already
exceeds the whole prefix. Surreal interpolation therefore produces a
filler in $D_p^{\WordsInc}$, including when either original side was
empty. If this residual alphabet were a set, using all of it as lower
constraints would require a strictly larger point within that same
set, a contradiction. It is therefore proper.

For the extension assertion, start a deterministic back-and-forth with
the supplied set partial isomorphism. At each stage take the first
unmatched source point in the fixed global well-order, and place its
image in the cut specified by the present partial isomorphism. The
image can be chosen as the first eligible point in the fixed global
well-order. Then perform the corresponding inverse insertion for the
first unmatched target point. The strict cut constraints automatically
exclude previously used points. At a limit set ordinal take the union
of the preceding partial maps. The histories and partial maps are sets
at every stage, and both directions are eventually exhausted.

For uniformity, membership in the resulting bijection is expressed
by existence of a set-length initial history obeying these deterministic
rules. The nodes, initial match, stage ordinal, and history are all set
variables. Only the original alphabet definitions and global well-order
are class parameters. The same elementary formula works for all the
specified instances. As in the repository's uniform prefix constructions
(\cref{swo:fs:lem:backforth,swo:sh:wv:tree-isomorphism}), this avoids choosing an arbitrary class isomorphism
independently for each node. The recursion has set-valued stages and
does not require $\ETR$ or Class Choice.
\end{proof}

The extension assertion allows a single point of the source alphabet
to be matched with any single point of the target alphabet. This
freedom, applied along one distinguished branch, is the key to the
next theorem.

\subsubsection{Transitivity on supplied class branches}

\begin{theorem}[Branch transitivity of the ordered trees]
\label{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity}
Work in $\GBC$. For either $\mathscr K=\Words$ or
$\mathscr K=\WordsInc$, let $F,G:\Ord\to\No$ be two supplied class
branches. There is a class automorphism $A:\mathscr K\to\mathscr K$
preserving lengths, prefixes, and lexicographic order such that
\[
                   A(F\res\alpha)=G\res\alpha
                   \qquad(\alpha\in\Ord).
\]
In particular, it preserves the order of the immediate successors of
every node.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each pair of nodes $p,q$ of the same length $\alpha$, use
\cref{swo:bw:ta:residual-isomorphisms} to define an increasing bijection
\[
                      h_{p,q}:D_p\longrightarrow D_q.
\]
When $p=F\res\alpha$ and $q=G\res\alpha$, begin the deterministic
construction with the single prescribed match
\[
                         F(\alpha)\longmapsto G(\alpha).
\]
These are admissible unused entries because $F,G$ are branches.
For every other pair $p,q$, begin with the empty partial map.
The condition selecting the seeded case is elementary in the set
parameters $p,q,\alpha$ and the class parameters $F,G$.
Thus one class relation gives all the $h_{p,q}$ simultaneously.

For a source word $f$ of set length $\alpha$, define its image $g$
by set recursion. Begin with the empty target prefix and set
\[
                    g(\xi)=h_{f\res\xi,\,g\res\xi}(f(\xi))
                    \qquad(\xi<\alpha).
\tag{S29.20}\label{swo:bw:ta:recursive-map}
\]
Take unions at limit stages. Each chosen letter belongs to the target
residual alphabet, so the output is injective in $\Words$ and
increasing in $\WordsInc$. Set Replacement supplies the output graph.
Restrictions of a construction are the unique constructions for the
corresponding shorter input words. The resulting class map $A$ thus
preserves lengths and prefixes.

It is also bijective. Given a target word $g$, reconstruct a source
prefix $p$ recursively. At position $\xi$, the target prefix
$q=g\res\xi$ is known and the next source letter is uniquely
\[
                             h_{p,q}^{-1}(g(\xi)).
\]
This belongs to $D_p$, so the reconstruction remains in the required
tree. It is inverse to \eqref{swo:bw:ta:recursive-map} at successors and at
limits. Hence every target node has exactly one source node.

To check lexicographic order, proper-prefix comparisons are preserved
by the already proved prefix and length assertions. Otherwise let
$\xi$ be the first unequal coordinate of two words. They have the same
source prefix $p$ and therefore the same target prefix $q$ at that
stage. Their next entries are transformed by the same increasing map
$h_{p,q}$, which preserves the comparison. This proves the order
assertion and also its restriction to immediate successors.

Finally, set induction on $\alpha$ proves
$A(F\res\alpha)=G\res\alpha$. At each successor stage the appropriate
$h_{p,q}$ contains the prescribed match, and at limits both sides are
the unions of their shorter restrictions. The graph of $A$ is defined
from the unique set recursion histories, with the fixed class
parameters already described. No family of class-valued outputs is
collected into a class of classes.
\end{proof}

For any supplied branch $H$, its image under a tree automorphism is
itself an admitted class branch, defined by
\[
             A_*H(\xi)=A(H\res(\xi+1))(\xi).
\]
The prefixes are coherent, and elementary comprehension gives the
graph. The inverse tree automorphism supplies the inverse branch
operation. This formulation is available within the stated class
framework without replacing the virtual collection of branches by an
undeclared higher-sort object.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Corollary~9.3, ``Exhaustivity is additional information'']\label{swo:bw:ta:exhaustivity}
{\itshape
There is a length-, prefix-, and lexicographic-order-preserving class
automorphism of $\Words$ carrying the prefixes of an exhaustive
bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$ to those of a nonexhaustive injection.
Consequently exhaustivity of proper-class branches is not an invariant
of this ordered prefix-tree structure.}
This is source~27's \cref{swo:sc:cor:nonintrinsic}, here with target branch $\alpha\mapsto\alpha$. Source~25's \cref{swo:ph:thm:invisible} proves more: the core and all its cylinders can be preserved as well.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~29's proof]
Global Choice gives an exhaustive enumeration $b$ of the surreal class.
Apply \cref{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity} to $F=b$ and to
$G(\alpha)=\alpha$, where ordinals are regarded as surreals.
The latter branch omits, for example, $-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Numerical cofinality is also additional information]
\label{swo:bw:ta:cofinality}
An automorphism of the ordered increasing-word tree $\WordsInc$ can
carry a numerically cofinal proper-class branch to one whose range is
bounded above by zero.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take
\[
                F(\alpha)=\alpha,
                \qquad G(\alpha)=-\frac{1}{\alpha+1}.
\]
Both are strictly increasing class functions. Every surreal is smaller
than some ordinal---its sign length gives an ordinal bound---so $F$
is cofinal in the numerical surreal line. Ordered-field arithmetic
makes $G$ strictly increasing, and every one of its values is negative.
Apply \cref{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity} for $\WordsInc$.
\end{proof}

The structures in these corollaries name lengths, prefix extension,
and successor orders. They do \emph{not} name the common evaluation
relation assigning a literal surreal label to each successor. In
particular, equality of labels used at different nodes is not part
of the stated reduct. The automorphisms can change that information.
If label evaluation were named, it could express exhaustivity directly.
Similarly, the ambient set membership relation on the codes is not
being asserted invariant under these tree automorphisms.

The automorphism in \cref{swo:bw:ta:exhaustivity} is an automorphism of the
set-word tree, not an automorphism of $\Hsl$: its induced branch map
fails to preserve the domain of exhaustive enumerations. The conclusion
therefore complements the repository's core-automorphism extension obstructions
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension,swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic}), while making a distinct assertion about a
richer prefix structure.

\subsubsection{Why the full tree over a set carrier behaves differently}

\begin{proposition}[Terminal nodes over a set alphabet]
\label{swo:bw:ta:set-alphabet}
For a fixed set alphabet $X$, consider the full tree of all injective
ordinal-length $X$-words, with all possible set lengths. Its terminal
nodes are exactly the exhaustive enumerations of $X$. Every
prefix-tree automorphism therefore preserves exhaustivity.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If a word omits a label $x\in X$, appending $x$ is a permitted
one-letter extension. If its range is $X$, no label is available for
such an extension, and any proper longer word would have to supply
one at the first new coordinate. This proves the characterization.
Terminality is preserved by every automorphism of the prefix relation.
\end{proof}

For an infinite set alphabet of cardinality $\mu$, the entire tree is
a set: every injective domain is below $\mu^+$, so its nodes occur in
a set-sized collection of function spaces. A truncation changes the
argument. For instance, a tree cut off at height $\mu$ has terminal
height-$\mu$ nodes that may omit labels. In the surreal class tree,
every node has set range and therefore has unused surreal labels.
There is no terminal set node at the end of an $\Ord$-length branch.
This is exactly where the set-carrier characterization ceases to apply.

\subsubsection{Local descriptions and a family preserving exhaustion}

Every length- and prefix-preserving automorphism $A$ of $\Words$
that preserves lexicographic order determines increasing bijections
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 h_p &: \No\setminus\ran(p)
               \longrightarrow\No\setminus\ran(A(p)),\\
 A(p\cat\langle x\rangle)
     &=A(p)\cat\langle h_p(x)\rangle.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Surjectivity on the immediate successors follows from bijectivity of
$A$ and preservation of prefixes. Conversely, a uniform collection of
increasing maps between the relevant source and target residual
alphabets, used coherently as in \eqref{swo:bw:ta:recursive-map}, determines
such an automorphism. \Cref{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity} shows that
this local description alone imposes no preservation of exhaustion.

There is nevertheless a broad concrete family for which exhaustion is
preserved, allowing the relabelling of a tail to depend on its entire
initial set prefix.

\begin{proposition}[Fixed-stage continuation by residual bijections]
\label{swo:bw:ta:fixed-stage}
Fix a set ordinal $\delta$ and a length-, prefix-, and
lexicographic-order-preserving automorphism $B$ of the injection tree
through height $\delta$, including that height. For every node $p$ of
length $\delta$, specify uniformly an increasing bijection
\[
             k_p:\No\setminus\ran(p)
                    \longrightarrow\No\setminus\ran(B(p)).
\]
There is a class automorphism $A$ of the full injection tree agreeing
with $B$ through height $\delta$ and continuing each tail after $p$
by the same entrywise map $k_p$. Its induced operation on class
branches preserves exhaustivity in both directions. Such uniform
families $k_p$ exist in $\GBC$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For words of length at most $\delta$, use $B$. For a longer word $f$,
put $p=f\res\delta$, take $B(p)$ as the initial target word, and define
\[
                A(f)(\xi)=k_p(f(\xi))\qquad(\delta\leq\xi<\dom(f)).
\]
The original tail avoids $\ran(p)$, and its image avoids
$\ran(B(p))$; injectivity of the tail is preserved. Thus the resulting
word is a node. Restrictions are compatible at and on both sides of
$\delta$. An inverse is obtained from $B^{-1}$ on the initial prefix
and the appropriate $k_p^{-1}$ on its tail, proving bijectivity.

A first disagreement before $\delta$ is preserved by $B$. If two
words agree through $\delta$, the same increasing $k_p$ acts at any
later first disagreement. Proper-prefix comparisons are also preserved.
Therefore $A$ has all the asserted tree and order properties.

Now let $F$ be any supplied class injection, and let $p=F\res\delta$.
Its tail takes values in $\No\setminus\ran(p)$. The range of $F$
is all of $\No$ if and only if that tail exhausts this residual
alphabet. Since $k_p$ is a bijection onto the residual alphabet of
$B(p)$, this holds if and only if the image tail exhausts its own
residual alphabet, which is equivalent to exhaustivity of $A_*F$.
The same argument proves the reverse direction.

Finally, apply \cref{swo:bw:ta:residual-isomorphisms} with empty initial
matches to obtain the $k_p$ uniformly from $p,B$, and a fixed global
well-order. Their elementary class definition supplies the required
family without a choice of class-valued stages.
\end{proof}

At $\delta=0$ this includes uniform entrywise increasing relabellings
of the entire surreal alphabet. At positive set stages it permits
different residual relabellings after different prefixes. The fixed
bijection on an entire tail provides the coverage argument that is
absent from unrestricted coordinate-dependent choices. The theorem is
a sufficient construction, not a classification of every
exhaustion-preserving automorphism.

\begin{corollary}[Agreement through any prescribed set stage]
\label{swo:bw:ta:bounded-stage-agreement}
For every automorphism $A$ of the ordered injection tree and every set
ordinal $\delta$, there is an exhaustion-preserving automorphism
$\widetilde A$ agreeing with $A$ on all nodes of length at most
$\delta$. Nevertheless some automorphisms of the full tree do not
preserve exhaustion.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Restrict $A$ to the tree through height $\delta$ and apply
\cref{swo:bw:ta:fixed-stage}. The second assertion is
\cref{swo:bw:ta:exhaustivity}.
\end{proof}

Thus the failure to preserve exhaustive proper-class branches cannot
be diagnosed from the action through any one fixed set height, even
when that entire height and all earlier levels are retained. The
corollary is stated as a uniform approximation theorem about supplied
class maps; it does not presuppose an internal class of all
class automorphisms.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:bw:ta:fixed-stage,swo:bw:ta:bounded-stage-agreement} and
source~27's \cref{swo:sc:thm:localbounds} and antichain transformations are
different sufficient families for preserving exhaustion; none classifies the
exhaustion-preserving subgroup (sources~25, 27 and~29 each ask for it:
\cref{swo:ph:n16.1}; source~27's Question~12.6; source~29's Question~13.7).

% ---- hand chunk XIII coreaut
\section{Automorphisms of the core and the failure of extension (sources 20 and 21)}\label{swo:xiii:sec:coreaut}

\merge\ Sources~20 and~21 were written before Part~VIII and prove again, each
independently, most of Part~VIII's \cref{swo:viii:sec:automorphisms}: the
classification of cut orbits by characters (source~20's Theorem~5.3 is
source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits}; source~21's Theorem~9.8 is its
$(\Ord,\Ord)$ case and \cref{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity}), the extension
criterion (source~20's Theorem~5.8 and source~21's Theorem~9.4 are source~17's
\cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}), and the existence of non-extendable
automorphisms (source~20's Corollary~5.6 is \cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic};
source~21's Theorem~9.10 is \cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension}, and its
Theorem~9.12 follows from \cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic}). Those statements are
printed as notes with the sources' proofs. New here are source~20's localized
failure (\cref{swo:lm:aut:thm:localfailure}: the automorphism can fix any set of
core points and be supported in one interval), its disjointness of relabelled
cores (\cref{swo:lm:aut:prop:labelmoves}, which sharpens
\cref{swo:gs:prop:relabelling}), and source~21's explicit cut with no crossing
first-level cylinder (\cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:vertical-cut}).

Both sources say they answer the repository's extension question
(\cref{swo:n16.4}) negatively. At the time this was so against their pins
(\code{d5bd4a67b} and \code{109aaca15}, which predate Parts~VI--VIII); at this
report's present state Part~VIII has already answered that question in part,
negatively (\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}~(c)), and the two sections are
second routes to it, except for the three new results named above. Source~20
writes $\Omega$ for ``no set-sized witness'', which Part~VIII writes $\Ord$.

% ---- source 20, Section 5
\subsection{Source 20: automorphisms of the core and the failure of extension}\label{swo:lm:aut:section}

% ---- source 20 (batch-83 manuscript 02), lines 1252-1714

The bounded-support core has an exceptionally homogeneous abstract order,
but its position among global well-orders carries additional information.
We now separate these two structures. The principal new conclusion is
that an automorphism of the core need not extend even when only one
additional exhaustive enumeration is to be included. This failure can
occur while any prescribed set of core points is fixed pointwise.
It answers negatively the unrestricted extension question posed in the
repository and the previous continuation (\cref{swo:n16.4}; source~18).

Throughout this section we work in $\GBC$ and fix a baseline class
bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. Write $\Pbd(b)$ for the ordinary class of
normalized set codes for permutations of $\Ord$ with set support, and
$E_c$ for the global enumeration evaluated from $c\in\Pbd(b)$. Codes are
ordered by their evaluations. We use the established core theorem:
$\Pbd(b)$ fills every cut specified by sets, including cuts with an empty
side, and is class-order-isomorphic to $\No$. We also use its stronger
uniform interpolation form, whose upper and lower input families may be
set-indexed families of arbitrary exhaustive global enumerations. The
back-and-forth principle underlying the core theorem is classical in
the study of the surreal order \cite{Ehrlich2012}; the arguments below
record the relevant class-theoretic details explicitly.

\subsubsection{Class cuts and their automorphism orbits}

\begin{definition}[Strict cuts and set characters]
\label{swo:lm:aut:def:character}
A \emph{strict class cut} of $\Pbd(b)$ is a nonempty proper initial class
$L\subseteq\Pbd(b)$ having no greatest element. Its upper side is
$U=\Pbd(b)\setminus L$. Define
\[
 \chi(L)=\bigl(\cf_s(L),\ci_s(U)\bigr),
\]
where $\cf_s$ is the least cardinality of a set cofinal subset when one
exists, and is the marker $\Omega$ otherwise; define $\ci_s$ dually.
The marker $\Omega$ means only ``no set-sized witness.'' It is not a
set cardinal and is not used as an object containing all ordinals.
\end{definition}

If a class without a greatest element has a set cofinal subset, the
usual set-theoretic cofinality argument, applied to that subset, gives
a strictly increasing cofinal sequence of infinite regular length.
The dual statement applies to coinitiality. The upper side of a strict
cut can instead have a minimum, in which case its character is $1$.
In particular, the strict cut below a core point is included in our
convention. A closed principal initial segment is excluded because
it has a greatest element.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~5.2, ``Saturated sides'']\label{swo:lm:aut:lem:sides}
{\itshape
Let $C$ be a class linear order filling every set cut. A nonempty
initial class $A\subseteq C$ with no set cofinal subset also fills
every set cut, including empty sides. Dually, a nonempty final class
with no set coinitial subset has the same property. Every such class
is class-order-isomorphic to $\No$ in $\GBC$.}
For the sides of a core gap this is the first part of source~17's \cref{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity} (and source~21's \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:cut-sides}); source~20 states it for every class order filling set cuts, and its second paragraph is the back-and-forth of \cref{swo:prop:universal}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Let $P,Q\subseteq A$ be sets with $P<Q$. If $Q$ is nonempty, a point
of $C$ between them belongs to $A$, because it lies below a member of
the initial class $A$. If $Q$ is empty, the absence of a set cofinal
subset gives a point of $A$ strictly above all of $P$. This includes
the case $P=Q=\varnothing$. Thus $A$ has the full set-cut property.
