It cannot be a set: applying that property with lower side all of $A$
would produce a point of $A$ above itself. The final-class statement
is dual.

For the isomorphism, Global Choice provides set-like enumerations of
the two proper classes. Alternately extend a set-sized partial order
isomorphism to include the next point of each enumeration. The
previous lower and upper images form sets, so the required new point
exists. Choose the least eligible point in a fixed global well-order.
At each ordinal stage the partial map is a set, and at a set limit
its earlier stages have a set union. The resulting class is the union
of the unique compatible set computations. This is ordinary
set-valued transfinite recursion with class parameters, rather than
recursion with a class-valued state; no $\ETR$ or class-choice scheme
is needed.
\end{proof}

Every nonempty open interval $(a,b)$ of $\Pbd(b)$ also fills every set
cut: adjoin $a$ to the lower constraints and $b$ to the upper
constraints. It is therefore another copy of $\No$. This observation
will permit the later construction to be confined to a prescribed
interval.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~5.3, ``Complete cut-orbit classification'']\label{swo:lm:aut:thm:orbits}
{\itshape
Two strict class cuts $L,L'$ of $\Pbd(b)$ are carried to one another
by a class order automorphism of $\Pbd(b)$ if and only if
$\chi(L)=\chi(L')$. The possible pairs are exactly
\[
 (\Omega,1),\qquad
 (\lambda,\Omega),\qquad
 (\Omega,\lambda),\qquad
 (\Omega,\Omega),
\]
where $\lambda$ ranges over infinite regular set cardinals. The first
pair consists precisely of strict cuts below core points.}
This is source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits}, with the marker $\Omega$ in place of source~14's character symbol $\Ord$. Source~20 realizes $(\Omega,\Omega)$ by the repeated-label cut of \cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated}, source~14 by a successor-prefix cylinder edge.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
An automorphism and its inverse send sets to sets by Class
Replacement. They therefore preserve cofinal and coinitial set
witnesses and their least possible cardinalities. This proves
necessity.

At least one coordinate of $\chi(L)$ is $\Omega$. Otherwise take a
set $A_0$ cofinal in $L$ and a set $B_0$ coinitial in its upper side.
Set-cut interpolation gives $A_0<z<B_0$. If $z\in L$, cofinality of
$A_0$ contradicts the first inequality; if $z\notin L$, coinitiality
of $B_0$ contradicts the second. The endpoint and regularity
observations following \cref{swo:lm:aut:def:character} give the displayed
list of possible forms.

To prove sufficiency, construct isomorphisms between the two lower
sides and between the two upper sides, then join the maps. A side
whose relevant character is $\Omega$ is a copy of $\No$ by
\cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:sides}. Suppose instead that the initial sides $L,L'$
have the same set cofinality $\lambda$. Choose increasing cofinal
sequences $(a_\xi)_{\xi<\lambda}$ and
$(a'_\xi)_{\xi<\lambda}$. Begin back-and-forth with the entire
\emph{set} partial isomorphism
\[
                 a_\xi\longmapsto a'_\xi
                 \qquad(\xi<\lambda).
\]
For a new $x\in L$, the already mapped points below and above $x$
give a set cut in the ambient target core. Some $a_\xi$ is strictly
above $x$, so its image $a'_\xi$ is an upper constraint. Every
realizer of the cut consequently lies in $L'$. The inverse step is
identical. This produces the required side isomorphism. For final
sides with equal set coinitiality, use the dual argument. If both
upper sides have a minimum, map the minima to one another and apply
\cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:sides} to the open final tails. Each stage again has
only a set partial map. Joining the two side isomorphisms preserves
all comparisons across the cut and gives a class automorphism.

Strict principal cuts realize $(\Omega,1)$. For an infinite regular
$\lambda$, choose an increasing sequence
$(a_\xi)_{\xi<\lambda}$ in $\Pbd(b)$ and put
\[
 L=\{x\in\Pbd(b):(\exists\xi<\lambda)\ x<a_\xi\}.
\]
The sequence is cofinal in $L$. If fewer than $\lambda$ points were
cofinal, choose an index bound for each of them; regularity would
bound all these indices below $\lambda$, a contradiction. Thus
$\cf_s(L)=\lambda$. Its complement has no set coinitial subset by
the preceding interpolation obstruction. This gives
$(\lambda,\Omega)$, and the dual construction gives
$(\Omega,\lambda)$. Finally the explicit cut in
\cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated} below realizes $(\Omega,\Omega)$.
\end{proof}

The theorem is about individually supplied class cuts and class
automorphisms. It does not form an ordinary class whose elements are
all cuts. It is nevertheless a complete classification of the action:
any two allowed cut parameters having the same displayed characters
are conjugate.

\subsubsection{A represented cut and an unrepresented cut in one orbit}

For an exhaustive enumeration $e:\Ord\to\No$, write
\[
                  L_e=\{c\in\Pbd(b):E_c<_{\lex}e\}.
\]
If $e$ is not evaluated by a core code, its two strict comparison
sides partition $\Pbd(b)$.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~5.4, ``The character of a noncore enumeration'']\label{swo:lm:aut:lem:exhaustive}
{\itshape
If $e$ is an exhaustive global enumeration outside the chosen core,
then $\chi(L_e)=(\Omega,\Omega)$.}
This is source~17's \cref{swo:gs:prop:class-characters} (source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:characters}) for exhaustive noncore enumerations.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
For a set $A\subseteq L_e$, uniform core interpolation applied to
the rows indexed by $A$ and the one upper row $e$ gives a core row
strictly above every member of $A$ and strictly below $e$. Thus $A$
is not cofinal. The dual argument excludes a set coinitial subset
above $e$. Smaller and larger first labels give nonempty sides.
\end{proof}

Such enumerations exist in $\GBC$. For example, compose $b$ with
the class permutation interchanging each consecutive pair
$2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+1$ of ordinals. The support is a proper
class, so the resulting enumeration has no code in the bounded-support
core.

For an injective set prefix $p:\delta\to\No$, let
\[
 C_p=\{c\in\Pbd(b):E_c\restriction\delta=p\}
\]
be its convex cylinder. Every such cylinder is nonempty. A prefix
\emph{straddles} a cut when its cylinder meets both sides. The
established prefix-recognition theorem says that a strict class cut
is represented by an injective $\Ord$-word precisely when it has a
straddling cylinder at every set-ordinal length. That word is unique.
It represents a set-like global well-order precisely when it is
surjective. A raw class well-order has the same cut as the injective
enumeration of its canonical initial $\Ord$-block, so raw
representability satisfies the same prefix criterion, without the
surjectivity requirement (source~18, \cref{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut};
\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition,swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}).

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~5.5, ``A local deleted-label cut'']\label{swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated}
{\itshape
Let $p$ be an injective set prefix and choose
$x\in\No\setminus\operatorname{ran}(p)$. Form the noninjective set
word
\[
 q=p\mathbin{{}^\frown}\langle x\rangle,
 \qquad
 t=p\mathbin{{}^\frown}\langle x,x\rangle.
\]
Every core row differs from $t$ before $t$ ends, and hence
\[
                   D_t=\{c\in\Pbd(b):E_c<_{\lex}t\}
\]
is well-defined. It is a strict class cut of character
$(\Omega,\Omega)$, lying inside $C_p$, and is represented by no
injective $\Ord$-word and by no raw class well-order of $\No$.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:ex:repeated-label-cut} (source~15's repeated-label case, \cref{swo:cb:n7.7}), with its character computed.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
A core row cannot agree with both occurrences of $x$, so ordinary
first-difference comparison partitions the core into initial and
final sides. All codes below $C_p$ are on the lower side and all
codes above it are on the upper side. Within $C_q$, the side is
decided by whether the next label is less or greater than $x$.
Fresh labels on either side, followed by prefix completion, show
that both parts are nonempty.

Let $A\subseteq D_t$ be a set. The members outside $C_q$ lie below
that cylinder. For the members inside, collect their next labels,
all of which are less than $x$. Choose a surreal $y<x$ strictly above
every collected label and outside $\operatorname{ran}(q)$. Such a
fresh realizer exists: the realizers of any surreal set cut form a
proper class, since a set of all realizers could itself be adjoined
to the lower constraints to obtain a still larger realizer. A set
of forbidden labels cannot exhaust that class. Complete
$q\mathbin{{}^\frown}\langle y\rangle$ to a core row. It remains
in $D_t$ and lies above all of $A$. Thus the lower character is
$\Omega$. The upper side is dual.

If $\delta=\operatorname{dom}(p)$, the cylinder $C_q$ straddles
$D_t$ at length $\delta+1$. At length $\delta+2$, every injective
prefix already differs from $t$, and all its completions compare
with $t$ in the same direction. There is therefore no straddling
cylinder of that length. Prefix recognition excludes an injective
representative. The canonical initial-block description excludes
a raw representative as well. Equivalently, any putative
representative would be forced to begin with $p,x,x$, contrary to
injectivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Corollary~5.6, ``Representability is extra structure'']\label{swo:lm:aut:cor:notintrinsic}
{\itshape
The strict cut of every exhaustive noncore enumeration is carried
by some class automorphism of $\Pbd(b)$ to a cut represented by no
raw class well-order. Thus the bare core order does not distinguish
these two kinds of cuts.}
This is \cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic} with a repeated-label cut as target; source~15's \cref{swo:cb:thm:automorphism} uses a first-label cut and source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension} the cut of a nonexhaustive word.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Apply \cref{swo:lm:aut:thm:orbits} to
\cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:exhaustive,swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated}.
\end{proof}

Omitted-range injective branches also have character
$(\Omega,\Omega)$. For a set of core rows below such a branch,
Class Replacement bounds all their first-disagreement coordinates.
Follow the branch beyond that bound, choose a fresh smaller next
label, and complete the prefix to a core row. This improves the
entire set while remaining below the branch; the upper side is
dual. Consequently one orbit contains
exhaustive branches, branches with residual tails, and nonbranch
cuts caused by a repeated label. The prefix-recognition criterion
therefore describes the order \emph{with its specified cylinder
structure}; it cannot be recovered as an invariant of the bare
ordered core.

\subsubsection{Nonextension while fixing arbitrary set data}

\begin{theorem}[Localized failure of one-point extension]
\label{swo:lm:aut:thm:localfailure}
Let $e:\Ord\to\No$ be an exhaustive enumeration outside $\Pbd(b)$,
and let $S\subseteq\Pbd(b)$ be any set. There is a class order
automorphism $\varphi$ of $\Pbd(b)$, fixing $S$ pointwise, for which
there is no raw class well-order $R$ of $\No$ satisfying
\[
       \{d\in\Pbd(b):E_d<_{\lex}R\}=\varphi[L_e].
\]
In particular, $\varphi$ has no order-embedding extension from the
one-point enlargement $\Pbd(b)\cup\{e\}$ into the raw comparison
structure, and no automorphism extension to either $\Hsl$ or
$\Hall$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Partition $S$ according to its comparison with $e$. Uniform
interpolation produces core points $a,d$ such that
\[
 \{s\in S:E_s<e\}<a<e<d<\{s\in S:e<E_s\}.
\]
Empty outer sides are allowed. The interval $I=(a,d)$ contains no
member of $S$. Choose a prefix $p$ of $e$ extending beyond the
first disagreement of $e$ with each endpoint. Then
$C_p\subseteq I$. Choose a fresh $x$ and let $D_t$ be the
deleted-label cut from \cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated}.

The lower and upper sides of $L_e$ within $I$ have no set cofinal
and coinitial subsets, respectively. For example, given a set on
the lower side, adjoin $a$ and interpolate below $e$; this produces
a larger member still in $I$. The upper side is dual. The
construction in \cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated} produces its improving
points inside $C_q\subseteq I$, so the two sides of $D_t$ within
$I$ have the same characters. By \cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:sides}, all four
sides are copies of $\No$. Join isomorphisms of corresponding
sides to obtain an automorphism of $I$ carrying its first cut to
its second. Extend it by the identity outside $I$. The resulting
$\varphi$ fixes $S$ and satisfies $\varphi[L_e]=D_t$.

If a raw order $R$ were the image of $e$ under an order-embedding
extension, then for every $c\in\Pbd(b)$,
\[
       E_{\varphi(c)}<_{\lex}R
          \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E_c<_{\lex}e.
\]
Its strict core cut would therefore be $D_t$, contradicting
\cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:repeated}. The same contradiction excludes the
displayed cut identity directly, without constructing an
encompassing object of all raw orders.
\end{proof}

This is stronger than the existence of a single bad automorphism.
Any set of prescribed core data can be retained, and the failure
can be confined to a core interval containing the cut of $e$.
Accordingly, representedness is not an isomorphism-invariant
property of the core order even after an arbitrary set of core
parameters has been named. The theorem also identifies the exact
limitation of set-sized partial homogeneity: extending a partial
isomorphism within the core does not control its behavior at
proper-class cuts.

The one-point formulation is legitimate already in $\GBC$.
Replace the additional point by one new set marker and compare it
with core codes using the class parameter $e$. The impossibility
asserts that no individual class relation $R$ can realize its
required image comparisons. No ordinary class containing all
class relations, and no function whose ordinary arguments are
classes, is required.

\subsubsection{Exactly what an extension must preserve}

Write $\mathsf{Exh}_b(L)$ for the assertion that a strict cut $L$
is the strict core cut of an exhaustive $\Ord$-enumeration. This
is a predicate of a \emph{class variable}, not a subset of an
ordinary class of all cuts. Prefix recognition gives the following
equivalent formulation using only set quantifiers with $L$ as a
class parameter:
\begin{enumerate}
\item at every ordinal length there is a straddling injective
set prefix;
\item every surreal belongs to the range of some such prefix.
\end{enumerate}
The straddling prefix at any fixed length is unique, since two
disjoint convex cylinders cannot both cross an initial cut.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~5.8, ``Extension criterion for the set-like order'']\label{swo:lm:aut:thm:extensioncriterion}
{\itshape
Fix a class automorphism $\varphi$ of $\Pbd(b)$. It has an extension
to the set-like global comparison structure, given by one
elementary transformation of each supplied class enumeration, if
and only if
\[
 \mathsf{Exh}_b(L)
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathsf{Exh}_b\bigl(\varphi[L]\bigr)
\]
for every strict class cut $L$. If the extension exists, it is
unique. Here the displayed statement quantifies over class
parameters; the conclusion does not assert an ordinary class
function having arbitrary classes as its elements.}
This is source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}, with the predicate $\mathsf{Exh}_b$ in place of source~17's $\mathscr R_b$; the two predicates agree by \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Necessity follows by comparing the image of an enumeration with
the images of all core rows, and then applying the inverse
extension.

For sufficiency, supply any exhaustive enumeration $e$ as a class
parameter. Form the class cut $\varphi[L_e]$. By the hypothesis
it has a straddling prefix at every ordinal length and its
uniquely recovered word is exhaustive. Define its image $e'$ by
\[
 e'(\alpha)=x
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{there is an injective prefix }p:\alpha+1\to\No\\
 \text{straddling }\varphi[L_e]\text{ with }p(\alpha)=x.
 \end{gathered}
\]
All quantified variables in this definition are sets. Membership
in the image cut is the elementary condition
\[
 d\in\varphi[L_e]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (\exists c\in\Pbd(b))\,
       \bigl(\varphi(c)=d\ \wedge\ E_c<_{\lex}e\bigr).
\]
Elementary class comprehension therefore produces $e'$ for every
supplied $e$, by the same formula. The prefix criterion proves
that it is the unique exhaustive enumeration with that cut.

Core density gives, for distinct exhaustive enumerations,
\[
              e<f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_e\subsetneq L_f.
\]
Indeed a core row strictly between them witnesses strict
inclusion. The construction consequently preserves and reflects
order. At a core row it agrees with $\varphi$, because the strict
cut below $c$ is carried to the strict cut below $\varphi(c)$.
The analogous construction with $\varphi^{-1}$ gives its inverse.
Finally any extension must carry $L_e$ to $\varphi[L_e]$, and
density makes the exhaustive representative unique.
\end{proof}

For one supplied noncore $e$, the corresponding criterion is
sharper still. An image in $\Hall$ exists exactly when
$\varphi[L_e]$ has a straddling prefix at every ordinal length;
an image in $\Hsl$ exists exactly when the recovered word is
also surjective. For the entire raw structure, preserving these
cuts alone is insufficient: several raw orders can have the same
canonical initial $\Ord$-block. An extension must additionally
identify the orders of their residual fibers, with the required
uniformity. This is the remaining structural question, after the
unrestricted extension assertion has been refuted.

\begin{proposition}[Numerical relabeling moves a chosen core]
\label{swo:lm:aut:prop:labelmoves}
Let $h$ be a nonidentity increasing class automorphism of
$(\No,<)$. The evaluated bounded-support cores based at $b$ and
$h\circ b$ are disjoint. In particular, no nonidentity numerical
relabeling stabilizes one chosen core.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If a row belonged to both cores, it would differ from each
baseline on only a set of coordinates. Thus $b$ and $h\circ b$
would differ on a set of coordinates, and Class Replacement would
imply that $h$ moves only a set of surreal labels. If $x<h(x)$,
then every $y$ with $x<y<h(x)$ satisfies
$h(y)>h(x)>y$. The proper-class interval $(x,h(x))$ would consist
entirely of moved labels, a contradiction. If $h(x)<x$, every
$y\in(h(x),x)$ satisfies $h(y)<h(x)<y$, giving the same
contradiction.
\end{proof}

Numerical relabeling still gives a natural isomorphism between
the two different cores and a natural transformation of global
enumerations. The proposition explains why it does not account
for the nontrivial internal automorphisms of one fixed core.

\merge\ Source~20's last paragraph before \cref{swo:lm:aut:prop:labelmoves}
calls the extension question for the whole raw structure ``the remaining
structural question''. Source~19's \cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:aut} answers it in an
external set-sized model: a core automorphism extends to the raw order exactly
when it preserves the isomorphism types of all residual fibres. Source~25 asks
the elementary question about two baselines that \cref{swo:lm:aut:prop:labelmoves}
answers for relabelled ones: two cores coincide exactly when their baselines
eventually agree, and are otherwise disjoint (its Question~16.6,
\cref{swo:ph:n16.6}).

% ---- source 21, Section 9
\subsection{Source 21: core automorphisms, a concrete obstruction to extension}\label{swo:fu:fnd:sec:automorphisms}

% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 1564-2056
The bounded-support core carries much of the local order geometry of
\(\Hsl\), but its abstract order does not determine which of its large
cuts are represented by exhaustive enumerations.  This distinction gives
a concrete negative answer to one of the repository's extension questions:
some automorphisms of the core do not extend even to order embeddings
from \(\Hsl\) into \(\Hall\).  We first establish a cut reconstruction
lemma, then give an exact extension criterion for the set-like fragment
and two successive forms of the obstruction.

\subsubsection{The core and its cuts}

Work in \(\GBC\), and fix a baseline class bijection
\(b:\Ord\to\No\).  Write $\Pbd(b)$ for the genuine class of normalized set-support codes, ordered by the
lexicographic comparison of their evaluations.  If \(d\in \Pbd(b)\), write
\(E_d:\Ord\to\No\) for the corresponding global enumeration.  Concretely,
one can code a permutation of an ordinal, extend it by the identity, and
compose with \(b\).  Normalization removes the duplicate codes obtained by
adjoining an identity segment.  Thus distinct points of \(\Pbd(b)\) have
distinct evaluations.

The following established core properties are used below
(Part~IV: \cref{swo:gl:completion,swo:gl:interpolation,swo:gl:pbd-no}): every injective set prefix extends to an \(E_d\); \(\Pbd(b)\)
realizes every separated cut given by two sets of its points, with empty
sides allowed; and \(\Pbd(b)\) is order-dense in \(\Hsl\).  The same density
argument applies to injective \(\Ord\)-words whose ranges need not be all
of \(\No\).  In particular, \(\Pbd(b)\) is an \(\eta_{\Ord}\) class order
without endpoints.  The class version of the back-and-forth underlying
this characterization is also central to the usual uniqueness theorem
for the surreal order \cite{Ehrlich2012}.

For an injective class function \(F:\Ord\to\No\), define
\[
 L_F=\{d\in \Pbd(b):E_d<_{\lex}F\},\qquad R_F=\Pbd(b)\setminus L_F.
 \tag{S21.$\ast$}\label{swo:fu:fnd:eq:word-cut}
\]
These are ordinary classes of set codes.  When \(F=E_d\), the lower
class is the strict lower cut of that core point, and the upper class
includes the point itself.  Otherwise both sides are strict.
For an injective set word \(p\), put
\[
 C_p=\{d\in \Pbd(b):p\subseteq E_d\}.
\]
We say that \(C_p\) \emph{crosses} a class \(L\subseteq \Pbd(b)\) if it meets
both \(L\) and \(\Pbd(b)\setminus L\).

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~9.1, ``Elementary reconstruction from a core cut'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:lem:reconstruction}
{\itshape
Let \(F:\Ord\to\No\) be injective.  For every injective set word \(p\),
\[
       C_p\text{ crosses }L_F
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\subseteq F.
\]
Consequently \(F\) is recovered from \(L_F\) and \(b\) by
\[
\begin{split}
 F(\alpha)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 &\exists p\;[\dom(p)=\alpha+1,\ p\text{ injective},\\[-2pt]
 &\hspace{42mm}p(\alpha)=x,
               \ C_p\text{ crosses }L_F].
\end{split}
\]
The defining formula has only set quantifiers and the displayed class
parameters.  In particular, two injective \(\Ord\)-words with the same
core cut are equal.}
With \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:represented-cuts} this is the represented-cut theorem \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition} (\cref{swo:xiii:note:ninefold}); the lemma is its uniqueness and reconstruction clause.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
If \(p\not\subseteq F\), the first discrepancy between \(p\) and \(F\)
occurs before the end of \(p\).  Every evaluation extending \(p\) has
the same comparison with \(F\) at that discrepancy.  Thus all of \(C_p\)
lies on one side of \(L_F\).

Conversely, suppose \(p=F\restr\beta\).  Choose unused labels
\(x<F(\beta)<y\).  For example, choose \(x\) below, and \(y\) above,
the set \(\ran(p)\cup\{F(\beta)\}\).  Extend
\(p\cat\langle x\rangle\) and \(p\cat\langle y\rangle\) to core
enumerations.  The first is below \(F\) and the second is above it, so
\(C_p\) crosses the cut.  Applying this equivalence to words of length
\(\alpha+1\) proves the formula and uniqueness.
\end{proof}

The lemma applies equally to exhaustive and nonexhaustive words.  A
nonexhaustive word can therefore never induce the cut of an exhaustive
one.  This is a stronger statement than the mere absence of a core
point at the cut.  The reconstruction also works for principal core
cuts: arbitrarily long prefixes still have core extensions on both
sides of the represented enumeration.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~9.2, ``Which core cuts are represented by words?'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:represented-cuts}
{\itshape
Let \(L\subsetneq \Pbd(b)\) be a nonempty lower class with no greatest
element.  Then \(L=L_F\) for some injective
\(F:\Ord\to\No\) if and only if, for every ordinal \(\alpha\), some
length-\(\alpha\) prefix cylinder \(C_p\) crosses \(L\).
When this holds, the crossing prefix at each level is unique, these
prefixes are coherent, and their union is the unique representing word.
The word is exhaustive if and only if every surreal occurs in some
crossing prefix.  All these tests and the reconstruction use elementary
formulas with the class parameters \(L,b\).}
This is \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}, proved again (\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold,swo:xiii:note:ninefold}).
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Necessity follows from \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:reconstruction}.  For sufficiency,
first observe that two distinct cylinders of the same length cannot
both cross a lower class.  Their fixed prefixes have a first discrepancy,
so every point of one cylinder precedes every point of the other.
A point outside \(L\) in the earlier cylinder and a point inside \(L\)
in the later cylinder would contradict downward closure.

Thus there is a unique crossing prefix \(p_\alpha\) at each level.
Every restriction of a crossing prefix also crosses, since its cylinder
contains the original cylinder.  Consequently
\(p_\beta\restr\alpha=p_\alpha\) whenever \(\alpha<\beta\).
Define \(F(\alpha)=p_{\alpha+1}(\alpha)\).  Existence and uniqueness
of these set prefixes give an elementary definition of the graph;
there is no choice of a class-valued stage.  Coherence shows that
\(F\restr\alpha=p_\alpha\), and therefore \(F\) is injective.

Take a core point \(E_d\ne F\), and let \(\delta\) be their first
discrepancy.  If \(E_d<_{\lex}F\), then \(E_d\) precedes every point
of the crossing cylinder \(C_{p_{\delta+1}}\).  That cylinder has a
point in \(L\), so downward closure gives \(d\in L\).  If
\(E_d>_{\lex}F\), the cylinder has a point outside \(L\) below
\(E_d\), so \(d\notin L\).

There remains only the possibility \(E_d=F\).  The comparisons just
proved show that, if \(d\in L\), it would be the greatest point of
\(L\).  The hypothesis excludes this.  Thus \(L=L_F\) also in that
case.  Finally, \(\ran(F)\) is the union of the ranges of the crossing
prefixes, which proves the exhaustivity criterion.
\end{proof}

The no-greatest-element hypothesis is essential for this formulation.
For a core point \(E_d\), both
\(\{c:E_c<_{\lex}E_d\}\) and
\(\{c:E_c\le_{\lex}E_d\}\) have the same crossing cylinders at every
level.  Reconstruction gives \(E_d\) in both cases, but only the first
is its strict lower cut.  The second has greatest element \(d\).

\begin{note}[Source~21, Proposition~9.3, ``The first failed level of a cut'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:prop:first-failure}
{\itshape
Let $L$ be a proper nonempty lower class of $\Pbd(b)$ with no greatest
element. Suppose its first level with no crossing cylinder is a limit
ordinal $\lambda$. The coherent earlier prefixes have a union $p$ of
length $\lambda$. If $C_p$ lies on the upper side, then $L$ has set
cofinality exactly $\cf(\lambda)$. If $C_p$ lies on the lower side,
the upper side has set coinitiality exactly $\cf(\lambda)$.
Consequently a cut with no set-sized cofinal lower subset and no
set-sized coinitial upper subset (``large on both sides,'' as in
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:def:large-cut}) either comes from a full injective
$\Ord$-word, or first loses its crossing cylinder at a successor level.
In the latter case it is a cut between the next-label cylinders inside
one fixed set prefix.}
This is the limit case of the first-failure classification (source~13's \cref{swo:fs:thm:failure}, source~15's \cref{swo:cb:thm:terminal}, source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:firstfailure}, source~18's \cref{swo:sh:thm:cut-first-failure}) with source~14's characters (\cref{swo:tc:thm:characters}).
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Write $p_\beta$ for the unique crossing prefix at level $\beta<\lambda$.
Their restrictions agree, so their union is an injective set word
$p$. Its cylinder is nonempty and wholly on one side. Suppose
$C_p\subseteq \Pbd(b)\setminus L$. Choose a cofinal sequence of
$\cf(\lambda)$ many levels $\beta<\lambda$ and at each such level a
code $d_\beta\in L\cap C_{p_\beta}$. Global choice and class
replacement make these codes a set. Every $d\in L$ must disagree
with $p$ at some position $\delta<\lambda$, in the smaller direction.
For $\beta>\delta$ one has $d<d_\beta$. Thus the chosen set is cofinal.

Conversely, for a family of fewer than $\cf(\lambda)$ codes in $L$,
their disagreement positions with $p$ are bounded below $\lambda$.
A lower-side point in a later crossing cylinder is strictly above
the entire family. Hence the cofinality is exactly $\cf(\lambda)$.
The other case is the order dual.

If a large cut ever fails the crossing test, it has a least failing
level. Level zero crosses, and the preceding argument excludes limit
levels. At a successor level $\alpha+1$, the unique length-$\alpha$
cylinder still crosses, but each of its next-label cylinders lies
entirely on one side. Their numeric ordering gives precisely the
stated next-label cut.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The exact extension criterion}

Let \(h\) be a class automorphism of \(\Pbd(b)\).  For a class
\(L\subseteq \Pbd(b)\), its image
\[
                    h_*L=\{h(d):d\in L\}
\]
is an ordinary class.  The expression
\[
          \mathcal C_{\mathrm{exh}}=\{L_E:E\in\Hsl\}
\]
will be used only as virtual notation for the represented exhaustive
cuts.  It does not assert that this collection of classes is itself a
class of \(\GBC\).

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~9.4, ``Extension criterion'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:extension-criterion}
{\itshape
A class automorphism \(h\) of \(\Pbd(b)\) extends to an order automorphism
of \(\Hsl\) if and only if \(h_*\) carries the represented exhaustive
cuts onto themselves.  Explicitly, the condition is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\forall E\in\Hsl\ \exists F\in\Hsl\quad L_F=h_*L_E,\\
 &\forall F\in\Hsl\ \exists E\in\Hsl\quad L_F=h_*L_E.
\end{aligned}
\]
The extension is unique.  The first condition alone gives an order
embedding of \(\Hsl\) into itself extending \(h\).
In the two-sorted formulation, the extension is a uniform operator on
class parameters.  Its output is elementarily reconstructed from
\(h,b,E\); neither \(\ETR\) nor Class Choice is required.}
This is source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}; source~21 adds that the first condition alone gives an extending self-embedding of $\Hsl$.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Suppose \(\Phi\) is an extending order automorphism.  For \(d\in \Pbd(b)\),
\[
 E_d<_{\lex}E
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 E_{h(d)}<_{\lex}\Phi(E).
\]
Hence \(L_{\Phi(E)}=h_*L_E\).  Surjectivity supplies the second condition.
The same cut equation is necessary for an extending order embedding.

Conversely, given \(E\), form \(h_*L_E\) by elementary comprehension and
apply the formula in \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:reconstruction}.  The first condition
asserts that the reconstructed word is an exhaustive enumeration \(F\),
and the lemma makes it unique.  Thus this construction defines \(\Phi(E)\)
without making a choice from a collection of class witnesses.

If \(E<_{\lex}E'\), order-density of the core gives
\(L_E\subsetneq L_{E'}\).  Applying \(h\) preserves this proper inclusion,
so the represented output cuts satisfy
\(L_{\Phi(E)}\subsetneq L_{\Phi(E')}\), which implies
\(\Phi(E)<_{\lex}\Phi(E')\).  For a core point \(E_d\), the image of
its strict lower cut is the strict lower cut of \(E_{h(d)}\); therefore
\(\Phi(E_d)=E_{h(d)}\).  The second condition gives surjectivity.
Finally, every extension must satisfy the cut equation, and reconstruction
makes its value at each input unique.
\end{proof}

\Cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:represented-cuts} makes the criterion explicit in the
prefix language.  For each input \(E\), the transformed lower cut
\(h_*L_E\) must have a crossing cylinder at every ordinal level, and
every surreal must occur in some such crossing prefix.  These tests
characterize an extending embedding.  Applying the same tests to
\(h^{-1}\) as well characterizes an extending automorphism.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Corollary~9.5, ``Restriction to the core'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:cor:stabilizer}
{\itshape
In an enlarged universe where the displayed collections are sets,
restriction identifies
\[
 \Aut(\Hsl;\Pbd(b))
 \cong
 \operatorname{Stab}_{\Aut(\Pbd(b))}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{exh}}).
\]
Here \(\Aut(\Hsl;\Pbd(b))\) denotes the automorphisms carrying the core onto
itself.  In \(\GBC\), the same assertion is understood as the corresponding
criterion for uniform operators.}
This restates \cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion} as an identification of groups in an enlarged universe.
\end{note}

The criterion is exact, but it deliberately retains the represented-cut
family as additional data.  The next result shows that this data cannot
be discarded.

\subsubsection{Homogeneity of large cuts}

\begin{definition}
\label{swo:fu:fnd:def:large-cut}
A class cut \((L,R)\) of \(\Pbd(b)\) is \emph{large on both sides} if
\(L,R\) are nonempty, partition \(\Pbd(b)\), satisfy \(L<R\), and
\(L\) has no set-sized cofinal subset while \(R\) has no set-sized
coinitial subset.
\end{definition}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~9.7, ``Each side is an \(\eta_{\Ord}\) order'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:lem:cut-sides}
{\itshape
If \((L,R)\) is large on both sides, both \(L\) and \(R\), with their
induced orders, are proper-class \(\eta_{\Ord}\) orders without endpoints.}
This is the first part of source~17's \cref{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity} (source~20's \cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:sides}).
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Neither side can be a set, since it would then be its own set-sized
cofinal or coinitial subset.  Consider set constraints \(A<B\) in \(L\).
If \(B\ne\varnothing\), interpolate them in \(\Pbd(b)\).  The resulting
point lies below an element of \(L\), and hence belongs to \(L\).
If \(B=\varnothing\), the set \(A\) is not cofinal in \(L\), so some
point of \(L\) lies strictly above all of \(A\).  This also handles
\(A=\varnothing\).  The proof for \(R\) is dual.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~9.8, ``Conjugacy of large class cuts'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:cut-conjugacy}
{\itshape
Any two class cuts of \(\Pbd(b)\) that are large on both sides are carried
to one another by a class automorphism of \(\Pbd(b)\).}
This is the $(\Ord,\Ord)$ case of source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits} and the second part of \cref{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Write the cuts as \((L_0,R_0)\) and \((L_1,R_1)\).
By \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:cut-sides}, the two left sides are proper-class
\(\eta_{\Ord}\) orders, as are the two right sides.  Global Choice
supplies set-like enumerations of these genuine classes of set codes.
We give the standard back-and-forth for the left sides.

At stage \(\alpha\), the partial isomorphism is a set.  Insert the first
unused point of \(L_0\), placing its image between the images of all
already mapped points below and above it.  These are set constraints, so
\(\eta_{\Ord}\)-interpolation supplies a point.  The strict inequalities
make it fresh.  Then perform the reverse insertion for the first unused
point of \(L_1\).  A fixed global well-order selects the interpolants.
At a limit stage take the union of the preceding partial maps.  Since
the stage is an ordinal, its history and the resulting map are sets.
The union over all ordinals is an isomorphism \(L_0\cong L_1\).

The same construction gives \(R_0\cong R_1\).  Join the two maps.
Their domains and ranges partition the core, and the cross inequalities
are preserved because the left side precedes the right side in each cut.
The result is the required automorphism.

Every stage of this recursion is set-valued.  Its existence is the
ordinary class-parameter recursion available in \(\GBC\), rather than
an application of \(\ETR\).
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~9.9, ``Cuts induced by nonskeleton words'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:lem:word-cut-large}
{\itshape
If an injective \(F:\Ord\to\No\) is not the evaluation of any point
of \(\Pbd(b)\), the cut \((L_F,R_F)\) is large on both sides.}
This is source~17's \cref{swo:gs:prop:class-characters} for noncore injective words (source~20's \cref{swo:lm:aut:lem:exhaustive} for exhaustive ones).
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Let \(T\subseteq L_F\) be a set of core codes.  For each \(d\in T\),
the first discrepancy \(\Delta(E_d,F)\) is an ordinal.  Class Replacement
gives an ordinal \(\beta\) strictly above all these discrepancies.
Follow \(F\) up to \(\beta\), choose a fresh label smaller than
\(F(\beta)\), and extend this set prefix to a core enumeration.
The result lies below \(F\) but above every \(E_d\) with \(d\in T\):
at the first discrepancy of \(E_d\) with \(F\), the new enumeration
still agrees with \(F\).  Hence \(T\) is not cofinal in \(L_F\).

For a set of codes in \(R_F\), choose a fresh label larger than
\(F(\beta)\) instead.  This produces a point above \(F\) and below
all the specified upper points.  Taking empty sets of constraints shows
that both sides are nonempty.  The hypothesis excludes an equality
case at a core point, so the upper side has no principal boundary.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~9.10, ``Nonextendable core automorphisms'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:nonextension}
{\itshape
There is a class automorphism of \(\Pbd(b)\) that has no extension even to
an order embedding \(\Hsl\to\Hsl\).  Consequently the stabilizer in
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:cor:stabilizer} is a proper subgroup of \(\Aut(\Pbd(b))\).}
This is source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension}, with the same pair-swapped $E$ and the target word $\alpha\mapsto\alpha$; source~21 states the failure for order embeddings $\Hsl\to\Hsl$, and source~17's argument gives that too, since it uses only the cut equation.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Define an exhaustive enumeration \(E\) by swapping every adjacent pair
of positions of \(b\):
\[
 E(2\cdot\alpha)=b(2\cdot\alpha+1),\qquad
 E(2\cdot\alpha+1)=b(2\cdot\alpha).
\]
Here ordinal multiplication has \(2\) on the left.  The two-element
blocks partition \(\Ord\), so \(E\) is a bijection.  Its support is
all of \(\Ord\), and therefore \(E\) is not a core evaluation.

Let \(F(\alpha)=\alpha\), regarding each ordinal as a surreal.
This word is injective but not exhaustive; for example, it omits \(-1\).
It too is not a core evaluation.  By \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:word-cut-large}, both
\((L_E,R_E)\) and \((L_F,R_F)\) are large on both sides.
By \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:cut-conjugacy}, choose \(h\in\Aut(\Pbd(b))\) with
\(h_*L_E=L_F\).

An extending order embedding \(\Phi\) would satisfy
\(L_{\Phi(E)}=h_*L_E=L_F\).  The reconstruction lemma would then
force \(\Phi(E)=F\) coordinate by coordinate.  This is impossible,
because \(\Phi(E)\) must be exhaustive and \(F\) is not.
\end{proof}

Thus all large class cuts lie in one orbit of the abstract core
automorphism group, whereas exhaustive represented cuts form a proper
part of that orbit.  The distinction between exhaustive and
nonexhaustive branches is not recoverable from the core order alone.
This obstruction already occurs in the set-like fragment; no residual
tail of an unrestricted class well-order is needed.

The result is existential and the construction uses the stated class
parameters and Global Choice.  It does not classify the extendable
subgroup, prove parameter-free definability of the automorphism, or
assert that every automorphism of \(\Hsl\) preserves a chosen core.
In a full inaccessible-universe model it becomes an ordinary set
theorem: a saturated core of size \(\kappa\) has conjugate
\((\kappa,\kappa)\)-cuts, some represented by bijections of length
\(\kappa\) and some represented only by nonexhaustive injective words.

\subsubsection{An obstruction even to extension into the unrestricted order}

A nonexhaustive word can still be the initial \(\Ord\)-word of an
unrestricted class well-order, by placing its omitted labels afterward.
To rule out extension into \(\Hall\), one therefore needs a cut that
is not represented even by an injective \(\Ord\)-word.  Such a cut has
a particularly simple definition.

\begin{proposition}[A large cut with no crossing first-level cylinder]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:prop:vertical-cut}
The class
\[
                    K=\{d\in \Pbd(b):E_d(0)<0\}
\]
is a proper lower cut, large on both sides, and no one-letter prefix
cylinder crosses it.  Consequently \(K\ne L_F\) for every injective
\(F:\Ord\to\No\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lexicographic comparison makes \(K\) a lower class.  A completion of
\(\langle-1\rangle\) belongs to it, and a completion of
\(\langle0\rangle\) does not, so the cut is nonempty and proper.

Let \(A\subseteq K\) be a set of codes.  The set of first entries
\(\{E_d(0):d\in A\}\) lies strictly below \(0\).  Surreal
set-cut interpolation gives a label \(z\) strictly above all those
entries and strictly below \(0\).  A core completion of
\(\langle z\rangle\) lies in \(K\) above every point of \(A\).
Thus no set is cofinal in the lower side.

Now let \(B\subseteq \Pbd(b)\setminus K\) be a set.  Form the set
\[
           U=\{E_d(1):d\in B,\ E_d(0)=0\}.
\]
Choose \(x\) below every element of \(U\cup\{0\}\), and complete
the injective prefix \(\langle0,x\rangle\) to a core point.
It lies in the upper side.  It precedes every row in \(B\) starting
with a positive label by comparison at position \(0\), and every row
in \(B\) starting with \(0\) by comparison at position \(1\).
Hence no set is coinitial in the upper side.

For any one-letter prefix \(\langle a\rangle\), its entire cylinder
lies in \(K\) if \(a<0\), and its entire cylinder lies outside \(K\)
if \(a\ge0\).  None crosses.  The final assertion follows already
from \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:reconstruction} at level \(1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~9.12, ``No extension even from \(\Hsl\) into \(\Hall\)'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:no-raw-extension}
{\itshape
There is a class automorphism \(h\) of \(\Pbd(b)\) with no extending
order embedding \(\Hsl\to\Hall\).  In particular it has no extending
order embedding \(\Hall\to\Hall\).}
This follows from source~14's \cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic}, whose target is a cylinder edge, the trace of no unrestricted class well-order; source~15's \cref{swo:cb:thm:automorphism} uses a first-label cut $\{d:E_d(0)\in A\}$ with $A\cong\No$, of which \cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:vertical-cut} is the case $A=\{x:x<0\}$.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Choose the exhaustive adjacent-pair-swap enumeration \(E\) used in
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:nonextension}.  Its core cut is large by
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:word-cut-large}.  The cut \(K\) of
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:vertical-cut} is also large, so
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:cut-conjugacy} gives a core automorphism \(h\) with
\(h_*L_E=K\).

Suppose \(\Phi:\Hsl\to\Hall\) were an extending order embedding.
For every core code \(d\), order preservation gives
\[
 E_d<_{\lex}E
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 E_{h(d)}<_{\lex}\Phi(E).
\]
Thus the unrestricted class well-order \(\Phi(E)\) would induce
exactly the cut \(K\) on the core.  By \cref{swo:fu:gl:initial-cut}, every
unrestricted class well-order induces the same core cut as its canonical
initial injective \(\Ord\)-word.  This contradicts
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:vertical-cut}.  An extending embedding on all of
\(\Hall\) would restrict to one on \(\Hsl\), so it too is impossible.
\end{proof}

The two obstructions locate different boundaries.  The cut of a
nonexhaustive word fails the exhaustivity test in
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:represented-cuts}, but does have crossing cylinders at
every ordinal level.  The cut \(K\) fails already at the first level.
The latter failure cannot be repaired by adding a residual tail to a
class well-order.  These examples do not say that every large cut is
unrepresented: \(L_E\) itself is a large represented cut.

For the unrestricted order, preservation of initial-word cuts is a
necessary extension condition.  A sufficient general extension theorem
would also have to control the residual fibers that those cuts do not
distinguish.  The exact set-like criterion in
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:extension-criterion} avoids that additional issue because
the core cut uniquely determines an exhaustive enumeration.

% ---- source 19, Section 9
\section{Residual data and the completion of the raw order (source 19)}\label{swo:rs:rf:sec:completion}

\merge\ Source~19's Sections~9--11, printed whole. The inherited facts it
starts from, display~(S19.14), are \cref{swo:cf:fibers} for the fibres and the
uniqueness clause of \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition} with
\cref{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage} and source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers}
(Part~IX) for the kernel of the trace map. \Cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction}
answers source~15's question ``Completion with residual data''
(\cref{swo:cb:n13.5}) in an external set-sized formulation, and
\cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:aut} source~15's ``Automorphism extension''
(\cref{swo:cb:n13.6}), source~14's ``Automorphisms of raw trace fibers''
(\cref{swo:tc:n14.7}), source~20's \cref{swo:lm:n11.2} and source~21's
\cref{swo:fu:rq:full-extension} in the same formulation. Source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:rf:lem:endpoints} is the class version of source~21's set-level
endpoint lemma (\cref{swo:fu:set:fiber-ends}, Part~X).

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 1644-1923
The first-block theorem does more than exhibit an obstruction to a naive
completion: it specifies the data that a faithful completion must retain.
We first recall the established fiber statement, then derive an exact
reconstruction at a size level where all the objects involved are sets.
The resulting description is exact, although computing the order types of
all residual fibers remains a separate problem.

Fix a baseline bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$ and its class $\Pbd(b)$ of
normalized bounded-support permutation codes.  Write $E_c$ for the
enumeration evaluated from $c\in\Pbd(b)$.  For a raw class well-order
$R$, let $F_R:\Ord\to\No$ enumerate its initial set-like part, and put
\[
 B_R=\No\setminus\operatorname{ran}(F_R),\qquad
 t(R)=\{c\in\Pbd(b):E_c<_{\mathrm{lex}}R\}.
\]
The previously proved first-block and represented-cut theorems give
\[\tag{S19.14}\label{swo:rs:rf:eq:kernel}
 t(R)=t(S)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_R=F_S,
 \qquad
 t^{-1}(t(R))\cong\WO(B_R).
\]
These are inherited results.  Their second isomorphism is restriction to
the residual alphabet; its inverse appends a residual well-order after
the fixed word $F_R$.  The fibers are convex.  Distinct initial words are
separated by a core row: at their first ordinal disagreement their common
prefix is a set, so a fresh numerical surreal can be inserted strictly
between the two unequal labels and the resulting prefix completed to a
core enumeration.

An exhaustive initial word has a singleton fiber, as does a word omitting
one label.  A word omitting $n$ labels has a finite fiber with $n!$ points.
Only the exhaustive word in the first two cases is set-like.  Moreover a
principal core cut $\Pbd(b)_{<c}$ has exactly the representative $E_c$,
because that enumeration is exhaustive.

\subsection{An external set-sized formulation}

Fix an externally set-sized two-sorted model
$\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal S)$ of $\GBC$.  The baseline is an admitted class
of this model.  Let $\Hall^{\mathcal M}$ be the external set of its admitted
raw class well-orders, and interpret $\Pbd(b)$ externally as the set of
its core codes.  All comparisons are those computed in $\mathcal M$.
No transitivity, $\omega$-standardness, or $\beta$-model assumption is
needed in this subsection.  Internal linearity and the internal density
and absence of endpoints of $\Pbd(b)$ yield actual external statements
about these interpreted orders.

For a residual carrier $B$, the notation $\WO^{\mathcal S}(B)$ means the
external set of admitted relations satisfying the model's class-well-order
predicate.  It need not be the collection of all externally well-founded
relations on the external carrier.  This distinction permits the theorem
to cover nonstandard models without an implicit absoluteness assumption.

Let $\mathcal Q=\operatorname{DC}(\Pbd(b))$ be the ordinary external
Dedekind completion of the dense order $\Pbd(b)$.  Concretely its
points are all external subsets $q\subseteq\Pbd(b)$ which are nonempty,
proper, initial, and have no greatest member, ordered by inclusion.  A core
point $c$ is identified with $\Pbd(b)_{<c}$.  Thus $\mathcal Q$ is
conditionally complete, has no endpoints, and contains $\Pbd(b)$
densely.  For $q\in\mathcal Q$ set
\[
 H_q=\{R\in\Hall^{\mathcal M}:t(R)=q\}.
\]
Each $H_q$ is empty or is a convex copy of
$\WO^{\mathcal S}(B_q)$ for the uniquely recovered initial word.
Different nonempty fibers compare exactly as their indices in
$\mathcal Q$.  In particular, this gives a lexicographic-sum description
of $\Hall^{\mathcal M}$ over its represented core cuts.

\begin{definition}[Completion convention for a nondense order]\label{swo:rs:n9.1}
For a nonempty external linear order $L$, let
$\operatorname{DC}(L)$ retain every old point and adjoin one point for
each proper unfilled Dedekind gap
\[
 L=A\sqcup B,\qquad A<B,
 \qquad A,B\ne\varnothing,
 \qquad A\text{ has no greatest point},\quad
 B\text{ has no least point}.
\]
Let $\operatorname{IC}(L)$ additionally acquire a least point if $L$
had none and a greatest point if $L$ had none.  Then
$\operatorname{IC}(L)$ is a complete bounded chain.  Existing adjacent
pairs are retained; they are not split by new points.
\end{definition}

Taking all downsets of a nondense order would not enforce this convention:
it can separate distinctions which are already realized by an old point
or an adjacent pair.  The convention above is the gap-filling Dedekind
completion relevant to the raw well-order space.

\begin{theorem}[Reconstruction by completed residual fibers]
\label{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction}
For each $q\in\mathcal Q$ define
\[
 K_q=\begin{cases}
 \{\ast_q\},&H_q=\varnothing,\\
 \operatorname{IC}(H_q),&H_q\ne\varnothing.
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 K=\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}K_q,
\]
where the sum is lexicographic.  Embed
$\Hall^{\mathcal M}$ by retaining each of its points in its own fiber.
Then $K$ is canonically its Dedekind completion
$\operatorname{DC}(\Hall^{\mathcal M})$ relative to this embedding.
Every old adjacent pair remains adjacent.  For any $x<y$ in $K$, either
an old raw order lies strictly between them, or $x,y$ themselves are an
adjacent pair of old raw orders.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Convexity and the comparison of different fibers make the displayed map
an order embedding.  To prove conditional completeness, let
$A\subseteq K$ be nonempty and bounded above, let $P$ be its projection
to $\mathcal Q$, and put $q_0=\sup P$.  If $q_0\notin P$, then
\[
 \sup A=(q_0,\min K_{q_0}).
\]
Every member of $A$ has smaller first coordinate, and any candidate with
smaller coordinate is exceeded by a member of $A$ by the definition of
$q_0$.  If $q_0\in P$, the nonempty section $A_{q_0}$ has a supremum
$z$ in the bounded complete chain $K_{q_0}$, and
\[
 \sup A=(q_0,z).
\]
These arguments also establish minimality of the proposed upper bound.
Infima are dual.  The sum has no endpoints because $\mathcal Q$ has none.

If $x<y$ have different first coordinates $q<r$, choose a core index
strictly between $q$ and $r$.  Its original core point lies strictly
between $x$ and $y$.  If they belong to the same fiber, the ordinary
interval-completion property supplies an old fiber point between them
unless they are adjacent old points.  Adding a missing fiber endpoint
does not create adjacency, since the original fiber had no endpoint on
that side.

It remains to check that the new points represent exactly old unfilled
gaps.  An internal gap point of $\operatorname{IC}(H_q)$ has old fiber
points cofinal below and coinitial above.  An added lower endpoint has
old fiber points coinitial above, while core points with smaller indices
are cofinal below; an added upper endpoint is dual.  If $H_q$ is empty,
core points on either side of $q$ approach the new singleton from both
sides.  Thus every new point has no greatest old predecessor and no
least old successor.  Conversely conditional completeness supplies a
point in every old proper unfilled gap.  Exactly the required gap points
have therefore been added, giving the canonical completion isomorphism.
\end{proof}

The interval endpoints in this theorem are essential.  For example,
suppose $H_q$ has no least point.  Core points with indices below $q$ must
have a supremum in the full completion.  Their supremum is the new lower
endpoint of the completed fiber, not an arbitrarily selected residual
well-order.  The analogous statement holds at the upper endpoint.

\subsection{Which boundary points are already present?}

\begin{lemma}[Extrema of the residual well-order space]
\label{swo:rs:rf:lem:endpoints}
Let $B$ be an admitted linearly ordered carrier with
$\WO^{\mathcal S}(B)\ne\varnothing$.  This external well-order space has
a least point if and only if the numerical order on $B$ is itself an
admitted class well-order.  In that case this numerical order is the
least point.  It has a greatest point if and only if the reverse
numerical order is an admitted class well-order, in which case that
reverse order is the greatest point.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $R$ is least.  If $a<b$ numerically but $b$ precedes $a$ in $R$,
conjugate $R$ by the transposition interchanging these labels.  This
gives an admitted well-order which agrees with $R$ before the old
position of $b$ and then has the smaller label $a$.  It is smaller in
the raw lexicographic comparison, a contradiction.  Therefore $R$
agrees with numerical order on every pair, so that order is an admitted
well-order.  Conversely, the numerical well-order always selects the
least remaining numerical label.  At its first disagreement with any
other well-order it is therefore smaller.  Reverse the comparisons for
the greatest-point assertion.
\end{proof}

Consequently the lower boundary of a represented completed fiber is new
exactly when its numerical residual alphabet is not a class well-order;
the upper boundary is new exactly when the reverse numerical order fails
to be a class well-order.  These tests use the model's admitted predicate,
while their conclusions concern actual external endpoints.

The empty, one-point, and standard finite residual cases require no
boundary additions.  An internally infinite residual numerical
well-order has an old minimum and acquires a new upper endpoint; a
reverse well-order acquires a new lower endpoint.  When neither direction
is a class well-order, both boundaries are added.  Both directions can
be class well-orders only when the carrier is internally finite: an
infinite carrier would yield, by successive least-element selection, an
$\omega$-sequence increasing in one direction and decreasing in the
other.  Without $\omega$-standardness, internal finiteness must not be
silently replaced by external finiteness.

\begin{proposition}[Exactly which suborders embed into the core completion]
\label{swo:rs:rf:prop:transversal}
Let $H'\subseteq\Hall^{\mathcal M}$ contain the core.  It has an order
embedding into $\mathcal Q$ fixing the specified core embedding if and
only if it meets each $H_q$ in at most one point.  In that case the
embedding is the trace map and is unique.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A point of the dense completion $\mathcal Q$ is uniquely determined by
its comparisons with the core.  Hence two raw points with the same
trace cannot have distinct images.  Conversely the trace map is an
order embedding whenever it is injective, because different fibers
compare by their cuts.  These facts also prove uniqueness.
\end{proof}

Choosing one representative from each represented cut therefore gives
a suborder whose completion is $\mathcal Q$.  Appending the restriction
of the baseline to each residual alphabet supplies a parameterwise
selector.  This is an ordinary external selector here; internally it
does not form a class whose elements are arbitrary classes.

\subsection{Automorphisms and the required decorations}

For $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Pbd(b))$ let
$\overline g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal Q)$ be its unique extension,
given on cuts by $\overline g(q)=g[q]$.  Decorate each $q$ by the order
type of $H_q$, with the empty fiber counted as a separate decoration.
Let $G$ be the subgroup of core automorphisms preserving these
decorations.

\begin{theorem}[The exact extension criterion]
\label{swo:rs:rf:thm:aut}
A core automorphism $g$ extends to an automorphism of
$\Hall^{\mathcal M}$ if and only if $g\in G$, equivalently if
\[
 H_q\cong H_{\overline g(q)}\qquad(q\in\mathcal Q).
\]
Writing $\operatorname{Aut}(\Hall^{\mathcal M};\Pbd(b))$ for
automorphisms preserving the core setwise, there is a short exact sequence
\[
 1\longrightarrow
 \prod_{H_q\ne\varnothing}\operatorname{Aut}(H_q)
 \longrightarrow
 \operatorname{Aut}(\Hall^{\mathcal M};\Pbd(b))
 \longrightarrow G\longrightarrow 1.
\]
In the external set setting this sequence splits noncanonically.
Every such raw-order automorphism extends uniquely to its Dedekind
completion from \Cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $h$ extends $g$, comparison with each core point gives
\[
 t(h(R))=g[t(R)].
\]
Thus $h$ maps $H_q$ isomorphically onto $H_{\overline g(q)}$, proving
necessity.  Conversely, ordinary external Choice selects isomorphisms
between the corresponding nonempty fibers.  Their union is an
automorphism of the lexicographic sum.  At principal core cuts the
maps are forced singleton maps, so the union restricts to $g$.

An automorphism fixing the core pointwise fixes every trace and hence
acts independently within its fibers; every such independent family
does give an automorphism.  This identifies the kernel and proves
exactness.  To obtain a noncanonical splitting, choose one representative
chain $L_d$ for every occurring nonempty fiber order type and fixed
isomorphisms $\phi_q:H_q\to L_d$.  Lift $g\in G$ on $H_q$ by
\[
 \phi_{\overline g(q)}^{-1}\circ\phi_q.
\]
The intermediate identifications cancel under composition, so these
lifts form a homomorphic section.  No canonical choice of the
$\phi_q$ is asserted.  Extension to the completion is the usual unique
extension of an automorphism to its filled Dedekind gaps.
\end{proof}

Merely preserving which cuts are represented is therefore weaker than the
required criterion.  The entire residual fiber type, including its
adjacencies and endpoint behavior, is the necessary decoration.  The
external Choice used to select fiber isomorphisms is ordinary set Choice;
the theorem does not infer an internal higher-order choice principle.

% ---- source 19, Section 10
\section{Why residual classification is not automatically self-similar (source 19)}\label{swo:rs:rf:sec:recursion}

\merge\ Over $\No$ itself the trace of an injective word is injective
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}); source~14's trace-fibre theorem
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers}, Part~IX) is that case. Over a general residual
alphabet the next statements show that two initial words can share a trace,
never three. Source~19 writes $\mathcal C_X$ for a core of exhaustive
enumerations of a proper linearly ordered class $X$; it is not the core of
$\No$.

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 1928-2167
The initial-word theorem is exact, but an iteration must retain the
numerical residual alphabet.  Deleting a set from $\No$ preserves fresh
separators.  Deleting the entire proper range of an $\Ord$-word need not
do so.  We can, however, describe the possible failure quite sharply.
Work parameterwise in $\GBC$, or with admitted words in one fixed class
realization.  For a proper linearly ordered class $X$, choose a core
$\mathcal C_X$ of exhaustive $\Ord$-enumerations such that every
injective set prefix has a core completion.  A bounded-support core of
a fixed baseline has this property.  Write $\tau_X(U)$ for the strict
lower trace of an injective admitted $\Ord$-word $U$ on this core;
the trace need not be a normalized cut for a general alphabet.

\begin{lemma}[Exact criterion for an unseparated pair]
\label{swo:rs:rf:lem:greedy}
Suppose $U<V$ first differ at $\alpha$, with common prefix $p$ and
next labels $a<b$.  There is no core enumeration strictly between
$U$ and $V$ if and only if all three conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item No label of $X\setminus\operatorname{ran}(p)$ lies strictly
      between $a$ and $b$.
\item For every $\beta>\alpha$, $U(\beta)$ is the greatest label
      of $X\setminus\operatorname{ran}(U\restriction\beta)$.
\item For every $\beta>\alpha$, $V(\beta)$ is the least label
      of $X\setminus\operatorname{ran}(V\restriction\beta)$.
\end{enumerate}
When these hold, neither word is exhaustive, no injective admitted
$\Ord$-word lies strictly between them, and
$\tau_X(U)=\tau_X(V)$.  Thus they also characterize equality of the
two strict lower traces.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A label between $a$ and $b$, appended to $p$, gives a core separator.
If $U$ later chooses a label below some unused label, complete its
prefix through that larger alternative.  The result exceeds $U$ but
remains below $V$ because its label at $\alpha$ is still $a$.
A later failure to choose the least unused label in $V$ gives the dual
separator.  This proves necessity.

Conversely a word strictly between them must share $p$ and at
$\alpha$ select $a$, $b$, or an intermediate label.  The third option
is excluded.  A word selecting $a$ is at most $U$, since $U$ selects
the greatest unused label at every later stage.  A word selecting
$b$ is at least $V$.  This proves the stronger absence of any
injective admitted word strictly between them.

To handle the strict-trace endpoint issue, suppose $U$ were exhaustive.
Its tail after $a$ would then be the reverse numerical class well-order
of $X\setminus(\operatorname{ran}(p)\cup\{a\})$.  The later tail of
$V$ is numerically strictly increasing and has proper range.  Start
beyond the possible occurrence of $a$ and take
$V(\beta_0+n)$ for $n\in\omega$.  Class Replacement makes this an
available set sequence, descending in the reverse numerical well-order,
a contradiction.  The dual argument excludes exhaustive $V$.
Consequently neither word equals a core enumeration.  Absence of a
strict core separator is therefore exactly equality of their strict
lower traces.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[At most two initial words over an arbitrary residual cut]
\label{swo:rs:rf:prop:doubleton}
There cannot be three distinct admitted injective $\Ord$-words over
$X$ with the same core trace.  In an external interpretation, each
nonempty raw trace fiber is therefore either
\[
 \WO^{\mathcal S}(B_U)
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \WO^{\mathcal S}(B_U)+\WO^{\mathcal S}(B_V),
\]
where the two-word case is the ordered pair described in
\Cref{swo:rs:rf:lem:greedy}.  Residual well-order completions are supplied
by $\GBC$.  This assertion is independent of the baseline among cores
having the stated prefix-completion property.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For three words with equal trace, apply \Cref{swo:rs:rf:lem:greedy} to
the outer pair.  The middle word contradicts its absence of intervening
injective words.  For raw orders the trace is the trace of their initial
word, and the orders with one fixed initial word form exactly its
residual well-order space.  Distinct initial-word fibers compare in the
order of their words.  These facts give the displayed possibilities.
The criterion mentions only the numerical alphabet and the two words,
which proves baseline independence.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An alphabet criterion for failure of core separation]
\label{swo:rs:rf:prop:alphabetcriterion}
Keep the hypotheses above: $X$ is a proper linearly ordered class, all
words and class isomorphisms are admitted in the fixed realization, and
every injective set prefix extends to an exhaustive row of
$\mathcal C_X$.  The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Two distinct admitted injective $\Ord$-words over $X$ have
      the same strict lower trace on $\mathcal C_X$.
\item For some set $S\subseteq X$, the numerical order of $X\setminus S$
      has an admitted initial segment of type $\Ord$ and an admitted
      final segment of type $\Ord^*$, with admitted class isomorphisms
      witnessing these types.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently all distinct admitted injective words are separated by a
core row exactly when no such set deletion exists.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For the first implication, let $U<V$ be a pair from
\Cref{swo:rs:rf:lem:greedy}, with common set prefix $p$ and unequal
labels $a<b$.  Delete
$S=\operatorname{ran}(p)\cup\{a,b\}$.  The range of the later
greedy-minimum tail of $V$, with $a$ removed if present, is an initial
numerical segment of $X\setminus S$ of type $\Ord$.
Indeed any smaller residual label must have been selected earlier in
that tail.  Removing at most one label preserves its proper, set-like
well-order type.  Dually the later greedy-maximum range of $U$, with
$b$ removed if present, is a final segment of type $\Ord^*$.
These ranges and their canonical enumerations are admitted class
constructions from $U,V,p$.

Conversely let $J$ be the initial $\Ord$-segment and $K$ the final
$\Ord^*$-segment of $Y=X\setminus S$.  They are disjoint: a common
point would place an increasing $\omega$-sequence from the remaining
tail of $J$ inside $K$, contradicting the well-ordering of $K$ in
the reverse numerical direction.  Well-order $S$ as a common set
prefix $p$, and let $a<b$ be the first two labels of $J$.  They are
consecutive in $Y$.  After $p$, form $U$ by choosing $a$ and then
enumerating $K$ downward; form $V$ by choosing $b$ and then enumerating
$J\setminus\{b\}$ upward.  Each concatenation has type $\Ord$ and
is an admitted injective word.  The first tail always selects the
greatest unused label because $K$ is final; the second always selects
the least because $J\setminus\{b\}$ is initial in $Y\setminus\{b\}$.
\Cref{swo:rs:rf:lem:greedy} therefore gives equal strict core traces.
\end{proof}

The following example realizes the two-word obstruction even if the
comparison core is enlarged to all exhaustive set-like enumerations.

For $\alpha\in\Ord$ put
\[
 \ell_\alpha=1-\frac1{\alpha+2},\qquad
 r_\alpha=2+\frac1{\alpha+2},\qquad
 Y=\{\ell_\alpha:\alpha\in\Ord\}
    \cup\{r_\alpha:\alpha\in\Ord\}.
\]
Here $\alpha$ is viewed as its ordinal surreal, and every displayed
arithmetic operation is a surreal field operation.  The left labels
increase in type $\Ord$ inside $[1/2,1)$; the right labels decrease in
type $\Ord^*$ inside $(2,5/2]$.  Every left label lies below every right
label, so the numerical order of $Y$ has type $\Ord+\Ord^*$.

\begin{proposition}[Different initial words with the same residual core cut]
\label{swo:rs:rf:prop:residualcounterexample}
There are injective $\Ord$-words $U<V$ over $Y$ with different ranges
whose strict lower traces on all admitted exhaustive set-like
enumerations of $Y$ coincide.  Each word is the initial word of a raw
well-order of $Y$.  Moreover $Y$ occurs as a residual alphabet after
one proper initial block in a raw well-order of $\No$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Take
\[
 U=(\ell_0,r_0,r_1,r_2,\ldots),\qquad
 V=(\ell_1,\ell_0,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ldots).
\]
The first expression means the unique $\Ord$-collapse of the order
consisting of $\ell_0$ followed by the $r_\alpha$ sequence; this is valid
because $1+\Ord$ has type $\Ord$.  The second expression is the
increasing left sequence with its first two labels transposed.
Both words omit proper subclasses of $Y$, and $U<V$ at the first label.

Let $E:\Ord\to Y$ be any admitted exhaustive set-like enumeration.
If $E(0)=\ell_0$, then $E\ne U$ since $U$ omits every $\ell_\alpha$
with $\alpha\ge2$ (and also $\ell_1$).  At their first later
disagreement, $U$ chooses the greatest still-unused numerical label:
it is sweeping the right block downward from its maximum.
Consequently $E<U$.

If $E(0)=\ell_1$, then $E\ne V$ since $V$ omits the right block.
At their first later disagreement, $V$ chooses the least still-unused
numerical label, so $E>V$.  If $E(0)>\ell_1$, that inequality holds
immediately.  There is no label below $\ell_0$ or strictly between
$\ell_0$ and $\ell_1$.  Therefore
\[
 \{E:E<_{\mathrm{lex}}U\}
 =\{E:E(0)=\ell_0\}
 =\{E:E<_{\mathrm{lex}}V\},
\]
where $E$ ranges over exhaustive set-like enumerations.
Appending an admitted residual well-order to either word gives its
raw completion, with that word as initial set-like block.

Finally $\No\setminus Y$ is proper: it contains all negative ordinals.
Restricting the baseline and collapsing the resulting set-like order
gives a bijection $F:\Ord\to\No\setminus Y$.  Its raw completions
have residual alphabet exactly $Y$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An explicit interior completion point]
\label{swo:rs:rf:prop:interiorgap}
In an external set-sized interpretation of the preceding example, the
shared raw trace fiber of $U,V$ is exactly
\[
 \WO^{\mathcal S}(\{\ell_\alpha:\alpha\ge1\})
 \; + \;
 \WO^{\mathcal S}(\{r_\alpha:\alpha\in\Ord\}).
\]
The junction between these summands is a proper unfilled Dedekind gap
of $\WO^{\mathcal S}(Y)$.  It supplies an interior new point of the
completed residual fiber, in addition to any points added at its
outer boundaries.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The two residual alphabets are exactly the labels omitted by $U$ and
$V$, respectively.  \Cref{swo:rs:rf:prop:doubleton} excludes a
third initial word with their trace, so their raw trace fiber is the
displayed convex sum.  The first alphabet is numerically of type
$\Ord$, and the second of type $\Ord^*$.  By
\Cref{swo:rs:rf:lem:endpoints}, the first summand has no greatest point
and the second has no least point.

The downward closure of the first summand and the upward closure of
the second partition the full raw order of $Y$: the two summands
together form a convex trace fiber, and there is no further raw point
between them.  The first closure has no greatest point and the second no
least point, giving the claimed unfilled gap.  Its completion point
has raw orders on both sides.  Since $Y$ is realized as a residual
alphabet of $\No$, the point also occurs inside the interval completion
of an actual raw surreal-order fiber in
\Cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction}.
\end{proof}

Thus the original surreal theorem cannot simply be reapplied inside
every residual fiber.  On this residual alphabet, equality of traces
on its own set-like core merges different initial $\Ord$-words.
The merger is limited to two words by
\Cref{swo:rs:rf:prop:doubleton}, but its two residual well-order
spaces must both be retained.  A recursive theory must preserve this
prefix-and-alphabet structure; the set/proper-class distinction alone
is insufficient to make the process self-similar.

% ---- source 19, Section 11
\section{Persistent external cuts absent from the class realization (source 19)}\label{swo:rs:rf:sec:externalbranches}

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 2172-2279
The full external completion in \Cref{swo:rs:rf:thm:reconstruction} uses
all external cuts of the core, whereas the internal represented-cut
theorem takes an admitted cut as a class parameter.  This is a strict
distinction in every externally countable model, even for cuts whose
every internally bounded prefix exists.

\begin{theorem}[Continuum many omitted amenable branches]
\label{swo:rs:rf:thm:missingbranches}
Let $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal S)$ be any externally countable two-sorted
model of $\GBC$.  Its external core completion contains
$2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct cuts which have an internally set-coded
straddling prefix at every internal ordinal but are represented by no
admitted raw class well-order.  These cuts can be induced by external
exhaustive bijections
\[
 F:\Ord^{\mathcal M}\longrightarrow\No^{\mathcal M}
\]
whose restriction to every internal ordinal is coded by a set of $M$.
No $\omega$-standardness assumption is required.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Externally enumerate all admitted subclasses of $\Ord$ as
$A_0,A_1,\ldots$, and enumerate all internal ordinals as
$\delta_0,\delta_1,\ldots$.  Set $\gamma_0=0$.  At stage $n$ put
\[
 \eta_n=\max^{\mathcal M}(\gamma_n,\delta_n),\qquad
 \gamma_{n+1}=\eta_n+2.
\]
These lengths are independent of the following free choices and are
externally cofinal in the interpreted ordinal order.

For an external binary sequence $s\in2^\omega$, build coherent
internally set-coded binary functions
$p_n:\gamma_n\to\{0,1\}$.  Start with the empty function.  Extend
$p_n$ by zeros on $[\gamma_n,\eta_n)$, and set
\[
 p_{n+1}(\eta_n)=1-\mathbf1_{A_n}(\eta_n),\qquad
 p_{n+1}(\eta_n+1)=s(n).
\]
Each step is a finitely specified internal set construction.  Their
coherent external union defines the characteristic function of an
external subclass $A_s\subseteq\Ord^{\mathcal M}$.
For every internal ordinal $\alpha$, choose $n$ with
$\alpha\leq^{\mathcal M}\gamma_n$; its restriction to $\alpha$ is
then the internal set $p_n\restriction\alpha$.  This is the claimed
amenability to internally bounded initial segments.  At $\eta_n$ it
differs from $A_n$, so $A_s$ is not admitted.  Distinct $s$ give distinct
classes at the free coordinates $\eta_n+1$.

Use the internal partition of the ordinals into pairs
$(2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+1)$, with ordinal left multiplication
by $2$.  In the baseline $b$, swap the two values of a pair exactly
when $\alpha\in A_s$.  This defines an external exhaustive bijection
$F_s:\Ord^{\mathcal M}\to\No^{\mathcal M}$: the coordinate
permutation is an involution on disjoint pairs.  Every internally
bounded initial restriction is coded in $M$, because it uses only an
internally bounded restriction of $A_s$ and of the admitted baseline.
If $F_s$ were admitted, elementary class comprehension from it and $b$
would recover $A_s$, a contradiction.

Although the model's ordinals may be externally ill-founded, $F_s$
and an admitted core row $E_c$ have a least disagreement.  They cannot
be equal, since $F_s$ is not admitted.  Choose one disagreement
$\delta$.  Both restrictions through $\delta+1$ are coded internal
sets, so their nonempty disagreement subset has an internally least
member.  Every earlier internal ordinal lies in that restriction;
hence this is also their least disagreement in the external interpreted
ordinal order.

Define
\[
 q_s=\{c\in\Pbd(b):E_c<_{\mathrm{lex}}F_s\}.
\]
First-difference comparison makes $q_s$ initial.  Fresh labels and
core completion make it nonempty, proper, and without a greatest
member.  For any internal ordinal $\alpha$, the prefix
$F_s\restriction\alpha$ is coded in $M$.  Complete it once with a
fresh label below $F_s(\alpha)$ and once with a fresh label above.
The two core points lie on opposite sides of $q_s$ in its prefix
cylinder.  Thus its prefix criterion persists at every internal ordinal.

Suppose an admitted raw order $R$ represented $q_s$.  Its admitted
initial word $F_R$ cannot equal $F_s$.  Their least disagreement exists
by the same bounded-restriction argument.  A fresh core separator
strictly between the two unequal labels, after their common set prefix,
distinguishes their lower core cuts.  This contradicts $t(R)=q_s$.
Thus $q_s$ has empty raw fiber.  It cannot itself be an admitted class
cut, since the internal persistent-prefix theorem would then assemble
an admitted representing word.

Finally, distinct free-bit paths give different $F_s$.  Their least
disagreement exists by the same argument, and a core separator makes
their cuts distinct.  There are $2^{\aleph_0}$ paths, proving the
claim.
\end{proof}

These missing cuts are not terminal cuts of the internal first-failure
classification.  Their crossing prefixes persist throughout the
model's ordinal range; the obstruction is that their coherent global
branch is absent from the class realization.  Their singleton fibers
in the external completion are therefore an additional, explicitly
exhibited source of completion points.

Here amenability means that internally bounded restrictions, and hence
intersections with internal sets of ordinals, are coded in the model.
It does not assert that adjoining $A_s$ or $F_s$ to the class realization
preserves $\GBC$, Class Replacement, or the relevant comprehension closure.

% ---- source 27, Section 8
\section{The exact least ordinal support bound (source 27)}\label{swo:sc:sec:support}

\merge\ Source~27's Section~8, printed whole. Its first subsection re-derives
source~17's exact reserve cardinal (\cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve}; display (S27.13)
is (S17.7)), which it credits, and is printed as text. Its
\cref{swo:sc:thm:leastheight} answers the ordinal half of source~17's question
``Ordinal and birthday optima for supported completion''
(\cref{swo:gs:n15.10}) and Part~VIII's ``Ordinal support bounds \ldots\ remain
open'' (\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}~(f)); birthday bounds and the forced-prefix
length remain open (\cref{swo:xiii:sec:status}). Its first example extends
source~17's \cref{swo:gs:n7.2}.

% ---- source 27 (batch-83 manuscript 13), lines 1452-1622
Completing a set prefix to a global enumeration is a recurring step in
the preceding constructions. A generic proof takes a sufficiently large
cardinal block and completes a partial permutation there. The repository
has already optimized the \emph{number} of additional moved positions
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve}). We now optimize their
\emph{ordinal location}. A support of two very high ordinals is small in
cardinality and large in height, so these are genuinely different problems.

\subsection{Forced motion and the cardinal reserve}

Let $A\subseteq\Ord$ be a set and $h:A\to\Ord$ injective. Write
\[\tag{S27.12}\label{swo:sc:eq:support-data}
\begin{gathered}
 D=\{a\in A:h(a)\ne a\},\qquad R=h[D],\qquad S=D\cup R,\\
 u=|R\setminus D|,\qquad v=|D\setminus R|,\\
 \tau(h)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&u=v,\\
 \max(\aleph_0,u,v),&u\ne v.
 \end{cases}
\end{gathered}
\]
Cardinals are identified with initial ordinals. The prescribed fixed
points $A\setminus D$ are disjoint from $R$, by injectivity of $h$.

Every extending permutation $\pi$ must move each point of $S$. This is
immediate for $D$. If $r\in R\setminus D$, some distinct prescribed
point already maps to $r$, so $\pi(r)=r$ would violate injectivity.
For an extension with set support, put $T=\supp\pi\setminus S$.
Removing the prescribed bijection
$h:D\to R$ leaves a bijection
\[\tag{S27.13}\label{swo:sc:eq:reserve-match}
 (R\setminus D)\cup T\ \longrightarrow\ (D\setminus R)\cup T.
\]
Consequently $u+|T|=v+|T|$. If $u\ne v$ are finite, finite cancellation
forces $T$ to be infinite. If $u\ne v$ and one is infinite, the rule for addition of
well-ordered infinite cardinals forces $|T|\ge\max(u,v)$. This proves
$|T|\ge\tau(h)$.

Conversely, a fresh set $T$ of size $\tau(h)$ outside $A\cup R$ makes
the two sides of \eqref{swo:sc:eq:reserve-match} equipotent. Any bijection between
them, combined with $h$ on $D$ and the identity elsewhere, completes the
partial injection. This is the earlier exact cardinal reserve result.
Because all sets here are well-orderable subsets of ordinals, its
pointwise existence argument needs no choice for arbitrary sets; it is
available in $\ZF$. A uniform simultaneous choice of matchings is a
separate assertion.
