\subsection{A necessary and sufficient cutoff criterion}

\begin{theorem}[Completion below a specified ordinal]\label{swo:sc:thm:supportcriterion}
Let $\beta$ be an ordinal. There exists a permutation $\pi:\Ord\to\Ord$
extending $h$, with $\supp\pi\subseteq\beta$, if and only if
\[\tag{S27.14}\label{swo:sc:eq:supportcriterion}
 S\subseteq\beta
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 |\beta\setminus(A\cup R)|\ge\tau(h).
\]
The second condition is automatic when $\tau(h)=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose such a permutation exists. Its forced support contains $S$.
The remaining moved set $T$ misses $R$ by definition and misses
$A\setminus D$ because those points are prescribed fixed. Thus
$T\subseteq\beta\setminus(A\cup R)$. The reserve argument above gives
$|T|\ge\tau(h)$, proving both necessary conditions.

Conversely, choose $T\subseteq\beta\setminus(A\cup R)$ of cardinality
$\tau(h)$. Choose a bijection in \eqref{swo:sc:eq:reserve-match}; both sides
are well-orderable and have equal cardinality. Its domain, $D$, and the
complement of $S\cup T$ partition $\Ord$, and their proposed images
partition $\Ord$ as well. The resulting piecewise map is therefore a
permutation. It extends $h$, fixes every point outside $S\cup T$, and
has support contained in $\beta$. Some reserve points may happen to be
fixed, but the lower bound forces the cardinality of the moved reserve
to remain $\tau(h)$ when that cardinal is nonzero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A closed formula for the least bound}

Let $f:\Ord\to\Ord\setminus(A\cup R)$ be the increasing enumeration
of the fresh ordinals. It is canonically defined by
\[
 f(\xi)=\gamma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \gamma\notin A\cup R\ \text{ and }\
 \otp\bigl(\gamma\setminus(A\cup R)\bigr)=\xi.
\]
The complement of a set of ordinals has type $\Ord$, so this formula
defines $f$ without a class-valued recursion. Put
\[\tag{S27.15}\label{swo:sc:eq:height-data}
 \delta_S=\sup_{s\in S}(s+1),\qquad
 \delta_T=\sup_{\xi<\tau(h)}\bigl(f(\xi)+1\bigr),
\]
with an empty supremum equal to $0$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact ordinal support optimum]\label{swo:sc:thm:leastheight}
The least ordinal $\beta$ for which $h$ extends to a permutation supported
in $\beta$ is
\[\tag{S27.16}\label{swo:sc:eq:leastheight}
 \boxed{\displaystyle\beta_{\min}(h)=\max(\delta_S,\delta_T).}
\]
This minimum is attained. The formula specifies a canonical optimum,
not a canonical completing permutation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We have $S\subseteq\beta$ exactly when $\delta_S\le\beta$. Since
$\tau(h)$ is an initial cardinal, the fresh set below $\beta$ has
cardinality at least $\tau(h)$ exactly when its order type is at least
$\tau(h)$. That is equivalent to
$f(\xi)<\beta$ for every $\xi<\tau(h)$, and therefore to
$\delta_T\le\beta$. The cutoff criterion now says that the admissible
$\beta$ are exactly the ordinals above both displayed bounds. Their
least member is their maximum, and the converse part of
\cref{swo:sc:thm:supportcriterion} attains it.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[The one-sided shift]\label{swo:sc:n8.3}
Prescribe $h(n)=n+1$ for $n<\omega$. Then $S=\omega$, $u=0$, $v=1$,
$\tau(h)=\omega$, and $f(n)=\omega+n$. Hence
\[
 \beta_{\min}(h)=\omega\cdot2.
\]
An optimum completion maps $\omega$ to $0$ and maps
$\omega+n+1$ to $\omega+n$, while retaining the prescribed shift on
$\omega$ and fixing all ordinals at least $\omega\cdot2$.
No finite reserve beyond $\omega$ can close this one-sided infinite chain.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Prescribed fixed positions can delay the reserve]\label{swo:sc:n8.4}
Add the requirements $h(\xi)=\xi$ for $\omega\le\xi<\gamma$, where
$\gamma\ge\omega$. The forced moved set and the cardinal reserve are
unchanged, but the first available fresh ordinals are now
$\gamma,\gamma+1,\ldots$. Therefore
\[
 \beta_{\min}(h)=\gamma+\omega.
\]
This example explains why $S$ and $\tau(h)$ alone do not determine the
ordinal optimum: the fixed domain $A\setminus D$ can block the reserve.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[High fixed points need not matter]\label{swo:sc:n8.5}
If $h$ is the identity on $A$, then $S=\varnothing$ and
$\beta_{\min}(h)=0$, however high the elements of $A$ lie. Adding only
finitely many fixed points outside $\omega$ to the one-sided shift still
leaves $\beta_{\min}=\omega\cdot2$, even if one of those fixed points
is arbitrarily high. The bound measures motion, not the height of the
input data.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Balanced infinite motion]\label{swo:sc:n8.6}
For $A=\{2n:n<\omega\}$ and $h(2n)=2n+1$, both $u$ and $v$ are
$\aleph_0$, so $\tau(h)=0$. Transposing each even number with the next
odd number gives the optimum $\beta_{\min}=\omega$. Equal infinite
boundary cardinalities require no reserve.
\end{example}

\subsection{Application and exact limits of the result}

For a prescribed injective surreal prefix $p:\alpha\to\No$, put
$h=b^{-1}\circ p$ with $A=\alpha$. Then
\cref{swo:sc:thm:leastheight} gives the least baseline coordinate bound below
which one can modify $b$ so that $b\circ\pi$ begins with $p$. This is
an exact optimization for a fixed baseline and a fixed prefix.

It does not optimize the birthday of the set code for $\pi$, the birthday
of an order-embedded surreal representing that code, or the numerical
size of the moved surreal labels. Nor does it select the prefix that
optimizes an interpolant between two given cuts. Those involve additional
choices and remain distinct research problems. The strict inequality in
``support contained in $\beta$'' is the reason for every successor
$s+1$ and $f(\xi)+1$ in \eqref{swo:sc:eq:height-data}.

% ---- hand chunk XIII realizations
\section{Class realizations: what labelled and marked enumeration spaces remember (sources 22, 27, 21 and 30)}\label{swo:xiii:sec:realizations}

\merge\ Part~VIII proved that, over a fixed set universe and baseline, an old
core cut is represented in a larger class realization exactly when it is in the
smaller one, and that every proper extension of the class part adds a global
enumeration and a represented cut
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute,swo:gs:thm:class-extension}); it left open what the
external order type of the admitted enumerations remembers
(\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}~(e)). Four sources answer as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Labelled availability recovers the whole class part.} Source~22's
\cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful}, printed first: with a common baseline $b$ and a
common class bijection $g:\Ord\to M$, inclusion of the admitted exhaustive
traces, or only of the pair-swap traces, is equivalent to inclusion of the class
realizations. Source~27 proves it with only $b$ shared, as a criterion for
order embeddings fixing the core (\cref{swo:sc:thm:markedmodels}), and source~30
with no baseline given in advance (\cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful}); both are
printed as notes with their proofs. The pair-swap code is the one source~17
uses for \cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension}.
\item \emph{External size.} The external collection of admitted enumerations
has the cardinality of the class part (source~21's
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational}; source~30's
\cref{swo:rt:fnd:cor:cardinality}).
\item \emph{Countable models: the bare order forgets.} The external order is
$\mathbb Q$ (source~13's \cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}, Part~IX, proved again as
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational}); it stays $\mathbb Q$ with the core as
a dense colour and the baseline fixed
(\cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:coloredcore}), and it does not detect $\ETR$
(\cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:etrinvisible}). Fixing the core pointwise recovers
everything (\cref{swo:sc:thm:markedmodels,swo:fu:fnd:cor:core-rigidity}).
\item \emph{A common baseline} exists in every $\GBC$-realization of a countable
model exactly when some $p$ has $V=\operatorname{HOD}_p$ there
(\cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:hod,swo:rt:fnd:cor:universalbaseline}, applications of
Williams's minimum-model theorem).
\end{itemize}
Source~21's section also proves the well-foundedness facts the comparisons need
(\cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:set-witness} is the scope statement already printed in
\cref{swo:sk:sec:foundations}).

% ---- source 22, Section 9
\subsection{Source 22: recovering an available class realization}\label{swo:rg:sec:realization}

% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 638-735
\subsubsection{The coding parameters and the model comparison}
Let $M$ be a fixed set universe, and let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ be class realizations over it such that $(M,\mathcal X)$ and $(M,\mathcal Y)$ satisfy $\GBC$. Comparisons between these class collections are made in the metatheory. Assume they share a global enumeration
\[
 g:\Ord^M\longrightarrow M
\]
and a baseline enumeration $b:\Ord^M\to\No^M$. Supplied parameters are part of the hypotheses, not claimed to be canonically definable in an arbitrary model.

We may arrange that the two labels in each consecutive pair of baseline positions are numerically ordered:
\[
 b(2\cdot\xi)<b(2\cdot\xi+1).
\]
Indeed, sort each pair of an existing baseline. Every ordinal is uniquely $2\cdot\xi+i$ for $i<2$; this is ordinal multiplication with the finite factor on the \emph{left}. The sorting transformation is elementary and available in both realizations.

Because $M$ and $b$ are fixed, the set-coded core $\Psupp(b)^M$, its ordering, all set-prefix nodes, and their incidence are identical in the two realizations. What may differ is which class cuts and which full class branches are available.

\subsubsection{Encoding an arbitrary class by pair swaps}
For an available class $A\subseteq M$, define its ordinal bit class by
\[
 a_A(\xi)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g(\xi)\in A.
\]
Define $e_A$ by leaving the $\xi$th baseline pair in its original order when $a_A(\xi)=0$, and reversing it when $a_A(\xi)=1$. Explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 e_A(2\cdot\xi)&=
 \begin{cases}b(2\cdot\xi),&g(\xi)\notin A,\\b(2\cdot\xi+1),&g(\xi)\in A,\end{cases}\\
 e_A(2\cdot\xi+1)&=
 \begin{cases}b(2\cdot\xi+1),&g(\xi)\notin A,\\b(2\cdot\xi),&g(\xi)\in A.\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
It is a class bijection $\Ord\to\No$, since each baseline label occurs exactly once.

\begin{proposition}[Pair-swap encoding]\label{swo:rg:prop:pairs}
The assignment $A\mapsto e_A$ is injective and elementary in the supplied class parameter $A$. On ordinal bit classes it preserves their first-disagreement lexicographic order. Moreover,
\[
 e_A\text{ is evaluated by a code in }\Psupp(b)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\text{ is a set}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
At the first bit disagreement $\xi$, the first label disagreement is at $2\cdot\xi$, where the zero bit yields the smaller baseline label and the one bit the larger. This proves order preservation and injectivity.

The supporting permutation moves exactly the two positions of those pairs with bit one. Its support is a set exactly when the one-bit ordinal class is a set. Since $g$ is a class bijection, class replacement in either direction identifies this condition with $A$ being a set. Uniqueness of the permutation relative to $b$ rules out an alternative supported representation of the same enumeration.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Elementary decoding from a lower trace]\label{swo:rg:thm:decoder}
For every available class $A$, its normalized lower trace
\[
 T_A=\{d\in\Psupp(b):d<e_A\}
\]
is available. From $T_A$, the common set-coded labelled incidence structure, and $b,g$, the class $A$ is recovered by an elementary formula. In particular, no satisfaction predicate or class-valued transfinite recursion is required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The trace is an elementary class definition from $e_A$ and evaluation. It is normalized by \cref{swo:rg:prop:global-density}. Apply \cref{swo:rg:thm:unranked} to reconstruct its unique word, which must be $e_A$. Then
\[
 g(\xi)\in A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 e_A(2\cdot\xi)=b(2\cdot\xi+1).
\]
Substituting the elementary crossed-prefix formula for the reconstructed value gives the promised decoder using only set quantifiers and the supplied class parameters. The existence of a crossed node long enough to read that coordinate is part of \cref{swo:rg:thm:unranked}, not an extra choice requirement.
\end{proof}

Call a normalized represented trace a \emph{binary-swap trace} when its reconstructed branch sends each pair of positions to the corresponding baseline pair in one of the two possible orders. Such a branch is automatically exhaustive, and the preceding decoder yields its unique class $A$. Thus the class sort can be represented by this specially recognized collection of traces; the entire family of exhaustive traces is more than is needed.

\subsubsection{Faithfulness for same-set class realizations}
In the metatheory, let $\mathscr B_{\mathcal X}$ be the collection of lower traces on the common core represented by exhaustive enumerations available in $\mathcal X$. Let $\mathscr S_{\mathcal X}$ be its subcollection of binary-swap traces. These are metatheoretic collections, not objects asserted to exist inside $(M,\mathcal X)$.

\begin{theorem}[Faithful reconstruction of the class realization]\label{swo:rg:thm:faithful}
With the fixed $M,b,g$ above, the following are equivalent:
\[
 \mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y,
 \qquad
 \mathscr B_{\mathcal X}\subseteq\mathscr B_{\mathcal Y},
 \qquad
 \mathscr S_{\mathcal X}\subseteq\mathscr S_{\mathcal Y}.
\]
In particular, equality of the admitted exhaustive traces, or just of the binary-swap traces, is equivalent to equality of the available class realizations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inclusion of class realizations preserves all class enumerations and their elementary lower traces, so it implies inclusion of each trace collection.

Conversely, suppose the exhaustive trace inclusion holds, and take $A\in\mathcal X$. Construct $T_A$ in $\mathcal X$. By hypothesis it is the lower trace of an exhaustive enumeration available in $\mathcal Y$, and hence it is itself an available class in $\mathcal Y$. The elementary decoder of \cref{swo:rg:thm:decoder}, performed in $(M,\mathcal Y)$ using the common incidence and parameters, recovers exactly $A$. The decoding formula has only set quantifiers. Its interpretation is identical in the two models because their set universe, trace, and coding parameters agree. Thus the decoded external subclass really is the same $A$, and $A\in\mathcal Y$.

If only binary-swap trace inclusion is assumed, the same argument applies because every $T_A$ is a binary-swap trace. This proves all equivalences. Applying the inclusion assertions in both directions proves the equality assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Membership reconstruction]\label{swo:rg:n9.4}
Over the fixed set sort $M$, the class-membership structure is recoverable from a sort of admitted binary-swap traces with core incidence and the parameters $b,g$. The decoder interprets $x\in A$ from the corresponding trace and the unique ordinal $\xi$ with $g(\xi)=x$.
\end{corollary}
This is a relative reconstruction statement. It is stronger than merely detecting that a proper same-set class extension adds some traces, which was established in the earlier continuation (source~17, \cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension}). It is not a reconstruction of $M$, of $b,g$, or of a class realization from the bare order type of $\Hsl$.

\subsubsection{Why this is not a diagonal paradox}
The input to $A\mapsto T_A$ is itself a class variable. The theorem does not give a set code for every $A$, nor a class function whose set-valued arguments enumerate all classes. A third sort may contain all these traces as objects, but then the sort and its axioms must be explicitly introduced. Inside $\GBC$, each encoding or decoding is a schema uniform in one supplied class parameter.

Indeed, an exhaustive uniform enumeration of all global enumerations is impossible. Suppose a single class graph $F(\xi,\eta)$ gave global bijections $F_\xi$ for every ordinal $\xi$ and covered every available global bijection. Define a bit class by
\[
 a(\xi)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_\xi(2\cdot\xi)\ne b(2\cdot\xi+1).
\]
The associated pair-swap enumeration $e_a$ differs from $F_\xi$ at position $2\cdot\xi$: when $a(\xi)=1$ it outputs the unequal upper baseline label; when $a(\xi)=0$ it outputs the lower label instead of the equal upper one. Thus $e_a$ is missing from the family. This is an elementary diagonal argument, and it coexists with \cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful} because the latter never supplies such a set-indexed exhaustive family.

\merge\ The pair-swap enumeration $e_A$ and the decoder of \cref{swo:rg:thm:decoder}
are source~17's construction in the proof of \cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension};
\cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful} turns that construction into a complete invariant.
The diagonal paragraph above is \cref{swo:gl:diagonal} in pair-swap form.

% ---- source 27, Section 9
\subsection{Source 27: the marked core detects the admitted classes of a model}\label{swo:sc:sec:models}

% ---- source 27 (batch-83 manuscript 13), lines 1627-1757
The same first-order set universe can support different collections of
admitted classes. Their unmarked external order types may conceal that
difference. Marking the common bounded-support core pointwise gives a
much more rigid invariant.

\subsubsection{Reconstruction from a trace uses only set quantifiers}

For a class injection $E:\Ord\to\No$, define its lower trace on the
core by
\[
 L_E=\{d\in\Psupp(b):E_d<_{\lex}E\}.
\]
For an injective set prefix $p$, let
$C_p=\{d\in\Psupp(b):E_d\text{ extends }p\}$.
Call $p$ \emph{straddling} if $C_p$ meets both $L_E$ and its complement.

The prefix $E\restr\alpha$ straddles at every set length $\alpha$:
append fresh letters on both sides of $E(\alpha)$ and complete to
core codes. No other prefix at that length straddles, since the
cylinders at a fixed level are linearly arranged and a lower cut
cannot cross two of them. Consequently the graph of $E$ is recovered by
\[\tag{S27.17}\label{swo:sc:eq:reconstruct}
 E(\alpha)=x\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \exists p\,[\dom p=\alpha+1,\ p(\alpha)=x,
 \ C_p\cap L_E\ne\varnothing,
 \ C_p\setminus L_E\ne\varnothing].
\]
Every quantified prefix and every witness code is a set. This is the
elementary part of the repository's more general represented-cut
recognition theorem (\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}). We need this formula, rather
than just an abstract appeal to density, when classes from different
models are compared externally.

\subsubsection{An embedding criterion for two class realizations}

Let $(M,\mathcal X)$ and $(M,\mathcal Y)$ be set-sized models of $\GBC$ with
the same first-order set structure. They need not be transitive,
and neither class part is assumed contained in the other. Suppose
they share a baseline $b:\Ord^M\to\No^M$. Let $H_{\mathcal X}$
and $H_{\mathcal Y}$ be their \emph{external} orders of admitted
set-like enumerations, and identify the evaluated canonical core
codes as distinguished elements of both orders.

\begin{note}[Source~27, Theorem~9.1, ``Embeddings fixing the core'']\label{swo:sc:thm:markedmodels}
{\itshape
There exists an external order embedding
\[
 J:H_{\mathcal X}\longrightarrow H_{\mathcal Y}
\]
fixing every common core element if and only if
$\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y$. Whenever such an embedding exists,
it is the literal inclusion on enumeration graphs. In particular,
an isomorphism fixing the core pointwise exists exactly when
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Y$.}
This is source~22's \cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful} in another form. Source~27 shares only the baseline $b$ (its decoder $d:\No\to V$ uses Mostowski collapses instead of a class bijection $g$), assumes no inclusion between the realizations, and states the criterion for order embeddings $H_{\mathcal X}\to H_{\mathcal Y}$ fixing the core, which must then be the inclusion. Source~22 fixes $b$ and $g$ and states inclusions of trace collections.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~27's proof]
If $J$ fixes the core, then for every $d\in\Psupp(b)$ and
$E\in H_{\mathcal X}$,
\[
 E_d<E\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E_d<J(E).
\]
The two lower traces are the same external subset of the common set-code
domain. Formula \eqref{swo:sc:eq:reconstruct}, evaluated in the same first-order
structure with the same predicates $L_E,b$, therefore reconstructs the
same graph in both expansions. Hence $J(E)=E$ and
$H_{\mathcal X}\subseteq H_{\mathcal Y}$.

To recover arbitrary admitted classes of sets, use a fixed definable
surjection $d:\No\to V$, available in set theory with Choice. Here
is its coding construction. A surreal sign word can encode an ordinal
$\alpha$, a distinguished $i<\alpha$, and a binary relation on
$\alpha$; unary sign headers and an ordinal-length binary table give
such a code. If the relation is well-founded and extensional, return
the image of $i$ under its Mostowski collapse; otherwise return
$\varnothing$. Every set has a code by well-ordering the transitive
closure of its singleton. No simultaneous choice of a code for every
set is made. The decoding map $d$ is the same elementary definition
in both class realizations.

For $C\in\mathcal X$, let
$Z_C=\{\alpha:d(b(\alpha))\in C\}$. Swap baseline positions
$2\cdot\alpha$ and $2\cdot\alpha+1$ exactly when
$\alpha\in Z_C$. The resulting enumeration $E_C$ belongs to
$H_{\mathcal X}$, hence also to $H_{\mathcal Y}$. Its pair
orientations, together with $b$, recover $Z_C$ by elementary
comprehension. Surjectivity of $d\circ b$ then recovers
\[
 C=\{x:\exists\alpha\,[d(b(\alpha))=x\ \text{and}\ \alpha\in Z_C]\}.
\]
Thus $C\in\mathcal Y$, proving $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y$.

Conversely, class inclusion includes each admitted enumeration, and
the same elementary first-disagreement formula preserves its order.
This inclusion fixes the common core. The first part of the proof
already establishes its uniqueness.
\end{proof}

The use of \eqref{swo:sc:eq:reconstruct} is substantive. Two classes from
incomparable realizations need not coexist in any common class model.
If $M$ is nonstandard, their external disagreement set need not have a
first element in its internal ordinal order. The proof does not
assume one: it transfers an elementary reconstruction formula with
shared parameters instead.

If $(M,\mathcal X)$ is externally countable, $H_{\mathcal X}$ is
countable, dense, and without endpoints. The usual back-and-forth
argument makes it isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$. Hence an unmarked
countable order can forget the class realization entirely, while
fixing the embedded core pointwise forces exactly class inclusion.
The marking is additional mathematical data, not a property extracted
from the pure order.

\begin{corollary}[The raw-order existence criterion]\label{swo:sc:cor:rawmarked}
Under the same hypotheses, a core-fixing external embedding of the raw
global well-order comparisons exists exactly when
$\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y$. Such an embedding fixes every old
set-like enumeration. No uniqueness is asserted on non-set-like fibers.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A raw well-order has the same core trace as its initial $\Ord$ block.
If that trace is the trace of an exhaustive enumeration $E$, formula
\eqref{swo:sc:eq:reconstruct} makes its initial block equal to $E$; no labels
remain for a tail. Thus $E$ is the unique raw realization of that
trace. A core-fixing embedding therefore fixes every set-like $E$,
and the pair-code argument gives class inclusion.

For the converse, a shared relation's internal well-foundedness is
absolute between same-set $\GBC$ expansions: it is equivalent to
absence of a set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence. Class inclusion
therefore includes the old raw well-orders, and elementary labelled
comparison preserves their order. It fixes the core.
\end{proof}

\merge\ The remark before \cref{swo:sc:cor:rawmarked} that a countable
$H_{\mathcal X}$ is $\mathbb Q$ is source~13's \cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}
(Part~IX) and source~21's \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational} below.

% ---- source 21, Section 11
\subsection{Source 21: model dependence and preservation}\label{swo:fu:fnd:sec:models}

% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 2540-2832
Changing the admitted classes can change the collection of global
enumerations even when every set remains fixed.  Nevertheless, the
abstract external order can forget much of this change.  In particular,
every externally countable \(\GBC\) model gives the same abstract
set-like enumeration order, namely \(\mathbb Q\).  Naming a common dense core
reveals a much finer distinction.  We prove these statements after
separating the relevant notions of well-foundedness and preservation.

\subsubsection{Shared relations and well-foundedness}

We use two standard facts from second-order set theory: realizations
with the same sets agree about well-foundedness of shared class
relations, and well-foundedness is preserved from a transitive
submodel with the same ordinals.  See
\cite[Observations~4.12--4.13]{Williams}.  Their elementary
proofs explain exactly why they apply here.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~11.1, ``A set witness to ill-foundedness'']\label{swo:fu:fnd:lem:set-witness}
{\itshape
In \(\GBC\), a class relation \(R\) is ill-founded if and only if
there is a set function \(f:\omega\to\dom(R)\) such that
\[
                      f(n+1)\mathrel R f(n)
                      \qquad(n\in\omega).
\]
Consequently, well-foundedness of a fixed class relation is expressible
with only set quantifiers and the class parameter \(R\).}
This is the scope statement printed in \cref{swo:sk:sec:foundations} (the Hilbert's-tenth review's patch) and in source~11's \cref{swo:sec:formalization}, and the equivalence of \cref{swo:ix:note:wellfounded} (Part~IX); source~25 states it in \cref{swo:ph:sec:foundations}.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
The range of a descending sequence is a nonempty class with no
\(R\)-minimal element.  Conversely, suppose that a nonempty class
\(A\) has no \(R\)-minimal element.  Fix \(a_0\in A\), and use a
set-like global well-order to select an \(R\)-predecessor in \(A\)
at each subsequent step.  Every nonempty class of possible
predecessors has a first point in that global order.  Ordinary recursion
with the displayed class parameters produces the sequence, and Class
Replacement makes its restriction to \(\omega\) a set.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Changing classes while keeping the sets]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:prop:same-sets-wf}
Let \((M,\mathcal X)\) and \((M,\mathcal Y)\) be \(\GBC\)
realizations of the same first-order model.  They agree about
well-foundedness of every relation in \(\mathcal X\cap\mathcal Y\).
They also agree about the labeled lexicographic comparison of any
shared class well-orders of a fixed shared carrier.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The first assertion follows from \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:set-witness}: the
possible set sequences and their membership relations are identical.
For the second, the largest common labeled prefix and the two first
residual labels have elementary definitions in the shared carrier and
relations.  Those definitions quantify over the same set domain and
therefore have the same interpretation.  For set-like enumerations,
one can equivalently use their least ordinal of disagreement.
\end{proof}

No transitivity or external well-foundedness assumption is needed for
this agreement statement.  Both models can agree about a relation that
is externally ill-founded.  The assertion concerns their common
interpretation, not its correctness in a larger metatheory.

\begin{proposition}[Preservation with the same ordinals]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:prop:same-ordinals}
Suppose \((M,\mathcal X)\subseteq(N,\mathcal Y)\) are transitive
\(\GBC\) models with \(\Ord^M=\Ord^N\), and old classes are retained
as the same relations on old elements.  Every old class relation that
\((M,\mathcal X)\) regards as well-founded remains well-founded in
\((N,\mathcal Y)\).

On a fixed old carrier, inclusion therefore preserves the old labeled
lexicographic well-order space and its comparisons.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that \(N\) has a descending \(\omega\)-sequence through an
old relation \(R\).  In \(N\), the ranks of its entries are bounded by
some ordinal \(\beta\).  This ordinal belongs to \(M\), since the
models have the same ordinals.  All the entries lie in the ground set
\(A=\dom(R)\cap V_\beta^M\), increasing \(\beta\) if necessary.
By Class Separation, \(R\cap(A\times A)\) is a set relation in \(M\).
The ground model regards it as well-founded and constructs its rank
function into an ordinal.  Transitivity makes that same rank function
a witness to well-foundedness in \(N\), contradicting the descending
sequence.

For an old fixed carrier, the numerical labels and the two relation
graphs have not changed.  Their common labeled prefix and first residual
labels are consequently unchanged.  Thus the same first discrepancy
gives the same lexicographic comparison.
\end{proof}

This applies to ordinary set-forcing extensions and, more generally,
to class-forcing extensions satisfying the stated hypotheses.  It
does not assert the preservation of every second-order axiom, the
existence of a uniform forcing relation for arbitrary class forcing,
or that every \emph{new} abstract class-well-order type was already
present.  Those are separate questions with stronger hypotheses and
genuine recursion issues \cite{GHHSW,HamkinsWoodin}.

\begin{proposition}[A sufficient condition for external correctness]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:prop:height-cf}
Let \((M,\mathcal X)\) be a transitive \(\GBC\) model, and let
\(\theta=\Ord^M\) be its ordinal height in the metatheory.
If \(\cf(\theta)>\omega\), every internally well-founded class
relation is externally well-founded.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
An external descending \(\omega\)-sequence would have its entries'
ranks bounded below \(\theta\), by the cofinality hypothesis.  Restrict
the relation to a ground rank segment containing those entries.
This is a well-founded set relation in the transitive model \(M\),
so its ground ordinal rank function also witnesses external
well-foundedness.  This contradicts the sequence.
\end{proof}

The rank-cut case is the familiar sufficient condition in
\cite[Observation~1.14]{Williams}.  For height of countable
cofinality, the rank bound can fail.  A transitive model is correct
about its well-founded \emph{set} relations, but transitivity alone
does not ensure correctness about all admitted class relations.
A transitive realization with this additional correctness property is
called a \(\beta\)-model.

\subsubsection{The carrier also changes under forcing}

There is an essential qualification to any claimed inclusion between
surreal well-order spaces in different universes.  If a forcing
extension adds a new subset \(r\subseteq\omega\), it adds the new
surreal sign sequence of length \(\omega\) whose positive signs occur
exactly at positions in \(r\).  Hence
\(\No^M\subsetneq\No^N\).  An old enumeration
\(E:\Ord\to\No^M\) is no longer onto \(\No^N\), so it is not
literally a point of the new \(\Hsl(\No^N)\).

After choosing auxiliary enumerations, there are straightforward
comparison embeddings.  For unrestricted class well-orders, fix a
class well-order \(T\) of
\(D=\No^N\setminus\No^M\) and send \(R\) to \(R+T\).
Every old label precedes every new one, so the first labeled discrepancy
of two old orders remains their first discrepancy after extension.

For set-like orders, this sum generally has a proper-class initial
segment.  Instead choose a set-like enumeration \(d\) of \(D\),
indexed by \(\Ord\) when \(D\) is proper or by a set ordinal when it
is a set.  Interleave \(E(\alpha)\) at slot \((\alpha,0)\) and,
where defined, \(d(\alpha)\) at slot \((\alpha,1)\), with
\(\alpha\) the primary coordinate.  Every initial segment is a set,
so the resulting well-order is set-like and has type \(\Ord\).
At the first old discrepancy all preceding new-label slots agree;
thus lexicographic comparisons are preserved.  These constructions
require the stated auxiliary data.  They should not be mistaken for
a canonical inclusion or a functorial choice independent of that data.

\subsubsection{Proper expansions of the class realization}

Now fix the sets.  Let
\[
       (M,\mathcal X)\subseteq(M,\mathcal Y),\qquad
       b\in\mathcal X,
\]
be \(\GBC\) realizations, and use the same normalized core \(\Pbd(b)\)
in both.  Its codes and evaluations are identical because the set part
and the baseline are identical.  Write \(H_{\mathcal X}\) and
\(H_{\mathcal Y}\) for the externally interpreted collections of
admitted set-like global enumerations.  For set-sized two-sorted models,
these collections are ordinary sets in the metatheory.

\begin{theorem}[A class expansion as an extension by cuts]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:class-expansion}
The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(H_{\mathcal X}\) is an order-dense suborder of
      \(H_{\mathcal Y}\).
\item \(H_{\mathcal X}=H_{\mathcal Y}\) if and only if
      \(\mathcal X=\mathcal Y\).
\item For \(E\in H_{\mathcal Y}\), its lower cut \(L_E\) in the common
      core belongs to \(\mathcal X\) if and only if its enumeration
      graph \(E\) belongs to \(\mathcal X\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both orders contain \(\Pbd(b)\), which is dense in \(H_{\mathcal Y}\).
Old comparisons are unchanged by \cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:same-sets-wf}; this
proves (i).

For (ii), choose a class bijection \(v:\Ord^M\to M\) in
\(\mathcal X\), using Global Choice.  Given any \(A\in\mathcal Y\),
define a class subset of the internal ordinals by
\[
                  B_A=\{\alpha:v(\alpha)\in A\}.
\]
Encode \(B_A\) by swapping the \(\alpha\)-th adjacent pair of \(b\)
exactly when \(\alpha\in B_A\).  Denote the resulting enumeration
by \(E_A\).  This is an element of \(H_{\mathcal Y}\).  If its graph
belonged to \(\mathcal X\), the orientations of its pairs, together
with \(b\) and \(v\), would recover \(A\) by elementary comprehension.
Thus a new class supplies a new admitted enumeration.  The converse is
immediate since enumeration graphs are classes.

For (iii), an admitted \(E\) defines \(L_E\) by elementary
comprehension.  Conversely, if \(L_E\in\mathcal X\), apply the
elementary reconstruction formula of \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:reconstruction}
inside \((M,\mathcal X)\).  Its set quantifiers have the same domain
as in \((M,\mathcal Y)\), so its resulting class graph is exactly \(E\).
Hence \(E\in\mathcal X\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Rigidity when the core is fixed pointwise]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:cor:core-rigidity}
If \(\mathcal X\subsetneq\mathcal Y\), there is no weakly increasing
map \(H_{\mathcal Y}\to H_{\mathcal X}\) fixing every point of the
common core.  In particular there is no such isomorphism or monotone
retraction.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Suppose \(r\) is such a map.  If \(r(E)>E\), choose a core point
\(E_d\) strictly between them.  Monotonicity gives
\(r(E)\le r(E_d)=E_d\), a contradiction.  If \(r(E)<E\), choose a
core point between them and use \(r(E_d)\le r(E)\), again a
contradiction.  Thus \(r(E)=E\) for every input, which is impossible
for a point in \(H_{\mathcal Y}\setminus H_{\mathcal X}\).
\end{proof}

The core therefore detects a proper expansion through newly represented
cuts, provided its individual points are identified.  This does not
imply that the abstract unmarked enumeration order detects the expansion.

\subsubsection{The external countable order is always rational}

\begin{theorem}[External size and countable classification]
\label{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational}
For every set-sized two-sorted \(\GBC\) model \((M,\mathcal X)\),
the metatheory has
\[
                      |H_{\mathcal X}|=|\mathcal X|.
\]
If the entire two-sorted model is externally countable, then
\[
                (H_{\mathcal X},<_{\lex})\cong(\mathbb Q,<).
\]
Neither assertion requires transitivity, \(\beta\)-correctness, or
\(\omega\)-standardness.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The inequality \(|H_{\mathcal X}|\le|\mathcal X|\) follows because
the enumeration graphs are members of \(\mathcal X\).  Fix internal
bijections \(v:\Ord^M\to M\) and \(b:\Ord^M\to\No^M\).
The binary pair construction in \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:class-expansion} gives
an external injection \(A\mapsto E_A\) from \(\mathcal X\) into
\(H_{\mathcal X}\), since the graph of \(E_A\) determines \(A\).
Cantor--Bernstein proves the cardinal equality.

In the countable case, the \(\GBC\) theorems that \(\Hsl\) is a
linear order, is dense, and has no endpoints hold in the model.
Their class quantifiers range over exactly the externally admitted
class objects in \(\mathcal X\).  Thus they say precisely that the
external relation on \(H_{\mathcal X}\) is a countable dense linear
order without endpoints.  The usual back-and-forth for countable
orders identifies it with \(\mathbb Q\).
\end{proof}

There is no conflict with the internal statement that no uniformly
set-indexed family is cofinal in \(\Hsl\).  An external countable
listing of all its admitted points need not be encoded by a uniform
family inside the model.  Nor is there a conflict with the diagonal
obstruction to an internal exhaustive class list: an external list is
not an internal decoder.

This theorem gives a concrete limitation on attempts to recover truth
resources or class-comprehension strength from the unmarked order.
Whenever the relevant two-sorted models are externally countable,
their set-like enumeration orders are all isomorphic to \(\mathbb Q\), even
though their admitted class collections can differ.  The named dense
core retains finer information through \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:class-expansion}.

Finally, \(\omega\)-standardness plays a different role in the
unrestricted order.  The preceding rational classification transfers
internally proved density directly to the admitted class objects.
By contrast, an interval that the model regards as finite can have
externally infinitely many points when its claimed size is a
nonstandard natural number.  Statements about external finite-tail
condensation must therefore be read with their separate standardness
hypotheses.  The distinction between Global Choice and selection of
class witnesses is likewise unaffected: our cut reconstructions are
explicit and unique, and do not use a Class Choice principle
\cite{ClassChoice2026}.

\begin{note}[\merge; overlaps in source 21's Section 11]\label{swo:xiii:note:fu-models}
\Cref{swo:fu:fnd:prop:same-sets-wf} combines \cref{swo:fu:fnd:lem:set-witness}
with the elementarity of labelled comparison used in \cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute}.
In \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:class-expansion}, item~(iii) is source~17's
\cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension} and item~(ii) its last clause; item~(i) and
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:cor:core-rigidity} are new. In
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational}, the second assertion is source~13's
\cref{swo:fs:prop:countable} (Part~IX); the first, $\card{H_{\mathcal X}}=\card{\mathcal X}$,
is new, and source~30 proves it again (\cref{swo:rt:fnd:cor:cardinality}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 30, Section 9
\subsection{Source 30: what labelled enumeration spaces remember about their class universe}\label{swo:rt:fnd:sec:realizations}

\merge\ Source~30's Section~9, printed whole; source~30 cites none of
sources~13--29. Its class realizations $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ are printed
$\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ and its core $\mathcal B_b$ is printed $\Psupp(b)$
(as a family of enumeration graphs). Its Proposition~9.1, Theorem~9.2 and
Corollaries~9.3 and~9.4 are results of sources~22 and~21 and are printed as
notes with source~30's proofs. \Cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:coloredcore}~(1),
\cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:etrinvisible}, \cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:hod} and
\cref{swo:rt:fnd:cor:universalbaseline} are new against the repository;
source~30 calls the last two ``applications of known class-theoretic
machinery''.

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 2506-2978
The repository proves that enlarging the available classes, while keeping
the sets and a baseline fixed, necessarily adds a new global enumeration
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension}).
There is a stronger converse formulation: inclusion of the available
\emph{labelled} enumeration families detects inclusion of the entire class
collections. In fact, the much narrower family obtained by independently
swapping fixed adjacent pairs already contains all this information. This
observation gives a precise positive answer to the reconstruction question
with labels retained. It also explains why reconstruction from the pure
external linear order is a substantially different problem.

The arguments in this section use two distinct levels of language. Within
\(\mathsf{GB}\), each subset of the ordinals and each enumeration is one
class variable, and the constructions below are elementary formulas in
those variables. When comparing class realizations, we work externally
with a fixed \emph{set-sized} model \(M\) and collections
\(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\subseteq\mathcal P(M)\). The external collection of
their class graphs is then an ordinary set in the metatheory. No internal
class whose elements are proper classes is introduced.

\subsubsection{An elementary coding by pair orientations}

Fix a class bijection
\[
 b:\operatorname{Ord}\longrightarrow\No.
\]
Its existence already entails Global Choice, by the repository's theorem
over the choiceless \(\mathsf{GB}\) base (\cref{swo:cf:choice}). For each ordinal \(\alpha\), sort
the two labels \(b(2\cdot\alpha),b(2\cdot\alpha+1)\) numerically:
\[
 u_\alpha=\min\{b(2\cdot\alpha),b(2\cdot\alpha+1)\},\qquad
 v_\alpha=\max\{b(2\cdot\alpha),b(2\cdot\alpha+1)\}.
\]
Thus \(u_\alpha<v_\alpha\). Define the pair-normalized baseline \(c\) by
\[
 c(2\cdot\alpha)=u_\alpha,\qquad
 c(2\cdot\alpha+1)=v_\alpha.
\]
Here multiplication is ordinal multiplication, with the finite ordinal
on the left. The intervals
\([2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+2)\) partition \(\operatorname{Ord}\).
All of these definitions are elementary in the original baseline.

For a class \(A\subseteq\operatorname{Ord}\), let \(E_A\) be the
enumeration obtained by reversing exactly the pairs indexed by \(A\):
\[\tag{S30.9.1}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:encode}
 \begin{aligned}
 E_A(2\cdot\alpha)&=
 \begin{cases}v_\alpha,&\alpha\in A,\\u_\alpha,&\alpha\notin A,\end{cases}
 \\
 E_A(2\cdot\alpha+1)&=
 \begin{cases}u_\alpha,&\alpha\in A,\\v_\alpha,&\alpha\notin A.\end{cases}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Each pair is still used once and distinct pairs are disjoint, so every
\(E_A\) is a class bijection. Conversely, the elementary predicate
\(\operatorname{Pair}_c(E)\) says that \(E\) is a function on the ordinals
and, for every \(\alpha\),
\[\tag{S30.9.2}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:pairpredicate}
 \bigl(E(2\cdot\alpha),E(2\cdot\alpha+1)\bigr)
 \in\{(u_\alpha,v_\alpha),(v_\alpha,u_\alpha)\}.
\]
This predicate itself guarantees that \(E\) is a global bijection. Its
unique orientation class is
\[\tag{S30.9.3}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:decode}
 A_E=\{\alpha\in\operatorname{Ord}:E(2\cdot\alpha)=v_\alpha\}.
\]

\begin{note}[Source~30, Proposition~9.1, ``Pair coding with an elementary inverse'']\label{swo:rt:fnd:prop:pairs}
{\itshape
In \(\mathsf{GB}\) with the displayed baseline, the transformations
\(A\mapsto E_A\) and \(E\mapsto A_E\) are mutually inverse, uniformly
elementary transformations between ordinal classes and classes satisfying
\(\operatorname{Pair}_c\). If \(A\ne B\) and
\(\delta=\min(A\mathbin\triangle B)\), then
\[
 E_A<_{\mathrm{lex}}E_B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \delta\in B.
\]}
This is source~22's \cref{swo:rg:prop:pairs} with its decoder \cref{swo:rg:thm:decoder}, with the baseline pair-normalized; the Boolean structure below is source~30's.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~30's proof]
The inverse assertions follow directly from
\eqref{swo:rt:fnd:eq:encode}--\eqref{swo:rt:fnd:eq:decode}. A nonempty ordinal class has
a least member: after choosing any witness, minimize within the set of
ordinals below that witness. Before position \(2\cdot\delta\), the two
enumerations agree. At that position the enumeration whose orientation
bit is zero has value \(u_\delta\), and the other has value
\(v_\delta>u_\delta\). This proves the comparison formula.
\end{proof}

The coding also retains Boolean operations. Associate to \(A\) the class
permutation of surreal labels
\[
 T_A=E_A\circ c^{-1}.
\]
It either fixes both labels of a pair or exchanges them. Therefore
\[\tag{S30.9.4}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:boolean}
 T_A^2=\operatorname{id},\qquad
 T_A\circ T_B=T_{A\mathbin\triangle B},\qquad
 T_{\operatorname{Ord}\setminus A}
   =T_{\operatorname{Ord}}\circ T_A.
\]
Intersection is recovered by the elementary operation that exchanges a
pair precisely when both input permutations exchange that pair. Thus the
orientation family records the Boolean algebra of available ordinal
classes, including symmetric difference as actual permutation
composition. Boolean operations alone do not characterize which families
form a model of class theory: comprehension and Class Replacement impose
additional requirements.

\subsubsection{A faithful invariant of class realization}

Let \((M,\mathcal X)\) and \((M,\mathcal Y)\) be models of
\(\mathsf{GBC}\) with exactly the same first-order structure. They need not
be transitive, and neither class collection is initially assumed to
contain the other. Write
\[
 \mathcal E(\mathcal X)
 =\{E\in\mathcal X:(M,\mathcal X)\models
 E:\operatorname{Ord}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\No\}.
\]
This is external notation for a collection of graphs. Internal ordinal
arithmetic, surreal labels, and coded ordered pairs are all interpreted
in \(M\). If a baseline \(c\) is common to the two realizations, write
\[
 \mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)
 =\{E\in\mathcal X:(M,\mathcal X)\models\operatorname{Pair}_c(E)\}.
\]

\begin{note}[Source~30, Theorem~9.2, ``Reconstruction from labelled enumeration availability'']\label{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful}
{\itshape
For any two such realizations,
\[\tag{S30.9.5}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:faithful}
 \mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal E(\mathcal X)\subseteq\mathcal E(\mathcal Y).
\]
If a pair-normalized baseline \(c\) belongs to both realizations, these
conditions are also equivalent to
\[
 \mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)\subseteq\mathcal K_c(\mathcal Y).
\]
In particular, equality of either labelled availability family implies
equality of the complete class collections.}
This is source~22's \cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful} (and source~27's \cref{swo:sc:thm:markedmodels}). Source~30 needs no baseline given in advance: it takes one from the assumed inclusion of enumeration families, and the class bijection $g$ from that baseline.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~30's proof]
The forward implications use elementary comprehension and the fact that
being a bijection between the displayed classes is a first-order
assertion with set quantifiers and the specified class graph. Its truth
is unchanged when the first-order structure and graph are unchanged.

Suppose now that \(\mathcal E(\mathcal X)\subseteq\mathcal E(\mathcal Y)\).
Choose \(b\in\mathcal E(\mathcal X)\). The assumption makes it a common
baseline, and pair normalization gives a common \(c\). The standard
coding proof of the baseline--Global Choice equivalence supplies a class
bijection
\[
 g:\operatorname{Ord}^M\longrightarrow M
\]
uniformly definable from \(b\); hence the same \(g\) is available in
both realizations. One can instead use a common class surjection, obtained
by decoding ordinal presentations of rooted well-founded extensional
relations, since injectivity is not needed below.

Take any class \(X\in\mathcal X\), and form its ordinal code
\[
 A_X=\{\alpha\in\operatorname{Ord}^M:g(\alpha)\in X\}.
\]
Elementary comprehension in \((M,\mathcal X)\) gives \(A_X\), and then
\(E_{A_X}\in\mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)\). The assumed enumeration
inclusion puts \(E_{A_X}\) in \(\mathcal Y\). Applying the elementary
inverse \eqref{swo:rt:fnd:eq:decode} in the latter model recovers \(A_X\), and
the formula
\[\tag{S30.9.6}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:allclasses}
 x\in X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists\alpha\in\operatorname{Ord}^M\,
 \bigl(g(\alpha)=x\ \wedge\ E_{A_X}(2\cdot\alpha)=v_\alpha\bigr)
\]
recovers \(X\). Consequently \(X\in\mathcal Y\), proving
\(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y\).

If the common baseline is given at the outset, the same proof uses only
the inclusion of \(\mathcal K_c\). Every quantifier in the reconstruction
formula ranges over sets of \(M\); no quantification over an exhaustive
family of classes is hidden in the construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~30, Corollary~9.3, ``External size'']\label{swo:rt:fnd:cor:cardinality}
{\itshape
For any set-sized \(\mathsf{GBC}\) model \((M,\mathcal X)\) and a
baseline \(c\in\mathcal X\), the external sets
\(\mathcal X\), \(\mathcal E(\mathcal X)\), and
\(\mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)\) are equinumerous.}
This is the first assertion of source~21's \cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational}, with $\mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)$ added.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~30's proof]
The map \(X\mapsto E_{A_X}\) in the preceding proof injects all of
\(\mathcal X\) into \(\mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)\), while
\(\mathcal K_c(\mathcal X)\subseteq\mathcal E(\mathcal X)
\subseteq\mathcal X\). Apply Cantor--Bernstein externally.
\end{proof}

The reconstruction conclusion of \Cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful} also holds
when the recorded objects are the labelled
set-like well-order relations rather than their enumeration graphs.
The transformations in both directions are elementary: transport ordinal
order along the enumeration, or assign to each label the ordinal order
type of its predecessor set. It also holds for the availability family of
\emph{all} labelled class well-orders. For the latter statement one uses
the standard first-order characterization of internal class
well-foundedness; see \cite[Section~2]{Williams2019}.
Indeed, a nonempty ill-founded subclass yields a nonempty ill-founded
\emph{set} of labels: start with one label, and at each finite stage adjoin
all predecessors within the given ill-founded subclass of least possible
rank; then take the union. This
construction uses ordinary set-valued recursion. Therefore two
\(\mathsf{GB}\) realizations with the same sets agree about the
well-foundedness of a class relation they share. This is an internal
absoluteness statement, and does not assert external well-foundedness.

\begin{note}[Source~30, Corollary~9.4, ``The represented-cut version'']\label{swo:rt:fnd:cor:cuts}
{\itshape
Fix a common baseline and its set-coded support core. If two realizations
have the same available represented trace cuts of that core, then they
have the same classes. Inclusion of those represented-cut families
likewise reflects inclusion of the class realizations.}
This is the trace form of source~22's \cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~30's proof]
The repository's recognition theorem (\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}) constructs the unique enumeration
from its represented core cut by an elementary formula. Conversely, the
cut is elementary in the enumeration. These operations are absolute
between realizations with the same sets and baseline. Apply
\Cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful}.
\end{proof}

Thus a formalization may safely use the pair predicate and its elementary
decoder as a small interface to arbitrary classes. The statement is
uniform in any individually supplied class, or in a supplied uniform
family. It does not furnish a same-level class of all pair-swap
enumerations: the repository's diagonal theorem (\cref{swo:gl:diagonal}) still rules out an
exhaustive class-indexed evaluator. The positive reconstruction and the
negative enumeration theorem describe different operations.

\subsubsection{Why the pure external linear order loses this information}

For an externally countable model of \(\mathsf{GBC}\), its admitted
enumeration family is externally countable. Its lexicographic order is
dense without endpoints. To see density, take the first disagreement of
two enumerations, retain their common set prefix, choose an unused
numerical label strictly between the two disagreeing labels, and complete
the extended prefix to a global enumeration. The surreal set-cut
property supplies the fresh label, and the baseline supplies the
completion. Choosing a smaller or larger first label gives the absence
of endpoints. Cantor's classification of countable dense linear orders
therefore makes this external order isomorphic to \((\mathbb Q,<)\).

\begin{proposition}[A core preserved setwise and a core fixed pointwise]
\label{swo:rt:fnd:prop:coloredcore}
Let \((M,\mathcal X)\) and \((M,\mathcal Y)\) be externally countable
\(\mathsf{GBC}\) models with the same sets and a common baseline \(b\).
Let \(\Psupp(b)\) be the common family of its internally set-supported
permutations, viewed as enumeration graphs.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The core \(\Psupp(b)\) and its complement are dense in each
       enumeration order. There is an external order isomorphism
       \(F:\mathcal E(\mathcal X)\longrightarrow\mathcal E(\mathcal Y)\)
       with \(F[\Psupp(b)]=\Psupp(b)\) and \(F(b)=b\).
 \item If such an order isomorphism fixes every member of
       \(\Psupp(b)\) pointwise, then \(\mathcal X=\mathcal Y\),
       and the isomorphism is the identity on enumeration graphs.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Core density is the repository's prefix-completion theorem
(\cref{swo:gl:completion,swo:gl:interpolation}). For
complement density, choose a prefix cylinder inside any prescribed open
interval, and a core enumeration \(q=b\circ\sigma\) in that cylinder.
Choose an ordinal bound beyond the prefix length and the support of
\(\sigma\). Define a class permutation \(\tau\) that fixes positions
below a sufficiently large such bound and exchanges every later adjacent
pair. Then \(q\circ\tau\) still lies in the cylinder. Beyond the bound,
\(\sigma\) is the identity and \(\sigma\circ\tau\) moves every point
of a proper-class tail. Thus \(q\circ\tau\notin\Psupp(b)\).
All these constructions are elementary from the baseline and set
parameters and work in each realization.

Each enumeration order is therefore a countable dense linear order
with two dense colors: membership and nonmembership in the core. The
usual back-and-forth proof of Cantor's theorem applies with colors
preserved. Start with the one-point partial map \(b\mapsto b\), and
extend alternately through countable external lists of the two domains;
every required open interval contains an unused point of the required
color. This proves the first assertion.

For the second, let \(E\in\mathcal E(\mathcal X)\). An isomorphism
fixing the core pointwise makes \(E\) and \(F(E)\) determine the same
cut of the common core. The repository's elementary uniqueness theorem
for represented cuts (\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}) implies that their labelled enumeration graphs
are identical. This uniqueness also follows directly by taking a set
prefix through a disagreement and placing a common core enumeration
strictly between the resulting two prefixes. Consequently the two
enumeration families coincide. \Cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful} yields
\(\mathcal X=\mathcal Y\).
\end{proof}

Thus even a distinguished baseline point and a unary predicate for the
support core are insufficient to reconstruct a countable class
realization. The stronger requirement that the embedding of that core
be fixed pointwise retains precisely the represented-cut information.
The same back-and-forth may begin with any finite common suborder of the
core fixed pointwise, so naming finitely many additional core points
does not remove this loss of information.

\begin{proposition}[Pure order does not detect truth or ETR]
\label{swo:rt:fnd:prop:etrinvisible}
Suppose \((M,\mathcal Y)\) is an externally countable model of
\(\mathsf{GBC}+\mathsf{ETR}\), and \(M\) has a parametrically definable
global well-order. Put \(\mathcal X=\operatorname{Def}(M)\), allowing
set parameters in definitions. Then
\[
 (M,\mathcal X)\models\mathsf{GBC}+\neg\mathsf{ETR},\qquad
 \mathcal E(\mathcal X)\cong\mathcal E(\mathcal Y)\cong(\mathbb Q,<)
\]
as external pure linear orders, while
\(\mathcal E(\mathcal X)\subsetneq\mathcal E(\mathcal Y)\) as
labelled graph families. Moreover, relative to a common definable
baseline, the external isomorphism can preserve the support core
setwise and fix the baseline point.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The definable classes of a first-order model satisfy \(\mathsf{GB}\),
and the definable global well-order supplies Global Choice. Every class
in \(\operatorname{Def}(M)\) belongs to \(\mathcal Y\) by elementary
comprehension. Elementary transfinite recursion constructs a truth
predicate for the set universe, including satisfaction with set
assignments, by recursion on formula complexity;
this is a standard consequence of \(\mathsf{ETR}\)
\cite{GitmanHamkins}. Tarski's undefinability theorem excludes such a
full satisfaction predicate from \(\operatorname{Def}(M)\), even with
a set parameter.
Hence the smaller realization fails \(\mathsf{ETR}\) and is properly
contained in the larger one. \Cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful} gives strict
inclusion of their labelled spectra. Both pure orders are countable,
dense, and have no endpoints, giving their external isomorphisms with
\(\mathbb Q\). \Cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:coloredcore} supplies the
additional preservation assertions.
\end{proof}

This proposition is conditional on the displayed model hypothesis; it
does not derive the consistency of \(\mathsf{GBC}+\mathsf{ETR}\) from
\(\mathsf{ZFC}\). The separation between definable-class models and truth
extensions is standard \cite{WilliamsBeta}; its application here
pinpoints the information discarded by forgetting coordinates. No claim
that the external isomorphism is available internally is needed.

\subsubsection{Exactly when a definable baseline exists}

Global Choice and a definable global choice function are different
requirements. Fix one set parameter \(p\), and let
\(\operatorname{HOD}_p\) mean the sets whose transitive closures consist
of sets definable from ordinal parameters and the \emph{single named
parameter} \(p\). This convention is explicit because notation such as
\(\operatorname{HOD}(p)\) is also used with other parameter conventions.

\begin{theorem}[Definability threshold]
\label{swo:rt:fnd:thm:hod}
Over \(\mathsf{ZF}\), the following are equivalent for classes definable
by first-order formulas from the fixed set parameter \(p\):
\begin{enumerate}
 \item there is such a class well-order of \(\No\);
 \item there is such a set-like class well-order of
       \(\No\);
 \item there is such a bijection
       \(\operatorname{Ord}\longrightarrow\No\);
 \item \(V=\operatorname{HOD}_p\).
\end{enumerate}
The formulation of existence of a definable class is metatheoretic;
for any specified definition, the constructions produce specified
definitions of the other objects. In particular, parameter-free
definability has threshold \(V=\operatorname{HOD}\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply the repository's bare-\(\mathsf{GB}\) choice proof (\cref{swo:cf:choice}) to the given
definable relation. Its operations use elementary comprehension and
ordinary set-valued recursion, so every resulting class remains
definable from \(p\). In particular it gives a \(p\)-definable global
well-order of \(V\); refining by rank makes it set-like. Each set is
then the unique object at some ordinal position of this order, and so
is definable from that ordinal and \(p\). Every set, including every
member of its transitive closure, is consequently ordinal-definable
from \(p\). Thus \(V=\operatorname{HOD}_p\).

Conversely, the canonical ordinal-definition codes give a
\(p\)-definable well-order of \(\operatorname{HOD}_p\). Concretely, a
code records a rank \(\theta\), a formula number, and a finite tuple of
ordinals, and asserts that the formula defines one object in the set
structure \(V_\theta\) with parameter \(p\). Order the codes first by
a bound containing their ranks and ordinal parameters, and then by
canonical well-orders within that set of codes; assign each object its
least defining code. Satisfaction for the \emph{set} \(V_\theta\) is
uniformly definable in \(\mathsf{ZF}\). This construction therefore
uses no truth predicate for \(V\). If \(V=\operatorname{HOD}_p\), it
well-orders all sets; birthday or rank refinement and restriction then
give the required set-like surreal well-order and enumeration.
The remaining implications are the usual transport and collapse of
a set-like well-order.
\end{proof}

The parameter-free surreal statement is explicitly discussed by Hamkins
\cite{HamkinsChoice}. The parameter-relative formulation makes
precise what is required when a formal development proposes to replace
an explicit class baseline by a definition in the language of sets.
For a set model \(M\), it follows that
\[\tag{S30.9.7}\label{swo:rt:fnd:eq:defmodels}
 \mathcal E(\operatorname{Def}(M))\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 M\models\exists p\,[V=\operatorname{HOD}_p].
\]
Allowing arbitrary set parameters in \(\operatorname{Def}(M)\) is
essential to the quantifier on the right.

\subsubsection{A common baseline across all class realizations}

The preceding reconstruction transfers precise existence results about
class realizations to availability of global surreal enumerations.
Williams proves that a countable \(M\models\mathsf{ZFC}\) has a
\emph{minimum} \(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realization exactly when it has a
parametrically definable global well-order
\cite[Main Theorem~1]{Williams2019}. Here minimum means contained
in every realization; it is stronger than merely having no smaller one.

\begin{corollary}[Universal availability is definable availability]
\label{swo:rt:fnd:cor:universalbaseline}
Let \(M\models\mathsf{ZFC}\) be countable and
\(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realizable. With the intersection taken externally over
all its \(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realizations,
\[
 \bigcap_{\mathcal X:\,(M,\mathcal X)\models\mathsf{GBC}}
       \mathcal E(\mathcal X)
   =\mathcal E(\operatorname{Def}(M)).
\]
Consequently there is a global surreal enumeration admitted by every
realization exactly when
\(M\models\exists p\,[V=\operatorname{HOD}_p]\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A definable enumeration belongs to every realization. Conversely, suppose
that one enumeration \(b\) belongs to them all. The classes definable
from \(b\) and set parameters form \(\operatorname{Def}(M;b)\).
This is a \(\mathsf{GB}\)-realization, since it is contained in a given
\(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realization and its defining operations and Class
Replacement are inherited there. It has Global Choice because it
contains \(b\). Since every realization contains \(b\) and is closed
under elementary definitions, \(\operatorname{Def}(M;b)\) is contained
in every realization. It is therefore a minimum
\(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realization.

Williams's theorem implies that \(M\) has a parametrically definable
global well-order. Hence \(\operatorname{Def}(M)\) itself is a
\(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realization. The assumed universal availability of
\(b\) now puts \(b\) in \(\operatorname{Def}(M)\), proving the
reverse inclusion. Equation~\eqref{swo:rt:fnd:eq:defmodels} gives the final
equivalence.
\end{proof}

The countability hypothesis enters through the cited minimum-realization
theorem and should not be silently removed. This corollary and
\Cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful} are applications of known class-theoretic
machinery and the elementary pair construction; they are not claims to
new consistency theorems. They sharpen the repository's class-extension
analysis (\cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute,swo:gs:thm:class-extension}) in two ways: even a narrow labelled subfamily detects the whole
class collection, and the existence of a baseline common to all
realizations has an exact definability criterion.
Equivalently, every nondefinable global surreal enumeration admitted by
one realization of a countable set model can be omitted by another
\(\mathsf{GBC}\)-realization of those same sets.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:coloredcore}~(1) refines source~13's
\cref{swo:fs:prop:countable} and source~21's
\cref{swo:fu:fnd:thm:countable-rational} by a back-and-forth with two dense
colours fixing the baseline; item~(2) is the isomorphism case of source~27's
\cref{swo:sc:thm:markedmodels}. Together with \cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:etrinvisible}
it answers \cref{swo:st:n14.8} for externally countable models: the bare order,
even with the core named as a set and the baseline as a point, detects neither
the class realization nor $\ETR$.

% ---- source 25, Section 13
\section{Unrestricted class well-orders and other readings (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:raw}

\merge\ Source~25's Section~13, on the scope of its theorems. Its
Proposition~13.1 is \cref{swo:cf:lex} and is printed as a note.

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 776-826

The main homogeneity theorem concerns injective $\Ord$-words and their exhaustive subclass. It must not be silently applied to non-set-like well-orders, arbitrary repeated words, or numerically increasing words. We now state how those interpretations fit around it.

\subsection{Direct comparison without ordinal enumeration}

Let $R,S$ be class well-orders of the same labelled class $X\subseteq\No$, where well-order means that every nonempty admitted subclass has a least element. Write $\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)$ for the class of strict $R$-predecessors of $x$. Define $I(R,S)$ to consist of those $x$ for which
\[
 \operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\operatorname{Pred}_S(x)
\]
and the restrictions of $R,S$ to that common predecessor class agree. This is an elementary formula with the supplied class parameters. No quantification over possible initial-segment classes is needed.

\begin{note}[Source~25, Proposition~13.1, ``Largest common labelled prefix'']\label{swo:ph:prop:raw-prefix}
{\itshape
The class $I(R,S)$ is initial in both orders, and $R,S$ agree on it. If $R\ne S$, its complement has distinct least elements $u$ under $R$ and $v$ under $S$. The rule
\[
 R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u<v
\]
using the numerical order of the labels defines a strict linear comparison on supplied class well-orders of $X$. For set-like global well-orders, it agrees with first-disagreement comparison of their $\Ord$-enumerations.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex} (source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:fulllex}); source~25 recalls it with its proof.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
If $x\in I(R,S)$ and $yRx$, then $y$ is in the common predecessor class of $x$. Agreement on that class shows that $y$ has the same predecessors in the two orders and that their restrictions agree there. Thus $y\in I(R,S)$. The same argument works for $S$, proving initiality. For two points in $I(R,S)$, comparison with their predecessor classes shows agreement of the orders.

If $I(R,S)=X$, the orders coincide. Otherwise the class well-order property gives the two least points outside it. They cannot be the same point $w$: then the predecessor class of $w$ in both orders would be exactly $I(R,S)$, with identical restrictions, putting $w$ in $I(R,S)$ after all.

For transitivity, compare $I(R,S)$ and $I(S,T)$ as initial segments of $S$. They are nested. If the first is properly shorter, $S$ and $T$ still agree at the next point where $R$ separates from $S$; hence the comparison of $R$ with $T$ is that of $R$ with $S$. The symmetric argument applies if the second is shorter. If they coincide and $R<_{\lex}S<_{\lex}T$, their next labels satisfy $u<v<w$. Thus the distinct next labels $u,w$ decide $R<_{\lex}T$ as well. Trichotomy and asymmetry are immediate from distinct next labels.

For exhaustive set-length words or full $\Ord$-enumerations, the labels before the first unequal coordinate form exactly this common prefix. Hence the two definitions agree.
\end{proof}

This direct comparison is part of the maintained report (\cref{swo:cf:lex}). Its important foundational feature is that a proper-class common prefix causes no recursion problem. One compares the supplied relations directly rather than first trying to assign them class ordinal types.

\subsection{Set-like is a genuine restriction}

A class well-order is \emph{set-like} when each point has only a set of predecessors. A proper-class set-like well-order has type $\Ord$ in GBC; the rank of each point is the set ordinal determined by its predecessor set, and these ranks exhaust $\Ord$. This gives the enumeration interpretation used for $\Hsl$.

Unrestricted well-orders may have a proper-class initial block followed by further elements: $\Ord+1$, $\Ord+\Ord$, and more elaborate supplied class well-orders are examples of possible types. They have no enumeration by $\Ord$. Global choice provides enough coding to transport such orders to the carrier $\No$, but does not turn them into set-like orders.

Numerically well-ordered subclasses also need not be set-like. \Cref{swo:ph:prop:class-universal} embeds a supplied class order of type $\Ord+\Ord$ into the numerical surreal line. Its range, with inherited numerical order, has that same non-set-like type. A claim that every increasing proper-class word has a set-like range would therefore require an additional hypothesis; a full injective $\Ord$-word has a set-like range in its \emph{enumeration} order, which need not coincide with the numerical order.

\subsection{Termination, arbitrary words, and increasing subsets}

When comparing exhaustive well-orders on one fixed carrier, a word cannot be a proper prefix of another exhaustive word. The position of a termination marker is irrelevant there. It becomes important for varying ranges, arbitrary words, and injective words of different lengths. An end-first convention places a proper prefix before all its extensions; a central marker places some next letters below and others above termination. These can produce different local characters and saturation behavior, as studied in the earlier reports (\cref{swo:part:conventions}; sources~13 and~23).

The prefix geometry used here avoids that ambiguity. Nodes are ordered by extension, siblings by their numerical next labels, and full branches are compared at a genuine first disagreement. The new theorems therefore do not depend on selecting a termination marker for the entire node set.

The family of numerically increasing words is not preserved by our automorphisms, as \Cref{swo:ph:sec:invisible} shows. Nor is the injective extension lemma automatically valid after imposing monotonicity on each word: the next label must then be above all earlier labels, which adds cross-coordinate restrictions absent from its proof. Arbitrary repeated words remove the injectivity restriction but no longer literally enumerate well-orders of their ranges. Each variation warrants its own theorem rather than a notational substitution.

\subsection{Relation codes, order types, and quotients}

One can fix a well-ordering of label pairs and compare characteristic functions of relations at their first unequal bit. In a set-like class pair order, a nonempty difference class has a least coordinate. This yields a valid code-dependent comparison, but generally not the common-prefix comparison in \Cref{swo:ph:prop:raw-prefix}. It orders the \emph{bits describing the relations}, not the next labels in their enumerations.

Passing to unlabelled isomorphism types changes the problem again. Set-sized well-order types have canonical representatives in $\Ord$, but a type-then-label ordering deliberately prioritizes length or type and need not preserve enumeration lexicography. For class well-orders, one must not form an ordinary class of proper-class equivalence classes. Work with supplied representatives and a definable equivalence relation, a higher sort, or an explicitly larger universe. The label relation of \Cref{swo:ph:sec:labels} avoids this issue by representing each label class with its unique root edge.

% ---- source 25, Section 14
\section{A size and recursion audit (source 25)}\label{swo:ph:sec:foundations}

% ---- source 25 (batch-83 manuscript 11), lines 829-898

\subsection{Four different levels that should not be collapsed}

For clarity, the objects in this article occupy the following levels.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.24\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Object & Legitimate representation in the global argument\\
\midrule
One prefix or support code & A set, hence an element of an ordinary class\\
The core and prefix tree & Ordinary classes of such sets; their incidence is a class relation\\
One full enumeration or raw order & A supplied class relation, not an element of the core unless represented by a support code\\
All full enumerations, automorphisms, or cuts & Predicates on class variables; a literal collection requires a higher-level interpretation\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

Kelley--Morse theory strengthens class comprehension, but its classes still have sets as elements. It does not authorize a same-level class whose members are all classes. A higher sort or a universe shift is needed when such a collection is to become an object.

\subsection{Why the back-and-forth does not need ETR}

The homogeneity proof uses the following operations, all at the indicated sizes.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.29\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Operation & Size and principle used\\
\midrule
Collect disagreement ordinals & Class replacement on a set of indices produces a set of ordinals\\
Build the forced prefix & A set-length function; values are specified by elementary formulas with class parameters\\
Choose a core completion & A set support code; global choice selects the least successful code\\
One back-and-forth history & A set partial map between set codes at each set stage\\
Take a limit history & A union over a set ordinal of set partial maps\\
Take the final automorphism & Elementary comprehension of the union of the set-valued recursion\\
Transform one supplied branch & Formula \eqref{swo:ph:eq:branch-action}, with the branch as a class parameter\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

A set-valued recursion with an elementary class parameter can be expressed by saying that a value occurs in a set-sized correct initial history. Uniqueness of the histories follows by ordinary set transfinite induction, and their existence by set recursion with the fixed parameters. Elementary comprehension then collects the compatible stages into a class. The stage value is never a new arbitrary class.

By contrast, a recursion assigning an entire class to each stage, such as an iterated truth predicate of class length, falls under materially stronger recursion principles. The class-game and class-forcing literature makes these distinctions precise \cite{HamkinsRecursionPrinciple,GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}. The present proof does not infer a class-valued recursion theorem merely from the availability of $\Ord$ as an index class.

\subsection{No uniform enumeration of all global enumerations}

\begin{note}[Source~25, Proposition~14.1, ``Diagonal obstruction to exhaustive class coding'']\label{swo:ph:prop:diagonal}
{\itshape
No uniformly class-indexed family of global enumerations, with its index an ordinary class of sets, contains every member of $\Hsl$.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:diagonal} (source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:diagonal}), proved with a guard step at odd positions instead of a pair swap.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~25's proof]
By global choice it suffices to treat a uniform family $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Ord}$, allowing repetitions and padding a smaller family if necessary. Construct an injective word $d$ in two-position blocks. At position $2\cdot\alpha$, choose an unused label different from $e_\alpha(2\cdot\alpha)$. At position $2\cdot\alpha+1$, choose the least-indexed still unused label in the baseline enumeration $b$.

At each set stage the used labels form a set, so both choices exist. This is set-valued recursion. The second choice guarantees exhaustiveness. Indeed, for any $\beta$, the labels $b(\gamma)$ with $\gamma<\beta$ have all been used by some set-ordinal stage once they have each been used; a supremum of those set-many stages exists. At the next guard step, $b(\beta)$ is used unless it has already appeared. Transfinite induction on $\beta$ proves that every baseline label eventually occurs. Finally, $d$ disagrees with $e_\alpha$ at coordinate $2\cdot\alpha$ for each $\alpha$.
\end{proof}

This earlier diagonal mechanism (\cref{swo:gl:diagonal}) explains why the class of support codes can be dense without representing every global enumeration. The availability of a dense coded core is not an exhaustive coding theorem.

\subsection{Cuts and the Burali--Forti boundary}

The small-cut property used in \Cref{swo:ph:lem:fresh} allows only set-sized option families. An unrestricted rule filling every proper-class cut would already demand a surreal strictly greater than every surreal, by taking all of $\No$ on the left and nothing on the right. This is impossible. Similarly, the proper class $\Ord$ must not be treated as one of its own set ordinals. The proper-class scope of the enumeration domain is not a license to use it as a set-length prefix.

A cut of $\Psupp(b)$ is one supplied class of core codes. The totality of all such class cuts is not an ordinary class of sets. The trace decoder in \Cref{swo:ph:prop:trace-extension} acts on one supplied cut, and its uniform variants act on a supplied class-indexed family. This is enough for the results proved here.

\subsection{Class realizations and external models}

For a model $(M,\mathcal X)$ of GBC, the words and automorphisms in the global theorems are those admitted by its class realization $\mathcal X$. The homogeneity construction from admitted uniform parameters yields an admitted class map. Its statement does not refer to every externally imaginable subset of $M$.

With an inaccessible cardinal $\kappa$ in an ambient set theory, the full-class interpretation $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ makes the collection of internal classes an ordinary set in the ambient universe. All its internal full words can then be collected externally, and ordinary external maps between them can be discussed. This is a legitimate larger-universe interpretation, not a proof that GBC internally has a class of all classes. Inaccessible cardinals are not required for the regular set theorem of \Cref{swo:ph:sec:sets}.

For fixed class relations in GBC, well-foundedness is equivalent to the absence of a set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence. In the nontrivial direction, a nonempty class with no minimal element lets global choice select a descending sequence by set recursion. Consequently, enlarging the class realization while keeping the set universe and a fixed relation unchanged does not change that relation's well-foundedness. What can change is which class relations and full branches are available. This scope distinction is also recorded in the repository's review notes (this report's README, ``Other discrepancies'', and \cref{swo:sk:sec:foundations}).

Finally, ``all definable classes'' requires an explicit metatheoretic or syntactic interpretation. Formula codes alone do not supply an unrestricted internal truth predicate. Restricting to a stated formula family, supplying the relevant satisfaction relation, or working externally over a fixed model avoids conflating definability with a same-level exhaustive class coding.
