\section{Direct comparison and set-interval condensation once more (source 23)}\label{swo:xiv:sec:condensation}

\merge\ Source~23's Sections~9--10 recall the direct comparison of class
well-orders and the canonical decomposition into set-interval blocks before
its new constructions (\cref{swo:xiv:sec:histories}). Both are earlier
results, printed as notes; the text around them is kept, including the
warnings on what the raw order adds to the set-like one, and the iteration of
condensation by explicit set witnesses.

% ---- source 23 (batch-83 manuscript 05), lines 871-1262
\subsection{Source 23: direct comparison beyond ordinal-class enumerations}\label{swo:tm:sec:rawcompare}

A set-like well-order on $\No$ has a class enumeration of order type
$\Ord$. A raw class well-order need not: examples include copies of
$\Ord+\Ord$ and lexicographic products of ordinal classes. Simply asking
for the first \emph{ordinal coordinate} of disagreement can miss an entire
proper-class common prefix.

The repository gives a direct comparison (\cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}).
Here is the mechanism, with its foundational boundary made explicit.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Proposition~9.1, ``Largest common labelled initial part'']\label{swo:tm:prop:rawcomparison}
\emph{
For two class well-orders $H,K$ of the same labelled class $X$, there is an
elementarily definable largest common initial part on which the two
relations agree. If $H\ne K$, let $a$ and $b$ be the first remaining
labels in $H$ and $K$. Then $a\ne b$, and the rule
\[
 H<_{\lex}K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a<_X b
\]
defines a strict linear comparison on raw well-orders, when $X$ has a
fixed linear label order. No elementary transfinite recursion axiom is
required.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex} (source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:fulllex}) with the
same proof; Part~IX prints the five batch-81 proofs
(\cref{swo:ix:sec:reproved}).
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~23's proof]
Declare $x$ to belong to $P$ when its predecessor classes in $H$ and $K$
are equal and the two relations agree on that predecessor class. This is
an elementary formula with class parameters: equality of predecessor
classes and agreement of relations use only quantification over set
objects. If $x\in P$, every predecessor of $x$ belongs to $P$; the
relations agree on $P$. Any common labelled initial part has this
property and is contained in $P$.

If $P=X$, the orders agree. Otherwise the nonempty complement has an
$H$-least point $a$ and a $K$-least point $b$. Were $a=b$, its predecessor
class would be $P$ in both orders and it would belong to $P$, a
contradiction.

For transitivity, compare the common parts $P_{H,K}$ and $P_{K,M}$ as
initial segments of $K$. They are comparable by inclusion. If one is
properly smaller, the first disagreement with the third order is the
same as the earlier disagreement. If they are equal, the three next
labels satisfy the transitive numerical comparison. This proves
transitivity; trichotomy and asymmetry follow directly.
\end{proof}

The proposition remains a predicate-level statement about a fixed finite
number of class relations. It does not collect every such relation into
an ordinary class.

\subsubsection{Why the raw order has phenomena absent from the set-like part}

A raw order can have a proper-class common prefix with only two labels
$a<b$ left over. The two orders ending respectively in $(a,b)$ and
$(b,a)$ are adjacent in the outer lexicographic order: there is no third
permutation of the remaining carrier. This construction uses a well-order
of $\No\setminus\{a,b\}$ as the common prefix. The repository gives the
more general exact finite-tail adjacency analysis (\cref{swo:cf:adjacency};
source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation}).

By contrast, if two exhaustive $\Ord$-enumerations differ after a set
prefix, fresh surreal labels between the differing values remain
available. Their interval contains many further enumerations and, as
\Cref{swo:tm:sec:densecomplexity} will show, raw orders of arbitrarily
prescribed condensation complexity.

\subsection{Source 23: set-interval condensation without classes as elements}\label{swo:tm:sec:condensation}

The classical finite condensation of a linear order identifies points
with a finite interval between them; see, for example, Brown and
Su\'arez \cite{BrownSuarezFinite}. We use a size-relative analogue for class
well-orders: replace ``finite'' by ``a set.'' These are not the same
operation, and finite-condensation theorems are not invoked as proofs of
the class claims below.

\begin{definition}\label{swo:tm:n10.1}
For a class well-order $H=(X,<_{H})$, put
\[
 x\sim_H y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [\min_H(x,y),\max_H(x,y)]_H\text{ is a set}.
\]
Let $B_H$ be the subclass of points that are least in their
$\sim_H$-class. The \emph{set-interval condensation} of $H$ is
$D(H)=H\upharpoonright B_H$.
\end{definition}

Saying that the displayed interval is a set means that there exists a set
whose members are exactly the points satisfying the interval formula.
No powerclass is required.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Theorem~10.2, ``Canonical block decomposition'']\label{swo:tm:thm:block}
\emph{
The relation $\sim_H$ is a convex equivalence relation. Every block has a
least point, and $B_H$ represents the quotient as a class well-order.
Every block is either a set ordinal order or a copy of $\Ord$. Every
nonfinal block is a copy of $\Ord$; a set-sized block can occur only as
the final block.}
This is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition} (Part~IX), proved
there and by source~16 (\cref{swo:ds:thm:blocks} with
\cref{swo:ds:cor:finalset}) and source~18 (\cref{swo:sh:thm:class-division})
by the same rank argument; source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:blocks} below is a
fifth copy.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~23's proof]
Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. If $x\sim_H y$ and $y\sim_H z$,
the interval from $x$ to $z$ is contained in the union of the two given
set intervals; Separation makes it a set. Convexity follows by the same
argument. Each block is an admitted nonempty subclass and has an
$H$-least point $b$.

For $x$ in this block, the interval $[b,x)_H$ is a set well-order.
Assign to $x$ its ordinal order type. This is a class order isomorphism
from the block onto an initial segment of $\Ord$. If the block is a
set, the range is a set ordinal. If the block is proper, the range cannot
be a set, by Class Replacement applied to the inverse; hence the range
is all of $\Ord$.

Suppose a block $C$ is a set and some point lies after it. The class of
points strictly after every member of $C$ has a least element $d$.
For $c\in C$, the interval $[c,d]_H$ is contained in $C\cup\{d\}$:
a point between them outside $C$ would be strictly after the whole convex
block and contradict minimality of $d$. Thus $c\sim_H d$, impossible.
Therefore a set block must be final.

The representative of a block is an ordinary set object. Restricting
$H$ to these representatives supplies the quotient order without ever
using a proper block as an element of a class.
\end{proof}

In particular, every raw well-order is canonically a lexicographic sum of
$\Ord$ blocks, possibly with one final set-ordinal block. The index order
of those blocks can itself be a complicated raw well-order. This is a
structural decomposition, not a claim that every raw order has only a
set number of blocks.

\subsubsection{Iteration with explicit witnesses}

To keep every stage on the original domain, start with equality
$E_0$. Given a convex equivalence relation $E$, define its condensation
successor by
\[\tag{S23.3}\label{swo:tm:eq:successor}
 x\,D(E)\,y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists S\text{ a set}\ \forall z\in[x,y]_H\ 
 \exists s\in S\ (zEs),
\]
where the interval is written with its endpoints in increasing order.
Thus a set of representatives meets all $E$-classes in the interval.
At a limit stage take the union of earlier equivalences.

The witness in \eqref{swo:tm:eq:successor} can be converted into a set of least
representatives using Class Replacement. Accordingly it says exactly
that the interval in the represented quotient is a set. This formula
is elementary once $E$ is a class parameter.

For a general raw order, asserting a uniform hierarchy of class-valued
relations along an arbitrary class well-order is a genuine recursion
principle. $\GBC+\ETR$ is a sufficient setting; elementary transfinite
recursion has strength beyond $\GBC$ \cite{GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}.
We make no claim here that full $\ETR$ is necessary for this particular
operator. The next section avoids the issue for a large explicit family
by writing down every stage simultaneously.

\merge\ Source~23's successor rule \eqref{swo:tm:eq:successor} with unions at
limits is the convention of equivalence relations; sources~15, 20 and~29
iterate nested classes of least representatives and intersect them at limits
(\cref{swo:cb:cce:sec:histories,swo:lm:con:section,swo:bw:ch:history-def}).
Source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:quotient-limits} shows that the two conventions
define the same history. Whether $\ETR$ is needed for general inputs is
settled in the form of an equivalence by source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence}, not by $\ETR$ itself (\cref{swo:xiv:sec:status}).

\section{Local size of intervals in the unrestricted order (sources 20 and 27)}\label{swo:xiv:sec:local}

\merge\ Source~11's diagonal theorem (\cref{swo:gl:diagonal}) says that no
uniform class of set codes exhausts the set-like order. Source~20 localizes
it to intervals of the unrestricted order and finds an exact dichotomy: an
interval $[R,S]$ has a set-indexed exhaustive coding exactly when the
residual carrier $Y(R,S)$ after the common prefix is a set, and otherwise no
uniform family indexed by any class of sets exhausts even the open interval.
The resulting equivalence $\equiv_{\mathrm{set}}$ has convex blocks
$\WO(K_R)$, and its quotient is dense but not set-cut-filling. Source~27
proves the stronger omission: a uniform family misses a whole convex copy of
$\Hall(\No)$, so no uniform family is dense in the raw comparison. Both are
new against the repository.

% ---- source 20 (batch-83 manuscript 02), lines 1722-2142
\subsection{Source 20: A local size dichotomy for the unrestricted lexicographic order}
\label{swo:lm:loc:section}

The global failure of exhaustive set coding has a sharper local form.
An interval can have an ordinary set of codes, or it can defeat every
uniform family indexed by a class of sets.  The distinction is determined
by exactly one geometric feature: how many labels remain after the
endpoints' common prefix.  Throughout this section we work in $\GBC$.
Several of the structural lemmas only use $\GB$ once the displayed
well-orders have been supplied.

We use the elementary comparison of labelled class well-orders established
in this report (\cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}) and source~18
(\cref{swo:sh:thm:class-lex}).  If $R\ne S$ are class well-orders
of $\No$, their maximal common labelled prefix has carrier $C(R,S)$.
The first labels after this prefix are distinct; their numerical
comparison decides $R<_{\mathrm{lex}}S$.  We put
$C(R,R)=\No$ and write
\[
 Y(R,S)=\No\setminus C(R,S).
\]
The common prefix carries a relation as well as a carrier.  Thus equality
of prefix carriers below always includes agreement of their induced
orders when that agreement is needed.

A \emph{labelled class prefix} $p$ consists of a class $A_p\subseteq\No$
with a specified class well-order.  Its cylinder
\[
 \operatorname{Cyl}(p)
 =\{R:R\text{ extends }p\text{ as a labelled initial segment}\}
\]
is notation for a predicate on class relations.  It is convex under
the native lexicographic comparison.  In particular, its members need
not have set codes, and the braces do not assert that these members
form an ordinary GB class.  Whenever $\No\setminus A_p$ is nonempty,
a completion exists: append a fixed global well-order of the remaining
labels.

\subsubsection{Final set tails and interior cylinders}

For a class well-order $R$ of $\No$, put
\[
 K_R=\{x\in\No:\{y\in\No:xRy\}\text{ is a set}\}.
\]
This definition uses only set quantifiers with $R$ as a class parameter.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~6.1, ``The maximal final set tail'']\label{swo:lm:loc:final-tail}
\emph{
The class $K_R$ is either empty or a set.  It is final in $R$ and is
the unique maximal final subset of $R$ that is a set.  If it is
nonempty, it is the final set block in the canonical set-interval
decomposition of $R$.}
This is source~16's \cref{swo:ds:cor:finalset} (Part~IX), whose $A_R$ is the
present $K_R$, with the same argument; the uniqueness and maximality clauses
are explicit here.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Finality follows because a tail after a later point is contained in the
tail after an earlier point.  If $K_R$ is nonempty, let $k$ be its
$R$-least member.  Then
\[
 K_R=\{k\}\cup\{y:kRy\},
\]
which is a set by the definition of $k$.  Every final set $T$ lies in
$K_R$: for $x\in T$, the tail after $x$ is contained in $T$.

For the block assertion, recall that two labels lie in one canonical
block precisely when the closed interval between them is a set
(\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}; source~18's \cref{swo:sh:thm:class-division}).  All of $K_R$ lies in one such block.  If
$zRk$ belonged to that block, the union of $[z,k]_R$ and the set tail
after $k$ would make the tail after $z$ a set, contradicting the
minimality of $k$.  Conversely every point of a final set block has a
set tail.  Thus the two descriptions agree.
\end{proof}

The next lemma is the main local argument.  It is useful because the
unused numerical alphabet can be a very thin proper subclass of $\No$;
one cannot assume that it contains a numerical separator between two
specified labels.

\begin{lemma}[An interior cylinder with a proper residual alphabet]
\label{swo:lm:loc:proper-cylinder}
Suppose $R<_{\mathrm{lex}}S$ and $Y(R,S)$ is a proper class.  There
exists a labelled class prefix $p$ such that
\[
 \varnothing\ne\operatorname{Cyl}(p)\subseteq(R,S),
 \qquad \No\setminus A_p\text{ is a proper class}.
\]
This conclusion uses only $\GB$ and the supplied class well-orders,
apart from the use of Global Choice to choose an arbitrary completion
of the resulting prefix.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $C=C(R,S)$, let $Y=\No\setminus C$, and let $a<b$ be the first
labels of $R,S$ respectively after $C$.  Consider an ascent in the
$R$-tail,
\[
 aRxRy,\qquad x<y,
 \qquad \{z:xRz\}\text{ a proper class}.
 \tag{A}
\]
If such a pair exists, transpose the labels $x,y$ in $R$ to obtain
an order $T$.  At the first changed position, $R$ has label $x$ and
$T$ has label $y>x$, so $R<T$.  Both still start with $a$ immediately
after $C$, whereas $S$ starts with $b>a$, so $T<S$.

Take for $p$ the prefix whose labels are $\{z:zRx\}$, in their
$R$-order, followed by $y$.  Every completion of $p$ has the same two
strict comparisons just described.  Its residual carrier is
\[
 \No\setminus A_p
 =\{x\}\cup\bigl(\{z:xRz\}\setminus\{y\}\bigr),
\]
which is proper.  This supplies the desired cylinder.  Dually, a
descent
\[
 bSxSy,\qquad x>y,
 \qquad \{z:xSz\}\text{ a proper class}
 \tag{D}
\]
gives a cylinder inside $(R,S)$ by transposing $x,y$ in $S$.

Suppose neither (A) nor (D) exists.  By
\cref{swo:lm:loc:final-tail}, the class
\[
 Z=Y\setminus\bigl(K_R\cup K_S\cup\{a,b\}\bigr)
\]
is proper.  If $uRv$ are in $Z$, then $aRu$, the tail after $u$ is
proper, and failure of (A) implies $u>v$ numerically.  Hence $R$ on
$Z$ is strictly numerically decreasing.  Failure of (D) similarly
implies that $S$ on $Z$ is strictly numerically increasing.

The restriction of each relation to $Z$ is a class well-order.
Recursively take the first $\omega$ elements of $(Z,S)$: at every
finite stage the complement of the finitely many selected elements
is nonempty, and its $S$-least member is uniquely specified.  Ordinary
set-valued recursion with class parameters yields a set sequence
$(z_n)_{n<\omega}$.  Its entries strictly increase numerically, so
$z_{n+1}Rz_n$ for every $n$.  Its range is a nonempty available
subclass with no $R$-least element, a contradiction.  Thus (A) or
(D) exists, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

\merge\ Source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder} (Part~IX) finds, by the
same ascent--descent alternative, a cylinder with \emph{infinite} residual
carrier inside an interval joining two finite-condensation blocks; the lemma
above is its proper-class analogue, with the final set tails $K_R,K_S$ in
place of the maximal finite tails.

\subsubsection{Uniform coding and its diagonal obstruction}

For precision, a \emph{uniform $I$-indexed family} of class well-orders
means a single class relation $F\subseteq I\times\No\times\No$,
where $I$ is a class of sets and the section
\[
 F_i=\{(x,y):(i,x,y)\in F\}
\]
is a class well-order for each $i\in I$.  A predicate on class
well-orders has an exhaustive such coding if every available
well-order satisfying it is one of these sections.  This last
condition is an assertion with class quantifiers; it is not an
application of elementary comprehension to a collection of classes.
Set-indexed coding means that $I$ is a set.

\begin{lemma}[A diagonal inside every proper-residual cylinder]
\label{swo:lm:loc:cylinder-diagonal}
If $\No\setminus A_p$ is proper, no uniform family indexed by any
class of sets exhausts $\operatorname{Cyl}(p)$.  More strongly, for
every uniform class-indexed family $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ of well-orders
of $\No$, some member of $\operatorname{Cyl}(p)$ differs from every
$R_i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $Y=\No\setminus A_p$.  Global Choice supplies a class bijection
from $\Ord\times\{0,1\}$ to $Y$.  Thus $Y$ is partitioned into
disjoint pairs $\{u_\xi,v_\xi\}$ for $\xi\in\Ord$; name their
labels so that $u_\xi<v_\xi$ numerically.  Global Choice also supplies
a class injection $\sigma:I\to\Ord$.

Define an ordered pair at every ordinal $\xi$.  If $\xi=\sigma(i)$,
put $u_\xi,v_\xi$ in the opposite order to their order in $R_i$.
The index $i$ is unique.  At other coordinates use the order
$(u_\xi,v_\xi)$.  This rule is elementary in the given class
parameters.  Append these pairs, in increasing ordinal order, after
the prefix $p$.  The result $T$ is a class well-order of $\No$:
a nonempty subclass either has a least member in the prefix, or has
a least pair index and then a least member of that finite pair.
It belongs to $\operatorname{Cyl}(p)$.

For each $i$, the two labels in pair $\sigma(i)$ occur in the
opposite relative order in $T$ and $R_i$.  Hence $T\ne R_i$.
The construction has produced one ordinary class relation from the
given uniform family, without enumerating any collection of classes.
\end{proof}

\merge\ The pair-swap diagonal is the one of source~11's \cref{swo:gl:diagonal}
and source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:diagonal}, run inside a cylinder; source~27's
\cref{swo:sc:thm:omittedcopy} (\cref{swo:xiv:sub:families}) strengthens the
conclusion from one omitted order to a whole omitted convex copy of
$\Hall(\No)$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact local coding dichotomy]
\label{swo:lm:loc:dichotomy}
For two distinct class well-orders $R<_{\mathrm{lex}}S$ of $\No$,
the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $Y(R,S)$ is a set;
\item the closed interval $[R,S]$ has a uniform set-indexed
      exhaustive coding;
\item the open interval $(R,S)$ has a uniform exhaustive coding indexed by
      a class of sets.
\end{enumerate}
If these conditions fail, every proposed uniform class-indexed
family omits a well-order strictly between $R$ and $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $Y=Y(R,S)$ is a set and let $p$ be the common labelled
prefix.  The cylinder of $p$ consists precisely of the orders obtained
by appending a well-order of $Y$.  All such well-orders form the
ordinary set $\WO(Y)\subseteq\mathcal P(Y\times Y)$.
Concatenation gives a uniform family of class relations indexed by
this set.  Every order in $[R,S]$ extends $p$ by prefix convexity.
Filter the index set by the elementary native comparisons
$R\leq F_i\leq S$.  Separation with the supplied class parameters
gives a set of indices coding exactly the closed interval.  Filtering
with strict comparisons gives the open interval, proving (1)$\Rightarrow$
(2)$\Rightarrow$(3).

If $Y$ is proper, \cref{swo:lm:loc:proper-cylinder} gives a
proper-residual cylinder inside $(R,S)$.
\Cref{swo:lm:loc:cylinder-diagonal} constructs within that cylinder a
well-order omitted by any proposed class-indexed family.  This
contradicts (3), and proves both the remaining implication and the
last assertion.
\end{proof}

This is a sharper conclusion than an estimate of cardinality.  In GB
there is no ordinary cardinal assigned to the collection of all class
well-orders.  The theorem instead gives a precise dichotomy in terms
of legitimate uniform presentations.  In particular, for these
intervals, allowing a proper class of set indices does not enlarge
the family of intervals that can be exhaustively presented.

\subsubsection{The convex blocks of locally set-sized intervals}

Define
\[
 R\equiv_{\mathrm{set}}S
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 Y(R,S)\text{ is a set}.
\]
Equality satisfies this convention because $Y(R,R)=\varnothing$.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical local-size blocks]
\label{swo:lm:loc:blocks}
The relation $\equiv_{\mathrm{set}}$ is a convex equivalence
relation on the predicate of class well-orders of $\No$.
The block containing $R$ consists exactly of the orders obtained by
keeping the labelled prefix on $\No\setminus K_R$ and replacing
the final well-order of the set $K_R$ arbitrarily.  Consequently its
native lexicographic order is represented by the ordinary set order
$\WO(K_R)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Symmetry and reflexivity are immediate.  For transitivity, the common
prefixes of $(R,S)$ and $(S,T)$ are initial segments of the same
order $S$, so one is contained in the other.  The shorter is a common
labelled prefix of $R,T$.  If both original residuals are sets, so
is the residual after this shorter prefix, and hence so is
$Y(R,T)$.  Convexity follows from prefix convexity: an order between
$R,S$ extends their common prefix, so its common-prefix residual
with either endpoint is a subset of $Y(R,S)$.

Suppose $R\ne S$ and $Y(R,S)$ is a set.  Let $a$ be the first
$R$-label outside their common prefix.  Its strict $R$-tail is a
subset of $Y(R,S)$, so $a\in K_R$.  Hence the common prefix already
contains every label of $\No\setminus K_R$, in its original
$R$-order.  Conversely, if $S$ keeps that prefix and appends any
well-order of $K_R$, then $R,S$ share that prefix and their
first-disagreement residual, if any, is contained in the set $K_R$.
This proves the block description.  The numerical first difference
inside the common set tail is exactly the usual comparison on
$\WO(K_R)$.
\end{proof}

If $K_R=\varnothing$ or $|K_R|=1$, the block is a singleton.  If
$|K_R|=n<\omega$, its size is $n!$.  If $K_R$ is infinite of
cardinality $\mu$, its size is $2^\mu$: the upper bound follows
from coding a relation by a subset of $K_R^2$, and independent
orientations of $\mu$ disjoint pairs give the lower bound.  The
ordered structure for an infinite tail depends on its numerical
alphabet, so cardinality alone does not classify these blocks.
Every set alphabet $K\subseteq\No$ occurs as such a final tail:
well-order $\No\setminus K$ in type $\Ord$ and append a well-order
of $K$.

We may discuss a quotient comparison using representatives and
$\equiv_{\mathrm{set}}$.  The notation $[R]$ in the next statement
is only an abbreviation for this equivalence relation.  It does not
make an equivalence class of class relations into a set or an
ordinary class element.

\begin{theorem}[A dense quotient that does not fill countable cuts]
\label{swo:lm:loc:quotient}
The quotient comparison by $\equiv_{\mathrm{set}}$ is dense and
has no endpoints.  Nevertheless there are two uniformly coded
countable families whose quotient classes form an unfilled cut of
character $(\omega,\omega)$.  Thus deleting all locally set-sized
blocks does not produce a surreal-like set-cut-filling order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $R<S$ belong to different blocks.  Their residual is proper, so
\cref{swo:lm:loc:proper-cylinder} gives a proper-residual cylinder inside
$(R,S)$.  Choose three different labels from its residual, sort them
numerically, and form completions $T_0<T_1<T_2$ beginning with these
respective labels after the prefix.  Their first disagreements leave
the entire proper residual unused, so the three completions lie in
three different blocks.  Convexity of the blocks gives
\[
 [R]<[T_1]<[S].
\]
To obtain blocks on both sides of any $R$, choose first labels
numerically below and above the first label of $R$, and complete
them.  Their disagreement with $R$ occurs before any common label,
leaving the proper residual $\No$.

For the countable gap, use the proper numerical alphabet
\[
 Y=(\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\})
   \cup\{\alpha:\alpha\in\Ord,\ \alpha\geq\omega\}
   \cup\{-\alpha:\alpha\in\Ord,\ \alpha\geq\omega\}
 \subseteq\No.
\]
Its complement is proper as well: for example, the labels
$\alpha+\tfrac12$ for infinite ordinals $\alpha$ are in that
complement and are pairwise distinct.  Choose one class well-order
$p$ of $\No\setminus Y$ and use it as a prefix.  For each positive
integer $n$, let $R_n$ extend $p$ with first remaining label $-1/n$,
and let $S_n$ extend it with first remaining label $1/n$.  Append a
fixed global order of the unused labels in each case.  These
constructions are uniform in $n$, and
\[
 [R_n]<[R_{n+1}]<[S_{m+1}]<[S_m]
 \qquad(n,m\geq1).
\]
All the displayed classes are distinct because different first
labels after $p$ leave the proper residual $Y$.

Suppose a class $[T]$ lies above every $[R_n]$ and below every
$[S_n]$.  In particular, $R_1<T<S_1$, so prefix convexity forces
$T$ to extend $p$.  Let $y\in Y$ be its first remaining label.
The inequalities imply
\[
       -1/n\leq y\leq1/n\qquad(n\geq1).
\]
No member of $Y$ satisfies these inequalities: a nonzero rational
fails one of them by the Archimedean property of $\mathbb Q$, and
an ordinal or negative ordinal of magnitude at least $\omega$
fails already for $n=1$.  This is a contradiction.

The downward closure of the $[R_n]$ and the upward closure of the
$[S_n]$ therefore partition the quotient comparison.  The first
family is cofinal on the lower side, and the second is coinitial on
the upper side.  Neither side has an endpoint because the displayed
sequences are strictly monotone.  No finite family can be cofinal or
coinitial on the respective side, proving the exact character
$(\omega,\omega)$.  These closures are again predicates on
representatives; the proof does not collect quotient objects.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The external cardinal form of the local dichotomy]
\label{swo:lm:loc:full-model-size}
Let $\kappa$ be strongly inaccessible in an ambient ZFC universe and
interpret classes using $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$.
The raw order of all internal class well-orders of the internal
surreal carrier is then an ordinary ambient set order.  For any
two distinct members $R<S$, its open and closed intervals satisfy
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 |(R,S)|\leq|[R,S]|<\kappa,
     &\text{if }Y(R,S)\text{ is an internal set},\\[3pt]
 |(R,S)|=|[R,S]|=2^\kappa,
     &\text{if }Y(R,S)\text{ is internally proper}.
 \end{array}
\]
Thus $\equiv_{\mathrm{set}}$ is exactly the external condensation
relation defined by $|[R,S]|<\kappa$.  Its quotient has $2^\kappa$
points, and every open quotient interval with distinct bounds has
$2^\kappa$ points.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The full-model size check, proved again in
\cref{swo:lm:con:full-model}, identifies internal sets with ambient
subsets of cardinality less than $\kappa$.  The surreal carrier
has ambient cardinality $\kappa$.  If $Y(R,S)$ is an internal set
of cardinality $\mu<\kappa$, the common-prefix cylinder is coded
by a subset of $\mathcal P(Y(R,S)^2)$.  Its cardinality is less
than $\kappa$ by the strong-limit property, proving the first case.

If the residual is internally proper, its ambient size is $\kappa$.
By \cref{swo:lm:loc:proper-cylinder}, the open interval contains a
cylinder whose residual also has size $\kappa$.  Independent
orientations of $\kappa$ disjoint pairs in that residual give
$2^\kappa$ distinct completions in the cylinder.  All are available
because this is the full-class model.  Conversely every raw
well-order is a relation on a carrier of size $\kappa$, so there
are at most $2^\kappa$ such orders.  This proves the second case
and the condensation characterization.

The whole raw order has $2^\kappa$ elements, again by pair coding
and the relation-coding upper bound.  Each equivalence block has
fewer than $\kappa$ elements by \cref{swo:lm:loc:blocks} and the
strong-limit property.  Hence there are $2^\kappa$ blocks: fewer
blocks, even allowing $\kappa$ elements per block, could not cover
$2^\kappa$ elements.  Finally, for $[R]<[S]$ the raw interval
$(R,S)$ has $2^\kappa$ elements.  Discarding the two endpoint
blocks removes fewer than $\kappa$ elements.  Grouping the
remaining elements into blocks of size less than $\kappa$ still
leaves $2^\kappa$ distinct blocks strictly between $[R]$ and $[S]$.
\end{proof}

\merge\ Source~20's Section~10 uses the same full model to re-prove
source~11's nonembedding \cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding}, by counting
$2^\kappa$ disjoint six-point blocks against a dense subset of size
$\kappa$; that passage is printed with source~20's foundations.

Two condensation operations have now appeared and must be kept
separate.  In \cref{swo:lm:loc:full-model-size} the points being condensed
are \emph{whole well-orders}, and the retained blocks describe local
interval sizes in their lexicographic order.  The next section
condenses intervals \emph{inside one supplied well-order}, whose
points are surreal labels.  The common set/class boundary does not
identify these different orders or their quotients.

\subsection{Source 27: uniform families miss whole convex copies of the raw order}\label{swo:xiv:sub:families}
\label{swo:sc:sec:families}

The bounded-support core is a dense ordinary class of set codes for the
set-like interpretation. Could a more elaborate ordinary class of codes
be dense in the raw comparison? The answer is negative. A diagonal
argument leaves enough unused labels to retain a convex copy of the
entire raw order, rather than just producing one omitted object.

\subsubsection{The diagonal construction}

\begin{theorem}[An omitted convex copy]\label{swo:sc:thm:omittedcopy}
Work in $\GBC$. Let $I$ be any ordinary class, and let
$\mathcal R(i,x,y)$ be a uniform family of binary relations on $\No$.
There is a convex family of raw class well-orders, described by explicit
operations on class variables, that is order-isomorphic to $\Hall(\No)$
and contains none of the relations $R_i$.

In particular, no uniformly class-indexed family of raw well-orders meets
every nonempty open interval of the raw comparison.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Reserve $A=(0,1)\subseteq\No$ and put $B=\No\setminus A$. The map
that prefixes the signs $(+,-)$ is a numerical order isomorphism
$\varphi:\No\to A$. The complement $B$ is a proper class. Global Choice
provides a bijection $c:\Ord\to B$ and an injection $j:I\to\Ord$.

The ordinal pairs
\[
 \{2\cdot\alpha,\,2\cdot\alpha+1\},\qquad \alpha\in\Ord,
\]
partition $\Ord$. Here $2\cdot\alpha$ is left ordinal multiplication.
Write $x_\alpha=c(2\cdot\alpha)$ and
$y_\alpha=c(2\cdot\alpha+1)$. List these pairs in order of $\alpha$.
Within pair $\alpha=j(i)$, choose its orientation opposite to the
truth value of $R_i(x_\alpha,y_\alpha)$: put $x_\alpha$ before
$y_\alpha$ exactly when that truth value is false. There is at most one
such $i$ because $j$ is injective. Orient all unassigned pairs by a fixed
default. This elementary definition gives a class bijection
$h:\Ord\to B$ and its induced well-order $P_h$.

For every class well-order $Q$ of $A$, form $h+Q$, placing all of $B$
first in the order $P_h$, then all of $A$ in order $Q$. Its initial
set-like block is exactly $h$, since every point of $A$ has the proper
class $B$ before it. Thus these orders constitute the convex fiber
\eqref{swo:sc:eq:raw-fiber} (source~11's \cref{swo:cf:fibers}). Restriction to $A$ and concatenation with $h$
identify its raw comparison with $\Hall(A)$; conjugation by $\varphi$
identifies the latter with $\Hall(\No)$.

Every member of this fiber differs from $R_i$ on the ordered pair
$(x_{j(i)},y_{j(i)})$. Therefore the whole fiber is omitted, even though
the input sections were not assumed to be well-orders.

For the final claim choose $a_0<a_1<a_2$ in $A$ and well-orders
$Q_0,Q_1,Q_2$ of $A$ beginning with these respective labels. Global
Choice completes the residual carriers. Then
$h+Q_0<h+Q_1<h+Q_2$. Convexity puts the nonempty ambient interval
$(h+Q_0,h+Q_2)$ inside the omitted fiber.
\end{proof}

The conclusion is stronger than failure of exhaustive coding. A uniform
family might omit many points and still be dense; this theorem rules that
out for the raw comparison. It does not rule out cofinal or coinitial
uniform families: varying the first numerical label through $\No$ gives
such families immediately. It also does not contradict density of
$\Psupp(b)$ in $\Hsl$, because the fiber used above has a proper-class tail
and contains no set-like global well-order.

The reference to a ``convex family'' is shorthand for a predicate on
class variables together with the transformations $Q\mapsto h+Q$ and
restriction to $A$. It is not a claim that this family is a class of sets.
Every step in the proof is elementary comprehension with class
parameters, supplemented by Global Choice for the two enumerations.

\subsubsection{The set analogue at birthday cutoffs}

The same mechanism has a useful set version, where ordinary counting
can replace class diagonalization.

\begin{theorem}[Many disjoint convex copies]\label{swo:sc:thm:setcopies}
Let $X$ be an infinite linearly ordered set of cardinality $\mu$.
Suppose a convex subset $A\subseteq X$ is order-isomorphic to $X$ and
$B=X\setminus A$ has cardinality $\mu$. Then $\WO(X)$, with
enumeration lexicography, contains $2^\mu$ pairwise disjoint convex
copies of itself. Every subset of size less than $2^\mu$ misses one
such copy, and its order-topological density and cellularity both equal
$2^\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are $2^\mu$ bijections $h:\mu\to B$: independent pair swaps
give the lower bound, while $\mu^\mu=2^\mu$ gives the upper
bound. For each such $h$, consider the completions $h+Q$ with
$Q\in\WO(A)$. They are a prefix cylinder and therefore convex.
Restriction identifies the cylinder with $\WO(A)\cong\WO(X)$.
Distinct bijections have distinct length-$\mu$ prefixes, so their
cylinders are disjoint.

Each cylinder contains three points in increasing order, hence a
nonempty ambient open interval. Selecting one such interval per cylinder
gives $2^\mu$ disjoint nonempty open intervals. Every dense subset
must meet all of them. Since $|\WO(X)|=2^\mu$, both bounds are exact.
A set of fewer than $2^\mu$ points meets fewer than that many disjoint
cylinders, proving the stronger omitted-copy assertion.
\end{proof}

For every infinite ordinal $\theta$, this theorem applies to
$X=\No_{<\theta}$. The cone
$A=(0,1)\cap \No_{<\theta}$ consists precisely of $(+,-)\concat s$ for
$s\in \No_{<\theta}$ and is isomorphic to $X$. Finite prefixing preserves
every infinite birthday cutoff: for finite $\alpha$ the new length is
finite, while for infinite $\alpha$ one has $2+\alpha=\alpha$.
The complement contains the whole negative-sign cone, also isomorphic
to $X$, and therefore has the same cardinality. No inaccessible-cardinal
assumption enters this statement about a fixed set of sign sequences.

The exact density formula overlaps the earlier corpus (source~16's
\cref{swo:ds:thm:density}, its ``Moreover'' clause). The point of the
argument here is its stronger geometric form: small subsets miss an
entire convex self-copy. The class theorem replaces the unavailable
hypercardinality count by an explicit diagonal on a uniform family.




\begin{note}[\merge; how the omission results compare]\label{swo:xiv:note:omission}
Four uniform-coding obstructions are now printed. Source~11's
\cref{swo:gl:diagonal} and source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:diagonal} produce one
global enumeration omitted by a given uniform family; source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:loc:cylinder-diagonal} produces one omitted order inside every
cylinder with proper residual carrier, hence inside every interval whose
residual $Y(R,S)$ is proper (\cref{swo:lm:loc:dichotomy}); source~27's
\cref{swo:sc:thm:omittedcopy} omits an entire convex fibre isomorphic to
$\Hall(\No)$, so a uniform family is not even dense in the raw comparison.
Source~27's theorem does not decide the local question of source~20's
dichotomy (its omitted fibre is chosen by the diagonal, not inside a
prescribed interval), and it does not contradict density of the core in the
set-like order: its fibre has a proper-class tail and contains no set-like
order, as source~27 says.
\end{note}
