\section{Complete condensation histories (sources 20, 23 and 29)}\label{swo:xiv:sec:histories}

\merge\ Part~IX printed source~15's explicit histories: for every class
well-order $J$, the polynomial order $P(J)$ has an elementary history indexed
by $J+1$ whose stages are proper and whose appended last stage is a
singleton (\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:anyhistory}). Three batch-83 sources go
further. Source~20 proves that a \emph{supplied} nested history of an
arbitrary class well-order $W$ terminates by the stage $W+1$, names $\ETR$ as
a sufficient existence principle, and computes the exact heights in full
models. Source~23 re-proves source~15's polynomial histories in the
equivalence-relation convention and places copies of them inside every
interval between two distinct set-like global enumerations. Source~29 gives
each point of a well-order with a terminating history a finite polynomial
address, and proves over $\GBC$ that the existence of canonical histories for
all inputs is equivalent to strong comparability of class well-orders. All
three take the same nested-representative operator $D_W$ and the same limit
convention, up to source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:quotient-limits}, which
identifies source~23's union of equivalences with the intersection of
representatives used by sources~15, 20 and~29.

% ---- source 20 (batch-83 manuscript 02), lines 2143-2414
\subsection{Source 20: complete condensation histories: a bound and an exact model}
\label{swo:lm:con:section}

The canonical set-interval decomposition is elementary.  A supplied
uniform history of successive decompositions can also be analysed
elementarily.  The issue of obtaining that history for an arbitrary
input is separate.  The preceding continuation realized arbitrary
class well-orders as first-level block-index orders, analysed removal
of initial blocks through ordinary ordinal stages, and supplied a
polynomial example isomorphic to its own first condensation
(source~18; \cref{swo:sh:thm:block-spectrum,swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block}).  Those results do not by themselves supply
a uniform history of iterated quotients for every input.  Here we
prove that a complete history
always terminates when it is run long enough, specify one sufficient
recursion hypothesis, and calculate its exact height in full-class
models.

\subsubsection{A precise limit convention}

Let $(X,W)$ be a nonempty class well-order.  For a nonempty subclass
$A\subseteq X$ containing $m=\min_W X$, define $D_W(A)$ to be the
least representatives of the equivalence relation
\[
 x\sim_A y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{z\in A:\min_W(x,y)\leq_W z\leq_W\max_W(x,y)\}
 \text{ is a set}.
\]
Thus $D_W(A)\subseteq A$ and it contains $m$.  This is an elementary
operator on classes with $W$ as parameter.  In particular, if
$A\ne\{m\}$ and $s$ is the least member of $A\setminus\{m\}$,
then $s\notin D_W(A)$, because $[m,s]_{W\restriction A}=\{m,s\}$.

A \emph{nested representative history} uses $A$ itself as the carrier
at each stage, rather than replacing it by an unspecified isomorphic
copy.  At successor stages apply $D_W$, and at nonzero limit stages
intersect all earlier retained subclasses.  The limit convention is
essential: abstract order isomorphism types alone do not retain the
information needed to form these intersections.

\begin{theorem}[Termination by the input order]
\label{swo:lm:con:termination}
Work in $\GB$.  Suppose a single class relation uniformly codes a
nested representative history $(H_i)_{i\in(X,W)+1}$, with
\[
 H_m=X,
\]
successor stages given by $D_W$, and nonzero limit stages given by
intersection.  Here one fresh final stage $*$ has been appended to
the index order $(X,W)$.  Then
\[
       H_*=\{m\}.
\]
More precisely, for every $x\in X$,
\[\tag{S20.1}\label{swo:lm:con:retention-bound}
 H_x\subseteq\{m\}\cup\{y\in X:x\leq_W y\}.
\]
For arbitrary $W$, elementary transfinite recursion along $(X,W)+1$
is a sufficient hypothesis for the required uniform history to
exist.  No necessity or reverse-mathematical equivalence is asserted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The recursion rules imply that the retained classes are decreasing
and all contain $m$.  Transfinite induction along $W$ is available
in GB for formulas with the supplied history as a class parameter:
a nonempty class of counterexamples would have a least member.
We prove \eqref{swo:lm:con:retention-bound} by that induction.

At the first stage $x=m$, the assertion is immediate.  Suppose $x$
is the immediate successor of $t$.  By induction, no member of
$H_t$ lies strictly below $t$ except possibly $m$.  If $t\ne m$
and $t\in H_t$, it is therefore the immediate successor of $m$
in the induced order on $H_t$, and is deleted by $D_W$.  All earlier
members other than $m$ have already disappeared.  If $t=m$, there
are no earlier nonminimal members to delete.  In either case
$H_x=D_W(H_t)$ contains no $y<_W x$ except $m$, as required.

If $x$ is a nonzero limit point of the index order, take
$m\ne y<_W x$.  There is $t$ with $y<_W t<_W x$; the inductive
bound excludes $y$ from $H_t$, hence from
$H_x=\bigcap_{t<_W x}H_t$.  This proves the bound at limit stages.

If $W$ has a greatest element $\ell$, the bound at $\ell$ gives
$H_\ell\subseteq\{m,\ell\}$.  Its condensation is $\{m\}$,
which is the appended successor stage.  If $W$ has no greatest
element, every $y\ne m$ has some index $x>_W y$, and the bound at
that stage excludes it from the final intersection.  The final
stage is again $\{m\}$.

Finally, the rule for $H_i$ is elementary in the earlier part of the
history: one tests whether the index is first, a successor, or a
limit, and then applies the corresponding displayed rule.  The
principle of elementary transfinite recursion along $(X,W)+1$
therefore supplies a class coding the history.  This uses the
standard meaning of ETR, whose stages may themselves be classes;
its distinction from ordinary set-valued recursion is discussed in
the primary literature on class recursion
\cite{GHHSW,GitmanHamkins}.  The termination proof
itself needed only GB and the already supplied history.
\end{proof}

The theorem does not contradict an isomorphism
$W\cong D_W(X)$.  The retained subclasses decrease even when their
abstract order types repeat.  In particular, no nontrivial retained
class is literally a fixed point of $D_W$: its second member is
always deleted at the next stage.  A purported nonterminating
history that keeps replacing a quotient by an arbitrary isomorphic
copy has changed the specified limit convention.

\subsubsection{The exact ordinal calculation}

An external set theorem gives a completely explicit calculation.
Let $\kappa$ be any infinite initial cardinal and let $\theta>0$
be an ordinal.  On a suborder of $\theta$, condense intervals of
cardinality less than $\kappa$, retain least representatives, and
intersect retained carriers at limits.  Write $H_\alpha(\theta)$
for the resulting ordinary transfinite history.  Exponentiation in
the next theorem is \emph{ordinal exponentiation}.

\begin{theorem}[Multiples of ordinal powers]
\label{swo:lm:con:ordinal-formula}
For every ordinal $\alpha$,
\[\tag{S20.2}\label{swo:lm:con:multiples}
 H_\alpha(\theta)
   =\{\kappa^\alpha\cdot\beta:
                         \kappa^\alpha\cdot\beta<\theta\}.
\]
Consequently the first singleton stage has exact height
\[\tag{S20.3}\label{swo:lm:con:height}
 h_\kappa(\theta)
       =\min\{\alpha:\theta\leq\kappa^\alpha\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First observe that, on an ordinal $\gamma$, condensation by intervals
of cardinality less than $\kappa$ keeps exactly the points
$\kappa\cdot\delta<\gamma$.  Indeed, ordinary left division by
$\kappa$ writes each point uniquely as
$\kappa\cdot\delta+\rho$, with $\rho<\kappa$.  Within one
$\kappa$-segment every closed interval has size less than $\kappa$.
An interval meeting two different segments contains a final segment
of the earlier $\kappa$-segment and therefore has size at least
$\kappa$.  This argument does not require regularity of $\kappa$.

At $\alpha=0$, equation \eqref{swo:lm:con:multiples} simply says that the
retained carrier is all of $\theta$.  If it holds at $\alpha$, the
map $\beta\mapsto\kappa^\alpha\cdot\beta$ order-isomorphically
identifies an initial ordinal segment with $H_\alpha(\theta)$.
Applying the preceding division observation to this induced order
keeps precisely the indices $\beta=\kappa\cdot\delta$.  Their
images are
\[
 \kappa^\alpha\cdot(\kappa\cdot\delta)
       =\kappa^{\alpha+1}\cdot\delta,
\]
proving the successor step.

Let $\lambda$ be a nonzero limit ordinal.  Every multiple of
$\kappa^\lambda$ is a multiple of $\kappa^\alpha$ for
$\alpha<\lambda$: write $\lambda=\alpha+\delta$ and use
$\kappa^\lambda=\kappa^\alpha\cdot\kappa^\delta$.
For the converse, suppose $x$ is a multiple of every
$\kappa^\alpha$ for $\alpha<\lambda$.  Divide it by
$\kappa^\lambda$:
\[
 x=\kappa^\lambda\cdot q+r,
       \qquad r<\kappa^\lambda.
\]
Continuity of ordinal exponentiation gives an $\alpha<\lambda$
with $r<\kappa^\alpha$.  The term $\kappa^\lambda\cdot q$
is itself a multiple of $\kappa^\alpha$.  Thus the displayed
expression is the left division of $x$ by $\kappa^\alpha$, with
remainder $r$.  Since $x$ was a multiple of that power, uniqueness
of division implies $r=0$.  This proves that the intersection of
all earlier retained classes consists exactly of the multiples of
$\kappa^\lambda$, establishing the limit step.

The right side of \eqref{swo:lm:con:multiples} always contains $0$ and
contains another point exactly when $\kappa^\alpha<\theta$.
This proves \eqref{swo:lm:con:height}.  The set in that minimum is
nonempty, since $\alpha\mapsto\kappa^\alpha$ is increasing and
$\kappa^\theta\geq\theta$.
\end{proof}

For example,
\[
 h_\kappa(\kappa)=1,\quad
 h_\kappa(\kappa+1)=2,\quad
 h_\kappa(\kappa^\omega)=\omega,\quad
 h_\kappa(\kappa^\omega+1)=\omega+1.
\]
The last pair makes the role of an appended terminal point especially
clear: the class-limit intersection may retain that point as well
as the minimum, requiring one more condensation.

\begin{corollary}[Exact heights in a full-class model]
\label{swo:lm:con:full-model}
Let $\kappa$ be strongly inaccessible in an ambient ZFC universe,
and use the full two-sorted model
$(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$.  If an internal class well-order
of its surreal carrier has ambient ordinal type $\theta$, then
$|\theta|=\kappa$, and its canonical nested condensation history
has ambient height $h_\kappa(\theta)$ from \eqref{swo:lm:con:height}.
The possible heights are exactly
\[
                   0<\alpha<\kappa^+.
\]
There is no single internal class-well-order schedule that bounds
the heights of all such input orders.  The bound by the input order
in \cref{swo:lm:con:termination} can be attained.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
In this full model, a subclass of $V_\kappa$ is an internal set
exactly when its ambient cardinality is less than $\kappa$.
Inaccessibility bounds the cardinality of every $V_\beta$ for
$\beta<\kappa$; conversely, regularity bounds the ranks of fewer
than $\kappa$ many elements of $V_\kappa$.  This is the standard
full-model size check used in the earlier continuation (source~18;
\cref{swo:sh:sec:foundations}).  All
ambient subsets are available as classes, so internal class
well-orders are actual well-orders externally.  The surreal carrier
has ambient cardinality $\kappa$.  Its order type therefore satisfies
$\kappa\leq\theta<\kappa^+$, and the condensation is exactly
the one computed in \cref{swo:lm:con:ordinal-formula}.

The bound $h_\kappa(\theta)\leq\theta<\kappa^+$ gives one
inclusion for the height spectrum.  Conversely, if
$0<\alpha<\kappa^+$, the ordinal $\theta=\kappa^\alpha$ has
cardinality $\kappa$ and has height exactly $\alpha$, because
ordinal exponentiation with base $\kappa>1$ is strictly increasing.
For completeness, the cardinality assertion follows by induction:
ordinal multiplication at a successor stage preserves cardinality
$\kappa$, and at a limit below $\kappa^+$ the union has at most
$\kappa$ terms, each of size at most $\kappa$.  A bijection transfers
this ordinal order to the surreal carrier, giving an available
internal class relation.

Any internal class well-order schedule has an ambient order type
less than $\kappa^+$.  The displayed spectrum contains a larger
height, proving the absence of a universal schedule in this model.
For attainment of the input-order bound, take an ordinal fixed point
\[
                    \theta=\kappa^\theta
\]
of cardinality $\kappa$.  One exists by starting with
$\theta_0=\kappa$, setting $\theta_{n+1}=\kappa^{\theta_n}$,
and taking $\theta=\sup_{n<\omega}\theta_n$.  Each stage and the
supremum have cardinality $\kappa$, and continuity gives the fixed
point.  Strict increase of exponentiation shows
$\kappa^\alpha<\theta$ for every $\alpha<\theta$, so
$h_\kappa(\theta)=\theta$.  Such an input retains more than one
point at every earlier stage and first becomes a singleton at its
appended final stage.
\end{proof}

The last corollary is an external classification in a specified
full-class model.  It is not a claim that a GB universe contains the
ordinal $\kappa$ naming its own height, nor that it can collect all
class well-orders and their histories into one class-valued object.
The remaining foundational question is sharp: which fragment, if
any, of elementary transfinite recursion is necessary for every
supplied class well-order to admit the nested history?  The
termination theorem answers what happens to a history once it
exists; it does not settle that existence principle over GB or GBC.

\begin{note}[\merge; the existence question is answered over $\GBC$]\label{swo:xiv:note:strength}
Source~29 answers this question, which source~20 also asks as its
\cref{swo:lm:n11.5}, over $\GBC$: the principle $\CTH$ that every class
well-order admits its history on the schedule $W+1$ is equivalent to strong
comparability $\CWO$ of class well-orders (\cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence}).
Since $\ETR$ implies $\CWO$ (Hamkins--Woodin), $\ETR$ remains sufficient;
whether it is necessary is not settled: source~29 leaves Hamkins and
Woodin's Question~7, on converses among these principles, open. Source~29
does not treat the question over $\GB$ without global choice. Source~20's \cref{swo:lm:con:termination}
is source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:input-bound}, and its height formula is
recovered there from finite normal forms (``A concrete full-model check in
\cref{swo:xiv:sub:strength}).
\end{note}
\merge\ (4 October 2026, batch~96.) Answered over $\GB$ as well. Sources~34
and~35 (Part~XVI) prove independently that $\CTH$, $\CWO$ and the two
polynomial forms are equivalent over $\GB$ with $\ZF$ sets and no form of
choice (\cref{swo:bo:hist:equivalence,swo:fc:gb-comparability}); source~29's
only use of global choice, the well-foundedness of $P(\Gamma)$
(\cref{swo:bw:ch:polynomials}), is replaced by a choice-free proof
(\cref{swo:bo:power:GB,swo:fc:thm:finite-support}; \cref{swo:xvi:note:hist}).
Whether $\ETR$ is necessary remains open.




\begin{note}[\merge; the polynomial orders in four sources]\label{swo:xiv:note:polynomials}
Source~15's $P(J)$ (\cref{swo:cb:n6.1}), source~18's $(\mathcal P,\triangleleft)$
for $J=\omega$ (\cref{swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block}), source~23's
$\mathsf P(\Gamma)$ and source~29's $\mathcal P(\Gamma)$ are one class: finite
partial functions from the exponent order to the nonzero ordinals, compared
at the greatest exponent of disagreement. They are printed $P(\Gamma)$ here.
Source~23 compares them by \eqref{swo:tm:eq:polyorder}; source~29 uses them
as the codomain of its finite normal forms.
\end{note}

\subsection{Source 23: ordinal-polynomial models of every prescribed hierarchy}\label{swo:tm:sec:polynomial}

Let $\Gamma=(G,<_{\Gamma})$ be a given set or class well-order. A member
of $P(\Gamma)$ is a finite partial function from $G$ to the nonzero
ordinals. Evaluation outside its finite domain is defined to be zero.
Thus we may conveniently write $p:G\to\Ord$ with finite support, but
\emph{the object $p$ is its finite graph}. For $p\ne q$, the finite
union of their supports has a greatest point of disagreement $\delta$, and
we define
\[\tag{S23.4}\label{swo:tm:eq:polyorder}
 p<q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p(\delta)<q(\delta).
\]
This is reverse lexicography on finite supports, not on arbitrary
infinite-support words.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Lemma~11.1, ``Polynomial order is a class well-order'']\label{swo:tm:lem:polywell}
\emph{
In $\GBC$, $P(\Gamma)$ with \eqref{swo:tm:eq:polyorder} is a class well-order.
It is proper whenever $G$ is nonempty.}
This is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:lem:polynomialwellorder} (Part~IX), and
source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:polynomials}; the three proofs map a descending
sequence to ordinals by a base larger than all coefficients (source~15
uses an additively indecomposable base, source~23 an infinite base,
source~29 the order type $\delta^\alpha$).
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~23's proof]
The greatest-disagreement comparison is a linear order: in a comparison
of three finite graphs, work in the finite union of their supports,
where ordinary finite lexicography applies.

Suppose a nonempty admitted subclass had no least point. Global choice
would recursively select a strictly descending sequence
$p_0>p_1>\cdots$. The sequence is a set, by set recursion and Class
Replacement. The union of its supports is a set well-ordered by
$\Gamma$, say of order type $\alpha$. Its coefficients form a set of
ordinals, so choose an infinite ordinal base $b$ larger than all of them.
Reindex the support set by $\alpha$. The map
\[
 p_n\longmapsto
 \sum_{\xi\in\supp(p_n)}^{\text{decreasing }\xi} b^\xi\,p_n(\xi)
\]
is strictly order-preserving into the ordinals.
Indeed, at the highest differing exponent $\delta$, every finite sum
of lower terms is less than $b^\delta$; this follows successively from
coefficients being below $b$ and the laws of ordinal exponentiation.
A larger coefficient at $\delta$ therefore dominates all lower terms.
We obtain a descending sequence of ordinals, a contradiction.

For any fixed $g\in G$, varying the coefficient at $g$ embeds $\Ord$.
Thus the carrier is proper when $G$ is nonempty.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~23, Lemma~11.2, ``The first block removes the least coordinate'']\label{swo:tm:lem:polystep}
\emph{
Suppose $G$ is nonempty with least point $g_0$. Two polynomials have a
set interval between them if and only if they agree at every coordinate
strictly above $g_0$. Consequently
\[
 D(P(\Gamma))\cong P(\Gamma\setminus\{g_0\}),
\]
where the order on the remaining coordinates is inherited.}
This is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:lem:deleteleast} (Part~IX), with the
same proof.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~23's proof]
If they agree above $g_0$, all points between them agree there too.
Only the coefficient at $g_0$ varies between two fixed ordinals, giving
a set interval.

Otherwise let $\delta>g_0$ be their greatest disagreement, with $p<q$.
Keep every coordinate of $p$ above $g_0$ fixed, and vary its coefficient
at $g_0$ through all ordinals greater than or equal to its original
value. Every resulting polynomial lies between $p$ and $q$, since the
higher disagreement at $\delta$ still places it below $q$. These give
a proper class of points in the interval.

The least representative of a block has coefficient zero at $g_0$.
Deleting that coordinate identifies the representative order with the
stated polynomial order.
\end{proof}

Adjoin a formally tagged new greatest stage $\top$ to $\Gamma$ (using a disjoint tagged copy of its old carrier). For $t\in G$, let
$I_t=\{\gamma:\gamma<_\Gamma t\}$ and put $I_\top=G$. Define
\[\tag{S23.5}\label{swo:tm:eq:Et}
 pE_tq\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall\gamma\in G\setminus I_t\ (p(\gamma)=q(\gamma)).
\]
The quantifier ranges over set objects $\gamma$; $p,q$ are finite graphs.
This is one elementary definition with parameter $\Gamma$, and defines
a class family on the set-coded stages of $\Gamma+1$.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Theorem~11.3, ``Prescribed-hierarchy theorem'']\label{swo:tm:thm:polyhierarchy}
\emph{
Let $\Gamma$ be any given class well-order, including a set well-order.
The family \eqref{swo:tm:eq:Et} is its polynomial order's set-interval
condensation hierarchy. More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item At the first stage, $E_t$ is equality. Each $E_t$ is a convex
 equivalence relation.
\item Its represented quotient is
 $P(\Gamma\setminus I_t)$.
\item If $t$ has immediate predecessor $s$ in the stage order, then
 $E_t=D(E_s)$.
\item At every nonzero limit stage $t$, including a limit final stage,
 $E_t=\bigcup_{s<t}E_s$.
\item $E_\top$ is universal, and every $E_t$ for $t\in G$ is
 nonuniversal. In particular, collapse occurs exactly at the final stage.
\end{enumerate}
These particular hierarchies are available in $\GBC$ without $\ETR$.}
This is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:anyhistory} (Part~IX), stated for
the equivalence relations $E_t$ with unions at limits instead of nested
classes of representatives with intersections; the two conventions agree by
source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:quotient-limits}. Source~23's form adds the
explicit quotient $P(\Gamma\setminus I_t)$ at every stage and allows $\Gamma$
to be a set well-order. Source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:polynomials} is a third
copy.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~23's proof]
For each initial segment $I_t$, equivalence means equality on the
remaining tail. This is a convex equivalence, and its least representative
is obtained by deleting all coefficients in $I_t$. Its quotient therefore
has exactly the stated polynomial order.

At a successor stage the remaining tail loses its least coordinate.
\Cref{swo:tm:lem:polystep} proves precisely the successor clause, including
when $I_s$ is a proper class. At the first stage no coordinate has been
removed, so equality is obtained.

At a limit stage, if $pE_tq$, their finite set of differing coordinates
is contained in $I_t$. A finite subset of this initial segment is already
contained in some $I_s$ with $s<t$: take a stage strictly above its
greatest member, which exists because $t$ is not a successor. Thus
$pE_sq$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. If there are no differing
coordinates, any earlier stage suffices. The same proof applies when
the predecessor segment of $t$ is proper.

At the final stage all coordinates are deleted. Before that stage,
the zero polynomial and the polynomial with coefficient one at coordinate
$t$ remain inequivalent. No recursion theorem was used: the displayed
formula supplies the family and the preceding arguments verify its
recursive specification.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Every set ordinal, and beyond}

For $\Gamma=\alpha$ a set ordinal, we may say that the collapse rank is
exactly $\alpha$. Every positive set ordinal is therefore realized by a
proper-class well-order. For finite $n$, the order is the usual finite
lexicographic ordinal-class power, with the highest coordinate compared
first. Its successive condensations delete one least coordinate at a time.

For $\Gamma=\omega$, the quotient at every finite stage $n$ is
isomorphic to $P(\omega)$ because $[n,\omega)$ has order type
$\omega$. Nevertheless the union of the finite-stage equivalences is
universal: two finite graphs have bounded support. This gives a
particularly transparent warning against declaring a hierarchy stable
merely because its successive quotient order types are isomorphic.
(\merge\ Source~15's \cref{swo:cb:n6.5} and source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block} make the same point with the same order;
\cref{swo:ix:note:selfsimilar}.)

For $\Gamma=\Ord$, the tail after any set ordinal stage is again
order-isomorphic to $\Ord$. Consequently every set-stage quotient is
isomorphic to $P(\Ord)$, and no set stage collapses it. The final
stage of $\Ord+1$ does collapse it, by the same finite-support argument.
The final stage has a proper class of predecessors, but its relation is
explicitly defined, not obtained by an unlicensed recursion.

Taking, for example, $\Gamma=\Ord+\Ord$ continues the hierarchy beyond
that first class-length block. The theorem is always relativized to a
\emph{given} admitted $\Gamma$. It does not assert a same-level class
containing the hierarchies of all class well-orders.

\subsubsection{Transport to surreal labels}

Under global choice, every proper ordinary class admits a set-like
$\Ord$-enumeration. Hence for nonempty $\Gamma$ there is a class bijection
between $P(\Gamma)$ and $\No$, and its well-order may be transported
to the surreal carrier. The transported ordering is generally unrelated
to the numerical ordering of the labels.

Thus the theorem supplies actual raw well-orders \emph{of all surreal
numbers}, not just abstract orders on an unrelated large carrier. The
choice of transport affects the outer lexicographic position but not the
condensation hierarchy of the transported relation.


% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 3238-3946
\subsection{Source 29: the exact strength of complete condensation histories}\label{swo:xiv:sub:strength}
\label{swo:bw:ch:section}

The elementary comparison of two labelled class well-orders does not
require an isomorphism between their unlabelled order types.  The
repository's common-prefix construction makes this distinction explicit
(\cref{swo:cf:lex}).  Iterating the canonical set-interval decomposition of one
class well-order is a different problem.  The preceding continuation, source~20,
proved termination conditional on a supplied uniform history, gave
elementary transfinite recursion as a sufficient existence principle,
and asked for the exact strength of that existence assertion
(\cref{swo:lm:con:termination}, \cref{swo:lm:n11.5}).

We now identify it with \emph{strong class-well-order comparability}.
The central construction assigns a finite ordinal-coefficient address
to every point of a well-order with a supplied terminating history.
These addresses form an initial segment of a class of formal
polynomials.  A common history for two convex suborders therefore gives
their initial-segment comparison.  Conversely, comparability places
any class well-order inside a polynomial order with an explicit
condensation history.

All results in this section are over \(\GBC\), unless a weaker
setting is explicitly stated.  No collection of classes is treated
as an ordinary class of members.  A history, an embedding, or a
family of maps is always one supplied class relation.  Formal sums
and appended endpoints use tagged copies of their carriers; an
arbitrary class carrier might be the entire universe, so a ``new
endpoint'' must not mean an untagged set outside that carrier.

\subsubsection{The operator, the schedule, and the existing termination bound}

Let \(W=(X,<_{W})\) be a nonempty class well-order and put
\(m=\min_W X\).  Here ``class well-order'' means that every nonempty
admitted subclass has a least element.  Given a nonempty subclass
\(A\subseteq X\), define
\[\tag{S29.21}\label{swo:bw:ch:small-interval}
 x\sim_A y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{z\in A:\min_W(x,y)\leq_W z\leq_W\max_W(x,y)\}
 \text{ is a set},
 \qquad x,y\in A.
\]
Let \(D_W(A)\) be the subclass of least representatives of these
equivalence classes.  The assertion that a displayed interval is a
set is expressed by the existence of a set with exactly its members.
Thus both \(\sim_A\) and \(D_W(A)\) have elementary definitions
from the supplied class parameters.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~11.1, ``One-step block facts'']\label{swo:bw:ch:blocks}
\emph{
The relation \(\sim_A\) is a convex equivalence relation.  Each of
its blocks has a least element and, in its induced order, is either
a set ordinal or a copy of \(\Ord\).  A set-sized block can only
be final.  In particular, a block followed by another least
representative has type \(\Ord\).}
This is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition} (Part~IX) for the
induced order on $A$, and source~23's \cref{swo:tm:thm:block}, with the same
proof.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~29's proof]
Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate.  An interval between two
points is contained in the union of the intervals from those points
to a third point, which proves transitivity.  Taking subintervals
proves convexity.  Each block is an admitted nonempty subclass and
therefore has a least point \(a\).  For a point \(x\) in that block,
its predecessors within the block are exactly the set interval
\([a,x)_W\cap A\).  Their ordinal order types give a canonical
rank map whose range is an initial subclass of \(\Ord\).

If that range is bounded by a set ordinal, Class Replacement applied
to the inverse rank map makes the block a set.  Otherwise the range
is all of \(\Ord\).  This proves the order-type assertion without
assigning a set ordinal to a proper class.  Finally, if a set block
were not final, let \(y\) be the least point after it.  Adjoining
\(y\) to the block would give a set interval from its minimum,
contradicting the maximality of the equivalence block.
\end{proof}

This is the canonical set-interval decomposition already used in
the project (\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}; source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:con:section}).  Its simultaneous definition
requires no history of class-valued states.

Let \(\Gamma=(I,<_{\Gamma})\) be a nonempty class well-order,
and append a final stage \(*\).  Every \(i\in I\) has an
immediate successor in \(\Gamma+1\), denoted \(i^+\).  A
nonzero limit stage means a stage other than the first which has
no immediate predecessor; its predecessor class need not be a set.

\begin{definition}[Canonical history]\label{swo:bw:ch:history-def}
A canonical condensation history for \(W\), with schedule
\(\Gamma+1\), is one class
\[
 H\subseteq (I\cup\{*\})\times X
\]
whose slices satisfy
\begin{align*}
 H_{\min\Gamma}&=X,\\
 H_{i^+}&=D_W(H_i) \qquad(i\in I),\\
 H_\lambda&=\bigcap_{i<_{\Gamma+1}\lambda}H_i
       \qquad\text{at every nonzero limit stage }\lambda.
\end{align*}
The final stage is included in the successor or limit clause as
appropriate.  The history is \emph{terminating} if
\(H_* =\{m\}\).  The principle \(\CTH\) asserts that every
nonempty class well-order \(W\) has such a history with the
specific schedule \(W+1\).
\end{definition}

The slices are decreasing and all contain \(m\), by elementary
transfinite induction with \(H\) as a class parameter.  The same
kind of induction proves the following bound from the preceding
continuation.  We include the argument because the distinction
between existence and termination is central to the equivalence.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Proposition~11.3, ``Termination for the input-order schedule;
earlier result'']\label{swo:bw:ch:input-bound}
\emph{
In \(\GB\), a supplied canonical history on the schedule
\(W+1\) satisfies
\[\tag{S29.22}\label{swo:bw:ch:retention-bound}
 H_x\subseteq \{m\}\cup\{y\in X:x\leq_W y\}
 \qquad(x\in X),
\]
and its final slice is \(\{m\}\).}
This is source~20's \cref{swo:lm:con:termination}, which source~29 credits;
the proof is the same induction.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~29's proof]
Induct along the supplied class well-order \(W\).  The first-stage
bound is immediate.  If \(x\) is the successor of \(t\), the
inductive bound has already excluded all points below \(t\)
except \(m\).  If \(t\ne m\) remains in \(H_t\), it is the
immediate successor of \(m\) there.  Its interval from \(m\)
has two points, so \(D_W\) deletes \(t\).  This proves the
bound at \(x\); the case \(t=m\) is immediate.

At a nonzero limit \(x\), each \(m\ne y<_W x\) lies below
some \(t<_W x\).  The inductive bound excludes \(y\) from
\(H_t\) and hence from the intersection at \(x\).  If \(W\)
has a greatest element \(\ell\), the bound leaves at most
\(\{m,\ell\}\) at stage \(\ell\), and the appended successor
condenses it to \(\{m\}\).  If \(W\) has no greatest element,
every \(y\ne m\) is excluded at some later stage, so the final
intersection is again \(\{m\}\).
\end{proof}

An appropriate instance of \(\ETR\) supplies the history because
the displayed successor and limit rules are elementary in the earlier
history.  This is class-valued recursion, not merely a recursion
whose values and earlier histories are sets.  The standard distinction
is developed in the class-recursion literature
\cite{GitmanHamkins,HamkinsWoodin}.  The remaining arguments first
work with an already supplied history.

\subsubsection{Greatest retained predecessors and finite changes}

The essential new observation concerns projections onto retained
carriers.  A decreasing family of arbitrary subclasses need not have
the property below; the successor rule forces it.

\begin{lemma}[Canonical floor maps]\label{swo:bw:ch:floors}
For every stage of a supplied canonical history and every \(x\in X\),
the greatest retained predecessor exists:
\[\tag{S29.23}\label{swo:bw:ch:floor}
 p_i(x)=\max_W\{a\in H_i:a\leq_W x\}.
\]
These maps are uniformly elementary in \(H,W\).  For \(i\leq j\),
\[\tag{S29.24}\label{swo:bw:ch:projection-identities}
 p_j(x)\leq_W p_i(x),\qquad
 p_j(p_i(x))=p_j(x),\qquad
 p_i(p_j(x))=p_j(x).
\]
Each \(p_i\) is nondecreasing as a function of \(x\).  At every
nonzero limit stage \(\lambda\), the earlier floors of a fixed
point stabilize:
\[\tag{S29.25}\label{swo:bw:ch:limit-floor}
 \exists i_0<\lambda\ \forall i\,
 (i_0\leq i<\lambda\ \Longrightarrow\ p_i(x)=p_\lambda(x)).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Prove existence by elementary transfinite induction.  At the first
stage the floor of \(x\) is \(x\).  Given \(p_i(x)=a\), let
\(b\) be the least representative of the \(\sim_{H_i}\)-block
containing \(a\).  A representative between \(b\) and \(x\)
would have to lie between \(b\) and \(a\), by the defining property
of \(a\).  It would therefore lie in the same block as \(b\),
contrary to least-representative uniqueness.  Thus
\(p_{i^+}(x)=b\).

At a nonzero limit \(\lambda\), the earlier floors are nonincreasing
because the retained carriers are nested.  The class of their values
is nonempty and has a \(W\)-least value \(b\), attained at some
stage \(i_0<\lambda\).  Every later floor below \(\lambda\)
equals \(b\).  Also \(b\in H_{i_0}\), so nesting places it in
every earlier slice.  It follows that \(b\) belongs to the limit
intersection.  Any point of that intersection below \(x\) is at
most \(p_{i_0}(x)=b\).  This proves both existence and
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:limit-floor}.

The induction assertion uses only set quantifiers and the supplied
classes.  In particular, the class of earlier floor values is defined
directly by the greatest-predecessor formula; no family of newly
chosen class maps is assumed.  Once existence is proved, the same
formula defines all \(p_i\) in a single class relation.

Monotonicity in \(x\) is immediate.  If \(i\leq j\), every
\(H_j\)-point at most \(x\) is an \(H_i\)-point and is at
most \(p_i(x)\).  This proves the first composition identity.
The second follows because \(p_j(x)\) itself lies in \(H_i\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Each point changes its floor only finitely often]
\label{swo:bw:ch:finite-changes}
For every fixed \(x\), only finitely many stages \(i\in I\)
satisfy \(p_{i^+}(x)\ne p_i(x)\).  No new floor value first
appears at a limit stage.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The limit assertion is \eqref{swo:bw:ch:limit-floor}.  If the class of
successor changes were not finite, repeatedly taking its least next
member would give increasing stages \(i_0<i_1<\cdots\) with
\[
 p_{i_{n+1}}(x)\leq_W p_{i_n^+}(x)<_W p_{i_n}(x).
\]
These are uniquely chosen set-valued steps.  Ordinary recursion along
\(\omega\), with the supplied classes as parameters, and Class
Replacement produce a set-coded descending sequence in \(W\), a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

The finiteness is pointwise, not a finite bound on the length of the
whole history.  It is also internal finiteness when the theorem is
interpreted inside a nonstandard model of class theory.

There is a precise quotient interpretation of the limit convention.
Put \(xE_i y\) when \(p_i(x)=p_i(y)\).  The maps \(p_i\) are
monotone surjections onto \(H_i\), so \(E_i\) is a convex
equivalence relation.

\begin{corollary}[Continuous identification at limits]
\label{swo:bw:ch:quotient-limits}
At a nonzero limit stage,
\[
                E_\lambda=\bigcup_{i<\lambda}E_i.
\]
Thus no pair of original points is first identified at a limit.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
An earlier identification persists by
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:projection-identities}.  Conversely, if the two floors
agree at \(\lambda\), choose an earlier stage after both
stabilization stages in \eqref{swo:bw:ch:limit-floor}.  Their floors
already agree there.
\end{proof}

Consequently the limit quotient is the directed quotient limit of
the earlier stages.  This can be stated without collecting a category
of all class orders: for any supplied class order \(Y\) and any
uniform compatible family of monotone maps \(f_i:H_i\to Y\),
there is a unique map from \(H_\lambda\) through which they
factor.  Define it by restricting the first \(f_i\) to
\(H_\lambda\).  Equation \eqref{swo:bw:ch:limit-floor} and compatibility
verify the factorization; surjectivity of each projection gives
uniqueness.  This answers one natural version of the earlier question
about alternative limit conventions (source~20's \cref{swo:lm:n11.6}): retaining the canonical quotient
maps gives exactly the nested-representative limit.

\subsubsection{A class of formal ordinal-coefficient polynomials}

For a class well-order \(\Gamma=(I,<_{\Gamma})\), let
\(P(\Gamma)\) be the ordinary class of finite partial
functions from \(I\) to nonzero set ordinals.  Missing coefficients
are read as zero.  Order these functions by the coefficient at the
\emph{greatest} exponent where they differ.  This is a finite-support
comparison, not a claim that \(\Ord\) is a set-valued base for an
ordinary exponentiation operation.  The empty function, denoted
\(0\), is the least polynomial.

\begin{note}[Source~29, Lemma~11.7, ``Polynomial well-orders and their explicit histories'']\label{swo:bw:ch:polynomials}
\emph{
The order \(P(\Gamma)\) is a class well-order in
\(\GBC\).  It has an elementary canonical terminating history on
the schedule \(\Gamma+1\), namely
\[\tag{S29.26}\label{swo:bw:ch:polynomial-history}
 K_i=\{q\in P(\Gamma):
                 \supp(q)\subseteq\{j:i\leq_\Gamma j\}\},
 \qquad K_*=\{0\}.
\]}
This combines source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:lem:polynomialwellorder} and
\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:anyhistory} (Part~IX), and source~23's
\cref{swo:tm:lem:polywell,swo:tm:thm:polyhierarchy}; source~29's
well-foundedness proof computes the set order type $\delta^\alpha$ instead of
mapping into an ordinal base.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~29's proof]
If the polynomial order had a nonempty subclass without a least
element, Global Choice would produce a descending \(\omega\)-sequence.
The union of its finite exponent supports is a set \(A\), whose
induced \(\Gamma\)-order has a set ordinal type \(\alpha\).
Class Replacement also bounds all coefficients occurring in that
sequence by a single set ordinal \(\delta\geq2\), chosen strictly
above every coefficient.

The sequence would therefore lie in the set order of finite-support
\(\delta\)-valued functions on \(\alpha\), with the same
greatest-difference comparison.  This is a well-order of ordinary
ordinal type \(\delta^\alpha\): the successor step is an ordinal
sum of \(\delta\) copies of the preceding order, and at a limit
every finite support is bounded in an earlier exponent segment.
Ordinary set transfinite induction proves the assertion.  The
descending sequence is impossible, so the class polynomial order
is well-founded.

At stage \(i\), the \(K_i\)-polynomials with the same coefficients
strictly above \(i\) form exactly one small-interval block, varying
their \(i\)-coefficient through \(\Ord\).  Within such a block
every bounded coefficient interval is a set.  If two higher parts
differ, arbitrarily increasing the \(i\)-coefficient of the smaller
polynomial stays below the larger polynomial.  Their interval
therefore contains a proper class.  The least representative of a
block has coefficient zero at \(i\), proving the successor clause
in \eqref{swo:bw:ch:polynomial-history}.  At a nonzero limit, retaining
only exponents above all earlier thresholds is exactly the
intersection rule.  The final threshold leaves only the zero
polynomial.
\end{proof}

All polynomial objects are sets: a polynomial has a finite domain of
set-valued stage labels and finitely many set ordinal coefficients.
The possibly proper-class size is in the collection of available
codes and in its ordering, not in an individual code.

\subsubsection{Finite normal forms from a supplied history}

For a history with schedule \(\Gamma+1\), define
\[\tag{S29.27}\label{swo:bw:ch:digits}
 c_i(x)=\otp\bigl(
    \{z\in H_i:p_{i^+}(x)\leq_W z<_W p_i(x)\},<_{W}\bigr).
\]
The displayed interval is a set.  Indeed, the successor construction
in \cref{swo:bw:ch:floors} identifies \(p_{i^+}(x)\) as the least
representative of the small-interval block containing \(p_i(x)\).
The digit is zero exactly when these two floors coincide.
By \cref{swo:bw:ch:finite-changes},
\[\tag{S29.28}\label{swo:bw:ch:normal-form}
 \operatorname{NF}_H(x)
       =\{(i,c_i(x)):i\in I,\ c_i(x)>0\}
       \in P(\Gamma).
\]
This finite graph is a set, and its dependence on \(x\) is given
by one elementary class formula.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical finite normal form]
\label{swo:bw:ch:normal-form-theorem}
For a supplied terminating history \(H\), the map
\(\operatorname{NF}_H\) is a class isomorphism of \(W\) onto
an initial segment of \(P(\Gamma)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We first record precisely how to insert a digit.  Suppose
\(b\in H_{i^+}\), and let \(z\in H_i\) be the point of ordinal
rank \(\rho\) in the small-interval block beginning at \(b\),
whenever that point exists.  Then
\[
 p_i(z)=z,\qquad p_{i^+}(z)=b.
\]
For every later stage, the floors of \(z\) agree with the floors
of \(b\), by \eqref{swo:bw:ch:projection-identities}.  At every earlier
stage \(j<i\), both relevant floors of \(z\) equal \(z\),
because \(z\in H_i\subseteq H_{j^+}\).  It follows that
\(\operatorname{NF}_H(z)\) has the same digits as
\(\operatorname{NF}_H(b)\) above \(i\), has digit \(\rho\)
at \(i\), and has zero digits below \(i\).  The digits of
\(b\) at and below \(i\) are themselves zero.  This is an exact
one-digit insertion rule.

Now fix an actual normal form.  At the last stage the floor of its
point is \(m\).  Read its finitely many nonzero digits in decreasing
stage order, starting from that anchor.  At each step the one-digit
rule says to take the unique point of the indicated ordinal rank
in the indicated block.  For an actual code, this point exists by
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:digits}.  Limit stages introduce no additional changes,
by \eqref{swo:bw:ch:limit-floor}.  The successive anchors therefore
reconstruct the original point.  Uniqueness at each rank proves
that \(\operatorname{NF}_H\) is injective.  These are finitely
many uniquely specified choices of sets, not a choice of class
isomorphisms.

It remains to prove order preservation and, crucially, that the
image is an initial segment.  Let
\(q<\operatorname{NF}_H(x)\) be any polynomial, and let \(i\)
be their greatest exponent of disagreement.  Their higher digits
are identical.  Reading those common higher digits reconstructs
the same anchor
\[
                    b=p_{i^+}(x).
\]
Write \(d=c_i(x)\) and \(c=q(i)\), with a missing digit of
\(q\) read as zero.  The comparison says \(c<d\).
In the \(H_i\)-block beginning at \(b\), the point \(p_i(x)\)
has rank \(d\).  Hence there are points \(a,a'\in H_i\) of
ranks \(c,c+1\), respectively, with
\[\tag{S29.29}\label{swo:bw:ch:cap}
             a<_W a'\leq_W p_i(x)\leq_W x.
\]
Taking \(a\) inserts the digit \(c\), leaving all smaller
digits zero.

Process the remaining nonzero digits of \(q\) in decreasing order.
For a lower exponent \(j<i\), both the current anchor and the
fixed cap \(a'\) belong to \(H_{j^+}\).  Initially this follows
from \(a,a'\in H_i\), and it remains true after each insertion
because the exponents decrease.  The cap is a later least
representative.  Therefore the \(H_j\)-block beginning at the
current anchor is nonfinal and has type \(\Ord\), by
\cref{swo:bw:ch:blocks}.  Every requested set ordinal digit is available
inside that block, and its point is still strictly below \(a'\).
The one-digit insertion rule proves that the step changes exactly
the requested digit and preserves the previously inserted higher
digits.  After the finitely many steps, the resulting point \(y\)
satisfies
\[
          \operatorname{NF}_H(y)=q,
          \qquad y<_W a'\leq_W x.
\]

Thus every polynomial below an actual code is itself an actual code,
and its decoded point is smaller.  When \(q\) is the normal form
of another given point, injectivity identifies that point with
the constructed \(y\).  The two linear orders therefore have
exactly the same comparisons.  The same argument for arbitrary
\(q\) proves initiality of the image.
\end{proof}

The initiality conclusion is stronger than an order embedding.  It
is the step that will give \emph{strong} comparability, rather than
merely an embedding as an arbitrary suborder.  The cap in
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:cap} guarantees that every finite collection of lower
digits can be filled without leaving the input order.

The theorem also explains how a history can have very large height
while every point has a finite address.  The exponents themselves
are labels in a supplied class well-order, and may have proper
classes of predecessors.  They have not been replaced by set
ordinals.  Only the coefficients and the finite address are sets.

\subsubsection{Restricting a history to a convex suborder}

To compare two input orders, we need their histories on the same
schedule.  The following restriction rule supplies them from a
single history of their sum.

\begin{lemma}[Anchored convex restriction]
\label{swo:bw:ch:convex-restriction}
Let \(Y\) be a nonempty convex subclass of \(W\), and put
\(a=\min_W Y\).  From a canonical history \(H\) on \(W\)
define, on the same schedule,
\[\tag{S29.30}\label{swo:bw:ch:anchored-history}
 J_i=\{a\}\cup\{y\in H_i\cap Y:a<_W y\}.
\]
Then \(J\) is the canonical history of the induced order on \(Y\).
If \(H\) terminates, so does \(J\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first-stage clause is immediate, and intersecting the displayed
subclasses at a limit gives the same formula at that limit.  For the
successor clause, fix \(x\in H_i\cap Y\) with \(a<_W x\),
and put \(u=p_i(a)\).  By the greatest-predecessor property,
the global and local intervals from their respective anchors are
\begin{align*}
 [u,x]_W\cap H_i
     &=\{u\}\cup\{z\in H_i:a<_W z\leq_W x\},\\
 [a,x]_W\cap J_i
     &=\{a\}\cup\{z\in H_i:a<_W z\leq_W x\}.
\end{align*}
Convexity of \(Y\) ensures that the tails displayed on the two
lines coincide.  The two intervals are sets simultaneously.

A witness above \(a\) that \(x\) is not a least representative
is a witness in both orders.  A global witness below \(a\)
gives a local set interval by restricting its tail and inserting
\(a\).  Conversely, a local witness equal to \(a\) can be
replaced by \(u\), using the displayed equality of tails.
Consequently the retained representatives strictly above \(a\)
agree exactly.  The point \(a\) is the local minimum and is
always retained.  This proves the successor clause.

At the final stage, a singleton global carrier contributes either
the same minimum or no point above \(a\).  Formula
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:anchored-history} therefore gives \(\{a\}\).
\end{proof}

Bare intersection with a noninitial convex interval is insufficient:
it can discard the interval's own minimum.  The anchor in
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:anchored-history} is the necessary correction.  For an
initial segment, the anchor already is the global minimum, so ordinary
restriction is enough.

\begin{corollary}[The exact criterion for a fixed schedule]
\label{swo:bw:ch:schedule-criterion}
For nonempty class well-orders \(W\) and \(\Gamma\), the
following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(W\) has a supplied canonical terminating history on
      \(\Gamma+1\);
\item \(W\) is class-isomorphic to an initial segment of
      \(P(\Gamma)\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The forward implication is \cref{swo:bw:ch:normal-form-theorem}.  For the
reverse implication, restrict the explicit history
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:polynomial-history} to the given initial segment and pull
it back through the supplied isomorphism.  Initiality and
\cref{swo:bw:ch:convex-restriction} verify the recursion clauses.  The
zero polynomial belongs to every nonempty initial segment, so the
pulled-back history terminates at its minimum.
\end{proof}

This criterion uses an actual initial-segment embedding as its
witness.  It does not invoke a class of order types or compare
unspecified cardinalities of class histories.

\subsubsection{Equivalence with strong class-well-order comparability}

Write \(\CWO\) for the assertion that, for every two class
well-orders, one is class-isomorphic to an initial segment of the
other, allowing the whole order as an initial segment.

\begin{theorem}[Exact strength of canonical histories]
\label{swo:bw:ch:equivalence}
Over \(\GBC\), the following principles are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\CWO\): strong class-well-order comparability;
\item \(\CTH\): every nonempty class well-order \(W\) admits
      its canonical history on the input-order schedule \(W+1\);
\item every nonempty class well-order admits a uniformly coded
      canonical terminating history on some class-well-order
      schedule \(\Gamma+1\);
\item every nonempty class well-order \(W\) is class-isomorphic
      to an initial segment of \(P(W)\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(2) implies (3).}
This is \cref{swo:bw:ch:input-bound}: the specified input-order history
terminates at its appended last stage.

\emph{(3) implies (1).}
Let \(R,S\) be two nonempty class well-orders on disjoint tagged
carriers, and form their ordered sum \(T=R+S\).  Apply (3) once,
to \(T\), obtaining a terminating history with some schedule
\(\Gamma+1\).  Its two anchored convex restrictions give
terminating histories for \(R\) and \(S\) on that same
schedule.  By \cref{swo:bw:ch:normal-form-theorem}, both are isomorphic
to initial subclasses of \(P(\Gamma)\).

Two initial subclasses of the same linear order are comparable by
inclusion: if neither included the other, choosing a point in each
set difference would contradict initiality in one direction or the
other.  Composing the map onto the smaller polynomial range with
the inverse map on the larger range gives the required initial-segment
isomorphism.  The maps and their ranges are elementary classes
defined from the one supplied history.  There is no choice of a
class witness for each member of a proper collection.  An empty
input order is handled separately and trivially.

\emph{(1) implies (4).}
We give an explicit argument that avoids assigning ordinals to class
well-orders.  First observe that every class order embedding
\(f:W\to W\) satisfies \(x\leq_W f(x)\) for all \(x\).
Otherwise choose the least counterexample \(x\).  Since
\(f(x)<_W x\), order preservation gives
\(f(f(x))<_W f(x)\), making \(f(x)\) an earlier counterexample.
Consequently there is no class order embedding \(W+1\to W\):
if \(a\) were the image of the appended last point, the restriction
to \(W\) would give
\[
                   a\leq_W f(a)<_W f(*)=a.
\]

Let \(\Gamma=W+1\).  The polynomial order
\(P(\Gamma)\) is a class well-order.  It contains an
embedded copy of \(W+1\), sending each exponent \(t\) to its
coefficient-one monomial \(e_t\).  Comparability between \(W\)
and \(P(\Gamma)\) cannot give an initial embedding
of the latter into \(W\), since composition would embed
\(W+1\) into \(W\).  Thus it supplies an initial-segment
embedding
\[
                   f:W\longrightarrow P(\Gamma).
\]
Its range lies strictly below \(e_*\).  If a polynomial at least
\(e_*\) lay in the range, initiality would put \(e_*\) and
every \(e_x\), for \(x\in X\), into the range.  Applying
\(f^{-1}\) to these monomials would again embed \(W+1\) into
\(W\).  The polynomials strictly below \(e_*\) are exactly
those supported on the original \(W\)-exponents, namely
\(P(W)\).  Hence \(f\) gives (4).

\emph{(4) implies (2).}
Apply \cref{swo:bw:ch:schedule-criterion} with \(\Gamma=W\).
Concretely, if \(f\) is the supplied initial-segment isomorphism,
define
\[
 H_i=\{x\in X:
          \supp(f(x))\subseteq\{j:i\leq_W j\}\},
 \qquad H_*=f^{-1}[\{0\}].
\]
This is one elementary class relation.  The polynomial history,
initial restriction, and pullback prove all the required clauses.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The surreal carrier alone suffices]
\label{swo:bw:ch:surreal-suffices}
In \cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence}, the history principle (2) is unchanged
if it is asserted only for class well-orders of the whole surreal
carrier \(\No\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Under Global Choice, a proper class with the restriction of a
set-like global well-order has type \(\Ord\).  Therefore every
proper class carrier has a class bijection with \(\No\).
Transporting a supplied order through that bijection, applying the
surreal-carrier history principle, and transporting both the label
and stage coordinates back gives the input-order history on the
original proper carrier.  For a nonempty set carrier, every interval
is a set, so the first successor stage is already its singleton
minimum and all later stages remain there.  Thus set carriers add
no further requirement.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{What the equivalence settles, and what it leaves separate}

The result identifies the exact condensation-history existence
principle with a familiar class-theoretic comparison principle:
\[
 \GBC\vdash\CTH\longleftrightarrow\CWO,
 \qquad
 \GBC+\ETR\vdash\CTH.
\]
Hamkins--Woodin prove that \(\ETR\) implies strong class-well-order
comparability and explicitly ask about converses among the relevant
ranking and comparison principles
\cite[Theorem~6 and Question~7]{HamkinsWoodin}.  Their Question~7 is
not settled here.  In particular, the presence of class-valued stages
does not by itself prove that \(\ETR\) is necessary.  Our theorem
provides an exact equivalence to \(\CWO\), without claiming an
equivalence to arbitrary elementary transfinite recursion.

It also preserves the distinction with native labelled lexicography.
The largest common labelled prefix of two supplied relations is
elementarily definable, and their next labels can be compared without
\(\CWO\) or a condensation history (\cref{swo:cf:lex}).  The stronger
principle arises when all the iterated quotient information is required
uniformly through a complete schedule.  These are different tasks.

\paragraph{Uniqueness and changes of the class collection.}
Two histories for the same input and schedule agree wherever both are
defined.  A least stage of disagreement is impossible: the first,
successor, and limit clauses all determine the slice from earlier
slices.  This is elementary induction with the two histories supplied
as parameters.  Consequently an extension of a GBC class collection
with the same sets may supply a previously unavailable history, but
cannot change an already available one.  The recursion clauses,
set-interval tests, and finite normal forms are elementary in the
shared classes and sets.  This is a uniqueness statement about
individual histories, not a class-valued choice function assigning a
history to every well-order.

\paragraph{A concrete full-model check.}
In a full inaccessible-universe interpretation
\((V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))\), the polynomial order
\(P(\Gamma)\) has ambient ordinal type
\(\kappa^\alpha\) when \(\Gamma\) has ambient type \(\alpha\).
Its coefficients range over the internal ordinals, externally
\(\kappa\), and its supports are finite.  Thus
\cref{swo:bw:ch:schedule-criterion} becomes exactly
\[
          \theta\leq\kappa^\alpha,
\]
where \(\theta\) is the ambient type of the input order.
This recovers the earlier exact height formula
\(\min\{\alpha:\theta\leq\kappa^\alpha\}\) for the relevant
nontrivial histories (source~20's \cref{swo:lm:con:ordinal-formula,swo:lm:con:full-model}).  The present proof
explains that calculation through canonical finite normal forms,
while remaining meaningful in arbitrary GBC realizations where
external ordinal types are not available internally.

\paragraph{Formalization boundary.}
A direct formalization can separate four interfaces: a class well-order
on set labels; a supplied history relation; the set-sized interval-rank
operation; and elementary comprehension and Class Replacement.
The floor-map and normal-form theorems then require no new recursion
axiom.  The finite polynomial codes belong to the set sort, and their
comparison uses only a finite support and the supplied stage order.
The existence theorem is a separate equivalence between two
second-order assertions, \(\CTH\) and \(\CWO\).

In a universe-relative type-theoretic implementation, the same proof
can be expressed with explicit smallness and an enclosing universe.
In a formalized two-sorted model, all claims of well-foundedness,
finiteness, and set-sized intervals must retain that model's
interpretation.  Neither approach permits forming an ordinary class
whose members are all class well-orders, all histories, or all of
their isomorphism classes.




\begin{note}[\merge; one height calculation, five times]\label{swo:xiv:note:heights}
In the full model $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ at an inaccessible
$\kappa$, internal set-interval condensation is condensation by intervals of
ambient cardinality below $\kappa$. Source~15's full-universe check
(\cref{swo:cb:cce:sec:histories}) and source~18's (\cref{swo:ix:note:selfsimilar})
identify one condensation with left division by $\kappa$; source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:con:ordinal-formula,swo:lm:con:full-model} iterate it to the
history $\{\kappa^\alpha\cdot\beta<\theta\}$ and the height
$\min\{\alpha:\theta\le\kappa^\alpha\}$, with every height $0<\alpha<\kappa^+$
attained and no universal schedule; source~23's universes section
(\cref{swo:tm:prop:boundedpoly}) computes that $P(\Gamma)$ has type
$\kappa^\beta$ when $\Gamma$ has type $\beta$, and source~29's ``concrete
full-model check'' above turns \cref{swo:bw:ch:schedule-criterion} into
$\theta\le\kappa^\alpha$. These agree. Source~20's corollary is the only one
to state the height spectrum and the attainment of the input-order bound.
\end{note}


\merge\ Source~23's Section~12 transports these polynomial orders into the
lexicographic order of all class well-orders of $\No$. Its
\cref{swo:tm:thm:densecomplexity} is new against the repository and against
Part~IX: it follows from the convexity of the fibres over a fixed set-like
head (source~11's \cref{swo:cf:fibers}) and source~15's polynomial histories,
but neither is stated with it.

\subsection{Source 23: arbitrary raw complexity inside global lexicographic intervals}\label{swo:tm:sec:densecomplexity}

Let $\Hsl$ be the virtual order of exhaustive class bijections
$e:\Ord\to\No$, and let $\Hall$ be the virtual order of all raw
well-orders on $\No$, both compared by the numerical label order.

\begin{lemma}[A set prefix is absorbed]\label{swo:tm:lem:absorb}
For every set ordinal $\sigma$ and every nonempty class well-order
$\Gamma$,
\[
 \sigma+P(\Gamma)\cong P(\Gamma)
\]
as class well-orders.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first set-interval block of $P(\Gamma)$ is $\Ord$, obtained by
varying only the least coordinate. The order $\sigma+\Ord$ is
isomorphic to $\Ord$: map the first block identically onto the ordinals
below $\sigma$ and the following ordinal $\xi$ onto $\sigma+\xi$.
The latter enumerates the ordinal tail beginning at $\sigma$.
Replace the first block by this isomorphism and leave the rest unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dense realization of prescribed raw hierarchies]\label{swo:tm:thm:densecomplexity}
In $\GBC$, let $e<f$ be two distinct members of $\Hsl$, and let
$\Gamma$ be any nonempty admitted class well-order. There exists a raw
well-order $H$ on $\No$ such that
\[
 e<_{\lex}H<_{\lex}f,
 \qquad H\cong P(\Gamma).
\]
In particular, every such interval realizes every positive set-ordinal
collapse rank and every prescribed class-indexed hierarchy of
\Cref{swo:tm:thm:polyhierarchy}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\delta$ be the first ordinal where $e$ and $f$ disagree, and let
$p=e\upharpoonright\delta=f\upharpoonright\delta$. This is a set
prefix. Choose a fresh surreal $c$ with
\[
 e(\delta)<c<f(\delta),\qquad c\notin\ran p,
\]
using \Cref{swo:tm:lem:fresh}. The remaining label class
$Y=\No\setminus(\ran p\cup\{c\})$ is proper. Transport the well-order
$P(\Gamma)$ to $Y$ by a class bijection and place it after the
prefix $p\cat(c)$.

The first disagreement with each endpoint occurs at the label $c$, so
$e<H<f$ regardless of the order chosen on $Y$. Its internal order type
is $(\delta+1)+P(\Gamma)$, which is $P(\Gamma)$ by
\Cref{swo:tm:lem:absorb}. The hierarchy is invariant under this
isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The precise density assertion]\label{swo:tm:n12.3}
The theorem concerns intervals whose endpoints are set-like exhaustive
enumerations. It does not assert the same statement for every nonempty
interval of $\Hall$: finite residual intervals and adjacent pairs are
counterexamples. Nor does it identify the condensation rank as an
invariant definable from the outer lexicographic order alone.
The extra structure is the relation encoded by an outer-order point.
\end{remark}

A useful consequence is that a research program restricted to the
canonical first set-like head cannot capture all internal order types
appearing locally in the raw enlargement. Beyond that head one encounters
hierarchies of any prescribed admitted well-ordered length. Nevertheless,
all the witnesses in the theorem are constructed by one fresh-letter
choice followed by a specified tail; the proof does not require a
simultaneous choice of tails for all possible class parameters.
