\subsection{Source 19: the exact external spectrum in countable class models}
\label{swo:rs:sec:cm-spectrum}

The distinction between internal and external finiteness yields a complete
answer to the countable-model question.  It also reveals a useful contrast:
the pure order has only two isomorphism types among countable GBC
realizations, but these types have the same first-order theory, and that
theory itself has the largest possible number of countable models.

Let $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)$ be an externally countable two-sorted
model of $\mathsf{GBC}$.  Its classes are the members of its admitted
class sort $\mathcal X$.  Write ${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ for
the external set of admitted class relations which $\mathcal M$ regards
as well-orders of its whole surreal carrier, and
${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ for the subset which it regards as
set-like.  Compare them by the labelled common-prefix lexicographic
comparison computed in $\mathcal M$.  This produces an actual external
linear order.  No external well-foundedness of the individual relations
is assumed.

For a countable nonempty collection $\mathcal A$ of nonempty order types,
let $\sigma(\mathcal A)$ denote the shuffle obtained by densely colouring
the rational order with those types and replacing each rational by the
corresponding chain.  Put
\[
 \mathcal F=\{n!:n\in\mathbb N\}=\{1,2,6,24,120,\ldots\},
 \qquad
 I_\infty=\omega+\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]
Here $\mathbb N$ is the external standard set of natural numbers, and
$\mathbb Z$ denotes its usual order.  The order $I_\infty$ has a first and a
last element.  Its external finite-distance components are an initial
$\omega$, a final $\omega^*$, and copies of $\mathbb Z$ densely indexed
between them.

\begin{theorem}[Exactly two countable GBC order types]
\label{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types}
For an externally countable model $\mathcal M$ of $\mathsf{GBC}$,
\[
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}\cong
 \begin{cases}
  \sigma(\mathcal F),&\mathcal M\text{ is }\omega\text{-standard},\\
  \sigma(\mathcal F\cup\{I_\infty\}),&
              \mathcal M\text{ is }\omega\text{-nonstandard}.
 \end{cases}
\]
In both cases ${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}\cong\mathbb Q$.
The two unrestricted orders are nonisomorphic but elementarily equivalent
in the pure language of linear orders.
\end{theorem}

The assertion concerns two possible types among GBC realizations,
conditional on the existence of the respective kinds of model.  It does
not say that their common first-order theory has only two countable
models.  We prove the classification first, and then give the stronger
first-order comparison.

\begin{note}[\merge; which clauses are earlier, and the two other proofs]\label{swo:xiv:note:countable}
Two clauses of \cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types} are in Part~IX: the
$\omega$-standard formula is source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}, and
${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}\cong\mathbb Q$ is source~13's \cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}
(the second clause of source~18's theorem), both by the proofs repeated
below. The $\omega$-nonstandard formula, the nonisomorphism and the
elementary equivalence are new against the repository and answer source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:n19.8}. Source~20 proves the same three clauses
(\cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy}) and source~21 as well
(\cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:nonstandard,swo:fu:fc:prop:elementary}); the three
proofs use the same nonstandard-interval lemma and the same finite-game
threshold. Source~19 obtains the elementary equivalence from the stronger
\cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-common-theory}, which needs no countability.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{The internal finite-tail partition}

The next constructions are first carried out internally in GBC.  They
apply to an infinite linearly ordered class whenever well-order completions
are available; for the surreal carrier, Global Choice supplies them.
They are parameterwise constructions of individual classes, not an
internal collection containing all class orders.

\begin{note}[Source~19, Lemma~12.2, ``The maximal finite terminal tail'']\label{swo:rs:lem:cm-tail}
\emph{
Every class well-order $R$ on an infinite carrier $X$ has a unique finite
terminal segment $T_R$ such that $R$ restricted to $X\setminus T_R$
has no greatest element.  Every finite terminal segment of $R$ is contained
in $T_R$.  Write $n(R)=|T_R|\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence} (Part~IX), with
the same proof; source~19 adds that in an $\omega$-nonstandard model the
stopping value may be nonstandard (the paragraph after the proof).
Sources~20 and~21 repeat it (\cref{swo:lm:mod:tail,swo:fu:fc:lem:tail}).
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~19's proof]
If $R$ has no greatest element, take the empty tail.  Otherwise remove
the greatest element and repeatedly remove the greatest remaining
element while one exists.  If the process did not stop at an internal
finite stage, ordinary set-valued recursion with class parameter $R$
would produce an internal descending $\omega$-sequence.  Class
Replacement makes its range a set, contradicting well-foundedness.
At the stopping stage the selected finite set is terminal and its
complement has no greatest element.  Each last-element or predecessor
step was unique, so the tail is unique, and every finite terminal
segment is among its initial sequence of removals.
\end{proof}

In an $\omega$-nonstandard model the stopping value $n(R)$ may be
nonstandard.  The lemma is an internal assertion and does not claim
that an external iteration through the standard natural numbers stops.

Let $B_R$ be the cylinder obtained by keeping $R$ unchanged on
$X\setminus T_R$ and permuting its $n(R)$ terminal labels.  These
cylinders partition the admitted orders: every member has the same
maximal terminal set and the same preceding prefix.  Each cylinder is
convex and has first and last elements.  Internally it is a finite chain
of size $n(R)!$.  More explicitly, the finite set of permutations of
$T_R$ belongs to $M$, and each permutation defines a class relation by
elementary comprehension.  Sorting the terminal labels in their ambient
order identifies their lexicographic permutations with the internal
finite linear order of size $n(R)!$.  Every admitted order in the
cylinder arises in this manner.

\begin{note}[Source~19, Lemma~12.3, ``Adjacency has finite residual carrier'']\label{swo:rs:lem:cm-adjacency}
\emph{
If $R<S$ are adjacent, their residual carrier after the first common
labelled prefix is finite.  In particular, an adjacency step cannot
leave the cylinder $B_R$.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:adjacency-finite-residual} (Part~IX) with
the same proof, and the finite-residual half of source~11's adjacency
criterion \cref{swo:cf:adjacency}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~19's proof]
Let $C$ be the common prefix, $Y=X\setminus C$, and let the first
unequal labels be $a<b$.  Keeping $C$ and the next label $a$ fixed,
the rest of the $R$-order must be the largest possible completion:
a larger completion would lie between $R$ and $S$.  Consequently each
successive label is the greatest unused label, so the reverse ambient
order well-orders $Y\setminus\{a\}$.  Dually, the ambient order
well-orders $Y\setminus\{b\}$.  Thus on
$Z=Y\setminus\{a,b\}$ both an order and its reverse are well-orders.
This forces $Z$ to be finite.  Otherwise successively taking the least
unused label would give an internal ascending $\omega$-sequence in one
order, hence a descending sequence in the other.  Therefore $Y$ is
finite.  It is a finite terminal segment of $R$, and so is contained
in $T_R$ by \Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-tail}.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~19, Lemma~12.4, ``Every prescribed internal tail occurs densely'']\label{swo:rs:lem:cm-dense-tails}
\emph{
Between two distinct cylinders there is a cylinder with
$n(R)=n$, for every prescribed $n\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder} followed by
\cref{swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail} (Part~IX), with the same two-change
argument, now read internally so that $n$ may be nonstandard; source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dense-colours} and source~21's \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:colors}
are the other copies.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~19's proof]
Take $R<S$ in different cylinders, with common prefix $C$, residual
carrier $Y$, and first unequal labels $a<b$.  The residual $Y$ is
infinite, since otherwise the two orders would belong to one finite-tail
cylinder.  We first find a whole cylinder inside $(R,S)$ with infinite
residual carrier.

One possible change is to keep an $R$-prefix through its label $a$,
then, at a later position outside $T_R$, replace the next label $x$
by a numerically larger unused label.  Its cylinder lies above $R$
and below $S$, and its residual is infinite.  A second possible change
does the dual operation in $S$: after retaining its label $b$, replace
a later label outside $T_S$ by a smaller unused label.

At least one change is possible.  Otherwise, on the infinite class
\[
 Z=Y\setminus\bigl(\{a,b\}\cup T_R\cup T_S\bigr),
\]
every earlier $R$-label would be numerically greater than every later
one, and every earlier $S$-label would be numerically smaller than
every later one.  The ambient order on $Z$ and its reverse would both
be well-orders, contradicting the argument in
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-adjacency}.  The new cylinder is different from
both endpoint cylinders, because its first disagreements with them
occur while the residual carrier is infinite.

In that residual carrier choose an $n$-element set $F$.  Well-order
the remaining carrier without a greatest element: use its infinite
initial cardinal if it is a set, or a set-like well-order of type
$\mathrm{Ord}$ if it is proper.  Append this order after the chosen
prefix and then append the labels of $F$.  The maximal finite terminal
tail is exactly $F$, as required.
\end{proof}

For the surreal carrier the full order has no endpoints: change the
first label upward or downward and complete the remaining carrier.
Every cylinder has endpoints, so its quotient has no endpoints either.
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-dense-tails} makes this quotient dense.  When the
class sort is externally countable the quotient is consequently a
copy of $\mathbb Q$.

\subsubsection{What a nonstandard finite interval looks like externally}

\begin{lemma}[The external shape of a nonstandard finite interval]
\label{swo:rs:lem:cm-nonstandard-interval}
In an externally countable nonstandard model of arithmetic, let $c$
be a nonstandard natural number.  The external order of the internal
interval $[0,c]$ has type
\[
 I_\infty=\omega+\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]
The arithmetic available in any GBC model suffices.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Declare $x\sim y$ when their arithmetic difference in absolute value
is a standard natural number.  This is precisely external finite
distance in $[0,c]$.  The component of $0$ consists of its standard
successors and has type $\omega$.  The component of $c$ consists of
its standard predecessors and has type $\omega^*$.  Every other
component has arbitrary standard predecessors and successors, and all
its members are obtained by those finitely iterated steps from any
chosen one.  It has type $\mathbb Z$.

The quotient has a first and a last component.  It is dense.  Indeed,
if $x<y$ belong to different components then $y-x$ is nonstandard,
and
\[
 z=x+\left\lfloor\frac{y-x}{2}\right\rfloor
\]
is at nonstandard distance from both endpoints.  A standard bound on
either half would give a standard bound on $y-x$.  Hence
$[x]<[z]<[y]$.  The open interval between the endpoint components is
a countable dense order without endpoints, so is a copy of
$\mathbb Q$.  This gives the displayed decomposition.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the isomorphism assertions in
\Cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types}]
In an $\omega$-standard model every $n(R)$ is standard, so every
cylinder has actual finite size $n(R)!$.  Their quotient is countable
and dense without endpoints, and every factorial size occurs densely
by \Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-dense-tails}.  Countable colour-preserving
back-and-forth gives $\sigma(\mathcal F)$.

In an $\omega$-nonstandard model the cylinders with standard tail
length again have actual factorial size.  If $n(R)$ is nonstandard,
then $n(R)!$ is nonstandard, and
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-nonstandard-interval} gives external type $I_\infty$.
These are all the possibilities.  Prescribing one fixed nonstandard
tail length shows that the $I_\infty$ colour occurs densely, and each
standard factorial colour is dense as before.  The same coloured
back-and-forth gives $\sigma(\mathcal F\cup\{I_\infty\})$.

For the set-like suborder, the first unequal ordinal position has a
set-sized common prefix.  Choose an unused surreal strictly between
the unequal next labels and complete the prefix to a global
enumeration.  The surreal set-cut property permits avoidance of the
set of previously used labels.  This gives internal and therefore
external density.  Varying the first label gives no endpoints, and
external countability gives $\mathbb Q$.  This argument never assumes
$\omega$-standardness.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Recovering the cylinders from the pure order}

The internal finite-tail partition is visible in the external pure
order through a single first-order formula.  This observation removes
any dependence on a hidden choice of presentation in the comparison
that follows.

Define
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{Adj}(x,y)
   &\;\Longleftrightarrow\;x<y\ \wedge\
               \neg\exists z\,(x<z<y),\\
 S(x)&\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
     \neg\exists y\,\operatorname{Adj}(y,x)
     \ \wedge\ \neg\exists y\,\operatorname{Adj}(x,y),\\
 E(x,y)&\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
     \neg\exists z\,
       \bigl(((x<z<y)\vee(y<z<x))\wedge S(z)\bigr).
\end{align*}

\begin{proposition}[Intrinsic cylinder equivalence]
\label{swo:rs:prop:cm-intrinsic}
In the external unrestricted order of any set-sized two-sorted GBC
model, $S$ picks out exactly the singleton cylinders, and $E(x,y)$
holds exactly when $x$ and $y$ belong to the same finite-tail cylinder.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A singleton cylinder has no immediate predecessor or successor,
because the quotient is dense.  In a larger internally finite
cylinder every point has at least one immediate neighbour inside
that cylinder, including its endpoints; the internal finite linear
order gives these neighbours even when it is externally infinite.
Thus these cylinders contain no $S$-points.  Consequently $E$ holds
within a cylinder.  Between distinct cylinders,
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-dense-tails} with tail length zero gives an
$S$-point, so $E$ fails.
\end{proof}

In the standard case $E$ is external finite condensation.  In the
nonstandard case a $I_\infty$-class contains many external finite-distance
components, so $E$ is strictly coarser.  In particular the two orders
in \Cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types} are not isomorphic: the second has
infinite $E$-classes and the first does not.  The sentence asserting
that every $E$-class is finite can be written in
$L_{\omega_1,\omega}$, using a countable disjunction of the finite
size formulas.  It is not a first-order sentence.

\subsubsection{One complete first-order theory for all GBC realizations}

The first-order comparison does not need external countability.

\begin{lemma}[Finite-game threshold]
\label{swo:rs:lem:cm-ef-threshold}
Let $h_r=2^r-1$.  Two finite chains of sizes at least $h_r$ are
$r$-equivalent.  The same conclusion holds if either chain is
replaced by an infinite discrete linear order with first and last
elements, in which every point other than an endpoint has its
corresponding immediate predecessor and successor.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the $r$-round Ehrenfeucht--Fraisse game.  With $s$ rounds left,
maintain the following invariant in each interval between matched
points, including the two end intervals: either the two intervals
have the same finite size below $h_s$, or both have at least $h_s$
points.  Initially the invariant holds.

For a short interval use its unique finite order isomorphism.  In a
large interval, if the newly selected point is within fewer than
$h_{s-1}$ points of one end, match that exact finite distance from
the corresponding end.  Otherwise choose a point leaving at least
$h_{s-1}$ points on each side.  The identity
$h_s=2h_{s-1}+1$ guarantees enough room.  Finite successor and
predecessor steps are available because the intervals have endpoints
and are discrete.  These choices preserve the invariant with
$s-1$ rounds left and therefore preserve the final finite order
pattern.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform complete theory]
\label{swo:rs:thm:cm-common-theory}
For every externally set-sized two-sorted model $\mathcal M$ of
$\mathsf{GBC}$, the pure external order
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ has the same complete first-order
theory
\[
 T=\operatorname{Th}\bigl(\sigma(\mathcal F)\bigr).
\]
In particular, the standard and nonstandard countable orders of
\Cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types} are elementarily equivalent.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix a quantifier rank $r$.  Colour a cylinder by its exact finite
factorial size if that size is below $h_r$, and merge all other
cylinders into one large colour.  Only finitely many colours remain.
Each occurs densely in the quotient: for the large colour prescribe
any standard factorial size at least $h_r$.  The quotient has no
endpoints.

In a finite game, match a newly visited quotient class to a class of
the same colour in the appropriate interval between previously
matched classes.  Density and absence of endpoints always permit
this.  Corresponding small cylinders are identical finite chains.
Corresponding large cylinders are $r$-equivalent by
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-ef-threshold}, since every internally finite
cylinder is externally discrete with endpoints.  Play a fixed
$r$-round winning game inside each matched pair of cylinders.
There are at most $r$ moves inside any one pair, and the quotient
matching preserves the order between pairs.  This gives an
$r$-round winning strategy for the whole orders.  As $r$ was
arbitrary, their complete theories agree.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A proper elementary suborder and an omitted type]
\label{swo:rs:cor:cm-elementary-suborder}
In the nonstandard countable order, the union $L_{\mathrm{fin}}$
of its genuinely finite $E$-classes is a proper elementary suborder
isomorphic to $\sigma(\mathcal F)$.  The partial type
\[
 p(x)=\{\text{the }E\text{-class of }x\text{ has at least }m
                       \text{ members}:1\le m<\omega\}
\]
is nonprincipal over $T$.  The standard shuffle omits it; every
point in a $I_\infty$-class of the nonstandard shuffle realizes it.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Deleting the $I_\infty$-coloured quotient points leaves a countable dense
order without endpoints in which all finite factorial colours are
dense.  Thus $L_{\mathrm{fin}}\cong\sigma(\mathcal F)$.
For elementarity fix a finite tuple from this suborder and a
quantifier rank $r$.  Repeat the preceding quotient matching while
fixing its parameter classes, and use the identity within those
finite parameter classes.  The same finite-game argument works for
every $r$ with the tuple fixed, proving elementarity.

The type is finitely satisfiable because factorial sizes are
unbounded, and its realization and omission are immediate from
the class sizes.  Were it isolated by a formula consistent with
the complete theory $T$, that formula would have a realization in
the standard shuffle and force a realization of $p$ there, a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The standard shuffle is the prime model]
\label{swo:rs:cor:cm-prime}
The standard shuffle is a countable atomic, and hence prime, model
of $T$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a finite tuple, specify its partition into $E$-classes, the
order of these classes, the finite size of each class, and the
exact position of each tuple entry in its class.  Each condition
is first-order expressible.  Their finite conjunction specifies
a single automorphism orbit: apply coloured-quotient
back-and-forth and the unique isomorphisms of the finite chains.
Consequently it isolates the tuple's complete type, establishing
atomicity.

For completeness, primeness follows by an elementary enumeration
argument.  Enumerate the standard shuffle and embed its elements
one at a time into any model of $T$.  At each step the isolated
type of the next finite tuple is consistent with, and extends,
the previously isolated tuple type; its existential realization
therefore follows from that preceding type.  The resulting union
is an elementary embedding.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The common theory has many other countable models}

The GBC classification is more restrictive than elementary
equivalence.  One can make this precise without appealing to an
abstract model-spectrum theorem.

\begin{theorem}[All countable orders occur inside countable models of $T$]
\label{swo:rs:thm:cm-many-models}
For every countable linear order $A$, put
\[
 J_A=\omega+\sum_{a\in A}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]
There is a countable model $L_A$ of $T$ with exactly one infinite
$E$-class, of type $J_A$.  Moreover,
\[
 L_A\cong L_{A'}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\cong A'.
\]
Consequently $T$ has $2^{\aleph_0}$ pairwise nonisomorphic
countable models.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Start with a rational quotient densely coloured by the finite
factorial sizes, choose one quotient point, and replace its chain
by $J_A$.  All other classes retain their prescribed finite
chains.  The order $J_A$ is infinite, discrete, and has first
and last elements.  The threshold argument of
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-ef-threshold} therefore applies.  After merging
the large colours at any fixed rank, all quotient colours remain
dense.  The same finite-game proof gives $L_A\models T$.

The formula $E$ recovers the displayed classes exactly, because
the singleton classes remain dense between them.  Thus an
isomorphism must preserve the unique infinite class.  Its external
finite-distance quotient is $1+A+1$: the endpoint components
are $\omega$ and $\omega^*$, and the interior components are
the indicated copies of $\mathbb Z$.  Removing the endpoint
components recovers $A$.  Conversely an isomorphism $A\cong A'$
extends to their $J$-classes, and a coloured rational
back-and-forth fixing the distinguished quotient point gives
$L_A\cong L_{A'}$.

There are $2^{\aleph_0}$ nonisomorphic countable linear orders.
For an explicit family, encode a binary sequence $(a_n)$ by
$\sum_{n<\omega}(\mathbb Z+(2+a_n))$.  Its finite-distance
components alternate a copy of $\mathbb Z$ and a finite chain
of length $2$ or $3$; their quotient has type $\omega$, so it
recovers the sequence.  This gives the lower bound for models
of $T$.  The upper bound is the usual count of relations on a
countable domain.
\end{proof}

The arithmetic midpoint in
\Cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-nonstandard-interval} explains why these other
models do not produce additional countable GBC realizations.
Within an internally finite nonstandard interval, its external
finite-distance quotient must be dense, forcing the interior
index order to be $\mathbb Q$ in a countable model.  The
prescribed-tail construction additionally forces such $I_\infty$-classes
to occur densely whenever the model is nonstandard.  These
conditions go beyond what the pure first-order theory can express.

\subsubsection{What the result does and does not forget}

For countable GBC realizations, the pure unrestricted order
remembers $\omega$-standardness up to isomorphism and forgets it
at the level of first-order theory.  Its theory is even independent
of the external size of the class model.  The theorem does not
classify expansions by the set-like predicate, evaluation at
surreal labels, birthday restrictions, named baselines, or coding
and definability information.  Those structures remain natural
places to look for dependence on the underlying set universe
and class realization.

All constructions above use elementary class comprehension,
ordinary set-valued recursion with supplied class parameters,
and Global Choice for completions.  They require neither ETR
nor an internal class of all class orders.  The quotient and
model-theoretic games are external set constructions, with their
scope explicitly fixed at the start.



% ---- source 20 (batch-83 manuscript 02), lines 2415-2910
\subsection{Source 20: two external order types for countable class models}
\label{swo:lm:mod:section}

The earlier continuation, source~18, classifies the raw
lexicographic order of an externally countable, $\omega$-standard model
of $\GBC$ as a shuffle of finite factorial chains
(\cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}). It asks what happens
when the model has nonstandard natural numbers (\cref{swo:sh:n19.8}). We now give the exact
classification in that case, including its external finite-condensation
blocks and its first-order theory. The classification concerns the
\emph{pure external linear order}; it discards the labels, the class
membership relation, and the predicate of set-likeness.

Let $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)\models\GBC$, with both sorts countable
in the ambient metatheory. Let ${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ be the external set of
those $R\in\mathcal X$ that $\mathcal M$ regards as class well-orders
of its surreal carrier. The comparison $R<S$ means that $\mathcal M$
satisfies the elementary labelled first-disagreement formula. Thus
``well-order'' and ``finite'' inside a construction below are initially
\emph{internal} notions. We never assume that $R$ is externally
well-founded. Internal linearity of the comparison nevertheless makes
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ an actual external linear order.

For a countable nonempty family $\mathcal A$ of countable order types,
write $\sigma(\mathcal A)$ for its \emph{dense shuffle}: colour
$\mathbb Q$ so that every colour in $\mathcal A$ is dense, and replace
each rational by a copy of its colour. The usual colour-preserving
back-and-forth proves uniqueness of the resulting order type. Put
\[
 \mathcal F=\{1,2,6,24,120,\ldots\}=\{n!:n\in\omega\},
 \qquad
 I_\infty=\omega+\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]
The sum in $I_\infty$ means a rationally ordered family of copies of
the integer order; it does not mean an ordinal product.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~8.1, ``Countable-model dichotomy'']\label{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy}
\emph{
For every externally countable $\mathcal M\models\GBC$,
\[
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}\cong
 \begin{cases}
   \sigma(\mathcal F),&\mathcal M\text{ is }\omega\text{-standard},\\[2pt]
   \sigma(\mathcal F\cup\{I_\infty\}),
       &\mathcal M\text{ is }\omega\text{-nonstandard}.
 \end{cases}
\]
These two orders are not isomorphic, but they are elementarily
equivalent in the language containing only $<$. In the nonstandard
case, the union of the blocks of standard finite size in the displayed
shuffle is an elementary suborder isomorphic to $\sigma(\mathcal F)$.}
This is source~19's \cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types} without its set-like
clause, together with the first clause of source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:cor:cm-elementary-suborder}; source~20's proof follows in the
lemmas below, the proof after \cref{swo:lm:mod:interval} and
\cref{swo:lm:mod:elementary}.
\end{note}

The proof separates an internally finite terminal permutation block
from an externally finite-distance block. Conflating these two
equivalence relations would give an incorrect classification.

\subsubsection{A coarse equivalence that remains valid internally}

For each admitted $R$, there is an internally finite terminal set
$T_R$ such that $R$ on $\No^{\mathcal M}\setminus T_R$ has no greatest
element. Write $n_R=|T_R|^{\mathcal M}\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$.
The following argument recalls the terminal-tail result with the
nonstandard interpretation made explicit.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~8.2, ``Internal terminal tails'']\label{swo:lm:mod:tail}
\emph{
The set $T_R$ exists uniquely and contains every internally finite
terminal segment of $R$.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence} (Part~IX) and
source~19's \cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-tail}, with the same proof.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Work inside $\mathcal M$. If there is no greatest label, take
$T_R=\varnothing$. Otherwise start with the greatest label and
successively take its immediate predecessor whenever there is one.
If this does not stop at some $n\in\omega$, ordinary set recursion
with the class parameter $R$ gives an $R$-descending sequence of
length $\omega$. Class Replacement makes its range a set, contradicting
the class well-order property. At the stopping stage the selected
finite terminal segment has a remainder with no greatest element.
Every finite terminal segment is obtained by finitely many of the
same uniquely determined predecessor steps, proving uniqueness and
maximality. In a nonstandard model the stopping value $n$ can be
nonstandard; the argument does not assert termination after a
standard finite number of external steps.
\end{proof}

For unequal $R,S$, let $C(R,S)$ be their largest common labelled
prefix. Its definition is elementary in the class parameters: a label
$x$ belongs to it exactly when the two predecessor classes of $x$
are equal and the two relations agree on that predecessor class.
Define an external relation on ${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ by
\[
 R\mathrel{E_{\mathcal M}}S
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 R=S\ \text{ or }\
 \mathcal M\models
 ``\No\setminus C(R,S)\text{ is a finite set}.''
\]
The formula on the right quantifies over a set coding the residual
carrier and a natural number. It does \emph{not} quantify over a
set of class relations or assert the existence of a finite sequence
whose entries are classes.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~8.3, ``The internal permutation blocks'']\label{swo:lm:mod:permutation}
\emph{
$E_{\mathcal M}$ is a convex equivalence relation. Its block through
$R$ consists exactly of the admitted orders that keep the prefix
$R\restriction(\No^{\mathcal M}\setminus T_R)$ fixed and permute
the internally finite set $T_R$. As an external linear order this
block is isomorphic to
\[
 [0,n_R!)^{\mathcal M}
   =\{i\in\omega^{\mathcal M}:\mathcal M\models i<n_R!\}
\]
with the model's natural-number order.}
This is the internal form of source~18's \cref{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks}
(Part~IX), as in source~19's paragraph after \cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-tail} and
source~21's \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:blocks}. Source~20 adds the coding argument
that identifies the external block with the model's interval $[0,n_R!)$,
including when $T_R$ is externally infinite.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
If the first-disagreement residual is internally finite, it is a
terminal segment in $R$, hence is contained in $T_R$ by
\cref{swo:lm:mod:tail}. The two orders therefore agree on the prefix outside
$T_R$. Conversely, two orders with that fixed prefix can first
disagree only inside $T_R$, so they are $E_{\mathcal M}$-equivalent.
Permuting $T_R$ leaves a remainder with no greatest element, so it
does not change the maximal terminal set. This proves transitivity;
reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. Convexity follows because
a fixed labelled prefix defines a convex lexicographic cylinder.

There is also a precise coding justification for the asserted block
size. Internally let $P$ be the set of permutations of $T_R$.
For $p\in P$, elementary class comprehension defines the order $R_p$
obtained by concatenating the fixed prefix with $p$. The construction
can be presented as one class of triples $(p,x,y)$ whose $p$-slice is
$R_p$. Its slices are classes, not elements of a set. Conversely,
the restriction of any admitted order in this cylinder to the set
$T_R$ is a set relation, by class separation, and hence is an
internal permutation code in $P$.

Inside the model, the lexicographic order on this finite set of
permutations is a chain of size $n_R!$, and therefore has an order
isomorphism with $[0,n_R!)$. The external interpretations of this
set isomorphism and of the slice construction give the claimed
external isomorphism. In particular, when $T_R$ is externally
infinite we are using the model's internally coded permutations,
not all externally existing permutations of its external carrier.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~8.4, ``Every internal tail size is dense in the coarse quotient'']\label{swo:lm:mod:dense-colours}
\emph{
The quotient ${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}/E_{\mathcal M}$ is a countable dense
linear order without endpoints. For every fixed
$n\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$, the blocks whose maximal terminal tail
has internal size $n$ occur densely in this quotient.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder,swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail}
(Part~IX) read internally, and source~19's \cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-dense-tails},
with the same argument.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
All constructions in this paragraph are performed inside the model.
Take $R<S$ in different $E_{\mathcal M}$-blocks. Let $C$ be their
common prefix, let $Y=\No\setminus C$, and let $a<b$ be their first
unequal numerical labels. The residual $Y$ is internally infinite.
We first find a prefix cylinder contained in $(R,S)$ whose residual
carrier is internally infinite.

One possible construction changes, in $R$, a label
$x\in Y\setminus(\{a\}\cup T_R)$ to a larger unused label while
retaining the prefix before $x$. The resulting cylinder stays above
$R$ and below $S$: the original next label $a$ is retained. Because
$x$ is outside $T_R$, the unused carrier at that position is
internally infinite, and remains so after choosing the replacement.
A second possible construction changes, in $S$, a label
$x\in Y\setminus(\{b\}\cup T_S)$ to a smaller unused label.
It has the symmetric properties.

At least one construction is possible. Otherwise, on the internally
infinite class
\[
 Z=Y\setminus(\{a,b\}\cup T_R\cup T_S),
\]
the restriction of $R$ would equal the reverse numerical order,
whereas the restriction of $S$ would equal the numerical order.
Both would be class well-orders. An infinite class cannot be
well-ordered in both directions: successively choosing the least
unused label in one direction produces an $\omega$-sequence
descending in the other, again with a set range. This contradiction
establishes the required cylinder. The first disagreements with
both original endpoints have infinite residual carriers, so its
members lie in blocks distinct from the endpoint blocks.

Let $P$ be its fixed prefix and $Y'$ its infinite residual carrier.
Given any $n\in\omega$, choose an $n$-element set $F\subseteq Y'$.
Well-order $Y'\setminus F$ without a greatest element. If this
carrier is a set, use an infinite initial cardinal as order type;
if it is a proper class, use a set-like well-order of type $\Ord$,
available from Global Choice. Append that order after $P$, and
then append $F$ in any order. Its maximal finite terminal tail is
exactly $F$. This construction works equally for a nonstandard
internal $n$.

Returning to the metatheory, these statements give density and
density of every indicated colour. Varying the first surreal label
below or above a given first label gives a different coarse block,
since the first residual is the entire internally infinite carrier.
Thus the quotient has no endpoints. It is countable because the
admitted class sort is externally countable.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{What an internally finite nonstandard interval looks like}

The arithmetic ingredient is classical; compare the decomposition of
countable nonstandard arithmetic models in \cite{Kach2004}. We give
the bounded-interval proof, since it identifies exactly which external
blocks occur here.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~8.5, ``The external type of a nonstandard finite interval'']\label{swo:lm:mod:interval}
\emph{
If $N\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$ is nonstandard, then externally
\[
 [0,N)^{\mathcal M}\cong I_\infty.
\]}
This is source~19's \cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-nonstandard-interval} for the
half-open interval $[0,N)$, with the same midpoint argument; source~21's
\cref{swo:fu:fc:lem:nonstandardinterval} is the third copy.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Two points of this interval have a finite external interval between
them exactly when their internal difference is a standard natural
number. The block containing $0$ consists of the standard natural
numbers and has order type $\omega$. The block containing $N-1$
consists of
\[
 N-1,\ N-2,\ N-3,\ldots
\]
and has order type $\omega^*$. These blocks are disjoint because
$N$ is nonstandard. A point outside them has nonstandard distance
from both endpoints; adding and subtracting standard integers
gives its entire finite-distance block, of type $\mathbb Z$.

The quotient of the remaining blocks is countable, dense, and has
no endpoints. If $a<b$ lie in different such blocks, $b-a$ is
nonstandard, and the model's integer midpoint
$\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor$ has nonstandard distance from both. It
therefore gives a strictly intermediate block. Given an interior
block represented by $a$, the points
$\lfloor a/2\rfloor$ and $\lfloor(a+N-1)/2\rfloor$ give interior
blocks respectively below and above it. Finally
$\lfloor N/2\rfloor$ gives at least one interior block. The quotient
is consequently isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$, proving the formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof of the isomorphism assertions in
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy}]
If the model is $\omega$-standard, \cref{swo:lm:mod:permutation} gives
precisely the finite chains of sizes $n!$. The colours $n=0$ and
$n=1$ both give the singleton type and can be merged. By
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dense-colours}, the quotient is a densely coloured copy
of $\mathbb Q$, proving the first formula.

If the model is $\omega$-nonstandard, standard $n$ still give these
same finite factorial chains. For every nonstandard $n$, the number
$n!$ is nonstandard, and \cref{swo:lm:mod:interval} identifies its block
with $I_\infty$. Merge all these nonstandard colours into the one
colour $I_\infty$. This colour is dense: choosing any one
nonstandard $n$ already gives a dense subcolour by
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dense-colours}. The standard factorial colours remain
dense. The countable colour-preserving back-and-forth now yields
$\sigma(\mathcal F\cup\{I_\infty\})$.

The standard shuffle has only finite finite-distance blocks,
whereas $I_\infty$ contains an infinite such block. Thus the two
external orders are not isomorphic. This conclusion needs no
assumption that a class well-order in the model is externally
well-founded.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[External finite condensation]
\label{swo:lm:mod:finite-condensation}
In the nonstandard case, the external finite-distance blocks of
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ have exactly the following order types:
\[
 1,2,6,24,120,\ldots,\quad \omega,\quad\omega^*,\quad\mathbb Z.
\]
The uncoloured finite-condensation quotient is $\mathbb Q$.
However, its block-type colours are not all dense: each coarse
$I_\infty$-block contributes a closed quotient interval whose first
point has colour $\omega$, whose last point has colour $\omega^*$,
and whose interior is a rational order entirely coloured $\mathbb Z$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Inside a coarse standard block, the entire finite chain is a single
finite-distance block. Inside a coarse nonstandard block, the proof
of \cref{swo:lm:mod:interval} gives its bottom $\omega$-block, its top
$\omega^*$-block, and its rationally indexed $\mathbb Z$-blocks.
No finite-distance block crosses between coarse blocks: between any
two distinct coarse blocks there are infinitely many others, by
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dense-colours}. These are therefore all the possibilities.

Any two distinct points of the finite-condensation quotient either
come from different coarse blocks, when coarse density supplies an
intermediate point, or come from the same $I_\infty$-block, when
\cref{swo:lm:mod:interval} supplies one. There are no endpoints and the
quotient is countable, so it is $\mathbb Q$. The colour description
follows from the same decomposition. In particular, replacing the
classification in \cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy} by a dense shuffle of the
displayed finite-distance block types would be wrong.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Elementary equivalence and an explicit elementary suborder}

The new infinite block cannot be detected by a single first-order
sentence because a sufficiently long finite factorial chain has the
same bounded-depth order behaviour. We make this argument precise,
including parameters.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~8.7, ``The finite-chain threshold strategy'']\label{swo:lm:mod:ef-threshold}
\emph{
Put $t_r=2^r-1$. A chain of at least $t_r$ elements that is finite
externally, and an internally finite chain of at least $t_r$ elements
in $\mathcal M$, satisfy the same $r$-round Ehrenfeucht--Fra\"iss\'e
game conditions in the pure order language. More generally, the
Duplicator wins whenever every corresponding gap between previously
matched points has either equal size below $t_r$, or size at least
$t_r$ on both sides.}
This is source~19's \cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-ef-threshold}, with the same
strategy; source~21 uses it inside the proof of
\cref{swo:fu:fc:prop:elementary}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Every nonempty gap in either chain has a least and a greatest point;
for the internally finite chain this assertion holds externally
because the internal endpoints are actual elements. Its size below
any fixed standard finite bound is also absolute. Maintain the
stated gap condition with $r$ remaining moves. The assertion for
$r=0$ is just preservation of the order of the selected points.

Suppose the next move divides a gap. If its size is less than
$t_r$, the corresponding gap has exactly the same finite size, and
the same-position response leaves identical gaps. Otherwise both
gaps have size at least
\[
 t_r=2t_{r-1}+1.
\]
If fewer than $t_{r-1}$ unselected points lie on one side of the
chosen point, match that finite distance from the corresponding
endpoint. The other remaining gap is large enough on both sides.
The two small-side cases cannot both occur. If neither occurs,
choose a point with at least $t_{r-1}$ unselected points on each
side in the corresponding gap. Such a point exists by the displayed
inequality, for example by counting $t_{r-1}$ points from its left
endpoint. The condition with $r-1$ remaining moves follows.
Induction gives the strategy.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~8.8, ``An elementary standard part of the external order'']\label{swo:lm:mod:elementary}
\emph{
Suppose $\mathcal M$ is $\omega$-nonstandard, and let
\[
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}_{\mathrm{std}}
 =\{R\in {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}:n_R\text{ is a standard natural number}\}.
\]
This is a union of coarse blocks, and
\[
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}_{\mathrm{std}}\cong\sigma(\mathcal F),
 \qquad
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}_{\mathrm{std}}\preccurlyeq {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}
\]
as pure linear orders. Standardness in this definition is an
external condition, not a claimed internal predicate.}
This is the first clause of source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:cor:cm-elementary-suborder} (its $L_{\mathrm{fin}}$ is the present
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}_{\mathrm{std}}$), with the same quotient-matching
proof; with \cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy} it gives the countable case of
source~19's \cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-common-theory}.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
The standard factorial colours are dense in the coarse quotient,
so restricting to them gives a densely coloured rational order.
This proves the isomorphism assertion.

Fix a finite tuple of parameters in ${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}_{\mathrm{std}}$
and a standard number $r$ of game rounds. Pair every coarse block
containing a parameter with itself, matching the whole finite
chain identically. During the game maintain an order-preserving
matching between the finitely many coarse blocks visited so far.
Each paired pair of blocks is either two identical-size finite
factorial chains, or one $I_\infty$-block and a finite factorial
chain of size at least $t_r$.

If a move visits a new coarse block, choose a fresh matching block
in the corresponding open interval of the other quotient, or in
the corresponding ray. Every standard factorial colour is dense
and unbounded there. Match a finite block by its same size. Match
an $I_\infty$-block by any factorial size at least $t_r$. Start the
local strategy of \cref{swo:lm:mod:ef-threshold} in the selected pair of
blocks. If the move visits an already paired block, continue its
local strategy. At most $r$ moves occur in any one pair, and moves
in different blocks are compatible because the quotient matching
preserves order.

This supplies a winning strategy for every finite $r$, with the
given parameters fixed. The Ehrenfeucht--Fra\"iss\'e criterion
therefore gives the elementary inclusion. Together with the
previous isomorphism results, this proves the elementary-equivalence
assertion of \cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy}.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Corollary~8.9, ``A type that distinguishes the two countable orders'']\label{swo:lm:mod:successor-type}
\emph{
Let
\[
 \operatorname{Succ}(x,y)\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
 x<y\ \land\ \neg\exists z\,(x<z<y).
\]
The partial one-variable type asserting that $x$ begins a chain of
$k$ successive immediate successors, for every standard $k$, is
finitely satisfiable but omitted in $\sigma(\mathcal F)$ and is
realized in $\sigma(\mathcal F\cup\{I_\infty\})$.}
This is the phenomenon of the second clause of source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:cor:cm-elementary-suborder}, with a different nonprincipal
type: source~19's type bounds the size of the class of $x$ under its formula
$E$, source~20's counts immediate successors; source~20 adds the dual type
and the points realizing both.
\end{note}
\begin{proof}[Source~20's proof]
Arbitrarily long finite factorial chains witness finite
satisfiability. In the standard shuffle every point belongs to a
finite block, and successive immediate successors cannot cross a
coarse boundary, so no point realizes the whole type. In an
$I_\infty$-block, every point of its bottom $\omega$-block realizes
it. Dually there is a type asserting arbitrarily many successive
immediate predecessors, realized in the top $\omega^*$-block.
Every point in one of the middle $\mathbb Z$-blocks realizes both
types simultaneously.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Decidability of the common pure-order theory]
\label{swo:lm:mod:decidability}
The common first-order theory of the two orders in
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy}, in the language containing only $<$, is
decidable.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Given a sentence $\varphi$, compute its quantifier rank $r$ and put
$t_r=2^r-1$. Let $s_r$ be the least factorial in $\mathcal F$ that
is at least $\max\{1,t_r\}$, and form the finite, effectively
computable set
\[
 \mathcal F_r=\{s\in\mathcal F:s<t_r\}\cup\{s_r\}.
\]
The quotient-matching strategy used in \cref{swo:lm:mod:elementary},
together with \cref{swo:lm:mod:ef-threshold}, shows that both original
orders are $r$-equivalent to $L_r=\sigma(\mathcal F_r)$.
Indeed, pair a newly visited block of size less than $t_r$ with
the identical finite size, and pair any larger block, including
$I_\infty$, with size $s_r$. Conversely, every block size appearing
in $L_r$ is available densely in the original order. All paired
blocks are either isomorphic or above the local $r$-round threshold.
It therefore suffices to decide whether $L_r\models\varphi$.

For completeness, this last decision is effective as follows.
Consider a rational dense linear order $D_r$ with unary predicates
$P_s$, for $s\in\mathcal F_r$, partitioning it into dense colours.
Let $K=\max\mathcal F_r$. Represent $L_r$ as the pairs $(q,i)$ with
$0\leq i<K$ and
\[
 D_i(q):=\bigvee_{\substack{s\in\mathcal F_r\\i<s}}P_s(q),
\]
ordered lexicographically, first by $q$ and then by $i$.
This is an effective finite-tag interpretation: for fixed tags,
equality translates to equality of the rational coordinates and
equality of the tags, and
\[
 (q,i)<(q',j)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 q<q'\ \lor\ (q=q'\land i<j).
\]
Translate an existential quantifier over a point into the finite
disjunction
$\bigvee_{i<K}\exists q\,(D_i(q)\land\cdots)$, translating the
subformula with that tag fixed. Boolean operations and universal
quantifiers are handled recursively. This produces a sentence in
the finite language of $D_r$.

The theory of a dense linear order without endpoints partitioned
into finitely many dense colours has effective quantifier
elimination. To eliminate one existential quantifier, put the
quantifier-free formula into disjunctive normal form. In each
conjunction, the quantified point either equals a parameter, lies
in an interval between parameters, or lies in an outer ray. Test
the equality cases directly. For a nonempty interval or ray,
existence is equivalent to compatibility of the finitely many
colour conditions, since every permitted colour is dense and
unbounded. Inconsistent order or colour conditions give false.
These tests are finite Boolean combinations of comparisons and
colours of the parameters. Repeated elimination reduces the
translated sentence to true or false and decides $\varphi$.
The procedure concerns the pure-order reduct only; it does not
decide the class theory or an expansion by evaluation or
set-likeness predicates.
\end{proof}

Thus the two pure countable order types record whether the model's
natural numbers are standard, but their first-order theories do
not. Within either side of the dichotomy, the bare order loses all
further information about the particular model and its admitted
classes. In particular, it cannot recover the model's arithmetic,
its class realization, or which labelled well-orders were originally
supplied. These conclusions concern the reduct to $<$; an expansion
retaining set-likeness, label evaluation, internal permutation ranks,
or the internal natural-number sort can retain substantially more
information. The expanded structures remain separate research
questions. No claim of elementary equivalence for those expansions
is made here.



% ---- source 21 (batch-83 manuscript 03), lines 2059-2536
\subsection{Source 21: finite tails, intrinsic blocks, and countable realizations}
\label{swo:fu:fc:sec}

The largest-common-prefix comparison and the exact adjacency criterion
are baseline results of the audited repository
(\cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:cf:adjacency}).  We now
derive a more complete description of the resulting finite blocks,
their automorphisms, and their behavior in countable models.  The proofs
are included; no claim of historical priority is needed.  A crucial
qualification is that an internally finite block need not be externally
finite in a nonstandard model.

Throughout this section, the carrier is $X=\No$, although the local
arguments apply to any infinite linearly ordered carrier admitting the
required well-orders.  Write $L=\Hall(\No)$ when speaking virtually.
For a two-sorted model $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)\models\GBC$, write
$L^{\mathcal M}$ for the \emph{external} collection of its admitted class
well-orders, equipped with the externally interpreted lexicographic
formula.  Assertions involving quotient sets, automorphism groups, or
topological derivatives are made in such an external realization.  Their
finite-variable ingredients remain formulas of class theory.

\subsubsection{The canonical terminal tail}

The blocks in this section are blocks \emph{of the lexicographic order
of well-orders}.  They must not be confused with the set-interval blocks
inside an individual non-set-like class well-order.

\begin{definition}[Maximal finite terminal tail]\label{swo:fu:fc:def:tail}
For an admitted class well-order $R$ on $X$, let
\[
 T_R=\{x\in X:\{y\in X:x\le_R y\}\text{ is a finite set}\}.
\]
When working in a model, ``finite'' in this formula means finite in that
model.  Put $C_R=X\setminus T_R$, let $P_R=R\restr C_R$, and write
$n(R)=\card{T_R}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~10.2, ``Existence of the maximal finite tail'']\label{swo:fu:fc:lem:tail}
\emph{
The class $T_R$ is a finite final segment, possibly empty.  Its complement
$C_R$ is nonempty and has no $R$-greatest element.  Moreover,
$n(R)=0$ exactly when $R$ has no greatest element.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence} (Part~IX);
source~21 obtains $T_R$ by one comprehension instead of the predecessor
recursion.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Elementary comprehension defines $T_R$.  If it is nonempty, let $x_0$ be
its $R$-least element.  The final segment beginning at $x_0$ is finite
by definition, and every point of that segment also has a finite final
segment.  Minimality of $x_0$ shows that this segment is exactly $T_R$.
Since $X$ is infinite, $C_R$ is nonempty.  If it had greatest element $c$,
the final segment beginning at $c$ would consist of $c$ together with
$T_R$, contradicting $c\notin T_R$.  Finally, a nonempty finite final
segment has a greatest element, while the greatest element of $R$, if
present, belongs to $T_R$.
\end{proof}

Let $B(R)$ consist of the orders obtained by retaining $P_R$ as an initial
labeled prefix and appending an arbitrary permutation of $T_R$.  This
family requires no choice of a class for each permutation.  If
$n=n(R)$ and $\pi:n\to T_R$ is a set bijection, its member is given by
the single elementary formula
\begin{align*}
 xR_\pi y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad&
 (x,y\in C_R\text{ and }xRy)\\
 &{}\lor(x\in C_R\text{ and }y\in T_R)\\
 &{}\lor(x,y\in T_R\text{ and }\pi^{-1}(x)<\pi^{-1}(y)).
\end{align*}
The set of bijections $n\to T_R$ together with this formula defines one
uniform class relation encoding the whole family.  Thus ordinary
$\GBC$ comprehension suffices; no class-choice principle is being used.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~10.3, ``Exact terminal permutation blocks'']\label{swo:fu:fc:thm:blocks}
\emph{
Let $E(R,S)$ mean that $R=S$, or that the complement of the maximal
common labeled prefix of $R,S$ is finite.  Then
\[
 E(R,S)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\in B(R).
\]
In particular, $E$ is an equivalence relation.  Its classes are convex
chains of size $n(R)!$, ordered as the ordinary finite lexicographic
permutation order; here $0!=1$.  Each class has a least and a greatest
member.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks} together with
source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation} (Part~IX), in the internal form of
source~20's \cref{swo:lm:mod:permutation}; source~21 adds the single uniform
formula $R_\pi$ coding the whole block.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
If $S$ permutes $T_R$ after $P_R$, the common-prefix residual is contained
in $T_R$ and is finite.  Conversely, suppose $R,S$ share an initial
labeled prefix $P$ with finite residual carrier $F$.  Every point of
$F$ has finitely many successors in both orders.  A point of $P$ has
finitely many successors in $R$ exactly when it does in $S$: the
restrictions to $P$ agree, and both remaining carriers equal the same
finite set $F$.  Consequently $T_R=T_S$, and the orders agree off this
set.  This proves the equivalence and transitivity.

A fixed-prefix cylinder is convex: an order that first departs from the
prefix compares with every completion of the prefix in the same
direction.  Hence $B(R)$ is convex.  Its uniform set codes are the
permutations of the $n(R)$-element set $T_R$, and lexicographic comparison
of the codes is exactly comparison of their appended finite words.
The least and greatest append the labels in increasing and decreasing
native order, respectively.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Corollary~10.4, ``Intrinsic finite condensation'']\label{swo:fu:fc:cor:intrinsic}
\emph{
In an $\omega$-standard model, or in an external realization where these
tails are genuinely finite, $E(R,S)$ holds exactly when the closed
lexicographic interval between $R$ and $S$ is finite.  Thus the possible
finite-condensation block sizes are
\[
                         1,2,6,24,120,\ldots.
\]
For a nonsingleton block its intrinsic size $n!$ recovers $n\ge2$.
Singleton blocks combine the possibilities $n=0$ and $n=1$.}
This is the external reading of source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation}
and source~18's \cref{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks} (Part~IX), with the same
proof.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
An $E$-class is finite and convex.  Conversely, list a finite interval as
$R=T_0<T_1<\cdots<T_k=S$.  Each consecutive pair is adjacent in the full
order.  The baseline adjacency theorem says that its common-prefix
residual is finite.  Transitivity of $E$ gives $E(R,S)$.  In a model this
argument uses $\omega$-standardness precisely to turn the internally
finite residuals supplied by that theorem into externally finite sets.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{A dense quotient with every factorial color}

The following result uses the explicit internal equivalence $E$.  It is
valid internally even when $\omega$ is nonstandard.  Statements about a
virtual quotient are abbreviations for their formulations using a finite
number of class variables.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~10.5, ``Density of each tail length'']\label{swo:fu:fc:thm:colors}
\emph{
The quotient by $E$ is dense and has no endpoints.  Between any two
distinct $E$-classes, for every $n\in\omega$, there is a class represented
by an order with maximal finite tail of length exactly $n$.  In
particular, the tail lengths $0$ and $1$ are separately dense, although
both give singleton blocks.}
This is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail} (Part~IX) and source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-dense-tails}. Source~21's proof differs: it passes to the
greatest and least members $R^+$, $S^-$ of the two boundary blocks and uses
their non-adjacency, instead of the two-change argument.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Suppose $B(R)<B(S)$.  Let $R^+$ be the greatest member of $B(R)$ and
$S^-$ the least member of $B(S)$.  They cannot be adjacent, because the
adjacency theorem would put them in the same $E$-class.  Choose
\[
                         R^+<T<S^-.
\]
The class of $T$ differs from both boundary classes.  This already proves
density of the quotient.

For the prescribed tail length, compare $T$ with each boundary.  The
two common prefixes are nested initial segments of $T$.  Let $C$ be
the larger one and let $t$ be the first $T$-label after $C$.  The residual
$X\setminus C$ is infinite: otherwise $T$ would be $E$-equivalent to
the corresponding boundary.  Thus
\[
                          Y=X\setminus(C\cup\{t\})
\]
is infinite.  Every completion of $T\restr(C\cup\{t\})$ remains
strictly between $R^+$ and $S^-$, because this prefix includes the two
first disagreements determining those inequalities.

Choose an $n$-element set $F\subseteq Y$ and a countably infinite set
$Z\subseteq Y\setminus F$.  One can obtain these sets from successive
least elements of the restricted order $T$: ordinary set recursion with
the class parameter and class replacement suffice.  Let
$K=Y\setminus(F\cup Z)$.  Complete the fixed prefix by
\[
              (T\restr K)\; +\; \text{an $\omega$-ordering of $Z$}
              \; +\; \text{an ordering of $F$}.
\]
Concatenation of these finitely many class well-orders is again a class
well-order.  The displayed $\omega$-part has no greatest element, so
the maximal finite terminal tail of the result is exactly $F$.  This
construction is uniform in its set parameters and does not choose from
a family of nonempty collections of classes.

Finally, the full lexicographic order has no endpoints: replace an
order's first label by a smaller or larger surreal and put the remaining
labels afterward.  Since every $E$-class has endpoints, the quotient
also has no endpoints.
\end{proof}

The proof deliberately does not presume that native surreal density
survives an arbitrary proper-class prefix.  Such a prefix may already
have exhausted all labels in a native open interval.  What is used is a
later completion cylinder with infinite residual carrier.

\begin{definition}[Rational shuffle]\label{swo:fu:fc:def:shuffle}
For a countable list of nonempty countable order types $A_i$, let
$\sigma(\{A_i\})$ denote the lexicographic sum over a copy of $\mathbb Q$
partitioned into dense color classes $Q_i$, with each point of $Q_i$
replaced by a copy of $A_i$.  Back-and-forth for countably colored dense
orders shows that its isomorphism type does not depend on the chosen
dense partition.
\end{definition}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Corollary~10.7, ``Countable standard realization'']\label{swo:fu:fc:cor:standard}
\emph{
If $\mathcal M\models\GBC$ is externally countable and $\omega$-standard,
then
\[
                    L^{\mathcal M}\cong
                    \sigma(\{1,2,6,24,120,\ldots\}).
\]}
This is the first clause of source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle} (Part~IX), with the same
proof.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
By \cref{swo:fu:fc:cor:intrinsic,swo:fu:fc:thm:colors}, the external condensation
quotient is countable dense without endpoints, with every listed block
size dense.  The colored back-and-forth theorem identifies its quotient
with the corresponding colored rational order, and the finite blocks
then determine the lexicographic sum.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Automorphism lifting and a failure of reconstruction}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~10.8, ``Automorphisms of finite blocks'']\label{swo:fu:fc:thm:aut}
\emph{
In the setting of \cref{swo:fu:fc:cor:intrinsic}, let $D$ be the external
finite-condensation quotient and color $d\in D$ by its block size $c(d)$.
Then
\[
                         \operatorname{Aut}(L,<_{\lex})
                         \cong \operatorname{Aut}(D,<,c).
\]
The induced map on the quotient determines the automorphism uniquely.}
This is the automorphism clause of source~18's \cref{swo:sh:n16.9}
(Part~IX), with the same proof; the orbit description in the next paragraph is
its orbit clause.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
An increasing automorphism preserves finiteness of closed intervals,
hence preserves the condensation equivalence and the size of each
class.  Conversely, a color-preserving quotient automorphism lifts by
the unique increasing bijection between each finite block and its
target.  The union of these bijections is an increasing bijection of
$L$.  Uniqueness follows from rigidity of finite chains.
\end{proof}

In the countable standard realization, two points are in the same
automorphism orbit exactly when their blocks have the same size and they
have the same rank inside those blocks.  Sufficiency follows by extending
a one-point color-preserving map on the rational quotient; necessity
follows from \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:aut}.

\begin{corollary}[A greatest element is not intrinsic]
\label{swo:fu:fc:cor:notrecoverable}
In a countable $\omega$-standard realization, there is an automorphism
of the pure lexicographic order taking a represented well-order with no
greatest element to one with a greatest element.  Such an automorphism
cannot be induced by any fixed relabeling bijection of the surreal
carrier.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:colors}, choose orders of tail lengths $0$ and $1$.
Both are singleton blocks, and colored rational-order homogeneity maps
one block to the other.  Lift that map using \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:aut}.
\Cref{swo:fu:fc:lem:tail} distinguishes existence of a greatest element in the
represented orders.  Relabeling preserves the abstract order type of
every represented well-order and therefore cannot have this effect.
\end{proof}

\merge\ The automorphism is the one used in the proof of source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable}, which exchanges a set-like
order with one of type $\Ord+1$; the clause on relabelings is source~21's.

This is a concrete limit on recovering enumeration structure from the
pure lexicographic order.  It also answers an automorphism question more
strongly than merely exhibiting numerical relabelings.  The countable
homogeneity argument must not be silently transferred to arbitrary
uncountable class realizations.

\subsubsection{The nonstandard correction}

External countability does not imply $\omega$-standardness.
Consequently, an unconditional claim that every countable realization
has the finite-factorial shuffle type would be false.  The correction
has an exact form.

\begin{note}[Source~21, Lemma~10.10, ``An externally infinite finite interval'']\label{swo:fu:fc:lem:nonstandardinterval}
\emph{
Let $\mathcal M$ be externally countable, and let $N\in\omega^M$ be
nonstandard.  The external order on the internal arithmetic interval
\[
                      I_N=\{i\in\omega^M:i<^M N\}
\]
has type
\[
                   I_\infty=\omega+\sum_{q\in \mathbb Q}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]}
This is source~19's \cref{swo:rs:lem:cm-nonstandard-interval} and source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:mod:interval}, with the same midpoint argument.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Externally declare $i\sim j$ if their internal arithmetic difference
is at most some \emph{standard} natural number.  The class of $0$ is
the standard natural numbers and has type $\omega$.  The class of
$N-1$ consists of $N-1-k$ for standard $k$ and has type $\omega^*$.
Every other class has type $\mathbb Z$: it consists of the elements $i+k$ for
standard integers $k$, and both distances to the endpoints are
nonstandard.

The quotient of the interior $\mathbb Z$-classes is nonempty, countable, dense,
and has no endpoints.  If $i<j$ represent distinct classes, $j-i$ is
nonstandard, so the internally computed midpoint
$\lfloor(i+j)/2\rfloor$ represents a strictly intermediate class.
For an interior $i$, the element $\lfloor i/2\rfloor$ gives a class
strictly between the initial class and that of $i$; the symmetric
construction works near the upper endpoint.  The interior quotient
therefore has type $\mathbb Q$.  Taking the ordered sum of its classes proves
the formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Theorem~10.11, ``Exact countable nonstandard realization'']\label{swo:fu:fc:thm:nonstandard}
\emph{
If $\mathcal M\models\GBC$ is externally countable and
$\omega$-nonstandard, then
\[
                   L^{\mathcal M}\cong
                   \sigma(\{1,2,6,24,120,\ldots,I_\infty\}),
 \qquad I_\infty=\omega+\sum_{q\in \mathbb Q}\mathbb Z+\omega^*.
\]
In particular it is not isomorphic to the order in
\cref{swo:fu:fc:cor:standard}.}
This is the $\omega$-nonstandard clause of source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types} and of source~20's \cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy};
the nonisomorphism is proved by the same finite-condensation invariant.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
Use the external interpretation of the internal equivalence $E$.
\Cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:blocks} states internally that each class is the finite
permutation order on $n$ labels for some $n\in\omega^M$.  Its ordinary
lexicographic rank gives an internal order isomorphism with $I_{n!}$.
The uniformly coded family preceding \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:blocks} includes
every such permutation.  Conversely, a class order on an internally
finite set is a set relation, hence corresponds to one of these
permutation codes.  Thus this internal isomorphism is also an external
bijection between the entire $E$-class and $I_{n!}$.

For standard $n$ the block is the actual finite chain of size $n!$.
For nonstandard $n$, its internal factorial is nonstandard, and
\cref{swo:fu:fc:lem:nonstandardinterval} gives the external type $I_\infty$.
The external quotient by $E$ is countable dense without endpoints by
\cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:colors}.  Every standard factorial color is dense.  Fix
one nonstandard $n$; the same internal theorem says that its prescribed
tail length occurs between every two distinct classes, so the external
color $I_\infty$ is also dense.  Colored back-and-forth proves the asserted
shuffle representation.

The $I_\infty$ blocks have externally infinite finite-condensation classes
of types $\omega$, $\mathbb Z$, and $\omega^*$.  None joins a neighboring
$E$-block: the endpoints of a maximal terminal permutation block have
no immediate neighbors outside it, by the internal adjacency theorem.
The finite-factorial shuffle has only finite condensation classes.
This intrinsic distinction proves nonisomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exactly what is being transferred]\label{swo:fu:fc:rem:transfer}
The preceding theorem does not assume that every admitted class
well-order is externally well-founded.  Internal well-orderhood and the
proved internal formulas supply the external linear order, its explicit
$E$-blocks, and the dense-color witnesses.  It is precisely the external
notion of finite condensation that changes in a nonstandard model.
Calling its $I_\infty$ blocks ``finite-condensation blocks'' externally would
therefore be incorrect.
\end{remark}

\begin{note}[Source~21, Proposition~10.13, ``Different orders, the same elementary theory'']\label{swo:fu:fc:prop:elementary}
\emph{
The two countable orders
\[
 A=\sigma(\{1,2,6,24,\ldots\}),\qquad
 B=\sigma(\{1,2,6,24,\ldots,I_\infty\})
\]
are elementarily equivalent in the pure language $\{<\}$, although
they are not isomorphic.}
This is the countable case of source~19's \cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-common-theory}
and the elementary-equivalence clause of source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:mod:dichotomy}. Source~21's strategy differs: it plays an
$I_\infty$-block against a single finite factorial block of size at least
$2t_r+1$ instead of merging large colours.
\end{note}

\begin{proof}[Source~21's proof]
We give a winning strategy for every finite Ehrenfeucht--Fra\"iss\'e
game.  The displayed shuffle blocks are an auxiliary device for the
strategy; no block predicate or color is added to the language.
With $r$ rounds remaining, put $t_r=2^r-1$.  Match the finitely many
blocks containing selected points in quotient order.  Inside every
matched pair, require each corresponding gap between selected points,
including the initial and final gaps, to have either the same size
less than $t_r$, or at least $t_r$ points on both sides.

The standard finite-chain splitting argument preserves this invariant.
Indeed, $t_r=2t_{r-1}+1$.  In equal short gaps copy the position exactly.
In a pair of long gaps, if the new point leaves fewer than $t_{r-1}$
points on one side, copy that distance from the corresponding endpoint;
the other side still has at least $t_{r-1}$ points.  If both resulting
sides are long, choose a point leaving at least $t_{r-1}$ points on each
side.  This works in $I_\infty$ as well: every nonempty gap determined by finitely
many selected points has a least and a greatest element, and successor
or predecessor steps realize every required finite endpoint distance.

When a move enters a previously unmatched finite block, choose a fresh
block of exactly the same size in the other quotient interval.  Such
blocks occur densely, and one can copy the selected position.  When a
move enters a previously unmatched $I_\infty$ block, with $r$ rounds left after
this move, choose a fresh finite factorial block of size at least
$2t_r+1$.  Match the selected point by copying a side of size less than
$t_r$, if present; otherwise leave at least $t_r$ points on both sides.
The dense factorial colors always supply the required block in the
correct quotient interval.  Existing matched gaps satisfy the weaker
invariant for the new number of remaining rounds.

After the last round the matching preserves order and equality.  Thus
the strategy wins every finite game, proving elementary equivalence.
Nonisomorphism was proved by the external finite-condensation invariant
in \cref{swo:fu:fc:thm:nonstandard}.
\end{proof}

\merge\ The following group description of the nonstandard order is
source~21's alone.

There is also a useful group description.  In the nonstandard
countable order, let $F$ be the set of points having an externally finite
condensation class.  Its convex components are the standard factorial
blocks, and the convex components of its complement are the $I_\infty$ blocks.
Indeed, between any two distinct $E$-classes there are blocks of both
kinds.  Thus this partition is intrinsic, even though individual
nonstandard tail lengths are forgotten.  After choosing identifications
of its $I_\infty$ blocks, one obtains
\[
 \operatorname{Aut}(L^{\mathcal M})\cong
 \left(\prod_{q\text{ colored }I_\infty}\operatorname{Aut}(I_\infty)\right)
 \rtimes \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Q,<,\text{colors}).
\]
The kernel and quotient are intrinsic; the displayed splitting uses
the chosen identifications.  Similarly,
\[
             \operatorname{Aut}(I_\infty)\cong
             \left(\prod_{q\in \mathbb Q}\mathbb Z\right)\rtimes \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Q,<).
\]
To verify the last formula, the initial $\omega$ and final $\omega^*$
condensation classes are rigid.  The interior quotient is $\mathbb Q$ and each
of its classes is $\mathbb Z$, whose increasing automorphisms are exactly
integer translations.  A quotient automorphism and one translation
per class give all automorphisms.

\subsubsection{One derivative removes all permutation interiors}

Let $L'$ denote the set of nonisolated points in the external order
topology.  The topology here belongs to the external order of admitted
class relations; it does not require a class of classes inside $\GBC$.

\begin{theorem}[The first derivative]\label{swo:fu:fc:thm:derivative}
For an external model realization as above, $L'$ consists exactly of
the singleton $E$-blocks and the two endpoints of every nonsingleton
$E$-block.  It has no isolated points, so
\[
                             L''=L'.
\]
The isolated points of $L$ are dense, and $L'$ is closed and nowhere
dense.  In either countable case,
\[
                         L'\cong\sigma(\{1,2\}).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In a linear order without endpoints, a point is isolated exactly when
it has both an immediate predecessor and an immediate successor.
The internal finite permutation chain has these two neighbors at every
rank other than its endpoints, including nonstandard internal ranks.
These remain actual neighbors externally.  At an endpoint there is no
neighbor on the exterior side: such an adjacency would extend the
maximal terminal block.  Thus precisely the stated points survive.

The quotient by $E$ is dense without endpoints.  Consequently every
neighborhood, within $L'$, of a retained endpoint or singleton contains
retained points from other blocks.  This proves $L''=L'$.  By the
density of the color $6$, every neighborhood of a retained point also
contains an interior point of a six-element block, which is isolated
in $L$.  The isolated points are therefore dense.  Their union is open,
so $L'$ is closed; the same density makes its interior empty.

Finally, in a countable realization the dense quotient contains
densely many singleton blocks and densely many nonsingleton blocks.
After the latter are replaced by their endpoint pairs, colored
back-and-forth yields $\sigma(\{1,2\})$.
\end{proof}

Thus the first derivative forgets the distinction between the two
countable raw orders, although external finite condensation detects it.
For uncountable realizations the principal remaining invariant is the
colored quotient: its isomorphism type, saturation, and automorphism
group need not be fixed by the preceding local arguments.



% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 2982-3026
\subsection{Source 30: A compactness observation about finite condensation}
\label{swo:rt:sec:finite-condensation-compactness}

This observation concerns ordinary set-sized linear orders, for example
the external countable orders in a countable class-model realization.  It
does not treat a virtual collection of classes as the domain of an
ordinary first-order structure.

\begin{proposition}[Finite factorial blocks are not first-order protected]
\label{swo:rt:prop:factorial-compactness}
Let $L$ be a linear order containing finite adjacent chains of arbitrarily
large length.  Then the complete first-order theory
$\operatorname{Th}(L,<)$ has a countable model with an infinite
finite-condensation class.  In particular, if every finite-condensation
class of $L$ is finite, that property is not preserved by elementary
equivalence.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Expand the language by constants $c_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z$, and add
\[
 c_i<c_{i+1}\quad\text{and}\quad
 \neg\exists z\,(c_i<z<c_{i+1})
 \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z)
\]
to $\operatorname{Th}(L,<)$.  Every finite subset of these axioms is
realized by placing the finitely many relevant constants consecutively
inside a sufficiently long adjacent chain of $L$.  Compactness gives a
model of the complete theory with all these constants.  Downward
L\"owenheim--Skolem gives a countable such model.  Every interval
$[c_i,c_j]$ for finite integers $i<j$ consists of the finitely many named
successive points.  Hence all the $c_i$ belong to one finite-condensation
class, which is infinite.
\end{proof}

Factorial terminal blocks supply the hypothesis because $n!$ is
unbounded in $\omega$.  Thus an external classification as a dense
shuffle of finite factorial chains cannot by itself serve as a
first-order characterization of lexicographic well-order spaces.  It
requires the external structural condition or a suitable infinitary
language.  This conclusion does not contradict an exact classification
within a previously specified family of countable class-model
realizations: compactness may produce orders outside that family.




\merge\ Source~30's proposition is classical compactness, and its source does
not cite the other countable-model manuscripts. Source~19's
\cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-many-models} constructs such models of the common theory
explicitly, one for every countable order $A$, and the $\omega$-nonstandard
$\GBC$ realizations of \cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types} are models of the same
theory with infinite finite-condensation classes. Together they show why the
external finiteness condition in source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle} cannot be replaced by a
first-order axiom, as source~19's paragraph after
\cref{swo:rs:prop:cm-intrinsic} also says.

\cref{swo:sc:thm:fullrank}, which states as an equivalence what this report
used only in one direction: the full structure $(V_\kappa,\mathcal
P(V_\kappa))$ satisfies $\GB$ exactly when $\kappa$ is strongly inaccessible,
