\subsection{Source 27: foundations that avoid size paradoxes}
\label{swo:sc:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Four safe levels of discourse}

\textbf{A fixed set.} For $X=\No_{<\theta}$ or any other set of labels,
$\WO(X)$ is a subset of $\mathcal P(X^2)$. All relation-table spaces,
all their subsets, their order topologies, and their Dedekind cuts are
ordinary sets. This is the cleanest environment for cardinal spectra,
topology, computation, and first formalization milestones. An infinite
birthday cutoff does not require an inaccessible cardinal.

\textbf{Definable classes in set theory.} In $\ZFC$, the sign-sequence
description defines a proper class $\No$. One can state a schema about
each formula defining a class relation, prove uniform constructions
from specified formula parameters, and quantify over set-coded words.
One cannot quantify over all arbitrary classes as objects of $\ZFC$.
Syntax codes do not erase this distinction: a universal satisfaction
predicate for the universe is not supplied by the set of formula codes.

\textbf{Two-sorted class theory.} In $\GBC$, individual class relations
are variables of the second sort. Formulas such as
$R<_{\mathrm{raw}}S$ and statements quantifying over class well-orders
are legitimate. A uniformly given family has one graph
$\mathcal R(i,x,y)$ with set indices $i$ in an ordinary class.
This setting supports the comparison, residual maps, prefix
automorphisms, and diagonal theorem proved above.

\textbf{An external model or a higher type.} If $(M,\mathcal X)$ is
a set-sized model in a surrounding theory, its admitted classes are
elements of the external set $\mathcal X$. The external collection of
admitted well-orders is then a set, with an ordinary topology and
automorphism group. Alternatively, a higher-order theory can explicitly
add a sort for collections of classes. Either route must specify its
semantics and comprehension principles; neither follows merely from
writing braces around a class-variable predicate.

Kelley--Morse theory strengthens the permitted comprehension formulas,
but its classes still have sets as members. It does not automatically
turn an arbitrary collection of classes into a class. Work on
hyperclass forcing makes such higher-level distinctions explicit
\cite{AntosFriedman}; that literature is context for the additional
type level, not an axiom needed by the theorems here.

\subsubsection{Why Global Choice is visible}

Global Choice provides an ordinal enumeration of every proper class,
including $\No$. Its standard equivalent formulations distinguish it
from ordinary set Choice \cite{HamkinsGC}. In this particular setting,
the repository proves the stronger converse: over $\GB$, the existence
of any class well-order of $\No$ implies Global Choice
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}). Thus the baseline is not innocent notation.

For perspective, the set-code surjection $d:\No\to V$ used above
explains the mechanism once set Choice is available. A well-order of
$\No$ lets one choose the least code of each set and hence obtain a
global choice procedure. The choiceless version in the repository also
establishes the required set Choice by set-valued rank recursion.
We do not reclassify that established equivalence as an open question.

Set-sized results in \cref{swo:sc:sec:tables,swo:sc:sec:support} need much less.
The explicit increasing-word split needs no choice at all; its
homogeneous class-order identifications use Global Choice. The support
optimum is a pointwise theorem about well-orderable sets of ordinals;
only its use as a uniform completion procedure requires a fixed
selection mechanism.

\subsubsection{Set-state recursion and genuinely class-valued recursion}

An ordinal-length process whose state and earlier history are sets at
every set stage is available by ordinary recursion with class parameters.
One constructs each set-length run, proves uniqueness, and takes its
elementarily definable union. The residual isomorphism lemma follows
this pattern. The fact that the final graph is a proper class does not
make each intermediate state a class.

Elementary transfinite recursion, $\ETR$, addresses stronger situations
in which individual stages can themselves be classes and later stages
refer to entire earlier class slices. Truth-predicate and class-game
examples illustrate this distinction in the primary literature
\cite{GitmanHamkins,HamkinsWoodin}. We use no inference from ``a
recursion has length $\Ord$'' to ``it requires $\ETR$.'' Conversely,
we do not justify a simultaneous choice of class isomorphisms merely
by calling it ordinary recursion. The uniform graph construction in
\cref{swo:sc:lem:uniformresidual} is the required justification.

\subsubsection{Full rank models: an exact inaccessible-cardinal criterion}

An inaccessible cardinal is a convenient way to replace the whole
two-sorted universe by a full rank model. Its precise role can be
stated as an equivalence.

\begin{theorem}[Full rank semantics]\label{swo:sc:thm:fullrank}
In ambient $\ZFC$, the full two-sorted structure
\[
 (V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))
\]
satisfies $\GB$, with the usual set part including Infinity, if and
only if $\kappa$ is strongly inaccessible. In that case it also
satisfies $\KM$ with Global Choice.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose the full structure satisfies $\GB$. Its set part makes
$\kappa$ a limit ordinal above $\omega$. If
$\cf(\kappa)<\kappa$, an external cofinal map
$f:\cf(\kappa)\to\kappa$ is an available full class, with domain
a set of $V_\kappa$. Its range has unbounded rank below $\kappa$ and
is not a set of $V_\kappa$, contrary to Class Replacement.
Hence $\cf(\kappa)=\kappa$, so $\kappa$ is a regular cardinal.

If $2^\lambda\ge\kappa$ for some cardinal $\lambda<\kappa$,
ambient Choice gives a surjection $\mathcal P(\lambda)\to\kappa$.
Its graph is also a full class, and its domain belongs to $V_\kappa$.
Class Replacement would put its range $\kappa$ in $V_\kappa$,
again impossible. Thus $\kappa$ is an uncountable regular strong
limit cardinal.

Conversely, at a strongly inaccessible $\kappa$, every set in
$V_\kappa$ has external cardinality below $\kappa$. Any full class
function on such a set has fewer than $\kappa$ values, whose ranks
are bounded below $\kappa$ by regularity. Its range is therefore in
$V_\kappa$. Standard rank closure supplies the set axioms, and this
argument supplies Class Replacement. Every subset is admitted as a
class, so even impredicative class comprehension holds. An external
well-order of $V_\kappa$ supplies a Global Choice class.
\end{proof}

The theorem characterizes \emph{full rank initial-segment models}.
It does not say that all Henkin models of $\GBC$ require inaccessible
cardinals, nor that a set of surreals cut off at an arbitrary birthday
is invalid. A singular birthday fragment is a legitimate set order;
it is generally not the set part of a full class-theoretic universe.

\subsubsection{Internal versus external well-foundedness}

There are three separate assertions: a relation is well-founded on
sets of a model, it is well-founded on that model's admitted classes,
and it is well-founded externally. Under $\GBC$ the first two agree,
by the descending-sequence argument, but they need not agree with
the third. Even transitivity of the set part is not by itself the
full correctness condition for class well-foundedness
\cite[Section 3]{HamkinsWoodin}.

For shared relations in two same-set $\GBC$ expansions, their internal
well-foundedness agrees because their set-coded descending sequences
agree. Their admitted relations may still differ, which is precisely
what \cref{swo:sc:thm:markedmodels} detects. The distinction prevents two
common errors: assuming that adding classes must destroy old internal
well-foundedness, and assuming that an internal ordinal enumeration
can always be traversed as an externally well-founded sequence.

\subsubsection{An axiom and object ledger}

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.44\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.49\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule Construction or theorem & Sufficient setting and object type\\
\midrule\endfirsthead
\toprule Construction or theorem & Sufficient setting and object type\\
\midrule\endhead
All well-orders on a fixed set $X$ & $\ZFC$; a set of set relations.\\
Terminal-cut factorization & $\ZF$ or elementary class definitions; a
map on set-coded words.\\
Pointwise minimum ordinal support & $\ZF$ with definable-class notation;
all matching sets are well-orderable.\\
Direct raw labelled comparison & $\GBC$; an elementary formula on two
class parameters. No hyperclass is formed.\\
Uniform residual isomorphisms and branch transport & $\GBC$ with a
baseline; one graph on set tuples, assembled from set runs.\\
Omitted convex copy for every uniform family & $\GBC$; diagonalization
on an ordinary class index, with a formula on residual class orders.\\
Dense core in raw relation-table order & $\GBC$ and a set-like scan;
an ordinary class of set codes.\\
Marked-model embedding criterion & An external theorem about two
set-sized $\GBC$ models with common sets and baseline.\\
All subsets and topology of an admitted order & A surrounding universe
where the admitted class part is a set, or an explicitly stronger type.\\
Full $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ semantics & Exactly an ambient
strongly inaccessible $\kappa$ for the usual $\GB$ axioms.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

an inaccessible full model $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ is an optional
external illustration (sources~19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 28, 29), as in
\cref{swo:ec:thm:inaccessible}. Each source's own wording is kept below.

% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 494-521
\subsection{Source 19: set-like global enumerations and their core}\label{swo:b83:sub:rs-core}

\merge\ Source~19's Section~3.1, printed whole (the rest of its Section~3 is a
note in Part~X). Its core $C$ is this report's core in the support coding,
$\Psupp(e)$; \eqref{swo:rs:eq:core} is \cref{swo:gl:pbd-no} with the separation
property of \cref{swo:gl:interpolation}.

Under Global Choice fix a set-like enumeration
$e:\Ord\to\No$. A bounded-support modification permutes some
initial set of positions and agrees with $e$ thereafter. Choose one
canonical set code for each such modification. These codes form an
ordinary class $C$ of sets, with an evaluation relation that produces
the associated global order. The earlier reports prove
\[\tag{S19.2}\label{swo:rs:eq:core}
 C\cong\No,
 \qquad
 \text{$C$ separates any two distinct exhaustive set-like enumerations.}
\]
They also prove the stronger parameterwise interpolation statement for
every uniformly set-indexed cut of set-like enumerations
\cite[\S19]{swoAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:gl:interpolation}). Uniformity means that the family is supplied
by one class relation with a set index; it does not mean an arbitrary
external set of class objects.

One elementary fact will be used repeatedly. Every injective set
prefix $p:\alpha\to\No$ extends to a member of $C$: choose a
large initial segment of $e$ containing all labels in $p$, put the
prefix first, and reorder the remaining set of labels before returning
to the unchanged tail. If a proper class word $F:\Ord\to\No$
is injective, then at every set stage there are members of $C$ on
both sides of $F$ sharing that prefix. Choose their next labels
slightly below and above $F(\alpha)$ and avoid the used set.


% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 522-616
\subsection{Source 19: raw class comparison and canonical blocks}
\label{swo:rs:sec:rawbaseline}

\merge\ Source~19's Section~4, printed whole; its two propositions are results
of Parts~III and~IX and are recorded as notes.

An admitted class well-order is a strict linear class order whose restriction to
every nonempty admitted subclass has a least element. In GBC one may
equivalently use the usual well-foundedness test on sets; this is a
statement inside the class model, not an assertion about all external
subsets \cite[\S3]{HamkinsWoodin}.

\begin{definition}[Common labelled initial segment]\label{swo:rs:n4.1}
For class well-orders $R,S$ of the same labelled carrier $X$, let
$C(R,S)$ consist of the labels $x$ for which
\[
 \operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\operatorname{Pred}_S(x),
 \qquad
 R\restr\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)
   =S\restr\operatorname{Pred}_S(x).
\]
Here $\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$. Each equality expands
to a first-order formula with $R,S$ as class parameters.
\end{definition}

\begin{note}[Source~19, Proposition~4.2, ``Elementary comparison; prior result'']\label{swo:rs:prop:rawcomparison}
\emph{If $R\ne S$, the class $C=C(R,S)$ is a proper initial segment
of both orders, the orders agree on it, and their first labels outside
$C$ are different. Define $R<_{\lex}S$ when the first remaining
$R$-label is numerically smaller than the first remaining $S$-label.
This is a linear order, expressed as a formula on class parameters in GB.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}; source~19 calls it a prior
result.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~19's proof.} If a label satisfies the defining property, every predecessor does too.
Thus $C$ is initial and the restrictions agree. Every common labelled
initial segment is contained in $C$. If $C=X$, the relations agree
everywhere. Otherwise take the least remaining label of each order.
The predecessor class of each is exactly $C$; equality of the two
labels would put that label in $C$, a contradiction.

For transitivity, the common prefixes of $R,S$ and of $S,T$ are
initial segments of $S$, so one contains the other. If containment is
proper, the earlier comparison decides $R$ against $T$ with the same
sign. If the prefixes coincide, compare the three next numerical
labels; the transitivity of the label order applies. Trichotomy and
asymmetry follow directly. No recursive matching of different labels
and no class of equivalence classes is used.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~19, Proposition~4.3, ``First block and full block decomposition; prior results'']\label{swo:rs:prop:blocks}
\emph{Let $R$ well-order a proper class $X$. Its labels with set-sized
predecessor class form a proper-class initial segment, possibly all of
$X$, of type $\Ord$.
More generally, declaring $x\sim_R y$ when the closed $R$-interval
between them is a set gives convex blocks of type $\Ord$, with
at most one final set-sized block. In GB,
\[
 R\cong (J_R\times\Ord)_{\lex}+\theta_R,
\]
where $J_R$ is represented by the actual least labels of the proper
blocks and $\theta_R$ is a set ordinal.}
This is the first block of \cref{swo:cf:core} and the canonical block
decomposition of Part~IX (source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}; also
\cref{swo:ds:thm:blocks,swo:sh:thm:class-division}); source~19 calls both prior
results.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~19's proof.} The first claim follows by enumerating each set predecessor segment
by its unique ordinal rank. This segment cannot stop after only a set
of labels: the least remaining label would also have set predecessors.
Every ordinal rank occurs, since a missing rank would yield a first
missing stage after a set initial segment. This yields its class
isomorphism with $\Ord$ by elementary comprehension.

For the full decomposition, set intervals are closed under finite
unions, proving transitivity of $\sim_R$. Each block has a least label
by class well-ordering. Within a block every predecessor segment from
that least label is a set. Thus its type is a set ordinal or $\Ord$.
A set block followed by another label would unite with the next label
to remain a set interval, contradicting maximality. Hence a set block
can only be final. The ranks within each proper block and the least
block labels give the displayed isomorphism. This simultaneous
construction does not iterate a class-valued quotient operation.
\end{note}

The quotient $J_R$ need not be simpler than $R$ up to isomorphism.
Earlier work gives fixed-point examples \cite{swoSrc16,swoSrc18} (\merge\ sources~16 and~18, Part~IX).
Consequently this decomposition alone does not justify a terminating
recursive classification.

\begin{remark}[Existence and choice]\label{swo:rs:n4.4}
Over GB without set choice, the existence of any class well-order of
$\No$ is equivalent to Global Choice \cite[Theorem 13.1]{swoAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:cf:choice}).
The forward implication uses its restrictions to the binary sign levels
to well-order every $\mathcal P(\alpha)$ uniformly, and then constructs
rank-wise well-orders of the universe by set recursion. In this article
the global constructions simply state GBC as their hypothesis.
\end{remark}



% ---- source 19 (batch-83 manuscript 01), lines 2764-2997
\subsection{Source 19: formalizations that preserve the intended subject}
\label{swo:rs:sec:formalization}

The foundational issue is not repaired merely by replacing the word
``set'' with ``class.'' A class theory has its own sorts and its own
comprehension principles. The earlier sections illustrate three distinct
tasks: comparing supplied class relations, constructing one class from
supplied parameters, and studying a domain whose elements are arbitrary
classes. They require different formal interfaces.

\subsubsection{A size ledger}

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.29\textwidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Object & Safe internal treatment & Safe external treatment\\
\midrule
A surreal sign sequence & A set with an ordinal domain & An element of
the model's interpreted surreal carrier\\
$\No$ itself & A proper class & A set in a containing universe when
the entire model is a set\\
A global well-order $R$ & A class relation; allowed as a class parameter
& One element of the external set of admitted relations\\
All global well-orders & A predicate on class variables & The actual
external set $\Hall^{\mathcal M}$\\
The bounded-support core & A class of canonical set codes & A set of
codes with an interpreted evaluation relation\\
A supplied core cut & A class subset of those set codes & A subset of
the external core\\
All external core cuts & No claim of a same-level class of such objects
& A subset of the power set of the external core\\
The decorated completion & A parameterwise or explicitly higher-sort
construction & An ordinary set-theoretic lexicographic sum\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

A two-sorted model need not be transitive, $\omega$-standard, or a
$\beta$-model. Its assertions of well-foundedness concern the objects
and subclasses that it admits. An external descending sequence might
be absent from its set sort. None of the external model theorems
silently replaces admitted well-orders by relations that are actually
well-founded in the containing universe.

\begin{note}[Source~19, Proposition~13.1, ``The uniform coding obstruction'']\label{swo:rs:prop:diagonal}
\emph{In GBC there is no class relation $A\subseteq I\times\Ord$, with
$I$ a class of set indices, whose rows enumerate every admitted binary
class on $\Ord$.}
This is source~11's diagonal non-coding theorem (\cref{swo:gl:diagonal}), here
for rows that are binary classes on $\Ord$, by the same diagonal class $D$
along a class surjection onto the index class.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~19's proof.} If $I$ is empty the assertion is immediate. Otherwise Global Choice
gives a class surjection $b:\Ord\to I$: enumerate a proper $I$
in type $\Ord$, or enumerate a set $I$ and repeat a fixed value
after its enumeration ends. Elementary comprehension forms
\[
 D=\{\alpha\in\Ord:(b(\alpha),\alpha)\notin A\}.
\]
For every $i\in I$, choose $\alpha$ with $b(\alpha)=i$.
Then $D$ differs from the $i$th row at $\alpha$, a contradiction.
\end{note}

Pair-swapping a fixed global enumeration transfers this obstruction to
uniform exhaustive coding of all set-like global orders. It explains
why the core is useful but cannot contain every global enumeration.
It also explains the model-relative missing branches of
Theorem~\ref{swo:rs:rf:thm:missingbranches}. A single externally specified
family can exist as a set in a larger universe without being a
uniformly admitted family inside the original model.

\subsubsection{Why the elementary constructions do not require ETR}

In ordinary set recursion, the object constructed at every ordinal
stage is a set, and the history below a fixed set ordinal is a set.
With a fixed class parameter, GB proves the appropriate set recursion
and Class Replacement. Unique compatible initial solutions can then
be assembled by an elementary formula: a pair belongs to the final
class precisely when it appears in some set-sized initial solution.
This applies to birthday-controlled insertion, deterministic
back-and-forth on partial set maps, and the set-valued recursive
choices used throughout the global core construction.

By contrast, an elementary transfinite recursion with class-valued
stages asks for a class $S\subseteq\Gamma\times V$ satisfying
\[
 S_\gamma=\{x:\varphi(x,S\restr\gamma,Z)\},
\]
where each $S_\gamma$ may already be a proper class. This is the
principle $\ETR_\Gamma$, not a consequence obtained merely by
calling the operation a recursion. Already $\omega$-length class-valued
recursions can construct truth predicates. The distinction and its connections
with determinacy and class forcing are developed in
\cite{GitmanHamkins,GHHSW,HamkinsWoodin,Williams}.

The common labelled prefix is elementary because equality of the
two predecessor relations expands into quantification over labels.
The simultaneous set-interval block decomposition is elementary
because one uses actual least block labels and set intervals. Neither
construction attempts to recursively find an arbitrary isomorphism
between differently labelled class well-orders. Such abstract
comparison is the subject of stronger principles; for example,
Williams's Lemma~3.17 uses an ETR hypothesis \cite{Williams}.

The model-theoretic shuffle proofs likewise use only ordinary
set-valued constructions internally. The use of an external
finite Ehrenfeucht--Fra\"isse game does not assert that the entire
external family of plays or strategies belongs to the class model.

\subsubsection{Four workable foundational routes}

\paragraph{Bounded ZFC mathematics.}
Fix $X$, $\alpha$, or a birthday bound. Then every enumeration,
cut, automorphism, and completion is a set. The infinite-tail spectrum,
restriction classification, and bounded completion normal forms
can all be formalized here. No inaccessible cardinal or class theory
is needed for these results. This is the most direct route for
the first machine-checked development.

\paragraph{GBC with supplied class parameters.}
State results as formulas about $R,S,F,C$ and supplied uniform
families. Define the comparison, first block, set-interval quotient,
and trace cuts with elementary comprehension. When a theorem mentions
all class well-orders, it universally quantifies a class variable;
it does not create a new class containing those relations as elements.
This route closely matches the elementary global proofs.

\paragraph{External models.}
Fix a set-sized structure $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)$ in a
containing ZFC universe. Its class sort is now an external set, so
$\Hall^{\mathcal M}$, its automorphism group, its power set,
and its Dedekind completion are ordinary mathematical objects.
This is the route used by the decorated-completion and model-spectrum
theorems. The resulting object is model-relative; it is not a
replacement for the class of all actual surreals in the containing
universe.

A useful full-class example is $(V_\Omega,\mathcal P(V_\Omega))$
for a strongly inaccessible $\Omega$ in an outer universe. It gives
strong comprehension internally. Such an example is a sufficient
semantic setting, not a hidden assumption behind the set-sized
theorems. In this model the set-like global orders correspond
externally to $\Omega$-length exhaustive enumerations of the
bounded surreal carrier, while arbitrary admitted well-orders can
have any external order type of cardinality $\Omega$.

\paragraph{An explicit higher sort or universe hierarchy.}
One may introduce a sort of collections of classes, or work in
nested universes and state exactly which objects are small at which
level. This permits a domain of global orders and families of their
cuts directly. It changes the ambient language or universe, and
the additional comprehension or size assumptions must be listed.
KM permits stronger quantification over classes in comprehension;
it does not make proper classes into elements of other classes.

These routes are complementary. A proof can first be established as
an ordinary theorem about a set linear order, then interpreted in a
larger universe, or instantiated with the external orders of a class
model. What must be proved separately is that the interpretation has
the intended admitted relations and the intended smallness predicates.

\subsubsection{A Lean development tied to inspected repository sources}

The inspected revision contains
\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/SignSequence.lean}
and \texttt{SignSequenceCutOperation.lean} \cite{b83ProveItLeanFoundations}.
The first defines
\[
 \texttt{SignSequence.\{u\} : Type (u + 1)}
\]
and proves \texttt{birthdays\_bounded}, \texttt{not\_small}, and
\texttt{small\_bounded}. The last declaration makes a fixed
birthday-bounded fragment small relative to $u$; the first requires
an explicit \texttt{Small.\{u\}} hypothesis on the indexing type.
The cut-operation file proves
\texttt{exists\_separator\_of\_small\_sets}, with explicit
\texttt{Small.\{u\}} instances for both option subsets.
These are exactly the size-sensitive facts needed by the elementary
order theory. They do not yet certify the new results of this article.

Lean's universe hierarchy and impredicative propositions do not erase
these distinctions \cite{LeanUniverses}. A predicate on a large type
may be perfectly well-formed without its extension being small in
the smaller universe. In particular, writing a relation on
\texttt{SignSequence.\{u\}} does not prove that its predecessor
types are \texttt{Small.\{u\}}. Set-likeness should be recorded as
that explicit condition. Likewise, an external Lean well-foundedness
predicate on a type is not automatically the internal well-foundedness
predicate of a chosen GBC model.

The following module boundaries are proposals; no modules with these
names are claimed to exist in the inspected repository.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.25\textwidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Proposed layer & Main statements & Why it comes here\\
\midrule
Labelled enumeration order & First disagreement, prefix cylinders,
literal residual lexicographic sum & Common set-level interface\\
Binary codes and fusion & Prefix-free sign code; constant-subcylinder
lemma; fusion into one fiber & The main embedding mechanism\\
Fixed-type spectra & Cardinal-layer division; deletion scheduler;
lower and upper weighted ranks & New ZFC classification\\
Completion codes & Full branches, numerical splits, limit boundaries;
canonical comparison & Exact bounded arrangement, beyond characters\\
Restriction maps & Three- and four-label witnesses; exact classification
& Small, independently reusable theorem\\
Class-model interface & Two sorts, admitted comprehension and replacement,
evaluation of formulas & Internal/external interpretation boundary\\
Raw comparison and core & Common labelled prefix; bounded-support codes;
first-block trace & Parameterwise class results\\
External reconstruction & Decorated completion and automorphism extension
& Ordinary theorem on the external set order\\
Model invariants & Tail cylinders, nonstandard intervals, EF games
& Exact external classification and common theory\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The finite restriction theorem is an attractive first target: it needs
no surreal arithmetic and has short explicit witnesses. The next
high-value target is the fusion lemma, because it isolates the main
reason for strict nonembedding results. The cardinal-layer theorem
then becomes a composition of independently checked encoders and
fusion costs. Formalizing the entire GBC metatheory should be a
separate project rather than an implicit side effect of introducing
a large type.

An alternative formalization may use a set-theoretic universe such as
a Tarski--Grothendieck model. Existing surreal formalization work gives
relevant experience with foundations and Conway normal forms
\cite{PakKaliszyk}. That work is methodological context here; the
present proofs are order-theoretic and do not require a formalized
normal-form theorem or surreal multiplication.

The results have different logical scopes. Keeping them separate is

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.35\textwidth}YY@{}}

The repository and same-day continuation results are identified where

\subsection{Source 20: a size-safe toolkit}
\label{swo:lm:base:toolkit}

\subsubsection{Signs, birthdays, and set cuts}

We use the sign-sequence presentation
\[
 \No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}.
\]
The birthday $\bd(x)$ is the domain length of $x$. At the first unequal
position, compare $-<\text{undefined}<+$. The birthday fragment
$\No_{<\theta}$ is a set for every set ordinal $\theta$.
Every set of surreal numbers has bounded birthdays. For an infinite
initial cardinal $\kappa$, put
\[
 \mu=|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}.
\]
This is an equality of cardinals, and it is not a claim that every ordinal
calculation involving $\mu$ can be replaced by cardinal arithmetic.

The basic surreal separation property is: if $A,B$ are sets and $A<B$, a
surreal lies strictly between them. Empty sides are allowed. It implies
the following strengthening used repeatedly.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~3.1, ``A fresh separator'']\label{swo:lm:base:fresh}
\emph{If $A,B,U$ are sets of surreals with $A<B$, there is a surreal $z\notin U$
such that $A<z<B$.}
This is source~11's \cref{swo:lem:delete} (a set can be avoided), with the
same one-line proof.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} Let $U_0$ be the members of $U$ lying strictly between $A$ and $B$.
Then $A\cup U_0<B$. Choose $z$ between these two sets. If $z\in U$,
the inequalities would imply $z\in U_0$, contrary to $U_0<z$.
\end{note}

Every nonempty open numerical interval of $\No$ is a proper class. Otherwise
apply \cref{swo:lm:base:fresh} with that interval as the forbidden set. The same
argument shows that deleting a set preserves the set-cut property.

\subsubsection{What the class theories permit}

Here $\GB$ means G\"odel--Bernays theory whose set part is ZF, without
Global Choice built into the abbreviation; $\GBC$ adds Global Choice.
All global baseline constructions in this article take place in GBC.
A class well-order is a strict linear class relation for which every
nonempty available subclass has a least member. It is \emph{set-like}
when every strict predecessor class is a set.

An individual member of $\Hsl$ or $\Hall$ is a class relation. Consequently
``$R\in\Hall$'' abbreviates a predicate on a class variable. It does not
assert membership in a GB class containing other proper classes. A
uniform family $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ is one class relation
\[
 T(i,x,y)\quad\text{with row }R_i(x,y),
\]
where the indices $i$ are sets and $I$ can itself be a set or a class.
This is what ``set-indexed'' and ``class-indexed'' mean below.

In GBC, ordinary recursion with \emph{set values} along $\Ord$ is available:
each set-ordinal initial history is a set, and the compatible local
histories define one class. It does not require full elementary
transfinite recursion. In contrast, a recursion whose value at each stage
is an entire class may require $\ETR$, even when the stage order is small.
The distinctions among $\ETR_\omega$, $\ETR_{\Ord}$, and full $\ETR$ must
not be suppressed \cite{GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Proposition~3.2, ``Set-like global orders'']\label{swo:lm:base:setlike}
\emph{In GBC, a proper-class set-like well-order is uniquely isomorphic to
$\Ord$. In particular, a set-like well-order of $\No$ is equivalent to
a class bijection $\Ord\to\No$.}
This is the identification of set-like class well-orders with class bijections
$\Ord\to\No$ used throughout this report (the reading of $\Hsl$ in
\cref{swo:sec:notation}).

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} Send each label $x$ to the ordinal order type of its predecessor set.
The range is an initial subclass of $\Ord$. If it were bounded, the inverse
map on a bounding ordinal would make the original carrier a set by Class
Replacement. Hence the range is all of $\Ord$.
\end{note}

The existence of a class well-order of all surreal labels already has
choice strength. Over $\GB+\mathrm{AC}$ it is equivalent to Global Choice:
sets can be coded by well-founded extensional relations on ordinals, those
relations by sets of ordinals, and those by surreal sign sequences.
Choosing the least code in the supplied surreal well-order produces a
global choice operation. The repository proves the stronger equivalence
over GB without assuming set choice separately
\cite[Theorem 13.1]{swoAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:cf:choice}). The further results below do not need
that strengthening.

\subsubsection{The set-sized baseline}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~3.3, ``Fixed carrier spectrum; earlier result'']\label{swo:lm:base:spectrum}
\emph{Let $X$ be an infinite linearly ordered set of cardinality $\mu$.
Then $|\WO(X)|=2^\mu$, every linear order of cardinality at most $\mu$
embeds in $\WO(X)$, and
\[
 \alpha\emb\WO(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\alpha<\mu^+
 \qquad(\alpha\text{ an ordinal}).
\]
The same upper bound holds for reverse well-ordered suborders.}
This is \cref{swo:sw:setspectrum} (the reals report's spectrum theorem for every
infinite alphabet); source~20 calls it an earlier result.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} There are at most $2^\mu$ relations on $X$. Partition $X$ into $\mu$
two-element pieces and enumerate those pieces in a fixed ordinal order.
Choosing independently which member of each pair appears first embeds
the binary lexicographic cube $2^\mu$ into $\WO(X)$ and proves the lower
cardinality bound. If $L$ has cardinality at most $\mu$, enumerate its
elements by coordinates below $\mu$. The characteristic functions of its
initial segments are nested, distinct, and lexicographically ordered as
$L$; the pair construction then embeds $L$ into $\WO(X)$.

Suppose a strictly increasing sequence of enumerations has length
$\mu^+$. On a tail, its first entries stabilize: a monotone sequence in
an alphabet of size $\mu$ cannot keep changing through a regular
$\mu^+$-sequence. Repeating this observation stabilizes each successive
entry on a tail. At any limit stage below $\mu^+$, regularity supplies a
common tail for all earlier requirements. The stabilized prefix cannot
exhaust $X$, since then the strictly increasing tail would be constant.
Continuing would therefore give an injection from $\mu^+$ into $X$, a
contradiction. The decreasing case is identical with inequalities reversed.
An ordinal below $\mu^+$ has size at most $\mu$, so the embedding direction
has already been proved.
\end{note}

For $\No_{<\kappa}$, the cutoff is therefore $(2^{<\kappa})^+$, not automatically
$\kappa^+$. The recent continuation also computes density, cellularity,
point characters, and proper-gap spectra for the minimal stratum
\cite{swoSrc18} (\merge\ printed in Part~VI); those more detailed formulas are not needed by
the new class-level theorems here.

\subsubsection{Variable set words are still a class of sets}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Proposition~3.4, ``Explicit compression of dictionary words'']\label{swo:lm:base:wordcode}
\emph{All set-length words over $\No$, with prefix-first dictionary order,
admit an explicit order embedding into $\No$, without Global Choice.
If $w=(x_i)_{i<\alpha}$, its code has birthday
\[
 \sum_{i<\alpha}\bigl(1+2\cdot\bd(x_i)+2\bigr).
\]
Here all sums and products inside the birthday expression are ordinal.}
This is source~11's explicit word code (\cref{swo:sw:code}), with the same
pair-doubling of signs.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} Replace each minus sign of $x$ by the pair $--$, each plus sign by $++$,
and append the pair $-+$. Call the resulting prefix-free sign word $c(x)$.
Because $--<-+<++$, this transformation preserves numerical comparison,
including the case where one original sign sequence ends first.
Code $w$ by concatenating, for each entry, one plus sign followed by
$c(x_i)$. Unequal entries are decided within their prefix-free entry codes.
If one whole word ends first, the next sign of the longer code is a plus,
so the shorter code is smaller. The displayed length follows by counting
the signs in each block.
\end{note}

This compression includes injective words, hence all well-orders of
variable set-sized surreal subsets. It does not encode arbitrary class
relations by sets; every individual input word in the proposition is a
set. Nor is it an isomorphism with $\No$, as the limit-prefix example in
\cref{swo:lm:base:interpretations} shows.

\subsubsection{Comparison of arbitrary class well-orders}

For class well-orders $R,S$ of the same labelled carrier $X$, let $C(R,S)$
consist of those $x$ such that their strict predecessor classes agree and
the two relations agree on that predecessor class. Membership in $C(R,S)$
is elementary with class parameters: all its quantifiers range over labels.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~3.5, ``Largest common labelled prefix'']\label{swo:lm:base:commonprefix}
\emph{The class $C(R,S)$ is an initial segment of both orders, their restrictions
to it agree, and it contains every common labelled initial segment.
If $R\ne S$, it is proper in $X$ and the labels
\[
 a=\min_R(X\setminus C(R,S)),\qquad
 b=\min_S(X\setminus C(R,S))
\]
are distinct.}
This is the largest common labelled prefix of \cref{swo:cf:lex} (source~12's
\cref{swo:st:thm:fulllex}).

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} If $x\in C(R,S)$, each predecessor $y$ of $x$ has the same predecessor
class and inherited predecessor order in both relations. Thus $y$ also
belongs to $C(R,S)$. For two members, comparison can be read inside the
predecessors of the later one, where the relations agree. Conversely,
a common labelled initial segment has the same predecessors and relations
at every one of its points, so it is contained in $C(R,S)$. If the two
next labels were equal, their common predecessor class would be exactly
$C(R,S)$, and that label would itself belong to the class, a contradiction.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~3.6, ``Native class lexicography; earlier result'']\label{swo:lm:base:rawlex}
\emph{For $R\ne S$ in $\Hall(X)$, define $R<_{\lex}S$ when $a<b$ numerically,
with $a,b$ from \cref{swo:lm:base:commonprefix}. This is a strict linear comparison
and agrees with enumeration lexicography when both orders are set-like.
It requires no comparison theorem for abstract class well-order types.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}; source~20 calls it an earlier
result.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} Trichotomy follows from $a\ne b$. For transitivity, the prefixes $C(R,S)$
and $C(S,T)$ are initial segments of the \emph{same} well-order $S$, hence
one contains the other. If one is shorter, the corresponding earlier
divergence determines the comparison of $R$ and $T$ as well. If they are
equal, compare the three next labels and use numerical transitivity.
For set-like orders the common prefix is a set, and its ordinal length
is exactly the first differing coordinate of the canonical enumerations.
\end{note}

Equality of predecessor \emph{sets alone} would be insufficient: the
enumerations $(0,1,2)$ and $(1,0,2)$ give the same predecessor set at $2$
but disagree before it. Agreement of the inherited relations is essential.

\subsubsection{The bounded-support core}

Fix a baseline class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. A normalized core code is
a set permutation $\pi:\lambda\to\lambda$ such that
\[
 \lambda=\sup\{\xi+1:\pi(\xi)\ne\xi\}.
\]
The empty permutation represents the baseline. Extend $\pi$ by the
identity above $\lambda$ and evaluate the resulting enumeration as
$E_\pi=b\circ\widehat\pi$. The ordinary class of codes, ordered by their
evaluations, is denoted ${\Pbd(b)}$. Equivalent terminology is the class of
enumerations eventually equal to $b$, represented by their unique set codes.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~3.7, ``Uniform completion'']\label{swo:lm:base:completion}
\emph{Every injective set prefix $p:\delta\to\No$ extends to an enumeration
represented in ${\Pbd(b)}$. One completion can be selected uniformly in $p$.}
This is source~11's supported completion (\cref{swo:gl:completion}).

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} The set injection $b^{-1}\circ p$ takes values below some ordinal. Choose
an infinite initial cardinal $\gamma$ larger than both that bound and
$\delta$. The domain and range complements in $\gamma$ both have size
$\gamma$, so a bijection between them extends the injection to a
permutation of $\gamma$. Use a fixed global well-order to choose one such
set bijection, extend by the identity, and normalize.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~3.8, ``Core interpolation and identification; earlier result'']\label{swo:lm:base:core}
\emph{In GBC, the class order ${\Pbd(b)}$ is isomorphic to $\No$. More strongly,
between any two uniformly set-indexed separated families of injective
class words $\Ord\to\No$ there is a core enumeration. Empty families are
allowed on either side.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:interpolation,swo:gl:pbd-no}; source~20 calls it an earlier
result.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} Call the two families $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(B_j)_{j\in J}$. When both
are nonempty, Class Replacement bounds all cross first-disagreement
ordinals by a set ordinal $\beta$. Build an injective prefix and keep only
rows still agreeing with it active. At the current coordinate, the active
left values form a set $L$ and the active right values a set $U$, with
$L\le U$ pointwise. If their intersection is empty, choose a fresh strict
separator using \cref{swo:lm:base:fresh}, append it, and stop. If their
intersection is the singleton $\{z\}$, append $z$ and discard all rows
with another value. The comparison invariant is preserved. Two common
values would contradict the cross inequalities. At limits take unions.
Both sides cannot stay active through $\beta$, so the procedure stops
with a set prefix. If one side was empty, separation is possible at once.
Complete the prefix using \cref{swo:lm:base:completion}.

Thus every separated pair of sets of core codes has a strict interpolant.
The core is a proper class, since transpositions involving arbitrarily
large ordinals have distinct codes. Enumerate it and $\No$ by $\Ord$ using
Global Choice. Alternating extensions of a set-sized partial isomorphism
give an isomorphism: at each step the required lower and upper images
are sets, so interpolation supplies a fresh image. The histories remain
sets at every set stage. This is the usual class back-and-forth argument,
not an invocation of class-valued ETR.
\end{note}

We call a class order with this set-cut property an $\eta_{\Ord}$ order.
The same back-and-forth proof shows that any two such proper class orders
are isomorphic, that set-sized partial order isomorphisms extend to
automorphisms, and that every class linear order embeds into one under
Global Choice. The classical surreal universality and homogeneity
background is discussed by Ehrlich and Hamkins
\cite{Ehrlich2012,HamkinsEmbeds}. The new automorphism theorem later in this
article concerns the much stronger demand of extending an automorphism
to the ambient space of global well-orders.

For an injective set prefix $p$, write
\[
 {\Pbd(b)}(p)=\{c\in{\Pbd(b)}:E_c\restr\dom(p)=p\}.
\]
These nonempty prefix cylinders are convex. The core is dense in
$\Hsl$, but it need not meet an interval between arbitrary non-set-like
raw orders. A common proper prefix with a small residual carrier is one
basic reason. This distinction drives the local-size results below.

\subsubsection{Which core cuts encode class orders}

The new automorphism results require a precise account of represented
cuts. We record the relevant earlier criterion, with its proof, so that
the dependence on enumeration structure is visible.

\begin{note}[Source~20, Lemma~3.9, ``The first ordinal block'']\label{swo:lm:base:firstblock}
\emph{For $R\in\Hall(\No)$, the class
\[
 B_R=\{x\in\No:\{y:yRx\}\text{ is a set}\}
\]
is a proper initial class and, with its induced order, has type $\Ord$.
Let $f_R:\Ord\to B_R$ be its canonical enumeration. For every core
code $c$, comparison of $E_c$ with $R$ is the same as comparison of
$E_c$ with $f_R$. Thus the strict core cut of $R$ depends only on $f_R$.}
This is source~11's canonical first block (\cref{swo:cf:core}) with source~16's
observation that the core cut of a raw order is that of its first block
(\cref{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}).

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~20's proof.} The class is initial and set-like by definition. If it were a set, its
complement would be nonempty, and the least point of that complement
would have exactly $B_R$ as its predecessor set. It would then belong
to $B_R$, a contradiction. Apply \cref{swo:lm:base:setlike}. If $E_c$ and $f_R$
differ, their first differing ordinal coordinate already determines
the raw comparison with $R$. If they agree everywhere, $f_R$ is onto
$\No$ because $E_c$ is, so $R$ is exactly that core order.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~20, Theorem~3.10, ``Recognition by straddling prefixes; earlier result'']\label{swo:lm:base:recognition}
\emph{Let $L$ be a nonempty proper initial class of ${\Pbd(b)}$ with no greatest
element. The following are equivalent in GBC:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $L=\{c:E_c<_{\lex}f\}$ for an injective class word
$f:\Ord\to\No$;
\item for every set ordinal $\delta$, some injective prefix of length
$\delta$ has a cylinder meeting both $L$ and its complement;
\item $L$ is the strict core cut of a raw class well-order of $\No$.
\end{enumerate}
The injective word in (1) is unique. The cut has a set-like representative
exactly when this word is onto. Recovery of the word uses only elementary
comprehension with $L$ as a class parameter.}
This is the represented-cut theorem of Part~VIII, source~14's
\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition} (\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold} lists its six
earlier proofs); clause~(3) is source~16's raw-trace corollary. Source~20 calls
it ``the relevant earlier criterion'' and gives its proof, a seventh route by
straddling prefixes; Part~XIII uses it.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Second route (source~20).} At most one cylinder of any fixed length straddles $L$: distinct
cylinders are disjoint and ordered, so two straddlers would place a point
outside an initial class below a point inside it. If straddlers exist at
all lengths, uniqueness forces their prefixes to cohere. Define $f(\alpha)$
as the last value of the unique straddling prefix of length $\alpha+1$.
This is an elementary definition from uniquely specified sets. Coherence
proves injectivity. At the first difference between a core row and $f$,
the straddling cylinder one coordinate longer determines which side of
$L$ that row occupies. If $E_c=f$, the code $c$ cannot lie in $L$:
a larger member of $L$ would give the opposite comparison. Hence (1)
follows.

Conversely, for every set prefix of an injective class word, continue
to its next value, choose fresh labels on either side of that value,
and complete the two prefixes in the core. They lie on opposite sides
of the word's cut. Thus every length has a straddler and (1) implies (2).
The same first-difference argument proves uniqueness of the word.

By \cref{swo:lm:base:firstblock}, a raw representative gives an injective word,
so (3) implies (1). Given an injective word, append a fixed well-order
of its unused labels. Its initial word is still the first ordinal
block: all later points, if present, have the proper range of $f$ among
their predecessors. The resulting raw order has the required cut. It is
set-like exactly when there are no unused labels. If some other set-like
representative existed, uniqueness of the word would force it to be the
same nonexhaustive word, which is impossible.
\end{note}

The test quantifies over all ordinal \emph{lengths}, each of which is a
set. It does not choose one class at each stage. This is why recovery is
elementary even though the recovered word is a class. The later symmetry
theorem will show that the cylinder structure in this test contains
information absent from the bare linear order of the core.



% ---- source 20 (batch-83 manuscript 02), lines 3151-3352
\subsection{Source 20: formalization without paradoxes}
\label{swo:lm:form:section}

\subsubsection{Four workable foundations}

There is no single formalization that silently turns all rows of the
interpretation table into the same object. Four complementary approaches
are useful, and their relationships explain several apparent paradoxes.

\paragraph{Ordinary set theory at a fixed stage.}
Choose a set alphabet $X$ or a birthday cutoff $\No_{<\theta}$. Its relations,
well-orders, enumeration strata, order topologies, and Dedekind cuts are
ordinary sets. The fixed-carrier theorem, sharp filtration criterion,
ordinal condensation formula, and countable topological example fit this
framework directly. One can also work with a set-indexed family of such
stages. A proper-class inverse limit is an additional statement; it is not
automatically supplied by existence of all its individual stages.

\paragraph{Two-sorted class theory.}
In GB or GBC, the labels are sets, individual global well-orders are
classes, and their comparisons are formulas with class parameters. A
uniform family has one relation on set indices and set labels. This
supports birthday gluing, the core construction, class automorphisms,
local coding obstructions, and analysis of a supplied condensation
history. One may quantify over class variables in an assertion without
using those variables as members of a new class.

\paragraph{Stronger comprehension and recursion.}
KM permits stronger class comprehension, but its second sort still does
not consist of objects allowed to be members of ordinary classes. It
therefore does not turn ``all class well-orders'' into a GB-style class
of elements. ETR supplies class-valued recursion histories along specified
well-founded class orders. Our termination theorem identifies what happens
to such a history once it exists; it does not prove that its existence
has the exact strength of full ETR. The known distinction between
set-valued recursion and class-valued ETR is essential here
\cite{GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}.

\paragraph{A containing universe or an explicit model.}
In an outer universe, fix a set model $(M,\mathcal X)$ of a two-sorted
class theory. The admitted classes are now external objects, so their
well-order space and any desired quotient are external sets. The full
model $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ at an inaccessible cardinal
provides particularly transparent cardinal calculations. Countable
models provide the shuffle classifications proved above. These are two
different external realizations, not inconsistent answers to one
unqualified cardinality question.

\subsubsection{What an inaccessible full model actually contains}

Let $\kappa$ be inaccessible in the ambient universe and consider
$(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$. Its internal surreal carrier is,
externally, $\No_{<\kappa}$ of cardinality $\kappa$. All its ambient subsets
are available as classes. A subclass of this carrier is an internal
set exactly when its ambient cardinality is less than $\kappa$.
Consequently the external full well-order space is
\[
 \WO(\No_{<\kappa}),
\]
while its internally set-like part is
\[
 \WO_\kappa(\No_{<\kappa}).
\]
Indeed an actual well-order of a carrier of size $\kappa$ is internally
set-like precisely when all its predecessor segments have size below
$\kappa$, which forces its type to be exactly $\kappa$.

Both spaces have cardinality $2^\kappa$, but their geometry differs.
The minimal stratum has a dense set of size $\kappa$: choose a completion
for each injective prefix of length below $\kappa$. There are only
$\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$ such prefixes, and every nonempty order
interval contains one of their cylinders. Fresh separators exist because
$\No_{<\kappa}$ fills cuts of size below $\kappa$.

The full order has $2^\kappa$ disjoint nonempty intervals. Reserve three
labels and vary the enumeration of all other labels in $2^\kappa$ ways.
For each common exhaustive prefix, its six possible final permutations
form a convex six-point block. An open interval between the first and
last point of each block is nonempty, and the different blocks are
disjoint. An embedding into the minimal stratum would give
$2^\kappa$ disjoint nonempty intervals in an order with a dense subset
of size $\kappa$, which is impossible. This re-proves the earlier
full-model nonembedding result \cite{swoAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding}) and locates the new
interval and condensation calculations in the same concrete model.

There is no conflict with class universality of $\No$. Internally,
universality concerns class orders \emph{whose elements are sets}.
Externally the full well-order space has $2^\kappa$ points, whereas the
internal surreal carrier has only $\kappa$. Similarly, the new one-point
nonextension theorem does not deny that a new class order can embed into
$\No$: it denies an embedding satisfying all comparisons already fixed
by a specified automorphism on an entire proper-class core.

\subsubsection{Changing the class collection while keeping the sets}

Suppose $(M,\mathcal X)$ and $(M,\mathcal Y)$ are GBC realizations of
the same first-order set model. For a relation available in both class
collections, well-foundedness has the same truth value in both models.
In GBC a failure of class well-foundedness is witnessed by a set-coded
descending $\omega$-sequence; the sets, and hence all such witnesses,
are unchanged. This is the precise absoluteness used here
\cite[Observation 4.12]{Williams}; related stronger results appear
in \cite[\S3]{HamkinsWoodin}.

The common native comparisons are stable as well, because their
definitions use only set quantifiers and the supplied class relations.
With a common baseline $b$, the set-coded core and its evaluations are
also unchanged. What can change is which additional relations, class
cuts, automorphisms, or uniform histories are available. Thus class
extensions may add new points to the surrounding well-order space;
they do not make an old shared well-order ill-founded merely by adding
more classes.

An external branch through the stages of a countable model need not be
an admissible internal class. The gluing theorem uses Class Replacement
to bound the birthdays of a descending sequence. Omitting admissibility
would remove that step. The countable shuffle theorem respects this
boundary: its back-and-forth is external and its external enumeration
need not belong to the model.

\subsubsection{A practical route in Lean}

The pinned ProveIt sources contain useful universe-aware interfaces.
They were inspected at the revision on the title page; this article did
not run a Lean build or add a Lean theorem.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.29\textwidth}P{0.30\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Existing file & Inspected declarations & Appropriate use\\
\midrule
\texttt{SignSequence.lean} &
\texttt{SignSequence}, \texttt{birthdays\_bounded},
\texttt{not\_small}, \texttt{ordinalOrderEmbedding} &
Carrier, relative smallness, birthday bounds, and ordinal labels\\
\texttt{SignSequenceCut.lean} &
\texttt{exists\_cut\_separator\_}\newline
\texttt{of\_birthday\_lt},
\texttt{small\_cut\_fillers} &
Separators with explicit universe and birthday bounds\\
\texttt{SizeObstructions.lean} &
\texttt{SmallCutData}, \texttt{HasSmallCutFillers},
\texttt{noUnrestrictedCuts} &
Distinguishing small cut filling from the inconsistent unrestricted form\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The files lie under
\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/}
\cite{ProveItSigns,ProveItCutFill,ProveItSize}. In particular,
\texttt{SignSequence.\{u\}} lives in \texttt{Type (u+1)}, and
\texttt{not\_small} rules out its being small relative to universe
$u$. The fact that it has a Lean type is not a proof that the entire
carrier may be used as one of the small index types in a cut theorem.

The most direct formalization begins with a generic linearly ordered
carrier and well-order relation codes. Prove common-prefix comparison,
its transitivity, restriction reversal examples, two-label persistence,
and the finite-change theorem before specializing to surreals. These
arguments use no surreal arithmetic. The next layer formalizes coherent
filtrations and the countable-witness condition, followed by the set-sized
ordinal condensation formula. This yields useful verified results without
first constructing a full class-theory library.

For genuine class statements there are two honest routes. One can work
relative to explicit universes and retain every smallness condition, or
formalize a two-sorted model with a class-code type and an evaluation
relation. In the second route, ``internally well-ordered'' must be expressed
using the model's interpretation. Substituting Lean's external
\texttt{WellFounded} for that notion would exclude the very nonstandard
models studied in \cref{swo:lm:mod:section}. In a full transitive model the two
notions coincide, which is why the inaccessible calculations are simpler.

Core automorphisms then require a general set-cut interpolation interface,
uniform set-valued recursion, and a precise coding of evaluations. The
one-point extension obstruction should be formalized with one new marker
adjoined to the class of core codes, as in \cref{swo:lm:aut:thm:localfailure}.
That formulation avoids constructing a type intended to mean ``every
proper class of the whole ambient universe.'' Complete condensation
histories should take the history as an input first; a separate theorem
can derive its existence from the selected ETR axiom or semantic model.

\subsubsection{The exact boundaries that prevent paradoxes}

The usual contradictions disappear when the quantifiers are kept in
their declared domains. A cut theorem realizes cuts with small sets of
constraints, not the cut having the entire carrier as its lower side.
A global enumeration enumerates surreal \emph{labels}, not all class
relations on those labels. A representative of a canonical block is an
actual least label; the whole proper block is not thereby made a set.
An external power set is formed in the containing universe, not in a
smaller universe that would regard its domain as proper.

Finally, first-divergence comparison never identifies arbitrary abstract
class well-orders with ordinals. It uses shared labels and compares two
initial segments of one supplied order. This is weaker than the general
problem of constructing isomorphisms between arbitrary class well-order
types. The literature proves ETR implications for that comparability
problem; those implications must not be promoted to equivalences without
a separate proof \cite{HamkinsWoodin,Williams}.

\subsubsection{Finite diagnostics supplied with the article}

The archive includes a standard-library Python program and its saved
output. The program checks all unordered pairs of permutations on
carriers of sizes two through five. It verifies the decisive-pair
persistence statement on every relevant restricted carrier and the
coordinatewise monotonicity of witnesses on every relevant nested pair
of carriers. It also evaluates finite surreal signs as exact dyadic
rationals to check the dictionary-word encoder independently of the
encoder's own sign comparison.

The saved run passes 58,255 decisive-pair restriction checks and 609,862
nested-witness checks, across 7,432 permutation pairs. It also passes
28,920 exact dyadic comparisons for 241 words with at most two entries,
each entry having at most three signs. The explicit nonmonotone
restriction example is reproduced in the output.

These are finite operational diagnostics. They establish no class
automorphism theorem, transfinite induction, cardinal calculation,
nonstandard-model classification, or ETR implication. Those conclusions
rest on the written proofs. No Lean build, additional axiom audit, or
machine verification of this article is claimed.

\subsubsection{Rebuilding and reusing the deliverable}

The main LaTeX file is self-contained and uses a conventional TeX Live
installation. It has no external figures, bibliography database, or
generated source dependencies. Compile with
\begin{verbatim}
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error \
  surreal_orders_limits_symmetries_models.tex
\end{verbatim}
Run the independent finite diagnostics with
\begin{verbatim}
python3 finite_diagnostics.py --output finite_diagnostics_results.json

\subsection{Source 21: a practical route to rigorous formalization}\label{swo:fu:sec:formalization}

The mathematics can be formalized in several compatible ways. The
best starting point is a small-carrier development that isolates
labelled order comparison from surreal arithmetic. The genuinely class
results should then be expressed in a chosen model of class theory or
through an explicit universe-relative smallness interface.

\subsubsection{An axiom and size ledger}

The following ledger records sufficient foundations used by the proofs.
It is not an assertion that every entry is optimal.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}P{.32\textwidth}P{.25\textwidth}P{.37\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Construction & Sufficient setting & Essential restriction\\
\midrule\endhead
Set alphabet, fibers, noncardinal invariants, fixed-cardinality coherence &
$\ZFC$ & The carrier and all indexing families in these sections are sets.\\[4pt]
Largest common labelled prefix & $\GB$, given the class well-orders &
Elementary comprehension; equality of predecessor classes uses set quantifiers.\\[4pt]
Canonical first block and set-interval blocks & $\GB$, given the class well-order &
Ranks of set intervals define all blocks simultaneously.\\[4pt]
Normalized core and uniform prefix completion & $\GBC$ &
One fixed baseline and explicitly coded set support.\\[4pt]
Set-cut interpolation and large-cut conjugacy & $\GBC$ &
Uniform set-indexed inputs; set-valued recursion, even when its length is $\Ord$.\\[4pt]
Represented-cut reconstruction and extension obstruction & $\GBC$ &
Cuts are individual classes of core codes; the family of all cuts is virtual.\\[4pt]
External countable classifications & A metatheory containing a countable two-sorted $\GBC$ model &
Its admitted class objects form a countable set externally; standardness is stated separately.\\[4pt]
Full inaccessible-universe interpretation & An inaccessible $\Omega$ in the metatheory &
The specific realization is $(V_\Omega,\mathcal P(V_\Omega))$; this is an additional model assumption.\\[4pt]
Uniform class-valued recursion & An appropriate $\ETR$ principle &
Not supplied by calling an ordinal-length construction ``recursion''; state the value size.\\[4pt]
Actual hypercollection of class well-orders & A larger universe or a third-order theory &
Comprehension and choice at the new level must be specified.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

For example, the canonical block theorem does not need class-valued
recursion because its equivalence relation is defined directly.
Conversely, an argument that selects an arbitrary isomorphism for each
of a proper collection of residual fibers does not become uniform just
because each individual isomorphism exists. A proof must either give
an elementary unique construction, assume a suitable higher-level
choice principle, or restrict its conclusion to individually specified
inputs. The cut-reconstruction proof of the extension criterion takes
the first route.

\subsubsection{The small-carrier formal core}

A first formalization can parameterize everything by a type $X$ with a
linear label order. A well-order presentation consists of a relation
$R:X\to X\to\mathrm{Prop}$, proofs that it is a strict linear order,
and well-foundedness. The following dependency order avoids involving
surreal addition, multiplication, or analytic constructions.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Define predecessor sets and the common labelled prefix. Prove
initiality, maximality, and existence of the two first outside labels
for distinct well-orders on the same carrier.
\item Define lexicographic comparison through these labels and prove
trichotomy and transitivity. Relate it to first disagreement for
ordinal-indexed exhaustive enumerations.
\item Prove convexity of prefix cylinders, partial-injection completion
inside a sufficiently large cardinal, and the first-cardinality fiber
decomposition. These results can be tested on finite carriers, but their
formal proofs should not be replaced by finite tests.
\item Add the elementary interval-size or short-chain hypothesis and
derive the agreement topology, point characters, density, and cellularity.
The noncardinal birthday theorem then becomes an application of the
three-symbol padding code and an ordinal product calculation.
\item Formalize the fixed-slot embeddings and prove their literal
composition equation. This supplies a useful coherence result before
introducing any proper-class model.
\end{enumerate}

The countable homogeneity theorem is a separate manageable milestone.
Its main ingredients are the uniqueness of a countable dense order
without endpoints, order sums, finite-prefix cylinders, and a
back-and-forth on countable structures. The Baire coding can be verified
as two continuous inverse maps on countable permutations; it need not
be derived from a broad descriptive-set-theoretic library.

\subsubsection{Using the repository's universe-relative surreal interface}

The audited repository already contains sign-sequence foundations for
bounded birthdays, small cuts, and size obstructions \cite{ProveItSigns,ProveItCutFill,ProveItCuts,ProveItSize}. The relevant files distinguish
smallness relative to a universe from unrestricted families. Their
existence does not confer formal status on the new results of this
paper.

The concrete universe parameters matter. In the pinned source,
\path{Surreal.Foundations.SignSequence} lives in
\texttt{Type (u + 1)}, while its birthday is an
\texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}}. The declarations
\path{SignSequence.birthdays_bounded},
\path{SignSequence.small_bounded}, and
\path{SignSequence.not_small} distinguish small families and bounded
birthday subtypes from the encompassing type. Numerical first
disagreement is exposed by \path{SignSequence.lt_iff}. Small-cut
interpolation is available through
\path{SignSequence.small_cut_fillers} and
\path{SignSequence.exists_separator_of_small_sets}; the latter requires
explicit \texttt{Small.\{u\}} instances for both option sets. The
constructor \path{SignSequence.cut} comes with
\path{SignSequence.cut_realizes} and
\path{SignSequence.birthday_cut_le_iSup}. Finally,
\path{Surreal.Foundations.noUnrestrictedCuts} rules out unrestricted
cut filling for any irreflexive relation by taking the whole carrier
as the left option set. These are source-audited interfaces, not a new
kernel check of the repository or of this manuscript.

One sound design exposes the following mathematical interface:
\begin{itemize}
\item a universe-relative ordinal type and sign sequences on small
ordinal domains;
\item a linear numerical order using centered termination;
\item bounded birthdays for small families;
\item a separator for every small separated pair of families;
\item the impossibility of replacing ``small'' by arbitrary families
of the encompassing surreal type.
\end{itemize}

There are then two different formal targets. The first is a theorem
about all well-orders of a particular type in a sufficiently large
universe. That is an ordinary type-theoretic theorem, with explicit
universe parameters. The second is a theorem inside a formalized
two-sorted set theory, whose class variables range over the classes
admitted by that model. One should not identify these targets merely
because both are written with an expression resembling ``all
well-orders.''

The main nonextension theorem is particularly suitable for a modular
formalization. Its abstract input is a genuine class order $S$ with
small-cut interpolation, a prefix completion operation, and an
elementary cut decoder. The output is an obstruction to extending an
automorphism. Surreal field structure is irrelevant. A final module can
instantiate the interface with the normalized surreal core.

\subsubsection{Definable codes are a restriction, not a substitute for all classes}

A formula code with set parameters can describe a definable class
well-order. Such codes are sets, but the evaluation of every formula
uniformly requires an appropriate satisfaction relation. Over a fixed
set model, satisfaction is an external set relation and this approach
is straightforward. For the entire set universe, an unrestricted
internal truth predicate cannot be inserted silently into $\GB$.
Restricting formula complexity, adding a suitable truth class, or
working externally with a fixed model are distinct options.

Even when evaluation is available, different codes can define the same
relation. Numerical lexicography then orders their evaluations, giving
a preorder on codes until extensional duplicates are identified.
Finally, a definable-code family need not exhaust the admitted class
relations, and \cref{swo:fu:gl:diagonal} prevents any internally uniform
set-code family from exhausting all global enumerations. The code
language and its interpretation are part of the formal object.
