\subsection{Source 22: foundations, raw class orders, and universe dependence}\label{swo:rg:sec:foundations}
\subsubsection{Global choice and the interpretation of a class well-order}
A class relation $R$ on a class $A$ is \emph{set-like} when every predecessor segment $\{y\in A:yRx\}$ is a set. A set-like class well-order of a proper class has order type $\Ord$, and its unique ordinal enumeration is available by elementary class definitions using its set predecessor segments. An unrestricted class well-order need not be set-like. Orders of types $\Ord+1$ and $\Ord+\Ord$ have points with proper-class predecessor segments and cannot be enumerated exhaustively by a single $\Ord$-word.

Global Choice supplies a set-like global well-order and hence the baselines used above. The maintained report proves the stronger choice equivalence, over $\GB$ without assuming set choice: the existence of a class well-order of the whole surreal class is equivalent to Global Choice \cite{swoAtPin,swoReadmeAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:cf:choice}). We use this as a previously established result, not as a new theorem. The explicit choice parameters in \cref{swo:rg:sec:core,swo:rg:sec:realization} therefore have genuine foundational content.

When ``well-order'' is stated internally in a two-sorted model, it refers to the model's available subsets or classes. Under $\GBC$, a fixed class linear order is well-founded exactly when it has no set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence. For the nontrivial direction, if an available nonempty subclass has no least member, use Global Choice to select a predecessor at each finite step; recursion on $\omega$ with class parameters and replacement yield a set-coded descending sequence. Conversely, the range of a descending sequence is an available subclass with no least member.

It follows that enlarging the class realization over the same set universe does not change well-foundedness of a \emph{fixed already available relation}. It can change which relations exist. External well-foundedness of a nonstandard model is a separate matter: an external descending sequence need not be a set of that model.

\subsubsection{Direct comparison without an ordinal enumeration}
The direct common-head construction from the earlier report \cite{swoAtPin} avoids forcing a non-set-like class order into an $\Ord$-enumeration. We spell it out because it explains why raw comparison itself does not require $\ETR$.

For class well-orders $R,S$ on the same labelled carrier $A\subseteq\No$, put
\[
 I(R,S)=\{x\in A:\operatorname{Pred}_R(x)=\operatorname{Pred}_S(x)
 \text{ and the two orders agree there}\}.
\]
Equality and agreement here are expressed by quantifying over elements, not by collecting proper predecessor classes into a set.

\begin{note}[Source~22, Proposition~10.1, ``Elementary raw lexicographic comparison'']\label{swo:rg:prop:raw}
\emph{The class $I(R,S)$ is the largest common labelled initial part of $R$ and $S$. If $R\ne S$, the complement has an $R$-least element $a$ and an $S$-least element $b$, with $a\ne b$. Declaring
\[
 R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a<b\text{ numerically}
\]
defines a strict linear comparison of the available class well-orders. The definition is elementary in $R,S$ and agrees with enumeration lexicography in the set-like case.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}; source~22 credits it to
the earlier report.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~22's proof.} If $x\in I(R,S)$ and $yRx$, then $y$ belongs to the common predecessor class of $x$. The agreement of the restricted orders there shows that the predecessor classes of $y$ agree and carry the same restricted order. Thus $y\in I(R,S)$; the argument is symmetric for $S$. Any common labelled initial part is contained in $I(R,S)$, proving maximality.

If $R\ne S$, this common part is proper. Its complement is an available nonempty class, so it has least elements $a$ and $b$ in the respective well-orders. If $a=b$, both predecessor classes would be $I(R,S)$ with agreeing orders, forcing $a\in I(R,S)$, a contradiction. Trichotomy and asymmetry follow from the numerical label order.

For transitivity, suppose $R<_{\lex}S<_{\lex}T$. The heads $I(R,S)$ and $I(S,T)$ are initial parts of $S$, so they are comparable by inclusion. If one is strictly shorter, the other comparison still agrees at the first disagreement of that shorter head, and that comparison decides $R<_{\lex}T$. If the heads are equal, the three next labels have the form $a<b<c$ numerically, so again $R<_{\lex}T$. When ordinal enumerations exist, the common head is exactly their common prefix.
\end{note}

One application of this construction, or extraction of one canonical set-like initial head, must not be confused with an arbitrary iteration whose successive states are proper classes. The latter can call for stronger recursion principles.

\subsubsection{Which orders embed?}
For set alphabets, \cref{swo:rg:thm:spectrum} gives the exact ordinal spectrum and universality for linear orders of size at most the alphabet cardinal. In the global setting, the ordinary-class universality statement is stronger but must be carefully typed.

\begin{note}[Source~22, Proposition~10.2, ``Ordinary-class universality'']\label{swo:rg:n10.2}
\emph{In $\GBC$, every linear order whose carrier is an ordinary class of sets embeds, by a class map, into $\No$, and hence into the set-coded core ${\Psupp(b)}$ and the virtual global enumeration order.}
This is the class universality of \cref{swo:prop:universal,swo:gl:universality};
source~22 says it is the usual surreal universality mechanism.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~22's proof.} Use Global Choice to enumerate the carrier in a set-like order, with domain a set ordinal or $\Ord$. At stage $\alpha$, the previously placed points form a set. Their images below and above the next element determine a separated set cut of $\No$. Choose a separator, for example by the canonical simplest-cut operation or by the fixed global choice, and place the next point there. Every initial recursion segment is set-valued, so ordinary transfinite recursion with class parameters gives the desired class embedding.

To embed $\No$ into ${\Psupp(b)}$, choose uniformly a supported completion of each singleton prefix $(x)$. First labels show that $x<y$ implies the completion of $(x)$ is below the completion of $(y)$. Compose the two embeddings.
\end{note}
This is the usual surreal universality mechanism, not a historical novelty \cite{Ehrlich2012,swoAtPin}. It does not quantify over a same-level class whose elements are arbitrary classes. In particular, it does not imply an embedding of the entire higher-order collection of raw well-orders into an ordinary class order.

\subsubsection{Why \texorpdfstring{$\GBC$}{GBC} is enough for the new reconstruction}
Four superficially similar operations have different strengths:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Set transfinite recursion with already supplied class parameters produces set-valued stages along each set ordinal; the compatible initial solutions can be collected by elementary comprehension.
\item The height of one cylinder is the order type of a \emph{set} of ancestors. No global class rank needs to be recursively constructed.
\item The branch reconstructed from a cut has a unique value at each coordinate, explicitly defined by the existence of a crossed \emph{set} prefix. It is obtained by comprehension, not by repeated choices of new classes.
\item A recursion with proper classes as successive states is a different assertion. Its solution is a class of pairs coding all stage memberships, and its existence is not automatically a theorem of $\GBC$.
\end{enumerate}
The distinction is substantive. Gitman and Hamkins connect elementary transfinite recursion for class relations with clopen determinacy for class games \cite{GitmanHamkins}. Gitman, Hamkins, Holy, Schlicht, and Williams identify the class forcing theorem with $\ETR_{\Ord}$ over $\GBC$ \cite{GHHSW}. None of these stronger principles is silently used in \cref{swo:rg:thm:height,swo:rg:thm:unranked,swo:rg:thm:decoder,swo:rg:thm:faithful}.

\subsubsection{Three safe frameworks}
\paragraph{Set fragments in $\ZFC$.}
Fix a birthday cutoff and an enumeration ordinal. Every carrier, function space, and relation space is a set. All results of \cref{swo:rg:sec:alphabet,swo:rg:sec:residual,swo:rg:sec:finite,swo:rg:sec:infinite} live at this level. Singular cutoffs are allowed; inaccessible cardinals are not assumed.

\paragraph{Classes in a two-sorted theory.}
In $\GBC$, set prefixes and support codes form ordinary classes. Enumerations and raw relations are class variables. Incidence and evaluation are ordinary class relations with set-coded arguments. Assertions about all enumerations are formulas with class quantifiers, not definitions of an ordinary class of enumerations. Stronger comprehension in $\KM$ does not by itself turn classes into members of classes; it changes the allowed formulas and resulting class existence, not the basic sort distinction.

\paragraph{An explicitly larger universe or additional sort.}
In an external universe, the classes of a fixed set model may form a set, and their functions and relation spaces can then be ordinary set objects externally. Alternatively, a higher-order theory may introduce a sort of collections of classes. Both approaches are legitimate when the ambient theory, available collections, and permitted maps are stated. Their conclusions must not be read back as same-level class constructions in $\GBC$.

A $\ZFC$ treatment by definable-class schemata is also possible. A supplied definition can be substituted into the elementary constructions. However, syntactic codes of formulas are not a uniform truth predicate, and ranging over all formula codes does not automatically produce a definable evaluator for all classes.

\subsubsection{A full inaccessible-universe interpretation}
Suppose, in an external metatheory, that $\kappa$ is strongly inaccessible and consider
\[
 (V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa)).
\]
This is a full class model of the relevant class axioms. Its surreal carrier is externally the set $\No_{<\kappa}$, of size $\kappa$. Its set-like global well-orders correspond exactly to exhaustive length-$\kappa$ enumerations of that set. Indeed, set-likeness says that each predecessor class has size less than $\kappa$; an external well-order of a $\kappa$-sized set with this property has order type $\kappa$. Unrestricted class well-orders correspond to all external well-orders on that labelled set, including types $\kappa+3$ and longer.

Since $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology} gives density and cellularity $\kappa$ for the set-like enumeration order, while its $\kappa+3$ raw stratum has $2^\kappa$ pairwise disjoint open intervals. This yields another proof of the earlier nonembedding phenomenon \cite{swoAtPin} (\merge\ \cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding}).

\begin{note}[Source~22, Corollary~10.3, ``A stratum obstruction to raw-to-set-like embedding'']\label{swo:rg:n10.3}
\emph{In the full inaccessible-universe interpretation, the unrestricted raw enumeration order does not order-embed into the set-like enumeration order.}
This is source~11's full-model nonembedding theorem
(\cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding}); source~22 obtains it again from its
invariant table (Part~X), a different route.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Second route (source~22).} Choose in each of $2^\kappa$ distinct length-$\kappa$ cylinders of the $\kappa+3$ stratum three increasing points. Under an order embedding, their outer-point intervals remain pairwise disjoint nonempty intervals, because each contains the image of the middle point. This would force cellularity at least $2^\kappa$ in the target, whose cellularity is $\kappa$. No assertion about equality of a suborder's order topology with its inherited topology is needed.
\end{note}

At the opposite external size extreme, if both sorts of a model $(M,\mathcal X)$ are externally countable, its available global enumeration order is externally a countable dense order without endpoints. An external back-and-forth gives an isomorphism with $\mathbb Q$. That map need not be available in the model. This explains why an external order-type statement alone cannot replace the labelled reconstruction of \cref{swo:rg:thm:faithful}.

\subsubsection{The forbidden constructions}
A hypothetical surreal realizing the cut $(\No,\varnothing)$ would be greater than every surreal, including itself. Therefore only set-sized, or suitably universe-small, cuts may be filled without contradiction. Similarly, the collection of all ordinal lengths is not a set, and a set of all support codes cannot have unbounded heights. The diagonal argument in \cref{swo:rg:sec:realization} rules out an exhaustive uniform class parametrization of all global enumerations by set-valued indices. These are distinct size obstructions, and none is repaired by merely changing notation from ``set'' to ``class''.

\subsection{Source 22: a concrete, universe-explicit formalization program}\label{swo:rg:sec:formalization}
\subsubsection{Actual inspected interfaces}
The ProveIt sign carrier uses a lower universe for ordinal lengths and a larger universe for the entire carrier. The following source interface was inspected at the pinned revision \cite{ProveItSigns}:
\begin{lstlisting}
structure SignSequence : Type (u + 1) where
  birthday : Ordinal.{u}
  signAt : Ordinal.{u} -> SignType
  signAt_ne_zero_iff : forall i, signAt i != 0 <-> i < birthday
\end{lstlisting}
This display transliterates logical symbols for readability; the repository uses Lean's usual Unicode syntax. Its actual namespace is \code{Surreal.Foundations}. Inside \code{SignSequence}, the inspected declarations include
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.43\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Existing declaration & Role in the present mathematics\\
\midrule
\code{lt\_iff} & First-disagreement characterization of numerical order.\\
\code{birthdays\_bounded} & Bounds the birthdays of a lower-universe-small family.\\
\code{not\_small} & The complete sign carrier is not small in the universe of its ordinal lengths.\\
\code{small\_bounded} & A fixed birthday bound gives a small fragment.\\
\code{IsPrefix}, \code{truncate} & Prefix and restriction operations, separate from numerical order.\\
\code{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt} & A separator at a prescribed birthday above all option birthdays.\\
\code{small\_cut\_fillers} & Realization of separated small cuts.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The last two declarations occur in \code{SignSequenceCut.lean}, in the namespace
\begin{center}\code{Surreal.Foundations.SignSequence}.\end{center}
See \cite{ProveItCutFill}. Their parameter types explicitly use \code{SmallCutData} and \code{HasSmallCutFillers}. The file constructs the separator through a complete lexicographic order of bounded Boolean words. It does not assume a field structure or an unrestricted cut operation.

These source declarations are existing inputs, not formalizations of the new theorems. No Lean compiler or repository build was run for this manuscript, and no new Lean proof file is supplied. The formalization ledger of the earlier report likewise does not claim that its own global enumeration results have been kernel-checked \cite{swoReadmeAtPin}.

\subsubsection{Set-sized modules first}
A first implementation should be independent of surreal arithmetic. It should expose an abstract linear alphabet, ordinal coordinate intervals, and a bijective enumeration subtype. The first-disagreement comparison can reuse a lexicographic function-order interface. The mathematical dependencies suggest the following sequence.

\paragraph{Prefix and residual module.}
Define extendible prefixes, residual carriers, and the order type of the remaining coordinate interval. Prove concatenation and restriction inverse, then cylinder convexity. The theorem must retain the complement-cardinality hypothesis rather than assuming that an arbitrary long partial injection extends.

\paragraph{Characters and finite blocks.}
Express the lower and upper sides as ordered sums over first-disagreement coordinates. Formalize the cofinality of a sum with no last index and with a last index. Derive character transfer, then the finite $n!$ block description and the adjacency lemma. This isolates the infinite reasoning from finite permutation enumeration.

\paragraph{Topology and cardinal arithmetic.}
State richness as an alphabet hypothesis. Count short injective prefixes; distinguish an open cylinder, a convex cylinder, a $\pi$-base, and a base. The two separate lower-bound constructions---many short cylinders and many late residual intervals---then prove \cref{swo:rg:thm:topology}. Instantiate richness for the bounded sign carrier only after the abstract result is complete.

\paragraph{Unranked tree incidence.}
Formalize an abstract node/core incidence relation with extension, incompatible-cylinder separation, and fresh strict refinement. Prove that inclusion recovers prefix, that each ancestor collection is small, and that its ordinal order type recovers height. A bounded-height set version should be checked before passing to a class-model interface.

\subsubsection{Do not identify all function types with available classes}
Both \code{Ordinal.\{u\}} and \code{SignSequence.\{u\}} live at a level capable of containing their lower-universe-small fragments. The type of all functions between those types is a perfectly legitimate object in a sufficiently large type universe. It is nevertheless not automatically the class sort of a specified $\GBC$ model. A model may admit only some such external functions as classes.

Accordingly, the global layer should use an explicit two-sorted model or an explicit predicate of admissible class graphs, together with comprehension and replacement interfaces. A uniform family is represented by one admissible relation with set-valued indices. The trace decoder takes an admissible class parameter and constructs another admissible class by a verified elementary formula. In a higher-universe full-model implementation, label the conclusions as external statements about that full collection.

Universe polymorphism prevents type-in-type errors; it does not automatically express all the subtleties of an arbitrary class realization. Conversely, no new large-cardinal hypothesis is needed merely to prove the abstract set-alphabet theorems in Lean. The inaccessible cardinal in the preceding section belongs to one particular model comparison, not to their proof dependencies.

\subsubsection{Useful interfaces rather than unsupported code claims}
The following is a proposed mathematical specification, not compiled Lean:
\begin{lstlisting}
ResidualCylinder:
  input:  an extendible injective prefix p of an alpha-enumeration
  output: an order isomorphism from enumerations of the residual
          alphabet onto the cylinder of p

RecoverHeight:
  input:  cylinder incidence with distinct nodes and fresh refinement
  output: the unique ordinal type of the set of strict ancestors

DecodeTrace:
  input:  a normalized class cut crossing a proper class of nodes
  output: its unique injective ordinal-class word, defined by
          crossed set prefixes, together with a coverage criterion
\end{lstlisting}
These specifications expose the actual proof obligations: extendibility, small ancestor sets, uniqueness, and admissibility of the defining formulas. Writing a declaration named after a theorem without proving these obligations would not constitute a formalization.


% ---- source 22 (batch-83 manuscript 04), lines 968-972
\subsection{Source 22: conclusion}
There are two independent sources of complexity. In set-sized enumeration spaces, a prefix of length below the alphabet cardinal remains flexible, whereas a full cardinal-length prefix may leave an arbitrary residual order. That elementary distinction produces a complete cardinal-topological classification of fixed-length strata, finite factorial blocks, and a sharp contrast between finite and countable tails.

In the global problem, the decisive distinction is between an ordinary class of set codes and the higher-order collection of available class words. Retaining cylinder incidence recovers the missing ordinal ranks; retaining labels allows exhaustive branches to be recognized; and retaining the admitted traces over fixed parameters recovers the available class predicates themselves. Each step has an elementary definition with an explicit size boundary. None requires a same-level class of all well-orders, an unrestricted surreal cut, or an implicit class-valued recursion.

\subsection{Source 22: finite regression checks and reproducibility}\label{swo:rg:app:checks}
The accompanying \code{code/finite\_checks.py} uses only the Python standard library. It checks finite first-disagreement comparisons, residual-cylinder convexity and factorial size, recovery of prefix inclusion and height in an injection tree with spare labels, pair-swap order preservation and trace decoding, and the forced-last-label counterexample when spare labels are absent. Its machine-readable output is \code{data/finite\_checks.json}. The delivered run passed 1,388,197 assertions, including 533,417 ordered word-pair cases, 16,071 residual cylinders, and all 267,289 node pairs in a 517-node finite injection tree. The pair-swap decoder was checked on all 16 four-bit words inside an ambient order of 40,320 permutations.

These checks do not verify uncountable cardinal arithmetic, transfinite cofinalities, small-cut filling, class comprehension, or model reconstruction. They guard the finite combinatorial mechanisms used in the written proofs. Their code is deterministic, and the recorded assertion counts can be reproduced by running
\begin{lstlisting}
python3 code/finite_checks.py --output data/finite_checks.json
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The LaTeX source has an internal bibliography and no external image or font-file dependencies. A working build script, source audit, status note, and checksum manifest are included in the archive.%

\subsection{Source 23: embedding spectra and what the new results do not change}\label{swo:tm:sec:spectra}

\subsubsection{Fixed set carriers}

For an infinite linear alphabet $X$ of cardinality $\mu$, let
$\WO(X)$ consist of complete ordinal enumerations of $X$, and
$\WO_\mu(X)$ of those of length exactly the initial ordinal $\mu$.
The following baseline is already in the repository and its companion
reals report \cite{swoAtPin,ProveItReals}. We include a proof to isolate it from the
new termination theorems.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Theorem~8.1, ``Fixed-set baseline'']\label{swo:tm:thm:setspectrum}
\emph{Both orders have cardinality $2^\mu$. They contain an embedded copy of
every linear order of cardinality at most $\mu$. Their increasing
ordinal embedding spectrum, and their decreasing ordinal embedding
spectrum, consist exactly of the ordinals $\beta<\mu^+$.}
This is \cref{swo:sw:setspectrum}; source~23 calls it a baseline ``already in
the repository'' and includes a proof.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~23's proof.} The upper cardinal bound follows by representing each well-order as a
relation on $X$. Partition $X$ into $\mu$ two-element sets and write
each as $\{a_i,b_i\}$ with $a_i<b_i$. For a binary word of length
$\mu$, enumerate the $i$th pair as $(a_i,b_i)$ for bit zero and
$(b_i,a_i)$ for bit one. Concatenating the pairs has ordinal length
$2\cdot\mu=\mu$. The first different bit decides the first different
label. This embeds the binary lexicographic cube $2^\mu$ and proves
the lower cardinal bound.

For a nonempty linear order $J$ with $|J|\leq\mu$, list its elements, with
repetitions if needed, as $(x_i)_{i<\mu}$. Associate to $x\in J$ the
binary word $c_x(i)=1$ exactly when $x_i<x$. If $x<y$, then
$c_x\leq c_y$ coordinatewise and the inequality is strict at an index
listing $x$. Hence $x\mapsto c_x$ is a lexicographic embedding. Compose
with the pair coding. The empty order embeds trivially.

For the upper ordinal bound, suppose $(f_\eta)_{\eta<\mu^+}$ were
strictly increasing in $\WO(X)$. Construct by recursion a common eventual
prefix of length $\alpha$ for every $\alpha<\mu^+$. At a successor
stage the next values on a tail of the family are nondecreasing in $X$.
A nondecreasing $\mu^+$-sequence with at most $\mu$ distinct values
is eventually constant: otherwise the change stages would be cofinal in
$\mu^+$, contradicting its regularity. At a limit stage less than
$\mu^+$, take the supremum of the earlier stabilization stages.

No eventual common prefix can already exhaust $X$, because by
Lemma~\ref{swo:tm:lem:noprefix} all later enumerations would then coincide.
Thus the recursion yields an injection $\mu^+\to X$, a contradiction.
The decreasing case uses nonincreasing next values. The lower spectrum
bound follows from the universality already proved.
\end{note}

The global word orders discussed above are ordinary proper classes, not
one of these fixed-set orders. Under global choice they all embed into
$\No$, whether or not they are saturated, by the usual forth construction
along an $\Ord$-enumeration. Conversely singleton words embed $\No$ into
each of them. Thus they are equimorphic. Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:termination} and
Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:increasing} show why equimorphism alone loses essential
local information.

\subsubsection{Birthday cutoffs}

For an infinite cardinal $\kappa$, the sign sequences of length below
$\kappa$ form the set $\No_{<\kappa}$ of cardinality $2^{<\kappa}$.
Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:setspectrum} therefore applies with
$\mu=2^{<\kappa}$. If $\kappa$ is regular, a family of fewer than
$\kappa$ options has birthdays bounded below $\kappa$, so the usual
sign-cut construction gives the corresponding small-cut saturation of
this stage. At singular stages the birthday bound needs separate care.

The repository develops a finer singular strong-limit dichotomy for
binary coding length (\merge\ \cref{swo:st:thm:transition}). We do not use that dichotomy or re-prove its
optimality here. Neither its correctness nor any purported strengthening
is needed for the termination or condensation theorems.

\subsubsection{The set-coded core of the global enumeration order}\label{swo:tm:sec:core}

The class of set words must not be confused with the virtual order $\Hsl$ of
all class bijections $\Ord\to\No$. Nevertheless, an ordinary class of
set codes is already dense in the latter and interpolates every uniformly
set-indexed cut. This is a prior result of the repository \cite{swoAtPin}; the
following proof connects it to the bounded-prefix method used above.

Fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. A set-supported permutation of
$\Ord$ is coded canonically by its set of moved pairs, with identity
understood elsewhere. Let $\Psupp(b)$ (source~23's $P_b$) be the ordinary class of these codes,
ordered by comparing their evaluations $b\circ\pi$. Distinct codes have
distinct evaluations.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Lemma~8.2, ``Completing a set prefix'']\label{swo:tm:lem:completeprefix}
\emph{Every injective set word $p:\alpha\to\No$ extends to $b\circ\pi$ for a
set-supported permutation $\pi$ of $\Ord$.}
This is source~11's supported completion (\cref{swo:gl:completion}), for
source~23's support-graph codes.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~23's proof.} Put $u=b^{-1}\circ p$, an injection from $\alpha$ into $\Ord$ with set
graph. Choose an infinite cardinal $\kappa$ strictly above all ordinals
in its domain and range and with $|\alpha|<\kappa$. The two complements
$\kappa\setminus\alpha$ and $\kappa\setminus\ran u$ both have
cardinality $\kappa$. Any bijection between them completes $u$ to a
permutation of $\kappa$. Extend that permutation by the identity above
$\kappa$, then retain only its moved pairs as the code.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~23, Theorem~8.3, ``Uniform small cuts have core separators'']\label{swo:tm:thm:core}
\emph{Suppose $I,J$ are sets and $(e_i)_{i\in I},(f_j)_{j\in J}$ are
\emph{uniformly presented} class bijections $\Ord\to\No$, with
$e_i<f_j$ for every $i,j$. Some evaluation of a code in $\Psupp(b)$ lies
strictly between the two families. Consequently $\Psupp(b)$ is set-cut saturated
and isomorphic to $\No$ in $\GBC$; its evaluations are dense in $\Hsl$.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:interpolation,swo:gl:pbd-no}; source~23 calls it ``a prior
result of the repository''.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~23's proof.} Uniform presentation means that each indexed family is given by a class
relation on index, ordinal position, and surreal value. It permits Class
Replacement on set index domains. If both sides are nonempty, let
$\delta_{ij}$ be the first disagreement of $e_i$ and $f_j$. Choose a set
ordinal $\beta$ above all $\delta_{ij}$. Every prefix cylinder meeting
both families has length less than $\beta$. All such prefixes therefore
belong to a set: restrict the uniformly given words to set positions
below $\beta$, collect their set restrictions, and use Replacement.

As in Lemma~\ref{swo:tm:lem:crossing}, these crossing prefixes form a chain.
Their union $p$ is an injective set word, and all constraints outside its
cylinder are correctly oriented. If its cylinder meets both families,
its lower and upper sets of next labels are strictly separated: a shared
next label would yield a longer crossing prefix. Choose a fresh separator
$a$ of those sets. If only one family meets the cylinder, choose $a$
strictly above, or strictly below, its set of next labels as required.
If neither meets it, choose any unused $a$. No input word terminates at
$p$, since every input has domain $\Ord$.

In every case all comparisons are decided by the prefix $p\cat(a)$.
Complete it by Lemma~\ref{swo:tm:lem:completeprefix}; any completion preserves
those decisions. When an index set is empty, an appropriate fresh first
label bounds the other family's first labels, and the same completion
works. When both are empty, the baseline itself suffices.

Applying this to sets of codes proves saturation of $\Psupp(b)$. It is a
proper class, since every possible first surreal label is attained by
the completion lemma. The back-and-forth argument of
Corollary~\ref{swo:tm:cor:iso} gives $\Psupp(b)\cong\No$. Taking two singleton index
sets proves density in the virtual enumeration order.
\end{note}

This theorem realizes \emph{uniformly set-indexed} cuts, not arbitrary
class-indexed cuts and not an external collection of unrelated classes.
The index sets being small is what bounds the first-disagreement positions.
Also, the ordinary class $\Psupp(b)$ is not an exhaustive coding of $\Hsl$;
Section~\ref{swo:tm:sec:foundations} gives the diagonal obstruction. There is no
conflict between a surreal-sized dense core and a strictly higher-level
domain of all admitted global enumerations.

% ---- source 23 (batch-83 manuscript 05), lines 1265-1531
\subsection{Source 23: why the constructions do not create a class paradox}\label{swo:tm:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Three levels that must not be conflated}

The word orders $\WordsAll_\varepsilon(\No)$, $\I_\varepsilon(\No)$, and
$\WordsInc_\varepsilon(\No)$ are ordinary classes: each element is a set function
on a set ordinal. The polynomial carrier $P(\Gamma)$ is also an
ordinary class, even when $\Gamma$ is proper, because its elements are
finite graphs. Class parameters are used to define membership, but they
do not become members.

By contrast, an exhaustive $\Ord$-enumeration of $\No$ is a proper-class
function. The expressions $\Hsl$ and $\Hall$ abbreviate predicates on
such functions or relations. A map between all their members requires
an explicit interpretation: a uniform formula transforming class
parameters, a higher sort, or an external map over a set-sized model.
These meanings are not interchangeable.

The condensation quotient presents a third common hazard. A block may
be a proper class, so the expression ``the class of all blocks'' is not
an ordinary class in $\GB$. The least-representative construction in
Theorem~\ref{swo:tm:thm:block} removes this hazard. The successor operation
\eqref{swo:tm:eq:successor} likewise quantifies over a set transversal, not a
set of proper-class objects.

\subsubsection{Global choice and the scope of class universality}

Global choice supplies a set-like well-order of the universe and hence
$\Ord$-enumerations of proper classes. It supports the forth and
back-and-forth constructions used here. The repository proves the
stronger equivalence that a class well-order of $\No$ exists exactly
when global choice holds, over its stated $\GB$ conventions \cite{swoAtPin}.
We rely on the forward global-choice construction; no new proof of that
choiceless equivalence is claimed.

Under global choice, every admitted class linear order embeds into
$\No$: enumerate its domain and at each set stage fill the cut determined
by images already chosen. This standard class-universality argument is
explicitly discussed by Hamkins \cite{HamkinsUnivChoice}. It does not say that
there is one class of \emph{all} class linear orders or a uniform map
on such a collection. We also do not infer any converse choice principle
from universality alone.

\subsubsection{No exhaustive class of set codes for global enumerations}

The following diagonal makes the relevant obstruction concrete. It is
consistent with, and independent of the new local word constructions;
it is also part of the earlier report's foundational picture \cite{swoAtPin}.

\begin{note}[Source~23, Proposition~13.1, ``Uniform-code diagonal'']\label{swo:tm:prop:diagonal}
\emph{There cannot be an ordinary class $D$ of set codes with a uniform class
evaluation $F(d,\alpha)$ such that every exhaustive class bijection
$\Ord\to\No$ equals $F(d,-)$ for some $d\in D$.}
This is \cref{swo:gl:diagonal}, by the same pair switch along a class surjection
onto the codes.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~23's proof.} Assume otherwise and choose a class surjection
$i\mapsto d_i$ from $\Ord$ onto $D$; global choice supplies it, allowing
repetition if $D$ is a set. Fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$.
Partition the ordinal positions into consecutive pairs
$(2\cdot i,2\cdot i+1)$. On each pair put the two values
$b(2\cdot i)$ and $b(2\cdot i+1)$ in the order that makes the first
one different from $F(d_i,2\cdot i)$.

This defines an exhaustive class bijection $g$ by an elementary formula,
with no recursive choices. It differs from $F(d_i,-)$ at position
$2\cdot i$ for every $i$. Since every code is listed, $g$ has no code,
a contradiction.
\end{note}

A bounded-support core can nevertheless be an ordinary class of set codes
and be isomorphic to $\No$. Such a core is not an exhaustive coding of
all class bijections. The termination theorem constructs other ordinary
class orders isomorphic to $\No$; it does not evade this diagonal.

\subsubsection{Set-valued construction versus class-valued recursion}

The fresh-separator lemma uses two small cuts. The crossing-prefix proof
uses a bounded set of supplied prefixes. Direct raw comparison uses an
elementary common-part predicate. Polynomial condensation uses one
explicit formula. None requires a general recursion whose values are
arbitrary classes.

A generic iteration of \eqref{swo:tm:eq:successor}, a recursively chosen class
at each stage, or a truth predicate for a class structure is different.
The literature on elementary transfinite recursion makes this distinction
precise \cite{GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}. A proof that an explicit formula
satisfies a recursive specification is not a proof of the unrestricted
recursion scheme. Conversely, it is unnecessarily strong to assume
$\ETR$ merely because a verified explicit example has a class-length
indexing order.

\subsection{Source 23: bounded universes and a concrete interpretation}\label{swo:tm:sec:universes}

\subsubsection{Ordinary ZFC approximations}

A set cutoff avoids higher-order collections. Choose a set of surreal
labels $X$, a set ordinal bound on word lengths, and any chosen relation
codes. All resulting carriers and relation families are sets. The
class theorems cannot simply be copied without their smallness margins:
lengths may reach the bound, required fresh labels may leave $X$, and
set-cut saturation becomes saturation only for families below an
appropriate cardinal.

For example, the proof of the termination theorem needs the union of a
small family of prefixes still to have allowed length. Regularity of a
length bound is a natural sufficient hypothesis. The finite checks in the
package deliberately do not replace this requirement by a finite
analogue and then claim a transfinite conclusion.

\subsubsection{A full inaccessible-universe model}

Let $\kappa$ be strongly inaccessible and work externally with the
full two-sorted structure whose sets are $V_\kappa$ and whose classes
are all subsets of $V_\kappa$. Internally, ordinals form a proper class;
externally that class has order type $\kappa$. Internal set-sized
families have external cardinality below $\kappa$, and every such
family of elements of $V_\kappa$ belongs to $V_\kappa$.

The internal surreal sign carrier has external size $\kappa$, and its
set-cut property becomes saturation for families of size below
$\kappa$. Its set words also have external size $\kappa$.
The full global enumeration collection is now an external set of
bijections $\kappa\to\No^{V_\kappa}$, with cardinality $2^\kappa$.
It is not an internal ordinary class enumerated by $\kappa$ set codes.
This is a concrete setting in which Proposition~\ref{swo:tm:prop:diagonal}
has an ordinary cardinal shadow.

\begin{proposition}[Polynomial orders become ordinal powers]\label{swo:tm:prop:boundedpoly}
In this full model, if an admitted class well-order $\Gamma$ has external
order type $\beta$, then $P(\Gamma)$ has external order type
$\kappa^\beta$, with \emph{ordinal} exponentiation. Internal
set-interval condensation is the operation of collapsing intervals of
external cardinality below $\kappa$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
After externally reindexing $\Gamma$ by $\beta$, the polynomials are
finite-support functions $\beta\to\kappa$. They form the usual ordinal
base-$\kappa$ expansions below $\kappa^\beta$, compared at their highest
different exponent. This can also be proved without an expansion
algorithm: at a successor exponent the order is the sum of $\kappa$
copies of the preceding order, and at a limit it is the union of the
initial suborders with bounded finite support. These are exactly the
successor and limit equations for ordinal exponentiation.

A subclass of $V_\kappa$ is an internal set exactly when it has external
size below $\kappa$. The forward direction follows from inaccessibility;
for the converse, regularity bounds the ranks of fewer than $\kappa$
objects and places their set in $V_\kappa$. Apply this to the intervals.
\end{proof}

For $\Gamma=\omega$, the concrete example is $\kappa^\omega$.
Its finite successive condensations again have order type
$\kappa^\omega$, yet their limit equivalence is universal. Thus the
class construction has an entirely familiar ordinal realization once
the size level is fixed. The inaccessible hypothesis is a sufficient
external model for this explanation, not an axiom needed by the
$\GBC$ proofs of the explicit constructions.

\subsubsection{Model dependence}

In a two-sorted model with fewer available classes, ``all global
enumerations'' means only the available class functions. An arbitrary
external enumeration or isomorphism need not be internally available.
Likewise, external countability of a model does not make its internal
proper classes into internal sets. Statements about external order types,
internal uniform transformations, and a higher-order powerclass must be
labelled separately. No conclusion about all such class realizations is
being inferred from the full inaccessible case.

\subsection{Source 23: a size-explicit formalization program}\label{swo:tm:sec:lean}

\subsubsection{Interfaces that actually exist}

The inspected repository includes the following relevant interfaces
\cite{ProveItCutFill,b83ProveItSmallCutData,swoAtPin}. The statements here describe their source;
no build was run in this investigation.

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.48\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.45\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Source interface & Role in the proposed development\\\midrule\endhead
\texttt{SignSequence.lean}: universe-indexed sign carrier and bounded
birthdays & Separates the large carrier from lower-universe families.\\[4pt]
\texttt{SignSequenceCut.lean}:\newline
\texttt{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt} & Supplies a separator
at a prescribed birthday strictly above option birthdays.\\[4pt]
\texttt{SignSequenceCut.lean}:\newline
\texttt{small\_cut\_fillers} & The abstract small-cut property needed
for the termination proof.\\[4pt]
\texttt{SmallCutData.lean}:\newline
\texttt{ofSmallSets}, reindexing, and
\texttt{HasSmallCutFillers.}\allowbreak
\texttt{exists\_separator\_of\_small\_sets} & Converts
predicate-based sets of options to explicitly small indexed data.\\[4pt]
\texttt{SizeObstructions.lean}:\newline
\texttt{noUnrestrictedCuts} & Prevents an accidental same-size
unrestricted cut-filling axiom.\\\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

In particular, a Lean type named \texttt{Set X} does not mean that every
such set is small at the cut-index universe. The explicit
\texttt{Small} hypotheses are the mathematical content of the size
boundary. An attempt to fill all cuts indexed at the carrier's own size
would admit the cut with every element on the left and nothing on the
right, an immediate contradiction.

\subsubsection{The first formalization milestone}

A practical first development should stay abstract. Take a linearly
ordered carrier $A$ in a larger universe, with small-cut fillers indexed
in a lower universe. Represent a word by a lower-universe ordinal length
and a map from its initial segment to $A$. Record or prove smallness of
the index type. In the injective version add injectivity as a predicate,
not as a new carrier with silently different size.

The proof dependency order is:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove the two-cut fresh-separator lemma and preservation under a
small forbidden family.
\item Define an external marker cut, its extended letter comparison,
word lexicography, concatenation, and convex cylinders.
\item Construct the small set of prefixes of a small family of input
words. Prove uniqueness of a crossing prefix at each length and the
bounded union lemma.
\item Formalize the maximal-prefix separator proof, retaining separately
the endpoint-child case and the no-small-approach case.
\item Instantiate with the sign carrier, then prove the increasing-word
counterexample using an explicit countable increasing family.
\end{enumerate}

No surreal field arithmetic is needed. This produces a useful checked
theorem before attempting virtual orders or internal models of set theory.
The article's exact character theorem can follow afterward, since it needs
cofinality definitions and cardinal minimality beyond the separator proof.

\subsubsection{Polynomial and raw-order formalization}

There are two complementary routes. In a universe-relative type theory,
finite-support polynomials can be represented by finite maps into a large
ordinal type. The set-interval predicate should be replaced by
\emph{lower-universe smallness} of interval types. Proving that a higher
coordinate disagreement contains a copy of the large ordinal carrier
then proves non-smallness. This is the type-theoretic version of
Lemma~\ref{swo:tm:lem:polystep}.

For literal $\GB$ or $\GBC$ claims, formalize a two-sorted model and
interpret the constructions inside it. The theorem about arbitrary
class well-orders needs an admitted-subclass well-order predicate, not
only the absence of a small descending sequence under unstated choice.
The quotient should be the subtype of least representatives. The family
$E_t$ should be defined directly by tail agreement; proving its recursive
laws is then a theorem, not an axiom asserting an iteration exists.

A higher-universe representation of all relations on a given type is
also legitimate. It creates a larger type of codes and must not be
identified with a same-level proper-class collection. Universe raising
solves the typing problem by changing the size level, not by eliminating
Cantor-style obstructions.

\subsubsection{Verification boundary}

No new Lean or Rocq source is supplied as verified code. The package's
Python program tests finite lexicographic comparisons, cylinder convexity,
crossing chains, finite-support ordering, and tail-equivalence identities.
It cannot certify class well-foundedness, small-cut saturation, the
absence of a set cofinal family, or a transfinite limit step. The ordinary
proofs in this article are the evidence offered for those assertions.

\subsection{Source 23: conclusions and result ledger}\label{swo:tm:sec:ledger}

The main distinction is not between a small order and an unimaginably
large one. It is between different carriers, different continuation rules,
and different logical levels. For arbitrary and injective set-length
words, the termination cut controls all local point characters and exactly
when the order becomes surreal-like in the strong saturation sense.
For increasing words, the continuation restriction defeats every fixed
marker. For raw class well-orders, a safe quotient construction reveals
arbitrarily long explicit condensation hierarchies, and those structures
occur inside every interval between distinct set-like enumerations.

\subsection{Source 24: a formalization plan tied to the inspected ProveIt sources}\label{swo:pc:sec:lean}

The source inspection was deliberately narrow; the concrete module described below is cited as source code\,\cite{ProveItSimplicity}, not as verification of the new results. The relevant report's README identifies the existing well-order study as an unformalized research report. The current work was not inserted into the repository and the repository was not built. We inspected an actual foundation module rather than treating a prose claim that the surreal library exists as verification of the new theorems.

\subsubsection{A concrete existing interface}

At the pinned revision, the file
\begin{quote}\small
\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/SignSequenceSimplicity.lean}
\end{quote}
imports the sign-option theory and proves, in namespace
\path{Surreal.Foundations.SignSequence}, declarations including
\begin{quote}\small
\path{isPrefix_of_minimum_birthday},\\
\path{existsUnique_prefix_of_ordConnected},\\
\path{existsUnique_minimum_birthday_of_ordConnected},\\
\path{ordConnected_separators},\\
\path{existsUnique_simplest_separator}.
\end{quote}
The last declaration has the essential shape
\begin{lstlisting}
(c : SmallCutData.{u, u + 1} SignSequence.{u} (\x y => x < y))
(hc : exists x, c.IsRealizedBy x)
  : exists unique x,
      c.IsRealizedBy x and
      forall y, c.IsRealizedBy y -> IsPrefix x y
\end{lstlisting}
This display is an English-like rendering of the inspected signature, not a compilable Lean replacement. Most importantly, \code{hc} is an \emph{existence hypothesis}. The theorem gives a unique simplest separator once existence is supplied; it does not itself prove that every cut has a separator. The explicit small-cut universe parameters are also part of the interface, not removable decoration.

\subsubsection{Recommended separation of modules}

A new development should begin with an arbitrary infinite alphabet and only later instantiate it with surreal birthday cutoffs. One possible module organization is the following; all names here are proposed, not claims about files already present.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}p{.34\linewidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Main obligations\\
\midrule
\path{WellOrders/Enumeration} & Labelled well-order equivalence, fixed-length words, absence of proper-prefix ambiguity for a fixed carrier.\\
\path{WellOrders/PrefixExtension} & Complement cardinalities, ordinal-tail type, completion of short injections.\\
\path{WellOrders/PrefixTopology} & Convex clopen cylinders; equality of prefix and order topologies under thickness.\\
\path{WellOrders/ForwardCompletion} & Prefix uniformity, Cauchy-filter stabilization, injective completion, exhaustion requirements.\\
\path{WellOrders/ExhaustionTree} & Child partition, exact branching, regular-limit unions, the homeomorphism of Theorem~\ref{swo:pc:thm:regular}.\\
\path{WellOrders/PermutationContinuity} & Bounded-image predicate; continuity criteria; complete two-sided uniformity.\\
\path{WellOrders/CountableCompletion} & Complete metric, real-line completion, explicit dense $G_\delta$ representation and gap cardinality.\\
\path{Surreal/ThickCutoffs} & Sign-cone interval lemma and cardinality at all infinite birthday cutoffs.\\
\path{ClassOrders/CommonPrefix} & The predecessor formula and raw lexicographic transitivity with explicit class-model semantics.\\
\path{ClassOrders/UniformFamilies} & Uniform family coding, Class Replacement bounds, small-net rigidity, class completion schemes.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

Here \emph{ordinal tail type} is a real obligation: a prefix of length $\alpha<\mu$ leaves a tail of type $\mu$ because $\mu$ is initial. The corresponding statement for arbitrary fixed ordinal lengths is false in that simple form. Likewise, the formalization of the regular tree must expose the use of regularity at every limit stage.

\subsubsection{Suggested proof boundaries and audit points}

The general alphabet layer needs no surreal arithmetic. It requires an infinite cardinal, an ordinal or chosen well-ordered index type of that cardinality, a set of labels, and ordinary cardinal comparison. For the order topology, add thickness. The surreal-specific layer then discharges exactly that alphabet interface through signs.

The finite executable model should remain separate from the theorem layer. Enumerating finite permutations can test that a child-cylinder partition is disjoint and exhaustive at finite levels, but it cannot establish regular-limit closure. Testing finite partial injections can catch a reversed composition or a mistaken inverse, but it cannot distinguish regular from singular cardinalities. The distinction belongs in quantified cardinal and ordinal lemmas.

For a class-model formalization, represent a class as a predicate or relation on the universe of the model and specify which predicates are admitted in its class part. Do not identify the full ambient function type with the internal class collection unless a full-class model is the intended semantics. If a higher-universe formalization is chosen instead, write every smallness assumption explicitly; a Lean \path{Set} of large objects is not automatically small in the universe used by a small-cut theorem.

A useful audit sequence is: first verify all fixed-set theorems; then verify the cutoff instantiation; then verify statements about a single uniformly coded class family; only afterwards address a higher-sort domain of all class relations. This order keeps the most delicate logical issue out of otherwise elementary topology proofs.

\subsection{Source 24: conclusions}

The natural lexicographic enumeration spaces have more than one completion, and the difference is mathematically informative. Forward stabilization preserves injectivity but can lose labels. Inverse stabilization prevents that loss. Dedekind completion is larger again: it also fills cylinder edges and numerical gaps. The three constructions agree on many finite tests while diverging sharply in transfinite settings.

For regular minimal enumeration cardinalities there is an explicit generalized Baire model, with branching $\mu^{<\mu}$. At the countable surreal cutoff the topology is completely metrizable and familiar, while the order has continuum many missing real-line completion points. At singular cardinalities the bounded-set ideal becomes visible through discontinuous right translations and inversion. These are structural results about the requested lexicographic orders, not consequences of pretending that the surreals form a set.

At the global level, the same subject is rigorous once the size level is kept explicit. A class of set codes can supply every short prefix but cannot enumerate all global well-orders. Set-indexed approximation is rigid; class-indexed approximation is expressive. Arbitrary class well-orders admit an elementary labelled comparison even when their common prefix is a proper class, but their tails require a theory beyond ordinal-class words. These distinctions are the central safeguards against paradoxes and the most useful guide to further formalization.

\subsection{Source 24: finite regression checks and reproducibility}\label{swo:pc:app:tests}

The accompanying Python program uses only the standard library. It checks finite analogues of the mechanisms most vulnerable to indexing mistakes: first-disagreement comparison, convexity of prefix cylinders, disjointness and coverage of the least-unused-label child partition, independent pair-block binary coding, finite partial-injection extension, and central-termination sign-cone comparisons. It also checks the first several instances of the escaping-label example and the identities relating forward and inverse permutations.

The recorded run passed on 5,913 finite permutations and 16,071 prefix cylinders; it checked 10,158 child partitions, 20,775 lexicographic comparisons, 3,618 partial-injection extensions, and 3,255 interval-cone extensions. Full counts and the precise test scope are in \path{data/finite_checks.json}.

These checks are deliberately described as regression tests. Every finite injection from a finite set to itself is already surjective, so a finite experiment cannot reproduce the missing-label completion boundary. Nor can a finite permutation distinguish regular from singular cardinality. The limiting examples and the class results are established by the written proofs, not by extrapolation from the test data.

The package contains the standalone LaTeX source, the compiled PDF, the verification script and its JSON output, a build script, a source-audit note, and a checksum manifest.%

\subsection{Source 25: a concrete formalization program}\label{swo:ph:sec:formalization}

\subsubsection{Existing interfaces actually inspected}

The pinned repository revision contains a universe-indexed sign-sequence carrier \cite{ProveItSigns}. Its relevant declaration is
\begin{lstlisting}
structure SignSequence : Type (u + 1) where
  birthday : Ordinal.{u}
  signAt : Ordinal.{u} -> SignType
  signAt_ne_zero_iff : forall i, signAt i != 0 <-> i < birthday
\end{lstlisting}
This display transcribes the interface using ASCII arrows; it is not an independently compiled source file. Numerical order is lifted from the lexicographic order of zero-extended sign functions. The module includes \code{lt\_iff}, \code{birthdays\_bounded}, \code{small\_bounded}, \code{not\_small}, and a separate \code{IsPrefix} relation. In particular, numerical order and simplicity are not conflated.

The inspected cut module \cite{ProveItCutFill} supplies two relevant declarations:
\begin{lstlisting}
exists_cut_separator_of_birthday_lt
small_cut_fillers
\end{lstlisting}
The former constructs a separator of a specified birthday strictly above all option birthdays. These are precisely the inputs needed for Lemma~\ref{swo:ph:lem:fresh}; the homogeneity theorem does not require surreal arithmetic.

The repository research article is not itself a Lean development of the results proved here. This task did not run the repository's Lean build, and no new theorem in the present article is claimed to have been kernel-checked.

\subsubsection{The first target should be the regular set theorem}

Theorem~\ref{swo:ph:thm:regular} is a good initial formalization target because its structures, branch spaces, and automorphism groups are ordinary types of set-sized objects. The class theorem should not be simulated by silently treating all large-universe objects as small.

A reusable development can abstract over an ordered alphabet $X$ and a fresh-cut extension property. It should then separate six mathematical layers.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.29\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Principal obligation\\
\midrule
\code{PrefixProfile} & First disagreement, prefix equivalence, profile preservation, and induced node action\\
\code{SupportedCompletion} & Extension of partial injections using an explicit reserve and a support bound\\
\code{ProfileExtension} & The maximum and no-maximum cases of Lemma~\ref{swo:ph:lem:onepoint}\\
\code{CoreHomogeneity} & Set-sized back-and-forth, partial-bijection invariants, and branch transport\\
\code{LabelCoherence} & Root-edge representatives, coordinatewise normal form, and small-support rigidity\\
\code{ExhaustiveExtension} & Core trace injectivity, the represented-trace criterion, and the nonextension witness\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

These are proposed module names, not declarations reported as already present. The most valuable early milestone is the no-maximum case of the one-point lemma. It is easy to test only successor divergences and accidentally omit the genuinely transfinite content.

\subsubsection{Proof data worth exposing explicitly}

A partial-configuration record should contain its domain and range, a bijection between them, the proof of pairwise first-disagreement equality, and the proof of order preservation. The fixed noncore markers should be treated as additional supplied constraints, not incorrectly inserted into the type of core codes.

The extension lemma should return a \emph{prefix witness} first, with proofs of injectivity and all profile constraints. Supported completion should then be a separate operation. This factorization makes the two independent sources of existence clear: alphabet cut filling and permutation completion. At singular lengths either source can fail for different reasons.

The inverse branch action needs its own proof. A function preserving prefixes injectively need not be a tree automorphism; the construction must retain surjectivity on the core and derive an inverse node map. Similarly, the trace criterion requires preservation of represented cuts in both directions, not only that exhaustive cuts map into exhaustive cuts.

The edge-label relation can be formalized on the subtype of immediate-successor pairs. Its canonical representative is a root edge, so no quotient of proper classes or higher-universe equivalence classes is needed. The coordinatewise normal-form theorem is then a transfinite induction on the prefix length.

\subsubsection{Universe discipline for the eventual class analogue}

In the repository's sign interface, ordinals of universe $u$ and the full sign carrier inhabit the next universe, while a fixed birthday fragment is small relative to $u$. A theorem using \code{Small.\{u\} I} must not be generalized to an arbitrary higher-universe index type without a new proof. The small-cut property only accepts the intended lower-universe option families.

A universe-relative analogue of the main theorem would need an explicit notion of small support, a chosen enumeration or appropriate presentation of the alphabet, and the exact closure principle required by its back-and-forth. It is not enough to replace \texttt{Ord} with \texttt{Ordinal} in an informal proof. Lean's universe hierarchy is a size-management mechanism, not automatically a model of every GBC class statement.

For a direct foundational formalization, one may instead work inside a formal model of set and class theory, with elementary comprehension and class replacement explicit. That approach is heavier but makes the ``no ETR'' claim an actual theorem about axioms. The regular set theorem and the class-theory theorem are complementary targets rather than interchangeable encodings.

\subsection{Source 25: conclusions and theorem ledger}\label{swo:ph:sec:conclusions}

The ambiguity in the original question is productive when made explicit. Fixed set carriers yield ordinary set orders with bounded ordinal spectra. Full surreal enumerations form a higher-level domain, but a set-coded core and an ordinary class of prefix nodes make a large part of their geometry accessible in GBC. Raw class well-orders require direct relation comparison rather than a fictitious enumeration of every class type by $\Ord$.

The new structural conclusion is that the supported core and its complete unranked prefix geometry are still not enough to identify exhaustive branches. Their symmetries have a precise configuration classification, and all noncore injective branches lie in a single orbit. Exhaustiveness becomes visible only after adding information that links labels across nodes. The natural equality-of-edge-labels relation does more than recover coverage: together with the supported core, it removes every automorphism.

\subsection{Source 25: repository and literature audit}\label{swo:ph:app:audit}

\subsubsection{Snapshot and scope}

The repository was inspected at revision
\begin{center}\path{7ff7736ecf3a0adc8536b2d083cf819e1ba39ace}.\end{center}
The targeted sources were the maintained surreal-well-orders article and its README, and the foundational Lean files \code{SignSequence.lean} and \code{SignSequenceCut.lean}. The repository source includes continuation material in addition to the originally merged manuscripts; we do not infer a current compiled page count from the README's historical description.

The audit was not a line-by-line review of the entire repository, and it did not build Lean, validate all prior manuscript claims, or modify any remote file. The principal dependencies needed here---fresh separation, supported completion, core density, prefix recovery, and the class-order comparison---are either explicitly identified with inspected interfaces or re-proved in the body of this article.

The Library continuations consulted for provenance were the cut-reconstruction manuscript, the second continuation on spectra and extension obstructions, the residual-geometry manuscript, and the termination-and-condensation manuscript listed below. Their titles and relevant research questions were retrieved to avoid presenting an already supplied result as a fresh contribution. We do not claim to have independently reviewed all proofs in those manuscripts.

\subsubsection{Literature scope}

The Kanovei--Shelah paper was checked for the actual index space used in its construction, which explains the correction in Section~2. The class-recursion references distinguish elementary set-valued recursion from ETR and related stronger principles. Ehrlich's survey \cite{Ehrlich2012} provides historical context for the surreal continuum; the specific new prefix-homogeneity and rigidity arguments are not attributed to that survey.

Historical novelty has not been established by an exhaustive literature search. Theorems marked as continuation results are claimed relative to the inspected material, and their validity must be judged from their stated hypotheses and proofs.

\subsection{Source 25: executable checks and reproducibility}\label{swo:ph:app:checks}

The archive includes a deterministic Python program using only the standard library. It tests finite restrictions of ordered prefix recodings over rational labels, the maximum-attained one-point construction in both directions, the first-disagreement/prefix-equivalence identity, finite supported completions, and a cross-node label-coherence counterexample.

The recorded run used seed \code{20261003} and 2,500 trials. It passed 269,329 assertions, broken down as follows.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Yr@{}}
\toprule
Checked finite mechanism & Assertions\\
\midrule
Profile preservation in sampled prefix recodings & 36,847\\
Fresh injective extension prefixes & 2,500\\
Forward one-point profile extension & 13,587\\
Backward prefix injectivity & 2,500\\
Backward one-point profile extension & 13,587\\
Prefix equivalence from first disagreement & 184,235\\
Finite supported completions & 16,071\\
Failure of cross-node label coherence & 1\\
Two-sided fresh-cut example & 1\\
\midrule
Total & 269,329\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

A finite sampled recoding is not asserted to be an automorphism of the entire rational injection tree. It tests the local finite profile mechanism. In particular, these checks do \emph{not} verify the no-maximum limit case, proper-class recursion, global homogeneity, the exhaustive-branch non-invariance theorem, cardinal arithmetic, or Lean kernel correctness. The JSON result file records these exclusions explicitly.

The inspected declaration has the shape

    forall i, signAt i != 0 <-> i < birthday

The carrier is the sign presentation, with termination represented by zero. Its inspected declarations include \texttt{lt\_iff} for first-disagreement numerical comparison, \texttt{ofSigns}, \texttt{ordinalOrderEmbedding}, \texttt{birthdays\_bounded}, \texttt{not\_small}, and \texttt{small\_bounded}. The same file distinguishes \texttt{IsPrefix} from numerical comparison and proves \texttt{simpler\_wellFounded} for proper-prefix simplicity.

The repository README additionally records small-cut results in neighboring files. Those declarations were reported there, but their full proofs were not re-audited for this continuation. No theorem about the new non-Borel boundary is being represented as an existing Lean theorem. The article's proposed module names below are plans, not claims that files with those names already exist.

\subsubsection{Separate the general alphabet layer from surreal arithmetic}

The principal construction can be formalized before any surreal theory. A minimal interface is an index type with a well-order and a cardinal/minimal-length condition, a label type of the same cardinality, and a prefix-agreement relation. At the level of schematic Lean definitions, the core data are as simple as
\begin{lstlisting}
universe u

def InjectiveWords (I X : Type u) :=
  {f : I -> X // Function.Injective f}

def PermutationWords (I X : Type u) := I ~= X

def PrefixAgree {I X : Type u} [LT I]
    (a : I) (f g : I -> X) : Prop :=
  forall i, i < a -> f i = g i
\end{lstlisting}
\noindent\merge\ Transliterated to ASCII; the source prints Lean's Unicode symbols.
These type-level sketches do not implement the cardinal hypotheses or proofs and were not compiled for this article. The substantive obligations are not these wrappers. They are cardinal complement calculations, cofinal block decomposition, the topology generated by cylinders, and the proof that the omitted-label map is continuous.

A suitable development should avoid making ``cardinal $\mu$'' both an arbitrary well-ordered type and an initial ordinal without an explicit bridge. The proof of Lemma~\ref{swo:nb:lem:extension} must retain the fact that every proper prefix has smaller cardinality and that its residual tail has order type $\mu$. At a nonminimal domain the corresponding statement is false, as Proposition~\ref{swo:nb:prop:successor} illustrates.

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.31\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Main obligations\\
\midrule
\texttt{Words/MinimalPrefixes} & Initial-cardinal tail reindexing; extension of short injections; two unused-label extensions.\\
\texttt{Words/PrefixTopology} & Clopen cylinder base, Hausdorffness, local character, thick-alphabet order-topology equivalence.\\
\texttt{Words/PrefixCompletion} & Coherent stabilized prefixes, complete injection uniformity, density, open exhaustion requirements.\\
\texttt{Words/OmittedLabelCode} & First-mismatch partition, disjoint reservoirs, marker bijections, exact omitted range, continuity and order preservation.\\
\texttt{Words/SingularBoundary} & Small non-Borel Cantor set; continuous-preimage contradiction; complete-metric $G_\delta$ criterion.\\
\texttt{Words/ClosedUniversality} & Compact image closedness and the closed-trace argument; countable clopen-base embedding.\\
\texttt{Words/BoundedImages} & Closed forward-bounded injection space, dense $G_\delta$ bounded subgroup, closure-trace equation.\\
\texttt{Surreal/ThickCutoffs} & Sign-trunk construction and the two cardinal parameters $\kappa$ and $2^{<\kappa}$.\\
\texttt{ClassOrders/CommonPrefix} & Admitted-class semantics, elementary prefix formula, raw comparison and transitivity.\\
\texttt{ClassOrders/UniformFamilies} & Support reserves, diagonalization, Class Replacement bounds, set-indexed net rigidity.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{The smallest trustworthy boundary proof}

The first-mismatch identity~\eqref{swo:nb:eq:releaseunion} and the ordered markers are finite-coordinate combinatorics. Their transfinite use requires a separate cardinal block lemma. Once that lemma is available, the range calculation and continuity proof do not require a developed theory of surreal addition, multiplication, or analytic functions. The only specifically surreal input is thickness of the birthday alphabet.

For the final non-Borel step, a formalization can either use a library perfect-set theorem for Borel Cantor subsets, if the relevant version is available in the pinned environment, or isolate it as a named imported theorem whose proof must be supplied. It should not introduce an unproved new axiom while presenting the resulting theorem as kernel-verified mathematics. The two cases in Lemma~\ref{swo:nb:lem:nonborelset} also require the ordinary choice-based cardinal alternatives for the continuum and the Bernstein recursion in the equality case.

The complete-metric criterion is proved in Appendix~\ref{swo:nb:app:gdelta} precisely to avoid a hidden Polish/separability assumption. Its necessity direction is sufficient for the main negative result. Formalizing that direction first would minimize dependencies while retaining the full conclusion.

For the global part, a sound first target is a class model represented by a carrier of sets, an explicit predicate selecting admitted class relations, and the relevant comprehension/replacement axioms. Alternatively, work one universe higher and label the theorem as an external, universe-relative statement. Using the full ambient function type as if it were automatically the internal class part would erase the distinction that the proof is meant to preserve.

\subsection{Source 26: conclusions}\label{swo:nb:sec:conclusion}

The singular boundary of the minimal enumeration space is now visible on a very small and explicit test family. Compactly many injections, each omitting at most one label, already force non-Borelness of exhaustiveness. As a result, the complete-metrizability question has a cardinal-independent negative answer at every uncountable countable-cofinality length. Together with local character and the countable case, this yields an exact classification rather than merely an example of a bad metric.

The closed-trace theorem strengthens the conclusion when the enumeration cardinal exceeds the continuum. The $\beth_\omega$ surreal cutoff satisfies all needed assumptions in $\ZFC$ and turns the abstract alphabet theorem into a statement about the numerical lexicographic order of labelled surreal well-orders. It is a Baire, metrizable, densely ordered space with extensive closed-subspace universality and no nonempty completely metrizable open part.

These advances coexist with, rather than replace, the earlier order spectra and class-theoretic constructions. Fixed carriers, variable carriers, numerical increasing words, nonminimal lengths, raw class well-orders, and quotient order types remain distinct objects. At the global level, uniform coding is a powerful rigorous substitute for a nonexistent ordinary class of all class relations, but diagonalization marks its limit. Keeping the alphabet, length, topology, and logical level explicit is both the main defense against paradoxes and the clearest route to further formal verification.

\subsection{Source 27: comparing global well-orders without a class of classes}
\label{swo:sc:sec:classcomparison}

\subsubsection{Well-foundedness and set-likeness}

A class relation $R$ on $X$ is a class well-order if it is a strict linear
order and every nonempty admitted subclass has an $R$-least element.
In $\GBC$, equivalently, every nonempty set subclass has a least element.
Indeed, if a nonempty class $A$ had none, Global Choice would recursively
choose a descending $\omega$-sequence in $A$; its range is a set, a
contradiction. This equivalence concerns classes admitted by the model.
It does not identify an internally well-founded relation in a nonstandard
model with an externally well-founded one.

The relation is \emph{set-like} if $\pred_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$ is a set for
every $x$. A set-like class well-order on a proper class has order type
$\Ord$: each predecessor set has a set ordinal type, these ranks form
an initial subclass of $\Ord$, and a bounded range would make the
carrier a set. Conversely, any class bijection $\Ord\to X$ transports
ordinal order to a set-like class well-order.

An arbitrary class well-order need not be set-like. A well-order of type
$\Ord+1$, realized on $\No$ using Global Choice, already supplies a
counterexample. This explains why a naive instruction to compare the
``first unequal ordinal entries'' is incomplete in the raw interpretation.

\subsubsection{An elementary common-prefix formula}

The next construction is an established foundation of the repository
\cite{swoAtPin}; we reproduce it because the new large-family theorem
depends on its exact strength.

\begin{definition}\label{swo:sc:def:commonprefix}
For class well-orders $R,S$ on the same labelled class $X$, put
\[
 C(R,S)=\{x\in X:\pred_R(x)=\pred_S(x)
 \text{ and }R,S\text{ agree on }\pred_R(x)^2\}.
\]
Here agreement means agreement of the two class predicates on all pairs
in the common predecessor class. No power class is formed.
\end{definition}

\begin{note}[Source~27, Theorem~3.2, ``Direct labelled comparison'']\label{swo:sc:thm:rawcomparison}
\emph{In $\GBC$, $C(R,S)$ is the largest common labelled initial segment on
which $R$ and $S$ agree. If $R\ne S$, let $a$ and $b$ be the respective
least elements outside it. Then $a\ne b$, and
\[
 R<_{\mathrm{raw}}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a<_X b
\]
defines a strict linear comparison of class well-orders. Its formula uses
only set quantifiers with $R,S$ as class parameters. No $\ETR$ is needed.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}; source~27 calls it ``an
established foundation of the repository''.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~27's proof.} If $x\in C(R,S)$ and $yRx$, then $y$ belongs to the common predecessor
class. Any predecessor of $y$ lies in that class, and agreement there
shows that $\pred_R(y)=\pred_S(y)$ with the induced orders equal.
Thus $y\in C(R,S)$, and the same argument applies to $S$. The orders
agree on $C(R,S)$ because $uRv$ with $v\in C(R,S)$ is equivalent
to $u\in\pred_R(v)=\pred_S(v)$, and hence to $uSv$.
Conversely, every common
labelled initial segment with agreement is contained in $C(R,S)$.

If $C(R,S)=X$, the two orders are equal. Otherwise its complement has
least members $a,b$ in the two well-orders. Both predecessor classes are
exactly $C(R,S)$. If $a=b$, the definition would put this point in
$C(R,S)$, a contradiction.

For transitivity suppose $R<S<T$. The common prefixes $C(R,S)$ and
$C(S,T)$ are initial segments of $S$, hence one contains the other.
If the first is properly shorter, the first divergence of $R$ from both
$S$ and $T$ occurs there, with the same smaller label. If the second is
shorter, use the symmetric argument. If the prefixes coincide, the three
next labels satisfy $a<b<c$. In every case $R<T$. Totality and
asymmetry follow directly from totality of $<_X$.
\end{note}

This theorem constructs a \emph{formula} $R<_{\mathrm{raw}}S$ on class
variables. It does not assert the existence of a class containing all
such $R$. General isomorphism comparison of unrelated class well-orders
is a different problem and can require stronger principles
\cite{HamkinsWoodin}. The labelled identity comparison avoids that task.

\subsubsection{The first set-like block and its convex fibers}

Let $I_R$ be the elements whose $R$-predecessor class is a set. It is an
initial segment. Its inherited order has a canonical enumeration
$c_R:\Ord\to I_R$: for every set ordinal one can perform the set-length
recursion choosing the next element, and uniqueness assembles the
prefixes. Equivalently $c_R(\alpha)=x$ exactly when the set
$\pred_R(x)$ has order type $\alpha$. This also proves uniformity for
a uniformly given family $R_i$.

For a fixed class injection $h:\Ord\to X$, consider all raw well-orders
with $c_R=h$. If $Y=X\setminus\ran h$, these are exactly the orders
\[\tag{S27.2}\label{swo:sc:eq:raw-fiber}
 h+Q,\qquad Q\text{ a class well-order of }Y.
\]
Every point of $Y$ has all of $\ran h$ before it, so none belongs to the
initial set-like block. Two different blocks $h,k$ first disagree at a
set ordinal, and that disagreement decides comparison of \emph{every}
order in their respective fibers. Therefore each fiber is convex.
Within one fiber, comparison is precisely raw comparison of the tails
$Q$. These are formula-level statements, and remain meaningful when the
fibers are collections of class variables.

The fiber may have one point, finitely many points, a set-sized order,
or an entire raw class-order comparison, depending on $Y$. This residual
information is why replacing every raw well-order by its first ordinal
block loses much more than redundant notation.

\subsubsection{A set-coded core for the set-like interpretation}

Fix a baseline class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. A permutation $\pi$ of
$\Ord$ with set support is completely represented by the set graph of
its moved points. The associated enumeration is $E_\pi=b\circ\pi$.
Let ${\Psupp(b)}$ denote the ordinary class of these canonical codes, compared
by their enumerations. Distinct codes have distinct enumerations.

Every injective set prefix extends to such an enumeration: translate it
by $b^{-1}$ to a partial injection of ordinals and complete that injection
to a permutation with set support. An explicit optimum is obtained in
\cref{swo:sc:sec:support}. Between two set-like enumerations, take their common
set prefix and insert a fresh numerical label strictly between their
first unequal labels, then complete. A set of used labels cannot exhaust
a surreal interval, so a fresh label exists. Hence the core meets every
nonempty interval of the set-like comparison.

More strongly, the repository proves that ${\Psupp(b)}$ fills every separated
cut specified by a \emph{uniform set-indexed} family of core elements,
and in $\GBC$ it is isomorphic to $\No$ \cite{swoAtPin}. This is a
property of an ordinary class of set codes. Theorems below show why it
cannot be promoted to a dense uniform family for the entire raw order.
