\subsection{Source 27: a concrete formalization route}
\label{swo:sc:sec:formalization}

The best first machine-checked development is a generic library of
well-ordered words and relation scans. It should depend on an ordered
alphabet and explicit size parameters, then specialize to the surreal
carrier. This keeps the proofs reusable and makes the size distinctions
visible in the interfaces.

\subsubsection{What ProveIt already provides}

At the pinned revision the independent sign carrier is defined as
\texttt{SignSequence : Type (u + 1)}. It has an ordinal birthday
in \texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}}, a sign at each such ordinal, and the condition
that the sign is nonzero exactly below the birthday. Its numerical
order is lifted from lexicographic order on the zero-extended signs.
The inspected declarations include the following
\cite{ProveItSigns,ProveItCutFill,ProveItCuts,ProveItSize}.

\begin{longtable}{@{}P{.44\textwidth}P{.49\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule Existing declaration & Role in a future development\\
\midrule\endfirsthead
\toprule Existing declaration & Role in a future development\\
\midrule\endhead
\texttt{SignSequence.lt\_iff} & First-disagreement characterization of
the numerical order.\\
\texttt{ordinalOrderEmbedding} & The all-plus embedding of ordinals
into the sign carrier.\\
\texttt{birthdays\_bounded} & Every small indexed family has a strict
ordinal birthday bound.\\
\texttt{small\_bounded} & Each bounded-birthday subtype is small in
the lower universe.\\
\texttt{not\_small} & The whole sign carrier cannot be resized to
the lower universe~\texttt{u}.\\
\texttt{small\_cut\_fillers} & Existence of a strict separator for
small separated cuts.\\
\texttt{exists\_separator\_of\_small\_sets} & A set-interface form
of small-cut interpolation.\\
\texttt{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt} & A separator at
a prescribed birthday above all option birthdays.\\
\texttt{noUnrestrictedCuts} & Formal obstruction to demanding
strict separators for arbitrary large cuts.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The first entries are in \texttt{SignSequence.lean}; the last four
are in the cut and size modules named in \cref{swo:sc:sec:scope}. We inspected
their source statements. This article does not claim to have rebuilt
ProveIt or machine-checked its new lexicographic theorems.

\subsubsection{Universe levels should remain part of the statement}

Lean's universe hierarchy provides a disciplined way to say that a
carrier is too large for one universe while still being an object
in a larger one \cite{LeanUniverses}. It does not identify all universe
levels or provide a type of every type. In the inspected development,
both \texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}} and \texttt{SignSequence.\{u\}} live in
\texttt{Type (u + 1)}. The lower universe~\texttt{u} controls the
small well-ordered representatives; \texttt{Small.\{u\}} asks whether
a type can be resized to that lower universe. Predicate types and
collections of predicates on a fixed carrier do not each automatically
require a new universe. The crucial distinction is between a construction
with explicit fixed universe parameters and an unbounded totality across
all universe levels. Relation types, family indices, and the model in
which a class interpretation is made should retain their actual universe
parameters in every theorem interface.
An order embedding of a bounded universe's word type into a larger
surreal type is compatible with all the negative results above. It
does not establish an embedding of a literal collection of every
proper-class relation into the same foundational level. Similarly,
proving a small-cut property does not permit instantiating it with
the whole carrier as a small set.

\subsubsection{Recommended theorem interfaces and implementation order}

\textbf{Stage 1: generic words.} Represent a word by a well-ordered
domain and an entry function, or by an ordinal and entries on its
initial segment. Use an explicit sum type for the terminator; do not
use a distinguished alphabet element unless taking a stated quotient.
Prove first-difference uniqueness, linearity, common-prefix rules,
convexity of cylinders, and prefix-freeness for exhaustive injections.
The split map of \cref{swo:sc:thm:incfactor} should be formalized here, as
an exact order isomorphism independent of any surreal arithmetic.

\textbf{Stage 2: set relations and scans.} A scan is an order-indexed
bijection onto ordered pairs; retain its ordinal type in the data.
Define the characteristic table and its order embedding into a binary
power. Formalize adjacent-pair coding, stabilization of a
$\mu^+$-sequence of binary words, and the exact spectrum.
Then prove the prefix-neighborhood lemma and the two scan-topology
theorems. The six-coordinate construction is a small, concrete
counterexample generator with a genuinely transfinite consequence.

\textbf{Stage 3: permutation completion.} Separate forced moved points
from available reserve points. The main reusable equivalence is
\eqref{swo:sc:eq:supportcriterion}. Formalize the finite and infinite cardinal
cancellation cases, followed by increasing enumeration of fresh
ordinals and \eqref{swo:sc:eq:leastheight}. Keep the existence of a matching
separate from selecting one computationally. The exact finite optimizer
in the accompanying diagnostics is a test of the specification, not
a proof of the infinite reserve case.

\textbf{Stage 4: an explicit class model.} For the class theorems,
formalize a two-sorted model or a fixed universe-bounded interpretation.
Expose an interface for elementary comprehension, Class Replacement,
and a set-like global enumeration. Prove the common labelled prefix
formula and its linearity without introducing a class of class
relations. Define a family as a single relation with a set index
argument. The diagonal theorem can then be formalized directly.

\textbf{Stage 5: set-state recursion and prefix automorphisms.} Prove
one lemma assembling compatible unique set-length runs. Apply it first
to the residual back-and-forth, then to the local-map evaluator.
This isolates the exact foundational step and prevents accidentally
assuming a principle of class choice. The branch-transitivity theorem,
the coverage bounds, and the cross-node label classification then
follow with short structural arguments.

\textbf{Stage 6: external model comparison.} Express the trace
reconstruction formula and prove its invariance for models sharing
their first-order set structure and the displayed class predicates.
The marked-model theorem should be an external theorem about these
models, not an internal quantification over a universe's own entire
semantic apparatus.

These stages form a dependency order, not a promise of an existing
implementation. The source audit is deliberately explicit about which
items are already Lean declarations and which are proposed new modules.

\subsection{Source 27: finite diagnostics, proof status, and reproduction}
\label{swo:sc:app:checks}

The archive includes a Python program using only the standard library.
It checks all effective oriented scans on three labels, the explicit
enumeration-versus-table reversal, finite versions of the six-point
fiber construction, the exact increasing-word factorization at every
cut of a finite alphabet, and the finite support optimum by exhaustive
permutation search. The program writes a JSON record of counts and
results. Its checks remain active when Python optimization is enabled.

These checks have a limited and explicit role. They detect mistakes in
orientation, prefix termination, partitioning, and support-height
conventions. They do not prove regularity arguments at $\mu^+$,
infinite reserve requirements, Global Choice, any class recursion
claim, or absence of a uniform class family. Those conclusions rest
on the mathematical proofs in the article. In particular, the finite
support search always has balanced finite boundary cardinalities;
the $\omega$-shift obstruction cannot be discovered by extrapolating
that test alone.

The theorem statements and their foundational assumptions were reviewed
independently during preparation. This is not external peer review and
does not change their status to machine-checked mathematics. The
stronger general-gap cut-classification proposal was not proved and
is left in \cref{swo:sc:sec:questions}, rather than included among the
theorems.

The LaTeX source is self-contained and uses an internal bibliography.
Compile with
\begin{quote}\ttfamily
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error\newline
\hspace*{1em}surreal\_lexicographic\_orders.tex
\end{quote}
Run the finite diagnostics with
\begin{quote}\ttfamily

\subsection{Source 28: a formalization plan tied to the inspected repository}\label{swo:ge:sec:lean}

\subsubsection{Separate the generic theorem from its surreal instance}

The new algebra and topology use only a set of coordinates, an ideal of allowed control sets, and permutations. A Lean development should first formalize that generic layer. Surreal-specific code is needed only to supply a thick linearly ordered alphabet and to connect its numerical order topology with the generic prefix topology. This avoids importing arithmetic or real-closed-field results into proofs that do not use them.

A sensible dependency order is as follows. First implement injective partial maps, exhaustive completions, and prefix agreement. Then implement an admissible control ideal, its agreement topology and uniformity, and the exact translation and inversion criteria. Next prove the maximal-subgroup theorem and the symmetric-ideal envelope theorem. The bounded ideal then supplies the singular normalizer and closure results; the small-set ideal supplies the character and complete-group statements. Finally instantiate the order-topological interface at a birthday cutoff.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}P{.25\linewidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Main obligations & Dependencies to keep explicit\\
\midrule
\texttt{PartialInjection} & Small and bounded extension lemmas & Cardinality of both complements; reserve construction.\\
\texttt{AgreementIdeal} & Neighborhoods, uniformity, control ideal & Finite unions, singleton coverage, complement size.\\
\texttt{PermutationContinuity} & Exact criteria and maximal subgroup & Internal transposition witnesses.\\
\texttt{GroupEnvelope} & Symmetric ideal and minimality & Conjugation of pointwise stabilizers.\\
\texttt{BoundedPermutation} & Self-normalizer and one-sided closure & Singular cofinality; enlarged bounded support.\\
\texttt{SmallSetCharacter} & Exact character and diagonal lower bound & Cofinal small-subset families, not just ordinal cofinality.\\
\texttt{AgreementCompletion} & Injection completion and two-sided limits & Stabilization on whole control sets.\\
\texttt{SurrealEnumeration} & Thickness and order-topology instance & Sign cones, universe-indexed alphabet size.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

These are proposed module names, not claims that such files already exist in ProveIt. No uncompiled code with admitted proofs is presented as a verified implementation.

\subsubsection{What the inspected Lean file actually proves}

The inspected source~\cite{ProveItSimplicity} is
\begin{quote}\small\raggedright
\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/SignSequenceSimplicity.lean}.
\end{quote}
In the namespace \texttt{Surreal.Foundations.SignSequence}, it proves, among other declarations,
\begin{quote}\small\raggedright
\path{isPrefix_of_minimum_birthday},\\
\path{existsUnique_prefix_of_ordConnected},\\
\path{existsUnique_minimum_birthday_of_ordConnected},\\
\path{ordConnected_separators},\\
\path{existsUnique_simplest_separator}.
\end{quote}
The final theorem has an explicit existence premise for the separator of a
\texttt{SmallCutData.\{u, u + 1\}} cut. It establishes a unique simplest separator \emph{given existence}. It must not be used as an independent proof that every permitted small cut is filled. The minimum-birthday theorem similarly concerns a nonempty order-convex set.

There are also two unrelated prefix notions to keep separate: a surreal sign prefix, relevant to birthday and simplicity, and an enumeration prefix, relevant to the coordinate topology studied here. A theorem about one is not an instance of a theorem about the other without an explicit map and proof.

\subsubsection{Universe discipline and class semantics}

A Lean expression of the form \texttt{Set A} denotes predicates on the type \texttt{A}; it does not, merely by its name, impose the set-versus-proper-class distinction of $\GBC$. A universe-indexed surreal carrier is a type at a specified level. To model global class statements, one should either formalize a two-sorted class model inside the type theory or state external comparison results for a smaller universe embedded in a larger one.

Set-level filter completeness can be formalized in the usual way once its carriers are genuine types. The global small-net and coherent-prefix results should be separate theorems about a model and a supplied class relation. Their hypotheses include Class Replacement or the corresponding semantic closure property. Treating a type of all class relations as an ordinary internal class would reproduce precisely the foundational error the manuscript avoids.

\subsubsection{A feasible first verification target}

The shortest useful verified chain is: conjugation of pointwise stabilizers; the ideal continuity criteria; maximality under the finitary-subgroup hypothesis; and the ideal-envelope theorem. These do not need ordinal arithmetic. A second chain formalizes the bounded extension lemma and the singular normalizer argument, with Lemma~\ref{swo:ge:lem:parts} as a separate cardinal-combinatorial result. The cofinality diagonal in Theorem~\ref{swo:ge:thm:character} is an independent, compact target.

This modular sequence would provide checked mathematical advances before tackling the larger surreal and class-model interfaces. The current manuscript supplies the proofs and dependency map, not a completed new Lean development or a repository-wide verification certificate.


% ---- source 28 (batch-83 manuscript 14), lines 1059-1066
\subsection{Source 28: conclusion}

The lexicographic study becomes more informative, not less, when its competing interpretations are separated. For a fixed thick set of labels, the minimal enumeration order has a prefix topology. At singular enumeration size, that topology sees bounded positions rather than all small coordinate sets. Its failure to support the full permutation-group structure is therefore a precise filtration phenomenon, not a defect in surreal arithmetic.

The boundedness-preserving subgroup has a strong algebraic position: it is maximal under the finitary hypothesis and self-normalizing. Its forward closure and completion are exactly describable, while the inverse-bounded locus provides a dense complete metric subspace at countable cofinality. The canonical group envelope replaces bounded control by arbitrary small-set control. Its large character is forced by a direct diagonal argument, and its two-sided completeness has an explicit inverse-stabilization proof.

At the global level, every set of ordinal coordinates is bounded, so the singular obstruction does not transfer unchanged. The real issue is logical size: a virtual domain of class enumerations is not a class of such enumerations. Uniform coding, supported set codes, model-relative class semantics, and the direct common-prefix comparison allow the subject to be studied without making that identification. These distinctions also determine a realistic route to formal verification and a focused list of remaining problems.

\subsection{Source 29: formalization without paradoxes}\label{swo:bw:sec:formalization}

The choice of foundation is part of the statement of the problem.
The preceding results suggest four workable approaches, each useful
for a different portion of the theory.

\subsubsection{Four routes and their scope}

\begin{longtable}{P{0.19\textwidth}P{0.36\textwidth}P{0.37\textwidth}}
\toprule
Framework & What it treats directly & Boundary that must remain explicit\\
\midrule
\endhead
$\ZFC$ with set bounds & Birthday fragments, fixed strata, binary
codes, countable topology, and every specified set-word construction
& A class is represented schematically by a formula; there is no
internal quantifier over all definable classes or universal truth
predicate.\\[5pt]
$\GBC$ with supplied classes & Global enumerations, numerical class
carriers, uniform families, raw comparison, and set-valued class
constructions & The full collection of class relations is not an
ordinary class. A history supplied as a class parameter is different
from a theorem that it exists.\\[5pt]
Higher-order class theory & Collections whose members are classes,
and maps or completions on these collections & The additional sort
and its comprehension axioms must be specified. $\KM$ strengthens
class comprehension but still does not make proper classes members
of ordinary classes.\\[5pt]
External or universe-relative model & All available objects of a
specified model can be studied as external sets; type universes
separate carriers from collections of relations & Internal size,
external size, internal well-foundedness, and external correctness
must not be identified. Enlarging the universe changes the object.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

For a ZFC-only development, the first milestone should be fully
set-sized: fix $\theta$ and $\alpha$, construct $\No_{<\theta}$ and
$\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\theta})$, and prove the desired theorem uniformly in
those parameters. Statements about all set ordinals then form ordinary
first-order theorems. A statement about all \emph{definable class}
well-orders is instead a schema, unless one moves to a specified
external model with a satisfaction relation available outside it.
Coding formulas alone does not supply an internal satisfaction
predicate for arbitrary formulas of the same universe.

For GBC, the most economical discipline is to keep all relation
arguments explicit. The common-prefix comparison in
\Cref{swo:bw:gl:comparison} uses two supplied classes. The branch
automorphism in \Cref{swo:bw:ta:branch-transitivity} uses two supplied
branches and one fixed global scan. The condensation normal form
in \Cref{swo:bw:ch:normal-form-theorem} uses a supplied history. Each can
be described by one elementary class formula after its parameters
are available.

By contrast, asserting a solution to every elementary recursion
with class-valued slices along an arbitrary class well-order is
the principle $\ETR$, not a routine consequence of the ordinary
set recursion theorem \cite{GitmanHamkins,HamkinsWoodin}. The new
$\CTH\leftrightarrow\CWO$ equivalence identifies exactly the
existence principle for the particular complete condensation histories
used here. It neither proves that arbitrary class recursion follows
from comparability nor requires such recursion once a history has
already been supplied.

\subsubsection{What the inspected Lean code already provides}

The repository has genuine Lean files supporting the sign-sequence
foundation. Their existence and statements were inspected at the
pin; they were not rebuilt in this task. All five files below lie in
\begin{quote}\small
\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/}.
\end{quote}

\begin{longtable}{P{0.36\textwidth}P{0.56\textwidth}}
\toprule
File & Relevant support actually present\\
\midrule
\endhead
\texttt{SignSequence.lean} & A carrier in \texttt{Type (u+1)} with
birthdays in \texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}}, numerical first-disagreement
order, bounded birthdays, ordinal embedding, and non-smallness.\\[5pt]
\texttt{SignSequenceCut.lean} & Small-cut fillers and separators at a
prescribed birthday above the birthdays of the constraints.\\[5pt]
\texttt{SignSequenceCutOperation.lean} & Canonical small-cut operations,
birthday bounds, density, and absence of endpoints.\\[5pt]
\texttt{SignSequenceSimplicity.lean} & The unique simplest separator
\emph{assuming an existing separator}; the existence hypothesis is
not an unrestricted cut-existence theorem.\\[5pt]
\texttt{SizeObstructions.lean} & A lower-universe indexing discipline
for small cuts and impossibility of unrestricted cut filling.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

In particular, the assertion named
\texttt{existsUnique\_simplest\_separator} must not be used with its
separator-existence premise omitted. The small-cut theory and the
non-smallness theorem fit together: allowing every subset of the
carrier as a lower cut would demand a point above the entire
carrier. The obstruction is a formal mathematical statement, not
a limitation to bypass with an unchecked universe coercion
\cite{b83ProveItLeanFoundations}.

A Lean universe-relative surreal type is also not a paradoxical
set of all surreals at its own universe. Its birthdays range over
ordinals at a smaller universe, and the carrier lives at the next
level. One may form relations or collections in a larger type
universe, but then the resulting construction is explicitly relative
to those universe parameters. No identification of a type with
the totality of all types is involved.

\subsubsection{A practical sequence of formal milestones}

The most useful initial formalization is a generic first-difference
library rather than a large class-theory encoding. The following
milestones have exact mathematical specifications.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Set ordinal words and explicit termination.}
Represent a word with its ordinal domain and a function on that
domain. Prove existence of the first disagreement, strict-order
transitivity, prefix-free comparison of bijections, and the three
orders obtained from termination below, between, or above labels.
Keep zero padding as a preorder until the stated quotient or reduced
representatives have been constructed.

\item \textbf{The native birthday spectrum.}
Formalize \Cref{swo:bw:bs:lem:fusion,swo:bw:bs:prop:finite-tail,swo:bw:bs:prop:limit}.
The crucial invariant is that the target prefix contains actual
signs, not padded termination symbols. At a limit, take the union
of the source prefixes and verify the ordinal identity
$2\cdot\lambda=\lambda$. This proves the full spectrum in
\Cref{swo:bw:bs:thm:spectrum} without any class quantification.

\item \textbf{The canonical word factorization.}
Formalize \Cref{swo:bw:wp:factorization} over an arbitrary ordered alphabet
split as $L+R$. The proof only needs the ordinal initial segment
of lower-side entries and its residual tail. The proper-class
corollary ${\mathbf{T}_{\min}}^{\mathrm{op}}\mathbin{\times_\lex}{\mathbf{T}_{\min}}$ can then depend explicitly
on supplied local alphabet isomorphisms.

\item \textbf{Residual fibers and finite tails.}
Prove the exact decomposition over an injective prefix into
well-orders of its unused labels, before introducing any cardinal
coding. For countable alphabets, formalize
$P_{\omega+n}\cong E_n\mathbin{\times_\lex} n!$ and the adjacent endpoint
pairs. This separates the combinatorial core from the descriptive
set theory.

\item \textbf{Two named topologies and two named Borel structures.}
The discrete coordinate topology and the order topology must be
distinct definitions. The theorem that comparison is
$\Delta^0_2$ in one coding must not rewrite the Borel structure
of the other. The same discipline applies to the topological
product Borel structure and the tensor sigma-algebra generated
by measurable rectangles.

\item \textbf{Condensation from a supplied history.}
Prove the floor identities, finite support, and initiality of
the normal-form image with the history as a parameter. Only
after these lemmas are complete should an existence axiom
such as $\CWO$ or $\ETR$ be connected to the construction.
This order of development makes the exact logical dependency
visible in the theorem statements.
\end{enumerate}

These are proposed modules and proof targets, not newly compiled
Lean developments. Their advantage is that most of the difficult
mathematics can be checked in set-sized or universe-relative
form before the final class-theoretic packaging is attempted.

\subsubsection{The restrictions that prevent paradoxes}

The restrictions are concrete. A surreal's sign sequence has a set
ordinal domain. A Conway normal form has set support. A member
of a GB class is a set. A comparison between two class relations
does not create a set of all class relations. A uniformly indexed
family has one specified class code. A power collection of classes
belongs to a higher sort or to an external model. A class
well-order with a proper-class predecessor segment is not assigned
a set ordinal rank at that point. Finally, a nonprincipal cut
between proper classes is not filled merely because every
set-sized cut is filled.

With these conditions retained, the phenomena proved here are
compatible rather than contradictory. The same set-prefix tree
can support very different class branches, and an ordinary class
core can be universal for all ordinary class linear orders while
failing to contain the entire higher-order family of global
enumerations.

\subsection{Source 30: small cuts, class comparison, and the inherited tools}\label{swo:rt:sec:tools}

\subsubsection{Sign sequences and set-sized cuts}

Write $\No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^{\alpha}$ as a class
definition, not a set union. The birthday $\bd(x)$ is its sign length.
For an infinite cardinal $\kappa$,
\[
|\No_{<\kappa}|=\sum_{\alpha<\kappa}2^{|\alpha|}=2^{<\kappa}.
\]
Cardinals are identified with initial ordinals when they serve as
coordinate lengths. Ordinal and cardinal multiplication remain
different operations.

We use the standard small-cut lemma: for sets $L<R$ of surreal
numbers, there is a simplest separator, whose birthday is at most
$\sup\{\bd(z)+1:z\in L\cup R\}$. The usual sign construction proves
this by meeting each lower and upper requirement before or at that
bound. It includes empty option sets and gives upper and lower
bounds for every set of surreals. These facts and birthday estimates
are implemented on the inspected sign carrier
\cite{b83ProveItLeanFoundations,Ehrlich2012}.

The word \emph{set} is indispensable. Taking all of $\No$ as lower
options would require a surreal larger than itself. A small-cut
theorem cannot be generalized to arbitrary class options.

\subsubsection{Class theory and recursion}

We take $\GB$ to have ZF as its set part and no choice axiom;
$\GBC=\GB+\GC$ includes set choice. A class has sets as elements.
Although the language has class variables, elementary class
comprehension permits only set quantifiers in the defining formula,
with class parameters.

Ordinary recursion with set values and set-sized initial histories
is available with fixed class parameters: solve on each set-sized
domain and assemble by uniqueness. A recursion assigning a proper
class at each stage is different. $\ETR$ supplies additional
elementary class-valued recursions; it is not a synonym for ordinary
transfinite recursion \cite{GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}.

A \emph{class well-order} is a strict linear class relation for
which every nonempty admitted subclass has a least member. It is
\emph{set-like} when each predecessor class is a set. In GBC, for
linear class relations, well-foundedness is equivalent to absence
of a descending $\omega$-sequence. From a nonminimal subclass,
choose successively its baseline-least smaller member; ordinary
recursion produces such a sequence. Equivalently every nonempty
set subset has a least member. This formulation also gives
absoluteness for an existing relation between class realizations
with the same sets.

\subsubsection{The choice requirement is exact}

\begin{note}[Source~30, Theorem~3.1, ``Inherited choice equivalence'']\label{swo:rt:thm:choice-baseline}
\emph{Over $\GB$, the following are equivalent: global choice; a class
well-order of $\No$; a set-like class well-order of $\No$; and a
class bijection $\Ord\to\No$.}
This is source~11's \cref{swo:cf:choice} (over $\GB$ without set choice);
source~30 recalls its argument. (\merge\ ``Uniformly'', not ``coherently'':
the orders $w_\alpha$ need not extend one another, \cref{swo:rem:answered-choice}.)

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~30's proof.} We recall the choiceless argument of \cite[statement labelled
\texttt{swo:cf:choice}]{swoAtPin} (\cref{swo:cf:choice}). A supplied well-order $W$
of sign sequences recursively gives well-orders $w_\alpha$ of
$V_\alpha$. At successors, the unique ordinal enumeration of the
already ordered $V_\alpha$ identifies its subsets with sign
sequences of one fixed length; transport $W$ to order its power
set. At limits compare rank first, then use the existing order
on that rank. All stages are sets. Selecting the least element
of a nonempty set in a sufficiently large $w_\alpha$ gives
global choice.

Conversely global choice selects a well-order of each birthday
layer. Their birthday-ordered concatenation is set-like. The
ordinal ranks of a set-like well-order of the proper class $\No$
form an initial subclass of $\Ord$. This range cannot be a set,
by class replacement, so it is all of $\Ord$. Its inverse is the
required bijection. A bijection conversely transports the ordinal
order to a set-like one.
\end{note}

This is existence in the class sort, not first-order definability.
We sharpen the distinction later. Background and classical
choice equivalences appear in \cite{HamkinsChoice,HamkinsGC}.

\subsubsection{Comparing arbitrary class well-orders directly}

For class well-orders $R,S$ on the same labelled class $X$, let
$P_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$ and define
\[\tag{S30.3.1}
x\in C(R,S)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
P_R(x)=P_S(x)\ \text{ and }\
R\!\upharpoonright P_R(x)=S\!\upharpoonright P_R(x).
\label{swo:rt:eq:commonprefix}
\]
All equalities expand into quantification over set elements.
Elementary comprehension therefore forms this class.

\begin{note}[Source~30, Proposition~3.2, ``Inherited common-prefix comparison'']\label{swo:rt:prop:class-comparison}
\emph{For $R\ne S$, $C(R,S)$ is their largest common labelled initial
segment. Its complement has different least points $a$ in $R$
and $b$ in $S$. Comparing $a$ and $b$ in the native label order
defines a strict linear comparison of class well-orders.}
This is \cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}.

\smallskip\noindent \emph{Source~30's proof.} If $x\in C(R,S)$, all its predecessors also belong, with the same
induced order. Any common labelled initial segment satisfies the
formula, proving maximality. Equal residual minima would themselves
satisfy the formula, a contradiction. For transitivity,
$C(R,S)$ and $C(S,T)$ are nested as initial segments of $S$.
If one is shorter, that earlier disagreement controls the third
comparison. If they coincide, use transitivity on the next labels.
\end{note}

No ordinal is assigned to a proper-class prefix. In particular
the construction applies to transported orders of type
$\Ord+\Ord$ and their tail rearrangements. This is a comparison
formula on class variables; it is not a class containing all the
relations as elements.

\subsubsection{Embedding benchmarks}

Write $\BB_\theta=(\{0,1\}^{\theta},<_{\lex})$. For infinite
$|X|=\mu$, pair orientations give
$\BB_\mu\hookrightarrow\WO_\mu(X)$. Every linear order of
cardinality at most $\mu$ embeds into $\BB_\mu$ by coding its
initial segments on a well-ordered list of its labels.

The preceding reports prove the complete fixed-set benchmark (\merge\ \cref{swo:sw:setspectrum}):
$|\WO(X)|=2^\mu$; all linear orders of size at most $\mu$ embed;
and an ordinal embeds exactly when it is below $\mu^+$.
At birthday stages the minimal stratum satisfies
\[\tag{S30.3.2}
\WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})\equi\BB_{\rho_\kappa}.
\label{swo:rt:eq:prefix-benchmark}
\]
The next section states the precise prefix-coding ingredients
needed from this theorem and proves the new residual extensions.
An embedding classification does not determine order topology:
equimorphic orders may have different endpoints, jumps, and
completions. This distinction is central to the later results.

\subsection{Source 30: formalization without size paradoxes}\label{swo:rt:sec:formal}

The distinctions in the theorems suggest a practical formalization
architecture. Its purpose is to make a theorem's domain and
quantifiers visible in its type, so that an innocent-looking change
of representation cannot silently change the mathematics.

\subsubsection{Three sound routes, serving different questions}

\paragraph{Set stages in ZFC.}
All of the residual coding, countable topology, and Borel results
are ordinary set mathematics. Fix $\No_{<\kappa}$, an ordinal domain
$\alpha$, and the relevant set of bijections or relations.
Power sets, products, spaces of codes, and quantification over
all those codes are legitimate. No inaccessible cardinal, global
choice, or class theory is needed. Ordinary choice is used to
select well-orderings and codes for a set-indexed collection of
residual alphabets.

For this part, a theorem should take an ordinal-indexed domain
as data. A bare bijection between that domain and its cardinal
does not preserve the first-disagreement order. The singular
scheduler and the regular code-sum lemma are precisely the
places where erasing the ordinal structure would invalidate
the proof.

\paragraph{Two-sorted GB/GBC.}
To study the whole surreal class, express a global enumeration
by a formula about one class graph. Express its lexicographic
comparison with a second graph by another formula. For a
uniform family use one class relation
$F(i,\xi,x)$, with the index $i$ ranging over sets. The
partial-table extension theorem has the safe shape
\[
\forall J\,\forall p\,
\bigl(\text{$J$ is a class well-order and $p$ is a valid set table}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists W\,\text{desired properties}\bigr).
\]
The proof supplies $W$ by elementary definitions from its
parameters. It never creates a class containing $J$ or $W$
as an element.

This route is adequate for the elementary reconstruction and
approximation theorems. The present arguments use set-valued
recursions with set-sized initial histories. More general class
recursions, whether their values or dependency histories are
proper classes, require separately stated principles such as ETR. Class forcing is another area where strength
must be specified: the unrestricted class forcing theorem is
equivalent over GBC to $\ETR_{\Ord}$ \cite{GHHSW}.
That theorem is background for a future forcing analysis,
not an assumption hidden in our extension arguments.

\paragraph{A containing universe or an external model.}
An actual topology on a collection of classes, an automorphism
group of that collection, or an intersection over all class
realizations is cleanly formulated in a metatheory in which
the model $(M,\mathcal C)$ is a set. Then $\mathcal C$ and its
subcollections are ordinary sets there. State explicitly
whether a support, sequence, or isomorphism is internal to $M$
or merely exists externally.

For example, a model-internal set may be externally countable
without belonging to any prescribed small internal rank.
Conversely the whole internally proper surreal class is a
set externally. Allowing its whole relation table as an
external support makes the observation topology discrete,
destroying the density result. This is a change of topology,
not a contradiction.

One may alternatively posit a third sort of collections of
classes, with explicitly stated axioms. Merely passing from
GB to Kelley--Morse does not do that: KM strengthens class
comprehension but still does not make proper classes elements
of ordinary classes. A higher sort must be introduced as
such. There is no need for it in the set theorems or in the
elementary class formulas proved here.

\subsubsection{Why an exhaustive same-level evaluator is impossible}

The pair construction gives an immediate diagnostic for an
incorrect size claim. Suppose one class relation $F(\alpha,\xi,x)$
uniformly listed every global enumeration as $E_\alpha$ for
$\alpha\in\Ord$. Use the normalized pairs $u_\alpha<v_\alpha$
from \cref{swo:rt:fnd:prop:pairs}, and form by elementary comprehension
\[
A=\{\alpha:E_\alpha(2\cdot\alpha)=u_\alpha\}.
\]
At position $2\cdot\alpha$, the pair enumeration $E_A$ is
$v_\alpha$ if $E_\alpha$ is $u_\alpha$, and is $u_\alpha$
otherwise. In either case they differ. Thus $E_A$ is omitted.

Under global choice a purported exhaustive class of set indices
can be reindexed by $\Ord$ (with repetition if the index domain
is a set), giving the same contradiction. There is therefore no
uniform exhaustive same-level evaluator. This familiar diagonal
argument is entirely compatible with
\cref{swo:rt:fnd:thm:faithful}: that theorem recovers each individually
supplied class from a corresponding enumeration; it does not
list all classes.

Likewise, enumerating formulas is not an automatic escape.
For a fixed formula, satisfaction in a given set structure is
available. A uniform predicate evaluating every formula in the
whole universe supplies additional truth strength; Tarski's theorem
prevents it from being definable in the same language.
Stronger class theories can supply truth for a fixed language,
without thereby listing all available classes. A metatheoretic
schema of separate definitions does not itself supply one uniform
internal evaluator.

\subsubsection{The Lean interface actually present in ProveIt}

The inspected files lie under

\path{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/}.
\end{quote}
Their source, rather than a proposed module name in a report,
is the basis for the following inventory.

\begin{center}\small

\midrule\endhead

\texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}} and a zero-extended sign function.
\path{birthdays_bounded} bounds small families;
\path{not_small} proves the carrier is not small at level $u$.\\[4pt]
\path{SignSequenceCut.lean} &

of a prescribed birthday above all option birthdays;

\end{center}

These declarations are in the namespace
\path{Surreal.Foundations}, with carrier-specific results in
\path{Surreal.Foundations.SignSequence}. Their universe-relative
form is mathematically essential. The fact that all surreals
at one level can be treated as a type at a higher level does
not make that type small at the original level. A proof of
small-cut filling must retain its smallness hypotheses.

We inspected these declarations but did not rebuild the
repository or extend its Lean development. No theorem in the
new residual, topology, or reconstruction sections is being
reported as Lean-verified. The following is an implementation
plan, with proof obligations, rather than claimed existing code.

\subsubsection{A dependency-respecting implementation plan}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Separate the representations.}
Define different types for a well-order relation, a bijective
ordinal enumeration, a partial injection, and a relation table
with its scan. Define conversion maps explicitly. The
first-disagreement theorem should say which order each
conversion preserves. It should not install one undifferentiated
order instance on every code.

\item \textbf{Formalize prefix-free binary coding.}
Prove the sign code $-\mapsto00$, $+\mapsto11$, termination
$\mapsto01$ is prefix-free and order-preserving. State the
concatenation theorem with ordinal sums of code lengths.
Its regular-cardinal specialization and its constant-length
padding specialization should be separate lemmas.

\item \textbf{Verify the singular scheduler.}
Give the max-coordinate schedule its actual ordinal order
type and prove that the first occurrence of a row precedes
every larger-index row. Establish exhaustiveness, injectivity,
and first-disagreement preservation separately. This is the
most delicate set-theoretic component of the embedding proof.

\item \textbf{Use residual alphabets as dependent data.}
After a prefix $p$, the remaining alphabet is
$X\setminus\ran(p)$. A selected code depends on that set.
The proof that equal prefixes select equal codes is as
important as the existence of the codes. The upper and lower
embeddings can then be assembled block by block.

\item \textbf{Name all three topologies.}
On fixed countable enumerations, distinguish the full
discrete-product topology, the lexicographic order topology,
and the pulled-back relation-table topology. Their Borel
sigma-algebras agree in some cases and diverge in others.
Using the wrong ambient topology would turn a false
continuity statement into an apparently routine proof goal.

\item \textbf{Formalize the finite-tail decomposition first.}
The order equivalence $P_{\omega+n}\cong E_n\times n!$ is a small
interface from permutation combinatorics to topology.
Build the split-order Borel lemma and its countable-fiber
exception formula above this interface.

\item \textbf{Develop class results through set nodes.}
Formalize the partial-table rank extension for sets.
Then use a supplied model of class theory, or an explicit
universe-relative surrogate, to prove the branch and
stabilization statements. Pair coding and its decoder are
elementary and make a suitable first reconstruction theorem.
\end{enumerate}

This order of work provides useful certified results before
requiring a full formal theory of arbitrary class realizations.
Finite testing of a scheduler or a code checks indexing
conventions, but cannot replace the proofs of regularity,
class replacement, or absence of exhaustive evaluators.

\subsubsection{Assumption ledger}

\begin{center}\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}P{0.42\textwidth}P{0.49\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Result or construction & Foundation used\\
\midrule\endhead

ZFC; ordinary choice for set-indexed code selections.
Regularity and strong-limit hypotheses occur exactly where stated.\\[4pt]
Every fixed type at $\kappa<\aleph_\omega$ &
ZFC, without CH or GCH. All smaller infinite cardinals are
regular, and larger residual alphabets use the native padded code.\\[4pt]
The GCH classification of every fixed type &
ZFC+GCH. It is a conditional classification, not a ZFC assertion
that all singular residual cardinals are strong limit.\\[4pt]

GB without prior set choice; inherited theorem with explicit
set-valued rank recursion.\\[4pt]
Common-prefix class comparison &
Elementary class comprehension with supplied well-orders;
no class ordinal or ETR is introduced.\\[4pt]

are sets.\\[4pt]

for comparison of realization collections.\\[4pt]

\end{center}

\subsection{Source 30: verification and the scope of the conclusions}\label{swo:rt:sec:verification}

The mathematical review was organized around independent
failure modes: ordinal length rather than cardinal length;
the change of residual alphabet after a prefix; topology
versus a particular measurable presentation; class-valued
versus set-valued recursion; and internal versus external
collections. The final regular, singular strong-limit,
mixed-block, finite-tail, table-extension, and
reconstruction arguments received separate proof review.
Review is additional scrutiny, not a substitute for a
formal proof or external peer review.

The archive includes a small executable check of the
finite mechanisms: the three scans of six labelled orders,
prefix-free sign coding, pair orientations, and the finite
partial-table extension criterion. It exhaustively compares
acyclicity of partial orientations with existence of an
extending permutation on carriers through size five.
The resulting record is included.%
\footnote{\merge\ Shipped as \path{code/30-tables-verify_finite.py} and
\path{data/30-tables-verification_results.json}, with \path{code/30-tables-build.sh}
(it compiles the unshipped \code{surreal\_well\_orders.tex} beside itself),
\path{30-tables-source_audit.txt} and \path{30-tables-proof_review.txt}. The
checker writes \path{verification_results.json} beside itself unless
\code{--output} is passed (\cref{swo:b83:sub:checks}).} These checks validate
finite conventions only; no finite test establishes the
transfinite scheduler, Borel nonmeasurability, class
replacement, or the model-theoretic conclusions.

The classifications proved here concern precisely the
representations and hypotheses stated. GCH gives a full
fixed-type embedding classification at infinite cardinal
birthday cutoffs. The unconditional theorem already covers every
fixed type at each infinite $\kappa<\aleph_\omega$, and every
residual block above the birthday cutoff. Only the regime of
singular non-strong-limit residual cardinals at most $\kappa$
remains outside the stated exact formulas.
Even a complete embedding classification leaves the
topological distinctions at $\omega+1$ and $\omega+2$
visible. At the global level, relation tables can make all
types locally indistinguishable while labelled enumeration
availability recovers the entire class universe. Both
phenomena are compatible because they retain different
information.

further part. In the external order of every set-sized $\GBC$ model the
singleton blocks and the finite-tail permutation blocks are first-order
definable (\cref{swo:rs:prop:cm-intrinsic}); existence of a greatest element
is not invariant (\cref{swo:fu:fc:cor:notrecoverable}).
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.8}, source~12's \cref{swo:st:n14.8}, and
the open item ``what the unlabelled external order type remembers'' of
\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}~(e)}: answered in part for the pure order. Among
countable models it remembers exactly whether $\omega$ is standard
(\cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-two-types}); its first-order theory is the same for all
set-sized models (\cref{swo:rs:thm:cm-common-theory}). Expansions by the
set-like predicate, labels or baselines are not classified here (source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:n11.3,swo:lm:n11.4}, source~19's \cref{swo:rs:n14.9}).
\item \emph{Source~17's \cref{swo:gs:n15.9}, the condensed unrestricted
order}: answered in part, for countable models: its finite-condensation
quotient is $\mathbb Q$, with the colour arrangement of
\cref{swo:lm:mod:finite-condensation} in the nonstandard case. For the coarser
condensation by set-sized residuals, source~20's quotient is dense without
endpoints but has an unfilled cut of character $(\omega,\omega)$
(\cref{swo:lm:loc:quotient}).
\item \emph{Uniform coding of the unrestricted order} (no earlier question):
an interval $[R,S]$ is exhaustively coded by a uniform set-indexed family
exactly when its residual $Y(R,S)$ is a set (\cref{swo:lm:loc:dichotomy}), and
no uniform class-indexed family is dense in the raw comparison
(\cref{swo:sc:thm:omittedcopy}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{The problem and the contributions}\label{swo:gcz:sec:intro}

Global choice makes a single selection simultaneously throughout the universe.
Ordinary Choice supplies selections for each set-sized family. With Replacement
available, these principles often have the same consequences about sets. Removing
Replacement changes the problem: a family described by a formula and indexed by
\(\omega\) need not itself be a set. A uniform selection from that family can
then produce information that ordinary Choice cannot assemble.

Glazer proved that global choice with expanded Separation is not conservative
over \(\ZC\), both with and without Foundation \cite{gczGlazer}. We use the
countable-family incidence obstruction in his Propositions 3.8 and 4.11; we do
not reconstruct his symmetric-extension countermodels. Our contribution to that
argument is to show that a selector on countable inputs already supplies the
uniform presentations needed for its contradiction.

The relevant ProveIt source is the report on surreal well-orders
\cite{gczAtPin}. Its Theorem 13.1, label \code{swo:cf:choice}
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}), gives over
\(\GB\) the equivalence between global choice, class well-orders of \(\No\),
set-like such well-orders, and an \(\Ord\)-enumeration of \(\No\). Its
Question \code{swo:ge:n10} (\cref{swo:ge:n10}) asks how image bounding and uniform choice separate
over weaker class theories. We analyze particular mechanisms in that question;
the question's other reconstruction and extension schemes remain open.

The two parts of the article are related, but their logical settings differ.
The countable-selection theorem is a theorem about a first-order theory with an
additional operation symbol. The rank-model results are semantic classifications
of specific two-sorted structures with all external subclasses admitted. No
identification of these two settings is assumed.

\subsection{The localized theorem}

Write \(\GC_{\le\omega}\) for a total operation \(c\) satisfying
\[
 X\ne\varnothing\ \wedge\ X\injto\omega\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c(X)\in X.
\]
Separation must be allowed to mention \(c\). The main refinement is
\[
 \boxed{\ZC+\GC_{\le\omega}+\Sep(c)
       \text{ is not conservative over }\ZC.}
\]
The corresponding statement with Foundation also holds. Moreover, replacing
``at most countable'' by ``countably infinite'' does not restore conservativity.
The proof is in \cref{swo:gcz:sec:nonconservative}.

There is a genuine obstacle to the naive proof. Repeatedly deleting the selected
element for \(\omega\) steps need not exhaust a countable set. A selector can
list one infinite part first and leave another part untouched. Nor may we simply
continue through all countable ordinals: the relevant ordinal types need not
exist in Zermelo set theory. We instead collect all compatible partial
well-orders inside a fixed power set and then normalize the resulting order
against a single set of order codes.

\subsection{The exact classification}

For a limit ordinal \(\lambda>\omega\), put
\[
 S_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}{}^\alpha 2,
 \qquad \bd(s)=\dom(s).
\]
Here \(\bd(s)\) is the ordinal length, or birthday, of a binary sign sequence.
The following table previews the classification. Every cardinal condition is
evaluated in the external \(\ZFC\) universe.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}X p{0.39\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Principle in \(\RM_\lambda\) & Exact condition on the height\\
\midrule
Global choice; a birthday-monotone set-like well-order of \(S_\lambda\)
& Every limit \(\lambda>\omega\)\\[4pt]
A class bijection \(\Ord\longleftrightarrow S_\lambda\)
& \(\lambda=\kappa\) is a cardinal and \(2^{<\kappa}=\kappa\)\\[4pt]
Such a bijection with nondecreasing birthdays
& \(\lambda=\kappa\) is a strong-limit cardinal\\[4pt]
A class injection \(V_\lambda\injto S_\lambda\); equivalently,
every set well-order has an ordinal order type
& \(\lambda=\kappa=\beth_\kappa\)\\[4pt]
Class Replacement on every ordinal domain
& \(\lambda\) is an uncountable regular cardinal\\[4pt]
Full Class Replacement
& \(\lambda\) is strongly inaccessible\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The fourth row is an equivalence \emph{within this family of full-class rank
models}. It is not asserted over every weak class theory. The table also concerns
the sign-sequence carrier; at arbitrary cutoffs we do not assert closure under
the surreal field operations.

\subsection{What is new, what is inherited, and what remains open}

The bounded proof of the well-ordering theorem used below is classical in
method. Its application to a uniform presentation theorem, and thence to the
countable-input refinement, is the main additional deduction. Targeted searches
did not find that refinement explicitly stated; this is not a proof of priority.
Restricted global-choice principles have an established literature, including
Enayat's treatment of global finite choice \cite{gczEnayat}.

The distinction between well-orders and ordinal order types without Replacement
is also established. Hamkins discusses ordinal abstraction and the example
\(V_{\omega_1}\) in his account of Rin's work \cite{HamkinsRecursionPrinciple,gczRin}.
Carneiro's discussion addresses set-like class orders without Replacement
\cite{gczCarneiro}. The contribution of our second part is the simultaneous exact
classification of the displayed coding and replacement properties, including
their different thresholds and explicit separating heights.
The usual global-choice equivalences over \(\GB\) are collected in
\cite{HamkinsGC}; the beth-fixed-point background also has prior discussion
\cite{gczBethDiscussion}.

\section{Axioms, classes, and bounded constructions}\label{swo:gcz:sec:axioms}

\subsection{The first-order base theory}

Following Glazer's convention, \(\Zer\) comprises Extensionality, Empty Set,
Pairing, Union, Power Set, Infinity, and the Separation schema. Including Empty
Set explicitly is harmless; the other usual formulations derive it. Set Choice
is added to obtain \(\ZC\). We write \(\ZC_{\mathrm F}\) when Foundation,
in the form that every nonempty set has an \(\in\)-minimal member, is added.
No form of Replacement or Collection is part of these base theories.

All occurrences of \(X\injto D\) mean that there exists a \emph{set graph}
of an injection. A set well-order is a strict linear order on a set such that
every nonempty subset has a least member. We do not replace its underlying set
by an ordinal unless that replacement has been justified.

When a class operation \(c\) is named, \(\Sep(c)\) means Separation for every
formula of the language containing \(c\), with set parameters allowed. A formula
defining a unique set-valued operation gives a definitional expansion: formulas
using the new operation can be translated into the original expanded language.
Consequently, such a definition transports Separation, but does not introduce
Replacement.

\subsection{Fixed bounds}

Fix a well-ordered set \((D,<_{D})\), and define
\[
 \Small_D(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\injto D.
\]
A \(D\)-restricted selector chooses from every nonempty \(D\)-small set.
For definiteness it returns \(\varnothing\) elsewhere. Its restriction to the
subsets of a fixed \(D\)-small set \(X\) can be represented by a set:
\[
 \{(A,x)\in\Pow(X)\times X:
             A\ne\varnothing\text{ and }c(A)=x\}.
\]
This follows by Separation. The restriction's being a set does not imply that
the family of all such restrictions, as \(X\) varies, is a set.

We shall also use the set of codes
\[\tag{S31.1}\label{swo:gcz:eq:codes}
 \mathcal C_D=\Pow(D)\times\Pow(D\times D).
\]
A code records both a carrier and a relation. Recording the carrier is essential:
the empty relation alone cannot distinguish different singleton orders. Ordinary
Choice supplies one fixed well-order \(\prec_D\) of \(\mathcal C_D\).
No choice of a code for each \(X\) has yet been made.

\subsection{A bounded-existence convention}

Every set introduced in the first part will have an explicit containing set.
For example, a proposed graph from \(X\) to \(D\) is separated from
\(X\times D\); a family of relations on \(X\) is separated from
\(\Pow(X\times X)\). Cartesian products themselves exist by the ordinary
Pairing, Union, Power Set, and Separation construction.

These bounds are more than presentation details. A statement of the form
\(\forall n\in\omega\,\exists!X\,\varphi(n,X)\) need not provide a set
containing all the values \(X\). On the other hand, if a containing set \(B\)
is already known, then its graph is a subset of \(\omega\times B\), and
Separation suffices. Our argument repeatedly uses the second situation while
avoiding the first.

\section{Uniform presentations from restricted selection}\label{swo:gcz:sec:uniform}

\subsection{A selector-compatible well-order}

\begin{lemma}[Bounded well-order construction]\label{swo:gcz:lem:thread}
Let \(X\) be a set and suppose \(c(A)\in A\) for every nonempty
\(A\subseteq X\). In \(\Zer+\Sep(c)\) there is a unique well-order \(W_X\)
of \(X\) satisfying
\[\tag{S31.2}\label{swo:gcz:eq:choiceorder}
 a=c\bigl(X\setminus\pred_{W_X}(a)\bigr)
 \qquad(a\in X).
\]
The relation \(W_X\) is uniformly definable from \(X\) and \(c\).
No ordinal collapse, Replacement, or Foundation is used.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Call \((A,R)\) a \emph{thread on \(X\)} if \(A\subseteq X\),
\(R\) well-orders \(A\), and
\[
 a=c\bigl(X\setminus\pred_R(a)\bigr)\quad(a\in A).
\]
The ambient set in this equation is always \(X\), even for a proper partial
domain \(A\). The set \(\Thr_X\) of threads is separated from
\(\Pow(X)\times\Pow(X\times X)\).

We first prove that any two threads \((A,R)\), \((B,T)\) are comparable by
initial segment. Let \(C\subseteq A\cap B\) consist of those \(x\) whose
predecessor sets in the two orders are equal and on whose predecessor set the
two orders agree. If \(x\in C\) and \(yRx\), then \(yTx\), and agreement
below \(x\) implies agreement of the predecessor sets and orders below \(y\).
Thus \(y\in C\). The symmetric statement holds, so \(C\) is an initial
segment of both orders, with the same order on it.

If both threads continue beyond \(C\), let \(a\) and \(b\) be the respective
first points beyond it. Their predecessor sets are exactly \(C\), whence
\[
 a=c(X\setminus C)=b.
\]
The predecessor orders agree, so this common point belongs to \(C\), a
contradiction. One thread is therefore an initial segment of the other.

Separate from \(X\) the union \(A_*\) of all thread domains, and from
\(X\times X\) the union \(R_*\) of their relations. Comparability makes
\(R_*\) a linear order on \(A_*\). To verify well-ordering, let
\(Y\subseteq A_*\) be nonempty. Choose \(y\in Y\) and a thread containing
\(y\). Let \(z\) be the least element of the nonempty intersection of its
domain with \(Y\). Any other thread is an initial segment or an extension of
this one; its new points cannot lie below \(z\). Thus \(z\) is least in
\(Y\) for \(R_*\).

Every thread containing a point \(a\) has the same predecessors of \(a\)
as the union. Consequently \((A_*,R_*)\) is itself a thread. If
\(A_*\ne X\), append \(c(X\setminus A_*)\) to its end. The resulting
well-order is a thread with a larger domain, contradicting the definition of
\(A_*\). Hence \(A_*=X\), proving existence. Two full-domain threads must
coincide by initial-segment comparability, proving uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why ordinary iteration is insufficient]\label{swo:gcz:rem:iteration}
Let \(X=\omega\times\{0,1\}\). A selector on subsets of \(X\) can select
the least available \((n,0)\) whenever any such point remains. Successive
finite deletions then visit only \(\omega\times\{0\}\). The compatible
well-order can have type \(\omega+\omega\), so its first \(\omega\)
positions need not enumerate \(X\). The next theorem produces an injection
into \(\omega\) without asserting that this particular well-order has a
countable ordinal representative in the weak theory.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Normalizing against one set of order codes}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform presentation theorem]\label{swo:gcz:thm:uniform}
Fix \((D,<_{D})\) and a well-order \(\prec_D\) of \(\mathcal C_D\).
Over \(\Zer\) with Separation in the relevant expanded language, the following
existence principles are interconvertible by uniform definitions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item a selector \(c\) for every nonempty \(D\)-small set;
\item a class assignment \(X\mapsto i_X\) which supplies a set injection
      \(i_X:X\injto D\) for every \(D\)-small set \(X\).
\end{enumerate}
In \(\ZC\), the needed order \(\prec_D\) exists by ordinary Choice.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume (i). Every subset of a \(D\)-small \(X\) is \(D\)-small, so
\cref{swo:gcz:lem:thread} constructs \(W_X\). Form by Separation
\[
 \mathcal A_X=\{(A,R)\in\mathcal C_D:
                 R\text{ well-orders }A\text{ and }(X,W_X)\cong(A,R)\}.
\]
This set is nonempty. Indeed, an existing injection \(u:X\injto D\) transports
\(W_X\) to its image; both the image and the transported relation are separated
from \(D\) and \(D\times D\). This argument uses the existence of a
particular \(u\) only to prove nonemptiness. It does not choose such a \(u\)
uniformly.

Let \((A_X,R_X)\) be the \(\prec_D\)-least code in \(\mathcal A_X\).
There is a unique order isomorphism
\[
 i_X:(X,W_X)\longrightarrow(A_X,R_X),
\]
because a well-order has no nonidentity order automorphism. For completeness,
two isomorphisms would have a least point of disagreement; their values there
have the same predecessor set and therefore are equal, a contradiction.
The isomorphism graph is a subset of \(X\times D\). The assertions defining
the least code and its unique isomorphism constitute a uniform definition of
\(i_X\). Set its value to \(\varnothing\) on nonsmall inputs.

Conversely, assume (ii). For nonempty \(D\)-small \(X\), the image
\(i_X[X]\) is a nonempty subset of \(D\). Choose the unique element of
\(X\) mapped to its \(<_{D}\)-least member. This uniformly defines a
selector. All image and inverse graphs here have displayed set bounds.

In either direction, the new operation has a unique set value specified by a
formula in the old expanded language. Substitution of this definition translates
each instance of Separation involving the new operation into an available
instance of Separation. This verifies the assertion about the whole expanded
theories, not just about an isolated operation.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Uniformity is not compatibility under restriction]\label{swo:gcz:n3.4}
The theorem does not say that \(i_Y=i_X\restr Y\) when \(Y\subseteq X\).
Nor does it assert a definitional equivalence that recovers an original selector
after a round trip. It gives uniform constructions establishing equivalence of
the two existence principles, with a fixed set of code-ordering parameters.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Uniform countable enumeration]\label{swo:gcz:cor:enumeration}
Under \(\ZC+\GC_{\le\omega}+\Sep(c)\), a single class definition assigns
to every nonempty countable set \(X\) a set surjection \(e_X:\omega\to X\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{swo:gcz:thm:uniform} with \(D=\omega\). Let
\(m_X=\min i_X[X]\), and define
\[
 e_X(n)=
 \begin{cases}
  i_X^{-1}(n),&n\in i_X[X],\\
  i_X^{-1}(m_X),&n\notin i_X[X].
 \end{cases}
\]
The graph is a subset of \(\omega\times X\), and its range is \(X\).
\end{proof}

\section{Incidence coding without Collection}\label{swo:gcz:sec:coding}

The next theorem captures what a uniform presentation makes possible. Its
hypothesis is weaker than requiring a different incidence trace for every
label: equal traces need only determine the same target value.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded trace compression]\label{swo:gcz:thm:compression}
Work in \(\Zer\) with Separation for all the named class parameters. Let
\(I,D,T\) be sets. Suppose:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item \(i\mapsto X_i\), for \(i\in I\), is a class assignment of sets,
      and a uniform class definition gives set injections \(u_i:X_i\injto D\);
\item \(A\) is a class, \(E(x,a)\) a class relation, and \(F:A\to T\)
      a class surjection;
\item whenever \(a,b\in A\) satisfy
      \[
       \forall i\in I\,\forall x\in X_i\,
           \bigl(E(x,a)\leftrightarrow E(x,b)\bigr),
      \]
      one has \(F(a)=F(b)\).
\end{enumerate}
Then there is a set partial surjection
\[\tag{S31.3}\label{swo:gcz:eq:partial}
 Q:\Pow(I\times D)\rightharpoonup T.
\]
If \(\Pow(I\times D)\) is well-orderable, then
\(T\injto\Pow(I\times D)\). In particular this last conclusion holds in
\(\ZC\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For \(a\in A\), define its trace by Separation from \(I\times D\):
\[\tag{S31.4}\label{swo:gcz:eq:trace}
 H_a=\{(i,d)\in I\times D:
           \exists x\in X_i\,[u_i(x)=d\ \wedge\ E(x,a)]\}.
\]
For each \(i\) and \(x\in X_i\), injectivity gives
\[
 E(x,a)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (i,u_i(x))\in H_a.
\]
Thus \(H_a=H_b\) implies the hypothesis in (c) and hence \(F(a)=F(b)\).
Now separate from \(\Pow(I\times D)\times T\) the relation
\[\tag{S31.5}\label{swo:gcz:eq:tracegraph}
 Q=\{(H,t):\exists a\in A\,[H=H_a\ \wedge\ F(a)=t]\}.
\]
It is single-valued by the preceding observation and surjective onto \(T\)
because \(F\) is. To get an injection in the other direction, well-order
\(\Pow(I\times D)\), and assign to each \(t\) its least \(Q\)-preimage.
The resulting graph is again a subset of a fixed set product.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Compression from a restricted selector]\label{swo:gcz:cor:smallcompression}
In \(\ZC+\GC_{\le D}+\Sep(c)\), the same conclusion holds when (a) is
replaced by the assumption that every \(X_i\) injects into \(D\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use \cref{swo:gcz:thm:uniform} to define \(u_i=i_{X_i}\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The logical point of the compression theorem}

Neither \(\{X_i:i\in I\}\), nor \(\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\), nor the
collection of traces \(\{H_a:a\in A\}\) was obtained by Replacement. The
first two may fail to be sets. The third can, when needed, be separated from
\(\Pow(I\times D)\). The proof does not first collect the class of labels
and then take its image. It directly defines a bounded relation whose fibres
are determined by the trace.

Empty rows \(X_i=\varnothing\) cause no problem: their injection has empty
graph and contributes no coordinate. This is a small advantage of formulating
the theorem using injections instead of surjections onto the rows.

The target-separation condition also permits quotient labels. A class may have
many labels describing the same trace, provided their target values agree. Thus
the method applies to incidence presentations with redundant codes, not just
to extensional representations of individual objects.

\subsection{What ordinary set Choice already provides}

If the family of rows is an actual set, ordinary Choice supplies simultaneous
injections. To see the bounded reason, let \(U\) be the union of that family.
Every candidate injection into \(D\) is a subset of \(U\times D\). The
sets of candidate injections therefore form a subfamily of
\(\Pow(\Pow(U\times D))\). Choice on this set-sized family provides a
selection. Consequently, the new phenomenon concerns class assignments whose
values have no common set bound. It is not a failure of ordinary countable
choice inside \(\ZC\).

\section{Countable global selection is nonconservative}\label{swo:gcz:sec:nonconservative}

\subsection{The external input from Glazer}\label{swo:gcz:sub:glazerinput}

We use the following precise interface to Glazer's countermodel theorem
\cite[Propositions 3.8 and 4.11]{gczGlazer}. There is a pure set-theoretic
obstruction sentence \(\Theta\), with separate versions for \(\ZC\) and
\(\ZC_{\mathrm F}\), realized in his respective models. Its definable data
include countable sets \(X_n\), an extensional incidence class on their
class union, and a class surjection onto a set carrier \(T\) satisfying
\[
 T\not\injto\Pow(\omega).
\]
Extensionality of incidence means that equal traces imply equal labels and
hence equal target values. The inequality is the part of his cardinal
obstruction used here.

This formulation suppresses unnecessary ordinal representatives. If a target
is given by a prewell-order on a set \(B\), its quotient can be represented
as a subset of \(\Pow(B)\): separate the equivalence classes from that power
set. The argument therefore does not assume that a von Neumann
\(\omega_2\) exists internally. The published construction, rather than any
new forcing assertion in this article, supplies the countermodels.

and~4.11]{gczGlazer}. This write has not checked them against Glazer's paper:

exactly this form is unreviewed, and source~31 names expert review of the
