% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 189-296
\section{Foundations: classes, definability, and well-foundedness}
\label{swo:bo:sec:foundations}

\subsection{The base theories and the object language}

We use the two-sorted formulation of G\"odel--Bernays theory. Sets are
members of classes; proper classes are not members of other classes.
Elementary comprehension permits formulas with set quantifiers and
supplied class parameters. Class Replacement says that the image of a set
under a class function is a set. The notation $\GB$ here includes the
usual ZF set axioms but does not assume Global Choice; none of the
choice-free proofs below needs a choice axiom for arbitrary sets.
$\GBC$ adds a global choice function, equivalently in this setting a
set-like global well-order. The letter $G$ will denote such a well-order
when one is used.

A class relation on $X$ is represented by a class of coded pairs of sets.
One relation suffices to code a family: its section at a set index $i$
is a class. This does not turn the family into a class whose members
are themselves proper classes. Appended endpoints and sums use tagged
sets, such as $(0,x)$ and $(1,\varnothing)$. An arbitrary carrier can
already equal the whole universe, so an untagged ``new set outside the
carrier'' is not a legitimate general construction.

\begin{definition}[Class well-order]\label{swo:bo:n2.1}
A class well-order is a strict linear order $<_{W}$ on a class $X$
such that every nonempty admitted subclass of $X$ has a least member.
A relation is \emph{set-like} if the predecessors of each individual
point form a set.
\end{definition}

The word ``admitted'' refers to the class part of the model. An internal
class well-order is not automatically externally well-founded when the
model is set-sized. A transitive model of class theory is a
$\beta$-model if its assertions of class well-foundedness are externally
correct. We invoke this extra hypothesis when taking external order types.

Over $\GBC$, class well-foundedness is equivalent to the absence of a
set-coded infinite descending sequence. Given a subclass without a least
point, use $G$ to select a predecessor repeatedly; ordinary recursion
on $\omega$ and Class Replacement produce a descending set sequence.
Conversely, the range of a descending sequence has no least member.
This standard distinction is discussed in \cite{GitmanHamkins,HamkinsWoodin}.
Over $\GB$ alone we retain the subclass-minimum definition and do not
use the reverse implication without an additional selection argument.

\begin{lemma}[A first-order criterion for linear orders]\label{swo:bo:found:settest}
In $\GB$, a class linear order is a class well-order if and only if
every nonempty \emph{set} subset of its domain has a least point.
Consequently a common class linear order has absolute well-foundedness
between two $\GB$ realizations with the same sets.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Only the reverse implication needs proof. Suppose a nonempty admitted
subclass $C$ has no least point. Below any $x\in C$, take the least
ordinal $\rho$ such that $C_{<x}\cap V_\rho$ is nonempty, and then take
the order-least point of that set. The hypothesis supplies this latter
minimum, so the selected predecessor is unique. Starting from any one
point of $C$, ordinary set-valued recursion yields an infinite
descending sequence. Its range is a set subset with no least point,
a contradiction. The criterion quantifies only over sets and the
given relation; hence it is unchanged in a same-set class extension.
\end{proof}

This lemma is specific to linear orders: their set-sized restrictions
provide unique choices. It does not silently identify the set-subset
criterion with absence of descending sequences in arbitrary choiceless
settings.

\subsection{Four meanings of definable}

The formulas defining a class order can have no parameters, set
parameters, ordinal parameters, or specified class predicates. These
give different spectra. An order defined from a truth class is not thereby
definable in the pure language of set theory. Nor does the fact that each
member of an external list is definable give one formula that evaluates
every definition in that list.

The principal elementary constructions preserve their input parameters.
If $A$ and $B$ are defined using $p$, their tagged sum, product, and
finite-support power are defined using $p$. Our hereditary $\Omega$
system uses no extra predicate: its terms are finite trees with ordinal
labels. The diagonal theorem later uses a uniform relation already
supplied, while its truth specialization explicitly enlarges the language.

For a ZFC-only presentation, each such construction can be read as a
metatheoretic scheme about specified defining formulas. Statements
quantifying over all classes, such as $\CWO$, require a class theory
or an external interpretation. A universal internal predicate that
evaluates every pure set-theoretic definition cannot be assumed.

\subsection{Induction is not the same as class-valued recursion}

Induction along a supplied class well-order is elementary: if the class
of failures of an elementary property were nonempty, its least member
would contradict the induction step. This proves uniqueness and many
structural assertions. It does not create an unknown class-valued
history. A history satisfying
\[
S_i=\{x:\varphi(x,S\mathbin{\upharpoonright}i,A)\}
\]
is a new class whose sections may all be proper classes. The principle
$\ETR$ asserts the existence of such solutions along class well-orders.
Even a length-$\omega$ class-valued recursion can require more than
$\GBC$, as the recursive construction of a full truth predicate shows.
In contrast, recursion on a finite tree, or on $\omega$ with uniquely
specified set values, is available in the elementary arguments below.

% ---- source 35, its Section 2
\subsection{Source 35: foundations and the meaning of length}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 227-245
\label{swo:fc:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{The base theory and class parameters}

Throughout the choice-free results, $\GB$ means the two-sorted
G\"odel--Bernays theory with ZF for sets, elementary class comprehension
allowing class parameters, and class Replacement.  No form of Choice
is built into this notation.  We write $\GBC$ for its extension by
Global Choice.  This convention is stated because authors differ on
whether the abbreviation $\GB$ includes set Choice.  $\KM$ denotes
Kelley--Morse class theory; any additional choice or collection
principle will be named when used.

A \emph{class presentation} $W=(X,<_{W})$ consists of a class of sets
and a class relation on those sets.  In a model $(M,\mathcal X)$,
all the classes mentioned belong to $\mathcal X$.  A class is never
silently an element of another class.  Expressions involving families
of classes mean one class of tuples with set-valued indices.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Definition~2.1, ``Class well-order'']\label{swo:fc:n2.1}
\emph{A class presentation $W=(X,<_{W})$ is a class well-order if $<_{W}$ is a
strict linear order and every nonempty admitted subclass of $X$ has a least
element. It is set-like if, for every $x\in X$, the predecessor class
$W_{<x}=\{y\in X:y<_{W}x\}$ is a set.} This is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:n2.1}; source~35 calls the pair $(X,<_W)$ a \emph{class
presentation}, a class of sets with a class relation.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 256-268

The word ``admitted'' matters in model-theoretic discussions.  The
internal assertion is interpreted using the model's sets and classes.
In an external full model the quantification includes every subset of
the carrier.  For fixed relations on a fixed set universe satisfying
the usual choice assumptions, well-foundedness has a first-order
description by absence of a set-coded descending sequence.  Consequently
one should not claim that changing only the class collection in two
same-set $\GBC$ realizations automatically changes well-foundedness.
The later formalization section explains the distinct issue of a
transitive set model being externally wrong because it is missing a
descending sequence as a \emph{set}.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Proposition~2.2, ``The exact boundary of set-likeness'']\label{swo:fc:prop:setlike}
\emph{In $\GB$, a set-like class well-order is isomorphic to a set ordinal if
its carrier is a set, and to $\Ord$ if its carrier is proper. Every
proper-class well-order has an initial subclass isomorphic to $\Ord$. If it is
not set-like, it has an initial subclass isomorphic to $\Ord+1$.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:setlike} (Section~XVI.3), by the same proof:
the rank $x\mapsto\otp(W_{<x})$ maps onto an initial subclass of $\Ord$, which
is all of $\Ord$ for a proper carrier by Class Replacement applied to the
inverse; the points with set-sized predecessor classes form the initial copy
of $\Ord$, and its first successor caps a copy of $\Ord+1$. Source~35 adds
that the rank function is elementary because the isomorphism certifying each
value is a set. Sources~32 and~33 prove it as \cref{swo:dc:thm:setlike,swo:dh:prop:setlike};
in this report it is the class-carrier form of source~11's canonical initial
part (\cref{swo:cf:core}) and of the first block of
\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 295-333

\subsubsection{Two notions of comparison}

An order embedding is an injective class map preserving and reflecting
the strict order.  Write $A\emb B$ if one exists.  Write $A\iemb B$
if an embedding exists whose image is an initial subclass of $B$;
the entire target is allowed.  Write $A\iprec B$ if its image is
proper.  When we say that one order is \emph{longer} without further
qualification, we mean this proper-initial-segment comparison.

The existence of an arbitrary suborder embedding is weaker as a
\emph{witness}: it need not itself identify an initial segment.  Under
strong class-well-order comparability, the two usual comparisons can
be related as for set ordinals.  We do not assume that principle while
constructing elementary examples.  A class isomorphism, denoted $\cong$,
must be a class available in the chosen formalization.

\begin{lemma}[Rigidity and the successor obstruction]
\label{swo:fc:lem:successor-obstruction}
In $\GB$, every order embedding $f:W\to W$ of a class well-order into
itself is inflationary: $x\leq_W f(x)$.  There is no embedding
$W+1\emb W$.  Between two class well-orders there is at most one
isomorphism onto an initial subclass.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If the class of counterexamples to inflationarity is nonempty, let
$x$ be its least element.  From $f(x)<x$ and order preservation,
$f(f(x))<f(x)$, contradicting minimality.  If an embedding of $W+1$
into $W$ maps its final point to $a$, its restriction $f$ to $W$
satisfies $a\leq f(a)<a$, again impossible.  For uniqueness of initial
isomorphisms, a least point of disagreement would have two different
images with exactly the same predecessor class in the target; strict
linearity forbids this.
\end{proof}

This elementary obstruction replaces several tempting but unjustified
appeals to a universal ordinal rank for class well-orders.

\merge\ The first two assertions of the lemma are source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:basic:anti} (Section~XVI.3), proved in the same way, and
sources~32 and~33's \cref{swo:dc:lem:nocompress,swo:dh:lem:inflation,swo:dh:cor:successor};
source~35's \cref{swo:fc:lem:no-successor-embedding} is a second proof of the
second. The third, uniqueness of an initial-segment isomorphism, is stated as
a lemma only here; source~34 uses it after \cref{swo:bo:her:history} and
source~32 notes it after \cref{swo:dc:lem:nocompress}. It is printed whole
because \cref{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion} uses it.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 334-363
\subsubsection{The symbol \texorpdfstring{$\Omega$}{Omega} and the absence of a paradox}

We use $\Omega$ as a typographical symbol for the \emph{presentation}
$(\Ord,\in)$ when it occurs in class-order arithmetic.  It is not
a member of $\Ord$.  For example, a carrier for $\Omega+1$ is
\[
 (\{0\}\times\Ord)\ \cup\ \{(1,0)\},
\]
with every point of the first tagged copy below the final point.
The pair $(1,0)$ is a set.  Its predecessor class is proper.  A carrier
for $\Omega\cdot\Omega$ is $\Ord\times\Ord$, ordered by the second
coordinate first and by the first coordinate within each block.
Neither construction asks for a set containing all ordinals.

Similarly, $\Omega^{[\Gamma]}$ below is a class of \emph{finite set codes}.
An exponent label $i\in\Gamma$ is a set, even when its predecessor
class in $\Gamma$ is proper.  The exponent label need not be an
ordinal.  Finite support is what makes the object a legal set code.

\begin{remark}[Set-valued and class-valued recursion]\label{swo:fc:n2.4}
A recursion on $\omega$ whose next value is a uniquely specified set
can be carried out in $\GB$ with supplied class parameters.  One takes
finite approximations and uses class Replacement to obtain the
set-coded sequence.  A recursion on $\omega$ whose stages are newly
constructed \emph{classes} is different: $\GB$ does not in general
supply one class coding the entire sequence.  The Tarskian recursion
for truth is the familiar warning.  The finite-trace constructions in
this paper repeatedly use the former fact and never assume the latter
without a stated principle \cite{GHHSW}.
\end{remark}

% ---- source 32, its Section 2 (its Section 1.2 is printed in Section XVI.1)
\subsection{Source 32: well-ordering, set-likeness, and comparison}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 128-129
\label{swo:dc:sec:foundations}

\begin{note}[Source~32, Definition~2.1]\label{swo:dc:n2.1}
\emph{A class well-order is a strict linear order $<_W$ on a class $\dom W$
such that every nonempty admitted subclass of $\dom W$ has a least element; it
is set-like when $W_{<x}=\{y\in\dom W:y<_W x\}$ is a set for every
$x\in\dom W$. An embedding preserves and reflects the strict order; an initial
embedding additionally has an initial-segment image. One writes $A\emb B$ and
$A\iemb B$ only when the witnessing map is an admitted class.} This is
\cref{swo:bo:n2.1} with the two comparison relations of source~34's
Section~1.2 (XVI.1.2). Source~32 writes $D_W$ for the domain of $W$, printed
$\dom W$ here, because $D_W$ is the condensation operator of Parts~IX and~XIV
and of Section~XVI.5; it writes $\preccurlyeq_{e}$ and $\preccurlyeq_{i}$ for
$\emb$ and $\iemb$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 137-147

In GBC the apparently second-order well-order condition has an elementary test in the supplied class parameters. The following familiar equivalence is also used in the class-order literature \cite{HamkinsWoodin}.

\begin{lemma}[The descending-sequence test]
\label{swo:dc:lem:descending}
For a strict linear class order $W$, the following are equivalent: every nonempty admitted subclass has a least point; every nonempty set subset has a least point; and there is no set function $f:\omega\to \dom W$ with $f(n+1)<_W f(n)$ for every $n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion implies the second. A descending sequence has a set range with no least point, so the second implies the third. Conversely, let $S$ be a nonempty admitted subclass with no least point. Fix a set-like global well-order of the universe. Choose its least point in $S$ as $f(0)$; after choosing $f(n)$, choose the globally least element of $S$ below $f(n)$ in the $W$ order. Recursion of length $\omega$ with set values and class parameters, followed by Class Replacement, gives a set function $f$. It is descending. This is ordinary set-valued recursion, not class-valued elementary transfinite recursion.
\end{proof}

\merge\ Source~32's \cref{swo:dc:lem:descending} is the $\GBC$ equivalence
already printed in Part~IX (source~15's paragraph ``Exactly where recursion
principles enter'' in \cref{swo:cb:sec:foundations}) and stated
by source~33 as \cref{swo:dh:lem:wftest}; source~35 recalls it in
Section~XVI.8 (its Section~9.3) and source~34 in \cref{swo:bo:diag:truth}'s
preamble. Over $\GB$ without global choice, source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:found:settest} gives the equivalence of the first two clauses for
linear orders; the third clause, absence of descending set sequences, is not
claimed there to be equivalent without choice.

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 148-149
Consequently, validity of a supplied class-order presentation can be tested by a first-order formula with its domain and relation as class parameters. This fact will later let us filter invalid fibers of a uniformly presented family without impredicative class comprehension.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~2.3, ``The exact set-like boundary'']\label{swo:dc:thm:setlike}
\emph{Every set-like class well-order is isomorphic either to a set ordinal or
to $\Omega$. Moreover, every proper-class well-order has a canonical initial
segment isomorphic to $\Omega$}, namely
$I_W=\{x\in\dom W:W_{<x}\text{ is a set}\}$. This is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:basic:setlike} and source~35's \cref{swo:fc:prop:setlike}, by the
same rank collapse and the same least point outside $I_W$; source~32 works in
$\GBC$, although the proof uses no choice.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 163-165

This gives the precise answer to the first threshold question: longer orders are possible exactly because they are not set-like. No additional element of $\Ord$, and no inconsistency, is involved.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Lemma~2.4, ``No self-compression'']\label{swo:dc:lem:nocompress}
\emph{If $W$ is a class well-order, no admitted embedding $W+1\to W$ exists;
every admitted self-embedding $f:W\to W$ satisfies $x\leq_W f(x)$.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:anti}. Source~32's proof takes the least $x$
with $f(x)<_Wx$, puts $y=f(x)$, and derives $y\leq_W f(y)$ from minimality and
$f(y)<_W f(x)=y$ from order preservation; for $W+1$, the image $a$ of the new
point satisfies $g(a)<_W a$ for the restriction $g$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 175-176

Uniqueness of an initial-segment isomorphism follows from the same least-disagreement argument. Existence is another matter: GBC does not permit one simply to collect all class partial isomorphisms and take their union. That proposal uses quantification over classes inside the proposed defining formula. Under ETR, class well-orders are comparable by initial embeddings \cite{HamkinsWoodin}; our explicit constructions below do not assume this comparison principle.

% ---- source 33, its Section 2
\subsection{Source 33: foundations, well-foundedness, and size}\label{swo:dh:sec:foundations}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 243-261
\subsubsection{The base theory and the meaning of a class presentation}
Our default base theory is $\GBC$: G\"odel--Bernays set theory with global
choice, including the usual set axioms of $\ZFC$. Set variables range over
sets; class variables range over the available classes. Elementary class
comprehension permits formulas with set quantifiers and named class
parameters. Class replacement says that the image of a set under a class
function is a set.

A \emph{class order presentation} is a pair $(D,R)$ of classes, with
$R\subseteq D\times D$. Elements of $D$ are always sets. A function between
presentations is represented by a class graph of ordered pairs of sets.
An isomorphism type will be discussed externally or by comparing presentations;
we do not form an internal class whose elements are proper-class relations.

Global choice supplies a set-like global well-order $G$ of $V$, which we fix
when needed. Its restriction to any nonempty class has a least point. This
last assertion follows by choosing one point, intersecting the class with its
set-sized $G$-initial segment, and applying ordinary set well-ordering.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Definition~2.1]\label{swo:dh:n2.1}
\emph{A class well-order is a linear class order for which every nonempty
available subclass has a least element; it is set-like if every proper
principal initial segment $D_{<x}=\{y\in D:yRx\}$ is a set.} This is
\cref{swo:bo:n2.1}; source~33 writes a presentation as a pair $(D,R)$ of
classes.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 271-275

There is an important first-order test for this definition. The equivalence
below is standard in the class-recursion literature \cite[\S3]{HamkinsWoodin}; the
proof records exactly the use of choice and replacement needed later.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Lemma~2.2, ``The descending-sequence test'']\label{swo:dh:lem:wftest}
\emph{For a linear class order $R$ on $D$, the following are equivalent in
$\GBC$: (a) every nonempty available subclass of $D$ has a least point;
(b) every nonempty set subset of $D$ has a least point; (c) there is no set
function $f:\omega\to D$ with $f(n+1)Rf(n)$ for all $n$. Consequently
well-orderhood is expressible by a first-order formula with $D,R$ as class
predicates.} This is source~32's \cref{swo:dc:lem:descending}, by the same
argument: from a subclass $C$ without least point, choose $x_0\in C$ and then
the $G$-least member of $\{y\in C:yRx_n\}$; finite approximations define the
$n$th value by an elementary formula, and Class Replacement on $\omega$
collects the values into a set function. Source~33 stresses that only an
ordinary set-length sequence of sets is constructed, with no class-valued
stages. Over $\GB$, (a)$\Leftrightarrow$(b) is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:found:settest}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 299-309

\begin{remark}[Internal versus external well-foundedness]\label{swo:dh:n2.3}
The word ``set'' in \cref{swo:dh:lem:wftest} refers to the sets of the model under
consideration. An external descending sequence need not belong to that model.
Thus a general transitive class model can misjudge well-foundedness. The
inaccessible-rank models used in \cref{swo:dh:sec:spectra} are verified separately to
avoid this problem. We do not silently identify internal well-foundedness with
external well-foundedness.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Set-like orders stop at Ord}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Proposition~2.4]\label{swo:dh:prop:setlike}
\emph{A set-like class well-order is isomorphic either to a set ordinal or to
$\Omega$; in particular a proper-class set-like well-order has type $\Omega$.}
This is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:setlike}, by the ordinal collapse
$\rho(x)=\otp(D_{<x})$; if its range is a proper initial segment of $\Ord$, its
least omitted ordinal bounds it, and Class Replacement applied to the inverse
makes $D$ a set.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 322-332

An order beyond $\Omega$ therefore needs at least one point with a proper class
of predecessors. That requirement is not an inconsistency: it simply places
the order outside the set-like case of \cref{swo:dh:prop:setlike}.

\subsubsection{Embeddings, initial embeddings, and rigidity}
Write $A\emb B$ if an available class order embedding $A\to B$ exists, and
$A\iemb B$ if one exists with initial image. The first relation is enough for
our diagonal results. We do not assume, in $\GBC$, that arbitrary class
well-orders admit an initial comparison.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Lemma~2.5, ``Inflation of a self-embedding'']\label{swo:dh:lem:inflation}
\emph{If $f:W\to W$ is an order embedding of a class well-order into itself,
then $x\leq_W f(x)$ for every $x\in W$.} This is the first assertion of
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:anti}, with the same least-counterexample proof.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Corollary~2.6, ``The successor obstruction'']\label{swo:dh:cor:successor}
\emph{For every class well-order $W$, $W\emb W+1$ and $W+1\nemb W$; in
particular, there is no greatest class well-order under embeddability.} The
nonembedding is the second assertion of source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:anti};
source~33's proof restricts $h:W+1\to W$ to $W$ and applies
\cref{swo:dh:lem:inflation} at $a=h(\mathrm{top})$, and the empty $W$ is
immediate.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 357-359

This proof is useful precisely because it needs neither a universal
comparison theorem nor a class recursion along $W$.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 297-424
\section{The boundary at \texorpdfstring{$\Omega$}{Omega} and elementary arithmetic}
\label{swo:bo:sec:basic}

\begin{theorem}[The set-like boundary]\label{swo:bo:basic:setlike}
In $\GB$, every set-like class well-order is isomorphic either to a
set ordinal or to $\Omega$. Every proper class well-order $W$ has
a canonical initial copy of $\Omega$, consisting exactly of its
points with set-sized predecessor classes. If $W$ is not set-like,
it has an initial copy of $\Omega+1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a set-like order define $r(x)=\otp(W_{<x})$. Each value is
a set ordinal, and $r$ is an isomorphism onto an initial subclass
of $\Ord$. A bounded initial subclass is an ordinal; Class
Replacement applied to the inverse map then makes the original
carrier a set. An unbounded initial subclass is all of $\Ord$.

For general $W$, let $S$ consist of the points with set predecessor
classes. It is an initial subclass and is set-like. If $W$ is
proper and $S$ were a set, the complement would be nonempty and
have a least point $b$. Its predecessors would be exactly $S$,
contradicting $b\notin S$. Thus $S$ is proper and has type
$\Omega$. If its complement is nonempty, its first point caps the
claimed initial copy of $\Omega+1$.
\end{proof}

This theorem excludes a set-valued increasing rank map from a genuinely
longer class well-order into $\Ord$. It does not exclude class
rankings into another long order. In particular, assigning every point
the set ordinal ``number of its predecessors'' would simply assume
away the phenomenon being studied.

\begin{lemma}[No backward self-embedding]\label{swo:bo:basic:anti}
For a class well-order $W$, every class order embedding $f:W\to W$
satisfies $x\leq_W f(x)$. There is no class order embedding
$W+1\to W$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $f(x)<_W x$, choose the least such $x$. Then
$f(f(x))<_W f(x)$ makes $f(x)$ an earlier counterexample.
For an embedding of $W+1$, let $a$ be the image of its endpoint.
The restriction to $W$ would imply
$a\leq_W f(a)<_W a$. The empty order is immediate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Sums and products}

Define $A+B$ by tagged concatenation. Define $A\cdot B$ on pairs
$(b,a)$, comparing $b$ first and then $a$; thus it is $B$ copies
of $A$. More generally, a uniformly given family $(A_b)_{b\in B}$
has a sum $\sum_{b\in B}A_b$. For a nonempty subclass of the sum,
first choose the least occupied index and then the least point in
that fiber. This proves well-ordering in $\GB$ without class choice.
The coordinate maps prove, with explicit isomorphisms,
\[
(A+B)+C\cong A+(B+C),\qquad
(A\cdot B)\cdot C\cong A\cdot(B\cdot C),
\]
\[
A\cdot(B+C)\cong A\cdot B+A\cdot C.
\]
Commutativity and distribution of $(A+B)\cdot C$ over its left
summands are not asserted; set-ordinal examples refute them.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{L{0.24\textwidth}L{0.35\textwidth}L{0.29\textwidth}}
\toprule
Presentation & Concrete model & Distinguishing feature \\
\midrule
$\Omega+1$ & Ordinals followed by a tagged endpoint & A proper-class
predecessor segment with a final point \\
$\Omega\cdot2$ & Two consecutive ordinal blocks & The second block
has no last point \\
$\Omega\cdot\omega$ & Countably many ordinal blocks & Has a
set-coded countable cofinal sequence \\
$\Omega^2$ & Pairs of ordinals, outer coordinate first & Proper-class
many ordinal blocks \\
$\fsp\Omega\Omega$ & Finite ordinal-coefficient polynomials with
ordinal exponents & Contains every $\Omega^\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Ord$,
as an initial segment \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

In the last two lines the superscripts mean the finite-support
construction defined below. A cofinal set in $\Omega\cdot\omega$
does not collapse its carrier to a set: the initial segments bounded
by that set can themselves be proper classes.

\subsection{Canonical division by \texorpdfstring{$\Omega$}{Omega}}

\begin{theorem}[One-step block decomposition]\label{swo:bo:basic:blocks}
Every class well-order $W$ has a canonical decomposition
\[
W\cong\Omega\cdot Q+\delta,
\]
where $Q$ is a class well-order and $\delta$ is a set ordinal,
possibly zero. The representatives and the isomorphism are elementary
in $W$, and the construction is valid in $\GB$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Declare $x\sim y$ when the closed interval between them is a set.
The relation is an elementary, convex equivalence relation. Every
block has a least point $r$, and each of its points has a set
predecessor interval within the block. Its local rank
$\otp([r,x))$ identifies the block with a set ordinal or with
$\Omega$, by \Cref{swo:bo:basic:setlike}.

If a block were a set and not final, the class of points following
it would have a least point $z$. The interval from the block's
minimum to $z$ would be that set with one point adjoined. This
contradicts distinctness of the blocks. Let $Q$ be the class of
least representatives of all proper blocks, with the inherited order.
There is at most one set block, and it is final; take its order type
as $\delta$, or take $\delta=0$ if it does not exist. Local ranks
give the displayed isomorphism uniformly.
\end{proof}

This is a canonical decomposition of a supplied order, not an
automatic transfinite iteration of decompositions. The question
whether all successive quotients can be supplied as one history is
the subject of \Cref{swo:bo:hist:section}. The one-step construction
and the polynomial examples already appear in ProveIt
\cite{xviAtPinBO}; they are included here to make the refinement
self-contained.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:bo:basic:setlike} is source~35's \cref{swo:fc:prop:setlike},
source~32's \cref{swo:dc:thm:setlike} and source~33's \cref{swo:dh:prop:setlike};
\cref{swo:bo:basic:anti} is source~35's \cref{swo:fc:lem:successor-obstruction}
(first two clauses), source~32's \cref{swo:dc:lem:nocompress} and source~33's
