\cref{swo:sh:thm:class-division}), and here again by sources~35, 32 and~33
(\eqref{swo:fc:eq:omega-division}, \cref{swo:dc:thm:division,swo:dh:thm:division});
source~34's remainder $\delta$ is Part~IX's $\theta_R$ and source~35's $\rho_W$.

% ---- source 35, its Section 3 (Section 3.1; Sections 3.2--3.6 are printed in Section XVI.4)
\subsection{Source 35: arithmetic of presented class well-orders; sums and products}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 370-441
\label{swo:fc:sec:arithmetic}

The operations in this section act on \emph{presentations}: a class of
set-valued labels together with a class ordering relation.  They do not
turn proper classes into elements of a larger same-level class.  Write
$\Omega$ for the presentation $(\Ord,{<})$.  An expression such as
$\Omega\cdot\Omega$ denotes a specified class order; an equation between such
expressions means a class order-isomorphism.  All the direct constructions
and their well-ordering proofs below work in $\GB$, with the convention
that a class well-order gives a least element to every nonempty available
subclass.  Global Choice is unnecessary for these results.

The repository already develops the ordinal-coefficient polynomial
construction $ P(\Gamma)$ and uses it to analyze condensation
histories~\cite{xviAtPinFC}.  Here we place that construction inside a
general arithmetic, allow arbitrary class well-ordered coefficients, and
give a choice-free proof of well-foundedness.  Class expressions of the
form $\Ord^\Gamma$ also occur in the literature on elementary transfinite
recursion~\cite[Section~9]{GHHSW}.  The finite-support definition makes
the meaning and the required resources explicit.

\subsubsection{Sums and products}

For class well-orders $A$ and $B$, their sum $A+B$ has the disjointly
tagged domain
\[
 (\{0\}\times A)\cup(\{1\}\times B),
\]
with every point of the first copy before every point of the second.
Their product $A\cdot B$ has domain $A\times B$ and comparison
\[
 (a,b)<(a',b')
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 b<_B b'\ \text{ or }\ (b=b'\text{ and }a<_A a').
\]
Thus $A\cdot B$ consists of copies of $A$ indexed by $B$.  A nonempty
subclass of the product has a least occupied $B$-coordinate, and its
fiber there has a least $A$-coordinate.  This proves the well-ordering
claim without a recursion or any choice principle.  The sum is even
more immediate.

The same argument handles a \emph{supplied uniform family}.  More
precisely, let $I$ be a class well-order, let $D\subseteq I\times V$ be a
class, and let a class relation specify a well-order $A_i$ on each fiber
$D_i$.  The tagged domain $D$, with the $I$-coordinate compared first,
is the sum $\sum_{i\in I}A_i$.  There is one class of pairs and one
class comparison relation.  No class whose members are the classes
$A_i$ is being formed.  Choosing the least occupied index and then
the least point of its fiber proves that this sum is well-ordered.

Reassociation and retagging give explicit isomorphisms
\begin{align*}
 (A+B)+C&\cong A+(B+C),\tag{S35.1}\\
 (A\cdot B)\cdot C&\cong A\cdot(B\cdot C),\tag{S35.2}\\
 A\cdot(B+C)&\cong A\cdot B+A\cdot C.
 \tag{S35.3}\label{swo:fc:eq:class-distributivity}
\end{align*}





For example, the product reassociation sends $((a,b),c)$ to
$(a,(b,c))$; both comparisons prioritize $c$, then $b$, then $a$.
These verifications use only the displayed definitions, so there is
no hidden comparison theorem for arbitrary class orders.

The direction in \eqref{swo:fc:eq:class-distributivity} matters.  The other
distributive law already fails for set ordinals:
\[
 (1+1)\cdot\omega\cong\omega,
 \qquad
 1\cdot\omega+1\cdot\omega\cong\omega+\omega.
\]
The familiar noncommutativity of ordinal arithmetic persists as well.
It is helpful to record the order of the factors before simplifying
an expression.

% ---- source 32, its Section 3.1 (Sections 3.2--3.3 are printed in Section XVI.4)
\subsection{Source 32: ordinal arithmetic with explicit class presentations; uniform sums and products}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 179-210
\label{swo:dc:sec:arithmetic}

\subsubsection{Uniform sums and products}

A family $(W_i)_{i\in I}$ of class orders will always be \emph{uniformly coded}: there are classes $D$ and $R$ such that
\[
\dom W_i=\{x:(i,x)\in D\},\qquad
x<_{W_i}y\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (i,x,y)\in R.
\]
This is not a class function whose values are proper classes. Its elements are ordinary set tuples, and it is a legitimate object of GBC.

\begin{proposition}[Uniform sum theorem]
\label{swo:dc:prop:sums}
If $I$ is a class well-order and $(W_i)_{i\in I}$ is a uniformly coded family of class well-orders, then
\[
\sum_{i\in I}W_i
\]
is a class well-order on the pairs $(i,x)$ with $x\in \dom W_i$, ordered first by $i$ and then within the fiber.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a nonempty subclass of the sum, its occupied indices form an admitted nonempty subclass of $I$. Take the least occupied index and then the least point in that fiber. Both choices use elementary comprehension and the well-order hypotheses.
\end{proof}

The binary sum $A+B$ is the two-fiber special case. The ordinal product $A\cdot B$ is the sum of copies of $A$ indexed by $B$; on $\dom A\times \dom B$, the \emph{second coordinate has priority}. Rearranging finite tags and tuples gives explicit admitted isomorphisms
\[
(A+B)+C\cong A+(B+C),\quad
(A\cdot B)\cdot C\cong A\cdot(B\cdot C),
\]
\[
A\cdot(B+C)\cong A\cdot B+A\cdot C.
\]
Commutativity and the other distributive law are not asserted. These are ordinal, not cardinal, operations.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:dc:prop:sums} is the sum argument of source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:sec:basic} and of source~35's Section~3.1 (in
\cref{swo:fc:sec:arithmetic}), printed as
a numbered statement because sources~32 and~33 cite it so; source~33's
\cref{swo:dh:prop:sums} is the same proposition.

% ---- source 32, its Section 5
\subsection{Source 32: canonical division by \texorpdfstring{$\Omega$}{Omega} and class cofinality}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 333-343
\label{swo:dc:sec:division}

\subsubsection{Set-interval blocks}

For $x,y\in W$, let $[x,y]_W$ denote the closed interval between them, regardless of which is smaller. Define
\[\tag{S32.5}
\label{swo:dc:eq:setinterval}
x\sim_W y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [x,y]_W\text{ is a set}.
\]
The predicate on the right is elementary: it asserts the existence of a set with exactly the specified members. In particular, it does not quantify over a collection of proper classes.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Lemma~5.1]\label{swo:dc:lem:blocks}
\emph{The relation $\sim_W$ is a convex equivalence relation. Each block has a
least point, and the induced order inside each block is set-like. Every
nonfinal block is proper. Consequently there can be at most one set-sized
block, and if it exists it is final.} This is the block lemma of Part~IX and
Part~XIV (source~15's \cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:decomposition}, source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:n13.2}, source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:blocks}), proved inside
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:blocks} and as source~35's
\cref{swo:fc:lem:condensation-blocks} and source~33's \cref{swo:dh:lem:blocks},
by the same argument: transitivity from the union of two set intervals,
set-likeness because the predecessors of $x$ in its block lie in the set
interval from the block's least point $r$, and, if a nonfinal block $B$ were a
set, the least point $z$ after it would satisfy $[r,z]_W=B\cup\{z\}$, a set.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 355-373

Least representatives solve the size problem in forming the quotient. Instead of putting proper-class blocks into another class as elements, form the class of their least points. An original point determines its representative by an elementary formula. The resulting quotient is an ordinary class relation on sets. This is the block-representation method already used in the repository \cite{xviStatusTwentyThree}; the following division formulation makes its consequence explicit.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical $\Omega$-division]
\label{swo:dc:thm:division}
For every class well-order $W$ there are a canonically presented class well-order $Q$ and a set ordinal $\alpha$ such that
\[\tag{S32.6}
\label{swo:dc:eq:division}
W\cong\Omega\cdot Q+\alpha.
\]
Here $Q$ is the order of least representatives of the proper set-interval blocks; $\alpha$ is the type of the final set block, or $0$ when there is none. The pair is unique up to an admitted isomorphism of $Q$ and equality of $\alpha$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{swo:dc:lem:blocks}, every proper block is set-like and therefore has type $\Omega$ by \cref{swo:dc:thm:setlike}. The rank of a point $x$ within its block is the ordinal type of the set of block predecessors of $x$. The formula defining this rank is uniform in the block representative and $x$. If a final set block exists, apply the ordinary set-order collapse to it and call its type $\alpha$.

Assigning each point its block representative and its local rank gives the required admitted isomorphism. For the empty order take $Q=0$ and $\alpha=0$. For a nonempty set order there is just one set block, so $Q=0$ and $\alpha=\otp(W)$.

To verify uniqueness, observe that in any presentation $\Omega\cdot Q+\alpha$ the copies of $\Omega$ are exactly the proper set-interval blocks. Points from distinct copies have a proper interval between them, because it contains a final part of the earlier copy of $\Omega$. All intervals within a copy are sets, and the final ordinal $\alpha$, when nonzero, is the unique set block. An isomorphism preserves set-sized intervals: images of sets under an admitted class function are sets, and the inverse gives the converse. It therefore induces an isomorphism of the proper-block representative orders and an isomorphism of the final set blocks. Ordinary ordinal uniqueness gives equality of the remainders.
\end{proof}

\merge\ \Cref{swo:dc:thm:division} is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:blocks}
with the uniqueness clause of source~18's \cref{swo:sh:n13.4} (Part~IX), proved
in the same way: an admitted isomorphism and its inverse preserve set-sized
intervals by Class Replacement. Source~33's \cref{swo:dh:thm:division} states
the same canonicity. In \cref{swo:dc:prop:cofinality}, the description of the
least cofinal size is source~18's \cref{swo:sh:n13.5} in other words; the first
clause, an increasing cofinal map $\Omega\to W$ when no set is cofinal, is
proved here only by source~32 (its recursion along $\Ord$ uses a set-like
global well-order).

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 374-396

The theorem is not a global Cantor normal form theorem. In particular, $Q$ may be another non-set-like proper-class order, and iterating the quotient construction introduces a separate recursion problem. Nevertheless, it provides a canonical first structural invariant for every supplied $W$, with no ETR assumption and no global comparison theorem.

\subsubsection{Cofinality need not measure class size}

A subclass $C\subseteq W$ is cofinal if every point of $W$ lies at or below some member of $C$. Proper-class well-orders can have a last point, a countable cofinal set, or no set cofinal subset at all. For example,
\[
\Omega+1\text{ has cofinality }1,\qquad
\Omega\cdot\omega\text{ has cofinality }\omega,
\]
whereas $\Omega$ has no set cofinal subset. The hereditary order $\Eps(\Omega)$ has a countable cofinal set by \cref{swo:dc:thm:hereditary}.

\begin{proposition}[Set cofinality or an $\Omega$-sequence]
\label{swo:dc:prop:cofinality}
If a class well-order $W$ has no set cofinal subset, it has an admitted increasing cofinal map $\Omega\to W$. If it does have a set cofinal subset, its least possible set cardinality is $1$ or an infinite regular cardinal.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In the first case $W$ is proper. A set-like global well-order restricted to its domain gives an enumeration $e:\Ord\to \dom W$. Recursively choose $f(\xi)$ to be the $W$-least point strictly above $e(\xi)$ and all earlier values $f(\eta)$, $\eta<\xi$. The collection to be bounded is a set. Since no set is cofinal, a strict upper bound exists. This is set-valued recursion with set histories along $\Ord$, available in GBC. The result is increasing and is cofinal because it bounds every value of $e$.

In the second case, choose a set cofinal subset $C$. Its induced order has a set ordinal type $\lambda$. If $W$ has a greatest point, one point is enough. Otherwise the cofinality of $W$ equals the ordinary cofinality of $\lambda$: a cofinal subset of $\lambda$ gives one in $W$, and any set cofinal in $W$ maps cofinally into $C$ by taking least upper bounds in $C$ point by point. Ordinary ordinal cofinality is an infinite regular cardinal.
\end{proof}

The first clause does not say that $W$ has order type $\Omega$. A cofinal suborder is not necessarily an initial suborder. In $\Omega^{[\Omega]}$, for example, the monomials indexed by ordinal exponents are cofinal, although the whole order is much longer than its initial set-like segment.

% ---- source 33, its Section 3.1 (Sections 3.2--3.3 are printed in Section XVI.4)
\subsection{Source 33: an explicit arithmetic of class well-orders; uniformly indexed sums}\label{swo:dh:sec:arithmetic}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 364-368
Disjoint tags are implicit in all constructions. Define $A+B$ by placing every
point of $A$ before every point of $B$. Define $A\cdot B$ on pairs $(b,a)$,
with $b\in B$, $a\in A$, by comparing the $B$-coordinate first. Thus
$A\cdot B$ consists of $B$-many consecutive copies of $A$.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Definition~3.1, ``Uniform family'']\label{swo:dh:n3.1}
\emph{A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of class order presentations is uniform if
there are classes $U$ and $S$ with $\dom(A_i)=\{x:U(i,x)\}$ and
$x<_{A_i}y\leftrightarrow S(i,x,y)$; the index collection $I$ is itself a class
of sets, whose members are codes or labels, not proper classes.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:uniform} (Section~XVI.7) and source~32's
uniformly coded families before \cref{swo:dc:prop:sums}.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Proposition~3.2]\label{swo:dh:prop:sums}
\emph{If $I$ is a class well-order and $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a uniform family of
class well-orders, then the lexicographic sum $\sum_{i\in I}A_i$ is a class
well-order, definable from the given data in $\GBC$.} This is source~32's
\cref{swo:dc:prop:sums}, by the same least occupied index and least point of
its fibre; the argument uses no choice (source~34's \cref{swo:bo:sec:basic}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 394-398

The statement includes a subtle restriction: merely being told, for each
index, that some class order exists does not supply the uniform pair of
predicates $U,S$. Even a set-indexed collection of class-valued choices must
not be treated as an ordinary set function.

% ---- source 33, its Section 4
\subsection{Source 33: canonical division by the order of all ordinals}\label{swo:dh:sec:division}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 509-518

\subsubsection{Set intervals and their blocks}
For points $x,y$ of a class linear order $W$, let $[x,y]_W$ denote the closed
interval between them, regardless of their order. Define
\[\tag{S33.4.1}\label{swo:dh:eq:setinterval}
        x\sim_W y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [x,y]_W\text{ is a set}.
\]
Being a set is expressed by the existence of a set with exactly the specified
members. Thus \eqref{swo:dh:eq:setinterval} is an elementary definition from $W$.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Lemma~4.1]\label{swo:dh:lem:blocks}
\emph{For a class well-order $W$, the relation $\sim_W$ is a convex equivalence
relation. Each block has a least point and is a set-like well-order. Any block
that is a set must be the final block of $W$.} This is source~32's
\cref{swo:dc:lem:blocks}, with the same proof.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 539-540

\subsubsection{The division theorem}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Theorem~4.2, ``Canonical $\Omega$-division'']\label{swo:dh:thm:division}
\emph{Every class well-order $W$ has a decomposition
\[\tag{S33.4.2}\label{swo:dh:eq:division}
 W\cong\Omega\cdot Q+\alpha,
\]
where $Q$ is a class
well-order and $\alpha$ a set ordinal. The factors are canonical: $Q$ is the
order of the least points of the proper-class set-interval blocks, and $\alpha$
the type of the final set-sized block, if there is one, or zero. The
decomposition and the displayed isomorphism exist in $\GBC$.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:blocks} and source~32's \cref{swo:dc:thm:division},
including its canonicity: source~33 sends $x$ to the pair $(r(x),\rho(x))$ of
its block minimum and $\rho(x)=\otp\{y:r(x)\leq_W y<_W x\}$, and proves
canonicity by observing that in any presentation $\Omega\cdot Q+\alpha$ the
displayed blocks are exactly the set-interval blocks. Its displayed
equation~(4.2) is this decomposition.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 578-596

\begin{example}\label{swo:dh:n4.3}
The canonical decompositions of $\Omega+\omega$ and $\Omega^2+17$ have
$(Q,\alpha)=(1,\omega)$ and $(\Omega,17)$, respectively. A nonempty set ordinal
has $Q=0$ and is its own remainder. The empty order has both factors zero.
\end{example}

The theorem is a genuine structural statement about arbitrary class
well-orders. It does not assume initial comparability of two unrelated
orders, nor does it recursively construct classes along $W$. Every point's
coordinate is the type of a \emph{set} interval.

\subsubsection{Why repeated quotients need coherent data}
One may iterate the operation of identifying set-interval blocks. At a limit
stage, however, knowing only the isomorphism types of the previous quotients
is insufficient: one needs to know \emph{which points have already been
identified}. The next section makes this precise with an explicit family.
It also avoids any implication that the existence of individually described
quotients automatically supplies a uniformly coded transfinite iteration.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 426-599
\section{Finite-support exponentiation without Global Choice}
\label{swo:bo:sec:powers}

\begin{definition}[Finite-support power]\label{swo:bo:n4.1}
Let $A$ be a nonempty class well-order with least point $0_A$, and
let $B$ be a class well-order. The carrier of $\fsp A B$ is the
class of finite partial functions $f:B\rightharpoonup A\setminus
\{0_A\}$. Missing values mean $0_A$. For distinct $f,g$, take
the greatest point $b$ in their finite disagreement set and put
\[
f<g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(b)<_A g(b).
\]
Write $ P(B)=\fsp\Omega B$. Its elements are formal polynomials
$\Omega^{b_0}a_0+\cdots+\Omega^{b_{k-1}}a_{k-1}$, where
$b_0>_B\cdots>_B b_{k-1}$ and $0<a_i\in\Ord$.
\end{definition}

The superscript $b_i$ is a point of the exponent order; when
interpreting the monomial's predecessor length, it represents the
initial segment $B_{<b_i}$. A polynomial is a finite set, even
when both available coordinates and available coefficients range
over proper classes. No class-valued function is being made an
element of the carrier. The greatest-disagreement rule is a strict
linear order by the ordinary finite lexicographic argument.

\begin{theorem}[Choice-free power theorem]\label{swo:bo:power:GB}
$\GB$ proves that $\fsp A B$ is a class well-order whenever $A$
and $B$ are class well-orders and $A$ is nonempty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be a nonempty subclass of the power. We construct its least
member directly. Regard each polynomial as a finite list of
exponent--coefficient pairs in decreasing exponent order. For a
chosen prefix $p$, let $C_p$ consist of those members of $C$ whose
lists begin with $p$. Maintain two invariants: $C_p$ is nonempty,
and every member of $C\setminus C_p$ is larger than every member
of $C_p$. The empty prefix satisfies these conditions.

If $p$ itself is in $C$, it is least in $C_p$, since each proper
extension has a nonzero next coefficient. It is therefore least
in $C$, and the construction stops. Otherwise each member of
$C_p$ has a next pair. Among the next exponents choose the
$B$-least one, say $b$. Among the corresponding nonzero
coefficients choose the $A$-least one, say $a$. These are uniquely
defined minima of admitted subclasses. Append $(b,a)$ to $p$.
The new $C_p$ is nonempty. A member rejected at this step has a
larger next exponent, or the same exponent with larger coefficient;
in either case it is larger than every retained member. Thus both
invariants persist.

If this process did not stop, ordinary recursion on $\omega$
would produce a sequence of uniquely defined finite prefixes.
All values are sets, so Class Replacement supplies the sequence
as a set. Its successive selected exponents strictly decrease in
$B$, because every retained polynomial lists its support in
decreasing order. The range of this sequence would be a nonempty
subclass of $B$ without a least member, contrary to the hypothesis.
Hence the process stops and yields the required least member of
$C$. No choices from unrelated subclasses are made.
\end{proof}

The difference from the repository proof is exact. A general
subclass without a minimum cannot in bare $\GB$ simply be turned
into a descending sequence by invoking Global Choice. The proof
above uses the already supplied well-orders of the coordinates and
digits to choose unique minima. This is the dependency removed in
the canonical-history theorem.

There is also an independent short route to the same result. For a
nonempty set of finite graphs, collect its exponent supports and its
digits into sets, including the zero digit. Their induced well-orders
have set ordinal types. The given graphs therefore sit inside an
ordinary set ordinal power, so that set of graphs has a minimum.
\Cref{swo:bo:found:settest} upgrades this set-subset assertion to the
full class well-order assertion in $\GB$. The explicit greedy proof
records a minimum-selection procedure and exposes the same absence
of choice directly.

\subsection{Arithmetic laws with concrete witnesses}

The finite-support construction agrees with ordinary ordinal
exponentiation on set ordinals. For a successor exponent, the
last coefficient arranges copies of the preceding power; at a
limit, every finite support lies below some earlier exponent.
These observations give the usual set transfinite proof.

For class well-orders, explicit splitting and flattening of finite
graphs prove the following laws without class-valued recursion:
\begin{align*}
\fsp A0&\cong1,& \fsp A1&\cong A,\tag{S34.1}\label{swo:bo:power:units}\\
\fsp A{(B+C)}&\cong\fsp AB\cdot\fsp AC,
\tag{S34.2}\label{swo:bo:power:sum}\\
\fsp{(\fsp AB)}C&\cong\fsp A{(B\cdot C)}.
\tag{S34.3}\label{swo:bo:power:iterate}
\end{align*}






In \eqref{swo:bo:power:sum}, restrict a finite function to the two tagged
pieces; the $C$ piece is the more significant coordinate. In
\eqref{swo:bo:power:iterate}, a finitely supported function with finitely
supported values flattens to a finite function on pairs $(c,b)$.
The greatest differing $c$, followed by the greatest differing
$b$, is exactly the product order. Empty inner functions represent
the zero digit. The inverse maps group the finite pairs into their
fibers, so these are isomorphisms, not just embeddings.

An initial embedding $j:B\to C$ induces an initial embedding
$\fsp AB\to\fsp AC$ by relabelling supports. If $A$ has at
least two points and the image of $j$ is proper, the latter
embedding is proper: the first missing exponent supports a new
coefficient-one monomial. This gives a reliable strict-growth rule.

\begin{proposition}[The exponent is not a power class]\label{swo:bo:n4.3}
For every set ordinal $2\leq a$, one has
\[
\fsp a\Omega\cong\Omega,
\qquad
\fsp a{(\Omega+1)}\cong\Omega\cdot a.
\]
By contrast, $ P(\Omega)$ has a proper initial segment of
type $\Omega$ and is strictly longer than it.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For set $a$, any polynomial has a greatest support exponent
$\beta$ unless it is zero. All smaller polynomials have support
in $\beta+1$ and digits below $a$. They therefore form a set.
The whole power is proper, since there are monomials at every
ordinal exponent. \Cref{swo:bo:basic:setlike} gives its type
$\Omega$. Equation~\eqref{swo:bo:power:sum} gives the second formula.
For base $\Omega$, the constant polynomials form an initial copy
of $\Omega$, and the monomial at exponent $1$ follows all of them.
\end{proof}

Thus $2^{[\Omega]}$ and $\omega^{[\Omega]}$ do not leap beyond
$\Omega$ under this definition. A notation that presents them as
larger has either changed the exponentiation operation or confused
order exponentiation with a collection of subsets. Full functions
from a proper class are not set-coded elements of an ordinary
class; functions of unrestricted support require a different
foundation and a separately checked order.

\subsection{A presentation language and a useful normal-form rule}

A safe presentation language begins with $0,1$, set ordinal
constants, and $\Omega$, and closes under tagged sum, product,
finite-support power, and explicitly supplied uniform sums. It can
also include the hereditary constructor in the next development.
Each expression denotes a concrete class relation. Equalities
between expressions are witnessed by class isomorphisms, and
the language need not choose a representative of every possible
isomorphism type.

For $f\in P(B)$ with decreasing support $b_0,\ldots,b_{k-1}$,
the strict predecessor class has the canonical presentation
\[\tag{S34.4}\label{swo:bo:power:segment}
( P(B))_{<f}\cong
\sum_{i<k}\fsp\Omega{(B_{<b_i})}\cdot f(b_i).
\]
Indeed, partition the predecessors by the first, most significant
coordinate at which they fall below $f$. At coordinate $b_i$ the
smaller coefficient has $f(b_i)$ choices in ordinal order, and
the lower coordinates form $\fsp\Omega{(B_{<b_i})}$. Concatenating
these pieces in decreasing significance proves the formula.
It explains exactly what the polynomial notation means as a
description of an initial segment.

For example, a point written
$\Omega^{\omega+2}\cdot3+\Omega^7\cdot\omega+5$ names the
initial segment with those three successive terms. It does not
claim that the ambient proper class order is a von Neumann ordinal.
Constants and finite trees give systematic descriptions, but the
comparison of arbitrary formula-defined presentations is not
replaced by a universal syntactic normalizer. The diagonal results
below show why that stronger objective has a real obstruction.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:bo:power:GB} removes the one use of global choice in
this report's proofs that polynomial orders are well-ordered: source~15's
\cref{swo:cb:cce:lem:polynomialwellorder}, source~23's
\cref{swo:tm:lem:polywell} and source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:polynomials} each
turn a subclass without a least element into a descending sequence by global
choice. Source~35 proves the same theorem with a different termination
argument (\cref{swo:fc:thm:finite-support} and its proof below); sources~32
and~33 prove it in $\GBC$ by the set-support localization of source~34's
second route (\cref{swo:dc:thm:power,swo:dh:thm:power}). The laws
\eqref{swo:bo:power:units}--\eqref{swo:bo:power:iterate} are source~35's
\eqref{swo:fc:eq:power-sum} and~\eqref{swo:fc:eq:power-product}, source~32's
\cref{swo:dc:thm:powerlaws} and source~33's \cref{swo:dh:prop:laws}; the
initial-embedding rule is source~35's \cref{swo:fc:lem:power-initial}; the
first identity of \cref{swo:bo:n4.3} is the third of source~35's
\cref{swo:fc:prop:boundary-identities} and source~33's \cref{swo:dh:prop:smallbase}.
Formula~\eqref{swo:bo:power:segment} is source~35's
\cref{swo:fc:prop:polynomial-cut}.

% ---- source 35, its Sections 3.2--3.6 (Section 3.1 is printed in Section XVI.3)
\subsection{Source 35: exponentiation by finite support, cofinality and continuity}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 444-465

Let $A$ be a nonempty class well-order, with least point $0_A$, and
let $B$ be any class well-order.  Define $A^{[B]}$ to be the class of
\emph{finite partial functions}
\[
 p:B\rightharpoonup A\setminus\{0_A\}.
\]
Every such function is a set: its graph contains finitely many ordered
pairs of sets.  Missing values are read as $0_A$.  Its finite domain is
written $\supp(p)$.  For distinct $p,q$, the finite nonempty set
\[
 \{b\in\supp(p)\cup\supp(q):p(b)\ne q(b)\}
\]
has a greatest element $b_*$.  Put
\[\tag{S35.4}
 p<q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p(b_*)<_A q(b_*).
 \label{swo:fc:eq:finite-support-comparison}
\]
The empty graph is the least element.  The brackets emphasize this
order-theoretic exponentiation; it is not the collection of all
class functions $B\to A$, or cardinal exponentiation.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~3.1, ``Choice-free finite-support theorem'']\label{swo:fc:thm:finite-support}
\emph{If $A$ is a nonempty class well-order and $B$ is a class well-order,
then $A^{[B]}$ is a class well-order. This is provable in $\GB$.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:power:GB}, proved independently. Both proofs build
the least member of a nonempty subclass $C$ greedily, appending at each step
the least next exponent and then the least next coefficient, and both keep
every discarded polynomial above every retained one. They differ in the
termination argument: source~34 collects the uniquely specified prefixes into
a set sequence by recursion on $\omega$ and Class Replacement, and derives a
descending sequence of exponents; source~35 avoids the $\omega$-sequence and
considers the class of last exponents of all finite histories obeying the
rule, whose least element would have to be followed by a smaller one. Its
proof is printed as a second route.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 472-658
\begin{proof}[Source~35's proof]
The comparison is linear.  One way to check transitivity is to put
the supports of three polynomials into one finite decreasing list
of exponents and compare their coefficient lists lexicographically,
starting at the greatest exponent.  This is an ordinary finite
lexicographic comparison.

Let $C\subseteq A^{[B]}$ be a nonempty class.  Write each polynomial
as its finite list of nonzero terms, with exponents strictly
decreasing.  We construct the beginning of a least member of $C$.
Start with the empty prefix $s$.  At every step the survivor class
\[
 C_s=\{p\in C:p\text{ begins with the list }s\}
\]
is nonempty.  If $s$ itself is a polynomial in $C_s$, stop.  It is
the least survivor: every proper extension adds a positive
coefficient at a smaller exponent.

Otherwise every survivor has a next term.  The class of their next
exponents is a nonempty subclass of $B$, so choose its \emph{least}
element $b$.  Among survivors having next exponent $b$, choose the
least next coefficient $a$ in $A$.  Append $(b,a)$ to $s$.
The new survivor class is nonempty.  Moreover, each discarded
survivor is greater than every retained survivor: at the first new
place of disagreement it has either a larger exponent, or the same
exponent and a larger coefficient.

This process must stop after finitely many steps.  To see this
without making an infinite sequence of choices, consider all
\emph{finite histories} obeying the rule.  They are set codes, and
the condition of being such a history is an elementary formula
with the supplied classes as parameters.  If no history terminated,
the class of last exponents of nonempty histories would be a
nonempty subclass of $B$.  Let $b$ be its least element and take a
history ending in $b$.  Its next extension exists by the rule, and
its new exponent is strictly below $b$, since exponents in a
polynomial decrease.  This contradicts the choice of $b$.

At termination, the resulting finite list is a member of $C$ and
is below every polynomial discarded at an earlier step.  It is
therefore the least member of $C$.  All selections used designated
least elements; Global Choice and elementary transfinite recursion
were not used.
\end{proof}

For set ordinals $\alpha\geq1$ and $\beta$, this construction has
ordinary ordinal type $\alpha^\beta$.  Indeed, a last exponent
splits the order into $\alpha$ successive copies of the preceding
power, and at a nonzero limit every finite support is contained
in an earlier exponent segment.  These are the usual successor
and limit equations, starting with $\alpha^{[0]}=1$.
Consequently the construction genuinely extends ordinal
exponentiation.  The empty base can be treated separately by the
usual conventions $0^0=1$ and $0^\beta=0$ for $\beta>0$; it is not
needed in the results below.

\subsubsection{The exponent laws are explicit isomorphisms}

For nonempty $A$, splitting a finite support between the two tagged
parts of $B+C$ gives
\[\tag{S35.5}
 A^{[B+C]}\cong A^{[B]}\cdot A^{[C]}.
 \label{swo:fc:eq:power-sum}
\]
The right-hand coordinate records the restriction to $C$.  A
difference there is more significant than every difference in
$B$, exactly as required by the product convention.  Joining the
two tagged graphs is the inverse map.  In particular,
\[
 A^{[0]}\cong1,\qquad A^{[1]}\cong A,
 \qquad A^{[B+1]}\cong A^{[B]}\cdot A.
\]

There is also a flattening isomorphism
\[\tag{S35.6}
 \bigl(A^{[B]}\bigr)^{[C]}
       \cong A^{[B\cdot C]}.
 \label{swo:fc:eq:power-product}
\]
An element on the left assigns a nonzero finite $B$-polynomial
$p_c$ to finitely many $c\in C$.  Send it to the finite graph on
$B\times C$ whose value at $(b,c)$ is $p_c(b)$.  Conversely, slice
a finite graph on $B\times C$ at its finitely many occupied
$C$-coordinates.  Empty slices are omitted.  The greatest
different $C$-coordinate determines the first comparison; inside
that slice, the greatest different $B$-coordinate determines the
second.  This is precisely greatest-difference comparison on
$B\cdot C$.  Thus both the bijection and its compatibility with
the order are verified directly.

These identities are available even when several operands and
their initial segments are proper classes.  They require no
recursion whose stages would themselves have to be classes.
They also do not assert the generally false identity
$(A\cdot B)^{[C]}\cong A^{[C]}\cdot B^{[C]}$.

\begin{lemma}[Preservation of initial embeddings]
\label{swo:fc:lem:power-initial}
An order embedding $f:B\to C$ induces an order embedding
\[
 A^{[f]}:A^{[B]}\longrightarrow A^{[C]},
 \qquad
 A^{[f]}(p)(f(b))=p(b).
\]
If the image of $f$ is initial, the induced image is initial.
If that image is proper and $A$ has at least two elements, the
induced image is proper as well.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The map transports a finite support and its coefficients; an
embedding preserves the greatest point of a finite difference
set.  Hence it preserves and reflects comparisons.
Suppose the image of $f$ is initial.  Every exponent outside it
is above every exponent inside it.  A polynomial with an occupied
outside exponent is therefore greater than every polynomial
supported in the image.  The latter polynomials consequently
form an initial subclass, and each has a unique finite inverse
image under the displayed map.
If the exponent image is proper, let $c_*$ be its least omitted
point and let $1_A$ be the least point of $A$ above $0_A$.
The monomial supported at $c_*$ with coefficient $1_A$ is the
least polynomial outside the induced image.  This also proves
properness explicitly.
\end{proof}

The polynomial operation used in the repository is exactly
\[
  P(B):=\Omega^{[B]}.
\]
Its coefficients are the nonzero set ordinals.  The lemma shows
that $ P$ transports initial embeddings, including their
properness.  Identity maps and compositions are preserved
literally by support transport.  This functorial behavior is
what makes the fixed-point constructions in the next part
possible.

Changing the \emph{base} deserves separate attention.  An initial
embedding $A\to A'$ also gives a coefficientwise order embedding
$A^{[B]}\to(A')^{[B]}$, but that particular map need not be
initial.  Already for $2\subset3$ and exponent $2$, the image
contains the monomial at exponent $1$ while omitting the constant
coefficient $2$ below it.  One must not infer initiality from
coefficientwise inclusion.  For set ordinals another initial
embedding exists by ordinary ordinal comparison; applying an
analogous comparison to arbitrary class orders requires its
own justification.

\subsubsection{What collapses to \texorpdfstring{$\Ord$}{Ord}, and what passes it}

A set-like well-order on a proper class has its canonical
ordinal-rank isomorphism with $\Omega$: each point has a set of
predecessors, its rank is a set ordinal, and the range is an
initial subclass of $\Ord$ that is a proper class.  It must therefore be all
of $\Ord$.  This observation gives useful simplification rules.

\begin{proposition}[Set-sized operands at the class boundary]
\label{swo:fc:prop:boundary-identities}
For set ordinals $\alpha$ and $\beta$,
\[
 \alpha+\Omega\cong\Omega,
 \qquad
 \alpha\cdot\Omega\cong\Omega\quad(\alpha>0),
 \qquad
 \beta^{[\Omega]}\cong\Omega\quad(\beta\geq2).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In $\alpha+\Omega$, the predecessor set of a point in the second
copy has ordinary type $\alpha+\gamma$ for some set ordinal
$\gamma$.  In $\alpha\cdot\Omega$, the predecessors of $(a,\gamma)$
have ordinary type $\alpha\cdot\gamma+a$.  Thus both displayed
orders are set-like, and their domains are proper classes under
the stated nonemptiness assumption.

For $\beta^{[\Omega]}$, a polynomial and all its predecessors
have their supports in some set ordinal $\gamma$.  There are
only set-many finite $\beta$-valued graphs on $\gamma$, so its
predecessor class is a set.  The monomials with coefficient $1$
at successive ordinal exponents show that the whole domain is
proper.  The same set-like classification applies.  More
explicitly, the power on exponents below $\gamma$ has type
$\beta^\gamma$, and these ordinary ordinals are cofinal in
$\Ord$.  The resulting identification agrees with ordinary
base-$\beta$ evaluation on each finite polynomial.
\end{proof}

\merge\ The third identity is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:n4.3}; the first two
are source~32's remark after \cref{swo:dc:thm:powerlaws} and source~33's
examples after \cref{swo:dh:prop:laws}. Source~35's continuity principle
\eqref{swo:fc:eq:power-continuity} is the last clause of source~32's
\cref{swo:dc:thm:powerlaws}. \Cref{swo:fc:prop:power-cofinality} and
\cref{swo:fc:lem:bounded-specialization} are proved here only by source~35;
the second holds over $\GB$ as well (\cref{swo:xvi:thm:choicefree}).

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 659-798

The reversed expressions behave differently.  The new endpoint
of $\Omega+1$ has a proper class of predecessors, and the first
point of the second block of $\Omega\cdot2$ has the same property.
Neither order is isomorphic to $\Omega$.  Their displayed first
copies of $\Omega$ are proper initial subclasses, so the sense in
which they are longer is witnessed directly.

In $\Omega^{[\Omega]}$, the constant polynomials form an initial
copy of $\Omega$.  The monomial with coefficient $1$ at exponent
$1$ lies immediately after that whole copy.  Moreover,
\[
 \Omega^{[2]}\cong\Omega\cdot\Omega
\]
is a proper initial subclass of $\Omega^{[\Omega]}$, by
\Cref{swo:fc:lem:power-initial}.  In particular,
\[
 \beta^{[\Omega]}\cong\Omega\quad\text{for every set }\beta\geq2,
 \qquad
 \Omega^{[\Omega]}\not\cong\Omega.
\]
The size of the coefficient collection changes the construction:
allowing all set ordinals as coefficients introduces proper-class
intervals.  There is no legitimate inference that a proper-class
base can be replaced by a sufficiently large set base for the
\emph{whole} order.

\subsubsection{Cofinality is a separate invariant}

A long class well-order may still have a set of cofinal points.
The exponent construction gives exact elementary examples of
both possibilities.

\begin{proposition}[Cofinality of a limit exponent]
\label{swo:fc:prop:power-cofinality}
Suppose $A$ has at least two elements and $B$ is nonempty with
no greatest point.  Then $A^{[B]}$ has a set-sized cofinal
subclass if and only if $B$ does.  Whenever these cofinalities
are set cardinals, their least possible cardinalities agree.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $1_A$ be the least nonzero coefficient.  The map sending
$b\in B$ to the monomial with coefficient $1_A$ at exponent
$b$ is strictly increasing and cofinal.  Indeed, choose an
exponent above the greatest exponent of any given nonzero
polynomial; its monomial is larger.  A cofinal set in $B$
therefore gives a cofinal set of the same size in the power.

Conversely, let $Q$ be a cofinal set of polynomials.  Take
the greatest support exponent of each nonzero member of $Q$.
These exponents form a set by Class Replacement.  They are
cofinal in $B$: if all lay below some $b$, the monomial at
$b$ would exceed every member of $Q$.  Their number is at
most $|Q|$.  The two constructions prove both assertions.
\end{proof}

In particular, $\Omega^{[\Omega]}$ has no set-sized cofinal
subclass, whereas $\Omega^{[\omega]}$ has cofinality $\omega$.
The latter is nevertheless longer than every finite power
$\Omega^{[n]}$: these powers are proper initial subclasses,
and the monomials at the finite exponents give a cofinal
sequence.  If the exponent instead has a greatest point,
$\Omega^{[B]}$ has no cofinal set.  For any proposed set of
polynomials, their coefficients at that point have a common
ordinal bound; a larger coefficient there produces a
polynomial above the entire set.  Thus passing from
$\Omega^{[\omega]}$ to $\Omega^{[\omega+1]}$ changes the
availability of a set-sized cofinal sequence.  Cofinality
and initial-segment length measure different features.

\subsubsection{Continuity and bounded interpretations}

Continuity is meaningful for a given uniform system.  Suppose
$(B_i)_{i\in I}$ is uniformly presented, $I$ is a nonempty class
well-order, the domains are nested, and each earlier order is
an initial subclass of every later one.  Then
\[\tag{S35.7}
 B=\bigcup_{i\in I}B_i,
 \qquad
 A^{[B]}=\bigcup_{i\in I}A^{[B_i]}.
 \label{swo:fc:eq:power-continuity}
\]
The first union is well-ordered: given a nonempty subclass,
take one of its points in a stage and take its least point
inside that stage.  All points outside the stage are later.
For the second equality, the finitely many exponents of a
polynomial lie together in a single stage.  This proves
continuity directly from finite support.

In particular, if $B$ is nonempty and has no greatest point,
\[
 A^{[B]}=\bigcup_{b\in B}A^{[B_{<b}]}.
\]
Some of the orders $B_{<b}$ may be proper classes; nevertheless
this family is elementary and uniform.  These assertions do
not supply an unspecified family of class stages, or a
supremum of every class well-order.  The existence and coding
of the diagram precede the union.

There is another useful verification principle when a notation
system consists of finite trees carrying ordinal labels.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-specialization principle]
\label{swo:fc:lem:bounded-specialization}
Work in $\GBC$.  Let $T$ be an elementary class of finite
ordinal-labelled terms with a class linear order.  Suppose
that, for arbitrarily large set ordinals $\kappa$, all terms
whose labels are below $\kappa$ admit a common
strictly order-preserving interpretation into a set ordinal.
Then $T$ is a class well-order.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If a nonempty subclass had no least element, Global Choice
would produce a descending $\omega$-sequence in it.  Its
terms use only a set of ordinal labels, whose union is
bounded by some set ordinal.  Choose a larger $\kappa$
with the asserted interpretation.  The entire sequence
then maps to a descending sequence in one set ordinal,
a contradiction.
\end{proof}

For nested ordinal-coefficient polynomials, the relevant
interpretation substitutes an ordinary ordinal $\kappa$
for the formal symbol $\Omega$, with every coefficient below
$\kappa$.  Ordinary base-$\kappa$ comparison verifies
order preservation on the bounded terms.  This principle
explains how set-ordinal mathematics can verify a class
notation system locally without collapsing its global
order type to a set ordinal.  For the finite-support
operation itself, \Cref{swo:fc:thm:finite-support} is
stronger in its axiomatic economy, since its direct
least-element argument already works without Global Choice.

All comparisons made in this section have explicit witnesses.
No step assumes that arbitrary class well-orders are
comparable by initial embeddings.  That additional issue
belongs to the foundational analysis, rather than to the
elementary support calculations.

% ---- source 32, its Sections 3.2--3.3
\subsection{Source 32: finite-support exponentiation and familiar expressions}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 213-232

Let $A$ have a least point $0_A$ and at least two points. Define $A^{[B]}$ to be the class of finite partial functions
\[
f:\dom B\rightharpoonup \dom A\setminus\{0_A\},
\]
read as total functions with default value $0_A$. For distinct $f,g$, their finite set of differing coordinates has a greatest point $b$. Declare
\[\tag{S32.1}
\label{swo:dc:eq:powerorder}
f<g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(b)<_A g(b).
\]
The empty function is the zero point. Only finitely many nonzero digits are stored, so every element is a set even when both parameters have proper-class domains.

\begin{lemma}[Set-sized digit representation]
\label{swo:dc:lem:digits}
For ordinary ordinals $a\geq2$ and $b$, finite-support functions $b\to a$ with the order \eqref{swo:dc:eq:powerorder} have order type $a^b$ in ordinary ordinal arithmetic.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use ordinary transfinite induction on the set ordinal $b$. At zero there is one function. At $b=c+1$, grouping by the digit at $c$ gives $a$ successive copies of the order at $c$, hence type $a^c\cdot a$. At a nonzero limit, every finite support lies below some $c<b$, and these smaller orders are nested initial segments. Their union has type $\sup_{c<b}a^c=a^b$. This also proves that the digit order is a well-order and that the displayed embeddings at smaller exponent bounds are initial. The same induction identifies the rank of a digit function with the finite sum $\sum a^{\beta_i}d_i$ in decreasing order of its occupied exponents.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~3.3, ``Explicit class exponentiation in GBC'']\label{swo:dc:thm:power}
\emph{For class well-orders $A$ and $B$, with $A$ having at least two points,
the finite-support presentation $A^{[B]}$ is a class well-order. Its
construction and proof require no $\ETR$ axiom.} This is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:power:GB}, in $\GBC$. Source~32's proof is source~34's second
route with descending sequences in place of set subsets: a descending set
sequence uses a set of exponents and a set of digits, whose collapses to
ordinals translate it into a descending sequence in an ordinary ordinal power
(\cref{swo:dc:lem:digits}), and \cref{swo:dc:lem:descending} converts this
into class well-foundedness. That conversion is where global choice enters;
over $\GB$, \cref{swo:bo:found:settest} replaces it.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 237-242
\begin{proof}[Source~32's proof]
Linearity and transitivity can be checked on the finite union of the supports of any three functions, using the corresponding finite lexicographic comparison. Suppose there were a descending set sequence of functions. The union of its finite supports is a set $S\subseteq \dom B$, and the set of all its coefficient values together with $0_A$ is a set $T\subseteq \dom A$. The induced well-orders on $S$ and $T$ have ordinary ordinal types $b$ and $a$. If $T$ contains only zero, there cannot be a strict descent. Otherwise $a\geq2$, and replacing coordinates and digits by their ranks translates the sequence into a descending sequence in the set well-order from \cref{swo:dc:lem:digits}. This is impossible. Apply \cref{swo:dc:lem:descending}.
\end{proof}

The same \emph{set-support localization} argument is useful more generally: a purported countable obstruction to a finite-coded class construction often uses only a set of labels. One can then reduce the obstruction to ordinary set mathematics without collapsing the entire proper-class order.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~3.4, ``Exponent laws by explicit maps'']\label{swo:dc:thm:powerlaws}
\emph{For the preceding presentations, $A^{[0]}\cong1$, $A^{[1]}\cong A$,
\[\tag{S32.2}\label{swo:dc:eq:explaws}
 A^{[B+C]}\cong A^{[B]}\cdot A^{[C]},\qquad A^{[B\cdot C]}\cong (A^{[B]})^{[C]}.
\]
If $j:B\to C$ is an initial
embedding, pushing supports forward along $j$ gives an initial embedding
$A^{[B]}\to A^{[C]}$, proper when $j$ is proper. If $B$ has no greatest point,
$A^{[B]}$ is the union of its initial suborders supported in $B_{<b}$, for
$b\in B$.} These are source~34's
\eqref{swo:bo:power:units}--\eqref{swo:bo:power:iterate} and the
initial-embedding paragraph after them, source~35's \cref{swo:fc:lem:power-initial}
and \eqref{swo:fc:eq:power-continuity}, and source~33's \cref{swo:dh:prop:laws},
proved by the same splitting, grouping and support transport; source~32
assumes $A$ has at least two points.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 262-285

We deliberately avoid the assertion that initial embeddings in the \emph{base} always induce initial embeddings of powers. Even for ordinary finite ordinals that assertion is false: the digit subset for $2^2$ inside the base-$3$ presentation of $3^2$ is not an initial segment.

\subsubsection{Which familiar expressions really get longer?}

For every set ordinal $\alpha$ and every nonzero set ordinal $a$,
\[
\alpha+\Omega\cong\Omega,\qquad a\cdot\Omega\cong\Omega.
\]
Indeed, the orders on the left are proper and set-like, so \cref{swo:dc:thm:setlike} applies. By contrast, $\Omega+1$ is not set-like, and $\Omega\cdot2$ consists of two genuinely successive proper-class blocks.

For every set ordinal $a\geq2$,
\[\tag{S32.3}
\label{swo:dc:eq:smallbase}
a^{[\Omega]}\cong\Omega.
\]
To see set-likeness, a predecessor of a given finite-support function can use no exponent above its greatest occupied exponent. The available exponents are therefore bounded by a set ordinal, and the coefficient alphabet is a set. There are only a set of possible predecessors. The order is proper because there is a distinct monomial at each ordinal exponent. Again \cref{swo:dc:thm:setlike} applies.

This absorption fails for a proper-class base. In $\Omega^{[\Omega]}$, the monomial at exponent $1$ has all ordinal constants as predecessors. Thus $\Omega^{[\Omega]}$ is not set-like. The constructions provide, among many others,
\[
\Omega,\quad \Omega+1,\quad \Omega\cdot2,\quad \Omega^2,\quad
\Omega^{[\Omega]},\quad \Omega^{[\Omega^{[\Omega]}]},\quad \ldots.
\]
The displayed tower steps are connected by explicit proper initial embeddings. No universal comparison theorem is needed to certify their increase.

\subsection{Source 33: finite-support exponentiation and first landmarks beyond Ord}\label{swo:dh:subsec:power}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 401-414
Suppose $A$ is a class well-order with least point $0_A$. Define $A^{[B]}$ to be
the class of finite partial functions
\[
                 p:B\rightharpoonup A\setminus\{0_A\}.
\]
Missing values are read as $0_A$. The empty function is zero. For distinct
$p,q$, let $b$ be the \emph{greatest} exponent at which they differ and set
\[
                  p<q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p(b)<_A q(b).
\]
The greatest differing exponent exists because the union of the two supports
is finite. This is reverse lexicographic comparison on the exponent positions,
not comparison at the first difference.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Theorem~3.3, ``Arithmetic closure'']\label{swo:dh:thm:power}
\emph{If $A,B$ are class well-orders and $A$ is nonempty, then the
finite-support presentation $A^{[B]}$ is a class well-order. For set ordinal
bases and exponents, it is the usual ordinal power. No elementary transfinite
recursion principle is needed for its construction or well-foundedness.}
This is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:power:GB} in $\GBC$, proved as source~32's

\subsubsection{First landmarks beyond Ord}
\begin{proposition}\label{swo:dh:prop:smallbase}
For every set ordinal $a\geq2$,
\[
                         a^{[\Omega]}\cong\Omega.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 2^{[\Omega+1]}\cong\Omega\cdot2,
 \qquad 2^{[\Omega\cdot2]}\cong\Omega^2.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A polynomial below a given element of $a^{[\Omega]}$ cannot use an exponent greater
than the largest exponent of that element. All such polynomials therefore
belong to a set of finite functions from one bounded ordinal into the set
$a$. Hence $a^{[\Omega]}$ is set-like. It is a proper class because every ordinal
can occur as the exponent of a monomial with coefficient one.
Apply \cref{swo:dh:prop:setlike}. The remaining identities follow from
\cref{swo:dh:prop:laws}.
\end{proof}

\cref{swo:bo:n4.3} and source~35's \cref{swo:fc:prop:boundary-identities}; the
two consequences $2^{[\Omega+1]}\cong\Omega\cdot2$ and
$2^{[\Omega\cdot2]}\cong\Omega^2$ are printed only by source~33 (the first is the
case $a=2$ of source~34's $a^{[\Omega+1]}\cong\Omega\cdot a$).

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 495-506

fixed point above finite towers of powers of $\Omega$. None of these expressions
turns $\Omega$ into a set ordinal.

\begin{remark}[Not cardinal exponentiation]\label{swo:dh:n3.6}
The class $A^{[B]}$ just defined contains \emph{finite} function codes. It is not
the collection of all class functions $B\to A$. The latter would generally
be a higher-order collection, not a class of sets in $\GBC$. Likewise, arbitrary
infinite-support reverse lexicographic orders need not be well-founded; a
support convention is part of a definition, not a cosmetic choice.
\end{remark}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 601-949
\section{The canonical-history theorem over GB}
\label{swo:bo:hist:section}

The repository already proves a substantial theorem over $\GBC$: canonical
terminating condensation histories, strong comparability of class well-orders,
and certain initial-segment polynomial representations are equivalent
\cite{xviAtPinBO}. Its proof constructs canonical floor maps and finite
normal forms. We retain that construction and its attribution. The contribution
here is a sharper foundation: the choice-free polynomial well-order theorem
proved above removes the only use of Global Choice in the arbitrary-carrier
argument. Consequently the equivalence holds over $\GB$, including when the
set universe does not satisfy Choice. This answers the repository's remaining
question about the $\GB$ version for the precise limit convention below.
It does not establish the converse from comparability to $\ETR$ discussed by
Hamkins and Woodin \cite{HamkinsWoodin}.

Throughout this section a class well-order means that every nonempty admitted
subclass has a least element. We do not substitute the potentially weaker
absence of a set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence over a choiceless base.
All constructions use elementary comprehension and Class Replacement. In
particular, a supplied history is a single class relation, not a collection
whose members are classes.

\subsection{Histories and their termination bound}

Let $W=(X,<_{W})$ be a nonempty class well-order with minimum $m$. For a
nonempty subclass $A\subseteq X$ containing $m$, let $D_W(A)$ be the class of
least representatives for the equivalence relation
\[
 x\sim_A y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [\min_W(x,y),\max_W(x,y)]_W\cap A\text{ is a set}.
\]
The preceding block decomposition applies to the induced order on $A$.
In particular, a block followed by another block has type $\Ord$.

Let $\Gamma=(I,<_{\Gamma})$ be another nonempty class well-order. Form
$\Gamma+1$ with a tagged new final stage $*$. Write $i^+$ for the immediate
successor of $i\in I$ in this extended order. A nonzero limit stage is a
noninitial stage without an immediate predecessor; it may have a proper
class of predecessors.

\begin{definition}[Canonical history]
\label{swo:bo:hist:definition}
A canonical history of $W$ on $\Gamma+1$ is one class relation $H$ with slices
\[
 H_{\min\Gamma}=X,\qquad H_{i^+}=D_W(H_i),\qquad
 H_\lambda=\bigcap_{i<\lambda}H_i
 \quad\text{at nonzero limits }\lambda.
\]
It is terminating if $H_* =\{m\}$. The principle $\CTH$ asserts that every
nonempty class well-order $W$ has a canonical history on its own input-order
schedule $W+1$.
\end{definition}

The displayed intersection is elementary: membership says that every earlier
set-valued stage label satisfies the appropriate slice predicate. Elementary
induction along the supplied schedule shows that the slices are decreasing
and contain $m$. The history's existence, however, is not supplied by that
induction.

\begin{lemma}[Termination on the input schedule]
\label{swo:bo:hist:termination}
In $\GB$, any supplied canonical history on $W+1$ terminates. More precisely,
\[
 H_x\subseteq\{m\}\cup\{y\in X:x\leq_W y\}\qquad(x\in X).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induct along $W$, using the given history as a class parameter. The first-stage
claim is immediate. At the successor $x=t^+$, the inductive bound has removed
all points below $t$ except $m$. If $t\ne m$ remains, it is the second point
of $H_t$, so its two-point interval with $m$ causes its deletion by $D_W$.
This proves the successor bound. At a nonzero limit $x$, each $m\ne y<x$ lies
below some $t<x$, and is absent from $H_t$ by induction.

If $W$ has a last point $\ell$, its slice is contained in $\{m,\ell\}$;
the final successor leaves only $m$. Otherwise every nonminimal point is
excluded by some later stage, hence from the final intersection.
\end{proof}

This is the repository's supplied-history termination argument
\cite{xviAtPinBO}. It is consistent with $W$ being isomorphic to its first
condensation: the slices are actual nested subclasses, so repeated abstract
order types do not prevent the specified limit intersection from shrinking.

\subsection{Canonical floors and finite addresses}

\begin{lemma}[Floors at all stages]
\label{swo:bo:hist:floors}
For each stage $i$ and point $x\in X$, there is a greatest retained point
at most $x$:
\[
 p_i(x)=\max_W\{a\in H_i:a\leq_W x\}.
\]
The maps are uniformly elementary in $H,W$, nondecreasing in $x$, and for
$i\leq j$ satisfy
\[
 p_j(x)\leq_W p_i(x),\qquad
 p_j(p_i(x))=p_j(x),\qquad p_i(p_j(x))=p_j(x).
\]
At every nonzero limit $\lambda$, the floors of each fixed $x$ stabilize
before $\lambda$ at $p_\lambda(x)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At the first stage the floor is $x$. Suppose $p_i(x)=a$, and let $b$ be the
least representative of $a$'s block in $H_i$. A representative strictly
between $b$ and $x$ would be at most $a$, by the floor property, and would
belong to the same block as $b$. This is impossible. Thus $p_{i^+}(x)=b$.

At a nonzero limit $\lambda$, the earlier floor values form a nonempty
admitted subclass of $W$. Take its least value $b$, attained at some
$i_0<\lambda$. Because the floors decrease, every subsequent floor before
$\lambda$ equals $b$. Nesting places $b$ in every earlier slice as well,
so $b\in H_\lambda$. Every point of $H_\lambda$ at most $x$ is at most
$p_{i_0}(x)=b$. This proves existence and stabilization.

This is elementary induction: the greatest-predecessor formula defines all
floors from the supplied history without selecting class maps. Nesting also
proves the two composition identities, and monotonicity in $x$ is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finitely many changes]
\label{swo:bo:hist:finite}
For each fixed $x$, only finitely many stages $i\in I$ have
$p_{i^+}(x)\ne p_i(x)$. No floor value first appears at a limit stage.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The limit assertion follows from \Cref{swo:bo:hist:floors}. If the class of
successor changes were not finite, taking its least remaining member would
uniquely define increasing stages $i_0<i_1<\cdots$ with strictly decreasing
floors. Ordinary set-valued recursion along $\omega$, followed by Class
Replacement, gives a set-coded descending sequence in $W$, a contradiction.
These are unique minimum choices, so neither form of Choice is used.
\end{proof}

Define the ordinal digit
\[
 c_i(x)=\otp\bigl(\{z\in H_i:p_{i^+}(x)\leq_W z<_W p_i(x)\},<_{W}\bigr).
\]
This interval is a set because its endpoints lie in one set-interval block.
The digit is nonzero exactly at a floor change. Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{NF}_H(x)=\{(i,c_i(x)):c_i(x)>0\}\in P(\Gamma)
\]
is a finite set graph. Its dependence on $x$ is elementary. Finiteness here,
like the theorem itself, is interpreted internally in a nonstandard model.

\begin{theorem}[Finite normal form with initial image]
\label{swo:bo:hist:normalform}
If $H$ terminates on $\Gamma+1$, then $\operatorname{NF}_H$ is a class order
isomorphism of $W$ onto an initial segment of $ P(\Gamma)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First establish a digit-insertion rule. Let $b\in H_{i^+}$, and let $z$ be the
point of ordinal rank $\rho$ in the $H_i$ block beginning at $b$, when such a
point exists. Then $p_i(z)=z$ and $p_{i^+}(z)=b$. At later stages, the floors
of $z$ and $b$ agree by \Cref{swo:bo:hist:floors}. At every earlier stage both
floors determining a digit equal $z$, since $z\in H_i$. Thus insertion adds
the digit $\rho$ at $i$, keeps the higher digits of $b$, and makes all lower
digits zero.

An actual code reconstructs its point uniquely. Start from the final anchor
$m$ and read its finitely many nonzero digits in decreasing stage order,
using the insertion rule. Each requested rank exists for an actual code.
\Cref{swo:bo:hist:finite} ensures there are no other floor changes, including
at limits. The resulting point is therefore $x$. This proves injectivity.

To prove initiality, fix $q<\operatorname{NF}_H(x)$ and let $i$ be the
greatest exponent of disagreement. Decoding the common higher digits gives
the anchor $b=p_{i^+}(x)$. Write $d=c_i(x)$ and $c=q(i)$, so $c<d$.
The $H_i$ block at $b$ contains points $a,a'$ of ranks $c,c+1$, with
\[
 a<_W a'\leq_W p_i(x)\leq_W x.
\]
Insert digit $c$, obtaining anchor $a$, and keep $a'$ as a fixed upper bound.

Process the remaining nonzero digits of $q$ in decreasing exponent order.
For each lower exponent $j<i$, the current anchor and $a'$ both belong to
$H_{j^+}$. Initially this follows from membership in $H_i$; after an insertion
at $k>j$, the new anchor lies in $H_k\subseteq H_{j^+}$. They are distinct
retained representatives. Therefore the $H_j$ block beginning at the current
anchor is nonfinal and has type $\Ord$. Every requested ordinal digit exists
inside it, strictly below $a'$. Insert that digit and continue.

After finitely many steps the resulting $y$ satisfies
$\operatorname{NF}_H(y)=q$ and $y<a'\leq x$. Thus every polynomial below an
actual code occurs with a smaller preimage. Applied to two actual codes,
this also gives exact order preservation, using injectivity and linearity.
The image is initial, as required.
\end{proof}

The fixed upper bound in this proof is essential: it guarantees complete
$\Ord$ blocks for all lower digits. Mere injectivity into a polynomial order
would not yield strong comparability.

\subsection{Restrictions and prescribed schedules}

\begin{lemma}[Anchored convex restriction]
\label{swo:bo:hist:restriction}
Let $Y$ be a nonempty convex subclass of $W$, with $a=\min_W Y$. If $H$ is a
canonical history on $W$, then on the same schedule
\[
 J_i=\{a\}\cup\{y\in H_i\cap Y:a<_W y\}
\]
is the canonical history of the induced order on $Y$. It terminates whenever
$H$ terminates.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The initial clause and the limit intersections follow directly. For a
successor stage fix $x\in H_i\cap Y$ with $a<x$, and let $u=p_i(a)$.
There are no $H_i$ points in $(u,a]$. Convexity gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [u,x]_W\cap H_i&=\{u\}\cup\{z\in H_i:a<z\leq x\},\\
 [a,x]_W\cap J_i&=\{a\}\cup\{z\in H_i:a<z\leq x\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
These intervals are sets simultaneously. A global witness below $x$ showing
that $x$ is not a least representative is also a local witness if it is
above $a$. If it is at or below $a$, restriction of its interval and insertion
of $a$ gives a local set interval. Conversely, a local witness above $a$
is global too, whereas the local witness $a$ can be replaced by $u$ using
the displayed identities. Hence the retained representatives strictly above
$a$ coincide. The local minimum $a$ is always retained, proving the
successor clause. A final global singleton contributes no point above $a$,
so the local final slice is $\{a\}$.
\end{proof}

Bare intersection with $Y$ would sometimes discard its minimum; the anchor
cannot be omitted. The earlier polynomial construction supplies, in $\GB$,
the explicit history
\[
 K_i=\{q\in P(\Gamma):\supp q\subseteq I_{\geq i}\},\qquad K_* =\{0\}.
\]
Condensation deletes the least available exponent; the limit intersection
retains exactly the exponents above every earlier threshold.

\begin{corollary}[Exact fixed-schedule criterion]
\label{swo:bo:hist:schedule}
For nonempty class well-orders $W,\Gamma$, a canonical terminating history
of $W$ on $\Gamma+1$ exists if and only if $W$ is class-isomorphic to an
initial segment of $ P(\Gamma)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The forward implication is \Cref{swo:bo:hist:normalform}. Conversely, restrict
the explicit polynomial history to the supplied nonempty initial range and
pull it back through the class isomorphism. \Cref{swo:bo:hist:restriction}
verifies the recursion clauses; the zero polynomial gives the final singleton.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The equivalence and its exact scope}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical histories over GB]
\label{swo:bo:hist:equivalence}
Over $\GB$, the following principles are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\CWO$: of any two class well-orders, one is class-isomorphic to an
initial segment of the other, allowing the whole order.
\item $\CTH$: every nonempty $W$ has a canonical history on $W+1$.
\item Every nonempty $W$ has a canonical terminating history on some
class-well-order schedule $\Gamma+1$.
\item Every nonempty $W$ is class-isomorphic to an initial segment of
$ P(W)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The implication $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$ is \Cref{swo:bo:hist:termination}.

For $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$, form the tagged sum $T=R+S$ of two nonempty orders.
Apply (3) once to obtain one history on a schedule $\Gamma+1$. Anchored convex
restriction gives histories for $R$ and $S$ on that same schedule. Their
normal forms have initial ranges in the same order $ P(\Gamma)$.
Two initial subclasses of a linear order are comparable by inclusion.
Compose the map onto the smaller range with the inverse map on the larger
range to obtain the required class initial-segment isomorphism. Empty inputs
are immediate. There is no simultaneous choice of histories for many orders.

For $(1)\Rightarrow(4)$, first observe that any class order embedding
$f:W\to W$ satisfies $x\leq_W f(x)$. Otherwise the least counterexample
$x$ has $f(x)<x$ and $f(f(x))<f(x)$, giving an earlier counterexample.
It follows that $W+1$ cannot embed into $W$: if the last point mapped to
$a$, the restricted embedding would give $a\leq f(a)<f(*)=a$.

Now put $\Gamma=W+1$. The choice-free polynomial theorem makes
$ P(\Gamma)$ a class well-order. The coefficient-one monomials $e_t$
embed $W+1$ into it. Comparability with $W$ must therefore give an initial
embedding $f:W\to P(\Gamma)$; the opposite direction would embed
$W+1$ into $W$. Its range lies strictly below $e_*$, since otherwise
initiality would put $e_*$ and every $e_x$ in the range, again embedding
$W+1$ into $W$ through $f^{-1}$. The polynomials below $e_*$ are exactly
$ P(W)$, which proves (4).

Finally, $(4)\Rightarrow(2)$ follows from \Cref{swo:bo:hist:schedule} with
$\Gamma=W$. Explicitly, pull the support-threshold polynomial history back
through the supplied initial-segment isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Uniqueness with a fixed schedule]
\label{swo:bo:hist:uniqueness}
Two canonical histories for the same input order and schedule agree at every
stage. Suppose the sets, input order, and schedule remain fixed while the
collection of available classes is enlarged, and both orders remain class
well-orders in the larger realization. Then an already available history and
its normal forms retain their values and agree with any newly available
canonical history on that schedule.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The class of disagreement stages is elementary in the two supplied histories.
If nonempty, it has a least member. That member cannot be the first stage,
whose slice is prescribed. At a successor the equal preceding slices have
equal condensations, and at a limit the equal earlier slices have equal
intersections. Each possibility contradicts disagreement. For the second
claim, the set-interval tests and recursion clauses quantify only over the
unchanged sets with the given classes as parameters. The old history still
satisfies those clauses, and the assumed well-ordering of the schedule in the
larger realization permits uniqueness to identify it with any new candidate.
The ordinal interval ranks defining the normal forms are unchanged as well.
\end{proof}

Thus a stronger class theory can supply a previously absent history without
changing an old one. This distinction concerns existence of one class witness;
it does not provide a class-valued operation selecting histories for a totality
of class well-orders. Over the choiceless base, preservation of an old
relation's class-well-order property under enlargement of the class collection
is not being assumed without a hypothesis.

The repository's four-way equivalence and the preceding normal-form machinery
are the mathematical starting point \cite{xviAtPinBO}. Our strengthening
consists of the $\GB$ polynomial theorem and the checked elimination of Choice
from the remaining dependencies. It gives neither a proof of $\CWO$ in
$\GB$ nor a proof that $\CWO$ yields arbitrary elementary transfinite
recursion. Suitable $\ETR$ supplies the required histories; the reverse
comparison remains separate \cite{HamkinsWoodin}.

There is also a necessary limitation concerning carriers. The repository
reduces the history principle to well-orders of the entire surreal class by
transporting arbitrary proper class carriers through a global bijection.
That corollary retains its Global Choice hypothesis. The choice-free theorem
above quantifies directly over the given class carriers and does not assume
that every proper class is bijective with $\Ord$ or with the surreals.

% ---- source 35, its Section 4
\subsection{Source 35: condensation, finite addresses, and comparison without Choice}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 805-839
\label{swo:fc:sec:condensation}

This section strengthens a result recorded in the ProveIt manuscript
\cite{xviAtPinFC}.  That manuscript proves, over $\GBC$, an equivalence between
complete canonical condensation histories and strong comparison of class
well-orders; its Part~XIV explicitly leaves the corresponding question over
$\GB$ without Global Choice open.  We prove the equivalence over the
choice-free base used here: the sets satisfy $\mathrm{ZF}$, and the class
axioms provide elementary comprehension and Class Replacement.  Neither
set Choice nor Global Choice occurs in the proof.  The principal repair is
the choice-free finite-support theorem, \Cref{swo:fc:thm:finite-support};
the remaining argument is established below with its class-existence
requirements explicit.  The normal-form construction itself, and the
equivalence over $\GBC$, are credited to the repository.

Throughout, a class well-order means an order in which every nonempty
admitted subclass has a least element.  In particular, we do not replace
this hypothesis by the absence of a descending $\omega$-sequence.  An
initial segment may be the whole order.  Class carriers always consist of
sets; a block or history slice can be a proper class, but never becomes
an element of another class.

\subsubsection{One condensation is elementary}

Let $W=(X,<_{W})$ be nonempty.  For a nonempty subclass $A\subseteq X$,
with its induced order, define
\[
 x\sim_A y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [\min_W(x,y),\max_W(x,y)]_W\cap A\text{ is a set}.
\]
The right side is elementary: it asserts that there exists a set whose
members are exactly the displayed interval.  Let $D_W(A)$ consist of the
least elements of the $\sim_A$-blocks.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Lemma~4.1, ``Set-interval blocks'']\label{swo:fc:lem:condensation-blocks}
\emph{The relation $\sim_A$ is a convex equivalence relation. Its blocks have
canonical ordinal rank maps, and each block is isomorphic either to a set
ordinal or to $\Ord$. A set-sized block, if present, is final. In particular, a
block followed by another block has type $\Omega$.} This is source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ch:blocks} for the induced order on $A$, with the same proof, and
source~32's and source~33's \cref{swo:dc:lem:blocks,swo:dh:lem:blocks};
source~35 notes that the rank of a point is the order type of a set that
already carries the supplied well-order, so no well-ordering of a set is
chosen.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 867-892

This gives the repository's canonical division theorem.  Let $B_W$ be
the ordered class of minima of the proper blocks of $W$, and let
$\rho_W$ be the ordinal type of the final set block, or zero if there is
none.  Then
\[\tag{S35.8}\label{swo:fc:eq:omega-division}
                     W\cong\Omega\cdot B_W+\rho_W.
\]
Here the product is a $B_W$-indexed sum of copies of $\Omega$.  The
isomorphism sends a point in a proper block to its block minimum and its
ordinal rank within that block; it sends the final set block to
$\rho_W$.  This is one elementary class map.  Thus the word
``canonical'' does not conceal a choice of one isomorphism for each
block.  When $W$ is a set, $B_W$ is empty and $\rho_W=\otp(W)$.
For a proper carrier, $B_W$ is nonempty.  Formula
\eqref{swo:fc:eq:omega-division} and its proof are already in
\cite{xviAtPinFC}; the quotient can be as complicated as an arbitrary
class well-order, so this single division does not finish the analysis.

\subsubsection{What a complete history asserts}

Let $\Gamma=(I,<_{\Gamma})$ be a nonempty class well-order and append a
tagged final point $*$.  Each $i\in I$ has an immediate successor $i^+$
in $\Gamma+1$.  A nonzero limit stage has no immediate predecessor; its
predecessor class need not be a set.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Definition~4.2, ``Canonical condensation history'']\label{swo:fc:n4.2}
\emph{A history for $W$ on $\Gamma+1$ is a single class relation
$H\subseteq(I\cup\{*\})\times X$ with $H_{\min\Gamma}=X$,
$H_{i^+}=D_W(H_i)$ for $i\in I$, and
$H_\lambda=\bigcap_{i<_{\Gamma+1}\lambda}H_i$ at nonzero limits
\textup{(}source~35's displays (9)--(11)\textup{)}. It terminates if
$H_*=\{m\}$, $m=\min_WX$; $\CTH$ says that every nonempty $W$ has such a
history on $W+1$.} This is \cref{swo:bo:hist:definition} and
\cref{swo:bw:ch:history-def}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 906-914

The recursion clauses are elementary in the earlier history.  Their
solutions, however, are class-valued histories; elementary comprehension
alone does not assert that a solution exists.  Once $H$ is supplied,
elementary induction along its schedule proves that the slices decrease
and all contain $m$.  It also proves uniqueness for fixed $W$ and
schedule: a least stage at which two histories differ is incompatible
with the corresponding recursion clause.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Proposition~4.3, ``Input-order termination'']\label{swo:fc:prop:input-termination}
\emph{Every supplied history on $W+1$ terminates; more precisely
$H_x\subseteq\{m\}\cup\{y\in X:x\le_W y\}$ for $x\in X$.} This is
\cref{swo:bo:hist:termination}, source~20's \cref{swo:lm:con:termination} and
source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:input-bound}, by the same induction along $W$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 936-938

\subsubsection{Floors and the finiteness of every individual address}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Lemma~4.4, ``Canonical floors'']\label{swo:fc:lem:canonical-floors}
\emph{For every stage $i$ of a supplied history and every $x\in X$, the
maximum $p_i(x)=\max_W(H_i\cap(-\infty,x]_W)$ exists; the graph of all these
maps is elementary in $H,W$; for $i\le j$,
\[\tag{S35.12}\label{swo:fc:eq:floor-identities}
 p_j(x)\le_W p_i(x),\qquad p_j(p_i(x))=p_j(x),\qquad p_i(p_j(x))=p_j(x);
\]
and at each nonzero limit
$\lambda$ the earlier floors of a fixed point are eventually constant, with
value $p_\lambda(x)$.} This is \cref{swo:bo:hist:floors} and source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ch:floors} with \eqref{swo:bw:ch:projection-identities}, by the
same induction; source~35 stresses that no new class is defined at an
induction step, the value class being defined by one formula from the single
supplied $H$.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Lemma~4.5, ``Finite changes'']\label{swo:fc:lem:finite-floor-changes}
\emph{For a fixed $x$, the class $\{i\in I:p_{i^+}(x)\ne p_i(x)\}$ is finite.
No new floor value first occurs at a limit stage.} This is
\cref{swo:bo:hist:finite} and \cref{swo:bw:ch:finite-changes}: an infinite
change class would yield, by a uniquely determined recursion collected by
Class Replacement (``not an application of Dependent Choice''), increasing
stages with strictly decreasing floors.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1001-1011

The limit rule also has an intrinsic quotient interpretation.  Put
$xE_i y$ if $p_i(x)=p_i(y)$.  The projection identities and eventual
stabilization give
\[
                         E_\lambda=\bigcup_{i<\lambda}E_i
\]
at every nonzero limit: if two limit floors agree, choose an earlier
stage after the stabilization stage of each floor.  Thus an
identification of original points never first appears at a limit.

\merge\ The remark above is source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:quotient-limits}. The
explicit history \eqref{swo:fc:eq:polynomial-history} is source~34's $K_i$
after \cref{swo:bo:hist:restriction} and source~29's
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:polynomial-history}; source~35's paragraph after it is the
fullest verification of its successor clause printed here.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1012-1046
\subsubsection{Polynomial histories and canonical finite normal forms}

Write $ P(\Gamma)$ for the class of finite partial functions from
$I$ to nonzero set ordinals, compared at the greatest exponent where
their coefficients differ.  Missing coefficients are zero.  By
\Cref{swo:fc:thm:finite-support}, this is a class well-order in the
choice-free base.  Its explicit history on $\Gamma+1$ is
\[\tag{S35.13}\label{swo:fc:eq:polynomial-history}
 K_i=\{q:\supp(q)\subseteq\{j:i\le_\Gamma j\}\},
                      \qquad K_*=\{0\}.
\]
Indeed, fixing all coefficients strictly above $i$ gives one
set-interval block of $K_i$: its $i$-coefficient varies through
$\Ord$.  Bounded intervals within this fiber are sets.  Between
different higher parts, the interval contains arbitrarily large
$i$-coefficients on the lower higher part and is proper.  Removing
the $i$-coefficient therefore selects exactly the block minima.  At a
limit, intersection of the support thresholds is the required threshold;
at the final stage only the empty polynomial remains.  The formula is
uniform and elementary, so this particular history needs no recursion
axiom.

Now let $H$ be a supplied terminating history for $W$ on $\Gamma+1$.
Define
\[\tag{S35.14}\label{swo:fc:eq:history-digits}
