 c_i(x)=\otp\bigl([p_{i^+}(x),p_i(x))_W\cap H_i,<_{W}\bigr).
\]
The interval is a set because its endpoints lie in the same
$\sim_{H_i}$-block.  Its rank is zero exactly when the two floors
coincide.  Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{NF}_H(x)=\{(i,c_i(x)):i\in I,\ c_i(x)>0\}
\]
is a finite polynomial.  This is a set-valued elementary class map.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~4.6, ``Finite normal form from a supplied history'']\label{swo:fc:thm:history-normal-form}
\emph{The map $\operatorname{NF}_H$ is an isomorphism from $W$ onto an initial
segment of $P(\Gamma)$.} This is \cref{swo:bo:hist:normalform} and source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ch:normal-form-theorem}, with the same proof: one insertion adds
the digit $\rho$ at stage $i$ and zeros below it; reading the finitely many
nonzero digits from the final floor $m$ reconstructs $x$; for $q$ below an
actual code, the points $a<_Wa'$ of ranks $c$ and $c+1$ in the block at
$p_{i^+}(x)$ satisfy
\[\tag{S35.15}\label{swo:fc:eq:normal-form-cap}
 a<_W a'\le_W p_i(x)\le_W x
\]
(source~29's \eqref{swo:bw:ch:cap}), and the fixed upper bound $a'$ keeps every
later block nonfinal, so every requested lower digit can be inserted below
$a'$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1105-1113

The upper bound $a'$ in \eqref{swo:fc:eq:normal-form-cap} is essential.  It
ensures that all subsequently requested smaller digits can be inserted
inside nonfinal blocks, even when the input order has a truncated last
block.  Consequently the theorem gives an initial-segment embedding,
which is stronger than an embedding into an arbitrary suborder.

\subsubsection{Restriction to a convex interval}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Lemma~4.7, ``Anchored restriction'']\label{swo:fc:lem:anchored-restriction}
\emph{If $Y$ is a nonempty convex subclass of $W$ and $a=\min_WY$, then
\[\tag{S35.16}\label{swo:fc:eq:anchored-restriction}
 J_i=\{a\}\cup\{y\in H_i\cap Y:a<_Wy\}
\]
is the canonical history of $Y$ on the same schedule, and it terminates
whenever $H$ does.} This is \cref{swo:bo:hist:restriction} and
\cref{swo:bw:ch:convex-restriction}, with the same two displayed intervals.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1142-1146

Intersecting with $Y$ without restoring its minimum would generally
fail.  For an initial segment the anchor is the global minimum, and
ordinary intersection suffices.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~4.8, ``Exact criterion for a fixed schedule'']\label{swo:fc:history-criterion}
\emph{For nonempty class well-orders $W$ and $\Gamma$, the following are
equivalent in $\GB$: $W$ has a canonical terminating history on $\Gamma+1$;
$W$ is class-isomorphic to an initial segment of $P(\Gamma)$.} This is
\cref{swo:bo:hist:schedule} and \cref{swo:bw:ch:schedule-criterion}, by the
same restriction and pullback; every nonempty initial image contains $0$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1165-1170

\subsubsection{The equivalence over the choice-free base}

Let $\CWO$ assert that any two class well-orders are comparable by a
class isomorphism of one onto an initial segment of the other.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~4.9, ``Choice-free history--comparison equivalence'']\label{swo:fc:gb-comparability}
\emph{Over $\GB$ with $\ZF$ sets and no form of Choice assumed, the following
are equivalent: (1)~$\CWO$; (2)~$\CTH$: every nonempty $W$ has a history on
$W+1$; (3)~every nonempty $W$ has a terminating history on some
class-well-order schedule $\Gamma+1$; (4)~every nonempty $W$ is
class-isomorphic to an initial segment of $P(W)$.} This is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:hist:equivalence}, proved independently with the same four
implications: (2)$\Rightarrow$(3) by termination; (3)$\Rightarrow$(1) from one
history of the tagged sum $R+S$ and its two anchored restrictions;
(1)$\Rightarrow$(4) by comparing $W$ with $P(W+1)$, which contains $W+1$ as
the monomials $e_t$; (4)$\Rightarrow$(2) by the explicit relation
$H_i=\{x\in X:\supp(f(x))\subseteq\{j:i\le_Wj\}\}$, $H_*=f^{-1}[\{0\}]$.
Source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence} is the same theorem over $\GBC$.
Source~35's choice-free input is its \cref{swo:fc:thm:finite-support}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1233-1259

This proves the characterization over $\GB$ requested in the
repository's open-item list.  It does not determine whether $\CWO$
follows from $\GB$, and it does not establish $\CWO\Rightarrow\ETR$.
Elementary transfinite recursion supplies the displayed history
equations, so the proof also gives
\[
                 \GB+\ETR\vdash\CTH\land\CWO.
\]
The converse from comparison to unrestricted elementary transfinite
recursion remains a separate question.

The axiom distinction matters for scope.  The theorem applies to every
\emph{supplied} class well-order on a class of set labels.  Transporting
all proper carriers to a single preferred carrier, such as the whole
surreal class, can require Global Choice and is not part of this
strengthening.  Similarly, the conclusion supplies an individual history
for each individual input; it does not produce a same-level class whose
members are all class histories.

Finally, finite addresses do not impose a finite or ordinal bound on the
length of an order.  Their exponents belong to the supplied class
schedule and can themselves have proper classes of predecessors.  What
the theorem controls is the finite amount of changing information
attached to each individual point.  The existence of a complete uniform
history, and hence of these addresses for every input order, has exactly
the comparison content expressed in \Cref{swo:fc:gb-comparability}.

% ---- source 32, its Section 6
\subsection{Source 32: condensation: general termination and sharp examples}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 399-402
\label{swo:dc:sec:condensation}

The repository asks whether iterating set-interval condensation eventually collapses every raw class well-order, while distinguishing its explicit polynomial examples from arbitrary recursion \cite{xviStatusTwentyThree}. There are really two issues: existence of an admitted hierarchy and termination of a hierarchy once available. The second has a general answer.

\merge\ The question source~32 quotes is the one of source~23's status file;
this report had answered it before source~32 was written
(\cref{swo:xvi:rem:termination}).

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 403-417
\subsubsection{An elementary condensation operator}

Let $E$ be a convex equivalence relation on $W$. Write $r_E(x)$ for the least point in the $E$-class of $x$, and let $Q_E$ be the class of these least representatives in their inherited order. Define
\[\tag{S32.7}
\label{swo:dc:eq:operator}
x\,\mathcal C_W(E)\,y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
[r_E(x),r_E(y)]_{Q_E}\text{ is a set}.
\]
This is again a convex equivalence relation, by \cref{swo:dc:lem:blocks} applied to $Q_E$ and then pulled back to $W$. It is coarser than $E$. All of \eqref{swo:dc:eq:operator} is elementary in $W,E$: least representatives and set-sized intervals are expressed by quantifying only over sets.

For a supplied class well-order of stages, a \emph{condensation hierarchy} begins with equality, applies $\mathcal C_W$ at successors, and takes unions of its previous equivalence relations at nonzero limits. Unions are along an increasing chain, so they are convex equivalence relations. Stage domains and relations must be coded by one admitted class; an external assertion that each individual stage exists is not enough.

\subsubsection{Termination by the order's own length}

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~6.1, ``Conditional general termination'']\label{swo:dc:thm:termination}
\emph{Let $W$ be a nonempty class well-order, and append a new greatest stage
$\infty$ to form $W+1$. Suppose an admitted condensation hierarchy
$(E_t)_{t\in W+1}$ on $W$ exists, using equality at the least stage,
$\mathcal C_W$ at successors, and unions at nonzero limits. Then $E_\infty$ is
universal. In particular, $\GBC+\ETR_{W+1}$ supplies a hierarchy that collapses
$W$ by its own order length.} This is source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:con:termination}, source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:input-bound} and
\cref{swo:bo:hist:termination}, for hierarchies of equivalence relations;
such hierarchies are the nested histories of those statements
(\cref{swo:xvi:rem:towers}). Source~32's proof follows; its invariant
\eqref{swo:dc:eq:terminationinvariant} is the retention bound
\eqref{swo:lm:con:retention-bound} read through that correspondence.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 422-456
\begin{proof}[Source~32's proof]
Let $w_0$ be the least point of $W$. We prove by class well-order induction on the stages $t\in W+1$ that
\[\tag{S32.8}
\label{swo:dc:eq:terminationinvariant}
x\in W\text{ and }x<_W t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\,E_t\,w_0,
\]
where all points of $W$ precede $\infty$. At the first stage the assertion is vacuous.

Suppose $t$ is the immediate successor of $s$. If $s=w_0$, the assertion needed is just reflexivity. Otherwise, the induction hypothesis says that all points below $s$ lie in the one $E_s$-block containing $w_0$. The quotient interval from that block to the block containing $s$ has at most two points: a point below $s$ already belongs to the first block, and there are no other points before $s$ to create intermediate blocks. A two-point or one-point interval is a set. Applying $\mathcal C_W$ therefore merges $s$ and all its predecessors with $w_0$, proving \eqref{swo:dc:eq:terminationinvariant} at $t$.

If $t$ is a nonzero limit, take $x<t$. There is a stage $s$ with $x<s<t$, since otherwise $x$ would be the immediate predecessor of $t$. The induction hypothesis gives $x\,E_s\,w_0$, and the union rule gives $x\,E_t\,w_0$. This also handles $t=\infty$ when $W$ has no greatest point. If $W$ has a greatest point, the successor argument handles $\infty$. Thus every point is equivalent to $w_0$ at the final stage.

For existence under ETR, code the history by a class of triples $(t,x,y)$. The first-stage, successor, and limit clauses above form an elementary recursion rule with parameters $W$ and its stage order. Formula \eqref{swo:dc:eq:operator} is elementary, so $\ETR_{W+1}$ gives the required class. The induction establishing that its sections are increasing convex equivalence relations uses the operator properties already proved.
\end{proof}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Status.} The termination implication itself is a theorem of GBC about any admitted hierarchy satisfying the stated clauses. ETR is a sufficient existence hypothesis. This is not an argument that bare GBC admits every such hierarchy, nor that this particular recursion operator has the full strength of ETR.\par\smallskip

The invariant \eqref{swo:dc:eq:terminationinvariant} avoids a potentially misleading strategy: it does not try to assign a decreasing external ordinal size to the successive quotients. A quotient may be isomorphic to the previous quotient for a very long time while the quotient \emph{maps} continue to identify new points.

\subsubsection{An explicit family attaining arbitrarily long bounds}

Here we re-establish the polynomial mechanism already present in the repository, so that the sharpness argument is self-contained. Fix an admitted class well-order $\Gamma$ and put
\[
P(\Gamma)=\Omega^{[\Gamma]}.
\]
For a stage $c\in\Gamma+1$, define directly
\[\tag{S32.9}
\label{swo:dc:eq:explicitcond}
p\,E_c\,q
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p(d)=q(d)\text{ for every }d\in\Gamma\text{ with }c\leq d.
\]
At the added last stage there are no such $d$, so the relation is universal. The formula defines the entire hierarchy at once, without ETR.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~6.2, ``Exact polynomial condensation length'']\label{swo:dc:thm:sharp}
\emph{The relations \eqref{swo:dc:eq:explicitcond} form a condensation
hierarchy on $P(\Gamma)$. For nonempty $\Gamma$, no stage belonging to $\Gamma$
is universal, while the added final stage is universal. Thus its first
collapse occurs at the stage of length $\Gamma$.} This is source~23's
\cref{swo:tm:thm:polyhierarchy} (Part~XIV), source~15's
\cref{swo:cb:cce:thm:anyhistory} and the explicit history $K_i$ of
\cref{swo:bo:hist:restriction}'s sequel, and source~33's \cref{swo:dh:thm:polycond};
the proof is the same: the least representative of an $E_c$-class clears the
coefficients below $c$; at a successor two representatives agreeing above $s$
span a set interval, while different higher parts leave a proper class of
coefficients at $s$ between them; at a limit a finite set of differing
exponents is bounded below an earlier stage; and the monomial at $c$ separates
zero from the next stage.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 470-478

\begin{corollary}[Isomorphic quotients can hide real progress]
\label{swo:dc:cor:selfsimilar}
For $P(\Omega)=\Omega^{[\Omega]}$, the quotient by $E_\alpha$ is isomorphic to $P(\Omega)$ for every set ordinal $\alpha$, but the quotient at the class-limit stage $\Omega$ is a singleton. In particular, no set-ordinal bound on condensation lengths can work for all explicit class well-orders.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
At stage $\alpha$, the retained exponent tail is $[\alpha,\Ord)$, which is isomorphic to $\Ord$ by the ordinary ordinal-tail correspondence. Transporting finite supports gives the asserted quotient isomorphism. Nevertheless the equivalence relations strictly increase: the monomial at coordinate $\alpha$ survives $E_\alpha$ and is identified with zero at $E_{\alpha+1}$. Formula \eqref{swo:dc:eq:explicitcond} is universal only at the final class-limit stage. For each proposed set bound, this same example survives beyond it.
\end{proof}

\merge\ \Cref{swo:dc:cor:selfsimilar} is the self-similarity of source~18's
\cref{swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block} (Part~IX) at every set stage, for
$P(\Omega)$ instead of $P(\omega)$, and the remark after source~20's
\cref{swo:lm:con:termination} that repeated quotient types do not stop a
history; source~33's \cref{swo:dh:n5.3} gives the case $\Gamma=\omega$.

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 479-480
This is a particularly important warning for a formalization: equality of quotient order types is not equality of equivalence relations, and it is not a reason to stop an iteration. The bonding maps contain indispensable information.

% ---- source 33, its Section 5
\subsection{Source 33: polynomial condensation and finite digits}\label{swo:dh:sec:condensation}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 599-645

\subsubsection{Ordinal-coefficient polynomials}
For a class well-order $\Gamma$, let
\[
 P(\Gamma)=\Omega^{[\Gamma]}
\]
be the finite-support order from \cref{swo:dh:subsec:power}. Its elements may be
written formally as
\[\tag{S33.5.1}\label{swo:dh:eq:polynomial}
  p=\Omega^{\gamma_0}a_0+\Omega^{\gamma_1}a_1+\cdots+\Omega^{\gamma_{m-1}}a_{m-1},
 \quad \gamma_0>_\Gamma\cdots>_\Gamma\gamma_{m-1},\quad
 0<a_i\in\Ord.
\]
This is a notation for a finite list of exponent--coefficient pairs. It does
not presuppose that a point $\gamma_i$ of $\Gamma$ is a set ordinal. Repeated
terms are combined only according to the chosen coding convention; in the
canonical presentation each exponent occurs once.

Write $\Gamma^+=\Gamma+1$ and denote its new greatest point by $\infty$.
For $b\in\Gamma^+$, define
\[\tag{S33.5.2}\label{swo:dh:eq:Eb}
 p\ E_b\ q
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p(\gamma)=q(\gamma)\text{ for every }\gamma\in\Gamma\text{ with }\gamma\geq b.
\]
At $b=\infty$ the condition is empty. At the least stage it is equality.
The family $E_b$ is a single elementary class relation in $b,p,q$.

\begin{definition}[Exact condensation tower]\label{swo:dh:def:tower}
Let $W$ be a nonempty class well-order. An \emph{exact condensation tower}
indexed by $\Gamma^+$ is a uniform family of convex equivalence relations
$F_b$ on $W$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),itemsep=1pt]
\item $F_b$ is equality at the least stage;
\item at a successor stage $a^+$, two points are $F_{a^+}$-equivalent exactly
      when the interval between their $F_a$-classes in $W/F_a$ is a set;
\item at a nonzero limit stage $b$, $F_b=\bigcup_{a<b}F_a$.
\end{enumerate}
Quotients are always represented by the minima of their classes. The tower
is \emph{exhausting} if $F_\infty$ is universal.
\end{definition}

For any $a\in\Gamma$, its immediate successor exists in $\Gamma^+$: either
there is a next point of $\Gamma$, or the next point is $\infty$. A nonzero
limit means a point with no immediate predecessor. These descriptions require
no external ordinal numbering of the stages.

\begin{remark}[\merge; towers of equivalence relations are nested histories]\label{swo:xvi:rem:towers}
Let $W=(X,<_W)$ be nonempty with least point $m$, and let $(F_b)_{b\in\Gamma^+}$
be an exact condensation tower in the sense of \cref{swo:dh:def:tower}.
Source~32's hierarchies (\cref{swo:dc:thm:termination}) are the same objects:
its operator \eqref{swo:dc:eq:operator} is clause~(ii). Put
\[
 H_b=\{x\in X:x=\min_W[x]_{F_b}\},
\]
the class of least points of the $F_b$-classes, elementary in the tower. Then
$H$ is a canonical history of $W$ on $\Gamma+1$ (\cref{swo:bo:hist:definition}),
its floors are $p_b(x)=\min_W[x]_{F_b}$, and the tower is exhausting exactly
when $H$ terminates. Conversely every canonical history $H$ arises in this way
from exactly one exact tower, namely $x\mathrel{F_b}y\Leftrightarrow
p_b(x)=p_b(y)$, which is source~35's equivalence $E_b$ after
\cref{swo:fc:lem:finite-floor-changes}.

\emph{Proof.} Each $F_b$-class is convex, so its least point $r$ is the
greatest point of $H_b$ below any of its members $x$: a point $z$ of $H_b$
with $r<_Wz\le_Wx$ would lie in the class of $x$ by convexity and so would not
be a least point. Hence $p_b(x)=\min_W[x]_{F_b}$. At the least stage $F$ is
equality and $H=X$. At a successor $a^+$, clause~(ii) says that $x$ and $y$
are $F_{a^+}$-equivalent exactly when the $F_a$-classes between theirs form a
set; these classes are represented by their least points, which are exactly
the points of $H_a$ between $p_a(x)$ and $p_a(y)$, so the condition is
$p_a(x)\sim_{H_a}p_a(y)$ for the relation $\sim_A$ that defines $D_W$
before \cref{swo:bo:hist:definition}. Every $F_{a^+}$-class is therefore the union of the $F_a$-classes whose
least points form one $\sim_{H_a}$-block, and its least point is the least
point of that block: $H_{a^+}=D_W(H_a)$. At a nonzero limit $\lambda$,
$F_\lambda=\bigcup_{a<\lambda}F_a$, so $x$ is least in its $F_\lambda$-class
exactly when no $y<_Wx$ is $F_a$-equivalent to $x$ for some $a<\lambda$,
that is, exactly when $x\in H_a$ for every $a<\lambda$:
$H_\lambda=\bigcap_{a<\lambda}H_a$. $F_\infty$ is universal exactly when
its one class has least point $m$ and no other, that is $H_\infty=\{m\}$.
Conversely, for a history $H$ the relations $p_b(x)=p_b(y)$ are convex by the
monotonicity of floors, satisfy~(i) and~(ii) by the computation just made, and
satisfy~(iii) by the stabilization of floors at limits
(\cref{swo:bo:hist:floors}; source~29's \cref{swo:bw:ch:quotient-limits}).
The two passages are inverse because $p_b(x)=\min_W[x]_{F_b}$. \qed

Consequently source~33's \cref{swo:dh:prop:exhaust} and source~32's
\cref{swo:dc:thm:termination} are source~20's \cref{swo:lm:con:termination},
and source~33's digit map is a normal-form map (\cref{swo:xvi:rem:digits}).
\end{remark}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Theorem~5.2, ``Exact polynomial condensation'']\label{swo:dh:thm:polycond}
\emph{The family \eqref{swo:dh:eq:Eb} is an exhausting exact condensation
tower for $P(\Gamma)$. For every stage $b$,
\[\tag{S33.5.3}\label{swo:dh:eq:quotients}
 P(\Gamma)/E_b\cong P(\Gamma_{\geq b}),
\]
with the quotient represented by truncating all exponents
below $b$. No stage $b<\infty$ is universal. All these assertions hold in
$\GBC$.} This is source~32's \cref{swo:dc:thm:sharp} and source~23's
\cref{swo:tm:thm:polyhierarchy}, whose clause~(ii) is the same quotient
formula; source~33's proof is the same truncation argument.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 679-687

\begin{example}[Stationary quotient types, nonstationary identifications]\label{swo:dh:n5.3}
For $\Gamma=\omega$, every finite-stage quotient
$P(\omega)/E_n$ is isomorphic to $P(\omega)$, since the tail $[n,\omega)$
has type $\omega$. Nevertheless $E_n$ is nonuniversal for every finite $n$
and $E_\omega$ is universal. Replacing a coherent tower by a list of quotient
\emph{types} therefore loses essential information.
\end{example}

\merge\ \Cref{swo:dh:n5.3} is the case $\Gamma=\omega$ of source~32's
\cref{swo:dc:cor:selfsimilar} and source~18's \cref{swo:sh:prop:selfsimilar-block}.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 688-772
The general phenomenon of prescribed long condensation is related to the
repository's existing work. The contribution of \cref{swo:dh:thm:polycond} here is
the explicit arithmetic presentation, uniform formula, and exact quotient
calculation used in the next theorem; priority for the broad realization
principle is not claimed.

\subsubsection{A finite-digit theorem for arbitrary supplied towers}
For an exhausting tower $(F_b)$ on $W$ and $a\in\Gamma$, the $F_a$-classes
inside the $F_{a^+}$-class of $x$ form one set-interval block of $W/F_a$.
That block is set-like by \cref{swo:dh:lem:blocks}. Consequently the position of the
$F_a$-class of $x$ within it is a set ordinal. Denote this ordinal by
\[\tag{S33.5.4}\label{swo:dh:eq:digit}
 r_a(x)=\otp\{C:\ C\text{ is an }F_a\text{-class in }[x]_{F_{a^+}},
                                  \ C<[x]_{F_a}\}.
\]
In \eqref{swo:dh:eq:digit}, the notation $C$ is shorthand for its least
representative, so the displayed collection is genuinely a set of sets.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-digit embedding]\label{swo:dh:thm:digits}
Suppose $W$ is nonempty and has a supplied uniform exhausting exact
condensation tower $(F_b)_{b\in\Gamma^+}$. Then
\[
       \supp_W(x)=\{a\in\Gamma:r_a(x)\ne0\}
\]
is finite for every $x\in W$, and the map
\[\tag{S33.5.5}\label{swo:dh:eq:digitmap}
          \Phi(x)=\{(a,r_a(x)):r_a(x)\ne0\}
          \quad\text{is an order embedding }W\longrightarrow P(\Gamma).
\]
The theorem is provable in $\GBC$ from the supplied tower; it does not assert
that $\GBC$ constructs every such tower.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: every digit is an ordinal.}
The set-likeness argument preceding the theorem proves that each predecessor
collection in \eqref{swo:dh:eq:digit} is a set well-order. Its ordinary ordinal
collapse is unique, so all digits are specified by one elementary formula
with the tower as a parameter.

\emph{Step 2: nonzero digits occur at only finitely many stages.}
Fix $x$. Start with $\sigma=\infty$ and with $z$ the least point of
$[x]_{F_\sigma}=W$. More generally maintain that $z$ is the least point of
$[x]_{F_\sigma}$. If $x=z$, every digit at a stage below $\sigma$ is zero:
$x$ occupies the first $F_a$-class in its $F_{a^+}$-class for each such $a$.

Otherwise, let $\tau\leq\sigma$ be the least stage at which $x$ and $z$
are equivalent. It is not the first stage, since $x\ne z$. It is not a
limit, since the limit rule would give equivalence at an earlier stage.
Therefore $\tau=a^+$ for some $a\in\Gamma$.
At stage $a$, the two points lie in different $F_a$-classes within one
$F_{a^+}$-class. Since $z<x$, we have $r_a(x)>0$.

For $a<b<\sigma$, the points $z,x$ are already $F_b$-equivalent, and $z$
is still least in the larger $F_{b^+}$-class containing them. Hence
$r_b(x)=0$. Replace $\sigma$ by $a$ and $z$ by the least point of
$[x]_{F_a}$. Repeat the argument inside that class.

If the process did not terminate, the successive selected exponents would
form a strictly descending $\omega$-sequence in $\Gamma$. The next selected
exponent and the new minimum are uniquely specified by elementary formulas.
As in \cref{swo:dh:lem:wftest}, ordinary set recursion and class replacement would
collect this into a forbidden set sequence. The process therefore
terminates after finitely many steps. The selected exponents are precisely
all stages with nonzero digit. Thus \eqref{swo:dh:eq:digitmap} is a finite set code.

\emph{Step 3: comparison is preserved.}
Let $x<y$ and take the least stage at which $x,y$ become equivalent. Again
it has the form $a^+$. At all stages $b>a$ their digits agree, because their
$F_b$-classes are the same. At $a$, their distinct $F_a$-classes lie in one
set-like block, and the class of $x$ precedes the class of $y$. Therefore
\[
                         r_a(x)<r_a(y).
\]
The greatest differing digit is exactly $a$, which is precisely the rule
for $\Phi(x)<\Phi(y)$ in $P(\Gamma)$. In particular, the map is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the theorem does not claim]\label{swo:dh:n5.5}
The conclusion is an order embedding. No claim is made here that this
specific digit map always has initial image. Converting arbitrary suborders
to initial segments is a separate comparison issue. Under a theory with
class well-order comparability, an initial embedding of $W$ into $P(\Gamma)$
can be obtained, but that assertion is not used in the proof above.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[\merge; the digit map always has initial image]\label{swo:xvi:rem:digits}
\Cref{swo:dh:n5.5} makes no claim that $\Phi$ has initial image, and
source~33's research question \cref{swo:dh:n12.7} asks for which supplied towers
it is initial. It always is; the remark and the first part of the question are
stale, and stay on record with this proof. Let $(F_b)_{b\in\Gamma^+}$ be a
supplied uniform exhausting exact tower on $W$ and let $H$ be the terminating
history of \cref{swo:xvi:rem:towers}, with floors $p_b(x)=\min_W[x]_{F_b}$.
Fix $a\in\Gamma$ and $x\in W$. The $F_a$-classes $C$ contained in
$[x]_{F_{a^+}}$ with $C<[x]_{F_a}$ are represented by their least points; these
lie in $H_a$, are at least $\min_W[x]_{F_{a^+}}=p_{a^+}(x)$ and are below
$\min_W[x]_{F_a}=p_a(x)$; conversely, a point $z\in H_a$ with
$p_{a^+}(x)\le_Wz<_Wp_a(x)$ lies in $[x]_{F_{a^+}}$ by convexity and is the
least point of an $F_a$-class below that of $x$. Hence
\[
 r_a(x)=\otp\bigl(\{z\in H_a:p_{a^+}(x)\le_Wz<_Wp_a(x)\},<_W\bigr)=c_a(x),
\]
the digit of source~34's normal form (\cref{swo:bo:hist:normalform}; source~29's
\eqref{swo:bw:ch:digits}), and $\Phi=\operatorname{NF}_H$. By
\cref{swo:bo:hist:normalform} (over $\GB$; source~35's
\cref{swo:fc:thm:history-normal-form}; source~29's
\cref{swo:bw:ch:normal-form-theorem} over $\GBC$), $\Phi$ is an isomorphism of
$W$ onto an initial segment of $P(\Gamma)$. So $\Phi$ is initial for every
supplied tower, without any comparison principle; initiality is the capped
reconstruction in the proof of \cref{swo:bo:hist:normalform}, which
\cref{swo:dh:thm:digits}'s proof does not attempt. The second part of the
question, a canonical compression map with a weaker axiom bound, is answered
by the same identification: $\Phi$ needs only $\GB$ and the supplied tower.
\end{remark}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 773-811
\subsubsection{Recursion gives a converse}
The principle $\ETR_\Lambda$ says that every elementary class recursion
along the specified class well-order $\Lambda$ has a solution. It is more
than a notational license to write a recursively defined family.

\begin{proposition}[Conditional converse]\label{swo:dh:prop:converse}
Assume $\GBC+\ETR_{\Gamma^+}$. If a class well-order $W$ embeds into
$P(\Gamma)$, then its exact condensation tower indexed by $\Gamma^+$ exists
and is exhausting. Consequently, in this theory,
\[
  W\emb P(\Gamma)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  W\text{ has an exhausting exact }\Gamma^+\text{-tower}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The successor operation in \cref{swo:dh:def:tower}, represented using block minima,
is elementary in the previous equivalence relation. The limit operation
uses an existential set quantifier over earlier stage labels. Thus the
stated recursion principle produces the exact tower $(F_b)$ of $W$.
Transport $W$ to the image of its embedding in $P(\Gamma)$.

We prove by class well-order induction that, for points of $W$,
\[
                         E_b\subseteq F_b.
\]
The first stage is immediate. At a successor, two points in a common
$E_{a^+}$-class meet only a set of ambient $E_a$-classes between them.
Within the interval of $W$, an occupied $E_a$-class lies inside a single
$F_a$-class by induction. Select the least point of its intersection with
that interval, then the least representative of the resulting $F_a$-class.
Class replacement on the set of ambient classes shows that the intervening
$F_a$-classes form a set. Hence the two points are $F_{a^+}$-equivalent.

At a limit the inclusion follows from the union rules. Since $E_\infty$
is universal, so is $F_\infty$. The reverse implication is
\cref{swo:dh:thm:digits}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[\merge; under $\ETR_{\Gamma+1}$ an embedding into $P(\Gamma)$ becomes initial]\label{swo:xvi:rem:converse}
Combine \cref{swo:dh:prop:converse} with \cref{swo:xvi:rem:digits}: in
$\GBC+\ETR_{\Gamma^+}$, if a class well-order $W$ embeds into $P(\Gamma)$ by
an arbitrary order embedding, then its exact tower on $\Gamma^+$ exists and is
exhausting, so $W$ is isomorphic to an initial segment of $P(\Gamma)$ by its
normal-form map. Thus in that theory the displayed equivalence of
\cref{swo:dh:prop:converse} reads $W\emb P(\Gamma)\Leftrightarrow W\iemb
P(\Gamma)$, and by \cref{swo:bo:hist:schedule} both say that $W$ has a
terminating history on $\Gamma+1$. Source~33 states only the embedding form;
the upgrade is this write's, by the two cited proofs.
\end{remark}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Proposition~5.7, ``Exhaustion under a sufficient recursion principle'']\label{swo:dh:prop:exhaust}
\emph{If $W$ is a nonempty class well-order and $\ETR_{W+1}$ holds, then the
exact condensation tower of $W$ indexed by $W+1$ is exhausting.} This is
source~20's \cref{swo:lm:con:termination} with its existence clause, and
source~32's \cref{swo:dc:thm:termination}, through \cref{swo:xvi:rem:towers}.
Source~33's proof inducts on stages $x\in W+1$, showing that all points
strictly below $x$ lie in one $F_x$-class: at $x=y^+$ the point $y$ lies in
that class or the next, and one condensation step merges the prefix through
$y$; at a limit any two points of the prefix lie below an earlier stage. It
calls this ``a sufficient axiom bound, not an optimality theorem''. The
existence of exhausting towers for all class well-orders is $\CTH$ by
\cref{swo:xvi:rem:towers}, hence equivalent to $\CWO$
(\cref{swo:bo:hist:equivalence}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 826-829

This is a sufficient axiom bound, not an optimality theorem. The explicit
polynomial towers of \cref{swo:dh:thm:polycond} require no such axiom because their
entire family is given by the single truncation formula \eqref{swo:dh:eq:Eb}.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 951-964
\section{Hereditary normal forms and a first fixed point}
\label{swo:bo:her:section}

Finite-support exponentiation admits an explicit fixed-point construction that
goes beyond every finite tower with base $\Ord$.  This section works in
$\GB$.  We write $\Omega$ as a typographical symbol for the class order
$\Ord$, not as a new set ordinal.  The construction uses the familiar
hereditary normal-form pattern from ordinal analysis: for example, hereditary
base-$\omega_1$ normal forms below $\varepsilon_{\omega_1+1}$ already appear in
Weiermann's discussion \cite{xviWeiermann}.  Finite supports and preservation
of initial segments also belong to the established framework of normal
dilators \cite{xviFreund}.  Our purpose is to give the proper-class
construction, its foundational justification, and its universal property
directly.  We do not claim to have invented hereditary ordinal notation.

\merge\ The hereditary system is new to this report; the four sources construct
it independently. Source~35's $\mathcal E$ (\cref{swo:fc:def:hereditary-terms})
is this $\Eps$, with the same terms and comparison, proved well-ordered over
$\GBC$ (\cref{swo:fc:thm:hereditary-fixedpoint}); source~32's $\mathcal H(A)$,
printed $\Eps(A)$, is the general base of \cref{swo:bo:her:generalbase}, over
$\GBC$ (\cref{swo:dc:thm:hereditary}); source~33 reaches the same fixed point
as the direct limit $\mathbb T$ of the finite towers (\cref{swo:dh:thm:fixedpoint}).
In this section $\Eps^{\le n}$ is source~34's $E_n$, the terms of height at
most~$n$, renamed because $E_i$ is a floor equivalence in Section~XVI.5.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 965-1309

\subsection{A class of finite codes}

\begin{definition}[Hereditary base-$\Omega$ terms]
\label{swo:bo:her:def}
The raw expressions are finite rooted ordered trees with ordinal
coefficients.  We write the empty tree as $0$, and a nonempty tree as
\[
 t=\bigl[(t_0,a_0),\ldots,(t_{k-1},a_{k-1})\bigr],
 \qquad k>0,
\]
where the $t_i$ are its exponent subtrees and the $a_i$ are nonzero set
ordinals.  Compare two raw expressions recursively by lexicographically
comparing their lists of exponent--coefficient pairs: compare exponents
first and coefficients second; after an identical prefix, the shorter list
is smaller.  A term is \emph{valid} when all its exponent subterms are valid
and
\[
 t_0>t_1>\cdots>t_{k-1}.
\]
Let $\Eps$ be the class of valid terms, with this order.  Its intended
display notation is
\[
 t=\Omega^{t_0}a_0+\cdots+\Omega^{t_{k-1}}a_{k-1}.
\]
\end{definition}

Every expression is a set.  The recursive comparison terminates because
each recursive call concerns smaller finite trees.  Validity, comparison,
and the finite set of subterms therefore have uniform first-order
definitions, using finite computation witnesses if desired.  In particular,
the definition does not invoke a recursion of length $\omega$ whose values
are classes.  This distinction matters: arbitrary class-valued recursion
can require additional axioms even when its indexing order is small.

For an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$, let $\Eps[\kappa]$ consist of
the terms all of whose coefficients are below $\kappa$.  It is a set of
finite codes.  Define an ordinal interpretation on this set by
\[\tag{S34.5}
\label{swo:bo:her:valuation}
 v_\kappa(0)=0,
 \qquad
 v_\kappa(t)=
 \kappa^{v_\kappa(t_0)}a_0+\cdots+
 \kappa^{v_\kappa(t_{k-1})}a_{k-1}.
\]
This is ordinary evaluation of a finite tree in set ordinal arithmetic.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-coefficient comparison]
\label{swo:bo:her:comparison}
For $s,t\in\Eps[\kappa]$,
\[
 s<t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 v_\kappa(s)<v_\kappa(t).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induct on the total size of the two trees.  By the induction hypothesis,
the interpreted exponent lists remain strictly decreasing, and comparison
of their exponents agrees with comparison of the subterms.  All
coefficients lie below $\kappa$.  The usual comparison theorem for
finite-support base-$\kappa$ representations therefore compares the two
ordinal values at exactly the first exponent--coefficient difference of
their lists.  If one list ends after an identical prefix, its remaining
value is zero and is smaller than the nonempty remaining sum of the other
list.  These are exactly the defining cases of term comparison.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Well-foundedness in $\GB$]
\label{swo:bo:her:wellorder}
The definable relation on $\Eps$ is a class well-order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strict linearity follows from the comparison lemma: the finitely many
coefficients in any two or three terms have a common cardinal bound, so
irreflexivity, trichotomy, and transitivity transfer from ordinal
comparison. Now let $S$ be any nonempty set of terms. The coefficients
appearing anywhere in $S$ form a set of ordinals. Choose an infinite
initial cardinal $\kappa$ above all of them; arbitrarily large
well-orderable initial cardinals exist in ZF. The comparison lemma
embeds $S$ into the ordinals, so $S$ has a least term. Every nonempty
set subset therefore has a minimum. \Cref{swo:bo:found:settest} implies
that every nonempty admitted subclass has a minimum as well. This last
step requires neither set Choice nor Global Choice.
\end{proof}

This proof uses a different ordinal interpretation for different bounded
collections of terms.  It never attempts an ordinal-valued order embedding
of the whole proper class $\Eps$.

\begin{example}[Reading and comparing terms]
\label{swo:bo:her:example}
Consider
\[
 s=\Omega^{\Omega+3}7+\Omega^{\Omega+1}\omega^2+19,
 \qquad
 t=\Omega^{\Omega+3}7+\Omega^{\Omega+1}(\omega^2+1).
\]
These are finite codes with ordinary ordinal coefficient labels.  The
leading exponent and coefficient agree.  At the next common exponent,
$\omega^2<\omega^2+1$, so $s<t$; the final coefficient $19$ cannot
change the outcome.  Under any sufficiently large cardinal interpretation,
the same comparison is an ordinary ordinal calculation.  No object called
the ordinal $\Omega+3$ is required inside the original universe: its
occurrence is itself an exponent subtree.
\end{example}

The class and its order are parameter-free definable, although individual
terms carry arbitrary ordinal data.  A fixed finite syntax with constants
from a set supplies only a set of terms.  Allowing all set ordinal
coefficients is what makes this notation system a proper class.  This is
compatible with ordinary definability: every particular term is constructed
from a finite tuple of ordinal parameters and a finite tree shape.  It does
not entail a truth predicate deciding which ordinals are definable without
parameters.  Thus the presentation keeps separate the definability of an
entire class order, the parameters describing one of its elements, and the
availability of a short written name for a coefficient.

\subsection{Height, initial segments, and finite towers}

Define the syntactic height by
\[
 h(0)=0,
 \qquad h(t)=1+\max_{i<k}h(t_i)\quad(t\ne0),
\]
and put $\Eps^{\le n}=\{t\in\Eps:h(t)\le n\}$.  Thus $\Eps^{\le 0}=\{0\}$,
while $\Eps^{\le 1}$ consists of zero and the constants $\Omega^0a$, and is
canonically isomorphic to $\Ord$.  Write $1$ for the constant with
coefficient $1$, and define the finite sequence of constructions
\[\tag{S34.6}
\label{swo:bo:her:tau}
 \tau_0=1,
 \qquad \tau_{n+1}=\Omega^{\tau_n}.
\]
Here the latter expression is the singleton root list
$[(\tau_n,1)]$.  Each $\tau_n$ is a finite term; the resulting
$\omega$-sequence is set-coded.

\begin{theorem}[Exact height cuts]
\label{swo:bo:her:height}
For every $n<\omega$,
\[
 \Eps^{\le n}=\Eps_{<\tau_n},
 \qquad
 \Eps^{\le n+1}\cong\fsp{\Ord}{\Eps^{\le n}}.
\]
Consequently the height stages are proper initial segments with order
types
\[
 1,\quad\Omega,\quad\fsp{\Omega}{\Omega},\quad
 \fsp{\Omega}{\fsp{\Omega}{\Omega}},\quad\ldots,
\]
and $\Eps=\bigcup_{n<\omega}\Eps^{\le n}$ has cofinality $\omega$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Only zero lies below the least positive term $1$, proving the initial-cut
claim for $n=0$.  Removing the root identifies $\Eps^{\le n+1}$ with finite
graphs whose exponent support lies in $\Eps^{\le n}$, with arbitrary nonzero
ordinal coefficients.  This proves the displayed isomorphism.
Suppose $\Eps^{\le n}=\Eps_{<\tau_n}$.  A term lies below the monomial
$\Omega^{\tau_n}$ exactly when all its exponent support lies below
$\tau_n$: a greater exponent makes it larger, while an equal greatest
exponent requires coefficient at least $1$ and also makes it at least
the monomial.  Thus $\Eps^{\le n+1}=\Eps_{<\tau_{n+1}}$.

The term $\tau_n$ has height $n+1$, so it belongs to $\Eps^{\le n+1}$ and
not to $\Eps^{\le n}$.  The cuts are therefore proper and the sequence
$(\tau_n)$ is strictly increasing.  Every finite tree has finite height,
so the cuts exhaust $\Eps$ and this sequence is cofinal.  There is no
largest term; a finite subset cannot be cofinal.  Hence the least possible
cofinality is exactly $\omega$.
\end{proof}

A proper class well-order can have set cofinality because it need not be
setlike.  Here the predecessor class of the term $\Omega$ already
contains a copy of every set ordinal.  The theorem also shows that every
exponent subterm of a nonzero term is smaller than the whole term: its
height lies below that of the term, and the height levels are initial.

\subsection{The fixed-point isomorphism and leastness}

\begin{theorem}[A definable fixed point]
\label{swo:bo:her:fixedpoint}
There is a canonical definable class isomorphism
\[
 \fsp{\Ord}{\Eps}\cong\Eps.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Sort the finite support of a graph in decreasing $\Eps$-order and make
its exponent--coefficient pairs the children of a new root.  This produces
a valid term.  Conversely, remove the root of a term to recover the finite
graph.  The constructions are inverse, and both orders compare the greatest
exponent at which a coefficient differs.
\end{proof}

Leastness has a precise formulation which requires neither a collection of
all class order types nor a general comparability theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Least initial pre-fixed point]
\label{swo:bo:her:universal}
Let $X$ be a class well-order, and suppose that
\[
 j:\fsp{\Ord}{X}\longrightarrow X
\]
is an initial order embedding.  There is a unique finite-term evaluation
$e:\Eps\longrightarrow X$ satisfying
\[\tag{S34.7}
\label{swo:bo:her:evaluation}
 e(0)=j(\varnothing),
 \qquad
 e\bigl([(t_i,a_i)]_{i<k}\bigr)
   =j\bigl(\{(e(t_i),a_i):i<k\}\bigr).
\]
This map is an initial order embedding.  In particular, $\Eps$ embeds
initially into every class well-order equipped with an isomorphism
$\fsp{\Ord}{X}\cong X$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Define $e(t)=x$ by the existence of a finite assignment of elements of
$X$ to all subterms of $t$, satisfying \eqref{swo:bo:her:evaluation} at every
node and assigning $x$ to the root.  Finite-tree induction proves existence
and uniqueness, simultaneously proving preservation and reflection of
comparison.  Indeed, already evaluated exponent subterms have the same
strict order as before, so the graph at the next root is well-defined;
finite-support comparison followed by the order embedding $j$ gives
exactly the desired comparison.  Elementary comprehension supplies the
class graph of $e$.  All witnesses in this definition are finite sets.

It remains to prove initiality.  Put $I_n=e(\Eps^{\le n})$.  Since $j$ is initial
and the empty graph is least, $I_0=\{j(\varnothing)\}$ is an initial
segment of $X$.  If $I_n$ is initial in $X$, the finite graphs supported
on $I_n$ form an initial segment of $\fsp{\Ord}{X}$.  The evaluation
equation identifies their image under $j$ with $I_{n+1}$.  Hence
$I_{n+1}$ is initial.  Their increasing union $e(\Eps)$ is therefore
initial as well.  Uniqueness follows from finite-tree induction on the
evaluation equation.
\end{proof}

The argument defines one evaluation class by finite witnesses and then
studies its restrictions.  It does not recursively assemble an
$\omega$-sequence of classes.  In this concrete sense, $\Eps$ is the
least fixed point of the base-$\Ord$ power constructor, already in
$\GB$.  The assertion neither supplies $\ETR$ along $\Eps$ nor
makes $\Eps$ a largest definable class well-order.

\begin{corollary}[An explicit long condensation history]
\label{swo:bo:her:history}
The order $\Eps$ has an elementary canonical history on $\Eps+1$.
Its first singleton slice occurs at the appended final stage.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Transport the explicit history of $P(\Eps)$ through the root
isomorphism. At a stage $t\in\Eps$, the retained terms are precisely
those whose root exponents are all at least $t$, together with zero.
This is the polynomial history used in \Cref{swo:bo:hist:section}.
The monomial $\Omega^t$ is a nonzero retained point, so that slice
is not a singleton. The final slice is $\{0\}$.
\end{proof}

The universal property also makes the meaning of ``least'' independent of
our chosen tree coding.  A different presentation with the same fixed-point
property and the same initial universal property receives an initial
embedding from $\Eps$ and supplies one in the reverse direction.  Their
composites are initial self-embeddings of class well-orders and hence are
identities: a least point of disagreement would contradict initiality.
The presentations are therefore uniquely isomorphic.  This is a statement
about specified class maps, not a quotient whose members would themselves
be proper classes.

There is also a precise distinction between reaching the fixed-point order
and naming it as one of its elements.  Every term lies below some
$\tau_n$, while the sequence of these terms is cofinal in $\Eps$.
Consequently no term denotes an initial segment of type $\Eps$ itself.
The fixed-point isomorphism concerns the whole class presentation.  To
continue beyond it one may use a new class-order construction, such as
$\Eps+1$ or the general-base construction below; the finite terms already
defined do not silently acquire an additional terminal element.

\subsection{Exact calibration in larger universes}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded-coefficient order type]
\label{swo:bo:her:calibration}
For an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$, the map $v_\kappa$ is an
isomorphism of $\Eps[\kappa]$ onto the least fixed point of ordinary
ordinal exponentiation $\xi\mapsto\kappa^\xi$.  This is the least
epsilon number strictly greater than $\kappa$.  In particular,
\[
 \otp\bigl(\Eps[\omega]\bigr)=\varepsilon_0,
 \qquad
 \otp\bigl(\Eps[\kappa]\bigr)=\varepsilon_{\kappa+1}
 \quad\text{if $\kappa$ is uncountable}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The coefficient-bounded height stages have ordinal types $c_0=1$ and
$c_{n+1}=\kappa^{c_n}$, by root removal and ordinary finite-support
exponentiation.  They exhaust $\Eps[\kappa]$, so its ordinal type is
$\lambda=\sup_{n<\omega}c_n$.  Continuity gives
$\kappa^\lambda=\lambda$.  Any fixed point bounds all $c_n$, by
induction, and therefore bounds $\lambda$.

If $\kappa^\xi=\xi$, then
$\xi\le\omega^\xi\le\kappa^\xi=\xi$, so $\xi$ is an epsilon
number.  Also $\xi>\kappa$: for $2\le\xi\le\kappa$ one has
$\kappa^\xi\ge\kappa^2>\kappa$, while $\xi=0,1$ are not fixed.
Conversely, let $\varepsilon>\kappa$ be an epsilon number.  Choose
$0<\delta<\varepsilon$ with $\kappa\le\omega^\delta$.  Since
$\delta\varepsilon=\varepsilon$,
\[
 \varepsilon=\omega^\varepsilon
 \le\kappa^\varepsilon
 \le(\omega^\delta)^\varepsilon
 =\omega^{\delta\varepsilon}=\varepsilon.
\]
For completeness, $\delta\varepsilon=\varepsilon$ follows by bounding
$\delta$ by $\omega^\eta$ for some $\eta<\varepsilon$ and using
$\eta+\varepsilon=\varepsilon$.

Finally, every uncountable initial cardinal satisfies
$\varepsilon_\kappa=\kappa$.  Indeed, for $\alpha<\kappa$ the
usual construction of the epsilon enumeration gives
$|\varepsilon_\alpha|\le\max(\aleph_0,|\alpha|)<\kappa$;
continuity, together with $\varepsilon_\alpha\ge\alpha$, now gives
$\sup_{\alpha<\kappa}\varepsilon_\alpha=\kappa$.  The next
epsilon number is consequently $\varepsilon_{\kappa+1}$.
\end{proof}

The bounded-coefficient sets must not be confused with the height cuts.
For example, the constant term $\kappa$ is excluded from
$\Eps[\kappa]$, whereas the larger term $\Omega$ is included.
Thus $\Eps[\kappa]$ is not initial in the full $\Eps$.
In a full class model $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ with
$\kappa$ inaccessible, all the finite codes in question belong to
$V_\kappa$.  Its internally defined $\Eps$ therefore has external
order type exactly $\varepsilon_{\kappa+1}$.  This supplies an exact
external measurement without turning that ordinal into a set of the
smaller universe.

\merge\ Source~34's general-base system $H(A)$ is printed $\Eps(A)$; $\Eps=\Eps(\Omega)$
up to the identification of $\Omega$ with its nonzero coefficients.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 1310-1330
\begin{corollary}[Other class bases]
\label{swo:bo:her:generalbase}
For every class well-order $A$ with at least two elements, the analogous
hereditary finite normal forms $\Eps(A)$ form a class well-order in $\GB$.
They satisfy $\fsp{A}{\Eps(A)}\cong \Eps(A)$ and the same least initial
pre-fixed-point property.  Their height stages are the finite base-$A$
towers and are cofinal with order type $\omega$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use nonzero elements of $A$ as coefficients. In any nonempty set $S$
of terms, all coefficients, together with the least element of $A$,
form a set. Collapse their induced well-order to an ordinal, choose
an infinite initial cardinal above that ordinal, and interpret all
terms of $S$ at that cardinal with the collapsed coefficients. This
preserves comparison and supplies a least element of $S$. Finite
triples establish linearity, and \Cref{swo:bo:found:settest} gives
class well-foundedness in $\GB$. Root removal, the least nonzero
coefficient, and finite evaluation prove the remaining assertions
exactly as above.
\end{proof}

% ---- source 35, its Section 5
\subsection{Source 35: hereditary notation and fixed-point completion}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1266-1289
\label{swo:fc:sec:fixedpoints}

The polynomial operator admits a systematic extension beyond every fixed
finite tower of powers.  Its first fixed point has finite descriptions,
and its existence does not require elementary transfinite recursion.
The more delicate question is whether an \emph{arbitrary supplied}
class well-order can be placed inside such a fixed point.  We prove an
exact criterion for that extension, and thereby obtain another
characterization of the repository's condensation-history principle.

Class notation for epsilon-like orders above $\Ord$ is established
proof-theoretic practice.  Jeon's note explicitly recalls Rathjen's
class order $E_0=\varepsilon_{\Ord+1}$ and its role in induction
principles \cite[Proposition~1.5]{xviJeonNote}; the cited source is
\cite{xviRathjen}.  The finite hereditary construction below belongs
to that tradition.  We use our own notation $\Eps$ so that its
precise meaning is fixed by a class-order construction, without
presupposing a universe of generalized ordinal objects.  The local
extension criterion in \Cref{swo:fc:local-fixedpoint} is an additional
result developed here; its priority outside the sources examined has
not been independently established.

\subsubsection{Finite hereditary \texorpdfstring{$\Omega$}{Omega}-terms}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Definition~5.1, ``Normalized hereditary terms'']\label{swo:fc:def:hereditary-terms}
\emph{An $\Omega$-term is a finite tree: the empty list is the term $0$, and a
nonzero term is a list $t=((t_0,\alpha_0),\ldots,(t_{r-1},\alpha_{r-1}))$ with
$t_0>\cdots>t_{r-1}$ and $0<\alpha_i\in\Ord$, whose exponent entries are
themselves terms, displayed as $\Omega^{t_0}\alpha_0+\cdots+\Omega^{t_{r-1}}\alpha_{r-1}$.
Lists are compared lexicographically from the first pair, comparing exponents
first and coefficients second; a proper common-prefix extension is larger, and
exponent comparisons use the same rule recursively. $\Eps$ is the class of
normalized terms.} This is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:her:def}, with the same
order. Source~35 writes $\mathcal E$, printed $\Eps$
(\cref{swo:xvi:sub:notation96}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1309-1357

The definition concerns finite trees labelled by set ordinals.  It
does not place a proper class inside another class.  Recursive
comparisons involve smaller finite trees, so normalization and
comparison can be expressed by the existence of a finite set-coded
computation trace.  Consequently both predicates are elementary
definitions in $\GB$.  In a nonstandard model, ``finite'' has that
model's internal meaning, as throughout this article.

Write $c(0)=0$ and $c(\alpha)=((0,\alpha))$ for $\alpha>0$.
These are the constant terms.  To avoid confusing syntax with an
actual proper-class element, write
\[
       u=((c(1),1)),\qquad M(t)=((t,1)).
\]
Thus $u$ is the term displayed as $\Omega$, while $M(t)$ is displayed
as $\Omega^t$.  The symbol $\Omega$ in the display is a constructor
symbol; $u$ itself is an ordinary set code.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded specialization]
\label{swo:fc:lem:hereditary-specialization}
Let $S$ be any set of terms, closed under taking exponent subterms.
There is an additively indecomposable set ordinal $\Lambda>1$ such
that the evaluation
\[
 v_\Lambda(0)=0,\qquad
 v_\Lambda(t)=\sum_{i<r}\Lambda^{v_\Lambda(t_i)}\alpha_i
\]
is strictly order preserving on $S$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose $\Lambda$ strictly above every coefficient occurring in $S$;
a sufficiently large power of $\omega$ suffices.  The displayed
evaluation is ordinary set recursion on finite trees.  Simultaneous
induction on the sizes of two trees proves preservation of comparison.
For the induction step, exponent comparisons have already been
preserved.  If $\gamma<\delta$ and $a<\Lambda$, then
\[
 \Lambda^\gamma a<\Lambda^{\gamma+1}\leq\Lambda^\delta.
\]
For $\delta>0$, the ordinal $\Lambda^\delta$ is additively
indecomposable, so a finite tail of lower-exponent summands remains
below it.  At exponent zero there is no lower tail.  Therefore the
largest exponent of disagreement, followed by its coefficient,
decides both the syntactic and the evaluated comparison.  This is
exactly the comparison rule in \Cref{swo:fc:def:hereditary-terms}.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~5.3, ``The first explicit polynomial fixed point'']\label{swo:fc:thm:hereditary-fixedpoint}
\emph{In $\GBC$, $\Eps$ is a proper class well-order, and assembling a
polynomial into one new root gives an elementary class isomorphism
$\rho:P(\Eps)\to\Eps$.} This is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:her:wellorder}, which
needs only $\GB$, and \cref{swo:bo:her:fixedpoint}. Source~35's well-ordering
proof applies \cref{swo:fc:lem:hereditary-specialization} to the subterms of a
set-coded descending sequence, which global choice produces from a subclass
without least element (first minimizing set-theoretic rank, then using the
global choice function); source~34 applies its \cref{swo:bo:her:comparison} to
an arbitrary nonempty set of terms and concludes by \cref{swo:bo:found:settest}.
The root map is the same.
\end{note}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Proposition~5.4, ``Exact tower cuts and cofinality'']\label{swo:fc:prop:tower-cuts}
\emph{Put $b_0=u$ and $b_{n+1}=M(b_n)$. Then $\Eps_{<b_0}\cong\Ord$,
$\Eps_{<b_{n+1}}\cong P(\Eps_{<b_n})$ and $\Eps_{<b_n}\cong P^n(\Ord)$. The
sequence $(b_n)_{n<\omega}$ is strictly increasing and cofinal in $\Eps$. In
particular, $\Eps$ has cofinality $\omega$.} This is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:her:height} with the index shifted: $b_n=\tau_{n+1}$ and
$\Eps_{<b_n}=\Eps^{\le n+1}$; the proof is the same (the cut below $M(b)$
consists of the terms whose root exponents lie below $b$). Source~35 adds that
the sequence is obtained by set-valued recursion on $\omega$, so its range is a
set.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1424-1430

The apparent tension between a proper-class carrier and a countable
cofinal set is useful.  It is the \emph{set-like} proper well-order
$\Ord$ that has no set cofinal subset.  An order with proper-class
initial segments can have set cofinality.  Here each $b_n$ is a set
code whose predecessors form the indicated, generally proper, class.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~5.5, ``Leastness with an explicit witness'']\label{swo:fc:thm:least-hereditary-fixedpoint}
\emph{Suppose $F$ is a class well-order and $\varphi:P(F)\cong F$ is a supplied
class isomorphism. There is a unique class map $v:\Eps\to F$ with
$v(0)=\varphi(\varnothing)$ and $v(t)=\varphi(\{(v(t_i),\alpha_i):i<r\})$; it
is an isomorphism onto an initial segment of $F$.} This is the case of
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:her:universal} in which the supplied initial embedding
$j:\Ord^{[F]}\to F$ is an isomorphism; source~34's hypothesis, an initial
pre-fixed point, is weaker. The evaluation is the same finite-trace definition.
For initiality source~34 inducts on the height levels $I_n=e(\Eps^{\le n})$,
source~35 by structural induction on $t$; its proof is printed as a second
route.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1443-1507
\begin{proof}[Source~35's proof]
Evaluate each finite tree from its leaves upward.  This defines one
elementary class map by finite traces, with $\varphi$ as a parameter.
Simultaneous induction on two trees shows that distinct exponent
subterms have distinct images, so the displayed finite graph is a
polynomial, and that comparison is preserved.  Uniqueness follows
from the same finite recursion.

We prove initiality by structural induction on $t$.  There is nothing
below $v(0)$.  For nonzero $t$, let $s$ be its largest exponent
subterm, and take $y<_F v(t)$.  Every exponent $a$ in
$q=\varphi^{-1}(y)$ satisfies $a\leq_F v(s)$, since
$q<\varphi^{-1}(v(t))$ in polynomial order.  If $a<v(s)$, the
inductive assertion for $s$ supplies its preimage under $v$; equality
has preimage $s$.  Decode these finitely many exponents and retain
their ordinal coefficients.  They form a normalized term $t'$ with
$v(t')=y$.  Thus everything below an image point belongs to the image.
No comparison principle for arbitrary class well-orders was used.
\end{proof}

This theorem gives a precise sense in which $\Eps$ is the
first fixed point of $A\mapsto P(A)$.  The existence of the
isomorphism is part of the fixed-point assertion.  An external
equality of order types in an enclosing universe would not supply
the class parameter needed by the proof in an arbitrary class model.

The use of bounded specialization also has a precise limitation.
Bounding every coefficient by a set ordinal produces a set of finite
trees, but generally does not produce an initial subclass of the full
term order.  A new, larger constant coefficient still denotes a term
below $u$.  Specialization is therefore a device for ruling out a
particular set-coded descending sequence.  The actual initial
subclasses used to measure the tower are the exponent cuts in
\Cref{swo:fc:prop:tower-cuts}, not arbitrary coefficient cutoffs.

\paragraph{An enclosing-universe check.}
In the full model $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ at a strongly
inaccessible $\kappa$, the internal coefficients range externally
over the ordinals below $\kappa$.  Evaluate terms at the ordinary
ordinal base $\kappa$.  The evaluation identifies $\Eps$
with the least positive solution of $\kappa^\lambda=\lambda$.
Indeed, the successive tower cuts have types
$\kappa,\kappa^\kappa,\kappa^{\kappa^\kappa},\ldots$, and
ordinary base-$\kappa$ normal forms show that their union contains
every ordinal below the supremum of this tower.  The supremum is
the first fixed point by continuity and strict increase of ordinal
exponentiation.

This is also the least ordinary epsilon number strictly above
$\kappa$.  If $\lambda=\kappa^\lambda$, then
$\omega^\lambda\leq\lambda\leq\omega^\lambda$, so
$\lambda$ is an epsilon number; the fixed point is larger than
$\kappa$.  Conversely, the first epsilon number $\epsilon>\kappa$
satisfies
\[
 \kappa^\epsilon=(\omega^\kappa)^\epsilon
       =\omega^{\kappa\cdot\epsilon}=\omega^\epsilon=\epsilon.
\]
Here $\omega^\kappa=\kappa$ and
$\kappa\cdot\epsilon=\epsilon$.  Since an uncountable initial
ordinal $\kappa$ also satisfies $\varepsilon_\kappa=\kappa$,
this ambient type is $\varepsilon_{\kappa+1}$.  The calculation
explains the familiar epsilon notation while retaining the necessary
distinction: internally $\Eps$ is a proper class order,
whereas externally the displayed epsilon number is a set ordinal.

\merge\ The enclosing-universe check is a second proof of source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:her:calibration} for uncountable inaccessible $\kappa$, and
source~33 states the tower $t_{n+1}=\kappa^{t_n}$ in its Section~9.2
(Section~XVI.8).

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1508-1515

\subsubsection{Completion from an initial polynomial embedding}

The next construction permits an arbitrary seed order, provided its
initial embedding into its polynomial order is supplied.  This
hypothesis isolates exactly the potentially missing comparison
information.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Lemma~5.6, ``Finite-support preservation'']\label{swo:fc:lem:P-initial}
\emph{If $f:A\to B$ is an initial embedding of class well-orders, mapping each
exponent through $f$ gives an initial embedding $P(f):P(A)\to P(B)$. This
operation preserves identities and composition, and preserves properness of
initial embeddings.} This is source~35's own \cref{swo:fc:lem:power-initial}
for the base $\Omega$, with functoriality added, and source~34's rule after
\eqref{swo:bo:power:iterate}; the proof transports finite supports, and an
exponent $b$ omitted by $f$ gives the omitted monomial at $b$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1534-1768

\begin{theorem}[Explicit fixed-point completion]
\label{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion}
In $\GBC$, suppose that $j:A\to P(A)$ is an initial
embedding of class well-orders.  There is a class well-order
$C(A,j)$, an initial embedding $\iota:A\to C(A,j)$, and a class
isomorphism
\[
             \Phi: P(C(A,j))\longrightarrow C(A,j),
\]
all elementary in the supplied parameters.  If $j$ is proper,
$\iota$ is proper and $C(A,j)$ has a definable increasing cofinal
$\omega$-sequence.  Moreover, $C(A,j)$ initially embeds into every
polynomial fixed point into which $A$ initially embeds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For notation, write
\[
 A_n= P^n(A),\qquad j_n= P^n(j):A_n\longrightarrow A_{n+1}.
\]
These symbols do not assume an arbitrary class recursion.  A member
of $A_n$ is a finite nested polynomial code, with at most $n$
polynomial levels and leaves labelled in $A$.  Empty polynomials
can terminate a branch earlier.  Tags distinguish leaves from
polynomial nodes.  Membership and comparison are verified on a
finite tree.  The map $j_n$ replaces every bottom-level $A$-label
$a$ by the finite polynomial $j(a)$ and retains the outer nodes.
This too is checked by a finite trace.  Thus one elementary formula
defines all stages and all maps uniformly in $n$.

Each $A_n$ is a class well-order and each $j_n$ is initial.  Uniform
finite induction is legitimate here: in $\GBC$, well-foundedness
can be expressed as the absence of a set-coded descending
$\omega$-sequence, an elementary assertion about the uniformly
defined stages.  Alternatively, a proposed descending sequence at
one stage uses only a set of bottom labels and coefficients; their
set well-order types and ordinary finite polynomial constructions
give a direct contradiction.  Initiality follows from
\Cref{swo:fc:lem:P-initial}.

For $n\leq m$, let $j_{n,m}$ be the finite composite from $A_n$
to $A_m$, with $j_{n,n}$ the identity.  On tagged pairs $(n,a)$,
put
\[
 (n,a)\sim(m,b)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 j_{n,k}(a)=j_{m,k}(b),\qquad k=\max(n,m).
\]
Each equivalence class has a unique representative at its least
stage.  Use those representatives as the carrier of $C(A,j)$.
Concretely, all pairs at stage zero are retained; a pair $(n,a)$,
$n>0$, is retained exactly when $a$ is not in the range of
$j_{n-1}$.  This is a class of set codes, not a class whose members
are equivalence classes.  Order representatives by comparison of
their images in a common finite stage.  Injectivity and compatibility
of the connecting maps prove that equality and order are well defined.

Let $\iota_n:A_n\to C(A,j)$ send a point to its least-stage
representative.  The maps are initial embeddings.  Indeed, a point
below $\iota_n(a)$ can be compared with it in a common later
stage; initiality of $j_{n,k}$ supplies a unique preimage in $A_n$.
Every point belongs to some $\iota_n[A_n]$.  Given a nonempty
subclass of the colimit, choose one of its points and a stage
containing that point.  Its intersection with that stage has a least
element.  Initiality shows that no point outside the stage can be
smaller.  Thus the colimit is a class well-order.

To construct $\Phi$, take a polynomial $p$ on the colimit.  Its
finite support is contained in one $\iota_n[A_n]$: take the maximum
of the finitely many least-stage numbers of its exponents.  Decode
the support into $A_n$, retaining the coefficients, to obtain
$p_n\in P(A_n)=A_{n+1}$, and put
\[
                        \Phi(p)=\iota_{n+1}(p_n).
\]
For the empty support choose $n=0$.  The result is independent of
the chosen stage because
$j_{n+1,m+1}= P(j_{n,m})$.  Choosing a common stage for two
supports proves that $\Phi$ preserves order strictly.  It is onto:
a point represented at a positive stage already is a polynomial on
the preceding stage; a point at stage zero can first be moved to
stage one using $j$.  This proves the fixed-point assertion.

If $j$ is proper, so is every $j_n$.  Let $d_n$ be the least
point of $A_{n+1}$ omitted by $j_n$.  The points
$\iota_{n+1}(d_n)$ increase strictly, and the $n$th one lies above
the whole image of $A_n$.  They are therefore cofinal.  Their
definition is uniform and set valued, so Class Replacement supplies
the corresponding set sequence.

Finally suppose $h:A\to F$ is initial and
$\varphi: P(F)\cong F$.  Finite evaluation gives initial
maps
\[
 h_0=h,\qquad h_{n+1}=\varphi\circ P(h_n):A_{n+1}\to F.
\]
Two initial embeddings from one class well-order into another must
agree: at a least disagreement, the smaller image would lie below
the other and hence would be the latter map's image of an earlier
point, contradicting injectivity and earlier agreement.  Applying
this uniqueness to $h_{n+1}\circ j_n$ and $h_n$ proves compatibility.
The maps therefore induce an initial embedding of the colimit into
$F$.  All evaluations and identifications above are finite set
computations relative to the supplied classes; no $\ETR_\omega$
instance has been invoked.
\end{proof}

For $A=\Ord$, take $j$ to send an ordinal coefficient to the
constant polynomial at the least exponent.  This is a proper initial
embedding.  Its completion is exactly the hereditary system above:
a finite stage has finitely nested polynomial roots, and identifying
constant expansions gives the normalized hereditary trees.  The
first point missing from the zeroth-stage image is $b_0=u$; the
first point missing from the next-stage image is $b_1=\Omega^u$;
the subsequent missing points are $b_2,b_3,\ldots$.  Thus the
general colimit construction and the explicitly indexed tower cuts
give the same order and the same cofinal sequence.

\subsubsection{The exact local criterion}

\begin{theorem}[Local fixed-point extension criterion]
\label{swo:fc:local-fixedpoint}
For any class well-order $W$, the following are equivalent over
$\GBC$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item there is a class initial embedding $W\to P(W)$;
\item there are a class well-order $F$, a class initial embedding
      $W\to F$, and a class isomorphism $ P(F)\cong F$.
\end{enumerate}
For nonempty $W$, these are also equivalent to the existence of its
canonical terminating condensation history on the schedule $W+1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The forward implication is \Cref{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion}.
For the converse, identify $W$ with its initial image $A\subseteq F$
and write $\varphi: P(F)\cong F$.  The monomial map
\[
                    g(b)=\varphi(\{(b,1)\})
\]
is an order embedding of $F$ into itself.  Every such embedding is
inflationary.  Otherwise its least counterexample $b$ would satisfy
$g(g(b))<g(b)<b$, making $g(b)$ an earlier counterexample.

Take $a\in A$ and $q=\varphi^{-1}(a)$.  If
$b\in\supp(q)$, then the coefficient-one monomial at $b$ is
at most $q$.  Hence
\[
                           b\leq_F g(b)\leq_F a.
\]
Initiality gives $b\in A$.  Thus $\varphi^{-1}$ maps $A$ into
$ P(A)$.  Its range there is initial: a polynomial below
$\varphi^{-1}(a)$ has image under $\varphi$ below $a$, which
belongs to $A$.  Transport back through the original embedding to
obtain $W\to P(W)$.  The last equivalence is exactly the
repository's fixed-schedule normal-form criterion proved in the
preceding section.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A fixed-point characterization of comparability]
\label{swo:fc:cor:FPE-CWO}
Let $\FPE$ assert that every class well-order initially embeds in
a class well-order $F$ with a supplied isomorphism
$ P(F)\cong F$.  Then
\[
                  \GBC\vdash\FPE\ \longleftrightarrow\
                  \CWO\ \longleftrightarrow\ \CTH.
\]
Requiring the initial extension in $\FPE$ to be proper gives the
same global principle.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply \Cref{swo:fc:local-fixedpoint} to each input and use the
repository equivalence between $\CWO$, $\CTH$, and the assertion
that every $W$ initially embeds in $ P(W)$.  For a proper
extension, apply that assertion to the tagged order $W+1$ before
taking its completion.  The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

This conclusion calibrates \emph{extending every input}, even though
one explicit fixed point already exists in $\GBC$.  It also avoids
an invalid inference from a countable display of class-valued stages
to a need for $\ETR_\omega$.  The special operator used here is
finitary and has uniform finite codes; arbitrary elementary class
recursions need not have that property.  No equivalence with full
$\ETR$ follows from this argument.

There is no hidden choice of a class witness for every member of a
proper collection.  The local construction takes one order and one
embedding as supplied parameters and returns one explicitly defined
completion.  The global principle quantifies over inputs and asserts
existence separately for each one.  It does not assert a single class
whose entries are all those completions, nor does it provide a
uniform satisfaction predicate for arbitrary formulas defining
orders.  This distinction is essential when translating the result
into a theory whose classes are precisely the definable classes of
a fixed set-theoretic model.

\subsubsection{A next fixed point, with no maximal endpoint}

\begin{corollary}[Successor fixed-point extension]
\label{swo:fc:cor:next-fixedpoint}
Given $B$ and a class isomorphism $\varphi: P(B)\cong B$,
$\GBC$ constructs a polynomial fixed point strictly extending $B$
initially.  It is least among polynomial fixed points properly
extending $B$, in the sense of supplied initial embeddings.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $A=B+1$, with appended point $*$.  Define an initial embedding
$j:A\to P(A)$ by
\[
         j(b)=\varphi^{-1}(b)\quad(b\in B),\qquad
         j(*)=\{(*,1)\}.
\]
The first part fills exactly $ P(B)$, and the second point is
the first polynomial after that initial subclass.  Thus $j$ is
initial and proper.  Its completion contains $B+1$ initially and
is a fixed point, by \Cref{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion}.
Any fixed point properly extending $B$ contains an initial copy
of $B+1$, by adjoining its least point outside the image of $B$.
The universal property of the completion therefore proves leastness.
\end{proof}

Consequently the first hereditary fixed point is not a final boundary.
It has a next fixed point, and every supplied fixed point has another
one beyond it.  Each externally specified finite repetition is
available from these explicit constructions.  Organizing all such
extensions along a prescribed arbitrary class index is a further
uniformity problem; it is not supplied merely by writing an indexed
epsilon or Veblen symbol.  A rigorous notation system must specify
its set codes, its comparison rule, the admitted embeddings, and the
existence principle used to assemble any genuinely transfinite family.

\merge\ \Cref{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion,swo:fc:local-fixedpoint,swo:fc:cor:FPE-CWO,swo:fc:cor:next-fixedpoint}
are proved here only by source~35; none of sources~32--34 and nothing earlier
in this report constructs a fixed-point completion. Source~35 keeps them over
$\GBC$ and asks whether they hold over $\GB$ (its question~10.6,
\cref{swo:fc:n10.6}); they do (\cref{swo:xvi:thm:choicefree}). The ``repository
equivalence'' used in the proof of \cref{swo:fc:cor:FPE-CWO} is
\cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence} over $\GBC$, and \cref{swo:bo:hist:equivalence}
over $\GB$.

\begin{theorem}[\merge; completion without choice]\label{swo:xvi:thm:choicefree}
The following hold over $\GB$, with $\ZF$ sets and no form of set choice or
global choice.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item Source~35's bounded-specialization principle,
\cref{swo:fc:lem:bounded-specialization}.
\item $\Eps$ is a class well-order and root formation is an isomorphism
$P(\Eps)\cong\Eps$ (\cref{swo:fc:thm:hereditary-fixedpoint}).
\item The fixed-point completion \cref{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion}: for
every initial embedding $j:A\to P(A)$ of class well-orders there are $C(A,j)$,
$\iota$ and $\Phi$ with all the properties stated there.
\item The local criterion \cref{swo:fc:local-fixedpoint}; the characterization
\cref{swo:fc:cor:FPE-CWO} in the form $\GB\vdash\FPE\leftrightarrow\CWO\leftrightarrow\CTH$,
with its proper-extension variant; and the successor fixed point
\cref{swo:fc:cor:next-fixedpoint}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Source~35's proofs use global choice only to infer that a linear order is a
class well-order from the absence of descending set sequences. Over $\GB$ use
instead source~34's \cref{swo:bo:found:settest}: a class linear order is a
class well-order exactly when every nonempty \emph{set} subset has a least
element. That condition quantifies only over sets, so it is elementary in the
order.

(1) Let $S$ be a nonempty set of terms of the class $\mathrm{Tm}$ of
\cref{swo:fc:lem:bounded-specialization}. The labels occurring in $S$ form a
set of ordinals, by Replacement, and so have a strict upper bound. By
hypothesis there is a larger $\kappa$ for which all terms with labels below
$\kappa$, in particular all members of $S$, have a strictly order-preserving
interpretation into a set ordinal. The member of $S$ with the least
interpretation is least in $S$, since $S$ is linearly ordered. Thus every
nonempty set subset of $\mathrm{Tm}$ has a least element, and
\cref{swo:bo:found:settest} applies.

(2) Source~35's $\mathcal E$ and source~34's $\Eps$ are the same class with
the same order (\cref{swo:fc:def:hereditary-terms}); this is
\cref{swo:bo:her:wellorder,swo:bo:her:fixedpoint}.

(3) In the proof of \cref{swo:fc:thm:fixedpoint-completion} the stages
$A_n=P^n(A)$ and the maps $j_n=P^n(j)$ are defined by one elementary formula
uniformly in $n\in\omega$, with $A$ and $j$ as class parameters, through finite
nested codes, and $A_{n+1}$ is literally $P(A_n)$ under this coding. Let
$\varphi(n)$ say: \emph{$<_{A_n}$ is a strict linear order on $A_n$, every
nonempty set subset of $A_n$ has a $<_{A_n}$-least element, and $j_n$ is an
order embedding of $A_n$ onto an initial subclass of $A_{n+1}$.} Every
quantifier of $\varphi$ ranges over sets, so $\varphi$ is elementary, and
$\{n\in\omega:\neg\varphi(n)\}$ is a set; if it were nonempty it would have a
least element. Hence internal induction on $n$ is available for $\varphi$.
$\varphi(0)$ holds because $A$ is a class well-order, $P(A)$ is linearly
ordered and $j$ is initial. Suppose $\varphi(n)$. By
\cref{swo:bo:found:settest}, $A_n$ is a class well-order; then
$A_{n+1}=P(A_n)$ is a class well-order by \cref{swo:bo:power:GB}, so it is
linear and its nonempty set subsets have least elements; $A_{n+2}=P(A_{n+1})$
is linear by the finite lexicographic comparison; and $j_{n+1}=P(j_n)$ is
initial by \cref{swo:fc:lem:P-initial}, whose proof only transports finite
supports. So $\varphi(n+1)$ holds, and $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n\in\omega$.
By \cref{swo:bo:found:settest} once more, applied with $n$ as a parameter, each
$A_n$ is a class well-order. This replaces the paragraph of source~35's proof
that invokes global choice (``Uniform finite induction is legitimate here: in
$\GBC$, \ldots''); its alternative route through a proposed descending sequence
also needs choice to produce the sequence.

The rest of source~35's proof makes no choice. The carrier of $C(A,j)$
consists of least-stage representatives, defined by an elementary formula, and
its order compares images in a common finite stage. A nonempty subclass of the
colimit has a point in some $\iota_n[A_n]$; the intersection of the subclass
with that stage has a least element because $A_n$ is a class well-order, and
initiality makes it least overall. The isomorphism $\Phi$ decodes finite
supports. If $j$ is proper, $d_n$ is the least element of the nonempty class
$A_{n+1}\setminus j_n[A_n]$, uniquely specified, and Class Replacement
collects $(d_n)_{n<\omega}$. For the universal property, the maps $h_n$ are
defined by finite evaluation uniformly in $n$; ``$h_n$ is an initial embedding
of $A_n$ into $F$'' is elementary, and induction on $n$ proves it by
\cref{swo:fc:lem:P-initial} and the isomorphism $\varphi:P(F)\cong F$;
$h_{n+1}\circ j_n=h_n$ because two initial embeddings between class well-orders
agree (\cref{swo:fc:lem:successor-obstruction}, whose least-disagreement proof
is choice-free).

(4) In \cref{swo:fc:local-fixedpoint} the forward implication is~(3). The
converse uses that the monomial map $g$ is an order embedding of a class
well-order into itself, hence inflationary (\cref{swo:fc:lem:successor-obstruction}),
and initiality; the final equivalence is \cref{swo:fc:history-criterion} with
$\Gamma=W$, which holds over $\GB$. For \cref{swo:fc:cor:FPE-CWO}, apply the
local criterion to each input and replace the $\GBC$ equivalence
\cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence} by its $\GB$ form \cref{swo:bo:hist:equivalence};
for the proper variant, apply it to $W+1$. \Cref{swo:fc:cor:next-fixedpoint}
uses only~(3) and the universal property.
\end{proof}

\merge\ This answers source~35's question~10.6 (\cref{swo:fc:n10.6})
