% ---- source 35, its Section 6
\subsection{Source 35: a systematic notation discipline}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1775-1810
\label{swo:fc:sec:notations}

The purpose of a notation is to make a specified family of orders
usable.  A notation should identify its carrier, its comparison rule,
the axioms proving well-ordering, and the meaning of its equality.
There is no need to pretend that every class order has one canonical
set-valued name.  The preceding results instead suggest several
compatible levels of notation.

\subsubsection{Order constructors and labelled normal forms}

At the first level, a term is an instruction for constructing a
presentation.  Constants name the empty order, the singleton order,
set ordinals, $\Omega$, and explicitly supplied class well-orders.
Binary constructors form $A+B$, $A\cdot B$, and the finite-support
power $A^{[B]}$.  A family constructor $\sum_{i\in I}W_i$ is permitted
only when its input is one uniform class relation.  An initial direct
limit constructor includes its actual connecting maps as data.
Consequently every constructor has a finite, well-typed specification.

At the second level, once an exponent order $\Gamma$ is fixed, a
polynomial code is
\[
 q=\bigl((i_0,\alpha_0),\ldots,(i_{r-1},\alpha_{r-1})\bigr),
 \quad i_0>_\Gamma\cdots>_\Gamma i_{r-1},\quad
 0<\alpha_j\in\Ord.
\]
The code is a set.  Its displayed notation may be written
\[
 \sum_{j<r}\Omega^{\langle i_j\rangle_\Gamma}\alpha_j,
\]
where $\langle i\rangle_\Gamma$ means the initial segment
$\Gamma_{<i}$, not an unexplained ordinal assigned to $i$.
This superscript convention is optional when $\Gamma$ is the ordinary
ordinal class, but indispensable for an arbitrary class exponent order.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Proposition~6.1, ``Meaning of a polynomial as a cut'']\label{swo:fc:prop:polynomial-cut}
\emph{For the preceding code $q\in P(\Gamma)$, its strict initial segment has
the explicit order decomposition
$P(\Gamma)_{<q}\cong\sum_{j<r}P(\Gamma_{<i_j})\cdot\alpha_j$. Thus the displayed
polynomial is an actual finite sum of class well-orders. The assertion holds
in $\GB$.} This is source~34's \eqref{swo:bo:power:segment}, by the same
partition of the predecessors of $q$ by the greatest exponent at which they
fall below it.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1835-1971

This proposition separates two objects that a compact notation often
conflates: $q$ is one set code, whereas the order denoted by the cut
below $q$ can be a proper class.  For example, the code with coefficient
$1$ at exponent $1$ and zero elsewhere is a set, but its predecessor
order in $ P(\Ord)$ is $\Omega$.  A notation system for orders beyond
$\Ord$ is therefore possible without any individual notation being
a proper-class object.

\subsubsection{Worked comparisons and arithmetic}

Finite polynomials with ordinal exponents provide the following
strict comparisons, all witnessed inside the same polynomial order:
\[
 \Omega+1\ <\ \Omega\cdot2\ <\ \Omega\cdot\omega\ <\
 \Omega^2\ <\ \Omega^2+\Omega\cdot\omega\ <\ \Omega^3.
\]
Here and in worked displays within one notation order, $<$ abbreviates
the proper initial-segment comparison of the represented cuts.  Compare
the greatest exponent of disagreement; if it agrees, compare its
ordinal coefficient.  No search through all lower exponents is needed.

For instance,
\[
 q=\Omega^3\cdot2+\Omega\cdot\omega+7,
 \qquad
 r=\Omega^3\cdot2+\Omega\cdot(\omega+1)
\]
satisfy $q<r$.  Their exponent-$3$ coefficients agree.  At exponent
$1$, the coefficient $\omega$ is smaller than $\omega+1$, so the
finite tail $7$ does not affect the comparison.

Ordinal addition is visibly noncommutative.  The identities
\[
 (\Omega^2+\Omega\cdot3+7)+(\Omega\cdot4+5)
   =\Omega^2+\Omega\cdot7+5
\]
and
\[
 (\Omega\cdot4+5)+(\Omega^2+\Omega\cdot3+7)
   =\Omega^2+\Omega\cdot3+7
\]
hold as presentation isomorphisms.  In the first calculation the later
$\Omega$-block absorbs the earlier finite tail.  In the second it absorbs
the entire earlier summand.  More generally, when adding a nonzero
right-hand polynomial, retain the left-hand exponents greater than its
leading exponent, add the two coefficients at that exponent in the
\emph{ordinal} sense, and retain the right-hand lower tail.  Each
coefficient sum is a set ordinal, so there is no carry into the class
base $\Omega$.

For products, the direction of the factors must remain explicit:
\[
 (\Omega+1)\cdot\omega=\Omega\cdot\omega,
 \qquad
 \omega\cdot(\Omega+1)=\Omega+\omega.
\]
The first has $\omega$ successive proper blocks.  In the second,
the initial $\omega\cdot\Omega$ is set-like and hence has type $\Omega$,
followed by one copy of $\omega$.  The equality
\[
 \Omega^{[\Omega+1]}\cong\Omega^{[\Omega]}\cdot\Omega
\]
comes directly from splitting the final exponent coordinate.  It
does not depend on a recursive definition taking a supremum over a
proper collection of class objects.

The absorption laws for a set base are particularly instructive:
\[
 2^{[\Omega]}\cong\omega^{[\Omega]}\cong\Omega,
 \qquad
 \Omega^{[\Omega]}\not\cong\Omega.
\]
The first presentations have set-sized predecessors and proper
carriers.  In the last one, the predecessor class below the monomial
at exponent $1$ is already proper, so the order is not set-like.
This is a structural proof of the difference, rather than a symbolic
rule about an imagined largest ordinal.

\subsubsection{Hereditary terms and the first exponential closure}

In the hereditary system of the preceding section, the exponents
themselves are terms.  Comparison descends through finitely many
subtrees until it reaches ordinal coefficients.  The following is a
typical legal term:
\[
 \Omega^{\Omega^2+\Omega\cdot3+5}\cdot\omega
 +\Omega^{\Omega+7}\cdot4+9.
\]
Its meaning is a cut in the class of hereditary terms.  The term's
finite tree is a set even though its first exponent already denotes
a proper-class order.

Let $\Eps$ be the complete hereditary term order.  The finite
tower markers give a strictly increasing cofinal sequence in
$\Eps$; every single term lies below some such marker.  Hence
$\Eps$ is longer than every finite tower stage and has a
specified isomorphism $ P(\Eps)\cong\Eps$.  The
notation $\Eps$ names the whole order, while a term $t$ names
one of its proper initial cuts.  This avoids representing the entire
fixed point by one of its own elements.

There are two useful ways of continuing.  One may introduce a new
named constant for the order $\Eps$ and construct its successor,
products, and powers.  Or one may apply the fixed-point completion
construction to $\Eps+1$, obtaining a larger exponential fixed
point.  Repeating a fixed, explicitly specified finite construction
is legitimate.  Claiming a universal class-valued recursion through
all class well-orders requires a further principle and is not built
into this syntax.

\subsubsection{What is effective, and what is only definable}

There are four distinct levels of computational content.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A \emph{mathematical class presentation} permits arbitrary set
ordinal coefficients.  These coefficients have exact mathematical
order, but they are not all finite strings.
\item A \emph{relative comparison procedure} compares hereditary
terms using a supplied comparison procedure for their coefficient
notations.  Finite structural recursion then suffices.
\item An \emph{effective notation language} restricts coefficients
to a chosen recursively presented ordinal system.  It has countably
many expressions and names only the corresponding selected cuts.
\item A \emph{proof-carrying presentation} stores, with each new
constructor, a proof of well-order preservation or an initial
embedding certificate.  This is the appropriate interface for a
formal mathematics library.
\end{enumerate}

The small executable artifact accompanying this article implements
the finite-tree comparison idea with nonnegative integer coefficients.
It also checks the finite-support split and flatten maps against
ordinary finite ordered sets.  Its task is to make the conventions
reproducible; it is not a decision procedure for arbitrary definable
class well-orders or a formal proof of the theorems above.

\merge\ The executable artifact mentioned above is shipped as
\path{code/35-completion-finite_notation_checks.py}, with its recorded output
\path{data/35-completion-finite_notation_results.json}
(\cref{swo:xvi:sub:delivery96}).

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1972-1990
\subsubsection{An interface for extensible notations}

A useful formal specification associates four items with each
presentation: a predicate for legal codes, a comparison relation,
a stated well-order theorem, and a semantics relating codes to
initial cuts.  A constructor additionally records how it acts on
class maps.  For example, the exponent-order constructor $ P$
acts on an initial embedding by replacing each exponent label by
its image.  This preservation law is what makes the completion
theorem possible.

A notation package should therefore expose more than a pretty
printer.  It should expose the explicit initial embedding of one
stage into the next, the inverse on its image, and the map that
interprets a finite code.  Such witnesses permit comparisons and
direct limits in weak class theory even where unrestricted class
well-order comparability is unavailable.  The definability theorem
in the next section shows why this disciplined extensibility is
preferable to promising one complete language for all class orders.

\subsection{Source 32: finite terms beyond every finite exponential tower}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 288-291
\label{swo:dc:sec:hereditary}

The finite-support construction can itself be iterated inside finite syntax. This gives an exponential fixed-point presentation without performing a class-valued recursion of unbounded length.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Definition~4.1, ``Hereditary digit terms'']\label{swo:dc:n4.1}
\emph{Fix a class well-order $A$ with least points $0_A<1_A$. A hereditary
$A$-term is either $0$, or a finite list $t=[(t_0,a_0),\ldots,(t_{m-1},a_{m-1})]$
where the $t_i$ are hereditary terms in strictly decreasing order and
$a_i\in A\setminus\{0_A\}$. Compare nonzero terms by their leading exponents,
then their leading coefficients, and then their remaining lists; an exhausted
list is smaller than a nonexhausted one. The term $0$ is least.} Source~32
writes $\mathcal H(A)$ for this presentation, printed $\Eps(A)$; it is
source~34's general base of \cref{swo:bo:her:generalbase}, and for $A=\Omega$
it is $\Eps$ up to identifying coefficients.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 299-301

This definition is a finite-tree definition, not a recursive specification along a proper-class well-order. Membership and comparison are computed by recursion on the finite heights of the input trees (or the maximum of the heights of two trees). The requirement that the exponent list decrease is checked using comparisons of strictly smaller trees. Terms are finite sets of labels and finite-tree structure.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~4.2, ``A hereditary fixed-point presentation'']\label{swo:dc:thm:hereditary}
\emph{In $\GBC$, $\Eps(A)$ is a class well-order and there is an explicit
isomorphism
\[\tag{S32.4}\label{swo:dc:eq:heredfixed}
 \Eps(A)\cong A^{[\Eps(A)]}.
\]
The constant terms form a proper initial copy of $A$. There is
a set-coded increasing $\omega$-sequence cofinal in $\Eps(A)$.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:her:generalbase} (over $\GB$), with the cofinality of

which preserves and reflects comparison by \cref{swo:dc:lem:digits}; a

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 327-330

For $A=\Omega$, these terms provide an explicit proper-class order above all finite towers based at $\Omega$, with an isomorphism to its own $\Omega$-power. More precisely, the segment below $v_n$ has the corresponding finite-tower presentation: root decomposition identifies the segment below $v_{n+1}$ with $A^{(\Eps(A))_{<v_n}}$, starting with the one-point segment below $v_0=1$.

This is a useful answer to ``how far can one stretch?'' but it is not an endpoint. Adjoining a last point produces a strictly larger order by \cref{swo:dc:lem:nocompress}. One can also repeat finite-term constructions over the new base. The significance is that these examples are already definable by finite syntax in GBC; their existence is not evidence that GBC supports arbitrary recursion along them.

\subsection{Source 33: coherent towers of powers and a fixed point}\label{swo:dh:sec:fixedpoint}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 832-912

\subsubsection{An explicit tower, not an arbitrary class recursion}
Define presentations
\[
       T_0=\Omega,\qquad T_{n+1}=\Omega^{[T_n]}
       \qquad(n<\omega).
\]
These can be coded uniformly by finite rooted trees: leaves carry ordinal
labels, a node carries a finite descending list of exponent subtrees and
nonzero ordinal coefficients, and a level label specifies the required
nesting depth. Validity and comparison are obtained by finite bottom-up
evaluation on the code tree. In particular, a set records the entire
finite evaluation at every node. No truth predicate for the whole universe
is required.

This description supplies one elementary definition of the family of
carriers and orders. First-order induction on $n$, using
\cref{swo:dh:thm:power}, verifies that every stage is a class well-order. This is
different from asserting that \emph{every} arbitrary class-valued recursion
of length $\omega$ has a solution.

Embed $T_0$ into $T_1$ by sending $\alpha$ to the constant polynomial
with coefficient $\alpha$ at the least exponent, with zero sent to the
empty polynomial. Call this $i_0$. Inductively, let $i_{n+1}$ replace every
exponent by its image under $i_n$, leaving coefficients unchanged. These
maps also have uniform finite-tree definitions.

\begin{lemma}\label{swo:dh:lem:towerinitial}
Every $i_n:T_n\to T_{n+1}$ is a proper initial embedding.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The constants form a proper initial segment of $T_1$. More generally, if
$j:A\to B$ has initial image, the induced exponent map
$\Omega^{[A]}\to\Omega^{[B]}$ has initial image: any polynomial below an image
polynomial cannot have a nonzero coefficient at an exponent outside the
initial image. If $j$ is proper, a monomial at the least omitted exponent
is not in that image. Apply induction.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The direct limit}
Take the disjoint union of all pairs $(n,t)$ with $t\in T_n$. Identify
$(n,t)$ and $(m,s)$ when their images agree at a common later finite stage.
Each equivalence class has a unique representative at its least level.
Use these least-level representatives as a class carrier $\mathbb T$.
Comparison is computed by lifting two representatives to the larger of
their levels. Thus both equality and order on $\mathbb T$ are elementary from the
finite-tree coding.

\begin{theorem}[A definable fixed point beyond finite towers]\label{swo:dh:thm:fixedpoint}
The direct limit $\mathbb T$ is a class well-order, every $T_n$ is a proper initial
suborder of $\mathbb T$, and there is a definable order isomorphism
\[
                              \Omega^{[\mathbb T]}\cong \mathbb T.
\]
This construction is available in $\GBC$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The coherent initial embeddings make each $T_n$ an initial suborder of the
limit. For a nonempty subclass $S\subseteq \mathbb T$, choose $x\in S$ and a stage
$T_n$ containing it. The intersection of $S$ with that stage has a least
point. Every point of $\mathbb T$ below $x$ already belongs to that same initial
stage, so this least point is least in $S$. Thus $\mathbb T$ is well-ordered.
Properness follows from \cref{swo:dh:lem:towerinitial}.

An element of $\Omega^{[\mathbb T]}$ uses only finitely many exponent points of $\mathbb T$.
All those points lie in a common finite stage $T_n$. Interpret the same
polynomial as a point of $T_{n+1}$, hence of $\mathbb T$. A different sufficiently
large choice of stage gives the same limit point, by the definition of
$i_{n+1}$.

This map is order preserving because any two finite supports can be put
into one stage. It is onto because every point of a stage $T_{n+1}$ already
is a polynomial over $T_n$, and every point of $T_0$ is represented among
the constants of $T_1$. It is therefore the required isomorphism.
\end{proof}

The fixed point is not a ceiling: $\mathbb T+1$ again strictly exceeds $\mathbb T$ under
embeddability. Further explicit notation systems can be built, but their
uniform definition and well-foundedness must be checked rather than inferred
from suggestive ordinal symbols. The diagonal theorem below rules out one
uniform system containing every definable possibility in its own language.

\merge\ Source~33's direct limit, which it writes $E$, is printed $\mathbb T$:
$E$ is a floor equivalence in Section~XVI.5 and $\Eps$ is the hereditary

embedding $i_0$ of $T_0=\Omega$ into $T_1$ is source~35's seed embedding $j$
for $A=\Ord$, its maps $i_{n+1}$ are $P(i_n)$, so $\mathbb T$ is source~35's

\section{Uniform catalogs and truth jumps}
\label{swo:bo:diag:section}

The preceding notation systems describe substantial families of orders.  A
different question is whether one uniform notation system can encompass every
available class well-order.  There is a direct obstruction, which also leads
to an explicit construction showing how an added truth predicate increases
the definable order spectrum.  The results in this section are proved as
structural consequences; no claim of historical priority is intended.

Write $C\emb D$ when there is a class order embedding of
$C$ into $D$.  This notation requires neither a cofinal image nor an initial
image.  In particular, we will not substitute the general class comparison
principle for an embedding argument.

\subsection{A diagonal sum for uniform families}

\begin{definition}[Uniform class family]\label{swo:bo:diag:uniform}
A uniform family $(C_i)_{i\in I}$ consists of class relations $D(i,x)$ and
$R(i,x,y)$: the domain of $C_i$ is $\{x:D(i,x)\}$, and its strict order is the
corresponding slice of $R$.  Thus the family is represented by classes of
\emph{set tuples}.  An external list of formulas is not, by itself, such a
uniformly interpreted family.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform-family diagonal]\label{swo:bo:diag:sum}
Work in $\GB$, and let $(I,<_{I})$ be an available class well-order.  If
$(C_i)_{i\in I}$ is a uniform family of class well-orders, then
\[
   \Delta=\sum_{i\in I}(C_i+1)
\]
is a class well-order.  For every $i\in I$, the order $C_i+1$ embeds as a
convex block of $\Delta$, while
\[
   \Delta\nemb C_i.
\]
If $I$ is proper, then $\Delta$ is proper.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use tagged set codes $\langle i,0,x\rangle$ for $x\in C_i$ and
$\langle i,1\rangle$ for the last point of its block.  Order these codes first
by $<_{I}$ and then by the order of $C_i+1$.  Elementary comprehension supplies
both the domain and the relation.

Let $S$ be a nonempty subclass of this order.  The class of indices of blocks
meeting $S$ has a least member $i$.  The intersection of $S$ with that block
has a least member, since $C_i+1$ is a class well-order.  That member is least
in $S$, proving well-foundedness.

The inclusion of the $i$th block is explicit.  If an embedding
$f:\Delta\longrightarrow C_i$ existed, its restriction to that block would
embed $C_i+1$ into $C_i$, contrary to the successor obstruction
\cref{swo:bo:basic:anti}.  This contradiction excludes \emph{every} available class
embedding, including one using additional class parameters.  Finally,
$i\mapsto\langle i,1\rangle$ injects $I$ into $\Delta$; if the latter were a
set, class replacement applied to the inverse would make $I$ a set.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No uniform cofinal catalog]\label{swo:bo:diag:catalog}
In $\GBC$, no uniform class-indexed family of class well-orders is cofinal for
order embedding among all class well-orders.  In particular, no such family
represents every class well-order up to class isomorphism.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Restrict a global well-order to the index class and apply
\Cref{swo:bo:diag:sum}.  Its diagonal sum embeds into no catalog member.
\end{proof}

This remains an obstruction when the proposed catalog is redundant or
ineffective.  What matters is uniform interpretation as actual class
relations.  If the family and its index order are definable from fixed
parameters, the diagonal sum is definable from the same parameters.
Consequently such a family cannot even be cofinal among all well-orders
definable from those parameters.  This does not prohibit partial notation
systems, bounded fragments, or interpretation using stronger parameters.
It identifies why simply enumerating formulas does not produce a universal
notation system: their intended interpretations have not thereby been
collected into one class relation.

\subsection{A well-order supplied by one truth predicate}

Fix a set-like global well-order $G$ of $V$ and a class parameter $A$; finitely
many class predicates can be combined into $A$ by tags.  We do not assume
that $G$ is definable from $A$.  Let $T$ be a full elementary satisfaction
class for
\[
   (V,\in,A,G).
\]
Here ``full'' means that $T$ evaluates all first-order formula codes with
finite set-valued assignments and satisfies the compositional Tarskian
clauses.  It is an additional assumed class, not something being defined in
the language whose truth it expresses.  The established connection between
truth predicates and elementary transfinite recursion provides the
foundational context~\cite{GitmanHamkins}.

The key to a uniform catalog at this stronger level is that class
well-foundedness has a first-order test in $\GBC$.  Namely, a class relation
is well-founded exactly when there is no set-coded descending
$\omega$-sequence.  In the converse direction, if a nonempty class has no
minimal member, $G$ selects a predecessor of each of its points; ordinary
set-valued recursion on $\omega$ yields a descending sequence.  This is not
class-valued ETR.  The sharper $\GB+\mathrm{DC}$ version is proved in
\cite[Section~4]{GitmanHamkins}.

Index pairs of domain and relation formulas, together with a packed set
parameter, by
\[
   i=(e,f,p),\qquad
   \varphi_e(x,p;A,G),\quad \psi_f(x,y,p;A,G).
\]
Restrict to valid syntactic codes of these arities, and order the resulting
proper index class $I$ by $G$.  Packing finite tuples into $p$ includes every
presentation with finitely many set parameters.

From $e,f$ one effectively obtains the code of a first-order formula
$\operatorname{WO}_{e,f}(p;A,G)$.  It asserts that $\psi_f$ is a strict linear
order on the $\varphi_e$-domain, and that no set function $s$ on $\omega$ has
all its values in that domain with
\[
   \psi_f\bigl(s(n+1),s(n),p;A,G\bigr)
   \quad\text{for every }n\in\omega.
\]
Consequently
\[
   \operatorname{Valid}(i)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   T\bigl(\ulcorner\operatorname{WO}_{e,f}\urcorner,p\bigr)
\]
is a uniform elementary condition using $T$.  Define $W_i$ by interpreting
$\varphi_e,\psi_f$ through $T$ when $i$ is valid, and by taking the empty
order otherwise.  Explicitly, its domain is given by
\[
   x\in W_i\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \operatorname{Valid}(i)\ \wedge\ T(e,x,p),
\]
with $x<_{W_i}y$ defined by $x,y\in W_i$ and $T(f,x,y,p)$.  By the
compositional clauses and the preceding test, every fiber is a class
well-order.  Invalid formulas cannot introduce an ill-founded summand.

\begin{theorem}[Relative truth jump]\label{swo:bo:diag:truth}
Under the preceding $\GBC$ assumptions, let
\[
   J(T;A,G)=\sum_{i\in I}^{G}(W_i+1).
\]
This is a proper class well-order definable from $T,A,G$.  For every class
well-order $C$ whose domain and order are first-order definable from $A,G$
and finitely many set parameters,
\[
   C+1\emb J(T;A,G),
   \qquad
   J(T;A,G)\nemb C.
\]
The first embedding identifies $C+1$ with a convex block.  In particular,
$J(T;A,G)$ is not class-isomorphic to any such $C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The satisfaction class uniformly interprets the fiber family, so
\Cref{swo:bo:diag:sum} applies.  A presentation of $C$ occurs at the index
formed by its formula codes and packed parameters.  Its fiber is exactly
$C$, which gives the asserted block and rules out every reverse embedding.
Each index contributes its last point, ensuring properness.
\end{proof}

This gives a precise sense in which truth increases the order spectrum:
one newly definable order dominates every earlier definable presentation and
cannot embed back into any of them.  It cannot itself have an $A,G$-definable
presentation with set parameters, since that presentation would be one of
the fibers to which the theorem applies.  The obstruction concerns order
types, not only the definability of a particular isomorphism.

In bare $\GBC$ these conclusions concern order embeddings.  If the ambient
theory additionally proves comparison, for example in $\GBC+\ETR$, then each
$C$ is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of $J(T;A,G)$: comparison in
the other direction is excluded by the reverse-embedding obstruction.
The argument needs no class choice or second-order comprehension to gather
the fibers.  Their simultaneous interpretation comes from the supplied $T$.

\subsection{Iteration and the scope of the notation}

Let $\Gamma$ be a class well-order, include its domain and relation among the
base predicates $A$, and suppose a $\Gamma$-iterated truth predicate $U$ is
available.  Its slice $U_\gamma$ is a truth predicate for
\[
   (V,\in,A,G,U_{<\gamma}).
\]
The earlier aggregate is represented by set pairs
$\langle\delta,z\rangle$; it is not a class whose elements are classes.
The construction above is uniform, so it defines a uniform family
\[
   J_\gamma=J(U_\gamma;A\oplus U_{<\gamma},G),
\]
where $\oplus$ denotes the tagged join of predicates.
Here the fixed syntactic translation between separate predicates and their
tagged join is understood when applying $U_\gamma$.

\begin{corollary}[Growth along iterated truth]\label{swo:bo:diag:iterate}
For $\delta<_{\Gamma}\gamma$,
\[
   J_\delta+1\emb J_\gamma,
   \qquad
   J_\gamma\nemb J_\delta.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
From $U_{<\gamma}$ and the set parameter $\delta$, one recovers the slice
$U_\delta$ and the restriction $U_{<\delta}$.  Thus the fixed formulas
constructing $J_\delta$ can be expressed using $A,G,U_{<\gamma}$ and parameter
$\delta$.  Apply \Cref{swo:bo:diag:truth} at stage $\gamma$.
\end{proof}

This conditional statement handles successor and limit stages alike.  It
assumes the whole truth iteration as one class; it does not infer that
iteration from the separate existence of its slices.  Arbitrary available
class well-order lengths of iterated truth belong to the established ETR
framework~\cite{GitmanHamkins}, while extensions obtained by adjoining truth
predicates are studied in class-theoretic potentialism~\cite{xviBartonWilliams}.

The symbols $J_\gamma$ therefore provide systematic relative notation for a
strictly increasing family in the stated embedding sense.  They do not
denote canonical absolute class ordinals: the ordering of formula codes and
parameters through $G$ affects the sum.  Their robust content is the
domination property and the definability environment in which they appear.
Determining whether weaker hypotheses suffice for such dominating orders,
or whether an appropriate domination principle recovers truth, remains a
separate question; no converse follows from the construction.

\begin{corollary}[Bounded-fragment jumps]\label{swo:bo:diag:bounded}
For each fixed natural number $n$, $\GBC$ admits an $A,G$-definable class
well-order $K_n$ dominating every class well-order whose domain and relation
have $\Sigma_n$ or $\Pi_n$ definitions in the L\'evy hierarchy of
$\mathcal L(\in,A,G)$, with arbitrary finite tuples of set parameters.
Each such $C$ satisfies
\[
   C+1\emb K_n,
   \qquad K_n\nemb C.
\]
There is no single $A,G$-set-parameter-definable uniform family of class
well-orders having these domination properties simultaneously for all $n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed $n$, partial satisfaction for syntactically normalized
$\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$ formulas is elementary definable.  Bounded matrices
can be evaluated in a transitive set containing their assignments, with
the predicates restricted to that set; the fixed number
of unbounded quantifier blocks is then interpreted directly.

Use this partial evaluator to interpret the candidate domains and relations.
Apply the first-order linearity and descending-sequence test to those
interpreted relations, replacing invalid fibers by the empty order.  Their
uniform diagonal sum gives $K_n$ by \Cref{swo:bo:diag:sum}; a full truth
predicate is unnecessary for this fixed fragment.

If all the resulting domination properties belonged to one definable
uniform family, that family would be cofinal among all $A,G$-set-parameter
definable class well-orders: every fixed defining formula has some finite
L\'evy complexity.  Its definable diagonal sum would contradict that
cofinality by \Cref{swo:bo:diag:sum}.
\end{proof}

Thus separate constructions for every fixed complexity bound must be
distinguished from an internally uniform sequence of those constructions.
No assertion of separation at each pair of adjacent complexity levels is
being made.

% ---- source 35, its Section 7
\subsection{Source 35: definability, uniform bounds, and complexity separation}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 1997-2021
\label{swo:fc:sec:definability}

An explicit notation can describe a very long class well-order without
describing all such orders.  The distinction becomes sharp when the
interpretation of the notations is itself one class relation.  We prove
that every uniformly interpreted family has a strict upper bound, even
for the comparatively weak relation of suborder embeddability.  Combining
this observation with partial satisfaction gives a separation theorem
for the complexity of presentations of class order types.

The separation below is a consequence of elementary coding and
well-foundedness; no claim of historical priority is made.  Its role
here is to strengthen the repository's obstruction to exhaustive
lists of labelled orders.  That earlier obstruction can omit another
presentation of an already represented type.  The obstruction below
escapes every represented type, and even every type embedding into
one of the represented orders.

\subsubsection{A uniform family is always bounded}

Throughout this section an embedding is an order-preserving injection
whose graph is an available class.  The notation \(A\emb B\) permits
an arbitrary suborder as image.  It does not assert the stronger
initial-segment relation \(A\iemb B\).

\begin{note}[Source~35, Lemma~7.1, ``An appended point cannot be absorbed'']\label{swo:fc:lem:no-successor-embedding}
\emph{In $\GB$, if $W$ is a class well-order, then $\neg(W+1\emb W)$.} This is
the second assertion of source~34's \cref{swo:bo:basic:anti} and of source~35's
own \cref{swo:fc:lem:successor-obstruction}. The proof differs: instead of the
least point moved downward, it iterates the restricted map from the image of
the appended point and obtains a descending set sequence. It is printed as a
second route.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2029-2042
\begin{proof}[Source~35's proof]
Suppose that \(f:W+1\longrightarrow W\) is an embedding, and let
\(*\) denote the tagged appended point.  Identify the original copy
of \(W\) with \(W\) only for purposes of this proof, and put
\(g(x)=f(x)\) on that copy.  Set \(a_0=f(*)\).  Since every original
point precedes \(*\), we have \(g(a_0)<_W a_0\).  Define
\(a_{k+1}=g(a_k)\) for \(k<\omega\).  Order preservation gives
\(a_{k+2}<_W a_{k+1}\) whenever \(a_{k+1}<_W a_k\).
Ordinary set-valued recursion and Class Replacement produce this
sequence as a set.  Its range has no \(W\)-least element, contradicting
well-foundedness.  The tags ensure that no set outside the original
carrier has been tacitly assumed to exist.
\end{proof}

\begin{note}[Source~35, Theorem~7.2, ``Strict bound for a uniform family'']\label{swo:fc:thm:uniform-family-bound}
\emph{Work in $\GB$. Let $I$ carry a supplied class well-order $\triangleleft$,
and let $(W_i)_{i\in I}$ be a uniform family of class well-orders. There is a
class well-order $U$, elementary definable from these data, such that for
every $i\in I$, $W_i\emb U$ and $\neg(U\emb W_i)$. In $\GBC$, the conclusion
applies to a family indexed by any class of sets, since Global Choice supplies
the required order of $I$.} This is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:sum} with
$U=\sum_{i\in(I,\triangleleft)}(W_i+1)$ (source~34's $\Delta$), and its last
clause is \cref{swo:bo:diag:catalog}'s proof; the proof is the same: least
occupied row, then least point in the row, and a row inclusion composed with
$U\emb W_i$ would embed $W_i+1$ into $W_i$ (\cref{swo:fc:lem:no-successor-embedding}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2078-2096

\begin{corollary}[No cofinal uniform notation system]
\label{swo:fc:cor:no-cofinal-interpreter}
In \(\GBC\), no uniformly class-coded family of class well-orders is
cofinal among all class well-orders under suborder embeddability.
In particular, no such family represents every class well-order type.
If strong comparability \(\CWO\) is additionally assumed, the bound
in \Cref{swo:fc:thm:uniform-family-bound} is also a strict upper bound
under initial-segment comparison.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the theorem to the proposed family.  Its output \(U\) embeds
into none of its members, which contradicts cofinality.  Under
\(\CWO\), comparison of \(W_i\) and \(U\) must give an
initial-segment embedding \(W_i\iemb U\): the reverse alternative
would in particular give \(U\emb W_i\).  Equality of types is
excluded by the same argument.
\end{proof}

\merge\ The first two sentences of \cref{swo:fc:cor:no-cofinal-interpreter} are
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:catalog}; the clause under $\CWO$ is source~34's
remark after \cref{swo:bo:diag:truth} for its truth jump.
\Cref{swo:fc:lem:ordinal-wf-test} is the ordinal-carrier case of the
equivalence of \cref{swo:dc:lem:descending}, proved without choice by
least-ordinal selection; source~34's \cref{swo:bo:found:settest} gives, over
$\GB$, the set-subset form for every linear carrier.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2097-2282
The hypothesis concerns a semantic interpreter, not just a collection
of strings.  A syntax class \(T\) together with one class relation
decoding the carrier and comparison relation of every term in \(T\)
is covered by the corollary.  Enlarging the alphabet, allowing
ordinal parameters, or admitting terms of set size does not remove
the obstruction if the result still has such an interpreter.  The
construction even gives an explicit next order: sum the successors
of all currently interpreted orders.  A proposed system cannot
both interpret that entire sum and remain exhaustive.

This does not prohibit useful notation systems for large fragments,
nor a metatheoretic scheme assigning a different defining formula
to each notation.  The latter need not supply a single internal
evaluation class.  It also does not turn arbitrary suborder
embeddings into initial-segment embeddings in \(\GB\); the final
assertion of the corollary deliberately exposes that extra premise.

\subsubsection{A definable test for well-foundedness on ordinal carriers}

The fixed-complexity argument needs to select the well-orders among
uniformly evaluated relations.  This selection does not require
a class quantifier.

\begin{lemma}[Ordinal-carrier well-foundedness]
\label{swo:fc:lem:ordinal-wf-test}
In \(\GB\), a strict linear class order \(R\) on \(\Ord\) is a
class well-order if and only if there is no set function
\(f:\omega\longrightarrow\Ord\) satisfying
\[
                         f(k+1)\mathrel R f(k)
                         \quad(k<\omega).
\]
Consequently this property is elementary in the class parameter \(R\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A descending sequence has a nonempty range without an \(R\)-least
member.  Conversely, suppose that an available nonempty subclass
\(B\subseteq\Ord\) has no \(R\)-least member.  Choose its least
member in the usual ordinal order as \(f(0)\).  Given \(f(k)\), take
the usual-ordinal-least member of
\[
                        \{\beta\in B:\beta R f(k)\}
\]
as \(f(k+1)\).  This class is nonempty by hypothesis, and the choice
is unique.  Set-valued recursion along \(\omega\), followed by Class
Replacement, gives the prohibited set function.  No choice of a
class witness is involved.
\end{proof}

For arbitrary class carriers, the corresponding equivalence is
established in the standard class-recursion literature over
\(\GB+\mathrm{DC}\), and hence over \(\GBC\)
\cite[discussion preceding Definition~6]{GitmanHamkins}.
The ordinal carrier permits the direct least-ordinal selection above.
In a nonstandard or externally ill-founded model, this is an internal
criterion: it refers to the model's own set functions and available
classes.  External well-foundedness must be stated separately.

\subsubsection{Strict separation at every fixed definability level}

Fix a standard finite \(n\geq1\).  A \(\Sigma_n\) presentation on
\(\Ord\) means a strict order relation given by a formula of the
set-theoretic L\'evy hierarchy, allowing a finite tuple of ordinal
parameters.  We use prenex representatives; over the present set
theory the customary versions of the hierarchy give the same class
of definable relations.

For this fixed \(n\) there is a first-order partial satisfaction
formula \(\operatorname{Sat}_{\Sigma_n}\) that evaluates all such
formula codes.  Its construction is a metatheoretic finite induction,
not a uniform truth definition for arbitrary \(n\).  The distinction
is explicit in the standard development: bounded truth is
\(\Delta_1\)-definable, and the fixed \(\Sigma_n\) truth predicate
is \(\Sigma_n\)-definable for \(n\geq1\)
\cite[Lemma~2.13 and Definitions~2.14--2.15]{xviJeonWalsh}.

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-complexity separation of class order types]
\label{swo:fc:thm:definability-separation}
For every fixed standard \(n\geq1\), there is a parameter-free
first-order definition of a class well-order \(U_n\) on \(\Ord\)
with the following properties, provably in \(\GB\).
If \(R\) is a class well-order on \(\Ord\) admitting a
\(\Sigma_n\) definition with ordinal parameters, then
\[
                         R\emb U_n,
                  \qquad \neg(U_n\emb R).
\]
In particular, \(U_n\) has no \(\Sigma_n\) ordinal-parameter
presentation up to available class isomorphism.  Restricted to
definable classes and definable maps, these statements are also
theorems of \(\mathrm{ZFC}\) understood as a scheme.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A potential presentation is coded by \(c=(e,\vec\alpha)\), where
\(e\) is a code for a \(\Sigma_n\) formula with the appropriate
free variables and \(\vec\alpha\) is a finite tuple of ordinals.
Define
\[
 \xi R_c\eta
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{Sat}_{\Sigma_n}
          (e,\langle\xi,\eta,\vec\alpha\rangle).
\]
Let \(I_n\) consist of exactly those codes for which \(R_c\) is a
strict linear order on \(\Ord\) and has no descending set function
of length \(\omega\).  This is an elementary class definition:
the displayed satisfaction formula has already been fixed, and
\Cref{swo:fc:lem:ordinal-wf-test} expresses the remaining condition
using only set quantifiers.  Every section indexed by \(I_n\) is
therefore a class well-order.

The codes can be treated as nonempty finite tuples of ordinals.
There is a parameter-free set-like well-order of all such tuples:
compare their maximum coordinates first, their finite lengths
second, and then use the lexicographic order at a fixed length.
Every nonempty subclass has a least maximum, a least length at
that maximum, and finally a least tuple in the indicated finite
lexicographic order.  The predecessors of a given tuple form a
set, since their entries are bounded by its maximum coordinate
and they belong to the set of finite sequences from that bound.
Restrict this order to \(I_n\).

\Cref{swo:fc:thm:uniform-family-bound} now constructs
\[
                          S_n=\sum_{c\in I_n}(R_c+1).
\]
Every input \(R\) in the theorem is one of its sections, by correctness
of the fixed partial satisfaction predicate.  Thus \(R\emb S_n\),
whereas an embedding \(S_n\emb R\) would contradict
\Cref{swo:fc:lem:no-successor-embedding}.

It remains to put the carrier on \(\Ord\) without adding a
definable global choice assumption.  The tagged carrier of \(S_n\)
is itself parameter-free definably coded by finite ordinal tuples.
Use the set-like tuple order just described on this carrier, and
assign to each point the ordinal order type of its predecessor set.
The assignment is definable and is an isomorphism with an initial
subclass of \(\Ord\).  The carrier is proper: \(I_n\) includes a
code for the usual ordinal order, whose row already has a proper
class of points.  Hence the image cannot be a set ordinal, since
Class Replacement applied to the inverse map would then make the
carrier a set.  The image is all of \(\Ord\).

Transport \(S_n\) across this canonical bijection and call the result
\(U_n\).  All definitions used only the fixed natural number \(n\),
which can be built into the defining formula; there are no set
parameters.  Transport preserves the embedding conclusions.
Finally, if a \(\Sigma_n\) ordinal-parameter presentation were
isomorphic to \(U_n\), that isomorphism would in particular embed
\(U_n\) into an input order, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The theorem separates order types, rather than merely the complexity
of different names for one relation.  Its negative conclusion allows
any admitted embedding, even one defined using additional parameters
or available as a nondefinable class.  It does not claim separation
of two consecutive syntactic levels: no optimal upper complexity
for the output formula has been asserted.  The same construction
can be made for any fixed syntactic fragment having a definable
partial evaluator, provided that its codes and permitted parameters
have a supplied well-order.

\begin{corollary}[The separation family has no uniform ordinal-parameter evaluator]
\label{swo:fc:cor:nonuniform-complexity}
There is no first-order formula \(H(n,\xi,\eta,\vec\gamma)\), with
one fixed finite tuple of ordinal parameters \(\vec\gamma\), whose
sections \(H_n\), for every standard \(n\geq1\), are class well-orders
on \(\Ord\) satisfying the negative conclusion of
\Cref{swo:fc:thm:definability-separation} at level \(n\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The fixed formula \(H\) is equivalent to a \(\Sigma_m\) formula for
some standard finite \(m\geq1\).  Its \(m\)-th section, with the
additional ordinal parameter \(m\), is itself a \(\Sigma_m\)
ordinal-parameter presentation.  The stipulated negative property
for that section would therefore prohibit its identity embedding
into itself.
\end{proof}

This is why the assertion \emph{for each fixed \(n\)} cannot be
silently rewritten as the existence of one definable sequence of
the resulting class relations.  The corollary has the stated
ordinal-parameter scope.  It does not, by this argument alone,
exclude a uniform definition using an arbitrary non-ordinal-
definable set parameter or a new truth predicate.

\begin{note}[Source~35, Proposition~7.7, ``Version with arbitrary set parameters'']\label{swo:fc:prop:definability-global-choice}
\emph{Fix an available global well-order $G$ of the universe. In the language
$\{\in,G\}$, and for each fixed standard $n\geq1$, there is a $G$-definable
class well-order strictly bounding all $\Sigma_n(\in,G)$-definable class
well-orders with arbitrary set parameters, under suborder embeddability. The
carrier and relation of an input presentation may both be defined by such
formulas. No single formula in this language, even with additional fixed set
parameters, uniformly provides such bounding orders for every standard $n$.}
This is source~33's \cref{swo:dh:thm:bounded} with its \cref{swo:dh:cor:nodefcofinal},
and source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:bounded} for $A$ empty; source~35's proof
evaluates the two formulas by the fixed partial satisfaction predicate, filters
by the $\GBC$ well-foundedness test, orders the codes by a set-like global
well-order definable from $G$, applies \cref{swo:fc:thm:uniform-family-bound},
and obtains the nonuniformity as in \cref{swo:fc:cor:nonuniform-complexity},
all fixed set parameters of a proposed uniform formula being among those
allowed in its own offending section.
\end{note}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2307-2313

Naming \(G\) is substantive.  Global Choice as a class axiom does
not assert that a global well-order is definable in the pure
membership language.  The proposition consequently gives a
relative definability theorem, whereas
\Cref{swo:fc:thm:definability-separation} on ordinal carriers gives
the unconditional pure-language version.

\subsection{Source 32: no uniformly definable family reaches the end}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 482-485
\label{swo:dc:sec:diagonal}

There is no largest class well-order, since $W+1$ always defeats $W$. A stronger statement excludes one uniformly coded family from being cofinal among all admitted class well-orders, even for the weaker arbitrary-embedding relation.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Theorem~7.1, ``Uniform diagonal domination'']\label{swo:dc:thm:diagonal}
\emph{Let $I$ be a nonempty class well-order and $(W_i)_{i\in I}$ a uniformly
coded family of class well-orders. Define
\[\tag{S32.10}\label{swo:dc:eq:diag}
 D=\sum_{i\in I}(W_i+1).
\]
Then $D$ is a class well-order,
every $W_i$ embeds into $D$, and $D$ embeds into none of the $W_i$. The theorem
is provable in $\GBC$ without class-order comparability or $\ETR$.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:sum}, with the same proof by
\cref{swo:dc:prop:sums} and \cref{swo:dc:lem:nocompress}; source~34 shows it in
$\GB$. Source~32's diagonal $D$ is source~34's $\Delta$; it is not the
condensation operator $D_W$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 498-508

Notice what the theorem does \emph{not} assert: the copy of $W_i$ used in the sum need not be initial. No initial comparison is required for the contradiction. In an external setting where these presentations are ordinary well-orders, the usual ordinal comparison converts the conclusion into the strict inequality of order types.

\begin{corollary}[A fixed finite syntax has a definable bound]
\label{swo:dc:cor:finitesyntax}
Fix finitely many first-order formula pairs for a domain and an order relation, with arbitrary set parameters and fixed admitted class parameters. There is one class well-order, definable from the same class parameters and a fixed global well-order, that does not embed into any valid well-order presentation defined by those formulas.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Encode each finite tuple of set parameters by one set. A finite disjunction of the given formulas provides a uniform family indexed by a finite formula tag and the parameter code. By \cref{swo:dc:lem:descending}, being a valid well-order is an elementary predicate on each fiber. Replace invalid fibers by the empty order. Global Choice well-orders the index class, and \cref{swo:dc:thm:diagonal} supplies the desired bound. All definitions involve only the given finitely many formulas, so no truth predicate for arbitrary formulas is being used.
\end{proof}

\merge\ \Cref{swo:dc:cor:finitesyntax} is the finite-list case of source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:diag:bounded}; source~32 uses it in \cref{swo:dc:thm:ceiling}.

\begin{note}[Source~32, Corollary~7.3, ``No universal admitted list'']\label{swo:dc:cor:nolist}
\emph{There is no admitted uniform class-coded family that contains, up to
admitted isomorphism, every admitted class well-order. More strongly, no such
family is cofinal for the relation $\emb$ among all admitted class
well-orders.} This is source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:catalog}, by restricting a

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 516-517

An external list of formulas does not contradict this result. It is easy externally to enumerate finite strings that might define classes. The missing internal object is a uniform satisfaction relation evaluating all those formulas. Confusing an external enumeration of syntax with an admitted family of semantic evaluations is precisely the mistake that the next two sections exploit constructively.

\subsection{Source 33: a diagonal theorem for uniform families}\label{swo:dh:sec:diagonal}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 915-916

\subsubsection{Strict domination without a comparison theorem}

\begin{note}[Source~33, Theorem~7.1, ``Uniform-family diagonal'']\label{swo:dh:thm:diagonal}
\emph{Let $(W_i)_{i\in I}$ be a uniform family of class well-orders, where $I$
is a nonempty class well-order. Define
\[\tag{S33.7.1}\label{swo:dh:eq:diagonal}
 D=\sum_{i\in I}(W_i+1).
\]
Then $D$ is a class well-order and, for every $i\in I$,
\[\tag{S33.7.2}\label{swo:dh:eq:strictdom}
 W_i\emb D,\qquad D\nemb W_i.
\]
The construction and proof are available in $\GBC$.} This is source~34's
\cref{swo:bo:diag:sum} and source~32's \cref{swo:dc:thm:diagonal}, with the same
proof (\cref{swo:dh:prop:sums,swo:dh:cor:successor}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 938-943

The theorem is stronger than a statement that a family has no maximum. It
produces one order that strictly dominates \emph{every member at once},
without choosing isomorphisms between members or comparing their lengths.
It also works when some fibers are empty.

\begin{note}[Source~33, Corollary~7.2, ``No uniform catalogue'']\label{swo:dh:cor:nocatalogue}
\emph{There is no class-coded family, indexed by sets, that contains up to
isomorphism every available class well-order. More strongly, no such family is
cofinal under embeddability among all available class well-orders.} This is
source~34's \cref{swo:bo:diag:catalog} and source~32's \cref{swo:dc:cor:nolist}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 955-973

This is an appropriate class-order version of the obstruction behind
Burali--Forti, but its proof does not illegally collect all classes as
objects. It quantifies over an already supplied uniform family and constructs
one new relation from it.

\subsubsection{What remains possible}
A language can have a set of finite expressions and a definable evaluator
for a useful fragment: sums, products, finite powers, or the coherent tower
of \cref{swo:dh:sec:fixedpoint}. The obstruction says that such an evaluator cannot
be cofinal among \emph{all} well-orders definable in the same language if
its evaluation is itself definable there. One must increase complexity,
add a truth predicate, weaken the coverage claim, or move to a stronger
semantic setting.

In a theory with initial comparability, \eqref{swo:dh:eq:strictdom} can be read as
strict inequality of the usual external ordinal-like lengths. In the base
theory it is deliberately stated using ordinary embeddings, where the
proof is unconditional.
