Construct useful finite-expression languages with verified evaluation and
well-foundedness proofs for long fragments beyond $\Omega$. Which fragments
have decidable equality or comparison? The no-uniform-cofinal-family
theorem gives a precise reason not to promise one self-contained system
covering all definable well-orders in its own language.
\end{question}

\subsubsection{Comparison, recursion, and the strength of histories}

\merge\ Source~34's R5, source~35's question~10.3, source~32's question~12.8
and source~33's question~12.10 are Hamkins and Woodin's Question~7, which this
report records as source~29's \cref{swo:bw:n13.8}: \textbf{open}. Over $\GB$ it
is now a question about any of the equivalent principles $\CWO$, $\CTH$ and
$\FPE$ (\cref{swo:bo:hist:equivalence,swo:fc:cor:FPE-CWO,swo:xvi:thm:choicefree}).
Source~34's R6 and source~35's question~10.5 ask the weak-versus-strong part
of the same question: open. Source~32's question~12.1 and source~33's
question~12.6 ask for the strength of the existence of condensation
hierarchies or towers: \textbf{answered}, and kept on record: it is $\CWO$,
over $\GBC$ by source~29 (\cref{swo:bw:ch:equivalence}) and over $\GB$ by
sources~34 and~35, because hierarchies and towers are nested histories
(\cref{swo:xvi:rem:towers}); only $\CWO\Rightarrow\ETR$ remains open.
Source~35's question~10.4 is source~15's \cref{swo:cb:n13.3}: open.
Source~34's R7 is open. Source~32's question~12.10, on removing global
choice, is answered for the arguments it names: the descending-sequence test
is replaced over $\GB$ by \cref{swo:bo:found:settest} for linear orders,
support localization and least-representative division need no choice
(\cref{swo:bo:power:GB,swo:bo:basic:blocks}), and the diagonal of an already
well-ordered uniform family is a $\GB$ theorem (\cref{swo:bo:diag:sum}); global
choice remains for ordering arbitrary index classes (\cref{swo:bo:diag:catalog}),
and how much set theory each argument needs is open.

\begin{question}[Source~34, R5: comparability versus elementary transfinite recursion]\label{swo:bo:R5}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2129-2135
Investigate the converse to $\ETR\Rightarrow\CWO$, and its
relationship with continuous ranking. This is Hamkins--Woodin's
published Question 7, not resolved by the present history
equivalence \cite{HamkinsWoodin}. The $\GB$ refinement isolates
an additional equivalent formulation that may be useful for
building separating models or extracting recursion.

\end{question}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2769-2785
\paragraph{The remaining recursion and comparison boundary}

\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.3: Does comparability yield elementary transfinite recursion?]\label{swo:fc:n10.3}
Determine whether strong class-well-order comparability implies
$\ETR$ over the usual base theories, or construct a separating model.
\end{question}

This is a classical open-question direction, not a problem solved by
the choice-free improvement.  The results here add an equivalent
fixed-point extension formulation over $\GBC$: every class well-order
has an initial extension admitting an isomorphism with its own
$\Omega$-power.  One may therefore try to recover iterated truth from
the completion witnesses, or show that those witnesses can exist
without all elementary recursion solutions.  A bare order isomorphism
need not provide a truth predicate; the missing reduction must be
proved rather than inferred from the height of the order.

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 838-842
\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.8: Comparison and recursion]\label{swo:dc:n12.8}
What are the reverse implications between ETR, existence of continuous class rankings, initial class-order comparability, and arbitrary-suborder comparability?
\end{question}
This is the family of comparison questions posed by Hamkins and Woodin \cite{HamkinsWoodin}. Our diagonal theorem uses neither comparison principle and therefore does not answer those reversals. Condensation existence may provide a new intermediate principle to test, rather than a presumed equivalence.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 1727-1738
\paragraph{Connections to published problems and formal systems}
\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.10: Comparison versus recursion: a published interface]\label{swo:dh:n12.10}
Hamkins--Woodin ask whether ETR, continuous rankings, initial comparison,
and weak comparison of class well-orders are equivalent over
$\GBC^-$ \cite[Question 7]{HamkinsWoodin}. Can the diagonal and condensation
methods isolate new implications or separating model constructions?
This article proves no reversal. The targeted search located the published
question but did not establish a complete up-to-date resolution of its
status; a project pursuing it should begin with a renewed specialist
literature check.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Source~34, R6: weak versus strong comparison]\label{swo:bo:R6}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2137-2142
Determine the exact strength of arbitrary-suborder comparability
relative to initial-segment comparability. The diagonal theorem
does not settle this question. A reversal must produce an initial
range or a genuine countermodel, rather than appeal to set-order
intuition.

\end{question}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2802-2815
\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.5: Weak comparison and ranking principles]\label{swo:fc:n10.5}
Which of the implications among ordinary suborder comparability,
initial-segment comparability, continuous class rankings, and
$\ETR$ reverse over $\GB$ or $\GBC$?
\end{question}

The successor-sum bound proved here uses ordinary suborder embeddings
and needs no universal comparison principle.  By contrast, fixed-point
completion uses an initial embedding certificate.  This distinction
may help formulate intermediate principles.  The relevant established
implications and the original Hamkins--Woodin question should remain
explicit when constructing models or proposed reductions
\cite{HamkinsWoodin}.

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 799-803
\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.1: Exact strength of condensation existence]\label{swo:dc:n12.1}
Over GBC, what is the strength of the assertion that every class well-order $W$ admits the set-interval condensation hierarchy along $W+1$? Is it weaker than full ETR, equivalent to a recognizable fragment, or equivalent to a natural class-order comparison principle?
\end{question}
The termination part is settled by \cref{swo:dc:thm:termination}; hierarchy existence is the remaining issue. A productive separation test would construct a GBC realization closed under this one elementary operator but not under arbitrary elementary recursions.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 1695-1702
\paragraph{Condensation, ranks, and recursion}
\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.6: The exact recursion strength of exhaustion]\label{swo:dh:n12.6}
Determine the weakest theory proving the existence and exhaustion of the
condensation tower for every class well-order. \Cref{swo:dh:prop:exhaust}
gives a sufficient order-dependent ETR assumption. Does an appropriately
uniform exhaustion principle recover a substantial recursion principle?
\end{question}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2786-2801
\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.4: Uniform finite condensation]\label{swo:fc:n10.4}
For every supplied class well-order $W$, does $\GB$ prove the existence
of one class coding all finite iterates of its set-interval
condensation operator?
\end{question}

Each externally fixed finite iterate is elementary.  The uniform
assertion is different, as the repository correctly emphasizes.
The finite-trace proof for repeated $ P$ does not answer this
question: $ P$ acts by local transformations of finite supports,
whereas set-interval condensation contains a global set-existence
test.  A promising approach is to analyze whether a single input
order can make its successive condensations encode increasingly
complex partial truth.  A negative result must construct such an
input and recover the truth information explicitly.

\begin{question}[Source~34, R7: restricted history principles]\label{swo:bo:R7}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2144-2152
Study histories only for orders of a specified definability
complexity, only on a specified family of code carriers, or only
on specified schedules. Track the existence of a well-order on
each carrier explicitly, so a restriction cannot become vacuous
when Choice fails. Determine when these fragments recover full
comparability and when they measure a weaker principle. The
whole-surreal-carrier reduction in the repository uses its
separate Global Choice analysis and is not a new open problem here.

\end{question}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 848-852
\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.10: Reducing choice and background strength]\label{swo:dc:n12.10}
Which arguments can be carried out without Global Choice, given well-ordered input domains? How much set theory is needed for support localization, least-representative division, and diagonal domination of an already well-ordered uniform family?
\end{question}
The direct least-element proof for sums is choice-free once the orders are supplied. Global Choice was used in the descending-sequence test and in ordering arbitrary parameter-index classes. Separating these uses may yield versions suited to choiceless GB or weaker set fragments.

For which supplied towers is the canonical map $\Phi$ of

criterion on tower fibers that proves initiality without invoking general
class comparison? A separate question is whether a different canonical
compression map has a weaker axiom bound.

\end{question}
The explicit examples realize every supplied class length as an exact collapse length. A classification therefore has to retain more information than the external cardinality of the domain or the repeated quotient's isomorphism type.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 1711-1718
\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.8: Minimal condensation lengths]\label{swo:dh:n12.8}
Under which hypotheses can one assign a minimal exhaustion length to an
arbitrary class well-order, compare these lengths, and do so uniformly
across a supplied family? The coherent-relation requirement must be kept;
the repeated quotient-type example $P(\omega)/E_n\cong P(\omega)$ rules
out a classification using quotient types alone.
\end{question}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 809-813
\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.3: Normal forms after repeated $\Omega$-division]\label{swo:dc:n12.3}
For which presentations does iteration of \cref{swo:dc:thm:division} yield a useful canonical normal form? Can one recognize the finite-support powers and hereditary term orders directly from their block structure? What hypotheses ensure uniqueness of more elaborate normal-form expansions?
\end{question}
The one-step division theorem is unconditional in GBC. Neither a universal Cantor normal form for all class well-orders nor a uniformly admitted iteration through all possible class lengths has been established here.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2905-2932
\paragraph{Condensation beyond finite polynomial forms}

\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.12: Classify isomorphism-level condensation fixed points]\label{swo:fc:n10.12}
Which class well-orders are isomorphic to their set-interval quotient,
and which can occur in nontrivial isomorphism-level cycles?
\end{question}

The example $ P(\omega)$ already shows that one-step condensation
can preserve the order type.  It does not show that the actual retained
subclass is unchanged.  Nor does it prevent a specified transfinite
history from terminating.  Any classification should retain the
quotient map, the literal retained representatives, and the
isomorphism type as distinct data.  This avoids the false inference
that every quotient must have a strictly smaller abstract length.

\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.13: Alternative limits with an explicit universal property]\label{swo:fc:n10.13}
What genuinely different class-order theories arise when limits of
condensation systems are defined by other universal properties or
additional completion operations?
\end{question}

The nested-representative limit and the union of its induced equivalence
relations already describe the same canonical process.  A new theory
must change something substantive, such as the admitted maps, the
identifications made at limit stages, or the ambient type level.  The
benefit should be an exact theorem or a preserved invariant, rather
than an alternative spelling of the same construction.

Replace ``is a set'' by a specified smallness ideal or by internal

finite-digit representation survive? Singular cutoffs require particular
care because the rank-bounding and replacement arguments used at an
inaccessible $\kappa$ may fail.
\end{question}

\subsubsection{Notation systems, fixed points, and support conditions}

\merge\ Source~35's question~10.6 is \textbf{answered} positively by this write
(\cref{swo:xvi:thm:choicefree}), and kept on record. Source~34's R4 and
source~35's question~10.8 ask for the same Veblen-style hierarchy of class-order
fixed points; with source~35's question~10.7 (completion for other functors),
source~34's R2 and R3, and source~33's question~12.14, they are open.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2816-2831
\paragraph{Fixed-point completions and their functorial behavior}

\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.6: A choice-free completion theorem]\label{swo:fc:n10.6}
Can the local fixed-point completion theorem itself be lowered from
$\GBC$ to $\GB$ in full generality, with a completely uniform proof
of well-ordering for the finite-trace direct limit?
\end{question}

The explicit finite-support constructor is now known to preserve
well-ordering without Choice.  The remaining point is the internal
uniformity of the iterated stages for an arbitrary supplied seed
embedding.  Proving each externally fixed stage is not by itself a
proof of the needed uniform assertion in a weak base.  This article
keeps the stated $\GBC$ hypothesis for the completion theorem instead
of using a metatheoretic iteration as an unstated class-existence axiom.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2832-2846
\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.7: Completion as a universal construction]\label{swo:fc:n10.7}
For which class-order functors $F$ does a supplied initial embedding
$W\iemb F(W)$ yield a least fixed-point extension by an elementary
finite-trace construction?
\end{question}

For $F= P$, finite support guarantees preservation of the direct
limit, while preservation of initial embeddings guarantees that every
predecessor of a point lies in a single stage.  These two properties
suggest sufficient hypotheses.  They should be phrased for one
uniformly supplied functor on codes and maps, without quantifying over
a nonexistent class containing all classes as elements.  Normal
dilators are a natural source of examples, but a claim about every
dilator must specify its coding and axioms separately.

\begin{question}[Source~34, R4: iterated fixed-point notation]\label{swo:bo:R4}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2121-2127
Develop a Veblen-style hierarchy of class-order constructors with
finite support and local certificates. State a well-foundedness
theorem for the complete proposed syntax before assigning it a
large symbolic ordinal name. Compare the resulting theory with
the support-based constructions used in ordinal analysis
\cite{xviFreund}.

\end{question}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2847-2860
\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.8: Successive fixed points and Veblen-style systems]\label{swo:fc:n10.8}
Construct explicit hereditary notation systems for successive
$ P$-fixed points, their common fixed points with other constructors,
and suitable Veblen-style closures.  Identify the exact comparison
and well-ordering proofs for each system.
\end{question}

The classical use of class epsilon notation shows that such growth
is a legitimate proof-theoretic direction.  The contribution needed
here is a coherent class-presentation semantics and verified
constructor laws.  A symbol resembling a familiar ordinal notation
is not enough to establish a class well-order.  Bounded specialization
and finite-support direct limits offer two complementary proof methods.

\begin{question}[Source~34, R2: support conditions beyond finite trees]\label{swo:bo:R2}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2104-2111
Determine which families of set-sized supports admit a coherent
replacement for greatest-disagreement comparison while preserving
class well-foundedness. An unrestricted infinite support need not
have a greatest differing coordinate. The finite-support proofs
identify exactly where such a replacement must supply additional
structure; a proposed extension should include counterexamples
showing why its support restrictions are needed.

\end{question}

\begin{question}[Source~34, R3: normalization of arithmetic inside the hereditary system]\label{swo:bo:R3}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2113-2119
Construct certified algorithms for addition, multiplication, and
exponentiation of the initial-segment notations represented by
finite trees, with an explicit interface for ordinal coefficients.
Prove the algorithms against class-order isomorphisms, not only
against a few specializations $\Omega\mapsto\kappa$.
Determine precisely which operations preserve finite normal forms.

\end{question}

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 1763-1770
\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.14: Higher-order extension without a final universe]\label{swo:dh:n12.14}
Which useful ordinal operations and comparison principles can be expressed
on unrolled or hyperclass order codes, and what are their exact collection
and recursion requirements? A satisfactory extension should reproduce the
appropriate diagonal obstruction at its own level rather than postulate
an absolute final ordinal of every universe.
\end{question}

\subsubsection{Diagonals and definability complexity}

\merge\ Source~35's question~10.9, source~32's question~12.6 and source~33's
question~12.1 ask the same thing: the least complexity of an order escaping a
fixed definability level; open. Source~35's question~10.11 is open. Source~33's
question~12.2 asks to remove the named global order: for orders on $\Ord$ with
ordinal parameters source~35 removes it (\cref{swo:fc:thm:definability-separation});
for arbitrary carriers and set parameters it is open. Source~34's R8 is the
same distinction between ordinal and set parameters, which source~35's
$\delta_{\mathrm{ord}}\le\delta_{\mathrm{set}}$ measures
(\cref{swo:fc:thm:definability-spectrum}); open.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2861-2875
\paragraph{Definability spectra and uniform bounds}

\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.9: Quantitative complexity of escape orders]\label{swo:fc:n10.9}
For a fixed finite $n$, what is the smallest definability complexity
of a class well-order that strictly dominates all $\Sigma_n$ ordinal-
parameter presentations in the sense of the successor-sum theorem?
\end{question}

Our construction proves an escape at some finite higher complexity.
It does not identify the least possible increase, and it does not
prove that every adjacent level of a chosen syntactic hierarchy has
a particular canonical representative.  Establishing sharp upper and
lower bounds would turn a qualitative nonuniformity theorem into a
finer ordinal-analysis tool.

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 828-832
\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.6: Syntactic complexity of diagonal bounds]\label{swo:dc:n12.6}
Given formulas of fixed quantifier complexity, how complicated must a formula defining a diagonal upper bound be? Can the valid-fiber filter and the global index order be optimized to produce a sharp complexity hierarchy?
\end{question}
The proof uses only a fixed finite list and an elementary well-foundedness test. Making the syntactic transformations explicit would both sharpen the mathematics and provide a suitable finite verification target for the repository's formula calculus.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 1656-1664
\paragraph{Definability and order-height spectra}
\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.1: Sharp complexity of the diagonal]\label{swo:dh:n12.1}
For a fixed syntax convention, what is the best explicit upper bound on the
complexity of the formulas defining $D_n$? \Cref{swo:dh:thm:bounded} proves
that no isomorphic $\Sigma_n(G)$ presentation exists. Can a matching small
additive increase in the Levy hierarchy be obtained, and can optimality
be shown for natural coding schemes?
\end{question}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2893-2904
\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.11: Optimal uniform-family bounding]\label{swo:fc:n10.11}
Given a uniform family, can one construct a more canonical or smaller
strict bound than its successor-sum, while staying in the same weak
theory and preserving useful functorial properties?
\end{question}

The successor-sum depends on an ordering of the index class and makes
no claim to be a least upper bound.  Removing that dependence may
require comparison witnesses or higher-order selection.  The problem
is therefore a useful test case for the difference between explicit
bounding and canonical classification.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 1665-1671
\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.2: The role of a definable global order]\label{swo:dh:n12.2}

\begin{question}[Source~34, R8: ordinal parameters versus arbitrary set parameters]\label{swo:bo:R8}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2154-2159

models in which ordinal parameters already give the same spectrum,
and models in which the two differ. Under an appropriate definable

\end{question}

\subsubsection{Definability ceilings and truth}

questions~12.3 and~12.4, and source~35's question~10.10 ask for the same
invariant, the definable ceiling $\Theta_L$ (source~32's $\delta_A$, source~33's

source~33's question~12.5 ask how large a truth jump is: source~32 shows that

the new ceiling is open.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2161-2167

the model and named predicates. Countable cofinality is now fixed

\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.4: Classifying definability ceilings]\label{swo:dc:n12.4}
For fixed inaccessible $\kappa$ and global predicate $G$, which ordinals occur as $\delta_A$? Are there natural sufficient conditions supplementing
\[
\kappa<\delta<\kappa^+,\qquad \cf(\delta)=\omega,
\qquad \kappa^\delta=\delta?
\]
\end{question}
Closure under hereditary finite term formation gives further necessary restrictions. It would be valuable to compare the ceiling with heights arising from admissibility, definable well-founded relations, or an appropriate unrolling, but no identification of these invariants is assumed in the proofs above.

Can $\delta_G$ be characterized in admissibility, fine-structural, or

constructible rank models? The manuscript proves countable cofinality,
arithmetic closure, and the epsilon-number property, but not an exact
ordinal notation for this ceiling.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Source~33, Research question~12.4: Dependence on the global-order predicate]\label{swo:dh:n12.4}
How much can $\delta_G$ vary as $G$ ranges over set-like global well-orders
of one fixed $V_\kappa$? What information can be coded into such a $G$
while preserving its order-theoretic role, and what external heights can
occur? Distinguish a change of predicate from a change of the set model.
\end{question}

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2876-2892
\begin{question}[Source~35, Question~10.10: Characterize the definability-sensitive cutoffs]\label{swo:fc:n10.10}
For inaccessible $\kappa$, analyze the external suprema of the
well-order types definable over $V_\kappa$ with no parameters,
ordinal parameters, real parameters, or arbitrary set parameters.
Which equalities between these suprema are forced by structural
properties of $V_\kappa$?
\end{question}

The counting argument gives strict bounds below $\kappa^+$, and
successor closure gives no maximum.  It does not calculate the
suprema.  These are external invariants of a specified structure and
language.  They should not be presented as internally definable
ordinals of $V_\kappa$, since many lie above its entire ordinal class.
Models with a definable global well-order may behave differently from
models where arbitrary set parameters carry information unavailable
from ordinal parameters.

Downward closure in the proof used the arbitrary point parameter $x$ of a presentation. Without that parameter, the spectrum need not be justified as an initial segment by the same argument. The first task is to specify the parameter class before comparing ceilings.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2176-2182
Hamkins and Woodin establish preservation results under specified
forcing hypotheses and formulate more general questions
\cite{HamkinsWoodin}. Study preservation of the explicit notation
systems and of $\Theta_{A,G}$ separately from preservation of
all class-order types. Old orders can remain well-founded while
new isomorphisms or new presentations become available.

\end{question}

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 843-847
\begin{question}[Source~32, Question~12.9: Changes of class realization and forcing]\label{swo:dc:n12.9}
How does the definability ceiling change when one enlarges the admitted predicates while retaining the same set universe? Which analogous invariants behave well when the set universe also changes by forcing?

The first situation includes the truth extension proved here. The second must be kept distinct: preservation results for class well-orders and ETR in the forcing literature impose their own hypotheses \cite{HamkinsWoodin}. A useful starting point is to formulate comparison maps between two explicitly specified spectra instead of presuming that all externally identical ordinal types have admitted isomorphisms.

\paragraph{Source~34's closing remark and source~35's practical sequence.}

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 2190-2195

The immediate mathematical deliverable is the choice-free history
theorem. The fixed-point and definability results supply two distinct
ways to extend the project: one builds increasingly expressive finite
syntax, while the other measures how the available class language
changes the range of order types.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 2933-2958
\paragraph{A practical sequence of next steps}

A sensible implementation sequence starts with the choice-free
finite-support lemma and explicit map laws, then verifies the
normal-form theorem, and finally formalizes fixed-point completion.
These steps have short dependencies and precise acceptance criteria.
The full reverse-mathematical separation problems should be pursued
after these constructive foundations are checked, because they rely
on subtler model existence and truth considerations.

For the repository, the immediate mathematical changes would be to
replace the polynomial well-order proof, lower the assumptions of the
specific canonical-history theorems, add the local fixed-point
criterion, and attach an explicit status note to each theorem.  A
separate module should contain the notation interface and its
constructor certificates.  This article and its archive are a
standalone deliverable; no repository mutation or publication is
part of the present work.

The resulting picture is precise: class-order arithmetic has many
explicit, arbitrarily extensible constructions; the canonical histories
available for all inputs are governed by strong comparability; and
uniform definability imposes its own barriers even when individual
presentations are elementary.  These three facts give distinct,
testable directions for further work.

% ---- source 12, lines 1551-1577
\subsection{Source 12's conclusion}

There is a rigorous full lexicographic order of all global surreal
well-orders, provided it is understood as a relation on class objects,
not as an ordinary class containing those objects. Its comparison needs
no universal enumeration of abstract class order types: the largest
common \emph{labelled} prefix is elementary and sufficient.

The set-like suborder has a particularly uniform geometry. It fills
set-indexed cuts, contains every class linear order even locally, and is
equimorphic with binary classes on $\Ord$. The unrestricted order adds
new proper-class prefix phenomena, including finite adjacent blocks.
The diagonal theorem prevents either construction from being exhausted
by a same-level class of set codes.

At set-sized birthday bounds the theory becomes quantitative. The full
well-order space of a carrier of cardinality $\mu$ has exact ordinal
spectrum below $\mu^+$ and binary rank $\mu^+$. The minimal surreal slice
has rank $\mu$, except at singular strong-limit cutoffs, where it has
rank $\kappa\cdot\kappa$. This is an order-theoretic effect of cofinal
blocks of code lengths, invisible to cardinal counting alone.

The inaccessible-rank interpretation shows exactly how these facts can
coexist: internal classes and the external collection of all such
classes occupy different levels. Respecting those levels removes the
apparent paradox without weakening the embedding and universality
questions into trivialities.

% ---- source 09, lines 1524-1546
\subsection{Source 09's conclusions}
The lexicographic well-ordering problem has three different answers,
depending on its carrier. On a fixed set of surreals of size $\kappa$,
the exact ordinal spectrum stops at $\kappa^+$. Allowing arbitrary
set-length words gives a class-universal dictionary order, but prefix
limits give it local order properties different from those of $\No$.
For set-like global well-orders, first disagreement again defines a
linear comparison. Existence of a global enumeration is equivalent to
global choice over $\GB$ with set choice, and all global enumerations
cannot be collected into an ordinary class of set codes.

The eventual-agreement core resolves the constructive side of the
global problem: it is a genuine class, it is isomorphic to the surreal
line, it realizes every uniformly set-sized cut of global enumerations,
and it is dense in every global interval. Bounded reflection explains
why set-indexed configurations can always be studied in a suitable
bounded permutation stage. The explicit missing branch and binary
diagonal identify two independent boundaries: arbitrary class-sized
cuts need not have solutions, and no single uniform class-indexed
coding covers all global enumerations.

These boundaries are not paradoxes. They are the information needed to
state theorems at the correct logical level.

% ---- source 08, lines 1818-1843
\subsection{Source 08's conclusion}

The global enumeration problem has a particularly clean answer once
the types of objects are separated. Set-like well-orders of $\No$ are
represented by class bijections from $\Ord$, and numerical
first-disagreement gives a rigorous virtual linear order. That order
is large enough to encode every class binary word, yet its set-cut
geometry is already witnessed by a single class of set-supported
perturbations. This code class is another copy of the surreal line.

At a fixed set carrier, the structure is different: its exact ordinal
spectrum stops at the successor of the carrier cardinal, and finite
permutation tails account for every jump. At varying set carriers,
termination introduces new local cofinalities. For non-set-like
well-orders, a further index convention or relation code is necessary.
None of these distinctions is optional bookkeeping: each changes a
mathematical conclusion.

The principal proofs are elementary in their stated foundations.
Their formalization should begin with bounded objects and the
repository's existing sign-sequence cut theorem, and only then pass to
the uniform class formulation. The dense-skeleton theorem provides a
concrete target: it combines first-disagreement combinatorics,
controlled set support, small-cut filling, and universe-aware
back-and-forth without requiring a paradoxical collection of all
classes.

\subsection{Source 13: conclusions and result ledger}\label{swo:fs:sec:conclusion}

The strongest organizing principle is not that a single enormous
well-order has been discovered. It is that different notions of
``all'' and different representations produce distinct linear orders,
while a small collection of explicit tools connects them safely.

The fixed-set layer has its own cardinal and ordinal spectra. The
ordinary class of set words depends decisively on termination. The
full set-like enumeration domain has a surreal-sized dense core but
no exhaustive uniform class of set codes. The raw order domain expands
individual branch fibers, not the entire cut space of that core. A
higher-level product can exceed the dense core's capacity even though
ordinary class-indexed sums are absorbed. Finally, pure order
isomorphisms can change the prefix presentation itself.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1927-1955
\subsection{Source 14: conclusion}
The strongest organizing distinction is not between large and small
cardinalities alone. It is between set-coded presentations, class-valued
branches, and raw class relations with further tails. Prefix cylinders
make that distinction mathematically visible.

Every normalized class cut of the set-supported core either stops at
a cylinder edge, stops at a genuine numerical gap, or follows an
injective branch through all ordinals. Exhaustive well-orders are exactly
the branches that cover the alphabet. Because this criterion reconstructs
a graph using only set quantifiers and old parameters, it yields a
no-new-realization theorem for old cuts. Raw well-orders have the same
trace precisely when their canonical initial branches agree, leaving
an explicit residual well-ordering problem in each fiber.

Support restrictions provide a different axis of complexity. Allowing
support of cardinality $<\kappa$ gives exactly the cut-filling threshold
$\cf\kappa$, and the failure beyond it has an attained support cost.
All these layers still contain a copy of the full surreal order. Thus
class universality, density in an ambient comparison order, and
saturation are genuinely different properties.

The resulting theory remains paradox-free because each ``all'' has a
specified sort, each prefix has a specified size, and each use of
surreal cut filling has set option families. The automorphism-orbit theorem sharpens this distinction: bare-order
symmetries can exchange exhaustive traces with nonbranch boundaries.
The principal open targets are now the exhaustive-trace stabilizer, finer support invariants, and the
interaction between raw tail structure and higher class realizations.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 1894-1919
\subsection{Source 17: conclusion}
The lexicographic ordering problem separates into several mathematically
substantial structures. On the minimal birthday-cutoff slice, the
relevant parameters are the cardinality $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ and two different
cofinalities $r=\cf\kappa$, $q=\cf\mu$. Point characters are $(q,q)$,
cylinder cofinalities are $r$, and three distinct cut mechanisms give the
exact gap spectrum. Exhaustiveness is also the key issue in fusion:
a coherent full-length injection need not be a permutation.

The same distinction persists at class scale. A single lower class cut of
a supported core determines an injective global word exactly when its
labelled cylinders straddle at every ordinal length. A separate coverage
condition distinguishes exhaustive words. Reconstruction is elementary,
but exhaustion is invisible to the bare core order: a core automorphism
can carry an exhaustive branch gap to a nonexhaustive one. The represented-
cut predicate is therefore genuine additional structure, and same-set
class extensions change it while leaving the code carrier unchanged.

For unrestricted class well-orders, a proper-class prefix can leave a
finite residual alphabet. The resulting maximal adjacency components are
exactly the factorial blocks of a finite final segment; their condensation
is dense without becoming an ordinary class of all class orders. Across
all these conclusions, typing the objects and bounding the recursion
histories are part of the mathematics, not merely notational cautions.

The proof dependencies are short. Set cuts yield fresh
coefficients after deleting a set. Fresh coefficients and
bounded-support completion yield strong interpolation.
Strong interpolation yields density, local cofinality
statements, the \(\No\)-isomorphism, and cut coding.
Independently, the predecessor comparison yields convex
cones, the canonical initial-part decomposition, and the
finite-residual jump theorem. Pair swaps supply both
positive binary embeddings and the diagonal obstruction.

The bundled Python script checks finite instances of
the two comparison rules and of the sign encoding. It
checks 465 coefficient-code comparisons, 79,800
word-code comparisons, and 266,272 pairs of finite
permutations, with the predecessor rule checked in both
directions and the adjacency criterion compared with the
finite lexicographic order. These checks help detect a
reversed delimiter or an incorrect finite comparison.
They do not verify an ordinal induction, a class
comprehension argument, or a cardinal nonembedding
theorem.

The article contains full mathematical proofs for the
claims it promotes to theorems. It does not claim that
the new results have been checked in Lean, that the
whole repository has been audited, or that every
research question listed here is a previously published
open problem.

\subsection{Source 09: verification and reproducibility}
\label{swo:ec:app:verification}
The accompanying \texttt{code/finite\_checks.py} uses only Python's
standard library. It checks finite versions of the pair-switch
lexicographic embedding, partial-prefix permutation completion, the
forced-prefix separator algorithm, support extension preserving first
disagreements, and the diagonal switch construction. Exact rational
arithmetic is used for the separator tests. A deterministic random seed
makes the sampled checks reproducible; other suites exhaust their
specified finite ranges.

\textbf{These checks do not verify any transfinite theorem.} Their role
is to detect indexing, orientation, and extension mistakes in the
finite combinatorial mechanisms. Proofs of the infinite statements
are the written arguments in the article. The recorded run passed 164,560 assertions, including 1,101 separator-family
cases. The test report is \texttt{data/finite\_checks.json}. The archive also contains a build
script and a theorem-status ledger.

To compile the article, run \texttt{bash build.sh} in the archive's root
directory. It makes three passes with \texttt{pdflatex}, resolves the
internal bibliography and cross-references, and writes build products
into \texttt{build/} before copying the finished PDF to the root.

\subsection{Source 08: finite regression checks}\label{swo:sk:app:tests}

The package includes \texttt{verify\_finite.py}, requiring Python 3.10
or later and only its standard library. Running it writes
\texttt{verification\_results.json}. The supplied run passed:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Y r@{}}
\toprule
Check & Instances \\
\midrule
Consecutive permutation pairs, sizes $1$ through $7$ & 5,906 \\
All increasing pairs of distinct permutations, sizes through $5$ & 7,432 \\
Pair-code order comparisons, bit lengths $0$ through $7$ & 21,845 \\
Sign words of lengths $0$ through $6$ & 127 \\
All sign-code order and prefix-free comparisons & 16,129 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The permutation test checks both directions of the adjacency rule on
all manageable pairs, not just a few positive examples. The sign test
compares the numerical convention $-<0<+$ with the binary blocks
$00<01<11$, including pairs in which one sign word is a proper prefix.
The pair-code test checks that every output is a permutation of the
correct finite alphabet and that comparisons agree with the input
binary order.

These tests can detect a reversed pair orientation, a wrong terminal
block, or a mistaken finite-tail rule. They cannot prove regularity
arguments, transfinite stabilization, set/class separation, or the
existence of a global isomorphism. Those depend on the mathematical
proofs in the text.

\subsubsection{Specific dependency choices}

The fresh-value lemma uses an already constructed small-cut interface.
The dense-core interpolation argument is written out rather than
attributed only to a theorem name. The global product obstruction
explicitly reuses the earlier report's density and inverse-evaluator
method. The cut and automorphism theorems do not require its
singular-cardinal classification, and the central-word theorem does
not require surreal arithmetic. Thus a later correction in a
nonessential prior theorem would not automatically affect the main
new proofs.

\subsection{Source 13: reproducibility and finite checks}\label{swo:fs:app:checks}

The archive contains the standalone \code{article.tex}, its compiled
PDF, a build script, a standard-library Python checker, its recorded
JSON output, and a status note. No external image or private font file
is required. The bibliography is internal to the TeX source.

The finite checks cover the following distinct mechanisms. First,
they build well-order relations on finite alphabets and compare the
common-predecessor formula with direct permutation lexicography.
Second, they test convexity of every finite prefix cylinder and the
uniqueness and coherence of crossing prefixes at all finite cut
positions. Third, they test finite prefix completion. Fourth, they
compare the central-word sign code with independent rational values
of finite surreal sign sequences.

The test alphabets for the last group are
$-2,-1,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1,2$, with all words of length at most three,
including repeated-letter words. Finite signs are evaluated as dyadic
rationals, not merely re-compared by a second copy of the same
lexicographic function. The reserved-marker condition is also checked
by exhibiting the collision that would result from admitting a
trailing zero as a letter.

These tests do not establish class comprehension, ordinal-limit
coherence, global choice, the back-and-forth theorem, or a
transfinite birthday bound. They are reproducible checks of finite
instances and independent representations, with the logical trust
boundary stated explicitly.

\begin{lstlisting}
# Run from the extracted archive directory.
python3 code/finite_checks.py --output data/finite_results.json
bash build.sh
\end{lstlisting}

The build script runs three LaTeX passes to settle cross-references
and the table of contents. A PDF inspection record and checksums are
included in the delivery's status files.

\subsection{Source 14: finite diagnostics and reproducibility}
\label{swo:tc:app:tests}
The accompanying \texttt{verification.py} uses only Python's standard
library. It checks finite instances of the following kernels:
relation-based common prefixes versus enumeration prefixes; convexity
of prefix cylinders; the chain property of crossing prefixes at every
finite cut; extension of partial injections on a finite support;
preservation of all comparisons under support compression; finite
self-delimiting sign and word codes; and pair-orientation coding.
The exact tested ranges, case counts, and pass/fail results are written
to \texttt{verification\_results.json} by the delivered execution.
The delivered run passed every diagnostic. Its principal counts are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Kernel & Tested cases or comparisons\\\midrule
Labelled common-prefix comparison & 15,018\\
Prefix cylinders / proper finite cuts & 2,371 / 867\\
Finite partial injections & 15,126\\
Compressed candidates / retained comparisons & 3,868 / 66,873\\
Numerical sign-code pairs & 16,129\\
Outer word-code pairs, two termination conventions & 320,000\\
Pair-orientation comparisons & 21,844\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Finite alphabets have endpoints and adjacent labels, unlike the residual
surreal alphabet. Therefore the finite crossing-prefix test checks the
chain lemma, not the full boundary trichotomy. The buffer argument for
infinite partial injections, cofinality at singular cardinals, Global
Choice, and class-model absoluteness are not experimentally verified.
Those assertions stand on their written proofs and remain appropriate
subjects for independent mathematical and formal review.

To reproduce the package locally:
\begin{lstlisting}
python3 verification.py
bash build.sh

\section{The other sources' title pages and abstracts}\label{swo:app:abstracts}

\merge\ The results these summaries announce are printed in the body; the
summaries are kept for the record.

\subsection*{Source 12}
\paragraph{Title-page summary.}

% ---- source 12, lines 86-111
\textbf{Main distinction.} An arbitrary class well-order of $\No$ need not
have order type $\Ord$. Nevertheless, two such well-orders have an
\emph{elementarily definable largest common labelled initial segment},
possibly a proper class. This supplies a lexicographic comparison in GBC
without invoking general class well-order comparability or ETR.

\medskip
\textbf{Principal quantitative result.} Put
$\No_{<\kappa}=\{s:\alpha\to\{-,+\}:\alpha<\kappa\}$ and
$\mu=|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}$, for an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$.
The minimal-length permutation order satisfies
\[
\WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})\equim
\begin{cases}
\BB_{\kappa\cdot\kappa},&\mu=\kappa\text{ and }\cf\kappa<\kappa,\\
\BB_\mu,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where $\BB_\gamma=(2^\gamma,<_{\lex})$ and $\equim$ means mutual
order-embeddability, not isomorphism.

\medskip
\textbf{Status.} This is an AI-assisted, unrefereed research manuscript.
Proofs are supplied for the stated results; historical priority is not
claimed. The accompanying exact finite tests do not verify the transfinite
arguments. No new Lean formalization is claimed.

% ---- hand chunk abs12_mid

\paragraph{Abstract.}

% ---- source 12, lines 117-143
We study the lexicographic order of well-orderings of the surreal numbers,
carefully distinguishing bounded sets of surreals, set-like global
well-orders, and arbitrary global class well-orders. For the full class
problem, ordinal-indexed enumerations are insufficient. We construct the
largest common labelled initial segment of two well-orders directly from
their relations, prove that comparison of their next elements defines a
linear order, and show that this construction needs only elementary class
comprehension once the well-orders exist. Over GB with set choice, the
existence of any class well-order of the surreals is equivalent to global
choice. The collection of all these well-orders is not itself an ordinary
class of GBC or Kelley--Morse theory; a diagonal theorem rules out any
uniform exhaustive coding by a class of sets.

For set-like global well-orders we prove density, interpolation for
set-indexed cuts, local universality for class linear orders, and mutual
embeddability with the lexicographic comparison of binary classes on
$\Ord$. For unrestricted global well-orders we classify adjacent pairs:
they arise precisely from finite residual permutations after a common,
necessarily proper-class, prefix. At a birthday cutoff $\kappa$, we obtain
an exact regular/singular dichotomy for the binary coding rank of
minimal-length enumerations. We also establish the exact ordinal and
binary-cube embedding spectra for the full set-sized order. Finally, a
full-class model based on an inaccessible rank explains exactly how the
bounded and global theories fit together, and provides a rigorous example
in which the full order and the set-like order have the same cardinality
and ordinal spectrum but different coding ranks. Explicit proof-assistant
interfaces and further research questions are included.

% ---- hand chunk abs09_head

\subsection*{Source 09}
\paragraph{Abstract.}

% ---- source 09, lines 98-124
The phrase ``the lexicographic order of all well-orders of the surreal
numbers'' has several mathematically different interpretations. We develop
three: exhaustive enumerations of a fixed set of surreals; all set-length
injective surreal words; and class bijections from the ordinals onto the
surreal numbers, representing set-like global well-orders. For an infinite
set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$, we give a self-contained proof that its
lexicographic well-ordering space has cardinality $2^\kappa$, contains every
linear order of size at most $\kappa$, and contains an ordinal precisely when
that ordinal is below $\kappa^+$.

For the global problem, we work in G\"odel--Bernays set theory with global
choice and do not pretend that a collection of proper classes is itself an
ordinary class. Fix a global enumeration $b$. Its eventually-equal
perturbations admit canonical set codes. We prove that their lexicographic
order is isomorphic to the surreal line, meets every set-prefix cylinder,
and interpolates every uniformly set-indexed separated pair of families
of arbitrary global enumerations. Thus every class linear order embeds
into this genuine class core. We also prove bounded reflection for
set-indexed families, construct an explicit unfilled
$(\Ord,\Ord)$-configuration, and diagonalize against every uniform
class-indexed list of all global enumerations.

A strongly inaccessible truncation gives a fully set-sized model of the
size distinction: the core has cardinality $\kappa$, whereas all length
$\kappa$ enumerations have cardinality $2^\kappa$. The article includes
foundational and Lean formalization plans, a repository audit, finite
verification code, and a focused research agenda.

% ---- hand chunk abs09_mid

\paragraph{Title-page status.}

% ---- source 09, lines 127-131
{\small\color{Gray}\noindent
Status: AI-assisted research manuscript; complete written arguments are
provided for the stated results. Not peer-reviewed or Lean-verified.
Classical ingredients and repository results are distinguished from the
constructions developed here. No claim of historical priority is made.}

% ---- hand chunk abs08_head

\subsection*{Source 08}
\paragraph{Abstract.}

% ---- source 08, lines 90-113
There is no single unqualified object called ``the lexicographic order of
all well-orders of the surreal numbers.'' We distinguish well-orderings of
a fixed set of surreals, well-orderings of varying set-sized subsets,
set-like well-orderings of the whole surreal class, and arbitrary class
well-orderings. For an infinite ordered set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$, the
exhaustive-enumeration order $\W(X)$ has size $2^\kappa$, contains every
linear order of size at most $\kappa$, and contains an ordinal $\beta$
exactly when $\beta<\kappa^+$. Its adjacent pairs arise precisely from
finite permutation tails.

For the whole surreal class, work in G\"odel--Bernays set theory with
Global Choice. The numerical first-disagreement comparison of class
bijections $\Ord\to\No$ is meaningful without treating classes as elements
of classes. Fix one such bijection $b$. We prove that every set-sized
separated family of global enumerations has a strict separator obtained
from $b$ by a permutation of set support. The class of canonical codes for
these perturbations is therefore order-isomorphic to $\No$. It is a dense,
set-cut-realizing skeleton inside the much larger virtual enumeration
order, and every class linear order embeds into it. The full virtual order
is equimorphic with the lexicographic order of class binary sequences, but
admits no class-uniform exhaustive parametrization. We supply proofs,
cutoff versions, counterexamples to tempting identifications, a
universe-sensitive Lean implementation plan tied to inspected ProveIt
sources, and a research agenda.

% ---- hand chunk abs08_mid

\paragraph{Status box.}

% ---- source 08, lines 115-123
\begin{resultbox}
\textbf{Status and scope.} The results below are mathematical derivations
with explicit proofs, not claims of historical priority. The manuscript
has not been independently refereed, and its new results have not been
checked by a proof assistant. Repository declarations are identified
separately from proposed extensions. The accompanying executable checks
cover finite coding and adjacency examples only. All uses of ``class''
are relative to the stated foundational model.
\end{resultbox}

\subsection*{Source 13}
\paragraph{Title page.} ``Further research report''. \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Surreal Well-Orderings: Cut reconstruction, asymmetric products, prefix non-rigidity, and size-safe foundations} (PDF metadata: ``Further Structure''). Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
We further investigate the lexicographic comparison of well-orderings of
the surreal numbers, separating set-sized alphabets, set-length words,
set-like global enumerations, unrestricted class well-orders, and
code-dependent alternatives. The central new result is an exact
prefix-cylinder criterion for a normalized class cut of a surreal-sized
dense core to be represented by an injective ordinal-class word. Exhaustive
words are characterized by an additional label-coverage condition. Cuts
that fail the criterion have a first failure of one of two precisely
described kinds: a next-label cut or a limit-prefix boundary.

We prove an asymmetric product phenomenon. The global enumeration order
absorbs a surreal left factor, and more generally admits every ordinary
class-indexed lexicographic sum of copies of itself. Its two-point split,
however, does not embed back in the full inaccessible-universe
interpretation, nor by a definable uniform transformation in
Kelley--Morse theory with global choice. Externally countable models give
the opposite answer for unrestricted external maps. A finite-block
recoding automorphism shows that the pure linear order does not recover
its prefix cylinders. Finally, replacing end-first dictionary comparison
by a central termination convention on the nonzero alphabet makes both
arbitrary and injective set-length word orders isomorphic to the surreal line.

The proofs specify their logical size levels. An implementation plan uses
the repository's actual universe-indexed sign-sequence and small-cut
interfaces, without claiming a new Lean formalization.

\paragraph{Title-page status.}
\textbf{Research status.} AI-assisted, unrefereed mathematical manuscript.
The proofs are presented for scrutiny; historical priority and kernel
verification are not claimed. This is a follow-up to the repository's
merged report, not a replacement or a certification of all its results.
The inspected repository snapshot is pinned in \Cref{swo:fs:app:audit}.
Finite checks accompany the article, but do not establish transfinite or
class-theoretic theorems.

\subsection*{Source 14}
\paragraph{Title page.} ``Research continuation''. \emph{Lexicographic Well-Orders of the Surreals II: Cut classification, support thresholds, and class-model absoluteness}. Prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
The earlier ProveIt reports identify a set-coded dense skeleton of the
lexicographic order of global surreal enumerations, but leave open which
cuts of that skeleton come from exhaustive enumerations. We answer the
prefix-structured version of that question. Every proper normalized class
cut of the skeleton has exactly one of three forms: an edge of a
set-prefix cylinder, a nonprincipal numerical gap after a set prefix, or
a coherent injective branch of length $\Ord$. The last form is realized
by a global well-order of set-like type exactly when its branch covers
every surreal. Reconstruction is elementary; a separate orbit theorem shows that
bare-order automorphisms can destroy exhaustive representability.

This yields an absoluteness theorem: enlarging the class part of a model
while retaining its sets and a fixed baseline enumeration cannot newly
realize an old skeleton cut by a global enumeration. New enumerations
have genuinely new trace cuts. For unrestricted labelled class
well-orders, the trace map forgets exactly the tail after the canonical
$\Ord$-long initial segment; its fibers are described explicitly.

A separate support analysis gives a sharp hierarchy. If $\kappa$ is an
infinite set cardinal, the permutations of a baseline with support of
cardinality $<\kappa$ form an $\eta_{\cf\kappa}$-order, but not an
$\eta_{(\cf\kappa)^+}$-order. A separated pair of $\cf\kappa$-long
families forces at least $\kappa$ moved coordinates, and this support
cost is attained in the full skeleton. Thus universality for ordinary
class linear orders can coexist with sharply limited saturation.

We distinguish fixed carriers, variable set domains, increasing
subclasses, global set-like orders, unrestricted class relations,
relation-code lexicography, and order-type quotients. The exposition
includes proofs, exact quantifier conventions, a repository audit,
universe-relative and Lean formalization plans, finite regression tests,
and a focused research agenda.

We continue the study of lexicographic orders of labelled well-orderings of surreal numbers, with particular attention to a distinction that appears at singular enumeration cardinalities: controlling a bounded initial segment is not the same as controlling an arbitrary small set of positions. For the minimal enumeration slice, this distinction separates the numerical order topology from a canonical topology compatible with all permutation operations.

We prove that the subgroup preserving bounded sets in both directions is maximal among subgroups containing the finitary permutations and carrying the inherited topological-group structure. At every singular cardinal it is self-normalizing. We determine its forward closure and completion, describe a dense inverse-continuity locus, and construct explicit permutations separating the one-sided boundedness conditions. The smallest group topology finer than the prefix topology is exactly agreement on arbitrary sets of size less than the enumeration cardinal. Its character is the cofinality of the small-subset poset, which is strictly greater than that cardinal in the singular case. It is complete for its two-sided group uniformity.

These results apply to surreal birthday cutoffs after verifying their thickness. We also distinguish fixed and varying carriers, inherited numerical well-orders, set-like and unrestricted global class well-orders, relation codes, and order-type quotients. Class arguments are formulated without a class of classes, and a formalization plan separates universe-indexed Lean mathematics from model-relative class semantics.

\paragraph{Source 29.} \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Surreal Well-Orders: Exact Birthday Spectra, Word Products, Topological Transitions, and Class Comparability}.

% ---- source 29 (batch-83 manuscript 15), lines 88-150
The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of the surreal
numbers'' refers to several different mathematical constructions. Some
are sets, some are classes of set codes, and some are higher-order
collections of class relations. We give a common framework for these
interpretations and extend the corresponding ProveIt research program.

Our first result recovers the exact birthday cutoff from the numerical
order: the binary lexicographic cube $\B_\beta$ embeds in
$\No_{<\theta}$ exactly when $\beta<\theta$. Consequently the birthday
fragments form a strictly increasing hierarchy under order embeddability,
even throughout a band on which their cardinality is constant. In
contrast, for every countable $\omega<\theta<\omega_1$ and every
enumeration length $\alpha=\Lambda+n$ of cardinality the continuum,
with $\Lambda$ limit and $n$ finite, the well-ordering stratum is
equimorphic to $\B_\Lambda\mathbin{\times_\lex} n!$. We extend the corresponding
residual-cardinal analysis to arbitrary noninitial birthday bounds and
state the remaining singular upper-coding gap explicitly.

For increasing set-length words, splitting at the termination cut gives
a canonical factorization. The centered surreal case has order type
${\mathbf{T}_{\min}}^{\mathrm{op}}\mathbin{\times_\lex}{\mathbf{T}_{\min}}$, where ${\mathbf{T}_{\min}}$ is the shorter-first order of
all set-length surreal words. This identifies three previously separate
zero conventions and describes the fourth by adjacent-pair expansion.
If proper-class numerical carriers are admitted, shorter-first adjacency
instead occurs exactly when a carrier acquires its unattained numerical
supremum. The longer-first class-carrier order remains dense.

At the countable alphabet $\No_{<\omega}\cong\mathbb{Q}$, finite terminal
tails produce a sharp progression in topology and measurable structure.
The native lexicographic and coordinate Borel structures agree at
$\omega+1$, differ at $\omega+2$, and are incomparable at every
finite successor $\omega+n$ with $n\ge3$. We also prove that the entire ordered set-prefix
tree fails to recognize exhaustive or numerically cofinal class branches.
Finally, over GBC, the existence of complete terminating canonical
set-interval condensation histories is equivalent to strong comparability
of class well-orders. The proof supplies finite ordinal-coefficient
normal forms from any such history.

Every assertion distinguishes isomorphism from equimorphism, supplied
classes from collections of classes, and elementary definitions from
class-recursion existence principles. The article ends with concrete
formalization targets and a revised research agenda.

\paragraph{Source 30.} \emph{Lexicographic Well-Orders of the Surreals: Residual Codes, Topological Transitions, and Class Reconstruction}.

% ---- source 30 (batch-83 manuscript 16), lines 68-116
The lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of the surreal numbers has
several mathematically inequivalent interpretations. After separating
them, we develop four continuations of the existing ProveIt reports.
We determine binary-cube equimorphism types for new fixed strata with
infinite remainders, including the previously isolated case $\mu+\omega$.
Finite descent through regular and singular strong-limit cardinal blocks
gives a complete fixed-type equimorphism classification under GCH.
An additional bounded-birthday argument classifies every fixed type
in ZFC at each infinite cutoff $\kappa<\aleph_\omega$.
We prove a sharp topological and measurable transition between the
countable strata of types $\omega$, $\omega+1$, $\omega+2$, and
$\omega+n$ for $n\geq3$; relation tables and enumeration codes cease to
be measurably interchangeable already at $\omega+2$. An exact
partial-table extension theorem shows that every admitted proper-class
well-order type is locally indistinguishable from every other by
set-sized relation data. Finally, the admitted \emph{labelled} global
enumerations recover an entire class realization, despite the severe
information loss of its external pure order. Sets, classes, and
metatheoretic collections are kept distinct throughout. The article
includes proofs, source and assumption audits, a formalization plan,
and a prioritized research agenda.

\paragraph{Source 31.} \emph{Countable Global Choice and Surreal Coding over
Zermelo Set Theory: A localized nonconservativity theorem and exact rank-model
spectra}.

% ---- source 31 (batch-89 manuscript 01), lines 75-100
We investigate an intersection of Elliot Glazer's work on weak choice principles
and ProveIt's research on surreal numbers and class well-orders. The first result
is a refinement of Glazer's nonconservativity theorem: a global selector required
to choose only from nonempty countable sets already produces new set-theoretic
consequences over Zermelo set theory with Choice, provided Separation is extended
to the selector. Selection on exactly countably infinite sets suffices as well.
The additional argument is a bounded uniformization theorem. It converts a
selector on sets embeddable into a fixed well-ordered set into a uniform assignment
of injections into that set, without Replacement or ordinal collapse. A general
incidence-coding theorem then connects this uniformization to Glazer's published
countermodel.

The second part studies the full-class structures
\(\RM_\lambda=(V_\lambda,\Pow(V_\lambda))\), for limit ordinals
\(\lambda>\omega\). Global choice and set-like well-orders exist at every such
height. Nevertheless, ordinal enumeration of binary sign sequences, enumeration
in birthday order, universal coding of sets by sign sequences, and full Class
Replacement have different exact thresholds: respectively
\(2^{<\kappa}=\kappa\), strong-limit cardinality, a beth fixed point, and strong
inaccessibility. We also determine replacement on each individual set domain
and the external cardinalities of internal proper classes. These results isolate
several mechanisms behind the usual global-choice equivalences. Full proofs,
strict separation examples, an axiom audit, and twelve further research questions
are included. The article claims a proved refinement and a structural synthesis;
it makes no claim of resolving unrestricted surreal transfer or of establishing
historical priority for every result.

\paragraph{Source 34 (base).} \emph{Beyond $\Ord$: Definable Class
Well-Orders, Canonical Arithmetic, and the Limits of Notation}. ``Research
report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov'', dated 4~October 2026.

% ---- source 34 (batch-96 manuscript 10), lines 56-82
The class of all ordinals is the endpoint of set-sized ordinal notation,
but it is not the endpoint of definable well-ordering. Tagged sums,
lexicographic products, and finite-support powers produce well-orders such
as $\Ord+1$, $\Ord\cdot\Ord$, and $\fsp{\Ord}{\Ord}$ without creating
a new set ordinal. We develop these constructions as relations on sets,
separate their explicit arithmetic from stronger class-recursion principles,
and give systematic notation by finite labelled trees.

The main refinement of the ProveIt program is a choice-free proof that
finite-support powers of class well-orders are well-ordered. It lowers the
repository's equivalence between canonical terminating condensation histories
and strong class-well-order comparability from $\GBC$ to $\GB$, for arbitrary
class carriers and the full subclass-minimum definition of well-ordering.
This resolves the corresponding base-theory question in the inspected
repository; it does not decide whether comparability implies elementary
transfinite recursion. Further results give a hereditary fixed-point notation
system, a uniform-family diagonal obstruction, a truth-relative construction
of longer definable orders, and an external cofinality theorem for definable
order spectra. In a full inaccessible-universe interpretation, all class
well-order types have external lengths below $\kappa^+$, while the hereditary
system has the exact length $\varepsilon_{\kappa+1}$.

Every substantive theorem is proved or explicitly attributed. The paper
distinguishes repository refinements and new combinations of arguments from
established literature, makes no claim of historical priority, and records a
formalization plan and a focused research agenda. The proofs are mathematical
proofs; no kernel-checked formalization is claimed.

\paragraph{Source 35.} \emph{Definable Class Well-Orders Beyond $\Ord$:
Arithmetic, canonical notation, fixed-point completion, and the limits of
uniform definability}. ``Research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov'',
dated 5~October 2026.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 67-100
The ordinal class is the end of the set ordinals, but it is not the end
of definable well-order presentations whose elements are sets.  A
proper-class well-order may have points with proper classes of
predecessors, giving familiar-looking expressions such as
$\Ord+1$, $\Ord\cdot\Ord$, and $\Ord^{\Ord}$ rigorous meanings.
We develop their arithmetic using tagged sums, lexicographic products,
and finite-support exponentiation, while keeping class presentations
separate from nonexistent set ordinals beyond $\Ord$.

The first contribution is a direct, choice-free proof that finite-support
exponentiation preserves class well-ordering.  It lowers the ProveIt
manuscript's equivalence between strong class-well-order comparability
and complete canonical condensation histories from $\GBC$ to $\GB$,
with no use of set Choice.  A second contribution, over $\GBC$,
characterizes precisely which orders have a fixed-point completion for
$ P(X)=\Ord^{X}$:
an order $W$ initially embeds into such a fixed point if and only if
$W$ initially embeds into $ P(W)$.  For nonempty $W$, this is also
equivalent to its canonical terminating history on $W+1$.
The proof uses finite traces
and an explicitly coded direct limit, rather than arbitrary class-valued
recursion.  We also prove a strict bounding theorem for every uniformly
coded family with a supplied well-ordered index class, and derive a hierarchy of definability
complexities of their presentations up to admitted isomorphism.

Hereditary ordinal-coefficient terms supply a concrete exponential
fixed point and a transparent comparison procedure.  Full-model and
definability-sensitive spectra explain the model-relative sense in
which such orders can stretch farther than $\Ord$.  The final sections
compare set-theoretic and type-theoretic formalizations and propose a
research program.  Existing polynomial and condensation results are
credited to the inspected repository; classical class-epsilon notation
is also credited.  The extensions are proved here, but no claim of
literature-wide priority or resolution of $\CWO$ versus $\ETR$ is made.

% ---- source 35 (batch-96 manuscript 11), lines 104-106
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} Class well-order; ordinal arithmetic; elementary
transfinite recursion; definability; canonical condensation; fixed point;
finite-support notation; G\"odel--Bernays set theory.

\paragraph{Source 32.} \emph{Beyond Ord: Definable Class Well-Orders. Explicit
arithmetic, condensation, definability ceilings, and truth jumps}; headed
``Foundations and order theory''. ``Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir
Reshetnikov'', dated 4~October 2026.

% ---- source 32 (batch-96 manuscript 08), lines 78-86
The ordinal class is the largest set-like well-order, but not the largest class well-order. We develop an explicit arithmetic of non-set-like well-orders without treating proper classes as elements of a same-level universe. Finite-support exponentiation and hereditary finite normal forms give orders far beyond $\Ord$ already in G\"odel--Bernays set theory with Global Choice. A canonical division theorem expresses every class well-order as $\Omega\cdot Q+\alpha$, where $\Omega=(\Ord,{<})$, $Q$ is a class well-order presentation, and $\alpha$ is a set ordinal.

Three further results organize the limitations of this arithmetic. First, a diagonal sum dominates every member of any one uniformly class-coded family, even without class-order comparability. Second, whenever a set-interval condensation hierarchy exists along $W+1$, it collapses $W$ by its final stage; elementary transfinite recursion supplies such a hierarchy. Explicit polynomial examples show that no set-ordinal bound suffices. Third, for an inaccessible $\kappa$ and the classes definable over $(V_\kappa,\in,G,A)$ with set parameters, the externally realized order types form an ordinal $\delta_A$ satisfying
\[
\kappa<\delta_A<\kappa^+,
\qquad \cf(\delta_A)=\omega,
\qquad \kappa^{\delta_A}=\delta_A.
\]
A full truth predicate for that structure makes $\delta_A$ itself representable. We give proofs, isolate the relevant axioms, relate the constructions to the ProveIt repository, and propose a formalization and research program.

\paragraph{Source 33.} \emph{Beyond Ord: Definable Class Well-Orders,
Arithmetic, Condensation, and Definability Heights}; headed ``Foundations /
research article''. ``Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov'',
dated 4~October 2026.

% ---- source 33 (batch-96 manuscript 09), lines 102-127
Proper-class well-orders can extend beyond the order of all set ordinals without
creating new set ordinals. We develop a size-safe calculus for these orders and
separate explicit constructions in G\"odel--Bernays set theory with global choice
from principles requiring elementary transfinite recursion. The structural
results include canonical division by the order of all ordinals, an explicit
condensation hierarchy for finite ordinal-coefficient polynomials, and a
finite-digit embedding theorem for orders equipped with an exhausting
condensation tower.

The main definability result is a uniform-family diagonal theorem. For each
fixed finite formula-complexity bound, it produces a class well-order definable
without set parameters, relative to a named global order, into which every
well-order of that complexity with arbitrary set parameters embeds, while the
constructed order embeds into none of them. Consequently, set-parameter-free
presentations are externally cofinal among all set-parameter-definable
presentations, but no definable uniform family can witness that cofinality.
At an inaccessible rank model $V_\kappa$, all full-class order types are exactly
the ordinals below $\kappa^+$; the smaller definable spectrum has a supremum
strictly between $\kappa$ and $\kappa^+$ of external cofinality $\omega$;
this supremum is an epsilon number closed under ordinal arithmetic.
Adding a truth predicate strictly increases that definability height.

The article supplies proofs, an axiom ledger, repository integration guidance,
and further research problems. Historical priority for the derived results is
not established, and no machine verification of the class-theoretic proofs is
claimed.
